https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing.
He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.
“We need to believe that we can win,” Pochettino said that day in September 2024. “That we can win not only a game: We can win the World Cup.”
It is the type of belief that feels almost alien to observers of the US men, the type of statement that American fans yearn to hear so badly from a coach yet also roll their eyes at. For years, fans of men’s soccer in the US have been desperate to taste glory, and for years they have developed an inferiority complex spurred along not only by results but by international perception. Even in the present day, with American players playing in Europe at the very highest level, the idea that the US could win a men’s World Cup feels borderline preposterous.
That never stopped Pochettino from espousing his belief that the US should believe they could make a miraculous run in 2026 and win the whole thing. It was a mantra he returned to frequently during his time leading the team, publicly and privately, even in the weeks leading up to the tournament. Pochettino even told Donald Trump that the US could win it all, perhaps planting the seeds for an assist turned own-goal down the line.
Belief is something that could attract even the most casual US fans, the type of newcomers whose previous experience with an American soccer coach came from Apple TV. Unfortunately for US fans, Pochettino’s actions never quite lined up with the inspirational speech.
There was the near-constant stream of rumors attaching Pochettino to clubs in England, rumors he never really went out of his way to quash even before they tied him to the Manchester United job he has now accepted. In many ways this type of thing is unavoidable and understandable: bringing on a high-profile coach and expecting peace and quiet is the footballing equivalent of dating a supermodel and expecting no one else to make an advance. Yet too often it felt as if Pochettino was the one stoking the fire; it was not uncommon to wake up in the States and find social media feeds populated with clips of the Argentinian espousing the valor of the Premier League and even floating the idea of returning someday.
This was never really shocking or unexpected and was far from offensive. Professional sports are fickle and players, coaches and administrators alike are wise to keep their options open and their bridges intact. Yet it was a bit galling to hear from someone brought in to galvanize the US’s players and fans ahead of a generational event: a home World Cup.
Pochettino also seemed sometimes frustrated by the very thing he was in part brought in to help change: American soccer’s sometimes awkward place in America itself. After losing the 2025 Gold Cup final to Mexico in Houston, he went out of his way to criticize the idea that the US would play in front of a pro-Mexico crowd on home soil, an issue that predates Pochettino by decades and may well never be solved, one even the most cursory research would’ve revealed prior to arrival. He fairly criticized the lack of stakes in Major League Soccer and suggested that US players are coddled throughout their youth development while at the same time butting heads with media who dared question the effects of a group-stage loss to Turkey at this summer’s World Cup. In reality, he faced far less pressure as the head coach of the USMNT than he would have in most any other major footballing nation.
All of it too often gave observers the feeling that Pochettino was never truly bought in. But then, there was the whiplash, which was palpable. As soon as one began to feel that way, there’d be a fresh injection of dopamine – the US’s 4-1 demolishing of Paraguay, for example, far and away their best-ever performance at a World Cup. And there was Poch, nearly in tears and belting out Country Roads, then speaking glowingly about America, American football and everything else that comes along with it. A few weeks later, they’d suffer a 4-1 drubbing at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 that will go down as among the worst-ever performances by the US at a World Cup. Certainly the most traumatic.
Athletes and coaches hate being asked about their legacies, in general. The question in and of itself sounds moribund, as if the person asked is about to ascend into the ether. Legacies, too, are tricky things – they often take years to materialize, and they’re sometimes just as quickly erased by shifting perceptions or the accomplishments of successors.
Pochettino does not seem to be the kind of person who would mind being asked about his legacy; he actually seems more like one who would already have one in mind before departure. Yet when asked by the Guardian on Friday to define his lasting impact, he struggled to do so at first. “I am not arrogant,” Pochettino replied with a smile and a laugh. “Well, not arrogant enough. I am a little bit arrogant.”
Eventually he relented. Pochettino’s lasting impact, the coach said, was largely down to relationships, to having done things the right way, in his mind.
“The most valuable feeling that we get isn’t one victory, or that we helped in the program,” he said. “It is that relationship in the program – even when you cross the sea, you look and smile because I think you share the values that are very important in life, more important than anything else. That is our principal that we respect always.”
Pochettino has always thought in big, broad, ambitious strokes and has executed those visions over the course of his career with varying degrees of success. In the United States, he arrived with varying goals: ensure a proper showing at a home World Cup, help change the perception of the game to the general public and lay down roots for long-term growth.
In some ways, Pochettino certainly succeeded. In others, he’s left the whole of American soccer wanting. It’s a fitting end for a coach who wanted so many people to believe – yet might never have felt that way himself.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Rubio targets ICC: 'Won't submit to sterile vision of radical judges'
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Hilal Saki
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Rubio targets ICC: 'Won't submit to sterile vision of radical judges'
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has targeted the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a speech to a conservative legal group on Friday, arguing for a muscular foreign policy and against international law restraining US actions.
During his speech to the Federalist Society in Washington, his first prepared remarks since Republicans were routed in the midterm elections on 3 November, Rubio said the goal of the US-Israeli war against Iran was to prevent Tehran from ever developing a nuclear weapon, which he said was particularly urgent because the Islamic Republic's "radical Shia clerics" had an "expansionist mentality."
He contrasted this with the government of North Korea's Kim Jong Un, whom Trump has met three times. "I'm not excusing the terrible things that have happened there," Rubio said of North Korea. "I'm just saying he (Kim) is not expansionist. He's not trying to invade Japan or, you know, China or whatever."
Rubio dismissed criticisms that the Trump administration has broken international law by such actions as seizing Venezuelan then-President Nicolas Maduro and striking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific that it says were carrying drugs.
The US, Rubio said, would not “submit to the sterile vision of radical judges or soulless global bureaucrats,” repeating his assertion that the court would try to prosecute US officials or service members that he used to justify sanctions against the ICC announced last month.
“Americans have never agreed to submit to the ICC's authority, but that court and its allies in the global bureaucracy have appointed themselves judge and jury and executioner of the international order,” Rubio said.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the Netherlands-based court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges.
The ICC has received strong backing from most member states, which include all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey.
Washington has denounced the court over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is "deprioritised."
The US sanctions, designed to stifle the ICC’s ability to operate, will take effect in April unless supporters of the Netherlands-based court can reach an agreement with the US to avert them.
Rubio suggested that if the court tried to enforce its rulings against Americans, Washington would respond with force. Quoting the Roman general Pompey, Rubio said the US response would be: "Stop quoting laws to men with swords.”
Report by Reuters

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Trump to discuss Iran war, but not Ukraine, at China summit
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Hilal Saki
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Trump to discuss Iran war, but not Ukraine, at China summit
US President Donald Trump will discuss the Iran war with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week but he is not expected to discuss Ukraine war, a US official said.
The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.
Report by AFP

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Hilal Saki
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Rubio says economic pain inflicted on Iran makes military action unnecessary
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that further US military action against Iran is unnecessary because the economic pain the Washington is inflicting on a "weakened" Tehran "is so great".
“And right now, frankly, the economic pain that we are inflicting on that regime is so great that there’s no need for military action because we’ve weakened them so much,” Rubio said in his address to the Federalist Society National Lawyers Convention in Washington.
“But I think victory is ensuring that they never have a nuclear weapon,” he added.
At the same time, Rubio acknowledge the economic pain Americans have experienced as a result of the war, which has driven up fuel costs and affected nearly every sector of the global economy.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Coyote officials thought they had killed after child attack seen alive in LA neighborhood
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A coyote that California wildlife officials believed they had euthanized after it bit a toddler and menaced residential pets in a trendy Los Angeles neighborhood was seen alive recently, neighborhood residents said.
Wiley, the name some Atwater Village residents gave to the coyote, had vexed the area with its increasingly aggressive and brazen behavior. The wild animal, which scampered through people’s backyards, was reportedly being fed by an unidentified man. Wiley’s presence drew local uproar after he bit a 16-month-old child.
The attack prompted California department of fish and wildlife officers to shoot Wiley in October, an intervention that appeared to cap the neighborhood saga.
That is until residents observed a limping Wiley back in Atwater Village in recent weeks.
When asked what went awry, the California department of fish and wildlife said in a statement provided to KTLA that officials shot Wiley on 16 October. The department’s officers could not locate the coyote’s body and concluded it had died.
The department returned to Atwater Village, where they shot Wiley for a second time, confirming on Tuesday that the coyote had been killed.
The twist in Wiley’s tale brought cold comfort to some residents, who feel that the coyote’s death could have been prevented.
“I don’t think he should have been euthanized because coyotes are predators, and they’re going to do what they’re going to do,” one neighbor, Ana Fishman, told KTLA. “And that’s not his fault. He should have been relocated. I think the fact that coyotes apparently, in the state of California, can’t be relocated is wrong.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US Coast Guard suspends search for woman swept out to sea in California
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Anna Betts
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The US Coast Guard announced that it has suspended its search for a 24-year-old woman who is believed to have been swept out to sea in California.
The woman, identified as 24-year-old Senah Park, was last seen near Panther state beach in Santa Cruz county at about 8.30pm local time on Sunday, authorities said earlier this week.
In a statement, the Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office said deputies responded to the beach at about 8pm on Sunday night, after receiving a report “of a woman who was believed to have been swept into the ocean”.
According to the sheriff’s office, a group of friends were on the beach when an “incoming tide knocked several of them over”. During that incident, Park “is believed to have been swept out to sea”, they said.
The San Mateo-Santa Cruz unit of California Fire CZU said firefighters were dispatched to the beach at about 8.30pm on Sunday. The unit said: “Four people had gone through the keyhole on the beach and when the tide rose, they became trapped.”
“Three people were able to escape the rising tide,” they said, adding: “One person, described as a woman in her twenties, was not able to escape and was believed to have been swept out to sea.”
Authorities said that an “extensive search” began on Sunday night, involving drones, ground crews, helicopters, and search and rescue teams.
In an update issued on Tuesday, the sheriff’s office said that its “fixed wing Air Unit and Drone Team have been searching the coastline and surrounding waters” for Park.
“While there are no significant updates to share at this time, our thoughts are with Senah’s family and friends during this incredibly difficult time,” the sheriff’s office statement on Tuesday said.
In a separate statement on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard said watchstanders at its San Francisco command center received a notification on Sunday night from Santa Cruz fire department personnel “of a confirmed person in the water near Panther State Beach”.
The Coast Guard said that watchstanders issued an urgent marine information broadcast and coordinated the launch of a 47ft motor lifeboat crew and MH-65 Dolphin helicopter aircrew for the search.
The agency said that it also coordinated “eight hours of search efforts across 95 square miles” and deployed assets including helicopter aircrews, boat crews, drones and more.
But, in the statement on Tuesday, the Coast Guard said that it had “suspended its search” on Monday afternoon.
“Suspending a search is a difficult decision,” Lt Max Holloway, San Francisco sector search and rescue mission coordinator, said in a statement on Tuesday. “Given the extensive search effort of the surrounding area and environmental conditions, we have suspended active search efforts pending further developments.
“We worked closely with our partner agencies and exhausted all available resources in our attempt to locate Ms Park,” he added. “Our deepest condolences are with her family and loved ones.”
The announcement comes as the National Weather Service’s San Francisco Bay Area and Monterey office warned on Tuesday that high surf is expected this coming weekend, with “dangerously large breaking waves” of between 20 and 30ft expected.
“It is highly advisable to stay away from beaches and off of jetties, piers, and rocks,” the NWS office said. “Remain out of the water. Never turn your back to the ocean!”
It also comes as in recent weeks parts of California have experienced historic high tides and record-breaking water levels, as the impacts of an exceptionally strong and still-strengthening El Niño continue to unfold.

https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ea.title: Manhattan’s East Side loses another movie theater to development
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ea.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/news/manhattans-ea.text:
Months after news broke that the Kips Bay AMC will shutter at year’s end, another East Side movie theater announced it has projected its last film.
Cinema 123 by Angelika closed on Oct. 30 after more than 60 years of business near the Queensboro Bridge on East 60th Street.
“As our final credits roll, we thank you for being part of our story,” the theater wrote in a social media farewell post with vintage photos of its 1976 marquee and line for “Rocky” and a 1986 photo that includes its former neighbor, the classic consumer electronics chain Crazy Eddie.
Cinema 123’s building was sold by owner Reading International to developer Roger Equities for $41 million in a deal that, according to public record, closed on the same day of the theater’s announcement.
Roger Equities currently plans to redevelop the approximately 8,000-square-foot, 1001 3rd Av. lot – located between East 59th and East 60th streets, and across from Bloomingdale’s flagship – into multifamily rental housing, the Commercial Observer reported.
A change of property ownership also caused the expected closure of the AMC Kips Bay 15, which was purchased by NYU Langone and is likely to be developed into a medical facility. That plan has prompted pushback from local elected officials who are seeking to preserve the theater.
Cinema 123’s sister locations, Angelika Film Center & Cafe on W. Houston St and Village East by Angelika on 2nd Ave. in the East Village remain open.
When Cinema 123 opened in 1962, it was the nation’s first ever twin-screen cinema. Following its initial success, it added a third screen in the 1980s. In more recent years it was beloved for still offering 70-millimeter film screenings.
Cinema 123’s closure will leave the AMC Orpheum 7 as the Upper East Side’s last remaining movie theater.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.title: Sotheby’s Hedreen Auction Proceeds Will Repay Loan, Not Fund University Museum: Report
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.text:
A $300 million art donation to Seattle University has been revealed to be more complex than originally reported.
On Monday, Sotheby’s will begin selling approximately 50 works from the collection amassed by Seattle real estate developer and philanthropist Richard “Dick” Hedreen, previously billed as the “largest art gift ever” to a US university. Hedreen said in September that the sale did not mean the promised gift was falling through. Rather, he suggested, the proceeds would help furnish Seattle University’s new art museum, where the collection was eventually expected to hang.
Records newly reported on by The Seattle Times, however, tell a different story: The works are being sold not to fund the museum, but to pay off a debt secured against the collection — a debt Hedreen says stands between him and fulfilling his pledge to the university.
What was originally framed as a donation, in reality, was a pledge: Hedreen, whose firm R.C. Hedreen Co. owns the Grand Hyatt among other Seattle properties, retained the right to buy and sell works from the collection until the gift was finalized. The Sotheby’s auction is expected to generate at least $100 million across a series of sales. As of writing, the overall value of the artwork set for Seattle University is unclear.
The sale spans an expansive sweep of art history. Works by Willem de Kooning, Rashid Johnson, Amy Sherald, and Jonas Wood will be offered alongside Old Masters by Bronzino, Jacopo Pontormo, Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, and Thomas Gainsborough. Leading Sotheby’s offerings is Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990), estimated at $20 million to $30 million. Cecily Brown’s 12-foot-wide Untitled (Shipwreck) (2017), estimated at $7 million to $10 million, is another highlight.
A news release from Seattle University stated: “Hedreen has given the university the renowned Hedreen Collection (named for himself and his late wife Elizabeth ‘Betty’ Ann Petri Hedreen, a Seattle University alumna) valued at $300 million, along with $25 million in seed funding to develop the museum.”
However, the Seattle Times reported that records show that the “seed funding” was actually provided through the private sale of a de Kooning painting. Estimated in 2024 to be worth $25 million, the work fetched $17 million.
The Sotheby’s sale proceeds will instead go toward paying off an outstanding loan secured against the collection. The borrowing dates to 2012, when Hedreen first pledged several artworks, including a pieces by Francis Bacon, de Kooning and David Hockney, as collateral for a Goldman Sachs loan. In 2025, that financing was replaced with a Bank of America loan secured by approximately 44 major artworks.
R.C. Hedreen Co. President David Thyer confirmed that the Sotheby’s sale is tied to financial pressures in the hotel and real estate markets. Income generated by the company’s properties, he said, is insufficient to repay the loan “in any reasonably foreseeable time frame.”
ARTnews has contacted Sotheby’s for comment.
Richard Hedreen’s son, Guy, said in a statement that his family’s “commitment to Seattle University has not changed.” His father, Guy added, “is not selling works from his collection in order to spend money on himself” or his business. Rather, the auction reflects his commitment to the university “by removing a debt that prevents him from translating his pledge intentions into an outright gift.”
Construction on the new art museum, originally scheduled to begin this past summer, has been pushed to 2027 as the project awaits permits. Designed by local architect Tom Kundig, the museum is intended to permanently house the Hedreen collection, alongside rotating exhibitions and academic programming.
Scott K. McClellan, Seattle University’s vice president for university affairs, said the school continues to believe the collection “presents a significant opportunity for the university, community and our broader vision for the arts.” He reiterated the “shared intention of Mr. Hedreen and the university” that Seattle University ultimately receive a collection of museum-quality works commensurate with the collection that formed the basis of the original commitment.
McClellan added that it had been “reasonable” for the university to expect Hedreen’s loan to be paid off by 2028, when the museum was originally scheduled for completion.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ke.title: Manhattan Landlord Sues Kehinde Wiley, Claiming He Owes $36,000 in Unpaid Rent
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ke.author: Harrison Jacobs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ke.text:
Artist Kehinde Wiley returned to the New York art scene last week with his first show in the city since he was accused of sexual assault in 2024. Now the famed artist and Obama portraitist faces a legal dispute of a different kind: real estate.
In a complaint filed in New York County Supreme Court, 115 West 11th Street LLC accuses Wiley of failing to pay rent on his apartment in its building since October 1. According to court documents filed November 6, the rent is $18,000 a month, and the landlord is seeking $36,000 in total.
Per the documents, Wiley has lived in the building since September 2023 and signed a lease renewal in July 2025, which was later extended through the end of September. The landlord contends that Wiley did not vacate the apartment when the lease ended and has continued to live there without paying the agreed $18,000 a month.
Wiley has not yet responded to the complaint. A summons, also filed November 6, requires the artist’s attorneys to respond within 20 days.
The complaint was filed on the same day Wiley’s new exhibition, “What the Light Becomes,” opened at Sean Kelly Gallery in New York. The show features a new series of portraits of contemporary New Yorkers. According to the exhibition text, the show is “conceived of as a love letter to New York and a return to the subject of the city that launched Wiley’s career.”
Sean Kelly Gallery did not respond to a request for comment from ARTnews by press time.
Wiley is one of the art world’s brightest stars and one of the few artists who are household names, thanks to his beloved official portrait of President Barack Obama. He has been tied up in the courts since 2024, when five people accused him of sexual assault or rape. Wiley has denied the allegations. He has said that his encounters with some of the accusers were consensual and that he did not know others. Only one accuser, Ogechi Chieke, has sued the artist, and that case is ongoing.
In a New York Times profile published last week, Wiley said of the allegations, “I’ve been through more pain—it’s really hard to imagine what it’s like to have people believe that. To look at you and think you’re a predator.” He added, “In my life, there has always been, by hook or by crook, some sense of grace that comes out of even the most challenging situations.”
Jennifer Barrett of Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, Wiley’s attorney in the Chieke lawsuit, did not respond to a request for comment by press time.
	The Daily Mail first reported the new lawsuit on Wednesday.
.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.title: Long-Lost Charles Le Brun Painting Returns to the New Palace in Potsdam
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.author: Anne Doran
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.text:
Lost for more than 75 years, a painting by French Baroque artist Charles Le Brun (1619–1690) is now returning to the New Palace in Potsdam’s Sanssouci Park. The news was reported first by the German Press Agency (dpa) following a statement by the Prussian Palaces and Gardens Foundation Berlin-Brandenburg (SPSG).
Court painter to Louis XIV after 1661 and the designer most responsible for the opulent style of the French monarchy, Le Brun created the work, a depiction of a sleeping Christ Child with the Holy Family, around 1655. It was acquired in the 1700s by King Frederick the Great (Frederick II) of Prussia for the New Palace, where it hung in one of the guest apartments.
In 1942, to protect it from Allied bombings, much of the art at the Picture Gallery of Sanssouci and the New Palace, including Le Brun’s painting, was evacuated some 60 miles northwest to Schloss Rheinsberg.
On April 29, 1945, the Red Army entered Rheinsberg. Russian troops occupied the building, and a short time later the majority of the paintings housed in the Schloss Rheinsberg were sent to the Soviet Union. However, according to the SPSG, not all of the works arrived there, with some entering private collections in Rheinsberg under “convoluted circumstances.”
Le Brun’s painting was documented as being at Schloss Rheinsberg until July 30, 1945. After that, according to a spokesperson from the foundation, the painting vanished—until it resurfaced at a Berlin auction house in 2021.
The return was made possible by the support of the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation and the Friends of the Prussian Palaces Association. On November 18, 2026 at 2:30 p.m., the “Holy Family” will be unveiled in the Upper Red Chambers of the New Palace.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.title: The ADAA Fair Is Back, and Sometimes Smaller Really Is Better
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/.text:
Art fairs should do two things: let visitors see art, ideally stuff they haven’t seen before, and help dealers sell that art to people who want to buy it. Simple enough. And yet, somewhere along the way, fairs became so enormous that seeing everything on offer began to feel like an endurance sport.
That’s one reason the newly rechristened Art Dealers Association of America Fair, which opened Thursday night at the Park Avenue Armory, was such a pleasure. With just 63 exhibitors, it’s small enough to navigate without a map, manageable enough to spend time actually looking at the art, and varied enough to reward a little wandering. These may sound like modest achievements, but anyone who’s spent six hours trudging through a convention center will appreciate them.
The setting helps. The Park Avenue Armory still has plenty of its old New York charm, something that’s increasingly hard to come by in an art fair. Organizers have also moved the bar to the center of the exhibition hall, improving the sightlines and making the whole affair feel more open. You can actually see what’s going on across the room, rather than navigating a maze of booths.
Of course, the fair’s return wasn’t entirely straightforward. Last July, the AADA abruptly canceled its 2025 edition, calling the decision a “strategic pause.” The organization subsequently retired the Art Show name and ended its decades-long fundraising partnership with the Henry Street Settlement, which had received more than $38 million through the fair’s benefit previews. The Whitney Museum of American Art is now the beneficiary, and the fair has returned with 12 fewer exhibitors and what seems to be emphasis on its national membership.
The reasons behind the sudden cancellation remain something of a mystery (and there were no shortage of rumors percolating about what happened with the fair’s old partner, Henry Street) but whatever the circumstances of its reinvention, the result is a fair that gets at least one of those two basic things right.
As for the selling, well, that’s up to the dealers.
Kinsey Robb, the ADAA’s executive director, was spritely and in good spirits at Thursday’s gala, quite literally shining even, thanks to her skirt, which was decorated with what she described as little chandeliers. It was a new purchase and even spent some time at the tailor before the evening’s debut. Organizing a fair, she explained, comes with plenty of highs and lows. Sometimes a little retail therapy helps.
Robb, who took over the association in September 2024, has spent much of the past year talking about making the fair more valuable to its members. But when I asked whether that meant exhibitors were actually paying less to participate, she offered a rather different definition of value.
“I think it’s sales, sure,” she said, “but the real benefit was the connections dealers make with one another and with collectors.” She described a collegial atmosphere during installation, with dealers more than pleased to see old friends and actually interested in what their neighbors were showing.
That might sound a little sentimental, but Robb makes a reasonable point. The association represents a large network of galleries, many of them small businesses whose concerns are rather different from those of the industry’s multinational behemoths. The fair, she argued, gives them somewhere to meet, exchange ideas, and share their expertise.
“It’s not my fair,” she said. “It’s the members’ fair.”
Fortunately, there was evidence that the members were doing business, too.
According to sales figures released by the ADAA following Thursday’s preview, Jonathan Boos reported two of the evening’s biggest transactions: Agnes Pelton’s The Well of Peace (1932), with an asking price of $2.4 million, and a Beauford Delaney painting priced at $1.6 million.
The action wasn’t confined to the million-dollar end of the market. AH Arts sold a Helen Frankenthaler work on paper for a reported $75,000, while James Barron Art placed works by Beverly Pepper, Kenneth Noland, and Kikuo Saito, with asking prices ranging from $40,000 to $85,000.
Contemporary art found buyers as well. Jessica Silverman reported selling eight works by Julie Buffalohead, priced between $22,000 and $50,000, while Charles Moffett sold all four of its Lily Stockman paintings at $20,000 apiece and four works by Julia Jo priced between $30,000 and $40,000.
Kraushaar Galleries, meanwhile, reported two six-figure sales alongside several works priced below $2,000. That’s a fairly remarkable spread, and perhaps a better illustration of the ADAA’s appeal than another speech about the importance of community.
Of course, these are dealer-reported sales, and asking prices don’t necessarily reflect what buyers actually paid. Still, they suggest that at least some collectors came to do more than admire the art and enjoy the open bar.
And there was plenty worth admiring. Here are five booths that caught my eye.
Gavlak
At Gavlak, two generations of artists offer very different takes on light, color, and the cosmos. Lita Albuquerque, a veteran of California’s Light and Space and Land Art movements, presents a series of luminous paintings in which gold-leaf discs appear to float against fields of saturated blue, black, and crimson.
In Goya’s First Breath (2025), a pale gold oval glows against a black background, looking something like a distant planet glimpsed through the darkness.
Across the booth, Jessica Cannon takes a more intricate approach. Her paintings are built from overlapping geometric forms and thousands of tiny marks that create shimmering, almost woven surfaces. In August Radii (2026), bands of peach, orange, pink, and green spiral around a central point, while Razor Moon (2026) offers a cooler composition of blues and purples.
The two artists make an excellent pairing. Albuquerque’s paintings seem to radiate light from within, while Cannon’s appear to catch and scatter it. They’re also the sort of works that reward seeing them in person, changing subtly as you move around them. Albuquerque’s paintings are priced between $90,000 and $125,000, while Cannon’s range from $25,000 to $40,000.
Peter Blum Gallery
Alex Katz is one of those artists whose work is so instantly recognizable that it’s easy to forget how much thinking goes into making something look so effortless.
Peter Blum’s booth, devoted entirely to Katz’s works on paper, offers a particularly enjoyable reminder. Spanning roughly seven decades, the presentation brought together early cut-paper collages and later charcoal and graphite drawings.
One particularly charming little collage, Untitled (ca. 1957–58), shows four figures relaxing on a nearly deserted beach. A thin strip of dark green landscape cuts across the horizon, while the figures, rendered in tiny scraps of colored paper, occupy only a fraction of the composition. Most of it is simply sand.
It’s all very Katz, despite measuring just five by eight inches. There’s something wonderful about how little he needs to establish a scene.
The more recent drawings, including studies of flowers, reveal the same economy of line. Very little unnecessary information, yet somehow everything you need is there.
Eric Firestone Gallery
Eric Firestone, as usual, put together an excellent booth of seven women associated with the New York School, including Helen Frankenthaler, Pat Passlof, Elise Asher, Miriam Schapiro, Sari Dienes, Adaline Kent, and Jeanne Reynal.
It’s a compelling collection of artists whose contributions to postwar American art were frequently overshadowed by those of their male contemporaries. More importantly, the works themselves are terrific, and the presentation makes a convincing case for how much experimentation was happening beyond the familiar names of Abstract Expressionism.
Among the highlights is a small, previously unexhibited 1951 landscape by Frankenthaler, made with oil and pencil on a piece of palette paper. It’s a fascinating glimpse of the artist before the breakthrough that would transform her practice the following year.
There’s also Dienes’s Burnt Totem (1961), a monumental assemblage made from discarded wooden hat forms, and Passlof’s Keeping Still Mountain, a large, restless abstraction whose title comes from the I Ching.
The booth is a firm nod to the fact that there is a lot of art history that remains to be reconsidered, even when the period in question has been studied to death.
Cristin Tierney Gallery
Maureen O’Leary’s paintings at Cristin Tierney are wonderfully strange. At first glance, her bright colors, simplified figures, and seemingly cheerful domestic scenes suggest something almost storybook-like. Spend another minute looking, though, and things become considerably less straightforward.
In Spring (2026), a backyard gathering unfolds around a barbecue, with children, animals, and plants crowded into a busy, brightly colored landscape. Flames leap from the grill while the surrounding figures seem to inhabit slightly different versions of reality. There are echoes of the Nabis and Post-Impressionists in the flattened perspective and improbable colors, but O’Leary’s world is distinctly her own.
What makes the paintings work is the tension between their familiar subject matter and the peculiar atmosphere she creates. These are scenes of ordinary life, but ordinary life as remembered in a particularly vivid dream.
The presentation coincides with The Linden Trees, O’Leary’s second solo exhibition at the gallery, which runs through December 19.
Piero Atchugarry
Sculpture can be a difficult proposition at an art fair, where space is limited and paintings tend to get most of the attention. But Piero Atchugarry’s solo presentation of Brazilian artist Túlio Pinto is worth seeking out.
Pinto works with stone, steel, and glass, arranging materials in configurations that appear to defy the laws of physics without actually doing so. A heavy stone rests on a chain made of glass. Elsewhere, an enormous steel beam appears to depend on another delicate glass chain to remain upright.
In Complicity #52, rust-colored steel beams grip enormous amber glass forms, while a large piece of rose quartz hangs precariously from one end. The whole structure looks as though it ought to collapse, which is precisely what makes it so compelling.
The four works on view span several years of Pinto’s practice, including pieces from his Complicity Vectors series and more recent Gravitas sculptures. They share an interest in balance, resistance, and the sometimes surprising strength of materials we ordinarily think of as fragile.
It’s a smart, physically engaging, and exactly the sort of thing that makes a smaller art fair worth visiting.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.title: Lightsaber Brandished by Darth Vader Auctioned for $4.9 M., Breaking Record for Star Wars Sales
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.author: Andy Battaglia
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/st.text:
A lightsaber wielded by none other than Darth Vader sold for $4.875 million in a Heritage Auctions sale, breaking the record for Star Wars–related memorabilia.
The treasure was used in Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Star Wars: Return of the Jedi (1983), and also holds the special distinction of having been the weapon central to the former’s famous “I am your father” scene, in which Luke Skywalker learns some surprising news from the figure who had long been his nemesis.
Heritage reported that the sale exceeded that of “Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber and severed hand effects rig” last year (for $3.75 million) and a poster painting for Star Wars: Episode IV—A New Hope in 2025 (for $3.875 million).
About the sale of the lightsaber, one of 27 offered up by Heritage, Brian Chanes, the auction house’s senior director of Hollywood and entertainment, told Los Angeles’s ABC7 Eyewitness News, “I’ve been doing this for 35 years and I’ve never seen a compilation of screen-used lightsabers like this; you know, from the original franchise to the sequels.” He continued: “It’s the one on the set. It’s from the most iconic sequence of the entire franchise. From a memorabilia standpoint this is like the holy grail.”
	About sales of the kind in general, Chanes added, “I always tell people that memorabilia, the m-e-m portion is your memories, what you remember when you first saw the first Star Wars film. It basically takes you to the happy place when you first saw it, and it’s a feel-good thing!”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fa.title: Fake UK Artist Visas Are Being Offered for $132,000, New Investigation Finds
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fa.author: Hikmat Mohammed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fa.text:
Several companies have been helping migrants apply for UK visas under the government’s Global Talent program by creating fake art portfolios, complete with fake published art criticism and art news, according to a new investigation published by the BBC Friday.
Nigerian art critic Molara Wood told the publication that she had found her name attached to fake online reviews praising the works of two obscure artists, just one instance of the materials created.
“There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists,” Wood told the BBC. Following the BBC’s investigation, two Nigerian men’s visas are in the process of being revoked, according to the Home Office. The two claimed to be fine art photographers in their visa applications.
One BBC reporter went undercover to research the companies offering packages through the Global Talent program. The firm said it could supply the reporter with artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation. The reporter had been reassured that the “fully inclusive” would grant them a visa without refusal—the package was priced at more than £100,000 ($132,000). The Home Office told the BBC that the company the reporter had dug out was already under investigation. A spokesperson for the Home Office said that they “will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system” and the “home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused.”
The government’s Global Talent program was launched in 2020 and was designed to attract creative workers, including scientists and artists. However, in recent years, it has become a way for companies to target wealthy migrants looking to move without going through the official route, which has become challenging in the UK following new immigration laws.
In another case, a woman said she worked with a company to help her secure a talent visa through the tech route. The company had used fabricated evidence for her application, including a fictitious mentoring award and materials falsely suggesting that she had been a keynote speaker at an event. In the end, her application was rejected.
The companies offering talent visas have been targeting all nationalities. The BBC found two companies in its investigation: iCareer Consultancy and its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, based out of London’s corporate hub, Canary Wharf, offering fake artwork and immigration advice. During a call with an undercover BBC reporter, an iCareer consultant said that four of his clients obtained a visa this year and that they can supply the reporter with an employee to pose as a client and network for them at gallery openings. The company also said that for £28,000 ($37,000), they can offer a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, boosting their chances of securing a visa.
iCareer told the BBC through its lawyers that it strongly denied “offering any visa services whatsoever” and that meeting with the consultant “was not authorized by iCareer.”
“We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him,” the company said.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/rh.title: Rhizome Announces Partnership With Electronic Arts Intermix Following Vimeo Censorship Concerns
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/rh.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/rh.text:
Earlier this week, Rhizome, the 30-year-old digital art nonprofit that has been affiliated with the New Museum since 2003, announced a pilot program with its internal video hosting platform video.rhizome.org, and Electronic Arts Intermix (EAI). Rhizome hopes to offer VRO, as it’s known, to other digital arts organizations and artists as an alternative to commercial video platforms like Vimeo.
“We think offering artists video hosting is something that could be meaningful for people in the community right now,” Michael Connor, Rhizome’s executive director, told ARTnews. “With the way that the web is going, it’s harder and harder to run a platform the way Vimeo operated a decade ago.”
Rhizome initially set up VRO in 2022, but their plans to offer the technology to others in the digital arts community kicked into high gear this summer following a breakdown in the relationship between Vimeo and EAI, a video and new media distributor with a collection of thousands of digital artworks by over 200 artists.
The trouble started in May, when EAI began receiving emails, which EAI executive director Rebecca Cleman believes were AI-generated, flagging their account for community guideline violations. Karl McCool, EAI’s distribution director, told ARTnews that the two works Vimeo initially flagged were Barbara Hammer’s 1970s films Dyketactics and Women I Love, two of EAI’s most requested films.
EAI wasn’t completely caught off guard by this, McCool explains. He’d heard from colleagues at similarly sized arts organizations, like Collectif Jeune Cinema, a French experimental film distributor, and Visual AIDS, which supports HIV+ artists, about issues they were having with Vimeo. And in December, Connor says he told Cleman to “watch out for Vimeo,” having also heard about problems with streaming controversial or explicit media.
Despite EAI’s repeated attempts to get in touch with Vimeo to explain the history and value of Hammer’s, and others’, artworks, neither McCool nor Cleman was ever able to speak with a real person at the company, and their account was shut down over Memorial Day weekend.
EAI finally connected with someone at Vimeo about a month later, and the account was temporarily reinstated—once they took down the videos that had been flagged by artists like Ellen Cantor, Carolee Schneemann, Peggy Ahwesh, and Alex Bag, in addition to Hammer.
ARTnews reached out to Vimeo, but did not receive a response about their policy for removing videos or suspending accounts by press time.
“One thing that struck us,” said McCool, “is that a lot of the videos were works by women. Because we know the catalogue inside and out, we know that there’s a lot of work by men that is arguably far more explicit. And those things weren’t flagged … I don’t know that they were deliberately targeting women, but it was really notable what they didn’t pick up on, like the two films of Bruce Nauman’s testicles, or the many films of Vito Acconci completely naked doing sexual sorts of things, or the two Lawrence Weiner films that are full of unsimulated sex.”
EAI proactively removed these videos as well, since their contact at Vimeo explained that the account would be reinstated only once. By this point, EAI was already working with Rhizome on the new platform and planned to transition away from Vimeo as soon as it was ready.
Cleman and McCool trace their recent issues with Vimeo to the company’s $1.38 billion acquisition by Bending Spoons, a tech conglomerate that also owns WeTransfer, Eventbrite, and Airtable, in the fall of 2025. It was then that Vimeo’s business model shifted significantly, Cleman wrote in an email to ARTnews, with a majority of their workforce being dismissed in favor of AI replacements. McCool explained that he and others at EAI reached out to contacts at Vimeo they had been in touch with as recently as a few weeks or months prior, and all had been let go.
McCool credits Rhizome with “heroic” efforts over the summer to build an alternative to Vimeo using PeerTube, an open-source video platform, that addressed all of EAI’s specific needs. “We couldn’t just use PeerTube like an alternative version of YouTube,” McCool explained. “We needed Rhizome’s help to build a version that was tailor-made for us. We had to ensure that videos could be embedded on our own website with certain digital rights management protections in place. We had to make sure these works aren’t easily copied or pirated. We had to have good captions in place. There were all these different considerations that we needed Rhizome’s help with.”
Rhizome delivered on building the service—pro bono, McCool notes—and EAI is now able to host their videos via VRO. Connor plans to continue advocating for the importance of independent infrastructure in keeping digital artwork reliably available online. “Rhizome is still a nonprofit,” Connor said. “We’re not trying to run a video-hosting business. But the work our developers did for EAI is really easily replicable if we have other institutions or artists that need their own channels. We see hosting artist videos as mission-aligned work.”

Iran says three tankers hit by mines in Hormuz catch fire
Iran's navy and Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that fires had broken out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorised route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Guards' navy said in a statement on the incident in the south of the waterway, carried by the Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.
A separate statement from Iran's conventional navy said another tanker "navigating through the unsafe and prohibited zone east of the Strait of Hormuz with its tracking and identification systems switched off, caught fire and was forced to stop after striking a naval mine".
The statements did not provide the names or origins of the vessels but the Guards said one of those hit in south Hormuz was a supertanker.
The Guards released footage on Friday of a large plume of smoke rising from a vessel it said was carrying liquefied gas and hit a mine in the south of the strait.

'What would be left of international legal order': Araghchi on US strikes
"If states were free to attack one another based on their own assessments of possible future threats, what would be left of the international legal order?" Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has asked in an opinion piece for Japan's Kyodo News.
"This question," Araghchi wrote, "goes well beyond the political dispute between Iran and the United States."
"It concerns one of the fundamental principles on which the international order established after the Second World War rests: the use of force is governed by law, and no state, however powerful, is entitled to place its own judgment above binding rules of international law," the article read.
He said the US-Israeli strikes constituted a clear violation of the prohibition on the use of force and an infringement of Iran's sovereignty.
"Their legality must be assessed against the U.N. Charter and established principles of international law, not against political arguments or justifications advanced after military operations have begun," he wrote.
He said the US had neither obtained UN Security Council authorisation nor established grounds for invoking self-defence under Article 51, which permits force in response to an armed attack.
The attacks on schools, sports stadiums, civilian infrastructure, and Iranian nuclear facilities subject to International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards raise further questions under international law, and they must be examined under international humanitarian law.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Eixão: Brasília precisa escolher entre a velocidade dos carros e a segurança das pessoas
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: André Pires
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A discussão sobre o Eixão expõe um confronto de concepções que Brasília precisa enfrentar. De um lado, a evidência científica sobre segurança viária e o direito das pessoas à cidade. De outro, uma lógica urbana herdada do século passado, que fez do automóvel a prioridade absoluta e dos cidadãos coadjuvantes do espaço urbano. O governo do Distrito Federal diz ter estudos técnicos próprios, discorda da decisão e vai recorrer. O debate é legítimo e deve ser feito com dados abertos, não com slogans.
Durante décadas, fomos levados a acreditar que uma cidade funciona melhor quando os carros circulam mais rápido. Essa ideia está tão enraizada que qualquer redução de velocidade é recebida, por alguns, como ataque à mobilidade. Mas é preciso perguntar: mobilidade para quem?
O Eixão foi concebido dentro de um modelo de cidade que priorizava a circulação dos automóveis. Isso faz parte da história de Brasília, mas não significa que o modelo deva permanecer intocável. A cidade cresceu, a sociedade mudou e o planejamento urbano precisa acompanhar.
A velocidade não é apenas uma questão de tempo. É uma questão de sobrevivência.
A diferença entre 80 km/h e 60 km/h pode parecer pequena para quem está ao volante, mas é enorme na física de uma colisão. Para o mesmo veículo, nas mesmas condições, a energia cinética a 80 km/h é cerca de 78% maior do que a 60 km/h, pois ela cresce com o quadrado da velocidade.
A evidência sobre pedestres é ainda mais contundente. Uma revisão sistemática com meta-análise, publicada em 2019 na revista “Accident Analysis & Prevention”, estimou que o risco de morte de um pedestre atingido chega a 50% quando a velocidade de impacto é de cerca de 59 km/h, e a 90% quando chega a cerca de 80 km/h. O mesmo estudo calculou risco de 5% a 30 km/h e de 10% a 37 km/h, e concluiu que os resultados sustentam limites de 30 a 40 km/h em áreas de grande circulação de pedestres.
Duas ressalvas são necessárias. Primeiro, esses números se referem à velocidade no momento do impacto, e não ao limite indicado na placa. Segundo, os autores apontam indícios de viés de publicação entre os estudos analisados. Ainda assim, o padrão é claro: o risco cresce de forma acentuada com a velocidade. E há uma consequência honesta a tirar disso: 60 km/h não torna uma via segura para quem atravessa a pé. Torna-a menos letal do que 80 km/h.
Não falamos de abstração acadêmica. Falamos de vidas humanas. Relatórios da Polícia Civil do DF citados na sentença apontam 264 vítimas de sinistros de trânsito no Eixão entre 2022 e 2025, das quais 20 morreram e 244 ficaram feridas. Durante a tramitação da ação, iniciada em 2024, novos atropelamentos fatais foram reportados ao juízo. Em 20 de outubro, menos de um mês antes da sentença, uma jovem de 18 anos morreu atropelada no Eixão Norte.
Diante desse cenário, o juiz Carlos Maroja determinou a redução do limite de 80 para 60 km/h, com a adequação da fiscalização eletrônica, um projeto para ampliar a segurança e a acessibilidade das travessias, com semáforos para pedestres, e um plano de limpeza, drenagem, iluminação e reforço de segurança nas passagens subterrâneas. A própria sentença estima um acréscimo de cerca de cinco minutos para percorrer o Eixão de ponta a ponta, e considera esse custo razoável diante da redução da letalidade. A decisão ainda cabe recurso, sobretudo no ponto questionável da inserção de semáforos, que violariam o tombamento urbanístico da capital.
A sentença também mostra que não há contradição entre reduzir a velocidade e cobrar passagens subterrâneas dignas. O próprio Departamento de Estradas de Rodagem do Distrito Federal (DER-DF) lembra que túneis sujos e mal iluminados colocam o pedestre em risco a qualquer velocidade, e o juízo considerou a insegurança dos túneis uma das premissas da decisão, que torna a travessia em nível, pela pista de alta velocidade, quase inevitável.
Infraestrutura abandonada não é solução. São pautas complementares, e também o é o investimento em transporte público: uma cidade precisa oferecer transporte coletivo digno, travessias seguras e condições adequadas a pedestres, ciclistas e motoristas.
Sustento, como opinião, que uma lógica urbana que coloca o automóvel no centro de todas as decisões tende a produzir dependência do carro, a estimular velocidades incompatíveis com a segurança e a ampliar desigualdades. Quem não dirige, quem depende do transporte coletivo, quem tem mobilidade reduzida e quem precisa atravessar uma via também tem direito à cidade. Brasília não pode ser refém dos automóveis.
A capital tem 66 anos e caminha para o centenário, em 2060. Temos a oportunidade e a responsabilidade de decidir que cidade queremos construir para os próximos cem anos. Vamos reproduzir uma lógica urbana do século passado ou ter coragem de planejar uma cidade mais humana, acessível, sustentável e segura?
A evidência precisa orientar as políticas públicas, mesmo quando suas conclusões contrariam hábitos consolidados. O planejamento urbano não pode ser guiado apenas pela percepção de quem quer chegar alguns minutos mais cedo. Precisa considerar riscos, desigualdades e, sobretudo, o valor da vida.
Reduzir a velocidade não resolve todos os problemas de mobilidade do Distrito Federal. Mas reconhecer seus limites não é motivo para rejeitar uma medida de segurança. É motivo para avançar em outras soluções, com planejamento, investimento e participação popular, e para avaliar, depois da implantação, se a medida funcionou.
Mobilidade não é fazer carros circularem mais rápido. É garantir que as pessoas vivam melhor. O Eixão não precisa deixar de cumprir sua função. Precisa deixar de ser pensado exclusivamente a partir da perspectiva dos automóveis. A cidade pertence às pessoas, não aos motores.
*André Pires é administrador, gestor público, gestor de projetos e militante do PDT.

UKMTO says seven Hormuz tanker attacks recorded in a week
At least seven tankers were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the week to 11 November, UKMTO said, with one strike leaving multiple crew injured in the Arabian Gulf.
The latest, on 11 November, hit a tanker’s engine room 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras al-Khaimah, and the crew was evacuated, UKMTO said in its weekly overview.
Of eight incidents reported, three vessels continued their voyage, three needed assistance and two had unknown outcomes. None was reported sunk.
On 7 November, US Central Command said it disabled the HUDA in the Gulf of Oman after its crew ignored warnings and tried to breach the US naval blockade.
UKMTO said the traffic through the waterway was about 65 percent below pre-war levels, with combined 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits, against 170 and 155 the previous week. It rated threat level in the strait is as severe.
In the Red Sea, no attacks have been reported since 24 August, but Bab al-Mandab transits remain about 24 percent below levels before the Houthis’ 22 July blockade announcement.
UKMTO has logged 163 conflict-related incidents since 28 February.

UN says IMO confirms 25 seafarer deaths since Iran war began
As many as 25 seafarers have been killed in 134 confirmed maritime incidents across the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the US and Israeli started war on Iran in February, according to Khalid Khiari, UN Assistant Secretary-General Khaled for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific.
Briefing the UN Security Council on Friday, Khiari cited figures from the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) covering incidents recorded up to November 11.
He said October saw the highest monthly number of incidents involving commercial shipping since February, warning that continued disruption was driving up energy, transport and insurance costs and threatening global food security.
“This situation cannot be allowed to become the new normal,” Khiari said, calling for an immediate end to attacks on civilian vessels and the restoration of safe maritime navigation.
Bahrain’s representative told the meeting that about 1,600 vessels had been affected by disruptions in the waterway, leaving more than 23,000 seafarers stranded aboard their ships.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: When tech founders leave, what happens to their companies?
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
When tech founders leave, what happens to their companies?
Nvidia could lose 30 percent of its value following cofounder Jensen Huang’s decision to step down, analysts warns.
In the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of the artificial intelligence giant Nvidia, the company has brought in a new interim chief, Colette Kress, who has been with the company since 2013.
Along with Kress, the AI bellwether appointed its first-ever board chair, Harvey Jones, a venture investor with three decades of tech industry experience.
The changes mark a major overhaul of Nvidia’s corporate structure and leadership, which Huang has dominated since cofounding the AI chipmaker in 1993. A powerful figure in Silicon Valley, he stepped down on Thursday following reports of his affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative and two employees that have drawn scrutiny from United States lawmakers, the company’s board and shareholders.
Despite the shakeup, the question remains how much of Nvidia’s nearly $4 trillion value was pegged to its longtime leader, who is synonymous with the company’s exponential growth. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, predicted that Nvidia’s value could decline 25 to 30 percent without Huang at the helm.
Historically, executives across corporate America have been beholden to shareholders, who hold executives accountable. In Silicon Valley, however, companies have often been built around a founder’s vision – as was the case for Nvidia.
Why do tech companies put so much faith in their founders?
Analysts have long maintained that the success of companies like Nvidia hinges on the success and vision of their founder. A report from Bain and Company found that founder-led companies perform 2.1 times better than companies that are not led by their founders between 2015 and 2025, and when it comes to tech, that jumps to 2.6 times.
“When it comes to succession, the data shows that, as great as these founders are, it’s incredibly rare for their successors to do as well as the original founder. So I wouldn’t necessarily call it a risk. It’s simply the evolutionary life cycle of building a company,” Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera.
Silicon Valley has long embraced this model, with companies such as Meta – Facebook and Instagram’s parent company – and Tesla built around the vision and personalities of their founders.
“It’s a common challenge among tech giants. You can ask: What does SpaceX look like without Elon Musk? What does Meta look like without Mark Zuckerberg? I think the same principle applies here, particularly in an emergency situation like this,” Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at the Eurasia Group, told Al Jazeera.
Musk came under scrutiny from the board at the electric vehicle maker as his attention was divided among a growing portfolio of businesses, which was a distraction from the company.
Musk’s increasingly public political activities with the administration of US President Donald Trump became a source of controversy for Tesla, with the company facing protests at its showrooms amid damage to its brand image and declining vehicle sales. In the first quarter of 2025, Tesla deliveries fell 13 percent year over year to their lowest level in nearly three years.
Ultimately, Tesla’s board opted not to remove him. However, his other company made changes to its governance structure that made it essentially impossible for the board to fire him when SpaceX prepared to go public earlier this year.
Musk was expected to retain approximately 82 percent of SpaceX’s total voting power after the IPO, despite selling shares to outside investors, a move that gave him control of who sits on the board, a role that is supposed to oversee the CEO. The Texas-based aerospace giant wrote into its charter that removal requires approval from holders of its special class of shares, and because Musk owns the majority of those shares, he can veto his own firing.
For Nvidia, Huang’s leadership often paid off. Nvidia invested heavily in graphics processing and helping build out data centre infrastructure amid a rapid expansion in the AI sector.
Nvidia has continued to make those kinds of investments. Just this week, the company agreed to purchase $10bn worth of shares in a private placement ahead of Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO next week.
Who is in charge of Nvidia?
Nvidia’s management structure was heavily centred around Huang. He had dozens of executives reporting to him directly rather than operating within a more traditional hierarchical chain of command.
Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang could be removed by the 11-person board of directors “with or without cause”, as they hold a majority of votes. Unlike other tech giants, Huang does not have outsized control. Huang owns about 3.6 percent of the company and does not have majority voting power.
Nvidia’s structure is unique among major Silicon Valley companies.
Meta and Alphabet, for example, have special stock arrangements that give their founders more voting power than their actual ownership stakes would normally provide. As a result, founders like Zuckerberg can maintain control over who sits on the board, which can make it more difficult for shareholders to challenge leadership decisions.
This means that while Huang had enormous influence over Nvidia’s direction, he did not have the same formal voting control wielded by other major tech founders.
The company appointed Kress as its interim CEO. She previously served as Nvidia’s chief financial officer.
What happens when a founder leaves?
Historically, when a founder leaves, it hurts the direction of the company and can sway its competitive advantage in the market, and it has happened several times in corporate history.
In the 1980s, after a power struggle between Apple founder Steve Jobs and then CEO John Sculley, the company struggled for a decade. By 1997, the tech giant was on the brink of bankruptcy, with nearly $1bn in losses that year.
“When Apple’s founder Steve Jobs left the company for the first time, Apple experienced a major downturn, eventually prompting the board to invite him back,” Lu said.
When Jobs returned to the company, the Cupertino, California-based tech giant’s luck began to change and led to the launch of its most well-known products, including the iMac and the iPhone.
Starbucks faced a similar setback after founder Howard Schultz stepped down as CEO in 2000. He handed leadership to Orin Smith, the company’s then-president and chief operating officer.
The Seattle-based coffee shop chain continued to grow under Smith, but struggled after he retired in 2005 and was replaced by Jim Donald. Amid slowing sales and increased competition, Starbucks lost more than 80 percent of its value.
In January 2008, Schultz returned as CEO and launched a turnaround effort that included closing hundreds of underperforming locations.
However, founder-led companies are not necessarily destined for a downturn when their founders leave.
Jobs, who left the company in 1985, returned in 1997 and led its subsequent turnaround before handing the reins to former CEO Tim Cook in 2011. Under Cook, Apple continued to grow, briefly surpassing a $5 trillion market capitalisation in July 2026.
At Microsoft, Bill Gates stepped down as CEO in 2000, with Steve Ballmer succeeding him. After Ballmer retired in 2014, Satya Nadella took over.
Nadella shifted the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant’s focus towards cloud computing and enterprise software – a move that helped its market capitalisation grow from approximately $302bn in 2014 to $3.88 trillion in November 2026.
Nvidia faces another issue, and that is that much of the AI sector’s growth is pegged to its powerful chips.
OpenAI, which is eyeing an IPO, has up to $100bn worth of planned financial agreements with Nvidia. Nvidia has also agreed to invest $10bn in Dario Amodei-led Anthropic through a private placement tied to its planned US IPO, which could take place as early as next week.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/amnes.title: Amnesty urges Pakistan-administered Kashmir to free activists and end crackdown
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/amnes.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/amnes.text:
Amnesty urges Pakistan-administered Kashmir to free activists and end crackdown
Army personnel patrol outside a polling station during the first phase of voting for the local legislature in Mirpur, Pakistan-administered Kashmir, on 27 July 2026 (AFP/Qayyum)
Amnesty International has urged the newly formed government in Pakistan-controlled Kashmir to release hundreds of activists arbitrarily detained under anti-terrorism laws for protesting against the rising cost of living.
In a letter to the newly elected Prime Minister Syed Iftikhar Ali Gilani, the rights group demanded that Gilani’s new administration improve the human rights situation by repealing the ban on the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC).
“In [the] wake of swift and systematic steps taken by authorities since June in the region to repress civic freedoms, we call upon your government and all relevant authorities to ensure that the human rights of all those inside the region are upheld,” wrote Isabelle Lassee, deputy regional director at Amnesty’s South Asia Regional Office.
“The arbitrary banning of Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots people’s movement, by proscribing it under the first schedule of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Anti-Terrorism Act, 2014 violates the right to association, freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."
Founded in 2023, JAAC is a coalition of traders, lawyers, students, civil society activists and local political figures who have campaigned against the high electricity bills, rising flour prices, heavy taxation and poor public services affecting Kashmiris in Pakistan-administered Kashmir.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Earlier this year, protests against the rising cost of living turned violent, leading to a harsh government crackdown and the banning of JAAC under anti-terrorism laws.
Since the ban, hundreds of activists, protesters and journalists have been placed on anti-terrorism watchlists and arrested over alleged links to the group or their coverage of demonstrations.
The ban has sparked widespread protests among Kashmiri diaspora communities in cities across Europe and North America.
The unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir has also presented a major challenge for the region's newly installed government.
Gilani, a member of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), became prime minister in August after being nominated by the party's central leadership, amid reported divisions within its regional ranks.
His appointment followed months of protests and political unrest, with demonstrators raising grievances over governance, economic conditions and their treatment by the authorities.
The crackdown has drawn international scrutiny, with UN experts and human rights organisations raising concerns about restrictions on civil liberties and the use of anti-terrorism legislation against activists.
