https://www.aljazeera.com/editorial/long.title: Young musicians connect a community across the Line of Control
https://www.aljazeera.com/editorial/long.text:
This feature is part of a series examining how artificial borders reshape daily life, divide families and force loved ones to navigate the human cost of political geography.
In the remote Tulail Valley close to the Line of Control in Indian-administered Kashmir, 25-year-old singer Aasim Yaseen was walking through his village, Buglinder, when a college student from a neighbouring hamlet stopped him.
The young man, Tanveer, took out his phone and played Sangh Mukh Shamah, a song Yaseen had recently released in Shina, their shared language.
The encounter motivated Yaseen.
“People here don’t consider music work,” he says.
“Sometimes I think about going into another profession, but then someone plays my song on their phone, and I keep going.”
Across Gurez in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, Drass in Indian-administered Ladakh, and Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, young musicians like Yaseen are sharing Shina songs on social media. They are helping keep their language alive and renewing ties within a community that has been divided for generations.
The songs cross the Line of Control, which divides Indian- and Pakistani-administered parts of Kashmir. But the musicians face financial pressures, unreliable internet connections and political restrictions on their movement.
Songs across a divided world
For Yaseen, that separation is part of his family history.
His grandfather has told him stories about Yaseen’s great-great uncle, who lived in Gilgit-Baltistan before Partition and stayed there as the region fell under Pakistani control. Yaseen says movement became extremely difficult after the Line of Control was established, and security concerns eventually led the relatives to lose contact.
“We were one family,” Yaseen says. “But we were divided into two countries.”
Gurez, the homeland of Indigenous Shina-speaking people, lies on historic routes linking the Kashmir Valley with Central Asia, including the Burzil Pass route to Astore in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan.
Gurez has no local crossing where families can visit relatives in Gilgit. Buses once connected Srinagar with Muzaffarabad and Poonch with Rawalakot, but neither route passed through Gurez.
Residents in Gurez and Drass say security restrictions make them wary of calling or messaging relatives across the Line of Control. They worry that making contact could attract suspicion. Sharing Shina songs online feels safer: People on the other side can listen without either person needing to make direct contact.
Artists began sharing songs on Facebook and YouTube in the late 2010s. By 2020, residents were using online Shina music to reconnect with a community scattered across the mountains.
A 35-year-old teacher from Purana Tulail village, who requested anonymity due to security concerns, says songs have become an emotionally powerful way to communicate.
“Songs became a medium,” he says. “Through music, we could convey a message without having to send it. When a singer from this side sings, our community across the border listens to it.”
Music at the border
In Buglinder, Yaseen’s family life is all about farming.
Outside the family’s wooden home, a zomo — a hybrid of yak and cattle — stands under a tree while chickens roam the yard. Inside, his mother prepares namkeen chai, Kashmir’s pink salted tea, on a clay stove. The family drinks it with local roti and desi ghee.
Yaseen crosses a bridge with the animal towards a neighbouring village on the hillside. Below him, the Kishanganga River flows through the valley before flowing into Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Above him, bunkers sit atop hills and fences run across the mountains. Cameras surveil the ridgelines, and security checkpoints line the roads. In winter, snow can close the roads for months, making it difficult to reach schools, markets and medical care.
After the April 2025 attack near Pahalgam, which killed 26 people, most of them tourists, India and Pakistan exchanged strikes. In Gurez, residents say they sheltered in bunkers or were evacuated to temporary camps. Many had to leave their homes and livestock behind.
Yaseen’s 71-year-old father, Abdul Rahim Sheikh, works the family farm and runs a small shop selling groceries and daily essentials. He herds cattle in a nearby mountain range lined with barbed wire, while Yaseen helps fence a potato field.
Later, Yaseen’s sister calls him back to the house. Guests from Mumbai have arrived. The family welcomes them with kehwa, a spiced Kashmiri tea, and introduces them to Yaseen in the kitchen, where he sings.
His audience is just a handful of guests, but his recordings help extend his reach much further.
A cultural map without borders
“Politically we are divided, but musically our hearts beat together,” says 38-year-old Salman Paras, a prominent contemporary Shina folk singer.
Paras was born in Sheikhpora Kilshay, a village in the Minimarg-Gurez area of Astore district, Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan. He grew up hearing stories of shared ethnic ties and separation from Gurez, where some families from Kilshay remained on the Indian-administered side after the region was divided.
He says his grandfather’s brother stayed behind in Gurez while the rest of his family migrated to Gilgit. Eventually, they lost touch.
Decades later, a Shina musician on the Kashmir side of the Line of Control came across Paras’s songs on YouTube and contacted him to say that relatives of his had been traced to Kangan, a town in central Kashmir where many Dard families migrated from Tulail.
Paras has not disclosed the musician’s identity for security reasons, and the families have yet to reconnect. But someone had recognised his family ties through his music.
His fusion of Shina folk and modern pop has brought the language to listeners beyond Gilgit-Baltistan. Paras’s song Karay Karay, recorded with Pakistani singer Ali Zafar, was accompanied by a video filmed during the cherry blossom season in Skardu and in the Katpana Desert, a high-altitude desert near the city of Skardu in Gilgit-Baltistan. It brought Shina to audiences beyond the mountainous region and has been viewed millions of times on YouTube. He’s also had recent performances in Dubai and Muscat.
“For a long time, many people didn’t take me seriously as a singer,” Paras says. “But when Ali Zafar introduced me, I sang proudly as Shina from Gilgit-Baltistan. People took notice.”
On November 3, Paras went live on Instagram, singing in Shina and several of its regional varieties. The session drew listeners from Gurez, Drass, Kargil and Gilgit-Baltistan.
During that live interaction, Imtiyaz Samoon, a Shina speaker from Gurez on the Indian-administered side, told Paras how deeply his music is loved in the valley. He said local singers often perform Paras’s songs at community events, and that his music has become part of gatherings throughout Gurez.
Paras responded, saying he wanted to collaborate with musicians on the Indian-administered side and, if the necessary permissions and visa could be arranged, perform in Gurez and Ladakh.
“If you look at the official map of Gilgit-Baltistan today, Gurez and Ladakh are missing,” he says, referring to Shina-speaking areas on the Indian-administered side. “But in my mind, I’ve drawn a cultural map that includes Chitral, Kohistan, Gurez and Ladakh. They are my people.”
Iftikhar Uddin Iftikhar, 29, a singer based in Gilgit, has watched a similar audience grow around his music.
He began learning music in 2015 under Shina folk singer Muhammad Amin Shah and released his first Shina album in 2018. He now collaborates with local performers, composes music and records in studios in Gilgit.
“Now I have friends across the border: Shina speakers in Kashmir and Ladakh,” he says. “They listen to my music. I never thought my songs would reach them.”
Iftikhar considers Paras an inspiration. He wants to build his career and forge a path for younger performers.
“Shina music is our identity,” he says. “I am not just promoting songs – I am keeping our language alive.”
The cost of keeping a language alive
Yaseen’s songs are finding listeners, but he still struggles to afford studio time.
He normally lives in Srinagar, more than 160km (100 miles) from home, where he studies music at Cluster University and performs at local events. When Tanveer approached him in Buglinder, he was visiting his family to help with the annual harvest.
His interest in singing began at school. Standing on a hill above a neighbouring village, he points towards his childhood school and remembers Rasheed Samoon, a teacher who gave him 10 rupees to sing his first poem, Aavo Mil Kar Kam Karain (Let’s work together).
Now, when he can afford it, Yaseen rents a studio in Srinagar. Producing a song, including studio time and production costs, runs him between 30,000 and 35,000 Indian rupees ($318–$372), he says.
Musicians share microphones, speakers, instruments and editing skills to reduce costs. For his song Malalak, released in April, for example, Yaseen shared the cost of video production and editing software with fellow musician Zia Ul Alam.
Younis Majeed, 27, from Izmarg village, is part of the same emerging generation of musicians in Gurez. He blends Shina folk melodies with contemporary beats. His song Tamah Hoon (I Have a Desire) has reached more than 21,000 viewers online.
“The internet lets us get to know each other again,” he says. “It reconnects us emotionally and culturally, both across and within borders.”
But the infrastructure supporting that connection is fragile. Some villages close to the Line of Control have little or no mobile coverage. Artists may have a smartphone but no quiet place to record, or they may be able to upload a song but not earn from it.
Further east, in Drass in Indian-administered Ladakh, 24-year-old singer Zain Drassi faces similar problems.
In early September, he performed with a local band at the Drass and Suru festivals. For him, the performances were a chance to bring a shared musical tradition back into public view.
“It was a small recovery of our cultural space after it had been limited for so long by war and political borders,” he says.
Drass was a key theatre of the 1999 Kargil War, and residents have lived with displacement and restrictions on movement. Today, Drassi says, local musicians also struggle to find the resources needed to make professional recordings.
“The internet has brought us closer to our people in Gurez and Gilgit, but practically we have different challenges,” he says.
Musicians can record vocals locally, he explains, but must travel elsewhere for composition, arrangements and professional production, seeking services in Srinagar, Bhaderwah or neighbouring Himachal Pradesh. Traditional instruments and musicians skilled in playing them are also difficult to find.
The younger performers are finding new ways to record and distribute Shina songs. Much of the repertoire they draw on, however, survived through singers and writers who had no digital audience.
The musicians who kept it alive
In Kangan, in central Kashmir, 53-year-old singer Yousuf Naseem has spent three decades preserving Shina through music.
Sitting on his veranda, he plays a six-stringed rabab. His songs carry memories of migration, loss and the home he left behind.
Born in Dangithal, near the Line of Control in Gurez Valley, Naseem remembers long winters, family storytelling and songs passed along by older relatives.
“The elders in our house were our library,” he says. “Whatever they hummed, we sang.”
During the 1999 Kargil conflict, his family was among those forced to leave Gurez. They resettled in Kangan.
“We lost everything,” he says. “But the songs travelled with us.”
Naseem began taking Shina music to new listeners in Srinagar. In Bohri Kadal, a historic market in the old city where many Dard families work as wazas, or chefs, he gave a shopkeeper a copy of his first cassette, Dardistan, and asked him to play it every morning.
His voice began travelling through the market.
“People would ask what language it was,” Naseem says. “It was Shina. For many, it was the first time they had heard it.”
While Naseem carried Shina music beyond Gurez, Fareed Ahmed Kaloo worked to preserve it within the valley.
At the Shina Cultural Centre near Dawar, young musicians gather as Kaloo, 67, adjusts his harmonium and begins to sing. He wears a traditional shoka and white pakol cap.
“Gilgit, Kargil, Gurez, Drass – our pride, our own,
This is our Golden Garden: Dardistan, our home.”
Kaloo leads the Habba Khatoon Dramatic Club, a cultural group founded in 1976 to preserve Shina folklore in Gurez.
“After Partition, our culture faded,” he says. “Kashmiri music dominated, and our Dardic roots went silent.”
For years, he travelled between villages on foot, carrying a harmonium and a tumbak naari, a clay percussion instrument. He performed at weddings, fairs and local gatherings, accepting food, a place to sleep or a small honorarium as payment.
“We didn’t do it for money,” he says. “We did it because someone had to, and no one else would.”
Some of the club’s earliest members have died. Others left amid cross-border shelling and never returned. Kaloo stayed, teaching folk songs to younger generations.
He now listens to new tracks on his phone and admires how musicians in Gilgit have developed their sound while retaining elements of traditional Shina music.
“They’ve gone far ahead of us,” he says with a smile. “As they should. Our songs must evolve, but never lose their roots.”
Words that travel
The connection between these generations also runs through the work of Masood Samoon, a 78-year-old Shina writer and linguist from Gurez.
For more than two decades, Samoon has written poetry that musicians have turned into songs. He wrote Yaseen’s songs Malalak and Sangh Mukh Shamah.
“Yousuf Naseem sang my songs,” Samoon says. “He took my words to Kashmir, to people who had never heard Shina before.”
“Now Aasim Yaseen sings them,” he adds. “My words travel farther now than I could.”
In Gurez and Drass, Shina has relied heavily on oral transmission, with limited support from formal education. But new primary-school textbooks introduced by the Jammu and Kashmir school board this year are intended to give the language a stronger place in classrooms.
A Srinagar-based linguist who specialises in Shina welcomes the books but says their impact will depend on how the language is taught and whether children continue to use it in everyday life. He requested anonymity for fear of repercussions.
“Written resources are valuable, particularly for a language spoken by a relatively small population, but efforts to preserve Shina must also support its continued use as a spoken language,” he says.
Samoon’s poems are part of that spoken life. They are performed by older singers, recorded by younger artists and heard by listeners who may speak different varieties of Shina.
He says people from one area may not understand every word sung in another dialect. Yet the songs continue to find audiences.
“Music is a boundless thing,” Samoon says. “Shina is the language of my heart. When musicians sing my words, I travel across mountains and borders – even when I cannot physically travel there.”
As evening settles over Srinagar, Yaseen sits with fellow musicians at Al-Bahr Studio, working on another Shina track. The lyrics draw on folk tradition. The beat is modern.
The language is the same one heard in Naseem’s cassettes, Kaloo’s village performances and Samoon’s poetry. But the route it takes has changed.
Yaseen hopes one day to share a stage with musicians in Gilgit. For now, he records in Srinagar, performs when he can and returns to Tulail with new songs.
“The border will remain,” he says. “But our songs will still travel.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/us-ai.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/us-ai.text:
US air travel thrown into chaos as nationwide flights grounded over 'radar instability'
Chaos was reported at airports across the United States on Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights following problems with radar and communications systems.
Passengers were stranded as hundreds of flights were diverted and thousands cancelled.
Officials said instability in radar systems made it unsafe to continue normal operations.
The FAA said in a statement that communications problems had affected multiple air traffic control centres and that technicians were investigating.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the disruption began at 3.36pm EST (8.36pm GMT), when radar and communications systems at facilities across the country became unstable.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
“We started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with airplanes,” Duffy said at a White House briefing.
He said more than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the ground stop was imposed. Those planes were allowed to continue to their destinations and land safely.
The FAA lifted the restriction at 8.15pm, but Duffy warned that restoring normal operations would take time.
“It's going to be slow,” he said, urging passengers to check with their airlines as carriers worked to reposition aircraft and crews.
The disruption came a day after a global Microsoft outage affected services including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, disrupting government operations and businesses worldwide.
Public services disrupted
The Microsoft outage began on Thursday and continued into Friday. Outage-tracking website Downdetector recorded nearly 130,000 reports of problems accessing Outlook shortly after 1pm on Thursday.
Microsoft attributed the outage to a technical problem with its infrastructure and said there was no indication of malicious activity or a cyberattack.
The outage disrupted public services in Britain, where a judge halted a trial in Manchester and sent jurors home because of delays.
British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to call in urgent requests.
The National Pharmacy Association also warned of delays in obtaining medication, as disruption to National Health Service systems threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.
In the US, the outage affected some law enforcement services. Colorado’s Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office said online bond payments had been disrupted.
“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” Microsoft wrote in a social media update.
However, officials said the Microsoft outage was unrelated to the nationwide flight disruption, while the company said it had no indication of a connection.
“Microsoft has no indication that the FAA nationwide ground stop is related to the recent service disruption,” a company spokesperson said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
How does Iran view shift in US approach after JD Vance ordered away?
Washington believes maritime blockade, overland border disruptions, air restrictions and isolating sanctions are working.
Tehran, Iran – Decision-makers in Iran are now considering the implications of Vice President JD Vance’s removal from the Iran file to focus on domestic issues, which analysts say could increase the chances of conflict between the two sides.
Vance has been the US’s chief negotiator in talks with Iran, but US President Donald Trump told him to direct his focus on alleged Democratic “corruption”, according to a post by Trump on Truth Social on Thursday. He added that a deal with Iran was no longer a priority for the government.
The vice president is believed to be viewed by Tehran as one of the more pragmatic figures in the Trump administration since the US and Israel launched their surprise war on Iran on February 28.
Nasser Hadian, professor of international relations at the University of Tehran, said that by assigning Vance to the case of alleged domestic corruption, Trump was mainly signalling a confrontation with the Democrats after their sweeping victories against the governing Republican Party in the midterm elections.
But the move may also serve Israel, which is reportedly eager for Trump to launch new strikes against Iran, after Vance blamed the Republicans’ humiliating defeat in the midterms on the war.
“Another signal is to Iran, essentially saying reaching a deal now is not a priority, and that the person known to have a relatively softer stance on Iran was redirected to other issues,” Hadian said.
The negotiator
Vance is believed to have been in favour of a negotiated resolution to the war, due to its rising economic costs for US citizens and their opposition to the war suggested in opinion polls.
The vice president was backed by Trump envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff when he negotiated the now-defunct memorandum of understanding with Iran in June, which briefly paused the war and resumed shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Rubio has, meanwhile, called Iranian authorities “insane” for their demands on ending the war. But he also acknowledged the cost of an all-out war and seeks to win via deepening economic pressure and isolation on all Iranians.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has faced an impeachment vote due to his role in the war, and Central Command chief Brad Cooper are reportedly in favour of renewed military action against Iran.
Vance wrote a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in late October, as regional mediators redoubled their efforts to bridge gaps between the two sides. Rezaei initially described the tone of the missive as positive, but by last week, he was addressing claims of progress and a possible direct meeting with Vance as “fake news about imaginary talks”.
“You lost the war and the election. Vance has conceded, Rubio is heading for the exit, Hegseth is about to be fired, and the CENTCOM commander is now a podcaster!” he wrote on X at the time.
‘With or without Vance’
Mediated contacts are ongoing between the two sides, but no breakthrough is expected. Tehran is demanding seven conditions and clear sequencing of concessions to end the war, but this is appearing to be unacceptable to the US.
Mohammad Saleh Sedghian, director of the Arab Center for Iranian Studies, pointed out that Trump has repeatedly highlighted alleged rifts within the Iranian negotiating team. But he said Iranian authorities were also questioning the reliability of another potential agreement with Washington.
“Even if you can imagine Mr Rezaei sitting down with Mr Vance, and reaching a deal? What guarantee is there that Trump will enforce it?” he told Al Jazeera.
The atmosphere of mistrust between the two sides is also complicating prospects of a deal, he added. This means that the ongoing US siege on Iran and harsh sanctions will continue, something that could cost Iran more than a relatively shorter military conflict with Washington, he added.
“The blockade and disruptions are significantly raising the costs for Iranian people. The current state of no war and no negotiated resolution is very dangerous,” Sedghian said.
Iranian reformist newspaper Shargh argued this week that Vance’s role concerning Iran is unresolved rather than definitely terminated, but also said the conflict could further escalate.
Conservative Farhikhtegan daily disputed the portrayal of Vance as genuinely antiwar, arguing that diplomacy, military force and economic pressure ultimately serve a common objective for the US in trying to coerce Iran to accept its conditions.
For now, the two sides are continuing to fight over control in the Strait of Hormuz, with retaliatory attacks on shipping and military installations.
On Friday and Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and regular army separately claimed several new incidents of vessels either hitting naval mines or being struck by projectiles after attempting “unauthorised” routes in the critical waterway.
The latest weekly report by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) on Friday reported eight incidents in and around the strait, mostly in the southern route near Oman.
UKMTO also recorded 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits through the strait during the week, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels.
Hadian believes that Iranian decision-makers will not tolerate the current situation indefinitely.
“The authorities will either go after their warships, their vessels, or their military bases,” he added. “The stronger the blockade becomes, including through maritime pressure and disruptions for overland borders and air travel, war becomes more probable.”
But Trump’s sidelining of Vance on the Iran issue will not radically alter the current situation, Hadian said, since Washington believes its tactic of economic pressure on Tehran can force it to make concessions.
“The US would have done this with or without Vance, and I believe it will continue to do this,” he said.

Spain vs England: UEFA Nations League – predictions, how to watch, teams
Spain, who are unbeaten in their last 43 competitive meetings, host England in Madrid on Sunday.
Who: Spain vs England
What: UEFA Nations League, Group A3
Where: Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid, Spain
When: Sunday, November 15, at 7:45pm (19:45 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream.
England have the chance to avenge their defeat and end Spain’s 43-match unbeaten record when they face the reigning world champions in Sunday’s final Nations League group encounter.
Spain staged a 3-2 comeback victory at London’s Wembley Stadium in late September, as Lamine Yamal scored an early opener and Mikel Oyarzabal finished the job.
Spain and England have both sealed their berth in the competition’s quaterfinals, with La Roja assured of the top spot should they avoid defeat on Sunday. England, meanwhile, will finish second if they fail to beat the two-time World Cup winners.
Teenage sensation Yamal, with four goals, and Mikel Merino, with three, have headlined Spain’s attacking charge, while newly-crowned Ballon d’Or recipient Harry Kane leads England.
Before Spain vs England, here’s everything you need to know:
How have Spain played in the Nations League?
Spain have a perfect record and lead Group A3 with 15 points.
They beat England 3-2 in the first game, an away trip, and followed it with a 4-1 rout of Croatia at home.
Then, they beat Czechia 3-1 at home, followed by a 2-1 away win over Croatia and a 2-0 away win over Czechia.
How have England played in the Nations League?
England are second in Group A3 with 12 points from five games, having won four times and lost once.
Their Nations League campaign started with a 3-2 home defeat to Spain before Thomas Tuchel’s side beat Czechia 2-0 and thrashed Croatia 7-0 in back-to-back away fixtures.
Later, they beat Czechia 3-0 at home and Croatia 2-1.
Tuchel eager to end Spain’s unbeaten run
Tuchel believes England are ready to end Spain’s unbeaten record when they face the world and European champions in Madrid.
While victory offers little more than the prospect of a more favourable Nations League quarterfinal in March, it would be a landmark moment for England if they could end Spain’s run of 43 matches without defeat.
“It (Spain) is a team that has forgotten how to lose, so of course it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost,” said Tuchel.
“I think we’re there, and I think we’re ready to win on Sunday.
“I know what it takes, and no one can ever guarantee it, but I think it’s the moment to check how far we are and to push our limit and proof of concept,” the German added.
“It’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength.”
‘We want to get to 44’: De la Fuente
De la Fuente said their unbeaten record provided his players with extra motivation.
“We want to keep setting new milestones, and this is another one,” he explained.
“None of us would probably ever have thought we’d even reach 35, because we already felt those were astronomical numbers, but having reached 43, you think, my goodness, we want to get to 44, of course we do.”
What happened the last time Spain and England met?
Spain came from behind to beat England 3-2 in an entertaining Nations League encounter on September 26, denying the hosts a cathartic win after their painful World Cup exit.
Yamal put Spain ahead in the second minute, but Anthony Gordon equalised, and Kane added another as England ended the first half with a 2-1 lead.
The Three Lions captain missed a penalty in the second half, though, allowing Spain to bounce back, as Alex Baena found the equaliser before Oyarzabal sealed victory in the 74th minute.
Spain vs England: Predictions
Opta’s supercomputer favours Spain for victory. They have a 59.6 percent probability of winning, while England’s odds of victory are 19.3 percent.
There is a 21.1 percent chance the game ends in a draw.
Form guide
(Last five matches; last game first)
Spain: W-W-W-W-W
England: W-W-W-W-L
Head-to-head
- Matches: 29
- Spain wins: 12
- England wins: 13
- Draws: 4
Team news and predicted lineups
Spain
Yamal is expected to face England after missing the last game with a knee problem. Nico Williams and Aymeric Laporte are doubtful
Probable Spain XI: Unai Simon; Marc Pubill, Pau Cubarsi, Dean Huijsen, Marc Cucurella; Dani Olmo, Rodri, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Mikel Oyarzabal, Alex Baena
England
Myles Lewis-Skelly returns from his suspension, while Ezri Konsa is also expected to return after missing the last game due to a knee injury.
Djed Spence (muscle) is doubtful, and Marc Guehi (muscle) remains out with injury.
Probable England XI: Jordan Pickford; Trent Alexander-Arnold, Ezri Konsa, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall; Elliot Anderson, Declan Rice; Morgan Rogers, Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon; Harry Kane

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war
Leaked Russian records reveal a war toll that falls hardest on older men, poorer regions and foreign recruits.
Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year.
Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria.
The records were obtained by two hacking groups, the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow.
Rosstat confirmed it had been hit by cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1, but said it found no evidence that its databases had been compromised or that protected data leaked.
Moscow does not officially publish its military death toll.
Deaths can take months, and sometimes years, to be registered, in Russia. Investigations for The Financial Times (FT) have concluded that once late paperwork is counted, the toll up to August will settle at about 550,000.
So what do the leaked records show, and what do they tell us about who is fighting Russia’s war? Here’s what you need to know:
What was leaked, and is it genuine?
The Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow said on November 1 that they had broken into Rosstat’s network.
The two hacking groups published their own analysis of the records and shared the files with several news organisations, though the data has not been independently verified.
However, media outlets and analysts say they believe it is real.
Janis Kluge, an expert on Russia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X: “There is no longer any doubt that the leaked Rosstat database is authentic. You can find any famous person who has died in recent years.”
However, in a later post he added: “The trickier question is: Was the data manipulated to increase the war death toll?” before adding, “This would [be] unbelievably difficult, so this is a highly unlikely conspiracy theory”.
What do the records show?
A death toll far beyond anything Moscow has admitted so far.
The files list about 410,000 deaths directly as war-related, and 42,000 more fighting-age men whose deaths were confirmed in court because their bodies have never been recovered.
The FT identified another 12,000 likely military deaths among men who died at or near the front, bringing the total to at least 450,000.
Where have most of those Russian casualties occurred?
About 120,000 of those with a recorded location died in the area containing Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, and a further 48,000 in Bakhmut, the FT reported.
Avdiivka is a small industrial city in the Donetsk region. After Russian-backed forces seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015, it became part of the so-called “contact line”, and Ukrainian forces spent years fortifying the city.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it was the subject of two years of bitter fighting before Russia took it in 2024.
After the fall of Avdiivka, Russian forces moved towards the coal-mining city of Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, capturing it in early 2026 after more than a year of gruelling battles that had left the city in ruins.
Bakhmut, a city in the Donetsk Oblast and situated at a vital intersection connecting eastern Ukraine with the rest of the country, was the site of the longest and bloodiest infantry battle of the war before falling to Russian and paramilitary Wagner Group forces in May 2023.
Who has been killed?
Older men from poorer, often minority regions.
The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 in 2025, and men aged 35 to 44 made up the largest group, with 158,000 dead, the FT reported.
Ethnic Russians constitute more than two-thirds of Russia’s population of 143 million. The rest are minorities – from millions of ethnic Ukrainians and Tatars to smaller Indigenous groups in Siberia and the Arctic.
Zabaykalsky Krai, home to a large community of Buryats, an Indigenous Mongolic people of southern Siberia, recorded about 12,300 deaths, roughly one for every 80 people in the region, the FT reported.
Bashkortostan, another region with a large minority population including Indigenous Bashkirs and Volga Tatars, recorded 15,800 deaths.
How many foreign fighters have been killed?
More than 4,000, and possibly far more.
The FT identified 4,141 probable foreign soldiers holding foreign citizenship among the dead.
Bloomberg News, using a wider definition that includes people born outside Russia, counted 11,335, with foreign deaths rising from about 630 in 2022 to more than 5,500 in 2025.
Deaths of Nepalis were concentrated in 2023 and 2024, and those of Colombians, Kenyans and Nigerians from late 2025, Bloomberg reported.
The FT counted the highest death toll from Uzbekistan at 807, followed by Tajikistan with 598. There were also 44 Nepali dead and 98 Colombians, the highest toll from Latin America.
About 340 Africans are among the dead, most of them killed since 2025, Bloomberg reported.
Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt had the highest tolls, with 127 deaths between them, according to the FT.
Furthermore, Ukrainian officials believe Russia deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to hold off Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region, but they do not appear in the leaked data.
Why are foreigners fighting for Russia?
Mostly for the money, and often after being misled.
An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army overall.
An Amnesty International report in September found that people from Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa had been promised well-paid civilian jobs and then forced into the army on arrival in Russia.
The rights group spoke with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.
It found local agents and misleading online job advertisements were being used to deceive foreign nationals in their home countries.
Nationals from 36 African countries are known to be fighting for Russia in the four-year war, Ukraine’s foreign minister said in November last year.
One South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was told to fly to Moscow, pick up a truck, and drive it to Poland.
His wife told Amnesty International: “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him. He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”
Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not then fulfilled, Amnesty reported.
In Kenya, where intelligence officials say more than 1,000 citizens have been recruited, agencies promised monthly wages of about $2,715 and bonuses of up to $9,309.
Moscow denies coercing anyone to fight in Ukraine.
What do these casualty figures mean for the war in Ukraine?
They indicate that Russia is struggling for manpower.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, posted an analysis of the leaked data, saying the figures likely understate Russia’s true losses because of reporting limitations.
It added that, as of July, Russia’s casualties are now outpacing its recruitment.
Kluge told The Moscow Times that the deaths also represent about half a per cent of Russia’s working-age population, which may have little economic impact, so the main significance is political.
He added, “You cannot say Russia is winning this war if it is losing population at this rate.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Joe Pinner
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful.
Children’s Village, Tocantins, Brazil
In Tocantins, central Brazil, the Canuanã school is a boarding school whose pupils come from remote farming communities across the region. In 2017, architects gave the school’s 540 boarders two new “villages” of dormitories, one for girls and one for boys.
The buildings are made from locally sourced timber and earth bricks. A vast canopy shades the complex, and perforated brick walls let air pass through, so the bedrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning even when temperatures reach 45C. Under the roof, rooms open on to shady, landscaped courtyards and airy verandas.
David Mikhail, the co-founder of Mikhail Riches, a UK practice specialising in sustainable design, says: “It is absolutely fantastic. So beautiful. It does a lot with little resource, which is the essence of a sustainable approach.” He adds: “I love the economy of it, and the huge sense of place they managed to evoke through such elegant and limited means.”
The architects have said their biggest challenge was convincing pupils and teachers that earth, brick and timber could feel modern rather than old-fashioned. They managed to do so by listening to students through 10 days of workshops to understand what they wanted from the design.
The Arc, Bali, Indonesia
The Green school in Bali is surrounded by jungle and promotes sustainability through learning in a natural environment. Since it opened in 2008, it has been built almost entirely in bamboo. Its gymnasium, the Arc, was completed in 2021.
Inspired by a mammal’s ribcage, the Arc’s bamboo arches span a 760 sq metre sports court without a single column interrupting the floor space. The arches support an undulating canopy, and natural ventilation comes from breezes that flow in at the base, while warm air escapes through vents at the top.
Bamboo is a highly sustainable building material because of how quickly it can regrow; large varieties reach building strength in just three to six years. “It is so fast-growing and sequesters a lot of carbon dioxide very quickly, so using it for building is a bit of a no-brainer if you can make it work,” says Mikhail. “And not only have they made it work, they’ve done it absolutely beautifully.”
Sara Kulturhus, Skellefteå, Sweden
Skellefteå, a small city just south of the Arctic Circle, is surrounded by 480,000 hectares (1.2m acres) of forest, and features wooden schools, a wooden road bridge, even a wooden multistorey car park. In 2021 it added Sara Kulturhus, a 20-storey cultural centre and hotel that is one of the tallest timber buildings in the world. It houses two theatres, a museum, an art gallery, the city library and a hotel.
The building is made of glulam – layers of timber glued together – and cross-laminated timber, a kind of super-sized plywood. The hotel rooms arrived as prefabricated wooden pods and were stacked into place. Building in wood saved a year in construction time compared with steel and concrete, while the timber came from trees harvested within 40 miles of the site, and replacement trees have since been planted.
“It promotes a love affair with wood and timber, and the localism of that in an area like Sweden is fabulous,” Mikhail says. “The lovely thing about cross-laminated timber is that the trees you use to make the panels don’t have to be elderly specimen trees. They can be relatively fast-grown and sustainably farmed.”
The Forest, Hobart, Australia
When the University of Tasmania was planning the redevelopment of its main campus in central Hobart, the architects chose to adapt what was already there rather than demolish it and start again. Two early 20th-century brick warehouses and a heritage-listed glass dome were stitched together into a single campus of classrooms and study spaces, which opened in February 2026.
At its heart is the glass dome, built in 1997. It is filled with about 3,200 native plants, including various species of ferns, and has an integrated watering, misting and fogging system that recreates rainforest-like growing conditions.
“You could argue the most sustainable building is actually no building, and the second most sustainable building is a refurbished old building,” says Mikhail. “That’s what this is: they’re taking existing structures and breathing new life into them, reimagining what they could be.”
Rammed Earth House, Cranborne Chase, UK
On the site of a former brickworks in the Wiltshire countryside, this house has been built from the ground beneath it. Rammed earth, which has been used since the Neolithic period, is a building material made of soil that has been compacted layer by layer into thick walls. Here, clay-rich soil was dug up and mixed with rubble from demolished outbuildings and local limestone.
The earth is “unstabilised”, meaning no cement has been added, which makes this one of only a few UK buildings made that way. Unstabilised earth could, in principle, simply go back into the ground if the house were ever demolished.
Rammed earth’s thermal mass also evens out temperature and moisture indoors, which the architects say will matter more as the climate warms. “As a piece of architecture, I think it’s phenomenal,” says Mikhail. “It’s an architect’s dream, and I’m slightly envious of it, I’ll be honest.”
“It’s like a beautiful piece of jewellery, and it riffs on lots of really lovely sustainable ideas.”

https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/debut-du-ras.title: Début du rassemblement parisien
https://www.humanite.fr/-/-/debut-du-ras.text:
C’est la fin de ce direct consacré à cette nouvelle journée de mobilisations, retrouvez nos reportages et analyses sur le mouvement social en cours sur notre site et dans nos éditions imprimées.
Acte V des mobilisations : vie chère, lycées, enfantisme, loi « permis de tuer »... La convergence des mouvements ce samedi 14 novembre
L'essentiel
- La mobilisation du 14 novembre s’inscrit juste avant une grande journée de grève interprofessionnelle et dans la fonction publique annoncée pour le lundi 17 novembre.
- Plusieurs mouvements convergent : l’Acte V des Gilets jaunes contre la vie chère, des organisations syndicales (CGT, FSU, FO), des collectifs de défense des droits humains opposés à la proposition de loi “permis de tuer” sur la présomption d’usage légitime des armes par la police, ainsi que la marche internationale contre les violences faites aux enfants et aux adolescents.
- À Paris, la manifestation relie la place de la République à la place de la Nation en passant par la Bastille à partir de 13 heures.
- Plus de 300 cortèges et rassemblements sont attendus à travers le pays, comme à Bordeaux, Lille, Rennes ou Angers.
- Le mouvement entend protester contre la vie chère, pour la hausse des salaires, celle des moyens alloués à l’Éducation nationale, mais aussi contre les violences faites aux enfants.
- Le ministre de l’Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, a déployé 70 000 policiers et gendarmes sur le territoire.
Le Direct
17h54
Fin de ce direct, un Acte VI samedi prochain, après le rendez-vous syndical du 17 novembre
17h47
200 000 manifestants en France selon l’intersyndicale jeune
L’intersyndicale jeune revendique également 100 000 personnes défilant à Paris. Le ministère de l’Intérieur en a dénombré 24 000 dans la capitale, 106 000 dans toute la France. En Loire-Atlantique la préfecture indique que des manifestants se sont introduits dans la zone interdite du centre-ville et que vingt-neuf interpellations ont eu lieu.
À Marseille, un cortège de plusieurs milliers de personnes a défilé, alors qu’aucune organisation n’avait déposé de parcours. Un acte VI se tiendra samedi prochain, selon Benjamin Ball, membre de la coordination des gilets jaunes.
17h36
Les forces de l’ordre en nombre dans les manifestations
Décidément, côté gouvernement, le ridicule ne tue pas. Alors que les autorités avaient mobilisé 70 000 policiers et gendarmes, prévoyant entre 30 000 et 60 000 personnes dans les rues de la capitale et de 50 à 60 défilés sur tout le territoire, le ministère de l’Intérieur a compté, au doigt mouillé, -il faut le croire !-, 8 900 personnes mobilisées réparties sur 55 actions dans tout le pays. Soit… 8 policiers pour un seul manifestant ! Voilà ce qui s’appelle sécuriser le terrain.
17h00
Le cortège arrive à Nation
La plupart des manifestants sont arrivés au bout du parcours, place de la Nation, entre 16h30 et 17h. Le cortège s’est en partie scindé un peu plus tôt, au niveau du carrefour entre le boulevard Diderot et l’avenue Daumesnil, à la suite d’un blocage mis en place par les forces de l’ordre.
16h38
Le témoignage d’Éléna, mère de famille et Gilet jaune
Eléna, mère de famille, est Gilet jaune depuis 2021. Elle manifeste tous les samedis, alors évidemment, elle est présente aujourd’hui pour dénoncer la baisse du pouvoir d’achat et la vie chère. Elle estime que, pour son cas personnel, « ça va » : elle et son conjoint parviennent à vivre décemment avec leurs deux salaires.
Mais elle voit ses parents « galérer » avec des retraites de misère, et dénonce également les violences policières qu’elle constate de ses propres yeux, depuis 2021.
16h31
Des conditions plus apaisées pour les Street Medic
Loïc, street medic présent dans le cortège parisien, confie à L’Humanité son soulagement de voir la manifestation du jour encadrée « par la gendarmerie » plutôt que par les CRS.
Une bonne nouvelle selon lui, car les gendarmes sont « mieux formés et reçoivent des ordres différents (…). Ils sont beaucoup plus sympas avec nous ». À sa connaissance, aucune intervention n’a été nécessaire jusqu’ici. « Pour l’instant, tout se passe très bien », indique-t-il.
Répartis en « 4 ou 5 groupes » et « reliés par radio », les street médic ont « un peu plus peur de la fin » de la manifestation, au moment où les manifestants se disperseront.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: How SAF successes in Sudan’s Kordofan could turn tide against the RSF
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
How SAF successes in Sudan’s Kordofan could turn tide against the RSF
The SAF successes in Kordofan are seeing the battle against the RSF turn in favour of the Sudanese government.
Khartoum, Sudan – The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) gained control over several strategically important villages and localities in west Kordofan this week, shifting the war against the rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in its favour.
On Friday, the Sudanese army took control of al-Khuwai, according to local media. This is one of the main towns in West Kordofan and a strategically important site in the army’s ongoing campaign against the RSF in the resource-rich state, which began several weeks ago.
So far, the offensive by the SAF and allied Darfur forces has succeeded in breaking the RSF siege on al-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, and surrounding areas.
It has also opened up new routes for the army in central and southwest Sudan, paving the way for significant SAF advances in South Kordofan, all the way to Babnusa and the approaches to North Darfur, including an important road linking al-Nuhud, the site of gold mines, and al-Khuwai.
The RSF, alongside its alleged allies in the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdelaziz Al-Hilu, still holds al-Nuhud and parts of South Kordofan. But its recent defeats in southern and western Sudan could weaken the paramilitary’s ability to coopt tribal groups in the region.
“The RSF’s shift from attack to defence will alter its military composition, which was built on demanding rapid tribal support,” Mohamed Ali, an independent Sudanese analyst, told Al Jazeera.
“The Kordofan region is not a social stronghold for the RSF; therefore, it is expected to withdraw from the region and reposition its forces in Darfur. This would give the army a strategic advantage in Kordofan and could make Darfur the new epicentre of the conflict sooner than expected.”
Tribal structures
The RSF’s main social and tribal support base is among the Arab communities of south and east Darfur, including areas around Nyala and el-Daein, along with border areas with neighbouring countries.
The RSF has relied heavily on mobilising tribes and civilians in areas under its control, said Mohiedeen Mohamed, an expert on Sudanese military affairs. This is particularly true when the paramilitary comes under attack from several fronts and reinforcements are desperately needed to hold the line.
But this informal coalition is also vulnerable to the changing circumstances in the war, with a number of tribal and other groups defecting from the RSF in recent weeks, as the SAF gains ground.
“When the RSF expanded into parts of the Kordofan region, it established alliances with certain tribal groups and local communities,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera.
“However, these alliances can be understood, at least in part, as arrangements driven by military and political necessity, rather than necessarily reflecting the longstanding social and historical integration.”
Humanitarian crisis
After the downfall of former Sudan President Omar al-Bashir in 2019, a power struggle between General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the head of the SAF, and his former ally in the RSF, Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo, emerged, developing into a nationwide conflict between the two sides in April 2023.
Fighting between the SAF and RSF has resulted in one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with about 150,000 people killed and more than 14 million of Sudan’s 53 million population displaced in the ongoing war.
Following SAF’s military successes in Khartoum and other areas, fighting has focused on the remote, impoverished but oil-rich and strategically important Sudanese provinces of Darfur and Kordofan.
The recent battles in Kordofan form part of a broader struggle over geography, economic resources, and supply routes connecting Sudan’s central regions with Darfur and beyond.
The RSF still consolidates control across all five states in Darfur, including el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, which fell to the RSF in October 2025 after a brutal siege and bloody reprisals that saw thousands of civilians killed, tortured, detained or raped.
The United Nations has identified Kordofan as the epicentre of Sudan’s conflict and said fighting in the area is complicating an already dire humanitarian situation.
Continued fighting has seen about 4.5 million civilians flee to Chad, Egypt, South Sudan, and other neighbouring countries.
Civilians are paying the highest price in the war, with drones targeting them and civilian infrastructure, including homes, schools, health facilities, power and water plants.
About 160 people were killed in drone attacks over several days in October in western regions of Sudan.
War of attrition
While both sides have been accused of using drones, analysts see the RSF’s use of drones as part of a wider strategy of intimidation and economic disruption, aimed at spreading fear and paralysing daily life in government areas.
“However, the military balance in Kordofan is shifting. The SAF’s growing air superiority, extensive use of drones, and changing ground tactics have enabled advances along unexpected routes, as demonstrated by the capture of Al-Khuwei,” said Mohamed. “These developments significantly reduce the RSF’s chances of regaining lost territory.”
Most humanitarian assistance operations in the region have halted due to the deteriorated security situation.
Omer Yousif, 55, a driver who works in aid delivery for an organisation called Tasami, said travelling through his native Kordofan has become an increasingly dangerous task. But he believes the humanitarian and security situation might improve if the SAF campaign in the region is successful.
“We were travelling to all of Kordofan region despite the danger because we wanted to help our people. I was captured last August by the militia and I was beaten. Some of my colleagues were tortured and killed,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Restoring the Kordofan region [to the SAF] means more aid can be delivered to both Kordofan and Darfur region.”
Al-Rasheed Mohamed, a military expert, told Al Jazeera the SAF offensive in Kordofan appears to have had some success in consolidating their gains in central Sudan, and opening a new route towards Darfur.
“Of course, the current operations along the western strategic axis are part of a broader military strategy linked to the overall plan to reclaim control of the entire country and restore Sudan’s sovereignty over every inch of its territory,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Although the advances have varied across different fronts, the overarching strategic objective remains the same – the army is now advancing and taking the initiative across these fronts, while the RSF has been pushed into a defensive position.”
Border areas
Control of Kordofan also brings considerable economic and strategic benefits, with the region being rich in agricultural products, including sesame seeds, groundnuts, hibiscus and gum arabic.
It is also home to the strategically important Heglig oilfield, a major oil processing and transit hub for Sudanese and South Sudanese crude, as well as gold.
“Ultimately, restoring state control and stability across Kordofan is not merely a territorial or security objective; it is a critical economic and national sovereignty priority,” Mohamed al-Nayer, a professor of economics at the University of Sudan, told Al Jazeera.
“It would enable [the] Sudan [government] to regain control of its natural resources, revive exports, restore oil production, increase foreign currency revenues, and lay the foundations for sustainable economic recovery in the short and long term.”
Kordofan’s proximity to South Sudan also gives it control over key border crossings, trade routes, pastoral corridors and critical oil infrastructure.
Whoever controls Kordofan would thus gain significant economic leverage and strategic influence with neighbouring South Sudan.
“Kordofan’s stability is equally important to South Sudan, whose oil exports depend on transportation through Sudanese territory to Bashayer Port,” said al-Nayer.
“Both countries therefore share a strategic interest in securing oil infrastructure, protecting border areas, and restoring cross-border trade.”
Of particular importance are the area’s strategic oil fields, particularly Heglig and Balila in West Kordofan, which produce 90% of Sudan’s oil. Control over these resources also grants the government linked to the SAF added national and international significance and legitimacy.
“Securing these fields and restoring oil production would help reduce Sudan’s dependence on imported petroleum products, strengthen public revenues, and support economic recovery,” alNayer added.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Tech’s biggest names sank a tax on billionaires’ wealth with $425m and a familiar playbook
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Dara Kerr
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In the hours after polls closed on election day, tech industry players began praising Sergey Brin, the co-founder of Google, on social media.
“Huge thanks to Sergey Brin here,” wrote Garry Tan, the CEO of Y Combinator. Venture capitalist Ilya Sukhar posted: “God bless Sergey Brin.” And David Marcus, a crypto entrepreneur, simply wrote: “Hero.”
They were all referring to Brin’s instrumental role in the defeat of California’s wealth tax ballot measure, known as Proposition 40. The proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires in the state was defeated by just over five points. Simultaneously, an opposition initiative that would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth, Proposition 42, put on the ballot by Brin and a cohort of the state’s ultra-rich, is poised to pass.
Brin, whose net worth is about $230bn, contributed at least $132m to the fight – more than any other donor. The runner-up was former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, who gave more than $48m. Millions more were donated by executives from Palantir, DoorDash, Stripe and Reddit, along with prominent venture capitalists. All told, Silicon Valley’s elite raised nearly $425m to sink the tax, according to campaign finance filings, making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history.
Over the last month, the campaign poured those dollars into highly produced ads and mailers that bombarded voters with warnings that the tax was dangerous and would hurt everyday people. Taglines from the campaign said Prop 40 was an “everyone tax”, “reckless experiment” and “you’re next”. While supporters of the tax said the money would go toward funding the state’s healthcare losses from Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents repeatedly sent the message to voters that it would make healthcare funding worse.
Even without Prop 40’s outsized opponents, the pro-billionaire tax campaign had a difficult task. It had to convince Californians that this specific one-time tax, chiefly geared toward healthcare funding, was the right way to address losses from Trump’s bill. The idea of zeroing in on billionaires ruffled feathers across the state with major political figures opposing it, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, and Xavier Becerra, the governor elect.
Then there was the funding. In comparison with the billionaires’ war chest, the pro-Prop 40 camp, sponsored by the union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), raised just more than $31m. They were outspent nearly 14-fold.
“All lies have a shelf life,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff for the SEIU-UHW. “Billionaire-funded propaganda may mislead voters about the consequences of these cuts today, but as hospitals reduce services, emergency rooms close and families lose access to care, the truth will become increasingly difficult to hide.”
The counties that voted to pass Prop 40 are typically more Democratic and where many of the state’s wealthy reside, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and other areas around the Bay Area. The counties that overwhelmingly voted against the measure were mostly red, rural and poor. While many of these counties swung blue in US House races this election, up to 80% of voters there voted no on Prop 40, according to the latest count.
Rob Lalka, a business professor at Tulane University and author of The Venture Alchemists: How Big Tech Turned Profits Into Power, compared the Prop 40 campaign with Uber and Lyft’s ballot measure crusade in 2020, where the companies spent more than $200m to defeat an initiative over labor rights for drivers. The ride-hailing companies used similar tactics, Lalka said, something he describes as “misleading propaganda and paying for endorsements”.
“The money also seemed astonishing at the time: the amount to influence the outcome, over $200m, was a massive sum,” Lalka said. “Money in politics has only increased in California throughout this decade. That’s the context for Prop 40 this election cycle.”
The colossal funding of political campaigns has broken records nationwide this midterm cycle, said Francesco Trebbi, a business and public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He pointed to Elon Musk dumping $446m into House and Senate races across the county, but noted that it was ineffective in places such as Texas: Musk’s mark, James Talarico, won.
“Maybe it was easier to decouple Prop 40 opposition from President Trump’s agenda, so Brin had an easier target to hit,” Trebbi said. Still, he added: “We need a lot more data and statistical evidence in order to conclusively finalize this discussion.”
Exit polls haven’t yet been released for Prop 40, which will give more details on voters’ decisions. In the meantime, the SEIU-UHW’s Jimenez said that despite the loss, the union and its allies are not going to give up on the long game: “If Sacramento fails to protect patients and deliver a real solution that makes billionaires pay their fair share, healthcare workers will pursue every available avenue, up to and including returning to the ballot in 2028 with a billionaire tax.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 to hit new space distance record of one light-day
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
NASA’s Voyager 1 to hit new space distance record of one light-day
The probe was launched in 1977 but it continues to relay space-related data back to a team of NASA scientists daily.
NASA has announced that its Voyager 1 probe will soon become humanity’s first object to travel one light-day from Earth.
On Wednesday, the robotic space probe will hit the milestone of travelling at least 16 billion miles since its launch in 1977, a distance equal to one light-day, or how far light can travel in 24 hours.
The probe completed its Saturn flyby in 1980, the end of its primary planetary mission, and is currently travelling at roughly 36,000 miles per hour (58km/h) in interstellar space, the vast gap between stars.
NASA expects it to take 18,000 years to travel a full light-year, and double that before it nears another star.
Plutonium-powered Voyager 1 was launched shortly before another probe, Voyager 2. Both continue to relay data back to Earth daily, including readings on the strength and direction of the magnetic field as well as on the surrounding pressure, dust and galactic cosmic rays.
Voyager 2 is expected to hit one light-day from Earth in 2035.
Both are kept active by a skeleton team of NASA engineers who send commands roughly once a week, and more if the probe gets into trouble.
In October, the team briefly lost communication with Voyager 1, and they have not yet figured out why.
Voyager 1 project manager Suzanne Dodd described Voyager 1 as “a national treasure” and told The Associated Press news agency that the two probes’ activities are akin to that of weather satellites.
The probe’s cultural impact has been significant. The famous “Pale Blue Dot” photo of Earth was taken by Voyager 1 in 1990.
“All of us — everyone on Earth — have been touched by these missions,” the Planetary Society’s Bill Nye said in a statement.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/three.title: Three Israelis emerge as possible successors to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, local media says
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/three.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/three.text:
Three Israelis emerge as possible successors to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, local media says
Three Israeli technology executives have emerged among the possible successors to Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of Nvidia after leading the artificial intelligence chipmaker for more than three decades.
Huang’s departure, announced on 12 November, took effect immediately. Nvidia’s board appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive while it searches for a permanent successor.
The company said it would consider both internal and external candidates.
Israeli media have named Michael Kagan, Nvidia’s chief technology officer; Eyal Waldman, co-founder and former chief executive of Israeli networking company Mellanox; and Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, as possible contenders.
Kagan co-founded Mellanox in 1999 and joined Nvidia after it acquired the company in 2020 for about $6.9bn.

He has since served as Nvidia’s chief technology officer, focusing on technologies that allow thousands of processors to communicate within large data centres.
Waldman also co-founded Mellanox and served as its chief executive before the acquisition. Unlike Kagan, he is no longer part of Nvidia’s management.
Ynet has also reported that he is in the succession discussions.
Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, is one of the key figures behind the company’s in-house chip development.
He joined Apple in 2008 and led the development of processors used in its products, including those underpinning its transition from Intel processors to Apple Silicon.
Controversy surrounding Huang
Huang’s resignation followed a series of reports about his personal relationships, including an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who US intelligence agencies reportedly suspect of being an intelligence asset for Beijing.
China has rejected the espionage allegation.
Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in an email to employees, apologising to his family and colleagues.
Nvidia subsequently announced an investigation into whether he had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation.
The company's board had been examining Huang’s position before his resignation, according to media reports.
Nvidia has not publicly said the reported relationships were the reason for his departure, nor has it established that company secrets or national security information were compromised.
The allegations have also raised questions about Nvidia’s business dealings in China, where its advanced AI chips have become a focus of US export-control policy.
Among the companies under scrutiny is Megaspeed, which reports have examined for its possible role in helping Chinese companies obtain restricted Nvidia processors.
Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised” but that its internal investigation would examine the available information.
Huang’s departure leaves Nvidia facing a leadership transition as its chips play a central role in the global AI race and its business becomes increasingly entangled in tensions between Washington and Beijing.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Canada’s Stelco to recall 175 workers after government pressure
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Canada’s Stelco to recall 175 workers after government pressure
Steelmaker promises back pay for workers whose layoffs its US owner blamed on tariffs, weak demand and imports.
Canadian steelmaker Stelco says it will recall all 175 workers laid off at its plant in Hamilton and pay them retroactively, following a weeks-long standoff that pitted workers and the Canadian government against its owner in the United States.
The announcement on Friday came shortly after Canada’s Industry Minister Melanie Joly said she would seek a court order to force Cleveland-Cliffs to sell Stelco unless she heard from management by the end of the day.
The company said in a statement on Friday that it had reached agreements with enough customers to restart its finishing operations and that workers would be recalled on December 1. They would receive back pay for the standard wages they would have earned while laid off.
The president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, Ron Wells, welcomed the announcement and credited pressure from workers, the union and the government.
At a news conference, he called the layoffs “illegal” and “immoral” which should never have happened.
Alongside him was Joly, who said the outcome sent a message to investors that Canada was “a country of the rule of law and that the law applies to everyone, notwithstanding the size of your wallet.”
“This fight was absolutely worth it,” she said.
Cleveland-Cliffs, which bought Stelco in 2024, announced in late September that up to 500 workers would be laid off at Stelco’s plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario, citing weak demand and difficult market conditions for cold-rolled and coated steel products used to make everything from cars to appliances.
It blamed US President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel, which made it more expensive in the US, as well as competition from cheaper foreign steel, which it argued was eating into domestic demand for Canadian steel.
Ottawa said the layoffs violated binding commitments the company made when it bought Stelco, including keeping the same number of Canadian unionised employees through 2029.
The government and the union also argued that Cleveland-Cliffs’ CEO Lourenco Goncalves violated a commitment to advocate for policies that would benefit the steel industries in both Canada and the US when he publicly supported Trump’s tariffs on steel, including Canada’s.
Goncalves’ open support for the tariffs raised questions, given that he also blamed them for Stelco’s financial troubles.
In its statement, Cleveland-Cliffs said its customers had committed to supporting its operations in Hamilton “despite the lack of response from the federal government to address the shortfalls in their tariff response program.”
It didn’t provide details on the agreements it had reached with customers or explain what had changed to make restarting operations viable.
Cleveland-Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.
