Diplomats from 18 Muslim-majority countries condemn Israeli strike on Nasser hospital
Top diplomats from 18 Muslim-majority countries strongly condemned an Israeli strike on the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis.
Countries that condemned the strike include Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan.
The attack left at least six people dead, including a child and a surgeon, prompting accusations from ministers that Israel is violating international humanitarian law.
In the joint declaration, the foreign ministers condemned ongoing assaults against Palestinians, warning that violence threatens to collapse the ceasefire in Gaza.
The countries accused Israel of blockading critical humanitarian assistance- specifically medical shipments and winter supplies-which they warned leaves infants and children exposed to failing water, sanitation, and healthcare systems as winter sets in.
Pressing for immediate compliance, the coalition called on Israel to strictly enforce the truce, facilitate unhindered aid deliveries, and fully honour its obligations under the ceasefire framework.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.title: Why US Democrats are expected to keep Schumer and Jeffries in power
https://www.aljazeera.com/news-analysis/.text:
Why US Democrats are expected to keep Schumer and Jeffries in power
The prospect of keeping the Congressional leaders in power is exposing long-running tensions in the party.
Over a week after Democrats rode a historic wave of support to retake the United States Congress, divisions within the party seem to be threatening to undermine its newfound political momentum.
Despite growing calls for a change in Congressional leadership, Democrats Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries appear likely to remain at the helm of their respective US Senate and House caucuses.
After amassing the most Democratic power in Washington since 2009, the two New Yorkers are seeking to retain their leadership positions as their party prepares to take control of both chambers in January.
Schumer, the US Senate’s 75-year-old minority leader, is vying to lead Democrats’ new majority in the chamber, a post he previously held during Joe Biden’s presidency. On the other side of the US Capitol, the 56-year-old Jeffries, as the current minority leader in the US House, is seeking the top role of speaker, placing him second in the line of succession for the US presidency.
But the prospect of keeping Schumer and Jeffries in charge has frustrated some Democrats, exposing long-running tensions between Democratic lawmakers who want to maintain continuity and those who believe their midterm victories offer an opportunity to fundamentally reshape the party’s priorities.
Here’s why Schumer and Jeffries could prevail:
An election victory buys political goodwill
Perhaps the biggest reason the top two Democrats in the US Congress will hold onto their posts: the party’s massive electoral gains.
Schumer’s supporters argue he helped Democrats secure at least eight Republican-held Senate seats, including victories in traditionally conservative states. The party is poised to hold as many as 56 seats in the next Congress, giving it a substantial majority not seen since former President Barack Obama’s first term in office.
“When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract”, Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego, with Schumer by his side, told reporters on Tuesday. “And this has been a really good election cycle for us”.
Schumer also played a central role in recruiting candidates who could compete in states where Democrats have struggled in recent elections, including former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown and former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper.
Adam Jentleson, a longtime US Senate aide and author of, Supermajority: How Democrats Can Build Lasting Power, argued Schumer’s electoral success makes it difficult for critics to mount a successful challenge.
“It’s hard to argue with somebody who just oversaw the biggest election the Democrats have had since Watergate,” Jentleson said during an interview with public radio station WBUR earlier this month.
“The only people who matter are the members of the Democratic caucus,” Jentleson said, explaining that lawmakers who had recently benefitted from the midterm results would have little incentive to remove the person who helped deliver those victories.
Schumer’s allies have made a similar argument. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who oversees the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, credited Schumer’s candidate recruitment and fundraising efforts for helping the party reclaim the US Senate.
“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership,” she said.
Schumer himself has expressed confidence that he has enough support to retain the position.
In an interview with The Washington Sun on Wednesday, he said he had secured more than enough backing from his colleagues.
“I am going to be elected leader, OK, and we’re united on the issues,” Schumer told the Sun. “We’re united.”
Schumer faces a challenge
Not every Democrat believes last week’s victories are enough to anoint Schumer as the party’s leader in the Senate in the next Congress.
Senator Chris Van Hollen announced on Thursday he would mount a challenge for the role after factions of the Democratic base, particularly progressives, have called for new leadership.
The Maryland Democrat attracted attention at the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term after he travelled to El Salvador to meet with his constituent, Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who had been deported to the country despite a judge’s ruling barring his removal.
That, according to a senior Senate Democratic aide who spoke with Al Jazeera, exemplified “the fight Schumer just doesn’t have”.
“This is not about any one individual, but it is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen said during a Thursday appearance on MSNOW, adding that US voters sent a message to “reject the status quo and to reject business as usual”.
Another Senate aide, who would only speak on condition of anonymity to talk freely about an internal matter, suggested Van Hollen’s bid may be more about extracting concessions from Schumer, like a promise to serve as a short-term “bridge” to a new generation of Democratic leadership.
An analysis by Al Jazeera showed that 12 Democratic senators have publicly committed to backing Schumer in next month’s leadership election. At least 10 senators, including independent Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, have said they will not. However, only half of those opposed to Schumer’s leadership have backed Van Hollen’s challenge.
In an interview with The Nation published on Wednesday, the Vermont independent senator acknowledged knowing Schumer for decades and even liking him personally. But he argued that personal relationships should not determine who leads the party.
“In this moment in American history, Chuck’s views are way out of touch with where the American people are at — and especially with where [the base of] the Democratic Party is,” Sanders said.
He added that Schumer was not in tune with Democratic voters on the issues, arguing the party needed a new and more ambitious direction.
Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin has also questioned Schumer’s leadership, calling for a concrete plan outlining how Democrats intend to use their newly won congressional power.
Slotkin went further on Tuesday, suggesting to reporters at the US Capitol that senators withhold a quorum — the minimum number of lawmakers required to conduct official business — if Schumer runs unopposed, until he presents a plan that gives members a meaningful voice in setting the party’s priorities.
Georgia Senator Raphael Warnock has also declined to commit to supporting Schumer, telling CNN on Tuesday that Democrats are at an “inflection point” and any senator who believes they should lead deserves an opportunity to make their case.
Still, there is a difference between public dissatisfaction and the votes needed to remove a leader. Senate Democrats select their leader through a private ballot, requiring only a simple majority of the caucus.
Tre Easton, vice president for public policy at the Searchlight Institute and a former deputy chief of staff for Democratic Senator John Fetterman, has also questioned the timing of the push against Schumer, arguing calls for new leadership would have carried more weight following the Democrats’ losses in 2024 rather than immediately after their electoral successes in 2026.
“The job of the leader in each legislative chamber here in the U.S. isn’t to articulate a vision for the party”, Easton said in a social media post. “It’s to keep each respective caucus together and count votes. Dassit”.
Jeffries faces a different kind of challenge
The outlook is considerably clearer for Jeffries, who is seeking to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes on January 3.
Unlike Schumer, Jeffries does not face a prominent challenger for his leadership position, despite criticism from some progressives over his approach to Trump and his longstanding support for Israel.
His backing from moderate Democrats has been particularly visible.
The New Democrat Coalition, a group of Democratic centrists representing 142 current and newly elected lawmakers, issued a statement on Tuesday endorsing his bid for speaker.
“Hakeem Jeffries is the right person at the right time to lead our party”, the group said. “He’s smart, strategic, and action-oriented, with strong relationships across the Democratic caucus”.
The coalition added that it “can’t wait to vote for Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker of the House on January 3, 2027”.
But support from the party’s moderate wing has not eliminated dissatisfaction among progressives.
Representative Pramila Jayapal, a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said she is withholding her support for Jeffries unless he commits to advancing Medicare for All, a proposal to establish a government-funded universal healthcare system.
Jayapal has also acknowledged that the lack of an alternative candidate complicates the leadership debate.
“You can’t beat somebody with nobody,” the Washington state Democrat told Talking Points Memo, adding that the emergence of a challenger would change the calculations of lawmakers considering whether to support Jeffries.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, meanwhile, was asked by CNN whether she supported Jeffries.
“The race is unopposed. Yeah,” she responded, suggesting that the absence of a challenger was an important factor in the debate.
The tensions in the US House have also been illustrated by the case of Don Leonard, an incoming Democratic congressman from Ohio who said he will withhold his support for Jeffries unless the party commits to specific policy changes.
Leonard, who has called for an end to US support for Israel and the war in Iran, alleged in a video posted to social media that senior House Democrats threatened to make his life a “living hell” in Washington and undermine his chances of re-election in 2028 if he continued attaching conditions to his support for Jeffries.
He has not identified the lawmakers involved, and the allegations have not been independently verified. House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar told reporters on Tuesday he did not know which senior Democrats Leonard was referring to.
Jeffries, who has denied reports that US House Democrats have been receiving calls to oppose his bid for the speakership, spoke to reporters on Thursday about frustrations within the party over his leadership.
“We take nothing for granted, because all of us in the House of Representatives are on a two-year employment contract”, Jeffries said. “And we have to continue to make our case both with respect to our track record up until this point, as well as, perhaps even more importantly, our vision for the future”.
The pressure will come after the leadership votes
The leadership contests are scheduled for November 18 and 19 for House Democrats and at an unannounced date in December for Senate Democrats.
If elected, both Schumer and Jeffries will likely continue to face competing demands from progressives seeking more aggressive action against Trump and from moderates representing districts and states where a more centrist approach may be politically important.
They will also have to contend with the practical limitations of governing. Even with control of both chambers, Democrats will not have the 60 Senate votes generally required to overcome a filibuster, meaning they will need Republican support for much of their legislation.
For now, however, the party’s electoral gains have given Schumer and Jeffries an argument for continuity.
“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer wrote in an X post on Thursday. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How a US extradition bid over Hamas allegations put a wealthy activist before a Spanish court
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Timothy Pratt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A two-hour hearing in Spain’s high court Friday on the US extradition request of wealthy leftwing activist and philanthropist James “Fergie” Chambers turned out to be a study in contrasts.
Chambers’s defense took most of the session to query the US citizen and detail irregularities in the Trump administration’s extradition request – several of which the Guardian has reported on – as well as the figures of Spanish law that would lead the three-judge panel to deny the request; while the prosecutor sped through his case, head down, asking Chambers no questions at all.
Notably, neither the judges or the prosecutor asked Chambers to address the insinuation in the extradition request that the wealthy activist had supported Hamas. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money laundering charge and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
But the defense’s queries did allow him to speak for the first time since his 10 July arrest in Ibiza about events at the center of the case: 2023 protests against Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit in Massachusets and New Hampshire and 2024 transfers of $7.2m to Tunisia, where he lived at the time. The latter was buttressed with testimony from a financial expert.
On the whole, Chambers painted a picture different from the depiction contained in the extradition request, that of a violent backer of Hamas on the run from the US. At one point, he noted that his family’s next door neighbor in Tunis was the US ambassador.
The court will decide next week on extraditing Chambers. If the decision is affirmative, Spain’s council of ministers can reverse the court’s decision. This means Chambers’s extradition may be among the last decisions made under Pedro Sánchez, the socialist prime minister, before national elections on 29 November.
Friday’s hearing began with Chambers’s defense asking about his wealth. A self-described communist and anti-imperialist, Chambers sold stock back to his family’s business, Atlanta-based Cox Enterprises, worth about $250m in mid-2023.
Then he started a foundation, he told the court. He and the foundation’s three-member board decide on funding and ensure that no projects seeking support are under US sanctions, Chambers said. The foundation has funded an estimated 100 progressive and humanitarian projects in 20 countries, according to his partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel – including, Chambers said Friday, organizations in Gaza working on issues such as “medical treatment for children, transportation out of dangerous areas and clean water and food”.
Two of the request’s three charges – riot and conspiracy to riot – are related to the late-2023 protests against Elbit.
Chambers detailed his participation in the protests: locking himself to a door, marching in the street and – in New Hampshire – standing in the road, speaking to the media and paying bail for four protesters who were eventually found guilty of misdemeanor charges and served 30 days in jail.
As for the $7.2m, the defense and a financial expert serving as a witness laid out how ten bank transfers from the US to Tunisia mostly went to sponsor the football club Club Africain – described by Chambers as “one of the largest football clubs in Africa” – and a sporting business Chambers launched while living in Tunisia.
“Is there any indication that the money went to support terrorist activities?” asked defense attorney Aitor Martínez. “None,” said financial expert Albert Deulofeu Schilt.
Then, in about 15 minutes of rapid-fire monotone, prosecutor Juan Hernández Villalba laid out a wholly different picture of Chambers as backing “an organized structure … aimed at repeatedly committing illegal acts … together with funds destined for terrorist organizations”.
He accused the defense of laying out the facts of the case “in a fragmented way … when what’s most relevant is an evaluation of the whole picture”.
“The extradition petition isn’t based on ideology or political statements, but on actions [Chambers] organized, financed and carried out, causing material damage,” Hernández Villalba asserted.
The actions against Elbit “were presented as a simple protest”, he said. “Nevertheless, the actions described by the US were planned for days … with objectively violent content.”
Given all this, the prosecutor said, “there are more than enough indications to consider … that [Chambers’s] funding was aimed at terrorism”.
Among the 100-plus people in varying time zones following Friday’s hearing on the court’s YouTube channel was Irish film-maker and journalist Sinéad O’Shea, whose documentary on Chambers called All About the Money makes its New York premiere this weekend. It covers the time period cited by the FBI affidavit underpinning the US request. O’Shea said that extradition case “builds a false narrative which begins with the protest in New Hampshire – a piece of vandalism at worst and for which people ended up serving 30 days. I saw myself the football club in which he invested in Tunisia and his donations to Palestinian and other charities are a matter of public record. It is impossible not to see this as a politically motivated case.”
Chambers’s views have been extensively profiled in US media. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
Dressed in dark jeans, a grey-blue shirt, a black jacket, with a close-cropped haircut and mustache, Chambers got the last word during the hearing.
“To this day I cannot understand why I have been in prison since July for what amounts to speaking emotionally and committing minor offenses of public disturbance,” he said.
“I’ve never had any contact with any terrorist organization. I’ve certainly never financed any terrorist organization … and for this my family has been torn apart. I missed my grandmother’s funeral last week. My five-year-old son asks where I am every day. And my wife will give birth, God willing, in March – and I don’t know if I will be by her side.”
“[All] because I have spoken my mind, and I had a lot more money than others who have spoken their mind, in my country. And that’s all it amounts to.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Bomb found at Illinois ethanol plant, prompting evacuations
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Residents were ordered to evacuate parts of an Illinois community on Friday after the mayor there said authorities found a bomb at a local ethanol- and alcohol-production plant.
The discovery reported at BioUrja Renewables in Peoria triggered a mandatory evacuation over a one-mile evacuation zone encompassing sections of that city as well as the adjacent municipality of East Peoria.
“It is real – this is a real thing,” Peoria’s mayor, Rita Ali, said, according to local news outlet WMBD. “We know that is a real threat. We know it is a bomb.”
Peoria’s police chief, Brad Dixon, said at a news conference early on Saturday that bomb technicians had rendered the object in question safe.
But Dixon asked for the public’s patience as investigators searched BioUrja Renewals’ expansive facility for other explosive devices, as the Peoria news outlet WEEK reported.
“We don’t know if there are other devices,” Ali remarked.
Meanwhile, Ryan Presley of the FBI, who is in charge of the bureau’s field office about an hour away in Springfield, Illinois, said agents would pursue whoever was responsible “tirelessly” and “bring them to justice”.
At about 7.05pm local time on Friday, the Peoria police department had announced that officers were “actively investigating a reported bomb threat at BioUrja Renewables”. The agency then urged “anyone who lives or works within a one-mile radius of the facility to immediately evacuate their homes and businesses until further notice”.
The police’s statement said the evacuation notice had been “issued out of an abundance of caution while officers and emergency personnel investigate the threat”, which officials initially referred to as a suspicious package. The city offered the Manual Academy school as a temporary shelter, and police said anyone who needed assistance evacuating their home or business could call for help.
In a separate statement, the municipal government of neighboring East Peoria acknowledged that the evacuation zone associated with the package at BioUrja Renewables extended into part of that city. The East Peoria government said it expected to provide an update at about 9am local time on Saturday, but in the meantime all evacuations would remain in place.
“This is not a hoax,” the Illinois state senator Dave Koehler said during the early Saturday news conference. “This has gone beyond that … This is serious. This is serious.”
Friday’s BioUrja Renewables case came amid a particularly chaotic day in the US marked by a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration-ordered nationwide ground stop at US airports that was in effect for about four hours, canceling or delaying more than 11,000 US flights.
The country’s nerves were also frayed by a tanker which struck a cruise ship docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday afternoon. First responders had to rescue passengers from the river’s water after the cruise ship turned on its side, and there were more than 30 injuries reported. But none of those injuries were critical, and there were no fatalities reported in association with the crash.

John Fetterman threatens to quit Democratic Party if next Senate leader is critical of Israel
Democratic Senator John Fetterman suggested on Saturday that he could leave his party if Senate Democrats chose a leader he considered insufficiently pro-Israel.
Fetterman singled out Senator Chris Van Hollen, a critic of Israel who on Thursday challenged Chuck Schumer, the septuagenarian hardline pro-Israel Democrat, for the Senate leadership. Van Hollen said the party needed new leadership after voters opted for change in this month’s midterm elections.
“Yeah, absolutely,” Fetterman said in a Fox News interview on Saturday when asked whether he had a red line that would make him “walk away” from the party.
“It would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being very anti, hostile to Israel,” said Fetterman, who has backed the Israeli genocide and ethnic cleansing in Gaza.
Democrats won 55 Senate seats in the midterms, giving them a comfortable majority. There had been speculation that Fetterman could defect to the Republicans if Democrats won just 51 seats, as many expected. With 55 seats, the party can retain its majority without him.

The Pennsylvania senator said he had yet to decide what he would do if Van Hollen became majority leader.
After visiting the Gaza border in September 2025, Van Hollen said: “In Gaza, the Netanyahu government is implementing its goal through the near-total destruction of civilian infrastructure and its use of food as a weapon of war.”
“These policies are part of a calculated effort to drive Palestinians out of Gaza by making it impossible for them to live there. Any talk of “voluntary departures” is a cruel hoax. Departure is not “voluntary” when the conditions needed to support life are extinguished,” he said.
Fetterman has made support for Israel a centrepiece of his time in office. He has visited Israel twice and met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at least four times, including in Washington.
His support for Israel was so pronounced that his own staff mockingly dubbed him the “senator from Tel Aviv”, according to a New York Magazine investigation. Most of his staff have since resigned.
The investigation also identified David Safier, an American Orthodox Jewish fundraiser, as Fetterman’s closest adviser and confidant.
Safier holds no official position in Fetterman’s Senate office but advises him on policy, raises money for him from pro-Israel groups and arranges calls with Netanyahu, the magazine reported.
A Wall Streert Journal investigation this September found that Fetterman reportedly cancelled a meeting with three paralysed military veterans from Pennsylvania, citing illness, only to turn up at his office shortly afterwards for a Fox News interview about Israel.
The incident was among several uncovered by the WSJ investigation that found the Fetterman repeatedly avoided constituents and routine Senate duties while prioritising media appearances and advocacy for Israel.

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Raphael Rashid
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra, to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe.
Eleven countries competed at the One Bangkok Forum in central Bangkok, and the show ran for two and a half hours including advertising.
The winner, who performs under the single name Carmelle, finished on 211 points, 41 clear of the hosts Thailand, with Vietnam third. She received the most votes from both the national juries and the public ballot.
Carmelle, 19, grew up beside the railway tracks in the Bicol region of south-eastern Luzon and has been competing in televised talent contests since she was 12.
Sobra-Sobra mixes pop and rap, is supported by traditional Philippine instruments, the kubing and kulintang, and is sung in Tagalog and English.
After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women”.
“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told the Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”
“It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are,” she told the Guardian before the final. “It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas.”
The show opened with a routine celebrating the host country, in which Muay Thai fighters shared the stage with drag performers on street food carts. The 11 acts were then driven on in tuk-tuks, each carrying their national flag.
Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên, a star at home for more than 20 years, performed first, among dancers costumed as lotus leaves. Mang x Daou represented Thailand, a duo assembled for the contest in the host country who performed a duet staged like a musical number.
Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai gave one of the most conventionally Eurovision performances of the night with Ananta Maya, a rock ballad staged with fire imagery and a large heart-shaped structure behind him.
He ended it by appealing for support for his country, which he said was “going [through a] very hard situation”. More than 1,500 people were killed and more than 5,000 were reported missing after a rock and ice avalanche near the Chinese border triggered catastrophic flash floods in August.
Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, originally a nine-member a cappella and beatbox group, sang without a single instrument. Three of their members were left out of the final due to a rule capping each act at six performers on stage.
Nyendra from Bhutan sang dressed in the gho, his country’s national dress for men, against a backdrop of Himalayan peaks. Mongolia’s Beck performed in a reinterpreted deel, also a national costume.
Half the result was decided before the show began. The 11 national juries voted at a dress rehearsal on Friday night and put the Philippines top with 93 points, ahead of Vietnam and Malaysia.
The other half came from viewers around the world, who could vote online but not for their own country, and who were given eight free votes each and the option to buy 10 more.
Laos’s entrant, Thinla, was unable to hear her own music during her performance, and her dress rehearsal was aired once all live performances were over. She finished fifth, with the night’s third-highest public score.
Carmelle receives no prize money but a trophy presented by Dara, the Bulgarian singer who won this year’s European contest, and will perform at Eurovision 2027 in Burgas.
Organisers have said the right to stage future editions will not automatically go to the winner, on the grounds that smaller countries lack the infrastructure.
Some of the clearest echoes of Eurovision’s camp traditions came through those who announced the votes.
South Korea’s jury points were read by Jo Kwon, a veteran pop star who has played Adam in the Korean production of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and the title role in Everybody’s Talking About Jamie.
The Philippines’ were read by Vice Ganda, a gay comedian who is one of the biggest stars on Philippine television.
Meanwhile, the guest performer was the Thai singer Jeff Satur, who reached a wider Asian audience through KinnPorsche, a 2022 series in the genre of male same-sex romance dramas that has a large following across Asia.
Organisers intend the Bangkok show to be the first of many regional editions, with the executive producer, Assaf Blecher, saying that 16 or 17 territories had expressed interest in competing next year, among them China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.title: ‘I’m still trying to find out who I am’: the little-understood plight of Forgotten Australians
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.author: Christopher Hopkins and Stephanie Convery
https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.text:
When Judy Leonard entered the orphanage, she was given a bed with a number. That was how the staff would refer to her. Not by her name, or even by one of the cruel nicknames the other children gave her, but by her allocated space in the dormitory: C2.
“I would like the readers to close their eyes,” Judy says now, “and imagine that it was them at age nine.”
Judy’s early childhood, along with those of her brothers and sisters, was spent playing in the streets and beaches in Melbourne’s west. Then the police arrived.
“We were classed as neglected,” Judy says. “Dirty, unwashed, uneducated.” She was bundled into a car with two siblings. “I remember looking back out of the car and seeing my mum and dad cry. And I’d never seen my father cry.”
For six months, the three siblings were locked away at Turana, an overcrowded accommodation (or “reception”) centre in Parkville for children in the welfare system. It doubled as a remand facility for “problem” children. Police were said to refer to it as “the rat bins”.
A judge later ordered the three children to an orphanage. They could come out again, he said, when their parents’ circumstances improved.
It would be years before Judy went home. In some ways, she never did.
Judy, now 79, is among the Forgotten Australians: more than half a million people who were placed in orphanages, institutions and other forms of out-of-home “care” before 1990. Many were subjected to physical, emotional or sexual abuse, and neglect. Depression and suicidality are among the wounds many of them carry.
Despite multiple government inquiries and a 2009 apology from then-prime minister Kevin Rudd, Forgotten Australians’ trauma and the ongoing effects of it remain little-known and poorly understood. For those facing the prospect of aged care, the horrors of their institutionalised childhood can rear up again, only to be met with incomprehension by those around them.
Judy
“I want people to look at me as a human being. Because this is not just my story, it’s thousands of people’s stories. I’m no different to you. But I went through life a little different,” Judy says.
“I had my freedom taken.”
In the orphanage, Judy began wetting the bed, for which she was bullied mercilessly. She had headaches from undiagnosed longsightedness. She also, unknowingly, had dyslexia – and was hit with a ruler every time she misspelled a word.
“You had to be on guard all the time,” Judy says. “When you’re like that, you come out of that orphanage with a type of understanding that is beyond the kids out here.”
Judy was 14 when she was allowed to go home.
Many years later, Judy and her husband, Henry, became carers of a two-year-old boy – the child of a friend in distress. Two weeks before his eighth birthday, he was taken by authorities.
“I swore I’d never have another kid ever again, because it just tore me to pieces,” Judy says. “The same as when I was in the home, when I left my parents.”
Dean
Dean Wise only recently learned he was a Forgotten Australian. He was in therapy, during a four-year battle with bowel cancer, when he saw a photograph on his psychologist’s computer of one of the institutions he’d been in.
“That was a confronting day, I must admit. I started bawling my eyes out,” Dean says.
At around age 12, and after repeatedly absconding from their foster home, he was separated from his sister and put into Baltara.
He had been fleeing sexual abuse, perpetrated by a man connected to his school. Being in the “reception centre” didn’t stop it: the man was seen as a trusted figure and allowed in to see Dean or take him on outings.
Dean says he tried to speak up about the abuse. He told his social worker, community services, police and school teachers. But “it fell on deaf ears”. The abuse ceased only when the man suddenly stopped visiting.
Finding other survivors through Open Place, Victoria’s support centre for Forgotten Australians, has given Dean community. But even at 57, “I’m still trying to find out who I am,” he says.
“I’m so tired. I’m physically exhausted. Getting diagnosed with the cancer, that just made it even harder.”
Dean is also angry. That’s partly why he’s telling his story.
“I’m doing it for the kids still going through the system and not being heard. Things have got to change. Simple as that. It’s got to change.”
Toni
Toni Brown always wanted to be like her bikie brother. She “took off from home”, hitchhiking from Melbourne to Sydney at age 12.
“There were bikers up there,” Toni says. “They used to park on Darlinghurst Road. That was all I knew.
“So one of them got hold of me – I’m 12, 13 – I fell in love – and I went to work for him on the streets.”
Toni, now 68, isn’t flippant about her experience as an underage sex worker, but her “worst years” came after police caught her. They sent her back to Melbourne and charged her with being “exposed to moral danger” – a “crime” frequently used to send victims of sexual violence to institutions. Toni was sent to a remand centre in Winlaton. It was ostensibly a training and rehabilitation centre for adolescent girls. In practice, it was a prison.
“You walked in the door, escorted by the officer. I had to strip,” Toni says. “They showed me to my room … but it was a cell. I had to sleep on the floor on a mattress because it was overcrowded.” Her bunkmate was a girl charged with the murder of two children.
During her seven months there, Toni was raped by an officer. Another officer witnessed the incident. “She turned her back,” Toni says.
“No wonder I got out and did what I did later. It was almost like I wanted to get back at everybody,” she says.
She returned to Sydney, and to sex work. When she was 16, she moved again and worked on a prawn trawler. “I could sit out and just be totally at one with the ocean … I got a drinking habit, a really bad drinking habit. But apart from that, that was what I think really started to make me stop and think about my life and what I’d done in the past. It started to wake me up.”
She came back to Melbourne in her early 20s, where she managed brothels and escort agencies.
Toni found the abuses of her past recurring later in life. They strained and sometimes fractured her relationship with her two sons, one of whom she was unable to see for many years. Still, she persisted. She drove taxis. She trained as a care worker and worked with kids whose challenges were just like hers had been.
These days, Toni dotes on her 11-year-old granddaughter, who she says once made a perfectly timed phone call that stopped her from taking her own life.
Richard
If you spent time in Melbourne’s gay clubs in the late 1990s and early 2000s, it’s likely you saw Richard Payne dancing on a podium. He was known as Grandpa Acid – not for the drugs (he wasn’t into those) but the music. Dancing was how he found euphoria.
After a decades-long career in agriculture, a marriage, a family and a divorce, Richard realised he was gay. It has been difficult for his family to come to terms with.
Richard was born with a cleft palate. His mother, an unmarried flight attendant, put him into care so she could work to pay for his medical needs. He was shuffled between hospitals and foster homes until he turned eight, when she relinquished his care to the state.
Then a wealthy landowner arrived, looking to adopt a child. “He took me down the street and bought me a great big lollipop,” Richard says. That sweet beginning didn’t last.
“He started doing things like making sure I’d wash myself properly. He’d come in the bathroom and he’d start washing me, and he started doing things,” Richard says. It escalated to violent rape. “He actually physically whipped me from head to toe and then penetrated me,” Richard says.
Confused and terrified, Richard fled back to the group home. He was turned away.
At 14, Richard was burnt in an industrial accident at his agricultural college and kept in intensive care for three months. “While I was there, the head doctor came in to see me,” Richard says. “He said, ‘Richard, how come you haven’t had your speech therapy treatment done?’” His adopted parents were “put on the spot and shamed to do it”.
Eventually, Richard confronted his abuser. “I slammed him up against the back of my ute and put my fist up and said, ‘If you ever touch me again, I’ll kill you.’”
At 21, Richard married into a relationship he describes as loveless, but that he committed to because he wanted a family. After the divorce, he went to his first gay club because a girl he had dated invited him. The men didn’t harass her there, she said.
He kept going back.
Then one night, a young man kissed him.
“I fell apart,” says Richard. “I was aching – I’d been aching all my life for somebody to show that they wanted me for who I am, what I am.”
In a letter he shared with Guardian Australia, Richard wrote that he felt his sexuality had been “robbed” from him in his youth. “This in turn resulted in my trying to dismiss the past and bury it,” he wrote.
“However you always know that one day you will have to relive it and that time is now.”
John
John Pinkard turned 80 this year. He has been attending Open Place for nearly a decade, but identifies as a member of the Stolen Generations. His memory is as sharp as a pin. But while he knows what happened to him in Tufnell Home, he can’t say for sure how old he was when he went in or how long he stayed.
Before Tufnell, John lived on the lam with his foster mother, who he just called “Mum”. His birth mother, a white woman ashamed of having fallen pregnant to an Aboriginal man, had abandoned him at a Brisbane hospital after giving birth.
Ann, the mother-in-law of his nurse, didn’t care about the colour of his skin. But the state government did.
“She told me that they physically tried to take me off her,” John says.
Ann took John home, but a sympathetic official quietly warned her that because she wasn’t married, they would try to take John away. So they fled into outback Queensland.
When things went bad in one place, they’d lob back to Brisbane. As John grew older, he learned how to identify government cars and how to hide. Once, he hid in the bulrushes of a swamp.
One day, John was coming home from school and forgot to look for the red rag on the windowsill that would let him know it was safe. Two men opened the door and grabbed him.
“There [were] lots of tears and carry on,” John says. “[Mum] pleaded with them not to take me like that, but she promised she’d take me up on Monday to the orphanage.”
John is emotional when he describes being left at Tufnell.
“We sat on the steps and Mum said to me, ‘John, I’ve got to leave you at this house for a short while, until I can get you back.’
“I saw Mum walk down the path and I saw her head going above the hedge – and the penny dropped. I made a run for the door and they had locked it.”
Minutes later, he says, “I got my first flogging.”
He remembers nuns erecting a makeshift boxing ring so they could watch the children fight. A priest, who took him behind red curtains, made him undress and sit on his lap. “He’d get me to put my hands down and get me to touch him,” John says. Afterwards, “maybe he’d give me a Mintie.”
He was allowed to return to Ann after she married, when he was about 10. That’s when she told him his father was an Aboriginal man who had raped John’s mother – a story he later learned was false – and said: “Don’t you ever own up to being Aboriginal.”
“I’ve lived a life without identity,” John says. “I’d been brought up as a white person, but I’d been looked upon as a coloured person.”
He also struggled to overcome his time in Tufnell. “I have been insecure with people – my wife, my children. I never told anybody about the abuse I got in the orphanage until I was about 50,” John says. “My wife said to me, ‘It’s like living with somebody in a glass cocoon. I can see you, but I can’t get through to you.’”
John remembers the phone call from his half-brother, about eight years ago, confirming his father was Aboriginal. “I just sat here and cried. Oh, God, at last! It’s out, I know, I know!”
And he found and met his mob: the Bundjalung people.
“I’ve had my recognition. I’m in a good place as far as knowing that I’m Aboriginal, Bundjalung people,” John says.
“I’ve been put down all my life, and now I know who I am.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
More than 100,000 rally across France in new Yellow Vest protests
Protesters chanted against declining affordability, the Macron government, police violence and poor school conditions.
More than 100,000 people have taken to the streets in France in another round of cost-of-living rallies organised by the “Yellow Vests” and various youth movements.
Saturday’s protests saw a decline in turnout compared with previous weekends and stayed largely calm, authorities said.
The Ministry of the Interior reported that 106,000 people took part in protests nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris – down from 146,000 people nationwide and 46,000 in Paris last week. Student unions place Saturday’s protest numbers higher, at 200,000 people, including almost 100,000 in the capital.
The country has been gripped by high-school blockades, mass demonstrations, and strikes for more than a month, with protesters rallying against falling educational standards, cost-of-living increases, low wages, and police violence.
A number of demonstrators also carried signs targeting President Emmanuel Macron, who has faced significant criticism from protesters.
Some rallies in recent weeks have seen violence at the fringes, and the first major protest on October 17 saw looting in cities across France. Since then, police presence at rallies and controls on transport and permits to protest have been expanded.
Marseille, France’s second-largest city, banned protests over the weekend, but the prefecture announced that some 3,500 people still took to the streets. Local media reported that tear gas and a water cannon were used against protesters and shared images of fires burning in a popular local square.
In Lyon, local media reported that roughly 8,000 people took to the streets. They shared images of masked protesters chanting in front of fires lit in the street and police charging and using tear gas.
Tear gas use was also reported in Nantes, Bordeaux and Paris.
More protests planned
Unions have called for a new day of strikes on Tuesday after rejecting a government promise to increase the minimum wage by 0.6 percent as “crumbs”.
If the demonstrations go ahead, they will take place on the eighth anniversary of the Gilet Jaune – which translates to “Yellow Vest” in French – movement, which rocked the beginning of the Macron government in 2018 with two years of protests triggered by rising fuel prices.
On Tuesday, the Yellow Vests will “celebrate their eight years where it all started: on roundabouts and toll booths all over France”, Yellow Vest protest tracking website 17octobregiletjaune.net writes.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Tens of thousands march in latest Portugal housing protests
These were the biggest protests against rising housing costs in Portugal since the social movement began weeks ago.
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of more than 30 towns and cities in Portugal to protest against surging rental prices, demanding urgent government action to address the country’s worsening housing crisis.
Organised by the Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) platform, demonstrations on Saturday took place under the slogan “They will not steal our right to a home,” with protests in Lisbon, Porto, Faro, Portimao, Coimbra, Braga and other locations. It was the biggest national demonstration since the social movement began weeks ago.
Participants, ranging from teenagers to retired people, walked behind large banners, with the Lisbon march punctuated by drums, music, and chanting.
Protesters called for caps to be placed on rent increases, greater legal protection for tenants against eviction, and more affordable housing. They also demanded the reversal of proposed changes to rental legislation.
Rita Silva, a spokesperson for Casa Para Viver, told Lusa news agency that the nationwide mobilisation showed the housing crisis was affecting the entire country, rather than being limited to major urban centres.
The platform, which brings together approximately 100 housing associations and grassroots organisations, is seeking tighter regulation on rental contracts, short-term tourist accommodation, and vacant properties.
The protests come after parliament approved the government’s proposed changes to provide greater flexibility in rental contracts and accelerate eviction procedures.
Housing campaigners warned the changes could weaken tenant protections amid rising rents and limited housing availability.
Portugal’s rising property prices
House prices in Portugal have risen much faster than incomes in recent years, statistics show. Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal posted the biggest jump in the European Union in the home price-to-income ratio, with an increase of 61 percent, followed by the Netherlands with 34 percent, the EU statistical office Eurostat said last week.
There is no indication that the rise in housing costs is slowing. Between the first quarter of last year and the first quarter of 2026, property prices rose by almost 20 percent, the National Statistics Institute, a government agency, said last month.
Rental prices, too, have climbed significantly, recording a 68 percent increase since 2020, according to the government. Much of this jump in real estate costs has been fuelled by foreign buyers and investment funds, as the country’s relaxed climate near the ocean has attracted many remote workers and retirees.
The government has responded to the protests by lowering taxes on new construction, restricting short-term rentals, and promising to build 145,000 new homes, but it acknowledged that the effects will not be immediate, as Prime Minister Luis Montenegro was urged by Casa Para Viver representatives to engage directly with them.
The protests in Portugal in recent weeks took their cue from demonstrations in neighbouring Spain last month over similar issues around housing and forced evictions. A wave of youth-led protests has swept Europe in the latter half of this year, with demonstrators across the continent denouncing rising prices and a lack of future prospects.

Saudi Arabia executes former child protester Jawad Qureiris
Saudi Arabia executed a man who was detained as a child, alongside another Saudi national from the Kingdom’s Shia-majority Eastern Province.
In a statement on Saturday, the Saudi Press Agency confirmed that Riyadh had executed Jawad Qureiris.
Hailing from a prominent Shia-majority family in the Kingdom’s Eastern Province, Qureiris was a former child defendant who was just 14 to 15 years old during the 2011-12 Arab Spring protests.
Qureiris’ family has a documented history of encounters with state security: one of his brothers was killed by security forces, while another was arrested at age 13 and faced capital charges related to alleged offences committed when he was nine years old.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Interior also announced that Fadel bin Hassan bin Abdullah Al-Safwani was executed on Saturday.
The ministry claimed the men were convicted of “terrorist crimes,” alleging they joined a foreign terrorist organisation, opened fire on security personnel and vehicles with weapons and explosives, possessed live ammunition, and provided logistical and financial support for operations within the Kingdom.
According to the SPA statement, the cases passed through specialised criminal courts, where the men’s legal responsibility was established before the verdicts were upheld by the Supreme Court and ratified via a royal decree.
Qureiris was arrested in December 2020 and charged with offences related to taking part in protests and organising on social media.
The late activist would have been 14 at the time of some of the protests in which he is alleged to have participated. His family said he was severely tortured until he gave a false confession to non-lethal terrorism offences that was used to convict him.
Since August 2025, Saudi Arabia has executed five men who were children at the time of their alleged crimes, all from Shia families in eastern provinces and all executed for offences related to demonstrations during and after the Arab Spring protests in 2011-12.
Jeed Basyouni, Reprieve's head of MENA death penalty projects, condemned the executions and said Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s “penalty for dissent is death- and we’ve seen very clearly in the last two years that this applies to children too.”
“Just like the other four young men executed recently for taking part in demonstrations when they were children, Jawad was tortured into making a false confession to so-called 'terrorist' offences and then tried, convicted, sentenced and finally killed in secret,” said Jeed Basyouni, Reprieve's Head of MENA Death Penalty Projects.
“The Crown Prince has pursued a vendetta against Jawad's family and others like it who dared to question his right to rule. This is a regime that uses capital punishment as a tool of political oppression and to settle personal scores. Saudi Arabia’s international partners must not stand by and let this happen, and should make urgent representations to halt the imminent execution of Youssef al Manasif."
The Eastern Province, a historic hotbed of anti-government demonstrations and home to the kingdom's vast oil reserves, has long been the focal point of state crackdowns against its Shia-majority population.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Pope Leo urges end to violence in Peru during visit to remote Andes town
In Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, the pope urges people not to respond to injustice with brutality.
Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited communities he once served as bishop.
“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.
Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.
Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Jujimori took office in July after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.
She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.
Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.
“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.
He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.
“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.
Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”
He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.
The pope, who holds both US and Peruvian citizenship, spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.

‘Loss of confidence’: US Navy fires commanders of warships deployed against Iran
The US Navy has fired several top officers without its customary public announcements, drawing criticism from lawmakers amid heightened security concerns at American military installations and tensions with Iran.
Those removed include the leadership team of the nuclear-powered attack submarine USS South Dakota. Its commander, second-in-command and senior enlisted sailor were relieved of their duties in October after the submarine reportedly struck something on the seabed.
The Navy also sacked Commander Caitlin Cunningham from her position leading the USS Michael Murphy destroyer on 27 September, citing a “loss of confidence”, according to a defence official.
The vessel had been deployed to support operations against Iran.
Admiral Brian Monahan, who served as attending physician to Congress and the Supreme Court for nearly 18 years, is also reported to have left his post amid an investigation.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Democratic Representatives Joe Courtney and Adam Smith said the Navy had failed to notify the House Armed Services Committee.
In a letter to acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and the service’s top uniformed officer, Admiral Daryl Caudle, they expressed “deep frustration” over the lack of communication.
“As a result of the Navy’s failure to communicate, what should have been a standard exercise in information sharing has instead raised questions about the Navy’s commitment to transparency and its commitment to a productive working relationship with Congress,” the lawmakers wrote.
The lack of public disclosure has also renewed scrutiny of the US military’s handling of information about the war on Iran.
The Associated Press has reported that restrictions on satellite imagery and limited official statements delayed public understanding of damage to 26 US military bases and other sites in the region following Iranian strikes.
The developments come as the US Air Force responded to suspected drone activity over RAF Lakenheath, a major US-operated airbase in eastern England, on Friday evening.
The incident prompted a security response, but no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, according to the Air Force.
Heightened tensions with Iran
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reportedly been pressing US President Donald Trump to resume military action against Iran.
Mossad chief Roman Gofman was in Washington on Friday for scheduled talks with CIA Director John Ratcliffe. He is also expected to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff in Miami, according to Axios.
Trump has so far favoured maintaining economic pressure and a naval blockade, although he has not ruled out further strikes.
On Thursday, Trump said the US did not need an agreement with Tehran and redirected Vice President JD Vance, who had played a central role in negotiations, towards domestic political issues.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Iran, meanwhile, told the International Atomic Energy Agency that discussions on restoring nuclear monitoring could not proceed while it faced threats of further military attacks, particularly against its nuclear facilities.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump ‘whiplash’ on deportations putting Afghans in turmoil: ‘People already survived a war’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sanya Mansoor in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to Afghanistan along with a larger group and possibly killed by the Taliban are experiencing “fragile relief” this weekend after it appeared that the Trump administration had put on hold plans to remove them within days.
Members of Congress and advocates have repeatedly warned that the deportations could effectively be a death sentence.
A flight originally scheduled to transport the group out of the US on election day earlier this month had stayed grounded after a federal judge issued a court order temporarily blocking its departure to Afghanistan or neighboring Pakistan. The whole group numbers more than 150 Afghans, the New York Times reported. And the AP previously reported that the federal government intends to route these detainees to their home country via Pakistan.
Then, as the temporary court order expired last weekend, immigration advocates battling to prevent the deportations talked of dreading that the detainees could be forced to leave the US during the week of 16 November . This prospect was based on a rescheduled removal date given for at least one Afghan man currently in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention who was due to be on the flight.
As that date loomed, suddenly there was another development amid frantic advocacy efforts.
Late on Tuesday, it was learned that that detainee, along with a handful of other detained Afghans on the original flight manifest, now no longer had a specified departure date issued by the US government.
Some immigration lawyers also reported that their Afghan clients had been moved from staging facilities to long-term detention facilities, suggesting they would not be forced onto a deportation flight in the coming days after all.
Amid some confusion and often few details from the administration, Shawn VanDiver, founder and president of the US non-profit coalition #AfghanEvac, said that a sensation of “fragile relief” had descended on the people involved.
Some of the Afghans in the targeted group have relatives who assisted the US war on Afghanistan after the terrorist attacks on the US on 11 September 2001 that drove out the Taliban, VanDiver said. He had already called Donald Trump’s efforts to remove Afghans from the US cruel and being done in “a heinous matter” as a scare tactic against others.
“In a matter of days, these allies were told they were being sent through Pakistan into the hands of the Taliban, then told they were safe, then told that nobody knows. That isn’t immigration policy. It’s whiplash inflicted on people who already survived a war,” he said. “These men and women kept their promise to America, and it’s time we kept ours by ending these removals for good.”
VanDiver has slammed any option to use Pakistan as a conduit for “forced rendition”.
Immigration advocates are hoping continued pressure will result in further delays and the ultimate cancellation of that flight and any others planned for the coming weeks. In the meantime, #AfghanEvac is pushing what will become the newly Democratic-controlled Congress in January to pass a bipartisan bill that has been drafted and would give Afghans who are already in the US temporary protected status (TPS) through July 2029, with a vetting process. The US supreme court in June allowed the Trump administration to strip such protections, including from Afghans.
Such legislation would “keep people we already vetted and brought here from being sent back to the Taliban while their cases are decided”, VanDiver said.
Among the passengers reported to be on the blocked flight were Afghans whose relatives helped American troops, women, at least one gay man and members of the minority ethnic Hazara group – some who have said they were previously beaten by the Taliban.
Human Rights First, the US-based human rights group, has warned about “grave, systematic dangers” for Afghans returned to Afghanistan. That includes “arbitrary detentions, executions, public flogging, and retaliatory violence”, as well as restrictions on basic freedoms for women and girls.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in response to questions and a request for comment that the agency complies with all lawful court orders and that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) does not comment on or confirm prospective removal operations, for operational security reasons, and the safety of its officers.
Sari Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said that the Trump administration’s targeting of Afghans reflects a broader trend of creating arrangements with other governments to send people back to war zones, security crises and countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with the US.
The US suspended relations with Afghanistan after the Taliban government took over in 2021, forcing a scrambled US evacuation.
The Trump administration has held secret talks with Iran about deporting Iranians via a third country, and last Sunday an attorney reported that the US deportation flight of Iranian nationals headed to Iran via Pakistan was abruptly canceled, according to the AP.
The Trump administration also is increasingly deporting immigrants to such “third countries”. The supreme court is still litigating in what circumstances the federal government can deport people to regions they have no connection to, though in late September, the court ruled on an emergency basis, allowing Trump to continue this practice.
Federal law is designed to prevent the US government from forcing someone to return to a country where they are likely to face torture.
The DHS said in a statement that immigrants sent to a third country “receive notice and an opportunity to challenge their removal unless the Department of State is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries” that they would be safe upon return.
More than 60 concerned lawmakers in Congress signed a letter to the DHS and the state department, citing relevant law and also calling for the cancellation of any deportation flights of Afghans or Iranians to their home countries, either directly or through any other country. “The United States is also bound not to return anyone to a country where they would face torture, and that obligation does not disappear because a flight makes a stop along the way,” the letter stated.
In another letter, New York congressman Gregory Meeks and US senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, both Democrats, wrote to Pakistan’s ambassador to the US, urging the Pakistani government not to collaborate in any operation to fly Afghans to Pakistan and then expel them over the border to Afghanistan. The Pakistani embassy did not respond to a request for comment.
The Afghans targeted are believed to have final removal orders, which means the US can legally deport them. But the fact that an immigrant failed to get asylum or prove to the Trump administration that they have a credible fear about returning to their home country does not mean they don’t face serious risks in their native country, critics argue.
The US state department advises Americans: “Do not travel to Afghanistan for any reason,” warning of “civil unrest, crime, terrorism, risk of wrongful detention, kidnapping, natural disasters, and limited health facilities”. The risks for returning Afghans are seen as much greater.
“We are talking about people who’ve already been tortured, people who came with evidence – some of the most compelling claims – and the idea that they could find themselves on this flight is pretty horrifying,” said Sarah Mehta, deputy director of immigration policy at the ACLU. “Why would we send Iranians to a war zone or Afghans to one of the most repressive regimes in the world knowing, indeed, that they are going to be targeted because of the very vulnerabilities that led them to flee in the first place?”
One Afghan national expected to be on any deportation flight, who has been detained in ICE custody since late 2024, fears returning because his wife is a former member of Afghanistan’s military before the Taliban took over, according to court documents. He is also part of the Hazara Shia group and said he has previously been severely beaten by the Taliban while they searched for his wife.
Shaw Drake, assistant professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law and co-counsel for the man, said the immigration judge’s not being swayed by these risk factors was “absolutely absurd”. Drake argues that his client had no notice or opportunity to present a claim of fear of persecution or torture in Pakistan.
The man’s mental health deteriorated when he was transferred to detention in El Paso, Texas, so much so that a federal court in New Mexico issued a stay for 14 days to ensure the government had enacted safeguards to protect him from the risk of suicide.
Another Afghan who could be put on a flight is a Hazara man who testified to immigration officials that he worried about being killed by the Taliban because he reported them to the police when they killed his father, according to US government documents. He said that a few years ago, he was captured, detained, tortured and threatened with death by the Taliban, whose members electrocuted him and beat him with sticks. US federal asylum officers acknowledged the detainee’s testimony but concluded there was insufficient evidence to show the Taliban would inflict severe mental or physical harm towards him if he were sent back.
Madhavi Narayanan, a lawyer at Human Rights First, who represents him, said: “It’s another confirmation that our immigration system is not equipped to help those who are fleeing persecution and genuinely seeking safety.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US blames system upgrade for longest nationwide FAA ground stop since 9/11
Sean Duffy, the country’s transportation secretary, said his agency is ‘going to hold people accountable’.
The top United States transportation official has said work being performed on an antiquated telecommunications system could be to blame for a rare, hours-long US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that halted all air traffic inside the country.
At a news conference in Washington, DC, on Saturday, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy spoke about routine maintenance that was performed on Friday to upgrade a router from copper to fibre at a “very remote location”.
Duffy said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router in question to start flooding other ones in the country’s air traffic control system.
“We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters at the Department of Transportation.
When those connection issues caused disruption in radar feeds and communications between air traffic controllers and aeroplanes, Duffy said a ground stop was ordered.
“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” he said.
The Transportation Department identified the contractor of Friday’s maintenance as L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company that has been tasked with modernising the communications system for the FAA.
“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”
Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”.
“They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”
In response to Duffy’s allegations, L3Harris told Al Jazeera it has been working “in close coordination with the FAA” and places safety and reliability as its “highest priorities”.
“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” a spokesperson for the company said. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”
Amid concerns that Friday’s ground stop was the result of a cyberattack, the US government said Saturday it did not “believe” that was the cause.
“Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said. “So, we don’t believe this was cyber at all.”
The head of the FAA, who also spoke at Saturday’s news conference, echoed the transportation secretary’s remarks, saying the system outage was caused by an equipment error.
“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said.
A root cause analysis would be shared with the public when it is available, he added.
As airlines and thousands of travellers begin the process of digging out from Friday’s groundstop, the longest and only second nationwide stop since 9/11, the FAA said full schedule integrity is expected by the end of Sunday.
“We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.”
Bedford said the FAA expects about 4,000 to 5,000 flights out of the 41,000 scheduled on Saturday to be cancelled.
“That will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” he said. “I do think the worst is behind us.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US suggested Ukraine cede parts of Donbas to Russia to become part of NATO
Zelenskyy rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality and said he refused to cede territory to Russia.
US negotiators have floated the idea that Ukraine should cede parts of eastern Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, after the latest rounds of Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi and Ireland.
This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised, Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?” he said. “That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda.”
Zelenskyy said the parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine the US asked about were areas Russia does not control. The Ukrainian president said he refused to cede territory.
“[Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe,” he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”
Putin has long said that Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.
Zelenskyy did say that if Ukraine received a comprehensive package, including security guarantees, military and reconstruction funds, and a recovery plan from the US and other partners, he would put the question about ceding parts of Donbas to a national referendum.
“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognising occupied territories as Russian. Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country’s constitution.
“If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in NATO right now anyway.”
Despite the diplomatic push to end the conflict, Russia and Ukraine reported numerous overnight attacks. Russian officials reported on Friday that about 1,200 Ukrainian drones were fired at the country, with oil infrastructure among the targets, while Ukraine reported attacks on a hospital and the port of Odesa.
At the summit in Ireland over recent days, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers – non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland – as well as EU officials. They would hold talks with US and Ukrainian officials, but not with Russia.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Italy fines Meta $880m over photo privacy
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Italy fines Meta $880m over photo privacy
Regulator said Meta’s ‘lack of cooperation’ and the large number of people affected contributed to size of the fine.
Italian regulators have fined Meta 805 million euros ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their consent.
The Facebook app on Android devices “accessed photos, videos and associated metadata stored on Italian users’ smartphones without specific consent and without informing them”, Garante, the Italian data privacy authority, said Saturday.
The issue relates specifically to the “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook” feature, which suggests photos and videos from the phone’s gallery for posting while browsing.
This feature violates the Italian law implementing the EU’s ePrivacy directive, the authority said.
Garante said the app’s process for collecting consent is too generic and does not allow users to fully understand the specific permissions they are allowing by accepting. The suggestions option was also enabled by default.
The figure of 805 million euros is by far the largest fine ever imposed by the Italian regulator.
Garante said Meta must fix the unclear consent notification and disable it being set by default, suggesting that roughly 20 million Italian Android users could have been affected by it.
The regulator also highlighted a “lack of cooperation” by Meta and said an earlier violation, which resulted in a 2019 fine, was a contributing factor in their decision.
The amount is roughly 0.47 percent of Meta’s global turnover.
The proceedings did not address the possible use of content to train artificial intelligence, which Meta denies.
Meta has not yet publicly commented on the matter, and it has the right to appeal the regulator’s decision.
