https://www.humanite.fr/societe/manifest.title: Nouvelle mobilisation mardi et samedi prochain
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/manifest.text:
Avant un nouveau rendez-vous syndical le 17 novembre, avec une nouvelle journée de grève et de manifestations pour le secteur public, après le refus vendredi par le gouvernement de relever le point d’indice des fonctionnaires, différentes organisations syndicales et de défense des droits humains vont défiler ce samedi 14 novembre 2026.
Cette nouvelle journée de mobilisation agrège plusieurs revendications distinctes, mais qui convergent ce samedi : pour la hausse des salaires, pour davantage de moyens à l’éducation, contre la proposition de loi sur la présomption d’usage légitime des armes par les forces de sécurité, qui revient, selon elles, à “un permis de tuer” et contre laquelle près de 50.000 personnes avaient déjà manifesté le 20 septembre dans toute la France, selon les chiffres du ministère de l’Intérieur.
Les manifestations de ce week-end interviennent alors que le gouvernement a annoncé une revalorisation du Smic au 1er décembre estimée très insuffisante par les organisations syndicales, de l’ordre d’une vingtaine d’euros, indexation automatique comprise. D’abord appelée par la CGT, Solidaires et la FSU, la journée d’action intersyndicale du 17 novembre voit ses rangs gonflés par l’annonce de la CFDT, vendredi, qu’elle rejoignait les autres syndicats, après avoir fait part de sa déception des propositions salariales de l’exécutif à la sortie du dernier entretien avec Sébastien Lecornu.
Les mobilisations des lycéens se poursuivent elles aussi, les blocages affectant plus de mille établissements la semaine dernière selon les syndicats d’enseignants, de proviseurs et de lycéens, loin de l’estimation minimaliste de quelques dizaines avancée par le gouvernement.
Quant à la manifestation enfantiste de ce  14 novembre, elle agrège désormais autour d’elle des collectifs pour le climat, la justice sociale et des lycéens. Plus d’une centaine de rassemblements sont prévus dans plusieurs villes à l’appel du Collectif enfantiste et du Mouvement du 26 septembre.
Pour en savoir plus :

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How ICE raids in Kansas meatpacking country sparked fury – and turned voters against Trump
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
José Del Real looked over the crowd from the stage in a park, at hundreds of his neighbors with furious signs tucked under their arms, voicing their anger at immigration agents who had descended on their town and started rounding up their friends and family. His daughters, in the front row, were crying.
Del Real, an army veteran who served two tours in Iraq, hadn’t voted in a decade. He thought it would not matter in this ruby red corner of Kansas. But the midterm election was weeks away. He draped an American flag over his shoulders, put on his Iraq veteran cap and ended his speech with a message: “None of this matters if you do not vote. Let’s go vote.”
They did. This county and two of its neighbors in south-western Kansas, Republican strongholds where a steady stream of immigrants have settled over the decades to work at feedlots and slaughterhouses, swung wildly to the left. The shift helped elect a Democratic US Senator from Kansas for the first time in nearly a century, signaling the limits of Donald Trump’s aggressive deportation agenda.
Since Democrats won back control of Congress in a decisive rebuke to Republicans, Trump has sent mixed messages about how he plans to handle immigration enforcement going forward. He suggested that his approach to deportations was too harsh but also named hardliner Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff. Both parties will be recalibrating their approach ahead of the next presidential campaign.
Here in Kansas, late September raids ignited a maelstrom of rage, turning many who had been apathetic, like Del Real, into determined voters.
Masked officers in tactical gear banged on doors before dawn. They stopped cars in the middle of intersections. Businesses shuttered. Families feared leaving their houses. Children stopped going to school. Some live-streamed themselves being detained. One man pleaded “God help me” in Spanish, his hands shaking, as he asked anyone watching to let his family know.
The resistance came not only from Democrats or the Latino population, which has grown to about two-thirds of Dodge City. Kansas’s embattled Republican senator, Roger Marshall, who would lose his reelection bid to Adam Hamilton, issued a statement pleading with the administration to consult local officials before launching raids.
Del Real regrets he didn’t vote in 2024, when Trump roared back into office pledging mass deportations.
“We had to see it in front of us,” Del Real said. “I had to see it in the flesh.”
This corner of Kansas is responsible for much of the country’s beef. The gates leading into Dodge City boast that it’s the “Queen of the Cowtowns” Its main street is named after the classic western set here, Gunsmoke. Murals celebrating cowboy history mix with evidence of a changing culture: storefronts showcasing quinceañera dresses, Mexican bakeries, city signs printed in both Spanish and English.
Del Real’s family came from Mexico when he was a kindergartner. Like most here, they came to work. The area – Dodge City and the region’s other hubs, Garden City and Liberal – is known as the Golden Triangle of Meatpacking, responsible for about a quarter of the US beef supply.
Some here thought their importance to the nation’s food might spare them from the administration’s deportation campaigns, said Amy Soberanes, a 25-year-old local organizer.
Soberanes, the daughter of Mexican immigrants, said she and others tried for years to get people – particularly their young, Latino neighbors – engaged.
But, from rural Kansas, immigration raids in places like Minneapolis and Chicago felt abstract.
Then they saw their own streets in social media videos.
People were furious, said Soberanes, who worried the daily protests could get out of hand. They told people not to slash tires or break windows, to store up their anger and take it out on election day.
“We’ll see them at the ballot box,” she recalls repeating.
Her phone rang and rang. People she’d hassled to vote for years asked: how do I register?
“If ICE hadn’t come, we would still be red, 100%,” she said. “And so I thank Donald Trump for sending immigration here.”
Answers about the immigration raids never came
No one knew immigration officers were coming.
Dodge City commissioner Rick Sowers said he and other city officials found out just like everyone else, through social media or masses of unmarked trucks on their neighbors’ lawns.
They scrambled to get answers from the federal government – who they were looking for, who was in charge, how long they would stay – and never did.
The Trump administration issued statements naming five “heinous criminals” they said had been arrested. But the Wichita Eagle dug into that claim and found none of those people were actually apprehended during the surge: Four had been deported months before and the fifth was already in prison, the newspaper found.
The agency said it detained 104 people from south-west Kansas.
Local officials have still never seen a list, Sowers said.
Local Republican chairman Scott Fischer, who describes himself as a supporter of strong borders, was surprised by the operation’s intensity.
“There was a little showmanship,” he said. “I don’t know why it was like that.”
He said he still considers the county red – it voted, narrowly, for Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson. The Associated Press called that race on Thursday: Masterson lost to Democrat Cindy Holscher .
But some Dodge City Republicans abandoned the party in the US Senate race.
Russell Arben Fox, political science professor at Friends University in Wichita, said swings as dramatic as that one couldn’t have happened without some white, moderate Republicans changing their minds.
More than half of Kansas voters in the Senate race disapprove of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is handling its job, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. That’s consistent with the 61% of voters who say this nationally.
Most of the Latino immigrants here are hard-working, family-oriented, faithful people – a perfect fit for conservative Kansas values, Fischer said, so local Republicans tend to have a nuanced view on immigration.
Some public officials have for years begged the federal government for reforms to provide a pathway for these workers who run the region’s economy.
“In general terms, mass deportation is not practical,” Fischer said. “When we say send them all home, what does that mean? Who is them?”
Dodge City residents came together to help during the raids
To many here, “them” this time meant relatives and friends. In this small town, nearly everybody is connected to everybody else, so they did what they could to help.
Oscar Soto delivered food to people afraid to leave home during the deportation raids.
He started calling it “the black week” after the black plague. That’s what it felt like to him, a pestilence that arrived suddenly.
His mother came here from Mexico, he said, and though she is here legally, she was terrified.
“It seemed unreal,” he said. “It was stuff that’s never been seen here, and it was day after day after day.”
He works at a family-owned grocery, and strung a garland of flags from around the world above the counter when it opened. Most customers are from Mexico and Guatemala, he said, but he wanted to signal that the store was for everyone.
Then he hung a big American flag from the ceiling. It means to him that anyone, from anywhere, can come here, work hard and build a life, free from fear.
That belief in the American dream was shaken for him when ICE arrived.
So he registered to vote for the first time aged 39.
He stood in line to cast his ballot, amazed by how many young, Latino voters were waiting along with him.

https://www.humanite.fr/feminisme/contra.text:
La vasectomie fait partie des méthodes de contraception masculine les plus sûres et les plus efficaces. Mais malgré une forte progression depuis 2010, la France accuse un énorme retard en la matière par rapport aux autres pays.
Et la vasectomie ? Cette méthode, considérée comme définitive, consiste à interrompre les canaux déférents qui transportent les spermatozoïdes. Il s’agit de la méthode de contraception masculine la plus répandue dans le monde : selon des chiffres des Nations unies datant de 2019, 16 millions de personnes utilisaient la vasectomie comme contraception dans leur couple (soit 2 % de l’ensemble des contraceptés).

https://taz.de/-Nachrichten-im-Ukraine-K.title: +++ Nachrichten im Ukraine-Krieg +++: Trump bietet Nato-Mitgliedschaft bei Gebietsverzicht an
https://taz.de/-Nachrichten-im-Ukraine-K.text:
+++ Nachrichten im Ukraine-Krieg +++: Trump bietet Nato-Mitgliedschaft bei Gebietsverzicht an
Der ukrainische Präsident macht publik, was sich der US-Präsident als Konfliktlösung vorstellt. Und jeweils mehr als 1000 Kriegsgefangene sollen ausgetauscht werden.
Selenskyj nennt Größenordnung für Gefangenenaustausch
Ein zwischen Russland und der Ukraine bei Gesprächen in Abu Dhabi vereinbarter Gefangenenaustausch umfasst nach Angaben des ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj jeweils mehr als 1.000 Gefangene auf beiden Seiten. Die genaue Zahl werde noch festgelegt, sagte Selenskyj am Freitag zu Journalisten. Er schätze, dass es auf eine Zahl zwischen 1.200 und 1.300 hinauslaufen werde. (ap)
Ukraine: Angriff auf russische Ölanlage in Region Samara
Das ukrainische Militär hat nach Angaben des Generalstabs eine Ölanlage in der russischen Region Samara angegriffen. Bei dem Angriff auf das Ölterminal Samara in der Nähe des Dorfes Proswet seien mehrere Lagertanks in Brand geraten, teilte der Generalstab am Samstag mit. Die Anlage sei ein wichtiger Teil des Netzwerks, über das Russland Öl auf die Weltmärkte exportiere, um den Angriffskrieg gegen die Ukraine zu finanzieren. Eine Reaktion des Kremls auf den Angriff am Freitag lag zunächst nicht vor. Laut dem ukrainischen Generalstab wurde auch der Flugplatz Lipezk-2 in der russischen Region Lipezk angegriffen. (ap)
Ukraine lehnt neutralen Status weiterhin ab
Die USA haben nach den Worten des ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj der Ukraine die Nato-Mitgliedschaft im Gegenzug für einen Gebietsverzicht in Aussicht gestellt. „Die Amerikaner haben eine Frage aufgeworfen: ‚Was wäre, wenn die Ukraine der Nato beitritt? Würde die Ukraine sich aus dem Donbass zurückziehen?‘ Das war das erste Mal, dass diese Frage gestellt wurde“, sagte Selenskyj am Freitag vor Reportern.
Der ukrainische Präsident fügte hinzu, dass Kyjiw über „spezifische Sicherheitsgarantien seitens der Nato und der EU“ diskutiere. Wenn diese im Zuge eines Abkommens zur Beendigung des Ukraine-Krieges vereinbart würden, werde er die Ukrainer darüber abstimmen lassen. „Ich habe nicht das Recht, diese Entscheidung allein zu treffen“, sagte Selenskyj.
Die vom russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin angestrebte Änderung der Sicherheitsarchitektur in Europa nannte Selenskyj „gefährlich“. So lehnt er einen neutralen Status und damit eine der Hauptforderungen Russlands zur Beendigung des Krieges weiter ab. „Wenn (der russische Präsident Wladimir) Putin davon ausgeht, dass die Neutralität der Ukraine festgeschrieben wird, dann wird dies nicht geschehen“, sagte Selenskyj laut der Nachrichtenagentur Interfax-Ukraine. Eine erforderliche Verfassungsänderung lehnte er ab.
„Wirkliche Sicherheit in Europa bedeutet die EU und die Nato. Das ist alles. Es gibt keine andere Sicherheit in Europa“, so Selenskyj.
Russland hat seit dem Überfall auf die Ukraine im Februar 2022 einen großen Teil der Donbass-Region im Osten der Ukraine eingenommen und beansprucht das gesamte Gebiet. Eine Nato-Mitgliedschaft des Landes lehnt Putin strikt ab.
„Sie setzen alles auf diesen Winter“, sagte Selenskyj weiter zur Kriegsstrategie der russischen Führung. Wenn der US-Kongress ein Gesetzespaket zu „Sanktionen und Waffen“ beschließe, dann wäre dies „die Art von Motivation, die Putin braucht“, um zu deeskalieren. (afp/dpa)
Russland: Ortschaft in der Region Saporischschja eingenommen
Russische Truppen haben eigenen Angaben zufolge die Ortschaft Tersjanka in der südostukrainischen Region Saporischschja eingenommen. Das berichtete die russische Nachrichtenagentur Interfax unter Berufung auf das Verteidigungsministerium in Moskau. (rtr)
Demokratische US-Senatoren stellen Forderung an Elon Musk
Demokratische US-Senatoren haben Elon Musk zur Aufbewahrung aller Unterlagen über die eingeschränkte Nutzung der Satellitendienste Starlink und Starshield in der Ukraine aufgefordert. Sie verlangten in einem Brief unter anderem Aufzeichnungen zur Kommunikation zwischen Musk und Führungskräften seiner Firma SpaceX sowie dem Weißen Haus und dem Pentagon. Die Einschränkungen würfen „ernste Fragen“ zur Kontrolle von SpaceX über Kommunikationssysteme auf, die für die nationale Sicherheit entscheidend seien, erklärten die Politiker. Die militärische Starlink-Version Starshield ist den ukrainischen Streitkräften zufolge unverzichtbar für die Kommunikation an der Front und für Drohneneinsätze zur Abwehr russischer Luftangriffe. (rtr)
Ex-IOC-Chef Thomas Bach: Russland soll zur Eishockey-WM zurückkehren
Der frühere IOC-Präsident Thomas Bach hat sich für eine Rückkehr Russlands bei der Eishockey-Weltmeisterschaft im kommenden Mai in Deutschland ausgesprochen. „Meine Meinung ist klar und die war immer klar: Es kann nicht an Staaten liegen, an Regierungen liegen, wer wann wie und wo und warum an Sportwettbewerben teilnehmen kann“, sagte Bach dem Sender Sport1. Der 72-Jährige wurde als Chef des Internationalen Olympischen Komitees eine Nähe zu Kremlchef Wladimir Putin vorgeworfen.
Bach begründete seine Sichtweise damit, dass die „Autonomie und Neutralität des Sports gewahrt werden“ müsse. „Es zählen die sportlichen Qualifikationen und nicht die politischen Einstellungen“, betonte der Fecht-Olympiasieger von 1976.
Um eine mögliche WM-Teilnahme Russlands ist eine heftige Debatte entbrannt. Der Internationale Sportgerichtshof Cas hatte mit einem Urteil russische Eishockey-Teams wieder zugelassen. Es folgten Boykottdrohungen mehrerer Länder um Weltmeister Finnland für Spiele gegen Russland. Der Deutsche Eishockey-Bund als Gastgeber dringt auf eine schnelle Lösung durch den Weltverband IIHF – ohne Russland als teilnehmende Nation.
Ausgerechnet die Ukraine könnte als sportlicher Aufsteiger bei der A-WM für Russland weichen. „Nun, das wäre mehr als problematisch, weil wie gesagt, die sportliche Qualifikation muss zählen und jemandem im Nachhinein die sportliche Qualifikation zu entziehen, das halte ich auch für höchst bedenklich“, erklärte Bach.
Russland hatte die Ukraine im Februar 2022 angegriffen, zuvor stand das russische Eishockey-Team bei den Olympischen Winterspielen in Peking im Endspiel und verlor dort 1:2 gegen Finnland. (dpa)
Dreiköpfige russische Familie durch ukrainischen Drohnenangriff getötet
Infolge eines ukrainischen Drohnenangriffs ist im westrussischen Gebiet Belgorod offiziellen Angaben nach eine dreiköpfige Familie getötet worden. Die Drohne griff dem operativen Stab der Region zufolge ein Wohnhaus in der Siedlung Proletarski im Landkreis Rakitnoje direkt an. Ein weiterer Mensch sei verletzt worden. Proletarski ist nur etwa 20 Kilometer von der ukrainischen Grenze entfernt. In der Region seien zudem bei ukrainischen Drohnenangriffen mindestens neun Menschen verletzt worden, hieß es.
Nach Angaben des russischen Verteidigungsministeriums wurden in der Nacht zum Samstag 29 ukrainische Drohnen abgewehrt. Ein Teil davon über der Region um die Hauptstadt Moskau. (dpa)
Russische Drohnenangriffe auf die Ukraine
Das russische Militär setzte wiederum gemäß einer Mitteilung der ukrainischen Luftstreitkräfte 96 Drohnen gegen Ziele in der Ukraine ein. Von diesen konnten demnach 81 abgefangen werden. Einschläge habe es an acht Orten gegeben. In Teilen des nordostukrainischen Gebiets Sumy kam es nach Auskunft des örtlichen Stromversorgers aufgrund russischer Angriffe zu Stromausfällen.
Ohne Angaben von Gründen wurde am Samstagmorgen die Straße über den Damm des Dnipro-Wasserkraftwerks in der südostukrainischen Großstadt Saporischschja für den Verkehr komplett gesperrt. Aus Sicherheitsgründen gab es vorher bereits immer wieder kurzfristige Einschränkungen. Die Stadt verfügt nur über zwei weitere Brückenverbindungen über die Insel Chortyzja auf das Ostufer des Flusses Dnipro. Saporischschja befindet sich nur etwas mehr als 20 Kilometer von der russisch-ukrainischen Frontlinie entfernt. (dpa)
Selenskyj beklagt anhaltende Drosselung von Starshield
Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj hat anhaltende Geschwindigkeitsbeschränkungen beim US-Satellitenkommunikationssystem Starshield beklagt. Diese Drosselung habe die Einsatzfähigkeit des ukrainischen Militärs im Land beeinträchtigt, sagte Selenskyj in seiner abendlichen Videoansprache. „Leider bleiben die Geschwindigkeitsbeschränkungen entlang der gesamten Frontlinie und in den vorübergehend besetzten Gebieten der Ukraine bestehen“, erklärte er. Er erwarte, dass das Verteidigungs- und das Außenministerium dieses Problem gemeinsam mit den zuständigen Stellen in den USA klären würden. (rtr)
Drei Tote bei russischen Angriffen auf zwei ukrainische Städte
Bei russischen Angriffen auf zwei ukrainische Städte sind nach Angaben regionaler Behörden drei Menschen getötet und mehr als 50 verletzt worden. In der südöstlichen Stadt Saporischschja traf ein Geschoss ein fünfstöckiges Wohnhaus. Dabei kam ein Rettungsarbeiter ums Leben, als bei den Bergungsarbeiten eine Betonplatte einstürzte, wie der Gouverneur der Region, Mychajlo Semikin, auf Telegram mitteilte. Unter den Verletzten seien sechs Kinder. In der Hafenstadt Odessa starben dem Leiter der Militärverwaltung, Serhij Lyssak, zufolge zwei Menschen bei einem Angriff auf ein Privathaus. Fünf weitere Personen erlitten Verletzungen. Die Angaben ließen sich von der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters zunächst nicht unabhängig überprüfen. (rtr)
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. https://www.humanite.fr/politique/attent.title: « Je vis en hypervigilance constante » : Sandrine Rousseau sur une liste du terroriste de Trappes
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/attent.author: Emilio Meslet
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/attent.text:
« Je vis en hypervigilance constante » : Sandrine Rousseau sur une liste du terroriste de Trappes
Publié le 14 novembre 2026
De l’absence de réaction des autorités à la banalisation des discours d’extrême droite dans les médias, en passant par le rejet de la pétition contre CNews et son quotidien sous haute tension, Sandrine Rousseau (députée Les Ecologistes) analyse les mécanismes de la violence politique et appelle à une solidarité citoyenne face aux intimidations.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Indigenous students retrace Lewis and Clark’s historic journey: ‘We can’t protect what we cannot see’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ashley Stimpson
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
In 1804, when Thomas Jefferson dispatched Meriwether Lewis and William Clark and their Corps of Discovery to explore the newly acquired land west of the Mississippi, the president’s primary aim was political: Americans needed to establish presence, power and trade routes in these territories before the Europeans beat them to it.
But Jefferson, an ardent naturalist, had a secondary agenda. He ordered that the expedition also survey the flora and fauna of these landscapes. On their two-year jaunt across the western half of the country, Lewis and Clark kept meticulous journals of the animals and plants they encountered: bison, horned lizards, sage grouse, prairie dogs, wild licorice and catfish, among them. These observations were pivotal in shaping an early understanding of North American biodiversity.
These “discoveries” were hardly new to the Indigenous tribes who had occupied the Great Plains and west for millennia, however. While European Americans tend to see the Lewis and Clark expedition as a triumphant achievement, many Native Americans remember it as an invasion, the bugle blast of forced removal and relocation.
“There are a lot of negative feelings about that history,” says Dan Buresh, a recently retired environmental science professor at Sitting Bull College on the Standing Rock Sioux reservation just outside Fort Yates, North Dakota. Nevertheless, when Buresh learned that ecologists with the Smithsonian National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute would be conducting another wildlife survey along Lewis and Clark’s historic route – this time using thousands of motion-triggered trail cameras installed by partner institutions across the country – he wanted his students to be a part of it.
Staff at the Smithsonian were on the same page. Unlike the first survey, when the many Native contributions to the Lewis and Clark expedition – which relied on tribal partners for navigation, diplomacy and protection – were downplayed or unacknowledged, the Smithsonian wanted to prioritize Native participation this time around. “Early on, we reached out to every tribal college along the trail,” says Brigit Rooney, the re-survey’s project coordinator. “Tribes were critical to the success of the Lewis and Clark expedition and we wanted to recognize those contributions by including current tribal members in the re-survey.” The Smithsonian’s Women’s Committee also raised money to enroll tribal students as paid interns, the only re-survey volunteers to receive a stipend.
In the end, seven tribal colleges signed up to run cameras, manage data and interpret the changes that have occurred over the last two centuries on their reservations, where this type of ecological knowledge is transmitted orally but rarely published.
“There are a lot of elders that are passing this information on from their childhood memories,” Buresh says. “This project allows us to ground-truth some of that, and to get the real-time data.”
At first, some residents of Standing Rock, which spans both Dakotas and is home to the Lakota and Dakota Nations, were hesitant about opening up their lands to outsiders. Buresh heard concerns from elders that the data would be used to, for instance, locate prime hunting spots. Others said they had felt burned in the past by scientists who had come to collect data and then not included tribal members on resulting studies.
“Sometimes, in the past, when we’ve shared this information, we didn’t really have full control over it afterwards,” says Tamiera Garter, a junior in environmental science and project intern who helped deploy the cameras. But Garter and fellow intern Precious Yellow Fat came to believe that gathering contemporary data was integral for their community, offering an opportunity to confirm or update the traditional ecological knowledge held by their elders. Some residents, for example, worry about the impact of climate change on the reservation’s wildlife, a concern that’s difficult to validate or address without data.
“We cannot protect what we cannot see or don’t understand,” says Yellow Fat, who recently graduated with a bachelor’s degree in environmental science. “Having those cameras out there will help us get insight on how we can manage the land and the species that live on it.”
“At the end of the day, it will protect our sovereignty,” Garter adds. “It will allow us to have more autonomy with decisions we make around management and conservation.”
The re-survey, which received funding from the Smithsonian’s Our Shared Future initiative, a commemoration of the country’s semiquincentennial, kicked off in early 2025 when Smithsonian staff digitized Lewis and Clark’s journals, geolocating hundreds of wildlife observations the survey party made along the way. In spring 2026, more than 50 research partners in 15 states activated camera arrays across the original route. Buresh, Yellow Fat, Garter and fellow students installed 16 across the 2.3m-acre (931,000-hectare) Standing Rock, which required several field days and a lot of hiking.
Before the photos even started rolling in, the experience was revelatory, say Yellow Fat and Garter, both members of the Lakota tribe.
“We saw a side of nature we don’t usually see,” says Garter. “I never saw the hills and grasses be so animated.” In addition to admiring chest-high grass and running from fearsome hailstorms, the students learned to identify birds and harvested quills from a dead porcupine to use in regalia and earrings. They got to spend time in sacred and historic sites they had learned about from their parents and teachers.
When the cameras began capturing images, Yellow Fat and Garter found stark ecological differences between the two watersheds – the Grand River in South Dakota and Cannonball River in North Dakota – on the reservation where they had spent much of their lives. They’ve seen close-up snaps of typically elusive bobcat and mule deer. They’ve puzzled over why certain animals show up at certain times, whether they’re looking for mates, food or cover. “We aren’t really just taking pictures,” Garter realized. “We’re trying to understand these animals.”
Bill McShea, the Smithsonian wildlife ecologist who conceived of the re-survey project, hopes the initiative will allow its tribal partners to get some overdue credit for taking good care of the wildlife in their charge. Indigenous tribes manage more land than the National Park Service, and previous studies have shown higher biodiversity on acres overseen by Indigenous stewards compared with other entities.
“If we look at where the bison are right now, where the good carnivore populations are right now, they’re on Indian reservations,” McShea says. “It’s because they have a better ethos toward wildlife than we do,” he adds, pointing to the spiritual role that animals play in many tribal cultures.
The re-survey is an extension of Snapshot USA, a nationwide wildlife-monitoring project McShea helped to launch in 2019 that partners with institutions around the country to track long-term trends in mammal population using camera traps. The ecologist modeled the program, in part, after the popular app eBird, which has gathered more than 200bn observations of birds since 2002 with the help of more than 100 million users.
“I was so jealous of the bird people. Bird people know everything about birds because they have 10,000 binoculars going out there every year and writing down what they see,” McShea says. “We had almost none of that information about mammals.”
To date, Snapshot USA has logged more than 1m records of mammals across all 50 states. These images are identified by AI and validated by volunteer scientists. The project has been largely successful in filling in gaps about mammal distribution, diversity and behavior, McShea says, except in sparsely populated parts of the country. “There just aren’t a lot of people in the Great Plains, so we have holes in our data there.”
When the semiquincentennial came along (as well as funding to celebrate the US’s natural history), McShea saw a poetic way to address those holes. The re-survey could commemorate Lewis and Clark’s original contribution to science, while also gathering data in parts of the country that Snapshot USA wasn’t capturing.
So far, re-survey partners have captured more than 5.5m images of a confirmed 67 species. There have even been some heartening findings among them, according to Rooney, the project coordinator: a slew of photos of American beavers, for example, a species that was being slaughtered for their fur by the millions in the early 19th century, resulting in their near extinction. Fishers – another small mammal in the weasel family – have shown up in Pennsylvania, where they were once completely wiped out by trappers. “The story we have in our heads about conservation is usually negative,” says Rooney, “but there are many positive stories to find.”
The trail cams took their last snaps at the end of October, and volunteers across the nation are now identifying the species that appear in each one uploaded to a dedicated project page. McShea says that once the project is complete, the data will be free and available to anyone who wants it, including land managers in charge of hunting regulations or scientists endeavoring to support endangered species.
Yellow Fat and Garter may be two of those scientists. Both are planning careers in natural resource management. Being part of this project, they say, has allowed them to hone their science chops while providing their tribes some of the recognition they deserve.
“I have no disdain for Lewis and Clark. I simply see them as researchers,” says Garter. “But we were some of the first stewards of the land, who understood how everything connected. So, for this opportunity to come back to us today, despite all we have been through as a people, it feels full-circle.”

https://taz.de/Mehr-Kosten-fuer-gesetzli.title: Mehr Kosten für gesetzlich Versicherte: Wer nicht warten will, muss zahlen
https://taz.de/Mehr-Kosten-fuer-gesetzli.text:
Mehr Kosten für gesetzlich Versicherte: Wer nicht warten will, muss zahlen
Kassenärzte-Chef Andreas Gassen erwartet, dass gesetzlich Versicherte künftig mehr selbst zahlen müssen. Grund seien auch Honorarkürzungen in der Ambulanz.
dpa/afp | Gesetzlich Versicherte müssen sich nach Angaben von Kassenärzte-Chef Andreas Gassen wegen Honorarkürzungen darauf einstellen, Behandlungen auch aus der eigenen Tasche zu zahlen – um so längere Wartezeiten zu vermeiden. „Niemand kann erwarten, dass die Praxen angesichts der Kürzungen einfach weiter machen wie bisher“, sagte Gassen dem Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland. „Ich gehe davon aus, dass es Angebote in der Privatsprechstunde geben wird, da wird ja jeder Termin vergütet“, sagte der Chef der Kassenärztlichen Bundesvereinigung (KBV).
„Gesetzlich Versicherte, die diese Option wählen, werden dann außerhalb der gesetzlichen Versicherung behandelt wie ein Privatpatient, müssen aber die Kosten als Selbstzahler aus der eigenen Tasche begleichen“, sagte er. Nur so sei die Finanzierung der Kosten zusätzlicher Fälle über das Budget hinaus möglich. „Die Praxen haben keine unendliche Leistungsverpflichtung“, stellte Gassen klar und warnte: „Wenn Fachgruppen 25 Prozent des Umsatzes verlieren, was teilweise der Fall ist, ist das ein existenzbedrohender Einschnitt.“
Das Sparprogramm der Bundesregierung für die gesetzliche Krankenversicherung (GKV) sieht umfangreiche Sparmaßnahmen vor. Nach Angaben von Gassen sind von den Honorarkürzungen im Umfang von drei Milliarden Euro insbesondere die Bereiche HNO, Orthopädie, Kardiologie, Radiologie und Rheumatologie betroffen. Vor allem hier werde es weniger Termine geben. „Ist das Budget aufgebraucht, werden sich die Patienten damit abfinden müssen, in ihrer Wunschpraxis vielleicht erst im nächsten Quartal einen Termin zu bekommen“, sagte er.
Kritik an den Aussagen von Gassen kam vom Spitzenverband der gesetzlichen Krankenkassen. „Hier werden gesetzlich Versicherte, die einen Arzt brauchen, in Geiselhaft genommen, damit Ärzte ihre Honorare steigern können. Dies ist ein skandalöses Verhalten“, erklärte die stellvertretende GKV-Vorstandsvorsitzende Stefanie Stoff-Ahnis. Die Kassenärztliche Bundesvereinigung habe die gesetzliche Aufgabe, die Versorgung von Kranken zu ermöglichen, nicht zu erschweren. „Niedergelassene Ärztinnen und Ärzte bekommen durch ihre Arztpraxen im Durchschnitt über 200.000 Euro im Jahr. Es gibt keinen Hinweis darauf, dass sich dies im kommenden Jahr ändert.“

Avant un nouveau rendez-vous syndical le 17 novembre, avec une nouvelle journée de grève et de manifestations pour le secteur public, après le refus vendredi par le gouvernement de relever le point d’indice des fonctionnaires, différentes organisations syndicales et de défense des droits humains vont défiler ce samedi 14 novembre 2026.
Cette nouvelle journée de mobilisation agrège plusieurs revendications distinctes, mais qui convergent ce samedi : pour la hausse des salaires, pour davantage de moyens à l’éducation, contre la proposition de loi sur la présomption d’usage légitime des armes par les forces de sécurité, qui revient, selon elles, à “un permis de tuer” et contre laquelle près de 50.000 personnes avaient déjà manifesté le 20 septembre dans toute la France, selon les chiffres du ministère de l’Intérieur.
Les manifestations de ce week-end interviennent alors que le gouvernement a annoncé une revalorisation du Smic au 1er décembre estimée très insuffisante par les organisations syndicales, de l’ordre d’une vingtaine d’euros, indexation automatique comprise. D’abord appelée par la CGT, Solidaires et la FSU, la journée d’action intersyndicale du 17 novembre voit ses rangs gonflés par l’annonce de la CFDT, vendredi, qu’elle rejoignait les autres syndicats, après avoir fait part de sa déception des propositions salariales de l’exécutif à la sortie du dernier entretien avec Sébastien Lecornu.
Les mobilisations des lycéens se poursuivent elles aussi, les blocages affectant plus de mille établissements la semaine dernière selon les syndicats d’enseignants, de proviseurs et de lycéens, loin de l’estimation minimaliste de quelques dizaines avancée par le gouvernement.
Quant à la manifestation enfantiste de ce  14 novembre, elle agrège désormais autour d’elle des collectifs pour le climat, la justice sociale et des lycéens. Plus d’une centaine de rassemblements sont prévus dans plusieurs villes à l’appel du Collectif enfantiste et du Mouvement du 26 septembre.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: James Blunt: ‘Do I have a nickname? Yes, it rhymes with blunt’
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Sian Cain
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
You were a punching bag for such a long time after You’re Beautiful became a massive hit, but your consistent good humour is deeply admirable. Does it ever get tiring?
It was a surprise, at the beginning. I was just a little guy with a dream. And when you achieve your dream, you think people would be happy for you. For them not to be happy for you, but angry with you, for your song, seems irrational, an overreaction. It is interesting how people generally want to tear people down for achieving their little dreams. But I’d had a real proper job before that [as a captain in the British army]. My friends might have been on operations in Afghanistan or Iraq, so if I were to complain to them at the time saying, “Oh, the Guardian said something really horrid about me and gave me three stars for my album” – they would be able to talk about who had lost their lives or limbs that day, and that put it all in perspective. And perspective is everything.
Then you start thinking really clearly. A journalist might say, “Hey, I read something negative about you online” – I can either start defending that or put it in perspective, which is: I’ve just played a concert to 15,000 people and those 15,000 people spent really hard-earned money to buy a ticket and booked hotels or flights to get there and queued up and, if it’s in England, queued in the rain. So am I really going to get upset by one negative tweet when 15,000 people really invested themselves in me? It’s all about perspective.
What is the best thing about owning two pubs?
The beer in my life is always free.
Are you very good at pulling a pint?
The staff in my pubs, because of who I am and the shame they sometimes feel, try to keep me out back doing the dishes rather than front of house. I understand why. It is how we roll.
Ed Sheeran and Carrie Fisher are the godparents of your children. What wisdom did you hope each of them would impart?
I hoped Carrie would look after herself. That’s why I asked her to be a godmother – I could see a destructive human being and I wanted her to care enough for herself that my son might know her. And it wasn’t to be.
And Ed and I had a very similar journey. We were singer-songwriters inspired by similar musicians, found ourselves managed by the same management, found ourselves signed to the same record label – but he just did it better. If you’re going to have your child be inspired by someone, point them in the direction of someone who does it better than you.
I understand you love a rave. How often do you get to one?
Not as much as I’d like, to be honest. I live in Ibiza and my favourite nightclub is a club called Pacha, which opened in 1973. When I was 13 years old, I was on a family holiday here and I walked past Pacha and told my friend, “I am going to live here, and I am going to go to that club.” The moment my first album, Back to Bedlam, became a hit, the first thing I did was buy a house in Ibiza, which is where I’m calling you from now. I later moved to Ibiza when I was a pariah in my own country and I wrote All the Lost Souls, a pretty dark and miserable second album. But the thing that kept me going was the dancefloor in Pacha … I wrote a song called 1973, the year Pacha opened. And then the DJ Pete Tong remixed it, so I would be in that club, listening to my own song, about the club that I was in – which is kind of mental.
There are other clubs I really love. Ushuaïa is like a Miami pool party and they’ll occasionally ask me to perform there. Sometimes I’ll drive down there, I park out the front, the security walk me to the stage and hand me a microphone, I’ll climb on to the stage, sing, crowd surf, go back on the stage, sing the final chorus, hand the microphone over, walk off the stage and drive home to put my kids to bed. That is either really rock’n’roll or really square, I am not sure which.
What is the best piece of advice you have ever received?
Don’t shit where you eat.
Who taught you that one?
Pretty much everyone I know.
What is the weirdest thing you have done for love?
Obviously I am a purveyor of saccharine songs, so I need to up my game when it comes to romance. So last Valentine’s Day, I hired a helicopter, flew over my house and threw 100,000 red rose petals at my wife in the garden below. I thought that was pretty good. She thought it was OK.
Who would you like to play you in the biopic about your life?
My mother really thought Tom Cruise but, if I’m totally honest, I know it’s more likely to be Alan Partridge.
What are you secretly really good at?
I do a really good gorilla impression. And! [James Blunt uses his brow to wiggle his scalp so it moves distinctly from his face] I actually have a wig that no one knows about. I don’t know anyone else can do that but I literally can move my whole scalp and hair as if it were a wig. It’s real. I haven’t managed to monetise it.
Do you have a nickname, and what is it?
Yes, it rhymes with blunt and it’s a tiny bit shorter. It’s character building!
Actually, it is bizarre that my name later became cockney rhyming slang for that. That’s one of my greatest achievements. I have a few things that I find genuinely an achievement – like I have a ski lift named after me in Switzerland, and a burger named after me. But to have cockney rhyming slang for your own name is amazing.
I have also heard about the James Blunt Museum, in a Herefordshire phone booth.
Yeah, a huge, huge deal for me as well. I have been known to go there just to give it a quick clean from time to time. It’s not too far, just a quick six-hour drive. I go there for the morning, clean it, head back home. It’s worth a visit if you find yourself in the northern hemisphere. I really recommend it.
Final question – you were just on Celebrity Traitors. If you could be on another reality show, what would it be?
I swore that I would never do a reality show. Ever. And I have lived and breathed by that proclamation. My manager doesn’t even bring me those shows. But my wife signed me up to this without telling me. And I really wish she hadn’t.
- James Blunt’s new album, Airplane Mode, is out now (Warner Music)

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: ‘You have to cope’: why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Elle Hunt
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
No one would think of Sasha* as lonely, least of all Sasha herself. The 38-year-old from Sydney has close and longstanding friendships, proactively keeps in touch and makes plans, and is engaged with her local community.
“All those things that you read about, about why men might be lonely – they don’t maintain one-on-one friendships, or they’re not good at reaching out, or their conversations aren’t deep and meaningful – none of those issues apply to me,” she says. “I’m a very socially connected person.”
Yet Sasha often felt lonely during her first year of motherhood, even when she was surrounded by other people. (All case studies’ names have been changed.) She attributes it now to the intensity of the experience. “It’s the identity shift of your first child, having no idea of what you’re doing, learning on the fly … You feel alone.”
We’re living through a global crisis of loneliness, with the World Health Organization (WHO) declaring it a priority for public health, but it’s hard to miss that the coverage and conversation has been overwhelmingly focused on men.
Global Google searches for “male loneliness” spiked suddenly in mid-2023, and have since seen frequent surges; interest in “female loneliness”, meanwhile, has remained a trickle.
In 2024, the UK government commissioned research on loneliness in boys and young men, even though – as the final report acknowledged – girls and women were more likely to report feeling chronically lonely. (Paradoxically, researchers suggested this was further evidence of the crisis in men, because they were less likely to speak up and seek help.)
In the media, it has been conceived as its own specific issue: “The male loneliness epidemic.”
“When I tell people that I study loneliness, sometimes they ask, ‘Oh, men’s loneliness?’” says Michelle Lim, a principal research fellow at the University of Sydney, chief executive of Australia’s Ending Loneliness Together campaign and an adviser to the WHO. “I have to say, ‘No, no – everyone’s loneliness.’”
From the relative lack of attention on women and girls, you might assume they’re doing fine, or at least better than men and boys. In fact, studies consistently show similar prevalence between genders. “There’s not really any difference … They’re equally both lonely,” Lim says.
Comparisons of men and women’s loneliness produce mixed, but insignificant results. Meanwhile, a recent systematic review of the current literature on loneliness among men in the US concluded that evidence of a “widespread epidemic … is absent”.
What is loneliness?
So why do we have the impression that men are especially or uniquely struggling, and why don’t we hear about the “female loneliness epidemic”? In part it reflects a broader misunderstanding, says Lim: “We do see this confusion about what loneliness is.”
Loneliness is defined as the sense that your social relationships are somehow lacking in quality, quantity or both. Social isolation – with which loneliness is often confused or conflated – is more objective, referring to an absence of connection.
Data tends to show that men are more socially isolated than women, meaning “they have fewer people they talk to”, Lim says. Because men also tend to value physical presence and “shoulder-to-shoulder” socialising above emotional intimacy and disclosure, “the assumption is that they are more lonely”, Lim goes on – but that is not necessarily the case, if they are satisfied with those interactions.
Women tend to be more connected, “but they might feel lonely within relationships”, she says. That might indicate interpersonal ambivalence or conflict, but it could also stem from feeling isolated and alone in their individual experience.
‘A very gendered experience’
Women are more likely to be carers than men are, they earn less on average, are less financially secure and are more vulnerable to adverse life events such as redundancy and divorce. “In many ways, they’re more socially disadvantaged, and that, we know, actually does predispose people to more loneliness,” Lim says. “It’s an equity issue.”
This became clear early in the Covid-19 pandemic, when loneliness started to gain more academic and media attention. Though both men and women reported feeling more lonely, the rise in women was much larger, which experts attributed to their increased workload, such as overseeing children’s schooling.
Spending more time on housework and caregiving not only means women have less time and ability to invest in their social connections; there is also likely to be the added loneliness of shouldering the burden, says Manuela Barreto, a professor of social and organisational psychology at the University of Exeter in the UK. “It’s a very gendered experience.”
Research has found that life transitions, such as becoming a parent, can promote loneliness, but the particular drivers likely differ for men and women, reflecting their different expectations and experiences.
Barreto suggests women are often more affected by children growing up and leaving the family nest, for example, due to the expectation or reality that “being a mother is much more central for women than being a father is for men”.
Menstrual health is another particular – and frequently underestimated – factor in women’s loneliness. A 2022 Japanese study found an association between loneliness and severe premenstrual symptoms in teenage girls. Regular pain can promote loneliness “in a very practical way”, Barreto points out, by preventing women from being fully present with others or even socialising at all.
Conditions such as endometriosis are described as lonely, worsened by lack of mainstream and medical understanding. “You have to cope, and deal with things by yourself,” says Barreto. “That really can make you feel very alone.”
That was the case for Sasha. She has endometriosis and spent two “very difficult years” trying for a baby through multiple miscarriages and ultimately IVF. “That was the first time in my life that I had felt lonely,” she says.
Miscarriage in particular, Sasha recalls as “the loneliest of experiences”, causing her to feel apart from her loved ones and withdraw socially. “It’s a type of grief that is really difficult for people who haven’t been through it to understand.”
By the time she gave birth to her daughter, Sasha was “physically and emotionally exhausted”. The shock of new motherhood – far from the easy, beatific state she’d expected – deepened her sense of alienation and ambivalence. “Particularly having a much-wanted baby you’ve really fought for, you think, ‘I’m not entitled to feel anything except joy,’” she says.
Even her partner could not relate, despite his best efforts. “He’s very involved but … my experience was very different to his,” Sasha says. “He was still going to work; his life hadn’t changed to the same degree.”
‘Like a feeling of panic’
Loneliness can also spring from self-comparison and feeling yourself to have deviated from the expected or accepted path – itself frequently gendered. For Laura*, 41, from Auckland, loneliness is “almost like a feeling of panic”.
She recalls going for dinner with a group of school friends and realising midway through that they’d spoken exclusively about their children. Laura was the only non-parent among them.
It wasn’t that she didn’t want to hear about their families, she says, and there was no deliberate effort to exclude her. “It was a simultaneous feeling that no one was particularly interested in what might be going on for me in my life, and also feeling shut out from this experience.”
Laura emphasises that she doesn’t feel lonely often. “It comes and goes, and is very much dependent on mood, what’s happening at work, who’s in my general orbit, the weather – all those factors that I think also affect mental health more generally.”
But her experience of loneliness is tied up with her life circumstances. Laura is single and lives alone, while many of her close friends have families or live far away. “I am in a very different life stage,” she says.
Laura works hard to expand her network and socialise solo, but it feels effortful; she misses the easy, unthinking companionship of a romantic partner or even flatmates. Not having “that default unit” – someone to commiserate or celebrate with and just share in her day-to-day experience – “comes with a sense of doing everything alone”, Laura says.
Sexist stereotypes add another layer of ambivalence, she suggests. “A man alone is self-sufficient, taking this bold, brave step, versus a woman living alone is a failure, left on the shelf … a weird, unlovable spinster.” It’s not that she believes this of herself, Laura adds. “It’s more my concern that that’s how other people will perceive me.”
Men have their own gendered drivers of loneliness, not least that expectation of being stoic and self-sufficient. In fact, that might be driving the attention on the male “epidemic”, Barreto suggests: because, stereotypically, men are supposed to be strong and unfeeling – the fact they might feel lonely is considered surprising and newsworthy.
While lonely women tend to internalise the problem and “get on with it”, Barreto goes on, the potential consequences of loneliness, for men, “can be a lot more severe”. Globally, rates of suicide are higher for males than females.
But there is not necessarily a straightforward association between a man feeling lonely and posing a threat to himself or others. The concept of a “male loneliness epidemic” also suggests a single, sweeping event, rather than a highly individual process. “Loneliness is a subjective experience, so it needs to be assessed in that way,” Barreto says.
Instead of comparing male and female loneliness, we need to augment our understanding of both, and non-binary individuals with them, she says. “We need to look at gendered life experiences, and link those to how they are hindering or facilitating our social connection … What is making men lonely, and what is making women lonely?”
By engaging with the specificity of those (and other) experiences, we may learn how to protect against loneliness and intervene effectively, Barreto says.
Already the data points to a productive path forward. A 2022 study of 30 countries found those that had higher levels of gender equality had lower rates of loneliness, for both men and women; the researchers hypothesised that equality was more conducive “to high-quality, close relationships”.
That dovetails with other research, showing loneliness to be a socioeconomic issue. Instead of looking to treat “male loneliness”, a better strategy might be improving social infrastructure and increasing living standards for everyone’s benefit. In the meantime, sharing individual experiences can help.
When Sasha became pregnant with her second child earlier this year, she knew she did not want to repeat the fraught, lonely time she had with her first. She engaged a therapist to protect her mental health and sought out honest, nuanced accounts of motherhood (she namechecks Matrescence by Lucy Jones) that made her feel seen.
“Happily”, Sasha says, her second postpartum experience has been easier. She has also made a point of speaking honestly about her difficult road to parenthood. Her motivation was to help others feel less lonely, but it eased the burden for her, too. “I found the more open I was, the more connected I felt.”

* names have been changed.

Stadtgespräch aus Moskau: Von Lügen und Siegesfantasien
Die Ohren spitzen genügt. Brutale Erfahrungen eines Insiders von der Front in der Ukraine, gehört im abendlichen Dunkel einer Moskauer Raucherecke.
W er behauptet, auf den Straßen der russischen Hauptstadt Moskau sei der Krieg gegen die Ukraine kein Thema, irrt. Es genügt die Ohren zu spitzen, um zu verstehen, dass das komfortable Hauptstadtleben keinesfalls völlig losgelöst von der brutalen Realität stattfindet.
In einem Viertel nicht allzu weit vom Zentrum entfernt sind die Lichter in den Büros längst gelöscht. Nach Feierabend herrscht in den wenigen Cafés und Restaurants Hochbetrieb. Ein junger Mann in Armeeuniform, die Haare kurz geschoren, steuert eine mit Regendach und improvisierter Sitzbank ausgestattete Raucherecke an. Im Schlepptau folgen ihm ein halbes Dutzend junger Männer in Zivil.
„Ich war so blöd und habe mich nach dem vierten Monat breitschlagen lassen und den Vertrag unterzeichnet“, platzt es aus dem Uniformierten heraus. Er war zum Grundwehrdienst eingezogen worden. Wehrpflichtige dürfen während ihrer einjährigen Dienstzeit nicht an die Front versetzt werden. Das russische Gesetz erlaubt es jedoch, sich mit Erreichen der Volljährigkeit als Zeitsoldat zu verpflichten – mit oder ohne militärische Grundkenntnisse. Ab dann stehen diese Personen den Streitkräften unbeschränkt zur Verfügung. Dem Diktat skrupelloser Vorgesetzter halten nicht alle Wehrpflichtigen stand. Unter den bestätigten Kriegstoten auf russischer Seite finden sich haufenweise 18-jährige Soldaten.
wochentaz
Dieser Text erschien zuerst in der wochentaz, unserer Wochenzeitung von links!
In der wochentaz geht es jede Woche um die Welt, wie sie ist – und wie sie sein könnte. Eine linke Wochenzeitung mit Stimme, Haltung und dem besonderen taz-Blick auf die Welt. Jeden Samstag neu am Kiosk und natürlich im Abo.
Niemand unterbricht den Monolog
„Wir wurden gleich nach Luhansk geschickt – das war heftig“, fährt der Uniformierte fort. Die ukrainische Region ist fast vollständig von russischen Truppen besetzt. Der Erzähler zieht an seiner Zigarette, die anderen schauen, soweit im Halbdunkel zu erkennen, gespannt in seine Richtung. „Wenigstens habe ich keinen Vertrag für eine Sturmabteilung unterschrieben, da kommt man nicht lebend raus.“
Dass er sich jetzt frei und ungezwungen in Moskau bewegen dürfe, erklärt er so: Dreizehn Jahre lang habe er eine Musikschule besucht, deshalb sei er nach Moskau verlegt worden und spiele jetzt im Orchester des Verteidigungsministeriums. Da gehe er jeden Morgen um 9 Uhr hin und dürfe um 14 Uhr wieder nach Hause. „Ich bin unbeschreiblich froh, dass ich hier bin.“ Die Erleichterung verleiht dem bislang nüchtern vorgetragenen Text einen leichten emotionalen Klang.
Niemand unterbricht den Monolog. Niemand erlaubt sich eine Frage. Aber vermutlich ahnen alle Anwesenden sowieso, dass ihr Bekannter – vielleicht kennen sie sich seit Schulzeiten, vielleicht erst seit Kurzem – ein prosaisches Detail unterschlagen hat: Der beschauliche neue Dienstort dürfte die Familie ein Vermögen gekostet haben.
„Alle wollen, dass dieser Krieg aufhört“
Bei der Erwähnung seines Umfelds am sicheren Arbeitsplatz redet sich der Erzähler allmählich in Rage. „Alle, die ganz Jungen bis hin zu den alten Fettbäuchen, alle wollen, dass dieser Krieg aufhört. Niemand will, dass er weitergeht.“ Nach wie vor ist nicht einmal ein Räuspern oder Hüsteln zu hören, die Zigaretten sind längst alle aufgeraucht. „Wenn ihr Leute kennt, die ihren Wehrdienst ableisten, dann müsst ihr ihnen einbläuen, dass sie ja keinen Vertrag unterschreiben – egal wie sehr sie geschlagen und gequält werden!“ Spätestens jetzt würde man gerne in die Gesichter der Umstehenden blicken.
„Sie lügen auf beiden Seiten“, fährt der Uniformierte fort. Er verfolge aufmerksam, wie über den Krieg berichtet werde. Ganz frei von Großmachtfantasien ist aber auch der fronterfahrende junge Musiker nicht. „Europa würden wir natürlich besiegen, aber zu welchem Preis!“
Der Konzertsaal einer Hochschule ist an diesem Abend fast bis auf den letzten Platz besetzt. Nach einem leichten Einstieg und einer grandiosen Darbietung von Verdis Gefangenenchor aus der Oper „Nabucco“ folgt der abrupte Übergang zu Liedern aus der Hochzeit des Stalinismus. Als das Orchester kurz vor dem krönenden Ende zum Radetzky-Marsch ansetzt, gerät das Publikum regelrecht in Ekstase.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: New Orleans officials file $1m lawsuit after ‘Mississippi miracle’ tanker crash
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
New Orleans port officials have filed a lawsuit seeking more than $1m in damages from the owner and operator of an asphalt tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship on the Mississippi River in the city on Friday.
In some of the first legal consequences of Friday’s crash, the port has also obtained a federal court order authorizing the seizure of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker. The Atlantic Asphalt slammed into the American Heritage cruise ship, causing the river boat to flip onto its side, injuring more than 30 people and setting off a frantic but successful effort to pull people out of the water.
The board of commissioners of the port of New Orleans filed the lawsuit in federal court late Friday, naming the Atlantic Asphalt tanker; its owner, Nave Shipping SA; and its management company, Thome Ship Management, as defendants.
Court documents state that the Atlantic Asphalt struck the American Heritage cruise ship at about 12.30pm Friday while passengers were disembarking at the port’s Thalia Street terminal.
The crash also left the terminal with extensive damage, according to the port’s lawsuit. The port estimates that repairs will exceed $1m, although officials are still determining the full scope of the destruction.
The port – beside repair costs – is pursuing compensation for cleanup operations, inspections and other expenses stemming from the Atlantic Asphalt’s crashing into the American Heritage.
Using a term for when a moving vehicle strikes a stationary object, the lawsuit alleges: “The allision occurred as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness of the Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping, Thome (and potentially other parties not yet identified with responsibility for the operation, condition, crewing and seaworthiness of the Atlantic Asphalt).”
“As a result of the foregoing,” the lawsuit also states, “the Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping, Thome (and potentially other parties not yet identified with responsibility for the operation, condition, crewing and seaworthiness of the Atlantic Asphalt) are solidarily liable for all damage sustained by the Board as described herein.”
The port furthermore requested permission from a federal judge to have the tanker seized and sold to help cover the costs of the damage. The judge, Wendy Vitter, approved the seizure request on Friday.
In its complaint, the port argued that the tanker and the companies overseeing its operations failed to comply with safety requirements and did not take appropriate precautions to prevent the collision with the stationary cruise ship.
The lawsuit maintains that the port bears no responsibility for Friday’s crash and seeks to hold the tanker’s owner and management company accountable for the resulting damage.
Port officials also indicated that additional defendants could be named in the case – and that the amount of damages sought could increase as further details emerge.
There were 197 passengers aboard the American Heritage at the time of Friday’s crash. Despite the severity of the collision, every passenger was accounted for, and no deaths or critical injuries were reported.
The city’s mayor, Helena Moreno, characterized the outcome as a “miracle on the Mississippi” – and attributed it to an effective performance by local, state and federal first responders.
In a news conference on Saturday afternoon, Moreno said that the American Heritage cruise liner may take several weeks to ultimately be removed from the site of the crash.
She added that members of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) had recently arrived in the city, with more expected to arrive later Saturday. Moreno said that “it took a little bit longer for their arrival” because of Friday’s nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that delayed and canceled thousands of flights.
Capt Melanie Burnham of the US Coast Guard, commander of the military branch’s New Orleans sector, on Saturday confirmed that the investigation into the previous day’s crash was ongoing.
She had said Friday that the Atlantic Asphalt had evidently experienced “some type of loss of steering” before the crash – but that it still needed to be investigated.
“Our top priority now is the safe removal of the hazardous material on board the American Heritage,” Burnham said on Saturday. “It’s still pretty early. We are estimating about 16,000 gallons [of fuel] are still on board the American Heritage.”
Burnham also confirmed on Saturday that the Atlantic Asphalt had been towed to a different location, and added that the scene of the crash would remain a restricted area for the foreseeable future.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Democrat wins Alaska governor’s seat for first time in nearly 30 years
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democrats have captured Alaska’s governor’s seat for the first time in nearly three decades, marking another major victory for their party in a midterm election period that has dramatically shifted political power across the US.
Former Alaska state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republican opponents, including a candidate backed by Donald Trump, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Alaska since 1998.
His victory – called by the Associated Press on Friday, 10 days after the polls closed – adds to a growing list of Democratic gains nationwide, bringing the party’s total to 30 US governorships. Democrats have also taken control of governor’s offices in several other longtime Republican strongholds, including Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.
Kreiss-Tomkins, widely known as JKT, secured the win having mounted a political comeback three years after departing the Alaska house of representatives.
The 37-year-old traveled extensively throughout the state during his campaign, building support around economic concerns and a promise to change the direction of Alaska’s government.
His platform centered on tackling affordability, ensuring full funding for public education, and requiring all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income taxes. He also pushed for a temporary halt to new datacenter developments until state lawmakers establish regulations governing their construction.
Throughout the campaign, Kreiss-Tomkins sharply criticized the leadership of outgoing the Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, arguing that Alaska had become “broken” during his eight years in office.
“Alaskans are hungry for change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “We’ve been running the same campaign since we launched in February, and I don’t take anyone’s vote for granted.”
Among his criticisms was the deterioration of the state’s ferry system, which Kreiss-Tomkins said had been left in disarray as service to numerous communities was drastically reduced. The ferry network serves as a critical transportation link for communities in south-east Alaska that lack road connections, including some with limited access to air travel.
Despite his criticism of the outgoing administration, Kreiss-Tomkins presented himself as a leader willing to work across political divisions. He pledged to assemble a cabinet that includes Democrats, Republicans and independents.
Unlike most states, Alaska allows voters to rank candidates by preference through ranked-choice voting – a system that also permits multiple candidates from the same political party to run against one another.
But Kreiss-Tomkins avoided the need for additional rounds of vote counting after winning more than 50% of first-choice votes, securing an outright victory.
The Alaska result comes just days after Democrats scored another major gubernatorial win in staunchly conservative Kansas, where the Democratic state senator Cindy Holscher narrowly defeated the Republican state senate president, Ty Masterson.
Masterson, who received Trump’s endorsement, faced a campaign in which Holscher repeatedly highlighted his ties to the Republican president. At the same time, Holscher maintained that she would remain willing to cooperate with the Trump administration on issues where common ground could be found.
The back-to-back victories in Alaska and Kansas underscore the scale of Democratic gains in what has become a nationwide electoral shift.
The party’s long-anticipated “blue wave” has now materialized, with Democrats flipping eight seats in the US Senate, gaining more than two dozen seats in the House and significantly expanding their control of governors’ offices after the 3 November midterms.
Such gains have handed Democrats a strong majority in Congress for the latter half of Trump’s second presidency, delivering a major shift in the balance of power in Washington and state governments across the US.
Meanwhile, with few ballots left to count for Alaska’s midterm US Senate election, Democrat Mary Peltola on Saturday was leading Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan, Alaska Public Media reported. That had prompted MS Now to characterize that Senate race as “leans Democratic”.
Beside Alaska and Kansas, the Democratic party won gubernatorial elections over Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, putting them in control of a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Gina Hinojosa is the first Democrat to be elected governor of Texas in 35 years – and also the state’s first Hispanic governor.
A major factor in the GOP’s midterm defeat is the unpopularity of Trump, whom most Republican lawmakers clung to even as polls indicated voters did not support his immigration crackdown, tariffs, the war with Iran or his signature domestic policy bill.
