Nach den Parlamentswahlen in Serbien: Gas geben, aber mit Bedacht
In Serbien jagt eine Festnahmen die andere. Fast täglich werden Strafverfahren eingeleitet. Juristen warnen vor allzu großem Übereifer.
Der Machtwechsel ist noch nicht einmal vollzogen, das neue Parlament soll sich erst am 17. November konstituieren. Doch schon zerfällt vor den Augen der nach Gerechtigkeit dürstenden Zuschauer in Serbien das Gerüst aus Korruption und Kriminalität des besiegten Regimes.
Seit die Studentenliste am 25. Oktober die vorgezogenen Parlamentswahlen gewonnen hat, vergeht kaum ein Tag ohne Festnahmen oder der Einleitung von Strafverfahren. Im Visier der Justizbehörden stehen Staatsanwälte, Polizisten, Kommunalbeamte, ehemalige Minister, Geschäftsleute, Bauunternehmer, Parteiaktivisten.
In Haft befinden sich bislang der Leiter der Kriminalpolizeidirektion, ein Kommandeur der Antiterroristischen Einheit, Gefängnisleiter, Eigentümer der ALTA Bank, der Direktor des Hydrometeorologischen Instituts Serbiens (RHMZ) und der Bürgermeister von Inđija.
Sie alle werden des Amtsmissbrauchs, der Geldwäsche und der Korruption verdächtigt. Die Staatsanwaltschaft für organisierte Kriminalität (TOK) hat ein Verfahren gegen den Chef des serbischen Geheimdienstes BIA, den scheidenden Justizminister und etwa 60 weitere Personen eingeleitet – unter anderem wegen illegalen Abhörens.
Warnung vor voreiligem Handeln
Das ist ein trauriges Bild unserer Staatsanwaltschaft“, sagt die Staatsanwältin Bojana Savović. Denn man sehe jetzt, was Staatsanwälte in den vergangenen 14 Jahren alles hätten tun können, jedoch nicht hätten tun wollen, weil sie sich dem politischen Druck gebeugt hätten. Sie hofft, dass das Tempo des Handelns nicht zulasten der Qualität der Anklageschriften gehe.
Auch die Rechtsanwältin Tanja Arsić warnt eindringlich: Die Staatsanwaltschaft dürfe keine Anklage erheben, solange die Beweislage nicht ausreiche. Sie dürfe nicht voreilig handeln, nur um schnelle Erfolge vorzuweisen. Denn das würde am Ende zu Freisprüchen für ehemalige Spitzenpolitiker führen. Ein solches Szenario wäre „katastrophal“.
Für die serbischen Demokratiekämpfer läuft es derzeit gut, doch die zukünftige Staatsführung wird sich schon bald mit einem logischen Paradoxon konfrontiert sehen, das als „Catch-22“ bekannt ist. Die parlamentarische Mehrheit und die künftige Regierung der Studentenliste müssen eine konsequente Gewaltenteilung zwischen Legislative, Exekutive und Judikative durchsetzen.
Es gilt, unabhängige staatliche Institutionen zu schaffen, die gegen politischen Druck gewappnet sind. Kurz gesagt: Der Rechtsstaat muss wiederhergestellt werden. „Es ist zur Gewohnheit geworden, dass eine Regierungspartei die nächste ablöst und den Staat für sich vereinnahmt – und die nächste Partei macht dann genau dasselbe“, erklärt Miloš Bešić, Professor an der Fakultät für Politikwissenschaften.
Nobles Ziel
„Die Lösung dieses Problems wäre das größte Ziel, das nach den Umbrüchen, die wir erlebt haben, erreicht werden kann.“ Denn die Studenten haben die Vision, dass ein Machtwechsel nur Sinn hat, wenn danach das ganze politische System verändert wird. Auf dem Weg zu diesem noblen Ziel müssten die Sieger der jüngsten Wahlen jedoch freiwillig jene Machtinstrumente aus der Hand geben, mit denen sie „höhere“ Ziele im Namen des „Allgemeinwohls“ durchsetzen könnten.
Damit würden sie ihre eigene Position in der Auseinandersetzung mit Vučićs Gefolgsleuten schwächen. Diese sind immer noch in jedem noch so kleinen Ort an der Macht und kontrollieren einen Großteil des Staatsapparats. Denn erstens gilt: Wenn die Justiz nach dem Buchstaben des Gesetzes und nicht nach politischen Direktiven arbeitet, sind Anschuldigungen das eine. Die Beweisführung vor Gericht und rechtskräftige Urteile sind jedoch etwas ganz anderes.
Zweitens räumt man durch ein striktes Festhalten am Rechtsstaat genau jenen Akteuren, die einem zuvor den politischen Spielraum beschnitten und gesetzeswidrig das Rückgrat gebrochen haben, die legale Möglichkeit ein, sich bei einem erneuten Griff nach der Macht wieder voll zu entfalten.
Stärkste Einzelpartei
Dieses Dilemma hatte sich in den ersten Jahren nach dem demokratischen Umbruch vom 5. Oktober 2000 in aller Deutlichkeit gezeigt. Bei den Parlamentswahlen Ende Dezember 2000 kam die ultranationalistische Serbische Radikale Partei (SRS) von Vojislav Šešelj auf lediglich 23 Mandate. Doch bereits im Dezember 2003 – gestützt auf genau jene neu geschaffenen demokratischen Errungenschaften – errang sie 82 Sitze und wurde mit Abstand stärkste Einzelpartei.
Neun Jahre später kehrten die ehemaligen Radikalen, nun im Gewand der Serbischen Fortschrittspartei (SNS), endgültig an die Macht zurück. Die damals wie heute viel beschworene Lustration – also die Säuberung des Staatsapparats von alten Kadern, die sich über das Gesetz hinweggesetzt hatten – blieb aus.

https://taz.de/Historischer-Dreier-beim-.text:
Historischer Dreier beim APEC-Gipfel: Treffen sich Trump, Putin und Xi …
… und reden doch nicht über den Ukraine-Krieg. Bei dem Gespräch am Rande des Gipfels in China am Donnerstag soll es um atomare Abrüstung und den Iran gehen.
afp | US-Präsident Donald Trump, Russlands Präsident Wladimir Putin und Chinas Staatschef Xi Jinping kommen in der nächsten Woche nach Angaben des Weißen Hauses zu einem historischen Treffen in China zusammen. Die Begegnung am kommenden Donnerstag im chinesischen Shenzhen ist das erste Dreiertreffen überhaupt zwischen den Staatschefs der USA, Russlands und Chinas, wie das Weiße Haus am Freitag mitteilte. Bei den Gesprächen soll es offenbar um nukleare Abrüstung und den Iran gehen – nicht jedoch um den russischen Angriffskrieg gegen die Ukraine.
Das Dreiertreffen findet demnach am Rande des Gipfels der Asiatisch-Pazifischen Wirtschaftsgemeinschaft (Apec) statt. „Der Präsident hat deutlich gemacht, dass er unter anderem den Abbau von Atomwaffen weltweit erörtern wird“, sagte die Sprecherin des Weißen Hauses, Olivia Wales, vor Journalisten.
Laut einem ranghohen US-Regierungsvertreter wird es bei den Gesprächen zwischen Trump und seinen Kollegen aus China und Russland auch um den Krieg im Iran gehen. Dagegen sei nicht davon auszugehen, dass Trump bei dem Treffen mit Putin und Xi auch auf den Ukraine-Krieg eingehen werde, sagte der Beamte am Freitag.
„Ich denke, der Präsident beabsichtigt in der Tat, bei dem trilateralen Treffen mit Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin über den Iran zu sprechen“, sagte der US-Beamte, der anonym bleiben wollte, Journalisten in einer Telefonkonferenz. Hinsichtlich Kiew und Moskau verfolge Washington jedoch eine „völlig andere Verhandlungslinie“. „China ist nicht wirklich Teil dieser Verhandlungslinie, daher erscheint es nicht angebracht, die Ukraine-Frage dort zu erörtern“, sagte der Regierungsvertreter.
Trump spricht auch separat mit Xi, aber nicht mit Putin
Wie aus US-Regierungskreisen verlautete, wird der Tech-Milliardär Elon Musk den US-Präsidenten auf der Reise nach China begleiten. An den Gesprächen mit Putin und Xi nimmt der Chef der Unternehmen Tesla und SpaceX demnach jedoch nicht teil.
Für Donnerstag ist den Regierungsvertretern zufolge zudem ein bilaterales Arbeitsessen sowie ein Treffen Trumps mit Xi geplant – es wäre das vierte Zusammentreffen der beiden Staatschefs seit Trumps Amtsantritt im vergangenen Jahr. Ein separates Vier-Augen-Gespräch zwischen Trump und Putin ist hingegen nicht vorgesehen.
Trump wird den Angaben zufolge zunächst am Dienstag auf den Philippinen eintreffen, um dort am Asean-Gipfel teilzunehmen. Anschließend reist er weiter nach Shenzhen.
Das Treffen von Trump, Putin und Xi in China war erwartet worden. Es weckte Befürchtungen, die Staatschefs könnten versuchen, die Einfluss-Sphären unter sich aufzuteilen. Trump hat im Ukraine-Krieg wiederholt prorussische Standpunkte vertreten und den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj kritisiert. China stellt sich im Ukraine-Krieg als neutral dar; die Ukraine und der Westen werfen China aber vor, Russlands Krieg entscheidend zu unterstützen.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Netanyahu says only a unity government can guarantee Israel’s security
Eisenkot, in charge of forming a government, dismisses the appeal as ‘tricks’ as talks and a Knesset speaker vote loom.
Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his call for a national unity government with his rival, Gadi Eisenkot, saying only such a government can guarantee Israel’s security.
In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said a meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”.
The prime minister said such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all”, claiming Tehran would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.
“Let’s meet in one room, without preconditions,” he said.
Within minutes, however, Eisenkot dismissed the appeal as a ploy.
A former army chief, Eisenkot said Netanyahu “knows he lost the election”.
“Netanyahu is calling for negotiations while they are already underway,” he said. “These tricks don’t work on me.”
Who has the numbers?
Neither side won a majority in the October 27 election. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc took 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s four-party bloc got 48 seats, and Arab-led parties won a record 19.
President Isaac Herzog last week tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, after 67 lawmakers, including those from Arab-led parties, endorsed him, while 46 backed Netanyahu.
Eisenkot has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. He has ruled out including Arab-led parties in his government.
Under Eisenkot’s plan for a minority “national emergency government”, his bloc’s 48 lawmakers would vote in favour against the 46 Netanyahu supporters, while the 26 lawmakers from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties could abstain. It would allow his government to be approved without an absolute majority in the Knesset.
Netanyahu has warned that such a government would lead to Israel’s “collapse”.
Points of contention
Netanyahu’s version would include Jewish parties from the centre and the right and exclude Arab parties. He and his allies have made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties “stole” the election.
On Friday, Eisenkot called Netanyahu’s campaign against them “racist”.
Eisenkot has said he could work with members of Netanyahu’s Likud party and with Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism if their commitment to unity is “sincere”, but he insisted on a “break with the extremists”, notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The Knesset will elect its speaker on Tuesday. The post is currently held by Netanyahu ally Amir Ohana, and the opposition has put forward Matan Kahana, a former military officer, in his place.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Explosion near Syria’s capital kills father and child
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Explosion near Syria’s capital kills father and child
Syria’s Internal Security Forces have launched an investigation into a suspected bomb attack in a suburb of Damascus.
Deadly car bomb blast kills two near Syria's capital
A blast from a suspected explosive device planted inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital, Damascus, has killed at least two people, including a child, and wounded one.
The explosion in Jaramana, on the southeastern edge of Damascus, on Saturday killed a man and his daughter, while a third person, said to be the wife of the man, was seriously injured.
Syria’s Internal Security Forces said they sealed off the area and opened an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the blast.
Jaramana is home to a large community of the Druze religious minority and has seen tensions between some Druze members and the Sunni majority backing President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government.
Witnesses described the vehicle as a Kia Rio parked between two apartment buildings in Jaramana, which is largely considered a quiet residential area, said Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from the blast scene.
Pett said the security situation in the capital remains complex, despite improvements since the regime of former President Bashar al-Assad fell two years ago.
“In the last couple of months, there were two very high-profile incidents,” she said, including a double-tap attack in July during French President Emmanuel Macron’s visit, which Syrian authorities attributed to a cell affiliated with ISIL (ISIS).
“There was also a deadly attack on what’s known as the Lawyer’s Cafe, near the Palace of Justice, which has been the scene of these high-profile trials of former members of the Assad regime,” Pett said.
She added that most of the bombings and security incidents have not necessarily targeted civilians but members and locations of security forces, which authorities have also blamed on ISIL.
Last year, Damascus joined the US-led international coalition against ISIL. The coalition was formed in 2014 and has carried out operations against the group in Syria and Iraq.
On September 27, the security forces said they had arrested four members of an ISIL cell involved in planning and carrying out several attacks in different parts of the country.
Last month, Syria’s security forces said they foiled a plot to target a police patrol in the Damascus countryside, saying an ISIL cell was preparing to carry out the attack, Syrian state television reported.
They said the group was responsible for explosions and assassinations in Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Homs.

https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Ioan Marc Jones
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
I expected to break. But I felt nothing. I did not cry, nor struggle to sleep. I seldom thought of him. I felt only guilt about how little I felt. Ours was a complex relationship. As a teen, I often resented my dad, occasionally despised him. I expected the world and found disappointment. But, as I grew older, I understood that he had struggles of his own. I learned to appreciate his decency and humour, his ability to make everyone laugh with only a few words. I loved my dad, from the first time he held me to the last time I held him.
But still, as weeks turned into months, I struggled to grieve. Then, when my partner and I rearranged our bookshelves, I found the first edition of Under Milk Wood that my parents gave us on our wedding day. I turned the cover and saw the note: “And all the bells of the tills of the town shall ring for our wedding.” It was my mum’s writing, but my dad’s idea. The man loved literature and poetry and considered Dylan Thomas, along with his dad and the Welsh rugby full-back JPR Williams, one of the best men to ever occupy our world.
I decided to re-read Under Milk Wood. I took in the first few lines and I suddenly missed him so entirely. My dad grew up in the most northerly village in Wales, on the shore of the Irish Sea, a place full of humour and surrealism. It made him a glutton for wordplay. Names in Under Milk Wood felt all too familiar: Dai Bread, the baker with two wives; Evans the Death, the undertaker; Nogood Boyo, the troublemaker. I heard my dad laugh at the Preacher’s words: “Will you take this woman to be your awful wedded wife?”
Thomas, like my dad, leaned into linguistic excess. Consider the sea, the jollyrodgered sea, dab-filled sea, still still sea, seesaw sea, seas barking like seals, seas green as a bean. I read the play in my old man’s voice, that London-diluted Welsh, with rolling Rs and whispering double Ls. It helped me access grief and mine proved a good grief: I laughed as I cried, cackled as I wept. My grief reminded me of all we’d lost, all we’d been lucky to have.
Small towns and villages possess their own mythology, secured by whispers, spread by gossips, growing wilder by iteration. I remembered my dad, sitting with me in the garden, a laugh so laughable it made me laugh, telling his child stories of his own childhood. A woman in his home town once grew a potato so big they had to build a chip shop round it. There was a crab who people knew on a first-name basis. Sledgehammer-wielding men could not break a boulder, size of a house, until my dad’s taid (grandfather), a stonemason, drew a small cross in white chalk. “Hit here,” he said, walking away. The boulder shattered into a thousand pieces.
Under Milk Wood brought the stories rushing back, with its own chronicles of absurdity. A sea-lawyer from Mumbles dies from blisters. It is always opening time in the never-closing Sailors Arms, because the clock has been stuck on half past 11 for 50-odd years. And Nogood Boyo was a fisher who never caught a fish, but did catch a woman called Mrs Samuels. Stories spread in winding whispers, embellished at every turn. The stories are seemingly implausible. But they are without doubt true, ask anyone.
I realised, spending time in Milk Wood, that there are no roadmaps for grief, nor a right way to grieve. Mine proved tragicomic: pain laced in laughter. And I’m lucky because next month, perhaps next year, I can pick up Under Milk Wood and it’s as if I get to see my old man again. I’ll listen to his stories. I’ll get to hear his voice. So, with that in mind, best to depart on the best part, Eli Jenkins’s prayer, and a stanza that truly captures my dad:
 
We are not wholly bad or good
  
Who live our lives under Milk Wood,
  
And Thou, I know, wilt be the first
  
To see our best side, not our worst.

https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.title: ‘Don’t lie to me to get free stuff’: how small businesses are fighting back against influencers
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.author: Zing Tsjeng
https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/n.text:
Nicole Flanagin remembers exactly the moment an influencer came after her business. It was the early hours of a March morning and the cat cafe owner in Lenoir, North Carolina, got a message. “At 1.37,” she says, “a friend sent me the link to this girl’s TikTok.”
The 41-year-old was already having a bad 24 hours. A mother of four, Flanagin also works at a pet rescue shelter and had spent the previous day unsuccessfully fighting for a dog not to be put down. She got home exhausted and promptly conked out in bed. Then she woke up to the message.
The video began innocuously enough with a local influencer sitting in her parked car. “For those of you who know me,” she stated, “I do reviews of local businesses. One very special thing about me is I don’t make bad reviews – but I’m kinda mad right now!” The woman had just taken her child to an unnamed cafe with “animals you can pet”, only to be coldly turned away because she had got its visiting hours wrong. In the influencer’s telling, she began bargaining with staff to try to let the girl into the area where the animals were kept. No dice. Her daughter started “literally bawling her eyes out … and they were just, like, standing there staring”.
Flanagin knew instantly that the woman was talking about her cafe, Brews and Mews – the only animal cafe in the area. The cats are fosters from local shelters, and children aged six and under can only visit during “Happy Meow-ers” sessions, to safeguard the cats’ time away from customers – particularly small, sticky‑fingered ones.
She looked up the woman’s account: she had more than 170,000 followers, some of whom had already started to comment favourably on the post. Flanagin knew it was only a matter of time before internet sleuths tracked down the name of her cafe. “I was, like, I’m going to get crushed. She’s going to close my business.”
But, amid her rising panic, Flanagin had a nagging feeling that something wasn’t quite right. “She attacked my employee and made out he was just staring at her kid wailing on the floor,” she says. But Brews and Mews hadn’t received an official complaint in its inbox. None of her typically conscientious employees had flagged the incident to her. So Flanagin looked up the CCTV. “I love a good receipt,” she tells me. “I’ve been through a divorce, honey.”
Time-stamped footage from security cameras in the cafe showed the influencer entering and having a conversation lasting less than 40 seconds with a staffer behind the till. She and her child briefly looked at the cats in the window before leaving quietly. There was little visible evidence of a toddler tantrum or, indeed, of a rudely gawking employee. “I started watching, and I was, like, ‘This did not happen.’” Flanagin says. A day and a half later, she decided to post the CCTV on the Brews and Mews TikTok page with an outraged comment about the lies the woman had told. That video now has more than 640,000 views.
The content creator later deleted her review and posted an apology video, where she explained: “I was upset as a parent and clicked that post button before I really thought about what would happen.” But the encounter clearly still rankles Flanagin. “Why is your opinion any more valid or important than mine or somebody else’s?” she says today of influencers. “I don’t regret defending myself.”
It may seem extreme to look up surveillance footage in order to prove a content creator wrong, but Flanagin is not the only small-business owner who has resorted to using CCTV. When singer Kelly Clarkson (a celebrity rather than an influencer) posted about what she regarded as bad service at the Art of Play shop in Brooklyn after being told a $15,000 mechanical bird she wanted to buy wasn’t for sale, it went around the world and surveillance footage was posted in response.
Flanagin’s fight was another skirmish on the frontline of a growing war between entrepreneurs and online content creators.The relationship is a complicated one: many business owners are thrilled to have the attention, and know that a post can make a difference. But, increasingly, they are feeling burned by influencers behaving badly, and are taking matters into their own hands. It has led to a takedown economy where the “fightback” can go as viral as a sponsored post. One such example relates to Binky Felstead from Made in Chelsea. When her assistant asked for a free cake for Felstead’s son’s third birthday, the baker snapped, went public, and caused a furore (and got an apology). Some independent shops are banning influencers altogether – and Borough Market in London has clarified its rules on filming, in a crackdown on the plague. How did we get here?
Before the rise of the creator economy, it was only Hollywood actors, star athletes and supermodels who expected celeb treatment. Now that rarefied circle has expanded to include social media influencers and many wannabes. They have sprouted across almost every sector: there are influencers for lawn care, Minecraft, dairy farming and more. But the nature of fame has fragmented, too. You could be lining up for a viral apple crumble next to the biggest food influencer in London and be none the wiser. Your son might be a fan of a Roblox creator with a millions-strong following and you might never recognise their username.
According to Forbes, the influencer economy is worth $250bn and is projected to almost double by 2027. Influencers can shift mountains of product and drive sales for the businesses they choose to work with. That can be transformational, particularly for those that struggle to afford traditional advertising. “Influencers absolutely catapulted my business to where it is now,” says Lucy Herron, the founder of the British shoe-wear brand Sloafer. “You can sell 50 pairs of shoes in 24 hours, and that is the difference between you being able to put a bit of money in your profit pot and not being able to pay your invoices.”
But depending on influencers as a marketing strategy is a double-edged sword. Diva-like behaviour can grow unchecked. Once, Herron sent a free pair of ballerina trainers (retail price £225) to an influencer best known for appearing on a reality show, expecting the customary thank you post on Instagram. Instead, the woman told Herron that she couldn’t publicly thank the brand because it might come to the attention of the tax authorities (according to HMRC, gifted products count towards your taxable income).
After months of back and forth, she reluctantly agreed to post a photo and tag Sloafer. Herron laughed in disbelief when she saw the picture. The woman had worn the black pumps with an all-black outfit and photographed herself standing at the back of a room, her face shrouded in darkness. “It was like collaborating with a ninja,” Herron says. “It sticks in your throat – they could buy a pair of my shoes in every colour and it wouldn’t dent their bank balance.” Still, Herron begrudgingly left a positive comment on the influencer’s page, thanking her for the post. “You have to keep playing the game,” she sighs. (Like all the business owners I spoke to, Herron didn’t want to name names.)
Influencers make for powerful recommendation engines and equally powerful enemies, adept at harnessing their followers’ outrage and weaponising the language of moral virtue. When Four Winds Craft Guild in Nantucket, Massachusetts, went viral after putting up a “no influencers” sign, some creators accused the owner of misogyny. One suggested that hating influencers was a “socially acceptable way to hate women”. “There are obvious valid reasons to criticise influencer culture,” argued the Canadian influencer Levi Coralynn in her video on the controversy, “[but] the conversation has now moved past hating on the industry and people just seem to hate women who participate in it.”
Herron has also been accused of sexism for calling out influencer culture on her social media accounts – particularly when she posted about unfollowing 250 female-owned accounts because she was fed up with sending shoes to influencers who never wore them. “It’s got nothing to do with internalised misogyny,” she tells me. “I’m trying to run a profitable business, and it’s bloody hard enough without someone taking the piss.”
Josh Wheeler, the founder of PR agency Be Broadcast, has worked with influencers for 15 years, often acting as an intermediary between them and brands and businesses. He says there is no one type of influencer most prone to bad behaviour. “I can think of nightmares and angels in all [categories].”
“The view from talent and people smelling the money around influencers is that [they are] the future, so everything has to be bent and broken around that influencer,” he explains. That can lead to mixed results for businesses who are pinning their hopes on an influencer’s reach. “There might be a campaign landing on Monday and the talent pulls out on Friday,” he recalls. “You’re, like, ‘OK, cool. Well, we’ve just spent three months on this.’ We’ve seen talent say to staff, ‘Don’t look me in the eye.’” Another was blacklisted after making “deeply inappropriate” comments about a member of Wheeler’s team on a briefing call. Still, he says, businesses sometimes treat influencers with kid gloves. “There is often a nervousness,” he says. “It’s like they forget they’re in charge.”
Perhaps because of this overweening power, a backlash is brewing against what some see as an increasingly noxious sense of entitlement among influencers. Big corporations can afford to put aside a budget to cover extravagant freebies and press trips, but small indies like Sloafer are “operating on knife‑edge profit margins”, Herron explains. Every pair of shoes sent to an influencer is one that they could sell to a customer, but “you’ve always got that thing in the back of your mind where you know a post could sell 20 pairs of shoes”, she says.
The tantalising possibility of the post that could revitalise your beloved establishment or save your brand is what keeps business owners coming back, says Hubert Zanier, the owner of Kipferl, a London-based restaurant and patisserie that serves Austrian food. In the hospitality industry, influencers have almost completely supplanted the role of the food critic when it comes to spreading the word about their businesses. “A lot of restaurants are struggling,” he says. “They all hope for that one viral post that makes the whole thing explode and pick up.”
Zanier knows this all too well. In 2024, a well‑known London influencer with 100,000 followers left him in the lurch after totting up a £300 bill at his restaurant. The first hint that something was off came when she asked to bring her family – something that Zanier normally wouldn’t accommodate (most restaurants will cover a plus one, but no more). She turned up with her partner, her parents and their dog – and proceeded to order two £38 bottles of red wine and almost £40 worth of schnapps. “My manager texted me and said, ‘Is that OK?’ I was, like, yeah, whatever – maybe we’ll get good coverage out of it.”
Instead, what happened was a months-long dispute between Zanier and the influencer, culminating in the latter calling him after Christmas to scream at him. “I was perplexed,” Zanier says. Typically, influencers will acknowledge a free meal on social media a few days after visiting a restaurant, he explains. But the creator fobbed him off for months. “She started to write really weird stuff, like ‘at the moment my creative juices are not flowing’.” Nine months on – Zanier is nothing if not persistent – the influencer finally gave up and offered to foot the bill. But when he sent it she phoned him up, furiously telling him: “This is absolutely outrageous.”
“I said, ‘I have a small business,’” Zanier recalls. “You exploited and abused my hospitality. I’ve invited you for lunch with wine and everything. I mean, we’re not friends. What’s the deal here?” The influencer conceded that she might include the restaurant in a write-up of European restaurants the year after – at which point he admitted defeat. “I just mentally wrote it off,” he says today. “But it was really, really unpleasant.” He still works with influencers, but is much more selective about who he invites to his restaurant. “I think they are part of the [food] industry now,” he shrugs. “Just because some of them might be black sheep, it doesn’t mean that they’re all crooked.”
But with such “rogue operators” (as Zanier puts it) circling the industry, it’s no wonder that some establishments are vigorously clamping down. When Borough Market security kicked out the food vloggers Bite Twice for filming there in November, it was said to have marked a “Frankenstein moment” for the hospitality business – the industry had created a monster and was now fighting back. The market now enforces rules against the scourge of content creators clogging up stalls and walkways with their equipment – anybody filming with more than a crew of two (presenter and cameraperson) or with professional-grade equipment must now seek clearance and carry their permit with them. It was hailed as a long-overdue rebalancing of the relationship between businesses and influencers – one that puts paying customers first.
Halfsies Cookie Company founder David Maffei usually spends seven days a week, sometimes up to 10 hours a day, baking in his New York kitchen – as a team of one. In Maffei’s eyes, influencers can provide useful PR for a small business like his. When the model Amber Lancaster posted about Halfsies to her half a million followers, he says, “We sold out for months.”
But influencer culture, he argues, has also spawned a generation of entitled imitators who believe that having a small following justifies A-list treatment from brands and businesses. The worst, he says, are those who fire off blandly friendly copy-and-paste messages to multiple companies, hoping someone will take the bait. “They’re, like, ‘Oh, I love your product. They’re such an integral part of my daily life!’” He now collates the cheekiest requests, along with his withering takedowns, on a Hall of Fame category on his Instagram.
“I’d love to include your amazing products in my bridal party boxes,” one such email request went. “Are you in for some bridal bliss? Let’s chat!” After Maffei pointed out that she had only 1,300 followers on Instagram, the bride-to-be argued, “I’m a beginner influencer.”
“And I’m a beginner astronaut,” Maffei replied. He posted screenshots of the exchange on the Halfsies Instagram account, where it received more than 17,000 likes and was even covered by People magazine. “Don’t lie to me to get free stuff,” he says.
“When you get those messages, it’s quite disheartening,” Anastasia Powers, a luxury balloon artist based in Essex, tells me. She has created dramatic displays for weddings, galas and corporate clients such as Zambrero and Twickenham rugby club. In other words, she’s not short of work – she is currently in the middle of talks with a celebrity DJ to create a display for his birthday – but still receives up to 10 freebie requests a month. “You’ve contacted me, so you can see the quality of my work – yet you want it for free and you don’t want to pay me my worth.” Powers sighs.
She founded Poptastic Balloon Company three years ago and is a one-woman business, doing everything from designing the display, driving to the location, and sizing and shaping the helium balloons to packing it all down at the end of the day. “Collaborations don’t pay for my petrol, my lights, my stock,” Powers says firmly. “They don’t put food on my table.”
She has a policy of turning down all influencer requests and says that other people in her industry are increasingly coming over to her way of thinking. She is in a WhatsApp group chat with fellow business owners to share intel about the worst offenders. “We’ll screenshot the messages, and we’ll all laugh,” she smiles. “Sometimes we’ll coordinate a reply and we’ll all send it to them, which is quite funny.”
Reshmi Bennett is the Michelin-trained founder of the luxury cake business Anges de Sucre, who made headlines for calling out Made in Chelsea’s Felstead after receiving an email requesting a “gifted” cake for her son Wilder. (Felstead is estimated to be worth between £1.4m and £3m and lives in a £3.6m south-west London house, which is, according to the Daily Mail, largely furnished with freebies.) The former banker turned chef was incensed: “Your whole persona is to be rich and fabulous, and here you are grifting for free stuff to pretend you’re rich and fabulous to your followers.”
Bennett’s cakes are expensive and artisanal work – she runs a team of three full-time staff and one part-timer to make towering creations that are hand‑delivered across London and Surrey. “Even though £100 is a lot for the average person to pay for a cake, the costs involved in us making the cake and getting it to the customer have just ballooned,” she explains.
Bennett took to Instagram to call Felstead out, even creating a joke fundraiser for the influencer to cover the cost of her son’s birthday cake. “Unfortunately,” Bennett noted on the now-deleted GoFundMe page, “our energy supplier is old-fashioned and continues to insist on being paid in actual money rather than exposure or engagement”. (A representative for Felstead later said: “This was a standard inquiry from Binky’s PA, offering social media exposure in exchange for a birthday cake.”)
Bennett, 42, has been burned by working for free in the past. An influencer with about 20,000 followers once asked for a birthday cake for her child. As the influencer was local to the area, Bennett hoped it might lead to more customers in the neighbourhood. But when the pictures were posted on Instagram, Bennett’s cake was one of many treats on a dessert table that included cookies, doughnuts and even cakes from her competitors. Worst of all, she only received a single inquiry as a result. It said: “Oh, hi, it’s my daughter’s birthday. Would you like to collaborate?”
“Piss off!” she laughs. “Work for free to get more free work? No thanks … I’ve set a filter in my inbox to put emails that have the word ‘sponsorship’ or ‘collaboration’ into spam.”
Cynics might observe that calling out these influencers can be a way to drive attention to your own brand. With the Clarkson case, the jury is out as to whether Art of Play’s response – contesting her account and jokily raising the price of the bird to $15m – was the right one. Still, negativity is the life force of the internet – one study has found that negative posts attract twice as much engagement as positive ones. In much the same way that “de-influencing” videos of creators criticising viral products became a trend in and of itself, negative posts about influencers have become their own cottage industry, with content creators on YouTube breaking down social media beefs for their followers.
But Bennett says that a no-holds-barred approach doesn’t always go down well if you’re a business trying to sell people your product. “I have got some stick,” she acknowledges. “It’s, like, you could just politely say no and move on. If I do, they just find someone else to [take my place], and it keeps that cycle going.” The answer, she says, is for small-business owners to speak out and share what it’s like to work with influencers – the good, the bad and the ugly. Wheeler, of Be Broadcast, advises businesses to be clear about their expectations when approaching influencers, including getting what they want in exchange in writing. “That early stage is genuinely vital to make sure that your experience doesn’t go pear‑shaped,” he says.
Back in Lenoir, North Carolina, Flanagin is gearing up for the morning shift at Brews and Mews. While she has received support from all over the world after she posted her video, the local community on Facebook have been firmly on the side of the influencer. Critics have said that she should have tried to handle it privately or not posted footage featuring the influencer’s children. “Locally, we’re the devil, yet we’re the first [place] that people call when they find a cat!” Still, her video is staying up. “I don’t regret it, honey. I said it with my whole chest,” she says. “And I would say it all day, every day, again and again.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Ronaldo-less Portugal thrashed 4-1 by Denmark in the Nations League
Rasmus Hojlund stars with brace as Denmark close in on a spot in the Nations League quarterfinals.
Portugal have been hammered 1-4 by Denmark, an embarrassing Nations League defeat in their first match without Cristiano Ronaldo, following the superstar forward’s retirement from international football.
Rasmus Hojlund starred with a superb brace on Saturday as second place Denmark close in on a spot in the quarterfinals with a brilliant display in Braga.
The Danes are on nine points from five fixtures, three behind Portugal, who were already sure of qualification for the last eight having won all four of their previous group fixtures.
A draw against third-placed Norway on Tuesday, 3-1 winners over Wales earlier, will see Denmark through.
Ahead of kickoff, Portugal paid tribute to Ronaldo, who announced his exit from the international game last week, with the team and mascots walking out wearing Ronaldo’s number seven and his name on their jerseys.
Fans held up a huge banner that read “Thank you, captain” as the teams entered the field, while applause rolled around the stadium once the match clock hit seven.
Ronaldo made his debut for Portugal in 2003 and went on to establish world records for goals and appearances in international football, netting 146 times in 234 matches.
The highlight of his international career was winning Euro 2016, but it ended badly when the 41-year-old fell out with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus over not being selected for a Nations League fixture in September.
That row led to the five-time Ballon d’Or winner being handed a 30-day suspension by the Portuguese football federation and his subsequent retirement, and Portugal, in a dismal display, looked like they needed prime Ronaldo.
Denmark were the better team from the first minute, and it was no surprise when the away team went in at the break thanks to Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg’s spot-kick in the 43rd minute.
Hojlund lashed home a brilliant volley four minutes after the restart, and seven minutes later left the home crowd shell-shocked with a strike of which Ronaldo would have been proud – the Napoli striker skipped past Ruben Dias before crashing home a powerful shot from the edge of the area.
Boos and whistles began to ring out at Estadio Municipal when Joachim Andersen headed in the fourth, and Bernardo Silva’s late consolation effort barely dampened the discontent.
Earlier on Saturday, Antonio Nusa opened the scoring for Norway just before the hour mark in Oslo with a fine low strike, before Andreas Schjelderup tapped home a perfect low cross from Erling Haaland, who rounded off the scoring from the penalty spot two minutes from time.
Wales briefly had hope of getting a result when David Brooks’s chipped finish halved the deficit in the 79th minute, but Craig Bellamy’s team will finish bottom of the group and risk being relegated to League B.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
Europe’s direct engagement with Moscow as part of Ukraine-Russia peace talks is edging closer to becoming a reality.
US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to move peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner told reporters Saturday that “both sides” know that compromises will be necessary to end the war, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on next steps.
Trump son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange.
The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not think it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.
The Kremlin has signalled an openness to negotiations with Europe, but it has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.
The five countries attending are the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland – the five countries that have signalled readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said that the bloc must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.
Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.
Zelenskyy said Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO.
The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Russia’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: US Olympic hero Kayla Harrison chokes out Amanda Nunes in fourth round to retain UFC title
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Kayla Harrison retained her UFC women’s bantamweight championship with a fourth-round submission of Amanda Nunes on Saturday night at Madison Square Garden, spoiling the comeback bid of the woman widely regarded as the greatest female fighter in MMA history.
Harrison (20-1) had plenty to prove in her first title defense against Nunes, who ended a three-year retirement for the long-awaited showdown. It was also Harrison’s first fight since June 2025, after spinal fusion surgery in January to address a neck injury forced the postponement of the bout.
Nunes (23-6) tried to wrestle with the two-time Olympic judo gold medalist and ended the first two rounds flat on her back. Harrison landed a series of short punches and elbows to the head that seemed to tire her out – she later acknowledged the difficulty of cutting weight to 135lb – as much as they damaged Nunes.
Harrison, who walked out to Eye of the Tiger while the fighter known as the Lioness stretched and bounced on her tiptoes ahead of Bruce Buffer’s introductions, wasted no time in the fourth round. Harrison grabbed Nunes by her right leg and tripped her to the canvas before taking her back and applying a rear-naked choke. Nunes quickly tapped out, to the astonishment of the packed Garden crowd.
“I think I’m still in shock,” Harrison said.
Nunes may be considered the greatest fighter in the sport’s history. Harrison staked her claim as the best right now.
Nunes walked out of the octagon on her own, while a victorious but weakened Harrison needed help returning to the locker room, championship belt firmly around her waist.
“I’ve got a lot of decisions to make when I get home,” Harrison said. “Every time I make weight, I say never again, so we’ll see.”
A UFC Hall of Famer, Nunes held championships in two weight classes, lost only once in 12 previous UFC title bouts and defeated the once-indomitable Ronda Rousey. She retired in 2023, citing burnout and a desire to spend more time with her wife as they raised their two young daughters.
She could return to retirement with her legacy as one of the sport’s greatest fighters secure.
Ciryl Gane successfully defended his UFC heavyweight championship against Josh Hokit in the main event.
US president Donald Trump has attended UFC events at the Garden in the past but was absent on Saturday night. Trump said last week he was offering UFC chief Dana White the job of White House press secretary, although he later said he was joking.
After bringing UFC to the White House lawn this summer, Trump brought White into the press briefing room on Monday. Trump briefly stood aside as White took questions.
White occupied his usual cageside seat and celebrated the promotion’s achievements over the decade since professional MMA was legalized in New York.
Conor McGregor won the lightweight championship in the main event of UFC’s debut card at Madison Square Garden 10 years ago. Georges St-Pierre, Daniel Cormier and Jon Jones are among the fighters who have won major championship bouts at MSG, where headlining the annual card has become a career goal for many champions.
Some fighters simply want to go out on top in New York.
Stephen Thompson had fans chanting his “Wonderboy” nickname during his retirement fight against Charles Radtke in a welterweight bout. Thompson, 43, who twice challenged for the welterweight championship, won by third-round stoppage with a spinning wheel kick to Radtke’s head. UFC played a video tribute to Thompson afterward.
“I told myself I wasn’t going to cry,” Thompson said, his voice catching. “We wouldn’t have this sport if it wasn’t for my fans.”
Thompson laid his gloves on the mat, the traditional symbolic farewell of a fighter entering retirement.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Francophone summit opens in Cambodia amid Rwanda-DR Congo rift
Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda clash over who should lead the organisation of French-speaking nations.
Leaders of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) are meeting in Cambodia amid a dispute between the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda over who should lead the association of French-speaking nations, which threatens to split the group.
The OIF is holding a three-day summit in the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh, through Monday. A loose confederation of 90 states and governments where French is spoken or widely used, the OIF has 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers.
French President Emmanuel Macron, who chaired the last summit in 2024 and will hand the chair to Cambodia, arrived on Saturday and met Prime Minister Hun Manet, The Associated Press news agency reported.
About 20 leaders are expected, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Vietnamese President To Lam, Rwandan President Paul Kagame and DRC President Felix Tshisekedi.
A fight over the top job
On Monday, leaders will choose the organisation’s next secretary-general for a four-year term.
Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo, who has led the OIF since 2018, is seeking a third term.
The DRC, however, which accuses Rwanda of backing the M23 armed group in the country’s east, has threatened to leave the OIF if she is re-elected. Congo, the United States and United Nations experts say Rwanda backs the M23, one of about 100 armed groups in the mineral-rich region.
Rwanda denies the allegations.
On Saturday, the DRC withdrew its candidate, Juliana Lumumba, the daughter of independence hero Patrice Lumumba, and backed Romanian former Prime Minister Dacian Ciolos to allow “consensus around a unifying candidacy”.
Rwanda’s foreign minister, Olivier Nduhungirehe, said Mushikiwabo would stay in the race. Mauritania’s Coumba Ba, a former minister, is also running, the AFP news agency reported.
Macron’s office said that most members agreed on the need for consensus and that he would take it up with his African counterparts. France is the biggest contributor to the OIF’s 2026 budget of 71.7 million euros ($79m).
Rwanda has said Macron asked Kagame to withdraw its candidate and that Kigali refused, AFP reported.
The DRC has a population of more than 110 million, roughly 40 million more than France, and is the most populous country where French is an official language. Its exit would be a blow to the organisation, which lost Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso, which announced their withdrawals in March 2025 following suspensions over military coups.
Cambodia in the spotlight
The summit’s slogan is “Reinvest in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability”. Activists see it as a chance to press Cambodia, a de facto one-party state, on rights.
UN Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews urged delegates to press for the release of detained activists. “No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions,” he said.
Macron arrived as France faces widespread protests at home. He is due to visit the Angkor World Heritage Site on Monday before leaving for Malaysia.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘We need to get back to class’: some teachers lose patience as France enters its eighth week of student protests
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Vincennes and Paris
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
For several weeks, Alex, 16, has woken at 4am and walked 90 minutes in the dark from his northern Paris suburb so he can help gather wheelie bins to blockade his high school in Vincennes.
In a tote bag, he brings some masks and some swimming goggles in case of police teargas. His parents, who work in the arts and vote left, support the French school student protesters who since September have blocked schools demanding repairs to dilapidated school buildings, more replacement teachers, a solution to overcrowded classes and more equality in the university application system.
“But this week, my mum woke up early and said to me: ‘Do you really think you need to blockade again today?’’ said Alex. “She supports me but is starting to think I’m doing too much. But how else can we make ourselves heard? We can’t stop now. It’s the only way the government will listen.”
His 17-year-old friend, also on the school barricade with dozens of pupils this week, said: “Any progress that has been won in France has been achieved through people demonstrating on the street.”
France is entering the eighth week of an unprecedented schools crisis. The biggest youth protest movement in decades has over the past two months seen hundreds of high schools barricaded with wheelie bins or shut amid security fears.
The government is now facing criticism of its handling of the crisis. It first responded with a security crackdown, mobilising riot police outside schools across France amid clashes that led to injuries from police weaponry, including children who lost a hand or an eye.
Then over the past two weeks, the government attempted to argue that its offer to decrease some class sizes and review the university application platform meant the movement was coming to an end.
But in recent days, the government has been accused by teachers’ unions of letting the protests fester into an increasingly dangerous mood of violence. Fireworks have been fired outside schools and inside classrooms in different parts of France.
A local councillor outside Paris was hit in the chest by a bottle of gasoline as she was trying to mediate outside a school. One education trade unionist said a school principal had bought a bulletproof vest for protection.
The government and teachers’ unions have said that individuals committing violence outside or inside schools were not the same people as students who were peacefully protesting for education rights.
But high school principals held their own demonstrations on Friday, saying they were struggling to cope with the confusion and chaos. At least 50 principals have made requests to quit their posts. More than 360 schoolchildren and 245 staff have been injured since the protests started.
So many weeks of classes have now been missed that one teacher, who demonstrated outside a central Paris police station this week after one of her pupils was arrested, said: “There is absolute uncertainty over how we can return to proper teaching. This is becoming an intractable situation with no end in sight.”
Thousands of French children in key baccalauréat (the French A-levels) exam years – even children who are not protesting directly – have now missed up to 150 hours of teaching at schools that have been barricaded daily or closed regularly for security reasons since the end of September. This is particularly acute in the Paris area, and in other cities such as Toulouse.
Online lessons have rarely fully replaced missed classes. Many teenagers are at home in their fourth or fifth week of no school. Some parents are beginning to wake early to stand outside schools themselves to try to individually stop wheelie bin barricades – sometimes leading to more clashes.
Police are increasingly stationed outside schools, sometimes hitting students’ hands with truncheons to make them loosen their grip on bins, as happened in central Paris this week.
“The French administration is trying to impose a kind of smokescreen of wishful thinking, that everything is alright, stiff-upper-lip, no problem, but everyone needs to face up to what is happening,” said Julien Roy, 52, who teaches history and geography at Lycée Balzac in the central city of Tours and represents the SNALC education union in Indre-et-Loire. “There is a crisis of trust. We need a de-escalation of violence and a path back to education.”
Roy’s school has been at the centre of the protests since the end of September when, on the pavement outside, a 16-year-old school student from a different school, lost the use of his eye after he was allegedly struck by a police rubber bullet.
“There is still constant tension,” said Roy. He added that in recent weeks firework mortars had been set off, sometimes aimed at staff, and fires had been started in bins and materials for molotov cocktails were found in a building opposite the school.
Police were regularly present. Staff felt individuals not connected to the school were involved in the violence. He said stress was taking a toll on staff: 10 colleagues were on sick leave, including his principal and deputy principal.
“We need to get back to class to teach our pupils again, some of whom are booing us,” Roy said. “We’ll have to sit down and talk about this, honestly and calmly, to get it out of everyone’s system so we can restore trust.”
He said: “There are children who are suffering, and many of them we’re not seeing because they are stuck at home. Some pupils approach school, see the police, panic and go away, because they can’t bear this atmosphere with police outside school. There are fragile teenagers with difficulties at school who can’t come in, and those children are shattered by this.”
He said: “What is lethal is that we’re leading children to conclude that it’s only through violence that they can be heard, that violence is legitimate and nothing can be gained through negotiation … this is going to leave an impact on society, creating future adults who are going to feel bitter and broken.”
At a high school in the Créteil area, an English teacher said: “I feel proud of my students’ peaceful protests. The children demonstrating are asking for the same thing teachers have wanted for years: more resources, more dignity in teaching environments. Teachers’ strikes haven’t been listened to, whereas students see they are having an impact.
“But with a presidential election next spring, and the start of electoral season, it’s difficult to imagine that this is going to stop. I do worry about students’ exams. One former colleague said to me that this school year could be a write-off.”
Students’ names have been changed

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: New York Democratic Socialists urge Ocasio-Cortez to run for US president
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
New York Democratic Socialists urge Ocasio-Cortez to run for US president
Delegates at NYC-DSA convention pass resolution formally calling on Congresswoman AOC to run in 2028 presidential race.
The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has voted to urge Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for United States president in 2028, a move that could serve as an early bellwether for the Democratic Party’s direction in the presidential race.
The resolution passed 291 to 123 at the chapter’s convention on Saturday. While it is not a formal endorsement by the DSA, it commits the New York City chapter to encouraging a presidential bid and building the groundwork for a potential campaign.
“If the US can elect Trump, I think we can elect Democratic Socialists,” Gustavo Gordillo, NYC-DSA co-chair, told Al Jazeera, referring to President Donald Trump.
The convention was held following a strong showing by DSA-endorsed candidates in the midterm elections. A record eight DSA-endorsed candidates were elected to federal office and will hold congressional seats in January.
Ocasio-Cortez, popularly known as AOC, is a longtime member of NYC-DSA, the chapter covering her home city. The New York City branch, which has about 15,000 members, has become one of the movement’s most influential. It endorsed Mayor Zohran Mamdani last year and has backed Ocasio-Cortez in all five of her congressional general elections since 2018.
That electoral influence has given the chapter a prominent voice in shaping the direction of progressive politics in the US.
“Now that we have put a mayor into City Hall and we’ve elected three socialists in the city, I think regardless of how a politician feels about DSA personally, they’re definitely looking at what we say and how we’re moving,” NYC-DSA co-chair Grace Mausser said. “We are one of the biggest political actors in the city, in the state, and the country, frankly.”
Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat representing New York’s 14th congressional district, rose to national prominence in 2018 after defeating a 10-term incumbent in a congressional primary. A prominent Democratic Socialist, she has advocated for policies including universal healthcare, tuition-free public college and labour protections.
The chapter has yet to finalise a national presidential platform. Mausser said it would be built around issues members encounter when speaking with voters.
“The top issues at the doors that we encounter are housing, healthcare, childcare – the hallmarks of affordability,” Mausser said. “Those would all become the core of a federal platform.”
The resolution text says the campaign would provide an opportunity for “continued crafting of a platform that engages the working class”. It also identifies public housing, stopping the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency, labour organising and “the anti-war and pro-Palestine movements” as priorities.
The NYC-DSA vote adds to mounting efforts on the left to persuade Ocasio-Cortez to enter the 2028 presidential race, following a debate within the national DSA over her possible endorsement and the launch of an independent campaign urging her to run, called “Ready for AOC”.
Ocasio-Cortez has previously she will decide on her political future after the midterm elections, leaving open the possibility of a 2028 presidential bid or a challenge for a US Senate seat.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Zimbabwe’s HIV gains face a test among young people
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Zimbabwe’s HIV gains face a test among young people
New prevention tools offer hope, but reaching young people remains a challenge.
Harare, Zimbabwe – When Shaun Moyo started nursing at Parirenyatwa Hospital in Harare in the late 1990s, the effects of the HIV epidemic were visible in the hospital wards and beyond them. Patients filled the wards, she recalls, while funerals had become a familiar part of everyday life.
Nearly three decades later, the picture has changed. Antiretroviral treatment has transformed the lives of people living with HIV. Condoms, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) and other prevention options also give young people more ways to protect themselves.
But Moyo, now a 48-year-old nurse working locum shifts at two major public hospitals in Harare, worries that some young people may not fully appreciate the risks.
Her concern reflects a wider challenge for Zimbabwe: how to protect hard-won progress against HIV while ensuring that young people understand, can access and are willing to use the prevention tools available to them.
Dr Misheck Ruwende, a Zimbabwean family physician and advocate for reducing HIV stigma, shares that concern. In a public address on Twitter in September, followed online by Al Jazeera, members of the public and other local journalists, Ruwende warned that the country risked losing some of the gains made over decades.
“The sad part is that this is coming at a time we have the best options to prevent HIV, from rapid testing, PrEP, condoms, PEP to injectables,” Ruwende said.
“It wasn’t like that in the late 90s to early 2000s. It looks like we are now reversing all this huge success we had notched in recent times,” he added.
The scale of Zimbabwe’s progress is clear in the national figures. UNAIDS estimates that annual new HIV infections fell from 79,000 in 2010 to 15,000 in 2023. Among people aged 15 to 24, infections declined from an estimated 27,000 to 4,400 over the same period.
But falling infections do not mean the threat has disappeared. The challenge is to sustain those gains among young people navigating relationships, economic pressures and uneven access to youth-friendly health services. It is a challenge shared across a region that continues to carry a heavy burden of HIV.
A generation that has forgotten the fear
For Moyo, the contrast between the epidemic she witnessed as a young nurse and the attitudes she encounters today can be difficult to accept.
“Seeing today’s youth who are blessed with condoms, ARVs and PrEP meds makes me furious,” she said. “In the 90s every weekend was a trek to cemeteries, not weddings.”
She believes the availability of effective treatment has changed how some young people perceive HIV. Because the virus is no longer the immediate death sentence it was once widely understood to be, she worries that some underestimate the consequences of infection.
Moyo recalled conversations involving her son and his friends on Facebook, where one comment suggested that “getting blood pressure is worse than HIV”.
Her observations are personal, not scientific evidence of changing attitudes among young people. But they point to a difficult public health task: explaining why prevention remains important even though treatment has made HIV a manageable chronic condition for many.
The concern is not confined to Zimbabwe. UNAIDS estimated that 210,000 adolescent girls and young women aged 15 to 24 acquired HIV worldwide in 2023. Some 160,000 of those infections were in sub-Saharan Africa, while nearly 60 percent of the global total occurred in Eastern and Southern Africa.
A regional warning
South Africa, Zimbabwe’s neighbour, illustrates the continuing scale of the epidemic in the region. UNAIDS estimated that 7.7 million people were living with HIV there in 2023.
Data from Gauteng province also point to concerns about sexually transmitted infections. Between April and December 2023, 167,109 males attended public health facilities in the province, and 67,400 were treated for Male Urethritis Syndrome (MUS), which is associated with sexually transmitted infections. The provincial health department reported that MUS incidence increased from 12 percent in 2020 to 15 percent in 2023. The condition is not itself a measure of HIV infections.
For Dr Linda-Gail Bekker, a South African HIV physician-scientist and co-author of the report on the PURPOSE 1 clinical trial, the response must combine scientific advances with prevention messages that speak to young people.
The Phase 3 trial examined lenacapavir, an injectable HIV prevention drug administered twice a year. In its primary analysis, none of the 2,134 women who received the drug acquired HIV.
The results highlighted the potential of long-acting prevention, but Bekker argues that medical advances must be matched by communication that resonates with young people.
“Beating the old drum about the horrors of HIV, and shouting to youths about condoms is not necessarily going to cut it,” she said.
She believes prevention efforts need to move beyond fear-based messages and give young people accurate information, accessible services and the freedom to make informed decisions without judgement.
Reaching young people differently
That task has become more difficult amid funding pressures. UNAIDS reported in March 2025 that disruptions to US-funded HIV programmes in Zimbabwe had affected services for key populations, including access to PrEP, testing and counselling.
Bekker has also raised concerns about whether prevention information reaches young people in ways they find relevant. Traditional pamphlets and warnings about abstinence or faithfulness may fail to engage those already making decisions about sex and relationships.
She argues that public health workers need to acknowledge young people’s realities and provide practical information about reducing risk, including through PrEP. Services must also be adolescent-friendly, allowing young people to ask questions and seek help without feeling judged.
In Harare, 23-year-old peer educator Angela Gutu is taking that message beyond the clinic.
Working with the Harare municipality, the health ministry, nongovernmental organisations and churches, she helps organise pop-up health services at markets, transport hubs, university campuses and sporting events. These are places young people already visit, bringing information and services closer to them rather than expecting them to navigate a formal health facility.
The distinction matters, Gutu says. For some young people, asking for an HIV test or screening for a sexually transmitted infection at a clinic can be intimidating. Fear of judgement or harsh treatment by health workers can discourage them from seeking help.
At the pop-up clinics, young people can access HIV self-testing kits and condoms, while mobile health workers provide referrals for PrEP and other services. Peer educators can help make those conversations less daunting, giving young people an opportunity to ask questions in an environment where they feel more comfortable.
“It’s about speaking young people’s lingo, taking away the HIV stigma,” Gutu said.
Her work reflects a growing recognition that making prevention services available is not enough. They must also be approachable, confidential and responsive to the concerns young people bring with them.
Taking healthcare beyond hospitals
Zimbabwe’s health authorities say they are also working to bring prevention and treatment closer to communities.
Dr Innocent Hove, Provincial Medical Officer for Harare Metropolitan Province, told reporters, including Al Jazeera, at an August meeting that tackling HIV among young Zimbabweans was an urgent priority.
The government is decentralising services including PrEP, PEP, HIV testing and treatment, as well as screening and treatment for sexually transmitted infections and tuberculosis.
Hove also pointed to mobile healthcare trucks being used to reach people in areas where conventional health facilities are difficult to access, including informal mining communities and remote artisanal gold-mining sites.
Such outreach could help people whose work, distance from clinics or financial circumstances make regular visits difficult. But its impact will depend on whether services are consistently available and reach those most in need.
For young people, access means more than knowing that PrEP or HIV testing exists. It means being able to obtain services without prohibitive costs, long journeys or fear of stigma.
Bongani, who plans to volunteer as a peer educator through the health ministry’s programme in January, wants to help make prevention information more accessible to his generation.
“My generation was born with the best array of HIV prevention tools. It’ll be a tragedy if AIDS deaths make a dramatic comeback due to our reckless behaviours,” he said.

Trump may not attack Iran as long as it doesn't provoke US, report says
President Donald Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, according to three people familiar with the matter.
Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict, which he launched in February with Israel.
But in meetings with his national security advisers and after a series of intelligence briefings, Trump said he was considering holding off on strikes, said the people, who, like others interviewed for this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.
He has also indicated sympathy for allies in the region who have asked him not to return to a full-fledged war.
"I could end it immediately, but at the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly," Trump told sports broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday.
Trump's private comments build on public remarks playing down the likelihood of major warfare resuming.
CALLS WITH SAUDI ARABIA AND TURKEY
In phone calls over the past two weeks, Trump asked for opinions from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, who both urged him not to resume attacks on Iran, according to a senior US official and another person familiar with the matter. They said Trump made no commitment either way.
Trump told bin Salman on 31 October that he was planning to attack after the elections, but the crown prince pleaded for him to hold off, arguing that economic sanctions against Iran were working, according to two more people familiar with the discussion.
Saudi Arabia's Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump has spoken with Erdogan three times since 28 October, according to Turkey's presidency. An official readout from the 7 November call stressed that tensions between Iran and the US need to end.
MILITARY OPTIONS
At the same time, the US military is ready to escalate if needed, three more people familiar with US planning said.
A third aircraft carrier is moving into the Middle East in the coming days to replace one of the two currently operating in the region, but all three carriers could stay if needed, the people said.
Trump could opt to bomb Iran's underground nuclear facilities, one of the people familiar with Trump's calls with the Saudi and Turkish leaders said. But the US has already struck those facilities, and it is unclear whether further strikes would be successful.
ISRAELI PRESSURE
Israeli officials have continued to lobby the administration to engage in another military campaign, according to a US official.
Trump signalled this week that the US has already achieved what it could from negotiations, but did not say whether he would resume strikes.
Report by Reuters

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
Fighting escalates in Yemen’s Marib and al-Jawf, as UN migration agency says more than 340,000 Yemenis displaced since August.
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis have said they intercepted two missiles and five drones targeting different parts of the country, allegedly launched by the Iran-backed rebel group.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards Riyadh,” Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, said in a post on X early on Sunday.
He said the coalition forces also shot down three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern region on Sunday.
Earlier on Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones “were intercepted and destroyed” in the Riyadh and southern regions.
Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), claimed to have shot down an armed Saudi coalition reconnaissance aircraft carrying out “hostile operations in the airspace of al-Jawf”.
In a post on X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-aligned group was able to “repel a number of Saudi military formations using several Yemeni-made surface-to-air missiles” and that it was the fifth aircraft the Houthis had shot down since the escalation began.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom’s authorities.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, as well as the East-West pipeline and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.
The interceptions come as the Saudi-led forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government also said they intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces had made gains against the Houthis during heavy fighting in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf, as fighting intensified in Marib.
Al-Nuzaili said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in the Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and that 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group had been destroyed.
The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes and 56 drone attacks, as well as 541 artillery strikes.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the Saudi-led coalition had launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in the Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
He said the Houthis targeted Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of the Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported that two women and two children were injured as a result of artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital controlled by the Houthis.
More than 340,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Security alert
As the fight between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise “heightened vigilance”, citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks.
The embassy said Houthi attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia had “caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions”, warning that hostilities could spread “rapidly”.
“Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia,” it said.
