Iraq PM sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran stronghold
Dismissals follow probe that uncovered illegal oil refineries and smuggling in a region run by Kataib Hezbollah, a pro-Iranian armed group.
Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed nine senior security officials over an alleged oil smuggling operation in the Jurf al-Nasr area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group.
Al-Zaidi chaired an emergency security meeting to review the findings of a committee investigating smuggling in Jurf al-Nasr, Babil province, military spokesperson Sabah al-Numan told the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
The move follows an investigation that uncovered illegal oil refineries and evidence of manipulation linked to the smuggling activities.
“In light of the investigation’s findings, [the prime minister] ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary,” al-Numan said.
The prime minister “also ordered the dismissal” of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil, he said.
The police chief of Babil province was among those dismissed.
Iran-aligned armed group
Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-aligned paramilitary group and one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, has recently issued several sharp statements against the prime minister, threatening his government and accusing him of corruption.
Senior Iraqi politicians previously told the AFP news agency that al-Zaidi had repeatedly said he was ready to confront groups refusing to disarm.
Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, said previous Iraqi governments had been careful not to address the issue of an alleged oil smuggling network worth up to $30m monthly.
“This area had effectively been run as a state within a state until now,” Smith said. “But that seems to have changed, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi saying that no inch of Iraq will be allowed to have oil smuggling operations like this.”
Two strategic oil pipelines running through the south of the country, just south of Baghdad, “had effectively been tapped into”, Smith said, citing a leaked intelligence report. “Oil was being siphoned off, stolen, and then sold on the black market in an operation worth tens of millions of dollars every month.”
On Wednesday, the INA reported that “intelligence documents” containing satellite images “showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction” in Jurf al-Nasr, accusing an unnamed group of tapping into a pipeline there.
Al-Numan said the investigating committee “confirmed the accuracy” of the information.
Akeel Abbas, a senior non-resident fellow at the Iraq Initiative within the Atlantic Council, told Al Jazeera that oil smuggling by various political factions and armed groups “is common in Iraq” due to “commercial rather than political or strategic” gains.
Abbas said the latest crackdown has more to do with “militia disarmament”.
“The prime minister cleverly decided to frame it as anticorruption. That is why a few days ago, there was a report leaked by the government about this operation,” he said.
The prime minister wants to “cut off the financial lifeline to this particular group that has been so resistant” to the government’s “militia disarmament” initiatives, he added.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Hundreds of men march in Switzerland to protest violence against women
Organisers say men must speak out, as Swiss study finds half of men aged 18 to 24 hold restrictive view of masculinity.
Hundreds of men have led a demonstration in Switzerland’s capital, Bern, to denounce misogyny and violence against women, saying men need to take a more effective role in fighting both.
The “Men Against Violence Against Women” rally outside parliament on Saturday follows persistent concerns that misogyny is too prevalent online among teenage boys and young men and that other men need to build a stronger counter-narrative.
The misogynistic views are pushed by the right-wing “manosphere” – a loose network of online forums and influencers that promote male supremacy and hostility to feminism. Such influencers were emboldened after Donald Trump won the US presidential election in 202 to justify and amplify misogynistic derision and threats online.
“We men are part of the problem – the problem being violence against women and queer people,” said Christoph Gosteli, a 42-year-old social worker who co-organised the rally with a group called maenner.
“That is why it is important for us to take a stand and say, ‘We no longer want to be part of the problem; we want to be part of the solution.’”
An academic and advocacy group survey released in June by the University of Zurich and MenCare, an umbrella group of Swiss men’s and fathers’ organisations, found that half of male respondents aged 18 to 24 held a “restrictive and dominance-based view of masculinity”, expressing concerns that “real men are increasingly marginalised in society”.
The study called for “a systematic and society-wide debate about ideals of masculinity that promote violence”, beginning in schools.
Swiss Justice Minister Beat Jans attended a conference earlier this month on the dangers of violent online abuse of women.
In a speech on November 2, he said that men commit four-fifths of violent crimes and that in rape cases, the share is “as high as 99 percent”.
“It is not all men. But we must also admit: It is almost always men,” Jans said. “Violence by men does not begin with the first blow; it begins with a disparaging remark. We men all have a duty.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
SpaceX’s Starship captured by launchpad arms in dramatic first
SpaceX officials say catch by mechanical arms shows Starship’s full reusability, crucial for rapid, low-cost recycling.
SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft has returned to Earth, caught midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.
The spaceship emerged from a cloudy sky on Saturday, descending slowly over Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 in Texas – the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space.
Soon afterwards, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk congratulated his “incredible team”.
SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates Starship’s full reusability, crucial for rapid, low-cost recycling.
However, with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.
Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.
SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it was not in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.
Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.
NASA, which is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the Moon later this decade, welcomed the achievement.
“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on X.
Starship completed 14 laps around the Earth, 265km (165 miles), outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.
It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
Starship, a 124-metre (407ft) behemoth, is the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, intended for Moon and Mars travel.
SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Andreeva to face Svitolina in WTA Finals showpiece as Sabalenka apologises
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Tumaini Carayol
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The rise of Mirra Andreeva has seemed inevitable ever since she burst on to the tour as a precocious 15-year-old more than three years ago, but this week, six months after her maiden grand slam triumph at Roland Garros, she has taken another massive step forward in her career. The 19-year-old will attempt to close out the most impressive week of her career by winning one of her most significant titles after thoroughly outplaying Jessica Pegula, the fifth seed, 6-3, 6-4 to reach the championship match of the WTA Finals at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.
A year ago, Andreeva surprisingly failed to qualify for the WTA Finals, missing out by a paltry six points after bizarrely deciding not to compete in the final tournament week before the event. The world No 3 has been utterly supreme in her long-awaited debut appearance, bulldozing through elite opposition to reach the final without dropping a set. She has conceded just 18 games in four matches this week, including a 6-4, 6-0 demolition of the No 1 seed Aryna Sabalenka, winning 11 games in succession from 1-4 down.
Andreeva will rise to No 2 in the WTA rankings for the first time in her career on Monday regardless of the outcome here. The world No 1, Elena Rybakina, and No 3, Sabalenka, will both be defending a large number of points at the Australian Open after Rybakina defeated Sabalenka in this year’s final, which means the No 1 ranking will almost certainly be a realistic target for Andreeva at the start of the 2027 season, particularly if she closes out this imperious week with a title.
The Russian will face Ukraine’s Elina Svitolina after Svitolina dominated the Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova in the second semi-final, rolling to a 6-2, 6-0 win. Svitolina, who also beat Sabalenka this week, will be attempting to win the WTA Finals for a second time after first lifting the trophy in 2018. This will be a rematch of their encounter earlier this week during the group stage, which Andreeva easily won 6-4, 6-0.
Elsewhere, Sabalenka issued a public apology on Saturday after being accused of making offensive remarks towards Svitolina during Friday’s match. An angry Sabalenka was caught on camera making a comment between points, which some social media users interpreted as an offensive insult against her Ukrainian opponent.
“My comment was not directed at Elina,” Sabalenka said in a social media post.
“I was frustrated with a small group of spectators who were aggressively cheering my mistakes, and I reacted emotionally in the moment. That said, I should have handled my frustration differently, and I apologise to anyone I offended. Elina played a great match, and I wish her all the best for the rest of the tournament.”
Any conspiracy theorist arguing that professional sport is scripted will perhaps end this week with a fresh spring in their step. This year’s WTA Finals, after all, began with an unexpected viral moment as Pegula’s stinging criticisms of Andreeva, whom she branded a “diva” after their practice, were caught on a hot mic and broadcast to the world. After Pegula apologised and both sides laughed off the incident, of course they would find themselves across the net for the first time in their careers in an official match at this tournament.
There are many positive things to say about the WTA Finals’ arrival in Indian Wells, particularly the strong crowds in an area so well accustomed to elite tennis, the unmatched desert landscape and the flawless temperature, but Indian Wells also notoriously presents challenging conditions in which to compete. From early on, heavy winds made it tough for both players to find rhythm and timing with both their serving and groundstrokes.
It took Andreeva some time to adjust to the conditions and she ended a messy early service game with a double fault to fall behind 2-1. However, as Andreeva began to demonstrate the full array of her numerous powers, she was by far the better player. Andreeva soaked up Pegula’s first strike with her brilliant defensive skills, consistently drawing errors from the American, but she also smartly chose her moments to step inside the court, take the ball early and redirect supremely off both sides. She served well in decisive games, effortlessly firing down 120mph service winners throughout the match. Pegula, for her part, has had to rely on her mental toughness in lieu of her top level for much of this week. Here she was simply too erratic and inconsistent against the WTA Tour’s newest diva.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Georgia football recruit Marcellus Young Casario dies at 18 after medical emergency
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Marcellus Young Casario, an 18-year-old Canadian high school football player who had committed to Georgia, died Friday following what his school described as a medical emergency.
Casario, a senior defensive lineman at Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School in northeast Georgia, was taken to hospital after an incident Friday morning. The school announced his death later that day but did not identify him until Saturday. No further details about the circumstances were released.
“Rabun Gap immediately followed our emergency response protocols, and local emergency personnel responded, transferring the student to the hospital,” the school said in a statement.
The school postponed its state semi-final playoff game against Cannon School scheduled for Friday night.
Originally from Halifax, Nova Scotia, Casario moved to Georgia to pursue a college football scholarship. The 6ft 5in, 255lb defensive lineman committed to the Bulldogs in June after receiving offers from several major programs.
Rated a three-star prospect, Casario was ranked the No 49 defensive end nationally by ESPN and was part of Georgia’s 2027 recruiting class.
“He was everything a coach wants in a player,” Rabun Gap coach Derek White said. “He was known for his relentless dedication, and his journey as a student-athlete was marked by hard work and true brotherhood with his teammates.”

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: German knives, English socks: 13 gifts beloved globally that Americans are missing out on
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Karen Yuan and Guardian staff
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
Our editors and writers have lived across the globe, from Abu Dhabi to Toronto to São Paulo. So when we asked them to share beloved gifts from outside the US, the answers were as varied as our home towns.
This is the stuff we bring home in our suitcases and press into friends’ hands. Take the “workhorse” German paring knives or the bright red tortilla press that makes homemade masa feel effortless. There’s a 3lb tub of Maldon salt that is absurdly whimsical yet practical, and a set of Australian linen sheets that get softer with every wash.
Some picks, such as El Dorado rum from Guyana, are a little piece of home. Others, including posters from Denmark’s Louisiana Museum, are just beautiful. And all of them are delightful discoveries that don’t require a plane ticket to bring home.
Germany
Mexico
Cast-iron tortilla press
There’s something really special about a fresh, homemade tortilla. They taste better than anything you can get at the supermarket and are shockingly (at least I was shocked) simple to make. To make your masa (dough), just add water to your harina (maize flour) and roll into little balls. Though you can realistically flatten these balls with a rolling pin and some parchment papers, a tortilla press gives you consistent thickness. Plus, the bright red finish brightens up any kitchen. Danielle Renwick
Australia
Hunter candles
I first discovered Hunter Candles when a colleague introduced me to their tucked-away storefront in Sydney’s tree-lined Surry Hills neighborhood. Their scents are fresh and never overpowering, with unique, earthy notes inspired by ingredients such as shiitake mushroom, river mint, blue gum trees, mountain ash and grapefruit rind (who would have thought!). I also love that customers in Australia can return empty candle glasses for refills. My favorite is Daisy, a bright scent with delicate florals and summery hints of peach. Maya Yang
Soft sheets from Dazed but Amazed
When I moved to Los Angeles, one of the first things that I bought was a linen sheet set from Dazed but Amazed, a small Australian company. The small-batch color combinations they offer are striking and unexpected; the sheets themselves get softer and softer with use. There’s a Pacific sensibility in everything the brand offers – they make my bedroom feel like it opens right on to the beach. Lois Beckett
UK
3lb tub of Maldon salt
For your friends with caviar taste on a McNuggets budget, let me introduce you to the 3lb container of the UK’s Maldon sea salt flakes. While small boxes of Maldon salt are widely available at grocery stores around the US, loyalists to the stuff (me) know that the 3lb tub is a whimsical necessity in any good kitchen. It’s not only a visually fun gift to receive (it comes with a cute little handle!), it’s absurdly practical! I use a smaller salt cellar on my counter, but knowing there’s plenty to refill it with at all times? A thrill! It’s also roughly $30, making it a cost-effective gift for someone desperately seeking seasoning in their life, a white elephant offering or a cheeky pre-holidays gift from you to you. Jenna Amatulli
Rock & Ruby socks
This sustainable knitwear brand, founded in east London during the pandemic, produces a beautiful array of striking, vintage-inspired socks. There are bold checks and tasteful stripes in a wide array of colors. I craved a pair as soon as I saw them. LB
Brazil
Pão de Queijo
I lived in Brazil in my 20s and 30s and to this day crave cheesy, gooey pão de queijo. This addictive treat, originally from the state of Minas Gerais, is a mix of tapioca flour, cheese and eggs. If I’m feeling particularly nostalgic I’ll pair them with some açai. I was delighted to find that this dry mix comes in bulk and tastes just like anything you’d find at a Brazilian padaria. DR
Italy
Bialetti Moka Pot
“Despite my Italian heritage, it took a temporary move to Rome to discover the magic of the moka pot. I instantly fell in love with this Italian coffee maker’s ability to brew a beverage on par with the $10 lattes found at my favorite cafes,” I wrote in my guide to achieving a perfect cup of iced coffee. In the chillier months, I rely on mine for achieving steaming cups of coffee, topped with frothed milk and a dash of cinnamon. It’s far less expensive than an espresso machine, but makes coffee nearly as strong.
 
While I own two sizes, the colored option would make for a particularly great gift (I have red). Lauren Gould
Canada
Mango puzzles
In the nearly 15 years I’ve lived in Toronto, I’ve never been more than 15 minutes by bike or streetcar from the city’s best outdoor spots: Trinity Bellwoods, or a ravine. These beautifully illustrated jigsaw puzzles that capture my favo(u)rite city scenes are a dream to play, each piece snapping easily into the next, and the poster is so lovely I have framed it. Jessie Willms
Canadian e-reader
If you’re looking for a non-Amazon alternative to the Kindle, let this be your sign to get a Kobo. (These e-readers are widely available outside Canada, but it’s nice to tell people that Canadian tech extends beyond the BlackBerry – RIP.) Then load it up with your favorite Canadian books, from Margaret Atwood to Rachel Reid to all the Emily St John Mandels. Does it also snow terribly from early December to May where you live? Get cozy under this quilt, in these sweatpants and this bunny hug (an endearing Saskatchewan regionalism for hoodie. Light a Province of Canada candle and read until spring. JW
Fable’s affordable ceramics
If you’re a millennial looking to (finally) upgrade and unify your tablewares, consider Fable. The Canadian company makes lovely ceramics that feel much more luxurious than their price point. The plates and bowls are a lovely foundation if you want to pair them with your existing eclectic tableware. While I would die to have all my tableware from Michelle Organ or Toni Darling Frank, budget (and my likelihood to drop breakables) prohibits it. A mix of makers big and small is the sweet spot. JW
Guyana
El Dorado rum
El Dorado rum comes from Guyana, where I’m originally from. Growing up, El Dorado was always a name we knew and took pride in. Guyana is known for its demerara sugar, and El Dorado rum is one of the great products that comes from the ingredient. When I give it as a gift, I love that I’m sharing a little piece of home and introducing someone to something special that represents my country. It’s a great rum. Keisa Caesar
Denmark
Posters from the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art
Scandinavia’s best contemporary art museum is tucked away in the Danish countryside, a short train ride outside Copenhagen. Luckily, its online store of stunning art prints ships to the US – and you can get them framed or unframed. There’s something for every art lover: reimagined maps and manuals of Dominican-American artist Firelei Báez, eerie figures of Kaari Upson, classic landscapes by David Hockney and more. For a holiday gift, I might choose one of these ocean plant cyanotypes by 19th-century British botanist Anna Atkins. LB

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: ‘I’m looking for faces which surprise me’: how Richard Avedon photographed the soul of his subjects
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
Richard Avedon had only taken a couple of frames when he accidentally hit his head on a light being held above him. The Dalai Lama burst into laughter. That was when Avedon snapped two more frames and announced: “Oh, I got it!”
Avedon’s assistant, Sebastian Kim, was baffled. “I was like, what the hell happened? There’s only four frames out of a roll of 12 frames,” he recalls in a phone interview. “I realised he knew at that moment that something had happened, a mistake had happened: he hit his head and the Dalai Lama lit up.”
Kim, 52, now an eminent photographer in his own right, is among the interviewees who feature in a new documentary, Avedon, directed by Oscar winner Ron Howard, which premiered at the Cannes film festival and is released on Netflix this week.
The film explores the six-decade career of the fashion and portrait photographer renowned for white backgrounds that stripped away distractions and for capturing figures ranging from Marilyn Monroe and Charlie Chaplin to civil rights activists, anti-war protesters and working-class Americans.
Avedon was raised in New York City. His father, Jacob Avedon, co-founded a specialty store on Fifth Avenue, which was lost overnight during the Great Depression. Avedon struggled academically, flunking out of high school despite winning a citywide poetry prize.
He once said: “My father wanted me to be strongly educated, strong physically, and to make a living. But I always felt that I flunked. I grew up thinking I was certifiably stupid. I couldn’t graduate high school. I flunked everything.”
In the second world war, Avedon joined the Merchant Marine. Assigned to the photographic unit, he took more than 100,000 ID card photos and performed autopsy documentation. Observing endless faces against white backdrops taught him that no two faces are alike.
At the New School’s Design Laboratory, Harper’s Bazaar art director Alexey Brodovitch provided Avedon’s foundational philosophy: “Astonish me.” When Avedon struggled to design a neon sign using traditional media, Brodovitch suggested using pipe cleaners or spaghetti, teaching Avedon never to be blocked by technical limitations.
Commissioned by Harper’s Bazaar magazine, Avedon brought theatricality to fashion. Observing Christian Dior’s 1947 The New Look collection, Avedon captured models moving, swirling and laughing across Paris streets, transforming fashion photography from static posing into dynamic visual storytelling.
His approach to portraiture was no less distinctive. Avedon’s studio aesthetic relied on a stark, seamless white paper backdrop, bounded by a bold black film border. He once explained: “It’s the existential white. The only thing you see is the geography of the face. One of the functions of art is to eliminate in order to make more powerful or stronger what the artist wants to get across.
“I remember once that I fasted for three days. I fasted with a friend. And she and I decided after the fast, how will we break the fast? We decided on a peach. I never tasted anything like that peach in my life. Because everything, because of the fast, becomes so precious. That’s a little bit about getting rid of the background.”
For his picture of Monroe in 1957, Avedon waited through hours of joyful posing until the actor collapsed into quiet exhaustion. Monroe slumped into a corner, allowing Avedon to capture her unguarded melancholy – a portrait often called Sad Marilyn.
He believed that models were active creative collaborators rather than decorative props. He once said: “I know perfectly well what I want before I leave the house in the morning but if the girl doesn’t feel that she’s part of it, if she feels that she is someone that’s hired for an hour, a stick of wood that’s going to be told to stand over there and do that, that’s exactly what you get out of her.”
By engaging sitters through conversation, music and playfulness, he created an atmosphere of mutual trust. Models like Penelope Tree and Lauren Hutton recall in the film that working with him was liberating, allowing them to drop their guards and express vulnerability in front of the lens.
Dallas Brennan Rexer, 54, one of the film’s producers, said: “He was trying to get into their head and into their soul, in a way, through his photos. It was the same process for him regardless, and the models that we interviewed spoke about how they weren’t treated as a model who was just there to hold the clothes on.
“They were a human that he connected to and he asked them questions and he tried to understand what they were thinking about and what they were feeling and tried to help get something out of them that radiated and gave them an energy. That’s what made the photos special. It wasn’t just that they were pretty and their clothing looked nice.”
Avedon photographed the Duke and Duchess of Windsor in their hotel suite. Aware of their polished public persona, he broke through their guard by claiming his taxi had run over a dog.
Rexer elaborates: “He knew how he felt about their politics and he didn’t want to allow himself to be used to make another polite pretty picture of them. He wanted to say something much more pointed and important. He used the photograph in a very clever and specific way. He captured the moment that he thinks said everything that needed to be said about them.”
Though Avedon achieved commercial success – directing television campaigns for Calvin Klein – he channelled his resources into politically charged documentary work.
In 1963, Avedon reconnected with his high school friend James Baldwin, with whom he had co-edited a school magazine. Together they published Nothing Personal, combining Avedon’s portraits of civil rights leaders and mental asylum patients with Baldwin’s rich prose.
Rexer explains: “Dick was at a place in his life where he was ready to get involved in something political and he wanted to do something meaningful on civil rights. Nothing Personal is a phenomenal book. The text that James Baldwin wrote is poetic and beautiful, but it also is so resonant today.”
Avedon’s asylum photographs were deeply personal, influenced by his sister Louise, who suffered from severe mental illness. He said: “I photographed things that frightened me so that I could understand them.”
But when Nothing Personal received a withering review in the New York Review of Books, Avedon was crushed. He admitted: “That review simply stopped me from working for about a year because I began to question myself as an artist.”
Yet Avedon continued his political involvement. During the civil rights movement, he quietly supported activists. Rexer notes: “In the background very quietly, Dick was sending film down to SNCC [the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee] because they were using photography to keep people accountable to what was going on in the south. Then they would send the film back, and he would take it to the lab and process it for them, quietly on the side to just keep the movement going.”
These efforts culminated in In the American West (1979–1984), commissioned by the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth, Texas. Over five summers, Avedon photographed working-class Americans against white paper. Avedon stated of the project: “I’m looking for faces which surprise me. I’m looking for a face that will hold the wall.”
In 1992, at age 69, Avedon became the first staff photographer in the history of the New Yorker magazine, hired by editor Tina Brown. He produced portraits of global figures and controversial fashion essays, such as the Mr and Mrs Comfort portfolio.
In a statement provided by Netflix, Howard observed: “He had to learn to bridge his commercial success and his creative endeavors, using his own resources to underwrite far riskier projects. He figured out how to lean into the popular to make space for the unusual ... In many ways, Avedon defied the idea that there must be a division between art and commerce, highbrow and lowbrow, beauty and brutality.”
Avedon’s internal contradictions are at the heart of Howard’s documentary, which draws from unprecedented access to personal archives held by the Richard Avedon Foundation, including hundreds of thousands of negatives, contact sheets and behind-the-lens footage.
Rexer says: “The archive is daunting at first because there were 16,000 sittings, and that can only mean hundreds of thousands of images, and so it’s a bit overwhelming in the first couple of months.”
Among the production team’s most extraordinary discoveries was a cache of casual audio tapes recorded inside Avedon’s studio during the 1960s and 1970s with collaborators like Marvin Israel and Doon Arbus.
Rexer says: “They would put a recorder on the table and hit record and forget about it. So you could be a fly on the wall. He was working out a lot of questions about truth and identity and self and all of the big things like beauty. They would have these wonderful lunches with these abstract conversations about it but then he could turn that into something concrete.”
Despite all the success, the workaholic Avedon lived in a constant state of anxiety and self-doubt. His son, John Avedon, says in the film: “He had a bull-like confidence in himself. At the same time, he was totally insecure. He absolutely suffered from performance anxiety, but then he absolutely performed. I think he had to be anxious in order to perform.”
For Rexer, this is the key to unlocking much of Avedon’s work. She explains: “You need to have the confidence to walk up to Henry Kissinger and say: ‘I’m taking your portrait right now and no, we’re going to do it this way and put your hands down and look into my lens.’
“But also the insecurity or the lack of know-it-allness to be able to ask questions and connect with his subjects and explore and make people feel comfortable too. It didn’t just come in big in the room. He made space for the people he was photographing. That’s beautiful.”
Avedon suffered a cerebral hemorrhage and died in 2004, aged 81, while in San Antonio shooting a project titled Democracy for the New Yorker.
For Kim, his influence remains profound. He says: “I credit him for making me the person that I am. The way that he shaped the person that I am, the photographer that I am. He has had such an impact on so many people. It was difficult, but I look back and it’s the discipline that creates character.”
- Avedon is available on Netflix on 11 November

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ballot-measu.title: What Ballot Measures Told Us About America
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ballot-measu.author: Ben Case
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ballot-measu.text:
What Ballot Measures Told Us About America
Last week’s votes on taxing billionaires, abortion and trans rights, and divestment from Israel offer a window into the American electorate’s political mood.
The blue tidal wave that swept congressional and local elections around the country is leaving a new political landscape in its wake. The generational scope of Democratic wins and unprecedented success of democratic socialist candidates notwithstanding, the president’s party almost always loses midterm elections, often by wide margins. How much do the election results reflect a shift in society’s politics, and how much do they reflect an extreme version of the standard two-party pendulum swing? And more importantly, where are the opportunities to push organizing to new horizons in this new terrain?
The results of ballot initiative votes are especially useful in analyzing the political realities on the ground. Ballot measures present a simple yes-or-no choice on a piece of legislation, making them excellent barometers of public sentiment. Between state and local ballots, Americans vote on hundreds of initiatives every cycle. Coming out of Election Day 2026, three ballot measures demand particular attention.
In California, a pioneering attempt to tax billionaires’ wealth to fund the hollowed-out health care system was drowned in almost $400 million in billionaire spending. Missouri saw the first Republican attempt to overturn abortion rights that were previously won at the ballot by packaging the rollback with transphobia; it was resoundingly defeated. And a whopping three-quarters of voters in Providence approved a measure to divest from countries and companies committing severe human rights abuses, making Rhode Island’s capital the largest US city to approve divestment from Israel.
Not Yet Taxing Billionaires in California
The California Billionaire Tax was as novel a proposition as it was consequential. Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill” made major cuts to Medicaid, with major coverage restrictions scheduled to take effect after the midterms, in January 2027. The cuts are expected to leave millions without insurance and put health care facilities at risk of closure. Billionaires’ fortunes have skyrocketed by hundreds of billions of dollars more since the bill’s passage.
In California, a union of hospital and health care workers put two and two together. In collaboration with leading progressive economists, the Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW) proposed a first-of-its-kind, one-time 5 percent wealth tax on the two hundred–odd billionaires living in California. The union projected that it would raise roughly $100 billion. Ninety percent of the revenue was earmarked for health care, with the remainder for education, food assistance, and administration.
Proposition 40, as it was designated once it qualified for the ballot, was written to be applicable to billionaires residing in the state on January 1, 2026, anticipating the capital flight argument that billionaires would simply move out. With the mind-boggling amounts of money billionaires have been making in recent years, the 5 percent wealth tax would still have left California’s billionaires vastly wealthier than they were just a year ago, while the state’s health care system would avoid disaster. Seems like common sense — unless you’re a billionaire who thinks taxation is oppression.
Yet the billionaires were not the only ones opposed to Proposition 40. Labor was mostly aligned behind UHW in the push, including the California Labor Federation, Teamsters California, and California Nurses Association. But it wasn’t unanimous: the California Teachers Association and the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California opposed. SEIU California remained neutral, despite Proposition 40 being proposed by one of its largest locals. Some prominent progressive advocacy groups like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California and the NAACP California/Hawaii State Conference joined unlikely forces with the likes of Peter Thiel against the billionaire tax.
The apparent split in left forces, particularly the elements of labor that opposed the billionaire tax, was prominently featured in ads from Building a Better California, a billionaire-backed organization opposing Proposition 40.
Many of Building a Better California’s attacks were focused on UHW president Dave Regan, who was on the receiving end of a litany of allegations, including resurfaced claims he used intimidation tactics in political negotiations seventeen years ago — all of which Regan frames as a transparent smear campaign aimed at distracting from the issue at hand.
Still, if the billionaire lobby’s goal was to sow mistrust around Proposition 40, the intra-left divisions and air of scandal around UHW certainly helped. To add insult to injury, UHW’s staff union declared a strike in the days leading up to Election Day, obstructing Proposition 40’s final get-out-the-vote push.
Ultimately, neither the measure’s necessity — even now, nobody seems to have an alternative plan for when the Medicaid cuts kick in — nor its meticulous construction ended up matching the unprecedented amounts of money the billionaire lobby dumped into this election. Opponents raised at least $378 million, overwhelming the pro-tax campaign and helping swing the popular vote away from Proposition 40. The billionaire lobby also financed two poison pill measures, Propositions 41 and 42, which could have blocked Proposition 40 even if it passed, provided they received more “yes” votes.
Proposition 40’s chaotic loss should not distract from its importance. The front line often doesn’t survive the battle, but in this case it opened an important new front. By organizing to put the issue directly on the ballot, UHW forced a public conversation about wealth taxes that put the idea on the political menu. Not only did Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna wholeheartedly endorse the measure, they had already introduced legislation for an annual federal billionaire wealth tax. California governor Gavin Newsom, in his haste to kill the California billionaire tax, was forced to admit that America needs a national minimum tax on the ultrawealthy (as long as it didn’t start in his state). United Airlines’ millionaire CEO, Scott Kirby, recently chimed in, advocating for a national wealth tax.
Proposition 40’s hard-fought loss is at once an illustration of how hard many billionaires will fight being taxed and how important it will be to tax them anyway.
Defending Abortion Rights and Defeating Transphobia in Missouri
Alongside the demonization of immigrants, attacks on transgender people have been a staple of reactionary scapegoating in recent years. In September, Elon Musk reportedly authorized more than $100 million in midterm spending by his PAC, which launched transphobic ads, including in Texas, Tesla’s headquarters. That strategy failed, as targeted Democrats swept in the midterms.
However, transphobic attacks also made it directly onto the ballot in multiple states, where they were largely successful. Majorities in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, and Washington approved restrictions on transgender students’ participation on school sports teams aligned with their gender identity. Another Colorado measure, banning gender-affirming surgeries for minors, also passed. Niche an issue as it may seem to many, the Right has found a foothold in youth sports.
Nevertheless, the biggest test of how far conservatives can leverage transphobia failed in Missouri, where Republican legislators tried using it as a lever to overturn abortion rights. The victory against this tactic is instructive for how the Left can defeat transphobic scapegoating at the ballot moving forward.
In 2024, Missouri residents voted to enshrine abortion rights in the state constitution. That vote, titled Amendment 3, had been proposed as a citizen initiative and won narrowly but decisively with 52 percent of the vote. It didn’t take long for Republicans in the state legislature to hatch a scheme to countermand the popular vote. The result was Amendment 3, part two.
This year’s Amendment 3 was a legislatively referred repeal of the citizen-initiated Amendment 3 from 2024. It combined a rollback of abortion rights with a constitutional ban on gender-transition procedures for minors, including surgery, puberty blockers, and hormone treatment, subject to specified medical exceptions. Rather than trying to change majority opinion on abortion rights, the antiabortion campaign focused its talking points on transphobia.
Voters also had to wade through the confusion. Not only had they just voted on abortion two years ago, but when a majority of Missouri voters checked “yes” on Amendment 3, they were voting to support abortion rights. Now, a “yes” vote on Amendment 3 meant the opposite.
It’s not the first time Republican legislators have attempted this kind of ballot title shell game, to little effect. It didn’t work in Missouri either. On Election Day, Missouri voters decisively rejected the new Amendment 3 with 55 percent of the vote — an even higher percentage than voted for abortion rights in 2024. To cement their rebuke, voters also passed a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment to protect the ballot initiative process from legislative tampering.
Had Missouri Republicans been successful in overturning a popular vote for abortion rights by leveraging transphobia, the same tactic would have been rolled out across the country. It still might, but now there is both strategy and precedent to defeat it. The coalition against the new Amendment 3 had to balance a focus on abortion rights with addressing attacks on trans youth.
A contingent of the campaign headed by PROMO, a Missouri LGBTQ organization, leaned into the opportunity to move the needle on trans rights for the long term. They committed to an intensive deep canvassing program aimed at changing hearts and minds — an approach that has worked on gay marriage and trans antidiscrimination votes over the past decade and a half. Therein lies the lesson.
The political Right has a fast-evaporating pool of persuasive appeals to the public. Following the Right’s trouncing in the midterm elections, conservatives can be expected to double down on anti-trans arguments as a foot in the door to a popular audience. Missouri shows that the best defense against transphobia is a good offense, both pointing out that scapegoating is designed to distract and also engaging in proactive public education to stand in unflinching solidarity against all forms of bigotry.
Divesting From Genocide in Providence
If elections over the summer indicated that Palestine had changed US politics, November signed, sealed, and stamped that reality. Explicitly pro-Palestine candidates won across the country, most prominently Abdul El-Sayed, who won a US Senate seat in Michigan despite what he described as $42 million in AIPAC spending against him. These wins proved beyond a doubt that questioning US support for Israel — a nearly unthinkable stance in mainstream politics only a few years ago — calling the genocide in Gaza a genocide, and advocating for an arms embargo against Israel are no longer liabilities for elected leaders.
Still, it is difficult to distinguish those who voted for El-Sayed because of his stance on Israel from those who supported him in spite of that stance. Such is the nature of two-party elections, when voters must shoehorn or project a variety of wants, needs, and hopes onto a single personality and often hold their noses about the rest. But devil’s advocates will find no solace this year, because there was one vote last Tuesday that was about Palestine and nothing else, and the results were not ambiguous.
Providence, Rhode Island, is the first US city to enact a binding divestment law by popular vote, targeting investments in countries and companies engaged in severe human rights abuses like genocide, ethnic cleansing, and apartheid — a campaign explicitly focused on divesting from Israel. It won by a landslide, with 75 percent of the popular vote. The effort was led by a local coalition that included Jewish Voice for Peace; Democratic Socialists of America; Reclaim Rhode Island, a housing justice and generally progressive organization; and American Federation of Teachers Local 6516, representing graduate workers at Brown University. (You can read more about the initiative in this Jacobin piece by two organizers from the campaign.)
Following the initiative win, Providence becomes the largest US city yet to approve divestment from Israel. It will join at least six other cities around the country in passing some form of divestment legislation — Hayward and Richmond in California; Dearborn, Michigan; Medford, Massachusetts; Belfast, Maine; and most recently Cambridge, Massachusetts. Providence does not have a proportionately large Muslim or Arab population, but it does have a sizable Jewish population. The overwhelming victory for divestment at the ballot cements beyond a doubt the swing happening in the American public not only away from Israel but toward decisive action against its genocidal policies.
It is also worth noting, with the California Billionaire Tax in mind, that while Providence marks a triumphant success for the Palestine solidarity movement in a watershed election, it was not the first attempt to divest from Israel by direct democracy. The first two attempts, both in Pittsburgh, lost court challenges and never made it to voters. The third, in Somerville, Massachusetts, won majority support a year ago, but was a nonbinding initiative. Somerville’s City Council has committed to pursuing a binding ordinance, and an ethical procurement proposal remains before it. Sometimes it takes time for game-changing policies with deep-pocketed adversaries to succeed at the ballot.
Alongside Question 7, Providence elected a mayor who endorsed the divestment initiative, twenty-eight-year-old democratic socialist David Morales, as well as a slate of allied city council members. Should Question 7 survive the court challenges that have already been threatened, it will be implemented by the new city government.
But even if it is somehow beaten back in the courts, the Providence vote will echo across the country and well beyond, showing that after three grinding years of misery in Gaza and across Palestine, firm policy against genocide is not only a viable position but an asset for candidates and elected officials.
American politics is changing fast. To make the most of it, it is helpful to understand how majorities vote when they get a chance to legislate key issues directly. Our moment requires taking big swings in redistribution and economic justice. At the same time, the closer those moves get to billionaires’ money, the more severe the reaction will become. Going up against those kinds of resources, setbacks are to be expected, but the worst thing we could do would be to interpret losses as undermining the necessity or viability of taxing billionaires’ wealth.
As the Right’s bid for legitimacy falters, it will lean harder into scapegoating and demonizing marginalized groups. Contra antipopulist liberal fantasies, American society is not hopelessly bigoted. People can be won over to both economic and social justice, but only if movements commit to the protracted work on both fronts as part of the same political project. And policy positions that appear to be third rails, like divesting from Israel used to be, can be transformed through mass organizing and popular pressure.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-power.title: A Sewer Socialist Proposal for the Climate: PowerNYC
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-power.author: Batul Hassan, Michael Paulson
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/public-power.text:
A Sewer Socialist Proposal for the Climate: PowerNYC
PowerNYC, a public clean energy developer in New York, could be Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s climate engine, lowering costs and creating a more resilient, greener electricity grid for New Yorkers.
Two years ago, then Assemblymember Zohran Mamdani launched his campaign for mayor with a series of on-the-street interviews of Donald Trump voters on Fordham Road in the Bronx. In the course of the following year, the cost-of-living crisis solidified as the uniting theme of his mayoral campaign, anchored by a clear agenda to bring costs down and build a city where New Yorkers can “afford to dream.” Last week, a big tent of Democratic politicians used this same message to rout the Right across the country — potentially opening the door to a new kind of politics that embeds climate action within economic populist agendas.
New York City is already providing a governing framework for legislators across the country seeking to translate campaign slogans into material improvements for working-class people. Through initiatives like discounted groceries at municipal grocery store pilots and a public stake in New York University’s Quantum Institute, the Mamdani administration has begun to demonstrate that the public sector can and must play a critical role in tackling the affordability crisis and meeting people’s everyday needs.
In this approach, Mayor Mamdani is drawing on a rich history of public ownership in the United States catalyzed by the New Deal. But in the modern era, we can only ensure that all New Yorkers can “afford to dream” if we tackle the climate crisis — a core driver of economic instability, high costs, and the foreclosure of a stable future.
A new report from Climate and Community Institute, Public Renewables Project, and Public Power NY, PowerNYC Development Corporation: The Case for a Public Renewable Developer in New York City, lays out a clear path for New York City to lead on climate action. Drawing on a New Deal–inspired approach to the energy sector, authors Jason Kowalski and Johanna Bozuwa make the case for New York City to take charge of its own energy future via a city-owned development corporation called PowerNYC. By rapidly deploying solar, battery storage, and thermal energy networks (TENs) across the five boroughs, PowerNYC would accelerate decarbonization to lower utility bills, ensure more reliable service, and phase out the fossil fuels driving the combined affordability and climate crisis.
Since the New Deal era, public development has built systems to service common needs from international airports to water and sewage systems across the country. Many of these systems still stand as durable remnants of a more ambitious era of governance.
PowerNYC Development Corporation applies this formula to twenty-first-century needs: it would leverage the public sector’s ability to coordinate and plan at scale to create a glide path for renewable energy projects that might otherwise languish in the limbo of private markets. Such an institution would fill a clear gap in New York City’s renewable energy landscape, delivering climate and economic benefits in the form of lowered emissions and utility savings.
Overlapping Energy Crises
New York City currently faces multiple overlapping energy system crises that are on track to get much worse in the coming years.
First, utility rates are becoming unaffordable for New Yorkers, who are now paying 11 percent more for their electricity bills than they did just last year, largely due to the costs of fossil fuel infrastructure and volatile natural gas prices. Second, the city’s supply of energy is constrained by an outdated grid, power plants reaching the end of their lifespan, and lack of needed transmission lines to bring renewable power from upstate New York, leading to blackouts in the summer and even higher risk of service interruptions in the future. Third, the cascading effects of fossil fuel generation threaten the well-being of New Yorkers through dangerous air pollution and increasingly catastrophic weather events.
To address these crises requires tackling the root cause of continued reliance on volatile fossil fuel markets and transitioning to green energy sources.
To date, the state has relied chiefly on market incentives to spur renewable energy development, but this strategy has fallen well short of meeting the state’s climate targets. And New York City has fallen way behind the rest of the state, with 90 percent of downstate electricity still coming from fossil fuels rather than renewables.
The technology to tackle such challenges exists, and renewable energy provides a cheap and clean alternative to polluting fossil fuels. But bringing projects themselves into fruition faces technical, bureaucratic, and cost barriers. Thousands of viable sites for clean energy projects scattered across public schools, hospitals, affordable housing, and other sites are currently underutilized due to the significant amount of time, expertise, and up-front resources required to turn a promising site into an operating clean energy project. Clean energy development is rarely a core competency of institutions or organizations with other primary purposes. While some of this market is served by private developers, navigating transaction costs, small project sizes, complicated sites, and other requirements and economic considerations often means such projects are deprioritized in the short term.
The burden of such delays falls on ratepayers and the public. This summer, heat waves overwhelmed the grid and left thousands of New Yorkers without power during the hottest days of the year. With winter temperatures around the corner, heating oil costs have risen nearly 70 percent since last year. Too often, working-class households are forced to choose between keeping themselves safe or paying their utility bills — even as the climate collapses around them.
We are now facing a stark choice: continue business as usual and suffer the consequences, or embrace a new approach that mobilizes the economic strength of the public sector to ensure the job gets done. As timelines for implementation of Local Law 97 (which mandated strict caps on emissions on large buildings in New York City), broader climate mandates, and escalating climate chaos loom, the city needs a public developer like PowerNYC to rapidly expand the deployment of green technology to electrify existing systems.
Introducing PowerNYC Development Corporation
PowerNYC would use its position as a public developer to create a financially self-sustaining engine of decarbonization for New York City. While many of the component parts and projects exist across agencies and other institutional actors, PowerNYC would consolidate the support available at various levels and provide a means to ensure renewable energy projects move from the page to implementation.
One major benefit of PowerNYC would be its ability to recycle capital to create a financially self-sustaining engine of decarbonization. After initial capitalization, its ownership of revenue-generating assets would allow it to back funding for further rounds of development. Applying this model to thermal energy networks and other green technologies would leverage the power of aggregated planning to ensure the public sector can tap into the same low-cost revenue sources from which private utilities already benefit.
For example, through PowerNYC, deploying battery storage across the five boroughs would allow the city to package a fleet of batteries’ worth of power to sell back to the electricity grid at peak demand times to displace the fossil power on which the city currently relies. The contract for such a deal could then be leveraged to secure further financing for ongoing development of renewable energy assets.
By accessing long-term, low-cost, stable financing, public developers like PowerNYC can unlock the potential for large-scale infrastructure projects while ensuring benefits are democratically distributed. Instead of taking a project-by-project approach, it would maximize the government’s ability to coordinate at scale with the goals of multiplying affordability benefits for ratepayers and expediting urgent climate action.
Research shows that deploying an initial 200 megawatts of distributed batteries alone via PowerNYC could generate New York City’s Con Edison ratepayers at least $170 million of savings annually by lowering capacity market costs and distribution costs. And publicly developed thermal energy networks, an alternative to gas pipe replacement, could create savings for National Grid customers in Brooklyn, Staten Island, and Queens who are currently paying for unnecessary gas infrastructure investments. Over time, its development mandate could expand to other clean energy and grid infrastructure needed to support decarbonization and affordability.
A Green Era of Public Institution-Building
No single city or even country can take on the planetary scale of the climate crisis alone, but the establishment of PowerNYC is a major opportunity for the largest city in the country to chart a new era of public institution-building to rapidly scale up climate ambitions.
Cities and states across the country have already embraced the potential of green public development. Nearly a decade ago, the Connecticut Green Bank established a similar, successful model for solar that has driven the state to the top of the national list for its percentage of public schools with on-site solar projects. Countries from Costa Rica to Denmark are using strong networks of public institutions to accelerate the planning and development of public power.
Public development is a proven method for bringing public goods to fruition. PowerNYC would use it to accelerate the deployment of green energy systems and begin to fix our toxic, cost-burdening energy system.
