Bahrain accuses Iran of attacking its territory to ‘settle’ score with US
Iran’s Foreign Ministry says its air attacks on countries cooperating with the US are justified under international law.
Bahrain’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denounced what it describes as “a resumption of Iran’s aggression” after the latest air attacks on its Riffa Air Base by Tehran.
In a statement, the ministry said the attacks on Sunday launched by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) violated international law and “no pretext can legitimise violations of state sovereignty”.
“Bahrain also rejects the use of its territory to settle accounts and holds Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences,” the statement added.
Bahrain’s military said its defence systems intercepted several Iranian “aerial attacks” targeting the kingdom. Its Riffa Air Base is used by the United States military.
The IRGC has not commented. It had said on Friday that it launched an attack on a US early warning radar facility in Bahrain and destroyed it. Bahrain said it intercepted two drones that day.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, noted that Iran had held back amid intermittent US attacks in the past weeks but in the past three days, it has fired twice at Bahrain.
“We were seeing the United States’s low-intensity warfare being conducted against Iran. From time to time, the US attacked Iran’s military assets – telecommunications towers specifically – in the southern part of the country,” he said.
But that appears to have changed. “It seems this is now the new rule of engagement,” Serdar added.
Iranian minister says attacks justified
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended Tehran’s attacks and accused Gulf countries of aiding US strikes against Iran.
“All the cases that indicate the role of the countries of the region in helping the US to attack Iran have been documented,” Baghaei said at a news conference on Sunday, adding that Tehran was taking diplomatic action and would “follow up on this issue seriously”.
He said missiles, drones and aircraft launched from military bases in neighbouring countries as well as logistical support provided to US forces were proof of these nations’ involvement.
“The responsibility of this group of countries in the region for the consequences … of the military aggression of the United States and the Zionist regime against Iran is clear,” Baghaei charged, referring to Israel.
Attacks on its neighbours, he said, were justified under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, which established the rights of states to defend themselves from attacks.
“No action has been taken by Iran against the sovereignty of these countries,” Baghaei said, arguing that Tehran’s attacks are “purely defensive in nature” and have targeted only US military bases and assets used to attack Iran.
Meanwhile, Jordan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates said in a post on X that it “condemned Iran’s brutal attacks on the sister kingdom of Bahrain as a flagrant violation of its sovereignty, a threat to its security, stability and territorial integrity”.
Egypt’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the country “reiterates its categorical rejection” of attacks threatening the region’s stability.
“The security of Bahrain and the Gulf states is closely linked to Egyptian national security and is one of the pillars of Arab national security,” the statement added.

Australia crush New Zealand to win fourth Women’s Rugby League World Cup
Australia dominated the first half and capitalised on the Kiwi Ferns’ errors to win 34-10 and clinch the trophy.
Winger Jaime Chapman collected a hat-trick as Australia crushed New Zealand 34-10 on Sunday with an emphatic first-half performance to clinch their fourth consecutive Women’s Rugby League World Cup title.
Two tries in the opening five minutes did the damage, and there were four more before half-time to send the Jillaroos to the break with a commanding 34-6 advantage.
Despite applying pressure, they were unable to add to their score as the humid conditions in Brisbane took their toll and errors crept in.
But Australia had done enough to ensure a fourth straight title, beating the Kiwi Ferns in the final each time, to reinforce their status as the sport’s powerhouse nation.
“I want to thank the Kiwi Ferns. It’s been such a great rivalry for so many years now, with so much respect between the two of our teams,” said Australia captain Isabelle Kelly, now a three-time World Cup champion.
“To my team … I’m just so humbled and honoured to be able to lead you guys. This has definitely been a dream come true, and I knew that we could get the job done.”
Before Australia’s global rise, New Zealand won the World Cup in 2000, 2003 and 2008.
“We didn’t quite get the job done today, but we are going to assert dominance back into this jersey,” said New Zealand skipper Raecene McGregor.
“The best of the Kiwi Ferns is yet to be shown, so stay with us.”
New Zealand had won only one of their previous 12 Tests against the Jillaroos dating back to 2017, and they were under the pump immediately.
A knock-on near the New Zealand try line just two minutes in allowed Australia to spread the ball wide, and Chapman dived over in the corner for her 11th try of the tournament.
With all the momentum, Australia pressured New Zealand into another mistake and capitalised, with Shaylee Bent crashing over for their second converted try.
Midway through the first half, they were 18-0 ahead, with another Chapman special on the back of a lightning break.
A sensational solo effort from Jessica Sergis stretched the lead further, with the five-eighth shrugging off three tackles to sprint the length of the field.
New Zealand finally got on the board when Shannon Mato barged across, but Chapman’s third came after she burst through two tackles to race away, putting Australia back in full control before Tamika Upton added a sixth before half-time.
Australia started strongly in the second half with only some desperate Kiwi defence keeping them at bay.
But it was a much tighter affair, with New Zealand’s Mackenzie Wiki crossing in the dying seconds for the only try of the half.

À quelques jours de l’arrêt de la cour d’appel de Paris le 30 novembre concernant sa condamnation à cinq années de prison par le tribunal correctionnel dans l’affaire dite du financement libyen de sa campagne, il fallait bien que Nicolas Sarkozy se rappelle à notre souvenir.

L’ancien président délinquant en appelle au rétablissement de l’ordre, conseille sa famille politique mais évoque aussi la venue du pape à Paris, la foi et le besoin de transcendance de l‘espèce humaine.
« Depuis trois millions d’années, l’homme est fait pour se mettre à genoux. https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: Siege on Hebron’s Beit Ula industrial zone threatens Palestinian economy
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
Siege on Hebron’s Beit Ula industrial zone threatens Palestinian economy
Israel takes measures to crush Palestinian business in the occupied West Bank.
Beit Ula, occupied West Bank – Fayez al-Amleh, 63, scans his factory in an industrial complex in this town northwest of Hebron and reflects on the recent Israeli measures that could cost him his business.
The production lines at TB.LOC, which produce security and fire-resistant doors, still slowly whir away. But they very nearly came to a halt when Israeli forces sealed the entrances to the Beit Ula industrial zone with earthen berms and stone barriers on November 4.
The measures have isolated roughly 60 Palestinian businesses from their customers and suppliers, which threatens the livelihoods of 2,500 workers employed in the industrial zone.
“Today, raw materials cannot get in, and we cannot get our products out of the industrial zone,” al-Amleh told Al Jazeera.
Hebron and the surrounding areas were hit hard by Israeli military operations after two Israeli soldiers were killed by suspected Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint near the Palestinian city on October 23.
Thousands of Palestinians were forced out of their homes during the 10-day siege on Hebron and returned only when Israeli soldiers left the city on November 2.
Siege on Hebron
The siege on Hebron, an economic hub for the occupied West Bank, led to losses of more than 12 million shekels ($3.8m) a day, according to Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari.
But just days after the siege on Hebron was lifted, the blockade on Beit Ula’s industrial zone began. This has significantly impacted the operations of al-Amleh’s factory and the lives of the 70 workers his business employs.
As a result, his employees have had their hours cut or moved to part-time work, reducing their take-home pay.
Since the closure, daily sales for al-Amleh’s business have dropped from 70,000 shekels ($21,988) to between 2,000 and 3,000 shekels ($628 to $942).
Beit Ula has facilities that shape metal and make doors, electrical cabinets, sponge, cardboard and construction materials. Their activities are connected to a wider network of commercial and service businesses that depend on the continued movement of supplies and goods.
Agricultural activities on the surrounding land have also been affected along with suppliers and traders whose daily business depends on the factories.
Israeli forces have carried out a series of measures around the town of Beit Ula, including the demolition of four industrial facilities and the establishment of a nearby settlement outpost.
These measures are viewed by Palestinians in the area as part of a broader Israeli effort to take control of land surrounding the industrial zone and threaten economic and agricultural activity in the area.
Al-Amleh said that if the siege on the industrial zone continues more factories could be forced to shut down. This would severely impact the economic viability of Beit Ula and nearby towns, which rely heavily on the industrial zone for employment and secondary businesses.
He rejected an allegation by Israel that Beit Ula is responsible for the movement of workers into Israel without work permits, the reason Israel has given for imposing restrictions on the industrial zone. Instead, he considers it to be a form of collective punishment against Palestinian businesses and workers based there.
Ayman al-Adam, who has worked at the industrial zone for about three years, said the Israeli blockade on Beit Ula threatens the incomes that he and hundreds of other employees rely on to support their families.
“This road closure is not just a closure. It is closing the doors of livelihood for all the workers,” he told Al Jazeera.
‘Economic warfare’
The Israeli military and settlers have embarked on a campaign of disruption and intimidation against Palestinian businesses across the West Bank in recent months.
Settler pogroms have seen West Bank olive farmers routinely attacked during this year’s harvest and Palestinian crops, olive trees and livestock stolen.
An expansion of Israeli checkpoints across the West Bank has also restricted the movement of goods and people, hitting Palestinian businesses hard.
Palestinian Minister of National Economy Mohammad al-Amour said the Israeli measures targeting economic facilities in the West Bank amount to a war on the Palestinian economy.
“About 60 economic facilities along with their workers and all aspects of their production have been completely isolated from the Palestinian economy,” al-Amour told Al Jazeera. “This situation has become a burden on the Palestinian economy instead of being a source of support and contributing to it.”
Mahmoud Allan, head of the North Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry, has appealed to authorities to halt the apparent Israeli campaign against Palestinian business.
“If this area is not reopened very quickly, some of the facilities that are major establishments in this licensed industrial zone in Beit Ula will be disrupted and forced to close,” he said.
“Factories can no longer operate normally. Workers have lost their income, and business owners are struggling to keep their businesses alive.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Black voters helped Democrats win in Georgia. Now they expect to be heard
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: George Chidi in Atlanta
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Stonecrest is resolutely middle class. About six out of 10 of its voters cast ballots in the 2026 election and about 90% of them voted for Democrats, according to election figures. And they have often been overlooked by Georgia’s Republican establishment.
The fundraiser Keisha Lance Bottoms held at the Privi event center and retreat in suburban Atlanta in September didn’t draw a lot of attention. But Stonecrest, by one measure the largest city in the United States with a non-Hispanic Black population above 90%, tends to roll under the radar.
It’s infuriating, said Vaughn Irons, Privi’s founder. “I think she came to speak to a community that often gets driven through and flown over.”
Black voting power helped secure victory for US Senator Jon Ossoff, Bottoms’ run for the governor’s race and a slew of down-ballot candidates. Now, those voters expect to be heard.
Culture war issues come with the change in partisan control of Georgia’s government; on abortion, on guns and on LGBTQ+ rights. But the customary politics of Georgia start and end with business, and that attitude is bipartisan.
Georgia’s Black voters have long wrestled with the Black Mecca paradox. Atlanta has long attracted Black professional talent from across the country and the world who were looking for strong African American political and cultural institutions and an economic environment perceived to give Black people an even shake.
But upward mobility for native-born Black Atlantans has been anemic. Black unemployment rates are lower in Atlanta than the nation overall. Georgia leads the nation for Black executive representation and recent income growth. But Georgia offers the worst chances for wealth of any state for a Black child born into poverty.
Activists have stood on soapboxes to shout at Georgia’s lawmakers about these economic issues for the last 20 years. In January, those voters will expect their government to answer them.
The opinions of Black voters – particularly Black women – have been ignored for years, said Tiffani Stephens, a voter in DeKalb county. “We’re taken as the pretty person and all we care about is clothes, shoes and makeup,” she said. “Where if you really know a Black woman, you know these are additives. We are of substance. Deep substance.”
Democrats didn’t just win the marquee political contests in Georgia this November. They won every statewide election from the lieutenant governor’s office down to the insurance commissioner. Democrats displaced a Republican majority on the electricity rate-setting public service commission. Almost all the statewide office holders will be Black women, including the incoming speaker of the Georgia house, state representative Carolyn Hugley of Columbus. Democrats are one state senator short of controlling both chambers.
“This was not just a magical thing. This took a long time, building the infrastructure for the south and particularly for Georgia,” said Deborah Scott, executive director of Georgia STAND-UP, a “think and act tank” non-profit advocating for job training and economic development for working families.
It has taken multiple failed election cycles, chipping away at layers of cynicism, to be ready for this moment, Scott said. Stacey Abrams, two-time gubernatorial candidate turned democracy activist, deserves some credit for Georgia’s political results in November. But it is also the product of meticulous relationship-building groundwork, particularly by organizations led by Black women, she added.
“If Stacey is the tree that all of these newly elected officials are sitting in, then the roots of that are community-based organizations and non-profit organizations like Georgia STAND-UP and the People’s Agenda, folks that have been doing the work for a long time.”
Describing the election results as a referendum on gas prices, or the war, or Donald Trump, is reductive, Scott said. Black voters assess their conditions holistically. “It’s not just about the gas prices are too damn high – which is true – but it’s also about the quality of life for regular Americans.”
The last two years have been radicalizing for some Georgia voters, Scott said. While highly-educated CDC employees found themselves impaled on the spear tips of HHS secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, nonprofits serving low-income communities like Scott’s have been scrambling to replace federal spending and a dearth of private grants, she said.
Before the election, activists have been squabbling for scarce resources, she said. Today, they are bathing in the afterglow of political unity.
For 20 years, Democrats have been shut out of major decisions about Georgia’s policy direction. The state has restrictive abortion laws and libertine gun laws. It is one of 10 states which did not expand access to Medicaid.
It has also attracted stunning amounts of foreign investment during Kemp’s two-terms in office, with car manufacturers, battery plants and chip makers locating to Georgia. But almost all of that state-directed economic development landed either in the north Georgia foothills or in rural south Georgia, like the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America manufacturing hub in Bryan county, rewarding white, Republican voters with jobs and political attention.
Scott speaks about the urgent need to encode voting rights protections in the Georgia constitution with one breath. In the next, she talks about deepening the port of Savannah, or the new Audi car plant being built near Macon.
“If you look at rural Georgia versus urban and suburban Georgia, it really is a tale of two states,” she said. “This is an opportunity for economic development in all of the regions around Georgia … it’s an opportunity to equalize the state. It’s Atlanta and the rest of the state. And of course, even in Atlanta, it’s the tale of two cities. Those that are born poor will not come out of it. There’s an opportunity for really affordable housing and real economic development.”
The city of Stonecrest, a suburb of south-eastern Atlanta, exists as a municipality because its Black, middle-class voters decided 10 years ago that they wanted their community to incorporate to serve them the way white middle-class voters are served 30 miles north in Sandy Springs. They wanted political leadership that matched their aspirations.
“As a small business owner, which I am, this is an opportunity to have a seat at the table,” said Kazemde Ajamu, who owns Akoma Coffee & Books at Stonecrest.
Ajamu is looking for Georgia to recognize microbusinesses and to better empower entrepreneurship for small business owners. “I feel good about the incoming governor-elect, that this gives us an opportunity to have a voice to speak to it, to create laws that help micro-businesses, mom-and-pops … That’s one example of having a seat at the table, having a voice, and someone that’s listening and can be proactive in that area.”
While Democrats have control over the apparatus of state government, there is no reason to believe that’s a permanent condition. Political competition will force Bottoms and the state legislature to pay attention everywhere, Irons said.
“Everybody’s interest is in growing, and having prosperity and better education,” Irons said. “The success of what’s likely to happen for the next governor is to create an environment where all parties that are serious about the growth and the prosperity of the state of Georgia can have a seat at the table.”
The accession of Bottoms as governor and Democrats in control of government agencies may mean that a place like Stonecrest is less likely to be overlooked, Irons said. But the former HUD official and economic development director for DeKalb county said that doesn’t alone solve problems.
“I think every community has to be ready for the investment that it wants,” Irons said. “And so you have a governor that you can access differently. I think Governor [Brian] Kemp probably was aware of the needs, but a different group of people had access, right? I think now that just because you have access doesn’t mean you don’t have your own responsibility to be ready.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Israel coalition talks put Arab party leader under pressure over Hamas
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Israel coalition talks put Arab party leader under pressure over Hamas
Mansour Abbas faces mounting pressure from Israel’s change bloc to denounce Hamas as a prerequisite for coalition role.
The question of whether Mansour Abbas, the leader of Israel’s United Arab List (Ra’am), is willing to recognise the Palestinian group Hamas as a “terrorist” organisation may determine whether his party will play a role in the country’s next government.
According to Israel’s Ynet news website, Abbas has signalled to parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that he would agree to the designation in exchange for a “genuine partnership” in a coalition led by Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming a new government after last month’s elections.
Eisenkot has made recognising Hamas as a “terrorist” group one of the conditions for joining his prospective coalition. He has also demanded that Abbas recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state – despite Abbas’s own identity as a Palestinian citizen of Israel.
But on Wednesday, Abbas denied that he had made a declaration on Hamas. Earlier in the week, he had simply reiterated Ra’am’s support for disarming Hamas, and condemning “terrorism”.
The demands concerning Hamas and recognising Israel as a Jewish state pose a problem for Abbas, whose party represents Palestinian citizens of Israel – around 20 percent of the population, excluding the millions who live under Israeli occupation in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
He wants to join the government – and has previously done so in the past, in 2021 – seeing it as a way to improve the lives of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and force Netanyahu and other far-right figures out of power.
But declaring Hamas a “terrorist” group would be seen by critics as tantamount to supporting the Israeli narrative, during a genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 74,600 Palestinians.
Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera that Eisenkot’s conditions are intended to make a partnership with Ra’am more acceptable to his Jewish Israeli supporters and coalition partners.
“Eisenkot is telling them practically that Ra’am’s votes will help him form the government, and that this partnership will take place according to the definition he wants for the state,” Jabareen said.
Including Ra’am’s eight seats in parliament would go a long way to helping Eisenkot secure a viable coalition. His own bloc has 48 seats, but Ra’am and another Arab-led party, the Joint List, recommended him to lead the government. The Joint List, however, is more unlikely to agree to any of Eisenkot’s demands, and therefore if it does support the prospective prime minister, it will be from outside the government.
Political jockeying continues in Israel, with other factors – such as who the ultra-Orthodox parties will back, and how many of Eisenkot’s coalition partners will be willing to accept any role for Ra’am – complicating matters.
Competing loyalties
During consultations with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on November 5, Abbas was asked why he would not use the “terrorist” designation when describing Hamas. The Ra’am leader said he needed the “space to be a bridge” between Jews and Palestinians.
“Leave me also a space to protect myself and my family,” he added, saying it was an issue of “life and death”.
Jabareen warned of underlying tensions even if an agreement over the designation was reached.
“There is also a security dispute,” Jabareen said. “Signing the classification of Hamas does not determine how Ra’am will act if the government decides to resume a wide war in Gaza.”
Then there is the question of recognising Israel as a Jewish state. Abbas has previously accepted that as a political reality, saying in 2021 that the country had been established as a Jewish state. But this year he clarified that accepting that as a reality did not mean endorsing it.
“The Jewish character of the state is an existing fact that was imposed on us, and we did not choose it,” he wrote in August.
Jabareen said Abbas was trying to navigate a complex situation, ensuring that he reflects the positions and beliefs of his Palestinian base, while being more acceptable and palatable to the wider Israeli public. The analyst, however, feels that this may have gone too far in the latter direction.
“Abbas is trying to be the most loyal to the government… he is looking at the Israeli voter more than he looks at his own voter,” Jabareen said. “He took legitimacy from his voter, and now he must see how he can correct the course with the Israeli voter.”
The prospect of Ra’am joining an Eisenkot government has also been seized upon by Netanyahu, who has repeatedly focused on the perceived threat of parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, portraying them as a danger to the state.
However, reports have emerged that Netanyahu’s close associate and former chief of staff, Natan Eshel, has contacted Abbas to gauge his stance on supporting Eisenkot.
“Publicly, Netanyahu is trying to make Ra’am’s support more politically costly for Eisenkot to secure, whether by encouraging opposition among Eisenkot’s partners or by making Abbas less willing to support him without concessions,” Jabareen said.
External support dilemma
Abbas’s options include joining Eisenkot’s coalition, supporting a minority government from outside, or joining the opposition.
“Supporting the government from outside it may reduce the cost of having an open partnership with Eisenkot, and give Abbas greater freedom to object to government decisions,” Jabareen said.
But there is another complication. Another leading member of Eisenkot’s bloc, Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, has repeatedly said he would oppose a minority government that is dependent on Arab-led parties.
Lieberman, a right-wing politician, has shown few signs of budging from his position, and has instead encouraged Eisenkot to partner with ultra-Orthodox parties – who were part of Netanyahu’s coalition during the last government – despite previous disputes over military conscription of Jewish religious students.
And then, even if Lieberman’s opposition is overcome, there is the potential for any future conflict, either with Palestinians or with regional states, to put any arrangement under strain, Jabareen warned.
“If it is just a short confrontation with Iran, then there is more of a chance of Abbas staying in any coalition,” Jabareen said. “But if it is a wider war in Gaza, or an escalation in Al-Aqsa or the West Bank, or even in Lebanon, that would put him under direct pressure from his supporters.”
Jabareen pointed to a similar dilemma in 2022, when Ra’am suspended its participation in the Israeli government coalition at the time over Israeli police raids and violence at the Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem.
“Would Ra’am stay silent on those issues just to keep the coalition together?” Jabareen asked. “I expect it would first voice its objections and, if the escalation continued, suspend its participation.”

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Surgery by fairy lights and truckloads of fruit: the sanctuary saving Cameroon’s chimpanzees
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Words and photographs by Marta Meinardi
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Every morning in central Cameroon, the primatologist Sheri Speede wakes to a daunting task. At the Sanaga-Yong sanctuary, which she founded in 1999, there are 75 chimpanzees to feed four times a day and monitor for physical or behavioural issues.
Of those, more than 30 need to be given routine birth-control medications, four are babies requiring round-the-clock care, and two are rowdy teenagers currently being integrated into new social groups.
A chimpanzee might wake up on the wrong side of the bed and decide to pick a fight, hatch a plan to rise in the group hierarchy, or refuse to take its medication. On any given day, Speede is therapist, meal-prepper, veterinarian and site manager all in one.
Originally a veterinarian in the US, Speede visited Cameroon in the late 1990s and, in 1997, met Jacky, a chimpanzee that had been kept in a small cage outside a hotel in Limbe for nearly 30 years. Known around town as the “mad chimpanzee”, Jacky had little prospect of release or rehabilitation. In August 1999, Speede brought Jacky to her newly founded sanctuary, where he became one of Sanaga-Yong’s first three residents.
Jacky is still there, estimated to be in his 60s. He and Speede have lived side-by-side for a quarter of a century – longer than many people live with their own children.
The problem, though, as it has been for decades, is that chimpanzees and other great apes are hunted as some of the most prized bushmeat species in the world. The practice is deeply rooted in traditional remedies, with a reported 36 conditions claimed to be healed by 22 chimpanzee parts. Female chimp reproductive organs are said to cure infertility in women; crushed bones, to heal fractures; sleeping on their skins, to offer protection during childbirth.
Poaching is often a two-for-one transaction. When mothers and mature adults are killed for meat, their infants are sold to wealthy clients who want a chimpanzee as a pet, or to the private zoo trade. Compounding this is the near-absence of government enforcement against wildlife trafficking.
In addition, the decades-long armed conflict in Cameroon has harmed biodiversity conservation in the country. Between the anglophone crisis – an ongoing armed conflict between the Cameroonian government in the south-west and separatist groups in the north-west – and the Boko Haram insurgency, many of the country’s conservationists and forests are being badly affected. Every time the government launches a counterattack on separatist groups in the north-west, civilian villages are burned and hundreds of people flee the violence, seeking shelter in the forests – forests that were once the natural habitat of endangered great apes.
Armed groups also often take up temporary residence in the shelter and secrecy of Cameroon’s dense forests. There, they set traps for bushmeat and carve out farms in previously protected areas. As armed groups regularly control the movement of people and goods in the area, regardless of what side of the conflict they are on, their presence greatly restricts the ability of conservationists to continue their work.
Cameroon is home to the Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee, of which conservation groups estimate somewhere between 3,500 and 9,000 remain in the wild. Classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, and one of humanity’s closest living relatives, the subspecies continues to decline as the bushmeat trade goes largely unpoliced by the Cameroonian government. Killing chimpanzees has been illegal in the country since 1994, but enforcement effectively began only in 2006, pushed by the Last Great Ape organisation (Laga). The NGO says it has recorded more than a hundred great ape confiscations – dead and alive – annually since then. An estimated five to 10 chimpanzees are lost for every one recovered.
That gap between law and enforcement has not closed. Paul Biya has led Cameroon’s government since 1982, making him one of the longest-serving non-royal heads of state, and under his administration the burden of humanitarian and conservation work has fallen largely to international organisations rather than the state.
Cameroon’s safeguarded chimpanzee population is mostly at three wildlife centres – Ape Action Africa, Sanaga-Yong Chimpanzee Rescue and Limbe Wildlife Centre. Together they house well over 200 rescued chimpanzees, with no plan or space to release them, for lack of enforcement to safeguard them and appropriate forested habitat. For this reason female chimpanzees at Sanaga-Yong are given birth control medication.
As the fight continues for chimpanzee conservation and stricter anti-poaching laws in Cameroon, Sanaga-Yong stands as a stronghold. The sanctuary has earned wide recognition for some of the best chimpanzee care in the world. It runs on a model that benefits the surrounding community, with all of its caregivers hired locally. In recent years it has taken on two Cameroonian veterinarians, Mael Firina and Christian Atonfack, who joined the team upon graduation from veterinary school. While many sanctuaries rotate through international staff, the goal here is to train both vets under Speede and visiting international veterinarians so that the sanctuary’s future veterinary care rests in Cameroonian hands.
That localisation of talent is increasingly the model for conservation. When the work of protecting a place is put in the hands of the people who live there, the odds of it lasting go up considerably.
“Conservation led by Indigenous peoples and local communities, based on their own knowledge and tenure systems, is far more likely to deliver positive outcomes for nature,” says Neil Dawson, a global development researcher at the University of East Anglia who has studied the role of Indigenous people and local communities in conservation. “In fact, conservation very often fails because it excludes and undervalues local knowledge and this often infringes on rights and cultural diversity along the way.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.title: « Une entrave au droit de grève » : la justice ordonne la levée du blocage de l’usine Lactalis de Cuincy et condamne trois représentants CGT
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.author: Eugénie Barbezat
https://www.humanite.fr/social-et-econom.text:
La justice a contraint vendredi 13 novembre la CGT de l’usine de produits laitiers Lactalis/Nestlé à Cuincy (Nord) à cesser immédiatement le blocage du site, brisant ainsi le mouvement de grève en cours depuis le 5 novembre. Le syndicat entend faire appel de cette décision.
Une augmentation des salaires significative, une prime exceptionnelle de 500 euros par salarié face à la hausse du coût de la vie, une indemnité de repas de 4,70 euros pour les équipes de jour et l’ouverture immédiate des négociations annuelles obligatoires (NAO) pour 2027.
Telles étaient, en substance, les revendications des salariés de l’usine de yaourts et desserts lactés basée à Cuincy, près de Douai, dans le Nord. Déterminés à obtenir satisfaction, 80 % des salariés de Lactalis Nestlé de Cuincy étaient en grève, avec leur syndicat CGT, depuis le 5 novembre.
Arguant dans un communiqué que « des discussions ont déjà permis la mise en œuvre de mesures répondant à certaines préoccupations exprimées » et que le droit de grève « en aucun cas ne peut justifier le blocage du site », la direction du site a tout simplement traîné les représentants des salariés devant les tribunaux.
Trois cégétistes condamnés à 1 000 euros d’amende
Le tribunal judiciaire de Douai, saisi en référé par Lactalis, a rendu vendredi 13 novembre une ordonnance enjoignant à la CGT du site « de libérer immédiatement tous les accès de l’usine, en particulier pour les véhicules de livraison entrant et sortant », selon le géant laitier. La CGT a alors appliqué cette injonction.
Mais le syndicat entend faire appel de cette décision, qu’il considère être une « entrave au droit à la grève », a déclaré à l’AFP Dominique Ben, représentant de l’union locale CGT de Douai.
Le tribunal a également condamné trois cégétistes locaux à payer 1 000 euros chacun et le syndicat lui-même 1 500 euros, une « honte » selon la CGT. Ces frais ont été demandés en vertu de l’article 700 du code de procédure civile, qui permet de demander à la partie condamnée le paiement des frais de justice de l’autre partie.
« Nous ne sommes plus dans un État de droit. La justice saigne ceux qui ont faim et protège les riches qui se gavent », s’indigne la fédération CGT de l’agroalimentaire dans un communiqué. Et de rappeler que pour leur patron, le milliardaire Emmanuel Besnier, 10e fortune de France, « les seules primes exceptionnelles et indemnités de panier jour pour l’ensemble des salariés, pour toute leur carrière, représentent à peine 0,12 % » des 14 milliards qu’il détient.
Aux côtés de celles et ceux qui luttent !
L’urgence sociale, c’est chaque jour la priorité de l’Humanité.
- En exposant la violence patronale.
- En montrant ce que vivent celles et ceux qui travaillent et ceux qui aspirent à le faire.
- En donnant des clés de compréhension et des outils aux salarié.es pour se défendre contre les politiques ultralibérales qui dégradent leur qualité de vie.
Vous connaissez d’autres médias qui font ça ?  
Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: Athletes rewrite the rules as Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics come to an end
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Athletes rewrite the rules as Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics come to an end
Hosts Senegal thrive, and exuberant athletes defy the shadows cast over the Games by politics and history.
Dakar, Senegal – At the last event of the Dakar Youth Olympics, sneakers shrieked across the floor as breakdancers faced off.
Baggy trousers carried national flags. B-boys and B-girls dropped into six-step footwork, spun through windmills and defied gravity in sudden freezes. Arms became legs, legs became arms, each move a challenge, each response a little more daring.
The competition on Friday, the last in the two-week games, was less about brute strength or speed than invention, creativity, balance and nerve. Each of the teenaged breakers was part gymnast, part basketballer, part boxer all at once, and they brought a fitting energy to the end of a Youth Olympics held on the world’s youngest continent.
Before Senegal became the first African country to host an Olympic event, France’s development agency lent the already heavily indebted West African country 80 million euros ($88m) for sporting facilities for the games. It came as young people across the region are increasingly questioning the former colonial power’s lingering influence.
At Dakar’s railway station, I watched French police helping secure the event. Above them stood a statue of two bronze soldiers – one African, the other French. The African one, named Demba, represents the colonial troops who fought and died for France during World War I. The French one, named Dupont, rests an arm on his shoulder, a gesture of fraternity that others see as colonial paternalism.
Beneath their gaze, politics and history still cast shadows over the games.
At the first swimming medal ceremony I attended, Russia’s 17-year-old Serafima Fokina stood on the podium, gold around her neck, singing her national anthem. Some spectators rose. Others remained seated.
For Russian athletes and their supporters, it was a moment of enormous symbolism: The Russian flag and anthem were back at an Olympic event for the first time since the country’s suspension after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Israel competed too despite its genocidal war on Gaza. A Senegalese man was arrested over a video opposing its participation that authorities described as threatening.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) insists on political neutrality, a principle it considers fundamental to the Olympic spirit.
“Youth athletes should not be held accountable for the actions of their governments,” the IOC said, arguing that sport offers them access to hope.
But neutrality is a delicate ideal in a world divided by war, and the flags they carried can never be separated from the conflicts beyond the podiums.
For Palestinian swimmer Alma Shaat, representing her country carried a different weight. She had a message for the children of Gaza.
“Any little girl in Palestine right now, specifically Gaza, I would tell her … to continue following her dreams,” she told me. “She’s not doing it only for herself, but she’s doing it for the people in Gaza and in Palestine.”
Senegal outperform France as China tops medal table
China ended up topping the medals table with 18 golds. Japan were second on 11 golds and Russia third with eight.
Eighty Senegalese athletes had travelled not to France or the United States but to China to train before the fames, part of China’s soft diplomacy. For Senegal it paid off – they finished sixth, five golds to their name, ahead of France.
At her final news conference of the games, International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry fought back tears. The Zimbabwean, who is the first African and first woman to lead the IOC, had helped bring the games to Dakar.
“I am so proud. I’m so grateful,” she said.
Yet it did not all go smoothly. At the Olympic village, the real test of unity came with the heat as athletes stayed in university dormitories without air-conditioning.
Outside the arenas, not everyone could get in. Events sold out. Transport was costly. But neighbourhood sports offered another way to join the celebrations in a city where children play football in the streets, and wrestlers train on the beach.
And sometimes divisions appeared to matter more than national pride.
I overheard a French-speaking Swiss journalist dismiss the prospect of covering a medal won by a German-speaking Swiss athlete. He also complained about the timing of events and the Olympic quota system, which limited participation to one athlete per country per event while giving greater representation to African nations.
But his complaints seemed strangely out of touch with the joyful spirit of the athletes, who were busy rewriting the rules. They had taken hold of the microphones and the cameras themselves. Each became a broadcaster, telling their stories through Instagram and TikTok, reaching audiences well beyond the television networks.
Back at the breakdancing finals, China’s Holy Rain faced Saturn of Chinese Taipei – two teenagers, one from mainland China, the other from Taiwan, dancing out their rivalry.
Amid the roar of the crowd, one spectator leaned towards another and shouted into his ear: “Imagine if their leaders could do the same.”
In the end, Japan’s Hiyo beat Ukraine’s 14-year-old Nikastar for the gold and Spain’s Mini Ali took bronze against Morocco’s Nawel.
Beneath their flags, rivals battled to the sound of hip-hop, then embraced. The flags remained. So did the divisions they represented. But for a few beats, neither seemed to matter.

https://www.humanite.fr/societe-2/attent.text:
Trappes : après l’attentat raciste, la solidarité face à la haine | RÉEL
Publié le 15 novembre 2026
Dans ce nouvel épisode de « RÉEL », le format de l’Humanité qui part à votre rencontre, Valadista s’est rendu à Trappes une semaine après l’attentat terroriste d’extrême droite qui a coûté la vie à Pengo Bossio Wangi et blessé cinq personnes, dont une enfant de 12 ans.
À rebours des discours anxiogènes des chaînes d’information en continu, l’association « Mamans du cœur » nous ouvre les portes de la ville pour redonner la parole aux habitantes et aux habitants. Traitement médiatique stigmatisant, discriminations à l’embauche, précarité, mais aussi entraide quotidienne et mobilisation citoyenne : immersion au cœur d’une commune qui oppose la solidarité à la haine.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/la-chro.author: Jean-Pierre Léonardini
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/la-chro.text:
Regards sur la scène actuelle
Après un long entretien avec l’artiste palestinien Mahmoud Al Hourani, qui s’implique ardemment dans la formation d’une nouvelle génération de marionnettistes dans le monde arabe, la revue Théâtre/Public consacre son dernier numéro aux « États de la scène actuelle 2024-2025 ». Y sont passées au crible de regards aiguisés certaines formes neuves qui, depuis une vingtaine d’années, continuent de modifier le travail théâtral et ses rapports avec le public.
La critique universitaire donne là le meilleur de la réflexion, sur les plans esthétique et éthique (autrement dit politique, au grand sens). Cela se manifeste aussi bien chez Arnaud Maïsetti, qui radiographie avec maestria deux « Exercices de conjuration », The Cloud, d’Arkadi Zaides, et Extra Life, de Gisèle Vienne, qu’avec Olivier Neveux, qui explore « les Moyens propres du théâtre » à partir de Monde nouveau, Les applaudissements ne se mangent pas, Pétrole et Pieuvre 1 + 2 & 3, œuvres respectivement dues à Nathalie Garraud et Olivier Saccomano, Maguy Marin, Sylvain Creuzevault et Françoise Bloch.
Ce ne sont là que deux exemples patents des qualités d’analyse d’une livraison exceptionnelle, à laquelle participe une pléiade de chercheurs de haut vol. Interrogés par Christophe Triau et Olivier Neveux, Hortense Archambault (MC 93) et Vincent Baudrillier (théâtre Vidy-Lausanne), anciens directeurs du Festival d’Avignon de 2004 à 2013, témoignent de ces années de changement des formes, qui ont radicalement modifié la donne théâtrale, fût-ce au prix de rudes empoignades.
En fin de parcours, dans les miscellanées (soit mélanges en dire familier) on découvre un beau portrait de l’artiste accomplie qu’est la Portugaise Regina Guimaraes, dont on peut lire ensuite la pièce Dure dictature, tandis que Clara Roman-Valussi, dans « Laboratoire Mystère Bouffe », analyse en détail les enjeux mémoriels et artistiques de ce spectacle fameux du Théâtre du Radeau, forgé par le si regretté François Tanguy. Pointue à bon escient, la revue Théâtre/Public, fidèle à son origine, fondée en 1974 par Bernard Sobel et l’Ensemble Théâtral de Gennevilliers, ne cède jamais à la facilité en cultivant l’exigence intellectuelle au plus haut degré.
Avis à la population ! Songez donc que la collection complète de Théâtre/Public constitue d’ores et déjà une archive inestimable sur les avatars du théâtre au regard de ses publics, ce dans une société qui, en ces domaines comme en tous les autres, ne cesse de se métamorphoser à vue d’œil.
Théâtre/Public, n° 261 (octobre décembre 2026), 16,90 euros, abonnement@theatrepublic.fr
Au plus près de celles et ceux qui créent
L’Humanité a toujours revendiqué l’idée que la culture n’est pas une marchandise, qu’elle est une condition de la vie politique et de l’émancipation humaine.
Face à des politiques culturelles libérales, qui fragilisent le service public de la culture, le journal rend compte de la résistance des créateurs et de tous les personnels de la culture, mais aussi des solidarités du public.
Les partis pris insolites, audacieux, singuliers sont la marque de fabrique des pages culture du journal. Nos journalistes explorent les coulisses du monde de la culture et la genèse des œuvres qui font et bousculent l’actualité.
Aidez-nous à défendre une idée ambitieuse de la culture !
Je veux en savoir plus !

Spitzenspiel der Frauen-Bundesliga: Die mit dem Kopf
Bernadette Amani trifft gleich zweimal für den FC Bayern gegen VfL Wolfsburg. Mit 4:1 endet das Spitzenspiel einseitig zugunsten der Meisterinnen.
Ist Wolfsburg gegen Bayern endlich wieder ein Top-Spiel auf Augenhöhe? Wer es nicht gerade mit dem FC Bayern München hält, hatte vielleicht aufgrund der starken Leistungen beider Teams in den letzten Wochen sogar darauf gehofft, dass durch einen Sieg des VfL Wolfsburg nochmal so etwas wie ein Hauch von Spannung im Titelkampf der 1. Bundesliga der Frauen einkehren würde.
VfL-Sportgeschäftsführer Dieter Hecking hatte vor der Partie sogar selbstbewusst angekündigt, dass die Wolfsburgerinnen gewinnen würden und den Bau eines neuen Leistungszentrums für die Frauen angekündigt, das 2029 fertig werden soll. Laut WAZ liegen die Kosten zwischen 10 und 15 Millionen Euro. VfL-Trainer Stephan Lerch hingegen schlug bezogen auf die Partie vorab bedachtere Töne an, und das Publikum hatte vielleicht eine Vorahnung. Es kamen gerade mal 9.015 Zuschauer:innen. Zum Vergleich: In der Regionalliga West der Frauen wurden für Sonntag rund 18.000 Menschen beim Spiel des BVB gegen Schalke im Stadion Rote Erde erwartet.
In dem, was ein Spitzenspiel sein sollte, kam der VfL selten nach vorn, 4:1 stand es am Ende für die Münchenerinnen. Der Eindruck lag nahe, dass diese sich ihre Herausforderungen inzwischen in Details suchen. Zumindest sagte Trainer José Barcala im Interview nach dem Spiel, dass ein Ziel gewesen sei, endlich mal nach Ecken gegen Wolfsburg zu treffen, das habe es unter ihm noch nicht gegeben.
Klara Bühl, Mitspielerin von Bernadette Amani
Das gelang gleich zweimal mit einer einstudierten Variante: Klara Bühl servierte von der Eckfahne sowohl das 1:0 (36.) als auch das 4:0 (81.) für Bernadette Amani. Die Kapitänin der Elfenbeinküste verwandelte beide Male völlig freistehend mit dem Kopf – als eine der kleinsten Spielerinnen auf dem Feld hatten ihre Kolleginnen alle Verteidigerinnen Wolfsburgs von ihr weggelockt. Bei ihrem ersten Tor zielte sie ziemlich genau vom Elfmeterpunkt unhaltbar unter die Latte. Beim zweiten Treffer aus kürzerer Distanz war Wolfsburgs Torhüterin Stina Johannes zwar noch dran, aber Amanis Kopfball kam mit zu großer Geschwindigkeit, um das Tor zu verhindern.
Vom defensiven Mittelfeld zur Goalgetterin
Es waren die ersten beiden Bundesliga-Tore von Bernadette Amani, die sonst im defensiven Mittelfeld mit ihrem klugen und umsichtigen Passspiel die unbesungene Taktgeberin in Bayerns Mittelfeld ist. Sie hält mit ihrem Positionsspiel und vielen kurzen Pässen das Spiel am Laufen und sorgt dafür, dass Bayerns Spielidee überhaupt aufgehen kann. Gegen den Ball verteidigt sie mit Auge, aber wenn es sein muss, darf es auch mal eine technisch saubere Grätsche sein. Auch in engen Champions-League-Spielen ist sie unverzichtbar.
Nach ihrem Wechsel vom spanischen Verein CD Tenerife zum FC Bayern im Januar dauerte es deshalb nicht lang, bis Amani eine Hauptrolle einnahm. Das mag daran liegen, dass wichtige Spielerinnen auf ihrer Position lange verletzt waren und zum Teil noch immer sind. Gleichzeitig ist der Einfluss ihrer Zeit in Spanien auf ihr Spiel unverkennbar und passt genau zu den Vorstellungen José Barcalas. Nach der Partie wurde Amani mitten im Live-Fernseh-Interview von einem Mitarbeiter des FC Bayern mit einem lauten „Vamos!“ aus der Übertragung geholt. Sie hüpfte danach lachend ins Teamfoto. „Extrem goldig“, sagte Klara Bühl, „Super schön, dass sie für ihre Leistung heute so belohnt wird, was sie die letzten Spiele abrackert.“
Während Wolfsburg in Partien wie dieser bis heute am Abgang von Lena Oberdorf zu knabbern hat, dürfte man sich in München schon darauf freuen, in Zukunft die Qual der Wahl zwischen Amani und ihr zu haben – oder einfach beide spielen sehen zu können.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia?
Ukraine’s NATO ambition has always been a red line for the Kremlin. Giving up territory has been a no-no for Ukraine. Will they make compromises?
The United States has pitched a new pathway for Ukraine to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), an aspiration that Kyiv has long held as a means to guarantee its defence against Russia, almost five years into their war.
But the administration of President Donald Trump has suggested that Ukraine would need to agree to give up all of the Donbas region in the country’s east, which Russian President Vladimir Putin has demanded as one of his conditions for ending the war.
The idea, according to Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, was communicated to him by Trump’s negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the latest round of US-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week.
After the Abu Dhabi round of talks, Kushner and Witkoff met Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed Zelenskyy in Dublin, before a meeting of European leaders in the Irish capital on Friday.
Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.
But the Kremlin has repeatedly said Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would demand “a harsh response” from Russia.
So will Washington’s latest pitch be acceptable to both Ukraine and Russia?
Here’s what we know:
What do we know about the US proposal?
On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that Kushner and Witkoff had suggested that Ukraine could become a NATO member if it ceded control of Donbas in the east.
He said, “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'”
“NATO is back on the agenda” since it is part of an “extremely difficult” conversation between Ukraine and Russia which would determine the future of European security, Zelenskyy said.
Putin has been against Ukraine’s NATO membership and has demanded that the alliance pull back its troops from countries bordering Russia.
“This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.
“Real security in Europe means the EU [European Union] and NATO. That’s it. There is no other security in Europe.”
Ian Lesser, distinguished fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the US, told Al Jazeera that Washington’s proposal, if accurate, is significant because it articulates very directly an approach long current in US administration circles that Ukraine should be prepared to make territorial concessions in the service of a settlement.
“The NATO element seems very doubtful. Surely attractive to Ukraine, but [it is] hard to imagine Moscow agreeing to this. And some NATO members will be doubtful too,” he said.
Chris Featherstone, a political scientist from the University of York in the United Kingdom, argued that the proposal was a major departure from previously held positions.
“The US has been very cautious about getting further involved in Ukraine, with the Biden administration giving military support, but clearly opposing any ideas of Western involvement on the ground. Trump has seemed to be very sympathetic to the Russian cause, and has had significant blow-ups with Zelenskyy, so this proposal is certainly a surprise,” he noted.
He told Al Jazeera that offering NATO membership in a peace settlement would give significant support to Ukraine should Russia reinitiate the conflict in the future.
“In the light of Trump’s repeated attacks on NATO, this could be seen as a recommitment to the alliance. However, there would be questions over whether Trump could bring other NATO allies to support the proposal,” he added.
What does the US proposal mean for Ukraine?
Ukraine applied to become a NATO member in September 2022, just months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country.
Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.
But NATO members remain divided over offering Ukraine alliance membership amid an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.
NATO members bordering Russia, like Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic about backing Ukraine’s ambitions. Several other nations in the alliance have also been supportive of an expedited process for Kyiv to join, amid concerns about corruption in Ukraine and while seeking an end to the war with Russia as a condition for the country to become a NATO member.
But under President Trump, the US has been far less receptive to Ukraine’s calls for NATO membership. Trump has publicly told Ukraine to give up on hopes of joining the alliance.
Yet, while the new proposal from Witkoff and Kushner revives Ukraine’s hopes of joining NATO, it demands a compromise that no government in Kyiv can easily make.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that the prospect of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for ceding territory had not been raised by members of the alliance before and reiterated that Kyiv would not give up any of its territories.
But he said if Ukraine received a peace deal which included security guarantees, the right to maintain a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army, and funds to rebuild the country, then he would hold a national referendum on the question of ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership.
Featherstone noted that Ukraine has been fighting for a long time and has consistently maintained that it will not relinquish its territory in a peace deal.
“The proposal from the Trump administration is clearly an attempt to test this Ukrainian position, in an effort to confront the impasse,” he said.
“NATO membership would give a level of security that Ukraine would likely welcome. However, this would be a big sacrifice of territory and sovereignty. After years of Trump’s questioning of the NATO commitment, Ukraine would need a strong statement of commitment to its defence should they be considering any proposal like this,” he added.
What does the US proposal mean to Russia?
The Kremlin has not yet responded to the latest US proposal.
But it has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. In fact, Putin has also cited the issue of Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason why Russia launched its war in 2022.
Despite Kushner and Witkoff’s meetings with Putin, the Kremlin has shown little appetite for a change in that position. Moscow has continued, throughout the war, to demand that Ukraine abandon its NATO ambitions and maintain a neutral and demilitarised status. Russia has also firmly opposed any deployment of Western troops or peacekeepers on Ukrainian soil.
In addition to demanding that Ukraine give up its NATO dreams, Moscow has also insisted that Ukraine should cede sovereignty over the Donbas region, in addition to parts of Zaporizhia and Kherson provinces that Russia already occupies.
Just as the new US proposal asks Ukraine to give up some territory in return for a NATO seat, it offers Russia a bargain — withdraw its red line on Ukraine’s NATO membership and get the Donbas in exchange.
Why is Donbas significant?
The region in eastern Ukraine has historically been the country’s industrial heartland and is therefore a critical economic engine.
A majority of people in the Donbas identify as ethnically Ukrainian, but a minority identifies as ethnically Russian. The Russian language is also widely spoken in the region — a legacy of Russian migration there in the 19th century and then under the Soviet Union.
Russia accuses Ukraine of discriminating against Russian-speaking and ethnically Russian people in the Donbas and has used this claim to justify its demand that Kyiv hand over the region to Moscow.
The region consists of the provinces of Luhansk and Donetsk. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has occupied almost all of Luhansk and most of Donetsk. In all, it controls about 88 percent of the Donbas region. But it has consistently demanded that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the remaining parts of the Donbas they currently hold.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director of geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, who previously served on the NATO secretary-general’s policy planning staff, told Al Jazeera the US proposal tests the extent to which the territory of Donbas really matters to Russia.
But he said the recent Abu Dhabi talks had shown that Russia wanted more than just territorial concessions from Ukraine.
“They [the Russians] want to discuss what they call a new European security architecture, which is a code name for Russia having veto [power] when it comes to NATO,” he said.
He noted that it was also interesting that the Americans did not put forward the idea of Kyiv ceding the Donbas to the Russians in exchange for NATO membership.
“But everything indicates that the Russians will never accept this,” he said, referring to the idea of Ukraine joining NATO.
“The Russians have no intention of actually coming to the negotiating table. They’re just bringing up new issues [currently about European security architecture] and broadening the agenda in order to make it look like they’re negotiating and appease the American leadership, while inflicting as much damage on Ukraine as possible,” he added.
What has the US said?
The US has not explicitly announced that it has suggested Kyiv should cede territory for NATO membership.
On Saturday, hours after Zelenskyy’s remarks to reporters, in a lengthy post on X, Kushner suggested that “the press has reported some of the maximalist positions proposed by both sides, along with strong political rhetoric”.
He highlighted that the conversations between Russia, Ukraine and the US were “private discussions” aimed at ending the war.
“Several new ideas emerged from these discussions and are now being explored. Some may lead to breakthroughs directly, while others may evolve into new proposals that help bridge the remaining gaps,” he said.
“In our private discussions, both sides understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war. Serious and constructive work continues among those of us committed to finding solutions,” he added.
Earlier, on Thursday, Kushner also told reporters that Putin has agreed to include Europe in peace negotiations.
“We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” he said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: India’s Under-19 Asia Cup win over Pakistan marred by post-match aggression
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
India’s Under-19 Asia Cup win over Pakistan marred by post-match aggression
India beat Pakistan by one wicket in a thrilling comeback in the final but follow it up with unsporting behaviour.
India have beaten Pakistan by one wicket in a nail-biting final of cricket’s Under-19 Asia Cup in Oman, but the comeback win was overshadowed by an on-field display of aggression and heated outbursts from the winning side.
The thrilling final on Saturday swayed between the two South Asian rivals before India scripted a last-ball win at the Oman Academy Cricket Ground in Al Amerat on the outskirts of the capital, Muscat.
Facing a steep target of 338 in the 50-over match, India staged a remarkable turnaround after slipping to 252-8 in the 42nd over as Manal Chauhan and Mohit Ulva rescued the run chase with a vital 57-run partnership for the ninth wicket.
The pair’s heroics gave India a record-extending ninth Under-19 Asia Cup title and their first one since 2021.
However, the winning side’s post-match celebrations quickly took an ugly turn as the players seemed to target Pakistan’s players with aggressive gestures that were later condemned by former cricketers and Indian fans on social media.
One Indian player was seen yelling and gesticulating angrily in the face of Pakistan wicketkeeper Hamza Zahoor, who did not respond to the aggression. Others kicked their legs in the direction of the Pakistan dressing room while the Indian team management tried to hold back the players.
India were lauded for their never-say-die spirit that saw them through but faced criticism for unsportsmanlike conduct.
Former Pakistan cricket captain Mohammad Yousuf emphasised the weight players carry when they step onto the pitch.
“You are not just representing your country. In fact, you are representing your upbringing, the values and the ethics your parents taught you as a child,” he wrote in a post on X.
“Therefore, always remain respectful and composed, whether in victory or defeat. True sportsmanship is reflected in the way you conduct yourself, regardless of the outcome.”
Former Indian cricketers and heads of state praised the team’s win but did not condemn their behaviour although several Indian cricket fans shunned the “uncalled-for” demeanour.
“India and Pakistan may be adversaries, and cricket may be fiercely competitive, but that is no excuse for such uncouth, crass and downright disgusting behaviour,” one Indian supporter wrote on X.
“The behaviour on display was a reflection of the culture of leadership this country has normalised. It’s a cricket match, not a war.”
“A country’s sporting culture is reflected not just in how its players win, but also in how they treat those who lose.”
Both sides skipped the customary post-match handshake, which has become a recurring feature in Pakistan-India cricket matches after political tensions spilled onto the pitch over the past year.
Last year, then-Indian captain Suryakumar Yadav and his players refused to shake hands with Pakistani team members during an Asia Cup clash in September and also decided not to accept the trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) President Mohsin Naqvi, who also serves as Pakistan’s interior minister.
When Pakistan faced India in the ICC Women’s World Cup 2025 in Sri Lanka, the teams steered clear of handshakes and repeated the practice at the ICC Women’s T20 World Cup this year in England as well as their group-stage match in the Women’s Asia Cup.
In September, the India women’s team refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi after winning the Asia Cup final in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.
Chauhan, Ulva heroics lift India to victory
On Saturday, lower-middle-order batter Chauhan’s 47 from 32 balls revived India’s run chase while Ulva guided India home with an unbeaten 49 off 26 deliveries and was the final-ball hero for his side as he hit a boundary when they required three runs to win.
“This tournament had not gone well for me, but I had belief that I would be able to deliver today,” Ulva said after the match. “I needed Manal’s support, which he provided.
“I knew it was my day and that I would take my team over the line. Number 10 has been a very lucky number for me as all my runs have come from here.
“We had belief in our batting that we could chase this down. This was a flat wicket, and we kept telling ourselves that if they could score this many, then we could too.”
Pakistan posted 337-9 after winning the toss and electing to bat. Opener Usman Khan led the scoring with 107 off 111 balls while Abdul Qadir made 80 and captain Farhan Yousaf scored 63.
India’s reply was built on a strong platform laid by captain Lakshya Raichandani, who scored 80 off 101 balls, and fellow opener Aaryavir Sehwag, the son of India great Virender Sehwag, who made 58 from 61 deliveries and struck nine fours and was named player of the tournament.
Aaryavir finished as the tournament’s leading run-scorer with 361 runs in five innings.
India’s lineup also featured wicketkeeper Anvay Dravid, son of former India captain and coach Rahul Dravid, who scored 19 runs.

Polls open in Cape Verde in race with first female presidential candidate
Joana Rosa and four other opposition candidates face off against President Jose Maria Neves, who wants a second term.
Voters have begun casting their ballots in Cape Verde, where President Jose Maria Neves is facing off against the West African island nation’s first female presidential candidate, Joana Rosa, in a vote hinging on slowing down persistent emigration.
More than 300,000 people are eligible to vote on Sunday from 8am to 6pm (09:00 GMT to 19:00 GMT) and will choose from six presidential candidates in a country known for its stability in the politically volatile region.
Neves, a member of the country’s oldest political party, the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde (PAICV), is tipped to be the favourite but faces his strongest challenger in Rosa of the Movement for Democracy party.
The 66-year-old served as prime minister for 15 years and became president in 2021. His party won 37 of 72 parliamentary seats in May, allowing Neves to appoint Francisco Carvalho, then mayor of the capital, Praia, as prime minister.
Rosa, an opposition candidate and former justice minister, is the first woman to run for president since independence in 1975. Her party governed for 10 years before the May vote.
The country runs a hybrid parliamentary-presidential system of government that sees the president enjoy veto authority and a mediating role.
Tourist haven
Cape Verde, a tourism haven located off the coast of Senegal, gained global fame this year after its men’s football team battled with much bigger nations to reach the World Cup knockout stages. In April, a cruise ship sailing off its coast was struck by a hantavirus outbreak.
Emigration has long been a problem because of a dearth of jobs. The archipelago has more people living in the diaspora than the 500,000 people residing on its islands. Most are in Portugal, its former coloniser, and the United States.
Nearly 77,000 diaspora Cape Verdeans are registered to vote at embassies abroad.
Neves has promised to organise a youth summit to address emigration if he is elected to a second term. Rosa, meanwhile, called for a government that allows young people “to build their futures here at home and prevent the continued exodus of young Cape Verdeans abroad”.
But many voters feel distant from the political class over concerns that it doesn’t understand their daily difficulties, Roselma Evora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde, told The Associated Press news agency.
Results are expected within two to three days.
Candidates must clinch more than 50 percent of the vote to win, or the top two candidates will face a run-off vote on November 29.

https://taz.de/Sicherheit-in-Syrien/!623.title: Sicherheit in Syrien: Explosion in einem Vorort von Damaskus
https://taz.de/Sicherheit-in-Syrien/!623.author: Julia Neumann
https://taz.de/Sicherheit-in-Syrien/!623.text:
Sicherheit in Syrien: Explosion in einem Vorort von Damaskus
In Syrien tötet ein Sprengstoff-Attentat im drusisch geprägten Jaramana zwei Menschen. Der Vorfall löst Spekulationen aus und fördert spaltende Narrative.
Mit Taschenlampen durchleuchtet der Zivilschutz das einstige Auto, das nur noch ein Haufen aus geschmolzenen Metallstücken und abgebrannten Kabeln ist. In dem Wagen war am Samstagabend ein Sprengsatz detoniert. Laut dem syrischen Innenministerium wurden ein 35-jähriger Vater und sein Kind getötet, die Mutter wurde verletzt. Die Explosion geschah in Jaramana, einem Vorort der Kapitale Damaskus, in der Nähe einer Batteriefabrik, berichtet der staatliche Sender Syria TV. Die Sicherheitskräfte haben das Gebiet abgesperrt und versprochen, eine Untersuchung einzuleiten.
Jaramana liegt rund vier Kilometer südöstlich vom Damaszener Zentrum entfernt. Der Vorort ist auch ein Verkehrsknotenpunkt zwischen der Flughafen-Zufahrtsstraße und der Innenstadt. In der Nähe dieser Straße soll die im Auto platzierte kleine Bombe explodiert sein.
Wer für den Anschlag verantwortlich ist, ist bisher unklar. Die Regierung erklärte, der Vorfall sei ein weiterer Angriff der islamistischen Gruppe Daesch, bekannt unter dem Eigennamen „Islamischer Staat“ (IS). In den vergangenen Monaten kam es in Damaskus und den Vororten zu mehreren Explosionen. Am 6. August war bereits ein Sprengsatz in Jaramana, in einem Passagier-Kleinbus auf der Hauptverkehrsstraße, explodiert. Dabei wurden 14 Menschen verletzt.
Spannungen sollen jüngst zugenommen haben
In der Stadt leben Christen und eine große Gemeinschaft der Drusen. In dem Vorort kam es in der Vergangenheit zu Konflikten zwischen Teilen der drusischen Gemeinschaft und sunnitischen Muslimen, die die derzeitige Regierung in Damaskus unterstützen. Die Drusenführer möchten Autonomie über ihr Gebiet und Waffen, die Übergangsregierung versuchte in der Vergangenheit gewaltsam das Gebiet einzunehmen.
Anfang 2025 kam es zu gewaltsamen Konflikten, im folgenden April und Mai zu tödlicher sektiererischer Gewalt wegen eines Abrüstungsabkommens zwischen Damaskus und den Drusenführern in Jaramana und im südlich gelegenen Suwaida. Im Sommer 2025 kam es dann zu Massakern, an denen auch Teile der Regierungstruppen beteiligt waren.
In den letzten Tagen sollen die Spannungen in Jaramana wieder zugenommen haben. Am Donnerstag protestierten Menschen in der Stadt dafür, dass die Täter der Suweida-Massaker zur Rechenschaft gezogen werden, berichtet der Sender Al Jazeera. In der Nacht auf Samstag hatten Sicherheitskräfte einen Mann festgenommen, der Symbole des Assad-Regimes verherrlicht haben soll.
50 Tote durch Explosionen unidentifizierter Täter
Solche Vorfälle lösen im fragilen neuen Syrien nicht nur Spekulationen, sondern auch spaltende, sektiererische Diskussionen aus. Ein Sicherheitsexperte sagte dem Sender Syria TV, der IS sei in der Region Jaramana nicht aktiv. „Selbst wenn man dem IS die schwerwiegendsten Vorwürfe machen wollte – alle Indizien deuten auf Drogenhändler und terroristische Banden hin, die in Suwaida und der umliegenden Region präsent sind.“ Er bemühte das sektiererische Narrativ, dass der Drusenführer al-Hijri in Suweida für die „Sicherheitslücke“ verantwortlich sei. Und beschwerte sich, dass Drusen sofort protestieren würden, „wenn etwa eine Kolonne von Fahrzeugen einer Spezialeinheit in Richtung Jaramana vorrückt.“
Al-Hijri unterstützte früher das Assad-Regime und nun die israelische Regierung. Seine Truppen kontrollieren Checkpoints an der Zufahrtsstraße nach Suwaida.
Das Syrische Netzwerk für Menschenrechte (SNHR) dokumentierte in den ersten neun Monaten 604 getötete Zivilist*innen in Syrien, darunter 50 durch Explosionen, deren Täter nicht identifiziert wurden. SNHR fordert, dass Beweismittel an Tatorten gründlich gesichert werden, sämtliche Tötungen von Zivilist*innen wirksam untersucht sowie die Täter strafrechtlich verfolgt werden – in rechtsstaatlichen Verfahren.
