https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Drone attacks on power stations plunge Sudan’s cities into darkness
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Drone attacks on power stations plunge Sudan’s cities into darkness
Sudan’s power stations are being targeted in waves of drone attacks, resulting in power outages.
Port Sudan, Sudan – Kamal Mohammed, 42, has spent years managing his diabetes. But prolonged power cuts in the al-Taqaddum neighbourhood of Port Sudan, where he lives, have made his life “catastrophic”, he says.
Kamal relies on regular insulin injections to manage his diabetes, but unstable electricity supplies make it difficult for him to keep track of the doses he needs or store the medication at the required temperature.
“I need an insulin dose every day, but sometimes I have to skip it when power cuts last so long that the refrigerator loses its cooling,” he said.
Drone attacks
Kamal’s story reflects the massive disruptions the war between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), which broke out in April 2023, has wrought on civilians across Sudan.
More than 14 million civilians have been displaced since 2023, including about 4.5 million to neighbouring countries, while more than 150,000 people are believed to have been killed.
The fighting between the SAF and RSF, two former military allies, has increasingly turned into a conflict in which civilians and civilian infrastructure are targets. Drone attacks killed more than 160 people in just a few days in western Sudan in October, while hospitals, displacement camps and markets have become targets.
Attacks on energy infrastructure have also severely affected healthcare infrastructure, aid groups and other services vital for civilian life.
The RSF has intensified attacks on power stations around Khartoum state over the past month, creating an energy crisis in the capital. There has been no clear schedule for the power cuts in Khartoum caused by the damage to energy infrastructure, but blackouts can last anywhere between six hours and a day.
Weapon of war
Between October 20 and November 2, 2026, there were at least 18 attacks on electricity infrastructure across at least nine states, leading to declining power generation capacity and fuel shortages.
Repeated drone attacks on power stations have seen electricity generation fall from about 4,400 megawatts before the war to about 1,100MW today, according to The Associated Press news agency.
Mohammed al-Husseini, a political analyst, noted that the RSF stepped up attacks on civilian infrastructure after the SAF captured strategically important towns in the Kordofan region and other areas in recent weeks.
“The attacks on power stations aimed to weaken Sudan’s economy and disrupt agricultural and industrial production, both heavily dependent on a reliable electricity supply, particularly as the country prepares for a new agricultural season,” al-Husseini said.
“The attacks also sought to disrupt essential services and deepen humanitarian pressures, given electricity’s role in supplying water, maintaining communications and keeping medical facilities, including dialysis centres, operational.”
The United Nations has warned about the harrowing effect these attacks are having on civilians already plunged into abject poverty due to the war.
“I don’t know where those drone strikes are originating from; we need help passing the message to whoever needs to hear it, that this must stop,” Denise Brown, UN resident and humanitarian coordinator, recently said.
“There is no defence for repeatedly hitting power stations and fuel stations. People who need lifesaving dialysis can’t get it. Women are giving birth with no lights in the hospital. Operations can’t take place.”
Civilian targets
With refrigeration no longer a viable option for storing insulin, some people are now buying ice to keep their medicine cool, but not everyone can afford this daily expense.
“I can barely afford my medication as my salary is not more than 150,000 Sudanese pounds [$14.4]. Buying even a small block of ice could cost me 7,000 pounds [$0.67] a day,” Kamal said.
Electricity supplies were far more stable before fighting began, he said. During the summer, power cuts were limited and rarely lasted more than four hours. Now they are frequent, and the pressure this has caused on the national grid has made utilities even more expensive for customers.
“Before the war, my monthly electricity bill was no more than 3,000 pounds [$0.28]. Now it can reach 100,000 pounds [$9.61], although sometimes it is lower because of the prolonged cuts,” said Kamal.
Those who can afford them have bought solar panels for a more reliable supply, but these systems cost between 4 and 6 million pounds ($385 to $577), putting them out of reach of most households in Port Sudan.
“I considered getting a solar power system to keep my insulin refrigerated, run fans for my children and charge our phones at home. But it is far beyond what I can afford,” Kamal said. “Every day, I have to look for somewhere with a generator where I can charge my phone.”
Energy crisis
The energy crisis has left businesses struggling to operate. Osama Omar, 22, is an engineering student who opened a laundry in the Deim Madina neighbourhood of Port Sudan about six months ago to cover his basic living expenses. But prolonged power cuts threaten his small laundry business, which relies heavily on electricity.
“For nearly a month now, the supply has become increasingly unreliable, with outages lasting more than 24 hours,” Omar told Al Jazeera.
He has tried to adapt his business to the rolling power outages, but their unpredictability makes this difficult, leaving laundry piling up at his premises. At times, he has had to turn down new orders.
“Running my business in Sudan already comes with many challenges because of the war, the unstable exchange rate and rising operating costs,” Omar told Al Jazeera. “But power cuts have become another war that Sudanese people are being forced to fight.”
The energy crisis is felt across the country, with camps hosting Sudan’s millions of displaced people being particularly hard hit.
Sabri Adam, deputy head of the committee overseeing al-Karama 3 displacement camp in al-Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile state, told Al Jazeera that the 3,000 residents there are struggling to cope with the situation.
“Many arrived with little more than the clothes they were wearing, leaving behind their homes and belongings,” he told Al Jazeera. “The camp has no electricity supply, relying on just three large floodlights for lighting – one near the communal toilets and two beside the water tanks.”
Those with chronic illnesses such as diabetes, who need to store their medication at certain temperatures, have been badly affected.
Azhar Abdullah, a displaced woman living in al-Karama 3, said the lack of access to water and electricity has worsened the situation for her 13-year-old daughter, who has a thyroid disorder that requires extra care.
“Her heart rate increases and she experiences severe pain when she has to wash clothes by hand or exert herself physically,” Abdullah told Al Jazeera. “I worry that her condition will deteriorate further, as she has to undertake strenuous tasks throughout the day amid the lack of basic services.”

https://taz.de/Sozialproteste-in-Frankre.title: Sozialproteste in Frankreich: Erneut Zehntausende Menschen auf der Straße
https://taz.de/Sozialproteste-in-Frankre.text:
Sozialproteste in Frankreich: Erneut Zehntausende Menschen auf der Straße
Den fünften Samstag in Folge fanden Demos gegen die Regierung statt. Der Protest blieb weitgehend friedlich; in Lyon wurde ein Fernsehteam attackiert.
afp/dpa | In Frankreich haben den fünften Samstag in Folge Menschen gegen die Regierung protestiert. Nach Angaben des Innenministeriums gingen landesweit rund 106.000 Menschen auf die Straße, darunter 24.000 in Paris – die geringste Teilnehmerzahl der vergangenen Wochen. Studentenverbände bezifferten die Zahl der Demonstranten auf 200.000, darunter fast 100.000 in der Hauptstadt. Landesweit waren 70.000 Polizisten im Einsatz.
In Paris wurde etwa gegen einen Gesetzentwurf protestiert, der Polizisten, die ihre Waffen einsetzen, weiteren Schutz gewähren soll. Andere forderten bessere Bildungsbedingungen, mehr Kinderrechte oder einfach ein besseres Frankreich.
Die Proteste verliefen weitgehend friedlich. In Paris, Bordeaux und Nantes setzte die Polizei jedoch Tränengas ein. Zuvor hatten einige Menschen unter anderem Feuerwerkskörper gezündet. Das Innenministerium meldete 219 Festnahmen. Zehn Polizisten seien leicht verletzt worden.
In Lyon musste die Polizei eingreifen, um ein Team von Fernsehreportern zu schützen, nachdem Demonstranten es angegriffen hatten, wie die örtlichen Behörden mitteilten.
„Es war sehr, sehr heftig, einer von ihnen hat mehrere Schläge abbekommen“, sagte ein Journalist, der den Angriff beobachtet hatte, der Nachrichtenagentur AFP. „Seine Kamera wurde zu Boden geworfen, ging kaputt, und danach haben sie sie an sich genommen und gestohlen.“
Der Protest hatte an Gymnasien seinen Anfang genommen. Schülerinnen und Schüler demonstrieren seit Wochen für mehr Lehrpersonal, Geld zur Sanierung maroder Schulen sowie gegen Ungerechtigkeiten im Bildungssystem.
Mitte Oktober lief der Protest mit Demonstrationen gegen hohe Lebenshaltungskosten zusammen. Aufgerufen hatte dazu unter anderem die Protestbewegung der Gelbwesten. Auch wenn sich mittlerweile weniger Menschen an Demonstrationen beteiligen, reißt der Sozialprotest nicht zwangsläufig ab. Für Dienstag haben Gewerkschaften erneut zum Streik aufgerufen.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: As told to Nick Ames
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
“Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona.
Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”
The highs and lows of Sir Bobby Robson’s remarkable England tenure are chronicled in a new book co-written by Butcher: Almost Immortal: When Bobby Robson’s England Gripped The Nation.
Your name instantly brings to mind you playing on for England with a bandaged head and bloodied shirt. With hindsight, should you have left the pitch? Sian Williams
I never contemplated leaving the pitch at all. As the captain of your country, playing in a crucial World Cup qualifier against the top team in our league, in our group, there’s no way. I said to Bobby: “If you take me off, I’ll hit you.” I don’t think I would have but I said: “No, don’t do it!” Initially, I felt the blood and it seemed like a bad one, quite severe, but when I was bandaged up I could still play and it wasn’t a problem. Heading the ball wasn’t an issue because you’re really fired up, the adrenaline’s there, so it didn’t concern me. There was no way I was going to voluntarily come off unless Bobby was of a mind to do that, but he knew my pain threshold very well and knew I would battle on. I had numerous injuries before, broke my nose in 1982, five weeks in hospital and lost a lot of blood. So he knew I had great fortitude. Things have changed dramatically now. From a medical point of view it would have been right to take me off, absolutely. But that was then and I think, as a captain, you have to lead. It’s nice that people remember me through that image, but I was just doing my job.
I once stayed at the hotel that forms part of the FA’s headquarters at St George’s Park. Above the bed, and hanging over my wife and me all night long, was a giant version of the photo of you covered in blood. It was a bit disconcerting – but what’s the strangest place you stayed in or visited while on England duty? Stu Egan
I’ve actually stayed in that room as well. Stu has told us what it was like for him and I have to say it wasn’t great for me either. I’m staring up looking at me with a bloodied head and thinking: “Oh my God, this has followed me around.” At least when you close your eyes and sleep you don’t have to see it, but I’m sorry he had to stay there.
I didn’t stay in many really strange places with England. When I was manager of Motherwell we had a Scottish Cup quarter-final and were in administration at the time. I was organising our travel myself and booked a hotel near Stranraer, online. It looked great, right by a golf course. But when we got there we realised it was a residential home for the elderly. The rooms had accessibility handles and low sinks. It wasn’t a horrible place at all, quite the opposite, it was very warm and caring. But it was strange coming down for breakfast seeing people being looked after by the nurses. We won 4-0 so it can’t have been bad for us.
Now that time has passed and Diego has left us, has your perspective on that afternoon in Mexico City softened at all, or do you feel a professional duty to history to never let the “Hand of God” be forgotten? Victor Segovia
My feelings haven’t changed and they won’t. But I’ve learned to live with it better, I’ve learned to get through it and I’m not so annoyed by the memory. You’re just disappointed it happened. It had an influence on the game because we went one down and I think a lot of the players were shocked by what happened. Half the team saw it, half didn’t. I was one of the ones who didn’t. It had a big part to play in the fact we didn’t get switched on again and conceded the second goal. I’m more disappointed because he beat me twice. You’ve got to respect the man and respect what he did for the second goal, and what he did in that game. He was the best player I’ve played against and one that I never really got near.
Maradona’s “wondergoal” – it was really an own goal by you as you did a desperate sliding tackle, wasn’t it? David
If I’d got a touch I’d have raised my hand straight away and admitted it was the best own goal I’d ever scored. He went past Peter Shilton and I managed to get back, but I couldn’t see the ball so I was kind of feeling around him with my left foot. I couldn’t get my right foot across, but I thought I could block it. I was so surprised when he made good contact and put it in the net because I thought: “I’ve got this.” You can see me afterwards on the TV, I’m banging my shinpads, I was so angry. I was more angry about that goal than I was the “Hand of God” goal. So I’d have loved to claim that one. I know it sounds bizarre but it would have been one of my greatest achievements. Would it still have been the greatest goal scored at a World Cup?
In the early 80s you had a brilliant side at Portman Road so I wondered if you have: “If only …” or “What if …” moments about that time. It has always felt to me that Ipswich left another big trophy or two out there. Stooze
We did. The 1980-81 season was arguably the best in our history. We lost the FA Cup semi-final, lost the league title on the last day of the season and then had to play the Uefa Cup final, which thankfully we won. It’s always at the back of your mind that you missed out on what you should have got, which was the treble. We should have done it. But I think the 66-game season was just too much for us, we didn’t have a big squad and struggled with injuries towards the end. But we came really close. Look at the teams Sir Bobby built, we were in Europe for nine seasons out of 10. There’s no particular moment I sit down and dwell on, but you know it’s there, so close but so far.
What was the one quality Bobby Robson had above all others and was he the best manager you played under? Carl Parrish
His man-management was top class. He knew how to get the best from his players, knew what buttons to press and got to know them very quickly. He could wield his strength, he was a really tough guy, but when he was friendly it was lovely. His face lit up and he made you feel really good through that man-management. He always used to say to me: “Whenever I pick you, you always do well.” When someone says that you feel really good about yourself. He knew what to say. But had an abundance of things that worked really well for him. His tactical knowledge, selection of players, the network he built up for the younger players to come through, so many things. He was the most complete manager in my eyes and I still think he’s the best. Wherever he went, home or abroad, he proved himself in a way no English manager has done.
What was it like playing alongside Des Walker with England? And how close were England to winning the World Cup in 1990? Ahmed Kheyre
Des was the best centre-half I played alongside for England; he was unbelievable. He prolonged my international career because he was my pace. You never beat Des Walker. He was OK on the ball, it wasn’t his strength, but he used to give it to people that had great ability in that area so he was very astute. He was very young at the time, but dependable, talked well, shouted, pulled you about, was dominant. He was one of the reasons I made it to Italia 90. As for how close we were, I think the semi-final was the best we played all tournament. As I was walking out I felt so serene, comfortable, like I was in a dream state. It was never normally like that, but I could see our boys’ faces: steely, determined, but relaxed. It was the best I’d ever felt before a game. I even successfully backheeled the ball to a teammate. It was one of the best moments of our lives. We didn’t get to the very best one, the final, but we were so close. You’re talking inches, the shot that came off the post right between Lineker and Beardsley. Beating Argentina in the final would have been the ultimate redemption.
Is it true that during your time at Rangers, the top away scorer at Ibrox was Butcher (og)? Anonymous
I think I scored more goals past Chris Woods, my own goalkeeper, than any other Scottish striker. They were crackers: pick that one out Woodsy. He was my roommate as well, so he would say: “I don’t want any more going past me.” But they were all good ones, put it that way. They weren’t just ricochets or anything else like that. Wow, they were proper own goals. If you’re going to hit it, hit it hard.
I’m a massive fan of you as a player but think I’m even more impressed by your work with veterans following the death of your son. What would be the biggest thing we could do to support veterans? Jim
We’ve got to have a specific centre for veterans, like a St George’s Park, which would be dedicated to their health and that of their families. That would be the ultimate aim for me. We need more, and bigger, facilities to focus on veterans’ mental health and respite for those around them. It would be ideal to create a military community where you’re not in service, but the families are together. It would enable the veterans to relax, get treatment, get better, get the toolbox that provides the coping mechanisms so that if something happens they know what to do and where to go. My son didn’t have that unfortunately: he stayed in his room and that was his safe place.
I enjoy my work with Combat2Coffee, which supports veterans and their families. It’s doing really well and the togetherness is great. It’s getting exponentially bigger and we’re about to open a veterans’ hub in Ipswich. It’s a special thing, you can just walk in off the street and get that support. I’m doing this because my son would have loved it, and it’s what he needed.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Ebony Riddell Bamber
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage.
When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan.
The majority studying in the department were young women, and a few of us were of African descent. Some classmates and I raised concerns within the department at the time, but nothing was ever done: his “freedom” of speech was something we had to just accept. Years after we left Leeds, a group of us felt so strongly about what we had experienced – and the university’s failure in its duty of care – that we wrote a letter about it.
I have been transported back to those Leeds seminar rooms after reading of the decision of Oriel College at the University of Oxford to allow Dr Nathan Cofnas to speak at an event organised by Oxon Universities’ Reform Society, a student group that supports Reform UK. Much like Ellis, Cofnas has persistently espoused views associated with scientific racism.
A blogpost published by Cofnas while he worked at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, claimed that “in a meritocracy, Harvard faculty would be recruited from the best of the best students, which means the number of black professors would approach 0%” and that Black people “would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. Though Cofnas’s right to his views were upheld by a tribunal, it found that the blogpost “created a hostile, intimidating, unwelcoming and degrading environment for members of the college, particularly black students”. Cofnas’s claims against Prof Jason Arday also led to the professor facing intense media scrutiny in the runup to his death.
For me, this story is a painful and sobering reminder that little has changed when it comes to universities’ care for their students, particularly Black students. In a statement regarding the Cofnas event, Oriel College said that the institution is “committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so. This includes the freedom to express views that many find deeply offensive.”
Perhaps the argument that platforming racist ideas is merely a “freedom of expression” issue persists because of a disconnect with the real experience of Black students – and faculty – who have to navigate university campuses under such circumstances. Nearly three decades on, I can still remember preparing myself for tutorials with Ellis. Trying to defend my right to exist, to be in that space. And I wasn’t the only one. Rehearsing arguments, sharpening comebacks, compiling data. Anything I could do to try to push back at whatever derogatory comment he would slip into his lecture.
I was brought up to be conscious, proud of my heritage and culture. Maybe I landed a blow or two, but the upshot was that it was exhausting. It was never enough. I was never going to change his mind, but I was not mature enough to realise that. And it chip, chip, chipped away at me, my self-esteem, my emotional wellbeing. At a time when I should have felt liberated, encouraged – and, yes, challenged – to explore, interrogate, critically analyse, I was being pushed into a box. The message was clear: know your place, Ebony.
Advocates of free speech may think that what I endured was OK, and similarly that Black and global-majority students at Oxford must simply suck it up with regard to Cofnas. But as a young Black woman on the receiving end of anti-Black as well as misogynistic speech from a person who had power over me, it felt like abuse.
And as for Oxford, while freedom of speech is indeed a fundamental human right, it also sits alongside an obligation, according to the UN, to “ensure the equal and non-discriminatory participation of all individuals in public life”. This means that universities must balance academic freedom with their duties under UK equality legislation.
It may be that Oriel College has considered both these obligations and done the necessary equality analysis, in which case it should share it transparently with students, academics and high-profile figures who have raised legitimate concerns. But otherwise, this just looks like yet another case of disregarding the safety of Black people who simply want to study, work and live their lives without their intelligence being questioned.
- Ebony Riddell Bamber is the programme director of the Scott Trust’s Legacies of Enslavement programme

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Iran says it targets US radar in Bahrain. What do we know?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Iran says it targets US radar in Bahrain. What do we know?
The Bahrain Defence Force says its air defence systems thwart several Iranian ‘aerial attacks’.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base in response to what it describes as hostile US actions.
Sirens sounded in Bahrain on Sunday as its Ministry of Interior urged residents to “remain calm” and “proceed to the nearest safe location”. It was the second time in three days that the IRGC claimed to have targeted a US radar system in Bahrain.
The US military said it intercepted two Iranian drones on Friday but has yet to comment on Sunday’s claim.
Here is what we know:
What happened on Sunday?
The IRGC said it struck the radar at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base, according to a statement carried by the IRGC-affiliated Fars News Agency.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued two alerts within about three hours, the first about 4:30am (01:30 GMT). The ministry warned of a “potential threat” and urged residents to seek shelter. It gave no further details about the threat.
The Bahrain Defence Force also said its air defence systems thwarted several Iranian “aerial attacks” targeting the kingdom.
In its statement, the IRGC said the Strait of Hormuz remained closed and claimed that US efforts to escort ships through the waterway had failed. It warned that any US attack would draw a more severe response.
What happened in Bahrain on Friday?
The IRGC said on Friday that it destroyed a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. The US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, saying it had shot down two IRGC drones and there were no injuries or damage.
In a statement carried by Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim News Agency, the IRGC called the operation a “serious warning” over what it described as aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported that Friday marked the first time since early September that Iran had claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.
Tehran has told the United Nations Security Council it would respond immediately to renewed US or Israeli attacks and has accused Bahrain and other Gulf states of supporting US military operations. Bahrain has called for the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and other countries in the region and demanded they stop.
Manama, Bahrain, is where the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet is based. A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks had damaged or destroyed buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.
What has happened in the Strait of Hormuz?
The IRGC’s navy said two oil tankers struck sea mines on Saturday while trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. In a statement carried by Iran’s state news agency IRNA, it said the vessels had switched off their navigation and tracking systems and were using what it called an “unauthorised” route.
The IRGC said two other tankers turned back towards the Gulf after receiving warnings from its maritime traffic control centre.
Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Mohammed Vall said on Saturday that there were “two similar incidents yesterday” and the number of tankers hitting mines has increased.
Vall said Iran claims that the Strait of Hormuz is under its “full control” and “only Iran and Oman have the right to control it”. The United States rejects that claim.
According to Vall, Iran blamed the incidents on the tanker owners and the countries backing them, saying they had failed to comply with the regulations Iran imposed on passage through the strait.
Where do efforts to end the war stand?
Diplomatic efforts to stop attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled with Iran’s parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, telling Al Jazeera that Tehran wanted to move beyond a state of “no war, no peace”.
Ghalibaf said in the interview last week that Iran has conveyed seven conditions for a deal through a Qatari mediator and was awaiting an official US response. The conditions he outlined included lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.
US President Donald Trump’s administration, meanwhile, has tightened sanctions and maintained the blockade on Iranian ports.
Saeid Golkar, the UC Foundation associate professor of political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, told Al Jazeera that limited exchanges could escalate into a wider war.
“Both sides may prefer to avoid a full-scale war, but the danger lies in miscalculation,” Golkar said.
“Iran may continue limited maritime and regional escalation to increase pressure while Washington could respond militarily. Such exchanges could eventually lead to a broader conflict that neither side initially intended.”

https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.title: Entangled Past: how descendants of enslaved and enslavers in Grenada embarked on journey of repair
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.author: Natricia Duncan Caribbean correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2026/no.text:
When the Grenadian historian Nicole Phillip opened an email from the then BBC journalist Laura Trevelyan in 2022, she uncovered a connection that stretched back centuries.
Their ancestors had stood on opposite sides of enslavement in Grenada: Phillip’s among Africans forcibly taken from their homes and enslaved, Trevelyan’s among the British families who profited from a system that inflicted unspeakable cruelty and inhumanity on generations of enslaved Africans.
That email sparked a journey of acknowledgment, reconciliation and repair that Phillip and Trevelyan say powerfully illustrates how slavery reparations can work in practice. Their new book, Entangled Past, outlines that journey and argues that their experience can offer a model for others.
The book was published in the same week that the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he was open to a formal British apology while ruling out financial reparations, and announced that Britain would enter a structured dialogue with the Caribbean, which is due to take place over the next year.
It describes the Trevelyan apology, the first of its kind in the British Caribbean, as “a concrete example of what can be achieved, when descendants of the enslaved and descendants of enslavers sit down together and ask how to confront the past and work towards a better future”.
Speaking to the Guardian, Trevelyan recounts how she first discovered her family’s involvement in enslavement when a cousin she had never met emailed her to say their ancestors had been identified as enslavers in a University College London database.
Her own research later revealed that Trevelyans had held shares in plantations in Grenada and enslaved more than 1,000 people. They were also compensated when enslavement was abolished.
“For me, as a journalist, it was just really a fascinating and absorbing story, because this is, right there, Britain’s hidden past. There’s Britain sweeping slavery under the carpet, and there’s our family part of it,” she says.
Six years on, Trevelyan was sending an email to Phillip.
“With some trepidation, I wrote to her saying that I was a descendant of absentee enslavers in Grenada and I’d like to talk to her about this because she’s both a historian and vice-chair of the reparations committee.
“And then I pressed send and I thought, what on earth is she going to think of this? I was a little bit anxious and I was pacing around.”
But in Grenada, Phillip was excited to receive it. “I wrote her back immediately. And I said, there is a big smile on my face. You are my favourite BBC journalist,” she says.
Phillip grew up surrounded by relics of Grenada’s colonial past, including plantation houses, mills and artefacts collected by her father. As a young adult, she looked out from her veranda at Beausejour plantation house and wondered about the secrets it held. She never imagined that one day she would visit the house with Trevelyan, a descendant of the family that once part-owned it.
But the journey between that first contact and the bond they now share was anything but comfortable or smooth.
Trevelyan described tough conversations with her family: “There were family members who disagreed entirely with the idea of apologising, feeling that it was nothing to do with them, all a long time ago, why dig up the past, and no good could come of it. Some worried about being sued, saying there had to be a good reason why Britain’s government had never apologised for slavery.”
Entangled Past does not shy away from uncomfortable aspects of the experience. In it, Trevelyan describes arriving in Grenada in 2023 for the apology feeling “extremely anxious and trepidatious”, and being “immediately alarmed” when the driver who collected her from the airport revealed why he had not displayed her name. “There’s a Rasta fellow on the radio denouncing your apology,” he told her, “and my wife doesn’t want any trouble.”
Trevelyan recalls being advised to expect the unexpected: people were still angry about enslavement and, as a descendant of an enslaver, she was putting a “face on enslavers”.
“And I thought that phrase, the gale is unavoidable, just really summed it up … People have every right to express their views in whatever way they wish, because it’s a complicated subject,” she says.
The day of the apology, Phillip says, was defined by protest and praise for the Trevelyans.
In their book, Phillip recounts arriving at the ceremony “purposefully adorned in the purple robes of my ancestors”, only to be greeted by Rastafarian protesters waving placards to the beat of drums. Some read: “Why sell us out again?”, “Stay focus on reparations not the sideshow” and “No house slave cannot negotiate for the Rastaman”.
Arley Gill, the chair of the Grenada reparations commission, was involved, alongside the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, in discussions with the family. He recalls protesters arguing that the Trevelyans’ offer of £100,000 was insufficient.
“Now our position, of course, is that £100,000 is a drop in the ocean,” he says. “But … we really don’t expect individual families to pay for all of the sins of the British empire.” But he said he believed that following the 10-point plan for reparations set out by the Caribbean community (Caricom) with regards to investment in education and health, it was a step in the right direction.
The £100,000 payment from Laura Trevelyan, with the Trevelyan Grenada Reparations Fund subsequently established by the wider family, is helping fund university education for Grenadian students.
Phillip says the benefits reach beyond individual recipients, who come from parishes where the Trevelyans part-owned sugar plantations.
“For these students, they are the first in their family to have a university degree,” she says, adding that many come from struggling households where women are the breadwinners.
“So it’s not just the person, it’s their family and their extended family, and by extension, the community that benefits when one person gets that opportunity to advance their education.”
Gill believes the process that preceded the payment offers lessons for the wider reparations movement. The dialogue, he says, was conducted on the basis of mutual respect. The Trevelyan family, he adds, were “not talking down to us”.
“So yes, I would say in short that that model is a workable model for families and institutions having a structured conversation with the ancestors of the enslaved.”
For Phillip, however painful and complicated the process may be, conversation remains essential. “Not talking about something doesn’t make it go away. It doesn’t help with healing.” Conversation, she says, is “a way of reconciling with the past and trying to find ways to move forward”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: What forced the US to ground all planes? A router switch, we now know
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
What forced the US to ground all planes? A router switch, we now know
US officials say a routine upgrade that went awry caused the mass disruption of air travel.
Airlines are still scrambling to return operations to normal after the longest and only second nationwide stop of flights in the United States since the attacks of 9/11 in 2001.
More than 5,000 flights were cancelled in the US on Saturday after over 9,000 were scrapped a day earlier as the knock-on effects continued from Friday’s abrupt ground stop. The stoppage was halted after more than four hours on Friday night, but airports and carriers were still grappling with large backlogs and resulting delays.
The decision to suddenly ground all planes on Friday initially triggered speculation of a cyberattack.
But officials have since ruled that out and named the reason for the weekend disruptions as a routine replacement of the communications routers that connect the US air traffic control system.
Here’s everything we know about what went wrong:
What happened?
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop of flights at 3:54pm East Coast time (20:54 GMT) on Friday, citing a telecommunications outage affecting air route traffic control centres.
The outage caused thousands of flights to be cancelled or delayed across the US.
The ground stop was removed at 8:15pm on Friday (01:15 GMT on Saturday), but hundreds of flights were still delayed or cancelled that night, according to the aviation analytics firm Cirium.
Aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations and land during the ground stop while international flights were handled on a case-by-case basis with some allowed to depart despite the restrictions.
What caused the ground stop?
A routine upgrade was being carried out – maintenance work that ultimately overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop, US officials said.
L3Harris, a contractor, was replacing a section of the system’s old and discontinued copper wire with new fibre optic lines in a remote location on Friday afternoon, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday.
The router in that location then started overloading the air traffic control system, causing communications disruptions. When officials couldn’t locate the cause of the overload, they grounded flights nationwide.
“When we see that, your safety is paramount. We shut down the airspace,” Duffy said.
The transportation secretary said “contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment” caused the router to start flooding other ones.
“We had 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds,” he told reporters.
The issue affected communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 en route centres.
The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS), a union representing FAA safety employees, said the issue was isolated to two routers that were updated on Friday. An official told the Reuters news agency it was believed the routers were in Arkansas and Texas.
An FAA official said the agency conducted a safety assessment before the work. The union said PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.
Ageing technology and equipment alongside a shortage of several thousand controllers have long been concerns plaguing the US air traffic control system.
Duffy on Friday called for $50bn in funding to upgrade these systems, up from his earlier request of $30bn after Congress approved $12.5bn last year.
So it wasn’t a cyberattack?
No.
White House officials had convened an emergency meeting in the Situation Room on Friday amid concerns that the incident was due to a cyberattack. But the US government has since said it did not believe that was the cause.
“Once we were able to isolate the work being done at this location, all of our systems came back online,” Duffy said. “So we don’t believe this was cyber at all.”
The FAA chief reiterated that view at Saturday’s news conference.
“We see zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said.
Who has been named responsible for the incident?
L3Harris, a US-based aerospace and defence company, is the contractor behind the systems upgrade, the US Department of Transportation said.
Three-fourths of the company’s revenue comes from US government contracts, largely from the military, The New York Times reported.
“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it … installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?” Duffy said. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”
Duffy added that L3Harris, which he said had performed decades of work for the FAA, “didn’t meet the moment”.
“They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it,” he said. “Frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”
In response to Duffy’s allegations, L3Harris told Al Jazeera it has been working “in close coordination with the FAA” and safety and reliability are its “highest priorities”.
“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the November 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” a spokesperson for the company said.
“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”
L3Harris said it has been “modernising” the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in “close coordination” with the FAA.
It added that it has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fibre optic system.
The FAA said it was doing additional testing with L3Harris to see if there are any further risks.
When will flights in the US be back to normal?
Bedford, the head of the FAA, cautioned that it could take time.
“We have crews and aircraft that are out of position for 12,000 flights that were lost,” Bedford said. “These crews, pilots and flight attendants need to get to their points of reconnection with their schedules.”
He stated that he thinks “the worst is behind us”.
Duffy said airlines were expected to restore their full schedules by Sunday night.
Airlines have issued travel waivers for passengers affected to rebook flights for later dates at no cost.
Tens of thousands of people remain stranded in airports across the country while others have been left to pay surge prices for hotels and rental cars as airlines scramble to resume flights.

https://taz.de/Ungarn-will-neue-Sportpol.title: Ungarn will neue Sportpolitik: Verheerende Verflechtungen
https://taz.de/Ungarn-will-neue-Sportpol.author: György Polgár
https://taz.de/Ungarn-will-neue-Sportpol.text:
Ungarn will neue Sportpolitik: Verheerende Verflechtungen
In Ungarn wird die Regierung das Sportsystem des Ex-Präsidenten Viktor Orbán abschaffen. Er begünstigte mit Steuergeldern politische Verbündete.
Als Ungarns Ministerpräsident Péter Magyar im Oktober mit der Abschaffung des sogenannten TAO-Systems eine fundamentale sportpolitische Kehrtwende ab Januar 2027 ankündigte, stieß die Entscheidung auf heftige Kritik der Opposition. Kein Wunder, denn die Weggefährten des abgewählten Premiers Viktor Orbán hatten vom verworrenen System profitiert.
Um den Sport zu finanzieren, hat sich das Orbán-Kabinett ein ausgeklügeltes Konzept ausgedacht: Die im Jahr 2011 eingeführte TAO (Akronym für „Társasági Adó“, ungarisch für „Körperschaftssteuer“) erlaubt Unternehmen, bis zu 80 Prozent ihrer Körperschaftssteuer nicht an den Fiskus abzuführen, sondern direkt an Sportvereine oder Verbände zu verschenken. Firmen können 100 Prozent dieser Spenden als Steuerabzug geltend machen.
Obwohl der Oberste Gerichtshof klarstellte, dass es sich bei diesen umgeleiteten Geldern um öffentliche Mittel handelt, funktioniert das System so, als ob es sich um Privatspenden handelt. Denn die erforderliche parlamentarische Kontrolle blieb aus. Begünstigt werden primär sechs populäre Mannschaftssportarten: Fußball, Handball, Basketball, Wasserball, Eishockey und Volleyball.
Die wirtschaftlichen Dimensionen sind nicht zu unterschätzen. Laut offiziellen Daten, die das Regierungsbüro im Oktober 2026 veröffentlichte, flossen über den TAO-Mechanismus in den letzten 11 Jahren schätzungsweise 3,5 bis 4 Milliarden Euro in den Sport. Der Löwenanteil davon landete direkt in Orbáns Lieblingssport, dem Fußball.
Sportprojekte für regierungsnahe Oligarchen
Kritiker – wie Oppositionspolitiker und Transparency International Hungary – bezeichnen das TAO-System als Paradebeispiel einer institutionalisierten Kleptokratie. Große Konzerne, die fast ausschließlich im Besitz von regierungsnahen Oligarchen und durch staatliche Aufträge zu Reichtum gelangt sind, leiteten ihre Körperschaftssteuer gezielt an Sportprojekte weiter, die von Politikern der regierenden Fidesz-Partei geführt wurden. So blieb das Geld im selben politischen und wirtschaftlichen Kreislauf.
Ein besonders symbolträchtiges Beispiel ist die Pancho Aréna in Orbáns Heimatdorf Felcsút, die im wahrsten Sinne des Wortes nur einige Schritte von seinem Privathaus entfernt steht. Das extravagante Heimstadion des dortigen Puskás Akadémia FC fasst rund 3.800 Zuschauer – in einer Gemeinde mit knapp 1.800 Einwohnern. Der Eigentümer des Klubs, der Baulöwe Lőrinc Mészáros, reichster Mann des Landes und Orbáns Jugendfreund, leitete TAO-Gelder seiner Firmen regelmäßig direkt an den Verein und finanzierte damit unter anderem den Bau des Stadions, der selbstverständlich vom eigenen Betrieb ausgeführt wurde. Der Klub selbst erhielt über die Jahre etwa 85 Millionen Euro aus dem TAO-Topf.
Um den Sportsektor finanziell nicht zu schwächen, soll die staatliche Sportförderung ab Januar weiterhin bei ca. 1,24 Milliarden Euro bleiben. Anstelle des bisherigen TAO-Steuererleichterungsmodells führt die Regierung nun eine weitere direkte Subvention in Höhe von etwa 400 Millionen Euro ein. Das Kabinett betont, dass die Gelder transparent fließen werden – insbesondere in den Nachwuchssport und die Infrastruktur erfolgreicher olympischer Sportarten statt fast ausschließlich in den Profifußball oder ausgewählte Großprojekte. Ab Januar soll jeder Forint lückenlos rückverfolgbar sein. Finanzierungszusagen werden an messbare Kriterien und strenge Prüfungen durch staatliche Kontrollorgane gekoppelt.
Die Opposition mahnte scheinheilig, dass sich die Entscheidungsgewalt von den spendenden Unternehmen zu staatlichen Regierungsstellen verschiebt, wenn der Staat das Budget direkt verteilt. Dadurch könnten nämlich neue Abhängigkeiten entstehen. Dabei haben sie gerade das ausgeblendet, was den TAO-Mechanismus zum Korruptionsmotor des ungarischen Sports machte: die Abwesenheit einer klaren und strikten parlamentarischen Kontrolle. Ihrer Meinung nach gefährdet dies die Finanzierung zahlreicher kleinerer Sportvereine sowie von Nachwuchsförderprogrammen. In Wahrheit gingen diese immer wieder leer aus.
Politische Amtsträger werden ausgeschlossen
Zudem wurde im Oktober ein Gesetzentwurf eingereicht, der Interessenkonflikte ausschließen soll. Demnach dürfen aktive politische Amtsträger unter anderem Minister, Staatssekretäre, Parlamentsabgeordnete oder Parteivorsitzende keine Führungspositionen in größeren Sportorganisationen bekleiden. Denn unter Orbán fungierte die Sportlandschaft als eine Art „Feudalbesitz“: Ein Verein oder Verband erhielt finanzielle Sicherheit und politische Fürsprache im Austausch gegen die absolute Loyalität seiner Führung gegenüber der Regierungspartei.
Die meisten Verbündeten Orbáns sind inzwischen zurückgetreten, da ihnen klar geworden ist, dass sie ihre bisherigen persönlichen und politischen Vorteile in Zukunft nicht mehr genießen werden. Gábor Kubatov, der Vorsitzende des populärsten und größten Sportvereins Ferencváros, sträubt sich allerdings noch. Er war bis vor Kurzem Vizepräsident von Fidesz und wurde bei der Vorstandswahl Ende Oktober erneut an die Spitze des Vereins gewählt. Er verkündete: „Unsere Liebe zu Ferencváros währt ein Leben lang. Sie lässt sich nicht durch irgendwelche Gesetze zerstören!“ Dass er bald gehen muss, müsste ihm klar sein.
Bei Ferencváros laufen obendrein polizeiliche Ermittlungen wegen mutmaßlicher Veruntreuung. Die Regierung hatte von 2016 bis 2027 insgesamt etwa 70 Millionen Euro aus der Staatskasse für den groß angelegten Ausbau einer multifunktionalen Sportanlage einkalkuliert. Der Komplex wurde jedoch nie fertiggestellt, obwohl der gesamte Betrag ausgegeben wurde. Die Politik hat dabei weggeschaut. Untersuchungen des neuen Kabinetts ergaben, dass Unsummen in Managementgebühren, die Verpflichtung von Fußballspielern und den Erwerb von Spielrechten geflossen waren.
Da der politische Rückenwind wegfallen und die bisherigen Geldkanäle versiegen werden, müssen die früher begünstigten Vereine und Verbände mühsam lernen, in einem echten, marktwirtschaftlichen Sponsorenmarkt zu überleben. Es ist nicht ausgeschlossen, dass einige von ihnen Konkurs anmelden werden.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: India pulled 500m people out of poverty. Many of them still barely survive
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
India pulled 500m people out of poverty. Many of them still barely survive
World Bank says India has pulled record numbers of citizens out of poverty, but millions among them are one shock away from being thrust back into destitution.
Rajsamand and New Delhi, India – Hema Prajapat, 25, says even “thorns growing inside her stomach” would not hurt as much as hunger does.
By the end of each month, her kitchen shelves are empty; her husband, Hari Prajapat, sinks deeper into debt; and an increasing share of their food supplies is set aside for their nine-year-old son, Divyansh.
But Hema’s family is no longer poor – at least on paper.
She spends 11,000 rupees ($117) a month on her household of three. That is about 49 percent more than the roughly 7,380 rupees ($78) monthly threshold for a family of that size, based on the World Bank’s poverty line.
India, the world’s most populous country, no longer counts its poor. It has not published an official consumption-based poverty estimate in more than a decade. That leaves the World Bank to provide internationally comparable estimates, using newer consumption surveys and its own poverty thresholds.
A recent World Bank report says India lifted nearly 500 million people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, with extreme poverty dropping from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent during the period.
The only comparable poverty-reduction effort on this scale was achieved by China, which lifted more than 800 million people out of extreme poverty over four decades.
Several economists have said India’s achievement is significant, and that the World Bank’s mechanism for calculating these numbers is beyond reproach, even as they have argued that the planet’s most populous nation still has a long way to go before it can claim to have defeated poverty.
Other economists have questioned the World Bank’s sweeping conclusions and India’s unwillingness under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government to carry out its own poverty estimates.
But masked by that largely academic and political split is the lived reality of millions of Indians who have crossed the supposed poverty threshold yet lead a life marked by persistent deprivation, and a precarity that leaves families one shock away from losing everything that matters to them.
“This poverty line, this bar, is very low. No person can live a dignified life [on this amount],” Hema told Al Jazeera, sitting in a small garden where she moonlights as a caretaker.
“Did they even get out of their AC cars?” she asked, taking a dig at the officials who prepared the report for the World Bank.
‘Money now vanishes’
India, home to 1.4 billion people, is one of the fastest-growing global economies – the fourth-largest by nominal gross domestic product (GDP), despite repeated recent shocks including the COVID-19 pandemic and the ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
It is also one of the world’s most unequal countries, with the top 1 percent of its population owning 40 percent of its wealth – a concern highlighted in the World Bank report as well.
Hema was 11 when she was married off to a man who belongs to a family of traditional clay-pot makers in Rajsamand district of Rajasthan state.
When pot sales could no longer meet their financial needs, her husband, Hari, started a street food stall selling pani puri, a popular Indian snack. That did not last long because of the pandemic.
Hema started to look for work.
For the past year, she has been cleaning houses and washing utensils in the neighbourhood for 5,000 rupees ($53) a month, but the deprivation did not end.
“We have to buy every single thing from the market,” she said. The family has no agricultural land.
The World Bank pointed to rising female labour force participation as one of the factors behind India’s improving poverty rates, although women’s access to secure and adequately paid employment remains a challenge.
“Since I started working, our home has seen some comfort, but the money is now vanishing faster, and we are even more in debt,” Hema said, adding that she is unable to figure out the maths behind it.
“The prices have multiplied in recent years, and whatever we earn falls short,” she told Al Jazeera.
The World Bank also noted that the Indian government’s provision of free or subsidised foodgrains to nearly 800 million citizens every month under its national food-security programme has helped tackle extreme poverty.
But a rising cost of living has meant that government subsidies and handouts are racing against growing economic pressures on families like Hema’s. India’s overall consumer prices rose by at least 51 percent between September 2016 and September 2025, according to the government’s Consumer Price Index. Wage rises in this period have not kept pace.
Some government schemes help, such as public schools for children or state-run hospitals that provide free or subsidised healthcare.
But Hema says free healthcare does not inspire much confidence in people. When her son Divyansh had a bad cold and the flu two months ago, she rushed him to a private hospital as waiting times at public hospitals are often longer, with crowded wards, overstretched doctors and limited resources.
“I was scared for him. His fever was getting worse,” she said.
Treatment at the private hospital cost Hema about 6,000 rupees ($64) – more than what she makes in a month. “I do not want my son to get used to private hospitals or their drugs. I cannot take him to one every time,” she said.
‘One shock’ away from poverty
Millions of Indian households that appear to be rising above the World Bank’s poverty threshold live on the edge, desperately trying to avoid being pushed back.
Santosh Mehrotra, a developmental economist in New Delhi, said the poverty threshold in India is too low. All it takes is “one shock” to be pushed back into it, he said. “That shock could be a pandemic, drought, flood, or even a wedding.”
Hema’s neighbour Sushila Salvi received one such shock.
In December last year, Salvi, 31, realised she was “finally pregnant” again – her second child after a gap of 14 years. Salvi did not trust government hospitals and wanted to get all her treatment at a private clinic.
In some ways, she had prepared for it. Over the previous eight years, she learned makeup skills and opened a small, one-seater salon in Kankroli, a small town in Rajsamand. She had been saving for her 14-year-old daughter’s higher education. The daughter currently goes to a government school.
“But when I got pregnant, I could not rely on government hospitals,” she said.
Maternal care cost her nearly 65,000 rupees ($695) and drained her savings. She had to pull her daughter out of extra tuition classes that cost her 600 rupees ($6) a month.
Mehrotra, who previously worked with the government on rural economies and poverty, said the World Bank’s poverty threshold is “also problematic because it does not draw a distinction between the rural and the urban populations” despite their different realities.
Seema Kumar, 37, lives on the outskirts of New Delhi and spends 20,000 rupees ($214) on her family of three.
She turns to loans when expenses spiral, such as during a festival or her 17-year-old son’s birthday.
But some shocks come unseen.
As India celebrated Diwali, a festival of lights, last week, and people burst firecrackers, air quality in New Delhi – one of the world’s most polluted cities – hit a record.
The next morning, as dense and toxic smog hung over the city, all three members of Seema’s family left for work. By evening, her son had developed a sore throat, everyone in the family had a runny nose, and Seema went to bed with a terrible headache.
“I could not buy a mask for my son, and they say I am not poor any more,” Seema told Al Jazeera.
Back in Rajsamand, as Hema swept the garden in her neighbourhood, she called Hari, her husband, reminding him that their child was due for a routine medical checkup that day.
Hari said he could not afford to refill petrol any more due to the increase in oil prices caused by the conflict in the Middle East. Hema offered to refill his motorcycle’s tank to go to the nearest hospital.
“My only hope is that my son makes something out of his life,” said Hema. “If I do not work for a single day – let alone a month – we can go back to the days of extreme poverty and deprivation.”

https://taz.de/Erfolg-fuer-Musks-Raumfah.title: Erfolg für Musks Raumfahrt: SpaceX fängt Riesen-Rakete Starship erstmals wieder auf
https://taz.de/Erfolg-fuer-Musks-Raumfah.text:
Erfolg für Musks Raumfahrt: SpaceX fängt Riesen-Rakete Starship erstmals wieder auf
Mit dem größten je gebauten Raketensystem will Elon Musk den Mars erschließen. Nun hat Starship einen Test absolviert – mit einem Erfolg und einem Rückschlag.
dpa | Erstmals hat das US-Raumfahrtunternehmen SpaceX die obere Stufe des Riesen-Raketensystems Starship nach einem Testflug ins All auf der Erde wieder aufgefangen. Rund 20 Stunden nach dem Start kehrte das Starship zum Weltraumbahnhof Starbase im US-Bundesstaat Texas zurück und wurde dort von Greifarmen am Startturm aufgefangen. Es war das erste Mal, dass SpaceX einen solchen Fangversuch unternahm – und bedeutet einen großen Fortschritt in Hinblick auf die Wiederverwendbarkeit von Raketen.
SpaceX sprach von einem „unglaublichen Erfolg“. Der Besitzer des Raumfahrtunternehmens, der Tech-Milliardär Elon Musk, würdigte die Verdienste seines „unglaublichen Teams“. Nasa-Chef Jared Isaacman gratulierte zu einem „spektakulären Start“ – das Auffangen der oberen Raketenstufe sei schon „fast wie Magie“ gewesen.
Rückschlag: Booster konnte nicht aufgefangen werden
Allerdings gab es bei dem 15. Testflug auch einen Rückschlag für SpaceX: Eigentlich hätte auch die untere Raketenstufe von Greifarmen am Startturm wieder aufgefangen werden sollen, doch das klappte nicht.
Der Booster namens Super Heavy kehrte zwar kurz nach dem Start zur Erde zurück, stürzte aber kontrolliert ins Meer und ging in Flammen auf. Angaben zur möglichen Ursache des Fehlschlags machte SpaceX zunächst nicht. Bei drei vorherigen Teststarts hatte das Auffangen der unteren Raketenstufe geklappt.
Starship setzte Satelliten aus
Die Starship genannte obere Raketenstufe schwenkte kurz nach der Trennung von der unteren Raketenstufe in eine Erdumlaufbahn ein und setzte Satelliten für Musks Internetdienst Starlink aus. Danach umrundete sie mehrfach die Erde.
Zuletzt hatte es im September einen Testflug des Starship gegeben. Dabei schaffte es das größte jemals gebaute Raketensystem erstmals in eine Erdumlaufbahn und stürzte dann rund drei Stunden später in einem Flammenball kontrolliert in den Pazifik.
Raketensystem ist größer als die Freiheitsstatue
Das Raketensystem Starship ist riesig und sogar größer als die Freiheitsstatue in New York. Es besteht aus zwei Teilen, die sich nach dem Start trennen: dem etwa 70 Meter langen Booster Super Heavy und der – ebenfalls Starship genannten – oberen Stufe, die rund 50 Meter misst. Beide Teile sind so konzipiert, dass sie nach der Rückkehr zur Erde wiederverwendet werden können – was vor allem logistische und finanzielle Vorteile hat.
Erstmals wurde das Raketensystem im April 2023 getestet – damals explodierte es nach wenigen Minuten aber komplett. Die weiteren Tests verliefen unterschiedlich erfolgreich.
Die US-Raumfahrtbehörde Nasa will mit dem Starship Astronauten zum Mond schicken, während SpaceX auch das Ziel verfolgt, eines Tages den Mars zu erreichen. Auch andere Raumfahrtfirmen in den USA - unter anderem Rocket Lab und die Firma Blue Origin von Amazon-Gründer Jeff Bezos – sowie andere Länder arbeiten an wiederverwendbaren Raketen. China holte im Sommer erstmals die Stufe einer Trägerrakete kontrolliert zurück.
