https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Will Iraq’s oil smuggling crackdown disarm militias without a conflict?
Iraq has dismantled an alleged smuggling ring in Jurf al-Sakhar which could financially squeeze militias and avert internal strife.
The Iraqi government has launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the Jurf al-Sakhar area, a stronghold of Iran-linked militias near Baghdad.
The campaign has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of top security directors, the Babil police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.
While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, analysts believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus.
At the heart of this confrontation is Jurf al-Sakhar – also known as Jurf al-Nasr – a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah group, believed to have close links to Iran.
For over a decade, Jurf al-Nasr has allegedly harboured illicit oil refineries. An intelligence report released last week claimed that the area was at the centre of a major corruption scheme involving oil revenues and Iran-linked militias.
That led Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to launch the crackdown, with an Iraqi security committee entering Jurf al-Nasr on Friday to investigate, following the arrest of other officials accused of graft. The formerly Sunni-majority area has long been considered outside government control since Iraqi militias seized the area a decade ago.
Michael Knights, head of MENA research at Horizon Engage, told Al Jazeera that Jurf al-Sakhar’s value is deeply rooted in recent developments in Iraq, when Iran-linked militias used the campaign against ISIL (ISIS) to stamp their authority in the country.
“Iran-backed militias illegally seized and renamed Jurf al-Sakr when they conducted sectarian cleansing of the Sunni residents in the area in 2014, under the cover of the anti-Daesh [ISIL] war,” Knights explained.
The town, about 60km (37 miles) from Baghdad, is at a critical point near the Shia pilgrimage route between the Iraqi capital and Karbala.
It was once the site of Saddam Hussein’s military industrial complexes, which made Jurf al-Nasr an ideal place for Iraqi militias to test, build and hide rockets, drones and missiles, said Knights.
“If full control is taken, which is unlikely, the government would be able to finally tell Iraqis that a militia had been removed from its base and the legal residents of the area allowed to return,” he said. “This would be like taking back the Bekaa Valley from Hezbollah.”
Knights said the actual financial impact on Kataib Hezbollah of the Jurf al-Sakhar crackdown could be less spectacular than expected, with the militia having other sources of revenue.
Analysts say that dismantling the smuggling networks is part of a wider project to bring weapons under the control of the state.
After some Iran-linked militias missed a deadline to disarm this year, PM al-Zaidi now appears to be using economic pressure to weaken these armed groups without directly confronting them.
Security and strategic expert Saif Raad told Al Jazeera that the anticorruption campaign in Jurf al-Sakhar is essentially a message from the PM that no group is above the law.
“This duality is over. Part of what happened now is that the Iraqi people knew these factions and knew why they hold onto weapons, and I believe this is a victory achieved by the government without a single drop of Iraqi blood,” Raad said.
“Jurf al-Sakhar has been around for, let’s say, more than ten years; for ten years no prime minister was able to enter this area.”
Averting armed conflict
A central focus of the government’s strategy is executing this crackdown without igniting a potentially explosive ‘Shia-on-Shia’ armed conflict.
The militia network which emerged following the US-led invasion of Iraq – and was emboldened during the campaign against ISIL – includes groups with widely divergent political and religious views. Some are closely aligned to Iran and accused of being proxies of Tehran, while others are closer to the federal government.
In a bid to prevent violence, Al-Zaidi reportedly cooperated with leaders of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), particularly with the Badr Organisation, before initiating the arrests and dismissals in Jurf al-Sakhar, Raad said.
Fadel Abu Ragheef, an Iraqi political analyst, told Al Jazeera that leveraging Hadi al-Amiri, leader of the Badr Organisation, was essential to neutralising the threat from the militias.
“The Badr Organisation is considered the largest combat force within the Popular Mobilisation Forces, so the process of focusing on this issue… is a fundamental part of strengthening the state project,” Raad observed.
“[The campaign] is a major shift in the process of strengthening the state and state institutions and making the Popular Mobilisation Forces an active and large part in controlling these groups [militias outside government control].”
Political analyst Ali Fadhlallah said that due to the structural nature of Iraq’s political and religious leadership, an internal war between the Shia factions was never likely to break out, particularly due to the influence Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani.
“The Shia component has very many large and positive factors that serve as a brake for any clash that is supposed to happen,” Fadhlallah said.
“The presence of the rational religious authority, which has always controlled the rhythm of the political process at dangerous crossroads, definitely has a very large role and it is monitoring the events… the issue of a [Shia-Shia] clash is unlikely, even in the most difficult and miserable circumstances.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: 20 years of Al Jazeera English: Our story is still being written
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
20 years of Al Jazeera English: Our story is still being written
As we celebrate our 20th anniversary, we remain committed to our values, the quality of our journalism and a willingness to evolve.
Twenty years ago today, on November 15, 2006, Al Jazeera English began broadcasting with a belief that the world needed a different perspective on the news. A perspective that would bring underreported stories to international attention and give people everywhere a greater opportunity to be seen and heard.
As we celebrate our 20th anniversary, that belief remains as important as ever.
The world has changed enormously over the past two decades. We have witnessed wars, political upheavals, economic crises, technological revolutions and profound changes in how people consume information. Through it all, Al Jazeera English has sought to do more than report events. We have worked to explain why they matter, explore their impact on people’s lives and help audiences understand an increasingly complex world.
Our journey has never simply been about building another international news channel. It has been about broadening the global conversation.
A different perspective on the world
From the beginning, Al Jazeera English sought to broaden international news coverage by bringing greater diversity of perspectives, voices and stories to audiences around the world.
We believed that events everywhere deserved attention, depth and serious journalism, regardless of where they took place. We also believed that people experiencing conflict, injustice, poverty and political change should not be merely subjects of news coverage, but voices within it.
This approach has helped define our editorial identity. It reflects our belief that no single perspective can fully explain our world, and that good journalism must question assumptions, examine different viewpoints and bring important stories to light.
At the heart of this philosophy is a simple principle: every human life matters, and every story deserves to be approached with dignity and fairness.
The people who made it possible
Behind every broadcast, investigation, documentary and breaking news story are people whose dedication makes our work possible.
Al Jazeera English brings together colleagues representing 78 nationalities, reflecting the diversity of cultures, experiences and perspectives that make our channel unique.
I think particularly of our journalists working in difficult and sometimes dangerous circumstances, often far from their families, determined to tell stories the world needs to hear.
I also think of the many colleagues working behind the scenes, whose contributions may not always be visible to audiences but remain essential to everything we achieve.
We must remember those who helped build this channel over the past two decades, including colleagues who are no longer with us. Their dedication and sacrifices are part of our history.
Our greatest achievement is not any single programme, interview or award. It is the collective effort of generations of people who have believed in the purpose of this channel.
Journalism in a changing world
The media landscape is changing at an extraordinary pace. Audiences have more choice than ever before, but also face an overwhelming volume of information, misinformation and competing narratives. Artificial intelligence is transforming how content is produced and distributed, while traditional viewing habits continue to evolve.
These developments present challenges, but also opportunities.
We must embrace innovation, explore new storytelling formats and meet audiences wherever they choose to engage with news. But technological progress must never come at the expense of what makes journalism valuable.
Technology cannot replace editorial judgement, human understanding, compassion or the responsibility to establish what is true.
Credibility is earned through consistent, rigorous journalism. Trust takes years to build and can be lost quickly. Neither should ever be taken for granted.
The next chapter
Today, as we celebrate our 20th anniversary, Al Jazeera English also unveils a new on-air look, marking the beginning of another chapter in our journey. But our ambitions extend well beyond what audiences see on their screens.
We want to strengthen our journalism, deepen our storytelling, develop fresh ideas and engage meaningfully with audiences around the world.
Equally important is building a workplace culture based on respect, trust, fairness, openness, collaboration and accountability. A place where people feel valued, ideas are welcomed and everyone has an opportunity to contribute and grow.
Great journalism requires talented people. Sustaining it requires an environment where they can do their best work.
Twenty years is a significant milestone, but not a destination.
We should be proud of what Al Jazeera English has achieved, while recognising that our continued relevance must be earned every day through the quality of our journalism, the strength of our values and our willingness to evolve.
The world still needs journalism that questions power, challenges assumptions, brings neglected stories to light and places humanity at the centre of its reporting.
That was our promise in 2006. Twenty years later, it remains our responsibility.
Our first 20 years have shaped who we are. What we do next will define who we become.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Hopkins’ late stunner sends Kansas City past Gotham and into NWSL final
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Bryan Armen Graham at Icahn Stadium
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
After a week dominated by a headline-grabbing stadium scheduling imbroglio, Gotham FC and the Kansas City Current finally got down to the vital business of their NWSL semi-final on Sunday afternoon, a frigid encounter at an unlikely venue on New York City’s Randall’s Island with a place in next Saturday’s championship match at stake.
Haley Hopkins delivered the knockout blow at the death, hitting an 89th-minute volley off the crossbar and in to seal a 2-1 upset that left Gotham FC’s title defense in tatters. Paired with Croix Bethune’s first-half free-kick stunner, the late winner sent fourth-seeded Kansas City past the defending champions into a championship showdown in six days against the Washington Spirit.
On a windswept afternoon where unyielding gusts undercut the warmth of a cloudless 50F sky, a physical opening stretch produced six fouls in the first eight minutes before either side threatened. Gotham recorded the first shot after 12 minutes when Jaedyn Shaw ran onto a Guro Reiten pass and missed wide right. Kansas City answered three minutes later, with Malawian star Temwa Chawinga firing wide left from the center of the area.
Twenty minutes in, Bethune won a free kick 25 yards out after a foul by Denise O’Sullivan. Stepping up with her left foot, she coolly curled her strike around the Gotham wall and inches inside the post. The goal from Bethune, the NWSL’s midfielder of the year two seasons ago with Washington, left the crowd in stunned silence before a smattering of boos echoed around the ground.
The popular Rose Lavelle came on after half-time for O’Sullivan to deafening swells and made an immediate impact, winning a couple of free kicks and nearly finding the equalizer with a left-footed shot from the center of the area that missed wide left. But opportunities came fewer and further between over the next quarter-hour as Kansas City tightened their defensive shell.
With their repeat bid hanging in the balance, Gotham found an equalizer against the run of play in the 69th minute when Midge Purce whipped in a cross that ricocheted between goalkeeper Lorena and defender Gabrielle Robinson before caroming off Laney Rouse into her own net – leveling the match at one apiece despite the hosts still not having registered a single shot on target. It was hardly a match for the artistry of Bethune’s silky opener, but the delirious home crowd was in no mood to quibble.
The contest appeared bound for extra time past sundown with temperatures plunging. But Gotham, having squeaked through last week’s quarter-final on another own goal, were suddenly within reach of a second straight NWSL final without having scored a goal of their own in either playoff match. Hopkins had other ideas, delivering the dramatic decider in the 89th minute before adding insult to injury by blowing kisses to the crowd from the touchline, provoking a cacophony of boos.
With its solitary grandstand, roofline lettering and towering floodlights, 5,000-seat Icahn Stadium gave the appearance of an 1890s English football ground dropped beneath the Triborough Bridge – an improbable stage for one of the biggest matches of the NWSL season.
Gotham had been forced to abandon their usual home at Sports Illustrated Stadium in Harrison, New Jersey, amid concerns over the deteriorating playing surface. The relocation capped a chaotic week for the league, which found itself juggling stadium availability, network television commitments and player safety at the most consequential stage of its season. Gotham’s regular ground, owned by MLS’s New York Red Bulls, had been booked for a friendly against Mexico’s Club América on Saturday, further complicating an already untenable situation.
Ultimately, the club prioritized a playable pitch over capacity. At one-fifth the size of their usual home, the municipal track venue where Usain Bolt made a creaky run-up to the Rio Olympics created an awkward compromise: world-class stars competing on a stage resembling a relic of football’s distant past. Sunday’s meeting also carried the unmistakable flavor of revenge. A year ago, Gotham entered the playoffs as the eighth seed and stunned top-seeded Kansas City in the quarter-finals, winning on a dramatic extra-time goal from Katie Lampson before going on to claim their second NWSL championship in three seasons.
This time the roles were reversed, with Gotham the top seeds and Kansas City arriving as dangerous floaters. The fourth-seeded Current had run off six consecutive wins entering Sunday, including a 1-0 extra-time victory over Angel City in the quarter-finals, settled by Michelle Cooper’s 96th-minute penalty. But one year after watching Gotham end their season in heartbreaking fashion, Kansas City returned the favor. Next stop: Washington, and a chance to claim the first NWSL championship in club history.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.title: Prince Harry tells Ukrainians they are ‘going to win war’ on surprise trip to Lviv
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.author: Harry Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text:
Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a surprise visit to the country.
The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had taken a risk in travelling to the country, but that he had felt “warmth” when arriving on Saturday.
It is the British army veteran’s fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in February 2022.
He spoke at a conference organised by the Superhumans Center, a clinic in Lviv that specialises in care and rehabilitation of those who have fought in the conflict. The prince has previously supported the group, which provides prosthetic limbs to those who have lost them in battle.
He said: “Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success.”
Harry watched wheelchair rugby players who hope to be in Ukraine’s team at next year’s Invictus Games, which will take place in Birmingham. Ukraine is aiming to send about 60 competitors to the event – its largest ever team.
The prince said the games for wounded military veterans, which he set up in 2014, could one day be held in Ukraine. “When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” he promised.
At the rugby match, Harry hugged a player he recognised – Valery Odainyk, who took part in the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025. The 41-year-old, who uses prosthetic legs, said he was “still an active serviceman”, and the prince expressed surprise he found time to train.
Odainyk said afterwards he had told Harry his involvement in his sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games”.
The prince visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, in September 2025 and in April this year. During the April visit, he called Ukraine “a country bravely and successfully defending Europe’s eastern flank” and said “it matters that we don’t lose sight of the significance of that”.
The 42-year-old spent a decade in the British army and served in Afghanistan, including as a helicopter pilot. He has described those years as the happiest of his life.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Iraq sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran group's bastion
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Hilal Saki
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Iraq sacks nine officials over oil smuggling in pro-Iran group's bastion
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.
"In light of the investigation's findings," Zaidi "ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary," his military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects.
The premier "also ordered the dismissal" of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babylon province, an interior ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the oil ministry.
Numan did not elaborate on the role of the sacked officials in the alleged smuggling operations.
A committee investigating the allegations entered Jurf al-Sakher on Friday, accompanied by members of Kataeb Hezbollah.
On Wednesday, the state news agency INA reported that "intelligence documents" containing satellite images "showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction" in Jurf al-Sakher, accusing the unnamed faction of tapping into a pipeline there.
According to Numan, the investigating committee "confirmed the accuracy" of the information.
Report by AFP

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: England fend off fiery Spain fightback after Anderson’s red to top Nations League group
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: David Hytner at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
It was the game to show Thomas Tuchel where his rebooted England team had got to; surely the ultimate test in international football. Spain in Spain. A world champion team who, in Tuchel’s words, had “forgotten how to lose.” Before this Nations League group decider, they had been beaten only once in 43 matches – on penalties against Portugal in the final of this competition last year.
What England produced for 65 minutes was extraordinary. What followed was equally so for different reasons. When it was over, England had made the most sensational of statements. Back in 2018, on their previous visit to Spain, England won 3-2 in Seville in the Nations League; it was one of Sir Gareth Southgate’s most famous results, an ignition point. It was the same scoreline and the same feeling for Tuchel on Sunday night.
England led 3-0. It was Harry Kane, of course, who put them in front from the penalty spot; the best player in the world damaging the best team. When Ezri Konsa and Ben White added the others, the travelling supporters were pinching themselves. With Jude Bellingham to the fore, England had run riot.
It was not over. Far from it. Everything changed when Jarell Quansah made a big error as the last man, robbed by Lamine Yamal, who got into the area and was fouled by Elliot Anderson. It was a red card for the England midfielder and a penalty for Spain. When Mikel Oyarzabal converted, it was the prompt for a siege.
Spain knocked hard at the door. They scored again through the substitute Nico Williams, created by an assist from the frankly ludicrous Lamine Yamal, a talent who sprinkles his magic liberally, and England were placed in grim survival mode. We have been here before under Tuchel and the equaliser looked on. The manager made a couple of defensive changes – Myles Lewis-Skelly for Kane and Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Bellingham was removed, too, and he departed shaking his head. Dan Burn came on towards the very end.
England held out. One of Tuchel’s major selection calls was to start James Trafford over Jordan Pickford in goal and he produced a remarkable stoppage-time double save to ensure England got the result they needed to leapfrog Spain and advance to the quarter-finals as the group winners. The second part of it was to deny Aymeric Laporte. It was a breathtaking moment; one to advance Trafford’s claim on the No 1 jersey. There were many others on a night that pulsed wildly from the outset – pretty much from when Spain paraded the World Cup trophy before kick-off. Had they not already had their homecoming with the gold? It was a power play.
England brought the swagger. They pressed hard on to the front foot. It was thrilling to see how they took on those in red and beat them, creating the sense of possibility. It was worth mentioning a spin move by Lewis Hall on halfway in the eighth minute when he could not afford to lose the ball. He did not, getting England up the field. There were other examples of the proactivity from other players; the desire to drop shoulders and surge forward, to be direct.
It was England who looked likely to score first and Spain needed a superb save from Unai Simón to deny Bellingham in the early going. He ran on to a Declan Rice corner, centrally placed and, with the ball slightly behind him, he had to dig out the half-volley rather than hit it more cleanly. Simón’s reflexes were nevertheless impressive. Gordon had a shot blocked by Martín Zubimendi. Kane fizzed another one just wide.
Spain kicked out a foothold in the 15th minute. It was Lamine Yamal, inevitably, who dragged them back into it. He nutmegged Hall and blasted away from him, Rice bringing him down to pick up a yellow card. What Hall did next spoke volumes about England’s approach, not to mention his courage. It was a slicing run from him, on a diagonal towards goal, which laid waste to a host of Spain players. He almost found Morgan Rogers with his cross.
It was an excellent first half for England; Rogers bristled with confidence on the ball, Bellingham threatened. They deserved to take a lead into the interval. Bellingham appeared to be fouled by Marc Cucurella, but Anderson did not stand on ceremony, driving a first-time pass up the inside right channel for Kane, who cut inside Pau Cubarsí to set up the shot.
Kane cleverly got his body between Cubarsí and the ball; the Spain centre-back had a problem. His challenge was necessary but clumsy; it was a clear penalty. Kane had a long wait while the video assistant referee checked for an Anderson foul on Cucurella as he followed through after his pass. It was accidental but nasty. Anderson got away with it. Kane had missed decisively in England’s 3-2 defeat against Spain at Wembley at the start of this competition. He made no mistake this time. It was his 93rd England goal.
England continued to push after half-time, especially Bellingham. He won the corner that led to Konsa heading in unmarked from a Rice outswinger and it was Bellingham who played in White, who was adventurous all night, for the third.
Nothing silly, Tuchel had to have thought. Quansah did something silly and the entire mood changed. Trafford made his first big save from the substitute Fermín López, but then it was 3-2 after Gordon was robbed in midfield. Spain went right to Lamine Yamal and his low cross for Williams was perfect.
Spain piled on the pressure. Williams went close. Lamine Yamal forced Trafford into a fine save, the goalkeeper denying Cucurella on the rebound. White made a saving tackle on Williams after a wonderful Lamine Yamal pass. Trafford saved his best until the last.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Somali-American Uber driver brutally assaulted in alleged hate crime in Minnesota
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Michael Sainato
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A Somali-American Uber driver was allegedly brutally assaulted by a passenger in Hopkins, Minnesota, on Saturday, in what his family says “appears to be a hate crime”.
The driver, Mohamed Yusuf, is currently hospitalized and fighting for his life, his family told the Somali Brief, a digital news site run by two Somali American journalists. The driver’s cousin, Abdinasir Ali told the outlet that the alleged attack took place early Saturday after a passenger in Hopkins, a suburban city south-west of Minneapolis, asked Yusuf’s name and then said he did not like the name Mohamed.
The passenger allegedly then choked the driver from behind, took control of the car and used it to assault the driver. “He was run over multiple times with his own vehicle,” Yusuf’s son, Mustafa Osman, told the Somali Brief.
The badly injured driver was later found “a mile down the road in a ditch”, with broken legs and ribs, two collapsed lungs and a spinal injury, his son said.
The Hopkins police department said in a statement they are investigating the assault after officers responded to a report of a suspicious vehicle at 1.20am on Saturday.
“Officers located an adult male suspect nearby and took him into custody,” the police department stated. They noted preliminary information indicates the incident involved an Uber ride share interaction and that the investigation remains ongoing.
“This is a pure hate crime,” one member of Yusuf’s family at the hospital told the Somali Brief. “Our politicians created this hostile environment.”
The alleged assault comes after Donald Trump made racist rhetoric and lies about Somali Americans in Minnesota a central focus of his midterm campaign rallies, and the president’s inflammatory claims have been echoed by Minnesota Republicans.
House majority whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota, recently said on a conservative podcast: “I’ve got basically the Somali civil war that’s come to the state of Minnesota.”
The Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair-MN), community leaders, elected officials and ride-share driver groups were planning a press conference on Monday at the Hennepin County Medical Center to call for justice.
“Mohamed Yusuf should be home safe with his family, not fighting for his life after an attack fueled by hatred towards his Somali identity,” said Omar Fateh, a state senator in Minnesota, in a statement on social media. “We need answers and an immediate and transparent investigation.”
SEIU Local 26, a local labor union that organizes rideshare drivers, said in a social media post on the alleged attack: “We are shocked, angered and saddened by the news of the alleged attack that happened this weekend on Mohamed, a Minnesotan and Uber driver.”
A GoFundMe created on behalf of Yusuf and his family has already raised over $140,000. “As a result of this senseless assault, he suffered severe injuries and is now in a coma, fighting for his life,” the family wrote in the appeal for financial support.
“We are shocked and horrified by the details of this senseless attack,” a spokesperson for Uber said in an email.
“We banned the rider from the Uber platform, and we are keeping the driver and his loved ones in our thoughts. We stand ready to assist law enforcement with their investigation.”

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: The unexpected power of fleeting friendships
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Tiffany Watt Smith
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
In Russian, a poputchik is a stranger you meet on a journey who you end up confessing everything to because you know you’ll never see them again. Like the English “fellow traveller”, poputchik was repurposed to describe Marxist sympathisers, but the original meaning intrigues me most.
The idea that we might safely unburden ourselves to strangers, or have their secrets bestowed upon us, is deeply embedded in Russian culture. It’s there in Leo Tolstoy’s The Kreutzer Sonata: as the windows tremble and the tundra passes in a hypnotic blur, Pozdnyshev tells his life story of marriage, betrayal and murder. Or in Venedikt Erofeev’s 1970s satire Moscow to the End of the Line, in which a retired cable fitter drunkenly hops a train and unfurls a sublime monologue on politics, society, love and, of course, vodka. A Russian friend jokes that this is “therapy, Soviet-style”.
Despite the fact that the proliferation of headphones and devices makes talking to strangers seem almost radical, most of us can probably tell our own poputchik tale. Perhaps we exchanged intimate secrets with someone on a car-share ride, or in an airport bar, or on that holiday when the coach broke down.
Earlier this year, on a long-haul flight to Toronto for work, I was seated among a group of excited young lads. My heart sank (though, for the record, they were impeccably behaved). Theirs must have too, finding a flustered, middle-aged bespectacled type in their row, instead of a pretty young thing to flirt with. We headphoned up and politely ignored each other, until at 4am, everyone gently snoring around us, my neighbour and I got to whispering. It turned out they were a group of Royal Navy submariners undergoing training off the icy Canadian coast.
Naturally I was dying to know all the details of their underwater life, but what I really remember was his shy admissions that he longed for a girlfriend – with months spent away it was hard to make a connection – and his worries about the talk he was due to give. In turn, I confided my fears around a recent career change. Then the lights pinged on, the cabin stirred and shifted, and we melted back into our separate worlds, wishing each other good luck when we disembarked. It was a disarming and expansive moment of shared vulnerability.
In our lonely and divided times, these fleeting intimacies with strangers are vital, though we’ve long been taught to dismiss them. Writing in the fourth century BC, Aristotle created a hierarchy of friendships that still haunts us today. At the top was the “perfect friendship”, a lifetime meeting-of-minds. At the bottom were a rag tag of convenient, pragmatic alliances, struck up to pass the time or for mutual assistance.
What made these lesser friendships unworthy was that they seemed disposable: “when the motive of the friendship is dissolved, the friendship is done away with,” Aristotle wrote with a disapproving sniff. It might be a stretch to describe someone I’d spoken to for an hour a friend, but if Aristotle was right, and the length of a relationship is the measure of its value, then fleeting connections ought to be the least worthy of our attention or interest.
Yet most of us recognise these connections can touch us in profound and lasting ways. Instead of Aristotelian hierarchies, perhaps it’s time to embrace the concept of “relationship anarchy”, which circulates in polyamorous communities. Relationship anarchists argue against ranking our romantic relationships, neighbours, long- and short-lived friendships, inviting us instead to see the singular value and qualities of each connection.
The evidence certainly suggests there are important benefits to even the most seemingly inconsequential connection with a stranger. Even small talk about, say, the weather can increase our sense of belonging and connection (it is more the form than the content that matters, researchers say). We frequently imagine that what distinguishes a close friend is that we can tell them anything, but just as often, we feel safe confiding in strangers, since they are less likely to judge or pepper us with intrusive follow-ups. In Shoji Morimoto’s 2023 memoir Rental Person Who Does Nothing, about his service offering company to strangers while they perform their chores, he observes: “There are a lot of important things that can be talked about with people you don’t know very well or even at all. Depth of discussion and depth of relationship don’t always go hand in hand.”
However sceptical we are of online spaces, and with good reason, they are one place we can exchange our secrets with strangers with relative ease. In the 1990s, trans people gathered in early internet chatrooms. Known only to each other by their handles, and often disappearing without warning, they forged temporary friendships that were nonetheless highly significant: in 1991, Terri Main, a 39-year-old trans woman, compared visiting CompuServe’s GenderLine forum to being enveloped in an “electronic hug”.
But while they can act as a lifeline, online encounters are different in important ways from real-world ones. So much in emotional connection happens unconsciously, a question of tone and rhythm, gesture, even smell. Real-world conversations also carry a different level of risk, since we can’t just log off when things go wrong, as they inevitably will (even Russian railway carriages had their fair share of opinionated bores, and other menaces). In the real world, we must learn to negotiate, to tolerate awkwardness and difficulty, to tactfully divert or withdraw. It is delicate, daring work, and its costs do not fall equally on all people. But if we neglect these social muscles entirely, they atrophy.
And there is so much to be gained, and to be learned. I don’t remember the name of the young man I met on the flight to Toronto. But I do remember exactly how the exchange made me feel. Connected and curious. Unburdened, Soviet-style. But most of all, awed by the extraordinary lives of others.
Tiffany Watt Smith is the author of Bad Friend (Faber). To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.
Further reading
Moscow to the End of the Line by Venedikt Erofeev (Northwestern University Press, £26.99)
Friends by Robin Dunbar (Little, Brown, £13.99)
Friendaholic by Elizabeth Day (4th Estate, £16.99)

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: The UFC is hard to like. Kayla Harrison shows why it’s harder to dismiss | Bryan Armen Graham
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Bryan Armen Graham at Madison Square Garden
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
If you don’t like what is being said, change the conversation. Amid the wreckage of an epic midterm beatdown, the diminished president of the United States spent part of last week channeling another Donald when he publicly floated longtime aide-de-camp Dana White – the Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive, Meta board member and public face of professional face-slapping – as the next White House press secretary. Trump’s kayfabe featured a support team of UFC bruisers to help White keep the Washington press corps in line, a fantasy lineup that included Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Khabib Nurmagomedov and one “Kayla Harris”. Surely he meant Kayla Harrison, the twice Olympic champion judoka from small-town Ohio who on Saturday night submitted the great Amanda Nunes in the co-main event at Madison Square Garden and made a credible claim for being the greatest female mixed martial artist the sport has ever seen.
Trump’s turn to White’s trademark bluster was a simple enough gambit to parse. In 2024, he rode the manosphere to an astonishing 63% backing among young white men, with White name-checking Joe Rogan, Theo Von, Adin Ross and the Nelk Boys from the victory podium like the heterodox heirs to Bill Buckley. Two years later, that support had cratered by 20 points in the midterms: the political equivalent of a 10-8 round. Suddenly, the prospect of White as some cauliflower-eared CJ Cregg seemed less like comic relief than a panicked attempt to inject a cycle of synthetic testosterone into Maga’s increasingly low-energy movement.
For those whose weekends don’t revolve around watching barefoot men and women kick and punch each other inside a steel cage, the performative West Wing sideshow doubled as native advertising for the UFC’s annual November extravaganza at the Garden – where a sold-out house of 19,740 spectators, mostly men, was finally assured by late Saturday afternoon once the few remaining obstructed-view seats in the deep 200s were snatched up for $308.50 apiece at the box office. Yet beneath the gruesome theater of 13 fights over nearly eight hours that bled into the wee hours of Sunday morning was a question of political expediency. Rogan, the UFC’s veteran color commentator and one of Trump’s most powerful media allies, had gone conspicuously mum on the president before the midterms, to his measurable detriment. Was White’s promotion, having tethered its fortunes so closely to Maga since 2016, contemplating a similar uncoupling now that the electoral winds had shifted?
In the parlance of Julia Masli: ha ha ha. There may have been fewer Maga hats and “YEW-ESS-AY!” chants than two years ago, when Trump feted his re-election cageside with Elon Musk and RFK Jr in his first appearance outside Mar-a-Lago. Yet any notion of a tactical retreat was scotched by the presence of Josh Hokit, who seized on his post-fight interview after a fight on June’s card on the White House South Lawn to peddle a vulgar conspiracy theory about Michelle Obama – and told reporters on Wednesday he had no regrets, boasting that Trump amplified it on Truth Social. Five months on, he was rewarded with a heavyweight title shot in the main event where he drew the loudest cheers of the night before bowing on points to the French fighter and actor Ciryl Gane.
The UFC was hardly about to abandon its oldest instincts. From its earliest days as a pay-per-view curiosity derided as “human cockfighting”, it has thrived on thumbing its nose at polite liberal consensus. Nowhere did the establishment resist more fiercely than here in New York, which banned professional MMA in 1997 and held out until March 2016 as the 50th and final US state to legalize it – and even then only after Democratic assembly members called it “a terrible, nasty, violent sport” and “a sad day” before reluctantly giving it the green light.
Three decades on, the promotion has turned cultural defiance into a slickly marketed juggernaut valued at more than $12bn, having cultivated the manosphere years before it had a name and given middle America a roster of homegrown heroes that boxing, its older and superior cousin-sport, increasingly struggled to provide. One industry executive described the UFC’s core audience to the Guardian as “white guys from the suburbs who grew up watching pro wrestling and aren’t married yet” – a demographic that would soon become one of the most coveted constituencies in American politics. The distance traveled from outlaw attraction to establishment property was underscored when Paramount Skydance, days after a highly scrutinized merger approved by Trump’s regulators, committed $7.7bn (£5.8bn) over seven years for its US broadcast rights.
White spoke at three Republican national conventions, defiantly brought the UFC back in May 2020 as the first major US sport to resume amid the Covid-19 shutdown, and in June staged a fight card on the White House grounds to mark the nation’s 250th anniversary and Trump’s 80th birthday, absorbing an estimated $30m (£22m) loss in the process. Having long served as a recruiting and morale vehicle for the US military, the UFC has seen its political and national-security ties become fully institutionalized: a proposed no-bid contract to train FBI agents under Trump loyalist Kash Patel, a state department sports-diplomacy agreement and a sponsorship deal with defense-tech contractor Anduril.
There is plenty to loathe about the UFC’s playbook even beyond its cozy synergy with Maga pageantry: its resistance to unionization, its intimidation and blacklisting of journalists, its stranglehold on fighter pay, which accounts for a smaller share of overall revenue than in any other major sport. (Only men’s tennis, where tensions over prize-money splits are approaching a breaking point, comes close.) Yet seeing Harrison’s name in lights in Times Square and throughout midtown Manhattan all week for one of the most consequential women’s bouts in the promotion’s 33-year history, it was also impossible to ignore the UFC’s most consistently redeeming quality: it has created a path to real money and celebrity for Olympians who devoted their lives to punishing sports that for years offered neither once the medals are handed out.
Few pieces of media have captured the lonely afterlife of Olympic glory more brutally than the opening five minutes of Bennett Miller’s 2014 drama Foxcatcher. The film shows Mark Schultz (played by a never-better Channing Tatum), the 1984 Olympic wrestling gold medalist in training for the world championships and the 1988 Games, delivering a motivational talk to a roomful of fidgety schoolchildren for a $20 check before smash-cutting to him waiting in a fast-food line and eating a burger alone in his car. For decades, that was the bargain struck by American wrestlers: sacrifice your youth to one of the world’s most unsparing disciplines, reach the absolute pinnacle only to discover that your life’s work has earned you neither a living nor an audience. Schultz himself fought at UFC 9 in 1996, becoming the first Olympic gold medalist to enter the octagon. At least 20 more Olympians have followed, mostly from wrestling and judo with a splash of taekwondo, including medalists like Ronda Rousey, Sara McMann, Yoel Romero, Henry Cejudo and Harrison, as the promotion gradually opened a genuine avenue to wealth and celebrity their original sports could scarcely offer.
None of this should allow White to be retconned into a trailblazer for women’s sports. Unlike Jake Paul, of all people, an unlikely ally who has spent years putting his ample fortune and promotional muscle behind female boxers, White flatly insisted in 2011 that women would never fight in the UFC, before finally seeing the light on the virtues of gender equality once Rousey became a bankable box-office attraction for a rival promotion. Even so, while the UFC’s ruthless business practices and Maga mien may offend their sensibilities, the spectacle of two baddies co-headlining a card that pulled in a $10.3m (£7.8m) live gate was enough to warm the hearts of everyone with an emotional investment in women’s sports from Billie Jean King to Coach Jackie.
For Harrison, the opportunity was transformative. Without the UFC, she might well have vanished into that quiet anonymity that swallows countless Olympians, her extraordinary story confined to a few niche sports pages and a two-week quadrennial window – even then at risk of being preempted by gymnastics, swimming or a Ryan Lochte gas-station scandal. Born in Middletown, Ohio – the same deindustrialized Rust Belt city that gave America vice-president JD Vance – Harrison was sexually abused as a teenager by her judo coach, Daniel Doyle, leaving her battling depression and suicidal thoughts. She went on to become the first American woman or man to win Olympic judo gold at London 2012, using her newfound spotlight to speak more openly about the abuse she had first disclosed before the Games in a powerful Sports Illustrated cover story.
Life kept landing blows. Her father took his own life in 2014, two years before her repeat gold in Rio. When her sister struggled with addiction, Harrison’s mother and stepfather took in her two young children. But after her mother suffered a stroke and her stepfather died in 2020, Harrison took over their care, eventually adopting them. By then she had overcome her initial disdain for MMA, trading the judo mat for the cage and winning two Professional Fighters League championships while navigating single motherhood. As she put it early Sunday morning in the bowels of the Garden, raising two kids leaves little room to dwell on dark days: “You still gotta open the bag of chips for them. Like, you wanna sit and cry on the floor, but they’re like, ‘Mom.’ I’m like, ‘Okay, guess I’m not gonna have a breakdown right now.’”
She joined the UFC in 2024 and needed just three fights to claim the bantamweight title once purpose-built for Rousey, submitting Julianna Peña 17 months ago. That set up Saturday night’s showdown with Nunes, her former training partner and the most decorated female fighter in UFC history coming off a three-and-a-half-year layoff. Harrison, now 36 and returning from career-threatening neck surgery that derailed their January meeting, admitted she would have gladly fought Nunes behind closed doors. The fame held little appeal beyond the platform it gave survivors of sexual abuse to find her Fearless Foundation.
On Saturday night, the clean, clinical judo that had first brought Harrison Olympic glory proved decisive all over again. Nunes bafflingly abandoned her advantage in the striking exchanges to grapple with the master judoka. She had Harrison wobbling in a frantic opening round, only to surrender dominant position after a beautifully executed throw. The pattern repeated in the second, with Nunes inexplicably pursuing takedowns before finding herself pinned beneath Harrison. By the third, Harrison’s fatigue was beginning to show, but Nunes had already allowed the champion to dictate the terms. In the fourth, Harrison finished the argument with a rear-naked choke applied with the sudden, predatory speed of an animal attack in an Attenborough documentary, forcing Nunes to tap. Afterward, Harrison crouched at the center of the octagon before dropping to her knees, looking for a moment as though she might cry. Instead, she seemed to find a moment of peace.
That platform simply does not exist in the insular world of American judo. By stepping into the octagon, she turned amateur-sport obscurity into main-event money, a place in the US sporting mainstream and her name and likeness on the marquee of the world’s most famous arena. Asked what her 13-year-old self would make of it all, Harrison laughed: “She wouldn’t believe me. She’d be like, ‘We did what? We do MMA? What? Like, we made how much money?’”
Harrison’s triumph under the bright lights of the Garden offered the clearest distillation yet of what the UFC is: a company stubbornly wedded to its rightwing bravado, a business model built on ruthless self-interest, and, right at the center of the cage, a woman who survived everything life threw at her finally getting paid – and seen.
