https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/f.title: Feds Characterize Trump As Mercurial King In Latest Bid to End Congestion Pricing
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/f.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/f.text:
New court, same losing argument.
The federal Department of Transportation continues to insist that the president and his agencies can do whatever they want, whenever they want, as the Trump administration tries without success to destroy congestion pricing in New York City.
In June, U.S. DOT appealed Judge Lewis Liman’s March decision in favor of the MTA, which sued the federal government over President Trump’s attempt to kill the Manhattan toll. In their brief, the feds asked court, not for the first time, to endorse the idea that Trump’s whims, rather that the law, have the final say over his government’s actions.
The brief contained two main arguments. The first, which will be familiar to longtime followers of this increasingly absurd legal saga, is that Liman never had the authority to hear the MTA’s lawsuit because it involves a dispute over a financial contract. If that were true, the entire case should have been heard by the smaller and more specialized Court of Federal Claims, not the larger and more general Article III court system.
The second and newer argument is similar to what the Trump administration argued in lower court: that the FHWA can do whatever it wants at any time. But instead of arguing that the president is a de facto sovereign who enjoys unlimited powers, Department of Justice attorneys argued that the FHWA can simply change its mind at any time.
“[E]ven if the Agreement were considered in [Administrative Procedure Act] terms — not as a contract but as a ‘regulatory grant of approval to build toll infrastructure on a federal aid highway,’ or perhaps as a similar agency action granting a benefit or establishing a federal program—the agency would have the inherent power to reconsider and revoke it,” the attorneys wrote.
The argument is consistent with the federal government’s longstanding position from the moment President Donald Trump kicked off his attempt to kill congestion pricing: that the president has inherent king-like powers to do whatever he likes. After Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy sent his first letter demanding New York end the toll in February 2025, Trump dubbed himself the King of New York. Ever since, the rest of the federal machinery has scrambled to stand up his argument.
Last January, in a hearing before Judge Liman, DOJ lawyer Eric Hamilton argued unconvincingly that the president and his agents possessed an absolute power to cancel contracts or agreements the federal government signs with other parties. Liman described that argument as “breathtaking” and “wrong.”
So the brightest legal minds still willing to work for the Department of Justice tried once more to convince the judiciary that American law allows the federal government to be an unreliable partner. Instead of insisting that the president can cancel contracts, DOJ lawyers argued that federal agencies can just change their mind about previous approvals. “The government must be empowered to adjust to changing circumstances or to changed priorities,” they wrote.
The problem with the new argument, as one legal expert pointed out, is the very same problem that tripped up Duffy when he tried to end congestion pricing: the agreement that authorized congestion pricing, the Value Pricing Pilot Program, lacks a kill switch and the overall law authorizing the program lacks a “revoke whenever you want” clause. 
Among the cases the federal government cited as precedent was California Sea Urchin Commission v. Bean, which involved a dispute over sea otter relocation program. That program followed an agreement with a specific clause that allowed the program to end under certain conditions — an arrangement found nowhere in the VPPP.
“It’s a stretch to say they have any inherent authority just to change their mind,” said NYU law professor Roderick Hills, Jr. “I don’t know of any case that said an agency can just always change its mind, regardless of the statute under which the initial decision was made, regardless of the correctness of the original decision.”
Hills said that precedent does allow for an agency to reverse itself if it can prove that it authorized a program based on an actual error. But since the FHWA didn’t rely on Duffy’s very first argument — which is that the VPPP never actually authorized cordon pricing — Hills was perplexed as to why the government cited case law that’s hinges so strongly on human error.
“Almost all the cases they cite involve an initial agency decision that was a mistake, or that the agency claimed was a mistake,” he said. “Since they don’t claim or identify any error that was made in the initial decision here, it’s hard to see how they can claim they have power to correct an error that they don’t indicate. How can you correct an error that doesn’t exist?” 
The argument is also out of place because the federal government didn’t raise it when the MTA sued the FHWA in district court. A district court will hear all sorts of weird legal arguments that a plaintiff or defendant puts forward. But at the appeals court level, judges only consider whether there the lower court’s ruling committed a legal error. A requirement known as “appellate preservation” requires a party in a suit raise the specific issue if it wants to be able to raise it on appeal.
Since the government never suggested in the lower court that it ordered an end to congestion pricing because a federal agency can just change its mind, the judges hearing the case could decide to ignore the argument entirely.
“The simplest thing to do would be not to rule on the merits at all, but say on second argument, you didn’t raise it below. It’s waived,” said Hills.
Because of these discrepancies, the Second Circuit may choose to exclusively analyze the federal government’s argument that the original VPPP contract, between the MTA and the FHWA, should be reviewed by the Federal Court of Claims, which considers federal disputes over contracts for money. Liman rejected that argument in the lower court.
There is no strong evidence that shows the dispute over congestion pricing is a contractual dispute over money. Furthermore, the MTA has been levying the tolls for nearly two years now and New York City has yet to fall. Both of these elements bode well for the MTA and the future of congestion pricing.
“Sean Duffy is the one who’s trying to change the status quo,” said Hills. “For almost two years, the MTA has been chugging along, and Sean Duffy’s been on the sideline saying, ‘Judge, stop that guy.’ In general, judges, like everybody else, don’t like to get involved with something unless there’s a good reason to get involved and change the status quo. 
Hills continued: “In this case, the legal arguments are weak, and the policy here seems fine. The Second Circuit has to hear the case. They have mandatory review, so they’ll have to say something, but after two 100-page opinions, I imagine that they won’t think they need to say a whole bunch.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Overhauls Homeless Outreach for Freezing Weather After Last Winter’s Cold Deaths
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Kaitlyn Schwanemann
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
New York City is revamping its homeless outreach programs for Code Blue weather emergencies, when real-feel temperatures outside drop below freezing overnight and become potentially lethal.
The move follows a brutal winter at the start of the year where at least 18 people died from cold exposure outdoors during a weekslong arctic stretch in January and February that posed an early crisis for the Mamdani administration and put unsheltered New Yorkers at risk. At the time, city officials scrambled to get vulnerable people indoors through increased outreach around the clock and opening more warming sites and low-barrier shelters.
As part of a $25 million investment, the administration is looking to hire 300 additional outreach workers who during frigid weather will fan out across zones where unsheltered people tend to stay, including encampments, parks and subway steps. Officials did not specify these areas, but said they represent about 75% of “known unsheltered locations” citywide.
Department of Social Services Commissioner Erin Dalton said her agency identified the zones based on 311 calls for homeless outreach and encampment responses, along with intel from canvassers who scour the streets throughout the year. She said DSS tested the approach last summer during extreme heat periods and recorded more than 2,000 “engagements” with people, more than 20 times as many on a given day compared to the previous summer.
“We’re going to implement this and then continue to improve. There’s no perfect plan,” Dalton told The City Reporter in an interview. “Weather is changing rapidly, and so we want to make sure that we can continue to innovate there.”
The overhaul includes hundreds more low-barrier beds in single- and double-occupancy rooms that New Yorkers can access through a relaxed intake process, as well as hiring dozens more nurses for outreach teams during freezing temperatures.
The city is also soliciting for on-demand transportation to speed up getting people into shelters, warming centers and drop-in sites, where they can get free food, showers and case management services. That is in addition to 50 NYC Health + Hospitals vans, each staffed with a nurse or nurse practitioner so people can get checkups, and 20 DSS warming buses at peak levels, officials said.
Not all 300 new canvassers will be deployed during every Code Blue event, according to the department, but they will be on standby for the most dangerous weather. Dalton added the city is interested in hiring more outreach workers with personal histories of street homelessness who can connect with unsheltered New Yorkers, and DSS will train them before they deploy into the field.
Advocates Hopeful for Retooled Strategy
Homeless advocates said they are pleased the administration plans to do more to find people in need who do not know about or trust city resources, including shelters. Some street-homeless people say they stay out of the shelter system due to concerns about safety and strict rules, even if that means living outside and risking the elements.
Andrew Chappotin, an activist with the nonprofit Safety Net Project who lived on the streets for three years until last winter’s fatal cold stretch, said he entered a Safe Haven shelter at the end of January even though he had negative experiences in local shelters before.
“I just couldn’t take the cold anymore,” Chappotin said. “This was the coldest weather I’ve ever experienced. My body did not do well this past winter.”
He said street outreach teams still need to build stronger relationships with unsheltered residents and better inform them about accessing help.
Adolfo Abreu, housing campaigns director for the advocacy organization VOCAL-NY, said he is excited about the revamped Code Blue program and hopes it is part of a broader effort to expand homeless outreach year-round.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Abreu said, has “outlined a very bold vision of a city that works for working families and as many people as possible. And a big gap in that vision has been how we’ve been kind of executing, delivering vital governmental services to our most vulnerable New Yorkers.”
Nearly 5,000 people were estimated to be living unsheltered in the city during an annual official count in March, an 11% jump from 2025. The survey is usually conducted in January, but was postponed because of the extreme cold.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani’s White Knight for Troubled Buildings Has Dismal Record of Violations
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently celebrated the transfer of ownership of three long-neglected rent-stabilized buildings in Brooklyn from Rubin Dukler, an owner who’d made frequent appearances on the city’s worst landlord list, to a new landlord named Mark Schwartz.
Schwartz is the mayor of Teaneck, New Jersey, and owns rent-stabilized apartment buildings across the city. Under the landlord swap that was cheered by the mayor and subsidized by the city, Schwartz has pledged to fix up the three Dukler buildings and provide tenants with decent living conditions they had long been denied.
In a Sept. 3 statement, Mamdani called the transfer “a new chapter” for the tenants and promised to work with the new owner “to put these 88 homes on a path toward stability and make clear that every New Yorker deserves a safe, well-maintained and stable place to call home.”
What the mayor did not mention was that Schwartz and his partners have racked up more than 1,400 open housing code violations deemed hazardous or immediately hazardous in the 28 buildings they now own or manage across the city, according to an internal city document obtained by The City Reporter.
Records show that the city Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) — the agency that will monitor Schwartz’s upgrade of the Dukler properties — has repeatedly cited Schwartz’s buildings for a sobering variety of squalid conditions. In the last four years alone, they have sued him or his partners 15 times to force required repairs.
And HPD has had to hire contractors to remedy conditions at their buildings because the owners failed to complete required repairs. The internal city document notes Schwartz and his partners currently owe the city $1.3 million for this work.
Of Mice and Mold
Tenants at 3569 Dekalb Ave., a 54-unit tenement near Woodlawn Cemetery in The Bronx that Schwartz and his partners have owned for many years, know all about this.
As of Nov. 2, that building had accumulated 268 open violations for conditions inspectors deemed hazardous or immediately hazardous, including 30 citations issued Aug. 26 for rat and mice infestations, non-functioning smoke detectors and toxic mold. Since Schwartz took ownership in 2018, the city has spent $21,500 to hire contractors to perform required repairs there.
“The roaches and the rats are crazy,” Maritza Diaz-Sanchez, 40, recently told The City Reporter, recalling a recent encounter when she said rats and mice ran through the lobby and up the staircase across her path. She pointed to a patch the building super had installed over a hole in the lobby floor to try and block additional furry guests.
“Two mouses and two rats,” she said. “It was a family.”
‘A Ton of Care’
In an interview, Schwartz admitted he was “embarrassed” by conditions at Dekalb Avenue, but insisted he’s aggressively moving to address all outstanding violations there and at his other properties across the city.
He said he’s had varying degrees of oversight of his buildings, relying at times on partners and third-party entities to stay on top of building conditions. This arrangement, he said, has not always obtained optimal results.
“When I handle it myself, they’re very clean. When, over the past years, over time in past years when others handle it, they don’t get taken care of as well as they should,” he said. “Every few years we give buildings back and forth to partners and third parties and it just doesn’t for the most part work out.”
“If I screw up I will say I screwed up,” he added. “If you rely on other people, you can’t say that.”
Last month Schwartz said he took control of 11 rent-stabilized buildings in which he says he had a small stake because he says he wants to better assist Mamdani’s efforts to preserve existing affordable housing.
“This administration and myself are getting very heavily involved in preservation. The rent-stabilized industry is a mess right now. The buildings need a ton of care,” he said. “I want to make sure our buildings are taken care of before I work with others. I’m very proud of our internal track record and the buildings we took over.”
Schwartz insisted he has “hit the ground” to remedy open citations: “We immediately began attacking all the violations and have made great progress.”
He has his work cut out for him. At one of those properties, a four-story property at 2044 Bergen St. in Crown Heights, a mile away from the Dukler buildings, Schwartz said he had been a “small partner” there for years but on Oct. 1 took full charge.
‘A Profitable Business Model’?
One of his first orders of business will be to address a lawsuit HPD filed last month. At the time there were 92 open violations in a building with 16 units, including 76 deemed hazardous. That represented a per-dwelling average of 4.75 hazardous violations — far in excess of the citywide average for rent-stabilized buildings of 0.05 violations per dwelling. Hazardous violations cited this year included roach and mice infestations and non-functioning self-closing doors and smoke detectors.
HPD alleged the owners had falsely certified that dozens of other violations had been remedied when inspectors discovered they were not. And they pointed out that the address of the building’s registered agent, Brian Dulitz, was a mail drop in a UPS store in Lower Manhattan. Dulitz has served as a registered agent on multiple Schwartz properties, including the Dukler buildings on Eastern Parkway.
HPD characterized the pattern of failure to address repair requests as deliberate, alleging the owners had “turned deferring maintenance of rent-stabilized buildings into a profitable business model.”
How Schwartz became the go-to guy in the Mamdani-supported landlord swap starts with him purchasing the mortgage on the Dukler properties in late 2024. Since then he said he’s moved to foreclose, but Duckler has continued to be the registered agent responsible for managing the three buildings.
Schwartz said in the summer of 2025, frustrated residents who had formed a tenants union after years of inaction from Dukler approached Schwartz about stepping in. Schwartz said he then began working with HPD — first under Eric Adams, then under Mamdani — seeking city subsidies to help him preserve and upgrade the 88 rent-stabilized apartments in the three buildings.
Rent Strike
On Sept. 4, the Dukler Tenant Union announced they’d reached an “agreement in principle” with Schwartz to rehabilitate their buildings with a long-term goal of converting them to co-ops that tenants would have the option to purchase.
The union said Schwartz agreed to cancel all arrears accumulated during a years-long rent strike in protest of Dukler’s failures, and that tenants will have some oversight over the upgrades to “ensure high quality renovations.” HPD will monitor contractors performing the rehabilitation.
“HPD is very hands-on,” Schwartz said. “The city is trying to expedite this for months. The city is begging to get this done by June. That would be a dream. I’m not going to lie to you. It is pressuring us.”
Asked to comment on Schwartz’s track record, the mayor’s office sent a statement from Cea Weaver, who runs Mamdani’s Office to Protect Tenants.
“Working alongside new ownership, the Dukler Tenant Union has negotiated a strong Memo of Understanding with Mark Schwartz so that they have another tool in their toolbox to hold building management accountable,” Weaver said. “As we do with any building, we will use each and every mechanism at our disposal to enforce the city’s Housing Maintenance Code and support both building owners who come to the table in good faith, and tenants who fight for their right to live in a safe, stable home.”
Schwartz said tenants were aware of his track record when they signed the memorandum of understanding, but when The City Reporter visited the Dukler buildings on Monday, tenants universally declined to comment about their soon-to-be new landlord.
Arielle Hersh, director of policy at the nonprofit Urban Homesteading Assistance Board, which helped organize the Dukler tenants, said she would not discuss Schwartz’s portfolio on the record.
Schwartz, for his part, said he’s enthusiastically working with the Mamdani team to make his takeover of the Dukler buildings work, but he noted the administration’s plans to greatly expand this tactic to other in-need buildings will require ample funding.
He estimated repairs alone at the Dukler buildings are expected to cost $150,000 per unit.
“I love their approach. I want to work with them on their approach,” he said, adding that “the Eastern Parkway package, it’s several hundred thousand per unit. That’s three buildings. How do you do this with hundreds of buildings? I don’t know where they’re going to get the money.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/g.title: GET OUT: E-Bike Battery Fires are a Crisis We Can No Longer Ignore
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/g.author: Charles Komanoff
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/g.text:
Back-to-back mass-death fires in Brooklyn and the Bronx have rocked the city these past two weeks, taking ten lives and ripping apart countless more, as reported in the Times, News, Post, Hell Gate, City Reporter, Gothamist, and of course Streetsblog. Substandard e-bike batteries likely triggered both conflagrations, an all-too-common occurrence that should shock street-safety and cycling champions into action.
Over the past decade, e-bike battery fires in New York City have killed dozens of residents and injured many more. They have rendered hundreds of apartments uninhabitable. Yet micromobility advocates have had little to say, treating this as an anomaly and not a core problem.
City government is complicit, too. On Oct. 28, three teens and their mother died from burns after their father’s e-bike erupted in flames in their Mott Haven apartment. The next day, Mayor Mamdani and Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore offered up pablum: don’t leave e-bikes in doorways, don’t charge them overnight and try to store them outdoors. We might just as well dispense with highway lane markers and beseech drivers to take it easy.
Officials took a similar tack after the Nov. 5 Brooklyn disaster, when another fast-moving fire, also apparently sparked by an e-bike battery, killed six residents of a two-story frame house in Sunset Park. The blaze marked the greatest loss of life from a single fire in New York City since the 2022 Twin Parks fire in the Bronx. Mamdani vowed to find a solution but omitted any specifics. Bonsignore was out of town and did not comment.
Even before the Mott Haven and Sunset Park blazes, e-bike-related fires across the five boroughs rose 41 percent from 2025. Batteries caused at least 406 fires this year, versus 241 over the same period in 2025 — a 68-percent increase. 
“Every single New York City resident should be furious,” said Brooklyn-based street-safety advocate and battery-swap entrepreneur Baruch Herzfeld. He’s right. We cyclists assert the moral high ground as we battle car and truck drivers and their elected enablers. We solemnly memorialize New Yorkers whom motorists kill on our contested streets. Yet this adjacent conflagration finds us largely silent.
This problem has persisted for so long that multiple mayors have “cracked down” on it, at multiple times in multiple ways, with little evident change. Between August and mid-September, the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection inspected more than 200 bicycle and micromobility shops and issued 136 violations that led to 77 summonses. But it was insufficient: the agency’s sweep primarily targeted vehicles equipped to exceed the city’s speed limit of 20 mph for scooters and 20 mph for e-bikes — not hazardous batteries.
This infernal calamity traces to the uncertified lithium-ion batteries that power thousands of e-mobility devices on the city’s streets. Extravagantly distant food delivery — enabled by the lack of a mileage surcharge — compounds the disaster by requiring longer and more frequent charging cycles. 
What Sets UL-Certified E-bike Batteries Apart
We think of batteries as mundane pieces of technology. Nobody fears the small metal disc that powers their wristwatch or the slightly larger cylinder in their television remote. E-bike batteries, by comparison, are complex devices that must operate over variegated conditions for long periods of time. That led Underwriters Laboratory to publish their first light-vehicle electric-battery safety standard, known as UL 2271, in 2013.
William Henry Merrill, an M.I.T.-educated electrical engineer and electrical inspector for the Boston Board of Fire Underwriters, founded UL in 1894. Now a multinational conglomerate with $3 billion in annual revenue, UL maintains safety standards for e-bike batteries. It is one of a few firms authorized by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration to certify their safety.
To win UL certification — those upper-case initials in a circle you’ve probably seen a thousand times but never really noticed — batteries must demonstrate that they can interrupt overheating, cut off power to battery elements in the event of over-charging or over-discharging, and prevent short circuits from triggering high-energy fires or explosions. In contrast, many uncertified batteries lack automatic shutoff controls or employ generic chargers that can overpower battery cells. They’re also less protected from damage from road jostling, moisture ingress and everyday wear-and-tear.
Many deliveristas ride cheaper e-bikes and scooters manufactured by obscure Chinese brands with cheap and swappable batteries. New York City has never recorded a fire caused by a UL-certified e-bike or other micromobility device. From all appearances, replacing the off-brand batteries with UL-certified batteries is both necessary and sufficient for fire-safe micromobility.
How to rid the city of substandard e-bike batteries
I propose a two-step solution:
- Enact a municipal ordinance authorizing the immediate seizure and confiscation of non-UL-certified lithium-ion batteries from residential, commercial and institutional buildings in the five boroughs. 
- Impose a steep surcharge on food deliveries administered by food-delivery app companies such as Doordash and Uber Eats. The levies will pay for a new FDNY-DCWP task force to hunt down the non-compliant batteries.
How big a surcharge? I approached this question by estimating the annual societal cost of e-bike battery fires and dividing that figure by the number of annual deliveries via e-bike. The result is a fee of $15 per delivery. (Yes, there would be parallel surcharges for deliveries by car or truck; and yes, the charge should graduate by distance.) 
To be sure, my $15 estimate is much less finely drawn than is my wont, owing to inexact figures on the frequency and societal costs of e-bike battery fire deaths, injuries and dwellings destroyed. It’s also a broad-brush figure, since not every e-bike is used for food-delivery. Case in point: the burning e-bike in Mott Haven was apparently gifted to the father — who remains in a medically induced coma — and probably wasn’t used for business purposes. 
Still, most deadly New York City e-bike fires are tied to the delivery sector. Moreover, that industry’s pockets are deep enough to pay for a municipal strike force to ferret out the thousands of non-compliant lithium-ion batteries used for micro-mobility — commercial or otherwise. The policy question is whether the entire calculated $15-per-delivery “fire externality” should be added to delivery prices, or a smaller amount.
Surcharge Calculations and Assumptions
If passed on to customers, a $15 surcharge would translate to a 40-percent rise from the average pre-tip, pre-tax price of $35-40. An increase of that magnitude would cut the demand for food delivery by half.1 That would be tough news for deliveristas, but good tidings for most New Yorkers, who for years have endured enormous collateral damage — both fire-related and street safety-related — from the sector’s unpriced dangers. Lesser surcharges would soften both the customer price increase and the impact on the delivery sector.
My calculations, assumptions and data sources are spelled out in a simple Excel sheet, available here, covering the past three years. For 2026, the largest damage cost, $144 million, stems from the 10 fatalities in the Mott Haven and Sunset Park fires. I arrived at this figure by multiplying U.S. DOT’s standard measure for the “valuation of a statistical life” — which was $14.2 million last year ($14.4 million with inflation) — by the number of deaths.
The second largest cost, $67 million, covers the far greater number of injuries. For the purposes of my calculation, I assessed the cost of each injury as five percent of the cost of a fatality, corresponding to U.S. DOT’s assessment of “moderate” injury costs. (The agency assesses serious, severe and critical injuries at roughly 10, 27 and 60 percent of fatal injury costs, respectively.)
The third largest cost, $16 million, concerns lost housing. I derived this figure from a 2024 report on “the economic, human and community toll” from e-mobility battery fires in New York City by Oxford Economics for UL Standards and Engagement, the non-profit arm of Underwriters Laboratory that devises safety standards.2
The three categories sum to $159 million for 2024, $193 million for 2025, and $227 million for this year. I have used the middle (2025) figure of $193 million and divided it by the annual rate of 13 million food deliveries. The result is $14.85, or $15 rounded.
If New York City were to surcharge app-operated food deliveries by that amount, the annual take would be close to the $193 million figure. That level of revenue could staff a thousand-person enforcement office, assuming fully loaded costs of $200,000 per employee. (The surcharge, and the task force, would shrink as the number of non-certified batteries diminished.) Alternatively, some of the revenue could support a trade-in program (as has been done with guns). The City could buy certified batteries at a bulk discount and give them to deliveristas in exchange for uncertified ones. 
Would this throw deliveristas under the bus?
In the short run, deliverista work-hours would surely shrivel along with the size of their industry. That shrinkage would be temporary, pending the eventual bounceback as non-UL-certified batteries disappear and the gross fire-damage figure dwindles — and, with it, the delivery surcharge. Authorities should press for a federal ban on the manufacture and importation of uncertified batteries, but that likely would take years — time the city doesn’t have.
Admittedly, this scheme is unabashedly draconian, at least at the “full price,” and stands in marked contrast to the “essential” designation of food-delivery in the Covid pandemic. As the strike force retrenched, the city could redirect some of the surcharge revenue to retraining and resettlement.
But when the smoke clears, we should see the facts clearly: what arose as a pandemic-era stopgap has transformed our streets to service some of the wealthiest New Yorkers. Requiring them to bear the true costs of their expensive and maladaptive habit isn’t exactly the French Revolution. It’s a way of prioritizing a safer city over extreme convenience.
Externality pricing can be a stern taskmaster. But what’s good in the case of congestion pricing should also be good for snuffing out e-bike fires that are hurting, and haunting, New Yorkers.

https://gothamist.com/news/developer-at-.title: Developer at Brooklyn collapse site had record of flouting orders from city agency
https://gothamist.com/news/developer-at-.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/developer-at-.text:
The developer of the property adjacent to the fatal Brooklyn building collapse had a record for cutting corners at the construction site, according to records from the city buildings department.
Those documents show that owner Robert Fischman sent a letter to neighboring landlords in June of this year to inform them of an upcoming disturbance: his company would begin excavating the empty lot at 2625 Bedford Ave. to make way for a new apartment building. It was one of many similar projects set to rise in the rapidly gentrifying neighborhood.
Five months later, the excavation site was the scene of a fatal disaster, after one of the apartment buildings next door at 1321 Flatbush Ave. crumbled into the dirt pit below. At least eight people have been pronounced dead as a result of the collapse and many more were injured, including multiple children on a day that public school students had off for the Veterans Day holiday. Rescue workers were still digging through the rubble Thursday morning for survivors.
The letter Fischman sent neighboring landlords lists the same phone number as his company, Berkoff Supply, an industrial hardware store in Brooklyn. A person who answered the phone at a number listed for Fischman hung up when contacted late Wednesday. An employee answered the phone at Berkoff Supply on Thursday but said Fischman was not available.
By the time Fischman had sent the excavation notice, the project team had already ignored commands from the Department of Buildings, according to records from the city buildings department.
The agency had previously issued the stop work order at the lot during demolition of an existing one-story building in March after determining that contractors had failed to install required safety precautions, including netting and sheds, said Department of Buildings spokesperson Andrew Rudansky. A month later, a buildings inspector found the owners had continued demolition work in violation of the order and issued another penalty.
At a press conference Thursday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the Brooklyn District Attorney's office is involved in investigating the collapse and that building inspectors had been dispatched across the five boroughs to check other related construction sites.
"A tragedy of this magnitude demands a comprehensive and thorough investigation. That includes both the construction site and the building that collapsed, that has already began with the Department of Buildings and law enforcement leading it," Mamdani said. "There are five main entities involved with this construction site who are associated with approximately 100 other sites across the city. Our Department of Buildings is commencing sweeps of those sites today."
Construction workers had been digging in the empty lot Wednesday before the adjacent structure collapsed, Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said at a press conference late Wednesday.
The lot is owned by a limited liability company tied to Fischman and Judy Swimer, according to property records. Swimer did not respond to a phone message. Architectural drawings filed in December last year reveal plans for a three-story complex on what was once a single-story commercial building. The developer later submitted new plans for a nine-story structure in September. Tigani said the buildings department had yet to approve those new plans. A permit was in place for the excavation work.
Structural plans filed by engineer Jeiming Wang of the firm LMW Engineering Group call for extensive excavation and bracing work to prevent neighboring buildings from collapsing, including steel, timber and concrete shoring. They also require the excavation contractor to use seismic monitors to track vibration and install crack gauges on surrounding buildings to monitor movements. Visual inspections were required, along with various oversight and reporting requirements under the supervision of a special inspector.
It’s unclear whether these precautions were taken. The Department of Buildings said it is still investigating what caused the collapse. Wang and the special inspector, MD Islam of Queens-based RI Consulting Services, did not respond to calls and emails on Wednesday.
The company Townhouse Builders was contracted to carry out the shoring work, according to a building permit issued to its owner, Mordchai Waisbrod, in September. Neither he nor the company responded to requests for comment.
This story has been updated with comments from Mayor Mamdani.
Other problems plagued the three-story apartment at 1321 Flatbush Ave., which is owned by a separate landlord, prior to Wednesday's disaster.
City records show inspectors documented a raft of hazards and that the owner Olufemi Falade had a long track record of deplorable building conditions. A judge sent Falade, to jail for 12 days in 2006 for violations at a different building, including vermin and exposed wiring.
Before its collapse, the building had 98 open housing code violations for unsafe electrical wiring, inadequate water supply to the sprinkler system, a lack of smoke detectors, water outages and a bed bug infestation among other problems, according to city data.
The property has cycled through the city’s tax lien sale process at least five times since 2017, due to its unpaid municipal debts, according to court and city property records.
Falade did not respond to a phone message.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: 8 Dead in Brooklyn Building Collapse As Search and Rescue Continues, Mamdani Says
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Andrew Giambrone, Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Eight people have died and 18 were injured after a three-story building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, collapsed into an adjacent construction site Wednesday afternoon, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday as rescue operations continued.
“There are no words for a loss of this magnitude,” Mamdani said in a statement. “My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.”
Those who died include six adults and two children, the mayor said at a press briefing Thursday afternoon. Two of the dead were workers at the construction site, and one person remains hospitalized in critical condition, he added.
City officials urged people to avoid the area where the building collapsed, at Flatbush and Bedford avenues. They said New Yorkers unable to reach someone they believe may have been affected by the catastrophe should call 311, while those outside of the city should call 212-639-9675.
Authorities were working to determine the cause of the collapse of the building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. into the open-pit construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. around 4 p.m. Wednesday. A third building, at 1323 Flatbush Ave., was damaged in the incident, with footage from the scene showing the side of that building ripped off and rubble from the collapsed building below.
“We have immediately launched a full investigation into how exactly this happened with our law enforcement partners, and we will be looking into all aspects of the building and the neighboring construction site,” Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said in a video statement late Wednesday.
Officials said Thursday they have issued vacate orders on three buildings on Flatbush Avenue and are sweeping other locations where the companies on the construction site were working when the building toppled. Regulators and the Brooklyn District Attorney’s office are probing the incident.
The city has not yet released the names of the victims.
At a church across from the disaster site Thursday morning, an anguished woman sobbed as she learned her husband, a construction worker, had died in the collapse. While exiting the church, she fell onto the sidewalk and others helped her get up.
“Mi esposo!” she cried.
Jose Gutierrez, a construction worker who came to the church to support the woman and the family, said he knew her husband from working at the same company. Gutierrez said the man’s body was extracted from the construction site around 6 a.m.
“We stayed here all night,” he said. “I came here to see my friend. I wish the situation was good.”
Officials said they were conducting structural stability inspections of nearby buildings. Multiple people were trapped when first responders arrived Wednesday at the scene, which drew more than 250 fire and emergency medical personnel.
Emergency management officials and the Red Cross have opened a reception center for displaced residents at the Flatbush YMCA at 1401 Flatbush Ave., authorities said.
Authorities said they shut down water mains around the site to facilitate the search and rescue operations, with about 100 buildings affected.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/a.title: As NYC Debates Amazon’s Delivery Model, Its Partner Fires 200 E-Bike Workers
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/a.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/a.text:
As NYC Debates Amazon’s Delivery Model, Its Partner Fires 200 E-Bike Workers
Just as the City Council debates reining in Amazon's business practices, the delivery giant threw workers of the job after canceling its contract with a Manhattan subcontractor.
An e-quad bike used to make deliveries in SoHo. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
This just isn’t working.
Amid a heated Council debate over reining in Amazon’s business practices, the delivery giant threw 200 e-bike delivery workers off the job this week after canceling its contract with a Manhattan subcontractor, Streetsblog learned from one of the laid-off employees.
Employees of Kaizen Management Solutions, a Delancey Street delivery service partner contracted by Amazon to fulfill same-day deliveries on electric cargo bikes, got the news on Wednesday night.
“Approximately 200 employees will be impacted,” said a letter sent to workers, which Streetsblog has seen. The positions will be terminated on Nov. 18. Employees will receive benefits until Jan. 31.
One of the laid-off employees told Streetsblog that Kaizen owner Ezra Tilaye said the firings came after Amazon terminated its contract with the company, one of Amazon’s many delivery service providers. Tilaye did not immediately respond to Streetsblog’s request for comment.
Amazon confirmed to Streetsblog that it did indeed terminate Kaizen’s contract, prompting the mass layoff.
The sudden layoffs could be a violation of the state’s WARN act, which requires employers with more than 50 employees to either provide severance or give workers at least 90 days written notice before layoffs affecting more than 25 people.
The closure of one of Amazon’s contracted Delivery Service Partners is not new for the e-commerce giant, which, despite its omnipresent company branding, does not directly hire delivery workers, but instead relies on a network of small companies to hire workers to fulfill deliveries. Workers are often seen on e-bikes or in vans blazoned with the Amazon logo, but they are not directly employed by Amazon but by companies like Kaizen.
Since 2018, Amazon has terminated contracts with 35 DSPs in the state, resulting in the loss of over 3,500 jobs, a report from the Teamsters Union found.
The firings come at a critical moment for Amazon’s business model in the city. The City Council is currently debating a bill, the so-called Delivery Protection Act, that would require Amazon to directly hire its delivery workforce. Supporters, who include Mayor Mamdani, believe the change is necessary to prevent these types of sudden layoffs.
“Mass layoffs and WARN Act violations at … captive DSPs highlight that they are not bona fide independent businesses but pawns of a giant corporation that needs to be held accountable for their operations,” said Paul Sonn, state Policy Program Director at National Employment Law Project, which worked with the Teamsters on its report. “New York City’s proposed Delivery Protection Act would do just that — and the City Council should act swiftly to approve it.”
The union, which has been pushing hard for the bill’s passage, said the situation at Kaizen is a prime example of why the Council should “close the loophole” allowing Amazon to evade responsibility for such firings.
“Amazon has spent millions of dollars on ads falsely claiming that this law will kill jobs. In fact, Amazon is New York’s biggest job killer,” said Teamsters spokesperson Matthew McQuaid.
Mayor Mamdani has released two videos this month in support of the bill, which a super-majority of Council members support.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin (D-Upper East Side) is still not ready to bring the legislation to vote. She told reporters at a press conference last month that she was still working through the bill’s “legal issues” with the city’s law department.
The bill has major street safety implications. Supporters say direct employment would hold Amazon accountable for what happens on the street while workers are delivering packages.
The Alliance for a Greater New York, which supports the bill, created an interactive tool that shows that Amazon-associated delivery vans drew 14,290 tickets from cameras and traffic enforcement agents between July 2021 and June 2025. And Amazon’s vehicles can be seen parking illegally and obstructing bike lanes all over the city.
On the other hand, Amazon is also one of the leading companies transitioning from dangerous trucks to safer electric cargo quads. But the company has threatened to pull its e-bikes out of the city if the bill passes, Streetsblog reported last month.
Amazon told Streetsblog it terminated its contract with Kaizen because of safety issues. Company spokesman Steve Kelly sent over the following statement only after Streetsblog inquired:
The safety of our employees, partners, and the communities we operate in is our top priority. Over the past year in New York City, we’ve talked a lot about the steps we and our partners take to support safety, the high standards we hold ourselves and our partners to, and the progress we’ve made together.
When a partner doesn’t put safety first, we take action. An investigation found that Kaizen Management Solutions put several e-cargo bikes back on the road before necessary repairs were done. That put its employees and others at risk. The investigation also found multiple breaches of contract involving fraud, including failure to accurately record drivers’ hours worked.
As a result, we’ve ended our partnership with Kaizen. We’re supporting the company’s affected employees by connecting them with other DSPs in the area.
Ninety percent of people living around the proposed bike route get to work without a car, but lazy reporters would rather write a "neighborhood divided" piece with no context.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: An expert guide to navigating the Fulton Center subway frankenstation
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Elizabeth Shwe, James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
Here’s a fun New York City puzzle: If a friend told you they were “getting off the train at Canal Street,” where exactly are they?
For a variety of reasons, it’s not uncommon for two or more subway stations to share the same name but not the same location. “Canal Street” is guilty of this, as is “86th Street” and “Wall Street.” And for much of the 20th century, “Fulton Street” was in that camp. (And it’s still true if you hop boroughs — there’s a Fulton Street station in Brooklyn.)
The Fulton Street 4/5 station came first, in 1905. Then the 2/3 station was built in 1918. The J/Z Fulton station opened in 1931. And finally, the A/C station arrived in 1933. By then, you had four stations, built and operated by three different train companies.
Fast forward to 2014, when the MTA — which has operated the city’s entire subway system since 1940 — opened the Fulton Center, one massive train hub that unifies all these lines and makes everything simpler. Except when it really doesn’t.
My Looped In co-host, Elizabeth Shwe, recently visited the eight-line, multi-level complex on a quest to cut through the confusion and become a Fulton Center super user.
She explains all the tips and tricks in this week's video, which you can watch here.
I had some questions of my own for her too:
James: Does the Fulton Center factor into your daily commute?
Elizabeth: Only when I have to transfer to the J/Z lines, which is unfortunate because the J/Z lines are the hardest to find. That’s because the J and Z platforms were built stacked on top of each other because Nassau Street they’re under is so narrow.
So, you really have to be careful and take the right stairs to get to the correct J/Z platform. My tip is to start on the A/C platform. If you want to go to the Brooklyn- and Queens-bound J/Z trains, you have to take one of the staircases closer to the west side, where you see a connection to the 4 and 5 trains. If you want to go the Broad Street bound J/Z trains, you have to take one of the staircases closer to the eastern 2 and 3 train side.
Another thing that trips people up: Unlike the rest of the lines at Fulton, the “Downtown” J/Z trains do not take riders to Brooklyn — those lines end at Broad Street. If you want to get to Brooklyn or Queens on those lines, you need to take an uptown train.
I once had a meltdown here trying to find the Brooklyn-bound J train. I kept ending up on the Broad street bound platform … which only takes you farther into the Financial District. That mix-up motivated me to study up on this cursed station.
James: Is the short answer to “why is this so confusing?” that the MTA combined three separate train lines into one superstation, and there’s only so much they move around
Elizabeth: Exactly. Fulton Center we know today is actually four separate subway stations built by three separate train companies at different times. Jodi Shapiro, a curator at the Transit Museum, told me that train companies didn’t want to make it easy for a commuter to transfer to a competitor line, which explains why the transfers feel so awkward.
And the Financial District has some of the oldest and most narrow city streets that twist and turn in ways that other parts of the Manhattan grid doesn’t, which meant train companies were pretty limited in where and how wide they could construct their subway lines. That explains why each subway line sits under different streets at different depths.
All those stations were pushed under one roof when Fulton Center opened in 2014.
James: I’ll admit I had never been to the Fulton Center until you told me about this project. It just never fit the patterns of how I move about town. But I took an inconvenient route one morning this week just to pass through, and my main takeaway was that there’s a Dunkin’ Donuts on one of the lower levels, but don’t fall for it; there’s a Krispy Kreme a couple levels up, if you’re willing to hike.
Elizabeth: Great tip, because I only saw the Dunkin' Donuts, since it’s on the first floor where you pass to get to the other subway stations.
James: Okay back to getting around: At some point I thought I was exiting through a turnstile and was confused when it didn't let me pass. Then I realized that somehow I had already left the subway system and needed to tap again to get back in. Is that a common mistake, or was I just not paying attention?
Elizabeth: You wouldn't know this if you don’t commute here often. Even though you can technically walk from Fulton Center to the World Trade Center station completely underground, it’s not a free transfer. So if you need to get to the E, R or W lines, expect to exit through a turnstile and pay the fare again.
James: What else should I know before returning?
Elizabeth: To me, the most confusing part of Fulton Center is that instead of the traditional mezzanine being the connection point to all transfers like at many other big stations, the A/C platform is usually a better place to orient yourself. My biggest tip is to think of the A/C platform as the backbone of the station. The J/Z platforms sit at their own levels and cut through the mezzanines, so going from the 4/5 trains to the 2/3 means heading down to the A/C platform, walking its length, and coming back up.
That means you might have to walk through a platform for a train you aren’t taking in order to get to the line you’re trying to ride.
James: You talked with people who’ve made 3D maps of the Fulton Center, do you look at one of those and think, "ah, I get it now?”
Elizabeth: Yes, they really did help! You can lose your orientation easily just walking up and down stairs and walking down the long corridor. But seeing a 3D map made it easy for me to conceptualize that the A/C platform is perpendicular to all the other lines, so it’s helpful to think of the A/C platform as your homebase where you can get to any transfer.
James: Is there anything else the MTA could do, in your opinion, to make it easier to navigate? Or is it one of those things where you as a commuter put in the work to really learn it, and then you get to feel smug about it, which every New Yorker loves?
Elizabeth: One suggestion for the MTA is to put a version of 3D maps and a “you are here” sign that may help people better situate themselves. Or even placing stickers on the floors pointing to the right direction for each different transfer.
But when I visited Fulton Center again, I noticed there’s plenty of signage, and they’re technically correct. It’s just that you have to stop and read them carefully.
When I reached out to the MTA about how confusing Fulton Station is to some commuters, they told me signage is present throughout the station and reminded me that there are station agents posted throughout the complex outside of the booths to help confused commuters.

https://gothamist.com/news/homeless-new-.title: Homeless New Yorkers’ healthcare costs plummeted after getting housed, study finds
https://gothamist.com/news/homeless-new-.author: Caroline Lewis
https://gothamist.com/news/homeless-new-.text:
An NYC Health and Hospitals initiative to help homeless patients find housing is paying off in the form of fewer emergency department visits and lower Medicaid costs, according to a new study by the public hospital system and its insurance subsidiary, MetroHealthPlus.
The study tracked Medicaid claims for 259 New Yorkers who received help finding apartments or supportive housing from NYC Health and Hospitals. Their healthcare costs dropped by an average of nearly $17,000 per person in the first two years after getting housed as they visited the ER and got admitted to the hospital less frequently, according to the study, conducted with the Wakely Consulting Group.
At the same time, the group’s spending on doctors’ visits and other non-emergency services such as substance use treatment increased, suggesting they were getting more preventive care.
The small study adds to a growing body of evidence suggesting that housing can help reduce emergency healthcare spending and utilization among people who were homeless, and comes as the city’s public hospital system continues to expand its housing efforts.
Under the Housing for Health Initiative, started by the Adams administration, the hospital system has been helping patients find permanent housing, while also using its land to build supportive housing developments and creating new transitional housing options for people leaving inpatient hospital stays who have nowhere to go.
“We have to think about our robust patient population that experiences homelessness,” said Leora Jontef, who leads NYC Health and Hospitals’ Housing for Health initiative. “This patient population is sicker than housed New Yorkers.”
NYC Health and Hospitals serves more than 60,000 patients a year who are homeless or unstably housed and many of them are what those in the healthcare field refer to as ‘frequent flyers’ — patients who visit the emergency department or get admitted for inpatient care over and over.
Among the study cohort, emergency department visits declined by about 40% in the first two years after getting housing placements, while inpatient stays dropped 36%.
The average number of days study participants spent in the hospital each year also got cut in half, dropping from an average of 10 days before finding housing to five days after being placed.
The biggest savings came from the decline in spending on inpatient care, which dropped from a monthly average of $1,278 per person before finding a housing placement to $492 during the first year of being housed.
The study also compared the cohort of newly housed patients with a group of New Yorkers enrolled in MetroHealthPlus who started out with similarly high levels of healthcare spending and utilization but remained homeless. Over time, healthcare costs for the group that received housing dropped below the group that did not.
However, healthcare spending among those that got housed was not lower than the broader homeless population enrolled in MetroHealthPlus overall, the study found.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Companies at Center of Brooklyn Building Collapse Have a Record of Safety Violations, Ignoring City Orders
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith, Katie Honan, Claudia Irizarry Aponte, Andrew Giambrone
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
As city officials scramble to figure out who is to blame for the stunning collapse of a Brooklyn apartment building into an adjacent construction site this week, questions are surfacing about the troubled track records of two of the contractors doing work there.
The three-story apartment building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. collapsed Wednesday afternoon into an empty lot next door at 2625 Bedford Ave. that was being dug out to make way for a planned apartment building. The city Department of Buildings said workers were down in the pit doing excavation when the late afternoon collapse occurred.
City officials said Thursday that eight people — including two children aged 9 and 10 — died and 19 more were injured, seven kids among them. Firefighters searched for survivors, braving treacherous conditions made worse by a torrential downpour, but wrapped up their mission late Thursday after concluding the search was complete. The dead included two construction workers, officials said.
At a press conference near the site, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the Buildings Department had identified five companies working at the collapse site that are “associated with 100 sites across the city.” The agency launched a sweep of those locations to ensure they’re in compliance with the city’s building code.
“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city who is responsible for this, we will hold them accountable,” the mayor vowed.
On Thursday evening, the Police Department released the names of the victims: Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Barry Mamadou, 23; Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 25; Edgar Sapon, 26; Ndiaye Mamdou, 31; and Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31.
Elite Concrete’s Record
Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani would not name the companies who had been working at or near the site, but records and interviews with workers revealed two: Elite Concrete, which was handling the excavation, and N Tech Design of America, which had performed demolition of the one-story building that existed at the empty lot before construction began.
Records reviewed by The City Reporter show Elite has been cited by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency that regulates construction safety, two times in the last four years over serious construction accidents.
In April 2023 an Elite worker fell 12 feet at a site at 32-03 39th Ave. in Long Island City after a steel deck collapsed, records show. OSHA accused Elite of failing to ensure workers had adequate fall protection and did not “determine if the walking/working surfaces in which its employees were to work on had the strength and structure integrity to support employees safely.”
Then, in August 2025, OSHA cited Elite again after a worker at a Jersey City, N.J., site was electrocuted using a steel trowel near a power line that wasn’t properly grounded. OSHA issued another violation, charging that workers at the site were exposed to empalement dangers because protruding steel bars known as rebar were not adequately covered.
In the Long Island City case, OSHA hit Elite with $32,000 in penalties which they reduced to $15,000 after the company contested the sanctions. In the New Jersey case, OSHA issued more than $11,000 in fines which Elite is contesting, records show.
Elite’s CEO, Eli Friedman, did not immediately respond to The City Reporter’s request for comment Thursday.
Defied Stop-Work Order
Another firm working the site was N Tech Design of America which did the demolition of a one-story building there that preceded the excavation work.
Last spring the Buildings Department slapped N Tech with $10,000 in fines after city inspectors discovered they were doing demolition without a permit, and then defied a stop-work order and continued working. The company paid the fine and work resumed in April after DOB granted them a permit.
Two years ago N Tech was sued by the owner of a Fenimore Street building in Brooklyn adjacent to where the firm was performing excavation work. The owner, James Farah, alleged that he found significant water and structural damage at his building that he blamed on N Tech’s excavation work.
Aramis Brown, who is listed as the licensee for N Tech, declined to comment.
On Thursday Crain’s New York reported that they had reviewed a Buildings Department document that said unsafe construction work at 2625 Bedford had caused the three-story building next door at 1321 Flatbush to collapse. After Crain’s inquired about that, however, DOB retracted the finding and said the cause of the collapse remained under investigation.
City Objections to New Building Plan
In addition to the two contractors, the buildings department has raised questions about plans by the owner, a limited liability company owned by Robert Fischman called W6 Facility X LLC, to erect a nine-story building at the site.
Buildings Commissioner Tigani said the department had earlier this year approved plans to build a three-story structure there, but last month Fischman amended his plans and sought approval for a nine-story structure that would rise 85 feet above the street.
In city records, the agency noted it has raised “objections” to this plan. But DOB spokesperson Andrew Rudansky said the department could not provide specific details about its concerns until the owner’s registered design professional — the developer’s architect — had a chance to respond.
Property records have also raised questions about the owner of the building that collapsed.
The building was built in 1930 and is owned by Isolag Realty Corp., tied to Brooklyn-based landlord Olufemi Falade. The building had 98 open housing violations as of Thursday, including 21 “immediately hazardous” and 40 “hazardous” violations for various conditions, according to city records.
The property appeared on the city’s tax lien sale list multiple times in the past decade. Falade was jailed for 12 days in 2006 for civil contempt for failing to fix reams of violations at other Brooklyn buildings he owned, the New York Times and New York Post previously reported. Public Advocate Jumaane Williams named him on the city’s “worst landlords” list, based on housing code violations, as recently as 2024.
‘An Excellent Young Man’
A Bushwick-based soccer club told The City Reporter one of its athletes died in the collapse.
José Luis Caguana Cosquillo was a construction worker at the Flatbush Avenue site. He leaves behind a pregnant wife and 4-year-old son, said Club Deportivo La Bahía leader Rodrigo Tubón. Caguana Cosquillo’s wife is due to give birth Friday, Tubón said.
Tubón, 50, hails from the same Ecuadorian village as Caguana Cosquillo and said he’d known his parents and relatives for many years. The young father would often come to games with his own burgeoning family, who lived in Bushwick.
“He was an excellent young man,” an emotional Tubón said in Spanish. “We lost the best guy on the team.”
The soccer club is discussing turning its scheduled championship game on Saturday into a fundraiser for Caguana Cosquillo’s family.
“Anything we can do to help,” Tubón said. “We’re all very shaken up by this. It’s unbelievable.”

https://hyperallergic.com/after-the-midt.title: After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins
https://hyperallergic.com/after-the-midt.author: Jasmine Wahi
https://hyperallergic.com/after-the-midt.text:
After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins
Democratic leaders need to understand that cultural funding cannot stop at large museums and institutions; it must reach the people whose labor makes it possible.
In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition.
As a curator and the co-director of an arts nonprofit, I’ve been asked what the results mean for the so-called “art world.” My first response was cynical: “not much.” At least not immediately. An election does not directly restore a canceled grant or pay an artist’s rent. And even a return to the funding landscape that existed before Trump took office in 2025 would leave us with a system that was already failing the people expected to sustain it.
Instead, the midterm election results should serve as an opening to hold Democrats in Congress accountable for making arts and cultural life materially sustainable, not simply to defend an inadequate system from further attack. That mandate concerns whose histories are told, who gets paid to make art, and who gets to define the country’s future. It also concerns whether the people doing that work can afford to keep going.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Juvenile Lockups Packed Beyond Capacity as Overtime Soars: Audit
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The city’s two juvenile detention centers are operating far beyond capacity, staff overtime has quadrupled and the average length of detention has nearly doubled, according to a new state audit.
The 69-page review also found that the number of probation officers declined by one-third between 2020 and 2026, even as juvenile caseloads increased.
“New York City is spending more money to keep young people in detention, and they are staying there longer,” state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli said in a statement.
“The city needs to address staffing shortages and overcrowding and also invest in prevention efforts, including after-school programs, mentoring and summer jobs, to give young people more opportunities and help keep them out of the juvenile justice system.”
Overcrowding at the two facilities has gotten so bad the city has been forced to use classroom space as housing units. Earlier this month, a state oversight agency stopped issuing waivers to allow ACS to use those common areas for housing.
The report — which covers 2019 through fiscal year 2026 — comes weeks after the Mamdani administration announced a series of changes aimed at addressing problems at the beleaguered facilities, Horizon and Crossroads.
The Administration for Children’s Services, which oversees the centers, says it is expanding alternatives to detention, increasing staffing and investing in educational and recreational programming.
Among the initiatives is a new intensive community monitoring program through the Department of Probation that will combine closer supervision with clinical assessments, family engagement, educational and employment assistance, and other community-based services. The program is intended to serve 150 young people who are transitioning out of secure detention or at risk of being placed there.
The administration is also increasing funding for community-based programs, expanding access to family therapy and making nonsecure detention available to some young people whom judges determine are appropriate candidates for a less restrictive setting.
ACS also announced plans to hire 56 additional youth development specialists and 85 employees dedicated to emergency response at Horizon and Crossroads.
The agency said it is investing in scanners, metal detectors and cameras to prevent contraband from entering the facilities, while expediting renovations and the installation of temporary classrooms to create more room for educational programming.
The state audit comes nearly ten years after state lawmakers passed the Raise the Age Law to transition 16- and 17-year-olds from the adult to juvenile criminal justice system.
In New York City, that meant transferring them from Department of Correction-run adult housing units on Rikers Island to the two secure detention centers operated by ACS.
But the department has struggled to staff and operate the centers as the number of young people facing criminal charges has ballooned over the past several years, according to a series of oversight reports and court filings.
In October 2024 the city’s Department of Investigation concluded that ACS’s point-based system to reward and punish the behavior of incarcerated youths, known as a behavioral management tool, had failed to adequately deter violence and contraband smuggling.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: ‘A Joke’: Missing State Aid Leaves CUNY Students Stressed
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Aisha Baiocchi
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
More than halfway through the Fall semester, some CUNY community college students are still waiting on financial aid awards from the state — weeks after officials said the problem was being solved.
The delayed funding is from the New York State Opportunity Promise Scholarship, the state-supported component of the City University’s Reconnect program, and covers tuition, fees and books for students at community colleges pursuing certain degrees. Last month, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced an expansion of the program to include new degree pathways and campuses.
One student at Kingsborough Community College told The City Reporter they had been reaching out to their university’s financial aid office about the funds since they first noticed the delays. The office told them the money had not yet been disbursed by CUNY’s central office.
GET THE CUNY SCOOP: Subscribe to our new weekly newsletter covering the City University of New York
The student included a screenshot of an email from the office saying they “still do not have confirmation” of when the money will be disbursed.
Students have taken to online message boards to complain about the missing funds — and the stress of not knowing when it will arrive. The money is a “last dollar” scholarship, meaning it makes up for shortfalls after other sources of aid have been exhausted.
A CUNY spokesperson echoed last month’s promises that the funds were one their way.
“NYSOP funds were distributed to campus accounts in the University’s Student Financial Aid system over the past month and will begin appearing in students’ accounts starting Monday,” Noah Gardy, CUNY press secretary said in a statement.
The university did not say how many students are still affected by delays in disbursements. Last month, a university official said hundreds of students had not received their scholarships.
“Nope, I called my Financial Aid office again today and was told that they still don’t have a date they can give me and that they actually haven’t heard ANYTHING from CUNY since the 7th last month,” one student wrote in a Nov. 5 Reddit post. “This entire situation is a joke.”
MORE: Past Due: Why CUNY Adjuncts Can’t Get Paid On Time
A Queensborough Community College student shared emails from their financial aid office from Nov. 10, saying they do not have a date for NYSOP disbursement yet but “expect it to be soon.”
Gardy said the university was working to prevent additional hold-ups. “While these delays will not affect registration, we regret any stress or uncertainty they may have caused,” he said. “We are reviewing our internal processes to prevent such delays in the future.”
CUNY Reconnect received $18.8 million from the most recent state budget. The program covers the cost of enrollment in 220 high-demand associates degrees at community colleges for adults between 25 and 55. It serves 10,000 students across the seven CUNY community colleges.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘É preciso regular o modelo de negócio e o monopólio das Big Techs’, afirma pesquisador
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Quem decide o que vemos nas redes sociais? Quem controla, armazena e monetiza as nossas informações pessoais? E que risco a concentração de poder das grandes empresas de tecnologia representa para a democracia? Essas perguntas motivam o trabalho do jornalista James Görgen, autor de “Notas da floresta digital – Geopolítica e desenvolvimento tecnológico em tempos de transição”, que já está nas livrarias.
O livro surge após quatro anos de análises sobre o avanço e a ameaça das big techs. A obra aborda a dependência do Brasil em relação aos gigantes da tecnologia sediados nos Estados Unidos e o que isso representa para a soberania nacional. Görgen é mestre em Economia Política da Comunicação e acompanha a agenda digital desde 1998.
Na conversa, o entrevistado comenta a necessidade de regular a atuação das plataformas e a resistência a essa regulação no Congresso. Também fala sobre a possibilidade de o Brasil construir a sua própria arquitetura digital e sobre alternativas como acordos com a China com transferência de tecnologia. Outros temas são a pressão dos Estados Unidos sobre o Pix e o papel do “Exército do Lula” em um governo sem maioria no Congresso.
O podcast De Fato é uma produção do Brasil de Fato RS em parceria com o SindBancários de Porto Alegre e Região.
Todo sábado, um entrevistado ou uma entrevistada debaterá os principais fatos em destaque no Rio Grande do Sul, no Brasil e no mundo.
