https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.title: ‘No one wants us any more’: how Hollywood turned its back on trans actors
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.author: Jason Lamphier
https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text:
At the start of 2024, Trace Lysette was feeling like she had reached the apex of her career. She had just been nominated for an Independent Spirit Award for best lead performance for her title role in the acclaimed drama Monica, earning a spot among A-listers like Natalie Portman, Jessica Chastain and Jeffrey Wright. She and her costar Patricia Clarkson had graced the cover of Variety and appeared on The Kelly Clarkson Show. She had landed a part in NBC’s Quantum Leap revival. Then everything came crashing down.
“I thought for sure I would have gotten some offers for a series regular on a TV show, which would have helped me finally buy a house,” recalls Lysette, who is trans. “But it didn’t come.” Instead, the calls stopped.
She describes the drought that followed as “a full-on ego death.” As she watched her savings dwindle, it was if someone had pulled the rug out from under her. “It’s almost like nothing I did had mattered, like it never happened,” says Lysette, who had also made waves with supporting turns in the groundbreaking series Transparent and the Jennifer Lopez hit Hustlers. “Everything I’d built, it just felt like: ‘Just kidding. We’re gonna take all that away from you.’” She estimates that she has auditioned for about seven parts in 2026 – a slow year for her, she says – but for nothing since the end of spring. She hasn’t had a lead role or major studio project since Monica.
Lysette is hardly alone. Vico Ortiz, a Los Angeles based transmasculine, non-binary and genderqueer actor best known for playing the non-binary pirate Jim Jimenez in the HBO Max series Our Flag Means Death, has noticed a shift in the industry as well. “We all used to be booked and busy, and then it was like: ‘Oh shit, we’re all getting dropped like flies,’” they tell me over Zoom, adding that the only big-budget network and movie roles they’ve auditioned for in the past two years have been for white cisgender femme-leaning “lesbian light” women (Ortiz is Puerto Rican).
The limited amount of prospects beyond short films and smaller fare has forced Ortiz and their trans and non-binary peers to re-evaluate their options. “No one wants us any more, and that affects our healthcare,” Ortiz says, “and that affects our chances to get gender-affirming care, should we want that, and it just spirals.”
In late September, Jack Haven, the trans star of Netflix’s Atypical and the 2026 queer Cannes film festival darling Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, made a public plea for help to qualify for Screen Actors Guild health insurance for the upcoming calendar year. “I guess what I’m asking is if you, or if anyone you know, can hire me on a set or production and pay me $4,000, I will do pretty much any job,” they said in a video posted to YouTube. After Haven published a follow-up video thanking supporters and announcing that they’d received “a lot of offers,” Lysette responded on X that she had lost her Sag-Aftra health insurance two years ago and that she, too, could use some gigs.
Even Oscar and Bafta nominee Elliot Page, fresh off his performance in Christopher Nolan’s commercial and critical smash The Odyssey, recently admitted that he doesn’t have his next project lined up. (Page recently came out as non-binary and uses he/they pronouns.) When asked if Hollywood was beating down his door on a September episode of the podcast On Film … With Kevin McCarthy, the actor, who came out as trans and non-binary in 2020, said that no, it wasn’t, before adding only half jokingly: “If someone wants to call me …” Earlier this year, Emmy winner Laverne Cox, arguably the most famous trans woman actor and advocate, told the Guardian that she had lost roughly 90% of her income in the past two years as acting opportunities, hosting contracts and corporate speaking engagements dried up. Meanwhile, Billions star Asia Kate Dillon, who is non-binary, wrote last month that acting opportunities were so scarce that they were looking for service work.
Just three years ago, trans actors popped up in a trio of summer movies with refreshing depictions that signaled progress. Transmasculine newcomer Zoe Terakes delivered a pivotal supporting turn in the A24 horror flick Talk to Me as a bully named Haley, whose gender identity was neither explicitly addressed nor initially apparent. In Greta Gerwig’s inescapable behemoth Barbie, trans actor and model Hari Nef portrayed a doctor Barbie with her transness not factoring into the part at all. And in Amazon’s adaptation of the bestselling queer romcom Red, White and Royal Blue, trans actor Aneesh Sheth had a small role as Amy, a bodyguard who was written as trans in Casey McQuiston’s novel, but whose gender was never mentioned in the film. As the Guardian reported at the time, these characters felt remarkable because their transness was not.
Now, it seems, the tides have turned. The findings in the annual Where We Are in Film report published by the LGBTQ+ advocacy organization Glaad in July were sobering. Of the 225 movies analyzed across the industry’s 10 major distributors – A24, Amazon MGM Studios, Apple TV, Lionsgate, NBCUniversal, Netflix, Paramount Skydance, Sony, The Walt Disney Studios and Warner Bros Discovery – zero included trans characters. The study called the results “unconscionable” and referred to major studios’ failure to spotlight trans stories as a misguided business decision “given that a supermajority of Americans (79%) agree that everyone deserves to be represented in media”.
“Gen Z represents the largest share of moviegoers in North America,” Glaad’s senior director of entertainment research and analysis, Megan Townsend, said in a press release at the time. “Gen Z also has the highest percentage of people who say they are part of the LGBTQ community, with Gallup reporting that more than one in five (23 percent) of Americans under the age of 30 are LGBTQ. If studios want to stay relevant with younger audiences and bring in box office dollars, they can’t afford to ignore nearly one-quarter of their most enthusiastic ticket buyers.”
Glaad’s latest Where We Are on TV report, released this week, is equally shocking. The study – which analyzed scripted broadcast, cable and streaming television from 1 June 2025 to 31 May 2026 – found only seven transgender characters (six women and one man) among the 369 LGBTQ+ characters tracked, marking a 79% decrease from the 33 trans characters counted last year. Since the record-high of 42 trans characters in the 2021-2022 season, the study has reported a year-over-year decline in the number of trans characters, but this year’s is the steepest drop that the media watchdog group has witnessed. In another alarmingly regressive twist, two of the seven trans characters counted were played by cisgender men.
Yet another blow to trans visibility: Because three of the characters tracked this year were on shows that had been cancelled and four were on limited series, none will return next year, effectively leaving no regular or recurring trans characters on television.
 
While the industry has been producing fewer TV shows since 2022’s streaming bust and the actors’ and writers’ strikes in 2023, that alone cannot account for such a severe downturn.
“About 10 years ago, you could feel that progress was starting, and then for it to just halt is very disheartening,” says Raina Deerwater, Glaad’s associate director of entertainment research and analysis and the lead author of the study. “There’s a complete absence in a way that there hasn’t been in a long time, and it’s scary.”
This plummet in representation arrives at a time when politicians and anti-LGBTQ+ activists are pushing misinformation and enacting laws and policies that threaten trans rights and safety. “Trans folks are being scapegoated,” Deerwater says, “and now they can’t even turn off the news and turn on whatever TV they watch for fun to get a trans story. The new stuff coming out is simply not inclusive of an entire population.”
 
Many in the industry argue that the dearth of parts for trans and non-binary performers is a kneejerk reaction to this post-Trump, anti-trans rhetoric and backlash.
“This administration has enabled people’s implicit bias – it’s been OKed by the masses,” says Lysette, who notes that not only are fewer trans stories being greenlit, but that transgender actors like herself who’ve scored both trans and cis roles now have little to no chance of getting either.
“There are reactionaries in the populace who don’t want to see any LGBT content for fear of their sensitivities,” says Rebecca Root, the trans British actor known for her leading role in the 2015 BBC Two sitcom Boy Meets Girl and her appearances in Netflix’s The Queen’s Gambit and the queer coming-of-age romcom Heartstopper. “So the studios think: ‘Well, the audiences don’t want to see trans things, so we won’t make trans storylines or have trans characters.’” Their fear of cancel culture leaves the decision makers in power paralyzed, she adds: “So they just say: ‘Well, we’d better not upset anybody.’”
Root credits The Queen’s Gambit writer-director Scott Frank for keeping her somewhat active in recent years by tapping her for two more roles, and she considers herself lucky for having been able to play both cis and trans characters over the course of her career. If she can barely fathom how much things have changed since she had her own series a decade ago, she has faith that the pendulum will swing back. “We’ve been here before, and we’ve got out of it before,” Root says. “We’ve come through on the other side, and we’ve lived through it. We will come through again.”
Standout performances from trans actors in projects this year that came out after the Glaad studies’ cutoff offer a silver lining: Josie Totah in Amazon’s new Carrie TV series; Yenesi in La Bola Negra; Miss Benny, Alaska Riley and Saturn Risin9 in Club Kid. Later this month, Euphoria star Hunter Schafer will lead Amazon Prime’s mega budget Blade Runner TV show.
Like Root, Ortiz remains hopeful about the future. While they’re hustling like they never have before, leaning on smaller indie projects and audiobook narration and voice acting, they, like many of their trans and non-binary friends, have developed a healthier relationship with Hollywood. “I’ve used this time to have a breakup with the industry, in a way,” they say. “I am seeing a lot more folks going independent and trusting their gut and still doing what they love to do, with or without these big networks behind them.
“We’re never going to be silenced,” Ortiz adds. “We’re going to find our spotlight. Whether you all like it or not.”

https://www.theguardian.com/games/ng-int.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
https://www.theguardian.com/games/ng-int.author: Keza MacDonald
https://www.theguardian.com/games/ng-int.text:
It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat.
The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.
One month before release, it is quiet at Rockstar’s headquarters. A lot of people have finished their labour on the game and are taking time off in the run-up to launch – a well-deserved rest after more than 10 years of development. Those who remain here are caught in the strange no man’s land between finishing a piece of art and releasing it into the world. When it does come out, GTA VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of entertainment ever made, projected to shift tens of millions of copies and earn billions in its first year; its predecessor, 2013’s GTA V, sold 230m copies. In the midst of a horrible time for the games business, full of studio closures layoffs and soaring development costs, a whole industry is relying on GTA VI to give it a shot in the arm. On one near-deserted floor, a screen shows a countdown to the release date.
For many players, meanwhile, the 13-year wait for a new Grand Theft Auto has become unbearable. When footage of GTA VI made its glitzy premiere on Netflix, it almost took the streaming giant’s servers down. Its first trailer has been viewed 300m times on YouTube alone. Across the world, people have booked days off work on 19 November to experience this event together – one of those increasingly rare shared global cultural moments in an age when we all live in our own algorithmic content bubbles.
There is a slightly strained atmosphere at Rockstar North, and not just because of the pressure of GTA VI’s impending release. Over in Glasgow, Rockstar is also defending a high-profile employment tribunal case over the dismissal of 34 of its employees last year, who claim they were fired because they were involved in union organisation efforts. The case was due to wind up in October, but will now drag on right up to Grand Theft Auto VI’s release. A few days before my visit, head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe was testifying in court as former employees and their reps at the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) protested outside.
Today, Kolbe is sitting in front of me with Rob Nelson, co-studio head of Rockstar North and one of the three creative leads on GTA VI, showing me what the studio has spent more than a decade and, by independent estimates that Rockstar will not confirm, more than $1bn making. On screen, Jason and Lucia – two young criminals on the run – are on their way from a bar to a nightclub, walking through downtown Vice City as the last vestiges of sunlight disappear and the streets become bathed in fluorescence. He is tall, square-shouldered, in a T-shirt and shorts; she has her hair up in a ponytail, wearing one of those merciless long-sleeved crop tops that almost nobody can pull off.
After dancing with each other at the club, part of a crowded mass of virtual people gyrating in neon UV-reactive mesh tops, they will each don a cap, sunglasses and a bandana over the face, and hold up a jewellery store before escaping into the night in a beaten-up car, the boot stuffed with holdalls filled with cash and sizeable firearms, evading the cops by driving right through a cornfield in an apt echo of Bonnie and Clyde.
Lucia is the first woman to have headline billing in a GTA game, part of a long lineage of criminal protagonists who range from the straightforwardly psychopathic (GTA V’s Trevor) to the unexpectedly sympathetic (GTA IV’s Niko Bellic, and San Andreas’s CJ). GTA VI is both her story and Jason’s. For some acts of this game you are locked into one character’s perspective, but most of the time you can switch freely between them. When they are apart, you can ensure they text and call each other. When they’re together, you can take them on little dates: to the gym, out to a bar, to a meditation retreat or to a liquor-store stick-up. You as the player become the steward of their relationship, and if you neglect it then there will be consequences. “You’re dropped into their lives,” Nelson explains, as Lucia speeds along a highway, Jason leaning out of the window to shoot at the tyres of the cop car pursuing them. “The relationship is yours to nurture or yours to lose. Whether it remains a romantic relationship is in your hands.”
This dynamic is not merely interesting – it is transformational for Grand Theft Auto. The series made its name on black humour and directionless violent mayhem, setting players free in virtual pastiches of New York, Miami or Los Angeles to crash stolen cars and terrorise pedestrians. GTA V in particular was an extravagant equal-opportunity offender, taking aim at everyone and everything from the US government to narcissistic tech bros, spoilt LA brats to hillbillies, the ultra-rich to caravan-dwelling wasters. Nobody has ever cared about anybody very much in a GTA game. Here, though, we are being asked not just to care about these characters, but to act out how they care for each other. When they are together, you can press a button to make them hold hands.
It is faintly unbelievable to see this game in action after it has existed for so long only as fervent rumour. GTA VI has been in development in some form since 2015, when the team took their first research trips to Miami (at this time, the game’s codename was Project Americas, reflecting a later abandoned ambition to set it across two continents). But it was only announced in December 2023, and has been delayed twice since. I get the impression that the people at Rockstar have basically been forced to put their metaphorical paintbrushes down. “They would never stop working on this game if they had the choice,” Kolbe says, somewhat ruefully. “It’s really hard to close it down,” Nelson admits. “If you step away and get a little bit of space from it, you can look at it objectively and go: ‘I’m proud of what we’ve done’. But ultimately, it is being taken away from you, and you do the best you can to finish it in the time that you’re told.”
Usually when shown a video game ahead of release, one is taken through a highly choreographed slice of the action designed to show it at its best, but that’s not what’s happening here. We’re simply tooling about in a densely populated Vice City, and almost anything I suggest, we can do. Walking out from Jason and Lucia’s flamingo-wallpapered apartment into the Florida sunshine, the first thing we see is a woman walking a dog. I ask if we can pet it; Nelson presses a button and Jason says: “Is it cool if I pet your dog?” “Course, she loves to greet her public,” the woman replies, before Jason stoops to give the pup a fuss. You can overhear pedestrians’ conversations as you pass by, and interrupting them might result in a bemused “Have we met?” or a stream of invective. Later, I see a gull sitting on a post by the beach and ask, just to be annoying, what kind of bird it is. Jason pulls out a pair of binoculars, the gull is recorded in a wildlife logbook, and I am told with pride that there are 62 types of birds to spot.
Of course we also do some crime. This is still Grand Theft Auto. But those who enjoy playing these games as a chaotic violent sociopath are in for a surprise here, because you have to be more careful than ever before. Jason and Lucia can’t just steal any car or bust their way into a bank; at the start they can only hotwire low-end vehicles and pick basic locks, working their way up to the higher-value jobs later. “These guys are a younger couple with their backs against the wall,” Nelson says. “Narratively, it doesn’t make a lot of sense for them to go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can.” Instead of whipping out an assault rifle in the middle of a crowded street and sending everyone scattering, you have to scope out your targets, whether it’s a gas station or an upscale mall boutique. You can disable security cameras or steal the footage, find back doors and safe codes so that you can get in without pulling a gun on anyone, and get out before witnesses arrive.
Fail to do these things and chaos ramps up quickly. After a couple of small-time crime sprees, we take Jason and Lucia to a well-protected jewellery store, where Lucia turns her pistol on the security guards for a few tense seconds before they surrender. Upstairs, though, where Jason is shoving money from the safe into a holdall, another guard decides to shoot rather than surrender. A desperate scramble ensues, in which Jason smacks the guy with the butt of a gun to knock him out while Lucia yells from the front of the store, and as they climb on to a stolen motorbike to make their getaway, the police arrive. The chase takes us halfway around the district, followed by cop cars and helicopters. When they eventually make it back to their car, Jason and Lucia stow the cash, change their clothes, and lie low in the outskirts of the city for a while to wait out the heat.
GTA VI is still very much a game about crime and criminals, but it strongly encourages you towards playing in-character and avoiding directionless rampages. In this way it is heavily inspired by Rockstar’s Red Dead Redemption 2 (2018), in which you play an outlaw in the old west who comes to regret his life of violence. For Nelson, one of the greatest challenges of GTA VI’s development has been figuring out how to encourage players to behave differently without restricting their freedom, which would be antithetical to Rockstar’s creative philosophy. Even with an unlimited budget, you can’t solve the central tension of the form: the balance between the story that developers are trying to tell, and the random whims of any given player.
“Crime is a fundamental part of GTA – at least, up until now, it has been. We’re trying to make sure we’re not punishing people for playing the game they are used to … [but] your actions will have some effect on how the game plays out.” I ask whether this is the first GTA game that tries to encourage a measure of empathy. “I would say so,” Nelson replies. “I would say that it’s a product of the story we’re trying to tell. We’ve tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to.”
Grand Theft Auto has forever been a lightning rod for moral panic over video game violence. In GTA III, infamously, you could hire a sex worker and then run her over to steal your money back. In the 00s the discovery of an explicit sex minigame hidden in the code of GTA San Andreas prompted class action lawsuits in the US. Haitian-American groups attempted to halt the sale of 2002’s GTA Vice City, VI’s spiritual predecessor, over its depictions of violence against those groups. US courts have consistently upheld Rockstar’s first amendment rights, but this history hints at a cultural double standard. It is widely accepted that film and TV can depict violence without endorsing it – few would seriously venture that Breaking Bad endorses cooking meth – but when it comes to video games, where the player takes an active role, they are often seen to be lionising the behaviour they depict.
As video game graphics have got more realistic – it is hard to see, in retrospect, how the now comically low-resolution puppet characters of 00s GTA games provoked such outrage – Grand Theft Auto has sought to contextualise its violence. Its cinematic storytelling and character development ambitions have grown exponentially, as have its budget and team size, which has quadrupled since GTA V. The entire history of games is a story of talented technical and creative people finding ways to work around technological constraints and make things that were never possible before, working magic with blocky characters and limited graphical power. But now the limitations that defined the scope of previous GTA games are essentially gone. The leash is off.
“What we have grappled with is the transition from being limited by technical constraints to being limited by human resource constraints,” Nelson says. “Like, how much can we physically build? You can keep going for ever … People say you can throw money at the problem, and you can to an extent, but it’s no guarantee of making something good.”
It’s true that with all that time, effort and money, Rockstar has been able to achieve a level of detail in GTA VI that is beyond anything I’ve ever seen in a game – even beyond Red Dead Redemption 2, which was so extravagantly, naturalistically detailed that someone went to the trouble of modelling horse testicles that retract in cold weather. In a GTA VI gas station, Nelson takes evident pleasure in showing me detailed eating and drinking animations as Jason wanders around with a doughnut in one hand and a six-pack of beer in the other – the liquid inside the bottles sloshes realistically as he walks, and the racks are stocked with fully illustrated magazines that you can take off the shelf and read through. Every one of the pedestrians you see outside has been designed by someone, even down to their clothes.
Why go to this trouble? In the PlayStation 2 era, Rockstar was releasing a new GTA game every couple of years; they weren’t radically different from one another in terms of gameplay, but their shifting settings and characters allowed the series’ makers to stretch their creative muscles. By contrast, it’s now been 13 years and two console generations since the last GTA. Why spend all this time on a single, ostentatiously gigantic project? It comes down to this, Nelson says: if you were a developer with these resources, the only developer with these resources, wouldn’t you go for the most ambitious thing you could?
“They could have made GTA 5.5, and done it faster,” says Kolbe. “Ultimately, that’s not what they wanted.”
Nelson nods: “You have to take big swings. It can’t be just more of the same.”
Grand Theft Auto VI is released for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on 19 November.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: ‘Risk multiplier’: super El Niño looms over Cop31 as climate pattern fuels global disasters
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Oliver Milman in Antalya
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
If the galloping pace of the climate crisis isn’t enough to spur countries to act at UN climate talks under way in Turkey, there is another major threat heightening its havoc: the strongest El Niño event in at least 1,000 years.
The “jaw-dropping” El Niño, a naturally recurring phenomenon where the eastern Pacific heats up every few years with temporary but global implications, has provided added urgency to wrangling at the Cop31 summit over climate funding for vulnerable countries that are having to scramble to respond.
Already, warping global weather patterns have fuelled huge wildfires and crop failures in Indonesia, coastal inundation in the US, severe drought in Sudan and severe flooding in countries including Ecuador and Somalia. “We are supercharging our weather and El Niño will be a risk multiplier,” said Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization.
Drought has ravaged the Marshall Islands, a small Pacific atoll country which relies heavily on rainfall for its water. “It’s a compounding crisis, we are trying to prepare but the drought has already hit and it’s on top of having to deal with rising seas that threaten our homes and drinking water,” said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy for the Marshall Islands, which has declared a state of emergency.
Last year, wealthy countries agreed to triple the amount of adaptation finance to poorer countries most vulnerable to floods heatwaves, wildfires and other damaging climate impacts. Yet just a fraction of the $305bn a year needed by 2035 is being delivered, with rich nations consistently lagging in providing climate finance.
This shortfall will be sharply felt in the coming year as El Niño takes its toll. “It’s so frustrating as countries that have done the least to cause climate change are being left with bills we can’t afford,” said Jetn̄il-Kijiner.
“This El Niño is adding stress and we have a limited capacity to respond,” she added. “We need a lot more money for adaptation and for loss and damage, billions more than we are getting right now. They [wealthy countries] say there’s no money but it’s going to AI, it’s going to the military. Just not on climate change.”
A cascade of different crises are expected to hit as the El Niño peaks in December and then reverberates throughout next year, which is almost certain, with the boost from El Niño, to be the hottest ever recorded. On land, there will be heatwaves, crop shortages and either too much or too little rain, while in the oceans corals will likely bleach through heat stress.
“It’s won’t be any joke, it will feel like accelerated global warming,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics. “We can fully expect there will be more humanitarian disasters linked to food, water, drought and in some places extreme floods. There doesn’t seem to be the right recognition of the scale of the threats.”
UN officials are particularly concerned about the situation in east Africa, due to the exacerbated drought which will force more people to move. The United Nations high commissioner for refugees (UNHCR) predicts there will be as many as 3m displacements across just four countries – Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan and Uganda – due to this El Niño.
“We are very concerned as the forecast for El Niño this year is the worst one ever,” said Antón Leis García, assistant high commissioner of UNHCR.
“There are so many places around the world where forced displacement is prevalent but if you were to zoom into just one area it would be the eastern horn of Africa,” he added. “The maize crop production in Kenya is already dropping by 40% which means there is less food for the refugees moving there and less capacity for Kenya to absorb more of them.”
Campaigners at Cop31 said this unfolding emergency means countries should quickly act.
“People living with the climate crisis cannot afford to wait for another round of diplomatic promises,” said Mohamed Adow, founder of Kenya-based thinktank Power Shift Africa. “You cannot protect a harvest with a pledge. People need resources on the ground.”

https://taz.de/Argentiniens-Kettensaegen.title: Argentiniens „Kettensägen“-Präsident: Javier Milei will noch einmal antreten
https://taz.de/Argentiniens-Kettensaegen.text:
Argentiniens „Kettensägen“-Präsident: Javier Milei will noch einmal antreten
Milei strebt eine zweite Amtszeit an und rühmt den wirtschaftlichen Aufschwung unter seiner Ägide. Doch seine Politik bringt erhebliche soziale Härten mit sich.
dpa | Argentiniens ultraliberaler Staatschef Javier Milei will sich bei der Präsidentenwahl im nächsten Jahr um eine zweite Amtszeit bewerben. „Für alle, die daran zweifeln, dass ich mich zur Wiederwahl stellen werde: Ja, ich werde mich zur Wiederwahl stellen“, sagte Milei bei der Eröffnung einer Ausstellung in einem historischen Museum hinter dem Regierungssitz in der Hauptstadt Buenos Aires.
Milei ist seit knapp drei Jahren Präsident der zweitgrößten Volkswirtschaft Südamerikas und ein enger Verbündeter von US-Präsident Donald Trump. Die entscheidende Stichwahl gewann er 2023 mit dem Versprechen einer radikalen „Kettensägen-Politik“. Eine medienwirksam in die Höhe gereckte Motorsäge wurde zu seinem Symbol für einen schlankeren Staatsapparat und eine deregulierte Wirtschaft.
Zwar ging die einst enorme Inflation während seiner Amtszeit nach einer Reihe von Reformen deutlich zurück und die Wirtschaft wuchs 2025 um 4,4 Prozent. Allerdings gibt es viel Kritik an den sozialen Härten, die mit Mileis marktradikaler Politik einhergehen. Zahlreiche Beamtenstellen wurden gestrichen, Subventionen gekürzt und Sozialprogramme abgewickelt. Nach einer offiziellen Statistik gilt ein Drittel der 46 Millionen Einwohner Argentiniens als arm, viele von ihnen sind auf staatliche Unterstützung angewiesen.
„Argentinien wieder groß machen“
Für die nächste Präsidentenwahl im Oktober 2027 sieht Milei sich selbst trotz aller Kritik in einer blendenden Ausgangsposition. „In den hundert Jahren vor unserem Amtsantritt hatte sich Argentinien immer mehr abgeschottet, und wir sind immer ärmer geworden“, sagte der 56 Jahre alte Ökonom. Nun wachse die argentinische Wirtschaft wieder. Trumps Motto „Make America Great Again“ hat sich Milei auf seine Weise zu eigen gemacht, wie er erneut deutlich machte: „Wir haben jede Menge zu tun, um Argentinien wieder groß zu machen.“

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Nick Robins-Early
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.
Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet.
The scandal has thrown Nvidia into crisis, cast a pall over the AI boom and even threatened the stability of the US economy. Huang’s downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats, and a glimpse into what intelligence experts say is a constant theater of corporate espionage secretly playing out every day throughout the US.
“The reason that this is making the news is because obviously you have one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the highest-profile CEOs in the world,” said Don Aviv, the CEO of corporate intelligence firm Interfor International. “But this happens all the time, across industries.”
As the AI boom and geopolitical competition with China have ramped up in recent years, the tech industry and security officials have tried to prevent exactly the type of plot that allegedly ensnared Huang. Corporate intelligence firms, AI companies and US officials have been on alert for espionage operations targeting tech executives – with some major tech firms warning employees to be skeptical of their personal relationships and holding investigations into how executives could be compromised.
OpenAI has even held training sessions specifically running through “honeypot” scenarios where a corporate spy or foreign intelligence asset pursues a sexual relationship with company staff in return for information or leverage, according to the Wall Street Journal. Aviv meanwhile estimated that his firm alone has conducted around a dozen investigations for significant companies into schemes involving honeypots, personal relationships, coercion or blackmail over the past three years.
Beyond a disastrous lapse in judgment from Huang, experts also describe the affair with a suspected spy as a massive failure of corporate oversight and a remarkable triumph for an alleged foreign influence operation. For all the concerns about digital infrastructure and the growth of cyber-attacks, intelligence analysts say that human error remains the most vulnerable part of most companies.
“The honeypot style trap is as old as the earth itself,” said Randy Watt, head of the corporate threat assessment and consulting firm SRW. “It speaks to a consistent weakness in humans that is exploitable.
“I guarantee you there are a whole number of executives in powerful corporations that are reviewing their relationships with girlfriends,” Watt added.
OpenAI, Meta and Google did not return requests for comment on their security practices. Nvidia did not comment on questions about Huang’s affairs or when the company learned about his involvement with the alleged spy. The Chinese government has denied any involvement in the affair or efforts at corporate espionage, with a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson earlier this week calling the reports “nothing but a smear against China”.
Silicon Valley’s long history of espionage
The fallout from allegations that China conducted a high-profile foreign intelligence operation against Huang has had global implications on the market and tech industry, with the Nasdaq falling 4% immediately after Huang’s resignation and Nvidia losing hundreds of billions in market value this week. Yet security experts say that while the impact of the operation is unique, the tactics and goals are not.
Silicon Valley, flush with incredibly valuable intellectual property and trade secrets, has long been a prized target for foreign spying operations. Throughout the cold war, Soviet agents conducted a decades-long effort to steal technological secrets from US tech firms, including major chip companies, that involved a complex web of international espionage.
During the 1970s and 80s, Soviet intelligence officers operated out of the Russian consulate in San Francisco as they carried out spying operations, according to former FBI special agent Rick Smith, who spent over two decades in the Bay Area working in counterintelligence. US officials estimated at the time that the Moscow Kremlin had mobilized thousands of spies in the country with the intent to steal intellectual property and help the Soviet Union copy American technology they could not produce themselves.
“Gaining access to our advanced technology continues to be their top priority,” William Casey, director of the CIA, warned in 1985.
Other countries and foreign nationals have also launched their own corporate espionage operations. North Korean spies created two businesses in the US with the intent of spreading malicious software to infect cryptocurrency developers, Reuters and cybersecurity firms reported last year. In October, US authorities arrested a Saudi national accused of planting a sophisticated listening device within the headquarters of OpenAI.
In recent years, however, it’s China’s government that has been most prominently accused of a multilayered effort to steal technological capabilities and IP from US tech firms.
A report from the nonprofit Center for Strategic and International Studies found at least 224 incidents of Chinese espionage in the US between 2000 and 2022, with over half of the plots directed at the theft of commercial technologies. In January, a federal jury in California convicted a former Google engineer of stealing confidential company information to benefit the Chinese government.
Some operations linked to China have even involved honeypot-style schemes where a suspected spy has pursued personal or sexual relationships with politicians and executives. The Washington Post obtained declassified FBI documents in August that showed that former California congressman Eric Swalwell admitted to “occasionally hooking up” with suspected Chinese operative Christine Fang.
The alleged Chinese operation involving Huang stood out to security experts, however, for both the extremely high-profile target and its apparent success.
Huang was first seen with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive who ran the Singapore-based Megaspeed datacenter firm, in late 2023. The two were together at a bar in Taiwan in 2024 and again at a conference in 2025, by which time the US commerce department was investigating whether Megaspeed was diverting AI chips to China in violation of export controls. In spring of this year, state secretary Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo reporting that the Nvidia CEO was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang ultimately appears to have helped facilitate the transfer of billions of dollars in advanced Nvidia chips to China.
“As an American, it’s not good, but I’m impressed with their skills,” Smith, the former FBI counterintelligence official, said. “What a target and a tremendous job by the Chinese.”
Huang was not only the head of what was once the world’s most valuable company, but he is also a close ally of Donald Trump who accompanied the president at White House dinners and on Trump’s official state visit to China. Huang has been an influential voice on tech policy, especially on export control and open source AI model issues, although it is unclear whether his extramarital relationship had any bearing on his views. Trump backed Huang after the scandal, calling him an “honorable guy”.
The Trump administration is also facing questions over why Alice Huang’s firm Megaspeed was spared from being placed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, Axios reported, despite intelligence outlining issues with the company. US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure to resign over perceived inaction in response to problems with Megaspeed.
Nvidia has since announced that it hired a top US law firm to conduct an investigation into Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, while Trump stated that the FBI would launch its own probe into the affair. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress and he now faces a lawsuit in California accusing him of misleading shareholders.
Easy access and social engineering
In order to combat the wave of corporate espionage and foreign influence campaigns, many companies have turned to intelligence and threat assessment firms to harden their security – several of which say they are expecting more demand for their services after the Nvidia scandal. These firms hold training and conduct investigations into what makes a company vulnerable, often focusing on the human elements of security.
“Everybody thinks it’s like what we see in Hollywood – surreptitious entry and listening devices and bugs and tails,” said Eduardo Jany, head of global security for a major US corporation. “It’s really more about social engineering.”
Malicious actors will seek out staff at companies that hold positions of influence or valuable information, frequently using what is publicly available through social media and data brokers to learn their personal information and create targeted plans. An employee with a substance abuse or gambling problem provides one avenue of exploitation, experts said, while a staffer who is lonely and seeking out relationships offers another kind of vulnerability.
Attempts at corporate espionage can also often come in the guise of business opportunities, as it appears was potentially the case with Nvidia and Huang, with spies posing as fellow tech executives or financiers.
“They’re looking at easy access and proximity from conferences and customer relationships,” Jany said. “They sidle up to our executives at any events or trade shows, or even make promises of investments.”
Corporations will sometimes hire firms to conduct what’s called penetration testing to check for weak points in their security, which involves using simulated attacks to uncover real vulnerabilities. One security expert described an example of his firm following an employee to the parking lot of a grocery store in order to gain access to their car and take a corporate ID card left hanging from their rearview mirror.
Dealing with C-suite executives like Huang tends to pose its own unique challenges for security and threat assessment firms, experts said. Top leadership at companies possesses far more autonomy and authority than the average employee, making it harder for underlings to confront them about misconduct or potential risks. CEOs can also be hostile to seeing themselves as fallible, with consultants having to sensitively approach the idea that their personal relationships may not be what they seem.
“These are really smart, accomplished people and you don’t want to come across telling them that they don’t know how to behave themselves or that they’re not sophisticated enough to know that they’re being taken advantage of,” said Brian Stephens, president of security risk advisory at the CEO advisory firm Teneo.
Executives can also protest that they’re not important enough to be a target or that everything about them is already public.
“It’s a defense mechanism to being told that the way you live your life is going to have to change,” said Elizabeth Buckley, Teneo’s head of cyber and technical solutions.
In addition to educating staff on protecting themselves from being exploited, security and risk experts emphasized that companies need robust mechanisms to flag concerns about misconduct or outside threats. One question facing Nvidia is who within the company knew about Huang’s relationships and whether any concerns were raised internally. Several corporate intelligence and security experts said it is unfathomable that someone at Nvidia would not be tracking the CEO’s whereabouts and who he was meeting with, especially on trips abroad.
Yet for all the training, oversight and security protocols companies can put in place, experts said that no amount of safeguards can totally replace personal judgment. While looming investigations will seek to answer what went wrong at Nvidia to lead to the current disaster, Huang’s downfall was of his own making.
“Jensen Huang lost his mind here,” Smith, the former counterintelligence agent, said. “But that often happens with romantic relationships.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now | Polly Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Polly Hudson
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
It has been a strange time to be a “woman of a certain age”, as Gregg Wallace so charmingly labelled us. Many of us were consumed by every detail of the Russell Brand trial and the David Walliams exposé. We were pleasantly surprised, albeit dazed – stunned even – by there being consequences for their behaviour, because that’s not how it usually goes, in our experience.
A few days ago, while spending time with a group of fellow certain-agers, among whom this was the main topic of discussion, as it has been pretty much everywhere I’ve been, I confessed to something of which I’m ashamed. If I had been the woman Brand was found guilty of raping – in an attack that was difficult even to read about – I worry that I would have felt powerless to complain about what had happened. I would have thought consent would be taken as a blanket statement that covered whatever followed, however horrifying and unwanted; that I’d made my bed, so was obliged to lie in it, come what may. My friends, it should be noted, felt the same. Thank God the heroic woman forced to endure Brand’s attack knew better.
After this week, much in my rear-view mirror looks different. For example, the brief relationship – although the word relationship is doing a lot of heavy lifting – I had with a 36-year-old man when I was 17. He was the DJ at the local high street nightclub that I was able to frequent, thanks to a terrible fake ID that was never closely inspected and a tangled web of lies to my parents about sleepovers at a friend’s. A group of us, all the same age, went to the nightclub as regularly as we could sneak out, as did a group of the DJ’s mates, all about 20 years our senior. We paired off and no one batted an eyelid. Boys of 17 were so childish: it was common knowledge that they matured more slowly than we did. It made sense that we were with older men.
Like most teenage girls, I was desperate to be treated as an adult, and the DJ obviously did that, with bells on. My association with him made me feel unbelievably cool, special and grownup, fully the sophisticated, worldly wise woman I had become, rather than the little girl my parents still saw me as. He had his own flat and a car, and he could come and go as he pleased. It seemed impossibly glamorous. I never for one second questioned what this man approaching 40 wanted with a kid, which is, much as I would have furiously denied it, what I was. Nor did I ever wonder why he wasn’t going out with women his own age, or what they sensed about him that I was blind to. I didn’t worry that what I was doing was dangerous, or ask myself if I was being exploited. Genuinely, until last week, it was just another tale in the folder marked idiotic teenage exploits. My friends were doing it too, it wasn’t unusual and no laws were being broken. It would have been illegal for the DJ to buy me an alcoholic drink in the club where we met, but there was no issue with him taking me home to spend the night with him after he played his last record.
Now, decades later, beyond belatedly, the person I’m most angry with is myself. Why didn’t I know better? It’s the same as when I heard from the Brand trial what women who were simply trying to get on with their jobs were subjected to, and it took me back to my time as a waitress. The male bosses would come up behind us waitresses when we had a stack of plates in each arm, and run their hands all over our bodies. None of the other teenage staff made a fuss about it, so I didn’t either. That was just what happened there. Oh, and to some degree, almost everywhere I’ve ever worked. I got used to dodging a grope, laughing off a suggestive remark, pretending not to understand advances from men with wives and kids at home, so as not to be seen as a troublemaker, difficult, someone uptight, who can’t take a bit of banter. Throughout all this, rather than doubt the men’s behaviour, the only actions I doubted were my own – what I’d worn, whether I’d given the wrong signals, or been too friendly. The misogyny is coming from inside the house.
I feel as if I’ve been blundering through life with my eyes closed. In light of the testimonies I’ve heard, the information I’ve taken in, so many intimate encounters are now reframed, blurry, uncertain. Blokes from my past who I thought were fine are rebranded – no pun intended – as dodgy and problematic. There were times when I felt bad or confused afterwards, thought that something wasn’t right, but I told myself I was being silly, oversensitive, weird. There were occasions when I ignored my intuition and my emotions and abandoned myself in favour of some man whose surname I probably no longer remember. It isn’t a case of not being brave enough to speak up: it’s much worse than that. It’s not even being aware there was anything to speak up about. I wish I could go back to the young woman I was then and apologise, for not taking better care of her, for letting her down so badly.
One way to reconcile how so many women’s histories have been altered in the wake of Brand and Walliams is to focus on hope, the positives. On what can change, now that some women, who are far more courageous than I am, have taught all of us how to know better.
 
Polly Hudson is a freelance writer
Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 (England and Wales), 0808 801 0302 (Scotland), or 0800 0246 991 (Northern Ireland), or visit 247sexualabusesupport.org.uk In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Prince Harry in Ukraine meeting Invictus 2027 hopefuls
British Royal says he’s ‘taken a risk’ in fourth surprise visit to Ukraine since 2022 to meet wounded veterans.
Britain’s Prince Harry has met wounded veterans and medics in Ukraine during a surprise visit.
The royal family member attended Ukraine’s National Invictus Games and a conference for medics in the western city of Lviv on Saturday. It was organised by Superhumans, a clinic that specialises in the rehabilitation of war-wounded.
“Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth,” Harry said, adding that he’d “taken a risk to come here”.
Ukraine has about 1.4 million combat veterans, more than 10 percent of whom have disabilities.
“You’re going to win the war,” the 42-year-old British royal said during his fourth trip to the country since the start of the conflict with Russia in 2022.
The prince watched wheelchair rugby players competing for a place in Ukraine’s team for next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham in England.
Around 500 people have registered to compete to qualify for the 60-member squad – the largest ever team – that Ukraine is planning to send to the 2027 event.
“You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success,” he said.
Prince Harry is the founder and patron of the Invictus Games Foundation, which he established in 2014 to support wounded, injured and recovering military service personnel and veterans through adaptive sports, e-sports and recovery programmes.
“When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” Harry told wounded veterans later on Saturday.
At a rugby game, he hugged Valery Odainyk, a contestant at the Invictus Games in Canada last year. The leg amputee is “still an active serviceman” in the Ukrainian forces.
“So when do you find time to train?” Harry asked in surprise.
The 41-year-old Odainyk said he told Harry that his involvement in disability sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games.”
They feature a mix of adaptive core and winter sports, such as alpine skiing, archery, track and field, cycling, wheelchair basketball, rugby and tennis.

Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
Eight arrests made in connection with an attempted arson, which Tallinn says was ordered by Russian intelligence.
Estonia will close its border crossings with Russia, after an attack on an Estonian defence company that Tallinn blames on Moscow.
The foreign minister made the announcement on Sunday, after eight people were detained overnight in connection with an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
Estonian authorities said the attacks had been ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence. There was no immediate comment from Moscow.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote on X, “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.
“Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia’s ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention.”
He did not specify how long the border closure would last.
Latvia’s Interior Minister Janis Dombrava thanked Estonia’s Internal Security Service on X, saying that several “Latvian citizens and non-citizens” were arrested.
“Since the collapse of the USSR, there have been people among us who are willing to commit serious crimes in Russia’s interests. We will continue our work to ensure that such people cannot endanger the lives of those who love Latvia and want to live in safety,” Dombrava wrote.
‘Shadow war’
Estonia, a European Union and NATO member state and a strong ally of Ukraine, currently has three open border crossings with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula.
Marko Mihkelson, chairman of the Estonian Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, told Al Jazeera that the arrests demonstrated that Estonia was “prepared to respond swiftly to such attacks”.
“It is essential that Russia’s state-sponsored campaign of terror does not remain merely a matter of diplomatic protests, either in Estonia or among our allies elsewhere,” Mihkelson said.
“Russia is waging a shadow war to divide Europe and undermine support for Ukraine. European countries must respond with asymmetric measures of their own. Closing borders with Russia is one such measure.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Exclusive: Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Elis Gjevori
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Exclusive: Toyota reviewing use of forklifts by Israeli military after MEE investigation
Toyota has said it is investigating the use of its forklifts by the Israeli military after Middle East Eye found photos and videos of the vehicles at weapons and munitions storage sites, serving supply lines for frontline units, and being used by the army’s Logistics Corps.
It comes after MEE uncovered details of a previously unreported 158m-shekel ($49.8m) contract between Toyota and Israel’s Ministry of Defense for the supply of forklifts that was signed in 2024 – the first full year of the Gaza war.
Toyota says that its vehicles are not intended for military use.
When asked about the contract, the company told MEE it had commitments in place with both the defence ministry and its official reseller in Israel to ensure that its technology and products were “for civil use only”.
But when MEE then shared footage posted on official Israeli military social media channels, which showed Toyota forklifts being used at locations including a missiles and ammunition depot in northern Israel, a Logistics Corps training base, and inside a munitions factory, it said it was investigating the images to determine whether those agreements had been breached.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/inegali.title: Mouvement lycéen : lettre ouverte d’un élève contre le mythe de la méritocratie
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/inegali.author: Tribunes
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/inegali.text:
Taho Lansalot-Devaux, lycéen de 15 ans, critique le discours sur le mérite qui ne sert qu’à légitimer les privilèges et masquer les effets des inégalités économiques, sociales et culturelles à la naissance. Il dénonce le rôle de la justice qui en réprimant la mobilisation vise plus à protéger l’ordre établi qu’à défendre les innocents.
À celles et ceux à qui l’on répète qu’ils n’ont que ce qu’ils méritent, et à tous ceux que les tribunaux de la respectabilité condamnent pour avoir refusé de plier,
On nous a vendu un catéchisme rassurant, répété de classe en classe et de tribune en tribune : la société serait une immense course d’obstacles, un stade équitable où chacun, muni de sa seule volonté et de son travail, finirait par récolter le fruit légitime de ses efforts. On appelle cela le mérite. C’est la plus belle fable que les dominants aient jamais inventée pour s’endormir l’esprit tranquille. Elle permet aux nantis de s’attribuer la paternité de leur réussite en y voyant la juste récompense de leur vertu, tout en intimant aux autres l’ordre de baisser la tête et de s’accabler eux-mêmes, en se persuadant que leur échec est le fruit de leur seule paresse.
Mais qu’on retire le vernis de cette grande mascarade pour regarder la réalité en face. Dès le berceau, les dés sont jetés, les cartes sont pipées, et les lignes de départ sont éparpillées sur des siècles d’inégalités et de privilèges hérités. Comment oser parler de mérite quand le destin d’un être humain se trouve balisé par le code postal de sa naissance, par le capital culturel et financier de ses parents, et par la violence feutrée des milieux qu’on lui assigne d’office ? Le mérite n’est que la légitimation morale du privilège : il transforme la chance en valeur, et l’injustice en fatalité.
Et lorsque la mécanique finit par broyer les corps, lorsque les individus, étouffés par cette violence sociale structurelle, finissent par céder, par déborder ou par refuser les règles d’un jeu qui les condamne, la machine change brusquement de visage : elle abandonne les belles promesses pour sortir son glaive.
C’est ici qu’intervient la seconde imposture : la justice punitive. Qu’on ne se méprenne pas : il ne s’agit ni de nier la réalité du tort fait à autrui, ni de prôner le chaos ou l’impunité générale. Le problème fondamental de la justice moderne n’est pas qu’elle sanctionne les actes, c’est qu’elle a radicalement renoncé à comprendre. En se transformant en un guichet aveugle de la vengeance d’État, de l’exemplarité théâtrale et de l’anesthésie sociale, elle évite soigneusement d’interroger la responsabilité de la structure qui produit, chaque jour un peu plus, la misère, l’exclusion et la colère. Elle traite les symptômes au lance-flammes tout en protégeant la maladie.
On érige des tribunaux à la chaîne, on enferme, on punit, on applique des barèmes de souffrance standardisés au nom de l’ordre public, comme si l’isolement cellulaire et la privation absolue de liberté pouvaient par miracle recréer du lien social et réparer les failles d’une communauté. Punir est devenu l’alibi suprême de l’État : cela le dispense d’avoir à rendre des comptes sur les conditions d’existence qu’il impose. On fait porter l’entière responsabilité morale de la crise à ceux qu’elle détruit en premier, transformant des drames éminemment politiques en simples faits divers faits pour nourrir l’appareil répressif.
On nous promet que le châtiment moralise, qu’il corrige, qu’il protège les innocents. Quelle immense lâcheté. La punition n’a jamais appris à vivre à personne ; elle n’est que la réponse paniquée d’un ordre établi qui tremble devant sa propre fragilité. Elle substitue la vindicte codifiée à l’effort exigeant de la responsabilité collective, et l’élimination temporaire des corps à la reconstruction patiente du tissu social.
Refuser cette double alliance du mérite et de la sanction, ce n’est pas céder au laxisme ou abdiquer toute morale ; c’est exiger la fin d’une gigantesque hypocrisie. C’est refuser de confondre la justice avec la vengeance des puissants, et la réussite avec la simple chance d’être né du bon côté de la barrière.
Tant que nous accepterons de jouer à ce jeu truqué où l’on trie les gagnants d’un côté et l’on châtie les vaincus de l’autre, nous serons les complices zélés de notre propre soumission. La véritable émancipation commence le jour où l’on piétine les faux bilans de compétences de cette société pour exiger, enfin, l’égalité inconditionnelle des vies.
Un esprit libre qui refuse l’absurde.
Le journal des intelligences libres
« C’est par des informations étendues et exactes que nous voudrions donner à toutes les intelligences libres le moyen de comprendre et de juger elles-mêmes les événements du monde. »
Tel était « Notre but », comme l’écrivait Jean Jaurès dans le premier éditorial de l’Humanité, le 18 avril 1904. 122 ans plus tard, il n’a pas changé.

Je veux en savoir plus !

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.title: Israel's data shows it allowed half of the promised aid trucks into Gaza
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/israe.text:
Israel's data shows it allowed half of the promised aid trucks into Gaza
Israel has failed to meet its commitments under the Gaza ceasefire deal, allowing in only around half the agreed volume of humanitarian and commercial goods each month since March, Israeli military data shows.
Data obtained by Haaretz newspaper showed a growing shortfall in food deliveries to Gaza, alongside severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair damaged infrastructure. Torrential rains have flooded displacement camps, leaving hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in increasingly dire conditions.
Under the ceasefire deal, Israel pledged to allow 4,200 vehicles carrying humanitarian and commercial goods into Gaza each week, equivalent to roughly 18,200 a month.
Deliveries were to include food, fuel, medical supplies and equipment, shelter materials and equipment to repair essential infrastructure.
Data supplied by the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (Cogat) to the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) show that Israel allowed about 4,700 trucks into Gaza in March, rising to 5,300 in April and more than 9,600 in May.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The number increased to more than 12,000 in June before falling to about 10,000 in both July and August.
Deliveries peaked at more than 13,000 in September, then dropped sharply to just over 6,500 in October.
Cogat disputed the findings, saying that the data presented was "inaccurate” and that Israel was meeting its humanitarian commitments “and beyond them”.
The figures mark a rare instance in which statistics supplied by Israel to the IGSC show that Israel has failed to fulfil its promises.
Cogat no longer releases detailed monthly statistics, publishing figures only for selected categories of supplies.
Flooding worsens crisis
The shortages have become more critical as winter rains flood makeshift shelters and damage displacement camps across Gaza.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said on Friday that about 46,000 households, representing an estimated 226,000 people, may have been affected by flooding.
More than 40,000 shelters were reported damaged, including over 9,000 destroyed beyond repair.
The UN warned that sewage-contaminated floodwater was creating public health risks.
Damaged health facilities, medicine shortages and disrupted services were compounding the emergency.
The World Health Organization has warned that about 950,000 displaced Palestinians are living in areas at risk of flooding, including more than 400,000 in particularly high-risk locations.
Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya on Saturday called for an emergency international campaign to provide shelter for Palestinians and secure the entry of tents, heating supplies, fuel and equipment to repair sewage and rainwater drainage networks.
In letters to Arab and Muslim countries, Hayya urged governments to pressure Israel to implement the ceasefire agreement, including its humanitarian provisions and a full withdrawal from Gaza.
He also called for unrestricted access for UN agencies and aid organisations and urged the UN Security Council to convene an emergency meeting.
Gaza's health ministry said Israeli violations of the ceasefire had killed 1,643 Palestinians and wounded 5,964 others as of Saturday.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Chris Van Hollen says he has path to win Senate leader over Chuck Schumer
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Marina Dunbar
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Democratic US senator Chris Van Hollen on Sunday escalated his bid to lead his party’s incoming Senate majority rather than Chuck Schumer, asserting that he has a path to victory amid a dedicated campaign that includes a series of television appearances.
Van Hollen, a Maryland progressive, appeared on Sunday on CNN, ABC and Fox News as he continues to make his case for why his peers in the Senate should reject Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus for nearly a decade.
On CNN’s State of the Union, he reaffirmed that he believes he has a path to victory, citing support and a widespread openness to change within the Senate Democratic caucus.
“This really is a response to the call of the voters, who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies, but they haven’t fully hired the Democrats,” Van Hollen said, alluding to how the US president’s Republican party lost control of Congress during the 3 November midterm elections.
“They’ve given us a chance, and I think we need to earn their trust. And I think that begins by not going back to business as usual.”
Van Hollen criticized reports that Schumer’s team may move the Senate caucus leadership election date earlier than 1 December. He contended that the caucus should have a debate about the group’s direction as the Democrats assume control of Congress in January for the second half of Trump’s second presidency.
Van Hollen also responded to a list that was reportedly leaked by Schumer’s team to the political news outlet the Hill that revealed the committed votes the New York senator claims to already have. Van Hollen said that some of those senators on the list have actually already pledged to vote for him instead of Schumer.
He also called for more “inclusion and democracy” within the Democratic caucus, accusing Schumer of trying to exclude the more progressive members of the party. Van Hollen alluded to victories by Democratic senators-elect whose candidacies Schumer did not support – Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine – and said they “would not be there” if Schumer had his way.
“He joined with Aipac and crypto to try to defeat them,” Van Hollen said, referring in part to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which opposed El-Sayed and Jackson.
Appearing on ABC News’s This Week, Van Hollen accused Schumer’s team of putting out misinformation by leaking the alleged list of supporters, equating it to an intimidation tactic.
“They’re essentially trying to instill fear in people who may say that they’re going to support me as a new leader,” he said. “We just had a great day for our democracy around the country. How about a little democracy in the Senate Democratic caucus?”
On Fox News Sunday, Van Hollen responded more directly to the Hill’s report, calling it “a bunch of nonsense”. The outlet reported being told by a Schumer confidant that Van Hollen has “no chance of winning” – and that progressives are only using his candidacy to gain leverage over Schumer to sign on to a “liberal wishlist of priorities”.
“This is a wide open race,” Van Hollen said. “The other team has been putting out numbers that are flatly wrong.
“They’re trying to create this false sense of momentum. If they really believed that they were ahead, they wouldn’t be trying to move up the elections.”
Van Hollen also said that the number of senator supporters he had as of Sunday was “15 and growing”.
“I agree with the American people and all our candidates who ran across the country that this is not about left versus right. It’s not about progressives or moderates or conservatives,” he said. “Those are old Washington labels. It’s much more about taking on a rigged economy, rigged in favor of the very wealthy and fueled by political corruption.”
The race will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades. The closed-door, secret-ballot election is slated for early December.
Schumer, the leader of the Democratic minority in the current Senate, had immediately responded to Van Hollen’s initial challenge for leadership in a social media post on Thursday, writing that he welcomed “any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”. But he added that he had “the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader”.
The Democratic caucus has privately deliberated about what message to take from the midterm elections – whether they truly represents an upswing in popularity for the party or if it was simply a firm rejection of Trump’s far-right policies.
Several of the incoming Democratic senators have voiced their desire for new leadership.
Beside El-Sayed and Jackson, that includes Senators-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota.
Bernie Sanders, the progressive senator from Vermont, also recently said that he would not support Schumer’s bid to serve as the Democratic leader.
Meanwhile, Scott Colom, the Democratic senator-elect who recently achieved a historic upset in Mississippi, said he was in “listening mode” when it came to who he would cast his vote for to lead his party’s Senate caucus.
“I’m going to figure out what are the things that people are doing well in leadership, what are the things they’re not doing well, and find out how we can work together to achieve results,” Colom said Sunday on NBC News’s Meet the Press.
Schumer did help recruit many of the party’s winning candidates and raised money for them.
But many say Democratic Senate candidates Angie Nixon in Florida and Jamie Davis in Louisiana could have won races they narrowly lost in their states had they been given more support from the party establishment, including Schumer.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Rory Carroll and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.
Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.
Meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.
The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.
At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.
US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.
Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.
However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.
A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.
In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.
There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.
The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.
Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.
Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.
The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.
“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.
The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.
In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend Aden on the southern coast.
“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.
The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.
A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.
