https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “reactive and risk-averse” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?”
This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “human bandwidth”. That is an extraordinary claim. Technology can help speed up identifying someone at risk of homelessness – but it does not supply a home. Better administration and adequate resources need each other.
Trust in institutions is waning. Reliability and fair outcomes matter. But the public also need ways to challenge decisions. Learning from business must not mean treating public scrutiny as “frictions” or neglecting the people whom markets fail to serve. Dame Antonia correctly identifies poor incentives, churn and inadequate training as issues. But who gets to the top also matters. A 2025 paper by Oxford University’s Erzsébet Bukodi and John H Goldthorpe, with Nottingham University’s Inga Steinberg, says access to elite civil service posts remains skewed to people from advantaged backgrounds. Progress towards widening access has reversed in the last 20 years. Whitehall risks overlooking the talent to govern an increasingly complex country.
The academics traced the backgrounds of 476 public service leaders between 1945 and 2022. Among officials reaching the top, the share from higher professional and managerial families fell from 56% before 1960 to 45% in 1980-99, then rose again. Those reaching senior posts in 2000‑22 resembled their pre-1960 predecessors in class origins. The paper also highlights how few people at the top have qualifications in Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) or quantitatively oriented disciplines such as sociology and demography. The latter could help officials understand the lives affected by policies they implement. Such a “cultural disconnect”, experts say, has caused major policy blunders.
Class privilege is linked to Whitehall’s cult of the generalist: those valued for intellectual dexterity rather than expertise. Privately schooled Oxford graduates dominated among top officials from privileged families, the vast majority of whom had studied humanities – the traditional grounding for Whitehall generalists. State-school entrants from other universities were more likely to have Stem or social science degrees. Better recruitment and promotion could help with the specialist knowledge Dame Antonia wants. Kate Bingham, the former vaccine taskforce chair, has warned that too few scientists are being recruited to shift Whitehall’s skillset. It’s time to look at the social selection that determines who gets to the top as well as reforming the system that shapes officials’ behaviour.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Andy Burnham
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
A generation of young people did not wake up one morning and decide they did not want to work. The fact that a million 16- to 24-year-olds are now not in education, employment or training (Neet) is not their fault. It is ours, as politicians.
We have failed to give them the support they need as they have grown up in a tougher world. This has become an economic catastrophe for the country – and a moral one too.
Sixteen years ago, the Conservative government took a deliberate decision to make young people bear the brunt of the cuts they chose to make. Those becoming adults today are the children of austerity. At four years old, with Sure Start centres closed, too many were already beginning school behind, without the support they needed to catch up. By 12, too many had seen youth clubs shut down and had fewer places to go in their communities with the closure of libraries and leisure centres. Teenagers in need of mental health support were told to wait months or even years. And, by 18, millions had passed through an education system that told them their technical talents were not worth as much as the abilities of their academic peers.
A country focused on the future would make young people its priority for investment – not the target for cuts. It would give all young people a path in life, giving them confidence and hope for the future. Britain has done neither. It is time to acknowledge that this failure has left too many young people ill-prepared for the challenging world they now face. And, of course, that has costs. Under the Conservatives, the welfare bill shot up by £114bn.
What is the Tory solution now? To punish those young people once again. The crude cuts they are proposing to the welfare bill would simply compound the mistakes they made in government. They would drive children into poverty and increase levels of family homelessness even further, piling further pressure on councils, the NHS and other public services. This is not “reform”. It is a path to higher public spending and broken services.
The way I see it is that we have two choices: we can either invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on; or we can continue to pay the price for failure.
I choose the first. The time has come for a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world. To bring down the welfare bill for good, we have to act at the different stages where young people can fall behind. We must intervene long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state.
Next week, Alan Milburn’s review into young people and work will be published. I want it to be a watershed moment. We have an opportunity to change the way we think about welfare and the way we think about childhood. Because the two cannot be separated.
For too long, we have waited until young people reach adulthood and then tried to deal with the problems that have built up over the years. Under this government, we will start much earlier, making sure children have the support they need at the moments that matter most.
It is what I call a whole-childhood approach. It means, in the early years, giving every child a proper start. Those who start school behind too often never catch up. To stop these children from falling through the cracks, we must build an education system which offers support with wider needs, such as mental health, and values all talents.
This brings me to a change I am determined to make as prime minister. I will build an education system in England based on the principle of parity between academic and technical routes, that gives all young people a path in life, a confidence in their abilities and tells them they are equally valued.
For too long, Britain has praised the graduation cap and looked down on the hard hat. New technical pathways in school will start to put that right. We will open up opportunities for young people to learn new skills and get good jobs where they live. When they approach adulthood, we will make sure they do not face a cliff edge. We will guarantee good work experience and employment opportunities.
The government will consider Milburn’s recommendations carefully and respond in full in the coming weeks. But I can say now that our response will not be in the manner of traditional Department for Work and Pensions reform. It will be societal and generational. We will rethink supporting childhood – shifting government spending from paying for failure to investing in success.
Of course, that support will have to come with responsibilities. If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can.
Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point. The system will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to receive. It will understand their ambitions and identify the help they need to achieve them.
This is the sustainable way to get the welfare bill down for good. It is how we build a more preventive and productive state and a country which allows every young person to grow up with hope.
- Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.title: Saturday Night Live: is John Mulaney the best modern host we have?
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.author: Zach Vasquez
https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio.text:
This edition of Saturday Night Live opens at the CIA headquarters. In the wake of the Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepping down after details of his extramarital affairs, including one with an accused Chinese spy, came to light, the agency has called together a meeting of the nation’s top tech billionaires: creepy Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson), robotic Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), awkward Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline), and the insufferable duo of Mark Zuckerberg (Andy Dismukes) and Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane).
An agent (tonight’s host, John Mulaney) attempts to school them on how not to get honeypotted. Per a helpful Venn diagram: “On this side we have beautiful women, and on this side we have people who would be interested in your shared opinions and interests. I cannot stress this enough: there is no overlap.” He fails to get through to the group (especially the middle-school-like Musk, whom he sprays with water to keep on track), so he hands things over to Jensen “Hide Your Wife” Haung himself, played by a returning Bowen Yang. Yang doesn’t attempt much of an impression, but he certainly looks the part thanks to some white hair dye and a black leather jacket.
A very solid and refreshingly narrative-driven cold open that makes excellent use of SNL’s cast, each of whom captures their awful tech overlord wonderfully.
Mulaney takes the stage for his monologue. This is the comic and former show writer’s seventh time hosting, which he loves because he says it feels like “there’s no host”. He performs a tight five about diagnosing his aging father as autistic (“He doesn’t know he’s autistic; he’ll find out when this airs”) and baby boomers being exactly as toxic as Gen Z (“My mother has three – not one, three – friends who have been banned from Facebook Marketplace for, and I’m quoting the email, hate speech”). He ends with a rant aimed at Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F Kennedy Jr (“You dumbass, your thing can’t be the measles”), doing a shockingly great and refreshingly mean-spirited impersonation of him. The vitriol Mulaney hurls towards Kennedy is palpable and very, very deserved.
Breaking news out of New York: a Turkish airliner has crashed during landing. A reporter at the scene interviews survivors, all of whom are Americans returning from that nation after receiving obvious cosmetic surgery: hair transplants, lip injections, penis enlargements, and BBLs. Former mayor Eric Adams (Kam Patterson) also pops up on his way back from Istanbul. An impressive array of ridiculous prosthetics.
Next up is an ad aimed at men with aging parents, an affordable alternative to live-in nurses and retirement facilities: Sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, not yours.” The difficult, thankless tasks fall on her, leaving the sons/brothers to live their best lives. A harsh and bleakly funny indictment of gendered family dynamics, and the best commercial sketch the show has done in a long while.
Four office drones unwind at the local bar after a stressful day at work, only to be intruded upon by their annoying co-worker, “worst person on earth” Kathy (Ashley Padilla). Seated one table over, drinking a massive virgin punch bowl, she continually butts in on their conversation (“We talking transpo? We talking transpo? We talking transpo?”). They attempt to ignore her, but her resolve proves stronger. The last minute or so of the sketch is a slow-burn waiting game, which is admirable, even if it does result in noticeable dead air.
Getting it Done is a reality television program where host Chris Gut (Culhane) visits small businesses across the country. On this week’s episode, he stops at a Rhode Island microbrewery. Drinks with Mulaney’s brewmaster opens something up in both men, leading to a sudden and surprising kiss. This unexpected gay experience has both men questioning who they are and what their hearts actually want. “Did the beer make me do it or allow me to do it?” wonders Gut. Culhane and Mulaney’s make-out sessions are sure to be shared far and wide on social media in the coming days. Also, kudos to all involved for the pitch-perfect aping of travelogue TV aesthetics, down to the handheld camera work and scene transition graphics.
Following the first performance from musical guest Phoebe Bridgers, it’s on to Weekend Update. On the subject of Huang, Colin Jost warns that Nvidia’s plummeting stock could crash the economy: “Which means Jensen Huang had a mid-life crisis so bad, you might lose your house in his divorce.”
Cast member Tommy Brennan joins the desk to play piano and sing a song about all the indignities of Thanksgiving. Intentionally rhythmically awkward – which has heretofore been Wickline’s schtick – the best bits are when he pauses singing to go into further detail about his awkward family gathering, which involves him catching uncle naked, his grandfather continuing to boycott the NFL because Colin Kaepernick took a knee during the national anthem, and his “gay and mean” sister coming out to their emotionally distant father.
It wouldn’t be a Mulaney episode without a big musical extravaganza about the seedier side of New York City. This time, Mulaney plays a handsome cab driver who, thanks to the city’s recent ban on horse-drawn carriages, is soon to be jobless. He and his horse Blackie (“Don’t worry, it is racial”) give one last ride through Central Park to two guys visiting from New Jersey. They run into a collection of fun city characters: obsessive marathon runners, dangerous pedicab drivers, aggressive religious vagrants, pervasive stoners, Park Slope cucks and Wall Street stockbrokers arguing over Mamdani, Mary Todd Lincoln herself, and in a rare case of cross-sketch world-building, Kathy from earlier (paying off the “We talking transpo?” line beautifully). The medley of tunes includes numbers from Little Shop of Horrors, Funny Girl, Annie Get Your Gun, Cats, West Side Story, Dream Girls and Hair. Yang reprising his role from Oh, Mary will likely get the lion’s share of press, but it’s Veronika Slowikowska who steals the show by revealing an insane pair of pipes during her parody of Don’t Rain on My Parade.
The musical theme continues in the next sketch, which is set at Woodstock, 1969. A group of friends grooving out to Sly and the Family Stone are interrupted by Mulaney’s mercenary hippie, who sees into the future and argues that they should all embrace the conservative sea change of the ‘80s: “When we get older, I think we should buy all the houses … also, we should have all the money … we should become ruthless corporate climbers, absolutely fetishize money in an almost pornographic way …” Like much of Mulaney’s monologue, this takes angry aim at baby boomer hypocrisy and hits dead center.
Bridgers returns for her second song – a haunting ballad made spookier with some glow-in-the-dark skeleton paint – to close out what is far and away the best episode of this season, arguably the best episode in a couple of seasons. Mulaney remains the greatest recurring host of this generation of SNL, someone who elevates every aspect of the show, in particular the writing. If only he could host every week.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/antifas.title: « Face au fascisme, il faut s’inspirer de la manière dont Gramsci posait les problèmes » : entretien avec l’éditeur Manuel Esposito
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/antifas.author: Elena Vedere
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/antifas.text:
En mai 2026, La Variation publiait « Que faire face au fascisme ? », un recueil de textes politiques et intimes d’Antonio Gramsci. Cette introduction à la pensée du philosophe qui co-fonda le Parti communiste italien (PCd’I) offre des pistes de réflexion pour lutter concrètement contre la montée de l’extrême droite.
Comment des textes écrits au début du siècle dernier pourraient-ils nous aider à penser notre présent ? Pendant l’entre-deux-guerres, Antonio Gramsci, intellectuel et co-fondateur du Parti communiste italien (PCd’I) en 1921, réfléchit longuement à la mise en échec de la gauche par le régime fasciste de Benito Mussolini. Il théorise plusieurs concepts clés, de l’hégémonie à la subalternité, qui ont refait surface dans le débat public ces dernières années.
Manuel Esposito a co-fondé, avec Justine Rabat, La Variation. Il revient sur la manière dont la pensée gramscienne, lorsqu’elle est lue près du texte – en considérant sa teneur marxiste et révolutionnaire – peut servir à l’émancipation collective. Ont déjà paru chez cet éditeur plusieurs recueils de Gramsci : Combattre le fascisme (2025) et Que faire face au fascisme ? (2026). Comment devenir libres ? sortira en janvier 2027.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: England stun Spain to end La Roja’s 43-game unbeaten run
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
England stun Spain to end La Roja’s 43-game unbeaten run
Spain suffer first defeat since March 2024 after losing 3-2 to England in Madrid despite grandstand finish.
England held on with 10 men to record a stunning win over Spain in Madrid in one of the great UEFA Nations League games.
The visitors had seen their hosts parade their World Cup trophy on the pitch before the game, but raced into a 3-0 lead inside an hour, before being reduced to 10 men on 65 minutes and having to cling on in a dramatic finale to pip Spain to top spot in Group A3 on goal difference.
It was a record 10th straight away win for the Three Lions, and it inflicted the first defeat on La Roja since they went down 1-0 in a friendly against Colombia in London in March 2024. The 43-game run saw them crowned European and World Champions along the way.
England produced a stunning start and might have been ahead inside the opening minutes, but Unai Simon made a brilliant reaction save to claw away Jude Bellingham’s close-range effort.
The visitors were irresistible in the first half, pressing high and denying the hosts time and space to find their rhythm, and Spain were unable to register a shot on target in the opening 45 minutes.
England led 1-0 at the break after Harry Kane latched onto Elliot Anderson’s pass in behind and drew a foul from Pau Cubarsi in the box. Following a brief VAR review into Anderson’s challenge on Marc Cucurella in the build-up, Kane stepped up to convert the penalty.
He fired to the right of Unai Simon to register his 93rd Three Lions goal on his 127th appearance in the final seconds of the half.
The visitors doubled their lead eight minutes after the turnaround as Declan Rice’s curling corner was met by a powerful downward header from the unmarked Ezri Konsa, his Arsenal teammate.
The hosts were in disarray four minutes later, when some slick counterattacking saw Bellingham slot through into space on the right of the box for the on-rushing Ben White to drill a low shot past Simon at his near post.
The game changed 25 minutes from time when Jarell Quansah was dispossessed in his own half, and Anderson was shown a straight red card for denying a goalscoring opportunity by putting his arm on Lamine Yamal as he raced into the box.
After VAR confirmed the decision, Mikel Oyarzabal sent James Trafford – recalled in place of Jordan Pickford in goal – the wrong way to give the hosts hope.
They piled on the pressure and reduced the arrears further on the break on 75 minutes, when Yamal’s first-time cross from the right was swept in off the post by substitute Nico Williams.
La Roja laid siege to the England goal in the closing stages as they sought a goal to extend their unbeaten run and claim top spot in Group A3. But Trafford produced a stunning double save in stoppage time, diving to his right to parry a shot from Fermin Lopez, then somehow bouncing up to turn the follow-up from Aymeric Laporte around the upright.
England held on to secure first place in the group on goal difference after both sides finished on 15 points.
Both sides will find out their Nations League quarterfinal opponents next March when the draw takes place on Friday. England is set to face one of the three A-Group runners-up, other than Spain, while La Roja will face one of the other three group winners.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/mossa.title: Mossad abducted Iranian general in Turkey, tortured him for weeks before killing him: Report
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/mossa.author: Elis Gjevori
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/mossa.text:
Mossad abducted Iranian general in Turkey, tortured him for weeks before killing him: Report
Israel kidnapped two Iranian officials and killed one of them in a decades-long search for an Israeli pilot whose fighter jet crashed in Lebanon while bombing the country in 1986, The New York Times reported on Sunday.
Israeli pilot Ron Arad was bombing Lebanese villages in 1986 when one of his missiles malfunctioned, forcing him to eject from his fighter jet.
Since then, Israel has been on a mission to find out what happened to Arad, leaving a trail of death and destruction in its wake which has left more than 40 people dead and dozens more wounded.
The NYT said that the search for Arad was rooted in the "Jewish tradition" to bring its soldiers back to Israel.
In December 2006, Alireza Asgari, a former general in the Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), became one of the first victims.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Asgari, who had served as Iran's deputy defence minister, arrived in Istanbul, Turkey and checked into the Ceylan Hotel near Taksim. Shortly afterwards, Mossad agents kidnapped him, the NYT reported.
Years later and tfter Iran requested information about Asgari's whereabouts, Israeli officials told their US counterparts that they had tortured him for several weeks, believing incorrectly he had information about Arad.
Asgari knew nothing about the Israeli pilot, the Israeli spy agency concluded. Mossad agents killed Asgari anyway and dumped his body in the Black Sea, according to the NYT.
At the time, Meir Dagan headed Mossad. A decision to kill a senior Iranian official would likely have required the Israeli prime minister's approval. Ehud Olmert held that position in 2007.
Iranian officials conducted their own investigation into Asgari's disappearance and found that Israeli agents had broken into his hotel room in Istanbul, drugged and kidnapped him. Investigators also found the vehicle used in the operation abandoned near the Black Sea.
Despite the lack of evidence linking Iran to Arad's disappearance, Israel went on to kidnap General Abdullah Saberi, an IRGC commander, while he was out for a morning run in Damascus in 2021.
Mossad operatives bundled Saberi into a refrigerator box and loaded him into a moving van.
After a lengthy interrogation involving torture, the Israelis dumped Saberi alive in Johannesburg, South Africa, in an attempt to conceal who was behind the kidnapping.
Saberi also knew nothing about Arad.
A joint Hezbollah-Iranian investigation subsequently concluded that Arad most likely died in 1988 in Nabi Chit, a village in eastern Lebanon, around two years after his plane went down, according to the NYT.
Investigators believed his captors had held him there and later buried him in the village. Israeli officials, however, remained obsessed with the theory that Iran knew what had happened to him.
In December 2025, Israel kidnapped Ahmad Shukr, a retired Lebanese security officer who, according to the NYT, left home to attend what he believed was a business meeting.
Lebanese officials believe Israeli agents abducted him. Shukr has not been seen alive since and his whereabouts are unknown.
Israeli officials now believe that Shukr killed Arad in retaliation for the killing of his brother by Israeli forces near Nabi Chit in 1988.
There is no evidence to support the Israeli theory.
Earlier this year, Israeli forces launched more than 40 strikes on Nabi Chit between 6 and 7 March, believing Arad was buried in a cemetery in the village.
The Israeli attacks killed at least 41 people and wounded more than 40 others, and Arad's body was not found.
Across Lebanon, Israeli attacks have killed at least 4,358 people between 2 March and early September 2026.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/centris.title: Teddy Riner, le cheval de Troie idéal du macronisme
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/centris.author: Sébastien Crépel
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/centris.text:
Teddy Riner, le cheval de Troie idéal du macronisme
La nouvelle coqueluche des médias a percuté comme un météore la campagne présidentielle. Soudain, tout le monde n’a d’yeux que pour Teddy Riner : et si c’était lui ? La France est habituée à ce que la course à l’Élysée ne se passe jamais comme le prévoient les oracles. Mais cette fois, la tornade médiatique s’abat avant que le vent ait eu le temps de tourner. À peine déclaré, le néocandidat voit son potentiel décortiqué par les sondages, tandis qu’une couverture médiatique impressionnante se met en place.
De là à dire que l’opération est trop bien ficelée pour ne pas être téléguidée, il n’y a qu’un pas que certains ont franchi en montrant du doigt Emmanuel Macron. Le judoka nie avec énergie, mais l’hypothèse semble plausible. Alors que la place du « centre » reste vacante faute de candidat qui parvienne à se démarquer, le chef de l’État sortant croit peut-être tenir le moyen de déjouer le destin en choisissant lui-même qui lui succédera. Riner est le cheval de Troie idéal du macronisme.
Profondément libéral économiquement, il reprend la formule brevetée par Macron du « ni droite ni gauche » mais avec un profil complètement différent, beaucoup plus populaire que le banquier de chez Rothschild. Teddy Riner est un immense champion dont les exploits rendent fiers les Français, un homme charismatique et chaleureux. L’élection d’un président noir face à l’extrême droite raciste serait aussi un précédent réjouissant pour tous les antiracistes.
L’opération Riner est séduisante : elle est pensée pour l’être. Rien ne dit qu’elle fonctionnera, car pour cela, il faudrait que le candidat en dise le moins possible sur son programme qu’on sait déjà pétri de contradictions intenables. On ne peut dire soutenir les mobilisations lycéennes et populaires qui appellent sur toutes les pancartes à abolir les privilèges du capital et, dans le même temps, défendre toutes les lubies de ce dernier : retraites par capitalisation, extinction des cotisations à la Sécu, fin des 35 heures… Riner en dit déjà trop ou pas assez.
Son CV est à son image : côté pile, un exemple et un symbole. Côté face, un businessman peu porté à la justice fiscale, ami des Balkany. Le « ni droite ni gauche » est un vernis écaillé.
Avant de partir, une dernière chose…
Contrairement à 90% des médias français aujourd’hui, l’Humanité ne dépend ni de grands groupes ni de milliardaires. Cela signifie que :
- nous vous apportons des informations impartiales, sans compromis. Mais aussi que
- nous n’avons pas les moyens financiers dont bénéficient les autres médias.
L’information indépendante et de qualité a un coût. Payez-le.
Je veux en savoir plus

Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK urge Israel to allow aid into Gaza
The countries accuse Israel of preventing tents and other vital supplies from entering Gaza, despite the humanitarian crisis.
Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom have urged Israel to allow immediate and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza, highlighting that recent floods have “brought further suffering” for Palestinians living there.
The countries’ foreign ministers co-signed Sunday’s joint statement, the latest international warning about the dire humanitarian situation in the besieged territory.
“People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance,” the statement said. “Yet 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza.”
For years, Israel has restricted entry and exports into Gaza, home to more than 2 million people.
But since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, Israel has placed the Palestinian territory under a full-scale blockade, limiting access to even essential supplies like food and water.
Under the Geneva Convention, denying civilians access to humanitarian aid can constitute a war crime.
“We today urge the Government of Israel to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza,” Sunday’s statement said.
Heavy rain this month swept away tens of thousands of tents in the territory, leaving many without shelter.
“This situation is entirely reversible”, Sunday’s statement said, “and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in”.
More than 1.9 million people have been displaced in Gaza, according to the United Nations, many of them suffering displacement multiple times.
As of November 1, the Global Shelter Cluster, a humanitarian organisation that coordinates with the Red Cross and the UN, estimated that Gaza residents need at least 1.7 million mattresses and 121,000 tents to face this season’s cold, rainy weather.
During Israel’s genocidal war, entire neighbourhoods and cities were levelled. Some of the structures that remain are unstable.
In September, at least 20 people were killed when a building they were sheltering in collapsed.
Shelter is only one factor in the ongoing humanitarian crisis, though.
Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been plunged into poverty since Israel began its genocidal war. The price of basic goods has soared as incomes have shrunk due to the war and Israel’s tightened siege.
Sunday’s statement follows a similar appeal from the UN’s Humanitarian Country Team of the Occupied Palestinian Territory on Friday.
“The devastating impact of the latest rainstorm in Gaza was preventable,” the team wrote.
“Children and adults were killed, critical services suspended, and thousands of family shelters flooded, swept away, or torn apart – not by the storm alone, but by policy decisions.”
The European Union also released a statement on Saturday, expressing “grave concern” over the humanitarian crisis.
It urged Israel to “allow immediate, unimpeded access” to humanitarian aid and “reopen all Gaza border crossings”.
Sunday’s joint appeal also called on all parties to “implement the Comprehensive Plan for Gaza”, a plan unveiled in 2025 that called for an immediate ceasefire between Israel and Hamas.
But attacks have continued, including on Thursday, when an Israeli air strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed six Palestinians.
Israel is the subject of an ongoing genocide case before the International Court of Justice, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, have been issued arrest warrants by the International Criminal Court.
They have been accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Israel's data shows it allowed half of the promised aid trucks into Gaza
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Elis Gjevori
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Israel's data shows it allowed half of the promised aid trucks into Gaza
Israel has failed to meet its commitments under the Gaza ceasefire deal, allowing in only around half the agreed volume of humanitarian and commercial goods each month since March, Israeli military data shows.
Data obtained by Haaretz newspaper showed a growing shortfall in food deliveries to Gaza, alongside severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair damaged infrastructure. Torrential rains have flooded displacement camps, leaving hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in increasingly dire conditions.
Under the ceasefire deal, Israel pledged to allow 4,200 vehicles carrying humanitarian and commercial goods into Gaza each week, equivalent to roughly 18,200 a month.
Deliveries were to include food, fuel, medical supplies and equipment, shelter materials and equipment to repair essential infrastructure.
Data supplied by the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (Cogat) to the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) show that Israel allowed about 4,700 trucks into Gaza in March, rising to 5,300 in April and more than 9,600 in May.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Mirra Andreeva holds nerve against Svitolina to win WTA Finals for first time
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Tumaini Carayol
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Mirra Andreeva had put herself on the brink of securing another effortless, straightforward set in one of the biggest finals of her career when she momentarily balked. Serving for the first set at 5-4, Andreeva nervously opened the game with two dire double faults before spraying two further unforced errors to hand over the break.
There have already been many times in Andreeva’s young career when similar sequences triggered epic, dramatic collapses, so prone the 19-year-old has been to losing her composure when things do not go her way. This time, she betrayed no negative emotions at all. Andreeva immediately retrieved the break and regained her momentum as she marched to a monumental victory, defeating Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win the WTA Finals at Indian Wells for the first time.
This is the perfect end to a year in which Andreeva won her first grand slam title at Roland Garros and established herself as one of the leading players of her generation. She will rise to a new high ranking of No 2 and she will sit just 293 points behind Elena Rybakina, who starts her 2027 season by attempting to defend the Australian Open title. Andreeva has put herself in the perfect position to attack the No 1 ranking at the beginning of the year.
Andreeva is also only the third player, after Serena Williams and Iga Swiatek, to win the WTA Finals without dropping a set and she is also the third teenager to win the title on her debut, after Chris Evert and Maria Sharapova. “It feels amazing to be part of this amazing group of people. I’m super privileged to put my name in that group. I’m really thankful to my team for helping me work every day, for pushing me to my limits, for forcing me to do stuff when I don’t want to do anything,” she said.
It was just eight months ago that Andreeva, the defending champion, departed these very courts at Indian Wells tearfully screaming “fuck you all” to the crowd as she suffered a total meltdown after losing in the second round to Katerina Siniakova. Her varied, intelligent game and excellent athleticism has never been an issue; the key to Andreeva’s breakthrough success this year has been her improved composure and emotional control in pressure-filled scenarios where she was previously prone to losing control.
Alongside her trophy and prize money, Andreeva earned a brand new Mercedes car as a result of her victory. Asked by Billie Jean King, who handed over the trophy, whether she can actually drive, Andreeva sheepishly admitted that she still does not have her licence. “This is an amazing motivation for me to get my drivers licence as fast as I can,” she said. “I still want to just try it, even give it a little spin, at least a couple of metres. If not, then, look, I have one, two, three, four, five people in my team who will drive and I can be a passenger princess for life.”
In a final between the top Russian and Ukrainian tennis players, the trophy ceremony required some thoughtful stage management. As she and all other Ukrainian tennis players have done since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Svitolina opted not to shake hands with Andreeva or take any trophy photos with her. After her runner-up speech, Svitolina opted to depart the stage and sit by the side of the court. However, when Andreeva congratulated Svitolina for her tournament and season, Svitolina did nod in acknowledgment of her words.
This was actually the second time this week that Andreeva and Svitolina found themselves across the net for each other. On Monday, Andreeva started her tournament by dismantling Svitolina 6-4, 6-0 in their opening round-robin match, a victory that set the tone for Andreeva’s blistering run through the draw. She closed it with her fifth spectacular performance of a week that has taken her career to new heights.
Elsewhere, the men’s world No 1, Alexander Zverev, opened the ATP Finals in Turin with a solid 6-4, 6-4 win over Rafael Jódar. In the second match of the day, the third seed, Ben Shelton, continued his good form by defeating his close friend Arthur Fils, the sixth seed, in an intense, bruising encounter, winning 6-2, 3-6, 6-3.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: US Treasury chief calls for outsider to lead embattled tech firm Nvidia
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US Treasury chief calls for outsider to lead embattled tech firm Nvidia
Scott Bessent gives Nvidia’s board 10 days to show the company’s compliance with US export controls.
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for an outsider to take the helm at Nvidia, the California-based technology giant that has faced scandal over its former chief executive, Jensen Huang.
Speaking on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures programme, Bessent said the company should look beyond its own ranks for Huang’s successor.
“This makes me think that, as the board conducts a search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company,” Bessent told Fox News. “Just [with] what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shake-up.”
Bessent’s comments come three days after Huang stepped down on Thursday, following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a woman US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia plays a leading role in producing chips and other computing components for artificial intelligence (AI).
As a result, the company has been at the centre of a technology race between the US and China, with the two superpowers competing for dominance in the growing AI sector.
Huang was long a key figure at Nvidia, as one of the company’s cofounders. Since 2025, he has also cultivated a close relationship with the second administration of US President Donald Trump.
In August 2025, for instance, Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen restrictions on the sale of H20 microchips to China, in exchange for the US government taking 15 percent of the sales.
But in late October, The New York Times revealed Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s clients.
The report cited unnamed US intelligence agents who believed Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to help the country’s firms navigate US chip restrictions.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Beijing has denied the allegations, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims. She reportedly left Megaspeed in 2025.
Tightening chip controls
For his part, Jensen Huang had long maintained that wider access to US technology would help Washington preserve its edge in the global AI race.
Bessent, however, questioned whether Nvidia had turned a blind eye to potentially illicit chip sales to bolster its financial results.
In Sunday’s television appearance, Bessent suggested a 10-day deadline for the company to show its compliance with US export controls.
“I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel,” Bessent said.
“I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?”
The controversy has encouraged a bipartisan push in Congress to tighten controls on US chip exports to China.
Lawmakers, including Republican Senator Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, have sought to use the annual end-of-year defence bill to close loopholes that Chinese companies can exploit to obtain advanced US-designed semiconductors.
But Bessent questioned the need for new laws, telling Fox News host Larry Kudlow that Washington’s existing export controls were sufficient but needed better enforcement.
“I don’t think we need the legislation,” he said. “We have all the rules we need; we just need them enforced.”
A new leader for Nvidia?
Since Huang’s departure, rumours have swirled about who might replace him at Nvidia’s helm.
The company’s board has floated Rene Haas, the chief executive of the semiconductor firm Arm Holdings, as a possible successor to Huang, according to the Financial Times.
Haas is no stranger to Nvidia, having spent several years at the company before joining the British chip designer.
Trump, meanwhile, has named former Apple chief executive Tim Cook as a potential candidate.
In a post on Truth Social on Thursday, Trump praised Huang’s work at Nvidia and said Cook was an ideal candidate to replace him.
“A Legend replaces a Legend,” Trump wrote.
But the Financial Times has suggested Huang may seek to return to his top-level post. In a report on Sunday, the publication said unnamed allies of his are rallying Silicon Valley executives to support his return to the company.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” one source told the Financial Times.
Currently, chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading Nvidia on an interim basis.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/pornograph.title: En Angleterre, des élèves veulent interdire l’utilisation de l’uniforme scolaire dans le porno
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/pornograph.author: Nadège Dubessay
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/pornograph.text:
Un groupe d’adolescentes anglaises d’un club de lecture féministe entend mener jusqu’au Parlement son combat pour interdire l’utilisation de l’uniforme dans l’industrie pornographique.
Dans ce collège au sud-est de l’Angleterre, certaines élèves du club de lecture n’ont plus vraiment le temps de lire. Depuis un an, les quinze adhérentes du petit club féministe de l’institut Cooper School, dans l’Oxfordshire, alertent et mènent campagne par tous les moyens contre la sexualisation des élèves, notamment dans l’industrie pornographique, via l’utilisation de leurs uniformes scolaires.
Elles entendent bien désexualiser ce qu’elles voient tous les jours, « pour que les mineures ne soient pas vues pour autre chose que des mineures », revendiquent-elles. Avec l’aide d’une professeure d’anglais, elles ont lancé une pétition et comptent bien porter les signatures et leurs propositions jusqu’au Parlement.
Élus de tous bords, mais aussi académiciens et associations ont été interpellés en ce sens. « Pourquoi sexualiser ce qui est censé protéger les élèves contre le harcèlement scolaire ? », résume dans une vidéo Kristan O’Flynn, la professeure d’anglais. L’objectif : que l’uniforme cesse d’être associé à l’érotisme, comme c’est aujourd’hui le cas dans l’industrie de la pornographie.
Déjà, en 2022, une pétition lancée par un autre club féministe du collège Sandbach High School, dans le Cheshire, avait été adressée au Parlement afin d’interdire la vente des uniformes scolaires dans les sex-shops.
Face aux violences sexistes et aux inégalités, l’information est une force
Ce que le patriarcat voudrait banaliser, invisibiliser ou réprimer, nous tenons à le documenter : les violences sexistes et sexuelles, les inégalités de salaire, les droits attaqués, les luttes féministes. Les vies bouleversées et les résistances collectives.
Ce journalisme demande du temps, des moyens, de l’écoute et de la rigueur. À l’Humanité, nous voulons le porter avec constance et détermination.
Aidez-nous à faire entendre ces voix. Soutenez l’égalité.

https://taz.de/Auch-Maenner-weinen/!6230.author: Jasper Nicolaisen
https://taz.de/Auch-Maenner-weinen/!6230.text:
Auch Männer weinen: Treptow Trashmetal
Warum nur weint der Mann im Auto? So wundert sich der freundliche Fremde. Wir werden es wohl nie erfahren.
T ief in Adlershof, wo die Novembersonne vermessen und sozialpädagogisch versorgt wird, von technisch-naturwissenschaftlichen Studiengängen der Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin und vom Jugendamt Treptow-Köpenick, da parkt zwischen weißen Konferenzwürfeln und herbstverfärbten Bauland-Wiesen, zwischen Asia-Imbissen für die Mittagspausen und Live-Love-Laugh-Cafes für Sozialarbeiterinnen, die zwischen zwei Terminen rauchen und pinkeln müssen, ein glatter schwarzer Audi.
Gedämpft durch die käferglänzende Karosserie dringt Trash-Metal heraus. Das Chassis wackelt im Blastbeat und eine Art Stimme oder dergleichen kreischt wie tausend cthulhuide Keilriemen. In dieser Hockdruckkammer kosmischen Grauens, inmitten des zweckmäßigen Stadtteils, sitzt ein junger Mann in tadellosem Anzug, befingert seinen Schlips und heult hemmungslos. Er merkt, dass wir ihn ansehen und schaut beiseite, aber es schüttelt ihn so sehr, dass keine Tarnung geht.
Er legt den Kopf aufs Lenkrad, mitleidheischend: Wir sollen so tun als wäre nichts. Den Wunsch erfüllen wir ihm, fragen uns aber im Weitergehen schon, was da los ist. Ging ein Forschungsantrag nicht durch, hat die Freundin die Postdoc-Stelle im fernen Indien angenommen? Hat die Sachbearbeiterin auf Sorgerechtsentzug entschieden oder hat es mit dem Pflegekind doch nicht gepasst? Nur, weil einer Anzug trägt, muss es ja nicht gleich um einen geplatzten Baudeal rund um eine der windigen Wiesen gehen. Wir werden es nicht erfahren. Treptow-Köpenick ist groß.
In der Platte schreien sie es raus, in der köllnischen Vorstadt hören es die Nachbarn und hier wird es im Auto an Kulturarbeiter delegiert, die aus den Tiefen der Selbstausbeutung gurgeln. Metal ist ja heute derart kulturell aufgewertet, das ist was für Leute, die jetzt an die kindness of strangers denken.

https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.title: Photos: Pope Leo visits Peru’s Amazon and Andean regions during 12-day tour
https://www.aljazeera.com/gallery/2026/1.text:
In Pictures
Photos: Pope Leo visits Peru’s Amazon and Andean regions during 12-day tour
The pope calls for the preservation of Indigenous traditions in Peru as he wraps a 12-day tour in Latin America.
Pope Leo XIV has criss-crossed Peru on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour, making stops in the Andean highlands and the Peruvian Amazon.
Sunday marked the last full day of his trip, which has seen him visit Uruguay and Argentina already.
The pontiff spent the morning in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire, delivering a speech at the Indigenous fortress of Saqsaywaman.
In his remarks, Leo praised the region’s traditional festivities and processions, which often blend Indigenous and Catholic spirituality.
“The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way,” he said.
Huge crowds also packed Cusco’s central Plaza de Armas to greet Leo. Though born in the United States, Leo acquired Peruvian citizenship in 2015, after living in the country for years and later becoming the bishop of Chiclayo, a major city in the north.
Leo is the first Peruvian citizen to become pope.
The visit to Cusco, a high-altitude city some 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested the 71-year-old pope’s stamina as he continues to recover from lung cancer surgery.
Leo, however, has shown no sign of fatigue since his 12-day, three-nation South American trip began on November 6.
In the afternoon, Leo flew to Pucallpa, a city near Peru’s eastern border, on the banks of the Ucayali River.
Pucallpa is considered a gateway to the Peruvian Amazon, and during his stay, Leo reinforced his late predecessor Pope Francis’s teachings on protecting the environment.
He also denounced the violence faced by Indigenous land defenders, who use their advocacy to confront deforestation, pollution and the threat of Indigenous expulsion.
“Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said. “The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice.”
Indigenous communities have long been threatened by illegal mining, deforestation and other forms of exploitation. Mining has also led to a water crisis in Peru, with pollution leading to an increased risk of heavy metal poisoning.
Leo is expected to return to Rome on Monday.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: NFL roundup: Cousins wins on Vikings return; Hutchinson injures knee celebrating sack
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Minnesota Vikings 24-10 Green Bay Packers
Kirk Cousins threw two touchdown passes to start his second stint with Minnesota (7-2) and Levi Drake Rodriguez had two of the Vikings’ eight sacks in a victory over the Green Bay Packers (6-4). Cousins went 21 of 31 for 207 yards just five days after rejoining the Vikings, who acquired him from the Las Vegas Raiders at Tuesday’s trade deadline. The last time Cousins had played at Lambeau Field or suited up for the Vikings, he tore his achilles tendon in a 24-10 Minnesota victory on 29 October 2023. Cousins rejuvenated an offense that had stalled under quarterbacks Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz.
New England Patriots 10-35 Detroit Lions
Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St Brown caught two touchdown passes in his German homecoming and Jahmyr Gibbs ran for 153 yards and two scores in a win over the New England Patriots, who lost quarterback Drake Maye to an ankle injury on their opening drive.
The Lions (7-2) have won five straight games but also lost edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson, who appeared to hurt his knee while celebrating the sack that knocked Maye out of the game. NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo later reported that the injury is believed to be serious.
We’ll know more when we get back in the States,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said. “Anytime you lose a player like that and you don’t know the entirety of it ... it hurts a little bit.”
Jared Goff threw three touchdown passes, along with two interceptions, completing 20 of 31 passes for 303 yards. St Brown caught a 56-yard touchdown pass in the first quarter to give Detroit a 7-3 lead. And his 28-yard TD reception – after teammates pushed him over the goalline in a scrum with Patriots defenders – made it 28-3 in the third quarter
The Patriots (5-5) have lost back-to-back games and three of their past four.
Buffalo Bills 31–12 New York Jets
Josh Allen runs for two touchdowns and throws a TD pass to DJ Moore to lead the Buffalo Bills to victory over the New York Jets. The win marks the Bills’ best start in 35 years, putting them at 8-1. James Cook’s 74-yard TD run in the fourth quarter helps seal the game. Jets quarterback Geno Smith leaves twice, first to be evaluated for a head injury and then with an ankle injury. Rookie Cade Klubnik steps in but the Jets manage only four field goals by Jason Sanders. The Jets (2-8) have lost five straight.
Kansas City Chiefs 35–13 Atlanta Falcons
Patrick Mahomes threw five touchdown passes, including one to newly acquired Josh Downs and two to rookie Emmett Johnson, and the Kansas City Chiefs (7-2) beat the struggling Atlanta Falcons (3-7) to move into a first-place tie in the AFC West. The Chiefs leaned on Johnson at running back after ruling out Kenneth Walker on Saturday because of a groin injury. Johnson had 22 carries for 101 yards and six catches for 70 yards in his first start. Mahomes completed 22 of 35 passes for 348 yards. Cyrus Allen and Andrew Armstrong each had his first career touchdown catch.
Jacksonville Jaguars 40–23 Tennessee Titans
Trevor Lawrence threw for 352 yards and three touchdowns, and the Jacksonville Jaguars pushed their winning streak to three games by defeating the Tennessee Titans. Parker Washington had seven receptions for 152 yards and a touchdown, Bhayshul Tuten rushed for 88 yards and a touchdown and Cam Little kicked four field goals as the Jaguars improved to 7-2. Cam Ward completed 28 of 39 passes for 231 yards and two touchdowns with an interception for the Titans (1-8), who dropped to 0-5 at home. Tennessee’s Joey Slye kicked field goals at 53, 54 and 50 yards. He also forced a fumble with a tackle on kickoff coverage, though the Jaguars recovered the ball.
Houston Texans 24–27 Cleveland Browns
Quinshon Judkins’ touchdown run with 53 seconds left capped a game-winning drive as the Cleveland Browns scored a comeback win over the visiting Houston Texans. The Browns (6-4) overcame a 17-point first-half deficit, grabbed a lead then lost it before Judkins rumbled in from five yards to end a 49-yard drive, allowing the AFC North team to win for the first time in three outings and improve to 4-0 at home. All six of the Browns’ wins have come on game-winning drives in the fourth quarter. Deshaun Watson beat his former team for the second time by going 25-for-40 for 312 yards with an interception. He rushed for 49 yards and a touchdown on eight carries. Harold Fannin Jr caught seven passes for 91 yards, including a 30-yarder to set up Judkins’ score. CJ Stroud was 20-for-38 for 211 yards with three touchdowns and an interception for the Texans (3-6). Nico Collins had nine catches for 94 yards and a score.
Miami Dolphins 22–24 Indianapolis Colts
Seth McGowan and Jonathan Taylor combined for 160 rushing yards and a touchdown to help the Indianapolis Colts hold off the visiting Miami Dolphins. Taylor ran for 83 yards on 16 carries and McGowan ran for 77 yards and a second-quarter touchdown on 12 carries as the Colts (3-7) snapped a five-game losing streak. Indianapolis’ defense made just enough key plays to thwart a late comeback attempt and hand the Dolphins (1-8) their third loss in a row. Kyle McCord completed 17 of 32 passes for 209 yards in his first NFL game as he started for Malik Willis, who was placed on injured reserve Tuesday.
Carolina Panthers 20–17 New Orleans Saints
Chuba Hubbard gained 172 yards from scrimmage and ran for two touchdowns, and Ryan Fitzgerald’s 54-yard field goal as time expired lifted the Carolina Panthers (4-5) to victory over the New Orleans Saints (3-6) with the NFC South Division lead at stake. The winning kick came after Saints cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry was called for a 30-yard pass interference penalty that gave Carolina the ball on the New Orleans 36-yard line with 21 seconds left. Hubbard rushed for 92 yards, and also gained 80 yards on five catches for Carolina, which improved to 4-5 despite committing 17 penalties for 152 yards. Alvin Kamara scored two short TDs for the Saints. New Orleans turned the ball over twice.

https://taz.de/Emma-Aicher-gewinnt-Slalo.title: Emma Aicher gewinnt Slalom in Finnland: Ein verdientes Rentier
https://taz.de/Emma-Aicher-gewinnt-Slalo.author: Elisabeth Schlammerl
https://taz.de/Emma-Aicher-gewinnt-Slalo.text:
Emma Aicher gewinnt Slalom in Finnland: Ein verdientes Rentier
Emma Aicher gewinnt den ersten Weltcup-Slalom des Winters in Levi, Finnland. Überraschend kommt das nicht, schließlich wurde sie in Schweden ausgebildet.
D as Rentier musste ein bisschen in der Kälte warten, ehe es seinen großen Auftritt hatte. Aber eisige Temperaturen ist es ja gewöhnt. Und dann war es so weit, nach der Siegerehrung für den ersten Weltcup-Slalom des Winters lernte es seine neue Patentante kennen. Emma Aicher nahm ihre Rolle ernst und hielt dem Zutraulichen Futter hin. Berührungsängste hatte die Skirennläuferin nicht. Warum auch? Zum einen kennt sie sich als gebürtige Schwedin mit Rentieren ein bisschen aus und zum anderen stürzt sich Aicher ja auch steile Pisten in hohem Tempo hinunter, was gefährlicher ist als ein enger Kontakt mit dem Bewohner Lapplands.
Zum ersten Mal seit 2012, seit dem Sieg von Maria Riesch, gab es am Samstag in Levi für eine deutsche Skirennläuferin ein Rentier. Es ist traditionell der Preis für die Siegerin beim alpinen Weltcup im finnischen Skiresort am Polarkreis. Ein Name für das Patentier hatte Aicher dann aber erst einmal nicht parat. Sie beschäftigt sich ja nicht damit, was kommen könnte, sondern nur damit, „was ich selbst beeinflussen kann“, und das ist gutes Skifahren.
Das hatte in den vergangenen beiden Jahren schon zu einigen Siegen in Abfahrt und Super-G geführt, aber im Slalom stand nicht nur Aicher, sondern der gesamten Konkurrenz zuletzt Mikaela Shiffrin im Weg. Die US-Amerikanerin hatte im vergangenen Winter neun von zehn Rennen in dieser Disziplin gewonnen, meist mit deutlichem Vorsprung, sich aber nun entschieden, die ersten beiden Torläufe des Winters auszulassen, jenen am Samstag in Finnland und den am kommenden Wochenende in Gurgl.
Aicher war dagegen erst vor einem Jahr, in Levi, zum ersten Mal auf das Siegerpodest im Slalom gefahren. An dem Ort, an dem sie auch im November 2021 ihre Weltcup-Debüt gab – und jetzt ihren ersten Sieg im Slalom schaffte, „mit zwei soliden Läufen“, wie sie selbst sagte. Aicher sprach von einem „Full-Circle-Moment“. Dass schon vor Saisonbeginn in eine Favoritenrolle im Kampf um den Gesamtweltcup spekuliert wurde, ließ Aicher kalt. Vermutlich ist sie genau deshalb so perfekt in den Weltcup-Winter gestartet mit dem dritten Platz im Riesenslalom in Sölden Ende Oktober und nun dem Sieg in Levi, einen Tag nach ihrem 23. Geburtstag.
Aichers Geburtsland ist ein Land der Slalomläufer
In Abwesenheit von Shiffrin waren andere Athletinnen als Top-Favoritinnen angetreten. Zum Beispiel Weltmeisterin Camille Rast aus der Schweiz, die einzige, die die Amerikanerin im vergangenen Winter geschlagen hat, es am Samstag aber nicht unter die besten Zehn schaffte. Oder die für Albanien startende Italienerin Lara Colturi, die schon häufig auf dem Podest stand, aber noch nie ganz oben. Wie vor einem Jahr wurde sie auch dieses Mal Zweite.
Überraschend kam Aichers Erfolg jedoch nicht. Sie hat ihre Karriere in Schweden schließlich als Technikspezialistin begonnen, wie dort alle Skirennläufer und Skirennläuferinnen. Die schnellen Disziplinen spielen dort bei der Ausbildung anders als in Deutschland und oder auch beim Nachbarn Norwegen keine sehr große Rolle. Schweden ist ein Land der Slalom- und Riesenslalomläufer, nicht der Abfahrer. In der schnellsten Disziplin gewannen bisher nur zwei schwedische Athletinnen Rennen. Anja Pärson und Pernilla Wiberg hatten aber erst zu den Besten der Welt im Slalom und Riesenslalom gehört.
Aicher startete als 16-Jährige bei ihren ersten FIS-Rennen, international ist dies die dritte Liga nach Weltcup und Europacup. Schon ihren vierten Slalom gewann sie, den fünften ebenfalls. Ehe Aicher ab der Saison 2020/21 für Deutschland startete, hatte sie auch noch einen Riesenslalomsieg errungen.
Dass sie auch auf den längeren Skiern und in den schnelleren Kursen unterwegs sein möchte, hat sie beim Deutschen Skiverband bald hinterlegt. Cheftrainer Andreas Puelacher förderte das, aber mit Auflagen: Das Hauptaugenmerk liege weiter auf dem Slalom, da müsse die Form stimmen, um sich in Super-G und Abfahrt ausprobieren zu dürfen, hatte vor drei Jahren die Vorgabe des Österreichers gelautet. Den Spagat hat sie hingekommen. Ziemlich gut sogar.

https://taz.de/Mord-im-Karnevalsverein/!.text:
Neuer Münster-„Tatort“: Mord im Karnevalsverein
„Narrenzeit“ ist ein richtig guter Trashmovie mit Feminismus und Longevity. Warum es mehr Tatorte braucht, die das eigene Genre aufs Korn nehmen.
Fürs Bunte sind im November die Narren zuständig. Im neuen Münster-„Tatort“ „Narrenzeit“ fällt einer allerdings gleich zu Beginn tot um: der Trainer der Münsteraner Gardetänzerinnen Martin Herrmann. Todesursache: vergiftete Bonbons.
Im Laufe der 90 Minuten, die in Teilen wie ein grellpoppiger Psychotrip inszeniert sind, stehen unter Verdacht: Frauen, die sich an Herrmann rächen wollen, weil er sie als Gardetänzerinnen abgelehnt hat. Die Anführerin der „Feministischen Front Münster“, die Herrmann unterstellt, in Frauen nur „tanzende, atmende Objekte“ gesehen zu haben. Die Chefin eines Longevity-Unternehmens. Und eine Echse namens Hans-Joachim.
Münster-„Tatort“: „Narrenzeit“, So, 20.15 Uhr, ARD
Die absurde Erzählweise und die entgrenzte Ästhetik, hinter der selbst die groteske Inszenierung des Professor Börne harmlos wirkt, ist das eigentliche Highlight dieser Folge: Da werden giftgrüne Bonbons auf dem Seziertisch zu rotem Sud zerkloppt. Es stehen ständig Karnevalstrommler auf der Straße, ohne Funktion. Es gibt eine völlig überflüssige Segelflugfahrt und eine überflüssig lange Kellerlabyrinthszene als Persiflage auf klassische Krimiüberflüssigkeiten und eine beatgetriebene Jazzmusik, die den Stimmungstreibersound von „Babylon Berlin“ nachäfft.
So sehr Fans der absurden Inszenierung hier auf ihre Kosten kommen so na ja sind manche Dialoge. Während die Kamera beispielsweise über den tätowierten Arm des zweiten Toten, eines Clubbesitzers, streift, sagt Kommissar Thiel: „Mit dem hab ich doch gestern noch geredet.“ „Mit dem Arm?“, fragt Professor Börne. „Mit dem Rest“, der Kommissar.
Alles nur nicht ernst
Der Münster-„Tatort“ versucht in dieser Folge mal wieder der Bierernsthaftigkeit des Sonntagabendproblemgrusels den Stecker zu ziehen und dabei trotzdem gesellschaftlich Problematisches zu verhandeln. In dieser Folge ist es unter anderem die „toxische Männlichkeit“, die nicht nur über die verdächtige Feministin, sondern auch über kleine Szenen vermittelt wird, beispielsweise wenn Professor Börne die neue Staatsanwältin mit „Häschen“ anspricht.
Es wird sicher bierernste Empörungsposts in den sozialen Medien geben, weil die Feministin nicht ganz so gut wegkommt. Wesentlich härter jedoch kriegt es die Longevity-Industrie ab. Die Problemmessage ist in diesem „Tatort“ aber absolut letztrangig. Genießen Sie einfach den Trashfaktor.

https://taz.de/Kuenstliche-Intelligenz-i.title: Künstliche Intelligenz in der Medizin: In die Apotheke statt zum Hausarzt
https://taz.de/Kuenstliche-Intelligenz-i.author: Daniela Barth
https://taz.de/Kuenstliche-Intelligenz-i.text:
Künstliche Intelligenz in der Medizin: In die Apotheke statt zum Hausarzt
Eine KI-Avatarin fragt in der Apotheke die Beschwerden ab, bevor ein Arzt per Video berät: Entlastet das Praxen oder ist es ein überflüssiges Experiment?
Freitag, kurz nach 16 Uhr. Niels, 47, Landschaftsgärtner, tritt in Arbeitskleidung an den Tresen einer Apotheke im niedersächsischen Rotenburg. Er klagt über Ohrenschmerzen, vermutlich eine Mittelohrentzündung, und bittet um etwas Stärkeres. Doch das gibt es nur auf Rezept, und sein Hausarzt hat längst geschlossen. Bliebe die Notaufnahme in der örtlichen Klinik, wo er jetzt lange warten müsste. „So viel Zeit habe ich schlicht nicht“, sagt er. Eine Sechs-Tage-Arbeitswoche sei für ihn normal. Apotheker André Große bietet ihm eine Videosprechstunde an, sofort. „Davon habe ich noch nie gehört“, ist Niels überrascht.
Nach kurzer Einweisung sitzt er allein in einer Kabine vor einem Monitor. Eine Frauenfigur fragt ihn nach seinen Beschwerden, wie schwer, links oder rechts, Notfall oder nicht? Angaben wie Brustschmerzen, Atemnot oder Sehstörungen können lauten Alarm auslösen, damit niemand ungesehen einfach geht und draußen umkippt. Dann darf Niels frei erzählen, in 58 Sprachen könnte er das machen. Ohne Eile, niemand hört zu. Seine Gesundheitskarte wird verschlüsselt ausgelesen, die Daten gehen erst an den Hausarzt, als der sich nach etwa zehn Minuten zuschaltet.
Der Arzt fragt nicht: „Was haben Sie denn?“ Stattdessen fasst er die Angaben zusammen, stellt ein E-Rezept aus und rät Niels, bei ausbleibender Besserung am Montag in eine Praxis zu gehen. Keine 20 Minuten dauert das Ganze. Als Niels draußen ist, wartet die Nächste: eine Mutter mit unruhigem Kind, akute Beschwerden, kein Arzt erreichbar, die Notaufnahme will sie meiden.
Avatar ist betont mädchenhaft
Die Frauenfigur auf dem Bildschirm ist eine künstliche Intelligenz namens Symptox, eine digitale Anamneseassistentin der Hannoveraner Hanntech GmbH. Der Avatar ist betont mädchenhaft. In psychologischen Tests, sagt deren Schöpfer Andreas Noack, fanden die meisten Testpersonen diese Figur am vertrauenerweckendsten.
Noack hat Hanntech 2006 gegründet. „Ich bin Erfinder, kein Entwickler“, sagt er. „Wir digitalisieren analoge Prozesse.“ Den Anstoß für Symptox gab ein Kinderarzttermin mit seiner Tochter: Der Papierbogen für die Anamnese, ein durch und durch analoger Prozess, müsste doch barrierefreier auszufüllen sein, dachte sich Noack. Und der Hausärztemangel vor allem im ländlichen Raum „bringt eine Mangelressource mit sich: Zeit“. Mit der vorliegenden Anamnese kann der zugeschaltete Hausarzt sofort entscheiden.
Seit 2024 ist die assistierte Telemedizin rechtlich geregelt, doch über die Vergütung konnten sich Apothekerverband und GKV-Spitzenverband lange nicht einigen. Im April 2026 entschied dann die Schiedsstelle, am 1. Juli trat das Apothekenreformgesetz in Kraft, seitdem läuft der Rollout von Symptox. Die Hausärzte loggen sich für Schichten ein. Sie sehen zuerst Fälle im Umkreis von 50 Kilometern, nicht aber, aus welcher Apotheke sie kommen. Dann entscheiden sie, ob sie sie annehmen. Im Pool sind laut Noack derzeit rund 300 Hausarztsitze, etwa 180 davon in Norddeutschland.
Einer von ihnen ist der Scheeßeler Allgemeinmediziner Jan Gerlach. Er hat den Rollout als eine Art Pilotarzt begleitet. Die Digitalisierung der Medizin nennt er sein „großes Hobby“, und so ist er mit Noack in Kontakt gekommen. „Ich mache bei Symptox mit, weil ich den Nutzen bereits aus meiner eigenen Praxis kenne“, sagt er. Dort gehört Telemedizin zum Alltag.
Jan Gerlach, Allgemeinmediziner aus Scheeßel
Bei Videovisiten im Altenheim schaltet er sich mit Patient und Pflegekraft vor Ort zusammen, Untersuchungen lässt er in die Praxis oder ins Homeoffice streamen. Anfangs gebe es manchmal Berührungsängste, viele fürchteten, nur noch von Robotern oder KI behandelt zu werden. Die Sorge verfliege, sobald er erkläre, dass die Technik die Ärzte nur unterstütze und ein echter Arzt berate und behandle. Bei den Älteren habe er sich gefragt, ob sie damit zurechtkommen. Dann sah er seine 80- und 90-jährigen Patienten im Wartezimmer mit dem Handy daddeln.
Für ihn hat das Netzwerk einen praktischen Nebeneffekt: Es helfe ihm, die eigene Sprechstunde in der Praxis besser zu organisieren. „Ich kann mich mehr um die relevanten Fälle vernünftig mit ausreichend Zeit kümmern.“
Er weiß, dass viele Kollegen sich Sorgen machen, um die Versorgung ihrer Patienten. Seine Haltung: Der Patient solle sich dort versorgen lassen dürfen, wo er möchte. Manche Patienten hätten eben Probleme, in eine Praxis zu kommen, aber eine Apotheke im Ort. Den Kollegen rät er, sich zu beteiligen. Es gebe mit der assistierten Telemedizin in Apotheken „wirklich gute Möglichkeiten, Patienten überall in Deutschland regelkonform zu versorgen“.
Bundesweit bieten derzeit rund 300 der knapp 17.000 Apotheken Symptox an, 30 sind es in Niedersachsen, im Landkreis Rotenburg sind es aktuell vier. Belastbare Nutzungszahlen gibt es also noch nicht. Der positive Effekt zeigt sich bisher in der Lücke, die Niels beschreibt: akute Beschwerden, geschlossene Praxen, volle Notaufnahmen.
Kritiker nennen assistierte Telemedizin „überflüssig“
Niedersachsens Gesundheitsminister Andreas Philippi (SPD) hält das System für zukunftsfähig, sieht Entlastung für Praxen und Notaufnahmen. Sein Ministerium verweist auf den Bereitschaftsdienst der Kassenärztlichen Vereinigung Niedersachsen, in dem sich rund 80 Prozent der Fälle bereits telemedizinisch versorgen ließen. Das Land fördere die Apotheken allerdings nicht, es handele sich um eine bundesgesetzlich geregelte Kassenleistung, bestehend aus einer über drei Jahre sinkenden Technikpauschale und einer Vergütung für die Arbeit. Das halte man angesichts der Investitionen der Apotheker in Hardware für rund 3.000 Euro und in Schulungen des Personals „nicht für unangemessen“.
Kritik kommt gleich aus mehreren Richtungen. Die Kassenärztliche Bundesvereinigung nennt nicht nur Blutentnahmen und Impfungen in Apotheken, die seit Juli offiziell erlaubt sind, „potenziell gefährlich“ – ihre Vorständin Sibylle Steiner hält die assistierte Telemedizin für „überflüssig“ und prophezeite in der Pharmazeutischen Zeitung, sie werde nicht funktionieren.
Christiane Qualmann, Vorsitzende des Hausärzteverbands Rotenburg/Verden, übt vor allem an der Vergütung Kritik: Die Reform entziehe den Praxen Honorare, mit denen andernorts Leistungen finanziert werden; es werde „nicht mehr Geld, sondern anders verteiltes Geld“, so Qualmann.
André Große, Apotheker
Für Apotheker André Große hingegen geht es um die Existenz. Für gesetzlich Versicherte ist die Sprechstunde kostenlos, aber die Apotheke erhält im ersten Jahr 30 Euro pro Vorgang, dann sinkt der Betrag sukzessive auf 21,50 Euro. Ärzte bekommen etwa 28,50 Euro. „Wir können von der reinen Logistik des Arzneimittels nicht mehr leben.“ Eine sinnvolle Alternative seien „Apotheken als kleine Gesundheitszentren“, „wie in der Schweiz oder anderen europäischen Ländern“.
Das E-Rezept, das der Hausarzt für Niels ausgestellt hat, muss nicht direkt in der Rotenburger Apotheke eingelöst werden, die freie Apothekenwahl bleibt. Indes wenig überraschend: Er löst es bei André Große ein. „Fixer geht’s ja kaum. Selbst wenn mein Hausarzt noch geöffnet hätte“, resümiert er, „hätte ich erfahrungsgemäß 45 Minuten bis eine Stunde warten müssen.“
Andreas Noacks erste Bilanz: Es funktioniere und werde genutzt, aber die Apotheken seien „noch nicht alle ausgelastet“. Apotheker Große vermutet, dass es noch Mundpropaganda brauche, bis sich der „Doc in the Box“, wie er es nennt, etabliert hat. Zum Gamechanger könnte die angedachte Pflicht zur Arbeitsunfähigkeitsbescheinigung (AU) am ersten Krankheitstag werden. Die AU könnte man sich ohne Wartezeit und Praxisbesuch in der Apotheke holen, die zugeschalteten Hausärzte dürften sie ausstellen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse

Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.title: Our five-year-old has hearing loss and may one day be blind. Here is where I find hope
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.author: Ali Stevens
https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text:
My daughter Poppy is five. She’s energetic and curious, loves dresses, books and creating new things and spends a lot of time playing with her big sister, Evie.
When Poppy was born, my husband, Ben, and I were focused on the usual joys of welcoming a new baby. A routine hearing screening showed something wasn’t quite right, although initially we were told it was probably fluid in her ears.
Poppy reacted to sounds around her and would startle if a door slammed, so we thought everything was fine. But further testing showed she had hearing loss and would need hearing aids.
It was difficult news, but we adjusted. Meeting people in the deaf community, families further along than us, made it feel far less frightening than the picture in my head. We learned about hearing loss, found the right support and started finding our feet.
When Poppy was seven months old, we decided to have genetic testing. We had been thinking about a third child and wanted to understand what had caused Poppy’s hearing loss and the chances of it happening again. We never expected what came next.
It was during Covid, so the test results came over the phone. I sat on my bed with a notepad, trying to write everything down so I wouldn’t forget. I think the only words I managed to jot down were “Usher syndrome”.
Usher syndrome type 2A is a rare inherited condition that causes hearing loss and progressive vision loss. It’s the leading cause of deafblindness in Australia and impacts about 1 in 6,000 children. Children are typically born with hearing loss, and then progressively lose their vision during their adolescence and early adulthood. There is currently no treatment for the vision loss.
The diagnosis landed like a second wave of grief.
It also settled the question about expanding our family: we decided against a third child, so we could focus our time, attention and resources on Poppy and Evie, and be ready for whatever the unknowns bring.
The guidance we were given was very broad, and it’s a bit of a blur. Essentially, it was “here’s the diagnosis, we’re so sorry, we’re here if you need us”. We have been told night vision problems typically start in the teens, and that her peripheral vision might narrow significantly around her 30s, though it varies.
For a while we buried our heads in the sand about the vision part. It felt like a problem we could tackle down the track and we’d only just started coming to terms with Poppy’s hearing loss.
With this new diagnosis, once again, we had to re-map all the things we had assumed our child would be able to do as she grew up. Would she be able to drive, study, work and travel independently? What would losing her sight mean for the choices she’d be able to make? What would it mean for our family?
There were so many unknowns.
But we’d been here before. After Poppy’s hearing diagnosis our minds had filled every gap with the worst possible version, until the deaf community talked us back down. We’d found our footing once. We knew we’d find it again.
A conference run by UsherKids Australia in Melbourne helped. A panel of teenagers and young adults living with Usher syndrome talked about their lives, some of them travelling the world, and told us what helps and what doesn’t. There were scientists, an audiologist, and advice on accessing the NDIS.
It helped us see that, while Poppy’s life will look a little different from her sister’s, she can still have friends, travel and study.
But the uncertainty hasn’t gone away. Almost five years on, Poppy’s future still riddles us with anxiety.
Nobody can tell us exactly when Poppy’s vision will begin to deteriorate, or how quickly. Right now, she shows no signs of vision loss, and she’s getting on with life like any other five-year-old. But Ben and I know what may be ahead of her. I’ve described it as a ticking clock: she can see now, but we don’t know when that might start to change.
Every parent lives with some version of this, a future they can’t control.
Parents start planning early. We imagine the “fourth trimester”: the kind of parents we’ll be, the kind of child we’ll have. For us, two diagnoses meant rewriting all of that. You can get stuck in grief, asking “why us?”, or you can shift your expectations and draw on the resources you have. We were fortunate to have the support and resilience to roll with the punches. A sleep regression passes, but this is a forever thing. So, we adapt every day, to give Poppy the best shot at thriving.
My way of coping has always been to go digging for more information, to understand what we’re facing. It’s what stops my anxiety filling in the gaps.
We don’t have a roadmap on what to tell Poppy, when or how, so we’re taking it as it comes. When she eventually has an appointment with an ophthalmologist, we’ll talk about checking how her eyes are working, the same way we talk about her ears. It isn’t something we’re avoiding. It’s just information a five-year-old doesn’t need to carry.
What gets me through is what gets every parent through: hope.
The research puts that hope firmly in sight.
Living in Melbourne, we don’t have to look far to see what medical research can achieve. In 1978, Graeme Clark and his team used their multichannel cochlear implant to produce hearing sensations in an adult with total hearing loss. That technology went on to transform hearing for people around the world. For families like ours, living with Usher syndrome, that history means a great deal.
Now we need the same progress with sight.
At the Centre for Eye Research Australia (CERA), also in Melbourne, scientists are working on gene and cell therapies for the vision loss in Usher syndrome. Until very recently, a treatment was considered impossible. Rapid advances are now putting new treatments in sight.
Recently, CERA’s head of genetic engineering, Prof Rick Liu, founded a spinout company, Adara Bio, which is developing a new RNA-editing platform called EDITRA.
Poppy’s type of Usher syndrome comes from a tiny spelling mistake in her genetic code. The faulty gene that causes vision loss is too large to fit into current gene therapies, which replace the damaged gene with a correct copy. Instead, EDITRA aims to fix the mistake by editing it with a treatment delivered to the eye in a single injection.
Prof Liu and his team are starting with Usher syndrome 2A because there’s currently no treatment available for children like Poppy. It’s still in the lab. But if it works, it could mean Poppy keeps her sight. About 19,000 Australians are affected by inherited retinal diseases like Usher syndrome, which are the leading cause of blindness among children and working-age adults.
We know there are no guarantees with research, and we don’t know whether a treatment will be available in time for Poppy. New treatments take years of work, and not every idea succeeds. But Melbourne’s experience with the cochlear implant shows why that work is worth doing: every piece of research becomes part of the chain that eventually leads to a treatment for Usher syndrome. I still believe that.
Poppy is five and has her whole life ahead of her. A cure wouldn’t change much for us today, but it would change everything about her future. It would banish the ticking clock that’s constantly there, and expand the possibilities for what that future could be.
