https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Africa CDC says Ebola outbreak in DR Congo ‘still not under control’
‘If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak,’ Africa CDC director says.
Africa’s top public health agency says the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is still not under control six months after it was declared.
“If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have,” Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told Reuters news agency on Sunday.
Since the outbreak was announced on May 15, more than 11,200 cases and 5,500 deaths have been recorded, according to government data.
Kaseya said that more than “80 percent of new cases emerge outside contact lists and over 65 percent of deaths” have occurred in the community outside health centres.
Cases have now been reported in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
“We are all in agreement today to say that this outbreak is still serious, and is still not under control,” Kaseya said.
The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which can trigger haemorrhagic fever.
It is the second-largest and second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, behind only the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. That epidemic infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.
Eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected in the ongoing outbreak, and many deaths have occurred outside treatment centres.
Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have led to a more rapid spread of the virus than in previous outbreaks.
Kaseya said coordination between DRC and donors remained a problem, calling it “a collective failure”.
Only $1.3bn of the $2.9bn pledged by donors to fight Ebola has been released, according to Kaseya.
“We are not pointing fingers,” he said, adding that Africa CDC was working closely with Kinshasa to ensure money isn’t wasted through duplication and that the DRC was working to digitise the payroll to health workers who “hadn’t been paid for months”.
Containment has been especially difficult because no vaccine or treatment has been developed specifically for the Bundibugyo strain, which kills about half of the people it infects.
Earlier this month, the World Health Organization (WHO) approved clinical trials of two new Ebola vaccines and said it expected results in early 2027.
“Transmission is slowing in several early epicentres, and clinical trials, including the Tumaini trial and new vaccine candidates, are advancing rapidly”, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote in a post on X.
The WHO said at least 3,000 people have recovered from Ebola virus disease in DRC and returned home.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Gen X is in worse health than boomers – and I have a few theories as to why | Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Emma Beddington
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
I almost choked on my bird-food breakfast recently, reading that gen Xers are in worse health than boomers. Research by the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies, on approximately 8,000 participants aged about 50 from the 1970 British Cohort Study, found that my generation is experiencing “worse physical and mental health across adulthood than earlier-born generations”.
Come on! How? We have better health education and pharmaceuticals than any previous generation, we’ve been browbeaten into cultivating our microbiomes and hitting our step counts, harassed to stand up (sitting’s worse than smoking!), jump around (protect your bones!) and pop creatine (unsure). Yet we’re still unhealthier than our elders?
Apparently: only 41% of the 1970 cohort rated their health excellent or very good compared with 50% of the 1958 lot surveyed in 2008, when they were in their early 50s. Meanwhile, a higher proportion of gen X reported having diabetes (9% v 6%) and were obese (32% v 26%). We also reported more symptoms of psychological distress.
Assuming we can discount fuzzy peach bath pearls or plaid shirts turning out to be mysteriously toxic, what’s happening to gen X? I have theories. For a start, this study uses self-reported health data. Maybe we’re more inclined to admit weakness and health worries? That might not be all bad – 10% more gen X than boomer women consulting a doctor about their mental health could, actually, reflect our greater openness rather than the fact we’re falling apart (it’s probably both).
A recent US study also found we’re the only generation currently drinking more now than before Covid. The researchers theorised it’s a stress-related hangover from the pandemic. And speaking of stress, demographic shifts mean many gen Xers are squished in a caring “triple-decker sandwich”: 56% have adult children at home (I bet all 56% are worried about their future); 34% with kids under 18 are also caring for ageing parents.
We also grew up in the golden age of UPFs. My husband’s madeleine de Proust is tinned ravioli and I remember my busy working mother gleefully buying our first M&S ready meal – chicken kiev, my madeleine. We might be fibremaxxing now, but we’re products of the era that birthed the Pop Tart: maybe the (kiev) chickens are coming home to roost?
But my strongest, grimmest hunch is that gen X aren’t special: we’re all less healthy. A 2024 UCL study found that while boomers are living longer, they’re doing so in poorer health than their parents, living with more chronic disease and a higher incidence of cancer, lung disease, type 2 diabetes and other serious conditions, a phenomenon the lead author, Laura Gimeno, described as “generational health drift”.
Down the cohorts, there’s the worrying rise in cancers among under-50s: in England, prostate cancer rates have quadrupled and bowel, kidney and uterine cancer diagnoses have more than doubled. This summer a damning report by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health warned that without drastic action, the UK is risking “raising one of the unhealthiest generations of children ever”. A King’s Fund analysis this year found that healthy life expectancy in England was more than two years lower in 2022–24 than in 2017-19.
This is compounded by income inequality (which in the UK is among the highest in Europe) and financial insecurity. Deprivation is starkly correlated with poor health outcomes across all generations – the same King’s Fund study showed a difference of almost 20 years of healthy life between the least and most deprived areas (69.2 and 49.8). In 2023, the Institute for Public Policy Research reported the UK was getting “poorer and sicker”, and while the economy is reportedly picking up, we’re still pretty poor and sick.
The gen X responders in the 1970 British Cohort Study rated health as more important than money. Hopefully our (mostly gen X) politicians feel the same and tackle the underlying issues – health and care services at breaking point, poverty, poor housing, pollution – with the urgency they need. The Centre for Longitudinal Studies started a new study this month following 30,000 UK babies. It would be wonderful if a few decades from now, as gen X staggers into decrepitude (if we’re lucky), it had good news to report.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
ASEAN, China fall short of agreeing on South China Sea code
Southeast Asian leaders also denounce violence in Myanmar and extend a ban on the country’s leader attending the bloc’s summits.
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have failed to conclude long-running negotiations on a code of conduct for the South China Sea during meetings in Manila, despite tentative agreement on about 80 percent of a draft, the Philippines’ foreign minister said.
“There is no conclusion yet,” Theresa Lazaro told reporters at the ASEAN summit on Sunday, adding that several key issues remain unresolved, including whether the code would be legally binding.
“The ASEAN countries plus China have also different views on how things are,” she added.
ASEAN and Beijing have been working on a code of conduct in the South China Sea, where they have overlapping claims, for more than two decades. The Philippines, as the current chair of the 11-nation association, had pledged to speed up the process and reach a deal by the end of this year.
Lazaro said she still hoped the code could be concluded under Singapore’s auspices, as the city-state takes over as chair next year.
Southeast Asian nations want the code to reflect international law, which some of them accuse China of ignoring. Beijing insists its actions have been lawful and professional.
China has laid claim to most of the South China Sea, clashing with the exclusive economic zones of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam, making a functional code essential to keeping tensions from escalating and managing maritime encounters.
An international arbitration tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects.
China and the Philippines, in particular, have faced off in a series of maritime confrontations in recent years.
The Philippines accuses Chinese ships of repeated aggressive actions inside its exclusive economic zone, including dangerous manoeuvres, firing water cannons and disrupting resupply missions. China accuses the Philippines of intruding on its territory.
Tensions escalated after Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022. Months of harsh words between the two countries over the sea preceded this weekend’s meetings.
Myanmar leaders still banned from summits
Separately, ASEAN extended a ban on Myanmar’s leader attending the bloc’s annual summits, saying the country failed to comply with a 2021 peace plan.
ASEAN leaders also decried Myanmar’s military and armed groups for continuing to attack civilians in the country’s long-running civil war.
Under the ban, Myanmar can be represented only by lower-level career diplomats, including at the summit in Manila. Myanmar was due to hold ASEAN’s rotating chair this year, but because of the civil strife, the role passed to the Philippines.
The stern rebuke followed a review of progress on the Five-Point Consensus for Myanmar, approved by ASEAN in April 2021 in a bid to ease the violence that erupted after Myanmar’s military seized power from the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in February that year.
The military coup triggered widespread pro-democracy protests that were brutally quashed, leading to armed resistance and a civil war that has spread over much of the country.
In Manila, ASEAN leaders expressed “deep concern” over insufficient progress in implementing the plan and urged all parties to “stop targeted attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure”.
There are “still certain bombings and displacement of Myanmar people, so step-by-step, we give it to them, how they’re going to tackle this issue, and we’ll monitor that,” said Lazaro, who is also ASEAN’s current special envoy to Myanmar.
Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, the former chief of the military, has made official visits to several ASEAN member states since assuming the presidency after elections in December and January, widely seen as having been rigged.
ASEAN has not discouraged those visits, but its leaders have emphasised that the peace plan remains “the main reference for addressing the political crisis in Myanmar”.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Toronto Tempo win WNBA draft lottery and No 1 pick with JuJu Watkins in play
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The Toronto Tempo won the WNBA draft lottery on Sunday, securing the No 1 pick in the 2027 draft and potentially the chance to select Southern California star JuJu Watkins.
The Tempo, who joined the league as an expansion team this past season, entered the lottery tied with the Houston Comets for the best chance of landing the top pick. Both teams had a 33% chance of winning.
The Comets, formerly the Connecticut Sun, will select second.
Washington had the third-best chance of landing the No 1 pick, holding the Chicago Sky’s first-round selection through a trade. The Mystics stayed at No 3.
Seattle will select fourth, followed by the Portland Fire at No 5. The Los Angeles Sparks will pick sixth and seventh, having acquired the latter selection in a trade with Phoenix. New York, Dallas, Indiana and Chicago follow, with the Sky also holding the 12th pick. Dallas, Golden State and Minnesota round out the first round.
The draft pool remains uncertain after the NCAA granted players a fifth year of eligibility. Players have until 2 April to declare for the draft, with those competing in the Final Four given additional time.
Toronto and Portland’s lottery odds were based on their records from their inaugural seasons, while those of the other five teams were determined by their records over the previous two seasons.

Pope condemns murders of Peru’s Indigenous leaders, deforestation of Amazon
The pontiff says he supports Indigenous efforts to protect their lands and demands justice for slain environmental defenders.
Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and condemned the “exploitation” of the world’s largest rainforest.
The pontiff urged Catholics on Sunday to oppose the deforestation and pollution caused by gold and oil production while meeting with a largely Indigenous audience in the Peruvian Amazon as part of his 12-day tour of South America.
The 71-year-old head of the Roman Catholic Church also expressed support for Indigenous efforts to protect their lands from illegal mining, logging and the “insatiable thirst for domination”.
“You know well the damage caused by indiscriminate deforestation and the pollution of rivers and other waters through illegal mining and oil spills,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries.
“These are not isolated accidents, but the consequences of the irresponsible exploitation of natural resources, which undermines the very existence of communities.”
He also backed their search for justice for the 57 murders that environmental groups estimate were committed from 2010 to 2024.
“Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said in the city of Pucallpa, in the Amazonian rainforest.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice!” he added to applause from the crowd.
Environmental challenges
Communities in Peru face mounting pressure from illegal logging, gold mining, coca cultivation and agricultural expansion.
According to a report published by Amazon Watch, an Indigenous rights and environmental advocacy organisation, communities that resist illicit commercial activity have faced rising violence, with 35 Indigenous leaders killed in Peru over the past 15 years.
In 2025, following a decade-long trial, Peruvian courts upheld a 28-year prison sentence for four timber merchants for the murder of four Indigenous people who opposed logging.
The most recent conviction came in August this year, when four people were jailed for up to 35 years for the 2023 murder of Indigenous leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado.
Deforestation has steadily shrunk the Peruvian Amazon, with the country losing about 200,000 hectares (494,200 acres) of natural forest in 2025, according to data published by Global Nature Watch.
While originally from the United States, Leo spent about two decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru and is also a Peruvian citizen.
The pope travelled to Uruguay and Argentina before his homecoming visit to Peru.
Leo is due to finish his Latin America tour in Peru’s capital, Lima, before leaving for Rome on Monday.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Harry Taylor
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Reports of artificial intelligence being used to sexually exploit children have risen by more than 8,400% in two years, research has found.
A report by the Edinburgh-based Childlight – Global Child Safety Institute says AI-related child abuse material, including deepfakes using “nudify apps”, had risen from about 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.
The images, although fake, can be used to blackmail children to demand money or more images.
The research examined reports of material by tech companies to the US-based organisation the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.
Prof Debi Fry, the global director of data at Childlight, said the findings showed the “shocking” level of child sexual exploitation.
The research focuses on east Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and North America. Previous studies have examined western Europe.
Fry said: “Our research reveals the shocking scale of child sexual exploitation and abuse and how rapidly the threats facing children are evolving, particularly online.
“But the findings also show where governments can make a difference. By bringing together evidence from surveys, police records and other sources, we can build a clearer picture of the risks children face, identify weaknesses in protection systems and help target resources and interventions where they are needed most.”
A report by the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) last month found AI-generated child sexual abuse material was growing online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.
IWF analysts have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the previous year. The UK-based NGO, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.
The problem had already risen in 2025, according to the IWF.
Childlight estimates more than 300 million children worldwide are the victims of at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse ever year.
It also estimates that about one in four children will be subjected to at least one form of abuse before their 18th birthday. The research also looked at offline sexual abuse reporting.
Almost a third of girls, and more than one in 10 boys were subjected to in-person sexual abuse during childhood in North America, the research found. This includes crimes such as sexual assault, rape and “upskirting”.
The recorded rate of reports and notices involving child sexual abuse material rose by 63% in the US between 2024 and 2025, compared with 18% in Canada.
Fry said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning. These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.
“While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.”
Paul Stanfield, the chief executive of Childlight, said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk.
“We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature. But there is nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse. We have the knowledge and tools to make a difference.
“We are calling on governments to recognise this as a preventable public health emergency, invest in better evidence and turn that intelligence into action. With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.”

Yemen hospital faces shutdown risk due to sege on Taiz
A hospital in the Yemeni city of Taiz has sounded the alarm over medicine and fuel shortages, warning that it is facing the risk of a shutdown if access to aid and supplies is not restored.
"For two months we have been calling and appealing to the international community, the humanitarian organisations: save Taiz, save health in Taiz, save the Yemeni-Swedish hospital. There is no fuel. We are at our last breath," said the hospital director Sami Al-Sharabi.
The Houthis have besieged Taiz for more than a month as they try to break into territory held by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
Since fighting reignited in the summer, nearly 330,000 people have been displaced.
"Save Taiz, save health in Taiz, save the Yemeni-Swedish hospital. There is no fuel. We are at our last breath." https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Founder of Guadalajara cartel dies in hospital after decades in prison
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Founder of Guadalajara cartel dies in hospital after decades in prison
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo was convicted of the 1985 murder of a US drug enforcement agent and a Mexican pilot.
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels, has died in hospital at age 80.
Local security authorities said Felix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died at about 2pm (20:00 GMT) on Sunday.
Felix Gallardo, a founder of the Guadalajara cartel, was convicted for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent, a crime that made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers.
Imprisoned since 1989, Felix Gallardo was held in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.
Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in the ensuing decades.
Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and a bodyguard for a local governor. Later, he gained a reputation as a powerful criminal capo known as the “boss of bosses”.
Felix Gallardo and others set up their cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and to forge an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar’s Medellin cartel.
His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials. His cartel also made innovations, such as using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero.
His legal battles stretched across decades. Arrested in 1989, Felix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel.
While already jailed, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar.
Camarena’s killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressured Mexico to arrest those involved.
In 2017, a federal court found Felix Gallardo guilty in the case and imposed a further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings.
His rise and fall were portrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 hit Netflix series Narcos: Mexico.
Felix Gallardo suffered poor health in his final years and was blind in one eye, practically deaf, and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence.
“Thirty-two years have passed,” he said. “That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime.”

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: Gender-diverse Australian sailors barred from US submarines despite Aukus deal, documents reveal
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Ben Doherty
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Aukus is effectively forcing the Australian navy to comply with a US ban on transgender people in the military with gender-diverse navy recruits prevented from starting a career in nuclear submarines because they would not be safe training on US boats.
Internal Australian defence force documents show transgender and non-binary sailors and officers are explicitly banned from Australia’s nuclear submarine training program because of US policies.
An internal defence briefing, released under freedom of information laws, said while ADF policy on equality and inclusion was unchanged, “US government policy is different”.
“ADF personnel undertaking duty in the US (including training) are required to comply with US policy,” the briefing said.
“Consequently, transgender and nonbinary ADF personnel and ADF career applicants are currently unable to commence the SSN [nuclear-powered attack submarines] training pathway.”
Australia, without a nuclear submarine fleet of its own, has hundreds of sailors and officers training on US nuclear submarines and on US bases.
At a women in defence event in October, Rear Adm Tish van Stralen was asked how the defence force was “managing the recruitment of gender-diverse and LGBTQ+ Australians into the nuclear submarine pathway” given the US directive.
Van Stralen, one of the highest-ranking women in the Australian navy, said the ADF was a diverse and equal opportunity employer.
But she said potential recruits for the nuclear submarine program were told the ADF was “subject to policies and laws in other countries, so we have to be very mindful”.
“We also have an obligation, a duty of care to our people, so we do not want to put our people into any sort of harm’s way or anything that might adversely affect them.
“I’m working very closely with navy at the moment and with the submarine agency around the training opportunities because it would be very difficult for me to put a gender-diverse person into that training at the moment.”
Van Stralen said the navy would seek alternative career paths for gender-diverse recruits prohibited from the nuclear submarine program. She said the UK, Australia’s other Aukus partner, had “more liberal policies” and that training opportunities “may arise in the UK”.
“We don’t want to disadvantage people because of it but we are subject to the laws and policies of the US when we are in their country.”
US moves came amid Aukus deal
The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, last year issued a directive to his department “to eliminate all diversity, equity and inclusion offices and initiatives”. He also has sought to ban transgender personnel from joining the US military – repeatedly using offensive slurs in public statements – and ordered that transgender personnel be purged from the services.
Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 – the first week of his second term as president – which banned transgender service personnel and said gender-diverse people were unfit to serve.
Announcing military cuts in September amid continued attacks on diversity, Hegseth declared that the US military would accept “no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals”.
Under the Aukus deal, it is proposed that Australia will buy three Virginia-class nuclear submarines from the US, beginning in 2032. In the lead-up to that, Australian sailors are training onboard US Virginia-class submarines and at US bases, while US-flagged nuclear submarines are porting in Australia.
Crewing Australia’s proposed nuclear submarine fleet is likely to prove one of the Aukus agreement’s most critical, sustained challenges. Virginia-class submarines have a complement of 135, more than double the crew for Australia’s diesel-electric Collins-class submarines.
Last week Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said the Aukus timeline presented the country with a significant “training challenge”.
“We just need to be training more people and that’s what we’re doing,” Marles said at HMAS Stirling, the West Australian port through which US nuclear-powered submarines have been rotating.
The Australian defence department did not respond to questions from the Guardian about the impact of adhering to the US policy directive, including how many Australian service personnel have been prevented from undertaking nuclear submarine training.
The government’s nuclear-powered submarine workforce strategy urges defence to “proactively expand the talent pool through active inclusion of underrepresented groups, including women, First Nations Australians, regional communities, and individuals who may not traditionally see themselves in technical or defence-related careers”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions
Trump has requested $50bn for upgrades, but Democratic lawmakers are asking for transparency before spending more.
Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours due to a reported equipment failure.
It was only the second time since the attacks on September 11, 2001, that such an order was given.
More than 9,000 flights were cancelled, and an estimated 1.5 million passengers were left stranded.
Officials blamed the disruptions on an upgrade gone awry. The routers used to communicate with aeroplanes in mid-flight had suddenly stopped working, and pilots were no longer able to speak on their usual frequencies.
As of Sunday, officials were still working to return the system to normal. “As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News, while acknowledging continued delays.
But the situation has led to scrutiny over whether the nationwide ground-stop could have been prevented.
While President Donald Trump has blamed a lack of funding from Congress, critics say billions of dollars have already been allocated for badly needed upgrades. The work, they say, is what has lagged behind.
Democratic lawmakers have also questioned the Trump administration’s choice of contractors to install the upgrades.
“Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years,” Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro said in a statement on Sunday.
“Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner.”
Spotlight on a defence contractor
Duffy has indicated that investigations are ongoing into what caused the malfunction on Friday.
But he has described the problem as starting at “a remote FAA location” where workers from the defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wire with fibre optic lines.
A router used for communication reportedly began to malfunction, sending out 1,000 attempts to log onto the FAA’s system every four or five seconds, overloading the entire network.
In an interview on Sunday with NBC’s Meet the Press, Duffy stopped short of blaming L3Harris.
“Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing the work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions,” he said.
Though Duffy did suggest he preferred to part ways with the company, which owns a significant chunk of the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure.
“I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network,” Duffy told Meet the Press. “I can’t cancel the network that they own, and I operate on.”
L3Harris has existed since 2019, following a merger between the Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies.
It is one of the largest defence contractors in the country, and its involvement with the FAA’s telecommunications network stretches back to 2002, when the Harris Corporation was awarded a billion-dollar contract to modernise the network’s systems.
But Friday’s mass grounding was not the first time L3Harris’s systems were involved in flight delays and problems with communications during an upgrade operation.
In November 2009, for example, the FAA’s network experienced a smaller outage as upgrades were being made to a router in Los Angeles, according to an agency investigation.
“The most notable impact to the flying public was the inability of the FAA to process electronic flight plan data,” a report explained.
“As a result, these flight plans had to be entered into the FAA air traffic control systems manually, causing the delay of over 800 flights that morning.”
In a statement after Friday’s grounding, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s current probe and had already replaced 70 percent of the system’s copper wire with fibre optics.
“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” it said.
Ageing FAA infrastructure
Critics point out that many of the problems associated with the FAA’s telecommunications systems predate L3Harris’s involvement and stem from ageing infrastructure.
The FAA has aimed for years to replace some 5,170 lengths of copper wiring dating to the 1960s, which is used by routers and other communication gear.
Ageing copper, however, is just one of the tech problems the FAA faces.
In a September report, the Government Accountability Office, an independent agency tasked with reviewing government departments, highlighted a series of areas in dire need of upgrades.
Computers used by air traffic controllers to display key information like flight approach paths and aviation warnings were using obsolete hardware, including screens from the 1980s and floppy disk drives.
Thousands of radios and specialised switches that allow radio communication over phone lines also rely on obsolete technology that is no longer manufactured.
The agency had been forced to look for replacement parts on the online marketplace eBay, according to Duffy.
The Government Accountability Office also pointed to the continued use of paper flight strips, slips of paper printed for each flight coming into an air traffic controller’s area of responsibility.
Those documents help decide how to coordinate movements like takeoffs and landings so planes do not collide. But the print-out system has already caused dangerous situations.
In August 2023, for instance, a printer used to print flight strips at San Diego International airport jammed. As air traffic controllers tried to fix it, a Southwest Airlines aircraft almost hit a Cessna jet by about 30 metres (100 feet).
Before Friday’s incident, the last national ground stop happened in January 2023, after the FAA’s Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) system stopped working.
Built in 1985, the NOTAM system was responsible for sending emergency messages out about dangerous weather, congestion or other safety issues.
Its failure prompted the FAA to undertake a major review. The Government Accountability Office ultimately found that, out of the 138 systems the FAA relied on, 51 were unsustainable, and another 54 were potentially unsustainable because of ageing technology.
Fifty-eight of those systems, according to the accountability office, had a critical impact on the safety of air traffic in the US.
Unmet upgrades and lack of oversight
In September, the Government Accountability Office reported that the FAA had failed to meet at least four of its 11 recommendations for modernising air traffic systems.
One reason for the failure was the complexity of the upgrades. The FAA reportedly has 11,389 individual upgrade projects on its agenda, and it has struggled to coordinate the repairs, leaving it unable to prepare for network-wide problems.
The accountability office also determined that the FAA failed to make upgrades because it was not properly overseeing work done by its contractors.
It also pointed to a lack of funding. Unlike many critical government agencies, the FAA’s budget is not mandated by law, so Congress has to approve spending for the agency each year.
Even if Congress does allocate funding, the Trump administration does not have to use all of the money right away, and Democrats have pointed to unspent funds as part of the problem.
Though Congress allocated $12.5bn for the FAA’s upgrades in 2025, the Trump administration has only committed to spending $4bn of that sum. Only approximately $1bn has been spent so far.
Still, Duffy has argued that the FAA needs at least $50bn in the wake of Friday’s grounding.
Democrats like DeLauro have called that sum a “ransom without a real plan to deliver”. She urged full transparency from Duffy and the FAA.
“No federal leader should be free to do their work without Congressional oversight,” she said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Zambia’s copper boom attracts billions in investment, but who benefits?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Zambia’s copper boom attracts billions in investment, but who benefits?
Workers’ rights, environmental concerns and local businesses remain at the centre of the debate.
Lusaka, Zambia – Zambia is attracting billions of dollars in mining investment as it seeks to become a significant supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition. But as foreign companies expand operations and new projects come on stream, questions are mounting over whether common Zambians are benefitting from the country’s growing mineral wealth.
President Hakainde Hichilema said more than $12bn had been invested in Zambia’s mining sector since 2022, as the government pushes to increase copper production and attract new investors.
Leading investors include Canadian companies First Quantum Minerals and Barrick Mining Corporation, India’s Vedanta Resources and China Nonferrous Metal Mining Group (CNMC).
Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH) has also emerged as a leading investor after committing $1.1bn to recapitalise Mopani Copper Mines, previously owned by Glencore. The investment gave IRH a 51 percent stake in the mine, with state-owned ZCCM Investments Holdings retaining 49 percent.
Alongside large-scale mining projects, the Copperbelt province has also seen the expansion of smaller Chinese-owned mineral-processing plants, some sourcing ore from artisanal and small-scale miners. Their growth has raised concerns about safety standards, regulatory oversight and environmental protection.
The government has sought to restore investor confidence through tax incentives and a more predictable fiscal framework, following years of frequent changes to mining tax policies under the former Patriotic Front government, which ruled Zambia between 2011 and 2021.
Unlocking mineral wealth and adding value
To accelerate mineral exploration, Zambia is undertaking a nationwide high-resolution aerial geophysical survey aimed at improving geological information and identifying previously unexplored mineral deposits. The survey is now about 98 percent complete, according to the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development.
The government has set an ambitious target of increasing annual copper production to 3 million tonnes by 2031, from less than 1 million tonnes in recent years.
“We can do with our copper, cobalt, nickel, lithium, manganese and rare earth metals, which we now know we have in this country for our people, what the UAE has done with oil and gas for its people and their economy,” Hichilema told delegates at the Zambia Mining and Investment Forum in Lusaka on October 19.
Beyond increasing production, Zambia is also seeking to expand value addition to copper, a key material in electric vehicles and renewable energy infrastructure.
Historically, the country has exported copper cathodes to China and other industrialised countries. But the government wants Zambia to play a more active role in the global transition to a low-carbon economy by developing domestic mineral processing and manufacturing capacity.
Africa’s two leading copper producers, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Zambia, are also exploring a partnership with South Africa to develop an electric vehicle battery manufacturing industry.
“DRC and ourselves are doing something on EV materials so we can build a joint venture with South Africa, which is ahead of us in the motor industry, so that the motor vehicles produced out of South African production lines have Congolese and Zambian inputs of the EV battery,” Hichilema said.
The proposed partnership reflects growing efforts by African mineral producers to move beyond exporting raw materials and capture a greater share of the value generated by the global energy transition.
However, turning these ambitions into reality will require more than increased mineral production. It will also depend on the development of local industries, skilled labour and infrastructure capable of supporting large-scale manufacturing.
Workers question their share amid mining boom
While foreign capital is driving an expansion of Zambia’s mining sector, trade unions say local workers are yet to see meaningful improvements in their working conditions.
“Inasmuch as the copper prices are going up and we have seen an increase in the amount of investments, we are experiencing same employment conditions – things are not any better for a mineworker,” Stephen Mwaanga, secretary of the National Union of Miners and Allied Workers, told Al Jazeera.
Despite higher copper prices, Mwaanga said, mining companies were also grappling with elevated production costs, including higher fuel prices, which he linked to the US-Israel war on Iran, affecting traffic via the Strait of Hormuz.
The wider Southern African region has also faced drought conditions associated with El Nino, putting additional pressure on electricity supplies. Zambia’s heavy reliance on hydropower makes the mining industry particularly vulnerable to reduced water levels, forcing the country to seek electricity imports and alternative sources of power.
Reliable electricity supplies are critical to sustaining the expansion of an industry that is central to Zambia’s economy.
“We need to strike a balance between improving the workers’ conditions of service and the challenges that these mining companies are facing,” Mwaanga said.
The challenge for the government is therefore not simply to attract more mining capital, but to ensure that increased production translates into better employment conditions and wider economic opportunities for Zambians.
Environmental costs of mining expansion
Beyond workers’ welfare, the rapid expansion of mining is raising concerns about its environmental consequences, particularly in communities already affected by pollution.
Eugene Mulenga, a human rights defender, fears the government’s drive to increase mineral production could place enormous pressure on the environment.
In February 2025, a structural failure at a tailings dam operated by Chinese-owned Sino-Metals Leach Zambia in Copperbelt released acidic, metal-laden mining waste into the Chambishi Stream. The pollution spread downstream into the Mwambashi and Kafue river systems, raising serious concerns about water quality, aquatic life and the livelihoods of communities dependent on the waterways.
A subsequent environmental assessment by the Zambia Environmental Management Agency documented the extent of the ecological damage and the effects of the discharge on affected waterways.
The incident exposed the environmental risks associated with mining expansion and renewed questions about the ability of regulatory authorities to monitor operations and enforce environmental standards.
Other pollution incidents have also been reported at mining operations, adding to concerns about the industry’s environmental footprint.
Zambia’s push to increase copper production to 3 million tonnes annually by 2031 has therefore intensified calls for stronger environmental safeguards and greater accountability from mining companies.
For common Zambians and local businesses, the benefits of the country’s growing mining investments also remain a subject of debate.
In an effort to ensure more mining-related spending circulates within the domestic economy, the government introduced local-content regulations, which require mining companies to allocate at least 20 percent of their annual procurement budgets for core mining goods and services to local suppliers in 2026. The threshold is scheduled to rise to 25 percent after one year, with further increases planned.
The policy is intended to strengthen indigenous businesses, create opportunities for Zambian suppliers and ensure a greater share of economic benefits from mining remains within the country.
But as Zambia positions itself to become a key supplier of minerals critical to the global energy transition, the question remains whether the investment boom will deliver meaningful improvements in citizens’ lives, particularly those living and working in mining communities.
For Mulenga, the economic ambitions must not come at the expense of communities whose livelihoods depend on the environment.
“What we have discovered is that most farmers and poor people who depend directly on these water bodies near the mining sites are being affected by the increasing mining activity,” he told Al Jazeera.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Eisenkot says Netanyahu can’t remain Israel PM amid alleged vote meddling
Members of an Arab-led party were reportedly arrested before Israeli elections based on unfounded evidence from the prime minister’s office.
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cannot “remain at the helm of government for even one more minute” amid reports alleging Netanyahu’s office engaged in electoral interference.
Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel’s new government, launched a scathing attack on his rival on Sunday, just a few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government.
“The conduct of outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his inner circle poses a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 published a report earlier on Sunday alleging Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, lodged a complaint with the police commissioner’s office against members of the United Arab List (Ra’am) party on the eve of Israel’s October 27 election.
Norden reportedly directed police officers to an alleged intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office.
Based on information from the source, about 14 police officers raided the homes of three Ra’am members without a warrant and arrested them on suspicion of bribery to incentivise voting, according to Channel 12.
Netanyahu subsequently launched a campaign against Arab-led parties throughout election day. After they won a record 19 seats, he made unproven accusations of electoral fraud.
The three men were released after police determined the information from the purported intelligence source was unfounded.
The Channel 12 report also alleged that David Zini, the head of Israel’s internal intelligence agency Shin Bet, requested the attorney general’s office to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli Knesset members on election day over suspected election interference, but the request was later rejected.
“I call for an immediate investigation into the affair and for the police and the Shin Bet to immediately clarify the details that have been published,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief.
Netanyahu’s Likud party called Eisenkot’s statement “outrageous incitement” against the prime minister.
On Friday, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections to cling to power.
Netanyahu renewed his appeal to Eisenkot to form a unity government on Saturday, but the opposition leader called the plea a “bluff”.
However, Eisenkot had confirmed talks between his Yashar party and the Likud party over the proposal for a shared government.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot’s bloc has yet secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

The EEOC Is Failing Workers While Hunting for Discrimination Claims From White Men
Investigators are rapidly closing out claims of workplace discrimination so that they can search for the kinds of cases chair Andrea Lucas most wants to find.
Earlier this year, Sebrina, a direct-care worker in Pennsylvania who works in group homes assisting clients with disabilities with everyday tasks, was discussing a client’s medications with a coworker. When she told her coworker that one of the clients does in fact need seizure medications, despite her coworker’s claim to the contrary, the coworker called Sebrina a “bitch,” she recalled. Another time, that same coworker called her “colored.”
Sebrina, who asked to use only her first name because she’s in the middle of legal action, reported the incidents, as well as the fact that one of her clients told her that he was being abused by a different caretaker, to her boss. That’s when she was abruptly suspended. She was accused of not following instructions for a particular client, but she says she had been begging to get the relevant instructions for months to no avail. Meanwhile, the coworker who called her the slurs was simply told to apologize to her. Eventually Sebrina was fired on July 13 for, she says, failing to attend a meeting scheduled for July 18.
On June 29, Sebrina filed an inquiry with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the federal agency tasked with protecting private-sector workers from discrimination, claiming she had been illegally discriminated against. An agency investigator started looking into it on August 14. When an EEOC investigator investigates a case, they typically spend months probing whether the case has merit, soliciting the employer’s response and gathering documents to either pursue an EEOC lawsuit or help the employee do so. Instead, five days later the agency sent Sebrina a “right-to-sue” letter, which closed out the EEOC case without any investigation and left her to pursue justice in the courts. “It just happened so fast,” Sebrina said. “I wanted him to investigate.” Instead, she was on her own with no more information than when she had started.
Related Articles
Three sources within the EEOC, plus three employment lawyers who regularly bring claims to the agency, told The Nation that what Sebrina experienced is increasingly common. Their comments and statements from the agency’s chair demonstrate that under the second Trump administration, the EEOC, created by the Civil Rights Act of 1964, has focused on representing aggrieved white men and people with anti-trans complaints while shutting out those whom it has historically served. Since she was appointed to lead the EEOC by President Donald Trump, chair Andrea Lucas has increased pressure on agency staff to field far more inquiries without growing the backlog of cases, three agency sources tell The Nation. At the same time, she’s pushed them to spend disproportionate resources on her personal priorities. The combination of those factors means that more and more people are experiencing what Sebrina did: Investigators in EEOC field offices are rapidly closing out claims of workplace discrimination without thoroughly investigating them so that they can search for and sink time into the kinds of cases Lucas most wants to find.
Democrats in Congress can hold hearings and bring Lucas in to testify about her priorities, but they aren’t empowered to change agency policies. In fact, Trump just nominated Matt Zandi, who most recently served as chief of staff to Harmeet Dhillon, until recently the head of the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division, as an EEOC commissioner, which if confirmed will give the Republican members of the commission a quorum and majority for at least two more years. It would also allow President Trump to fire the remaining Democratic commissioner, Kalpana Kotagal, as he did with the other two Democratic commissioners, while still maintaining enough members for Lucas to set the agency’s rules and agenda.
Workers get only 90 days after receiving an EEOC right-to-sue letter to file a case in court. Sebrina spent sleepless nights googling and scouring TikTok and YouTube for someone who might take her case in time. “Any and everything,” she said. Over 20 attorneys turned her down. “I cried,” she said. “My little baby saying, ‘Mom, you got to close your eyeballs or they’re going to dry.’” With just 30 days left, she decided to go pro se and try to file the paperwork in court on her own, but she had to figure out how to get the $200 filing fee waived. Her blood pressure was sky-high from the stress; her psychiatrist recently advised her to take a break to protect her mental health. “I’m just trying to stop the timer from ticking,” she said. “It’s just a lot that’s dropped on me.”
Early last year, Lucas created a list of her own personal priorities for the EEOC—including claims from people who believe they were adversely affected in the workplace by so-called diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, such as white men who believe a woman or person of color unfairly got a promotion instead of them, and claims that are “defending the biological and binary reality of sex,” such as cisgender women who feel discriminated against for sharing a bathroom with a trans woman—and told agency officials to seek out cases that lined up with them. Prior EEOC commissioners said that violated the agency’s processes and exceeded her authority. Lucas has also prioritized religious bias and national-origin discrimination against American citizens who believe a foreign-born person unfairly got an opportunity instead of them. She posted a direct-to-camera video on X.com last year soliciting complaints from anyone who is “a white male who has experienced discrimination at work.”
In response to a request for comment, an EEOC spokesperson, “Under Chair Lucas’s leadership, the EEOC continues to deliver significant results for American workers.”
The EEOC, which has a budget of just $455 million to cover the country’s 136 million private-sector employees, has always had to prioritize some complaints over others. Before Lucas became chair, however, those priorities were determined by looking at data showing what kinds of discrimination were most prevalent, an EEOC staffer with knowledge said. “Historically, people of color and women file the greatest number of charges, because they disproportionately face discrimination in the workplace,” so those complaints were prioritized (though the EEOC has always pursued discrimination claims of all kinds). Now the determination is driven by the administration’s political priorities. But the focus on white men, for example, is “not what our body of data reflects,” the EEOC employee said.
According to The New York Times, cases from white men claiming so-called reverse discrimination have been “accelerated through the process,” and the director of at least one district (the EEOC divides the country into 15 districts) told staff that such cases should be designated as deserving the highest level of resources and time. The director also said that such cases can’t be sent to mediation—a process in which the EEOC helps try to broker a settlement—and require “special permission” to dismiss. The EEOC employee I spoke with has heard from people directly involved that Lucas has fought back against staff attempts to reach settlements in these cases because she instead wants to bring litigation. Cases involving DEI and gender identity are getting extra resources, the EEOC employee said, and are all being assigned attorneys. Lucas herself has gotten far more actively involved in them than previous chairs would get in specific cases, according to the EEOC staffer with knowledge.
And yet staff told the Times that they have struggled to find complaints Lucas wants that have merit or strong evidence. That requires them to spend even more time trying to put a flimsy case together. So complaints without merit that fall into Lucas’s priorities are now supplanting other kinds with merit, the staffer with knowledge said, and staff is focusing on the demographics of who filed the complaint instead of whether the complaint itself is worthy.
In addition to being directed to find cases that Lucas wants to focus on, expectations for field staff have been raised to unrealistic levels, the EEOC employee said. Beginning October 1, Lucas directed EEOC investigators in the agency’s field offices to complete five intake appointments every day, two EEOC staffers said. An effective intake typically takes an hour and a half to two hours to complete, the staffer with knowledge said. At the same time, Lucas and Thomas Colclough, the EEOC’s director of field management, have told the directors of the agency’s field offices that anyone who walks through their office doors must be served. The change appears at least in part to be Lucas’s attempt to make it easier for white men to access the agency. Lucas herself has assured people on X.com alleging the kind of discrimination she’s focused on that they can walk into EEOC field offices and get quick responses. In one post, she said she was “aware of & working to increase our interview availability.” In another, she said she was working on ensuring that “all field offices are equally welcoming and available to walk-in appointments.” Prior to Lucas’s becoming chair, goals for the number of intakes completed each day were set by each local field office based on their capacity, and most workers had to get initial online appointments to ensure that there was enough staff capacity for each. Outside of rare instances, employees have never before been asked to do five a day, the staffer with knowledge said.
In response to a request for comment, an EEOC spokesperson said, “Chair Lucas is proud of the agency’s efforts to serve more workers by expanding intake appointments and walk-in availability. In Fiscal Year 2026, charge inquiries reached an all-time high, while charge receipts increased 11 percent—the highest level in more than a decade. These results underscore the growing demand for the EEOC’s services and the importance of Chair Lucas’s commitment to evenhanded enforcement, expanded outreach, and ensuring all American workers understand their rights under federal civil rights laws.”
All the extra time diverted to intakes is less time that staff can spend investigating inquiries and charges or developing promising cases to litigate. “People are spending so much time putting out the immediate fires,” the EEOC employee said.
Meanwhile, staffing is at a nadir. The agency received 270,000 inquiries last fiscal year, a 9 percent increase over 2024, but it had the lowest number of staff to handle that work since at least 2005. Staffing has continued to decrease this year—the agency has just 1,693 employees to police discrimination in all private workplaces, a 26 percent decrease from its peak under President Joe Biden and down by a third since a high-water mark in 2010. Just a few hundred of those employees are the investigators who both handle new inquiries and investigate them if they become actual charges.
At the same time, aggressive goals have been put in place for making sure the backlog of inquiries and charges doesn’t grow beyond a certain length, the EEOC staffer with knowledge said, even as employees are being forced to field more inquiries. That’s led to a mass closure of inquiries—in which EEOC investigators don’t even look into a complaint and simply issue a right-to-sue letter—and the neglect of complaints with merit or even the potential to make systematic change.
“Staff are closing charges in order to meet the goals, in order to keep the inventory [of pending inquiries and charges] artificially low,” the EEOC employee said. “The agency has become sort of a right-to-sue machine.”
The impact on Americans who have experienced discrimination at work has been stark. Steve Auerbach, founding attorney at the Law Office of Steven T. Auerbach, and Rachel McElroy, an attorney at the McElroy Law Firm, say that clients have received right-to-sue letters before the agency has even asked their employers for a position statement, which is typically the first step in assessing all inquiries. Charges Auerbach has filed with the agency have been closed out incredibly rapidly. “We’re looking at days, when in the past it was months, if not longer,” he said. “It was rare for me to even hear back for six months.” One inquiry that he filed in mid-June was issued a right-to-sue letter 18 days later; another filed in early August got one in just eight days. McElroy has similarly seen clients get right-to-sue letters in a matter of weeks, while a previous case waited years.

Beginning last year, Nathan Simmons, an attorney at Kaplan Law Firm, would file an inquiry only to receive an e-mail demanding more information—information that had already been included in his inquiry on behalf of his client. The agency has sometimes ignored his response and then immediately issued a right-to-sue letter. “The new policy completely undermines the purpose of the EEOC,” he said.
“I can’t rely on them to do their job right now,” Auerbach said of the EEOC. And, he said, it’s happening even to cases that appear to have merit. “I’m seeing it in instances where it’s both clear-cut and a pretty good case,” he added. McElroy agreed that the cases getting closed out are surprising. “They’re just your average EEOC charges,” she said.
Both Auerbach and McElroy have simultaneously experienced a huge increase in calls from workers seeking legal help after being quickly issued a right-to-sue letter by the agency—the week we spoke, McElroy had gotten three, when before she would only get such calls “every once in a while.” Auerbach called it “frightening” given that workers only get 90 days to file a lawsuit after getting such a letter.
Even when the EEOC decides not to take a case, its investigation is a crucial component of getting justice for employees. Auerbach noted that he’s reluctant to file a lawsuit without having heard the employer’s side of the story—something the agency is skipping over now as it scrambles to issue right-to-sue letters. “I’m counting on that to see if this is a meritorious claim, and I’m being deprived of that,” he said. “Not every dispute belongs in front of a federal jury.” Meanwhile, without the agency’s having done any investigation of a charge, attorneys must compile all the necessary documents and evidence before the 90-day window closes, which is not always possible.
It’s already difficult for workers to find an employment lawyer to take a case like this. First, there just aren’t enough of them. “A lot of the big billboard attorneys, they’re personal injury attorneys and medical malpractice attorneys,” McElroy pointed out. There are far fewer lawyers who take civil rights cases, and those that exist can only take on so many cases at a time. Many won’t respond to every call that comes into their office.
Many workers also can’t afford to take their employers to court on their own, even if they can find lawyers. Few workers who represent themselves get a favorable ruling. If the EEOC isn’t even looking into whether to pursue their cases itself, they may end up with no recourse in a worthy case. “To be shut out and ignored by the agency that’s congressionally tasked with listening to them,” Auerbach said, “it’s insult to injury.”
“Workers that are most in need of the agency’s services can’t in fact benefit from those services and get left behind,” the EEOC employee said. “If you have no actual way to enforce your civil rights, are they meaningful?”

L’ancien journaliste de Canal + comparaît aujourd’hui devant le tribunal de Nanterre, visé par trois accusations de harcèlement et d’agressions sexuelles sur d’anciennes collègues. À la suite du documentaire de Marie Portolano, qui avait révélé le sexisme systémique dans les rédactions sportives, l’inspection du travail avait saisi le parquet.
Une véritable déflagration. Au printemps 2021, la diffusion sur Canal + du documentaire Je ne suis pas une salope, je suis une journaliste, réalisé par Marie Portolano et Guillaume Priou, fait l’effet d’une bombe. Dans un sondage réalisé à l’époque par Odoxa pour RTL, 39 % des Français.es déclaraient avoir vu ou entendu parler du film.
Durant 76 minutes, près d’une vingtaine de journalistes sportives, dont des figures bien connues comme Vanessa Le Moigne, racontent le sexisme subi dans l’exercice de leur métier, notamment de la part de collègues et de supérieurs hiérarchiques. Comme Tiffany Henne, sommée quotidiennement par son chef de révéler son orientation sexuelle, persuadé qu’elle est lesbienne. Jusqu’au jour où il l’enferme...

https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/c.title: Cartoons from the frontlines
https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/c.author: Cartoon Movement
https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/c.text:
Ruslan Pikhota is a Ukrainian frontline cartoonist and an active-duty officer in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Before the full-scale invasion, he spent 15 years working in children’s publishing in Kharkiv. He volunteered in February 2022, served as an infantryman on the Donetsk and Kharkiv fronts, and was wounded near Bakhmut. He now serves with an unmanned systems unit.
Since the spring of 2022, he has created more than 550 drawings in trenches, dugouts, ruined buildings, and between military duties. His work documents frontline life, drone warfare, fear, loss, brotherhood, absurdity, and the black humour soldiers use to endure war. His English-language book, Smile under the Roar of Cannon Fire, was published in 2025, and his drawings have been shown in Prishtina, Geneva, and Grenoble. He is now developing this archive into a three-volume visual diary of the war.
We are delighted to welcome Ruslan to Cartoon Movement! As an introduction, we asked him to select what he considers to be his ten most telling drawings made at the front lines.
Drawing No. 519 — FOUR IN THE MORNING
At the front, you constantly feel Death nearby, until it begins to seem like another member of the unit. I imagined the beginning of their day at four in the morning: the soldier starts with coffee, while Death takes a strange pet for a walk.
Drawing No. 393 — WHEN YOU’RE IN A TRENCH
A soldier sitting in a trench always wants more behind him — more artillery, more armour, more aircraft. I drew a very simple infantry feeling: you are one small person in a hole in the ground, and suddenly no amount of support seems excessive.
Drawing No. 533 — WHEN THE SKY FILLS WITH MACHINES
When I first went to war, the sky was mostly empty. A few years later, it had become crowded with reconnaissance drones, FPVs, bomber drones and interceptors. The soldier remained, but the war around him changed.
Drawing No. 564 — WHEN MACHINES BECOME PREDATORS
When two FPV drones suddenly rise in front of a soldier, they stop looking like machines. In that instant, the mind reads them as something alive — predators preparing to strike.
Drawing No. 527 — WHEN DRONES CHANGE THE FOREST
Through drone cameras, I have seen entire battlefields wrapped in fibre-optic cable, birds’ nests made from it, and our own drones caught in cables left by others. The moose is invented, but the new web spreading across the landscape is real.
Drawing No. 541 — THE SEASONS OF WAR: AUTUMN
This drawing is rooted in what happened to my platoon near Kurdiumivka in December 2022. Under fire, we dug shallow shelters in the frozen ground and covered them with plastic, but when the temperature rose to 1°C and rain began, they filled with water while shelling and assaults continued. We remained there for 19 days; when we were finally pulled back to rest, only five of the original twenty-four men were still with the platoon.
Drawing No. 419 — BOTH RIFLES JAMMED
During an assault, Amigo, a soldier of Ukraine’s 3rd Assault Brigade, found his rifle jammed just as the Russian soldier facing him discovered the same thing. Rapira, another soldier from the brigade, intervened and saved Amigo. I later turned the real incident into a short comic: the black humour is invented, but the absurdity that produced it was not.
Drawing No. 562 — PILA: A MODULAR PROBLEM-SOLVING SYSTEM
Pila, a soldier of Ukraine’s 3rd Assault Brigade, lost an arm in the war. I did not want to portray him as a victim, so I imagined his prosthesis as a modular system — a weapon, a bottle, a flower or a fork, whatever the situation requires. Dark humour does not erase trauma; sometimes it gives a person control over it again.
Drawing No. 362 — MOTHER OF GOD: OKHMATDYT
After Russia’s missile strike on the Okhmatdyt Children’s Hospital in Kyiv on 8 July 2024, I saw a photograph of a woman comforting a young patient. I redrew the photograph and transformed it into an icon of the Mother of God and Child. Some events leave no room for satire; they can only be witnessed and remembered.
Drawing No. 396 — THE FIRST DAY AFTER THE WAR
I imagined the first day after the war at the Swallow’s Nest in Crimea. Russia’s war against Ukraine began in Crimea, and it will end there; the soldier has put down his weapon, but learning to live after the war will be another long journey.

As some of you might know, Cartoon Movement is a consortium partner in Horizon Europe project DELIAH (Democratic Literacy and Humour). In addition to researching humour, part of DELIAH’s mission is to raise awareness about the role of humour in our democracies. We try to do this in various ways: by writing about it, by giving workshops and now also by making a comic about it.
Over the last few months, we have worked with the renowned cartoonist Pedro X. Molina to create a four-page comic that explains what we currently know about how humour works in a democracy.
Depending on your device, you can choose to read the mobile version (just below) or the desktop version (below the mobile version).

Hi!

Below you’ll find our latest news, cartoon collections, and the most popular cartoons of the month. Enjoy! And no newsletter is complete without promoting our other newsletter, our daily editor’s choice.
Cartoon Movement at the Dutch Journalism Festival
The Dutch Journalism Festival (Nederlands Journalistiek Festival) is taking place on September 18 and 19 in Deventer, the Netherlands. The two-day festival features panels, workshops, movie screenings and live journalism. Cartoon Movement is also present with the workshop we delevoped for DELIAH: The Importance of Humour for Democracy: Good Humour versus Bad Humour
Unfortunately, the workshop is already fully booked. If you are interested, we did a similar workshop at the International Journalism Festival in Perugia in April, which was recorded:
Also, if you are planning to visit the festival, several Dutch cartoonists will be drawing live on Saturday to see who can make the best cartoon.
The state of democracy, in cartoons
The Kettering Foundation has published a collection of international cartoons with different perspectives on democracy. The collection, with cartoons from 19 renowned cartoonists, was put together by Tjeerd Royaards (cartoonist and editor-in-chief at Cartoon Movement), Terry Anderson (executive director at Cartoonists Rights), and Patrick Gathara (2026 CFK Global Fellow).
Satire translates complex political realities into stories, images, and jokes that ordinary people can engage with. In doing so, it lowers the barriers to political participation while creating space for critique that is often less threatening to audiences than overt political argument.
Patrick Gathara
