https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: The Guardian view on press freedom: authoritarians target journalism because it matters | Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Editorial
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Lina Attalah is an influential Egyptian journalist. Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October, resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month.
Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions.
On Monday, Russia finally succeeded in silencing the famed Novaya Gazeta, which had spent decades battling growing repression. Six of its journalists, including Anna Politkovskaya, paid for their coverage with their lives. But the newspaper continued until, stripped of its newsroom, donation platforms and right to publish, it was forced to turn the lights off. (The separate Novaya Gazeta Europe, founded by many of its alumni, continues.)
These cases are part of a wider pattern. Press freedom is at its lowest ebb for a quarter of a century, Reporters Without Borders said this spring, judging more than half of the 180 countries it surveys to have “difficult” or “very serious” conditions for journalists. The rising tide of war worldwide is also increasing the pressures and dangers: the Committee to Protect Journalists recorded a new peak of 129 deaths of reporters and other media workers in 2025. Unesco said last week that almost nine out of 10 killings of journalists go unpunished.
High-quality journalism has never been more necessary in a world of rising conflict, AI slop and malicious fabrications spreading on platforms run by big tech firms who barely nod to ethical responsibilities. As Ms Attalah herself has pointed out, the disappearance of professional media organisations enlarges the space for conspiracies and disinformation.
Yet while the US previously pressed the case of threatened journalists overseas, sometimes helping to ease their conditions, it is now led by a man who has called news media “the enemy of the American people”, whose FBI raided a correspondent’s home in January, and who is currently pursuing a $10bn lawsuit against the BBC. Donald Trump has also sought to dismantle federally funded organisations which were an important source of independent reporting on many repressive nations.
This week, an appeals court panel ruled that the administration had illegally fired the head of Voice of America. VoA, Radio Free Asia and Radio Free Europe have all struggled on thanks to dedicated staff, though hugely diminished. Recent elections in Serbia, Brazil and the US are evidence that journalism, alongside activism, can stem the erosion of democracy. Thousands of people protested in Turkey last month against Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s media crackdown. Large parts of the public still want the truth and, against the odds, courageous journalists worldwide persist in finding it out and sharing it. That authoritarians target them so relentlessly only testifies to their importance.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Senator-elect Scott Colom vows to ensure Trump follows through on his promises
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
After recently becoming the first Mississippi Democrat elected to the US Senate in more than four decades, Scott Colom pledged to try to ensure Donald Trump “follows through on the commitments” he made while successfully running for a second presidency in 2024.
Colom, while being interviewed by CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday, alluded to various campaign promises made by Trump – including lowering consumer prices, halting the seemingly endless wars waged under other presidential administrations, and fully releasing files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite.
But prices for fuel and other goods soared as Trump and Israel started war in Iran in February, a conflict which has dragged on for months – and critics have said many of the so-called Epstein files have been excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures by the president’s administration.
Voters “elected me to make sure he follows through on the commitments he made in 2024,” Colom said. “Well, I want to work … to actually accomplish that.”
Colom also said that he intended to support efforts to pass legislation restricting stock trading by members of Congress, saying it was important for Americans to know lawmakers at the US Capitol in Washington DC “aren’t making money instead of looking out for them”.
“We [have] got to look out for our families – not DC families,” Colom said.
In a separate interview with NBC News’s Kristen Welker on Sunday, Colom added: “I’m not here to look out for the billionaires. I’m here to look out for working people.”
Those remarks from Colom came after he unseated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith during the 3 November midterm elections to become the first Black US senator from Mississippi since 1875 – during the Reconstruction period after the American civil war.
Colom’s triumph over Hyde-Smith occurred about three years after she blocked the former state prosecutor’s nomination for a federal judgeship during Joe Biden’s presidency, which interrupted Trump’s two White House terms. In many ways Colom’s victory punctuated a midterm “blue wave” that saw Trump and his Republican party lose control of Congress to their Democratic counterparts for the latter half of his second presidency beginning in January.
With the outcome of the US Senate race in Alaska still pending on Sunday, the seat to which Colom was elected was among eight that the Democrats had flipped in that congressional chamber. Democrats had also gained more than three dozen seats in the US House during the midterms while significantly expanding their control of state governors’ offices, igniting hopes among the party’s supporters that it could impede Trump’s agenda for the rest of his time in power.
Trump has responded to the new political reality for the rest of his presidency by reminding the public that he has veto powers which he can wield to dictate policy with respect to matters such as the Iran war.
Asked by Bash to reflect on the historic significance of his win over Hyde-Smith, Colom replied: “It says that we have made a lot of progress in the journey to have people judged by the content of their character and not the color of their skin.
“I had faith that Mississippians would give me a chance … if I could get my values out there and a vision for our state out there,” Colom said. “And – you know – Mississippi proved me right.”
Colom appeared on both networks remotely from Atlanta, where he was stranded after his flight to Washington DC was cancelled in the chaotic aftermath of Friday’s nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop.
From Atlanta’s airport on Saturday night, Colom documented the frustrations of fellow travelers on social media.
The senator-elect said one traveler even made a reference to his viral campaign ad criticizing Hyde-Smith for once suggesting those concerned about rising beef prices could opt for cheaper sources of protein.
The campaign ad’s tagline was: “Pick another protein? … I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
As the clock passed midnight at the airport, Colom wrote that another passenger made a joke at the expense of Trump’s transportation secretary Sean Duffy, saying, “Pick another flight? … pick another transportation secretary.”

https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.title: La cultura taína sigue viva: exposición en el Bronx celebra legado de Bobby González
https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/la-cultura-taina-.text:
Share This Article
Una nueva exposición en el Museum of Bronx History explora la vida del poeta, narrador y educador puertorriqueño que dedicó casi cuatro décadas a preservar la cultura indígena y desafiar los estereotipos sobre el sur del Bronx.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 4 de noviembre. Traducido por Jacob Velez. Read the English version here.
Para Bobby González, la preservación de la historia indígena comenzó cerca de casa: en la bodega de su familia, ubicada en el sur del Bronx.
Mientras crecía cerca de las viviendas públicas Melrose Houses, González conoció a personas de diferentes comunidades indígenas que visitaban el negocio de sus padres. Esas conversaciones lo ayudaron a comprender mejor su propia herencia taína y despertaron en él un compromiso de por vida con la enseñanza de la historia indígena.
Ahora, tres años después de su fallecimiento, su trabajo es recordado en una nueva exposición en el Museum of Bronx History (Museo de Historia del Bronx).
La exposición, titulada “From the South Bronx Reservation: Bobby González, Taíno Indian” (“Desde la reserva del sur del Bronx: Bobby González, indígena taíno”), inaugurada el 8 de octubre y abierta hasta marzo de 2027, explora la vida del poeta, narrador y educador puertorriqueño que dedicó casi cuatro décadas a preservar la cultura indígena y desafiar los estereotipos sobre el sur del Bronx.
Nacido en 1951, González creció en una familia puertorriqueña cuyos padres emigraron a Nueva York después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Su padre trabajó como cocinero antes de abrir una bodega en la década de 1970, donde González y sus hermanos ayudaban a administrar el negocio familiar.
Según Stephen Payne, director de la Sociedad Histórica del condado del Bronx, la bodega desempeñó un papel importante en la formación de la identidad de González.
Entre los visitantes había personas de ascendencia cherokee, quechua, lenape y de otras comunidades indígenas. Sus conversaciones motivaron a González a aprender más sobre las comunidades indígenas de América y a explorar su propia ascendencia.
Esa experiencia influyó posteriormente en la expresión “South Bronx Reservation” (“Reserva del sur del Bronx”), que González utilizaba para describir la presencia indígena en su vecindario.
Payne explicó que la expresión también reflejaba similitudes entre el sur del Bronx y algunas reservas indígenas de Estados Unidos, incluidos problemas relacionados con la contaminación y la falta de recursos.
Para González, el vecindario era mucho más que el lugar donde había crecido. Se convirtió en la base de sus escritos, su poesía y su activismo cultural.
Su viuda, María Aponte González, lo recordó como alguien que siempre mantuvo una profunda conexión con su comunidad.
“Era una persona de espíritu muy amable”, dijo. “Nunca gritaba, nunca levantaba la voz”.
Describió a su difunto esposo como una persona accesible y tranquila, a quien los miembros de la comunidad acudían frecuentemente en busca de consejos.
González cofundó la organización cultural Taíno del Norte, organizó el festival anual Bronx Native American Festival y escribió varios libros, entre ellos The Last Puerto Rican Indian (“El último indígena puertorriqueño”). También viajó por todo el país para ofrecer charlas en escuelas, universidades y museos sobre la historia indígena.
Su misión era desafiar la creencia de que los taínos, un pueblo indígena que habitaba originalmente el Caribe, incluido Puerto Rico, habían desaparecido siglos atrás.
“Somos taínos, todavía estamos aquí”, dijo Payne, al recordar una frase utilizada por la organización que González ayudó a establecer.
Payne explicó que la exposición destaca cómo la identidad indígena continúa formando parte de las comunidades puertorriqueñas, particularmente en el Bronx, donde González se convirtió en una figura importante del movimiento de revitalización cultural taína.
La exposición también llega en un momento en que el Bronx atraviesa cambios demográficos. Payne señaló el aumento del costo de vida y cómo ha contribuido a que los residentes puertorriqueños abandonen el distrito o la ciudad, lo que resalta la importancia de que los miembros de la comunidad compartan sus historias.
“Es muy importante preservar esa parte de la historia mientras todavía haya personas en la comunidad que puedan hablar de ella”, dijo.
La exposición reúne pertenencias personales, escritos y otros materiales que González conservó a lo largo de su vida.
Aponte González, quien fue cocuradora de la exposición junto con el documentalista Edwin Pagán, seleccionó los objetos de su hogar.
“Todo lo que van a ver en la exposición es obra de Bobby”, dijo.
En lugar de centrarse en cómo otras personas describían a su esposo, quiere que los visitantes conozcan su legado a través de los materiales que él mismo había creado.
Entre sus contribuciones se encontraban talleres de poesía, incluida una serie de poesía recitada que ayudaba a poetas emergentes a desarrollar sus propias voces. También utilizaba títeres y narraciones para enseñar a los niños sobre la historia indígena y sus tradiciones culturales.
Aponte González puso en marcha el Proyecto Legado de Bobby González en 2024, después de conversaciones que había mantenido con su esposo sobre la preservación de su trabajo antes de que enfermara gravemente.
Describió la exposición como un proyecto que tardó dos años en desarrollarse, con el apoyo de Pagán y el Museum of Bronx History.
Para Payne, la exposición también refleja un desafío más amplio que enfrentan las instituciones históricas: preservar las experiencias de las comunidades trabajadoras, cuyos documentos y pertenencias personales suelen perderse debido a la inestabilidad de vivienda o la falta de recursos económicos.
Explicó que las familias que han sufrido desalojos o mudanzas frecuentes pueden haber perdido fotografías, documentos y otros materiales que ayudan a contar sus historias. En esos casos, las instituciones suelen recurrir a testimonios orales e investigaciones de archivo para recuperar historias que, de otro modo, podrían desaparecer.
La colección de González ofreció una oportunidad diferente, ya que él había conservado gran parte de su propio trabajo, que su viuda ha puesto a disposición a través del Proyecto Legado.
Más allá de celebrar sus logros, tanto Aponte González como Payne esperan que la exposición anime a las generaciones más jóvenes a conocer sus raíces culturales.
“Los jóvenes necesitan hacer espacio en sus mentes y estar abiertos a aprender”, dijo Aponte González.
Para Payne, el mensaje principal es que la historia indígena no debe entenderse únicamente como algo que pertenece a un pasado lejano.
Espera que los visitantes reconozcan que las comunidades indígenas continúan preservando, recuperando y desarrollando sus tradiciones culturales en la actualidad.
A través de los escritos, las narraciones y el activismo de González, la exposición ofrece a los visitantes la oportunidad de explorar esa historia viva mediante las experiencias de un hombre que dedicó su vida a compartirla.
La exposición estará abierta al público en el Museum of Bronx History, en 3266 de Bainbridge Avenue, en el Bronx, hasta marzo de 2027.

https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.title: NYC to Expand Homeless Outreach This Winter Following Last Year’s Deadly Cold
https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nyc-to-expand-hom.text:
Share This Article
The city is earmarking an extra $25 million to hire 300 additional outreach workers and open more low-barrier shelter beds, officials announced Friday. It comes after a brutal freeze killed 18 New Yorkers last winter.
The city will spend an extra $25 million to expand its homeless outreach efforts when temperatures drop this winter—hoping to avoid a repeat of last year, when a brutal stretch of historically cold weather killed 18 New Yorkers, many of them unhoused.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the additional funding at a press conference on Monday, part of a sweeping package of winter preparedness reforms that will also include “supercharged” plows and new snow blowers.
The $25 million will go to beefing up the Department of Homeless Services’ “Code Blue” operations, which kick in when temperatures dip below 32 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.
It’ll pay for 300 additional outreach workers, including nurses, to canvas city streets and implore people to come indoors. It will also open more public warming facilities, including heated buses and vans, and to creating another 800 “low barrier” shelter beds—sites with fewer entry requirements and less stringent rules than typical city shelters.
Those beds will be in single- and double-occupancy rooms, officials said, offering greater privacy than crowded—and sometimes, dangerous—group facilities that many street homeless New Yorkers are reluctant to enter.
“When we speak to homeless New Yorkers, we will hear that if only there was a low barrier single room bed, they would then be willing to go,” the mayor said.
Mamdani was newly inaugurated when last winter’s emergency cold conditions hit—what officials say included the city’s first blizzard in a decade as well nine consecutive days of below-freezing temperatures.
The cold killed at least 18 people, including several unhoused residents.
“I wasn’t here in the heart of last winter, but I’ve reviewed it, and I know how it went, and I learned a lot from it,” said Department of Social Services Commissioner Erin Dalton, who oversees the Department of Homeless Services (DHS). Mamdani appointed her to lead the agency in February.
Dalton said DHS will be making key changes to its cold weather response this year, including having its street outreach teams adopt a “broad geographic canvassing approach.”
This breaks from previous winters in which homeless outreach teams focused their efforts on a list of about 350 known street homeless New Yorkers, visiting their usual spots and urging them to take shelter. On most nights, the city was only able to locate about 15 percent of the people on that list, Dalton said.
She added that workers are already engaging with those folks before very cold weather sets in, but that “an approach built around a vulnerable list leaves way too many people in the street that aren’t known to us, and only covers a small portion of people.”
Instead, Dalton says, outreach teams will “walk the streets, encampments, parks, and subway steps where we know the vast majority of people experiencing homelessness stay,” and “engage every vulnerable person along the routes.”
The commissioner said DHS tested this broader canvassing approach over the summer during heat waves, and were able to reach far more people—”more than 20 times as many as on a given day” compared to the summer before.
While homeless advocates applauded the additional resources, they said many of the changes are long overdue.
“These are smart responses that will save lives. But these are also well-known action steps that have been called for for years,” VOCAL-NY, a grassroots group that organizes low-income and systems impacted New Yorkers, said in a statement Monday.
VOCAL leaders called on the city to invest more in permanent solutions to getting New Yorkers off the streets, like with additional city-funded rental vouchers and supportive affordable housing.
“That’s kind of the the ideal. It’s moving people into permanent housing,” Charles King, the CEO of the homeless nonprofit Housing Works, told City Limits last week, when the organization held a funeral mass for nine of the unhoused New Yorkers who died of hypothermia in last winter’s extreme cold.
“At the end of the day, giving a person a decent place to live is what all of us need.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Letter: Ian Berry obituary
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Judith Martin
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
By the time the photographer Ian Berry persuaded the Russian officer at the Czech border in 1968 that he was on the way to an architects’ conference, he had already been commissioned to contribute to Manplan, a groundbreaking series of photo essays in the Architectural Review in 1969-70.
Conceived by the journal’s visionary and somewhat eccentric editor/proprietor Hubert de Cronin Hastings, the eight editions, each with a specially commissioned photographer and editor, were not the publishing success that he had hoped for. Nonetheless, the series has since been described as “the bravest moment in architectural publishing”.
Berry’s contribution came in the second edition, called Society and Its Contacts, otherwise transport and communications, aiming to show what society needs, rather than what will pay best.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Shanghai next? City’s art scene leans into an uncertain future
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Lisa Movius
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Shanghai is a restless city. Its impatient hustle may spare its art scene from the plateau of middle age as it navigates a crisis of transition after the Covid years derailed its late 2010s momentum. Going into Shanghai’s annual art week (10-15 November), with two established fairs anchoring an explosion of art events across the city, its galleries, artists and institutions are assessing how the city’s art market can weather China’s economic slowdown and whether the cultural momentum of the past three decades can be sustained.
Art here doesn’t operate as an isolated system; it is constantly in conversation Cherry Xu, collector
“Shanghai has so many galleries, so many museums, so many eccentric little spaces that you could come in the middle of summer and still see art non-stop,” says Lorenz Helbling, who founded ShanghArt in 1996. One of the first contemporary art galleries in China, it now has locations in Shanghai, Beijing and Singapore. The Swiss transplant says the volume of artistic activity in the city of 25 million people can be compared to New York’s, though the scene can be harder to find. “You can make a lot of fun things here.”
The city’s two large-scale fairs, Art021 Shanghai (11-14 November) and West Bund Art & Design (10-15 November), established in 2013 and 2014 respectively, set the barometer and prime the mood. So far, Shanghai’s core galleries have largely survived China’s property crash and deflationary economy, but they need young artists and new collectors to continue buoying their businesses.
Lise Li, who founded Shanghai’s Vanguard Gallery in 2004, says the city is “still in an upward phase, just growing much more slowly than before”. During art week, Li’s gallery will participate in the second iteration of the boutique fair Hangover Shanghai (11-15 November) and in Art021, while showing the artist Tang Chao in the gallery and collaborating on a group show at the artist-run 33ml Offspace. Several artists represented by Vanguard are having big moments nearby: Liao Fei will simultaneously be showing at Hangzhou’s Imagokinetics and the artist group known as Jiū Society has an exhibition at Nanjing’s Beiqiu Museum of Contemporary Art.
Though the buzz of the 2010s has quieted, Li says, “there are quite a few more art institutions, and more newcomers are getting involved. The number of young artists is increasing rapidly; we see a lot of new faces every year. But most exhibitions are relatively conservative, which is rather a pity.”
The market has “changed considerably” compared to what now “might be called the ‘golden 15 years’ of China’s contemporary art market: the shift in the broader economic environment over the past few years has been impossible to ignore”, Otto Neu says. In 2022 he co-founded Nan Ke Gallery, which has a group show about art and literature on view during the fair week. “For artists and galleries alike, it is certainly a challenging moment. We probably have to work twice as hard as we did before simply to survive and keep things moving.”
Change, Neu adds, does not have to be negative. He cites the Chinese expression “great waves wash away the sand and leave the gold behind”, adding that “difficult periods can force an industry to become more focused, more rigorous and perhaps more honest about what really matters. In that sense, this may also be an important stage of maturation for Shanghai’s art scene.”
In addition to this month’s two international art fairs, Shanghai’s many resident artists—ranging from established figures like Ding Yi, Zhang Enli and Yang Fudong to mid-career and emerging talents—can rely on year-round programming at a healthy variety of homegrown and imported galleries. Western outfits like Almine Rech, Perrotin and Lisson maintain spaces in Shanghai, as do Asian powerhouses including Japan’s Ota Fine Arts and Korea’s Arario Gallery. ShanghArt has been joined by several influential local galleries, among them Antenna Space, Gallery Vacancy, Capsule Gallery and Don Gallery.
Major state-backed museums like the Power Station of Art, Museum of Art Pudong and West Bund Museum (which is partnered with the Centre Pompidou in Paris) have a complement of private museums that have proliferated since the 2010s. The Rockbund Art Museum, Long Museum and Yuz Museum are the best known, but smaller, newer, specialised or further-flung institutions like Fotografiska and the Museum of Glass, and non-profit spaces like Pond Society, Longlati and Prada Rong Zhai, have also enriched the Shanghai art ecosystem.
Vanguard Gallery’s Li credits Shanghai’s “open-city vibe” and its large base of collectors and visitors, along with the museums, galleries and artists, plus a citizenry curious “about fashion and new things, a strong history of business, and a diverse cultural structure. The main downside is that the cost of living is too high.” The lack of art information platforms, even in Chinese, is the other main challenge, she says.
The sense of openness is what drew the collector Cherry Xu to open her art-meets-fashion space Cheruby in the city last year. With new initiatives, “the boundaries between artists, designers, musicians and people working in fashion are becoming increasingly blurred”, she says, opening the art world to new audiences. “This kind of natural crossover between different fields is something very particular to Shanghai,” Xu says. “Art here doesn’t operate as an isolated system; it is constantly in conversation with design, music, fashion, technology and a broader youth culture, with these different communities influencing one another.”
Pragmatic chaos
Compared to Beijing’s art scene, Neu says, Shanghai’s creative community maintains a “healthy sense of distance. There is a certain independence between galleries, institutions, artists and collectors, which has shaped a rather distinctive ecosystem here”, a happy, pragmatic chaos of sorts. Beijing’s art scene is built on personal connections, Neu says, while in Shanghai, “between institutions, between galleries and even between galleries and collectors, there is often an understanding that business is business, friendship is friendship, and collaboration does not necessarily require complicated personal obligations or relationships”.
However, Neu adds that those divisions could become vulnerabilities in the current economic upheaval. “Perhaps this is precisely the moment when Shanghai’s art community needs to become a little more connected and cohesive than it has been in the past—not by giving up its independence, but by finding better ways to support one another,” he says.
Helbling says that Beijing is “more split up into scenes which work on their own”, while Shanghai has various circles that interact and are more permeable. He likens the city’s art community to its fairly compact geography, with the art neighbourhoods all within comparably easy reach of each other.
Twenty years ago, Shanghai was the upstart artistic challenger to Beijing, the political capital home to China’s leading art academy. Hong Kong’s concurrent cultural rise proved complimentary to Shanghai’s, and many in Shanghai say the expanding art activity in Korea, Japan and Singapore—as well as in mainland Chinese cities like Chengdu, Shenzhen and nearby Nanjing, Hangzhou and Suzhou—have been net positives for the local scene.
“This situation didn’t happen overnight; it’s the result of years of collaboration between Shanghai’s art institutions, galleries and fairs, as well as the collectors and artists living here,” Li says. “It’s not simply due to fairs or art weeks alone. The rise of art in new Chinese cities has also become developed, likely influenced by Shanghai and Hong Kong.”
Shanghai “was one of the earliest cities in China to develop a contemporary art market, and its relatively open culture and international outlook have given it a particular advantage”, Neu says. “Whether we are talking about collecting, aesthetic awareness or public understanding of contemporary art, Shanghai has accumulated more than two decades of experience and audience development. That kind of cultural infrastructure takes time to build.”
He adds that growing art scenes in other mainland cities represent “something very positive for Shanghai rather than a threat. A stronger regional art ecosystem ultimately creates more audiences, more conversations and more opportunities for everyone. Healthy competition and exchange between cities can only make the broader Chinese art scene more dynamic.”
Regionally, Xu says, Shanghai “has a very distinct local culture, its own audiences and creative communities, [while] its relationship with other Asian cities is becoming much more direct. It feels increasingly natural for artists, curators and other creative practitioners to live and work across different cities in Asia, and for us to look to what is happening in Tokyo, Seoul, Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok and elsewhere in the region, rather than instinctively treating Europe and the US as the only points of reference.” For Shanghai’s art week, Cheruby is showing a solo exhibition by the multidisciplinary Thai artist Tanat Teeradakorn.
More dialogue
“Shanghai has an interesting place within this network,” Xu says. “It has a relatively mature art infrastructure, but also very strong fashion, design, commercial, technological and popular cultures, and these worlds exist very close to one another in everyday life. It also has a large and increasingly young audience, so when an artist comes to Shanghai, they are encountering more than an established ‘art world’; they are entering a complex and fast-moving urban environment that is constantly being reshaped by new forms of consumption, technology and youth culture. That complexity creates a lot of possibilities.”
After helping to build the careers of some of Asia’s biggest art stars, Helbling now focuses on cultivating rising talents through more group shows and dialogue. “You always look at what artists are doing,” he says. “Many of them now operate between here and the West—educated here and in the West”, with networks and roots in both cultures.
After suspended mobility during the Covid years, dual-culture artists in Shanghai and across Asia have resumed their frequent travels between regions. Often the children of artists or collectors, young Chinese artists are very well versed in both Western and Asian artistic traditions, giving them a sophisticated perspective. “They have an interesting job to do to figure out what kind of art makes sense today,” Helbling says.
He recalls the “loneliness” of Shanghai’s 1990s avant-garde, now rendered “impossible” by contemporary art’s citywide popularity. Still, he views the 2000 internationalisation of the Shanghai Biennale, the first contemporary art fair SH Contemporary (2007-14), and the flowering of galleries and museums as all part of one era.
“There was from the 1990s when Shanghai opened up until the Covid time, and there is after Covid time,” he says. “The first 30 years, and now the second 30 years.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/michael-bloomber.title: New York's Most Eligible (?) Former Mayor Is Finally Off the Market
https://hellgatenyc.com/michael-bloomber.author: Hell Gate

He was a billionaire politician who is maybe not so politically relevant; she was his girlfriend of 26 years, a financial executive, whatever that means. Can we make it any more obvious? 
That's right: Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg and his longtime partner Diana Taylor finally tied the knot on Monday after more than a quarter century together. And what a quarter century it's been! 
"Twenty-six years after a chance seating assignment, Mike Bloomberg and Diana Taylor have married," a spokesperson for Bloomberg posted on the ex-mayor's X account. "The longtime couple exchanged vows today in a small, private ceremony at their home on the Upper East Side, joined by family, including his daughters, Emma and Georgina. The two first crossed paths when they sat next to each other at a Citizens Budget Commission meeting while he was first running for Mayor."
Extremely romantic origin story aside (we always thought it was strange that the Citizens Budget Commission only meets by candlelight at that cute hole-in-the-wall Italian spot down the block), Bloomberg and Taylor have been through a lot together over the last two and a half decades.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Tate Britain spotlights Bloomsbury artists Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant for the first time since 1999
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Andrew Pulver
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Bloomsbury Group seems to have been ever-present in UK culture since its inception in the early 20th century, just before the First World War. Lytton Strachey, John Maynard Keynes, Virginia Woolf, E.M. Forster, Vanessa Bell, Duncan Grant—their names are legion as representatives of a flowering of British intellectualism across the full spectrum of literary and artistic endeavours. While Roger Fry was arguably Bloomsbury’s most influential art-world voice, as the critic who essentially introduced European Post-Impressionism to Britain with a celebrated exhibition at the Grafton Galleries in 1910, Bell and Grant were the group’s most active and high-profile painters. The pair’s bracketing together for a new Tate Britain exhibition is also a result, no doubt, of their 40-year open relationship that saw them live and paint together—and each other—over many decades.
The Bloomsbury Group has largely retained its high profile over the decades, with feature films on many of its protagonists and even a BBC mini-series in 2015 called Life in Squares, named for the supposed Dorothy Parker gag that the group “lived in squares, painted in circles and loved in triangles”. Bell and Grant’s former home Charleston, near Lewes in East Sussex, has maintained a near-constant programme of exhibitions to keep the flame alive, the latest of which, Mad Bloomsbury (4 November-11 April 2027) examines the group’s engagement with mental health issues.
But the Tate show marks the first Bloomsbury-focused show at the national home for British art for over a quarter of a century. Thomas Kennedy, the curator of Modern British art at Tate Britain, thinks it is about time. “That means an entire generation of visitors have not seen an exhibition on Vanessa or Duncan’s work at Tate, and we felt that it was important for us to revisit their practices again after so long,” Kennedy says. “I don’t believe there’s ever been a major exhibition on Vanessa and Duncan together, and it’s so fascinating to see the ways they differ. We should recognise their individual accomplishments of course, but also the works they made together and how they influenced each other. We know about their relationship—she was married and he was gay—but this exhibition explores what that really meant in their artworks and in their life.”
Out of fashion
Looking back at that previous 1999 show, the cuttings files reveal that the turn of the millennium clearly marked a low point in critical opinion of the Bloomsbury artists; outright abuse might be the best description of some of the responses. The Guardian art critic Adrian Searle called them “a bit crap”, “lightweights” and “third rate”, while for the novelist Philip Hensher writing in The Independent, these “no-hopers” and their “rubbish” inspired simple “rage and loathing”.
But Kennedy is not having it. Bell and Grant, he says, “started experimenting with art in unique ways that hadn’t really been seen in Britain before”. He adds: “They created some of the first abstract works in Britain, which is sometimes very much overlooked. And they were creating these works together, and talking about art all day, every day, breaking the distinction between fine and decorative art with the Omega Workshops. What they were doing was really special.”
Bell, whose sister Virginia Woolf was even more celebrated in her field, is perhaps now the slightly more recognisable name of the two painters, though, as Kennedy points out, both Bell and Grant were considered leading figures during their lifetimes. Their close physical proximity, from when they moved to Charleston in 1918 to Bell’s death in 1961, meant their styles were often similarly adjacent, though Kennedy is clear on the differences. “Vanessa’s painting is more deliberate with very considered blocks of colour and very strong outlines, whereas Duncan’s is scratchier, more impulsive and it feels like he is experimenting more with more expressive techniques,” he says.
Kennedy adds: “However, later on, when they’re working on the Famous Women dinner service [a collection of 50 hand-painted plates], their styles are completely the same: the authorship has very much broken down and we can’t tell who did what. So much so that Roger Fry told them to paint in different studios to reassess their own way of making. It’s fascinating to see that push and pull between what they were taking from each other.”
In the end, it might be that the very thing that seemed to diminish the Bloomsbury Group for previous generations—their complex, near-incestuous love lives—is what is powering their current revival: to contemporary perspectives they now look like pioneers of unrepentantly queer lifestyles. Bell married fellow painter Clive Bell in 1907, then had a long relationship with Fry and had a daughter, Angelica, with Grant in 1918. Grant, for his part, had a string of male lovers while maintaining his domestic relationship with Bell. “They were looking towards non-monogamous relationships and accepting queer relationships. The latter, as you know, was illegal in the UK at the time,” Kennedy says. “Within the Bloomsbury Group they felt freedom—both artistically and the way they lived.”
• Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, Tate Britain, London, 12 November-11 April 2027

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.title: Kalshi Is Cozy With Trump — But It’s Ramping Up Dem Hires and Campaign Spending
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/kals.text:
Since the start of the year, the prediction betting site Kalshi has two hired former officials from Joe Biden’s White House as a policy adviser and a top lobbyist.
The company’s co-founders have also spent nearly $1 million on donations to federal candidates, with more than a third, or $377,000, going to Democrats like Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., according to a new report.
Kalshi’s spending spree shows how much prediction market sites have ratcheted up their presence in Washington as regulators craft rules for the industry. While the sites’ close relationship with the Trump administration has drawn headlines, the report from the progressive group Demand Progress details how the industry’s influence operation crosses party lines.
The push for bipartisan relationships began months ago, but it could pay dividends as Democrats take over both chambers of a Congress, said Ella Fanger, the corporate power policy adviser for Demand Progress. A betting market critic, Fanger predicted that the companies will keep trying to win allies on both sides of the aisle.
“They’ve been hopeful that they can have Democratic champions for their policy agenda,” she said, “and not just have Trump’s cronies sticking out their necks for them.”
The hiring spree of former Biden officials and spending on Democratic candidates come as prediction markets are facing increasing scrutiny over betting on elections and a spate of suspicious trades from Washington about policy moves and even military action.
On Tuesday, Democrats on Capitol Hill called for Trump to bar White House staffers from using the betting sites and, with Democrats taking Congress, many observers expect investigations into their use in Washington.
In a statement, Kalshi said it was willing to work “across the ideological spectrum.”
“Kalshi has had substantive conversations with policymakers over the past year regarding legislation that protects consumers, keeps minors off our platform, makes insider trading bans standard across the industry, and ensures the CFTC” — the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — “has the resources they need,” said the company’s head of government relations, John Bivona, a former Democratic congressional staffer and Biden White House official.
“We’ve come out in support of legislation introduced by members across the ideological spectrum,” Bivona said, “and we’ve worked with dozens of lawmakers from both parties on these priorities.”
Hiring Republicans — and Dems
Kalshi and its rival Polymarket are the dominant players in the prediction market industry, which has flourished since Donald Trump became president thanks to his administration’s hands-off approach to regulation.
The ties between the prediction betting sites and Trumpworld go all the way to the president’s inner circle, as evidenced by Donald Trump Jr.’s financial stakes at both competitors.
Polymarket has also hired as a lobbyist a Republican former top official at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The federal regulatory body has, under the Trump administration, sued states for trying to regulate sports betting as gambling.
The Demand Progress report covers Trump Jr.’s ties to the industry, but it also shines a light on the role of former Democratic congressional and executive branch staffers.
Kalshi’s hires have tended toward establishment Democrats. Among them are Stephanie Cutter, a political strategist whose work spanned the Obama and Biden administrations as well as Kamala Harris’s campaign for president. Cutter was tapped as a policy adviser for Kalshi in April. Bivona was hired by Kalshi as its head of government relations in January.
Tripled Lobbying Spend
Overall, Kalshi has spent $1.8 million on lobbying in the first half of 2026, compared to $615,000 in all of 2025, according to the Demand Progress report.
Polymarket spent a relatively meager $180,000 during the same period this year, compared to $360,000 last year.
Fanger, whose group is critical of the prediction markets’ attempts to neutralize state sports gambling regulators, said she is worried that a pliant Congress could approve the Trump administration’s favorable regulations.
“The concern is basically just that we could get legislation that would codify the rulemaking that the CFTC has already begun,” she said, referring to the agency’s efforts to formally exercise jurisdiction over sports, political, cultural, and weather betting contracts. “And we think that it’s important for states to be able to regulate this industry as gambling, which is what it is.”
The industry may need all the lobbyists it can get if progressives gain power in the next Congress. Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., who is angling to chair the House Financial Services Committee, said in a letter last week that she wants to “rein in predatory lending and predatory platforms, including prediction markets, so that our constituents keep more of their hard-earned dollars in their pockets.”
Waters is also a longtime foil to the crypto industry. Crypto currency interests alienated Democrats by spending tens of millions of campaign dollars on Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, who lost his seat to Democrat Sherrod Brown in the midterm election.
While crypto has lavished money on campaign spending through a super PAC, the prediction market industry has opted for a quieter campaign of smaller donations routed through more traditional channels.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: London’s Photographers’ Gallery to launch exhibition programme for emerging voices
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Simon Bainbridge
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Photographers’ Gallery in London is launching a 10-year programme to platform emerging talent through a series of biennial exhibitions. The initiative has been made possible by what the not-for-profit gallery describes as “a very generous grant” from the UK-based John Kobal Foundation.
Shoair Mavlian, the director of the Photographers’ Gallery, declined to specify how much the grant is worth, but she tells The Art Newspaper that it will cover all the costs of staging the shows in its second-floor space, newly named the John Kobal Foundation Gallery.
The initiative will see one artist selected every two years for an exhibition. The first solo exhibition will be announced later this year and will run from 23 June to 26 September 2027.
“The whole idea of the programme is based around giving an opportunity to someone who hasn’t had an institutional solo show before,” she says. “The Photographers’ Gallery is in a similar situation to all other museums in the UK in that we are pressured into having to always do blockbuster shows [to generate revenue]. And what this programme allows us to do is to take risks.”
The gallery received a renewed three-year grant from Arts Council England in 2023, as one of the funding body’s national portfolio organisations (NPO). This grant represents around 20% of the gallery’s revenue, says Mavlian, however, it has remained the same throughout years of rising operational costs and high inflation, and so like other UK arts organisations, the gallery has become more reliant on other sources of income. Its accounts for the year ending 31 March 2025 report £620,573 in admissions income, which is more than two thirds the value of its NPO grant over a single year.
“We are under this constant pressure to sell tickets and bring people through the door—which, of course, is important. But what that means is we then don’t always see the full breadth of photography that is being made today. We are often looking at things that are historic rather than looking at the contemporary.”
The John Kobal Foundation was established in 1990 a year before the death of the eponymous film historian and photography collector “to advance the public appreciation and awareness of photography”.
“We are delighted to support this important new initiative," says Michael Mack, the co-chair of the John Kobal Foundation, “which honours John’s vision of nurturing creativity and innovation in photography.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: How Did New York Become So Unequal?
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Joshua B. Freeman
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
A Tale of Two Cities
How did New York go from a center of social-democratic experiment to one of neoliberal devastation?
How Did New York Become So Unequal?
A new history of New York examines how it went from a center of social-democratic experiment to one of neoliberal devastation.
In 2013, Mason B. Williams published City of Ambition, in which he told the story of New York’s transformation during the New Deal era, when federal dollars from Washington powered Fiorello La Guardia’s expansive vision for the role of municipal government in everyday life. La Guardia’s alliance with Franklin D. Roosevelt, supported by an expanding labor movement and a network of left and liberal organizations, laid the basis for the New York I grew up in. Federal funds allowed the city to build the high school I attended, the subway lines I spent a lifetime riding, the highways, bridges, and tunnels that whisked me around the city and sometimes congealed me in traffic jams, the innumerable parks, playgrounds, beaches, swimming pools, and health clinics, and the public-housing system that currently has more than a half-million residents.
Books in review
City of Fortune: Inequality and the Making of Contemporary New York
Buy this book
Williams’s new book, City of Fortune, chronicles a transformation just as profound: the post-1970s-fiscal-crisis replacement of the local New Deal order with a New York version of neoliberalism. Williams shows in devastating detail how, over the past half-century, the city’s economy and municipal capacity for governance have grown at the same time that it has developed levels of poverty and inequality unprecedented in its modern history. It is the relationship between these trends—how “the systems that made [the city] work for some imposed costs and violence on others”—that is the central focus of his book.
Williams has digested the vast literature on modern New York, of which these trends are only a part. To it, he has added a massive research effort of his own, in scores of archival collections and publications, giving his volume an authoritative quality. His wide-ranging knowledge might bring to mind comparisons to the late historian Mike Wallace—and they would not be entirely unjust. But unlike Wallace’s encyclopedic accounts of life and change in New York, City of Fortune focuses on three particular issues to tell its story: policing, education, and housing. All three profoundly affected the lives of New Yorkers; all three were political flash points; and all three were intertwined with changes in both material conditions and ideological assumptions.
Like many other American cities in the 1960s and ’70s, New York suffered a massive increase in crime and the sense of danger and disorder that came with it. By the mid-1970s, the New York Police Department had been diminished by cuts in funding and personnel and seemed utterly ineffective in countering the trend. (Those of us who had cars stolen or apartments broken into during those years can remember how the police considered the idea of investigating such crimes laughable.)
But starting under Mayor Ed Koch, a new generation of police leaders and new crime-fighting strategies, many coming out of the academic world, reshaped police activity and remade life for millions of New Yorkers, especially men of color. Pursuing various iterations of “community policing” and “broken windows” theory, the NYPD aggressively combated even minor acts of disorder in neighborhoods targeted as centers of drug activity and crime, arguing that doing so would allow the natural mechanisms of community self-regulation to reemerge.
In the early 1990s, the crime rate in New York began to fall, and it would continue to do so until Covid-19 hit in 2020. How much police strategy had to do with this is unclear, since crime would soon decrease in other cities as well. Still, the NYPD doubled down on its intense policing in high-crime areas, which tended to be neighborhoods with large African American or Latino populations. “Stop-and-frisk” became the favored mode of policing, a practice both deeply racist in disproportionately targeting non-white men for searches without legitimate cause and a clear violation of the Fourth Amendment. Even as crime continued to drop, the city refused to reduce the pressure: In 2011, it recorded an astounding 685,724 stops.
In some precincts, there were more stops than residents. If you were young and Black, the relentless harassment could lead to jail time for petty offenses, job loss, or far worse. The swagger and sense of omnipotence that came with the official veneration of aggressive policing resulted in a series of tragic murders of innocent people by police officers that tore the city apart. Yet, Williams notes, the NYPD would only become more “impervious to reform.”
****In education, the city faced two massive challenges: the extreme racial segregation in its schools (among the worst in the nation) and their failure to provide huge swaths of students with a decent education. Rather than confronting segregation head-on—a politically difficult approach—the city began experimenting with “magnet schools” to draw students from both white and non-white communities to superior schools with superior resources. At roughly the same time, progressive educators like Deborah Meier began creating public schools that broke from the older, more rigid and hierarchical approaches to pedagogy and drew interested students from across relatively broad areas to alternative learning communities.
The idea of school choice, which encompassed both developments, proved ideologically promiscuous: It soon became a favored approach of leftists, liberals, and free-market conservatives. By the early 1990s, it was also the official policy of the New York City Board of Education. New schools (some dubbed “academies”) popped up like mushrooms, both within the regular public-school system and as charter schools, supported by foundation as well as taxpayer money.
Some of these new schools proved to be excellent, although they often created conflicts as they took over the buildings of older schools the way hermit crabs take over the shells of other creatures. They also helped keep middle-class white students in the public-school system—an explicit goal of city leaders. But in doing so, critics argued, they siphoned away resources as well as many of the best teachers and students from the rest of the system and left behind those who could not (or didn’t know how to) get into selective schools. Regardless of the reasons it was initiated, Williams notes, school choice often ended up reinforcing and deepening segregation and inequality.
New York’s housing market was plagued by segregation and inequality as well. “Nothing animated the city’s business community quite like rent regulation,” Williams observes, framing his discussion of housing around the never-ending contest over whether to expand, diminish, or eliminate rent control.
These limits on rent increases—a legacy of federal price controls during World War II—helped preserve a city made up largely of working- and middle-class renters during the postwar years, when America’s other major cities mostly shrank in size and vitality. In 1970, 1.3 million apartments in New York City built before 1947 were covered by the state’s strict rent-control law, while another 375,000 units built later were regulated by a looser rent-stabilization system the city set up in 1968. Rent regulations, by design, limited landlords’ profits and challenged the idea that owners of property had the right to do whatever they wanted with it. Landlords knew there was little point in arguing that they should be allowed to make more money—but the claim that rent control made it impossible to properly maintain their existing buildings and discouraged new construction carried more weight.
In 1971, with the support of Governor Nelson Rockefeller, the New York State Legislature instituted “vacancy decontrol,” which removed the limits on what a landlord could charge for a previously rent-controlled apartment after the former tenant had vacated it. The backlash against this victory for building owners was so intense that, three years later, the Legislature required that apartments leaving the rent-control system be placed, after a onetime opportunity to hike the rent, under rent stabilization, gradually shifting housing from the older regulatory system to the newer one. But rather than ending the battle, the decision simply changed the terrain on which it has continued.
For one thing, the mayor-appointed Rent Guidelines Board, which determines each year how much stabilized rents can be raised, became the object of intense lobbying by tenants and landlords, with hearings that are famously epic, unruly affairs. For another, real estate interests continued to chip away at the system, eventually winning laws that removed apartments whose rent was above a certain cap or whose tenants made more than a certain income (“luxury decontrol”). In 1997, Governor George Pataki and Republicans in the Legislature were set to gut the system beyond recognition, until a massive mobilization of tenants, backed by organized labor, largely forced them to retreat.
Despite how heroically tenants and their organizations have dug their heels in to maintain these restrictions on rent, the housing-affordability crisis in the city has only worsened. The removal of hundreds of thousands of apartments from the rent-regulation system, the failure to build enough new housing, and a growing population have combined to accelerate gentrification and make finding a place to live a nightmare for all but the well-off. “By 2011,” Williams writes, “for the first time in the city’s modern history, the median New York rental household was officially rent-burdened, paying more than 30 percent of its income in rent—and a third of households paid more than half.”
The three stories that form the spine of City of Fortune will be familiar to longtime New York residents, if not to outsiders, but Williams tells them with an impressive combination of lucidity and granular detail. He also makes two very important points about their dynamics that are not often brought out.
The first is the centrality of state politics to what happens in New York City. The system of rent regulation, for example, comes primarily from state law, though city ordinances are involved too. Its fate has remained in the hands of a Legislature made up mostly of people elected outside of the city and governors who looked to the suburbs for swing votes to keep them in office. The mayor may press the Rent Guidelines Board to limit increases on regulated units, but the state, if it chooses, could get rid of the entire system. Tax-abatement programs to encourage housing construction likewise come from Albany, not City Hall. So do charter-school authorizations and many of the regulations (including the testing regime) that shape the city’s school system. More broadly, the ability of the city government to create and maintain programs of all kinds, from policing to transit to healthcare access, depends on legal and financial relationships with the state and federal governments. The city cannot even change its income-tax rates, which are controlled by the state, to the frustration of the current mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Even with a DSA-led campaign to “Tax the Rich,” he failed to win state approval for a higher income tax on wealthy residents or a boost in corporate tax rates, ultimately settling for a modest surcharge on real estate taxes on expensive second homes.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The second point that Williams stresses is the continuity of public policy across parties and mayors. Though packaged and sold differently from administration to administration, practices like aggressive community policing (including stop-and-frisk) and school choice have proved remarkably durable, even with the mayor’s office occupied by such seemingly dissimilar characters as Ed Koch, David Dinkins, Rudy Giuliani, Michael Bloomberg, and Bill de Blasio. Williams never steps back enough to ask why this is so, though he does mention some factors in passing, including the power of institutional interests like the NYPD and the continuing influence of various lobbies and advocacy organizations.
Williams’s concentration on particular policy areas allows us to see the expanding impact of neoliberalism on everyday life, but it also limits his portrayal of the larger structures of economic and political power that shaped the evolution of the city. For example, the post-fiscal-crisis New York economy is quite different from its earlier incarnation, with the virtual disappearance of manufacturing—once a mainstay—and the increased importance of services, finance, and real estate. The new robber barons in the city, though they may be extracting wealth from across the globe and bringing it into New York, are also more attentive to municipal matters than their predecessors. And they are much more ideologically engaged: Issues like charter schools and school choice have become vehicles for delegitimizing the state and promoting free-market ideas (though when it comes to policing, the same folks are all for strong government).
The 1975 fiscal crisis, widely interpreted by politicians, business leaders, and the press as a verdict on the flaws of expansive egalitarian government, led to years of austerity. It also laid the basis for a consensus on the importance of attracting and catering to wealthy companies and individuals and maintaining an orderly city that would not offend them. This became the new common sense, the hegemonic idea sustaining the power of New York’s financial and real-estate elite. In myriad ways, it shaped public policy no matter who headed City Hall.
What did not happen in the years after the post-crisis recovery is as revealing as what did. While billions of public dollars were devoted to subsidizing high-end office construction, not a single new unit of public housing has been built in the past 35 years. During the same period, cities all over the world have built mass-transit lines or whole new systems; New York added only four subway stops, all serving wealthy Manhattan neighborhoods. As economic inequality and homelessness soared, with nearly one in seven public-school pupils homeless, the government failed to build the housing and provide the services needed for the displaced and resourceless.
City of Fortune is shocking not only for the details it recounts but also for its disturbing picture of the moral and political failures of New York’s leaders. How can a city like New York, with a landscape now punctuated by palaces for the ultra-wealthy—such as the $238 million penthouse that billionaire Ken Griffin counts as a second home—have 420,000 children living below the poverty line? How can a society go so wrong so quickly?
Williams sees some hope in the future and gives us a hint of what that future might look like. Ending his book on an upbeat note, he recounts an October 2019 rally in the Long Island City neighborhood of Queens, where Bernie Sanders, after suffering a heart attack, relaunched his presidential campaign with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at his side. In the crowd listening to Sanders’s moving appeal for solidarity across racial, religious, and national lines, Williams writes, was Zohran Mamdani, who had just launched his own campaign for the State Assembly.
Mamdani’s astounding election as mayor and his first months in office suggest that a new era might be beginning in New York. Unlike his opponents, Mamdani has a gut feel for the changes that took place in the city during the years Williams examines: the massive growth of inequality; the daily struggle of so many New Yorkers just to get by; the precarity of even young professionals in fields like higher education, culture, and the arts; and the extraordinary diversity of a city in which over 37 percent of the population was born outside the country (compared with 18 percent in 1970).
For progressives and ordinary New Yorkers, Mamdani is a breath of fresh air. Like Fiorello La Guardia, he is everywhere, filling potholes, shoveling snow, rallying with striking nurses, sharing iftar with city workers, riding his bike with Brooklyn parents taking their kids to school, and sitting in the nosebleed section of Madison Square Garden watching the Knicks. So far, he has been largely successful in avoiding pitfalls and inching toward fulfilling his campaign promises, which included freezing regulated rents, universal childcare, and free buses. But Williams’s account is a cautionary tale about the obstacles he faces: the limited power of the city in such crucial areas as tax policy and education; the fiscal challenges in an era when, unlike La Guardia’s, the federal government is determined to undermine blue-state cities rather than partner with them to better the lives of their residents; and the enormous power of the self-serving financial and real estate interests. It is too early to say if Mamdani and the movement that helped him win office will be able to break the link between the city’s growth and the grotesque inequality that Williams so ably chronicles. At stake is what it means to be a civilized society.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Peruvian senator calls for removal of large-scale replicas of Moche erotic sculptures from public park
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Graciela Ibáñez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A controversy over 3m-tall erotic sculptures in northern Peru reignited recently after a senator requested that the cultural ministry remove them from a public area. Located in a park outside the city of Trujillo, the sculptures are replicas of ceramics from the pre-Incan Moche civilisation.
“What happens when children see these images? Neurological and psychological factors are affected, because they see body dimensions that are completely different from how they see themselves,” Milagros Jáuregui, a conservative senator from the Renovación Popular party, said in a speech on 26 October.
The sculptures are located in Parque de la Fertilidad (Fertility Park), a public space where in 2021 then-mayor Arturo Fernández of the Moche district began installing giant fibreglass reproductions of ceramic depictions of sexual acts to promote tourism.
Known as huacos eróticos, the much smaller original ceramics date from the 3rd to 8th century AD. No more than 30cm in height, they were placed in tombs as burial offerings. But the debate about their much larger versions in the park goes beyond political prudishness.
“It’s a complicated issue,” the Peruvian archaeologist Walter Alva tells The Art Newspaper. “There’s freedom to express or re-create themes from the past, but these ceramics were created to be placed as offerings to the dead, with a sense of revitalising life. They are associated with both fertility and an entire system of beliefs.”
The Moche civilisation covered 700km of the coast of what is now Peru, between the regions of Piura and Ancash, centuries before the Inca dominated the area. “Moche art is primarily ceramic, and these vessels depict erotic scenes or concepts of sexuality from that era,” Alva says. “The sculptures in the park were created outside of their historical context.”
One of the greatest archaeological discoveries from the Moche civilisation was that of the Lord of Sipán near the city of Chiclayo—a discovery Alva made in 1987. A 3rd-century monarch, the Lord of Sipán’s body was found covered with gold along with eight other people, a dog and two llamas and nearly 500 objects including ceramic vessels, ornaments and textiles.
The Moche have the largest number of erotic representations among pre-Hispanic civilisations. The most complete collection of its ceramics is in Lima, at the Larco Museum of pre-Columbian art, which celebrated its centennial in July. Before the 1960s, children were forbidden from entering the room that housed the huacos. Today, minors must be accompanied by an adult. The institution’s Erotic Gallery is one of its most popular attractions.
Jáuregui, an evangelical pastor as well as a senator, believes these Moche sculptures should only be in closed spaces. “Displaying these types of images in public is harmful to children,” she told congress. “We should have them in museums, where high-school students can observe a part of our culture that is a national treasure with the help of teachers or some kind of tutor.”
