https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.title: Solstice Sonnet
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.author: Zeina Hashem Beck
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
Poems
                                        
                                    
                                     / 
                                                                            November 10, 2026
                                    
                
        
                            
                
                                
    
The Litani banks fill with phosphorus.
Here, the cricket repeats, somewhere, somewhere,
with its dark wings, its five eyes, its toothed legs.
Don’t mistake me for a recovered heart,
fascinated by the longest sunsets.
I am a green permanent resident,
which rings more eternal than citizen.
The summer solstice is about distance,
angles. Pulsing with airports & amens
under the fog, I give up on endings.
You point, articulate: Ta-mal-pa-is.
Try mountains if you’re searching for soul. Break—
but don’t trust me on this. Most days, I don’t
venture out in twilight like hungry deer.
Venture out in twilight like hungry deer!
But don’t trust me on this. Most days, I don’t
try mountains. If you’re searching for soul, break.
You point: articulate Tamalpais
under the fog. I give up on endings,
angles. Pulsing with airports & amens,
the summer solstice is about distance
which rings. More eternal than citizen,
I am a green permanent resident,
fascinated by the longest sunsets.
Don’t mistake me for a recovered heart
with its dark wings, its five eyes, its toothed legs.
Here, the cricket repeats, somewhere, somewhere—
a litany. Banks fill with phosphorus.
    
    
        
     
            
                            
                    
                                        
                        Zeina Hashem Beck is the author of the mirror sonnet collection This Was Supposed to Be About Beauty (Penguin, March 2027) and Sublingual: Failing in an Other’s Language (Haymarket, fall 2027), her debut nonfiction book. Her collection O (Penguin) won the 2023 Arab American Book Award for Poetry and was named a best book of the year by Literary Hub and the New York Public Library. She’s also the author of Louder than Hearts and To Live in Autumn, as well as the chapbooks 3arabi Song and There Was and How Much There Was. Her work has appeared in LARB, Lit Hub, Poetry, and elsewhere. She grew up in Lebanon and currently resides in the Bay Area.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Do Socialists Even Believe in Socialism Anymore?
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Mike Beggs, Ben Burgis, Bhaskar Sunkara
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Do Socialists Even Believe in Socialism Anymore?
The American left has a growing list of victories—and an unfinished argument about the society it wants to build.
We’ve all seen the cover. some of us even have a copy of it hanging in our living room: “The Red Apple.” The New York Post marked Zohran Mamdani’s November 2025 election with a Soviet-inspired cover that featured the incoming mayor carrying a hammer and sickle high above his head.
It was an image that those of us who grew up in New York during the Rudy Giuliani or Michael Bloomberg era couldn’t have imagined. The larger global context made it even more remarkable, demonstrating socialism’s advance in the United States even as it’s in retreat in much of Europe and Latin America. And since last year, Mamdani’s election has helped catalyze a string of socialist victories in congressional races. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has surged to over 120,000 members, and with the midterm results, the movement’s small congressional contingent is set to become dramatically larger.
What does socialism mean, though, to the socialists of our era? Their predecessors in early-20th-century socialist parties liked to talk about a “minimum program” of reforms within capitalism and a “maximum program” of reforms that go beyond capitalism entirely. Some even theorized a “transitional program” to bridge the gap between the two.
The “minimum program,” at least, is easy enough to see today. Socialist candidates for office talk about Medicare for All, jobs programs, and ending America’s wars overseas. In New York, Mamdani has conducted hearings on the misdeeds of negligent landlords, frozen the rent for millions of New Yorkers in rent-stabilized apartments, and established a Mayor’s Office of Worker Power to help people organize their workplaces. He’s worked to expand free childcare and taken the first steps to build public grocery stores in each of the city’s five boroughs. And through it all, the city’s economy has continued to boom.
To progressive allies of the DSA, these reforms are proof of the movement’s inherent pragmatism—in deeds, if not always in words. But others can reasonably ask if this generation’s socialists still believe in socialism at all.
When the leading DSA-affiliated politicians like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are asked to define socialism, they tend to talk about mitigating income inequality and giving everyone a dignified life. While these are certainly goals close to the heart of any socialist, it’s hard to see how they add up to socialism as a system, since they avoid the question at the core of socialism: the ownership of the means of production. Similarly, while the radicalism of some clauses of the DSA’s national platform—including the calls to abolish the Senate and to dismantle the carceral state—has been a lightning rod for criticism from the right, the document offers little detail about how a world beyond capitalism would work.
The DSA platform calls for public ownership of the largest corporations and essential industries. That would be a major transformation, but it could still leave much of the economy organized around private employers and wage labor. Even the section titled “Democracy at Work” is about trade unions, not who owns the means of production. And although the DSA declares a classless society its goal, it offers little explanation of how its demands for change within capitalism would get us there.
This blurriness about the “maximum program” can’t be chalked up to a lack of radical commitment or to strategic coyness. It reflects a real problem. On the one hand, capitalism is a brutally unequal system in which many struggle to take care of their families and spend much of their waking lives in jobs they despise. There are many good reasons to find it abhorrent. On the other hand, especially after the failures of state socialism in the Eastern bloc, many people who are deeply critical of capitalism aren’t entirely sure what an economically viable alternative to it would look like.
In light of that uncertainty, many progressives, and surely many readers of The Nation, wonder if it’s better to drop the socialism talk entirely. Politicians like Zohran Mamdani should abandon the historical baggage associated with socialism, their thinking goes, and just embrace social democracy and the great effort to tame, rather than replace, capitalism.
On one level, it’s easy to see their point. Social democracies like Denmark, Norway, Sweden, and Finland really were, at their peak, the most livable societies that human beings ever built. If the United States adopted the Nordic model in the coming years, it would be the greatest triumph of the American left since the Civil War and Reconstruction. That much should be obvious to anyone with progressive values. What might be less obvious is that it would still be a woefully insufficient response to growing levels of inequality and discontent.
Admittedly, one reason that socialists like ourselves stubbornly refuse to limit our horizons to social democracy is purely ideological. Even in the most expansive social-democratic welfare states, like Sweden in the 1970s, most of the working-age population worked for capitalist employers. Democracy stopped at the factory and office doors.
In the places where most adults spend their working days, we do not interact with each other as equals. The working-class majority have to do what they’re told by bosses or risk becoming unemployed. Often, workers’ best recourse against unreasonable demands is the power of exit. But even if they’re able to exercise that option, they will still have to find a new boss to submit to. They can choose their masters, but they can’t choose not to have a master. Meanwhile, some of their fellow citizens, due to nothing but accidents of birth, can live off trust funds without having to work at all.
For egalitarians, this is a deep injustice, and one that remains even when extensive public provision and a powerful labor movement have sanded off some of the system’s worst effects.
Even if we were willing to swallow this imbalance of power at the heart of the economy, though, there’s also a practical objection to stopping at social democracy. Thinking that’s as far as we can go sounds realistic, but it’s far from clear that capitalism as it exists in the third decade of the 21st century can sustain ambitious pro-labor policies and deep welfare-state commitments that would enable full employment and the truly comprehensive provision of public goods.
Michał Kalecki identified the underlying problem decades before it came to the fore. In his 1943 essay “Political Aspects of Full Employment,” Kalecki argued that while sustained full employment might be economically achievable under capitalism, it was politically unstable. Individual capitalists might occasionally welcome state policies to these ends in the short term to help restore demand for their products, but over time they would come to resist them. Tight labor markets weaken workplace discipline, strengthen workers’ bargaining power, and erode employers’ social authority—an environment, the business leaders feared, that would undermine capital accumulation.
Much of today’s progressive discourse ignores this lesson entirely. Full employment, expansive fiscal policy, and ambitious state investment are often presented by American progressives as stable end points within capitalism. Yet these policies will be bitterly contested by capital and, inevitably, will provoke crises.
Governments, for their part, can sometimes sustain such policies against the immediate wishes of business, especially when public order is at stake. But this autonomy is limited, since states remain dependent on private investment for growth, employment, and tax revenues. In an era of intensified global competition, and with aging populations already threatening the existing welfare states, it’s unclear that the Golden Age advances of the middle 20th century, when both labor and capital grew stronger, can return.
All this, of course, might sound like the case for an even more moderate reform program, one that avoids burdening capitalist job creators with excessive interference from labor but rewards workers with reasonable wages and protections in return. We draw the opposite conclusion. We think that people have the right to both the security of a welfare state and a voice in their workplaces. Precisely for that reason, socialists must not shy away from maximal demands: doing away with capitalism altogether.
The socialism of central planning and administrative allocation was a failure in the Soviet Union and similar societies. Learning from that history requires rethinking how egalitarian production and distribution can actually work.
If we need market mechanisms in at least some sectors of the economy, it doesn’t follow that we need capitalist property relations and the deep inequalities of power that go with them. We know that worker-owned and democratically governed firms can operate efficiently. Spain’s Mondragon Corporation, a federation of dozens of autonomous cooperatives, employs around 70,000 people. Its worker-members elect their governing bodies and participate in strategic decisions. If we could have a market sector where every company worked that way—where it was all Mondragons and no Amazons—we could have a prosperous modern economy without workplace authoritarianism and labor exploitation.
One reason cooperatives are rare under capitalism is that even relatively well-off workers who could pool their resources to start a business would be making a risky bet. It’s not rational for people with very limited resources to put all their financial eggs in the single basket of a venture that could go belly-up and leave them with nothing. Apologists for capitalism conclude that capitalist employment relations are morally innocent and mutually beneficial. Capitalists assume the risk and get the power, while workers surrender their power but get the security of a biweekly paycheck. We think that a better society would offer workers better options than the choice between economic insecurity and economic oppression.
In our vision of socialism, a large state sector provides universal public services such as education and healthcare, while a regulated market sector composed of democratic, worker-controlled firms produces ordinary goods and services in response to consumer demand. This means that workers do not have to risk their personal savings; public banks finance the companies, which must pay their members regular wages that meet minimum benchmarks. Worker-members also share any profits remaining after wages and other obligations have been paid.
Our model retains markets because prices, competition, and consumer choice solve real coordination problems. But it rejects capitalism on egalitarian and democratic grounds: A dynamic economy doesn’t require a separate class of owners with authority over production, investment, and the lives of ordinary workers.
This is no utopia. It wouldn’t automatically eliminate all forms of inequality, and it certainly wouldn’t eliminate all sources of political conflict. It would, however, be the first dominant form of human social organization since the Neolithic Revolution that did not divide society into a class of subordinated producers and a class of rulers living off the fruits of those producers’ labor. That’s the North Star that past generations of socialists understood themselves to be striving toward. It’s the vision that many of them died for, whether killed by strikebreaking Pinkertons or fighting as internationalist volunteers in the Spanish Civil War. We still think humanity has a chance to achieve that future.
DSA founder Michael Harrington used to say that radicals had to “walk a perilous tightrope.” We had to “be true to the socialist vision of a new society” and also “bring that vision into contact with the actual movements fighting not to transform the system, but to gain some little increment of dignity or even just a piece of bread.”
Harrington is not often invoked in DSA circles nowadays, but almost every socialist in the country is still trying to walk that tightrope, judging reforms both by the relief they bring and by the strength they give working people to fight for more. Universal healthcare would weaken workers’ dependence on employers for medical coverage. More public housing would reduce tenants’ dependence on private landlords. Stronger unions would give workers more power over their jobs. But turning these gains into steps toward socialism requires organizing and political agitation. That transformation won’t follow automatically from a popular mayor or a well-run sanitation department.
The New York Post cover was meant to be a warning about the society that Mamdani wants to build. We owe its readers a clearer picture of that society than a hammer and sickle can provide.

https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.title: I Am Yusuf, My Father
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.author: Mahmoud Darwish
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
I Am Yusuf, My Father
I am Yusuf, my father. My brothers do not love me,
Father, do not want me among them. They attack me,
pelting me with stones and words. They want me to
die, that they may say my eulogy. In my face they’ve
shut your door, and from the field they’ve driven me.
They’ve poisoned my grapes, Father. They’ve smashed
my playthings, Father. When the breeze blew and
ruffled my hair, jealous, they rose up against me, and
against you. But what have I done to them, Father?
Butterflies alighted on my shoulders, ears of grain
bent toward me, birds perched upon my hands. So
what have I done, Father? Why me? You named me
Yusuf, and they cast me into the well, but blamed the
wolf. The wolf is more merciful than my brothers…
oh, my father! Did I wrong anyone when I said that:
I saw eleven stars, saw the sun, and the moon, saw
them prostrate before me?
(Translated from the Arabic by Barbara Romaine)

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Collector Elie Khouri to create physical home for his private foundation in Dubai
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melissa Gronlund
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Dubai-based art collector Elie Khouri is building a space in the city for his eponymous foundation. The Elie Khouri Art Foundation (Ekaf) will be located in the coastal district of Jumeirah 1, in a villa renovated and redesigned by Counterspace, a firm led by the architect Sumayya Vally. The space, expected to open in 2028, will host public exhibitions and educational programmes.
Khouri is one of the Unite Arab Emirates (UAE)’s biggest and best-known collectors. Originally from Lebanon, he made his name as the chief executive officer of Omnicom Media in the Middle East and North Africa, and has been based in Dubai since the 1990s.
He began making plans for the foundation around five years ago, as one of the London-based Deflina Foundation’s collectors-in-residence, a programme launched in 2017 that considers collecting as a practice and seeks to support more ambitious implementation. With them he conducted feasibility studies to better understand what Dubai needs.
“The whole idea is to give back and foster exchange of ideas, challenge thinking and bring new perspectives,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “Dubai is about entrepreneurship. They support people like me, people coming to fulfil their ambitions. And what Dubai needs is private institutions, because that's how they will build their own version of culture.”
Despite Dubai’s large number of artists and galleries, it has never had a major museum, and private foundations have become a significant part of its infrastructure. The Jameel Arts Centre and Alserkal Avenue, each backed by individuals, are the two pillars of the art scene, in addition to smaller foundations such as Ishara, which focuses on art from South Asia.
Ekaf has an emphasis on global contemporary art, though one in which art from the Middle East will play an important role.
“We are here to support talent internationally,” says Khouri. “We're not about the region, but since we are in the Middle East, we also look at the best talent here. We have a responsibility to the ecosystem and the galleries.”
Ekaf will take Khouri’s collection, comprising works by more than 300 artists, as its starting point, drawing from it for initial exhibitions. Later shows will increasingly involve loans and collaborations. Ultimately, Khouri intends to establish an Ekaf collection that is separate to his personal holdings.
The veteran art strategist Caroline Louca, who was formerly at Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism and Christie’s Middle East, has been appointed as the director of the foundation. Louca and Khouri are looking to hire a curatorial team closer to the completion date for the museum.
Louca underlines that community engagement will be a major part of the foundation, with plans for talks, lectures and education streams. The foundation’s location, in Jumeirah 1, is a bonus in this respect. Jumeirah 1 is one of the oldest neighbourhoods in Dubai, where many affluent long-time residents live. Ekaf’s villa was home to an Emirati family in the 1980s, and Vally’s designs retain the elements of old-school Gulf architecture that is a source of nostalgia for many in the UAE.
"We are focusing on how we can make a place become part of the community—and not just focus on what we’re showing,” says Louca. “You can see beautiful artworks everywhere, but we want people to be a bit daring. We want them to walk in and ask questions—and not be embarrassed to ask questions—and then come back and ask more. If we can achieve that, it will be our barometer of success.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cultural-mar.title: How Cultural Marxism Became a Right-Wing Obsession
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cultural-mar.author: A. J. A. Woods
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/cultural-mar.text:
How Cultural Marxism Became a Right-Wing Obsession
The term “cultural Marxism” has become one of the main rallying cries for the international right. This lurid conspiracy theory about the influence of the Frankfurt School has little connection to reality, but that doesn’t make it any less dangerous.
In December 2021, the term “cultural Marxism” was added to the Oxford English Dictionary. It was, according to the OED, a phrase with a sinister and controversial past. Its etymology could allegedly be traced to 1930s Nazi propaganda; its first recorded English-language use was in a 1938 issue of a British Union of Fascists magazine.
Despite its dark history, this expression has recently surged in popularity. College campuses and city streets have been plastered with stickers that urge passersby to “smash” cultural Marxism. Prominent US Republicans, such as Texas Senator Ted Cruz and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have written book-length polemics to blame America’s decline on cultural Marxist ideologies.
Leaders in Latin America, like Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro and Argentina’s President Javier Milei, have vowed to rid their governments of this left-wing scourge. In the United Kingdom, Conservative Party MPs have said that cultural Marxists are “destroying” children’s souls and “snuffing out” the right to free speech.
Even the world’s richest man, tech-mogul-turned-Trumpian Elon Musk, has voiced concerns about a Wikipedia article that dismisses cultural Marxism as a “conspiracy theory.” This buzzword has now become a fixture in the lexicon of the contemporary Right — but what does it mean?
The Long March
“Cultural Marxism,” or the “cultural Marxism conspiracy theory,” is the political right’s attempt to explain why the culture of Western societies has changed over the past sixty years. According to this theory, a group of German thinkers known as the Frankfurt School (or the Institute for Social Research) invented the “ideologies” of multiculturalism, feminism, and environmentalism to trigger the demise of Western civilization.
When Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, and other Frankfurt School theorists fled Nazi Germany, they traveled to the United States and successfully injected their ideas into the 1960s student movement — or so the story goes. In the late twentieth century, their indoctrinated disciples performed a “long march through the institutions” (a phrase coined by German New Left activist Rudi Dutschke) to promote cultural Marxism in education, the media, the government, and the church.
More recently, right-wing activists and conservative pundits have used this theory to understand the rise of the Black Lives Matter movement, the increased visibility of LGBTQ+ communities, and the efforts to tackle the climate emergency. Even in countries outside the United States, conservatives have engaged in a “culture war” to defend their societies from this supposed menace.
What is cultural about this cultural Marxism? What is Marxist about cultural change? Conservative critics speculate that the Frankfurt School developed a fresh strategy of communist subversion in the 1930s. Instead of building a vanguardist party or seizing the factories, the Frankfurt School decided to infiltrate the cultural apparatus of bourgeois society to undermine Western capitalism.
Once ensconced in these positions of power, the critics maintain, cultural Marxists catered to the petulant demands of various minority groups — Black people, LGBTQ+ people, feminists — and dismantled the civilizational inheritance of the (white) majority. The Frankfurt School apparently believed that this strategy would cause a Marxist egalitarian utopia to emerge from the ruins of Western culture.
As the art historian Sven Lütticken observes, this alternative intellectual history relies on a theory of culture that mixes “conservative essentialism” with “schematic superstructuralism.” Culture, according to this right-wing conception, naturally reflects the values of a native populace. These values fuse a nation’s citizens into a harmonious unity that annuls antagonism and difference.
Yet this essentialist notion of culture cannot account for the drastic social changes that have taken place since the 1960s, because it treats the subordination of minorities as “natural” (or even as virtuous). Consequently, conservatives must conclude that an outside agent has seized the organs of cultural production to destroy the West.
In an act of self-defense, the opponents of cultural Marxism propose to eliminate every instance of “political correctness” or “wokeness” in public life through legislative reform, lifestyle changes, or violence. In this version of global events, the Frankfurt School and their devotees are blessed with a magical level of agency that can overcome all contradictions and countervailing forces.
A New Concept
Of course, no one can deny the historical existence and importance of the Frankfurt School. But why does this narrative of cultural degeneration focus so much on a collective of German Marxists? How does it continue to convince and excite the forces of political reaction? What is the genealogy of this idea we call the “cultural Marxism conspiracy theory”?
Some scholars suggest that “cultural Marxism” is simply an updated version of older antisemitic conspiracy theories like “Judeo-Bolshevism” or “cultural Bolshevism.” Of course, there are some eerie parallels between these earlier ideas and “cultural Marxism.” The British Union of Fascists translated Kulturbolschewismus as “cultural Marxism” in 1938, even if their use of the term was long forgotten by the time it was “recoined” in the early 1990s.
Contemporary far-right activists and authors tend to emphasize that several members of the Frankfurt School were Jewish, as if to suggest that these thinkers were genetically predisposed to operate as agents of cultural degeneracy. Even more damningly, the fascist online encyclopedia Metapedia once maintained an entry on cultural Marxism that presented the term as interchangeable with “cultural Bolshevism.”
It is ahistorical, however, to claim that “cultural Marxism” is nothing more than a rebranding of these previous tropes. This argument presupposes that Judeo-Bolshevism, cultural Bolshevism, and cultural Marxism are substantially identical, as though they share a transcendental essence that precedes their historical manifestations. It ignores the distinct trajectories of these ideas and implies that all right-wing politics are fundamentally the same.
The phrase “cultural Marxism,” as well as the conspiratorial narratives about the Frankfurt School that it often denotes, had its own bizarre history long before it ended up in the neo-Nazi thesaurus as a synonym for cultural Bolshevism. Where do we start? While I recognize the parallels between cultural Bolshevism and cultural Marxism, I do not think that the story begins in the 1920s or 1930s. For me, the 1960s is a better starting point for our analysis.
The history of cultural Marxism cannot be understood unless we reflect on the many overlapping shifts and realignments that stemmed from the ’60s. We must remember not to limit our notion of that decade to the spectacular images of May 1968 or Woodstock. As many scholars now agree, the 1960s were long — some claim that the 1960s lasted from 1955 to 1974 — and global.
It was a conjuncture that opened possibilities for revolution, dissent, and counterculture. However, it also involved the exercise of vast political power to defend social and racial hierarchies, control subversive energies, and protect modes of domination and exploitation.
Decades of Struggle
In his groundbreaking essay “Periodizing the 60s,” the cultural critic Fredric Jameson argues that the beginning of what would become known as the 1960s can be traced back to the struggles for national liberation and decolonization that broke out in 1950s Africa. Events in the Global South, such as the independence of Ghana and the Algerian War, ignited nearly two decades of struggle that shook the postwar global order.
Radicals in America and Western Europe drew inspiration from the successes of revolutionary and anti-imperialist movements around the world. They read Frantz Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth, Mao Zedong’s The Little Red Book, and Che Guevara’s Guerrilla Warfare. Students in the American New Left marched in the streets, held teach-ins, and occupied university buildings to protest their government’s military interventions in Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos.
The truly global nature of this 1960s revolt, with all its fissures and contradictions, gave rise to the hope that the “marginalized” and “minoritized” of the earth would be at the forefront of an unstoppable worldwide revolution. The days of an all-supreme Western civilization looked like they were coming to an end.
The 1960s saw the flourishing of new social and political categories of race, gender, and sexuality. Traditional modes of class-based struggle had lost their radical edge. The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947, as well as the merger between American Federation of Labor and the Congress of Industrial Organizations, tamed the labor movement in the United States and integrated unions into the anti-communist Cold War consensus. Uprisings against bureaucratic communism in the Soviet Bloc — Hungary, Poland, Czechoslovakia — demonstrated the need for a non-Stalinist and antiauthoritarian left.
New ways of doing politics were tested and elaborated. The slogan “The personal is political,” popularized by second-wave feminism, emphasized the importance of finding the links between individual experiences and wider structures of repression. Movements for Black power, women’s liberation, and gay liberation introduced a vibrant politics of identity that fused potent critiques of the existing order with daring visions of a liberated future.
They exposed the social exclusions, subordinations, and restrictions that underpinned the status quo of postwar capitalist societies. In the United States, these movements fought for the establishment of women’s studies, Black studies, and ethnic studies departments in American universities. Racial, sexual, and gender identities were embraced as epistemological bases for developing new forms of knowledge that could identify the multiple dimensions of power and oppression.
In the decades following the 1960s, many countries experienced something of a social and cultural revolution as women, racial minorities, and LGBTQ+ people acquired civil rights and started to play a more active and visible role in the public sphere. While these forms of equality and inclusion were usually partial and contradictory, they represented a significant liberalization of social life and an unsettling of old hierarchies.
The Cultural Turn
One of the most significant developments of the 1960s was the drastic expansion of “culture.” In the middle of the twentieth century, many “developed” countries transitioned from a predominantly industrial model of production to a largely service-and information-based one. During the rise of the postindustrial economy, culture burst into the foreground of day-to-day life.
The mass media — film, television, music, fashion, advertising, newspapers, and magazines — started to exert tremendous power and influence over the rhythms of everyday existence. The growing demographic of teenagers and young adults became an eager audience for the offerings of a new and exciting “youth culture.” The rise of this youth-oriented popular culture even altered conventional habits of speech, dress, and behavior.
These rapid changes spurred a “cultural turn” in humanities and social sciences scholarship. The thinkers of British cultural studies drew on the resources of Gramscian theory to rethink the nature of cultural production and consumption in postwar capitalist societies. Instead of assuming that mass culture turned people into passive consumers, these cultural theorists suggested that popular culture, especially youth subculture, constituted a site of potentially subversive political struggle.
As the forces of Western Marxism cut ties with Moscow, these intellectuals engaged with other radical causes and movements to promote a broad and populist form of cultural politics. Since the 1960s, cultural questions have become increasingly central to political debate.
It would be a mistake to believe that the 1960s were nothing but an outburst of liberal acceptance and youthful rebellion. From right-wing coups and neocolonial economic policies to police repression and state surveillance, the 1960s featured the use of extraordinary force to preserve arrangements of power and privilege.
Various right-wing and reactionary political movements ventured into this conjunctural terrain to defend the existing hierarchies of a supposedly pristine Western civilization. These forces required intellectuals who could explain away the causes of perceived cultural decline, organize their supporters into a coherent political identity, and offer compelling visions of conservative revival.
All cultural Marxism narratives derive from these efforts to resist and reverse the social changes that started to unfold in the long and global 1960s. It is important to understand how these intellectuals operated within their own political movements. How might we investigate the function and activity of these intellectuals? What kind of theory would illuminate the specific ideological practices that shaped their approaches to this cultural tumult? What this task requires, I suggest, is a return to Antonio Gramsci’s theory of intellectuals.
The Formation of Intellectuals
A central theme of Gramsci’s Prison Notebooks is a sustained and innovative rethinking of the concept of the intellectual. In a letter to his sister-in-law Tatiana Schucht, Gramsci remarked that he wanted to extend this concept beyond the limits of “the current notion that refers only to the preeminent intellectuals.” Instead of sticking to this abstract notion, Gramsci examined how specific types of intellectual were formed historically and how they functioned politically.
The sociologist Jerome Karabel describes this reorientation as a shift from a normative framework, which “treats intellectuals not as they actually are, but as they should be,” to an analytical one that identifies “the conditions and processes that shape the actual political consciousness and actions of different groups of intellectuals.” In the Prison Notebooks, Gramsci started from the “immediate, direct, and vivid impression” — the details of social practice and material circumstance — to reveal larger historical patterns.
His entries on intellectuals included several reminders about the importance of grounding one’s research in material reality. He specified that the formation and elaboration of intellectual strata did not “take place on the terrain of abstract democracy, but in accordance with very concrete traditional historical processes.”
The elements of cultural Marxism have been deconstructed and reconfigured time and time again as reactionary political forces across the world search for new ways to justify their opposition to equality, democracy, and justice. We will never understand these stories if we cling to the language of individual pathology.
Our approach to cultural Marxism must be rooted in the institutional, the conjunctural, and the structural. As Gramsci once put it:
Ideas and opinions are not spontaneously born in each individual brain: They have had a center of formation, of irradiation, of dissemination, of persuasion [that] has developed them and presented them in the political form of current reality.
It would be impossible — and uninteresting — to refute all the claims that every critic of cultural Marxism has made. After all, most cultural Marxism narratives include several factual observations, such as Herbert Marcuse’s endorsement of the “long march through the institutions” as a potential strategy for the post-1960s New Left. Yet these little facts are rarely used to provide us with an accurate account of either the Frankfurt School’s influence or contemporary social realities. Instead, they are mobilized to fuel political campaigns that seek to denigrate and disempower certain groups.
The Right has declared war on cultural Marxism. Only when we understand the practices — and weaknesses — of those reactionaries who have signed up for this war can we hope to resist their attacks and fight for a better future.

"This is the posture of a child: thrown into an already furnished world, in need of shelter yet wary of the rules on which shelter depends"
TO ENTER TOLIA ASTAKHISHVILI’S solo exhibition “Figure of the Child” is to descend beneath the surface. Curated by Fatima Hellberg and Manuela Ammer, the artist’s first solo museum exhibition does not merely inhabit two of MUMOK’s lower levels—it rebuilds them from within using drywall, tarpaulin, pipework, and light. The route begins in the foyer of Level -4, where Astakhishvili’s twenty-channel video Their own small gardens (2026) includes footage of the building’s inaccessible cellar and boiler room, and continues through a red polypropylene tunnel, Singing out of doors (2026), to the main exhibition space. Level -4 alone contains fifty-eight of the artist’s works, which often double as shelters for other artworks: huts and shelves that host pieces from the MUMOK collection, as well as contributions by members of the artist’s family and long-standing collaborators. In other words, the exhibition is like a house that has opened its door to everyone at once. Such generosity is the show’s first argument, and its first difficulty: Amid such a density of works, one may wonder whether each piece can be registered as itself, or whether it dissolves into an undifferentiated accumulation.
In such a situation, one has little to go on but their body. A museum ordinarily teaches the body to be quiet, upright, to keep a respectful distance from the object; here the works and their architecture unsettle that sense of discipline. With art everywhere the eye can see, even the floor becomes a display, and Astakhishvili’s dwellings and hiding places almost oblige the visitor to wonder, stoop, kneel, even crawl in order to see what else is there. This is, as the exhibition title suggests, the posture of a child, naming less a subject than a predicament: that of being thrown into an already furnished world, dependent on others yet capable of invention, in need of shelter yet wary of the rules on which shelter depends. The dwellings that thus command the body stand in loco parentis to more than the visitor. Hut 2 and Hut 3, like other architectural interventions elsewhere in the exhibition, were built to display the collection’s works—among them Nan Goldin’s Cibachrome print Honeymoon Suite, Nürnberg Eck, Berlin (1988), Picasso’s bronze Fernande (1906), and Medardo Rosso’s posthumous bronze cast Ecce Puer (1960).
Elsewhere, the shelter turns fully domestic. My emptiness (2025–26) re-creates the most intimate room of a house: a bathroom filled with excavated pipes, a bathtub, a shower tray, a light, and, hanging on one wall, a photograph in greenish tones by Kaucyila Brooke, taken from the series “Vitrinen in Arbeit’” (2002–2005), which documents Vienna’s Natural History Museum during renovation. One can walk in; mirrors add one’s figure to the scene so as to partake in the room’s intimacy. A wall seems to have once divided the bathroom into two parts; now gone, that division can still be felt via traces left behind. On the other side of that vanished line, Astakhishvili’s Hidden dreamer (2019–22)—a canvas worked in papier-mâché, pen, and paint—hangs on the wall.
The exhibition continues on Level -2, which adopts a lighter touch. From the staircase, one enters the space through a temporary corridor whose right side is a wall left standing from the preceding group exhibition, “The World of Tomorrow Will Have Been Another Present” (2025–26). Indeed, on the left, a wall text declares this floor to be a public space given over to events and invites visitors to make themselves at home, to play with what lies at hand, and to take care of the space as they would their own. Nearby are a wooden cabinet by Michael Kleine (Vitrine of dinner menu for June 19, 2026) and Heimo Zobernig’s shelf (2026), which itself holds small-scale sculptures by Veronica Brovall and Jonas Kuck together with several objects left over from the public programs of “Figure of the Child,” making it unclear which works belong to whom.
The corridor opens into a main room, sparer than the display downstairs, an environment in flux. Further remnants of the previous exhibition, along the right-hand side, carve out semi-secluded subspaces. On some days these spaces are occupied by public programs; on others they are left empty. In the open-plan part of the room, a table with paper and markers, benches left over from the opening dinner, and other material echoes from the ongoing events give the space the feel of a venue between special occasions. In one corner stands what appears to be a partial replica of a house, built at the start of the exhibition using plain construction board. Over the course of the show, the work, titled ideas are everywhere and in everything, 2026, has been filled with drawings and paintings by children. At the center, another unfinished house structure (the others are inside us, 2026) invites the audience in and, on occasion, is inhabited by visitors and by invited artists. A projector mounted on top of the structure casts nothing but a vast white field onto the wall, as though a film were about to play or had just ended.
This is all part of the “Tolia Curriculum,” a program that grew alongside the exhibition and unfolded both on this floor and in the museum’s cinema. Curated by Astakhishvili with Hellberg and realized with Marie-Claire Gagnon from MUMOK’s Exhibitions Department, these events began in May, while the installation was still under way, launching weeks of readings, screenings, movement sessions, and workshops for children and adults. During the first events, this space was little more than an armature, a world still coming into being. Once the show opened, the architecture was finalized, though still open to revision: Each event has given the floor a different spatial grammar.
Among the staggering thirty-one events, many bear the exhibition’s concerns closely. At Open Studio (May 23), visitors were invited to continue drawings the artist had started, authorship passing from hand to hand. On June 10, Simon Lässig’s presentation Microdrama traced, through texts and images, the emergence of the distinction between self and other in early childhood, and the ways it can be destabilized. James Richards’s film screening (June 18) carried a title, We came into this world wanting milk—everything else was made up as we went along, that read like a metaphor for the recurring child figure. Later events organized after the June opening extended that filial line of inquiry. Düsseldorf-based artist Keta Gavasheli’s First Utter, a listening/screening session in September, included cassette recordings, voice, movement, and acoustic guitar, growing out of the artist’s long-distance readings with her mother in Georgia. The performance circled motherhood, distance, and the unstable ground between memory and voice. Finally, the October screening of Jeff Preiss’s STOP, a film that follows his child’s growing up and transition over sixteen years, brought the exhibition’s titular figure to the screen in its most literal form.
Throughout the “Tolia Curriculum,” Astakhishvili’s most incisive gesture was to treat time, not space, as artistic material. The installation period, ordinarily compressed into as few days as possible and kept from public view, was entrusted to other artists and to the public as an open, durational event. Even for an artist whose practice has long been collaborative, to turn that interval into an open process meant forgoing authorial finality: making the work contingent on the program and the program on the hosting institution. Yet the plurality of perspectives assembled by the Curriculum was not confined to Level -2. Each program tacitly mediated how a visitor could encounter the exhibition below, drawing attention to its material and immaterial registers alike. A visitor who returned to Level -4 found its huts and hiding places inflected, after the fact, by what had been heard, drawn, or screened in the interim.
The mediation at work here differs from typical Kunstvermittlung (German for “art mediation”), which usually takes the finished exhibition as its point of departure and brings audiences into it by way of tours, talks, and workshops. The practice’s virtue is care; its limit is a tendency to leave the audience in the position of passive recipients, partaking in something already decided. Public programming, in the sense the Curriculum proposed, inverts that dynamic. Its premise suggests that the exhibition is incomplete without its public and that artistic practices can be shared as actively developing work rather than explained as finished concepts. Such a mode is scarcely visible in Vienna, where the repertoire of public programs seldom extends beyond the aforementioned lecture or guided tour, formats that transmit knowledge about a work while leaving its conditions untouched. The case for another approach to exhibition programming has never been stronger. At a time when public life is increasingly conducted through screens, and spontaneity is treated as a liability, the chance to draw, listen, or sit alongside strangers, and so to enact an exhibition together, acquires something close to political weight. An opening, with its glamour and free drinks, supplies the image of a community; the Curriculum materialized it, week after week.
In Deleuze and Guattari’s account of the wasp and the orchid1, two dissimilar beings become entangled: The orchid takes on the likeness of a female wasp, and the wasp, drawn to the flower, carries the orchid’s pollen onward. Neither imitates the other, but rather, each becomes a function of the other’s reproduction. What results is an arrangement neither could have produced alone. Something comparable took place at MUMOK. The installations turned into a venue, and the guests’ events entered the fabric of the work itself, each acquiring a vital function in the other’s apparatus. This kind of becoming is a process, however, and processes can be interrupted. Institutional critique has a habit of ending where it began: The museum temporarily accommodates the episodic, “childlike” disruption and then resumes its “adult” routines. The question now is whether and how MUMOK adapts this approach to its future programming now that the exhibition has closed, or lets it end here.
Michał Leszuk is a codirector of Kunstverein Kevin (Vienna) and a visiting lecturer in expanded museum studies at the University of Applied Arts Vienna.
“Tolia Astakhishvili: Figure of the Child,” and the accompanying “Tolia Curriculum,” ran from June 20 to November 1, 2026 at MUMOK, Vienna.
NOTES
1. Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia, trans. Brian Massumi (University of Minnesota Press, 1987), 10–12.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/el-sayed-spo.author: Sean Jacobs, Ivan Pech

Abdul El-Sayed’s Sports Fluency Is a Political Asset
Abdul El-Sayed’s ease in talking sports built rapport with skeptical voters and defies the stereotype of progressives hating what average people find fun. His knack for finding common ground is central to his broad political appeal.
One of Abdul El-Sayed’s greatest skills is his ability to deploy the language of sports to make his case. His fluency in sports allows him to find common ground with interlocutors and audiences, complicating the stereotype that progressives are anti-sports.
What makes him convincing and harder for his opponents to dismiss is that he played competitive team sports: El-Sayed was a hockey goalie in middle school. At Bloomfield Hills High School in the suburbs of Detroit, he played football and lacrosse and wrestled, becoming football team captain. These are sports conservatives embrace or consider quintessentially American. At the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, he continued playing sports at the club level, which is more competitive than intramural sports but separate from varsity athletics. As a Rhodes Scholar, he also played on and captained the University of Oxford men’s lacrosse team.
In a now-viral interview with Fox News’s Jesse Watters, El-Sayed did what so few progressive politicians manage: he disarmed a skeptical, even hostile, interlocutor not with talking points but with sports camaraderie. “We both played football and lacrosse. We both love America. We both love freedom,” he responded to the first question, before bantering about football ticket prices and ribbing his critics. The next night, Watters admitted to viewers, “I actually like Abdul. I probably shouldn’t like him, but I do.”
Hearts and Minds and the Home Team
By leaning into the language of sports, El-Sayed flips the script on the “bro culture,” especially among young men, that has long fueled right-wing politics and Trump-era masculinity. Rather than ceding that terrain, he claims it on his own terms. He repeatedly cast his opponent Mike Rogers as a subordinate “beta” in Donald Trump’s “alpha” orbit, turning the hierarchy of masculine posturing against them. Some skeptics, drawn in by his athletic bona fides, may find themselves unexpectedly receptive. It’s as if El-Sayed is saying: sports don’t belong exclusively to conservatives.
One of his most effective rhetorical strategies was to draw on the local loyalties and rivalries that shape Michigan’s fandom.
El-Sayed repeatedly invoked the long-standing rivalry between the University of Michigan Wolverines and the Ohio State Buckeyes, particularly their annual college football matchup, in which Michigan has the upper hand, sixty-two total wins to Ohio State’s fifty-three wins. His jabs at neighboring Ohio — and at J. D. Vance in particular — may seem strange and personal to outsiders, but they make perfect sense within Michigan’s political and cultural landscape. He was directing the taunt at Vance, an Ohio State alumnus who had repeatedly attacked El-Sayed with inflammatory racist and Islamophobic rhetoric. By turning the rivalry into a political jab, El-Sayed displayed local cultural fluency.
Some athletes agree. One high-profile supporter of El-Sayed is San Diego Padres pitcher Lucas Giolito. Front Office Sports previously reported that Giolito donated $1,250 to El-Sayed’s campaign. On election night, journalist Eli Kronenberg wrote on X that Giolito told him, “Although I don’t live in Michigan, I believe he’ll be a great progressive voice in the US Senate.”
On his book tour, Colin Kaepernick was asked which politicians he was most excited about. He answered quickly: “The ones that are interesting to me are obviously Mamdani in New York . . . [and] Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. I really like the approaches they’re taking. They’re staying very focused on the needs of the people. They don’t seem to be bought or swayed,” he said, adding that they represent a growing rejection of the establishment.
From the Field to the Campaign Trail
A few days before the election, former Michigan State long snapper Taybor Pepper, who played in the NFL for seven seasons, interviewed El-Sayed. After speaking with El-Sayed, Pepper wrote on X:
I understand why people want sports to be an escape from politics, but the reality is that throughout history, sports and politics have been deeply intertwined. From breaking racial barriers to fighting for equality and civil rights, athletes have played a pivotal role in pushing society toward meaningful social change.
Like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, El-Sayed supports English football club Arsenal FC, whose large, diverse global fan base has much in common with the New York Knicks, another of Mamdani’s passions.
This is not the first time El-Sayed has weighed in on sports’ cultural and political significance. In an April 2021 post on his now private Substack, The Incision, he analyzed the influence of big money on European football and fans’ successful resistance to major clubs’ attempts to commercialize the game further through the European Super League. He drew a parallel to the exploitation of the health care system back home: “If English soccer fans can stand up to fight for their soccer clubs, perhaps we too can fight for our healthcare, our prescription drugs, our schools, and our lives.”
In another post in October 2021, following the firing of former Raiders coach Jon Gruden over racist, homophobic, and misogynistic comments, El-Sayed argued that the problem was more systemic: “The toxic masculinity at the heart of America’s most popular sport — and men’s sports culture more generally — is way deeper than a few emails or a Jay-Z turnaround.”
Finally, about a month ago, El-Sayed’s campaign posted a short video on his social media in which one of his former high school football teammates, Nikita Sanches, speaks about El-Sayed as a teammate. Sanches, who was born in the Soviet Union and was a shy teenager when they first met, recalls how El-Sayed befriended him and took him under his wing. He also described how El-Sayed negotiated Islamophobia in the wake of 9/11. Sanches, now a chef, explains how, a year later, “we elected him our leader and our captain. Not just because he was our friend and our classmate, but because of the way he carried himself.” The same qualities that made El-Sayed a trusted teammate now help him use sports to connect with audiences beyond his political base.

The Palace of Westminster, which has housed the British Parliament since the thirteenth century, is at risk of a catastrophic fire if restoration work is not performed.
Dezeen reports that the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has determined that maintenance costs for Parliament, a UNESCO World Heritage site, will rise from £1.5 million to £2 million a week if delays around the building’s renovation continue. The government voted in 2018 to vacate the structure for restoration, but disagreements about how fully the House of Commons and House of Lords should leave during the potential decades-long renovation has suspended the work.
Two strategies have been recommended. PAC has asked MPs either to decamp fully from the building while the project is carried out—expected to take up to twenty-four years and cost up to £15.6 billion—or to “decant” gradually, which would result in the renovations taking sixty-one years with a cost up to £39.2 billion. Either option requires the approval of parliament.
“All options ahead involve extremely high figures with very big ranges,” PAC chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown said. “At a time of national fiscal constraint, we would expect the parliamentary authorities to examine these figures extremely carefully to see how they can be reduced before the vote.”
Clifton-Brown warns, however, that current fire risks could result in “Notre Dame-like flames” at the Gothic Revival-style palace, which was assessed to be at “constant risk of fire” in 2023. “Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof,” Clifton-Brown said, “resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life.”
According to the Guardian, ongoing maintenance to the Gothic Revival Palace has barely held at bay myriad issues: Leaking roofs; crumbling masonry protected by a maze of scaffolding; and a persistent risk outdated electronics causing a fire, necessitating round-the-clock fire patrols.
