https://jacobin.com/2026/11/kurds-uk-mig.author: Matt Broomfield
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/kurds-uk-mig.text:
Kurds Have Become Britain’s Latest Demonized Migrants
During the war against ISIS, the Kurds were feted in Britain as heroes. Today the stateless Kurdish population is increasingly demonized as a source of illegal immigrants and people smugglers.
A decade ago, the Kurds briefly figured in Western public consciousness as the feted heroes of the war against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS). In Britain as worldwide, audiences were fascinated by fetishized, orientalized images of “badass” Kurdish female fighters battling the Islamist terror group on the ground, backed by the UK and US militaries. Today the most populous stateless people in the Middle East are making headlines in the UK once again, but this time depicted as people smugglers, organized criminals, and unwanted illegal immigrants.
Broadly speaking, both migrants themselves and the smuggling networks who profit from their need to travel are hysterically depicted as united in highly organized, criminal, Islamic gangs that need to be “smashed” by the UK government. And a recent slew of right-wing media commentary has specifically focused on the Iraqi Kurdish groups, who are admittedly the current top dogs profiting from migrants seeking to make the treacherous journey between Calais and Britain.
This newfound attention feeds into BBC investigative journalism targeting Kurdish criminal networks in the UK allegedly running hundreds of illegal barbers and vape shops, which in turn leads to right-wing attacks on migrant-run high-street barbershops by Nigel Farage and Richard Tice of the far-right Reform UK party, and Robert Jenrick of the even further-right Restore UK. At the extreme, this discourse even leads to incidents like the attempted decapitation of one Kurdish barber by a Bristol neo-Nazi. As Western sympathy toward the Kurds occasioned during the ISIS war finally expires, media commentary and government policy is gradually setting up another marginalized ethnic group as the migration villains du jour.
Another Anti-Migrant Wave
For sure, it’s unlikely that axe-wielding fascists could or would distinguish a Kurd from a Turk or Arab. Likewise, the far-right politicians peddling anti-migrant narratives in Westminster have tended to refer conspiratorially to networks of “Turkish barbers.” Indeed, for better or worse, the Kurds — who number around forty million but have never had a recognized state of their own — have more often remained invisible in British public discourse.
The Kurdish ethnicity only made it onto the UK census for the first time in 2021, meaning that while official figures suggest there are around a hundred thousand Kurds in the UK, community representatives estimate the true figure is several times higher. Some Kurds are assimilated or prefer to refer to themselves as Iraqi, Iranian, Turkish, or Syrian for reasons of personal security or simple brand recognition: many of the UK’s nominally “Turkish” barbers or “Mediterranean” restaurants are actually Kurdish-owned.
On one level, the Kurds are thus simply being swept up in the latest broad wave of anti-migrant sentiment, targeting small boats in the English Channel and small businesses at home. And the same story is repeating itself elsewhere. There are rather fewer Kurds in the United States than in the UK or Europe, but there too recent Kurdish migrants report being caught up in new waves of anti-immigration sentiment. In Germany, cases of anti-Kurdish racism more than doubled in the past year, though this was primarily driven by Turkish, Iranian, and Arabic migrant communities themselves discriminating against the Kurds. Even Japan has seen its own tiny population of around three thousand Kurdish migrants become the key target of a specific xenophobic hate campaign spearheaded by the Asian country’s own far ight.
Kurdish Blame Game
The latest hysteria in the UK can’t be ascribed to the Kurdish ethnicity in particular. After all, the channel crossing has successively been controlled by groups from various nations: Iran, Iraq, Afghanistan, Albania. But this is just why increasingly frequent British media mentions of the Kurds in connection with organized crime are worth tracking.
While terms like “people smuggler” are weaponized by prosecutors and the media to smear and criminalize innocent migrants, Kurdish criminal organizations certainly do profit from the trade, sometimes on an exploitative basis. The Kurds’ long-term statelessness and the occupation of Kurdish-majority regions by Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Syria has left many of the Middle East’s estimated forty million Kurds occupying impoverished borderlands. Unsurprisingly, some turn to the grey- and black-market trade in legal or illegal goods to survive, including the Kurdish kolbar porters trekking through remote mountain passes between Iran and Iraq who are killed in their dozens every year. Decades of (legal) Kurdish migration have allowed these networks to extend to Europe, laying the foundation necessary to facilitate continued migration amid increasingly tough policing of UK and European borders, and create a profit for certain Kurdish individuals at the expense of others.
Throughout the Middle East, state violence against Kurds has often been linked to racialized depictions of Kurdish minorities as backward, uneducated mafiosos — as in the universally popular Turkish soap operas that frequently represent Kurds as villainous people smugglers and drug traffickers. Related negative stereotypes of Kurds are already somewhat more prominent in continental Europe, influenced by propagandistic Turkish depictions of the country’s domestic Kurdish opposition as narcoterrorists profiting from the European heroin trade, and may now be leaching into UK public policy. The shift recalls the vitriol previously directed toward Albanians during a prior surge in anti-small-boat rhetoric after 2022, and which academics argue directly contributed to UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) policy targeting migrants from the beleaguered Eastern European nation.
While the Albanians at least have a government that can robustly challenge Farage’s salvos, the stateless Kurds are left even more exposed. Ben Judah, the former adviser to Foreign Secretary David Lammy and centrist critic of UK migration policy, has suggested the Kurds’ weak geopolitical position should make it easier for Westminster to crack down on Kurdish migration networks. For Judah, despite the semiautonomous Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) “being under a de-facto Anglo-American security umbrella since the first Gulf War, there has been an unwillingness to put [people smuggling] first in our relations. . . . For Britain, the relationship as we know it should be on the line unless these authorities take this gravely seriously.”
In truth, this work is already being done. The FCDO has funded an anti-migration media campaign in the KRI, copying methods it previously deployed in Albania. More significantly, the BBC’s investigation into Kurdish migration networks led to the arrest of a leading Kurdish people smuggler in the KRI in coordination with the Iraqi Kurdish authorities. When I visited the KRI this summer, an official from the governing Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) stressed their ongoing cooperation with the British authorities to curb illegal migration, which was also the headline when Britain’s National Security Advisor visited the KRI earlier this week.
Though never numbering more than a few thousand per year, migrants from Iraq (most of them Kurdish) figured in the top five nationalities arriving in the UK via small boats from 2021 to 2023. They have since dropped out of the rankings. Relatedly, the latest figures suggest overall irregular migration out of the KRI has fallen by half in the past six months. None of this suggests an unmanageable crisis so much as the latest bout in the game of whack-a-mole in which one migration network loses control to another, and another set of desperate people are driven to seek a new life abroad, whatever the risks.
Expiring Partnership
In fact, the UK’s domestic shift against the Kurds comes amid related developments on the international stage. Judah correctly notes that the geopolitically isolated KRI, which was established by Western diktat following Saddam Hussein’s genocide against the Kurds and subsequent US-Kurdish cooperation during the two Gulf Wars, has long been reliant on these partnerships in order to survive. But rather than a cozy, mutually beneficial relationship, the Iraqi Kurdish authorities are currently being placed under severe security pressure by Westminster and Washington.
The US has withdrawn all its troops from the KRI and cut all security, essentially terminating the decade-old partnership that saw Kurdish ground troops defeat ISIS in coordination with Western air strikes, intelligence, and logistical support. The UK has unsuprisingly followed suit, withdrawing its own troops long stationed in the region. These moves repeat recent developments in neighboring Rojava (Syrian Kurdistan), where Kurdish forces that had lost twelve thousand fighters battling ISIS were this January forced to capitulate to the rule of a new Islamist government in Damascus after the United States finally terminated its cooperation with the Syrian Kurds. The Iraqi Kurds are now being left similarly exposed — not only to a potential ISIS resurgence but also to violent attacks by Iran-aligned militias in a febrile Iraq that is set to be the Middle East’s next battlefield and cross-border attacks from Iran itself.
Alongside their newfound status as migrant criminals, some Kurds are still making headlines as key Middle Eastern players — but no longer as heroic Western allies. Tehran has long repressed its own Kurdish population, executing hundreds in recent years. As the United States and Israel launched their disastrous war on Iran, US officials signaled and then rapidly aborted plans to arm unspecified Kurdish opposition groups. Donald Trump subsequently distanced himself from the proposal, announcing he was “very disappointed” with “the Kurds” who just “take, take, take,” adding “I think it’s a disgrace. . . . I’ll remember that,” and claiming that Kurdish forces illegitimately intercepted weapons shipments. As ever, these allegations were leveled at “the Kurds” in general, painting a whole people represented by a diverse range of political movements as mercenary and untrustworthy.
When I was in the KRI, both the governing authorities and exiled Iranian Kurdish armed groups stationed in the region strongly denied these allegations, with KDP spokesperson Hoshyar Siwaily telling me: “Although we are partners of the US, we would like to stay neutral, because this war is bigger than us. We don’t want to be part of it.” That hasn’t stopped Iran from launching more than seven hundred retributive strikes against the KRI, killing dozens of people — more than any other noncombatant country. The West is gradually closing the door on its erstwhile allies, even as Iran revenges itself on the Kurds.
Anti-Kurdish Alignment
With the Kurds abandoned by the West and targeted by the East, it’s little wonder that many still need to flee the region. The structural factors that drive Kurdish migration to the UK — and occasional involvement in criminality — are only likely to worsen in the coming years. Seriously tackling Kurdish migration to the West would mean tackling these regional “sources of conflict and insecurities” at their root. Conversely, however, the stage is being set to demonize those Kurds who flee future bouts of instability driven by the West’s regional interventions and repeated instrumentalization of the Kurdish cause. Western governments and right-wing media will find it increasingly convenient to join the likes of Iran in vilifying the Kurds, the one issue on which everyone in the Middle East seems to concur.
Below the line, commenters on right-wing news sites like the Daily Express and Daily Mail still generally confine themselves to the usual diatribes against migrants in general. But some are clearly picking up on the Kurds’ newfound prominence within this familiar rhetoric. Commenting on a story blasting the Kurdish networks between Calais and the UK as “brutal criminal kingpins,” one writes: “Saddam had the right idea about how to deal with these lot. . . . ” It’s a call to repeat the Iraqi dictator’s 1987–89 massacre of around a hundred thousand Kurds, a crime officially recognized as genocide.

https://gothamist.com/news/exclusive-vid.title: Exclusive video shows shocking moment Brooklyn building collapsed
https://gothamist.com/news/exclusive-vid.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/exclusive-vid.text:
Anderson Velez had just arrived in the Bronx for a painting job when he received a frantic phone call from his wife.
She was screaming, he said, begging rescue workers to pull their two sons from the rubble of their Brooklyn apartment building, which had collapsed minutes earlier.
All three survived, but his 9-year-old son was in intensive care after undergoing surgery on his skull and his wife has serious injuries to her ribs, spine and collar bone, he said Thursday.
Velez was left caring for his 2-year-old son. A video recorded by an in-home surveillance camera in the family’s apartment shows the boy being swept up in the rubble as a wall beside him gives way, revealing bright day light outside. He was pulled from the wreckage with scrapes to his forehead and legs.
“I am still in shock,” Velez said in the small lobby of a Brooklyn hotel the city is using to house people displaced by the disaster. “The truth is, I’m trying to be strong for my son, but I feel terrible.”
The shocking video reveals the moment his wife and their two children realized the building was collapsing.
The 9-year-old boy is seen holding a baby bottle and retrieving a gallon of milk from the refrigerator while the 2-year-old plays on the floor of the small third-floor apartment. Moments later, Velez's wife opens a door to the room screaming. The 9-year-old runs to his mother. A candle on a table can be seen visibly shaking and moving across the table’s surface. The younger boy moves slightly away from the wall before it caves in and the video cuts off.
“That movement, in my opinion, saved his life,” Velez said in an interview in Spanish.
Velez said he immediately returned to Brooklyn after his wife’s call.
“Everything was going through my mind. I was thinking about my children, hoping they were okay and that nothing serious had happened to them,” he said. “God heard me because I prayed so much for their health and well-being.”
Velez said he and his family had moved into the $1,500-a-month apartment at 1321 Flatbush Ave. earlier this month, after living in a homeless shelter.
He said his 2-year-old son “was completely covered in dirt” when rescue workers pulled him from the debris pile.
“His ears were full of dirt, his nose, his little mouth, his back — his entire body was covered in dirt,” he said.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said two of the eight people pronounced dead in the catastrophic collapse were kids, and several more were left injured.
Velez said his family knew the two children, who lived one floor below them.
A spokesperson for the Department of Buildings is still investigating the cause of the collapse of the three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. The near-century-old structure crumbled into an adjacent construction site, where the buildings department had previously penalized the development team for cutting corners and ignoring a stop work order.
Mamdani said buildings inspectors would conduct safety enforcement sweeps at more than 100 other projects linked to five companies involved in the botched construction project.

https://hyperallergic.com/protesters-urg.title: Protesters Urge Steven Spielberg to Boycott MoMA Over Leon Black’s Epstein Ties
https://hyperallergic.com/protesters-urg.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/protesters-urg.text:
Protesters Urge Steven Spielberg to Boycott MoMA Over Leon Black’s Epstein Ties
Activists rallied at the museum ahead of a benefit for the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, decrying the board member’s Epstein connections and his pro-Israel support.
Ahead of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) annual benefit for its Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center tonight, November 12, about 20 protesters assembled outside the institution to call on the gala's honoree, Steven Spielberg, to reject the recognition. The protest comes amid growing calls to oust Leon Black from the museum board over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
A letter sent to Spielberg by the feminist campaign group We Are UltraViolet, reviewed by Hyperallergic, urges the Academy Award-winning director to boycott MoMA until the institution severs ties with Black and renames the film venue.
“MoMA has benefited so handsomely from Black that they have named the very room you will be honored in, the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, in his honor,” reads the missive to Spielberg, authored by Elisa Bautista, campaign director of UltraViolet. For the past four iterations of the benefit, MoMA has funneled all proceeds into the film center, which was created in 2019 in recognition of a $40 million gift from the private equity tycoon.
“Mr. Spielberg, you do NOT want your legacy connected to accused abuser and Epstein associate Leon Black,” Bautista continues.
The letter makes reference to three sexual assault and misconduct accusations brought forth against the billionaire, all of which Black denies. One of the lawsuits was discontinued by the plaintiff, and an earlier lawsuit was dismissed by the court. A third lawsuit was allowed to move forward after a judge imposed a sanction. UltraViolet said it has not received a response from Spielberg's representatives.
Black left his role as CEO of his private equity firm Apollo Global Management in 2021, when news broke that he paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein’s first conviction for soliciting sex from a minor. Even though he stepped down as MoMA board chairman that same year, after Hyperallergic published an open letter signed by over 150 artists calling for his removal, Black remains a MoMA board trustee.
Public scrutiny of Black intensified in September, after the US House of Representatives unanimously approved a resolution to hold the MoMA trustee in contempt of Congress for defying subpoenas in an Epstein investigation. This month, Black sued California Representative Robert Garcia for defamation over public comments such as "Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”
Playwright and theater artist Gracie Gardner, who initially posted an open letter to Spielberg on her Instagram, said she was “amazed” by the public response.
“Steven Spielberg has made his career making stories about the dignity of women and children,” Gardner told Hyperallergic at tonight's protest. “It's totally disgusting that he's accepting an award [at the film center named after Leon Black], who's currently in contempt of Congress for not producing NDAs and his involvement in the Epstein files.”
Last month, Gardner co-performed a staged reading of former Barclays CEO and JP Morgan executive Jes Staley's deposition on Epstein to the United States House Oversight Committee in July.
At this evening's protest, others carried signs pointing to Black's connections to pro-Israel and Zionist organizations. Black has reportedly donated money to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which denies that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and Birthright Israel, which is accused of serving as a propaganda campaign for the Israeli government.
“I can personally say I'm Jewish and it's specifically because of my Jewish values that we're here. Never again means never again for anyone,” one demonstrator, Janet Goodman-Clarke, told Hyperallergic. “Leon Black not only is a Zionist, but he's also named ad nauseam in the Epstein files.”
MoMA has not replied to Hyperallergic's request for comment.
Artists, activists, and Epstein survivors have repeatedly gathered in front of MoMA demanding his ousting. Among those in attendance at today's action was Katie Fuller, arts educator and founder of the Time and Memory Project, who staged a separate protest calling for Black's removal in front of the museum with her sister in September.
Last month, Fuller teamed up with Epstein survivors, UltraViolet, and the Epstein-Trump Reading Room, created by the Institute for Primary Facts, to illustrate the extent of Epstein's network. The free, mobile installation displayed a timeline of President Donald Trump’s relationship with Epstein and contains thousands of books' worth of the released so-called “Epstein Files,” in which Black was mentioned over 8,500 times.
That protest included Dani Bensky, a dancer, educator, and Epstein survivor from 2004 to 2005. A few weeks after the action, Bensky wrote an op-ed for Hyperallergic condemning Black’s board position as “one of the starkest examples of institutional ignorance — a head-in-the-sand, look-the-other-way mentality that will inevitably give abuse of power a dark corner to grow and fester in.”
Besides his investments in MoMA, Black has held enormous sway in the art world. In a newly released book by William D. Cohan, Black disclosed plans to convert the Woolworth Mansion into a tax-beneficial art foundation, which is expected to house works from his estimated $5 billion art collection, an asset that Epstein helped leverage as bank collateral.
Gardner said she had one simple message for the attendees of tonight’s benefit gala: “If you know, you're human garbage. And if you didn't know, you can't say that after tonight, because we're out here saying hi to everybody with our signs.”

https://gothamist.com/news/why-brooklyni.title: Why Brooklynites Jeffries and Schumer are still favorites to lead Democrats in Congress
https://gothamist.com/news/why-brooklyni.author: Brigid Bergin
https://gothamist.com/news/why-brooklyni.text:
This column originally appeared in The Politics Brief, our weekly newsletter on the people, power and policies that shape New Yorkers' lives.
Sign up to get the full version where you can ask questions, share news tips and weigh in on the conversation. Hits inboxes on Wednesdays.
Outside the Beltway, there’s been an outpouring of pushback against electing House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries as speaker and Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer as majority leader. But political observers say it’s what happens inside the Beltway that counts, and that the two Brooklyn-based politicians are unlikely to be knocked off their leadership perches.
One big reason: no one has formally stepped up to challenge either lawmaker.
In the House, Jeffries' election as speaker would mark historic firsts. He is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House and the first speaker from New York City. While a handful of newly elected Democrats have not committed to supporting him — including incoming local Reps. Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier — no other lawmaker has emerged to challenge him.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who sits decidedly to Jeffries’s ideological left but has said she will support him, went on Instagram on Monday to explain how the internal leadership election works. The real vote takes place in a private Democratic caucus meeting through a secret ballot, she explained. If no one is challenging Jeffries, then members have no one else to vote for.
“ When you vote, it’s not this person's name, ‘yes or no’. That's not how this ballot looks,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “ The question needs to be, ‘Who do you actually want for the speakership? Who is running?’”
The behind-closed-doors process stands in contrast to how recent Republican House speaker elections have played out, spilling into acrimonious debate on the floor fueled by ideological divisions within the party and their razor-thin majority. In January 2023, it took 15 ballots to elect Rep. Kevin McCarthy speaker of the House, and then four ballots to replace him in October of that year with Rep. Mike Johnson.
Democrats are expected to hold nearly 260 seats when the next session begins in January. Jeffries only needs 218 to be elected Speaker. That means he has three dozen seats worth of negotiating room — a much more comfortable margin than House Republicans had in recent years.
“I think anything over 230 makes Hakeem’s life a lot easier A) in terms of getting elected, and B) in terms of passing bills without having to cater to the left wing of the caucus as much,” said Adam Carlson, head of the progressive polling firm Zenith Research.
In the Senate, Schumer’s prospects are more complicated.
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, the de facto leader of the left, said he would not be supporting Schumer and that “the time is now for change.” He held a press briefing Tuesday with Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who said she was undecided.
There are rumblings that the 75-year-old veteran lawmaker may face a challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who told reporters this week that he was in “listening mode” and had not ruled out running against Schumer.
“ If Van Hollen really throws his hat into the ring and goes full bore, I think he's the only one who can theoretically put together a coalition that could work, because he's an insider,” Carlson said.
New York’s junior Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who served as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said she was not "privy" to any conversations with Van Hollen and was standing firmly by Schumer.
“ He's done a great job marshaling our caucus these past two years to be laser-focused on cost, corruption and chaos,” Gillibrand said. She credited him with supporting candidates across the country who flipped at least seven Senate seats from red to blue, raising over $500 million for candidates.
“ I think people have a lot of gratitude towards Senator Schumer,” Gillibrand said, “and I think he'll win any Majority Leader race he has.”
Schumer would need a majority of the Democrats 54 to 56-member caucus to elect him majority leader. That’s roughly 29 votes.
Jeffries voiced strong support for his fellow Brooklynite.
“ Chuck Schumer was the quarterback of a team effort led by Senate Democrats and incredible candidates who ran all across the country,” said Jeffries, citing wins in Texas, Maine, Michigan, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina, Georgia and potentially in Alaska and Mississippi.
“I think the results of that election, the outcome, the decisive victory speaks for itself,” said Jeffries.
We want to hear from you
Do you support Jeffries for speaker and/or Schumer for Senate majority leader?
We'll share responses in next week's newsletter. (Sign up!)
This week in New York politics
- New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill selected Shirley Emehelu, a former prosecutor currently serving as New Jersey’s acting secretary of state, as her new lieutenant governor.
- With Democrats poised to take control of the House and Senate in January, some New Yorkers are hoping for a healthcare policy reset — even reversing the funding cuts to Medicaid and other safety net programs.
- After the results of the midterm elections, New York will be sending 20 Democrats and six Republicans to Washington in January as the state’s delegation in the U.S. House of Representatives.
- A federal judge has ruled that the Mamdani administration has to give immigration officials the names and birthdays of certain people living in a large, city-run homeless shelter in the Bronx.
- Voters in Elizabeth, New Jersey approved a measure that restores a $20 cap on future rent increases for rent-controlled units, at least for a year.
- New York Republicans are demanding a reckoning in their own party after a blue wave swept away many of their candidates on Election Day. Here’s what they’re saying.
- A New York appeals court struck down Nassau County's ban on transgender girls and women participating in certain sports competitions at county-owned facilities.

https://hyperallergic.com/print-center-a.title: Print Center and Women’s Studio Workshop Name New Leaders
https://hyperallergic.com/print-center-a.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/print-center-a.text:
Print Center and Women’s Studio Workshop Name New Leaders
Plus, SITE Santa Fe artists announced, awards for Lorna Simpson and Wolfgang Tillmans, and Penske Media partners with Amazon … because of course.
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Yukiko Yamagata to Helm NYC's Print Center
New York's Print Center, home to programs and exhibitions celebrating all the art that's pressed, proofed, and published, announced Yukiko Yamagata as its new executive director this week.
Her professional profile doesn't immediately scream “print nerd”: Yamagata most recently served as deputy director at Creative Time and previously worked at the Open Society Foundations, where she led a $15.8 million arts and culture fellowship program for socially engaged artists. But one of her earliest roles in the 1990s was as a senior curatorial assistant in the photo department at the Whitney Museum of American Art, and she is a current board member of Women Photograph, an organization focused on equitable practices in photojournalism and visual media.
Yamagata succeeds Judy Hecker, who announced her decision to step down earlier this year after a decade in the role, and is now executive director emerita.
Natalie Renganeschi to Lead Women's Studio Workshop
The Women's Studio Workshop in Rosendale, New York, dedicated to the printing arts as well as papermaking, bookbinding, photography, and more, has named Natalie Renganeschi as its fourth-ever executive director in the organization's 52-year history.
Renganeschi's career at WSW began in 2018, when she joined as a part-time employee while working as a high school art teacher. Now, she will oversee the nonprofit's major campus expansion, including the relaunch of its ceramics center.
“My path to leadership hasn’t been a traditional one, but it’s rooted in the ethos of WSW,” Renganeschi said in a statement. “Just as our mediums are steeped in process and the history of craft, working here is a sustained act of communal learning that allows for growth to come from below and within.”

https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-grand-j.title: Bronx grand jury to weigh charges against teen in fatal shooting of 15-year-old
https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-grand-j.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/bronx-grand-j.text:
A Bronx grand jury will consider Monday whether to indict a teen arrested in connection with the killing of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong, who was shot on his way to school last month, according to the district attorney’s office.
Prosecutors said Thierno Jalloh, 17, and two others were involved in Javits Frimpong's killing. Javits Frimpong was shot in the stomach as he walked to DreamYard Preparatory School around 9:30 a.m. on Oct. 29. The two others are still at large, officials said.
Jalloh briefly appeared in court Thursday on murder, manslaughter and weapons charges. He is being held in detention without bail and is expected back in court Monday.
According to the criminal complaint, someone who knows Jalloh identified him in surveillance footage connected to the crime during an interview with police several days later. Prosecutors said ballistic evidence and information from witnesses also tied Jalloh and two other people to the shooting. Those people had not been arrested as of Thursday afternoon.
Bronx Defenders, which is representing Jalloh, declined to comment after the court appearance.
Family members previously told Gothamist that the 15-year-old recently moved to New York from Ghana, following his father, who immigrated here in 2000. Prominent civil rights advocates, including the Rev. Al Sharpton and attorney Ben Crump, have condemned the killing and rallied around Javits Frimpong’s family.
Dozens of supporters for Frimpong’s family filled the sixth-floor courtroom for Jalloh’s brief appearance Thursday afternoon. Outside the courthouse, they shouted, “Justice for Javits.” Someone held a framed photograph of the 15-year-old with angel wings.
Thomas Frimpong, the boy’s dad, previously described his son as quiet. He said two students fought with his son a few days before the shooting and were suspended. The school told him his son was not to blame, he said.
Crump, who is now representing Frimpong’s family, said after the court appearance Thursday that prosecutors told his clients they do not believe the shooters went to Frimpong’s school or were involved with the bullying incident a few days earlier.
“Young people being able to get access to guns and cause irreparable harm — not only to Javits’ family, but also to themselves — I mean, it is a tragedy upon tragedy that everybody loses in this situation,” the attorney said. “It has to be a teachable moment to lead to a greater discussion about stopping gun violence in our community.”
Police arrested Jalloh Wednesday. Javits Frimpong’s sister, Millicent Frimpong, told Gothamist after the arrest that she was happy a suspect had been apprehended but that it did “not really” bring her any relief.
This story has been updated with a comment from Ben Crump.

https://hyperallergic.com/how-to-free-th.title: How to Free the Art World From Its Neoliberal Capture
https://hyperallergic.com/how-to-free-th.author: Nitasha Dhillon
https://hyperallergic.com/how-to-free-th.text:
How to Free the Art World From Its Neoliberal Capture
In “The Battleground of Art,” curator and activist Marco Baravalle dissects the art establishment's co-optation of radical politics and uplifts the stories of collectives that resist it.
We first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures, when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition. The group and our autonomous direct-action wing, Global Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.), had been invited by curator Okwui Enwezor to present our research and organizing against migrant worker exploitation in the construction of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. An artist boycott was underway, direct actions were escalating, and days earlier, on May 1, we had shut down the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.
Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan. These were not simply cultural centers; they formed the infrastructure for collective organizing, resistance, and enacting other worlds.
Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action. Drawing on his two decades of experience, Baravalle offers what we have called movement-generated theory and practice, rooted in the dialectic of doing and knowing. The book confronts the neoliberal capture of the art world, while also excavating histories and practices of abolition and autonomy that offer other possibilities.

https://gothamist.com/news/tornado-watch.title: Tornado watch in effect for 11 NJ counties, flash flood warning in Queens
https://gothamist.com/news/tornado-watch.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/tornado-watch.text:
A tornado watch was in effect for 11 New Jersey counties, and parts of Queens were under a flash flood warning until early Thursday evening.
The National Weather Service said that in addition to the possibility of a few tornadoes, also in Pennsylvania and Delaware, there was the potential of scattered hail up to the size of a ping pong ball and wind gusts reaching up to 70 mph.
The agency’s advisory about the tornado watch included areas as far north as Warren, Hunterdon, Somerset and Middlesex Counties, as well as several other areas in Central and South Jersey. As of mid-afternoon, the watch was in effect until 7 p.m.
The Garden State has seen an increasing number of tornadoes this year. So far, there have been five tornadoes in New Jersey, compared to two in all of 2025, and one in 2024, according to data from the New Jersey State Climate Office at Rutgers University.
A tornado warning had also previously been in effect for Southern Queens but expired after 2:30 p.m. However, the area was under a flash flood warning until 5:15 p.m. due to heavy rainfall in the area, according to the agency.
“We issued the warning as a potential heads up in case there are conditions that end up materializing with the heavy rain that is materializing over Queens right now, “ said David Stark, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service headquartered in New York.
Stark said that there wasn't a flash flood warning in effect for other parts of the city.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-p.title: NYC Council passes ban on 'surveillance pricing' that relies on personal data
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-p.author: Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-p.text:
The City Council passed a bill Thursday that bans companies in New York City from using surveillance pricing, which charges different prices based on algorithms or shoppers’ personal data.
Surveillance pricing means shoppers see a price based on their personal data like demographics, credit, browsing history or purchasing history. The bill prohibits surveillance pricing both online and in stores, although the practice is mainly used on the web.
Speaker Julie Menin described surveillance pricing as an “insidious and predatory corporate practice” that erodes privacy and fairness.
“It's a practice that worsens the affordability crisis, and today it's a practice that we are going to be ending,” she said during a press conference ahead of the vote.
In one investigation cited by the Council, Target shoppers saw a jump in pricing based on location data showing whether they were inside or outside a store. Shoppers found that a 55-inch SmartTV cost $499 on the Target app when inside a store, and $599 when in the store parking lot.
Uber, Lyft, Target, Instacart and airlines are among the companies that have faced scrutiny for alleged surveillance pricing. Many of the companies have denied using the practice.
Under the bill, the city would be able to issue fines of up to $1,000 for each transaction that violates the ban.
Menin’s proposal follows legislation approved by Albany lawmakers in June that prohibits surveillance pricing online and in stores, with some exceptions.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement that he supports the ban. He called surveillance pricing “just another way corporations are finding to squeeze working people.”
“New Yorkers’ personal data should never be used as a weapon against their own pocketbooks,” he added.
Business groups have warned that the ban could hinder discounts or loyalty programs for customers.
“If enacted, this law will make it harder for small restaurants with limited marketing budgets to reach customers, putting them at a disadvantage against national chains,” said Josh Gold, a spokesperson for Uber.
The company operates Uber Eats, which allows restaurants to offer discounts based on search history and previous orders.
Menin said the legislation would not affect discounts.

https://gothamist.com/news/feds-say-gang.title: Feds say gang members killed 12-year-old in East Flatbush drive-by, targeting a rival
https://gothamist.com/news/feds-say-gang.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/feds-say-gang.text:
Federal prosecutors have charged three men in the 2022 drive-by shooting that killed 12-year-old Kade Lewin in East Flatbush — saying the men were targeting an associate of a rival gang and fired into the wrong car.
Ousmane Diallo, Mayel Bussereth and Jonah Luc are members and associates of a Brooklyn gang called ICG Babiez, prosecutors wrote in court papers Thursday. A letter from prosecutors asks a federal magistrate judge to keep all three locked up until trial.
Court records showed none of the three had been assigned a lawyer as of mid-day Thursday.
“The senseless killing of a 12 -year-old boy in March 2022 is just one example of the violence ICG members and associates commit that endanger the lives of Brooklyn residents,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella, Jr. and prosecutors wrote in the letter.
Lewin was in the front passenger seat of a sedan parked near East 56th Street and Linden Boulevard when shots were fired into it from a black Mercedes-Benz on the evening of March 31, 2022, according to the letter. The boy was hit in the head and chest and died within 10 minutes, according to prosecutors.
A woman in the car was shot multiple times and survived, prosecutors said. An 8-year-old girl in the back seat was not hurt.
The men “misidentified the car that they believed the rival gang associate was in,” the letter states.
Prosecutors allege Diallo and Bussereth fired the shots. Each is charged with murder in aid of racketeering, along with assault and firearms charges, and faces a mandatory life sentence or death if convicted.
Luc is charged with assault and firearms counts, including causing Lewin’s death with a gun. Prosecutors say Luc admitted he was inside the Mercedes at the time of the shooting. He faces between 10 years and life imprisonment, and could face the death penalty.
A fourth person, identified in the letter only as “CC-1,” got into the driver’s seat of the Mercedes, prosecutors wrote. That person is not among the defendants.
Surveillance video followed the car from a Crown Heights apartment used by the gang, according to the prosecutors. They say it caught the car circling the block before the shooting and showed the men returning with their faces apparently covered.
Diallo, whom prosecutors call a leader of the gang, was on probation for a robbery when Lewin was killed.
He is now serving 14 years in state prison after pleading guilty to two attempted murders in Brooklyn, one of them about a year after the drive-by.
Luc is in New Jersey state custody for a probation violation. A jury convicted him in June of stealing government funds in a separate federal case.
Bussereth was on pretrial release in a gun case at the time of the shooting, according to prosecutors.

https://hyperallergic.com/a-toolkit-for-.author: Hyperallergic
https://hyperallergic.com/a-toolkit-for-.text:
A Toolkit for a Liberated Art World
Amin Husain and Nitasha Dhillon on Marco Baravalle’s new book, plus Jasmine Wahi on the continued fight for arts and culture after the midterm elections.
“Radical politics,” “marginalized communities,” “feminist art” … If you see these terms peppering wall labels at a major museum, there’s an excellent chance the institution behaves in direct opposition to those values and groups. Scholars Amin Husain and Nitasha Dhillon, who were also among the organizers of the historic Strike MoMA protests in 2021, know this pattern all too well. It’s part of the neoliberal capture of art institutions, which Italian curator and activist Marco Baravalle lays bare in his new book, The Battleground of Art. Read on for a review by Husain and Dhillon, who write that it’s a toolkit for building a better, freer art world.
Meanwhile, in the United States, that art world finds itself at a crucial turning point. In the wake of the midterm elections, longtime nonprofit arts leader Jasmine Wahi reminds us that the fight is only beginning. She opines today about the importance of holding Democratic officials accountable not just for redressing the damage inflicted by the Trump administration, but also for taking its responsibility to artists and culture workers seriously. “Rebuilding the same inadequate baseline is not enough,” she explains.
More in the news today, including public backlash against Egypt’s arrest of the editor of an independent publication and San Francisco-based painter Hiroshi Sato’s resistance against Silicon Valley and enshittifcation through his quietly subversive art. Heaven knows we could all use more of that.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins
In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition. | Jasmine Wahi

https://gothamist.com/news/with-search-f.title: With search for victims over, NYC officials look to what caused fatal building collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/with-search-f.author: Ryan Kost, Catalina Gonella, Brittany Kriegstein, David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/with-search-f.text:
It was a mild Veterans Day afternoon, and Katie Stevens, a teacher, had the day off. She’d left her windows open to let the cool fall air into her Flatbush apartment as she did her laundry.
At about 4 p.m., she heard what sounded like a car crash. A few minutes later came the sirens and then helicopters overhead.
Just down the block, near the corner of Bedford and Flatbush Avenues, a three-story apartment building had collapsed into a lot that construction workers had been excavating for a new development. Nearly all of the building had caved into the lot, shearing off the side of the neighboring building, exposing a stairway, a closet full of clothes and a bedroom set.
As Stevens approached the scene, she found a family crying on the sidewalk: “We may need everything right now,” they told her.
In the hours that followed, more than 250 firefighters and emergency service providers responded to the scene. Construction workers who had barely escaped themselves turned back to dig victims out of the rubble, Mayor Zohran Mamdani would later say. Councilmember Farah Louis described infants and toddlers being carried out on stretchers.
By Thursday afternoon, eight people were dead, including two children, and 18 others were injured. One person remained in critical condition. The rescue operation continued as a storm soaked the area in rain. By 4 p.m just as skies were clearing again, the FDNY declared the search and rescue operation over.
City officials said they began an investigation immediately after the collapse, one of the worst such disasters in recent city history. Gothamist reported Thursday that the developer of the site had a record for cutting corners on the project, according to records from the city buildings department.
The agency had issued a stop work order at the lot during demolition of an existing one-story building in March after determining that contractors had failed to install required safety precautions, including netting and sheds, officials said. A month later, a buildings inspector found the owners had continued demolition work in violation of the order and issued another penalty.
The five entities involved in the construction project are tied to about 100 others across the city, the mayor said, and building inspectors were beginning sweeps of those sites.
“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mamdani said.
In the immediate aftermath of the collapse, families gathered with their neighbors and loved ones on the sidewalk near the place that was once their home. Stevens, the teacher, said she took one young boy to a nearby clothing store to use the restroom. He kept asking her when he could go back home.
“I don't know, love,” Stevens recalled telling him. “But you are safe. Your family is safe. You're gonna be okay.”
Anderson Velez said he got a panicked phone call from his wife at home after he arrived for a painting job in the Bronx. She was screaming, he said, begging rescue workers to pull their two sons from the rubble of their Brooklyn apartment building, which had collapsed minutes earlier.
All three survived, but his 9-year-old son was in intensive care after undergoing surgery on his skull and his wife has serious injuries to her ribs, spine and collar bone, he said Thursday. Velez provided Gothamist with video of his apartment as the building collapsed.
“I am still in shock,” Velez said in the small lobby of a Brooklyn hotel the city is using to house people displaced by the disaster. “The truth is, I’m trying to be strong for my son, but I feel terrible.”
The Red Cross opened a reception center at a nearby YMCA for residents displaced by the destruction. At least seven households registered, though many spent their night on the sidewalks, wrapped in blankets, waiting for word about their loved ones.
The city’s public advocate, Jumaane Williams, described coming across a man on the sidewalk who appeared to be staring into space. The man was trying to find his wife. And so Williams and the local pastors asked if they might pray with him. He agreed, and they did.
“And so it was just amazing when his wife was found and taken out alive,” Williams said. “I'm hoping that that blessing, that miracle continues.”
But many were still left waiting.
On Thursday morning, rescuers continued the search as the community looked on. A demolition excavator worked through the rubble, piling the debris on one end of the lot — a mattress, a refrigerator and wood floor panels. Clothing and dozens of music records lay scattered across the site.
One woman collapsed to the ground after learning her husband was among the dead. “My husband, he died,” she yelled in Spanish.
“We’ve been waiting here all night. We went to four hospitals, and they haven’t given us any information,” Luis Siguencia said of his son, 22-year-old construction worker Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia Yupa, who had recently arrived from Ecuador.
“He wanted to get ahead,” Luis Siguencia said. “Because we all come here with the dream of getting ahead. He had his papers and everything.”
It wasn’t until Thursday afternoon that the Ecuadorean consulate general could confirm Gabriel had died in the collapse.
Kayla Chimborazo, who said she was Gabriel's stepsister, said her family spent the night “jumping from hospital to hospital, showing pictures, telling his name, his date of birth, to see if anybody has him.”
“We didn't even get a chance to see him,” Chimborazo said. “Even if there was that one possibility that he was still alive, we didn’t get to see him.”
Chimborazo described her stepbrother as “a sweet soul,” who was working to be able to provide for his wife and son in Ecuador. Chimborazo said she'd just seen him two weeks ago, at a family church gathering in New Jersey.
“He was really stepping up and starting a new start in life,” she said.
José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26, another construction worker from Ecuador, was also among the dead, the consulate reported.
His friend, Segundo Iza, stood vigil at the site of the collapse Thursday. He said he and Caguana Cosquillo had grown up together in Ambato, Ecuador. They’d met playing soccer.
Iza said his friend had moved to the U.S. four or five years ago. He had one son and another child on the way.
“He was someone who came here to achieve many dreams, to find better days for our children and our parents,” Iza said. “So it’s sad that our friend died here in New York.”
Eventually, the storm moved in, and with it, a heavy rain. The mayor spoke to reporters under a tent.
“These were our friends and our neighbors, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad and beyond,” Mamdani said. “ Let us continue to hold close those who have been plunged into unimaginable grief and pray for a full and rapid recovery for every New Yorker injured.”
The FDNY said late Thursday afternoon rescue operations had completed, and that it had determined there were no further victims.
An aunt to two of the men confirmed dead, Mamadou Bhoye N’diaye and Mamadou Bhoye Barry, gathered with her family that evening and grieved at the news.
“Right now my emotions are not good,” Kadidiatou Diallo said. “I just lost my nephews.”
Charles Lane contributed reporting.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Cidade de São Paulo tem mais de 28 mil imóveis sem luz após tempestade
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A tempestade que atingiu a cidade de São Paulo pouco depois do meio-dia desta sexta-feira (13) ainda causa consequências na vida dos paulistanos. Mais de 28 mil imóveis estão luz na capital paulista. Em toda a região metropolitana são mais de 33 mil locais sem energia, segundo dados da concessionária Enel.
Logo após a chuva, chegaram a ser 104 mil imóveis sem energia.
A Defesa Civil emitiu três alertas severos devido à tempestade, abrangendo as zonas sul, leste, oeste e central de São Paulo. Em seguida, a tempestade se deslocou, atingindo também a cidade de Guarulhos.
O Centro de Gerenciamento de Emergências (CGE), da prefeitura de São Paulo, indicou que a capital registrou pelo menos 11 pontos de alagamento. Já o Corpo de Bombeiros recebeu 22 chamadas para quedas de árvores, 17 para inundações e duas para desabamentos na região metropolitana.
Entre os pontos alagados estão a avenida Professor Luiz Ignácio de Anhaia Mello, em diversos pontos, inclusive no acesso à avenida Salim Farah Maluf. A Marginal Tietê também ficou alagada na altura da avenida Aricanduva. Todos esses pontos ficam na Zona Leste da cidade.
As avenidas Regente Feijó, no Jardim Anália Franco, Cassandoca, na Mooca, e a Radial Leste registravam pontos de alagamento. Semáforos foram desligados nas regiões do Tatuapé, Vila Prudente e Mooca. Na Zona Oeste, o túnel Dirce Camargo, no Itaim Bibi, chegou a ficar interditado.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: The McGuinness Boulevard Redesign Is Finally Complete
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Katie Honan
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
A long-awaited Brooklyn street redesign was finally completed Friday, after years of starts and stops and a supporting role in the bribery case of a former top aide to Mayor Eric Adams.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other elected officials celebrated the changes along a one-mile stretch of McGuinness Boulevard by cutting a ceremonial ribbon under the Pulaski Bridge in Greenpoint to cheers.
The changes, from Meeker Avenue to the bridge, add protected bike lanes, shorten pedestrian crossings and force turning vehicles to slow down. 
Mamdani vowed to restart the project three days into his term as mayor, and on Friday he thanked the advocates – many who lost loved ones to crashes – who kept pushing for it. 
“Even as the long pattern of wealthy interests trumping those of working people in this neighborhood repeated itself over and over, today that belief is finally vindicated,” he said. “My friends, we have completed the redesign of McGuinness Boulevard.”
The ceremony marked the end to a years-long back and forth on the street overhaul, first introduced by former Mayor Bill de Blasio and then squashed by former Mayor Adams, whose top aide, Ingrid Lewis-Martin, said the plan was only supported by outsiders. 
The City Reporter previously investigated the role siblings Gina and Tony Argento, owners of film production company Broadway Stages in the neighborhood, played in ending the project. The Argentos feared the reduction of traffic lanes would affect their trucks driving to and from the sound stages. 
More was revealed in a series of August 2025 indictments that alleged Lewis-Martin received cash, catering and a cameo on “Godfather of Harlem,” filmed at Broadway Stages, in exchange for stopping the redesign. 
Lewis-Martin and the Argentos were criminally charged over the scheme to influence City Hall. 
The largest push for a redesign of McGuinness Boulevard came after beloved teacher Matthew Jensen was struck and killed as he crossed McGuinness Boulevard just after midnight on May 18, 2021. 
He had just celebrated his birthday with seven friends, his cousin John Ogren said at Friday’s briefing.
“He was the happiest I’ve ever seen him. He had his dream job, he had his dream home,” he said. Jensen was struck by a speeding driver and thrown 75 feet with such a force his house keys were damaged, Ogren said, as he thanked everyone for the work to make the street safer.
“We gather as community because we care,” he said. “And because we care, we do.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ”Dark Horse’ é mais que um filme, é um esquema de lavagem de dinheiro’, avalia cientista político
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Ana Rosa Carrara
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A segunda fase da operação da Polícia Federal (PF) que apura desvio de emendas parlamentares para uso no filme “Dark Horse”, cinebiografia do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, agrava ainda mais a situação do deputado federal Mario Frias (PL-SP). A ação da PF teve como alvo Raphael Augusto Azevedo, ex-assessor de Frias.
Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, o cientista político Mateus de Albuquerque, professor da Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora (UFJF), avalia que cada fase da operação da PF ajuda a compreender o tamanho da engrenagem do esquema e evidencia que “‘Dark Horse’ é um filme, mas é, principalmente, lavagem de dinheiro”.
“É um esquema de transferência de verba pública para manutenção da família Bolsonaro”, resume.
Nesse sentido, Albuquerque destaca que os envolvidos lançaram mão da justificativa de que estariam realizando uma obra cultural para realizar os desvios de verba pública e tinham um nome forte para isso: Mario Frias. “Ele é ator, chefiou a cultura durante o governo Bolsonaro, deve ter mais intimidade com o ecossistema da cultura, que é cada vez mais profissionalizado, para mimetizar a forma com que se faz esse financiamento para transferir esse dinheiro para o seu fim, que fica cada vez mais evidente que era para sustentar [a moradia dos Bolsonaro] nos EUA”, argumenta.
O episódio, segundo o analista, também reforça a necessidade de rever a questão das emendas no Brasil. “É mais um exemplo de como o dispositivo de emenda, da forma como está no Brasil, pode ser usado para fins escusos”, continua.
Mateus de Albuquerque observa que há uma certa ironia quando se analisa a parte operacional do esquema, que, em sua lógica, se assemelharia à Lei Rouanet, tão criticada pelos bolsonaristas com base em desinformação. “Eles fizeram uma corruptela nefasta da Lei Rouanet, que não é um mecanismo de financiamento direto do Estado para produções culturais. Ela é um mecanismo de isenção fiscal para que empresas possam financiar obras artísticas”, afirma.
“O que o ‘Dark Horse’ faz: a busca por financiamento privado de maneira ilegal, irregular e, na prática, é um financiamento privado, porque a sua irregularidade se sustenta no elemento nocivo desse dinheiro privado que, na verdade, é público e foi roubado, convertido em dinheiro privado, através do Banco Master”, explica.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-alchemical.title: The Alchemical Possibilities of an Artist-Poet Collaboration
https://hyperallergic.com/the-alchemical.author: Phillip Pyle
https://hyperallergic.com/the-alchemical.text:
In 1982, Puerto Rican artist Papo Colo installed a book-shaped sculpture in the courtyard of El Museo del Barrio in Harlem. Commissioned as part of David Hammons’s Art in the Park program, it unfurled like an accordion across a series of 8-by-4-foot plywood panels co-authored by nearly 40 invited New York artists and poets. Four decades later, seven of those panels form the basis of Octopus and Others, an exhibition that addresses the porous boundary between the word and the image within the more experimental scenes of production from the ‘80s through today.
The first panel in the exhibition is by Colo himself and gestures toward the alchemical, even transcendent possibilities unleashed through the collaboration of artists and poets across distances, languages, and generations. “English Spanish $ Spanglish,” Colo scribbles in white paint against the black-coated plywood. “Vivas poetas individuales X-formed by Colo’s ceremony into collective.”

https://hyperallergic.com/botanical-arti.title: Botanical Artists Show Us What We Stand to Lose
https://hyperallergic.com/botanical-arti.author: Amy Levine-Kennedy
https://hyperallergic.com/botanical-arti.text:
Ascending to the third floor of NYC’s Society of Illustrators this fall is like entering a secret garden. The room is aglow with daylight and rare flora, not in situ, but in the 50 framed winners of its collaboration with the American Society of Botanical Artists’ 29th Annual International Exhibition. The works radiate with majesty, and the intricate sumptuousness is agonizing. Here, the threat of climate change looms.
With strong sun rays streaming in, the plant-potted upper patio of the Society of Illustrators is a jewel box of windowed light, a parade of watercolors on vellum or watercolor paper bask in the sunlight. Here is awe for Mother Earth and her plants — and these botanical artists — and for the meticulous, enchanting detail and outcry that cherish every bud, stem, leaf, petal, bark, seed, blade, stamen, and root.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Não vamos parar de trabalhar’, diz vereador do PT-SP ameaçado de morte
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: José Bernardes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O vereador João Ananias (PT-SP) registrou, nesta quinta-feira (12) um boletim de ocorrência após receber uma ameaça de morte por e-mail. O autor da mensagem fez menção direta à intenção de invadir o Palácio Anchieta, sede da Câmara Municipal de São Paulo, informou o número da sala do gabinete de Ananias e proferiu insultos.
O e-mail chegou no mesmo dia em que o vereador presidiu uma audiência para discutir orçamento das áreas de saúde e educação. A mensagem também fazia menção a um jogo de videogame. “Vou tirar a sua vida igual o Hitman. Conhece o Hitman?”. Hitman é uma franquia de videogames criada pela IO Interactive, lançada originalmente em 2000. A série acompanha Agent 47, um assassino profissional fictício, que recebe missões para eliminar alvos e utiliza estratégias como infiltração e disfarces para não ser identificado.
Em entrevista ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, João Ananias ressalta que a violência política aumentou muito após as eleições e que os alvos, majoritariamente, são os partidos progressistas. Ananias considera que a atuação na presidência de uma comissão relativa ao orçamento municipal possa estar gerando algum desagrado.
“A gente entende que isso tem a ver também com as audiências públicas que estão acontecendo na cidade de São Paulo. Por ser presidente da comissão, a gente está trabalhando para tratar de assuntos importantes da cidade. E, às vezes, tem pessoas que querem fazer cortes [para as redes sociais] no dia a dia e vêm aqui, tentam fazer suas agressões às políticas públicas progressistas”, avalia. “São pessoas que estão tentando virar políticos nas próximas eleições”, aponta.
O vereador relata que a presidência da Câmara disponibilizou escolta para ele e a equipe. “A pessoa que nos ameaçou está dizendo que vai vir atirar no próprio gabinete e, a partir do momento em que ele fala que fez uma arma só para me matar, a gente chega a um entendimento que de louco temos bastante”, afirma.
Para João Ananias, esse tipo de situação fragiliza a democracia. Ele lembra o episódio da ameaça de morte à deputada federal eleita Ana Elisa (PT-MG), que nem sequer assumiu seu mandato ainda.
“A cidade de São Paulo sempre foi muito democrática. Nós não podemos aceitar esse tipo de parlamentar que vai lá fazer corte, ganha eleição e depois vem aqui fazer baderna na Câmara Municipal. Não traz política de qualidade, não sabe a importância da política, da democracia. A gente precisa respeitar as divergências, as derrotas. E o que está acontecendo é que virou uma violência até institucional, porque tem parlamentar com cargo que não respeita a derrota. Mas gente não vai parar de trabalhar”, afirma
