https://taz.de/Nu-Metal-Band-Korn-auf-To.text:
Nu-Metal-Band Korn auf Tour: 30 Jahre alte Träume von Sex
Ist es Nostalgie oder ein neuer Boom? Die kalifornischen Gründerväter des Nu-Metal von Korn stoppen bei ihrer Jubiläums-Tour in Berlin.
Man muss es sich einfach als einen sehr großen Safe Space vorstellen, wenn über 10.000 Männer im deutlichen Überschuss zusammen mit den auch anwesenden Frauen den Refrain „All day I dream about Sex“ schreien. Und auch die weitere Textzeile „I don't know your fuckin' name. So what? Let's fuck.“ mitsingen können.
Im vergangenen Monat wurde das 30. Jubiläum des Albums „Life is peachy“ gefeiert. Ein Album der amerikanischen Nu-Metal-Band Korn, auf dem der Song „A.d.i.d.a.s“ ist, der die Textzeilen enthält. Und dessen Sänger hatte Samstagabend gerade herzliche Mittelfinger von der Bühne in jede Richtung der Uber-Arena in Berlin gestreckt, was die in die Jahre gekommene Masse jubelnd entgegnete. Denn dass man alt ist, erkennt man daran, dass man zu sogenannten Nostalgiekonzerten geht.
Korn ist auf Euro-Tour mit 17 Stationen. Und es ist alles wie früher. Im Moshpit des Innenraums hauen sich Männer herzlich ihre Körper aneinander. Es wird gestagedivt wie am Fließband. Frauen mit gestreckten Körpern und etwas labbrigere Männer, die sich auf tausend Händen zu den Musikern mit sehr langen dünnen Zöpfen am Kopf auf der Bühne tragen lassen. Sänger Jonathan Davis, als Asthmatiker immer wieder an der Sauerstoffmaske im hinteren Teil der Bühne, ist für seinen Gesundheitszustand immer noch erstaunlich agil unterwegs in seinen verschiedenen Gesangsstilen, die vom Growl über Scat-Rufen hin zu Emo-Ballade reichen.
Ein wenig an die Attitüde eines Wrestling-Moderators erinnernd, stapft er über die Bretter, auf die er sich einen Teppich hat legen lassen. Und auf den Rängen der Konzertlocation tanzen die Menschen, von denen sich vielleicht mehrere wundern, dass der Körper die Bewegungen von vor über 20 Jahre noch ganz genau kennt. Aber nein, hier sind nicht nur ältere Menschen.
Nu-Metal boomt im Internet
Denn im Jahr 2023 fiel es bereits auf: Laut Google Trends hat das Interesse an Nu-Metal seinen bisherigen Höchststand aus dem Jahr 2004 übertroffen. So hieß es damals auf Twitter und daraufhin in vielen Online-Artikeln. Es war die Zeit, als mehrere Veröffentlichungen Jubiläum feierten.
Alben der Hochzeit des Nu-Metals. Dem Genre, bei dem sich, so könnte man sagen, Growls, also grunzendes Schreien, mit emotionalen Melodien abwechseln. Dazu Drum-Exzesse und einfache, vor allem prägnante Gitarrenriffs, zu denen man hervorragend den Oberkörper nach vorne wippen kann, bis die Haare hinterherfallen.
Das Genre wurde von den kalifornischen Korn Mitte der 90er mit ihrem selbstbetitelten Album so richtig angezündet und darauf folgten grandiose Alben von Bands wie Staind, Deftones, Disturbed, Incubus, Slipknot, P.O.D., System of a Down. Korn veröffentlichte ihr kommerziell erfolgreichstes Album „Follow The Leader“ 1998. Doch nachdem der Jahrtausendwechsel überlebt war und das große Y2K-Chaos ausblieb, wurde das Genre mit Limp Bizkit und Linkin Park kommerziell immer erfolgreicher – allerdings nicht unbedingt besser.
Ab Ende 2009 schien das Interesse an Nu-Metal nachzulassen. Doch etwa im April 2021 passierte etwas, was man nicht unbedingt erwartet hätte, in der Schleifenhaftigkeit von Musiktrends aber auch nicht überraschte: Es begann wieder zu steigen. Und auf das große Comeback des Nu-Metals deutet nicht nur das ausverkaufte Korn-Konzert in Berlin an diesem Abend hin, sondern noch so einiges anderes.
So hart und dabei auch so weich
Auf TikTok wurden zuletzt viele Nu-Metal-Songs genutzt, angeblich weil sie in den kurzen Clips aufgrund von Wiedererkennbarkeit gut funktionieren. Etwa der Deftones-Song „Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away)“ erzielte dort große Beliebtheit bei Menschen, die in der Hochzeit der Band eher noch nicht auf der Welt waren. Als sie dann auch noch von Sängerin Billy Eilish erwähnt wurden, steigerten die Deftones ihre Zahlen auf Streamingplattformen um das Millionenfache.
Hipster Magazine wie 032C feierten die Band in ihrem Heft und die bei Menschen um die 30 als cool angesehene Marketing-Agentur Reference veranstaltete anlässlich der Art Basel Paris kürzlich ein Festival, bei dem der Korn-Gitarrist James „Munky“ Shaffer auftrat und Merchandise-Artikel mit Autogramm versah.
Und auch in dem bei jungen Menschen so beliebten Techno-Genre Hard Tech hört man den Nu-Metal-Trend. DJs spielen ganz ungeniert Remixe von Papa Roachs „Last Resort“ oder Slipknots „Duality“. Klar, denkt man sich, wenn man das so hört, und hätte es sich 2001 dennoch niemals träumen lassen.
Woran das liegt, lässt sich nur vermuten, aber es könnte schon mit der Kombi aus Härte und Weichheit zu tun haben. Dem entlastenden Schreien und den darauf folgenden Emotionen. Diesem Safe Space voller liebevoller Mittelfinger.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. https://taz.de/Veranstaltungsort-bUm-in-.title: Veranstaltungsort bUm in Berlin: Googles rebellische Er­b:in­nen
https://taz.de/Veranstaltungsort-bUm-in-.author: Jonas Wahmkow
https://taz.de/Veranstaltungsort-bUm-in-.text:
Veranstaltungsort bUm in Berlin: Googles rebellische Erb:innen
Häkelkurse, Co-Working und einer der letzten Zufluchtsorte der palästinasolidarischen Szene: Der Veranstaltungsort bUm muss zum Ende des Jahres schließen.
An einem grauen Mittwochmorgen führt bUm-Geschäftsführerin Eva Mörchen durch den ausgebauten Keller des ehemaligen Umspannwerks in der Ohlauer Straße. In einem großen Besprechungsraum packt gerade eine Gruppe überwiegend älterer Menschen ihre Sitzkissen zusammen. „Das ist unser wöchentlicher Meditationskurs“, sagt Mörchen. Der sei schon von Anfang an da gewesen, später habe eine der Teilnehmerinnen die Häkelgruppe ausgegründet. „Das sind auch Projekte gegen Einsamkeit, ohne dass wir sie so nennen“, sagt Mörchen.
Eine kleine Stahltreppe hoch führt Mörchen die taz durch die alte Maschinenhalle des Umspannwerkes. Heute bietet der Veranstaltungsraum Platz für 200 Menschen, Bühne und Technik sind schon da. An der Wand hängt ein Plakat für die Veranstaltung, die hier am Wochenende stattfinden wird: „Zündfunke. Kongress für einen Sozialismus von Unten“.
Das bUm ist ein unwahrscheinlicher Ort. In einem denkmalgeschützten Backsteinbau direkt am Landwehrkanal ist so eine Immobilie ein Traum für jeden Investor: Ansprechende Architektur, zentral gelegen in einem der hippsten Kieze Berlins, aufwendig saniert. In den vergangen sieben Jahren entstand hier ein Ort, befreit von Profitdruck, verankert in der Kiezkultur, der nicht nur kostenlose Räume für Häkelkurse bietet, sondern auch Bühnen für antikapitalistische und palästinasolidarische Kongresse.
Nun muss das bUm bis zum Ende des Jahres raus. Wie konnte es dazu kommen?
Mörchen schaltet auf einem kleinen digitalen Bedienfeld das Licht an. Die Decke der Maschinenhalle ist so hoch, dass über dem Saal noch Platz für einen Container mit Meetingräumen und Büros, der dort eingehängt ist – die bUm-Box. „Google hat das alles ausgebaut“, sagt Mörchen, „wir mussten nicht mehr viel machen.“
Googles gescheiterter Campus
2016 kündigte Google an, an diesem Ort in Kreuzberg einen Tech-Campus errichten zu wollen. Gegen das Projekt formierte sich Widerstand aus der Nachbarschaft und Berliner Zivilgesellschaft, der in einer kurzzeitigen Besetzung des Umspannwerkes gipfelte.
Kurz vor der Eröffnung aber zog sich der damals noch auf sein Image bedachte Konzern zurück und überließ die angemieteten Flächen der Zivilgesellschaft. Anfangs über die Spendenplattform „Betterplace“ – das Kürzel bUm steht eigentlich für „Betterplace Umspannwerk“. Schließlich zog sich auch die Spendenplattform zurück und das kleine Team um Eva Mörchen übernahm die Verwaltung der Flächen.
Google mischte sich nicht in die Belange des bUm ein, bezahlte aber die Miete über all die Jahre. Doch zum Ende des Jahres läuft der Mietvertrag aus. Verlängern will ihn der US-Techkonzern nicht.
Wieder unten im Keller angelangt, vorbei an schallisolierten Meetingboxen und einer Teeküche, sitzen etwa ein Dutzend Menschen konzentriert vor ihren PCs. „Wir haben rund 200 Mitglieder, die hier ihren Arbeitsplatz haben“, sagt Mörchen.
Co-Working ohne Kommerz
Ein Platz kostet hier nicht einmal 100 Euro im Monat, das ist rund ein Drittel dessen, was bei vergleichbaren Co-Working-Angeboten verlangt wird. Für viele der Nutzer:innen ist es die einzige Möglichkeit, wenn sie nicht zu Hause arbeiten wollen.
Dazu gehören auch Annamaria Olsson und Silke Georgia vom Verein Stories from the Beauty Parlor. Die beiden Frauen sitzen über den Bildschirm eines Laptops gebeugt an einem weißen Arbeitstisch „Wir betreiben Fundraising für feministische Projekte“, erklärt Olssen, weltweit sei Frauenarbeit systematisch unterfinanziert, nur 1 bis 2 Prozent der wohltätigen Spenden ginge an feministische Projekte, erklärt Olssen.
„Leider gehören wir selbst dazu“, sagt Olssen. Der Verein sei sehr klein und von Ehrenamtlichen getragen, teure Büros oder kommerzielle Co-Workingspaces könne man sich nicht leisten. „Die Alternative ist Isolation im Homeoffice“, sagt Olssen. In den vergangenen Monaten habe sie die Gemeinschaft im bUm schätzen gelernt, vor allem der informelle Austausch mit anderen Vereinen und Projekten.
„Es ist schade, dass wir bald alle gehen müssen“, sagt Mörchen. Zur Schlüsselübergabe mit Google am 17. Dezember habe man noch eine große Protestaktion geplant. „Wir dachten, wir schaffen es noch irgendwie, das bUm zu retten.“
Eigentümerin blockt
Mörchen erklärt, man habe versucht auf die Eigentümerin, eine internationale Immobilienfirma, zuzugehen. Das bUm habe ein neues Konzept erarbeitet, in dem ein gemeinwohlorientierter Betrieb durch kommerzielle Nutzung hätte querfinanziert werden können. 20.000 Euro Miete im Monat hätte man angeboten, aber die Eigentümerin hätte nicht einmal mit einem Gegenvorschlag reagiert. „Es kam weder eine konkrete Zahl noch ein konstruktives Gespräch“, berichtet Mörchen.
Eva Mörchen, bUm-Geschäftsführerin
Darüber, was danach kommt, schweigt sich die Eigentümerin aus. Gegenüber der taz ließ die Firma Anfragen unbeantwortet. Auch gegenüber dem bUm habe sich das Unternehmen nicht geäußert sagt Mörchen. „Wir hatten den Eindruck, dass sich Leerstand für die mehr lohnen würde.“ In den benachbarten, nicht vom bUm bewirtschafteten Flächen, stünden viele Büros leer.
Anlass zur Hoffnung gibt es wenig. In einem offenen Brief, den das bUm an diesem Montag verschicken will, fordert das bUm die Eigentümerin auf, wenigstens transparent über zu sein und künftigten Leerstand zu verhindern.
Aus den Parteien und der Bezirkspolitik hätten sie zwar viele Solidaritätsbekundungen bekommen, aber einen ernsthaften Versuch, das bUm zu retten, wurde nicht unternommen, sagt Mörchen. „Am Ende ist es eine Frage der politischen Prioritäten. Man hätte da kreativ sein können.“
Ankauf ausgeschlossen
Auf taz-Anfrage teilt das Bezirksamt Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg mit, man habe mit Unterstützung externer Expert*innen für gemeinwohlorientierte Immobilienentwicklungen geprüft, wie die Immobilie durch das Land oder einen Träger erworben werden könne. „Die Preisvorstellungen der Eigentümer ließen einen solchen Erwerb jedoch als nicht umsetzbar erscheinen“, teilt eine Sprecherin aus dem Bezirksamt mit.
Dass das bUm im Gegensatz zu anderen linken Projekten relativ geräuschlos geht, hat viele Gründe. Einer davon dürfte aber auch sein, dass sich das bUm in den letzten Jahren zum Rückzugsort der palästinasolidarischen Szene entwickelt hat, die von immer mehr Locations in Berlin ausgeschlossen wird.
In den Fokus der Berichterstattung geriet das bUm, als 2025 die Neuköllner Linke ein palästinasolidarische Kiezfest veranstaltete. Der Ortsverband lud den umstrittenen Palästina-Aktivisten Ibrahim Ibrahim ein, dem als Vertreter des Vereinigten Palästinensisches Nationalkomitee (VPNK) Hamas-Nähe vorgeworfen wird.
„Neuköllner Linke feierte mit Unterstützer einer Terrororganisation“ titelte der Tagesspiegel. Der CDU-Abgeordnete Timur Husein fragte in einer Anfrage nach der öffentlichen Finanzierung des bUms. Auch die taz sprach von dem Eventspace als eine „Bühne für Terrorversteher“.
Antisemitismus Vorwürfe
In einem Statement reagierte das bUm damals auf die Vorwürfe: „Gerade, weil palästinasolidarische Stimmen in Berlin massiv von Rassismus, Repression und Ausschluss betroffen sind, halten wir es für notwendig, diesen Gruppen Räume zu öffnen, in denen Trauer, Dialog, Aushandlung und vielfältige Positionen möglich bleiben.“
Grundsätzlich vermiete das bUm nur die Räume und greife nicht in die Programmatik ein. „Wir haben so viele Leute im Haus, wir können nicht für jeden eine Gesinnungsprüfung machen“, sagt Mörchen.
Sobald ein Thema aus Sicht des bUm berechtigt sei, dürfe es im Haus stattfinden. An Kontaktschuldlogiken wolle man sich hingegen nicht beteiligen, sagt Mörchen. Es zählt, dass die Hausregeln bei den Veranstaltungen eingehalten wird. Dazu zählt auch ein Verbot von Gewaltverherrlichung, rassistischen und antisemitischen Äußerungen. Ein Awareness-Team des bUm sei bei allen Veranstaltungen zugegen und achte unter anderem auch auf die Einhaltung der Hausordnung.
Auch mit dem sozialistischen Zundfünke-Kongress am Wochenende bleibt sich das bUm mit dieser Haltung treu. Dort treten die wegen ihrer kompromisslosen antizionistischen Haltung in Ungnade gefallene Linkenabgeordnete Vanessa Emde und der aus selbigen Gründen bereits aus der Partei geschasste Ramsis Kilani auf. Eine Presseakkreditierung haben die Organisator:innen der taz verweigert.
Google ermöglicht Palästinasolidarität
Ironischerweise ist es auch die durch Google ermöglichte Unabhängigkeit von staatlichen Geldern, durch die es sich das bUm leisten kann, angesichts des medialen und politischen Drucks nicht einzuknicken.
Mit dem sogenannten „BDS-Beschluss“ von 2019 fordert der Bund Kommunen und öffentliche Institutionen dazu auf, Vereinen und Akteur:innen öffentliche Räume und Förderungen zu versagen, wenn sie der gewaltfreien Boykott-Bewegung „Boycott Divest Sanction“ nahestehen. Laut dem Beschluss sei schon eine Infragestellung von Israels „Recht auf Landesverteidigung“ antisemitisch, Boykottaufrufe ebenso.
In der Praxis kann es ausreichen, wenn eine Organisation der BDS-Kampagne nahesteht oder ihre Inhalte unterstützt. So musste das durch öffentliche Gelder finanzierte Oyoun in Neukölln schließen, nachdem dort die antizionistische Jüdische Stimme für gerechten Frieden in Nahost eine Veranstaltung abgehalten hat. Im Februar 2025 sagte die TU eine Veranstaltung mit der UN-Sonderberichterstatterin Francesca Albanese ab, die dann im bUm stattfinden konnte.
„Generell ist die Frage, wer bekommt Zugang zu Räumen in der Stadt“, sagt Mörchen. Das gelte sowohl für die palästinasolidarische Bewegung als auch die hier arbeitenden Vereine und den Meditationskurs. Auch wenn das bUm nicht mehr zu retten ist, hofft Mörchen auf politische Lösungen, mit den gemeinwohlorientierte Räume in Zukunft langfristig gesichert werden können. „Strukturen, die seit sieben Jahren gewachsen sind, sollen über dem Recht auf Leerstand stehen“, sagt Mörchen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Portugal ohne Cristiano Ronaldo: Eine 7 für die Geschichtsbücher
Das portugiesische Nationalteam spielt nach 23 Jahren wieder ohne Cristiano Ronaldo. Und verliert. CR7 ist nicht anwesend und wird dennoch verehrt.
Wer hätte das gedacht, dass es doch mal passieren würde? Cristiano Ronaldo hat sich tatsächlich von der portugiesischen Nationalmannschaft verabschiedet. Wobei verabschiedet vermutlich etwas beschönigend formuliert ist hinsichtlich des öffentlichen Zerwürfnisses mit Nationaltrainer Jorge Jesus. Jedenfalls standen die portugiesischen Nationalspieler am Samstag beim Nationsleague-Spiel gegen Dänemark zum allerersten Mal seit 23 Jahren ohne ihren absoluten Superstar auf dem Platz. Und kassierten eine harte Heimniederlage.
„Desaströs“ sei die Leistung der Portugiesen gewesen, eine „Abreibung“ hätten sie bekommen, schreibt die Presse. Eindeutig war die Niederlage allemal: 4:1 hieß es am Ende für die Dänen und CR7 wird das vermutlich mit Genugtuung erfüllt haben. Nach 146 Toren in 234 Länderspielen hatte er in einer Videobotschaft das Trikot mit der Nummer 7 zurückgegeben und gesagt: „Ich habe es nie als ausschließlich meins empfunden.“ Sicher?
Die heilige 7
Hinter der geheuchelten Bescheidenheit weiß Ronaldo schließlich, dass die Nummer 7 so schnell keinen neuen portugiesischen Spieler finden wird. Beim Spiel gegen Dänemark trugen seine ehemaligen Kollegen beim Einlaufen jedenfalls alle das legendäre CR7-Trikot in Hommage an den Rekordtorschützen, mit dem Portugal 2016 zum ersten und einzigen Mal den EM-Titel holte. „Obrigado, Capi7ao“ hieß es auf einen riesigen Banner. Danke, Kapitän. Und nach der siebten Spielminute applaudierte das ganze Stadion.
CR7 war dabei zwar nicht körperlich anwesend, sein Geist wird es aber wohl noch lange bleiben. In diesem Rahmen muss das portugiesische Nationalteam sich nun neu sortieren. Es ist bestimmt eine Herausforderung, aber sicherlich auch eine Chance für viele neue talentierte Spieler, die bislang im Schatten des großen Weltfußballers standen.
Übrigens: Da die Nummer 7 offiziell nicht als Rückennummer bei einem Nationalteam gesperrt werden darf, hat der portugiesische Verband beschlossen, wenigstens das Layout der Ziffer zu ändern. „Die bisherige Nummer bleibt dabei als Symbol für eine Geschichte bewahrt, die niemals in Vergessenheit geraten wird“, heißt es.

https://taz.de/Olympische-Jugendspiele/!.title: Olympische Jugendspiele: Das historische Gold für Senegal
https://taz.de/Olympische-Jugendspiele/!.author: Helena Kreiensiek
https://taz.de/Olympische-Jugendspiele/!.text:
Olympische Jugendspiele: Das historische Gold für Senegal
Ringen ist im Senegal Nationalsport. Die 16-jährige Beachwrestlerin Elisabeth Diatta hat sich die Goldmedaille erkämpft.
Blitzschnell greift Elisabeth Diatta nach ihrer Gegnerin. Die Japanerin Kojima Reisa stemmt sich dagegen, versucht, die Senegalesin aus dem Ring zu drängen. Der Sand wirbelt auf, während die beiden jungen Frauen um jeden Zentimeter ringen, doch Diatta lässt sich nicht aus dem Gleichgewicht bringen. Sie löst sich aus dem Griff ihrer Gegnerin, setzt zum Gegenangriff an und schleudert sie mit einem gezielten Hüftwurf zu Boden.
Dann gibt es kein Halten mehr: Diatta reißt die Arme in die Luft, strahlt über das ganze Gesicht, springt vor Freude in die Höhe und lässt sich in den Sand fallen. Sie hat gewonnen. Und mehr noch, die 16-Jährige hat Geschichte geschrieben.
Mit ihrem Sieg im Beachwrestling gegen die Japanerin Kojima Reisa holte Diatta am Sonntag die erste Goldmedaille für das Gastgeberland Senegal bei den Olympischen Jugendspielen 2026. Und das auch noch im Beachwrestling, einer der beliebtesten und traditionsreichsten Sportarten des westafrikanischen Landes.
Elisabeth Diatta
Am Tag nach dem Sieg ist Diattas Stimme heiser. Viel kann sie nicht reden, die Stimme ist komplett weg. Die Anstrengungen der letzten Tage, der Freudentaumel, die körperliche und geistige Hochleistung während der Spiele fordern ihren Tribut. Doch auf ihre Leistung ist sie stolz, presst sie noch hervor.
In die Profi-Ringer-Liga
Diatta hat damit nicht nur sportlich einen historischen Erfolg erzielt. Ihr Sieg verschafft Senegal internationales Sportrenommee und hat zugleich Signalwirkung im eigenen Land. Denn Ringen ist hier weit mehr als nur eine Sportart. Laamb, wie der traditionelle Ringkampf auf Wolof heißt, ist Nationalsport und tief in der senegalesischen Kultur verwurzelt. Ob in offiziellen Arenen oder am Strand, sobald sich eine freie Sandfläche auftut, wird diese oft für Freizeit-Ringen und Übungen verwendet. Wer es bis in die Profiliga schafft, füllt ganze Stadien, wird als Star gefeiert und verdient gutes Geld. Neben Fußball gehört Ringen zu den beliebtesten Sportarten des Landes und war in diesem Jahr zum ersten Mal Teil der olympischen Disziplinen.
Die Tradition rund um den Sport reicht Jahrhunderte zurück. Mündliche Überlieferungen ebenso wie frühe Berichte europäischer Reisender und Missionare belegen, dass Ringkämpfe im Gebiet des heutigen Senegal bereits im 15. Jahrhundert ausgetragen wurden. Doch so tief der Sport in der senegalesischen Gesellschaft verankert ist, so sehr ist er bis heute eine Männerdomäne. Dass die erste Goldmedaille im Ringen nun ausgerechnet von einer jungen Frau gewonnen wurde, macht Diatta zur Vorreiterin – und zum besten Beispiel für die von den Olympischen Jugendspielen angestrebten Ziele: Begeisterung für Sport und gleiche Chancen für Jungen und Mädchen. „Senegalesische Mädchen sollen an sich glauben, denn Ringen ist nicht nur etwas für Männer“, macht Elisabeth Diatta Mut.
Insgesamt zehn Medaillen, davon fünf Mal Gold, kann Senegal verzeichnen und liegt damit auf Platz sechs der Medaillen-Rangliste. Deutschland sahnte insgesamt acht Medaillen ab, drei Mal davon das begehrte Gold, das die 17-jährige Judoka Jolina Reinhold, die 16-jährige Luna Fellinger im Taekwondo und die Handballmänner gewannen. Doch neben der Jagd nach Edelmetall dürften den jungen Athletinnen und Athleten auch die internationale Sportgemeinschaft und die ausgelassene Stimmung auf den Rängen in Erinnerung bleiben, neben kochenden Wettkampftemperaturen von durchschnittlich 36 Grad.
Neben Beachwrestling feierten auch Küstenrudern, Baseball5, Skateboarding und die chinesische Kampfkunst Wushu ihr Debüt im olympischen Programm. Erstmals trat zudem ein Flüchtlingsteam an. Und noch eine Premiere macht die Spiele in Dakar historisch: Zum ersten Mal überhaupt fand eine olympische Veranstaltung auf afrikanischem Boden statt. Dass dies auch das Bild des Kontinents als Gastgeber großer Sportereignisse verändern wird, ist für Kirsty Coventry, Präsidentin des Internationalen Olympischen Komitees (IOC), völlig außer Frage.
Russland ist wieder da
Auch Russland war bei den Jugendspielen in Dakar zum ersten Mal wieder auf der internationalen Sportbühne vertreten. Möglich macht dies eine 2025 formulierte Leitlinie des IOC, wonach junge Sportlerinnen und Sportler nicht für die Handlungen ihrer Regierungen verantwortlich gemacht werden sollen. Russlands Sportminister Michail Degtjarjow bezeichnete die Spiele bereits als wichtigen Schritt zur vollständigen Rückkehr des russischen Sports. Während Russland im Westen wegen seines Angriffskriegs gegen die Ukraine weitgehend isoliert ist, fällt die Wahrnehmung in vielen afrikanischen Ländern deutlich anders aus. Moskau hat seine Präsenz auf dem Kontinent in den vergangenen Jahren politisch, wirtschaftlich und militärisch gezielt ausgebaut – und viel an seinem Image gearbeitet. Einer Umfrage der Ichikowitz Family Foundation zufolge bewerten 83 Prozent der jungen Afrikanerinnen und Afrikaner den Einfluss Russlands in ihrem Land als positiv.
Politisch ging es auch bei der Eröffnungsfeier zu, als Israels Fahnenträger mit lautstarken Buhrufen empfangen wurde, während Palästinas Delegation deutlichen Applaus erhielt. Die Reaktionen spiegeln die Haltung wider, die Senegal im Gazakrieg wiederholt zum Ausdruck gebracht hat. Präsident Bassirou Diomaye Faye verurteilte das israelische Vorgehen deutlich und bezeichnete die Lage in Gaza als humanitäre Katastrophe. Im Land werden zudem zunehmend Forderungen laut, die diplomatischen Beziehungen zu Israel abzubrechen.
So sehr die Olympischen Jugendspiele für Völkerverständigung, Fairness und das Miteinander über Grenzen hinweg stehen sollen, ganz aus den Stadien verbannen lässt sich die Politik auch in Dakar nicht. Zugleich bieten die Spiele den teilnehmenden Ländern die Gelegenheit, sich jenseits politischer Konflikte in einem anderen Licht zu präsentieren. Für Senegal jedenfalls waren sie ein wichtiger Meilenstein und die Chance, sich international als verlässlicher Gastgeber großer Sportveranstaltungen zu empfehlen. Wo die nächsten Olympischen Jugendspiele stattfinden werden, ist bislang noch offen.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Why would anyone want a smart fridge?  | Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Dave Schilling
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
We are deep into the holiday season now, past Halloween and a mere two weeks away from American Thanksgiving.
I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much.
Grocery retailers are keen to take advantage of holiday-related binge eating, developing and releasing ever-more-depraved festive novelty foods to subdue us into carb-induced slumber.
In the UK, Marks & Spencer is expected to unleash hoards of weird, miniature packages of comical junk, affectionately known as “picky bits”, to prevent your digestive system from ever idling into park. “Ham and Barber’s Cheddar Crumpets”. “Twelve Mini Chicken Kyivs”. “British Melton Mowbray pork pie”. These dishes either sound like a thing a tertiary character orders in a Harry Potter novel or the last meal of a 60s British gangster.
In America, we have Trader Joe’s. There’s no fun name like “picky bits” for the plastic tubs of slop they sell in the refrigerator section. Instead, we turn to our spouses and partners and mumble: “Pick me up some of that crap.” Toffee-flavored cheddar cheese. Pumpkin spice yogurt dip. An advent calendar … for dogs.
I don’t begrudge anyone for cramming their shopping carts with intentionally whimsical perishable food products for depressed people. Overeating is a better use of your hibernation time than drunk-driving into an Arby’s at 2am. This is a holiday rite of passage: the junk food gauntlet. It’s as crucial to the festive season as a decorated tree and a surplus of good cheer.
But what if I told you that with the press of a button, the entire picky bits industrial complex could collapse before we even have a chance to open our canine advent calendars?
In France last month, supermarket refrigerators across the country were shut off remotely by Iranian terrorists. Other European countries have been hit with similar attacks, which occasionally lead to food having to be thrown out.
My entire body goes numb thinking about what it would do to US and British citizens if their supermarkets were similarly affected during the holidays. Can I muddle through another family get-together without a large, rapidly-warming bowl of chicken uncured bacon ranch dip to soothe my anxiety? Doubtful. The chaos would be unprecedented. It’d be like Judge Dredd, Blade Runner and The Purge rolled into one, but with worse catering.
You might be wondering how someone even hacks a fridge. Well, industrial fridges like the ones hacked in France are operated remotely via computer.
It makes some sense that large-scale operations like grocery stores need to have the ability to make temperature changes quickly, without a bunch of fumbling around with knobs and buttons. But internet-connected fridges are available to consumers, too. Refrigerators from brands such as LG and Samsung allow regular people to change the temperature of their fridge from a smartphone app.
My house is not nearly big enough to require me to adjust the settings on my appliances from another room. I only have six rooms (counting the bathrooms, with which I am very familiar during the holidays). Once again, technology aims to solve a problem that doesn’t exist.
All we’re doing is trying to get closer to the God-level control of everything at the push of a button. The issue with that is: if we are God to our machines, then the devil also exists, and he knows how to code.
Maybe there are a few useful applications of this technology for those of us who are supremely lazy. Some fridges have cameras and AI capabilities that tell you what food is inside, so that you might maintain a clean, tidy food storage system – one that tells you when your groceries are about to go bad.
As though your actual human eyes and hands don’t work. That old broccoli is in there. Do I need a computer to tell me what my poisoned nose already can sense? Yup, that’s rotten food. Confirmed. Until there’s a robot that can take the food out for me, move it to the compost bin, and hose down the interior, I’ll pass on the smart fridge.
I’ve already pointed out that computers have overwhelmed our cars, but this feels far more ominous. I need my holiday trash. I need my 2,000-calorie tandoori chicken bites. I can’t function without uncured ham and swiss cheese pockets.
This is existential. It goes beyond mere sustenance. This is my emotional support during trying times. If black-hat hackers can shut off my fridge and spoil my food, I might start picking my hair out or nibbling on one of my less crucial digits. If my mouth isn’t full of goop and slop, then I might be forced to have a conversation with an uncle. These are the things nightmares are made of.
The calamity is coming. Someone with more computer savvy will realize that the most vulnerable moment in our society is right now, during the holidays. The time when we need our buffalo chicken garlic bread bites the most.
The only solution is to rip the computers out and go back to the switches, toggles and tactile buttons that used to maintain our civilization. The alternative is risking a holiday season without parmesan-crusted chocolate chip cookies or peppermint orange chicken.
If you’re sweating right now, your blood pressure rising like a crimson tide, then you’re a normal human being. This is the proper response to a doomsday scenario otherwise unfathomable by the average mind.
Alternatively, we could go back to digging holes in the backyard and filling them with ice and food. Hackers can’t access your refrigeration hole. They can’t melt ice from thousands of miles away. We must go back to nature – potato cheese sticks and cookie dough ice cream bites preserved as the Lord intended.
Grab a shovel and get to work. Just make sure you have a functioning microwave.
- Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Tim Dowling
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout.
“I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”
Gout has been with us for as long as we know: in 1910 a case was diagnosed in a mummy found near a temple in Upper Egypt. It is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis – and, it is often said, the only curable one – resulting from raised levels of uric acid in the blood. Uric acid is produced when your metabolism breaks down molecules called purines, which are found in your body’s own cells and in certain foods you eat. Excess uric acid is normally processed by the kidneys and passed through urine, but persistently high urate levels can eventually lead to sharp crystals forming in the joints. The presence of these crystals can in turn trigger a profound immune response: inflammation, redness and pain. Eventually, hardened lumps of urate crystals called tophi can form under the skin.
High urate levels can have many causes, but they are not, in themselves, the sole cause of gout. “Virtually all people with gout will have a raised urate level,” says consultant rheumatologist Prof Edward Roddy. “But most people with a raised urate level don’t get gout.”
The pain of a gout attack is so debilitating that it can be hard to describe: the 19th-century writer and clergyman Sydney Smith said it felt “like walking on my eyeballs”. “Sometimes people think they’ve broken a bone – that’s quite a common thing,” says Roddy. “There is some qualitative research showing that people compare the intensity of the pain to having a heart attack or a kidney stone, and that women with gout compare the intensity of the pain to childbirth.”
It can also arrive, in the first instance, with little or no warning. “Often it comes on overnight,” says Roddy. “So somebody goes to bed pain-free, then they wake up and can’t put their foot to the floor.”
In the UK, Europe and the US, gout afflicts 2%-4% of the population. In the UK that equates to about 1.6 million people. “That is an awful lot more people in this country, for example, than have rheumatoid arthritis,” says Lucy Donaldson, director of research at Arthritis UK. She thinks persistent misunderstandings about gout can be a barrier to effective treatment. “There’s a lack of recognition about how common it is, and therefore people think it’s more isolated,” she says. “And, there’s a very judgmental attitude.”
Most sufferers will experience their first attack in the big toe, but if left untreated gout can spread to other joints in the foot and ankle, or the knee, or even hands, wrists and elbows. “You start to recruit different joints, and the flares become more common,” says Roddy. “Trying to avoid that happening is one of the important justifications for earlier treatment.”
Across the world gout affects about three times as many men as women (it is especially rare in pre-menopausal women). Certain ethnic groups, including Maori people, have a high susceptibility. “Some people may have gene variants that predispose them to having less tight control over urate levels in blood,” says Donaldson. But the genetic predisposition to gout is not perfectly understood. “Most of the focus has been on the genetics of uric acid levels,” says Roddy, “but we know less about the genetics determining crystal formation and inflammatory processes.”
Global incidence of gout is predicted to increase by 70% from 2020 to 2050; this is largely due to population growth and ageing. It’s more common among older people, but it’s also possible to suffer a first attack in one’s 20s. “There are reports coming in suggesting that the age of people developing gout is coming down,” says Donaldson.
If we still don’t hear too much about younger people getting gout, it could be because they often don’t seek treatment for the first flare. Painful as it is, gout tends to subside quickly.
“I just waited and eventually, a couple of days later, it went away,” says McAllister-Byrne, who is now 40. “A year or two after that, it would come back, and I’d wait for it to go. It’s only in the last two or three years that I went to the doctor.”
Historically, gout was understood as an affliction of leisure, of indulgence, even of quality. The Georgians thought it “a disease of the better sort, a superiority tax, a celebrity complaint,” according to the book Gout: The Patrician Malady. “Gout is the distemper of a gentleman,” Lord Chesterfield said, “whereas rheumatism is the distemper of a hackney coachman.” Gout was a hereditary trait that ran in good families; a badge of honour; a mark of distinction.
To some extent, those beliefs still colour our view of gout as a comical malady brought on by excess and idleness. “We’ve got the history of seeing pictures of people with a bandaged big toe in a bath chair,” says Donaldson. “And it often looks to be somebody who’s quite well off and clearly has quite a rich diet.”
“It definitely isn’t treated very seriously by other people,” says McAllister-Byrne, who says he had to endure unflattering comparisons to Henry VIII. “That’s what everyone always says, insinuating that it’s self-inflicted, from drinking lots of red wine and eating red meat.” He is in fact mostly vegetarian, and doesn’t drink regularly. McAllister-Byrne’s gout was probably part of his inheritance, however. “That’s what I think, because my dad has it.”
The National Institute for Heath and Care Excellence (Nice) guidelines for gout treatment call for patients with persistent flare-ups to be given urate-lowering therapy on a treat-to-target basis: that is, to establish a level of medication that will work and adjust the dose as required. Allopurinol is the most common prescription; febuxostat is another that will keep blood uric acid levels below a prescribed target of 360 micromoles per litre. Under that level, new crystals are prevented from forming and existing crystals in the joints should eventually dissolve. The risk of further gout attacks can be effectively eliminated.
That’s the theory, but it’s not always common practice in primary care. “Changing practice is like stopping a juggernaut sometimes,” says Roddy, who was instrumental in establishing the Nice guidelines in 2022.
“Not everybody’s treating to target,” says Donaldson. “They’re just giving a dose that they think is appropriate, but not then testing to see if it’s having the right effect. People were getting about 50% of what the effective dose should be in many cases.”
Very often the patients themselves do not follow up their initial treatment once the symptoms have abated, at least not until they’ve had several more painful flare-ups. As Roddy puts it: “The episodic nature of the condition contributes to suboptimal management.”
Then, of course, the stigma associated with gout can inhibit people from seeking treatment. It’s still regarded as a lifestyle disease, a consequence of a rich diet and too much drink. And while there are certain dietary risk factors – alcohol and foods rich in purine such as red meat and seafood can increase urate levels – the whole picture is much more complicated.
“Moderate wine consumption doesn’t really increase your risk,” says Roddy. “The risk is greatest with beer, and the reason for that is that beer is very rich in a compound called guanosine that the body breaks down to make urates.” But ultimately dietary precautions will not, on their own, alleviate gout. “There’s no good evidence that dietary modification makes much difference to urate levels,” says Roddy.
Apart from treatment, McAllister-Byrne hasn’t made any changes to his lifestyle. “When I was desperate during last year, I looked into it and I was like: I’m pretty much doing most of that,” he says.
The true causes of gout are a complex interplay of genetics, ethnicity, diet and related conditions including obesity, heart disease and poor kidney function. But the stigma associated with the historical disease persists. Could that be because, centuries on, we still call it gout?
We don’t diagnose people with apoplexy or dropsy any more, but we still have no better name for gout than gout, with all its ancient associations, misunderstandings and prejudices. A 2018 study found that when members of the public completed a questionnaire about gout, they were likely to believe it was caused by the patient’s own behaviour, but when it was called “urate crystal arthritis” (UCA), they were more likely to attribute it to ageing. Participants also considered UCA a more serious condition requiring medication, while gout was seen as more socially embarrassing.
Since starting treatment with allopurinol at the beginning of the year, McAllister-Byrne has had no further flare-ups of the disease. He is, however, reluctant to consider himself cured. “It’s managed, but it’s a sort of niggle in the back of my mind – if there were ever any issues, climate change or whatever, that stopped supply chains,” he says. “It’s made me think: should I stockpile some? Because quite quickly, I would be hobbling around.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.title: Sotheby’s $180 M. Van Gogh Sale Faces Eleventh-Hour Nazi-Era Restitution Claim
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.text:
With a $180 million painting by Vincent van Gogh due to go under the hammer Wednesday, Sotheby’s is pushing back against a last-minute restitution claim, citing details of a 1936 sale that the house says show the painting was sold voluntarily and for a good price.
The auction house told ARTnews that the archives of the art dealer Paul Cassirer confirm that van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), also known as Blossoming Chestnut Trees, sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, or about $22,000, in June 1936. Sotheby’s considers that a strong price for a van Gogh at the time. (Compare that to Verger avec cyprès (1888), a painting from the Paul Allen collection that fetched $117.2 million at Christie’s in 2022. That picture sold at Parke-Bernet in 1935 for $15,000.)
The new details come after the New York Times reported Friday that the heirs of Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher whose family fled Nazi Germany, had asked Sotheby’s to withdraw the painting from its November 18 auction. The heirs say the family was forced to sell the painting because of financial pressure brought on by Nazi persecution.
Their lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, challenged Sotheby’s to prove that the family received fair market value, according to an email shared with the New York Times, and would have sold the picture even if the Nazis had never come to power. “Otherwise,” he wrote, “no auction may take place.”
He also wrote that his client “is prepared to work toward a fair and just and just solution under the Washington Principles,” the guidelines accepted internationally for handling claims involving Nazi-looted art. ARTnews reached out to Schnabel for comment on evidence of duress, the family’s earlier restitution efforts, and what his client’s ideal outcome would be, but Schnabel did not answer before publication time.
The van Gogh is the star lot of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, assembled by the Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. The collection’s 12 Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings are expected to bring around $450 million. Sotheby’s has guaranteed the van Gogh, though the amount for that guarantee hasn’t been disclosed.
Sotheby’s wasn’t the only auction house eager to land the collection. According to people familiar with the negotiations, Christie’s also offered guarantees covering all the works, including the van Gogh. The figures are rumored to have been competitive with Sotheby’s and, in some cases, even higher.
For Sotheby’s, which has spent months promoting the collection, the timing could hardly be worse.
A Sale in Amsterdam
Samuel Fischer, who died in 1934, founded one of Germany’s most important publishing houses, with authors including Thomas Mann and Hermann Hesse. His son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, took over as the Nazis began banning many of the house’s authors. The family moved the business to Vienna in 1936, then fled Austria after the Nazi annexation in 1938. The Gestapo seized their Vienna home, library, and remaining art collection.
But the van Gogh’s history is different from that of the pictures the family lost in 1938.
According to the picture’s provenance, the family placed it with Cassirer’s Amsterdam gallery in 1932 or 1933, along with two Cézannes. It remained on consignment for nearly three years and traveled to both Rotterdam and Bern for exhibitions before being sold. The Netherlands was outside Nazi control at the time.
Luke Nikas, a lawyer representing Sotheby’s, told ARTnews that the van Gogh was sold to an independent buyer at fair market value. He also pointed out that the family held on to other paintings after the sale. Those were the works the Nazis eventually confiscated.
“The family had pursued and recovered works from the 1938 forced sale, but never the works they sold in 1936, such as this van Gogh,” Nikas said. He also described a postwar brochure published by Gottfried Bermann Fischer listing the paintings the family wanted to recover. Nikas said he has seen the document, and the van Gogh isn’t in it.
The two Cézannes tell another interesting part of the story. One is now at the Harvard Art Museums, where it has been on public display for years without a claim from the Fischer heirs. The other was offered at Christie’s in 2007, and again in 2017 when it sold for almost $6 million. In 2007, Gisela Bermann Fischer, who handled the family’s art claims until her death in 2014, told Christie’s that she wouldn’t oppose the sale.
There was a catch, though. In the same letter, as reported by the Times, she specifically reserved the right to challenge the sales of other family paintings she believed had been sold under duress. Sotheby’s told ARTnews that it had looked into the 2007 Cézanne sale but didn’t know about that reservation, which appeared in confidential correspondence between Bermann Fischer and Christie’s.
Sotheby’s restitution team has come in for scrutiny, too. As Julie Brener Davich noted in her Substack, the Appraisal, and as the New York Times reported in a follow-up Sunday, Lucian Simmons, who established Sotheby’s restitution department in 1997 and ran it for years, left for the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2024. Richard Aronowitz, who headed Sotheby’s European restitution work for 15 years, joined Christie’s in 2022. Both were also specialists in Impressionist and modern art. Two people familiar with Sotheby’s restitution operation told ARTnews that the department has almost doubled since it was run by Simmons.
What Counts as Duress?
The question here is whether a painting sold outside Nazi Germany to an independent buyer and at a good price can still be considered a forced sale. Nikas says New York law distinguishes between the terrible conditions Jews faced under the Nazis and a sale in which the buyer actually pressured the seller.
He pointed to two cases involving Picassos sold by Jewish families during the Nazi era.
In Zuckerman v. Metropolitan Museum of Art, a federal judge ruled in 2018 that a 1938 sale didn’t meet the legal standard for duress. An appeals court upheld the dismissal in 2019, though for a different reason: the family had waited too long to bring its claim. In Bennigson v. Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, a New York judge similarly ruled in 2024 that economic pressure caused by Nazi persecution wasn’t enough to establish duress when the buyer hadn’t contributed to it. The dismissal was upheld on appeal in 2025, again because of the delay.
That last point is interesting because Congress changed the rules earlier this year. In April, lawmakers amended the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act, or HEAR Act, eliminating laches, a legal defense that had allowed courts to throw out restitution claims because heirs had waited too long to pursue them. That makes it harder for museums, collectors, and auction houses to win qualifying cases simply by arguing that too much time has passed. It doesn’t change what counts as a forced sale, however.
Nikas said that distinction is crucial. Congress removed a defense based on delay, he said, but left the legal test for duress alone. He believes the 1936 sale fails that test.
Judd Grossman, a New York art lawyer who isn’t involved in the dispute but has experience with restitution cases, thinks the change has tipped the balance considerably toward claimants. “With this year’s amendments to the HEAR Act eliminating the equitable laches defense, which had prevented heirs from unfairly sitting on their rights before making a claim, the pendulum has swung dramatically in favor of claimants regardless of whether they have ever taken steps to vindicate their rights,” Grossman told ARTnews.
“Whatever the merits of the underlying title dispute, under this new statutory regime, we will see more of this sort of gamesmanship by claimants waiting to the very last minute to come forward before seeking their slice of the pie.”
With a $180 million van Gogh heading to auction Wednesday, Sotheby’s finds itself having to negotiate with the heirs of its former owner, or risk upsetting the biggest sale of the season.
Schnabel isn’t new to restitution claims. In 2016, he and provenance researcher Monika Tatzkow were already investigating Nazi-era losses involving paintings by Piet Mondrian when they approached the artist’s heirs and offered to look into other works. The family hired them, and their research eventually led to a restitution claim against the Philadelphia Museum of Art, according to a 2022 federal court opinion recounting the heirs’ allegations. Whether Schnabel approached the Fischers this time, or they approached him, isn’t clear.
Which brings us to the timing. Sotheby’s says it first heard from representatives of the Fischer heirs on Thursday morning, November 12. The Times contacted the auction house the following morning and published its story that evening. By then, the van Gogh had been publicly advertised for more than six weeks. The auction was only five days away.
Nikas questioned why the claim had arrived so close to the sale–the sale was first publicized in early October–though he said Sotheby’s was taking it seriously. The heirs may have good grounds for questioning what happened in 1936, but the timing gave Sotheby’s little room to respond before the allegations became public, which could have been the point.
There’s another question, too. Schnabel has asked Sotheby’s to establish not only that the family received a good price, but that it would have sold the painting even if the Nazis had never come to power. This may be difficult to prove in the case of a transaction that took place 90 years ago.
For now, Sotheby’s says the painting is still scheduled to be offered Wednesday night. The Blaquier family, meanwhile, says it is willing to talk. In a statement to ARTnews, the family said it had owned the painting for decades and respected the historical concerns involved.
“While the information available to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, the family welcomes constructive dialogue with the Fischer heirs and supports efforts to reach a mutually satisfactory resolution,” the family said.
Whether that happens before Wednesday remains to be seen.

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.title: Elon Musk joins 158,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.author: Guardian staff and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text:
Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company.
The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.
Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded, after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.
US lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have demanded Huang and Nvidia appear before Congress to explain whether US national security had been put at risk – with some in the president’s own party suggesting that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.
According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.
On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.
In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.
Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing.
The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”.
Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days.
Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.
Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”.
More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce.
The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”.
But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.
Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before Congress, according to officials, but no date has been set yet.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/cop-31/.title: Climat: les promesses intenables d’Ursula Von der Leyen
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/cop-31/.author: Gérard Le Puill
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/cop-31/.text:
Par Gérard Le Puill
Ancienne ministre de droite en Allemagne, Ursula Von der Leyen préside la Commission européenne depuis décembre 2019. Devant la COP 31 à Antalya , elle a promis une réduction de 50% des émissions de CO2 en Europe pour 2035, puis de 90% en 2040 et la neutralité carbone en 2050. Cette promesse ne prend pas en compte le bilan carbone des produits importés par l’Europe des 27, ce qui fait qui fait reculer la production industrielle et agricole des pays membres de l’UE suite aux nombreux accords de libre-échange négociés avec des pays tiers. Depuis 2022, Ursula Von der Leyen plaide pour un nouvel élargissement de l’Union européenne en tentant d’y faire entrer les pays suivants: Albanie, Bosnie-Herzégovine, Géorgie, Macédoine du Nord, Moldavie, Monténégro, Serbie, Turquie et Ukraine....

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/syria.title: Can Hezbollah salvage Syrian networks without clashing with Damascus?
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/syria.author: Reem Aouir
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/syria.text:
Can Hezbollah salvage Syrian networks without clashing with Damascus?
Earlier this month, Syrian security forces announced they had thwarted a plot to target the Homs oil refinery in central Syria, arresting a cell they said was affiliated with Lebanon’s Hezbollah.
The Homs refinery, alongside the Baniyas facility on Syria's coast, is one of the country's two oil refineries and a key supplier of petroleum products.
Syria’s General Intelligence Service said it carried out a “pre-emptive security operation” with the Internal Security Forces. The authorities identified the two detainees only by their initials, "MS" and "BSh", without disclosing when or where they were arrested. They also published photographs of what they said were explosive devices and equipment seized from the cell.
Hezbollah denied the allegations, reiterating that it does not have any presence on Syrian territory and is not involved in “any activity that undermines the security and stability of Syria”.
The statement said attempts to drag Hezbollah’s name into cases “that have nothing to do with it” wouldn’t change “the reality of its firm and clear position”.

The group also said its priority remained confronting Israel and its attacks on Lebanon and Syria, arguing that Arab and regional efforts should unite around confronting Israel’s “expansionist schemes”, and that the accusations “serve only the interests of the Israeli enemy”.
The latest allegations come amid a series of raids by Syrian forces targeting smuggling networks that Damascus says are linked to Hezbollah since the fall of Bashar al-Assad.
Neither the Syrian authorities nor Hezbollah have provided independently verifiable evidence to date establishing the alleged plot or the detainees' links to the group.
“The gap between the two accounts reflects a shift in the nature of the relationship,” Maher al-Tamran, a Syrian political writer and researcher, told Middle East Eye.
'I find it difficult to see what strategic benefit Hezbollah’s leadership could expect from authorising such an operation'
- Mohamad Hasan Sweidan, Lebanese political researcher
“Damascus is trying to establish a new equation based on the state’s monopoly over weapons and security decisions.”
Tamran said the alleged targeting of a vital economic facility went beyond a security operation, amounting to an attempt to undermine the state’s ability to provide energy and services and restore stability.
Mohamad Hasan Sweidan, a Lebanese political researcher and writer, meanwhile said Hezbollah was facing an “existential challenge” and that its priorities were preserving its ability to fight Israel, securing an Israeli withdrawal and ending the attacks on Lebanon.
“An attack on Syrian economic infrastructure would be particularly difficult to reconcile with those priorities,” he told MEE.
“It could give Damascus a stronger incentive to act against Hezbollah, deepen the group’s regional isolation and divert resources from the confrontation with Israel.”
Syria was already under pressure from the United States and some regional actors to act against the group, he said, and operations of this kind would only strengthen those demands.
“I find it difficult to see what strategic benefit Hezbollah’s leadership could expect from authorising such an operation.”
From a strategic ally to hostile territory
For decades, Syria was a crucial regional partner for Hezbollah, serving as the group's strategic link to Tehran and the overland route through which Iranian weapons and military supplies reached Lebanon.
As the Syrian uprising spread, Hezbollah became one of the former president's most important military allies, sending fighters to support government forces and helping to secure strategically important areas.
In December 2024, six days after the overthrow of Assad, Hezbollah’s secretary-general Naim Qassem acknowledged that the group had lost its military supply route through Syria.
He described the loss as “a detail in the resistance’s work”, and said the route could return to normal under a new government in Damascus, or the movement could “look for other ways”.
The loss did not necessarily end Hezbollah’s ability to obtain weapons, but it removed a supply channel that had operated for years with a friendly government's cooperation.
“For Hezbollah, Syria was never just a geographic corridor,” Tamran said.
“It was part of an integrated system that gave the group political, security and logistical cover, and linked the Lebanese front to Iran’s strategic depth. Losing Syria means losing an entire strategic environment, not just a route for moving weapons.”
Sweidan said the loss of the supply route “liquidates the continuous land corridor running from Tehran to the Mediterranean, and effectively ends the group’s role as an expeditionary regional force capable of deploying cadres freely across borders”.
“While basic armaments can always be acquired through unconventional means, the acquisition and integration of strategic game-changers, notably precision-guided missile conversion kits, heavy long-range rockets, advanced air defence systems and anti-ship capabilities depended heavily on Syrian state facilitation, protected military airfields and specialised military-industrial complexes,” he said.
Hezbollah also lost the Syrian hinterland, he added, which had provided “secondary depot storage, dispersed training grounds and secure fallback positions behind Lebanon’s narrow Bekaa Valley”.
Beyond geographical lines
In March 2025, deadly clashes broke out along the Syrian-Lebanese border after Damascus said Hezbollah had crossed into Syrian territory, abducting three members of its forces and killing them in Lebanon. Hezbollah denied involvement.
During the clashes, Syria’s defence ministry said its aim was to remove Hezbollah from villages near Qusayr, a Syrian town along a key supply route connecting the border region with Hezbollah areas in the Bekaa Valley.
'Syria’s borders are not just geographic lines, but social and economic spaces where family and tribal smuggling networks have formed over decades'
- Maher al-Tamran, Syrian political writer
The clashes ended after the two countries' defence ministers agreed to a ceasefire.
Later that month, Syrian and Lebanese officials met in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and agreed to strengthen security coordination and work towards demarcating their shared border.
But agreements between the two governments have not removed the challenges of securing the border shaped by years of smuggling, armed networks and overlapping groups and tribal ties on both sides.
“Syria’s borders are not just geographic lines, but social and economic spaces where family and tribal smuggling networks have formed over decades, some with overlapping ties to armed groups and local interests,” Tamran said.
Smuggling, he added, “cannot be treated as a purely security matter, separate from the local economy, poverty and the lack of jobs”.
For Damascus, reasserting control over the frontier is not simply about tackling illicit trade. It is also about preventing the re-emergence of the networks that allowed Hezbollah to move weapons and fighters through Syrian territory under Assad.
In July, Syria’s interior ministry said it would not allow Syria to be used “as a transit route or launch point for arms smuggling”.
'Strong reasons to prevent tensions'
Hezbollah may no longer have the protection of the Syrian state, but questions remain over whether local intermediaries, smuggling networks or weapons stockpiles survived the change in power.
“It is hard to speak of an organised Hezbollah military presence in the form we knew under Assad,” Tamran said.
“But it is also unrealistic to assume that the fall of the regime automatically made all of its extensions and local networks disappear.”
In October, the Syrian government and Hezbollah held secret talks in Turkey, according to Reuters.
One Syrian officials told Reuters that both sides agreed they held no hostility towards one another, and that Damascus assured Hezbollah it would not intervene militarily in Lebanon to disarm the group.
Syrian officials also asked Hezbollah to help stop “cross-border smuggling and dismantle its remaining sleeper cells, particularly in southern Syria”, the official said.
Hezbollah’s representatives “did not give a direct answer”, according to the official, but pledged not to interfere in Syria’s affairs.
Tamran said Hezbollah’s priority “may be to prevent Syria from becoming an environment hostile to its interests, more than trying to restore its former influence there”.
“I believe containment remains the most likely outcome,” Sweidan said. “The accusations and denials may continue, and there could be occasional security incidents, but both sides currently have strong reasons to prevent these tensions from developing into a sustained military confrontation.”
For Damascus, he said, a confrontation would consume military and financial resources, create more insecurity on the border and risk aggravating sectarian tensions. For Hezbollah, already facing continued Israeli attacks and occupation in south Lebanon, this would open up another front and further stretch its resources.
Less reliable alternative routes
Syrian authorities announced in May the coordinated arrest of an alleged Hezbollah cell accused of plotting to assassinate senior officials.
In July, the authorities said they had found long-range missiles, rockets and drones hidden in a tanker truck at al-Tanf border crossing with Iraq. The truck was heading for the Syrian coastal city of Baniyas.
The interior ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the shipment was intended to transit through Syria for Hezbollah in Lebanon.
'Hezbollah’s priority may be to prevent Syria from becoming an environment hostile to its interests, more than trying to restore its former influence there'
- Maher al-Tamran, Syrian political writer and researcher
Hezbollah dismissed the accusation as “fabricated narratives with no basis in fact”. Iraqi authorities said they would form a high-level committee to investigate.
“Hezbollah is more likely to seek alternative supply channels while exploring whatever limited opportunities may remain through Syria,” Sweidan said.
“Any continued use of Syrian territory would probably be more constrained and less reliable than before.”
Reports of shipments intercepted near al-Tanf were therefore “unsurprising”, he added.
“Its calculation is to recover military strength while limiting the visibility, scale and political costs of any activity that could provoke a confrontation with the Syrian leadership.”
Reuters reported on 26 October, citing Lebanese security sources, that Hezbollah had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to rebuild its military capabilities, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones.
“We have to distinguish between the ability to obtain funding and the ability to turn it into an integrated military force,” Tamran said.
“Nearly two years on, there is not enough public evidence that Hezbollah has succeeded in building an integrated alternative corridor to replace the old Syrian route.”
Sweidan said Hezbollah had found “alternative means of replenishing at least part of its arsenal”, pointing to the group’s use of FPV drones during the fighting with Israel.
“The more difficult question is whether the available alternatives can provide the volume, reliability and range of military supplies that Hezbollah previously obtained through Syria,” he said.
However, Tamran said the old corridor had also provided protection, storage and coordination, and that “these elements are hard to replace simply by finding other routes”.
A manageable relationship
The significance of the latest alleged plot, and any future attempts, lies in the context of the Syrian government's efforts to consolidate control.
As the new Syrian government seeks to distance itself from the Iranian axis associated with the Assad era and present Syria as a state capable of securing its borders and maintaining internal security, damage to essential economic infrastructure could deepen the country's economic difficulties, place further pressure on the population and undermine confidence in its Arab and western relations.
Any attacks would make it harder for President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government to establish stability, potentially benefiting actors opposed to the new political order, including former Assad loyalists, Iran and Hezbollah.
However, Sweidan said that “a weaker Syrian state would not automatically give Hezbollah back what it lost.
'Hezbollah is more likely to seek alternative supply channels while exploring whatever limited opportunities may remain through Syria'
- Mohamad Hasan Sweidan, Lebanese political researcher
“The former corridor depended on a political relationship with Damascus. Economic deterioration alone cannot recreate that relationship or reverse the new leadership’s regional alignment.
“Hezbollah could potentially exploit gaps in state control, but that would provide a much more uncertain arrangement than the support of an allied government.”
Sweidan added that further instability in Syria could have repercussions in Lebanon, including border clashes, displacement and worsening economic conditions.
“It could strengthen actors hostile to Hezbollah and create additional opportunities for Israeli intervention,” he said.
Those wider costs, he added, “would outweigh the possible benefit of occasional openings for weapons transfers”.
Hezbollah may have lost Syria as an open ally and military base, but it has not lost strategic value. While Hezbollah denies any activity there, questions remain over the border, smuggling networks and the legacy of its intervention in Syria.
“Syria remains of great strategic importance to Hezbollah, but its place in the group’s order of priorities has changed,” Tamran said.
Its immediate priority, he said, is to survive and rebuild its strength inside Lebanon, not necessarily to regain Syria militarily or politically.
“Hezbollah’s preferred outcome would presumably remain a supportive Syria,” Sweidan adds.
“Under the current circumstances, however, its more immediate interest is a manageable relationship with Damascus that prevents another front from opening.”
However, Tamran argued, “the paradox is that Hezbollah now needs Syria more strategically, but has less ability than ever to influence its decisions.”
Ultimately, Hezbollah’s presence in Syria has become smaller, more covert, and increasingly challenged.
