https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Mr Baxter, who ate our belongings – and broke our hearts
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Camilla Balshaw
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
The day we brought our 14-week-old cocker spaniel home in 2022, I was wearing a silk scarf I’d picked up decades ago in a vintage shop in Tokyo. I didn’t know it then but that rainy afternoon would be the last time I’d wear it. Three days later, it was in my new puppy’s mouth. Once he’d finished tearing my scarf to shreds, he gazed at me with soulful chocolate brown eyes, fluttering his long eyelashes.
No matter how fond I was of that silk scarf, how could I be angry? Puppies chew stuff. That’s what they do. Mr Baxter gnawed his way through four dog beds, blankets and multiple dog leads. Nothing was off-limits. Socks, shoes, trainers, gloves, flat caps, berets, the freshly printed chapters of my debut book, a nifty pair of 70s sunglasses. Fearless and lithe, he grabbed things we naively thought were out of reach, and woe betide anyone who tried to take them from him.
Mr Baxter didn’t have an auspicious start in life. Reared on a puppy farm and abandoned by a previous owner, he was adopted by us, half-starved and as thin as a pencil. The shelter called him Max, but this name didn’t suit him. There was an elegance to this anxious pup, so we renamed him Mr Baxter, although given his relentless, hyperactive chewing, perhaps Mad Max was more appropriate.
Desperate, we tried to understand our mischievous puppy. We read books about cocker spaniels. We turned to dog trainers and behaviourists for advice, who said: “Reinforce positive behaviour.” This meant a steady flow of his number-one dog treat: carrots. Much as he loved his vegetables, the carrots failed.
I began to wonder how long this might go on. Would Mr Baxter’s penchant for our possessions last forever? If I had to pinpoint my lowest moment, it was probably when Mr Baxter chewed through the sleeve of my Aran knit jumper.
I can’t recall the exact moment our steady, regular training finally paid dividends. This once unruly puppy simply became the most loyal and lovable companion, earning him the accolade of “Norfolk’s friendliest dog” from our neighbours.
Over time, we learned his real motivations were routine, walks – the longer the better (cocker spaniels are inexhaustible) – food and a tickled belly, not our possessions.
And yet there was always something otherworldly about the way he communicated through those deep, wise eyes. Perhaps he knew his time with us would be fleeting. We lost him at four years old. I’ll miss this free-spirited and curious force in our lives. I continue to wear my tooth-marked trainers that bear Mr Baxter’s presence, because sometimes the most precious memories in life come with a few teeth marks.
Named: A Story of Names and Reclaiming Who We Are by Camilla Balshaw is published by Bedford Square (£10.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

https://taz.de/News-Fatigue/!6228528/.title: News Fatigue: Nachrichten? Nein, danke
https://taz.de/News-Fatigue/!6228528/.author: Lilly Schröder
https://taz.de/News-Fatigue/!6228528/.text:
News Fatigue: Nachrichten? Nein, danke
Wer nicht weiß, was in der Welt passiert, kann sich schlecht für andere einsetzen. Aber macht es uns wirklich zu besseren Menschen, wenn wir informiert sind?
L -Ü-C-K-E-N-P-R-E-S-S-E, sagt er betont langsam, lässt den Blick in die Runde schweifen und lächelt selbstgefällig. Seit Beginn des Ukrainekriegs konsumiere er gar keine Nachrichten mehr, die öffentlich-rechtliche Lückenpresse komme ihrem Staatsvertrag nicht mehr nach, berichte nicht umfassend und objektiv, von den Privaten ganz zu schweigen. Die restlichen Mitglieder meines Zeichenkurses nicken eifrig. Auch sie würden keine Nachrichten mehr verfolgen, erzählen sie. Zu negativ, zu einseitig, zu deprimierend.
Ich schlucke und versuche es mit einem Gegenvorschlag: Wie wäre es mit Medien, die konstruktiven Journalismus betreiben, „Slow Journalism“ oder Lokalmedien? Da müsse man sich nicht nur mit dem Elend der Welt beschäftigen, sondern auch mit dem, was man vor der eigenen Haustür dagegen tun kann. „Mhmm“, murmelt eine. Sie bleibe dann halt doch eher auf Tiktok hängen.
Immer mehr Menschen schränken ihren Nachrichtenkonsum ein. Beim Digital News Report des Reuters Institute 2026 gaben 72 Prozent der Befragten an, dass sie zumindest gelegentlich aktiv Nachrichten vermeiden. 2024 waren es noch 69 Prozent. Der häufigste Grund: Die Informationen seien emotional belastend.
Ich verstehe, dass man sich nicht jeden Tag damit auseinandersetzen möchte, dass im Sudan Krankenhäuser bombardiert und Millionen Menschen vertrieben werden oder Trump seine rassistische Migrationspolitik mit ICE-Razzien, Massenverhaftungen und Abschiebungen verschärft. Aber es gibt auch Wege, gleichzeitig informiert und psychisch stabil zu bleiben, statt sich in Pandababy- und ASMR-Videos zu flüchten und das unter Selbstfürsorge zu verbuchen.
Rückzug in das Private
Es ärgert mich, wenn die düstere Weltlage als Legitimation dafür herhalten muss, sich vom politischen Geschehen abzuwenden und sich ins Private zurückzuziehen. Es ärgert mich, wenn mein Mitbewohner nicht weiß, wer Ajatollah Ali Chamenei ist, es ärgert mich, wenn meine Cousins nicht wissen, wer Gisèle Pelicot ist. Aber warum?
Schließlich ärgern sich meine Weinkenner-Freund*innen auch nicht darüber, dass ich von ihrem „Kulturgut“ nichts verstehe und irgendeine Plörre bestelle, Hauptsache billig. Auch meine Programmiererfriends sind nicht genervt, dass ich bis vor wenigen Wochen nicht wusste, wie man ein Word-Dok in ein PDF umwandelt.
Der Unterschied: Sich nicht zu informieren, ist unsolidarisch. Wer keine Nachrichten verfolgt, wird sich kaum Bündnissen anschließen, sich für andere Gruppen einsetzen oder politischen Widerstand mittragen. Jean-Philippe Kindler plädiert in „Scheiß auf Selflove, gib mir Klassenkampf“ dafür, „auf Abstand von sich selbst zu gehen“. Man könne keine Veränderungen anstoßen in einer Gesellschaft, die sich in die eigene Innerlichkeit zurückzieht, so Kindler.
Desinformiertheit macht ängstlich
Die Solidarität ist das eine, aber auch dem eigenen Seelenfrieden ist mit dem Nachrichtenverzicht nicht unbedingt geholfen, im Gegenteil. Die Welt wird dann zu einem diffusen Bedrohungsszenario, das einen jederzeit überfallen kann.
Eine Frau aus dem Zeichenkurs erzählt, dass sie Angstzustände bekomme, wenn sie im Radio unvermittelt eine Meldung höre. Nachrichtenfetzen, die sie beiläufig aufschnappt, könne sie ohne Hintergrundwissen kaum einordnen und katastrophisiere die Lage. Gleichzeitig kann auch das ständige Nachrichtenlesen zum Stressor werden.
„Warum informiere ich mich?“, frage ich mich. Wirklich aus Solidarität? Oder nicht auch, um mir ein Gefühl von Kontrolle vorzugaukeln? Um meine Neugierde zu stillen? Zu einer Gruppe dazuzugehören und mich in der Welt verankert zu fühlen? Um ein politisches Leben zu führen? Wahrscheinlich alles. Aber macht mich das zu einem besseren Menschen? Wohl kaum.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Ahmad Tibi elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Ahmad Tibi elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset
Leader of alliance representing Palestinian citizens of Israel says his election is a ‘rightful achievement’ for the Joint List.
An Arab member of Israel’s parliament, Ahmad Tibi, the chairman of the Joint List alliance, has been elected deputy speaker of the Knesset.
“This is a rightful achievement for the Joint List, which secured 11 seats” in the October 27 elections, Tibi told Al Jazeera on Monday.
He added that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir “attempted to prevent my election, but they failed despite their reckless incitement. The Joint List will be represented in all committees.”
Tibi, who was elected by his fellow Knesset members on Monday, is the leader of the Ta’al party, which is part of the Joint List.
The groups representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am) – made historic electoral gains in last month’s elections, securing a cumulative 19 seats in the 120-member parliament.
The bloc endorsed Gadi Eisenkot after President Isaac Herzog tasked him this month with forming the next government.
Palestinian-led parties are now focused on using their increased representation to address discrimination and other issues facing their community.
Call for criminal investigation
Tibi on Sunday called for a criminal investigation into Netanyahu and his aides, accusing them of engaging in “Mafia-style conduct” after an investigative media report accused them of interference in the parliamentary elections.
According to Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, contacted the police commissioner’s office before the Knesset elections, alleging that three activists from the Ra’am party in southern Israel were carrying large sums of cash and vouchers intended to sway voters.
Police relied on information from an intelligence source who was a former employee of the prime minister’s office to arrest the activists after raiding their homes without valid search or arrest warrants, the report said.
“No one is above the law, not even Netanyahu,” Tibi said on X.
Tibi was first elected to the Knesset in 1999 and previously served as its deputy speaker from 2006 to 2022.
Several Arabs have served as deputy speakers of the Knesset. Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, held the position between 2020 and 2022. Mohammad Barakeh, a former leader of the Hadash party, was appointed in 2003.
Other appointed Arab deputy speakers include Abdulmalik Dehamshe, a former Ra’am lawmaker, and Nawaf Massalha, the first Muslim to be appointed to the Knesset in 1988.

Du partenariat de la honte signé entre cinq pays européens et le Rwanda sur l’expulsion d’exilés au tollé causé en Israël par une enquête sur les mensonges de Benyamin Netanyahou, en passant par les tensions entre l’Estonie et la Russie, le rapport d’Amnesty International sur les conditions de travail chez Amazon ou encore l’avancée des Houthis au Yémen, retour sur l’actualité internationale de ces dernières heures.

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.title: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.author: Fiona Sturges
https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/n.text:
Kate Nash was standing on a fire truck in a showgirl outfit complete with white tights and pink G-string, shouting through a loudhailer about the music industry’s failure to pay artists fairly, when she wondered if she’d gone too far. It was 2024 and the truck, which made pit stops outside the London offices of Spotify and Live Nation, had a large black-and-white picture of Nash’s bum on the back along with the words “Butts for Tour Buses” – a reference to her newly launched OnlyFans account, which she was using to fund her tour.
That afternoon, she called her manager Kat. “I told her: ‘I’ve thrown a brick through the window at Spotify.’ She went: ‘What, literally?’ and I said: ‘No, but I’ve been standing outside their offices with a megaphone, so that relationship is over. I don’t think we’ll be making their New Music Friday feature.’ And we didn’t.”
Nash, the Brit award-winning singer and actor who rose to fame 20 years ago in the Myspace era, is not one to run away from a fight. Frustration and fury burned early in her career when she spoke up about the trolling from the tabloid press, which ran derogatory pieces about her appearance, and from strangers on the internet. She recalls receiving a message shortly before her chart-topping debut album Made of Bricks came out in 2007. “The title of the message was, ‘You are …’ and I opened it wondering: ‘Ooh, what am I?’ I thought it was fanmail. And this person said: ‘You are everything that’s wrong with music distilled into one slag.’ So it’s been a journey. It takes a long time to get to a place of ‘I don’t give a fuck’.”
It’s a crisp October day when Nash and I meet in a cafe near her home in north London. She is nursing a cold, though that hasn’t diluted her fervour when talking about the plight of working musicians. In the last 12 months, she has appeared before a parliamentary select committee to talk about the financial impact of Brexit on touring artists. “I’m in a position of privilege because I am making money from my catalogue,” she tells me. “But I still need to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour. I’ve got friends who are selling all their instruments and furniture to tour, or they’re not going on tour and they’re depressed.”
Nash bangs the table. “It makes me so mad!” she continues. “Where will we be in 20 years when we only have stadium acts? I’m not dissing those who do it, but I don’t want everything to be mainstream. I also want to see mid-level and small gigs. Without that, there’s no culture and no fanbase. It’s a broken system and I don’t think it’s fair.” She stops, and laughs. “Sorry, I get a bit passionate.”
To understand the roots of Nash’s fighting spirit, her forthcoming album offers some clues. Recorded in Spiddal on the west coast of Ireland, Cailín – it means “girl” in Irish – sees her exploring her Irish heritage through music that blends uilleann pipes, flutes and the tin whistle (Nash has played it since childhood) with punk and hip-hop. “I came in wanting to mess with trad Irish music and do something with it that hadn’t been done before,” she says.
Nash, whose mother is Irish, grew up in an Irish-Catholic community in north-west London, though she came to realise that “being half-English, I didn’t know about my own history, and I wanted to learn. It’s all quite emotional for me.” It wasn’t until she began recording, for instance, that she learned her grandfather was part of a group of men who tried to travel to Spain to fight Franco, though were intercepted en route and imprisoned at Curragh Camp in County Kildare. “We have a family motto: ‘I’m not looking for a fight, but if you’ve got one, I’m your man,’” Nash says.
Among the most arresting tracks on Cailín is her cover of Famine, Sinéad O’Connor’s song about the Great Hunger in Ireland that left a million dead. The lyrics tell how it was not a natural disaster, but a human-made catastrophe created by British rulers who shipped vital food supplies out of the country while the potato crop failed.
O’Connor, I note, was another singer who refused to be quiet about injustice. After she ripped up a picture of the pope live on US TV, she was told she had blown up her career, yet pop stardom wasn’t something she ever wanted. “I love that and I feel a connection to that,” Nash replies. “I’m not as pure as Sinéad in that sense as I have wanted success and, when I was 16, I was like: ‘I want to be famous.’ But as soon as that happened, I thought: ‘Ooh no, I don’t like this.’ I love being able to do creative work, but fame is slimy and gross.”
Nash says that at the height of her success after her first album came out, she sold out London’s Hammersmith Apollo and “felt nothing”. After her second album, My Best Friend Is You, came out she was dropped by her label via text. She took it as an opportunity to start doing things her way. In 2012, she released a punky single, Under-Estimate the Girl, which prompted the NME to declare: “Kate Nash has committed career suicide – and it sounds amazing.” She put out her next album independently and went on a tour, during which she worked almost exclusively with women behind the scenes and on stage. “That tour made me the woman I am. It was like being on a train with no driver, but it was fun and chaotic and wild. We played Shepherd’s Bush Empire, which was a big drop [in audience capacity from the Apollo], and it was the best night of my life because I was with a band I loved and we all cared about what we were doing,” she says proudly.
Since then, her career has been marked by ups and downs. In 2015, she discovered that her former manager had been misappropriating her money (after a protracted legal battle, they reached an out-of-court settlement). Nash ended up moving to the US – “I needed someone to smile at me and tell me to have a nice day” – where she auditioned for acting roles and took a job in a comic shop to help pay the bills (“I was saved by the nerds,” she grins). Then she landed the role of a lifetime in Glow, the hit Netflix series based on the real-life story of a group of female wrestlers in the 1980s. “It came at just the right time. I got strong, I learned how to throw people over my shoulder, and I laughed so hard my stomach hurt every day. With all those girls, there was a real camaraderie. We’re still in a WhatsApp group now.”
Glow was cancelled during the pandemic after three series – “I think it will come back one day, when we’re old and can’t fit into our leotards,” Nash laughs – and then came the actors’ and writers’ strikes, during which she didn’t work and “my mental health took a bit of a dive. I got obsessed with someone’s lost dog, which triggered my OCD. I was literally walking along railway tracks in LA looking for this dog, which, by the way, I found.” In late 2023, she decided it was time to come back to London and focus on her music.
Now, despite the precariousness of her business, Nash is content with where she is professionally. “I’m not for the masses and I’m aware of that and I’m comfortable with it. I don’t want to be palatable for everybody.” She says she has received as much support as criticism over her decision to go on OnlyFans to fund her music. “People say to me: ‘Sex sells.’ Music fucking sells! It contributes millions to the economy. It’s just not being distributed fairly.” But she remains hopeful for a future in which art wins out and performers are paid fairly.
“The music industry will not change itself, but the law will [force it to],” she says. “I see myself as the guy in The Shawshank Redemption. I’m doing these tiny scratches behind the scenes that people can’t see, and I’ll be doing that until I’m in a coffin. With these little scratches we will build the tunnel that will take us through the sewage and out to the other side.”
Cailín is released on 22 January via Kill Rock Stars.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Mark Hertsgaard
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The leader of the world’s fourth biggest economy, California governor Gavin Newsom, has explicitly endorsed a global phase out of the fossil fuels that drive climate breakdown.
Newsom told the Guardian that California is “100%” behind the efforts of the so-called Santa Marta coalition, a group of more than 50 countries that includes many of the world’s largest economies, to transition away from oil, gas and coal toward solar, wind, batteries and other non-carbon energy sources.
Speaking at the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday, Newsom said: “When you have a product that is obviously superior, which clean energy is for the climate and the economy, why wouldn’t you make that shift as quickly as possible?”
As the head of America’s most populous and economically powerful state, Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the administration of US president Donald Trump continues to boycott.
Newsom, a Democrat, is widely expected to run for president in 2028. His statement raises the possibility that the US, the world’s biggest economy and largest historical emitter of planet-warming gases, could join the Santa Marta coalition if he wins the presidency two years from now.
More than 80 countries wanted last year’s COP30 to begin to develop a global “roadmap” to phase out fossil fuels. A handful of petrostates led by Saudi Arabia blocked that effort, relying on the disputed notion that decisions at UN climate summits can only be made by consensus. Undaunted, countries favoring a roadmap met in April in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin designing a phase out on their own.
“Love it,” Newsom said of the challenge that this Santa Marta “coalition of the willing” is posing to the US and other states intent on keeping the world burning fossil fuels.
The coalition is in effect no longer allowing petrostates to employ procedural tricks and endless talk to prevent what scientists say is imperative: rapidly phasing out fossil fuels. Instead, this critical mass of countries, which includes Germany, France, Brazil and The Netherlands – with additional countries, perhaps including the UK, expected to join later in Cop31 – is proceeding on its own with roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels, hoping that its example and economic power will lead others to follow suit.
“You don’t ask drug dealers to vote for Prohibition, and you won’t get petro-states to agree to phase out fossil fuels,” said Mohamed Nasheed, the former president of The Maldives, who once convened a cabinet meeting underwater to dramatize the plight of low-lying island nations like his. “Countries wishing to phase out fossil fuels should just go ahead and do it,” Nasheed told the Guardian.
Newsom’s statement could add momentum to a CopP31 summit that has been widely expected to yield modest progress at best. The governor’s comments follow two political earthquakes that also raised hopes of a new era in global climate politics. First came the surprising re-election of president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil in October, then the crushing rebuke of Trump and his Republican Congress in the US midterm elections in early November.
What makes the Santa Marta coalition’s vision more than a pipe dream is the coalition’s economic might. Collectively, the 80-plus countries that wanted a phase out roadmap at Cop30 amount to the biggest economic superpower on earth.
If the coalition can begin implementing a credible transition away from fossil fuels, it “would send an unmistakable message that the age of oil, gas and coal is ending, and the smart money is shifting,” Mohamed Adow, director of the nonprofit Power Shift Africa, said in an interview. Governments and financial markets around the world would be put on notice that staying invested in fossil fuels will be an increasingly risky proposition that could leave them holding trillions of dollars of stranded assets.
Thus far, Germany, the world’s third biggest economy, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045. France, the world’s sixth biggest economy, and The Netherlands, the 18th biggest, have released phase out roadmaps as well.
California’s clean energy track record aligns with the one policy goal that, analysts say, Cop31’s final agreement might endorse: a commitment to obtain 35% of the world’s energy from electricity by 2035. California’s economy has run on 100% clean electricity nine out of every 10 days during much of 2026, with batteries emerging as “a game changer”, as Newsom described it. As the costs of clean energy continue to fall, Newsom expects more counties to follow California’s example because “the markets are moving in our direction”.
The midterms also brought to power scores of climate champions at the state and local level. In Texas, the US’s second largest state economy after California, the new governor is Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who shunned contributions from the fossil fuel industry that has long dominated her state. In all, 29 states will have Democratic governors who, among other things, could block datacenters.
Humanity is in “a final battle against the evil forces” trying to keep the world burning fossil fuels, said Johan Rockstrom, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research. As the Nepal glacier disaster and 50,000 extreme heat deaths in Europe this summer illustrate, climate breakdown is already wreaking terrible damage. Nevertheless, Rockstrom added, “89% of citizens across the world trust science [and] want action. We are a majority power that can have confidence we have a collective global community that really wants this to succeed--and that it isn’t too late.”
- Mark Hertsgaard is the executive director of Covering Climate Now and the environment correspondent for the Nation. He has covered UN climate summits since the 1992 Earth Summit

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: A super El Niño brings startling changes for marine life on California coast: ‘like nothing we’ve ever seen’
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Gabrielle Canon in Monterey Bay, California
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
On a picturesque autumn afternoon last week, the beaches of California’s Monterey Bay were teeming with life and death.
A cadre of shorebirds charged and retreated in a synchronized dance with the raging surf. Nearby, the receding tides had deposited lifeless bundles of feathers and bone, tangled in piles of glistening kelp. Swollen sea lion carcasses, their teeth bared in a quiet grimace, dotted the sand as beach picnickers and dog walkers enjoyed the warm, cloudless day.
The effects of a historic El Niño have officially reached Monterey Bay, according to scientists, and the mortality on display here may be a grim harbinger of more to come. The waters that hug California’s central coast are already undergoing startling changes.
The climate phenomenon, defined by unusually warm equatorial ocean conditions, is rapidly heating and expanding parts of the Pacific. Water temperatures are climbing off the charts, from the ocean’s depths to its surface. Record-smashing high tides are swallowing more of the shoreline. Plus, vital parts of a vibrant food web that feeds ocean diversity are disappearing, starving scores of species throughout the system.
These changes are compounding the impacts from the climate crisis and extreme marine heatwaves that have already stressed ocean ecosystems and their inhabitants.
“It is like nothing we’ve ever seen,” said Dr Jono Wilson, the science director for The Nature Conservancy’s oceans program. “We just are trying to figure out how to wrap our heads around the sheer scale of this event.”
Visual reports from divers, underwater cameras, and beach-goers have showcased how deeply underwater environments are changing. Waters clouded with nutrients cleared as they warmed, and an unusual array of visitors arrived from the southern seas.
The central coast has played host to schools of halfmoon fish that ventured far past their southern California range, translucent winged comb jellyfish generally spotted on dives near Hawaii, and Humboldt squid that are usually found in the eastern equatorial Pacific. Whale sharks common in the Sea of Cortez were seen in Malibu and juvenile garibaldi fish – brilliantly orange speckled with glowing electric blue splotches – were seen for the first time in Monterey Bay.
Despite the visible impacts near the shore, El Niño anomalies are even easier to spot at depth. A buoy moored at the mouth of Monterey Bay laced with sensors has been providing scientists like Dr Francisco Chavez, a senior scientist who leads the biological oceanography group for the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI), with insights from farther below.
Temperatures in the ocean layer called the thermocline, which acts sort of like a transition space between the sunlight-filled surface and the dark deep ocean, have been steadily rising in recent months. Chavez said they’ve now climbed 8C (14.4F) above average. That rivals what is being observed at the equator, where El Niño signals tend to be the strongest.
Researchers had to add more height to their graphs to accommodate how sharply the heat has risen. “It’s almost at room temperature 200ft below the surface,” said Dr Henry Ruhl, director of an ocean observing collaboration housed at MBARI. Meanwhile, scientists watched as important phytoplankton populations plummeted alongside the rising temperatures.
It’s not unusual for the waters to become less productive in winter, but the change was pronounced. “That’s a real indicator of the amount of biomass that’s there to supply marine food webs,” Ruhl said, adding that it dropped by an order of magnitude.
Warm water with fewer nutrients has had a pointed effect on kelp forests, essential ecosystems along the California coast that are still suffering from the last strong El Niño roughly a decade ago.
“Kelp is the key foundation species and it enhances the whole biodiversity of the system,” said Dr Scott Hamilton, a professor at San Jose State University and director at the Moss Landing Marine Laboratories just north of Monterey Bay. “We know when you lose the kelp, you can lose about 40% of the species that live in the kelp forest.”
The kelp is very sensitive to abrupt changes in its environment. Warm waters, fewer nutrients, and big wave events are all disruptive. During El Niño years, these are more likely to occur – sometimes all at once.
“We lost a lot of kelp just because the temperatures are just so crazy warm,” Hamilton said, adding that the air temperatures were cooler than the water. The kelp held on at first, but as the water warmed, it began to disintegrate and die off. “Last week, a lot of it just kind of melted,” Hamilton said.
When the kelp forest takes a hit, it’s like the first domino falling to set off a cascade of effects. And once the kelp is in decline, it has a much harder time bouncing back. Hungry sea urchins, deprived of their normal levels of nutrients, “start actively grazing around like little lawn mowers on the reef – any little baby kelp that pops up, they just mow it down”, Hamilton said. “That then keeps this very sort of food-limited system and no habitat for species, and it can perpetuate itself for long periods of time.”
Warm temperatures drive fish deeper into the ocean
Rising temperatures are also upending the food chain on the ocean’s surface and shore. Starved or starving seabirds have washed ashore between San Francisco and Los Angeles by the hundreds over the last few months.
Scientists believe that warming temperatures are driving the fish these birds depend on into deeper waters, but the exact cause of the mass mortality will take time to understand. Experts are afraid this may just be the beginning of an exceptionally challenging winter.
Brown pelicans and Brandt’s cormorants are being heavily impacted, and common murres have been among the hardest hit. The tuxedoed seabirds that resemble penguins and are related to puffins struggled in warming conditions even before El Niño conditions began to drive their food sources deeper. Marine heatwaves have had catastrophic impacts on their populations before.
During another exceptionally warm period between the summer of 2015 and spring of 2016, roughly 62,000 dead or dying murres were found on beaches stretching from California to Alaska, during a mass-mortality event that would ultimately claim an estimated loss of 4 million birds.
“We have already seen a lot of murres along the beaches,” Chavez said. “The fish they feed on are moving deeper.”
Experts won’t be able to track the full-scale impacts on these populations and many other species until next spring. Between now and then, Chavez said, it’s still hard to predict how events will unfold. But excessive warmth isn’t expected to fall off much over the next few months and that alone could wreak havoc on a variety of species, including fish, mammals, and birds. “Some will move,” he said, “and some will perish”.
Back at the Monterey Bay, Kriss Neuman pointed her foot at a pile of kelp – a large tangle of wobbly brown ribbons and bulbs lying limp on the beach – momentarily disbanding a cascade of tiny black flies, as she quickly jotted observations on to a clipboard.
As a principal ecologist for the scientific conservation organization Point Blue, Neuman’s research primarily focuses on the Pacific population of western snowy plovers – tiny tufts of white that speed across the sand on stilted legs or blend into the dunes.
Charting changes and impacts to their populations, which are federally protected under the Endangered Species Act, sometimes means counting the fresh piles of kelp on which they indirectly depend. “Kelp not only has this amazing productive life when it’s in the ocean – it has a second life when it comes to shore,” Neuman said.
Invertebrates and insects that come with the kelp or eat it when it’s on the sand feed the birds. “But it’s not enough to just have kelp in the system,” Neuman added. “There has to be a beach that is wide enough and high enough. In order to receive that kelp and for it to persist and kind of fire up the sandy beach food chain.”
The dueling challenges come to a head in El Niño years, as temperatures and nutrient declines take out the kelp forest and sea level rise chews away at the shrinking shoreline. But there’s a third element that could wreak havoc on bird populations that depend on the beaches: an issue Neuman refers to as “coastal squeeze”.
The coast has been armored with seawalls, steep berms, and other forms of protective hardscape added as cities and communities try to keep the rising tides from swallowing infrastructure. This has a negative impact on sandy beach ecology, which is also getting hammered by strong surf.
As their habitats get squeezed, “we expect to have fewer birds, less kelp on beaches driving the food web, and really narrow beaches,” Neuman said. “The predictions for sandy beach loss in California are pretty dire.”
‘There is still hope to save at least some of them’
Just north of the beaches, a small room lined with petri dishes, beakers, and buckets – and emitting a strong briny smell – may be the key to softening some of the threats to California’s coastal ecosystems.
Moss Landing Marine Laboratories research technician Bennett Bugbee held up a glass jar swirling with soft, small green kelp spores. Contained within them is the future of the food web.
Hundreds of plants could be grown from what’s in one little beaker, according to Bugbee. “And there are – what – thirty beakers on this table? So, there’s a lot of kelp we have at our disposal.”
As they grow, the kelp is moved from their beakers to tanks. Once they get about 4 to 6in long, they are relocated to basins outside near the shoreline so they can adapt under more variable conditions. For the final step, they are woven into ropes rigged to PVC pipes and placed in the ocean.
Even with careful cultivation in the lab, El Niño is adding obstacles to the process. Seawater the team pipes in for their tanks is becoming far too warm – Bugbee described it as feeling “like bathwater”. They are also having to think about how to move the tanks now housed near the shore farther inland if the tides continue to rise.
Even with the challenges ahead, Bugbee is cautiously optimistic. “Because we’ve been out there doing the work, seeing what’s going on, we’ve been able to adapt with the changing conditions,” he said. “ I think there is still hope to save at least some of them.”
The restoration process has already had successes. Kelp forests were decimated during the last El Niño, especially in the northern parts of California dominated by a species called bull kelp, of which more than 90% has been lost. “But there are some areas that have persisted,” Bugbee said of the work to rehabilitate the essential plant. “Just last year at our restoration site we had over 700% increase in kelp canopy, relative to control sites.”
It’s not just the kelp that could be spared the worst outcomes. Scientists in a range of fields are working diligently to build resilience into the most at-risk systems. Their findings will also add insights for how to protect communities on land and sea as the world continues to warm.
Research done during previous strong El Niño events and other marine heatwaves has provided a head start. “For the past 10 years, we have just been doing an incredible amount of work to prepare California and the West Coast for future El Niño’s and we’re at a much better spot right now,” Wilson said. “We have a lot of the tools and resources at the ready to help us recover.”

https://citylimits.org/opinion-dont-just.title: Opinion: Don’t Just Celebrate the City’s Seniors—Hire Them
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dont-just.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-dont-just.text:
Share This Article
“Elected officials are right to value older adults as engaged citizens and active participants in our democracy. But if government recognizes the value of older adults at the ballot box, it should also recognize their value in the workplace.”
Last year, while attending City & State New York’s annual New York Aging Summit, I listened as Ryan A. Murray, executive deputy commissioner and chief program officer of the New York City Department for the Aging, posed a simple question to the audience.
He first asked how many organizations offered internship programs. Nearly every hand in the room went up. He then explained what a “returnship” program was—a structured, paid program that helps experienced professionals return to the workforce after an extended absence—and asked how many organizations offered one.
Not a single hand was raised.
The silence in that room said more than any speech could have.
Although Executive Deputy Commissioner Murray directed his question to representatives of nonprofit and community organizations that advocate for older adults, there was one additional audience I wish had been asked the same question: elected officials.
Every year, elected officials honor older adults through proclamations, appreciation luncheons, awards, and speeches celebrating their lifetime of service. Those gestures are meaningful and appreciated. But they do little to address one of the greatest challenges many older New Yorkers face: finding meaningful employment.
After the celebrations end, many of those same older adults continue struggling to reenter the workforce because of age discrimination, outdated hiring practices, and the mistaken belief that experience has an expiration date.
If government truly values the wisdom, experience, and contributions of older New Yorkers, it should do more than celebrate them once a year.
Government shouldn’t just celebrate seniors—it should hire them.
This attention is understandable. Older adults are among the nation’s most civically engaged citizens. According to AARP, Americans age 65 and older have had the highest voter turnout of any age group for decades, while voters age 50 and older routinely account for more than half of the electorate.
Elected officials are right to value older adults as engaged citizens and active participants in our democracy. But if government recognizes the value of older adults at the ballot box, it should also recognize their value in the workplace.
Unfortunately, experienced workers age 45 and older often encounter significant barriers when attempting to return to the workforce despite decades of valuable experience.
Although laws such as the Age Discrimination in Employment Act prohibit age discrimination, many older workers continue to face hiring decisions influenced by outdated assumptions about technology, adaptability, or career longevity.
This isn’t just a perception. According to AARP, older workers historically remain unemployed longer after a job loss than younger workers, underscoring the need for innovative pathways back into the workforce.
Government is not immune from this challenge. Legislative offices, like many other employers, often have relatively few experienced workers despite the institutional knowledge, professional expertise, and life perspective they can bring to public service.
So what can elected officials do to better connect experienced workers with employment opportunities?
Some have already taken meaningful steps. In October 2025, for example, State Sen. Cordell Cleare hosted a job fair in Harlem specifically for job seekers age 50 and older. Initiatives like Sen. Cleare’s deserve recognition because they acknowledge the unique employment challenges experienced by older workers and provide valuable opportunities to connect them with prospective employers.
But job fairs, by their nature, depend on private employers to do the hiring. Government can go one step further by becoming part of the solution itself.
Rather than simply connecting experienced workers with employers, elected officials can establish returnship programs within government.
Imagine a six-month paid legislative returnship where experienced professionals work alongside elected officials assisting with constituent services, casework, community outreach, scheduling, communications, and legislative research while updating their professional skills and rebuilding their résumés.
Rather than asking the private sector alone to solve the problem, government should lead by example.
On the legislative side, Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie and Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins could establish a pilot returnship program by providing participating legislators with additional funding—for example, enough to support two temporary or part-time legislative aide positions during the January through June legislative session. Similarly, Gov. Kathy Hochul could establish pilot returnship programs within state agencies through an executive order or budget initiative.
New York already has experience creating innovative public-sector workforce programs. New York City’s Silver Star program, for example, allows retired city employees to return to part-time, project-based work without jeopardizing their pensions. While Silver Star serves retirees rather than unemployed job seekers, it demonstrates that government can successfully design flexible employment programs that tap into the experience of older adults. A statewide returnship program would build upon that concept by helping experienced professionals reenter the workforce.
To ensure the program remains focused on its intended purpose, several safeguards should accompany any pilot initiative. The New York State Department of Labor should centrally administer the application process and refer pre-screened candidates to participating offices for interviews and final hiring decisions.
Priority should be given to applicants age 45 and older who are unemployed, underemployed, returning to the workforce after caregiving responsibilities, retired individuals seeking to resume public service, or military veterans transitioning into civilian employment.
Participating offices should also submit an annual public report summarizing the number of applicants, interviews conducted, participants hired, program completion rates, demographic information, and the number of participants who later secured permanent employment. Public reporting would promote transparency, discourage favoritism, and provide lawmakers with data to evaluate whether the pilot should be expanded.
Although this proposal focuses on New York State government, the same concept could be adopted by county governments, municipalities, Congress, and even private employers seeking to benefit from the experience of older workers.
New York has no shortage of ceremonies honoring older adults. What it needs are more opportunities to put that experience back to work.
If government truly believes older New Yorkers still have valuable skills to contribute, it should prove it—not with another proclamation, but with a job offer.
Don’t just celebrate seniors. Hire them.
Leon Tulton is a Bronx community advocate and former legislative staff member.

https://citylimits.org/after-a-decade-ny.title: After a Decade, NYC Opened Its Waitlist for General Street Vendor Permits. Here’s What You Need to Know.
https://citylimits.org/after-a-decade-ny.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/after-a-decade-ny.text:
Share This Article
The city is adding 10,500 new merchandise vending permits next year—which grant vendors the right to legally sell goods, rather than food—after capping the number at just 853 for decades. “I said, ‘Oh my God, this thing is really happening,'” said Calvin Baker, a longtime Harlem vendor who was among the first to apply.
Some opportunities come along only once a decade.
For New Yorkers who earn their living as street vendors—an industry predominantly represented by immigrants, including many Latinos—that includes getting on the waitlist for a coveted city license.
For the first time in a decade, the city opened its waitlist last week for street vendor merchandise licenses, which grant vendors the right to legally sell goods, like jewelry, toys and clothing, rather than food.
“I said, ‘Oh my God, this thing is really happening,'” said Calvin Baker, a longtime Harlem vendor, describing how he felt when he was finally able to apply last week.
For decades, he and other vendors have fought against the city’s rigid 853-capped license limit, set in 1979. Since then, these licenses for non-veteran general vendors became available only when an existing license holder gave theirs up, leading to thousands of people selling merchandise on the streets without one—risking costly fines and potential criminal charges as a result.
Earlier this year, the City Council overrode former Mayor Eric Adams’ veto to pass a bill creating 10,500 new merchandise vending permits, and started taking applicants for a new waitlist last week.
“It was so good to see people that were on the line, on the struggle with me in the streets, fighting to get these licenses, sitting down there waiting for their turn to go fill out the application,” said Baker, 64, who sells hats, gloves and other apparel. “It was a blessing for me, man. I felt the peace of God. I felt satisfied.”
Previously, once a license became available, the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) would contact applicants from the existing waitlist, which closed in 2016.
But under the new law, the city will add another 10,500 licenses—including 3,478 Citywide General Vendor or called “white,” licenses, which allow for vending anywhere in the city, and 7,875 outer borough or “green” licenses—which will become available early next year.
“It is extremely difficult to predict, but it is fair to say that we estimate that thousands of people will apply,” said Mohamed Attia, director of the Street Vendor Project, the advocacy group behind the license expansion.
In August, DCWP started giving priority to applicants who were already on the 2016 waitlist, and began contacting them, sending them letters describing the next steps. They had until Oct. 29 to submit a license application, a DCWP spokesperson explained.
After that, the new 2026 waitlist opened on Nov. 2, and will close on Dec. 16. Vendors have to submit an application to join the list, and then wait for DCWP to tell them where they stand and what they need to do next. 
Baker was among the first applicants last Monday.
“It’s like you run the New York Marathon and you say, ‘Lord, how am I gonna do it? Can I finish this race?’ But then you get in it, and you finish it. The satisfaction that you feel from doing that. That’s the satisfaction I felt from filling out the application,” Baker described.
A DCWP spokesperson didn’t specify how many people have applied so far.
“DCWP is working hard to ensure the rollout of new general vendor licenses proceeds in a clear, orderly, and accessible manner,” a spokesperson said. “We know that street vendors are community fixtures—and we are proud to support these small businesses through best-in-class licensing services, proactive business education, and reforms to cut red tape.”
Where and how can a street vendor apply?
If you’re not already on the 2016 waitlist, you can apply to the new one online or by mail, and in very limited circumstances, such as “hardship cases,” in person.
Vendors can apply for either a white or green license, or both, in one application.
If you need help with your application, you can connect with the Office of Street Vendor Services at the Department of Small Business Services (SBS) by calling 888-SBS-4NYC (888-727-4692).
You can also get assistance in person by visiting NYC Business Solutions Centers during office hours (Monday to Friday, 9 a.m.- 5 p.m) at the following locations:
- The Bronx: 400 East Fordham Rd., 7th Floor, Bronx, NY 10458
- Brooklyn: 9 Bond St., 5th Floor, Brooklyn, NY 11201
- Lower Manhattan: 14 Wall St., 17th Floor, New York, NY 10005
- Upper Manhattan: 361 West 125th St., 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10027
- Washington Heights: 560 West 181st St., 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10033
- Queens: 90-27 Sutphin Blvd., 4th Floor, Jamaica, NY 11435
- Staten Island: 120 Stuyvesant Pl., 3rd Floor, Staten Island, NY 10301
Applicants can also make an appointment with the Street Vendor Project via email or phone (646-602-5679).
“There is a lot of misinformation and a lot of confusion about what this license is,” Attia explained.
“This license allows people to sell merchandise products out of the streets, the public sidewalks, out of a table, and there are so many rules around it,” he added. “So, if you are a food vendor, this license is not for you. If you have a retail business and you want to expand to some private events, some pop-up markets, this license is not for you.”
What are the requirements for applying?
The information requested from applicants is basic personal information, such as their name, address, phone number, and email. Additionally, it asks if a person has been selling general merchandise from January 2025 to Nov. 2, 2026.
Although most of the city’s street vendors are immigrants from different parts of the world, the application is only available in English. SVP said it is assisting applicants in seven languages.
The form also requires the submission of a photo ID, which may be a driver’s license, permits issued by a government agency, passport, or municipal ID card, among others.
One ironic feature of the process: previous civil or criminal summonses issued to the applicant can serve as proof of their vending experience (in addition to pictures showing the person vending, receipts for merchandise purchases, or a letter from an elected official, community leader, or nonprofit organization stating past vending activity).
SVP advocates see this as an acknowledgement that the prior system left many people without a way to sell legally, and as a reminder of how difficult it was to obtain a license under the old cap.
“The application was very easy,” Baker said. “”t took 10 minutes.”
Then what?
The waitlist application is separate from the license application, so joining the waitlist does not automatically result in a license.
DCWP will review the applications, assign each one a number, and contact applicants with information about next steps starting in February 2027.
“I’m looking for the ultimate. I’m looking for my license,” Baker said. “I will feel a lot better. I won’t have to always look around and worry about the NYPD running down on me, and just tossing my stuff any kind of way they want to without even having respect for your stuff.”
To reach the reporter behind this story, contact [email protected]. To reach the editor, contact [email protected]

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.title: Arizona Town’s Probe on Sex Abuse Claims Could Block Prison Firm Building New ICE Camp
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.author: John Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/ariz.text:
This story was published in partnership with LOOKOUT News.
An official from Marana, Arizona, is seeking clarification from the private prison giant Management and Training Corporation about its handling of sexual abuse allegations at the former state prison in the town, following an investigation from LOOKOUT and The Intercept.
In an October 28 letter, reviewed by LOOKOUT and The Intercept, Marana Finance Director and License Inspector Yiannis Kalaitzidis asked MTC Senior Vice President Mary Calvin for a written explanation of what the town official called an “apparent inconsistency” between state records and the facility’s 2023 Prison Rape Elimination Act, or PREA, audit, a report required by the federal law.
The request is part of the town’s review of MTC’s October 1 application for a business license to “Operate Marana Detention Facility.” The company ran a former Arizona state prison in Marana and plans to reopen it imminently as a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention camp.
The letter cites a September 29 LOOKOUT and Intercept investigation about how state records reference three allegations of sexual misconduct at the prison in 2022 and 2023.
PREA audits — which are required for jails, prisons, and detention centers at least once every three years — must record all allegations of sexual misconduct at detention facilities, whether they are substantiated or not. Certified in December 2023, MTC’s report for the Marana prison, however, recorded none.
Kalaitzidis noted in his letter that the audit says the finding of zero incidents was verified by the warden, chief of security, PREA compliance manager, and internal investigator. He also wrote that, despite the apparent reviews by several company officials, the report “does not appear to be certified or signed by any MTC personnel.”
The letter says the town of Marana is requesting the explanation as part of an investigation into whether MTC “made a material false statement in conducting the business” of the state prison facility, which would be grounds for denial of a business license according to the town’s code.
“The Town of Marana is currently reviewing MTC’s business license application,” said Andrea De La Cruz, the assistant town manager, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept by email. “As part of our review process and due diligence, the Town has contacted MTC to request additional information. The application remains under review, and no final determination has been made at this time.”
MTC did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Changing Political Context
Local residents and officials say the state, the federal government, and MTC left them out of meaningful discussions about reopening the prison as an ICE camp, LOOKOUT and The Intercept previously reported.
For now, a town business license is among the few levers local officials have.
In an October 2 letter from the local group Pima Resists ICE, or PRICE, to a Marana official who specialized in licensure, organizers cited not only the discrepancies between state investigations into sexual abuse and the PREA audit, but also alleged violations involving an escape from an MTC prison in Kingman, Arizona, in 2010, as well as abuses in a New Mexico immigration camp run by MTC as revealed in a 2017 DHS Office of Inspector General report.
The inquiry comes as Arizona’s political landscape is shifting. The midterm election gave Democrats control of both chambers of the state legislature as well as the governor’s office — a historic change in state power. Republicans will be in the minority at the state Capitol for the first time in 60 years.
That has Democratic lawmakers talking about taking on one of the most contentious laws in recent Arizona history. Following protests across the state, Democrats took up the cause of repealing a controversial 2010 anti-immigrant law known as Senate Bill 1070. In 2012, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down three of its provisions, leaving a requirement that police check the immigration status of people they stop under certain circumstances.
“I would absolutely love to see a repeal of SB1070,” state Sen. Analise Ortiz, a Democrat from Glendale, told LOOKOUT and The Intercept. “There are still parts of that law on the books that are enabling cities to collaborate with ICE to rip families apart, and that needs to stop.”
State Rep. Betty Villegas, D-Tucson, echoed Ortiz: “We already have bills aligned to focus on what other states have done to control ICE from coming into private property.”
Following the lead of neighboring New Mexico’s prohibition on local jurisdictions entering into contracts with ICE for immigrant detention camps, Villegas said Democrats in Arizona see an appetite for doing something similar in their own state.
Ortiz agreed, saying there is “likely an appetite” for something similar in Arizona, and that the Latino Caucus would address the issue.
Local nonprofits said lawmakers should also conduct a review of no-bid contracts like the one inked between the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, and MTC.
“This was literally handed to them with no review and no public input,” said Caroline Isaacs, the executive director of Just Communities Arizona, a nonprofit working on criminal justice reform. “We do not want the Democrats to wait until things get bad to investigate conditions.”
“We want them to do this now, before people get hurt.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
I’M BEN MUESSIG, The Intercept’s editor-in-chief. It’s been a devastating year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-ai-hone.title: Can New York Rein in AI and Profit From It, Too?
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-ai-hone.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-ai-hone.text:
On Tuesday morning, New York Governor Kathy Hochul announced another step in her mission to "rein in artificial intelligence" in lieu of federal regulation: The state is launching an academic research center focused on AI safety—the first one in the nation.
"They'll harness the highest computing power anywhere outside the private sector," Hochul said Tuesday. "Nobody can top this."
The New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research will employ about 80 "elite scientists" to independently test AI systems and bolster safety, Hochul said. Examples of their research includes developing methods to prevent AI agents escaping their sandboxes, like they did in the Hugging Face hacking incident, and working out how to best evaluate the safety guardrails that AI companies are deploying, said the Center's interim Co-Director Greg Morrisett. 
The Center will be powered by Empire AI, the state's $500 million AI computing center at the University of Buffalo, and is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder and Empire AI board chair Tom Secunda, plus a $25 million research investment from SUNY and the state. It's set to launch by the new year. When the RAISE Act comes into effect January 1, AI companies will be required to submit detailed safety frameworks on their models to the state, which will also be assessed by researchers at the center.

A bronze sculpture by renowned French German artist Hans (Jean) Arp valued at €145,000 ($160,000) was stolen from Galerie Ludorff’s booth at Art Cologne on November 8, the last day of the fair’s run. The Düsseldorf-based gallery has filed a criminal report with the police and is asking the public for assistance in finding the sculpture. Titled S’élevant (Rising), 1962, and standing just under a foot high, it is typical of the artist’s late oeuvre, which is characterized by smooth organic forms.
According to a press release on the website, the work was taken sometime between 4:55 and 5:10 p.m. “If you visited our booth during this period and took any photographs, we would be very grateful if you could share them with us,” wrote the gallery, which urged fair visitors and the broader art community to keep an eye out for the sculpture. “If you are being offered for sale the work described below at any point in the future or if you have any information regarding its whereabouts,” the gallery wrote, “please contact us or the police directly.”
Artnews reports that the work had been displayed unbolted on a plinth for the duration of the fair’s November 4–8 run, and that there had been four attendants on duty the day it was taken. Maya Hanke, Galerie Ludorff’s publicist and art fair manager told the platform that the fair’s security measures were inadequate. Among her complaints were a lack of security staff in high-traffic areas, and inconsistent bag checks on entry and exit. Fair representative Judith Leyendecker told the publication that fair officials were in contact with the gallery and were supporting the police investigation.

The organizers of SITE Santa Fe have revealed the theme and named the forty-two artists participating in the New Mexico biennial’s thirteenth iteration, to take place June 11, 2027–January 10, 2028. Titled “There Are Other Worlds,” the Ekow Eshun–curated exhibition aims to show how art might offer “Alternative ways of seeing, relating, and imagining,” per a curatorial statement.
The event will be divided into three sections: “Worlds Beyond,” inspired in part by the Transcendental Painting Group; “World in Common,” which will explore community-building among artists; and “Worlds Alive,” which will center the connections between flora, fauna, and humans.
Visitors can expect to see new commissions by Edgar Arceneaux, Firelei Báez, Raven Chacon, Lotus L. Kang, and Cauleen Smith. Among the other participating artists include John Akomfrah, Sanford Biggers, Frank Bowling, Olafur Eliasson, Nan Goldin, Shilpa Gupta, Sky Hopinka, Arthur Jafa, and Tavares Strachan.
“Uniting these practices is a shared sense that the world is never singular or fixed, but continually reshaped by how we perceive, imagine, and relate to one another. There Are Other Worlds invites us to look beyond existing realities to consider how alternative ways of being might come into existence.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/c.title: City to Close Bus-Clogged Lane on the Manhattan Bridge
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/c.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/12/c.text:
The city will close one of the Manhattan Bridge’s exit lanes to traffic in the coming months after a spate of high-speed deadly crashes at the span, Department of Transportation officials revealed on Tuesday. But buses routinely clog that particular lane, potentially limiting the closure’s ultimate impact on safety.
DOT plans to turn one of two lanes that connect the bridge to the Bowery into a bus stop, along with new markings, more Jersey barriers and painted curb extensions to discourage drivers from barreling downhill off the bridge into the densely-populated streets of Chinatown, the officials said at a presentation to Manhattan Community Board 3’s Transportation committee.
The plan is a start, transportation experts said, but they urged the Mamdani administration to be bolder and launch a larger-scale overhaul of the 1909 span’s highway-like approach.
“It would be nice to think bigger about the Manhattan Bridge and not just make small changes around the edges — and maybe we can still get there,” said Annie Weinstock, the director of programs at the group People-Oriented Cities. “It seems like they’re kinda formalizing what’s already happening.”
DOT plans to implement the changes this fall or winter, according to the agency’s presentation, in response to localsdemanding an intervention after motorists killed several people within feet from each other at the bridge’s exits over the last two years.
The right-most of the two lanes connecting the bridge to the Bowery will become a bus stop. Intercity buses routinely park up that lane already. The city plans to add so-called “lateral shift” designs to the off-ramp — basically making drivers swerve over and back — which discourages the speeding that happens on a straight shot.
The agency also plans to add more Jersey barriers and paint curb extensions to improve safety at a corner with heavy foot traffic.
Along just 14 blocks of Canal Street, between the Manhattan Bridge and the Holland Tunnel entrance, the city has recorded 806 reported crashes that injured 340 people in the last five years — about six per month.
DOT installed signs on the bridge to lower the speed limit on the approach from 35 miles-per-hour to 20 miles-per-hour and added Jersey barriers at the triangle where Cruikshank and Kwok were killed after the crash. But experts and victims’ friends and families have for a year urged the city to more radically transform the Manhattan Bridge to prevent the high-speed carnage from happening in the first place.
The agency has also been working on redesigning Canal Street for the past three years, reviving efforts dating back to 2002. But after pushback from parking and driving-obsessed opponents in Chinatown, officials slow-walked work on the more dangerous eastern end by postponing it until next year.
The agency’s plans for the bridge so far miss the mark for a bigger proposal to reclaim space at the entrance around its City Beautiful colonnaded arch. That’s especially the case now that the state’s congestion toll has cut car trips into the central business district, said Michael King, a former Department of Transportation director of traffic calming, who now runs the consulting firm Traffic Calmer.
“Now that we have congestion pricing, at some point the city’s gonna have to pull off the bandaid and make it a public space,” King said. “What are your priorities and what are your values. Are you going to have a real civic space… or does it have to be a highway on-ramp?”
“These little things are good and appreciated, but we can always do more and we always need to rethink the larger picture,” he added.
Weinstock and King have both studied the bridge extensively and in 2021 crafted a plan to repurpose the three-lane lower deck of the Manhattan Bridge entirely, replacing the space with bus and bike lanes.
The bridge features five lanes that feed into its namesake borough, but only two Brooklyn-bound lanes. The city chose to keep that design even after congestion pricing cut bridge trips by 20 percent.
The bridge and Canal Street are through-truck routes, and Bowery is a local truck route. Ninety percent of the streetscape at their intersection is devoted to cars. Nevertheless, pedestrians still outnumber motorists by nearly three-to-one there, and the city should seize opportunities to reduce big-rig traffic through these kinds of dense urban areas, according to King.
“If you accept that everything has to be driven through Manhattan in a giant truck, then yes? Ok, you have to have truck routes,” he said. “Maybe you don’t need trucks here. Can you really only get your stuff on a truck from the Holland Tunnel to the bridge?”
DOT spokesperson Mona Bruno said there had been “too many tragedies involving drivers treating this bridge exit as a speed ramp into residential Chinatown streets that are filled with pedestrians and cyclists.”
“We are moving quickly with a redesign start this year to naturally reduce instances of speeding among vehicles approaching Bowery and Canal Street, shorten crossing distances, and better protect pedestrians on sidewalks,” Bruno added.
Kevin Duggan joined Streetsblog in October, 2022, after covering transportation for amNY. Duggan has been reporting on New York since 2018, starting at Vince DiMiceli’s Brooklyn Paper, where he covered southern Brooklyn neighborhoods and, later, Brownstone Brooklyn. He is on Bluesky at @kevinduggan.bsky.social and his email address is kevin@streetsblog.org.
Just as the City Council debates reining in Amazon's business practices, the delivery giant threw workers of the job after canceling its contract with a Manhattan subcontractor.
