https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-city.title: New York City wind and rain make way for a cool and cloudy weekend
https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-city.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-city.text:
New York City will see a cold and gloomy end to the week, with wet and blustery weather expected to continue through much of Friday.
According to the National Weather Service, rain is expected to keep falling until Friday evening — though not with the same intensity as Thursday’s storms, which mainly affected parts of Brooklyn and Queens.
“We actually did have multiple reports of flash flooding in Southern Queens, with that thunderstorm that kept kind of training over the area for a couple of hours,” said meteorologist Matt Wunsch. “With that, JFK [airport] actually saw their second wettest day in November on record, with just over three and a half inches of rainfall for the day.”
Wunsch said a tornado warning went into effect at one point, though by the end of the day he said there were no reports of a tornado materializing anywhere in the five boroughs.
Though gusty winds are expected to persist throughout much of Friday — especially out at sea, where a gale force wind warning is in place — Wunsch said the forecast is looking less volatile than Thursday. He said snow is not likely.
“We should still see on-and-off rain pretty much through the day; anywhere from another quarter to a half an inch of rainfall is possible across the entire city, before the rain starts to kind of taper off as we get into the overnight tonight,” he said.
Temperatures will only reach the low to mid-40s, which is a lot chillier than the last several days.
The air will stay cool into Saturday and Sunday, with highs in the low-to-upper 40s, Wunsch said. Skies are expected to be dry with a mix of sun and clouds.

https://gothamist.com/news/top-nyc-mayor.title: Top NYC mayoral aide cast shadow over first Adams-era corruption trial
https://gothamist.com/news/top-nyc-mayor.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/top-nyc-mayor.text:
Few New Yorkers may recall Eric Ulrich’s role in Mayor Eric Adams’ administration. The once-up-and-coming Republican city councilmember lasted just 184 days as buildings commissioner before emerging as the focus of the first in a long series of corruption investigations into what state and federal prosecutors have described as a pay-to-play culture within the Adams administration.
Ulrich is charged with trading favors for cash and gifts worth more than $10,000.
But as the fourth week of his trial comes to a close in Manhattan, a more prominent figure from the Adams era has loomed large in recorded phone calls played throughout the proceedings. Adams’ former chief adviser Ingrid Lewis-Martin — who faces her own, unrelated corruption trial — has made frequent cameos in the prosecutors’ narrative as a behind-the-scenes fixer to whom local businesspeople turned when they wanted favors from Adams’ City Hall, like reopening a fire-damaged bakery in Williamsburg or getting a Brooklyn-based towing company back on the road.
“You’re a priority for me,” she said in one taped call with an Ozone Park restaurateur who fundraised for Adams’ mayoral campaign and was seeking help expediting a health inspection.
The recordings were made by the Manhattan District Attorney’s office, which obtained a court order to tap the phones of Ulrich and his associates — including pizza shop owner Joseph Livreri — for a full year starting in November 2021 as part of an investigation into illegal gambling. Livreri pleaded guilty to a bribery charge and told a Manhattan judge he gave Ulrich $4,000.
Lewis-Martin is separately charged with allegedly soliciting bribes, including $150,000 for her son, in exchange for steering migrant shelter contracts and speeding up buildings department approvals for developers. She has pleaded not guilty.
Her attorney, Arthur Aidala, did not respond to messages seeking comment on the role she played in Ulrich’s conduct, and she has not been charged in relation to the various indictments against him.
But it was Lewis-Martin who Ulrich name-dropped when he was trying to get a vacate-order lifted so Fortunato Brothers Bakery in Williamsburg could reopen in March 2022 following a fire. Ulrich, then serving as a mayoral adviser to Adams, frequently contacted then-New York City Buildings Commissioner Melanie La Rocca to fast-track approvals for the bakery after Livreri stepped in to help the bakery owner.
When a flurry of emails, calls and an in-person meeting with La Rocca proved insufficient, Ulrich telephoned her with a new sense of urgency.
“Sorry to bother you, but I got Ingrid asking me about it now,” Ulrich told La Rocca in a taped phone call from March 10, 2022, referring to Lewis-Martin.
During courtroom testimony, La Rocca told prosecutors she found it “puzzling” that someone with such a high stature in the administration would get involved in the bakery’s problems.
“It seemed like a rather mundane thing for a member such as Ingrid to be inquiring about,” La Rocca said in her testimony.
But prosecutors say Lewis-Martin had her hand in many other schemes to help businesspeople who offered bribes, like a bit role on a TV show and gifts for her son. She allegedly sabotaged a street redesign plan in Greenpoint in exchange for cash and free catering from Tony and Gina Argento, owners of a sound stage along the route. And she is accused of pushing through buildings department approvals for a hotel owner Mayank Dwivedi and real estate investor Pinky Vaid, who prosecutors say funneled tens of thousands of dollars to her son.
Other recorded calls played in the Ulrich trial reveal how Lewis-Martin was fielding requests from Joseph Livreri and another Adams fundraiser with ties to Ulrich.
Less than a month after Adams took office, Joseph Livreri called Lewis-Martin at home on behalf of a friend, Michael Mazzio.
In taped phone calls, Livreri urged her to give Mazzio’s towing company permission to pull stranded cars off the highway during a snowstorm on Jan. 29, 2022. Mazzio is facing trial alongside Ulrich and has been charged with bribery for giving Ulrich cash and a Mets season ticket package in exchange for help landing his daughter a city job.
Lewis-Martin agreed to call Adams’ then-chief of staff, Frank Carone, after talking with Livreri by phone, according to a taped phone call played in court. But minutes later, she told Livreri in another taped call that the city could not license Mazzio’s towing company because he was at the time suing the city.
“There's nothing I can do,” Lewis-Martin said. “I told Eric [Adams] and everybody. I sent some pictures.”
The next day, Ulrich griped about Livreri and Mazzio going over his head during yet another recorded conversation with his friend George Russo.
“I'm just saying to myself that I don't want them to think my people are needy. They're a pain in the a--, they’re not going to follow the rules,” Ulrich said.
But Ulrich’s “people” soon needed more help.
On Feb. 14, 2022, a city health inspector shut down Livreri’s Howard Beach pizzeria, Aldo’s, after finding mouse droppings and unrefrigerated calamari.
His brother Anthony Livreri called Ulrich asking for help to expedite a new inspection. Ulrich agreed, promptly notifying the commissioner of the mayor’s community affairs unit that the health department shut down “one of the mayor's favorite restaurants.”
Three days later, with the restaurant still closed, Ulrich called Livreri and put him on speakerphone with Lewis-Martin. Investigators recorded the call.
She agreed to help reopen the restaurant — a favorite hangout for Adams and his inner circle, including Lewis-Martin, during his victorious campaign a year earlier.
“Please do what you need to do so we can take care of you,” Lewis-Martin said in the taped call.
Before hanging up, Ulrich joked about how Livreri could repay Lewis-Martin: “She wants shrimp cocktail, just so you know, when you reopen.”

https://hyperallergic.com/the-secret-lif.title: The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife
https://hyperallergic.com/the-secret-lif.author: Matt Stromberg
https://hyperallergic.com/the-secret-lif.text:
The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife
Taking David Hockney’s painting of arts patron Betty Freeman as his subject, James Cahill tells the engrossing story of two friends who shaped the cultural landscape of 1960s Los Angeles.
In the summer of 1966, David Hockney began work on one of his most iconic paintings: “Beverly Hills Housewife,” a portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. She is depicted on her garden patio in front of her sleek, modernist house, which is framed by strips of blue sky and green lawn. A few status symbols surround her — a William Turnbull sculpture, a zebra-skin lounge designed by Le Corbusier, and a mounted antelope head— but the focal point is Freeman in her bright pink dress, gazing wistfully beyond the confines of the canvas.
Critic and novelist James Cahill uses the painting as a jumping off point to expound on the intertwined lives of both artist and muse, as well as to provide a fragmentary snapshot of Los Angeles in the 1960s, in his new book. With The Beverly Hills Housewife: Hockney’s Californian Muse and the World Beyond the Pool (2026), Cahill bounces between formal analysis of the painting, historical anecdotes, and inferences about the broader culture, zigzagging as if driving across LA without a map. Some of the detours prove less relevant to his central narrative than others, but they are nonetheless diverting pit stops on a thoroughly engrossing journey about the friendship between two complex individuals who played formative roles in shaping LA’s cultural landscape.

https://hyperallergic.com/tribal-groups-.title: Tribal Groups Urge Congress to Halt Bill That Threatens Sacred Sites
https://hyperallergic.com/tribal-groups-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/tribal-groups-.text:
Tribal Groups Urge Congress to Halt Bill That Threatens Sacred Sites
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would speed up permitting for major projects and could impact Indigenous sovereignty over culturally significant land.
Tribal organizations are urging legislators to halt the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that would speed up the permitting and review processes of major infrastructure projects and could severely undermine tribal sovereignty over sacred and culturally significant sites.
The United States Senate advanced the controversial bill for further debate on November 8 amid mounting criticism from Indigenous groups and historic preservation advocates, largely due to the act's narrowing of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966.
The law mandates federal agencies to weigh the impact of projects on historic properties, oftentimes with required tribal consultation, though BAAJA removes tribal nations from much of the review process. The bill text also curtails several other environmental acts, such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act, and pushes for shorter review timelines, the loosening of protections of sacred lands, and less federal oversight.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/labor-u.title: It’s Time for Labor to Join the Fight Against Data Centers and Tech Oligarchy
https://inthesetimes.com/article/labor-u.author: Stephen Lerner
https://inthesetimes.com/article/labor-u.text:
It’s Time for Labor to Join the Fight Against Data Centers and Tech Oligarchy
There’s no room for dithering—the U.S. labor movement has to choose now whether to be on the right side of history.
Stephen Lerner
We just experienced a once-in-a-generation political earthquake as President Donald Trump’s authoritarian administration and the broader Republican Party were dealt massive defeats at the polls, even in once solidly red states like Texas. Over the course of the midterm election season, data centers became a key issue, and the growing revolt against them and their Big Tech owners played a key role in Democrats’ “bluenami.” Yet as opposition to data center construction is beginning to reshape politics, giving rise to one of the most sweeping social movements of our time, the U.S. labor movement is currently split on the issue. For unions, incoherence around this issue could be toxic.
I have been an organizer in the labor movement since I dropped out of high school to join the United Farm Workers union on the grape and lettuce boycott in 1974. Over the past 50 years, I’ve lived through numerous moments forecasted as the labor movement’s decline or revival. With the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) reorganizing wealth, power, and work on an unprecedented scale, none compare to the moment we’re currently living through.
Across all of my organizing — from supporting a year-long strike for the International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union in the South to the Justice for Janitors (JFJ) campaign that organized more than 100,000 workers in the 1980s and 90s — one lesson has held true: unions grow when they are part of something larger than themselves. Movements for justice — whether it be economic, racial, or immigrant rights — give organizing what it needs most: hope, unity, and a vision of a world we can win. Workers join unions for more than a raise. They join to realize aspirations for justice and dignity.
Today, a massive buildout of data centers and a planned string of IPOs inflating the AI bubble are further concentrating wealth and power among a handful of Silicon Valley billionaires who back President Trump, while soaring costs of living, surveillance, and job insecurity weigh on the rest of us. Yet as we face these existential threats to workers, labor, democracy — and, as some experts and safety researchers warn, humanity itself — the labor movement is divided over whether to oppose the forces driving the coming upheaval when the AI bubble bursts.
Some unions have stayed silent on the issue, despite growing backlash against data centers and the tech oligarchy. At the June AFL-CIO convention, delegates approved a resolution that acknowledged the harms and threats to workers posed by AI, while maintaining that “responsible data center growth” was possible if done with union labor.
Seduced by the promise of high-wage union construction jobs, other building trades leaders have championed data centers as the best opportunity for blue collar workers in decades. In a New York Times op-ed titled “Electrical Workers Love Data Centers. You Should Too.,” Don Slaiman, community relations director of IBEW Local 26 — which represents electrical workers in the Washington, D.C. area — argued that data centers are beneficial in their provision of good union construction jobs, calling them the equivalent of the Roman “aqueducts of our era.” That promise may turn out to be a dangerous mirage.
The record of trade union density also informs the current moment. At the end of World War II, 80% of construction workers in the United States were unionized, most under master contracts. Only 11% of building trades workers are unionized now. The issue isn’t a shortage in construction jobs — it’s a shortage in unionized construction jobs. While the sector has grown by almost 7 million jobs since the end of World War II, union membership has continued to hover around just 1 million.
As density has declined, Project Labor Agreements (PLAs) have replaced master agreements, causing unions to focus on staffing the highest paying jobs covered by PLAs. The jobs — and therefore membership density — ride the waves of economic recession and prosperity. They lose union members when union work dries up and regain fewer when work picks back up. The migration of the limited number of unionized workers to the highest-paying PLA-covered jobs allows formerly unionized work to go non-union.
In the 1970s and 80s, construction of the Washington, D.C., Metro system absorbed the labor of unionized trades workers and accelerated the deunionization of non-mega-project construction. The building trades face the same danger with the data center buildout: a short-term boost leading to a long-term bust.
History suggests that it would instead be wiser for labor to make common cause with the anti-data center movement. Labor now faces a choice that may well decide its fate for the foreseeable future: to support one of the biggest and most broadly based popular movements in recent history — the fight against data centers and the tech oligarchs funding their development — or remain at odds with it. A recent poll found nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose data center development in their communities. In 10 states across the country this election, voters endorsed restrictions on data centers or opposed their development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures.
Protests against data centers have spread like wildfire over the last two years. Over 340 protests erupted across 42 states since January 2025, and some 220 new grassroots anti-data center organizations emerged within the span of only three months in 2026. That activism helped fuel the Democrats’ victories in Texas, Georgia and Ohio, three of the top six most data-center-heavy states. Candidates like Texas Gov.elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who beat a three-term incumbent, and U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence, who faced down the most expensive House race in the country this cycle, made opposition to data center construction core planks of their campaigns. 
By recognizing and joining hands with this movement, and standing together against the tech oligarchs who seek to define our future, labor can set the stage for its revival. By failing to do so, or, worse yet, allying with pro-data center forces against this metastasizing grassroots movement, labor risks accelerating its decline into irrelevance.
After all, labor’s great surges in membership, density, and power have come when it was in sync with broader social movements. In the 1930s, the children of sharecroppers and immigrants flocked into industrial unions because the Congress of Industrial Organizations (CIO) was bound up with the New Deal and its promise of dignity for workers. In the 1960s and 70s, workers inspired by the civil rights and women’s movements flooded into public sector unions. Those gains stabilized overall membership even as the private sector sank to its current 6%, down from a postwar peak of 35% overall. Nor is this pattern confined to the United States. Abroad, labor movements in Brazil, South Korea, and South Africa found that opposing authoritarianism sparked surging growth.
I’ve seen up-close how this kind of dynamic can play out. The success of the Justice for Janitors (JFJ) campaign we launched in the 1980s can be seen only in the context of the larger movement for liberation that thousands of immigrant workers rallied behind. Hundreds of thousands of janitors galvanized after the Los Angeles Police Department viciously attacked immigrant janitors who were striking to improve working conditions in Century City in June of 1990. Many attribute the movement’s success to its strong organizing in immigrant communities. Immigrant workers were fighting not only for their rights on the job, but for their dignity as human beings. JFJ was carried forward on the shoulders of communities that demanded to be seen.
The same dynamic played out earlier this year when the Trump administration sent armed immigration enforcement agents into Minneapolis to terrorize neighborhoods as part of its mass deportation plans. When unions joined in coalition with community organizations to resist, a movement culture started to coalesce. This model offers an alternative vision of how labor can approach the growing fight against AI data centers, and the tech oligarchy. Such deep alliance-building sets the table for mass organizing and growth through joining up with broader resistance.
I have seen what happens when workers feel like they’re part of something larger, and I have watched what happens when unions retreat to protect what they have. The first builds power, the second depletes numbers.
After this resounding election, we have now entered a “which side of history are you on” moment, one more consequential than any I’ve seen in the last 50 years. It is the labor movement’s task to act decisively in order to make sure it’s on the right side. Such an opportunity will not soon come again. 
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
Stephen Lerner is the architect of the Justice for Janitors campaign. Lerner is a labor and community organizer and helped found the Bargaining for Common Good network.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: João Palhares
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
As famílias camponesas que realizam a 3ª Feira Estadual da Reforma Agrária de Goiás na Praça Universitária, em Goiânia, foram surpreendidas, no início da tarde desse sábado (14), por provocações e xingamentos. Ao menos três grupos passaram pelo local para xingar, filmar e hostilizar assentados e acampados do Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra (MST). Em conversa com o Brasil de Fato DF, a coordenação do movimento disse que, ao ser abordado, um dos homens se declarou como fascista.
“Estão vindo aqui na feira para hostilizar as pessoas, para xingar, para provocar e, certamente, tentar arrancar alguma cena mais forte para poder dizer que as famílias são violentas”, explica a coordenação nacional do MST em Goiás.
Dois grupos de três pessoas também circulavam de carro no entorno da praça, passando repetidas vezes, enquanto uma dupla de moto fazia o mesmo. O episódio se soma a uma ofensiva ocorrida antes mesmo do início da feira, na sexta-feira (13), quando estudantes da Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Goiás (PUC Goiás) abordaram as famílias no alojamento, cedido em parceria com a instituição de ensino.
Uma agricultora que estava no momento da abordagem do grupo, mas prefere não se identificar, contou que a investida ocorreu quando a praça estava cheia. “Foi um momento tenso. A gente estava com vários visitantes aqui e causou um certo tumulto, um certo desconforto”, relata.
Como os feirantes são orientados a não ceder às provocações, foram os próprios visitantes que saíram em defesa das famílias e interpelaram o grupo. De acordo com ela, mesmo ouvindo que as pessoas não autorizaram o uso da imagem, os homens seguiram filmando as famílias presentes e tentando forçar as pessoas a gravarem vídeos com eles.
No fim da tarde, a situação estava tranquila, com a programação cultural e a venda de alimentos. As famílias seguiam orientadas a não responder às provocações. “Nós viemos para cá para fazer uma feira, para expor nossos produtos, para vender nossos produtos, mas também para dialogar como agricultor com o consumidor aqui da cidade sobre como é a vida lá no campo, como se produz comida”, defendeu a coordenação do MST.
O movimento analisa os vídeos gravados pelos grupos para identificar os autores e entrar com uma ação judicial contra eles. Na tarde de sábado (14), a coordenação também notificou a Polícia Militar do Estado de Goiás (PMGO) e pediu policiamento no entorno da praça para inibir novas investidas. Até o encerramento da programação, por volta das 22h, a reportagem identificou a presença de uma viatura nas imediações da praça.
O vereador de Goiânia Fabrício Rosa (PT), que esteve na feira no sábado, afirmou que o mandato vai tomar providências em relação aos ataques. Em abril, o parlamentar e o coordenador nacional do MST Leandro de Almeida Costa foram presos pela PMGO durante um ato pelos 30 anos do Massacre de Eldorado dos Carajás, em Santa Helena de Goiás.
A Polícia Militar informou, por meio de nota, que o policiamento da região “foi reforçado após o registro de episódios de hostilidade” contra os participantes da feira. “Até o momento, não houve registro de prisões relacionadas aos fatos.”
A PMGO disse ainda que “mantém o policiamento contínuo na região e acompanha as manifestações realizadas no local, com o objetivo de preservar a ordem pública e garantir a segurança de todos os envolvidos”.
A feira reúne cerca de 30 bancas com alimentos e artesanato de sete regionais do MST em Goiás, além de roda de viola, samba, dança afro e capoeira, e segue até este domingo (15) na Praça Universitária. “O ano que vem, 2027, certamente estaremos novamente aqui na Praça Universitária fazendo a nossa quarta Feira da Reforma Agrária”, projeta a coordenação em Goiás sobre a próxima edição.
Provocações
Assim como nas duas últimas edições da feira, na sexta-feira (13), as famílias do MST montaram barracas em um prédio desativado da Área 1 da Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Goiás (PUC Goiás), no Setor Leste Universitário, espaço que a universidade cede ao movimento. A presença das famílias provocou reclamações de estudantes de Medicina que utilizam o centro de aulas ao lado do prédio ocupado pelas famílias. Nas redes sociais, um jovem apontado como estudante do curso gravou vídeos na porta do alojamento. O principal questionamento do estudante estava relacionado à segurança dos alunos e ao incentivo da PUC às ocupações.
Segundo a coordenação, o vídeo gravado no alojamento chamava estudantes e outras pessoas a se mobilizarem contra as famílias. As ofensivas de sábado seriam desdobramentos dessa convocação. “Foi para lá provocar o nosso pessoal, fazer vídeo, com muito preconceito, estigmatizando, caracterizando o nosso pessoal como violento, como moradores em situação de rua, como se não fossem seres humanos”, explicou a coordenação do MST. Nas duas edições anteriores, as famílias ficaram no mesmo espaço, que não é usado pelos estudantes, sem nenhuma ocorrência.
“Nos preocupa muito um jovem estudante de medicina, que daqui uns anos vai ser médico, com esse nível de compreensão, caracterizando pessoas como bicho, e não como seres humanos. Que nível de atendimento um médico desse vai fazer quando tiver uma pessoa de uma classe menos favorecida?”, aponta a coordenação.
A movimentação se relaciona, de acordo com a coordenação, ao avanço da extrema direita no país, impulsionada por setores bolsonaristas que não aceitaram a derrota de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) para Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), reeleito em outubro para o quarto mandato. “Eles estão tentando emplacar [novas ofensivas]. À medida que um grupo produz conteúdo, eles tentam provocar para que outras pessoas, outros grupos venham”, complementa.
Em nota, a PUC Goiás defendeu a parceria e afirmou que a área cedida não é utilizada para atividades acadêmicas. O MST também se manifestou publicamente, agradecendo à universidade pelos três anos de parceria. O movimento também denunciou a divulgação, sem autorização, de imagens de famílias acampadas e assentadas, incluindo crianças.
