https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Voters Who Saved Democracy Are Being Written Out of the Story
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Tim Wise, Kimberlé Williams Crenshaw
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Voters Who Saved Democracy Are Being Written Out of the Story
The media downplayed the importance of Black voters for Democratic victories.
Here are some media headlines and hot takes after last week’s Democratic midterm victories. See if you can catch what’s missing from their framing.
First, CNN ran an exit-poll explainer under the headline “Women, young voters and independents: See where Democrats made inroads.” Time said the “distinct gains came from young, rural, and Hispanic voters.” The Washington Post told readers, “Democrats have a surprising group of voters to thank”: namely, rural voters in Republican strongholds. And Reuters reported, “Latinos drive Democratic gains.”
While those shifts were real, and the shift among Latinos was critical to Democratic fortunes in Texas, what each outlet neglected to mention is the centrality of Black voters to the party’s wins. And yet, these voters were the most crucial part of the story.
In Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Ohio, Michigan, and Mississippi—where Scott Colom appears set to become the first Black senator since Reconstruction—only the Black vote secured Democratic victories and flipped the Senate. In each of those states, exit polls show that white voters supported Republicans and would have gladly kept the chamber in GOP hands.
Even in Texas, although Latinos are the largest group of voters of color, at 25 percent of the total, with only 72 percent voting for James Talarico, and only 39 percent of white voters doing so, he needed the 12 percent of the electorate that was Black to turn out big, and they did, with 91 percent of their vote.
The extent to which the media downplayed the importance of Black voters to Democratic victories was stunning. For instance, Newsweek highlighted rural voters breaking for Democrats in South Carolina, while only noting farther down in the story that those rural voters were Black, while white rural folks mostly stayed home.
And The Washington Post, rather than crediting Black voters for Annie Andrews’s win there, ran a graphic highlighting the “significant improvements” Democrats made with less-educated whites, as if to suggest that had powered her victory. But this “improvement” moved these only voters from a 42-point Republican margin to a 21-point margin—hardly the key to Andrews’s victory, since this group still overwhelmingly rejected her.
The New York Times followed the same pattern, running a story proclaiming “White, Working-Class Voters Shifted Left,” noting, almost as an afterthought, that they still rejected Democrats by nearly 20 points.
And it wasn’t only in Senate races where the Black vote made the difference. In House races, white voters mostly supported Republicans nationally, meaning that here too, African American voters led the way, however much the media appears to have missed it.
This is no minor mistake, but rather anti-Blackness that refuses to give credit where it’s due. To the political press, those who drift away and come back are a story. Those who never left are like humidity in New Orleans, always there and not worth a headline. That tendency punishes Black Americans for being right first, seeing what Trumpism was in 2016, and voting against it consistently for a decade.
And when we see Black movement in the numbers, as with increased turnout, they still struggle to get credit. During an interview in which he was crediting every other possible constituency for the Democrats’ victories, a Vox interviewer asked Democratic political consultant David Shor about Black turnout. Only then did Shor acknowledge that the Black share of the electorate had risen four points in Georgia compared with the 2022 midterms. But even then, he immediately changed the subject back to the Latino vote in Texas, which wasn’t what the interviewer had asked about, and which also ignored the importance of Black turnout in that state.
This kind of erasure also harms those who did swing, because it hides who their allies are. Working-class whites who voted for Democrats spent years hearing that their problems were caused by “Black crime,” “DEI,” or government handouts to Black communities. In the end, they got nothing from those who offered them scapegoats without solutions. When they finally woke up, they joined a coalition that Black voters had been holding down the whole time.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But if the coverage never says so, these new arrivals may fail to realize that the people they were taught to fear are the ones who kept the door open for them. Black voters are the base of any coalition that can beat authoritarianism. Leaving that out of the story is how the right keeps working people divided.
Perhaps the most dangerous effect of erasing the importance of the Black vote is on Democratic priorities. Parties respond to stories about why they won. If the official story is that white rural voters or independents delivered the majority, the party will cater to them and, once again, treat the concerns of its most loyal voters as something that can wait.
But Black voters cannot afford to wait. In April, the Supreme Court gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has dismantled much of the federal civil rights apparatus, and the Justice Department’s Voting Rights Section has been hollowed out.
Restoring the Voting Rights Act is the Democratic Party’s best strategy for concretizing its gains. It won Senate seats in three (and likely four) Southern states, flipped House seats throughout the region, and held on to others, despite Republican attempts to gerrymander them away. A South where Black citizens can vote freely, in fairly drawn districts, is a South where those gains can last. And a South that is competitive for Democrats, where the promises of Reconstruction can finally be realized, is the recipe for lasting multiracial democracy.
Yes, President Trump will veto a new Voting Rights Act. But Democrats should pass it anyway, and they should make the veto a central issue in 2028.
But that won’t happen if the party believes the media framing about their victories. In state after state, Black voters didn’t just save the Democratic Party; they saved democracy. The least we owe them is the courage to tell the truth about that, and perhaps a thank you.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Art Basel offers compensation to dealers after early closure of Paris fair due to protests
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Georgina Adam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Art Basel will compensate dealers for the early closure of its Paris fair, held 20-23 October in the Grand Palais, the fair company announced today (11th November), on a French national holiday.
The fair was forced to shut down its Parisian outing two days early because of violent rioting in the French capital. Since then, dealers have been demanding compensation for their lost sales and booth fees. Indeed, soon after the closure the French Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) sent a strongly worded letter to the fair director, Karim Crippa. It accused the firm of not consulting with dealers—the CPGA represents 57 of the fair’s 211 exhibitors—and of showing “disrespect, even contempt” for them.
The closure hit the smaller dealers particularly hard, since the biggest galleries tended to make sales on the opening days, whereas the smaller dealers, mainly sited on the upper floor of the Grand Palais, depended on the two weekend days for business. The letter said it expected “concrete proposals” for this compensation.
Now Crippa has responded to the letter, with an offer of a reduction across the board of 20% of booth fees to all participants. He said: “We believe this approach offers a fair and considered way forward, reflecting our appreciation of the partnership we share and our commitment to strengthening it further.”
Philippe Charpentier of Mor Charpentier gallery, who is the president of the CPGA, tells The Art Newspaper that the compensation rate is what the committee expected.
Nonetheless, if one calculates in percentages, the fair was open for three-and-a-half days—it's ultra-VIP Avant-Première timeslot began 3pm on Tuesday 20 October, and the fair closed Friday—instead of the projected five and a half. The fair was therefore shortened by about 36%.
Speaking about the decision to close the fair early, Noah Horowitz, chief executive of Art Basel, tells The Art Newspaper: “We stand by the decision to close. We feel it was in the right interest of all the parties involved. It was a very difficult decision, but we stand by it.”
Asked about the decision to close for the two days—when unrest was only expected on the Saturday—he said: “Given the uncertainty surrounding the impact and the duration of the planned demonstrations and access to the Grand Palais, we simply couldn't be confident that conditions would allow us to reopen safely on Sunday. An event of this size and scale is incredibly complex, and some exhibitors had also expressed serious concerns about leaving artworks unattended in the Grand Palais on the weekend. We concluded that closing the fair early was in the best interests of the art, the staff and ultimately the visitors.”
Horowitz was not prepared to comment on other aspects of the closure, for example questions of insurance or the firm’s relationship with the Grand Palais, for which MCH paid €10.6m to rent the space for seven years in 2022. Horowitz said that MCH, the parent company of the Basel group of art fairs, was "fully committed to delivering the 2027 edition of the fair".

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Venice exhibition tells the story of the man who brought together contemporary artists and Murano’s master glassblowers
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Emma Park
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
In 1952, Egidio Costantini, an entrepreneur based in Venice, had a brainwave: to take the designs of contemporary artists and, with the collaboration of master glassblowers on the island of Murano, to make artistic sculptures in glass. This was a different approach from that adopted by traditional furnaces like Venini in their decorative glassware, which, although it increasingly involved international designers, was often produced in large, commercially dictated series.
Three years later, Costantini established the Fucina degli Angeli gallery to exhibit the results of his experiment. From then until the 1970s, when other glassmaking companies began to compete, Costantini played a pioneering role in the evolution of glass in Venice, acting as interpreter for more than 100 international artists to Murano’s master glassblowers.
An exhibition opening at the Peggy Guggenheim Collection in Venice this month, curated by the art historian Cristina Beltrami, will tell the Fucina’s story from the 1950s to the 1980s. It will also examine the little-documented but vital role played behind the scenes by Peggy Guggenheim herself, whose purchase of many items helped sustain the gallery financially and whose connections enabled Costantini to exhibit his glass across Europe and even in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. (As it happens, the collector is also the focus of an exhibition opening this month at the Royal Academy of Arts in London, about her Mayfair gallery of the late 1930s—Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector, 21 November-14 March 2027.)
More than 100 works, including glass, painting and sculpture, will be on display in Venice, as well as material from the Fucina’s archives, which have never before been studied in depth. These will be exhibited in 11 rooms organised by artist and theme, and will include glass translations of works by many luminaries of the period, from Max Ernst and Oskar Kokoschka to Lucio Fontana and Paul Jenkins.
Born in Brindisi in the south of Italy in 1912, Costantini established himself permanently in Venice, where he had been raised and educated, at the beginning of the 1950s. There he became a commercial agent for several of Murano’s glassworks. It was the time of Italy’s post-war economic boom and the city was teeming with creative energy. Costantini seems to have found no difficulty in assembling a group of Venetian artists to form the Study Centre for Painters in the Art of Glass, a collective that exhibited its work at the furnace of Ferro & Lazzarini in 1953.
A gift from Picasso
The next step was to involve international artists of even greater stature. Acting on his own initiative, Costantini had glass versions made of some ceramic sculptures by Pablo Picasso and then travelled to Picasso’s house in Vallauris, near Cannes, to show him the results. In return, Picasso gave Costantini a copy of the book Faunes et Nymphes de Pablo Picasso (1952). This survives in the archives with markings on the images of ceramic figures that were later reinterpreted as glass sculptures at the Fucina. But who made the markings remains a mystery.
The name “Fucina degli Angeli” (smithy of the angels) was proposed by the French writer and artist Jean Cocteau, a long-term friend and collaborator, apparently in reference to Costantini’s large family. The Austrian Expressionist artist Kokoschka contributed an emblematic sketch of two angels holding up an anvil, which he dedicated to the gallery and its founder, “who first succeeded in making me fascinated with the glass of Murano”.
Cocteau enjoyed designing extravagant mythological heads for the Fucina, as well as visiting the furnaces and discussing his ideas with the maestri. Both he and Jean Arp, the German sculptor and painter whose work also features in the exhibition, were “seduced by the colour” of glass and its richness, Beltrami says.
The results, though, may not have pleased everyone. The Swiss artist Walter Bodmer allowed his sketch Asymmetric Cat (1955) to be transformed into an oversimplified glass vessel. But after this, for reasons unknown, he never participated again.
The exhibition looks set to offer a fascinating insight into a very personal approach to collaborations between artist and craftsman, as well as an evocative record of an under-appreciated chapter in Venetian history.
• Fucina degli Angeli: Peggy Guggenheim and 20th-Century Artistic Glass, Peggy Guggenheim Collection, Venice, 14 November-29 March 2027

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Julia Stoschek Foundation to reopen Dusseldorf headquarters in 2027
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Catherine Hickley
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A month after closing its Berlin exhibition space, the Julia Stoschek Foundation, a nonprofit arts organisation set up by the German collector and businesswoman Julia Stoschek, announced it will reopen its Dusseldorf headquarters in April 2027.
The Dusseldorf space closed for renovation in 2025. The inaugural exhibition in the newly revamped space, called Selfish in Bed, is curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen, formerly the director of the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin, and features works by 43 artists from the foundation’s collection. The foundation’s more than 1,000-piece collection is focused primarily on time-based art—including video, film, moving-image installations, multimedia work, performance, sound work and virtual reality work.
“Seeing the collection continue to grow and welcoming new audiences two decades on brings me enormous joy,” Stoschek said in a statement. “And I can think of no better home for it than Düsseldorf, a city where art has been part of everyday life for generations.”
Stoschek’s Berlin space operated for ten years from June 2016 to October 2026. It hosted 22 exhibitions and drew 500,000 visitors. In April, the foundation said the closure was the result of a “strategic realignment” and that it would “now focus on international projects in order to make the collection accessible to a global audience.”
The Dusseldorf reopening marks the foundation’s 20th anniversary.
Selfish in Bed, which will run from 10 April to 19 December 2027, takes its name from a 2000 self-portrait by Sarah Lucas. Other artists who will feature in the exhibition include Wolfgang Tillmans, Bill Viola, Simon Fujiwara, Rosemarie Trockel and Tracey Emin.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: As war continues, local people mobilise to salvage southern Lebanon’s history
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sarvy Geranpayeh
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
“Wow. Can you hear the bombing?” Riad Al-Assaad asks The Art Newspaper, speaking from his village of Zrariyeh in southern Lebanon. An Israeli strike on a nearby village cuts short a conversation about his efforts to save what remains of the heritage in the country’s south: scanning its old buildings, recording its oral history and now rescuing its libraries. Despite a ceasefire, south Lebanon remains under Israeli occupation and at war, and its people say their history is being erased.
The south has lived with Israeli invasion and occupation for nearly half a century. Israel invaded in 1978 and pushed north to Beirut in 1982, the year Hezbollah formed to fight it, and it did not withdraw from the south until 2000. In 2006, the two fought a month-long war after Hezbollah captured two Israeli soldiers in a cross-border raid.
The present conflict began on 8 October 2023, the day after the Hamas attacks on Israel, with exchanges of fire between Hezbollah and Israel. It escalated in September 2024 into full-scale war, with an Israeli ground invasion and strikes on Beirut, before a ceasefire that November. Fighting resumed in March 2026, when Hezbollah fired on Israel after the US and Israel attacked Iran; a ceasefire agreement reached in US-led talks in June has not ended it. Strikes continue daily, and Israeli forces occupy around 600 sq. km of the south, reaching up to 10km into Lebanon, behind what the army calls the Yellow Line.
Zrariyeh has around 2,000 houses, Al-Assaad estimates. By his count, 65 have been destroyed in this war and more than 100 damaged. His father’s house, in the middle of the village, was hit twice: first by shrapnel, then by blasts that “levelled” neighbouring buildings and blew out its windows and doors. Like others who have repaired their homes “once, twice, three times”, he now covers the openings with plastic. “We are living in the nylon era,” Al-Assaad says. But what is at stake, he adds, is “our historical existence”.
The most visible part of that history is the south’s ancient monuments, and international protection has not kept them safe from the war. Since 2024, Unesco has granted 73 sites across Lebanon enhanced protection, which prohibits targeting them or using them for military purposes. In July, it inscribed the five castles of Mount Amel, all of them granted enhanced protection, on its World Heritage List and its list of sites in danger. Three of the castles, Beaufort, Dubieh and Chama’, are under Israeli occupation. Days after the inscription, the Israeli military detonated 700 tonnes of explosives about 800m from Beaufort, claiming it was destroying Hezbollah tunnels. In Tyre, a World Heritage Site since 1984, strikes have damaged columns, mosaics and the site’s offices and stores.
Ali Badawi, the ministry of culture’s regional director for south Lebanon, says his teams cannot reach the occupied sites and rely on low-resolution satellite images and footage released by the Israeli army. One broadcast showed Israeli soldiers in Beaufort’s historical halls watching the Fifa World Cup on televisions he believes were taken from the castle’s information centre. Unesco has allocated some funding for the restoration of Tyre, but elsewhere donors are holding back while the war continues. “We cannot do anything at the moment,” Badawi says. “We have to wait.”
Badawi lives in a village south of Tyre, close to Al Mansouri, an area that he says Israeli forces strike daily. “Sometimes at night we don’t sleep, because it is just explosion after explosion,” he says.
‘Constantly afraid, unsettled and distracted’
His colleague, Mohana Chahine, who manages the artefact stores at Tyre’s Al-Bass site, was seriously injured in an Israeli drone strike on 14 August 2024, weeks before the war escalated. She was driving home with her husband when a missile was fired at a motorcycle behind them, shattering the car’s windows and leaving her unable to move. Her husband pulled her from the car, and a second strike threw them both clear of it. After a month in hospital and further treatment in France, Chahine has completed her PhD and returned to work. “I go to work actively, but I am constantly afraid, unsettled and distracted,” she says. “I am constantly anxious about another war or being injured again.”
Beyond Tyre and the castles lies heritage that appears on no Unesco list: the old houses, mosques, churches and cemeteries of southern Lebanon’s villages. Joanne Farchakh Bajjaly, an archaeologist and former journalist, is the founder of Biladi, a heritage organisation that has monitored the south since October 2023. In 2025 it recorded 389 historical buildings in five villages—according to Biladi, 85% of them are now destroyed. It was preparing to publish a report last March, but the return of war halted that project and Biladi widened its survey instead. With architecture students from the Lebanese University, the organisation logged around 850 sites across 105 villages, occupied or under threat, from archaeological ruins to houses built before 1950. The full findings are being held for its delayed report, but Biladi shared some of them with The Art Newspaper. Among them: the loss of the area’s Shia religious sites—mosques, shrines, mausoleums or husseiniyas (halls for religious gatherings)—stands at around 98%.
In July Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said the army had completely destroyed 24 villages that were “hundreds of years old”, totalling 15,000 to 20,000 homes, by his estimate. Lebanese counts are higher.
“We have 38 villages that have been bulldozed to the ground. Nothing remains,” Bajjaly says, adding that villages still under attack, such as Al Mansouri, have not yet been assessed and the figure could rise. Badawi puts the total number of villages destroyed at around 50. Each village has an ancient centre built over older remains, he notes, some of them Byzantine, Roman or Phoenician, so the loss cannot be counted in homes alone. “It is not just a matter of number of houses. The historical fabric itself is destroyed.”
According to both Badawi and Bajjaly, historic cemeteries across southern Lebanon have also been bulldozed by Israeli forces. At shrines, Bajjaly says, the earth has been turned over and the dead dug up. “This is total desacralisation, and these are well-calculated gestures,” she says.
Olive trees have been destroyed, too. After seeing images of trees being uprooted, Badawi went to Naqoura in early 2025 and found a field stripped of its old trees. In September a French Lebanese businessman filed a lawsuit in France accusing the Israeli military of war crimes, alleging that 600 trees his family had cultivated for 250 years were uprooted and taken to Israel. “When they remove 500-year-old olive trees, this is not anymore an issue of security,” Al-Assaad says.
The aim, Bajjaly believes, is “to kill the relationship between the people and their land and their history, and therefore to make it clear for them that there’s no return”.
The artist Oussama Baalbaki knows all too well what that means. His late father, the renowned painter Abdel Hamid Baalbaki, began building the family’s house in their ancestral village of Odaisseh, close to the border, in 1984, two years after Israel’s invasion of Beirut displaced them. With the village under occupation, his parents built it “over a very long period, with limited financial means and amid occupation, recurring war and displacement”.
His father, an amateur collector, hoped the home would become “something like a museum, or a cultural centre for literature and poetry”, and filled it with manuscripts, rare books, sculptures, paintings and antiquities. “Most important of all, the house shelters, beneath the trees of its garden, the tomb of my mother and father,” Baalbaki says.
In October 2024 the house was “rigged with explosives, along with every neighbourhood of the village, in a systematic, annihilating manner”, Baalbaki says of the detonation, which was captured on video. His siblings visited the ruins in February 2025 to salvage what they could, but the village is now occupied and out of reach. “We lost our connection to the land of our ancestors,” he says, “and were left wandering in a torn space of imagination and time.”
The house had looked out over a valley towards a bare plateau, a view that shaped two generations of paintings. “This natural horizon imprinted itself on my father’s paintings and, in time, passed into my own,” Baalbaki says.
In Al Qantara, the family village of the artist and film-maker Ahmad Ghossein, the landscape itself has gone. His father returned there when the Israeli occupation ended in 2000, built a house and retired among his olive trees and chickens. When fighting began in 2023, he refused to leave, answering his son’s pleas from Beirut with photographs and videos.
“He was sending me all the time images of the sunrise, every morning, to say, ‘I’m fine’,” Ghossein says. He held out until September 2024, and even then went back whenever a ceasefire allowed. This March, Ghossein says, the village was blown up by Israeli forces and the hill it stood on levelled. “It’s not that you don’t find your house, you don’t find the land. It became white sand.”
Ghossein has made his father’s daily photographs, videos and WhatsApp voice notes into a four-screen video installation, The Sound of Silence. It was shown at the Beirut Art Center and at Frieze London in October, and is due to be shown at Art Jameel in Jeddah. The footage is as his father shot it: the garden, the chickens, the road to the village, never the war. The question behind the piece, Ghossein says, is: “Can you do something about a place that doesn’t exist anymore?” His father, who now lives in Beirut, is “lost, more or less”, facing the reality that he may not go back for a long time.
But Ghossein refuses to be cast as a victim. “Yes, it’s horrible. Yes, it’s a disaster. Yes, they are erasing,” he says. “But I’m just continuing. This is a resistance by itself.”
Rescuing private libraries
Al-Assaad’s answer is to save what can still be carried or recorded. He owns a construction company, which in wartime becomes “like a civil defence company”, handing out food, medicine and fuel. Working with the culture ministry, he supplies architectural scans of old mosques and houses in the border villages. “We can’t remove them. We can’t sandbag them,” he says, but they can be documented for future generations.
With Biladi he is now also rescuing private libraries: family collections handed down through generations. In Zibqin, known as the village of poets, they have found around 20. The two largest were lost under rubble; one of them, with around 6,000 books, was burned by an incendiary bomb, he says. From another damaged home the team is recovering up to 2,000 volumes, many of them handwritten. Each book is cleaned, photographed, catalogued and moved to safe storage until its owner can reclaim it. He is appealing to anyone in the south with a library at risk to get in touch. “We don’t have the luxury of time,” he says. “We don’t have the luxury of doubt.”
Bajjaly fears what happens to a people’s past when nothing physical is left to hold it. “Is the history of south Lebanon going to turn into a myth? ‘We had a house here. We had a mosque here’,” she says. Documentation is her answer, a way “to give back to the population a proof of their own existence”. Biladi’s survey will go to the ministry of culture, which she says is pressing for heritage to be part of any rebuilding. “Any plan of reconstruction for south Lebanon that does not include heritage would be a continuity of the destruction,” she says.
Baalbaki says the uprooting will be temporary. “We will return to our land. But with what imagination will we return, and to what landscape?”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Prize dedicated to African women artists expands to Senegal, announces 2026 winners
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gameli Hamelo
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Ghanaian-French artist Kwama Frigaux and the Senegalese Fatoumata Sy have been announced as the joint winners of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize. The prize, founded by the London and Accra-based Gallery 1957 in 2021 to support women artists in Ghana and its diaspora, has this year expanded to include artists from Senegal, in partnership with Institut Français du Sénégal. Frigaux and Fatoumata have been awarded $5,000 each, as well as a three-month residency (in Senegal for the Ghanaian and in Ghana for the Senegalese), and solo exhibitions.
The prize is named after the former Ashanti queen mother, renowned for her anticolonial resistance when Ghana was under British rule. The call for applications for this year’s edition opened in June and ran until September, and was open to Ghanaian and Senegalese women artists aged 18 or older, based either in their home countries or in the diaspora. The winners were announced during Accra Cultural Week (29 October -2 November), which is organised by Gallery 1957. On view there until 5 December 2026 is The Lore of Care: Maternal Acts of Devotion, a solo show by Theresah Ankomah, the winner of the 2025 Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize.
Frigaux and Sy were selected by a jury comprising Touria El Glaoui, the founder of the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair; the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey; Marie Hélène Pereira, a senior curator at Berlin’s Haus der Kulturen der Welt; Jeanne Barral, a curator at the Fondation Cartier; the collector Alexa Waley-Cohen; and Dominique Heyse-Moore, the senior curator of contemporary British art at Tate Britain.
Runners up of the prize participate in a mentorship programme, which provides support on topics such as grant applications and entrepreneurship. Mentors this year include the Nigerian artist Modupeola Fadugba and Aisha Ayensu, the founder of the Ghanaian luxury fashion brand Christie Brown.
"I think [it's] an incredible programme that helps drive the longevity of [the prize's] impact,” Leila Zakhem, the director of the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize, tells The Art Newspaper. “And it really creates a beautiful community.”
Zakhem explains that her team considered several countries for the expansion, including Nigeria. A key part of this search was finding a "very good implementing partner." The Institut Français du Sénégal, which is "a non-commercial space [has] a lot of credibility,” she adds, “and they were very excited to partner with us on the prize.” Zakhem says that she hopes the expansion will help develop and create a bridge between art communities in English- and French-speaking West Africa.
The planned next steps for the Yaa Asantewaa Art Prize are to expand further into West Africa, and then potentially beyond, with winners selected from different regions of the continent. “The goal is eventually to be the leading Pan-African female art prize on the continent,” Zakhem says.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: As Route 66 shifts into its centennial year, preservation efforts accelerate
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Allison C. Meier
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
US Route 66 officially started on 11 November 1926 with the launch of the nation’s first federal highway system. With the spread of affordable automobiles after the Second World War, it became a destination. A unique vernacular culture formed along its almost 2,500 miles running through eight states from Chicago, Illinois to Santa Monica, California, from neon signs enticing travellers to themed motels to roadside attractions with concrete and fibreglass sculptures.
Route 66 was decommissioned in 1985, with the new highways bypassing its Art Deco service stations and mid-century diners. Now, 100 years after its debut, there are efforts across the country to preserve what survives from what was once the “Main Street of America”.
Linking diverse cultures
“We want to let people outside of Route 66 know that it’s more than what you think it is,” says Rhys Martin, manager of the Preserve Route 66 Initiative at the National Trust for Historic Preservation. “Most people think of ’57 Chevys and cheeseburgers and Marilyn Monroe, and there’s a lot of that, but there’s so much more. It ties together so many diverse cultures, from Native American to African American. In my home state of Oklahoma, it goes through the Asian District [in Oklahoma City], which sprung up around Vietnamese refugees during the war. In West Hollywood, Route 66 has a huge LGBTQ presence.”
Grants from the Preserve Route 66 Initiative reflect that range of history, which is often overlooked in the nostalgia for its Americana. There are structural repair needs, like at the Fanning 66 Outpost in Cuba, Missouri, which hosts a 42ft-high rocking chair (the world’s largest until 2015), as well as storytelling projects, such as mapping Native American experiences along the corridor, as it passes through many tribal and ancestral lands yet has had little representation of their voices. Care for the road extends to the scarce sections of its original pavement. Through local advocacy, what is known as the Ribbon Road in Ottawa County, Oklahoma, which has the last segment of a 9ft-wide design made for Model Ts, was partially protected from resurfacing this year.
These are the same roads that the Model Ts went west on during the Dust Bowl to seek a better life Rhys Martin, Preserve Route 66 Initiative
“You might think a pavement’s not art, but when you get out and look at it, especially compared to what it is today, it is very different,” Martin says. “I have come to really appreciate it from a craftsmanship perspective, but also a longevity perspective. These are the same roads that the Model Ts went west on during the Dust Bowl to seek a better life, and the fact that I get to drive these same roads tells a story.”
Advocacy is under way to give National Historic Trail designation to Route 66, with a bipartisan bill introduced last year. Martin notes that Route 66 is now similar to how it was before 1926, when it was a loose network of roads, and this legislation would help bring together its fragmented parts.
“It gets people to sit at the same table, like the state Route 66 associations, the National Park Service and the Department of Transportation, so that we can find ways to work together for corridor-wide initiatives and to help elevate preservation needs,” he says. “The corridor continues to evolve, and buildings are threatened all the time with demolition or augmentation beyond recognition, and being designated as a National Historic Trail is not a roadblock. But it is something to say, this is important and we need to take care when the fabric of the road might be forever altered.”
Local groups, municipalities and individuals are stewarding Route 66’s relics. Martin is also the president of the Oklahoma Route 66 Association, which is restoring a U-Haul painted by the late artist Bob Waldmire, who illustrated maps and postcards of the road’s built and natural wonders. The city of Catoosa in Oklahoma acquired the beloved roadside Blue Whale in 2020 from the family of Hugh S. Davis, who in 1972 sculpted the 80ft-long attraction from concrete as a gift for his wife. Last May, a new Blue Whale Visitor Center opened with retro illuminated signage.
The city of Albuquerque opened a Route 66 Visitor Center last April and its park features a collection of restored roadside signs. Among them is the first major project from the Friends of the Orphan Signs (FOS), an organisation that since 2010 has worked on revitalising abandoned signs, particularly in Albuquerque’s underserved neighbourhoods.
Lindsey Fromm, the executive director of FOS, says that many of these signs are for places that were razed during the city’s removal of derelict buildings: “There were areas of Route 66 with dozens of towering empty signs.”
Most Route 66 sign restorations return them to their former glory; FOS reimagines them as public art. Revivir (2012) at the new visitor centre was created with students who designed visuals responding to local nature that were bordered with purple neon.
“While artists lead these sign projects, they will collaborate with communities, archives, the surrounding environment, or will collect histories and stories to create the work that is displayed, so that it speaks to the immediate moment and surrounding community who live, work and travel by the sign,” Fromm says.
Projects like this are not just about preserving places for tourists but Route 66’s role in daily life. These grassroots and national efforts recognise that even though it is no longer a main thoroughfare, it is still a vital place of connection from the Midwest to the Pacific, for communities both urban and rural, and between the visitors and residents brought together on their journeys.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/13/a.title: A Brooklyn Artist Built A Tower To Memorialize Victims Of Road Crashes
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/13/a.author: Sam Brule
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/13/a.text:
Michael Freedman next to screenshots from Crashscape. Photo: Sam Brule
The landscape of New York City is really a crashscape.
Brooklyn artist Michael Freedman has made the horror of road violence a three-dimensional experience with Crashcape, a new app that superimposes virtual images of crashes onto the very roadways where they occurred.
Point your phone at any intersection and Freedman’s app will render each crash that has been recorded there since 2022 as a 30-foot cube covered in Freedman’s own artistic renderings of the carnage. The more crashes, the more boxes.
The more impact for Freedman’s virtual memorial.
“I really wanted the cubes with the paintings around them to actually physically ‘block’ the intersections, so you could see these cubes and see the cars and trucks driving through the memorial,” Freedman said.
Freedman will demonstrate the app alongside an exhibition of his original paintings on Sunday in Gowanus for the annual World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims — an event to bring attention to the scale of a problem that most New Yorkers don’t even think about: Through Nov. 8 of this year, 176 people have been killed and 43,239 have been injured, according to NYPD data. That’s an injury every six hours.
“It’s not something that you want to pay attention to,” said Freedman, who also created Crashcount to create a frequently updated map of road violence. “And that’s why we have World Day of Remembrance.”
Why we don’t know
Why did activists even create a World Day of Remembrance for the victims of road violence — and why does Freedman fight so hard to broaden understanding of the daily carnage? It’s a long story.
A century ago, car makers used their growing influence to change the narrative about crashes, not only by shifting blame to pedestrians — aka “jaywalkers” — but also by encouraging the media to treat crash deaths as private family grief to be kept out of public view. That shift took car violence off the front pages and diluted the public debate of the growing concern of road carnage.
“We deprive [crashes] of the power that they need to compel us,” historian Peter Norton told Streetsblog in 2022.
The city’s first permanent memorial to traffic victims didn’t come until 2022 — long after tens of thousands of New Yorkers had been sacrificed to America’s freedom to drive, not to mention the hundreds of thousands who were badly injured by car drivers, their lives altered forever.
Car drivers do indeed get some benefit from their cars, but the cost of that benefit is borne by our entire society in pollution, congestion, rage, sprawl and crashes. The last one is Freedman’s main focus.
His exhibition at Littlefield includes the Crascape app, plus four oil paintings, each of which detail a specific crash with a title that references the distance of the crash from the Downtown Brooklyn performance space. For instance, the painting depicting the killing of Victor Hidalgo by an FDNY driver is called “258 Feet from Here.”
Another painting, “1,104 Feet from Here,” refers to nanny Arcellie Muschamp, who was killed by a pickup truck driver at Fifth Avenue and Union Street in 2011.
Freedman can’t paint all the horrors — there have been 52 reported crashes on the streets surrounding the venue since 2022 — but they all show up as stacks of cubes on Freedman’s Crashscape app.
And the tower grows.
“We’re not fixing the problems,” Freedman said. “We’re letting them fester.”
Obviously, there are some efforts: Then-Mayor Bill de Blasio created New York City’s Vision Zero plan in 2014 and started building out the bike network. Mayor Eric Adams failed to meet legal benchmarks for bike and bus lanes, but he did add scores of miles to both systems. And Mayor Mamdani has been reducing speed limits on some streets, as well as some small neighborhood segments.
But the bottom line — the deaths — are nowhere near zero. In fact, 210 people were killed in crashes in New York City last year, and that was considered a good year.
Amid this persistent failure, Freedman said he always asks people at events whether they know anyone who has been in a crash.
“Almost everybody does,” Freedman said.
“The Distance From Here,” noon to 1 p.m. at Littlefield (635 Sackett St. between Nevins Street and Third Avenue). Event includes a walk to Victor Hidalgo’s ghost bike. Families for Safe Streets is also hosting an event for World Remembrance Day for Road Traffic Victims, with more info available here.
Sam Brule is a senior at The New School. He’s previously worked at the New School Free Press, the Sopris Sun in Colorado, and most recently amNY. When he’s not writing, he works as a bike messenger.
