https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/t.title: Transportation Advocates Split on Senate’s Big Permitting Bill
https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/t.author: Kea Wilson
https://usa.streetsblog.org/2026/11/11/t.text:
The Senate’s massive new permitting reform bill could unlockmore highways and other fossil fuel-powered infrastructure even as it boosts transit — and transportation advocates are split on whether to support it in the context of a larger mobility culture that makes it all too easy to build auto-centric projects and snarl multimodal ones in red tape.
The Senate voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act on Monday, bringing the so-called BAAJA one step closer to passage and unleashing a firestorm of contradicting takes among proponents of sustainable and equitable development.
That’s because the 417-page legislation would essentially make it easier for communities to build just about anything they want, including AI data centers, ICE detention facilities, and oil wells, alongside green projects like solar farms and interstate transmission lines to deliver clean energy across the country.
Some advocates like Bill McKibbens questioned those trade-offs, calling the bill “a reflection of pre-election politics, when the GOP had all the power,” while others like Evergreen Action’s Pete Wyckoff called it “a big step forward for America’s clean energy economy.” President Trump, meanwhile, offered his full-throated support of the bill on Truth Social, calling it “a BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” (Capitalization, obviously, his.)
Advocates for transportation reform, though, had conflicting views on what the bill would mean for their issues Let’s wade into why.
The case against the BAAJA …
Most transportation reform advocacy orgs haven’t offered an official position on the BAAJA, but some broader sustainability groups have raised alarm bells about many of its biggest provisions – including those that would have huge implications for our national mobility culture.
For one, the bill would exempt many projects from the lengthy environmental review process currently required under the National Environmental Policy Act, including some highway widenings — at least if they don’t “alter the function or increase the capacity of the lifeline infrastructure by more than 20 percent,” the legislation states.
Some say that’s a sensible move that would push state Departments of Transportation to fix it first. Others, though, argue that highway agencies have a longtrackrecord of simply calling new interstate travel lanes “auxiliary lanes” on paper, to avoid triggering NEPA or more-stringent blue state laws— even if, to the naked eye, it sure looks like they’re expanding roads to fit more cars rather than adding a little more space for existing traffic to merge.
Moreover, those new “lifeline” exclusions would effectively allow highway agencies to hide how expansions-by-another-name will pollute, endanger, violate civil rights, and otherwise harm surrounding communities until it’s too late to stop them.
“The thing that folks need to understand about NEPA is that without the ability to hold DOTs accountable for providing complete and truthful information in the environmental review process, there is no guarantee that the public — or even the government itself — will fully reckon with the environmental and societal impacts of a highway expansion project,” added Tony Dutzik, associate director with the Frontier Group, an independent sustainability research group. “It just won’t happen.”
Even when road projects are still NEPA-eligible, the Senate’s new permitting bill would narrow the window advocates have to sue agencies for violating it from six years to just 150 days. As a result, only litigants with the time and resources to fast-track complicated lawsuits will have a chance to slap red tape on asphalt, and many grassroots groups would likely be out of luck.
It will also make many potential litigants ineligible to mount lawsuits, at least if they didn’t get wind of a project early enough to register a “substantive” comment proving they were facing “direct harm” from the project — two vague qualifications that some advocates say could be too easily get good suits tossed out by highway-happy judges.
Perhaps most disturbingly, David Bookbinder of the right-leaning Federalist Society noted that the bill would bar the federal government from taking any action to alter the operation of highways and other harmful infrastructure “at full capacity” after they’re built.
“In other words, a single federal permit or authorization under any one federal law effectively immunizes that project from adverse effects from changes in … any federal law at all,” he wrote in an open letter.
Taken together, some fear that the bill would functionally eliminate NEPA and raise emissions in the transportation realm — though no one’s quite sure by how much. Even the most optimistic scenario modeled by the independent Rhodium Group predicted the law would bring about only a 4-percent dip in greenhouse gases by 2040; in the least-optimistic scenario, emissions wouldn’t fall at all. And neither model mentions the mobility sector, specifically.
With so much to lose and the Democrats about to gain control of the House and Senate, advocates like Erik Schlenker-Goodrich of the Western Environmental Law Center urged Congress to wait out the lame-duck session to fight for a better bill, rather than settling from a dangerous compromise.
“The false urgency imposed on senators by the bill’s sponsors exists for only one reason—to minimize scrutiny and prevent lawmakers and Americans from understanding the enormity of BAAJA’s power transfer away from the people and to the oligarch class,” Schlenker-Goodrich wrote. “There is a constructive conversation to be had in the 120th Congress to build out renewables infrastructure and deliver on the promise of affordability, while respecting people and place.”
… and the case for it
Even if it would kneecap NEPA, though, some transportation reform advocates are still standing up in support of BAAJA — in hopes it will blast us into a new era of transit abundance.
In an October essay for Eno Center for Transportation, former FHWA administrator Stephanie Pollack argued that “NEPA has largely become an obstacle to getting good projects built, rather than a tool for stopping bad ones,” noting that safety, repair, and locally-driven initiatives will have a much easier time breaking ground without the burdens of the law in its current form.
“Which projects did NEPA delay while I was at US DOT? Bridge repairs and transit investments, ports and roadway safety projects, congestion pricing for New York City, and a project to build a community grid in place of a highway in Syracuse, New York,” Pollack wrote. “Which projects moved through the NEPA process largely unchanged and without a successful court challenge? Pretty much every major highway expansion.”
The American Public Transportation Association agreed in its endorsement of the bill, noting that a lot of the bill’s changes are purely procedural, like removing requirements for agencies to duplicate their efforts when state and federal review requirements mirror eachother, and setting enforceable deadlines for federal agencies to move the process forward rather than letting projects languish.
President Paul Skoutelas noted that too often, transit, biking and walking projects get mired in this kind of bureaucracy for years, while highway projects sail through with little friction. Some DOTs are even permitted to perform their own NEPA reviews under the notorious NEPA “assignment” program — and many like Texas use it to rubber-stamp harmful highway projects their communities don’t want, rather than speed the delivery of ones they do, like new rail lines.
“Every year a project waits in review, costs go up and riders wait longer for the service they need,” Skoutelas said. “This bill provides public transit and passenger rail agencies the certainty they need to plan, build, and maintain their systems, and deliver improvements to riders sooner. We look forward to working with Congress to get it across the finish line.”
Supporters of BAAJA acknowledge that the political climate for permitting reform will likely shift when the new Congress gets sworn in. But after literal decades of inertia on such a critical issue, they say it’s time to seize the moment and get the bill done now.
“Legislation is always a compromise, and Republicans were able to extract significant concessions in this bill,” Evergreen Action Executive Director Lena Moffitt said in a statement published after the midterms. “[But] this bill weakens tools that advocates have used for decades to protect communities from the harms of the fossil fuel industry.
“The hard truth is that despite decades of advocacy, polluting fossil fuel projects and pipelines are still being built en masse, while transmission lines are not,” Moffitt continued. “If the status quo remains, and clean energy projects are not built faster, the toll of the climate crisis will only get exponentially higher.”
The big picture
Of course, advocates on all sides of the issue recognize that permitting form alone won’t be enough to undo America’s forced car-dependency crisis, at least absent other policy reforms.
After all, communities probably wouldn’t need to sue for NEPA violations if highway agencies were legally required to “track outcomes and make decisions based on those findings” in the first place, as Joseph Womble recently noted in a blog for Transportation for America. As it stands, though, DOTs can keep right on collecting federal money to expand their interstates, even if the last expansion that they swore would cure congestion did the opposite instead.
Transit agencies, meanwhile, rarely have the resources or political support they need to keep networks moving, never mind expand them. And the place to fix that capacity problem requires giving them more support in the next major federal transportation bill — not overhauling things at the permitting stage, which many transit projects never gather enough money to reach.
“We don’t just need streamlined processes and more resources to create a modern, safe, and sustainable transportation system that achieves its intended outcomes,” Womble wrote. “We also need new priorities for what we’re trying to build or accomplish in the first place — not just streamlining the building of the same expensive stuff that serves yesterday’s needs.”
At the end of the day, advocates like Dutzik argue that U.S. permitting law already privileges highways. Now, it’s on advocates to decide whether or not the BAAJA will take that proverbial thumb off the scale and give multimodal projects a fighting chance — or push it down even more by drowning the country in asphalt.
“So-called ‘permitting reform’ has been happening with transportation projects for quite a while,” added Dutzik. “It’s part of a larger and longer-standing pattern of shortcutting the necessary review of expensive and damaging projects at the expense of transparency and public awareness.”
Kea Wilson is Senior Editor for Streetsblog USA. She has more than a dozen years experience as a writer telling emotional, urgent and actionable stories that motivate average Americans to get involved in making their cities better places. She is also a novelist, cyclist, and affordable housing advocate. She lives in St. Louis, MO. For tips, submissions, and general questions, reach out to her at kea@streetsblog.org, or on Bluesky @keawilson.bsky.social.
We all know about the streetscape, but the stuff underground is what gives developers fits. We talk to a man who knows how to solve deep-seated problems.

https://gothamist.com/news/newark-ice-de.title: Newark ICE detention center passes fed inspection, despite rising 'deficiencies'
https://gothamist.com/news/newark-ice-de.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/newark-ice-de.text:
The Delaney Hall immigration detention center in Newark received a passing grade in a recent federal inspection, even as the number of deficiencies identified in a site visit nearly doubled compared to the tally from a prior inquiry.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement inspectors found 22 deficiencies at Delaney Hall during their mid-September inspection, up from 12 during an inspection in late August of last year.
The category with the highest number of concerns in the latest review was the facility’s prevention and investigation of sexual assault and abuse, with six deficiencies found, such as a lack of staff reporting investigation findings and conducting necessary reviews.
The ICE inspectors ultimately rated the facility as “acceptable/adequate.” Spokespeople for ICE and the GEO Group, the private prison company operating the site, could not be reached for comment on the findings. The site re-opened in May 2025, after the GEO Group operated the site as an ICE detention center from 2011 to 2017.
Delaney Hall earlier this year emerged as a flashpoint in the nation’s immigration debates, as hundreds of detainees inside the facility launched a hunger and labor strike, and protesters outside gathered in support, at times clashing with local and federal law enforcement officers.
The detainees’ concerns included inadequate food and lack of access to appropriate medical care and legal representation. A Gothamist investigation in June identified over 70 federal lawsuits in which detainees alleged medical neglect and deficiencies since its re-opening.
Recent lawsuits filed by state and local officials seeking entry for fire and health inspectors remain pending. State health inspectors’ review of the food service areas in late May found poor employee hygiene, unclean surfaces, and food stored at unsafe temperatures.
The findings come as ICE has come under fire for conditions at its detention facilities, as deaths of immigrants in ICE custody are at the highest level in over two decades.
The federal inspection, conducted Sept. 15 to 17, offers the most detailed official look inside the facility in the months after the strike and protests earlier this year. The inspection was conducted by ICE's Office of Detention Oversight, under its Office of Professional Responsibility. On an average day, there are about 820 people detained at the facility, according to the inspection.
Federal investigators found that facility staff didn’t report sexual assault allegations to appropriate ICE leaders, or conduct necessary reports after sexual assault investigations to determine if any policy changes were needed. It remains unclear who the assault allegations were against.
Investigators also found several cases in which detainees didn’t receive a necessary initial medical screening within 12 hours of arriving at the facility, or the comprehensive health assessment required within 14 days of arriving. In four of the 25 cases reviewed, investigators found detainees’ medications weren’t distributed properly.
Kathy O’Leary, the New Jersey coordinator for the Catholic social justice organization Pax Christi USA, said that she was surprised investigators found “so few” cases of detainees not receiving necessary medication, given that she routinely hears from detainees and their families that they don’t receive them.
“We haven’t heard of anything getting better,” O’Leary said.
She added that transparency has been "reduced significantly since May,” given stricter restrictions on who is allowed to visit detainees and which detainees local government officials are allowed to speak with.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: A Mumford & Sons member is opening a new venue in Williamsburg's Domino Sugar Factory
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
Williamsburg was Ben Lovett’s gateway to New York. The British multi-instrumentalist, known for cofounding the folk-rock band Mumford & Sons, fell for the city immediately upon playing his first show here at an art gallery on North 6th Street.
It was 2008, and the indie music scene was thriving. He moved to the city a couple years later and began frequenting the edgy music venues scattered throughout the neighborhood.
“I have some great memories of crowd-surfing to Twin Peaks at a Glasslands show,” he told Gothamist.
Glasslands closed in 2015. A considerable number of Williamsburg dance clubs and concert venues followed. While Lovett still finds much to admire in places like Baby’s All Right, he said the continued closures strengthened his desire to “protect” the music scene.
“These spaces are essential to our humanity,” he said. “I don’t think people would want to live in New York if all you did was live here and work here. What you do with your third amount of time, your third space … is really important to consider.”
And so, Lovett said, he decided to do something about it: He’s opening an all-ages venue on the Williamsburg waterfront called Domino. Set to open in April 2027, the 750-capacity space will occupy the ground floor of the historic Domino Sugar Refinery building. Visitors will enter on River Street and walk through its preserved structures, such as a 240-foot-tall chimney, to attend concerts, comedy shows, film screenings and other planned events.
Domino was already in the works when Lovett learned that another beloved venue, Music Hall of Williamsburg, would be closing its doors at the end of 2026. The musician, who is developing his new space through his company tvg Hospitality, said he hopes for it to help foster the city’s creative community. He said Domino is the eighth venue that he has either built or operated. He is partnering on it with Emerson Hospitality, which opened the West Village steakhouse Graciela over the summer.
“In the hospitality and entertainment industry, you’re providing a centerpiece for people’s lives,” Lovett said. Music venues like Domino are “where they’re going to go to form a new friendship or fall in love or hear a lyric that suddenly unlocks a feeling. I’m all about protecting these spaces as best as we can and not allowing them to become the next, like, Gucci store.”
Major developers have flocked to the Williamsburg waterfront over the years, sparking accusations of gentrification and public debates over who gets to use the space and how. Two Trees, the management company that owns the Refinery building, landed a state tax break on a different waterfront housing complex earlier this year.
Lovett said he believed Domino would be the final tenant in the Refinery building, which otherwise houses office space, a glass-domed penthouse for events and an Equinox fitness club. He wants his venue to be an accessible space amid Williamsburg’s ever-evolving landscape.
“We need to make sure that we’re not losing the cultural side of Williamsburg,” Lovett said. “So we’re going to work really hard to put a stake in the ground at Domino and make sure that people know Williamsburg is culturally as relevant … and important to the city as ever.”

https://hyperallergic.com/45-of-us-indep.title: 45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds
https://hyperallergic.com/45-of-us-indep.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/45-of-us-indep.text:
45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds
In addition to declining funding, the survey identified a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns and financial precarity.
Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week.
The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who said they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.
“Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on issues impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymized respondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.

https://gothamist.com/news/the-smallish-.title: The smallish MTA projects that could make a big difference for riders
https://gothamist.com/news/the-smallish-.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/the-smallish-.text:
This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
The transit team behind On The Way is in the middle of launching an hourly call-in show every Thursday at 1 p.m. For the inaugural episode, we opened up the phones and asked listeners to share their transit moonshots — the big ideas that would dramatically change life for commuters in the city.
But transit planners' dreams led us down another road: the practical plans sitting on the shelf at MTA headquarters that could also make a difference in riders’ commutes.
A 2023 report from the MTA lays out several affordable — at least by New York standards — projects that could add service for thousands of commuters.
Take the MTA’s $30 million idea to build a busway beneath the elevated M line tracks in Ridgewood. The bus-only route would run a half-mile from Palmetto Street and Onderdonk Avenue to Fresh Pond Road. A busway could help several routes bypass gridlocked local streets and make commutes for thousands of riders “more reliable and operationally efficient,” the MTA’s report states.
The MTA evaluated the plan favorably, writing that it scores “exceptionally well in cost effectiveness since it saves money operationally.”
Another plan floated in the same MTA report would restore an LIRR station in Elmhurst, Queens, that was demolished in the 1980s. The MTA estimates it could be rebuilt for $210 million and pull riders away from the area’s crowded subways. The neighborhood would have a new commuter railroad connection to Manhattan.
But the transit agency wrote in an assessment that the restored station would provide only “marginal benefits in an area already well served by transit.”
U.S. Rep. Grace Meng, whose district covers Elmhurst, disagreed. She said the MTA doesn’t account for the growing local population that will bring more demand for commuter railroad service.
“This would allow people to take advantage of mass transit, drive less and increase ridership on the train,” Meng said, adding that residents could commute to Penn Station or Grand Central Terminal in around 10 minutes.
Liam Blank, who chairs the City Club of New York transportation and infrastructure committee, said the MTA could “unlock a virtuous cycle” by pursuing smaller capital projects. He called busways “low-hanging fruit.”
“Right now, busway implementation is probably at the highest feasibility because [the MTA] has a friendly administration, in working with a friendly New York City [Department of Transportation],” Blank said.
This is not to say the MTA is ignoring smaller-scale projects. Over the summer, the agency released a plan to fix dozens of subway bottlenecks that strain service, including two major chokepoints in Brooklyn that are a familiar inconvenience for riders.
Fixing one of the bottlenecks at Nostrand Avenue would cost an estimated $410 million — that’s just chump change!
NYC transportation news this week
Paving the way for low-traffic neighborhoods. The city transportation department is using plastic bollards to push car traffic away from the streets around McGolrick Park in north Brooklyn, aiming to stop drivers from speeding through Greenpoint.
Speeding sanitation supervisors. A Gothamist analysis found that DSNY workers who oversee trash collection and issue tickets rack up hundreds of automated speed camera tickets each year.
Study links ADHD to subway surfing trend. People killed “surfing” on top of New York City subway trains tend to be teen boys diagnosed with ADHD, according to a new study published this week by researchers from NYU-Langone and the city hospital system.
Canal Street is getting a facelift. The Department of Transportation has split the Reimagining Canal Street project into two phases — one targeting west Canal Street and one targeting east Canal Street — with goals of adding new crosswalks, two-lane bike lanes, pedestrian areas lined with planters and concrete blocks and more. But it may take a while.
A new Newark Bay Bridge is coming. Work is underway to replace the outdated Newark Bay Bridge, which carries the New Jersey Turnpike extension into Hudson County and serves as one of the main connecting roads between the Garden State and New York City. Officials say it should be wrapped up by 2031 with minimal disruptions to commuters.
Penn Station plan could funnel taxpayer money to new venue for James Dolan. The federal government's plan to rebuild Penn Station could lead to heaps of taxpayer money being used to subsidize a new entertainment venue for the Madison Square Garden Company.
MTA chair optimistic with Democrats in control of Congress. President Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly withheld funding from New York and the MTA since he took office in 2025. But MTA Chair Janno Lieber says he has “more confidence that the existing projects will be funded” with a Democratic majority in both the House and Senate.
Brooklyn woman killed after falling from a moving SUV on the BQE. Police said Chasna Thelemaque opened the rear door of a Toyota RAV4 and tumbled out of the car at around 2:30 a.m. on Sunday and was struck by a Hyundai Elantra heading in the same direction.
Curious Commuter
Have a question for us? Use this form to submit yours and we may answer it in a future newsletter!
Question from Mike in Queens
Why isn't there any graffiti on subway trains anymore? I see photos of trains covered in it from the 1970s. It's not like graffiti disappeared from the city, but you don't see it on the subways.
Answer
During the 1970s and 1980s, graffiti was a huge problem for the MTA. Crews would “bomb” entire trains with paint and treat subway cars as canvases on wheels. But the transit agency eventually took a drastic measure in 1989, implementing a policy to pull any graffitied train from service, no matter the disruption to commutes. That’s why you don’t see cars covered in paint. To this day, when a train does get “bombed,” it is sent back to a yard where crews spend hours cleaning it with a pressure washer.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: LISTEN: From the Club to the Flophouse in Wang’s World
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Harry Siegel
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Film slows you down because you have 36 exposures on a roll of 35mm film. You can’t shoot like a machine gun; you have to be more thoughtful. And then there’s the craft of taking the film and going into the darkroom and developing it. There’s this revelation of seeing the negatives for the first time. There’s making contact sheets where then you study them with a loupe and a grease pencil, and you thoughtfully think about what you’ve done. It’s a very big commitment of time then to go into the darkroom and make the print. So every step of the process is thoughtful and slow and very different than shooting with an iPhone…
As his first career retrospective opens at the Bronx Documentary Center, photographer and filmmaker Harvey Wang sat down with The City Reporter’s Harry Siegel to discuss capturing an ever-vanishing city, what it’s like looking back over decades of his own work and much more.
Harry Siegel: It’s TBD NYC, covering the ABCs of arts, books, culture, film, photography, etcetera — here in the only city in the world.
I’m Harry Siegel, The City Reporter’s editorial director for audio, here with Harvey Wang, the photographer and filmmaker who is the namesake subject of Wang’s World, his first-ever career retrospective that’s opening this weekend at the Bronx Documentary Center and will be there through January 9th.
Harvey, you came on FAQ NYC off-cycle a couple of years ago for a look back at your book, Harvey Wang’s New York, that was an incredible snapshot, so to speak, of a vanishing city as of 1990. Lots of stuff has vanished since then, and now you’ve got your first career retrospective with lots of photos and also three screenings of your documentaries, feature, and short films. It’s great to have you on, and let’s jump right in.
Harvey Wang: Nice to be here.
Harry Siegel: Thank you. Yeah, we’re doing it in person this time, which I’m glad about. Last time was mid-pandemic, as I recall, and we did it over Zoom.
Harvey Wang: Right, right. So this time I have to wear pants.
Harry Siegel: Yeah, everyone’s got to suffer for their art. A career retrospective is a real honor, but I have to imagine it’s got to be at least a little weird. Do you want to talk about the show, what’s in it, and what it’s been like just going back through decades of your work?
Harvey Wang: Sure. I wanted it to cover my earliest work that I did as a high school student growing up in Queens and coming into the city with my Nikkormat camera and exploring—and be sort of an autobiography, in a way, of my journey through the city and my career. So there’s early work, which I can go into detail later. There’s pictures of my period of living in Chinatown from ’79 to ’83, where I was photographing Club 57 and the music scene and just life on the Lower East Side and the East Village, and that was the origin of my doing the Harvey Wang’s New York book—seeing businesses closing up and starting to do portraits, and then over a five-year period doing portraits all over the city, and that becoming the book for W.W. Norton.
But even before that book, I had worked on two projects. One was about retired baseball players, which was very, very cool. That was my first book that I did with Ed Kiersh, the writer, for Bantam, and we traveled all over America.
And it was so cool meeting old Yankees like Don Larsen, Pedro Ramos, and Roger Maris, as well as players from—you know, Hall of Famers. And in that era, those ballplayers didn’t have big pensions or contracts, so they had to go back to jobs. Mickey Lolich had a donut shop, Bobby Shantz had an ice cream stand. You know, it was really very interesting to see these old-time legends living a real life.
After that, I did a book called Rock Wives about women married to rock stars—you know, fascinating: Angela Bowie, Leslie Meat Loaf, Dee Dee Ramone’s wife Vera. So doing portraits and stories, those all happened before Harvey Wang’s New York.
So the exhibit covers those books as well as two collaborations I did with David Isay, the legendary radio documentarian and MacArthur genius who became a good friend. We traveled around the country doing a book called Holding On: Dreamers, Visionaries, Eccentrics, and Other American Heroes, full of incredible characters. And that was a wonderful time for me to be on the road with David. We were very simpatico; we really just had a great time. I would quietly sit back while he did his interviews—and he was a great interviewer and very, very well-prepared interviewer and very sympathetic—and then I would have my moment to do the portraits, and then we’d get in the car and move on to the next city, state. You know, it was a great journey for me.
And another book we did together was Flophouse: Life on the Bowery, which we could talk about. So deciding what to include in the show was, you know, I went through my career, the different bodies of work, including stuff I did in Appalachia in my college years, and the show brings us right up to date. I’m doing a new series of color work, and there’s a section for that as well.
Harry Siegel: You’ve shot a lot in black and white—how old are you?
Harvey Wang: I’m 70.
Harry Siegel: Kids today. So you started in, you know, this era of chemical photography. Do you want to talk a bit about shooting black and white and color, how you decided on that?
Harvey Wang: I started shooting black and white film and then very quickly had a darkroom, you know, in my high school years. My cousin Roberta taught me how to develop film and make prints, and actually her husband Ethan, who’s not a photographer, spent time with me in the darkroom in their apartment on Bergen Street in a home owned by Tom Anderson. They rented a top-floor apartment and they had a darkroom, and I learned how to print there.
But darkroom work became a big part of my attraction to photography. First of all, shooting in film slows you down because you have 36 exposures on a roll of 35mm film. You can’t shoot like a machine gun; you have to be more thoughtful. And then there’s the craft of taking the film and going into the darkroom and developing it. There’s this revelation of seeing the negatives for the first time. There’s making contact sheets where then you study them with a loupe and a grease pencil, and you thoughtfully think about what you’ve done. It’s a very big commitment of time then to go into the darkroom and make the print. So every step of the process is thoughtful and slow and very different than shooting with an iPhone.
And I was just tickled to death when I would make a beautiful print, and it was a fulfillment. It was something tangible. It was something I could hold and show and share, and then ultimately put in a box. And those boxes started to—when I went to college, I had like one box of contact sheets, and now, you know, of course there’s hundreds of boxes of contact sheets, and it’s a physical representation of my life because each contact sheet intermixed with work and projects are friends and relationships and eventually children. And they’re sequential, and they’re ordered, and they’re physical, and it somehow suited me to work in film, in black and white.
Harry Siegel: You put out a book and a documentary, I guess a decade ago now, called From Darkroom to Daylight about some of this and the transition to digital. And like 10 years later, we are through the looking glass all the way, no doubt. On the flip side of this, I’m interested how you feel about digital photography.
Harvey Wang: Well, first off, when things switched from analog to digital, it did create a bit of a hiccup in my career because I didn’t—I was reluctant to adopt it. I just had this strong, you know, attraction to black and white and darkroom work. But I have to say it’s pretty incredible what you can now do with digital tools, and especially, you know, doing a job, any kind of commercial work, when you can photograph something and deliver it that afternoon, you know, without going to a lab, without going into the darkroom. So it speeds things up.
And then Photoshop is remarkable. You can do things that are impossible to do in a darkroom. And for my latest work that involves shooting multiple images and creating, you know, in effect, collages or series of pictures, it would have been so cumbersome to do it using analog tools. So, you know, I think digital has really opened up the world.
But there’s also what I anecdotally understand that there’s a lot of younger people who are very attracted to shooting film, and they’re getting old film cameras and they’re finding labs, and it’s similar to the vinyl record thing. You know, like in a time when everyone can do a perfect picture with their iPhone, I think there might be a movement to search out for imperfection—you know, the happy accident. There are no happy accidents in digital, you know, unless you’re faking them in Photoshop.
Harry Siegel: There’s all the delay with analog. There’s this long delay and you don’t know what you’ve shot until you’re getting the images back, and it’s just a very sort of different—
Harvey Wang: Yeah, and I think it’s a reaction—you know, the slow food, vinyl records, analog photography. Maybe it won’t all die out totally.
Harry Siegel: Do you want to talk a bit about Club 57 and how you ended up there and the characters?
Harvey Wang: Sure. So I’ll go back to 1979. I was living in Chinatown at 22 Catherine Street, a five-story walk-up. I had four roommates—there were five of us in total.
We were each paying about 100 bucks for our rent. I paid a little more because I had two rooms; I had a darkroom and a bedroom combined, and then a little office. But one of my roommates was a guy named Kai Eric, and he was dating Ann Magnuson, and she was sort of one of the founders of Club 57, which was on 57 St. Marks Place in the basement of a church. And it was a wildly creative time.
The idea was sort of like, “Let’s get together and put on a show.” You know, it was sort of like we’ll have a monster movie club, and we’ll have live art performances, and we’ll have pop-up art shows—and Keith Haring was there, and Basquiat, and Lypsinka, and all of these creative people would congregate. And they had a monthly calendar, there was a Ladies Auxiliary, and all of these sort of silly things—Country Western Night. It was just like playing, but among people who were just really, really creative and inventive, and anything goes.
So I would start to hang out there and do pictures on various events and nights, and it was wild fun. I always kept myself a little bit on the outside being a photographer, not so much participating as observing, and which has kind of been my M.O. for a lot of my life—is I’ve used the camera to get places, but not necessarily participate. There’s pluses and minuses to that.
Harry Siegel: You can look people in the eyes and they can’t see yours.
Harvey Wang: Well, there’s that. And you know, it’s interesting to me that all of this contemporary stuff was going on, and I was taking pictures, but at the same time I was doing Harvey Wang’s New York, which is a kind of looking back. I was looking, you know, I was looking back: what is going to disappear?
Where’s the New York of my grandfather’s era? And yet this other stuff was happening that I kind of like was flitting through, but not getting too deep with. You know, there were documentarians and photographers who were, you know, photographing Keith Haring at work, for instance, but I just would photograph the things that were happening at Club 57.
Harry Siegel: And this is a little later now, but I have in my hand Flophouse: Life on the Bowery, which you mentioned is another of the projects you did with David Isay. There’s sort of an incredible contrast in my head between the Club 57 stuff and that sort of work, and the two very proximate but very different New Yorks. Do you want to talk a bit about shooting that and how you went about it?
Harvey Wang: Yeah, I’d love to actually, because it’s—the book Flophouse: Life on the Bowery, published by Random House in the year 2000, was mostly shot in 1998, 1999. It was an outgrowth of a radio documentary that David Isay and Stacy Abramson did about the Sunshine Hotel. And so they were drawn to kind of this fabled Bowery. You know, it was legendary; it was the premier Skid Row in America, and from the end of the 19th century until the 20th, it was the country’s most infamous Skid Row.
By the 1990s, when we did this book, there were only about eight flophouses remaining, and still offering the shabbiest of accommodations for, you know, under $5 in some cases.
Harry Siegel: Flophouses, SROs—all these are now themselves a sort of disappearing world, and we’re in this new sort of modern homelessness that’s pretty young, you know, since about 1980, prior to which, you know, there was a lot of men who were finding very cheap and scuzzy rooms, and then some overwork.
Harvey Wang: Yeah, and it’s incredible how New York changes so rapidly, but I never imagined—you know, the New Museum opened up next to the Sunshine Hotel, and a contemporary artist named Anna took me to the Sunshine. There are two residents left in the Sunshine Hotel right today. There are two residents left, and in the Providence Hotel, they’ve been tearing down all the cubicles, and I think it’s down to maybe 14 people. So really it’s a rapid end of an era—the era of the flophouse.
Harry Siegel: Bouncing around a little, do you want to talk about your films, doing that sort of work, and what’s going to be screening over the next couple of months?
Harvey Wang: Sure. Yeah, the first screening date is on November 21st. I’ll be showing From Darkroom to Daylight, which is my documentary about the transition in photography from analog to digital. I interviewed 50 photographers, including some really well-known ones like Sally Mann, and Elliott Erwitt, and Eugene Richards, Alex Webb, Taryn Simon, David Goldblatt from South Africa—some really, you know, really outstanding people who had different thoughts about this transition: some totally embracing digital tools and others firmly committed to analog. But I was trying to figure out my own place in the world, and that—it was kind of in a way, even though it’s full of interviews, it’s a personal film on trying to figure things out.
So that’s From Darkroom to Daylight, and that will be preceded by a short film about Sid Kaplan, who is a legendary character in New York. He was Robert Frank’s printer; he printed for Robert Capa, and Cornell Capa, and Weegee, and he has an East Village darkroom. Many years he taught at SVA. But I made a short film about him, so that will precede From Darkroom to Daylight.
And then on December 1st, I directed one feature film in my life. It’s called The Last New Yorker, appropriately. It starred Dominic Chianese and Dick Latessa. Dominic, of course, is Uncle Junior, and Dick Latessa had a long career on Broadway; he was in Hairspray and countless other plays—wonderful guy. And then the lead female character was Kathleen Chalfant, and she was a wonderful actress to work with and was so—you know, me being a first-time director—she was so gentle and kind and helpful, and an amazing professional who’d come to set knowing her lines.
The film is about two older friends who kind of—basically the film is about them wandering around and talking. And in the course of the film, Lenny, the character played by Dominic, loses his money in the stock market, but he also falls in love. And so it’s a sweet story of friends in their 70s, it’s a love story, it’s about a changing New York. A lot of the locations were places that have since disappeared, like Blarney Stone, and Lismore Hosiery, and a jewelry store on Canal Street, Molded Shoe Company, Eisenberg’s Coffee Shop—all these locations that were their world, but have since disappeared just like they were dinosaurs walking around New York.
So on January 9th, we’re having an evening of short films which will include The Cantor’s Last Cantata — about a cantor from a Reform synagogue in Borough Park who is about to retire and puts on a play with the congregation that’s based on a 1940s operetta. It takes place in Brooklyn, and it imagines that all the residents of Brooklyn wake from a dream to find that the Brooklyn Dodgers have beat the Yankees. So it’s a really great Brooklyn story, and it’s wonderful to see it performed by these alta kockers, and it’s a touching little film.
I’ll also be premiering another short film at that night about the legendary Tulsa, Oklahoma photographer Gaylord Oscar Herron. So this is kind of cool: in 1980, I bought a book at the Strand called Vagabond, and it was a photo book, and it just really, really affected me. Some photo books in my life have really, you know, had a big impact on me—Diane Arbus, Walker Evans, August Sander, these photographers I found, you know, their work influenced me. But this book Vagabond, I just was so moved by it because the photographs, he wrote text, his artwork—it was something very special. And I wrote him a fan letter in 1980. I wrote Gaylord Oscar Herron a fan letter. And then just five years ago, I got a response. So like, you know, 30 years later, I get a phone call from a woman who said, “I’m working with Gaylord Oscar Herron—you know, he’s now, you know, 80 years old—and I found your letter in his scrapbook. Would you like to talk to him?” So this is like, you know, 30 years later I get a response. So I ended up going to Tulsa and spending, you know, three, four days with him and filming him, and so I made a short film.
Harry Siegel: And it’s debuting.
Harvey Wang: And it’s debuting, yeah.
Harry Siegel: So we touched on Harvey Wang’s New York that came out in 1990, you know, and it’s capturing all these jobs and professions that were part of a vanishing New York—maybe, you know, those grandfather’s New York: mannequin makers, social dancers, sign painters, fish dealers, TV repairmen, and saddest of all, news vendors. 35 years later, like, who are today’s like pinsetters, knife grinders, bathhouse attendants, photoengravers?
Harvey Wang: It’s funny you should ask because in talking to the education director of the Bronx Documentary Center, they have a great program there: classes for teenagers, photography—they teach photography, filmmaking. And we were thinking that it would be nice to do an updated version of Harvey Wang’s New York with these teens in the Bronx. And so I asked AI. I said, “What jobs will AI make obsolete in the Bronx?” And, you know, I got a list. And so this is like an ongoing idea. Maybe I’ll work with these kids, we’ll try to like do an updated version of the jobs that are going to be, you know, made obsolete by AI in the Bronx—you know, let these Bronx kids do portraits and little oral histories.
Harry Siegel: I feel like that’s like asking AI, “When will I die?” But, uh—
Harvey Wang: Exactly. You know, people have always said to me—people, you know, I’ve spoken to groups and students over the years, and they often say to me like, “Oh, you did this book, I guess you can’t do another project like this.” And I always say that at any given moment, there’s going to be stuff that’s changing and disappearing, whether it’s a particular ethnic group being displaced from a certain neighborhood, or somebody—you know, there’s always going to be something.
Harry Siegel: Goodbye Italians.
Harvey Wang: Yeah. Exactly. I mean, there are very few—there’s what, one street left in Little Italy now? Yeah, so at any given moment one can go through the city and find something that’s disappearing.
Harry Siegel: Right. Before all of us disappear, what’s next for you after all this and having, you know, a couple months to be there and people appreciating what you’ve done, you having this opportunity to sort of go back through your own work? Like, do you have big ambitions or little ones for what’s next? What are you thinking?
Harvey Wang: Well, like I said, I’m working on a new series for my own enjoyment, and some of those works will be hanging, and I don’t know what people will think of them. My own 13-year-old son doesn’t think much of them; he says, you know, he appreciates the old black and white stuff. So, but I’m entertained and I’m happy to do it.
But you know, I talk to a lot of photographers my age, and one thing that we’re all concerned about is what happens to our work when we’re gone. And these things take up many cubic linear feet of shelving, and will it have a home in the future? Will it be dumpstered? You know, I have a relationship with the Museum of the City of New York, and they have over 800 of my pictures in their collection, and they plan to take in more. So for me, at least, I know that my New York work will have a home, and when I’m gone, it’ll be searchable, findable, and sharable. But there’s a lot of work that, you know, I want to make sure it finds a home.
I donated pictures to the Baseball Hall of Fame, I’ve donated pictures to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame for those other books I had mentioned. I did a project with Milton Rogovin, the Buffalo photographer who passed away at age 100, I think, but when he was 90 I did a thing with him, and I donated my work about Milton to the Burchfield Penney Museum. So that’s part of the goal of what, you know, we do at this age, is find homes for the old work.
Harry Siegel: Harvey, thank you so much for coming on and talking all this through. The show is Wang’s World, at the Bronx Documentary Center through January 10th, and I hope we’ll talk again soon. Thank you.
Harvey Wang: Thank you.

https://taz.de/Fluechtlingsabschiebungen.title: Flüchtlingsabschiebungen aus Europa: Dobrindt und seine Kollegen setzen auf Ruanda
https://taz.de/Fluechtlingsabschiebungen.author: Simone Schlindwein
https://taz.de/Fluechtlingsabschiebungen.text:
Flüchtlingsabschiebungen aus Europa: Dobrindt und seine Kollegen setzen auf Ruanda
Mehrere europäische Länder wollen abgelehnte Asylbewerber nach Ruanda abschieben. Aufnahme fänden sie in international finanzierten Einrichtungen.
Das Transit-Zentrum Gashora liegt rund 50 Kilometer südlich von Ruandas Hauptstadt Kigali, hoch oben auf einem Hügel zwischen zwei größeren Seen. Die 2015 mit Geldern des UN-Flüchtlingshilfswerks UNHCR errichteten Gebäude beherbergen Geflüchtete aus ganz Afrika, die UNHCR regelmäßig aus dem Bürgerkriegsland Libyen evakuiert und nach Ruanda bringt. In Gashora warten sie auf die Bearbeitung ihrer Asylanträge, die sie von dort aus für europäische Länder, die USA oder Kanada stellen.
Rund 700 Betten, Fußball- und Volleyballplätze, Billardtische, Nähstuben und Fahrschulen gibt es in Gashora, um den Geflüchteten die Zeit zu vertreiben. Über 3.000 Geflüchtete, zumeist junge Leute, haben seit 2019 das Zentrum durchlaufen. Rund 2.600 von ihnen wurden in sechs Jahren nach Genehmigung ihres Asylantrags in sichere Aufnahmeländer ausgeflogen.
Bald könnten in der Einrichtung, die im Rahmen eines Abkommens zwischen UNHCR, AU (Afrikanische Union) und Ruandas Regierung entstand, abgeschobene Migranten aus Europa aufgenommen werden. Ruandas Innenminister Vincent Biruta ist laut Angaben aus Kigali an diesem Montag in Wien, um den Migrationsdeal mit mehreren europäischen Staaten zu unterzeichnen – darunter Deuschland. Im Bundeshaushalt 2027 sind 20 Millionen Euro für das Modellprojekt vorgesehen, davon sollen laut Spiegel rund 40 Plätze womöglich in Ruanda finanziert werden.
Im August und September waren mehrfach Delegationen aus Deutschland, Österreich, den Niederlanden, Dänemark und Griechenland in Kigali, um einen solchen Deal einzufädeln, bestätigte damals Ruandas Regierungssprecherin Yolande Makolo.
Kaum Perspektiven in Ruanda
Makolo betonte in einem Interview mit lokalen Medien, dass Ruanda selbst auf eine lange Geschichte von Flucht und Migration zurückblicken kann. Der Völkermord gegen die Tutsi in Ruanda 1994 hatte in der ganzen Region zu einer Flüchtlingskrise geführt, Millionen von jungen Ruandern sind im Exil aufgewachsen. Derzeit beherbergt das kleine Land im Herzen Afrikas rund 100.000 Geflüchtete, die meisten aus den Nachbarländern Kongo und Burundi.
Aus Sicht Ruandas ist Gashora ein Erfolgsmodell für den Umgang mit Flüchtlingen. „Wir haben Tausende aufgenommen“, betonte Makolo: „Und viele von ihnen sind wieder gegangen – sie wurden in Drittstaaten umgesiedelt. Das hat sehr gut funktioniert.“ Die Geflüchteten haben jeweils die Wahl, entweder in Ruanda eine Aufenthaltsgenehmigung zu beantragen, Asyl oder Resettlement in Drittstaaten zu beantragen oder in ihr Heimatland zurückzukehren.
Nur die allerwenigsten wollen in Ruanda selbst bleiben, geben viele Geflüchtete in Gashora gegenüber lokalen Journalisten zu. Das kleine Land mit rund 15 Millionen Einwohnern kämpft mit einer hohen Arbeitslosenrate. Laut dem ruandischen Statistikamt liegt sie bei Jugendlichen im Alter zwischen 16 und 30 Jahren bei rund 19 Prozent. Rund 35 Prozent der Bevölkerung sind in der Landwirtschaft tätig, das Durchschnittseinkommen liegt bei nicht einmal umgerechnet 2 Euro pro Tag. Für Migranten ist es ökonomisch schwer, in Ruanda Fuß zu fassen.
Britisch finanzierte Einrichtung in Kigali steht leer
Großbritannien war das erste Land, das einen eigenen Migrationsdeal mit Ruanda schloss. Der „Ruanda-Deal“ von 2022 hatte am Ende einen Umfang von umgerechnet rund 840 Millionen Euro.
Doch nur vier Migranten wurden freiwillig nach Ruanda ausgeflogen, denn Anwälte und Menschenrechtsorganisationen gingen vor Gericht dagegen vor. Im November 2023 erklärte der britische Supreme Court den Ruanda-Deal für rechtswidrig, da Ruanda kein sicheres Drittland sei. Daraufhin verabschiedete die Regierung in London 2024 ein Gesetz, das Ruanda zum sicheren Drittstaat deklarierte, und die beiden Regierungen schlossen im April 2024 einen neuen Migrationsvertrag, der den Bedenken des Supreme Court Rechnung tragen sollte.
Die neugewählte Labour-Regierung in London sagte aber im Juli 2024 wenige Tage nach ihrem Amtsantritt den Deal einseitig wieder ab, ohne ihn formell zu kündigen. Ruanda zog vor ein internationales Schiedsgericht in den Haag, um ausstehende Zahlungen einzuklagen. Dieses entschied zu Beginn dieses Jahres, dass London die geforderte Summe nicht zahlen muss.
Für die Aufnahme von Migranten aus Großbritannien wurde 2022 das „Hope Hostel“ in Kigali renoviert. Ursprünglich gebaut, um Waisenkinder des Völkermordes 1994 zu beherbergen, wurde die staatliche Einrichtung im Zuge des Ruanda-Deals mit britischen Geldern zu einer schicken Herberge für 50 bis 200 Personen ausgebaut. Sie steht bis heute leer – und stünde damit theoretisch nun zur Verfügung.
Die Niederlande verhandeln auch mit Uganda
Auch mit dem Nachbarland Uganda versuchen europäische Länder einen solchen Deal einzufädeln. Federführend sind die Niederlande. Sie unterzeichneten im September 2025 eine Absichtserklärung mit Ugandas Regierung. Aufgrund von Unregelmäßigkeiten bei den Wahlen in Uganda im Januar 2026 wurde das Vorhaben dann erstmal „auf Eis gelegt“, sagen niederländische Quellen der taz.
Quellen aus Ugandas Flüchtlingsministerium bestätigen nun, dass die Verhandlungen nun wieder „enorm hart vorangetrieben werden“. Bei dem jüngsten Besuch europäischer Delegationen im September, angeführt von den Niederlanden, war von bis zu 10.000 Migranten die Rede, die Uganda in den nächsten Jahren aufnehmen soll. Als Gegenleistung würden die Niederlande in Uganda Schulen und Krankenhäuser bauen – vor allem in den zahlreichen Flüchtlingslagern des Landes.
Uganda beherbergt zwei Millionen Flüchtlinge, mehr als jedes andere Land Afrikas. Die meisten stammen aus umliegenden Krisenregionen, von Kongo bis Sudan. Das Land ist für seine liberale Flüchtlingspolitik bekannt. In Uganda erhalten sie unkompliziert einen unbegrenzten Flüchtlingsstatus sowie eine Arbeitserlaubnis und können sich permanent niederlassen. Anders als in Ruanda gibt es in Ugandas großen Flüchtlingscommunitys zahlreiche Möglichkeiten für Eritreer, Sudanesen oder Geflüchtete aus anderen Nationen, einen Job und damit ein Einkommen zu bekommen.
Das Problem: Ugandas Regierung verfügt über kein Transit- oder Aufnahmezentrum wie Ruanda, wo man Migranten aus Europa zeitweilig beherbergen kann. Dies müsste erst gebaut werden. Aus Regierungskreisen hat die taz erfahren, dass ein möglicher Deal zunächst vom Kabinett beschlossen und dann von Präsident Yoweri Museveni abgesegnet werden müsse. „Da sind wir noch nicht so weit wie in Ruanda“, heißt es gegenüber der taz.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. Im Friseursalon: Der Salon auf der Bühne
Ein Theaterstück spielt in einem Friseurladen. Das erinnert den Kolumnisten an seine eigenen Friseurbesuche und den Haarschnitt von Oma.
C hristian Specht, Jahrgang 1969, ist politisch engagiert und setzt sich für mehr Mitwirkungsmöglichkeiten von Menschen mit Beeinträchtigung in den Medien ein. Seit 2017 ist er der erste Mensch mit Beeinträchtigung im Vorstand der Lebenshilfe. Er hat ein Büro in der taz und zeichnet (un)regelmäßig den „Specht der Woche“.
In der Berliner Morgenpost war ein Artikel zu einem Theaterstück. Ein Musical: „Salon Rosie“. Das hat mich vom Bild her erinnert an „Eine linke Geschichte“ im Grips-Theater.
Ich weiß aber nicht, ob das stimmt. Ich fand den Schrank toll vom Bühnenbild und die Lampe. Den roten Vorhang auch, den habe ich aber nicht gemalt. Es geht wohl um einen Friseurladen, und ich mag alte Möbel.
Leider habe ich keine zu Hause. Zum Friseur gehe ich auch manchmal. Das gefällt mir. Immer derselbe, der ist nett. Und nicht so teuer. Manchmal unterhalten wir uns auch.
Ich glaube, mein Friseur kommt aus Kroatien. Wir reden über alles Mögliche, über Kroatien, den Kiez am Kottbusser Damm, Berlin. Sein Geschäft sieht allerdings ganz anders aus, moderner als auf meinem Bild.
Als Kind hat mir meine Oma die Haare geschnitten, zu Hause.

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/fabien.text:
Dans un contexte de fortes mobilisations sociales, la Fête de l’Humanité Normandie a rassemblé militants, syndicalistes et sympathisants les 14 et 15 novembre, dans l’agglomération rouennaise. Deux jours de rencontres et de débats pour prolonger les luttes et préparer les prochaines échéances politiques.
La Fête de l’Humanité Normandie faisait son retour dans l’agglomération de Rouen, ce week-end des 14 et 15 novembre. Militants communistes, syndicalistes et sympathisants se sont retrouvés pour deux journées de débats, de rencontres et de convivialité. « On est sur une belle diversité et une belle affluence cette année », s’est félicité Aurélien Lecacheur, secrétaire départemental du PCF en Seine-Maritime.
