https://jacobin.com/2026/11/snyc-youth-c.title: The Southern Negro Youth Congress’s Bold Push for Equality
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/snyc-youth-c.author: Robert Greene II
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/snyc-youth-c.text:
The Southern Negro Youth Congress’s Bold Push for Equality
Founded in 1937, the Southern Negro Youth Congress was a key player in the radical wing of the early phase of the civil rights movement.
“Behold the land, the rich and resourceful land, from which for a hundred years its best elements have been running away, its youth and hope, black and white, scurrying North because they are of each other, and dare not face a future of equal, independent, upstanding human beings, in a real and not a sham democracy.” This line was spoken by W. E. B. Du Bois near the end of arguably his greatest speech, titled “Behold the Land.” It was delivered on October 20, 1946, at a convention hosted by the Southern Negro Youth Congress (SNYC), where Du Bois thundered from the dais at Antisdel Chapel at Benedict College in Columbia, South Carolina. He and the SNYC had, for a brief moment, made the Palmetto State the center of the struggle for global human rights in the post–World War II years.
Founded in 1937, the SNYC represented the radical wing of the early phase of the civil rights movement. Its radical politics lay in the organization’s recognition of the links between racial and class problems in the US South and throughout the nation. At times, it made alliances on the ground with various Communist Party USA organizations in the South. While many historians have come to see the civil rights era as extending longer than the “classic” phase of 1954 until the mid-1960s, what makes the SNYC unique is how many of the issues they attacked would come up again during both the 1960s and the early decades of the twenty-first century.
As part of the youth wing of the National Negro Congress (NNC), the SNYC went well beyond organizing the black youth of the Jim Crow–era South. It offered them an opportunity to voice and do something about the growing frustration many of them felt living in the grip of Jim Crow segregation.
Through the course of the Great Depression and World War II, the SNYC pressured political and social leaders throughout the South. As they pressed for greater freedom for all people in the former Confederacy, the SNYC became a beacon of hope during the fight against fascism at home and abroad. The SNYC always linked the struggles against Jim Crow segregation at home to the rising tide of fascism, Nazism, and militarism abroad, even before the advent of the better-known “Double V” campaign among black Americans during World War II, pushing for victory over fascism abroad and Jim Crow at home.
The bread and butter of the organization was the organizing of previously disenfranchised workers in the South. Their earliest campaigns included the organizing of black tobacco farmers outside their first headquarters of Richmond, Virginia. At other points, the SNYC would participate in voter registration drives and work with unions to increase labor organizing across a region that, by the Great Depression, had earned a staunchly anti-labor reputation. Other efforts included the investigation of cases of murder in the South via private investigators, such as the case of William Daniel’s 1946 murder by Birmingham police. In short, like the NNC and other radical organizations of the Great Depression and World War II eras, the SNYC used virtually every method at their disposal to fight against Jim Crow segregation.
But the challenges facing the SNYC were more dangerous after America’s triumph in World War II. A rift formed between liberals and leftists after the war; the wartime exigency of the American-Soviet alliance gave way to fears of another world war, this time between the United States and its allies against the Soviet Union and a growing postwar Communist bloc. At the same time, anti-colonial campaigns were spreading like wildfire across Asia and Africa. This, coupled with black frustration at home due to renewed white backlash to civil rights, gave the SNYC ample reason to step up their efforts in a place like South Carolina.
Ahead of Its Time
By 1946, South Carolina already had a growing movement for radical human rights. The Progressive Democratic Party (PDP), led by black South Carolinians Modjeska Simkins, John Henry McCray, and Osceola McKaine, built a progressive black alternative to South Carolina’s white-supremacist Democratic Party of South Carolina. Registering black South Carolinians to vote, putting up their own slate of candidates for state and national office, and even traveling to the 1944 Democratic National Convention to challenge the legitimacy of the South Carolina Democratic Party, the Progressive Democratic Party presaged the better-known Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party (MFDP) by twenty years in using grassroots democratic traditions to attempt to upend the old system.
Their efforts to overturn the ironclad rule of the white-supremacist Democratic Party did not result in electoral victory. Osceola McKaine, the black nominee of the PDP who campaigned against incumbent Olin Johnston in 1944, fell short in his campaign. But McKaine’s own personal story is a reminder of why black South Carolina, in 1944, was so thoroughly galvanized to fight back against Jim Crow.
McKaine, a native of Sumter, South Carolina, served in the United States military during World War I. After his term of service ended, McKaine, tired of the hypocrisy of American calls to “make the world safe for democracy” abroad while not doing so at home, settled in Ghent, Belgium, and opened a successful nightclub. Forced to flee Belgium due to World War II, McKaine returned to Sumter determined to fight for democracy in his home state. He was defeated in 1944 by Johnston, who was governor of South Carolina when the state condemned to death fourteen-year-old George Stinney, who some believe is the youngest person condemned to death in US history.
The PDP, like the MFDP twenty years later, was important not due to victory at the polls but due to the organization’s ability to give voters hope who had had none for generations. Thousands of new black voters became part of South Carolina’s voting process for the first time since the immediate aftermath of the collapse of Reconstruction. Meanwhile, growing pressure to restore the right to vote for black citizens in the South was also enhanced by the 1944 Smith v. Allwright Supreme Court decision, which declared the all-white primaries of Southern Democratic parties unconstitutional.
Again, South Carolina played a crucial role in resisting this, with Governor Johnston himself calling a special session of the state legislature in 1944 to pass new laws to continue the white primary. It was not until another federal court case, Elmore v. Rice, originating with the challenge of black South Carolinian George Elmore and decided in 1947, that the white primary was broken.
What SNYC Represented
South Carolina, therefore, had already made itself the nexus of domestic political battles over racism and citizenship. But the state was also important as a site of international debate over the future of peace in the post–World War II landscape. One of the chief architects of the post–World War II foreign policy, which quickly became antagonistic toward the Soviets, was South Carolinian James Byrnes.
Often overlooked in twentieth-century American foreign and domestic policy history, Byrnes holds the unique distinction of being one of the few politicians in American history to hold virtually every possible office in the federal government. He served as congressman, and later senator, from South Carolina in the 1920s and 1930s. As a close friend to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Byrnes briefly served on the Supreme Court before being named director of the Office of Economic Stabilization, and later director of the Office of War Mobilization during World War II. In that role, Byrnes became one of the most important people in America’s war effort. Afterward, under President Harry Truman, Byrnes was named secretary of state in 1945.
But Byrnes coveted the presidency. As was the case with another South Carolinian, John C. Calhoun, in the nineteenth century, Byrnes’s ties to South Carolina and white-supremacist ideology became the chief impediments to higher office. Most notably, liberals and progressives within the New Deal–era Democratic Party stymied efforts to make Byrnes the vice president under Franklin Roosevelt during his 1944 campaign. Still, Byrnes remained a powerful force within Southern and national politics. And as the Cold War intensified, a massive campaign for social change in his home state made perfect sense.
The SNYC, committed as it was to racial justice at home and peace abroad, knew that targeting Byrnes’ home state was a major rallying point for the radical wing of American politics in the post–World War II years. Also, the fact that South Carolina was home to a growing radical movement for human rights helped make it a logical choice for the SNYC’s annual convention.
Bringing both foreign and domestic crises together, finally, was the saga of Isaac Woodard, which galvanized activists and brought global attention to South Carolina. A black World War II veteran blinded by police on February 12, 1946, in Batesburg-Leesville, South Carolina, Woodard’s case became a symbol of the brutal attacks on black veterans and their allies that occurred throughout the South after World War II. A backlash similar to the Red Summer of 1919, the post-1945 political and social environment was incredibly difficult and reactionary, but also presented incredible opportunities to SNYC leaders.
The SNYC needed a place to not only bring together their members but a location where a new, militant human rights movement was evolving on the ground. Columbia became that place, due in large part to the work of Modjeska Simkins in welcoming the organization to her hometown.
The 1946 convention in Columbia, South Carolina owed a great deal to Modjeska Simkins. A human rights activist born and raised in Columbia, Simkins had become, by 1946, one of the leaders of a radical human and civil rights movement in the Palmetto State. She became secretary of the South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP in 1941 after working tirelessly in black communities across the state as director of negro work for the South Carolina Tuberculosis Association, and after playing a pivotal role in the formation of the state conference in 1939.
Many years later, in an oral history interview with Jacquelyn Dowd Hall, Simkins argued that the SNYC represented something unique and powerful in the broader human and civil rights movements of the twentieth century. “The power structure,” Simkins stated, “has always feared the combining of the forces of black and white masses.”
This was what the SNYC represented. On the first insert page of the 1946 conference program, the Southern Youth Legislature, which was the organizing body within the SNYC that spoke for the organization, made their demands clear. “We meet in solemn session,” they began, as “militant, courageous Negro youth of the South. Youth. . . . which must and will be served. Youth. . . . dedicated to the struggle for freedom. Youth determined to achieve that freedom in its lifetime.” For members of the SNYC, the opportunity arose to finally make a serious blow against segregation. Or, as the title of Erik Gellman’s groundbreaking 2012 work on the National Negro Congress goes, a “death blow to Jim Crow.”
Some of the leaders of the 1946 conference, like Modjeska Simkins or Dorothy Burnham, would become better known throughout the twentieth century for their work in various strands of the civil and human rights movements. Others, such as Columbia SNYC leader Harold H. Poole or Benedict College student Ethel Bigby, are not as well known nationally or even regionally. But they all were pivotal leaders in a movement that, in 1946, seemed poised to tackle the crises that Dr Martin Luther King Jr so eloquently described a generation later: militarism, racism, and capitalism.
Alas, the Second Red Scare at home and the Cold War abroad destroyed the SNYC. The organization was constantly harassed by the FBI and local police forces in the South. Ultimately, the organization was also brought down, like others, due to its alliance with the 1948 Progressive Party campaign of Henry Wallace. Eugene “Bull” Connor — better remembered for his vicious treatment of activists in Birmingham in 1963 — created havoc for left-wing activists in Birmingham.
Its 1946 convention remains the high point of the organization’s history, leaving behind a legacy of activism in South Carolina and throughout the nation. Many of the members of the SNYC, or those affiliated with the organization, continued to be involved in activism deep into the twentieth century. For example, several of the founders of the legendary Freedomways magazine, which between 1961 and 1985 served as a key periodical for the black left, were veterans of the SNYC. Editors and writers such as Esther Cooper Jackson, Louis Burnham, and even Du Bois himself all had significant ties with the organization.
In that sense, the SNYC is part of the larger connective tissue of twentieth century radical social movements — and the 1946 convention in South Carolina was its moment of triumph.

https://citylimits.org/tras-una-decada-n.title: Tras una década, Nueva York abrió su lista de espera para licencias de venta ambulante. Esto es lo que debes saber.
https://citylimits.org/tras-una-decada-n.author: Daniel Parra
https://citylimits.org/tras-una-decada-n.text:
Share This Article
La ciudad añadirá 10.500 nuevas licencias de venta ambulante de mercancías el año que viene —que otorgan a los vendedores el derecho a vender legalmente productos, pero no alimentos— tras haber limitado el número a tan solo 853 durante décadas. “Dije: ‘Dios mío, esto está pasando de verdad’”, comentó Calvin Baker, un veterano vendedor ambulante de Harlem que fue uno de los primeros en presentar su solicitud.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 10 de noviembre. Traducido por Daniel Parra. Read the English version here.
Hay oportunidades que solo se presentan una vez cada década.
Para los neoyorquinos que se ganan la vida como vendedores ambulantes —un sector en el que predominan los inmigrantes, entre ellos muchos latinos—, una de ellas es entrar en la lista de espera para conseguir una codiciada licencia municipal.
Por primera vez en una década, la alcaldía abrió la semana pasada su lista de espera para las licencias de venta ambulante de mercancías, que otorgan a los vendedores el derecho a vender legalmente mercancía como joyas, juguetes y ropa, pero no alimentos.
“Dije: ‘Dios mío, esto está pasando de verdad’”, comentó Calvin Baker, un veterano vendedor ambulante de Harlem, describiendo cómo se sintió cuando por fin pudo aplicar la semana pasada.
Por décadas, él y otros vendedores han luchado contra el limitado número de licencias de la ciudad, restringido a 853 licencias desde 1979. Desde entonces, estas licencias para vendedores que no son veteranos solo estaban disponibles cuando un titular de licencia existente renunciaba a una, lo que ha llevado a que miles de personas vendan mercancías en las calles sin licencia, arriesgándose así a costosas multas y posibles cargos criminales.
A principios de este año, el Concejo Municipal anuló el veto del exalcalde Eric Adams y aprobó el proyecto de ley que creaba 10.500 nuevas licencias de venta ambulante, y la semana pasada comenzó a aceptar solicitudes para una nueva lista de espera.
“Fue maravilloso ver a gente que había estado en la primera línea, luchando conmigo en las calles para conseguir estas licencias, sentada allí esperando su turno para rellenar la solicitud”, dijo Baker, de 64 años, quien vende gorros, guantes y otras prendas de vestir. “Fue una bendición para mí, tío. Sentí la paz de Dios. Me sentí satisfecho”.
Anteriormente, cuando quedaba libre una licencia, el Departamento de Protección del Consumidor y del Trabajador de la ciudad de Nueva York (DCWP por sus siglas en inglés) se ponía en contacto con los solicitantes de la lista de espera existente, que se cerró en 2016.
Según la nueva ley, la ciudad agregará 10.500 licencias más —entre ellas, 3.478 licencias generales para toda la ciudad, también denominadas “blancas”, que permiten vender en cualquier lugar de la ciudad, y 7.875 licencias para los condados periféricos, o “verdes”—, que estarán disponibles a principios del próximo año.
“Es muy difícil de predecir, pero es justo decir que estimamos que se presentarán miles de solicitudes”, afirmó Mohamed Attia, director del Street Vendor Project (SVP por sus siglas en inglés), el grupo de defensa que impulsó la ampliación de las licencias.
En agosto, el DCWP comenzó a dar prioridad a los solicitantes que ya figuraban en la lista de espera de 2016 y empezó a ponerse en contacto con ellos, enviándoles cartas en las que se describían los siguientes pasos. Tenían hasta el 29 de octubre para presentar una solicitud de licencia, explicó un portavoz del DCWP.
Después de eso, la nueva lista de espera para 2026 se abrió el 2 de noviembre y se cerrará el 16 de diciembre. Los vendedores deben presentar una solicitud para inscribirse en la lista y, a continuación, esperar a que el DCWP les comunique qué deben hacer a continuación.
Baker fue uno de los primeros solicitantes el pasado lunes.
“Es como correr la Maratón de Nueva York y decir: ‘Dios mío, ¿cómo voy a hacerlo? ¿Podré terminar esta carrera?’. Pero luego te lanzas a ella y la terminas. La satisfacción que sientes al lograrlo. Esa es la satisfacción que sentí al completar la solicitud”, describió Baker.
Un portavoz del DCWP no especificó cuántas personas han presentado su solicitud hasta el momento.
“El DCWP está trabajando intensamente para garantizar que la puesta en marcha de las nuevas licencias generales para vendedores ambulantes se lleve a cabo de forma clara, ordenada y accesible”, afirmó un portavoz. “Sabemos que los vendedores ambulantes son un elemento imprescindible de la comunidad, y nos enorgullece apoyar a estas pequeñas empresas mediante los mejores servicios de concesión de licencias, formación empresarial proactiva y reformas para reducir la burocracia”.
¿Dónde y cómo aplicar?
Si aún no figuras en la lista de espera de 2016, puedes presentar tu solicitud para la nueva lista por Internet o por correo y, en circunstancias muy limitadas, como en casos de “dificultad severa”, en persona.
Los vendedores pueden solicitar una licencia blanca o verde, o ambas, en una sola solicitud.
Si necesitas ayuda con tu solicitud, puedes ponerte en contacto con la Oficina de Servicios a los Vendedores Ambulantes del Departamento de Servicios a la Pequeña Empresa (SBS) llamando al 888-SBS-4NYC (888-727-4692).
También puedes obtener ayuda en persona acudiendo a los Centros de Soluciones Empresariales de Nueva York (NYC Business Solutions Centers) en horario de oficina (de lunes a viernes, de 9 a.m. a 5 p.m ) en las siguientes ubicaciones:
- El Bronx: 400 East Fordham Rd., séptimo piso, Bronx, NY 10458
- Brooklyn: 9 Bond St., quinto piso, Brooklyn, NY 11201
- Bajo Manhattan: 14 Wall St., decimoséptimo piso, Nueva York, NY 10005
- Alto Manhattan: 361 West 125th St., segundo piso, Nueva York, NY 10027
- Washington Heights: 560 West 181st St., segundo piso, Nueva York, NY 10033
- Queens: 90-27 Sutphin Blvd., cuarto piso, Jamaica, NY 11435
- Staten Island: 120 Stuyvesant Pl., tercer piso, Staten Island, NY 10301
Los solicitantes también pueden concertar una cita con el Street Vendor Project por correo electrónico o por teléfono (646-602-5679).
“Hay mucha desinformación y mucha confusión sobre qué es esta licencia”, explicó Attia.
“Esta licencia permite a las personas vender productos en la calle, en las aceras públicas, sobre una mesa, y hay muchas normas que la regulan”, añadió. “Por lo tanto, si eres vendedor de comida, esta licencia no es para ti. Si tienes un negocio minorista y quieres ampliar tu actividad a algunos eventos privados o a mercados temporales, esta licencia tampoco es para ti”.
¿Cuáles son los requisitos para aplicar?
La información que se solicita a los solicitantes es información personal básica, como nombre, dirección, número de teléfono y correo electrónico. Además, se pregunta si la persona ha estado vendiendo mercancías generales desde enero de 2025 hasta el 2 de noviembre de 2026.
Aunque la mayoría de los vendedores ambulantes de la ciudad son inmigrantes procedentes de diferentes partes del mundo, la solicitud sólo está disponible en inglés. El SVP ha indicado que está prestando asistencia a los solicitantes en siete idiomas.
El formulario también exige la presentación de un documento de identidad con fotografía, que puede ser un carné de conducir, un permiso expedido por un organismo público, un pasaporte o un documento de identidad municipal, entre otros.
Un aspecto irónico del proceso: las multas civiles o criminales anteriores emitidas contra el vendedor pueden servir como prueba de su experiencia en la venta ambulante (además de fotografías en las que se vea a la persona vendiendo, recibos de compra de mercancía o una carta de un político electo, un líder comunitario o una organización sin ánimo de lucro en la que se acredite su actividad anterior como vendedor ambulante).
Los defensores de SVP ven esto como un reconocimiento de que el sistema anterior dejaba a muchas personas sin una forma de vender legalmente, y como un recordatorio de lo difícil que era obtener una licencia bajo el antiguo límite máximo.
“La solicitud fue muy fácil”, dijo Baker. “Tardé 10 minutos”.
¿Y luego qué?
La solicitud para la lista de espera es independiente de la solicitud de licencia, por lo que inscribirse en la lista de espera no garantiza automáticamente la obtención de una licencia.
El DCWP revisará las solicitudes, asignará un número a cada una de ellas y se pondrá en contacto con los solicitantes para informarles sobre los siguientes pasos a partir de febrero de 2027.
“Quiero llegar a lo más alto. Quiero mi licencia”, dijo Baker. “Me sentiré mucho mejor. No tendré que estar siempre mirando a mi alrededor y preocupándome de que la policía de Nueva York venga a por mí y tire mis cosas como les dé la gana, sin siquiera respetar lo que es mío”.
Para ponerse en contacto con el reportero de esta noticia, escriba a [email protected]. Para contactar a la editora, escriba a [email protected].

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Staff petition against major restructuring plans at Sydney's Chau Chak Wing Museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Elizabeth Fortescue
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A Sydney University proposal to restructure its prestigious Chau Chak Wing Museum has shocked and angered the museum’s curators, who fear the world-class collections in their custody will be put at risk. A petition circulating in the Australian cultural sector decries the planned cuts to eight positions across curatorial, collections and public engagement teams.
”The loss of these roles, and changes to organisational structure, risks diminishing the museum’s capacity to care for and develop its collections, deliver educational experiences, support academic research and maintain its standing as a leading university museum,” the petition says.
According to the petition, the proposed new management structure is “top-heavy”, with three executive-level salaried directors in an organisation with only about 30 staff. The key position of head of collections would also be removed.
The Art Newspaper understands morale at the Chau Chak Wing Museum has plummeted. But John Buchanan, the branch president of the National Tertiary Education Union at the University of Sydney, says the museum’s staff members were strongly unionised and would fight the changes.
“They’ve got deep expertise, and they’ve basically been told: ‘there’s going to be a spill-and-fill change process and get in line to apply for your job again’,” Buchanan tells The Art Newspaper. ”This is an unhelpful way of dealing with a complex problem in the creative workforce, and [the staff] are showing their creativity by being so effective in organising.”
According to a university statement in response to the petition, the proposed changes aim to strengthen the museum’s educational and exhibition programme. “They include realigning positions in education and public programs and curatorial work, while creating a more sustainable staffing structure to meet growing demand,” the statement says. It adds that the proposed overall number of full-time equivalent roles would remain unchanged.
Craig Barker, an archaeologist and the head of public engagement at the Chau Chak Wing Museum, believes that the proposal would refocus staff attention towards education and engagement. While he was generally in favour of that idea, Barker tells The Art Newspaper that this will swing staff attention away from curatorial and collection management. Academic research and international expert connections would suffer, Barker adds.
Barker says his role’s title would become “deputy director of business, education and experience”, and that he believes the focus would be on business. ”Our big frustrations are not that there’s a refocus towards public engagement. It’s something that we want, but it’s at the cost of what we have done so well and where we’ve built our reputation, which is in highest-quality curatorial research,” Barker says. “The fundamental question is: does the University of Sydney want an internationally recognised, world-class research and object-based teaching facility? Or do we just want a nice shiny building with pictures hanging on the wall?”
Ann Stephen, a senior art curator of the university art collection at the Chau Chak Wing Museum, says her job is under threat. She adds that curatorial knowledge is vital for collection care, research, publications and advising on acquisition and deaccession of works. ”Without recourse to such knowledge, artworks can be misattributed, over or undervalued, or simply not understood in terms of any wider context,” Stephen says. ”Exhibition programmes not informed by curatorial knowledge can become merely dumbed-down spectacles lacking historical research or insights.”
According to the University of Sydney's statement, formal consultation began in July and “feedback and proposed alternatives” are welcomed.
The modernist Chau Chak Wing Museum opened to the public on the university’s main campus in 2020 and is free to enter. The museum amalgamated the university’s three main collections: antiquities, natural history and art. The director of the Chau Chak Wing Museum is Michael Dagostino, who was chosen as the curator for the Australian pavilion at the 2026 Venice Biennale. The Chau Chak Wing Museum was also a venue of the 2026 Sydney Biennale.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Could Firenze Lai’s first UK solo show signal a shift in global market recognition for Hong Kong artists?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Vivienne Chow
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
In mid-October, coinciding with Frieze London and nearly four years after she relocated from her native Hong Kong to London, the artist Firenze Lai opened her first UK solo exhibition at White Cube Mason’s Yard. Featuring new works created in her adopted home, North and True North (until 14 November) is not just a milestone for her career, it also signals a potential shift in major galleries’ approach to Asia.
Lai is among a handful of Hong Kong artists represented by major Western blue-chip galleries today. Born in 1984 and educated in Hong Kong, the artist has exhibited internationally, including in the main exhibition of the 57th Venice Biennale in 2017. Her current show marks the first solo exhibition White Cube has staged by an artist originating from Hong Kong since it opened its outpost in the city in 2012.
The shift suggests the maturity of this generation of mid-career artists from Hong Kong, several of whom have relocated abroad fairly recently. It also raises hopes that Western blue-chip galleries are finally adopting a less siloed approach to Asia, in which global art markets were approached from a simplistic geographical perspective. This mindset of “keeping Asians in Asia” kept transnational relationships rare, the cultural strategist Adeline Ooi notes, but this is starting to change.
“People are much more cosmopolitan and international today. They are not just rooted within their region and bounded by their geographies,” says Ooi, the former director for Asia at Art Basel.
Taking a wider view
Major international galleries are taking a more sophisticated approach, rather than simply placing Asian artists in front of Asian collectors, says the Taipei- and New York-based art adviser Gladys Lin. “It’s about integrating that artist into the wider language of the gallery programme, so that collectors from different backgrounds can understand the work in relation to other artists, histories and conversations.”
Hong Kong has long been Asia’s biggest art market hub, with headline-grabbing auction sales for over half a century joined, since the 2000s, by a lively landscape of galleries and fairs catering to local collectors, and those from mainland China and the wider region. The city has hosted Art Basel Hong Kong since 2013, and Asian outposts of blue-chip galleries proliferated after the launch of the ArtHK fair in 2008. Artists from the city, however, have struggled to receive much attention in the global market, or even at home.
Leading multinational Western blue-chip galleries such as White Cube, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Gagosian and Pace have shown Asian artists internationally, but they tend to concentrate on bolstering their rosters with established names from Asian cultural powerhouses like mainland China, South Korea and Japan.
Hongkonger artists are increasingly exhibiting abroad, but primarily with smaller galleries. The Taipei-based artist Lee Kit works with galleries including Massimo de Carlo in London and ShugoArts in Tokyo. The UK-based Chris Huen Sin-kan showed with the now-defunct Simon Lee in New York and London, and more recently with Matt Carey-Williams.
While diaspora and émigré Hongkongers have more opportunities to cultivate overseas networks, artists based in the city are also widening their reach. Chang Ya Chin held her first solo show with Perrotin in New York in 2025, while Stephen Wong Chun-hei exhibited with Unit London in 2022 and Mother’s Tankstation in 2025, which also represents Lee Kit. The sound artist Samson Young performed his work Canon at Art Basel Unlimited in 2016, presented by Cologne’s Galerie Gisela Capitain and the now-closed Team Gallery. Wong Ping held a solo show at Tanya Bonakdar Gallery in New York in 2021, while Mak2 had her European gallery solo debut in 2023 with the now-defunct Peres Projects in Berlin.
However, representation by one of the global “big five” galleries remains rare for Hong Kong artists. White Cube began working with Lai in July 2025. “Her paintings have a singularity that speaks to the human condition, a universal theme that audiences everywhere can appreciate,” a spokesperson for the gallery says.
Lai was born and raised in Hong Kong, and has lived in London since 2022. Her visual language nonetheless remains rooted in her lived experience of her densely populated hometown. “We are not 100% Chinese, nor are we 100% British,” Lai says.
Moving to London changed how she approaches the canvas. The painter recalls that during her time in Hong Kong—where she built a solid career and a following for her dreamlike figurative paintings through a long-term and continuing collaboration with Guangzhou gallery Vitamin Creative Space—she tended to work on smaller canvases.
‘I needed a bigger canvas’
“After moving to London, I felt that I needed a bigger canvas. I have a lot more to say,” Lai says. Much of her poignant new work draws from deep emotional responses to her changing environment before and after relocating.
Lai says the current timing for global market recognition for Hong Kong artists makes sense. Those of her generation, born between the late 1970s and 90s, needed time to establish themselves and explore which galleries would be a good fit for their career. “I am proud of the fact that Hong Kong has produced a generation of artists who can have solo shows in London,” she says. “I’ve been told to give up many times. But I can now tell a 15-year-old [aspiring artist] that this is possible.”
It remains unclear how much long-term benefit a solo exhibition at a global gallery can bring to an artist’s career. “Who are the people paying attention to Firenze right now? If they are private collectors, who are they and what are their demographics? If it’s an institution, who are they?” Ooi asks. Expanding the following for her work will take time as much as exposure.
Lin says Lai’s move to London put her into a different art world, where she offers galleries a “compelling combination”. “She already comes with a collector base in Asia, an institutional history and more than a decade of critical exposure,” Lin says. “It’s not simply about bringing in Asian collectors, but about adding an artist who connects different collectors, institutional and geographical systems. For a global gallery today, geography can still be a useful entry point, but it cannot be the final framework.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/13/c.title: Council Speaker Slams Amazon For Delivery Worker Layoffs
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/13/c.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/13/c.text:
An e-quad bike worker grabs a package to deliver in SoHo. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
City Council Speaker Julie Menin slammed Amazon for terminating a contract with one of its Delivery Service Partners, effectively firing around 200 workers, and vowed to pass first-in-the-nation regulations against the delivery giant whose business practices have come increasingly under fire.
“I think it’s terrible,” Menin (D-Upper East Side) told Streetsblog at a press conference on Thursday. “To be clear, we are going to be regulating Amazon, we will be the first city in the country to regulate Amazon in a very significant way.”
Menin’s strong words came hours after 200 employees of Kaizen Management Solutions, a company contracted by Amazon to fulfill same-day deliveries, were unceremoniously fired, effective on Nov. 18.
The fired workers — who deliver Amazon-branded packages on Amazon-branded bikes and fans — are not actually employed by Amazon. Instead, the e-commerce giant relies on a network of Delivery Service Partners, small independent companies, to hire workers and make the deliveries. For most such DSPs, Amazon is the only client. When Amazon drops a contract, the DSP goes belly up.
And it’s a pattern. Since 2018, Amazon has terminated 35 DSP contracts in New York, resulting in the loss of over 3,500 jobs, a report from the Teamsters Union found.
A Council bill sponsored by Tiffany Cabán (D-Astoria) would force Amazon to directly employ its delivery drivers. The bill, known as the Delivery Protection Act, has a majority of Council support, but remains on Speaker Menin’s desk as she negotiates what she calls “legal issues” to get it over the finish line. (A spokesperson for Menin reiterated that the Speaker is committed to passing the bill.)
One of the laid-off workers said the Delivery Protection Act gets to the heart of the problem with Amazon: the company is not a vaunted job-creator.
“This DSP model is about Amazon’s bottom line,” said the worker, who requested anonymity because he needs to find another job. “The model that allegedly creates jobs just laid off 200 people right before the holidays. … I wish I could tell you I have another thing lined up but I don’t. They didn’t even give me a month to figure it out.”
The Kaizen employee has worked at various DSPs over the past two years. He said he started the job because he needed to find work fast after graduating college without a safety net.
“They say you don’t choose Amazon, Amazon chooses you,” he said, adding that the job market is “atrocious.”
Amazon told Streetsblog it terminated after an investigation found that Kaizen “put several e-cargo bikes back on the road before necessary repairs were done,” and that there were “multiple breaches of contract involving fraud, including failure to accurately record drivers’ hours worked.”
The laid-off employee called this a “crock of shit.”
“If that’s truly the case, then every single DSP needs to be shut down, and that’s not happening,” he said.
Workers have been sounding the alarm for years about the conditions of Amazon’s vans and electric cargo quad bikes, which are often leased by Amazon directly to the Delivery Service Partners.
Amazon’s vehicles are notorious for double parking, blocking bike lanes, and setting up make-shift loading zones. Supporters of the bill say forcing Amazon to directly hire its delivery drivers would make the company more accountable for their conduct, and financially accountable for tickets.
The Alliance for a Greater New York, which supports the bill, created an interactive tool that shows that Amazon-associated delivery vans drew 14,290 tickets from cameras and traffic enforcement agents between July 2021 and June 2025.
“You want to park anywhere you can fit so that you can hop out and deliver this package, but it comes at a price. Sometimes it’s a hydrant. … Sometimes you’ll just have to simply double park,” said LeAnn Rivera, an Amazon van driver for a DSP in Queens. “It’s unfair because the only reason I’m even doing things like this is because I have pressure to move faster.”
Rivera said job security is her “main reason” for advocating for the passage of the Delivery Protection Act.
“When it comes to people who aren’t for it, their main worry is the small business people [DSP owners] losing their business,” she said. “But you’re not safe as an owner because anything, literally anything, can happen.”
Just as the City Council debates reining in Amazon's business practices, the delivery giant threw workers of the job after canceling its contract with a Manhattan subcontractor.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gude-debs-bi.title: Eugene Debs’s Life Speaks to Today’s Socialist Movement
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gude-debs-bi.author: Nelson Lichtenstein
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gude-debs-bi.text:
Eugene Debs’s Life Speaks to Today’s Socialist Movement
Eugene Debs’s greatest achievement was not any particular vote tally. It was his making socialist partisans understand that the socialist movement arose out of the American political tradition’s most democratic currents.
Shawn Gude’s splendid new biography of Gilded Age Socialist Eugene V. Debs could hardly have arrived at a more propitious moment. Perhaps as many as half of all young people tell pollsters they prefer socialism to capitalism. Gude, a member of the 130,000-strong Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), calls that organization, whose activism and endorsements have put eight self-professed socialists in the new Congress, the “institutional descendant” of Debs’s Socialist Party of America. In his victory speech right after winning the New York city mayoral election in 2025, Zohran Mamdani, an unapologetic DSAer, quoted Debs: “I can see the dawn of a better day for humanity.” And when Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour in the months after Donald Trump’s 2026 election, their critique of the billionaire class echoed Debs’s blistering denunciations of Gilded Age wealth when the barnstorming five-time presidential candidate denounced the Rockefellers, Morgans, and Carnegies of his day.
Gude has written a Debs biography for our time. He emphasizes the rootedness of the Indiana railroad fireman in middle-American culture and Christianity, downplays more than other historians the ideological divisions endemic to the early twentieth century Socialist Party, and emphasizes the degree to which Debs, like Bernie Sanders and some of his contemporary comrades, could appeal to such a remarkably wide variety of constituencies. Gude’s biography also offers a full-bodied sense of Debs as a fragile and contradictory personality in which his constant travel, the crowd’s applause, and the opportunities thereby created for liaisons with the opposite sex, may well have compensated for a childless and increasingly distant marriage, as well as a distaste for the conflicts, political and personal, attendant upon leadership in any mass organization.
An American Democratic Socialist
The story of Eugene V. Debs’s life,” writes Gude, “is the story of one man’s radicalization — and of the country he helped radicalize in turn.” During the first decade of his working life, Debs was a conventional railroad unionist often hostile to strikes and largely uninterested or ignorant of the radical currents, social and ideological, that were on the rise in Gilded Age America. He disdained not only the violence of the 1877 rail strike but also the rise of the Knights of Labor, a more inclusive union formation. Debs happily endorsed the “Benevolence, Sobriety, and Industry” that were the watchwords of his Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen.
But soon enough he was mugged by capitalist reality, most dramatically in the depression of the early 1890s that sparked the great Pullman boycott and nationwide rail strike Debs led in 1894. Jailed by the federal government for defying a union-busting injunction, Debs, like so many other imprisoned radicals in Russia, Prussia, and far-flung colonies, now had the time and incentive to read his Karl Marx. After six months in a Woodstock, Illinois, jail, he emerged a socialist.
By the start of the new century, when Debs stood proudly as the nation’s most forceful and popular anti-capitalist tribune, the Socialist Party seemed as American as the corn its members grew in Oklahoma, the copper mined by its Montana adherents, the cars built by Flint autoworkers, the apparel sewn by Lower East Side immigrants, or the sermons and editorials offered by advocates of the Social Gospel. With more than a hundred thousand members, some 1,200 socialists held elected office, including eighty mayors in thirty-six states.
And as Gude rightly asserts, Debs’s great achievement arose not out of any particular vote tally — he would win almost a million votes when he ran for president in 1912 and 1920 — but by making socialist partisans, as well as many of their opponents, believe that the movement he championed arose out of the American political tradition’s most democratic currents, from the revolutionary struggle against the British monarchy to the abolitionist fight against slavery. He was one of America’s great critics of the plutocracy, but more Christian agitator than political tactician. When, in early 1919, Debs was imprisoned for his opposition to World War I, his moral stature was crowned with martyrdom.
As if to even more firmly link his life and fate with that of our own time, Gude references Debs as a “democratic socialist.” That is an anachronistic phrase when applied to the early-twentieth-century movement led by men and women of a Debsian persuasion. In the years before the rise of Stalinism, not to mention German “national socialism,” almost all socialists described themselves as just socialists, or perhaps social democrats, because inherent in the idea of socialism was the democratic control of both economy and polity. (Before 1917, the Bolsheviks were a faction within the “Russian Social Democratic Labour Party.”) Neither Debs nor many of his contemporaries spent much energy thinking about precisely how a nationalized railroad or steel mill would be governed, an issue that bedeviled radicals of a later generation.
It was Michael Harrington who popularized the phrase “democratic socialism” when, in the early 1970s, he proved instrumental in the formation of the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee, forerunner of today’s DSA. So while semantically inaccurate, Gude’s deployment of the phrase “democratic socialism” to the movement led by Debs serves to make abundantly clear the tutorial purpose of this biography.
Debs the Tribune
Debs was a socialist tribune, a clever and powerful wordsmith whose rhetoric combined outrage and moralism, denunciation and inspiration. He was not an original thinker, avers Gude, but that hardly prevented thousands from coming to hear him orate.
More than any other socialist of his time, writes Gude, Debs had a “seemingly intuitive sense of how to connect with the US working class in all its heterogeneity.” He was an abolitionist opposed to the Old World tyranny of aristocrats and kings.
“Workers weren’t just poor, they were serfs,” summarizes Gude in explaining the Debs appeal. “Capitalism didn’t just impoverish, it enslaved. . . . And through solidarity would come freedom.“
However, when it came to actually running the Socialist Party and participating in its internal debates, Debs was almost always absent, out campaigning or ill at home, even as his own sentiments and inclinations usually tilted left. Debs was a founder of the Industrial Workers of the World, which he projected as a far more encompassing and radical labor formation than the increasingly stolid American Federation of Labor. And Debs was ambiguous when it came to socialist party advocacy of those reforms that might serve the immediate interests of the working class.
Debs did not directly polemicize against the “sewer socialists,” notably those holding municipal office in Milwaukee, Butte, Reading, and other cities, where their innovative public health regimes proved enormously beneficial to thousands of residents. But he was not interested in forging the alliances and legislation that would advance such reforms as an integral component of socialism’s electoral appeal: “What we want is not to reform the capitalist system. We want to get rid of it.”
Here’s an instance where Debs hardly offers contemporary socialists much inspiration. Both Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani would fit easily on the Socialist Party’s right wing, not far from Milwaukee’s Victor Berger or New York’s Morris Hillquit, both of whom often bested Debs when it came to internal party debate. Mamdani boasts of filling thousands of New York City potholes and opening a set of city-owned grocery stores, and he seems to have forged a working relationship with a New York governor several steps to his right. Meanwhile, Sanders links a forthright denunciation of American capitalism with a set of concrete reforms whose realization requires a very messy set of alliances and incremental steps forward that Debs would assuredly find utterly distasteful. And of course, much of this twenty-first century politicking will take place within, rather than in opposition to, the Democratic Party.
Debs Portraits Past and Present
Gude did not exactly rediscover Eugene V. Debs, because his life and times have long attracted the attention of latter-day radicals, especially during those eras when the Left has been on the rise. It’s instructive therefore to compare the Gude biography with two other narratives that saw publication in years past when other varieties of American radicalism seemed to have much ideological and social wind at their back.
Ray Ginger published the first comprehensive biography in 1949, The Bending Cross: A Biography of Eugene Victor Debs. Ginger was just twenty-five and still in grad school on the GI Bill. It’s hard to know how he found time to write the book. At the University of Michigan, the army put him in all-day classes learning Japanese, and for a time after the war he worked in a Detroit auto factory. Meanwhile, Ginger had joined the Communist Party in 1944 or 1945, when both the party and the industrial union movement it championed were at their apogee.
Ginger’s biography is not a party-line publication, and there is some indication that he clashed with Communist officials when they read the nearly completed publication. Still, its structure and argument reflects a species of 1930s and ’40s Popular Front Marxism. The table of contents constructs a teleological scaffolding that moves ever upward in both consciousness and organization, from “The Railroad Brotherhoods,” (mere trade union consciousness) to “The American Railway Union,” (Congress of Industrial Orgnaizations–style industrial unionism), and on to “American Socialism” and then “World Socialism,” the longest chapter in a book written during a half-decade when fascism was vanquished and the Cold War began.
Ginger’s career was a tragic one. Harvard fired him in 1954 when his Communist ties became known, after which he took jobs in New York advertising and publishing, all the while writing book after well-received book, most on Gilded Age America. He taught at Brandeis in the 1960s, but lost his post there after an affair with an undergraduate. An alcoholic, he continued to teach and write at various universities until cirrhosis of the liver took his life in 1975 when he was but fifty years old.
While Ginger is as appreciative of the humanity and transcendence of the Debsian revolutionary visions as is Gude, he takes aim at the socialist tribune’s failure to combine his popular appeal with a necessary engagement with the Socialist Party’s complex and contentious inner life. Gude gives Debs something of a pass on this score, perhaps reflecting the high-profile role now being played by Bernie Sanders, who is not even a member of DSA, or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whose DSA linkages are complex and somewhat attenuated.
But when Ginger was writing his biography, you did not have to be a Leninist to understand the importance of forceful leadership. The progressive trade unions and the various left-wing parties of that day considered it vital to put forth public spokesmen and women fully engaged in shaping the program and politics of the institution over which they presided. Consider Dorothy Healey’s unorthodox leadership of the California Communist Party or Walter Reuther’s skillful rise to power in the United Auto Workers. Both were exciting speakers but also deeply enmeshed in organizational politics. Debs did none of that.
Although he was by far the most popular figure in the Socialist Party, after 1904, Debs refused to attend party conventions or serve on leadership committees. His absenteeism created a vacuum filled by Berger, Hillquit, and others to his right. “Comrade Debs is no doubt a great orator and a fiery revolutionist,” wrote one socialist “rightwinger” quoted by Ginger, “but he is also one of the poorest generals and tacticians that our movement has.. . . . He has shown himself utterly unreliable in the meeting of the practical problems of the day and the selection of his advisors.”
Ginger’s admiration for Debs was therefore mixed with a certain condescension. He called him “more Midwestern than a worn and rotting plow-handle buried deep in the soil of a Kansas farm.” It is not that Ginger wanted a Vladimir Lenin or a Leon Trotsky, but when the author asserted in the last sentences of his book that Debs’s “finite self seemed to merge with the agonized wanderings of the nameless multitude,” the assessment was not entirely complimentary.
Nick Salvatore’s 1982 study, Eugene V. Debs: Citizen and Socialist, turned much of Ginger’s critique on its head. Debs was indeed as American as that rotting Kansas plow-handle, and that’s the whole point. Salvatore’s perspective, largely echoed by Gude, had a twofold origin. As a militant unionist and civil rights activist, Salvatore, who died in 2025 after a distinguished career as a Cornell historian, was in the 1960s and ’70s looking for a way that could enable the New Left to speak American, to evoke a new radicalism out of native values and context. One could find that impulse in the 1962 Port Huron Statement and the Free Speech Movement at the University of California, Berkeley, where Salvatore a few years later wrote a dissertation that became his prize-winning Debs biography.
The rediscovery, by an older generation of historians, of an eighteenth to nineteenth century “republican” tradition gave Salvatore the tools to understand Debsian radicalism as contiguous with many of the main cultural and social currents emblematic of the Protestant small-town America that an earlier cohort of radicals — think H. L. Mencken and Sinclair Lewis — had once disdained.
Salvatore wrote a “social biography” steeped in the “new labor history.” He postulated that Debs’s radicalism arose out of the culture found in Terre Haute, his preindustrial hometown, wherein a “manly” independence, evangelical Protestantism, and a republican understanding of the responsibilities and privileges of a virtuous citizenship engendered a democratic America. Like E. P. Thompson and Herbert Gutman, pioneering historians of working-class formation, Salvatore found nineteenth century radicalism, socialist or otherwise, emerging out of the clash between those republican virtues and the oppressive structures engendered by Gilded Age industrial capitalism.
Encapsulating all this, Gude writes of Debs, “His genius was assembling a mix of ideological ingredients familiar in working-class circles — Christianity and labor republicanism, Marxism and the American revolutionary tradition — and alchemizing them” into an all-American vernacular. “I like the Fourth of July,” Debs told a crowd on his first run for president in 1900, “It breathes a spirit of revolution.”
Debs and the Race Question
There was however, one aspect of the Debs praxis that Gude shows to be very much at odds with the dominant culture and the sentiments held by many of his erstwhile comrades. Debs did once assert, “We have nothing special to offer the Negro, and we cannot make separate appeals to all the races.” Abolishing capitalism was the solution to the Negro problem, the woman question, and the persistence of antisemitism. Until then, it was fruitless to seek any sort of particular amelioration, because the ruling class itself fostered and advanced such discriminations and oppressions. “The Negro is not one whit worse off than thousands of white slaves who throng the same labor market to sell their labor-power to the same industrial masters.”
And not only that: thousands of dedicated socialists were also dedicated racists who saw poorly paid Asian immigrants and African American strikebreakers as debased elements of the working population not all that different from what Marx identified as the lumpenproletariat. This was an era when manliness and whiteness were seemingly intertwined.
But Debs would grow in moral and social intelligence when it came to the causes and remedies of American racism.
On speaking tours of the South he was appalled at the brutal racism and Jim Crow practices he observed. He probably read W. E. B. DuBois’s new book, The Souls of Black Folk, afterward asserting that “The whole world is under obligation to the negro and that the white heel is still upon the black neck is simply proof that the world is not yet civilized.” When the film Birth of a Nation was shown in Terre Haute, Debs was aghast at this cinematic celebration of the Ku Klux Klan.
He applauded the anti-racist agitation of the young black socialists A. Philip Randolph and Chandler Owen, and by the time of the bloody race riots of the World War I era, he saw that the battle against racial oppression did require something “special” on the part of socialists and other progressives. As early as the 1912 election, W. E. B. DuBois judged Debs the only candidate, who “by word and deed, stands squarely on a platform of human rights regardless of race or class.”
Debs’s salutary evolution on this issue put him far to the left of most socialists and trade unionists of his time. And that was just the problem, because Debs rarely sought to leverage his popularity to make his party adopt a truly progressive posture on an issue of such vital import to the twentieth-century American left. Thus, in the 1930s and ’40s, it would be the Communists and not the Socialists who would stand out as civil rights pioneers.
What American Socialists Can Accomplish
Despite the Debsian appeal of a century and more ago, as well as the contemporary enthusiasm engendered by its twenty-first century revival, American socialism was and is a minority current in both politics and culture. The obstacles to its success are legion: sectarian infighting of the sort that helped destroy Debs’s party right after the Bolshevik Revolution; the long-standing religious, racial, and occupational divisions within the working class; and of course the enormous power of capital and its many ideological and political handmaidens.
But I don’t think a socialist movement has to achieve majoritarian hegemony to make an impression on the polity. Conservative denunciations of “creeping socialism” have not been entirely unfounded, either in 1930s or today.
When Norman Thomas, who succeeded Eugene Debs as the Socialist Party’s Great Depression–era leader, complained that “[Franklin Delano] Roosevelt stole our program,” he was also boasting of how a few thousand organized activists can make their presence felt when circumstances combine to offer them historical influence and leverage. The same may be true today.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/uk-labour-is.title: Andy Burnham’s Criticism of Israel Is All Bark and No Bite
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/uk-labour-is.author: Jamie Maxwell
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/uk-labour-is.text:
Andy Burnham’s Criticism of Israel Is All Bark and No Bite
Andy Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, have adopted a more critical tone toward Israel in a bid to win back progressive voters to the Labour Party. But the fundamentals of Britain’s close alliance with Israel remain largely unchanged.
In September, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that his government was going to impose sanctions on British trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Miliband also referred to “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.”
The Israeli authorities responded by downgrading the 180-year old British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem — it is now merely a “mission” — and expelling twenty British diplomats, including the consul general.
Miliband’s announcement came two months after Andy Burnham replaced Keir Starmer as Labour Party leader and prime minister. He billed it as part of a “comprehensive reset” of Britain’s approach toward Israel: Britain would no longer “acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution,” Miliband pledged.
In reality, there has been no such reset: the fundamentals of Britain’s relationship with Israel remain largely unchanged.
Extraordinary Lengths
Naturally, Miliband’s move provoked a roar of condemnation from Israeli political elites. Israel’s president Isaac Herzog, who has been credibly accused by multiple organizations of aiding and abetting war crimes in the Gaza Strip, said that he was “disturbed” by the new sanctions. The Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar accused Miliband of “outrageous lies.”
Israel’s British supporters were also indignant. Britain’s Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis denounced Miliband’s program, claiming that it was “a dark day for Britain’s Jews,” and that Miliband was seeking to appease “those who harbour a dangerous obsession with the Jewish state.”
This is not the first time Mirvis, an indefatigable defender of Israel, has attacked the Labour government. In September 2024, he denounced a move by Miliband’s predecessor as foreign secretary, David Lammy, to limit the supply of British arms for the Israeli military: “This announcement feeds the falsehood that Israel is in breach of International Humanitarian Law, when in fact it is going to extraordinary lengths to uphold it.”
On that occasion, events proved that Mirvis had little reason to be concerned. The following year, British arms sales to Israel soared to reach the highest level on record. If we look more closely at the details of Miliband’s announcement, a similar picture of tough talk combined with very limited actions reveals itself.
Red Line, Green Line
The sanctions focus on the banning of imports into the UK of goods produced in “illegal” Israeli settlements, an expansion of UK licensing refusals for arms exports to Israel, and the nonspecified “strengthening” of penalties against settlers who “support or incite acts of violence against Palestinian communities.”
If we assume that all of these sanctions are actually implemented — Miliband opted for a grace period of up to nine months before the changes take effect — their impact on Israel’s economy would still be very limited. An Al Jazeera investigation found that, since Miliband’s announcement, his government has awarded more than $14 million in public sector contracts to firms that profit from West Bank settlements.
Miliband coordinated his sanctions package with eleven other Western countries, including Canada, Ireland, France, and Denmark, ten of which have recognized a Palestinian state. In theory, if those countries applied the sanctions in a maximal way, they could hit the sprawling and internationally connected network of Israeli finance, fin tech, and construction firms that facilitate the spread of Jewish settlements in the West Bank.
But that seems unlikely. In his Commons statement, Miliband made clear that his quarrel was with the settler movement and its sponsors in Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, not with Israel itself. “We will continue to support valued trade with green line Israel precisely because we support the two state solution,” he said. “For this reason, I wholeheartedly oppose the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions campaign.”
This argument draws a convenient distinction between “illegal” Israeli settlements outside the 1967 borders and Israel proper. (In fact, in line with Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention, which prohibits the transfer of civilian populations into occupied territories, all Israeli settlements are illegal under international law). By doing so, Miliband has carefully shielded the infrastructure of British support for Israel from the damage that a broader and more robust UK economic boycott could inflict.
A Lucrative Relationship
That infrastructure is substantial, because the UK is Israel’s largest European trading partner. Israeli companies supply billions of pounds worth of medicines to the National Health Service every year. Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest defense electronics manufacturer, operates multiple factories throughout the UK, while its subsidiaries export engine components to the Israel Defense Forces.
Israel’s state-owned defense giant, Rafael, owns and operates factories in Newcastle and Hampshire. Through Lockheed Martin and BAE Systems, the UK defense sector manufactures approximately 15 percent of the machinery present in every operational F-35 fighter jet, the aircraft of choice for the Israeli military as it has laid waste to Gaza. None of these economic linkages will be negatively impacted by the sanctions.
Israel even maintains investments in the North Sea through Ithaca Energy, which is owned by the Delek Group, a multibillion-dollar Israeli energy conglomerate. Ironically, it may benefit from those investments in the future if the Burnham administration gives the go-ahead for exploitation in the Rosebank oil field, a highly controversial, potentially climate-wrecking development west of Shetland. Ithaca owns a 20 percent stake in Rosebank; a decision on the field’s future is due imminently.
There is also a strong case that the UK has colluded directly on an institutional level in Israel’s campaign of slaughter in the Gaza Strip. As the investigative journalism organization Declassified has exhaustively archived, between December 2023 and March 2025, the Royal Air Force flew a minimum of 518 intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance flights over the Palestinian Occupied Territories, including Gaza.
Successive UK governments have insisted that these flights were part of a broader effort at “hostage location.” However, given Britain’s long history of intelligence cooperation with Israel, there is good reason to suspect that the Israeli military could also have used the information gathered during these sorties for other purposes. Miliband has made clear that British-Israeli intelligence sharing will go on despite the sanctions. “I’m confident that our security co-operation with Israel will continue,” he told the BBC in September. “We have important intelligence and security relationships with Israel.”
Burnham’s Pivot
Miliband’s discretely designed sanctions system performs a domestic political function as well as an external strategic one. By publicly picking a fight with Netanyahu ahead of the Israeli elections, and by criticizing his annexationist policies, Labour sent a signal to left-wing voters who had turned away from the party during the Starmer period, when UK criticism of Israel was, to say the least, less forthcoming.
Starmer was a latecomer to Westminster life who appeared to be largely devoid of the ruthless intelligence needed to succeed in the Westminster snake pit. He thought he could build a lasting coalition in the crumbling center ground of British politics. When it became clear that he couldn’t, Burnham stepped in with a plan to reinvigorate Labour by convening a progressive bloc of voters in opposition to the reactionary one rapidly coalescing around Nigel Farage and Reform UK.
In order to do this, Burnham needed to win over the young, left-wing, and vigorously pro-Palestinian parts of the UK electorate that had peeled off in recent years toward Zack Polanski’s “ecopopulist” Green Party. Hence the Labour government’s new and heightened anti-settler rhetoric and its willingness to characterize Israel’s actions against the Palestinians as “war crimes.”
Yet the superficiality of the rhetoric grates against the reality of Labour’s inertia in other areas. In 2025, Starmer’s government imposed a draconian ban on Palestine Action, a campaign group that targeted Israeli defense firms on British soil with acts of civil disobedience and vandalism. It is now legally defined as a terrorist organization, on a par with al-Qaeda and the Irish Republican Army. Since then, the British authorities have arrested more than 3,500 people and formally charged more than 2,250 for peacefully protesting against the ban.
Burnham has not committed to repealing the ban, which the UN Human Rights Commissioner Volker Türk has described as a “disturbing misuse of counter-terrorism legislation.” Last month, his Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood strongly defended the arrest of Palestine Action supporters, comparing them to “a group of skinheads standing outside a mosque.”
“Systematic Duplicity”
In fact, there are growing signs that Burnham may extend authoritarian restrictions on the expression of support for Palestine in British public life. This would include a prohibition on the display of pro-Palestinian symbols by teachers in schools. His government is also urging schools and colleges to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which conflates criticism of Israel with antipathy toward Jewish people.
In contrast to Miliband, who is Jewish and thought to be genuinely sympathetic to the Palestinian cause, Burnham is by instinct a classic Labour Atlanticist who views Britain’s relationship with Israel as a core component of the UK’s strategic loyalty to the United States.
As a junior minister in the Tony Blair government, Burnham was a supporter of Blair’s Iraq adventure who later voted against parliamentary inquiries into the war (though he has since recanted on both fronts). He has also been a member of Labour Friends of Israel since 2015: during his first pitch for the party leadership that year, he dismissed the campaign to boycott Israel as “spiteful.”
None of this will be sufficient to quell Israel’s anger in the face of a remarkably modest set of British sanctions, nor to persuade a skeptical and exhausted Palestinian public that the UK has suddenly become an ally. But British double-dealing on the issue is hardly new.
In his 1993 book Culture and Imperialism, Edward Said reflected on Britain’s pattern of double-talk in the early twentieth century, promising independence to the Arab inhabitants of Mandatory Palestine while simultaneously committing itself to the creation of an autonomous Jewish homeland in the region.
“The history of British imperial policy in the Middle East is a history of systematic duplicity,” Said wrote. “Making promises to all sides that could never be kept.” Time, as they say, is a flat circle — nowhere is this maxim more true than when it comes to the British role in Palestine.

https://hyperallergic.com/at-nycs-adaa-a.text:
At NYC’s ADAA Art Fair, Unlimited Shrimp and $2K Diebenkorns
The Art Dealers Association of America’s chummy five-day show returns to the Upper East Side after quietly canceling last fall’s edition.
There are many art fairs in New York City, but perhaps none are friendlier than the one hosted by the chummy Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA).
“We all know each other very well,” Dorsey Waxter, former president of the ADAA and partner at Van Doren Waxter gallery, told Hyperallergic. “We’ve vetted each gallery that comes into the association for levels of excellence and standards. And it’s not so big you can’t have conversations with dealers and find out things about what you’re looking at.”
Jovial conversations about pathbreaking newcomers and long-dead modernists abounded inside the Park Avenue Armory, which provided a needed refuge from the cold nor’easter pummeling Manhattan for Thursday night’s VIP preview.

The Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts, has appointed Caroline Shields chief curator. A specialist in nineteenth-century French art, Shields joins the Clark following her position at the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO), Toronto, where she has served as curator and head of the European art department since 2019. She will step into her new role this January; the exhibition “Pointillist Politics: Neo-Impressionism, Anarchy, Utopia,” which she co-curated, will go on view at the museum in June 2027.
“In Caroline Shields, we have found an excellent leader and a talented manager of curatorial projects. Caroline is well known to us for her exhibitions and scholarship, and we are confident she will expertly steward our ever-evolving collection,” said Clark director Esther Bell in a statement.
Shields arrived to AGO in 2017 as assistant curator of European art before rising to her current position. While at the museum, she notably curated a major exhibition pairing the works of American Impressionist Mary Cassatt with those of Canadian Impressionist Helen McNicoll. Before coming to AGO, she held curatorial roles at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; and the Musée d’Orsay, Paris. Shields holds a BS in geology and art history from Boston College and a Ph.D. in art history from the University of Maryland.
“I am deeply inspired by the Clark’s institutional commitment to audience engagement, art historical scholarship, and its world-class collection,” said Shields in a statement. “It is an honor to join the Clark’s extraordinary team of curators and staff across the Institute as it moves into its next chapter.”
Shields joins the Clark as it prepares to break ground on a new wing to house the collection of European art it received as a gift from late philanthropist Asa O. Tavitian.

Pathbreaking artist Lorna Simpson, known for her photographic works eschewing racist and sexist stereotypes and interrogating race, class, gender, politics, and history, has been revealed as the winner of the thirty-third Wolfgang Hahn Prize, presented by the Society for Modern Art at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne. The museum, which sponsors the prize, will put €100,000 (about $110,000) in member donations toward purchasing a work by Simpson for its collection. A solo exhibition of the artist’s work will go on view at the institution next year, and will be accompanied by a publication.
Born in Brooklyn in 1960, Simpson was the first African American woman to have her art exhibited at the Venice Biennale, in 1990. That same decade, she gained acclaim for works pairing text fragments with layered photographs, frequently of women with their faces obscured, forcing viewers to confront their own perceptions of Black women. She has since expanded her practice to include painting, drawing, film, collage, and installation, through which she continues to explore symbolic systems and the divide between the self and others’ perceptions.
Simpson was selected for this year’s prize by a jury comprising Naomi Beckwith, deputy director and chief curator of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York and artistic director of Documenta 16, and the Museum Ludwig board. The jury in a statement posited Simpson’s oeuvre as “a bridge” to the practices if contemporary artists including Carolyn Lazard and Diamond Stingily, whose works “reflect[ing] on the self-image of African American women” have recently entered the museum’s collection.
Inaugurated in 1994, the Wolfgang Hahn Prize honors established contemporary artists who are internationally recognized but are not yet considered to be as well known in Germany as they deserve to be. Previous winners include Francis Alÿs, Frank Bowling, Trisha Donnelly, Isa Genzken, Mike Kelley, Kerry James Marshall, Betye Saar, Cindy Sherman, Rosemarie Trockel, Lee Ufan, and Haegue Yang.

The Newark Museum of Art (NMOA) has agreed to restore ownership of a large brown jug made in 1852 by the enslaved South Carolina potter David Drake, also known as Dave the Potter, to the artist’s descendants. According to a press release, NMOA will purchase the work back for its permanent collection.
Amber Germano, NMOA’s senior director of registration and collections management, initiated a conversation with the family about restitution. “When I read about the family’s efforts to reunite Drake’s work with his descendants, I immediately knew it was important that we return the vessel in our collection,” she said. “Within a week of reaching out to the family, we were meeting with them. Hearing from them deepened my understanding of the artwork and the importance of restitution.”
“This is what moral leadership looks like,” said George Fatheree III, advisor to David Drake’s descendants, “and we invite other institutions with Mr. Drake’s work to engage with his family so we can move together towards justice.”
David Drake created the stoneware vessel at the Lewis Miles Stoneware Manufactory in Horse Creek Valley, near Edgefield, South Carolina, while enslaved by Miles. It is one of around forty known works by Drake associated with the manufactory and bears three fingertip impressions along the base and another on the applied strap handle. NMOA acquired the vessel at auction in 2022 and has had it on view in the long-term installation “Seeing America: 18th & 19th Century.”
The family began reaching out to institutions about restitution Drake’s work following the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s exhibition “Hear Me Now: The Black Potters of Old Edgefield, South Carolina” in 2022. To date, they have reached agreements with the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Telfair Museums in Savannah, the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, and the Virginia Museum of Fine Art.
