https://gothamist.com/news/first-code-bl.title: First Code Blue of the winter season arrives in New York City
https://gothamist.com/news/first-code-bl.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/first-code-bl.text:
New York City activated its first Code Blue of the season on Friday, opening warming centers overnight and relaxing shelter intake rules as temperatures and wind chills are expected to approach freezing, officials said.
The cold weather emergency runs from 4 p.m. Friday to 8 a.m. Saturday, according to the city Department of Emergency Management. Temperatures in Central Park are expected to fall to about 36 degrees, with windchills as low as 34, but colder air moving in after a storm could push both closer to freezing, the agency said, citing the National Weather Service.
It’s the first Code Blue since Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced an expanded plan this week, after more than two dozen people died outdoors or in their homes during a stretch of freezing weather last winter. The city promised $25 million in new funding, 300 more outreach canvassers, 800 more beds and 20 warming buses for the season, aimed to help New Yorkers sleeping on the street.
But last winter showed the danger isn’t limited to people living outside. Gothamist found that at least five of the people who died outside during the cold stretch that began in January had housing.
On Friday, six warming buses are scheduled to run overnight, from midnight to 5 a.m. Saturday at Bellevue, Elmhurst, Harlem and Lincoln hospitals and at Penn Station, according to city officials. Eight drop-in centers are open, and three of those hospitals are serving as warming centers from 4 p.m. to 8 a.m.
“When Code Blue is in effect, we make it as easy as possible for anyone to come inside,” Department of Social Services Commissioner Erin Dalton said in a statement.
Anyone who walks into a city shelter or drop-in center will be let in without the usual intake steps, she said.
NYC Emergency Management Commissioner Christina Farrell urged New Yorkers to check on older neighbors “and anyone who lives alone.”
She also warned that fire is the biggest risk of staying warm at home.
Officials are asking anyone who sees someone outside who may need help to call 311, and to call 911 if a person is in danger, seems confused or appears very cold. Warming locations are listed at on.nyc.gov/warm.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-lowre.title: US Government Bureaucracy Is Designed to Punish the Poor
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-lowre.author: Kelly McKowen
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-lowre.text:
US Government Bureaucracy Is Designed to Punish the Poor
In The Time Tax, journalist Annie Lowrey ably documents the myriad ways US public services harm poor and working-class people and alienate them from the government. Yet she downplays the class interests that benefit from these Kafkaesque arrangements.
For several years, I lived in Norway and enjoyed the privileges associated with membership in Folketrygden, or the National Insurance Scheme. One privilege that I still think about often is the relative frictionlessness of interacting with the Norwegian government.
Seeing a doctor, for example, was effortless, and once my low annual deductible (as of 2026, ~$300) was paid, all testing and treatment for the year was covered without my involvement or input. My taxes were — without my prompting — prepared for me and sent for my amendment and approval. There was never anything to amend, of course. And because of the country’s leveringsfritak, or “silent acceptance” law, I did not even have to sign or submit a return.
The great difference between how things are typically done in Norway and how they are done in my home country, the United States, was never clearer to me than it was one day when I had to visit the US embassy in Oslo to handle some paperwork. At that time, the embassy was housed in an angular, charcoal-colored Eero Saarinen building across the street from the Royal Palace. It was not only conveniently located but, despite its popular reputation as a “fortress,” simple and straightforward to access — entering the compound required flashing my passport and was about as easy as doing anything else in Norway.
Imagine my surprise, then, when I arrived at the office where I was to complete my task: from the uncomfortable seating and oppressive lighting to the interminable wait and general feeling of disaffection, it was such an uncanny recreation of an underfunded Department of Motor Vehicles or post office that it could have been a movie set. There was even a small, cheaply framed photo of the president. The juxtaposition of this experience — which seemed designed to frustrate — and my happy dealings with Norway’s bureaucracies was, in its own way, radicalizing.
I sense that Annie Lowrey, author of The Time Tax, has been similarly radicalized, albeit through extensive personal and journalistic exposure to the myriad forms in which people in the United States have their time wasted and disrespected — or “taxed,” as she puts it — in almost every conceivable interaction with the government. She is clearly and justifiably pissed, and her book endeavors to show that the problem is, though widespread and deeply rooted in a particular national history of racial exclusion and class oppression, fixable. There is a world, she argues, beyond our current patchwork of fool’s errands and wild-goose chases.
The Time Tax and Its Origins
But it is to this patchwork — and its associated “time taxes” — that most of the book is devoted. Through a mix of reporting, social scientific research, and reflecting on her own experience with an autoimmune condition, Lowrey has collected a cabinet of maddening curiosities: impenetrable forms, inexplicable rejections, multiyear wait times, and more. Page after page finds ordinary Americans trying to navigate a twisted institutional terrain seemingly designed by Franz Kafka or M. C. Escher. In the United States, you can buy, bid, and bet with the click of a button. Yet paying your taxes, voting, and getting benefits for which you qualify requires you to do American Ninja Warrior — with the proper forms of ID in hand.
Having cataloged the challenges people face when using public services in the United States, the first section of The Time Tax concludes with a tantalizing glimpse at the Estonian case, which, in many ways, resembles the Norwegian one with which I am more familiar (sans generous welfare state and strong labor rights). The story, as told by Lowrey, is that the small Baltic country, battered and bereft after exiting the Soviet Union, lacked the time, experience, infrastructure, and resources to recreate the comprehensive service architectures of other countries. So it didn’t. Instead, a generation of young and enterprising leaders leaned into speed, convenience, and digital integration to build an innovative e-government. In Estonia, Lowrey has seen the almost frictionless future of navigating government — and it works!
The Time Tax is at its most interesting and convincing when Lowrey is detailing the diabolical busy boxes that occupy millions of Americans. After the brief field trip to Estonia, the book could — and probably should — have ended with her proposals. It doesn’t.
Perhaps drawing inspiration from her subject, Lowrey decides that she requires more of her reader’s time to make her point. After a section break, we leave Estonia and arrive at . . . Fort Pillow in 1864? With Confederate general and future Ku Klux Klan Grand Wizard Nathan Bedford Forrest? It was disappointing to discover that The Time Tax was not in fact beginning its descent to a satisfying landing — it had been diverted to another destination: the past.
The middle third of the book draws on the extensive historical and social scientific scholarship devoted to the United States’ welfare system to recapitulate a story that will be familiar to anyone who knows the tortuous history of social provision in the United States. All the beats are there: Civil War pensions, Jim Crow, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and the Great Depression, Lyndon Baines Johnson and the Great Society, Ronald Reagan’s “welfare queens,” Bill Clinton and the “end of welfare as we know it.” Lowrey provides some useful context for twenty-first-century annoyances but breaks no new ground here, and the long historical detour saps the momentum of her opening chapters.
I worry that it also leads her to draw the wrong conclusions about her time taxes. She laments, for instance, that “diversity creates time taxes” and suggests that we are not Estonia due to “racial makeup.” Could it not be instead that time taxes transform diversity into inequality and hierarchy?
Cutting the Time Tax?
In any case, the final part of the book picks up the threads of the first to make a final appeal and offer Lowrey’s solutions. This appeal takes for granted that the reader has not been entirely swayed by their own experiences or by the book’s emphasis on aggravation, injustice, racism, and inequality. Instead, Lowrey makes a persuasive closing argument that time taxes also hurt our health, teach us the wrong lessons about citizenship and government, and undermine social trust.
She concludes with her blueprint for change. Her proposed fixes include measuring time taxes via “sludge audits,” federalizing what are today state-run programs, reducing the use of means-testing in favor of universalism, and abolishing work requirements and pro forma interviews. These changes would, in the aggregate, make using public services faster, easier, more convenient, more empowering, and ultimately more fulfilling.
But I hesitate to call these proposals “solutions,” because I do not think that they actually address the problem at the heart of The Time Tax. This problem is not time taxes per se but the success of actors who weaponize bureaucracy to undermine our access to the goods and services of the social citizenship for which previous generations have fought and even died. The status quo in the United States is a nightmare not because elites are unaware of the fact that universalism promotes greater public investment and trust in government — it is a nightmare because they are aware. The history of many hitherto existing time taxes is also the history of class struggles.
Lowrey knows this — I think. She condemns TurboTax for helping to kill Direct File, Florida Republicans for fighting the reenfranchisement of convicted felons, and Donald Trump for the disaster of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)–related cuts. She tells us that “time taxes are not just policy failures, but deliberate tools of social control.” And yet The Time Tax’s antagonist is without question “Uncle Sam” (her chosen shorthand for the government) and his “bureaucratic excesses.”
The issue is that while she lambasts “Uncle Sam” again and again, she is hesitant to center the private interests for whom that control is useful and profitable. In her long historical excursus, she can acknowledge that poll taxes and other discriminatory laws were used by racist white elites to exclude black people, make their lives precarious, and destroy governmental alternatives to foster dependency on actors who rarely had their best interests in mind. But while the past has opponents, for Lowrey, the present only has design flaws.
A smaller rhetorical point: Lowrey undermines her cause with the book’s core metaphor. Calling the problem the “time tax” might sell books to tax-wary Americans, but it could reinforce the pernicious idea that taxes do not benefit ordinary people. This is odd, as Lowrey herself acknowledges that a sustainable remedy to “the headaches, snafus, and frustration imposed by Uncle Sam” requires the expansion and improvement of administrative capacity — a development that would almost certainly require, well, greater taxes.
Finally, there is a problem of conceptual imprecision, which becomes apparent in the book’s first pages. Lowrey opens The Time Tax with a montage, juxtaposing disconnected scenarios for the purpose of creating a connective thread — the time tax — between radically different people, places, and challenges. But as she moves from losing the right to vote, to trying to get insurance to cover therapies for an autistic child, to attempting to open a soft-serve ice cream shop, to practicing cosmetology without a license, to handing out burritos to the homeless without a permit, I began to question whether each of these is in fact an example of the same problem. After a while, she more or less abandons any attempt to persuade you that a given obstacle is or is not a time tax. Instead, she just asserts it, identifying one or more annoyances and then adding something like “ — a time tax,” as if it were obvious.
All in all, The Time Tax is laudable as a collection of curios. It is less useful as a blueprint. Though Lowrey knows — and sometimes says explicitly — that this maddening status quo reflects the desires of certain powerful and well-resourced actors, she offers no proposals for organizing to muzzle, defang, or otherwise diminish their influence. She writes that “change does not happen without awareness, and awareness is not possible without numbers and stories.”
But it also does not happen without an awareness of who or what benefits from keeping you trapped in a thousand purgatories and a strategy for organizing against them. The path to a Norwegian-style welfare state is not just a matter of design — it is one of politics, and class politics in particular.

The Philips Collection in Washington D.C has received its largest ever individual gift. The $10 million donation comes from the Beatriz and Graham Bolton Global Vision Fund. According to a press release, it will be used to “strengthen the Phillips’s international presence as a world-class art museum.” This will include exhibitions, loans, and international partnerships with not only other museums but also embassies and cultural organizations. The gift will also support the Education and Responsive Learning department and will endow the Beatriz and Graham Bolton Chief of Education and Responsive Learning. The museum’s education and community engagement gallery will be named the Peggy Bolton Community Gallery, in memory of Graham Bolton’s late mother. The Boltons have been patrons of the Phillips for years. They’ve previously supported exhibitions and programs like the Intersections installations by Los Carpinteros and exhibitions of work by Zilia Sánchez, Daniel Canogar, and Bernardí Roig. Beatriz Bolton joined the Phillips Board of Trustees in 2022 and chairs its Institutional Culture and Civic Responsibility Committee. “Graham and I are thrilled to support the Phillips’s mission of being a welcoming home for all, especially its ability to bring people together through the universal language of art,” said Beatriz Bolton in a press release. “We are inspired by how the Phillips makes art accessible and meaningful to people from all walks of life, including through exhibitions and programs like Creative Aging. We are proud to support an institution that harnesses the power of art to enrich lives in ways that are deeply personal and lasting.” “This exceptional gift from Beatriz and Graham represents intentional and personal philanthropy at its finest, grounded in a spirit of deep partnership and responsiveness to the museum’s ongoing work and future potential,” said Elizabeth Racheva, the institution’s Chief Advancement Officer. “Their tremendous generosity—as global citizens themselves—will elevate the museum’s impact and international profile for generations to come.”

https://gothamist.com/news/former-nyc-ja.title: Former NYC jails chief testifies about Adams adviser's push to hire friend’s daughter
https://gothamist.com/news/former-nyc-ja.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/former-nyc-ja.text:
When Eric Ulrich asked then-Department of Correction Commissioner Louis Molina to consider hiring his friend’s daughter for an open position in February 2022, Molina said he set up a meeting that same week.
Ulrich, then a senior adviser to Mayor Eric Adams, called Molina to recommend the daughter of his friend Michael Mazzio, according to a recording played in court on Friday. By the end of Molina’s one-on-one “exploratory conversation” with the recent college graduate, Mazzio’s daughter had a conditional job offer for an entry-level analyst position.
“She had the job if she wanted it,” Molina testified in court Friday.
Prosecutors have since accused Mazzio of bribing Ulrich with premium season tickets to the New York Mets in exchange for favors, including helping to secure the job for his daughter. A trial is ongoing in Manhattan against both men, who have pleaded not guilty.
Phone calls played in Manhattan court on Friday reveal new details about how Ulrich convinced Molina to interview Mazzio’s daughter and followed up to ensure the hiring process was moving along.
“Mazzio’s the priority,” Ulrich said in a recorded phone call played in court on Friday.
“You got it,” Molina replied.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

The Whitney Museum of Art has deaccessioned Willem de Kooning’s Yellow River and put it up for sale at Christie’s 20th-century evening auction on November 17. The 1958 painting is estimated to sell for $12 million to $18 million.
The sale is intended to support future acquisitions, Artnet reports, and follows the museum’s rare move in 2023 to deaccession seven works from its collection, including a major painting, Cobb’s Barns, South Truro (1930–33), by Edward Hopper. At the time, the Whitney justified the sale in part by stating that the works were “duplicative within the collection.” It’s not clear how the museum arrived at the decision to part with the de Kooning.
David M. Solinger, who became a trustee of the Whitney in 1961, purchased the painting from Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959, where it was on view in a hotly anticipated solo show of de Kooning’s canvases and works on paper. Nineteen had sold by noon of the opening day. These works marked a critical moment in de Kooning’s development, when he began painting monumental, gestural compositions that the editor and curator Thomas B. Hess dubbed de Kooning’s “abstract parkway landscapes.”
Fairfield Porter wrote of this period in de Kooning’s career, “It is as though his painting reached a different level of consciousness than painting that refers to a theory of aesthetics.”
Solinger’s widow, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, gave Yellow River to the museum as a gift in 2023. Christie’s lot essay includes an anecdote from Frank Robinson, former director of Cornell University’s Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, that the painting hung for a time at the foot of Solinger’s bed so that it was the first thing he saw upon waking.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-t.title: NYC schools to review hiring practices after teacher's aide accused of jogger murder
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-t.author: Jessica Gould
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-schools-t.text:
The city education department will review its hiring practices after learning that the man accused of killing a Brooklyn jogger last month was previously hired as a paraprofessional, despite a documented history of mental health concerns.
Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced Friday that the city’s Law Department will conduct the independent review and deliver recommendations.
“The safety of our students and staff is our highest priority. We can leave no stone unturned and no path unexplored when it comes to protecting that safety,” Samuels said in a statement.
Sayed Mohassib, 27, is accused of fatally stabbing Katie Suarez as she jogged on the Shore Parkway Greenway on Oct. 30. Mohassib worked as a paraprofessional at PS 200, which is only blocks from the greenway that passes under the Verrazzano Bridge. He has pleaded not guilty.
According to city records, Mohassib was first hired by the education department in 2019. He then left the school system and graduated from the NYPD’s police academy in 2022. He only worked for the NYPD for a month before being granted military leave to join the U.S. Marines. He was then discharged from the Marines due to psychiatric issues. He tried to rejoin the NYPD in 2023, but NYPD supervisors were so concerned by his behavior he was taken to Bellevue Hospital, officials said.
Nevertheless, Mohassib was rehired as a paraprofessional in 2024, payroll records show.
Parents and local officials have demanded to know why Mohassib was allowed to work closely with public school children after the NYPD, where he had also worked briefly as a police officer, raised serious concerns about his mental stability.
The majority of the city’s paraprofessionals work closely with students with disabilities who have individualized education programs, commonly known as IEPs.
New York City Council member Kayla Santosuosso had earlier this week called for a review of the education department’s personnel policies in light of the murder.
“I’m looking at what happened that led up to this person continuing to be employed by the DOE and in such an intimate way with students,” she said. “My concern is that there seem to be numerous red flags along the way that some system within the DOE should have caught.”
Santosuosso said school staff who had worked with Mohassib in the past had also reached out to her office this week to say they had raised concerns about his behavior. The education department did not respond to requests for comments about why he continued to be employed despite those concerns, or after the NYPD had rejected him.
The city has been struggling with a shortage of paraprofessionals for years. The United Federation of Teachers is suing the city over legislation to raise pay for paraprofessionals in order to recruit and retain more candidates.
According to the criminal complaint, Mohassib denied killing Suarez but told investigators that he was sitting on a bench along the path and became “covered in blood.”
Surveillance footage of Mohassib running from the scene of the murder, entering his apartment building and then walking out about 15 minutes later to throw items in the garbage, according to a complaint.
Jessica Battaglia, a former teacher at the High School of Telecommunication Arts and Technology, who said she knew Mohassib when he was in ninth grade, said it was shocking to learn that the “sweet” kid she taught could be arrested for murder.
She said Mohassib stood out for his kindness to classmates, especially students with disabilities. “He was one of our favorite students, that’s why we’re so shocked,” she said. She remembered him winning awards that year at an end-of-year ceremony, and said the person she knew more than a decade ago would have been a “perfect” candidate for a job working with children with disabilities.
She noted the news reports that indicated someone missed multiple signs of his deteriorating mental health. “Why didn’t anyone help him before he hurt someone else?” she asked.

https://gothamist.com/news/engineers-que.title: Engineers question city-approved plans after Brooklyn building collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/engineers-que.author: David Brand
https://gothamist.com/news/engineers-que.text:
City-approved excavation plans at the site of Wednesday’s fatal apartment building collapse in Brooklyn did not require construction crews to install additional bracing to support the adjacent structure, according to a review of building records.
The plans instead called for cutting into the soil at a 45-degree angle away from the three-story apartment building’s foundation to a depth of roughly 15 feet. Every other building around the perimeter of the construction site was required to have reinforcing steel buttresses known as rakers, according to the plans.
The collapse killed eight people and injured 18 more. The development team behind the property had previously ignored a stop-work order earlier in the year, city records show. The absence of the bracing raises further questions about the safety of the construction work.
Three structural engineers who reviewed the engineering documents, known as “support of excavation” plans, said they were surprised to see that the buildings department approved the measures without the additional structural support, which can help prevent adjoining buildings from collapsing when excavation work is done.
“That’s a recipe for disaster,” said Abi Agheyere, a structural engineer and a professor at Drexel University. “You have to have shoring.”
Agheyere said the extra precaution should have been taken due to the age of the 94-year-old building, which sat atop a rubble foundation. A preconstruction plan drafted by the engineering firm Quiver League and submitted to the Department of Buildings also described the building facade next to the construction site as in “poor condition with noticeable cracks.”
Quiver’s report notes that its inspectors lacked detailed information about the apartment building’s foundation and other structural features, and that they were only able to assess the building from the sidewalk and other adjoining properties.
Quiver engineer Sepehr Rezaeimalek prepared the report. He did not respond to a phone message Friday.
Chris Cerino, past president of the Structural Engineers Association of New York, said he would have expected to see additional bracing in the drawings, or “underpinning” to support the foundation of the collapsed apartment building.
“I would have anticipated a different detail on that side of the site,” Cerino said in a text message after reviewing the plans.
Department of Buildings spokesperson Andrew Rudansky said the support strategy depicted in the approved plans is “standard industry practice” and that “similar excavation designs have been safely performed at other work sites across the city for decades.”
Rudansky also said the project engineer — in this case, Jieming Wang of LMW Engineering — is responsible for making sure the plans are safe for construction before submitting them to the buildings department.
“Upon that confirmation by the design professional engineer, plans go through a full plan exam at the DOB,” he said.
Rudansky said the department completed the full exam and found the designs complied with city requirements. He said investigators are now conducting additional reviews, with a special focus on the project’s “geotechnical report,” which evaluated the soil and rock at the construction site before excavation work began. The engineer who prepared the report, Michael Karantinidis of International Geotechnical/Structural Laboratories Inc., did not immediately respond to a message left at his office.
Rudansky did not say what was supposed to support the building that collapsed between excavation and pouring a new foundation at the construction site.
Wang submitted the excavation plans for approval in December 2025. At the time, the owner of 2625 Bedford Ave., a limited liability company tied to Robert Fischman and Judy Swimer, sought to construct a three-story apartment building on the site. The development team later submitted a new plan in September to build a nine-story complex, but the Department of Buildings had not yet approved the revised project proposal.
A person who answered the phone at Wang’s office extension Friday immediately hung up.
Buildings records indicate that special inspector MD Islam was contracted to monitor excavation. Records updated Thursday said Islam had requested to withdraw from the project after the building collapsed.
Islam did not respond to requests for comment or emailed questions about the withdrawal.
In the immediate wake of the catastrophe, the city’s Department of Buildings issued a full stop work order. A comment on its online portal attributed the collapse “to unsafe construction operations.” The agency later deleted the comment, Crain’s reported Thursday.
The Department of Buildings is investigating the cause of the collapse alongside the city’s Department of Investigation and the Brooklyn District Attorney’s office. The city is also conducting sweep inspections at building sites across the city where the same contractors have conducted work. On Friday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the inquiry had expanded to 160 properties involving six different entities.
The edge of the now-collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. was the only location in the construction site where the engineering plans did not require steel supports.
Agheyere said the beams add another layer of protection against collapse.
“There's nothing that stops it from spreading right into the hole,” he said.
Another engineer who reviewed the plans said steel reinforcement is not always required to support an adjacent building if excavation is done properly.
“As long as you're not digging under the foundation, you don’t necessarily have to put up steel or additional measures,” said Eugene Gurevich, from the firm RAND Engineering & Architecture.
He likened the structure of a building to a ladder, with two parallel sides serving as feet and wooden joists, framing and floors as the handholds.
“One leg of the ladder was kicked out from under it and pulled the whole ladder down,” he said.
In an interview, Carpenter’s Union Executive Secretary-Treasurer Paul Capurso said construction crews may have dug too deeply to prepare for a potential nine-story building, rather than the three-story structure approved by the buildings department.
“There is potential they could have changed their design on the fly,” Concurso said.

https://gothamist.com/news/dad-girl-kill.title: Families devastated by Brooklyn building collapse came to NYC for a new life
https://gothamist.com/news/dad-girl-kill.author: Brittany Kriegstein, Ryan Kost
https://gothamist.com/news/dad-girl-kill.text:
The people who died in the Flatbush building collapse came from opposite ends of the world. But their loved ones said they shared the same hope: to make a new life in New York City.
“We have no words,” Juan Carlos Zabala said of his lost family. “They were following the American dream.”
His cousin, Juan Daniel Sabala, 31, had a 9-year-old daughter, Nicole. Both died in the wreckage. Another cousin of the same family, 10-year-old Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, was also found dead.
The collapse killed five other New Yorkers and injured 18 more in what is among the worst residential building collapses in recent city history. Zabala — speaking to Gothamist from Spain — said Friday that his cousin’s wife was still hospitalized and receiving intensive care with the couple’s 3-year-old daughter. Many others were also waiting for updates from their surviving family and friends.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin read the names of the dead, beginning with Sabala and his daughter, during a news conference Friday at a shelter for the displaced.
“They were cousins, they were roommates, they were sons, they were daughters, they were children,” Menin said. “They were Juan Sabala and Gabriel Siguencia, and two cousins who lived together, Mamadou Ndiaye and Mamadou Barry. They were Nicole Sabala and Kevin Reyes, another set of young cousins. They were Edgar Sapon, a construction worker who leaves a wife and 6-year-old son. They were José Caguana, who would pick up his 4-year-old son from preschool, and his wife is expecting a second child soon.”
Zabala said the family had arrived in the country three or four years ago, and Sabala had been working for a cleaning company. But the last time they spoke, Zabala said, his cousin sounded anxious.
“Everything with ICE was really bothering them,” he said. “So they stayed shut inside, from work to home and home to work because they were afraid of being deported.”
The family was home on Wednesday because it was Veterans Day, Zabala said. He had been planning to come visit in December — but now was left processing what had become of his relatives.
“I have a lot of nostalgia and a lot of sadness … because I am also in another country that’s not mine,” he said. “We came with a dream, hoping for a better life. And at the end, we don’t know what will happen to us.”
Ndiaye and Barry shared their apartment with a married couple, Mamadou Mouctar Balde and his wife, Fatoumata Binta Bah. She is six months pregnant and was pulled from the rubble by emergency workers. A widely shared picture of the rescue by AP Photographer Ryan Murphy shows her lying on a stretcher, flanked by firefighters, her skin caked with white dust.
She remains hospitalized with serious injuries, according to Councilmember Farah Louis, but she and her baby survived.
Balde, speaking in French, said he’d left the apartment to buy groceries shortly before the building collapsed. When he came back, emergency services and the Red Cross were already there. He thought there’d been a traffic accident until a woman told him the building had come down.
“When she told me there had been a collapse, I didn’t know where I was anymore, because I know our building borders that site,” Balde said. He said he told the woman, “My wife is inside, my friends are inside.”
Two of the dead, Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia Yupa and José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, were construction workers from Ecuador. Caguana Cosquillo’s wife is set to give birth this weekend, said Winston Sanchez, who spoke on behalf of the men’s families.
“It is a sad day because it not only collapsed the building, it collapsed the lives of many relatives, brothers, fathers,” Sanchez said.
Investigations into what led to the collapse are underway. Attorney General Letitia James said she was standing ready to help however she can.
“The families in this community deserve answers about what led to this collapse,” James said.
Louis, who at one point struggled to hold back tears, went further:
“Buildings do not simply collapse without systemic failure,” she said, adding that records show “a building with nearly 100 open violations sitting next to an excavation site cited for violating a stop work order.”
The speakers noted that the mayor’s office has set up an emergency relief fund for those affected, and the Flatbush YMCA is collecting gift cards and checks. Other organizations have stepped up to collect donations as well.
This story has been updated with new information.

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-wants-ai-.title: MTA wants AI cameras on subway trains to spot people on the tracks
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-wants-ai-.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-wants-ai-.text:
The MTA wants to test out artificial intelligence technology that can automatically detect people or objects on the tracks ahead of subway trains, according to documents published by the agency last month.
The agency is seeking a company to install a camera system on the front of a train car that alerts the operator to any hazard on the right of way. The technology would also be able to track any erratic movement by passengers on the edge of subway platforms.
MTA documents show the agency plans to spend between $5 million and $10 million to test the technology, and the agency wants to eventually roll the technology out across its fleet of subway trains.
The technology could help prevent deaths in the subway system. An MTA track worker was killed earlier this year after being struck by a train, and dozens of people have died in recent years after being shoved or deliberately onto subway tracks.
“This project is part of the MTA's commitment to explore emerging technologies aimed at strengthening safety and improving service reliability across the transit system,” MTA spokesperson Michael Cortez said in a statement.
At the end of testing, the technology will be uninstalled from the train while the MTA assess whether it can be rolled out across the system.
The MTA has wrestled with track safety for years. In 2021, the transit agency launched a “track trespassing task force” to look at different ways to avert any intrusions. The agency reported 68 people died while trespassing on subway tracks that year.
At the urging of Gov. Kathy Hochul, the transit agency installed metal barriers on sections of platforms at more than 150 subway stations.
The Federal Railroad Administration in 2024 announced a $32 million grant to help transit agencies develop technology to keep people off of train tracks. That same year, researchers at the nonprofit Transportation Research Board developed a system that uses AI to detect people on the tracks.

https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-help-t.title: How to help the victims of the Brooklyn building collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-help-t.author: Karen Yi
https://gothamist.com/news/how-to-help-t.text:
New Yorkers are stepping up to help the families affected by the fatal building collapse in Flatbush, which left eight people dead and 18 others injured.
Several organizations, including the YMCA and local elected leaders, are asking for donations, gift cards and new toiletries to help the families displaced by the disaster.
The Red Cross opened a reception center at the YMCA for families in need of support and assistance. A spokesperson said eight families have registered, including 16 adults and six children. The city is also using a nearby hotel to house families who lost their homes or had to evacuate from nearby buildings.
“These families lost everything,” Councilmember Farah Louis, who represents Flatbush, said during a press conference Friday. She said her office was standing with families to “make sure you get the shelter you need, the relief you need and the resources you need to build back again.”
Here’s a list of ways to help.
New toiletries
Organizations are asking for new and unopened donations of toiletries. That includes toothpaste, toothbrushes, deodorant, soap, body wipes, tissues, tampons and pads, hairbrushes and baby wipes. Those donations can be dropped off at several locations:
- Flatbush YMCA at 1401 Flatbush Ave.
- Brooklyn Borough Hall at 209 Joralemon St. (enter via Adams Street)
- Councilmember Farah Louis’ office at 2253 Nostrand Ave.
- The organization D.R.U.M. at 1468 Flatbush Ave.
Gift cards
New Yorkers can also donate gift cards in $25, $50 or $100 denominations that will go directly to impacted families to use for groceries, clothing and other household essentials. Gift cards can be for food, phone service or cash. Those donations can be dropped off at several locations:
- Flatbush YMCA at 1401 Flatbush Ave.
- Brooklyn Borough Hall at 209 Joralemon St. (enter via Adams Street)
- Councilmember Farah Louis’ office at 2253 Nostrand Ave.
- The organization D.R.U.M. at 1468 Flatbush Ave.
Monetary donations
The Flatbush YMCA started a GoFundMe for contributions.
Anderson Velez, 35, whose wife and two children fell into the rubble and survived, also launched a fundraising page as his 9-year-old recovers in the hospital. The family had just moved out of a homeless shelter and moved into their apartment eight days before the collapse.
The family of one of the victims, Jose Luis Caguana, has also started a fundraising campaign. Caguana, 26, left behind a 4-year-old son and his wife, who is pregnant with their second child.
The Mayor’s Fund to Advance New York City is accepting donations for families here.
The Flatbush Building Collapse Emergency Relief Fund, created by The Flatbush Development Corporation and the Flatbush Tenant Coalition, is accepting donations as they meet with affected families to assess their housing needs.
Clothing
The Bridge Multicultural & Advocacy Project is asking for clothing donations. New Yorkers can drop donations at 1894 Flatbush Ave. on Monday, Nov. 16 and Tuesday, Nov. 17, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Mark Appel, the group’s founder, said the organization is accepting new or gently used clothing in good condition. In particular, they are looking for winter gear such as gloves, scarves and sweaters, as well as underwear. People are encouraged to drop off sizes medium to large, as well as kids’ sizes.
Toys
Community Board 17 is hosting an annual holiday party on Dec. 18 and will invite the families affected by the collapse. New Yorkers can contribute new toys or children’s gifts for the celebration, which can be dropped off at the Community Board 17 offices at 4112 Farragut Rd.
New and unused bedding
Sheets, pillows, pillowcases and blankets are being accepted at the following locations:
- Community Board 17 at 4112 Farragut Rd.
- Clarendon Road Church at 3304 Clarendon Rd.
- Lenox Road Baptist Church at 1356 Nostrand Ave.

Special Edition: Jesus
Mona Chalabi, Anne Anlin Cheng and Patty Chang, Miles Greenberg, Betsy James Wyeth, and the hottest memes about the Nvidia honeypot.
Framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.
In the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the issue as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago.
Down the street, a place that pretended to be a legitimate art gallery for a couple of months, showing the worst possible commercial art, has finally given up, and now it’s selling fur coats. A man in a cowboy hat walks past two girls dancing for a social media video. The air is chilly, and I think of buying myself a leather jacket.
And then I see her.
She looks at me with the most loving eyes as she holds a stack of perfectly folded laundry. She comforts me with her wide, auspicious smile, her jet-black hair, and her wrinkle-free, porcelain skin. I feel safe, accepted, and not judged. “Fast service, same day,” she promises because she’s just a model in an ad for a laundromat.
—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Hockney and His Beverly Hills Patron
A review of James Cahill’s book on the painter and the patron in “Beverly Hills Housewife,” the state of arts journalism, and why Tribal Nations are opposing a Congressional bill.
It’s a beautiful day to support indie publications! Last week, a survey conducted by Critical Minded and the Rabkin Foundation quantified the precarity of independent US-based art magazines amid a climate of censorship, corporate takeovers, and economic instability. It’s no wonder, when media companies decide to partner with Amazon on art initiatives (cough, cough, Penske). Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia breaks down the survey results and what they can teach us about the future of independent, critical arts journalism.
Speaking of which, Staff Writer Anna Lee reports on a coalition of Tribal Nations opposing a bill that would threaten Native sites if Congress passes it. Longtime Angeleno Matt Stromberg considers an engrossing if occasionally overwrought book by James Cahill that explores the influential friendship between David Hockney and Betty Freeman, the arts patron at the center of one of his most recognizable paintings. And if that isn’t enough, Aaron Short shares a wry dispatch from the preview of the Art Dealers Association of America’s art fair in New York City — the tickets may have been $250 a pop, but at least there were unlimited dumplings and champagne to sweeten the deal?
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
