https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.title: School phone bans result in ‘modest’ academic gains for students, study shows
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text:
A large-scale study published Tuesday found strict cellphone restrictions in US schools – ones that require students to put phones in locked pouches for the entire academic day – result in small academic gains.
And there could be further gains if schools continue banning phones, the researchers said.
The study, led by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, found the schools with strict phone restrictions saw “modest” improvements in academic growth, compared with students in similar schools without those restrictions. Analyzing test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools nationally, the study estimates the academic gains were equivalent to about an additional week or two of learning over a school year.
Student achievement has been falling globally since 2013, which is roughly when social media-enabled smartphones took off. The researchers sought to determine if the decline is being reversed now that schools have started taking phones away, said Harvard professor Thomas Kane, one of the study’s authors.
“Our answer is yes, phone bans do have a positive effect on growth. But it’s not a panacea,” Kane said. Learning loss was gradual over a decade, he noted, and it’s not surprising that gains would also be gradual. The study used math and reading test data for grades four through 10 from the past five academic years.
“While schools should not expect large boosts in achievement immediately, storing students’ phones seems to be a cost-effective way to add 1-2 weeks of instruction each year, which could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” the study says.
The boost is equal to about half the annual decline in test scores since smartphones became mainstream, the study said.
The emerging research illustrating that complicated reality comes as more than 40 US states have passed laws that restrict cellphones at schools, according to the Phone Free Schools State Report Card, which tracks state phone legislation.
The laws vary widely and often let schools design their own policies, resulting in a patchwork of rules and enforcement across the country.
The argument for school cellphone bans is simple: Phones offer endless distraction. Take them away and students can focus on classwork, engage with peers and, ultimately, learn more.
However, while schools can lock phones away in pouches or banish them to backpacks, the study published on Tuesday makes evident that they can’t shut out the digital world.
And the connection between phones and learning is not entirely clearcut.
A different study published in May concluded strict school phone bans had “close to zero” effect on test scores. It compared schools with bans with tens of thousands of other schools.
The National Bureau of Economic Research study looked at a different set of standardized test scores than Harvard’s study, as well as GPS phone activity, teacher surveys and data from Yondr, the leading provider of lockable phone pouches, at 4,600 schools that use the pouches.
The study had found “modest positive effects” in high school test scores over three years, particularly in math. But the report’s authors – researchers at Stanford, the University of Michigan, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania – were hesitant to conclude overall learning benefits from the bans.
Both studies point to a similar conclusion, said Stanford education economist Thomas Dee, an author of the NBER study. “The early results from school phone bans are largely disappointing and raise unresolved questions,” Dee said.
Noting that the Harvard study showed learning gains may accumulate over time, Dee said: “I hope they’re right. However, I’m not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.”
The reasons, Dee said, could be that students are still distracted on other devices at school. Or, he said, “it may be that we see these disappointing results because out-of-school phone use is harming child development.”
Whether schools or states actually enforce any existing bans is also a question, said Jean Twenge, a psychologist at San Diego State University and author of 10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World.
Ask any teacher – or teenager – and they’ll tell you that some phone bans are largely cosmetic. Teens come up with creative workarounds, including stowing burner phones or even phone-shaped rocks in their locked pouches. At schools that rely on students to keep phones in backpacks, adherence to the ban can be spotty.
“It happens pretty often that there’s a policy of no phones during the school day, bell-to-bell, and you go into the school and phones are everywhere,” Twenge said.
Even without phones, Twenge asked: “Do they have laptops at school? Are they just doing social media on laptops instead?”
Phone use outside school affects academics too, Twenge said. “If they have that phone available when they’re studying, how much are they really taking in?”
Kane, of the Harvard study, agrees the effect of cellphone use outside school is “the big question”. But researchers have not been able to investigate parents and educators’ suspicions that late-night binges on YouTube and other platforms are costly for students.
“I find it astonishing that social media companies know how much time kids spend on their platforms, but that data has never been linked to student outcomes,” Kane said. “We can’t provide answers until the social media companies share data.”

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/famil.title: Family of Palestinian journalist Mohammed Atiq demands his release
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/famil.author: Fayha Shalash
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/famil.text:
Family of Palestinian journalist Mohammed Atiq demands his release
The family of Palestinian journalist Mohammed Atiq has demanded that his place of detention be disclosed and that he be released, following his arrest by the Israeli army at dawn on Sunday.
Israeli soldiers raided his home in the town of Burqin, west of Jenin, blew open the door, and searched the premises before taking Atiq to an unknown location. His family has yet to receive any information regarding his whereabouts or the conditions of his detention.
Atiq’s arrest comes amid an ongoing campaign of pursuit and detention targeting Palestinian journalists due to their professional work.
The Journalists' Syndicate has reported that approximately 210 journalists including about 23 women have been arrested since 7 October 2023. Meanwhile, the Palestinian Prisoners' Club confirms that 38 journalists, including five women, remain in Israeli occupation prisons.
Atiq works as a photojournalist for several international outlets, including Middle East Eye. About a month ago, he was detained for several hours while filming the olive harvest in the village of Anza, near Jenin.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Ahmed Atiq, his father, told us that the family remains unaware of his son’s fate or where he is being held, noting that they have received no new information regarding his situation.
He explained that the military liaison office has informed the family that it is closely monitoring the case and will provide updates as they arise.
Atiq stated that the Israeli army raided the house at dawn on Sunday, blowing open the door. They searched the entire property, causing minor damage to some of its contents, and threw the journalist’s camera outside.
"The soldiers told Mohammed’s wife to get dressed, as she was also going to be arrested. Female soldiers entered the house as well, but they left once they learned she was eight-months pregnant," he added.
He noted that his 32-year-old son had previously been arrested in 2016 and had been detained on several other occasions, at military checkpoints and while out filming on locations.
To the family’s knowledge, he was not beaten during this latest raid.
He concluded by saying that the occupation forces took his son away in a military vehicle. Since then, the family has had no information regarding his whereabouts or the conditions of his detention. He demanded that his son’s fate and location be disclosed and called for his immediate release.
Violations against journalists
The Palestinian Prisoners’ Club (PCC) stated that the number of journalists held in Israeli prisons has reached 38, including five women.
It further noted that two journalists from the Gaza Strip have been subjected to enforced disappearance since 7 October 2023, with no clear information available regarding their fate or the conditions of their detention. More than 260 journalists have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza.
The PCC explained that Israel employs various pretexts to justify targeting journalists most notably allegations of "incitement" and the existence of "secret files", while also utilising administrative detention and the military judicial system to keep journalists in custody without fair trials or legal safeguards.
"The targeting of journalists is not limited to the West Bank; it extends to the territories occupied in 1948 [Israel], as seen in the case of journalist Saeed Hassanein, who has recently faced prosecution and legal proceedings due to his journalistic work and stances," the statement reads.
'Imprisoned journalists face violations that include physical assault, torture, abuse, the denial of fundamental rights, and harsh detention conditions'
- Palestinian Prisoners’ Club
In the same context, the Israeli Prison Service has kept the imprisoned journalist Bushra al-Tawil in isolation for over two months.
She is being held under harsh conditions, which include frequent raids on her cell, physical assault, abuse, the use of tear gas, constant surveillance, the denial of basic rights, and the obstruction of visits by her legal counsel.
"Beyond being prosecuted for their professional work, imprisoned journalists face violations that include physical assault, torture, abuse, the denial of fundamental rights, and harsh detention conditions, all of which constitute violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law," the PCC affirmed.
Omar Nazzal, a member of the general secretariat of the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate, told us that Israeli authorities have arrested approximately 210 journalists including about 23 women since 7 October 2023.
He described these arrests as part of a systematic effort to target journalistic work and prevent journalists from uncovering the truth and reporting on events on the ground.
He explained that the Journalists Syndicate is working on two levels to address the cases of detained journalists - the first approach is legal: coordinating with entities concerned with the affairs of prisoners and former detainees, and assigning four lawyers to handle the cases of journalists before Israeli courts.
Each lawyer is tasked with following the case of a specific journalist depending on their place of detention or location by providing legal representation and attending court hearings.
The second approach involves international and external advocacy: preparing periodic reports that document the conditions of detained journalists and the violations they face, then submitting these reports to the International Federation of Journalists and relevant United Nations bodies, particularly those focused on freedom of opinion and expression.
"These actions sometimes elicit responses and statements from international institutions, which in turn send letters to the Israeli authorities demanding the release of detained journalists or requesting clarifications regarding the conditions of their detention," he added.
However, he emphasised that these efforts have yet to yield tangible results on the ground, as campaigns of arrest, abuse, and the prosecution of journalists targeted precisely for their professional work and their exercise of freedom of opinion and expression continue unabated.
He noted that confronting these policies is a long-term struggle, requiring sustained union, legal, and international efforts, as well as intensified pressure on institutions dedicated to press freedom even if the practical outcomes have been limited thus far.
According to the latest statistics published by Palestinian prisoners' institutions, the number of Palestinian prisoners and detainees in Israeli prisons reached approximately 9,300 as of early November 2026.
This includes around 90 female prisoners and more than 350 children. The number of administrative detainees exceeded 3,000, in addition to 1,419 detainees from the Gaza Strip whom the Israeli authorities classify as "unlawful combatants".
These figures do not include all Palestinian detainees held in military camps and detention centres belonging to the Israeli military.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: At the origin of France’s education protests, students refuse to give up
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
At the origin of France’s education protests, students refuse to give up
Blockades continue at some schools in the Parisian suburbs, as students and teachers say little has improved in their classrooms.
Paris, France – On a cold, rainy morning in early November, students and teachers met outside the locked gates of Paul Eluard, a high school in Saint-Denis north of Paris. Some were wearing costumes. For 17-year-old Kamelia, dressing as a dinosaur helped her to maintain the joy and hope that coexisted with the anger driving the student movement in mid-September.
“Costumes are the fun part. They show that it’s not all about violence. There’s also good cheer and fun in all of this,” Kamelia told Al Jazeera. “Today there are huge protests all over France, and it’s very important. I got up early, and even though I’m a little tired, I came anyway.”
Four days after students at Paul Eluard returned from a mid-term break, they joined a national strike on November 5. Nearby, students from the trade school Bartholdi had blockaded the gates of their school. Although the size of the student protests peaked in early October, many young people, especially in the suburbs, are refusing to return to the classroom until some of their demands are met.
“Sometimes, we see rats in the courtyard and in the restrooms. The restrooms are a mess. We don’t have enough water; it flows very slowly. We don’t have enough to drink, and the restrooms are dirty. The hallways are dirty, the classrooms are dirty, and there are cockroaches,” 17-year-old Nohlan, a student at Bartholdi, told Al Jazeera outside the school’s blockade.
The movement started at a high school in Creteil, a suburb southeast of Paris in the Val-de-Marne region, on September 17, and rapidly spread to Saint-Denis, then the rest of France. Students blocked the entrances to their schools to protest poor classroom conditions and took to the streets.
“The movement started in the suburbs, then Paris followed suit. Now the whole world is watching us,” Kamelia said. “[In Saint-Denis], we’re basically ignored, even though we’re part of this country. But we’re here, and we are the future of this country.”
By the end of September, an estimated 400 schools across France, including some universities, had joined the student movement. Protests on October 17 in Paris saw an estimated 550,000 participants, according to the interior minister, while organisers put the number at 800,000.
Although this is not the first time in recent years that students in working-class suburbs have protested against school conditions, the scale of this year’s movement has been remarkable.
“It really started to gain momentum, and when everyone started to get involved, it was incredible. It really moved me because last year, we set up a few blockades, but no one heard about them,” Kamelia said.
Although students are at the heart of the movement, many teachers have since joined, expressing solidarity with their students and deploring the conditions under which they have to teach.
High school students are setting the pace for the movement, said Lucie Sabze, an English teacher at Paul Eluard.
“I’m impressed by the students, their demands and their political discourse, which is very lucid and very clear,” she told Al Jazeera. “I think the scale of the movement can be explained by a growing frustration.”
Teachers at Eluard are celebrating one “victory”. They had been calling for the resignation of the head teacher, who they accused of letting an officer from France’s notoriously violent motorised antiterrorism brigade into the school to arrest a student.
On Sunday, a government agency announced Xavier Artaud had stepped down “as a safety precaution”.
“Given the unacceptable public accusations made against the high school principal by name, he requested protective measures requiring his removal from the Saint-Denis area,” said the Academic Director of National Education Services.
Bruno Gbalou, an English teacher at neighbouring Bartholdi, noted that conditions have only deteriorated in recent years.
“It’s been about 15 years since I came back from England and started teaching here, and things have only gotten worse. So there are more students, but we have fewer resources,” Bruno Gbalou told Al Jazeera. “It’s not fair to the students, and it’s not fair to us, and that’s one of the reasons why we’re going on strike.”
In a statement to the media in early October, President Emmanuel Macron said the government planned to respond to students’ demands “in the most concrete way possible”.
“I understand the anxieties, sometimes the anger, that our youth can have, whether about the climate, technological changes or geopolitical situations,” Macron said.
But the students who spoke to Al Jazeera said they do not believe the government has offered them real solutions. The November blockade at Bartholdi in Saint-Denis was in response to a lack of solutions, said student Nohlan.
“There’s still no change. We’re hoping for change, but we’re waiting, and waiting,” he said.
Louis Boyard, a member of the French National Assembly for Val-de-Marne, the administrative area where the protest movement started, explained that the government’s policies have significantly reduced educational resources.
“Macron pursued a policy of austerity, and as a result, he gradually dismantled public education while providing massive subsidies to the private sector because he supports private education over public education,” Boyard told Al Jazeera. “Macron thinks that by sweeping the problem under the rug, people will just go home. That’s not true. The people speaking out can’t really afford to eat any more. One in three French people are skipping meals. People – young people – have gone too far in this movement to back down now.”
The left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is currently polling about 20 percent in France’s upcoming presidential elections, has been accused of weaponising the student movement for political gain. But Boyard insisted that the movement was organic, and that LFI had simply followed because the party is “always on the side of those who fight”.
“Whenever there’s a struggle led by young people, I participate because I believe that young people have every right to get involved and fight,” Boyard said. “The movement took off because all the high school students looked at each other and said: ‘We’re not being respected. So we’re going to make sure we’re respected’.”
When he was a high school student, Boyard participated in a blockade, prompted by an asbestos problem, in 2018. Thanks to the protests, the students were able to get the school rebuilt.
“I’ve already won a victory this way, and we were justified in doing it. [The current students], too, are justified in doing it,” Boyard said.
As she inflated her dinosaur costume to join the protests in the centre of Paris, Kamelia wanted to send a message of hope.
“Everyone is rising up – all the young people. We’re a generation who’s truly awakened. It makes me so happy,” she said.

À l'origine de l'affaire : une séquence diffusée sur CNews à l'automne 2025 où Erik Tegnér s'en prenait à Yaël Braun-Pivet, Alain Minc et Jacques Attali. Qualifiés d'antisémites par des experts et dénoncés par StreetPress, ces propos ont déclenché une procédure-bâillon à l'encontre du média indépendant. 
Absence du plaignant, lapsus révélateur de son avocat, citations de Bernanos, et coût financier des procédures pour la presse indépendante : décryptage complet d'une audience hors norme avec Johan Weisz-Myara, fondateur de Streetpress.
Face à l’extrême droite, ne rien lâcher !
C’est pied à pied, argument contre argument qu’il faut combattre l’extrême droite. Et c’est ce que nous faisons chaque jour dans l’Humanité.
Face aux attaques incessantes des racistes et des porteurs de haine : soutenez-nous ! Ensemble, faisons entendre une autre voix dans ce débat public toujours plus nauséabond.
Je veux en savoir plus.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.title: Artsy and Artnet Acquire First Thursday as Art-Tech Expansion Picks Up Speed
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ar.text:
Artsy and Artnet have another deal: The two art-market platforms announced the acquisition of First Thursday, a London-based startup that uses artificial intelligence to help galleries keep track of collectors, manage relationships, and, ideally, sell more art.
The purchase comes seven months after Artsy and Artnet joined forces under Beowolff Capital, the investment firm founded by Andrew Wolff. And just last week, Artnet announced a partnership with Kalshi, the prediction-market platform that allows users to bet on auction results, prompting a rather unenthusiastic response from parts of the art world.
The latest deal, whose financial terms weren’t disclosed, is a little less controversial. It also gives a clearer picture of what the combined company is trying to build: a single system that galleries can use to manage almost every part of their businesses.
Founded in 2023 by Callum Hale-Thomson, First Thursday specializes in what it calls “collector intelligence.” In practice, that means gathering years of emails, sales records, inquiries, and notes into one searchable place, then using AI to help dealers figure out which collectors might be interested in a particular work.
Hale-Thomson, whose parents are both artists, told ARTnews that the idea came to him after he spent six months working inside London galleries, effectively serving as their IT guy and watching how they operated. He found that many were sitting on years of valuable information without an easy way to use it.
“You’re sitting on an unbelievable trove of information,” he said, describing the emails, notebooks, and other records galleries accumulate over time. The problem was finding anything useful when it was needed.
First Thursday’s existing software helps with that. At an art fair, for example, a dealer can scan a visitor’s business card, record which painting caught their eye, and send a follow-up email directly from thier phone. The system can also bring together past correspondence and publicly available information about collectors, helping galleries identify potential buyers they might otherwise have overlooked.
Under the new ownership, Hale-Thomson and his team will help develop a broader gallery-management platform, scheduled to launch for select Artsy and Artnet partners in early 2027. It will combine collector records with inventory management, sales tools, invoicing, marketing, and online viewing rooms. Galleries will also be able to publish works to Artsy and Artnet directly from the system.
The initial focus will be smaller galleries, which often lack the money or staff to maintain sophisticated software.
Alex Forbes, who oversees global partnerships for Artsy and Artnet, told ARTnews that the smallest gallery partners will be able to use the core system without paying more than they already do for their Artsy subscriptions.
Larger galleries will be able to purchase additional features and access for bigger teams. Exact pricing will be announced when the platform launches.
“We want it to be the easiest to start out with for a small gallery,” Forbes said, while also making it useful for businesses with more complicated operations.
The move takes Artsy and Artnet further into a competitive market for gallery software, where established companies such as Artlogic already offer inventory and business-management tools. Last year, Artlogic merged with ArtCloud, another sign of consolidation in the art-tech business. (Artsy is already integrated with Artlogic and Artcloud, which, according to an Artsy spokesperson, the company will continue to support.)
Forbes acknowledged that galleries have different needs and that no single product will necessarily suit everyone. But he said the broader plan is to connect the company’s existing marketplaces and pricing data with the software that galleries use to run their businesses.
One potentially sensitive question is what happens to all that collector information. Artsy and Artnet say galleries will retain control of their data, which will remain private unless they choose to share it with the platforms.
For Hale-Thomson, who will remain with the business, the opportunity is to bring more sophisticated tools to galleries that haven’t traditionally been able to afford them.
And for Artsy and Artnet, the acquisition marks another step toward becoming something considerably bigger than two websites where people look at art, check prices, and occasionally buy something. Increasingly, they want to provide the software that keeps the business running.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: Cinema de afetos que revoam: Feito Pipa, de Allan Deberton
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Émerson Cardoso
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
Após dirigir três filmes de curta-metragem, Allan Deberton dirigiu o aclamado Pacarrete, em 2019, que conta com Marcélia Cartaxo no papel principal. Com essa obra que foi sucesso de público e de crítica, e foi amplamente premiada, ele inicia a trajetória de diretor de filmes de longa-metragem. Depois de Pacarrete, que se tornou um dos filmes mais relevantes da cinematografia nacional, ele dirigiu, em 2024, O meu melhor amigo — a ampliação de seu segundo curta-metragem, realizado em 2013.
Agora, no ano de 2026, ele oferece ao público seu terceiro filme: Feito Pipa. Essa obra obteve êxito desde o início, pois tem recebido prêmios nacionais e internacionais — e tornou-se o representante do Brasil no Óscar. Com direção, roteiro, fotografia e elenco extraordinários (Teca Pereira, Yuri Gomes e Lázaro Ramos, dentre outros, brilham), o grande mérito dessa obra, além de seus aspectos técnicos notáveis, tem a ver com a atmosfera sensível, afetiva e humana apresentada na relação de Gugu com a avó Dilma (Teca Pereira), com o pai Batista (Lázaro Ramos) e com os amigos (e inimigos) da escola.
Gugu é uma criança queer de 11 anos que ama futebol tanto quanto ama usar maquiagem e adereços coloridos. Órfão de mãe, ele encontra na avó o afeto, a acolhida, o amor e a cumplicidade que o pai (amoroso, mas pautado em posturas marcadas pelos ditames e convenções do patriarcado) não consegue lhe oferecer efetivamente.
A talentosa Teca Pereira encontra nesse filme um espaço perfeito para mostrar o quão intensa é sua atuação. Dilma, como a atriz a constrói, mostra-se destemida, livre e forte, porém, ao ser acometida pela doença que lhe tira a memória, a personagem ganha novas camadas — e Teca Pereira conduz com maestria esse processo de mudança da personagem.
Sem que o neto possa reverter, embora o tente, em sua solidão de criança comprometida a não perder a avó (que é seu mundo em plenitude), Dilma passa a ser apagada pela doença, momento em que a atriz mostra vulnerabilidade, singeleza e humanidade em seu olhar de profundezas inesgotáveis.
A relação de Dilma com Gugu é o grande acontecimento dentro da obra: avó e neto encontram um no outro companhia, afeto e, sobretudo, liberdade para serem o que são. Isso é de tal modo bem construído nesse filme que, quando a avó vai perdendo a memória e o neto vai perdendo seu mundo de proteção e amor, o espectador passa por uma profusão de sentimentos.
Gugu, interpretado brilhantemente por Yuri Gomes, é uma personagem solar e vívida em seu desejo de agir no mundo como herói, jogador de futebol, estudante etc. Quando a avó vai apagando-se, porém, ele também se apaga.
A cena em que a avó é levada a um abrigo, sob decisão de Batista (interpretado por Lázaro Ramos em uma atuação marcante), o mundo feliz de Gugu entra em colapso.
Vale ressaltar que Lázaro Ramos delineia com maestria a dualidade de sua personagem Batista, que é um homem que ama o filho, mas não aceita o seu modo de ser, marcado que está pelas convenções sociais.
Quando vai visitar a avó pela primeira vez, na companhia do pai, Gugu se veste sem os adereços, cores e brilhos de antes — ele está forçosamente condicionado a vestir-se quase como o pai, e as tonalidades de azul que usa, sendo essa cor simbolicamente representativa do masculino, mostra uma adequação às regras impostas pela figura paterna.
Após a avó ser tirada dele, tudo em sua vida perde a cor e aprofunda nele a sensação de ausência. Embora tenha amigos na escola, e possa contar com o pai e a madrasta Patrícia (muito bem interpretada por Georgina Castro), Gugu entristece, perde a alegria e passa pela necessidade de agir de forma destemida para reencontrar seu paraíso perdido (a cena final aponta isso).
Na coragem de Gugu reverbera a coragem de Eliane (que foi capaz de brigar contra homens poderosos, para que a barragem não fizesse desaparecer a cidade e, em decorrência disso, levou doze tiros). Ironicamente, à medida que a barragem faz reaparecer os escombros da antiga cidade, Dilma perde a memória. O que parece mais doloroso, dentro da narrativa, é que a avó passa a esquecer do neto — isso torna a experiência de perder a avó ainda mais dolorosa para ele. O carinho de um pelo outro se esfacela, porque a memória poderá tirar isso deles. Gugu vivencia, cada vez mais consciente da situação, a dor de ser esquecido pela pessoa a quem mais ama.
Allan Deberton, com Feito Pipa, oferece mais um filme grandioso para inserir-se no rol das grandes obras cinematográficas do país. Pacarrete e Feito Pipa dialogam por trazerem personagens femininas singularizadas pelo envelhecimento — e pela loucura, em Pacarrete, e pelo adoecimento que resulta no apagamento da memória, em Feito Pipa. Em ambas as obras, estamos diante de mulheres extraordinárias no que há de simples e de belo em suas condições existenciais.
Para finalizar, ainda comovidos, três itens não podem ser esquecidos dentro dessa narrativa delicada, profunda e sensível: 1) o encontro de almas entre o neto e a avó, com a coragem de ambos de serem quem são, 2) a simbologia da pipa, que ora voa e revoa no céu, ora está perdida e desamparada sem poder alçar os voos para os quais está “vocacionada”, e 3) a canção Time after time, de Cindy Lauper, que é onipresente no filme — e cria ecos que reverberam durante e após ele terminar.
E a pergunta que fica é: por que esse filme lírico, profundo e sensível acaba? Dito isso, Dilma e Gugu, com a humanidade complexa e a sensibilidade intensa que demonstram, não deveriam ir embora nunca, por isso muitas pessoas demonstraram a necessidade de revê-los várias vezes nas salas de cinema do país.
Dilma e Gugu ficam presentes na alma de quem os viu em suas peripécias entre cômicas e comoventes. A pipa que revoa, simbolicamente, fala-nos sobre a existência de amor e humanidade. Isso (e muito mais) torna esse filme inesquecível!
*Émerson Cardoso é doutor, mestre, especialista e graduado em Letras. Pesquisador em Literaturas de Língua Portuguesa e Francesa, Professor e Escritor. Publicou, dentre outras obras, os livros: O baile das assimetrias (2022), Jornadas (2023) e Romanceiros (que recebeu o I Prêmio Literário Demócrito Rocha de 2024). Organizou Juazeiro tem artistas, Juazeiro tem poesia: manifesto poético (2024).
**Este é um artigo de opinião. A visão do autor não necessariamente expressa a linha editorial do jornal Brasil de Fato.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120392.title: Koalition | Koalitionsausschuss wird zur Belastungsprobe für Merz
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120392.author: Patrick Lempges
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120392.text:
- Politik
- Koalition
Koalitionsausschuss wird zur Belastungsprobe für Merz
Merz verspricht Stromsteuersenkung, doch die SPD fordert eine Gegenfinanzierung. In der CDU wächst der Unmut über Koalitionspartner und Kanzler.
Es geht um fünf Milliarden Euro, aber längst nicht mehr nur um eine Steuer. Wenn sich die Spitzen von Union und SPD am Dienstagabend im Kanzleramt zum Koalitionsausschuss treffen, steht die von Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) versprochene Senkung der Stromsteuer für alle im Zentrum. Der Kanzler steht unter enormem Druck in den eigenen Reihen und hat abermals vorschnell eine Einigung angekündigt, obwohl die Gegenfinanzierung wohl weiter ungeklärt ist. Für Merz geht es daher wieder um seine Glaubwürdigkeit. Vor allem aber hat sich der Streit um die Stromsteuer zu einem Konflikt über die politische Ausrichtung der Union entwickelt: Welche Entlastungen sollen Vorrang haben, wer soll sie bezahlen und wie viel Sozialstaat darf die Haushaltskonsolidierung kosten?
Am Montag bekräftigte Merz nach einem Treffen mit dem CSU-Vorstand, die Stromsteuer solle 2027 auf das europäische Mindestmaß sinken. »Wir werden uns morgen einigen«, verkündete er. Doch ausgerechnet im Finanzministerium scheint man von der angekündigten Lösung wenig zu wissen. Auf die Frage danach, wie die angekündigte Lösung aussehen werde, hieß es aus Kreisen des Hauses: »Das wüssten wir auch gern.« Für die Ausweitung der Senkung fehlen im Haushalt bislang rund fünf Milliarden Euro jährlich. Eine Gegenfinanzierung fanden die Haushälter von Union und SPD nicht. Im Etat für 2027 mit einem Volumen von rund 561 Milliarden Euro ist das Versprechen nicht berücksichtigt.
Ein Drei-Personen-Haushalt mit 4000 Kilowattstunden Jahresverbrauch würde nach Berechnungen des Vergleichportals Verivox nach der Steuersenkung rund 90 Euro im Jahr sparen. Marcel Fratzscher, Präsident des Deutschen Instituts für Wirtschaftsforschung (DIW) hält die Maßnahme für sozial unausgewogen. Gerade Familien mit geringen Einkommen profitierten kaum.
Streit um Prioritäten
Die Stromsteuer ist für die Union mittlerweile eine Frage der politischen Handlungsfähigkeit. Union und SPD hatten die Senkung im Koalitionsvertrag vereinbart. Bislang wurde sie allerdings nur für das produzierende Gewerbe sowie die Land- und Forstwirtschaft umgesetzt. Dass die privaten Haushalte und auch weitere Wirtschaftsbereiche leer ausgingen, sorgt für erheblichen Unmut.
Der Ärger darüber entlud sich in der vergangenen Woche bei einer Sondersitzung der Unionsfraktion. »Da hat es auch ordentlich geknallt«, berichtete der CDU-Finanzpolitiker Mathias Middelberg im Deutschlandfunk. »Da haben gestern so ziemlich alle ihre Meinung gesagt.« Die Aussprache der Union dauerte deutlich länger als die der SPD.
Middelberg selbst, der dem Wirtschaftsflügel zugerechnet wird, stellte die Prioritäten der Regierung infrage. Er halte es für sinnvoller, die Stromsteuer zu senken, als die dritte Stufe der Mütterrente umzusetzen. Der Wirtschaftsflügel verspricht sich von der Stromsteuersenkung – gerade weil dies auch alle sonstigen Betriebe beträfe – ein Wirtschaftswachstum. Damit berührt er jedoch einen Konflikt, der innerhalb der Union schon länger schwelt: Die CSU hatte die Ausweitung der Mütterrente auf Eltern von vor 1992 geborenen Kindern durchgesetzt – es ist ihr Kernprojekt. »Die Mütterrente ist beschlossen, sie steht nicht zur Disposition«, erklärte CSU-Landesgruppenchef Alexander Hoffmann, auch Markus Söder lehnt es ab, die Rentenleistung zugunsten der Stromsteuersenkung wieder infrage zu stellen, unterstützt jedoch auch die Pläne zur Stromsteuersenkung.
Nordrhein-Westfalens Ministerpräsident Hendrik Wüst (CDU) fordert unmissverständlich die Senkung der Stromsteuer für alle. »Das muss jetzt passieren«, sagte er bei einem kleinen Parteitag der niedersächsischen CDU. Die zunächst auf einzelne Branchen beschränkte Entlastung sei ein Fehler gewesen.
Die Senkung der Stromsteuer wird von weiten Teilen der Union getragen, nur über ihre Finanzierung und Priorisierung zu anderen Projekten wird intern gestritten. Bereits Anfang November verlangten die Vorsitzenden der CDU- und CSU-Landtagsfraktionen gemeinsam, die Stromsteuer auf das europäische Mindestmaß zu senken. Auch der CDU-Arbeitnehmerflügel fordert die Absenkung, um die Lebenshaltungskosten in den Griff zu bekommen.
Merz unter Druck
Währenddessen kritisiert Pascal Reddig, Vorsitzender der Jungen Gruppe der Unionsfraktion, die Kommunikation des Kanzlers. »Wir sollten keine Ankündigungspolitik machen«, sagte er bei N-TV. Ein Thema dürfe nicht öffentlich so stark in den Vordergrund gerückt werden, wenn die Gegenfinanzierung ungeklärt ist. Die Debatte habe eine »extreme Glaubwürdigkeitskrise« ausgelöst. Reddig nahm auch die eigene Partei in die Verantwortung: Es sei schließlich nicht gelungen, fünf Milliarden Euro in einem Haushalt von mehr als 550 Milliarden Euro zu mobilisieren.
Noch schärfer fällt die Kritik im Brandenburger Ortsverband Großbeeren aus. Dieser forderte in einer Mitgliederversammlung einstimmig den Rücktritt von Merz als Kanzler und CDU-Vorsitzendem. Verbandschef Adrian Hepp begründete dies mit der ausgebliebenen Stromsteuersenkung. Merz habe ein zentrales Wahlversprechen gebrochen und lasse sich von der SPD »am Ring durch die Manege führen«. Hepps persönlicher Wunschkandidat für die Nachfolge heißt übrigens Markus Söder. Dass ausgerechnet die Stromsteuer zum Anlass einer Rücktrittsforderung wird, zeigt, wie viel Frustration sich in der Union aufgestaut hat und wie viel auf diese Auseinandersetzung projiziert wird.
Die Frage der Gegenfinanzierung
Hinter dem Streit stehen unterschiedliche Vorstellungen darüber, wie knappe Mittel verteilt werden sollen. Die Union setzt auf Steuersenkungen und fordert zugleich, Subventionen und staatliche Ausgaben zurückzufahren. Middelberg kündigte an, angesichts des geringen Wirtschaftswachstums müsse stärker bei Förderprogrammen, Finanzhilfen und Sozialausgaben gekürzt werden. »Da gibt es gar keinen anderen Weg«, sagte er. Auch die CDU- und CSU-Landtagsfraktionschefs sehen bei Rente, Gesundheit und Pflege »Reformbedarf«.
Die SPD wehrt sich aber gegen weitere Einschnitte bei Sozialleistungen und setzt auf Umverteilung. Sie kann sich höhere Körperschaft- oder Abgeltungsteuer auf Kapitalerträge vorstellen. Die Union lehnt das wiederum ab.
Der Sozialverband Deutschland warnt derweil davor, Mütterrente und Stromsteuersenkung gegeneinander auszuspielen. »Gesamtgesellschaftliche Aufgaben müssen verlässlich aus Steuermitteln finanziert werden«, sagte SoVD-Chefin Michaela Engelmeier.
Weitere Baustellen der Koalition
Neben den Steuern stehen weitere Konflikte auf der Tagesordnung. Bei der Rentenreform will Merz am Dienstag offene Streitpunkte klären und einen Zeitplan vereinbaren. Vor allem die mögliche Abschaffung der abschlagsfreien Rente nach 45 Beitragsjahren ist umstritten – die SPD und Ost-Landesverbände der CDU stemmen sich dagegen. Ein Kabinettsbeschluss vor der Weihnachtspause ist dennoch das Ziel.
Die SPD will zudem den Spritpreisdeckel von Wirtschaftsministerin Katherina Reiche (CDU) thematisieren. Ihr Entwurf sieht einen Höchstpreis erst vor, wenn Benzin und Diesel drei Wochen deutlich über dem EU-Durchschnitt liegen. Die SPD hält das für wirkungslos, fordert stattdessen tatsächliche Höchstpreise und begrenzte Margen. Klingbeil verlangt außerdem ein Bekenntnis zur Übergewinnsteuer, die Union lehnt sie national ab.
Die Vorsitzende der Partei Die Linke, Ines Schwerdtner, erklärte dazu, dass mit dieser Steuer die fünf Milliarden Euro für die Stromsteuersenkung schnell aufzutreiben seien: »Die Bundesregierung muss sich nur endlich an die Übergewinne der Mineralölkonzerne trauen.« In Deutschland könnten somit 6,7 Milliarden Euro abgeschöpft werden.
Ob sich der Koalitionsausschuss auf eine Finanzierung der Stromsteuersenkung einigen kann, ist offen. Merz hat sich mit seinem Versprechen selbst unter Zugzwang gesetzt. Eine Einigung ohne tragfähige Gegenfinanzierung würde den Streit nur vertagen. Scheitert er erneut, dürfte nicht nur der Unmut in der eigenen Fraktion wachsen. Auch die Frage nach seiner Führungskraft würde erneut aufbrechen. Mit Agenturen.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: first draft of agreement under pressure as climate negotiations enter final days
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Ajit Niranjan
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Welcome to day 2 of week 2, as the clock winds down with just four days left to hammer through thorny divisions with lots left on the negotiating table. Monday brought out a first draft of the agreement but it’s far from set in stone.
The 18-page document includes 144 separate items, including many that are still being hotly disputed. Language on the transition away from fossil fuels, calls to reel in overshoot (which under current policies is projected to surge past 1.5C to 2.7C of warming by 2100), and stronger financial support for developing countries were outlined as a way to “draw out parties”, Chris Bowen, climate and energy minister of Australia and lead negotiator of the talks told the Guardian on Monday.
In other words, changes are expected. Insiders aren’t planning for the next draft to come quickly and it’s possible (likely) that the talks will go into overtime this week.
New government data published on Tuesday reveals nature in the UK is continuing its steep decline.
The latest biodiversity indicators produced by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs show that 11 out of 15 species measures have deteriorated over the long term, with 10 of these also declining in recent years. Breeding birds, butterflies, and priority species are among those continuing to suffer.
The data on the decline in nature comes after the prime minister called for greater climate resilience at Cop31. Richard Benwell, chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said: “Today’s biodiversity indicators show that nature is still disappearing around us. Species abundance has fallen by 40% since 1970, priority species by an awful 80%, and most protected sites are damaged or degraded.
“We cannot build resilience while our natural defences are crumbling around us. Healthy ecosystems are our best protection against floods, droughts, and extreme heat. Restoring nature is not an optional extra in tackling environmental hazards – it is essential to save lives and livelihoods.
“The Government must match its climate leadership abroad with urgent action and serious investment in nature at home. Business as usual is failing. We need sustained funding and stronger action to restore wildlife, revive habitats, and protect the natural systems on which our safety, resilience and prosperity depend.”
A spectre is hanging over Cop31. The spectre of AI.
Artificial intelligence is threatening to massively increase power demand around the world. And with that, carbon emissions. But it is barely spoken about in the halls and meeting rooms of the UN climate summit
Or at least publicly. Behind closed doors is another matter. According to research, almost 500 people at Cop31 are from corporate groups and companies involved in the AI buildout.
Lighthouse Reports, a public interest investigative journalism platform, said it counted a total of 495 registered attenders from 86 companies associated with building out AI infrastructure.
Engineering, design and construction had the largest representation, with 161 attenders. Companies that offer power and electrical equipment to datacentres were the second largest group.
That was followed by 54 representatives of datacentre operators, hyperscalers, cloud and AI companies including Amazon (AWS), Alibaba (Alibaba Cloud), ByteDance, Google, NTT DATA, Microsoft, Equinix, EdgeConneX, Meta and NVIDIA.
Discussion of AI in Antalya has been limited. It has no specific agenda item. But at the beginning of the second week of the UN climate summit the Turkish presidency unveiled a voluntary “Antalya AI pledge”. It sought to encourage nations to commit to assess the growing environmental risks of the technology, while tapping its potential for finding climate solutions.
However, it fell flat among nations invited to a high level meeting to introduce it. The pledge received 80 endorsements. But barely 10 nations were among them while the rest were companies or civil society groups, AFP reported.
The pledge was then supposed to be launched at a press conference, which was cancelled and rescheduled. And then the replacement time was cancelled as well, this time with no time or date when it is supposed to take place. The Turkish and Australian Cop31 presidencies did not respond to a request for comment.
In any case, AI has not proven to be a reliable partner when it comes to climate information. A UN-backed study published on Monday found the mildest challenge from users quickly turns AI models into climate crisis deniers.
There are a lot of competing voices at Cop31. But for those willing to escape the florescent lights and the unceasing hum of activity within the Blue Zone conference centre, an oasis outsides offers the voices that may be missing from negotiations: bird song and forest sounds are pumped through a speaker surrounding a tranquil pond providing a welcome break from the din inside.
The display created by Turkey’s General Directorate of Forestry was mostly being used as a nice backdrop for sidebar conversations and smoke breaks around midday Tuesday, but at least a handful of people were spotted sitting in the grass solo, perhaps catching a bit of peace before the inevitable pull to head back inside.
Draft deal a 'shopping list' fundamentally at odds with delivery, EU negotiator warns
Speaking at a press conference just now, the EU’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, lamented the language on climate finance, trade and carbon capture (CCS) in the draft decision. He argued that the focus of this Cop was supposed to be on implementation. “It had the characteristics of a shopping list,” he said of yesterday’s text.
“That, in our view, is fundamentally at odds with the logic of implementation,” he added. “Delivering what we have already agreed on, that should be the focus. And that is why we do think that – particularly in the domain of finance, particularly in the domain of trade, also in the domain of CCS, and suggesting that might be the solution to everything – I think the cover decision does not go in the right direction and needs significant change.”
Hoekstra expressed his support for the Turkish co-host’s electrification push to get 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035. “The more, the better. The quicker, the better. The cleaner, the better.”
However, he indicated the EU was flexible on how clean that electricity should be, “if, to some degree, a bit of pragmatism is needed to bring others into the tent”.
The position was echoed by Darragh O’Brien, the climate minister of Ireland, which holds the rotating Presidency of the Council of the EU. He referenced the 700 million people who do not even have access to electricity, and the progress being made “not just exclusively” through renewables.
Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia biggest exporters of historical fossil fuel emissions
The co-host of the Cop31 climate summit is among the countries with the greatest responsibility for having exporting fuels that destroy a stable climate, according to new analysis by Carbon Brief.
Between 1850 and 2025, Australia shipped coal, oil and gas that added 28.1bn tonnes of CO2 to the atmosphere, the analysis found. Only Russia and Saudia Arabia bore greater responsibility, with exported emissions more than double Australia’s.
There is no standard way to divvy up the blame for fouling the atmosphere with planet-heating pollutants. Traditional measures focus on where the fuels were burned, and can even account for the carbon embodied in imported goods.
This new approach puts the spotlight on the countries that extract the fuels. A country such as Saudi Arabia shoots up the ranking when including exported emissions in the tally, with more historical responsibility than even India, a country with 40 times as many people.
While the two biggest historical polluters, the US and China, are net importers of fossil fuels, they still sit at the top of this table. The bulk of their climate damage comes from fuels they dug up at home.
Studies have found that fossil fuel-burning must drop drastically to keep the planet from heating to horrific levels. While the fossil fuel industry and exporting countries argue against cutting production before demand falls, and some activists have fought to shift the focus away from consumption to the companies supplying dirty energy, most economists I’ve asked about it have made the case that both sides of the equation would need to fall in tandem to avoid counterproductive rebound effects.
Thousands of miles away from where negotiators are grappling over how to address the serious impacts from a warming world, the California coast is experiencing a glimpse of what’s to come.
The severe effects of a historic El Niño have dramatically raised sea levels along the shores of the western US, and enormous ocean waves are chewing through swaths of the coastline. Beachside homes have been destroyed by the conditions that have also harmed marine ecosystems.
Meanwhile, ocean temperatures in the region have smashed through previous records, setting off a cascade of effects that may worsen over the next few months.
“It is like nothing we’ve ever seen,” Dr Jono Wilson, the science director for The Nature Conservancy’s oceans program told the Guardian last week, as scores of dead seabirds and marine mammals washed up on beaches, life supporting a vital food web ocean ecosystems depend on plummeted, and violent surf crashed into the coast. “We just are trying to figure out how to wrap our heads around the sheer scale of this event.”
As a storm system churned over the San Francisco Bay Area early this week, adding another layer of hazards to the swollen tides, behemoth waves flooded into parking lots along the beaches and prompted evacuation warnings in nearby communities. The federally-run National Weather Service forecasted waves between 25-35ft, with some up to 50ft. There have already been deaths in recent weeks, as beach-goers were ripped from the shore into the water.
A rare tornado warning was also issued in the region this week. Twin whirling water spouts were spotted over San Francisco waters, as forecasters warned a series of severe storms could bring torrential rains and the threat of flash flooding or debris flows over the next week.
This super El Nino, a climate phenomenon defined by unusually warm equatorial ocean conditions, is rapidly heating and expanding parts of the Pacific, compounding the impacts from the climate crisis and extreme marine heatwaves that have already stressed ocean ecosystems and their inhabitants. It’s expected to strengthen over the next few months, and California is bracing for more rising tides and extreme weather that could overwhelm infrastructure. Scientists have said that the impacts are but a harbinger of what lies ahead as the climate crisis unfolds.
Perhaps the cosiest corner of Cop31 is tucked against a wall filled with hopes for the future. At the children and youth pavilion participants are invited to leave a mark – even if it’s just a colourful scribble.
Popular AI chatbots quickly turning to climate denial, UN-backed study finds
Graham Readfearn
Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.
While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change”.
The report uncovered a strong tendency for AI models to be sycophantic, meaning the model is more interested in pleasing the user than standing by facts – an issue identified when people turn to AI chatbots for personal advice.
The report from Unesco and University College London was launched at the UN climate summit in Turkey on Monday, revealing the results of tests on 15 of the world’s most popular AI models.
Leona Verdadero, Unesco’s lead author of the report, said: “AI is not neutral. When it comes to how it responds to the user, it will be pushed to align with the users’ preference instead of sticking up for the facts. The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s [misinformation] shows it is weak and fallible.”
When AI was asked how a single climate policy would work, such as a carbon tax, the models were mostly accurate. But when asked how two climate policies could work together, accuracy collapsed to no better than random guessing, the researchers said.
Just three out of 40 major European cities currently meet revised EU limits for air pollution, with cities in southern and eastern Europe lagging behind their Nordic counterparts, a study has found.
Copenhagen, Greater Stockholm and Greater Helsinki were the only cities to meet all four limits for nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate matter air pollution, according to environmental group Clean Cities.
Athens and Bucharest came bottom of the rankings, with all 11 cities receiving the lowest grades concentrated in southern and central and eastern Europe. Athens recorded the highest average nitrogen dioxide concentration, at 37.6 micrograms per cubic metre.
The report found that measures including low-emission zones, electric buses, school streets and improved cycling infrastructure had helped some cities make significant progress. London, Paris and Stuttgart were among those to have reduced air pollution substantially over the past decade.
Barbara Stoll, founder and senior director of Clean Cities, said air pollution was “not inevitable” and that strong political leadership could make a significant difference.
She said relatively affordable measures, including expanding cycling networks and introducing school streets, could help cities improve air quality.
Australia was dubbed “Fossil of the Day” yesterday for what campaigners called a masterclass in climate hypocrisy.
The title, awarded by Climate Action Network (CAN) each day to a country blocking progress, singled out the Cop31 co-host for presiding over negotiations to rescue the climate while signing off on polluting projects.
Australian fossil fuel subsidies were estimated at 16.3bn Australian dollars this year, eclipsing the country’s annual climate finance offering by an order of magnitude. The government has also approved 38 coal and gas projects since taking office in 2022.
“With four days to go, the Presidency lacks sufficient urgency,” said Denis Cauchi, CEO of Climate Action Network Australia. “Australia professes to be a friend to the Pacific, yet at home they are expanding the biggest threat to the Pacific – coal and gas. You cannot call yourself a global climate leader while fuelling the biggest cause of the climate crisis – fossil fuels.”
The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to a key environmental initiative, with complainants arguing football’s governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action.
Fifa is a signatory to the UN’s Sports for Climate Action Framework, a coalition which seeks to persuade sporting organisations to “work together to achieve a climate-resilient future”. Under the framework, signatories agree to cut their greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and to “partner with key stakeholders to deliver joint climate action”. They can have their status as a signatory removed, however, if “sincerity in participation or ability to participate is a cause for concern”.
According to five organisations that have submitted a joint complaint to the UN, Fifa’s actions are inconsistent with its words. In a letter to executives at the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, they argue “being a signatory of the Framework means making a commitment to both organisational climate progress and climate leadership. On the basis of the facts laid out below, we assert that Fifa has a record of failure on each of these key commitments.”
The letter claims Fifa has undermined its commitments by expanding the size of its tournaments, with the men’s World Cup increasing from 64 matches in 2022 to 104 matches in 16 cities across three countries this past summer, making it what the complainants say is “the most polluting World Cup ever”. In 2030, by which time Fifa’s emissions should have been halved, the World Cup is due to be held in six countries across three different continents, with potentially 64 teams and even more matches.
The complainants acknowledge Fifa launched a climate strategy in 2021, committing it to halving emissions by 2030 and reaching net zero by 2040. “However,” the letter says, “that strategy is not clear on how exactly these targets will be achieved. The evidence indicates that Fifa has expanded, rather than reduced, its emissions in the years since, principally by choosing to expand the footprint of its major tournaments.”
A second part of the complaint argues Fifa has failed in its responsibility to “champion transformative climate action” by agreeing a multi-year commercial arrangement with the Saudi Arabian energy giant Aramco as a “major worldwide partner”.
There’s plenty to go through in the coming days beyond the key sticking points. As part of a complementary platform to the negotiations, Cop31 is organised into “thematic days” and Tuesday is slated for “Oceans, Seas, Nature and Land Use”.
Cop31 was dubbed a “Blue Cop” in anticipation that there would be substantial actions taken on oceans and that ocean-based solutions could be worked into climate commitments. At the start of the summit Ocean Conservancy vice-president, Dr. Fatima Candance, pointed to this year’s mascot – a loggerhead turtle – as an important symbol for the work. “But symbolism alone won’t deliver the action we need,” she said, urging leaders to move from “pledges to projects”.
Speaking of pledges, last year’s land use pledge to recognise or strengthen rights across 160m hectares in tropical forest countries by 2030 is also up for review on Tuesday.
More than 50 Indigenous Peoples’, local community and Afro-descendant Peoples’ organizations and allied civil society groups from around the world issued a joint letter on Monday urging international leaders to ensure territorial rights are protected not just on paper but on the ground.
“Success must be measured not only by hectares recognised, but by territorial rights upheld, governance strengthened and communities empowered to determine their own futures, free from unwanted extractive and large-scale industrial activities,” the letter states.
That includes support politically and financially, with calls for direct funding for Indigenous Peoples, local and Afro-descendant communities. The letter followed a report issued last week from a collective of organizations that showed how oil, gas, mining, logging, and industry are threatening territories.
“Without securing our territorial rights, human rights violations continue, conflicts escalate, and our territories that sustain life remain under threat,” said Dinamam Tuxa, Executive Coordinator, Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil (APIB) in a statement issued with the letter. “Demarcating Indigenous Peoples territories is not only a matter of justice; it is an effective climate policy.”
Welcome to day 2 of week 2, as the clock winds down with just four days left to hammer through thorny divisions with lots left on the negotiating table. Monday brought out a first draft of the agreement but it’s far from set in stone.
The 18-page document includes 144 separate items, including many that are still being hotly disputed. Language on the transition away from fossil fuels, calls to reel in overshoot (which under current policies is projected to surge past 1.5C to 2.7C of warming by 2100), and stronger financial support for developing countries were outlined as a way to “draw out parties”, Chris Bowen, climate and energy minister of Australia and lead negotiator of the talks told the Guardian on Monday.
In other words, changes are expected. Insiders aren’t planning for the next draft to come quickly and it’s possible (likely) that the talks will go into overtime this week.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/uk-im.text:
UK imposes sanctions on eight Israeli firms and a group blocking Gaza aid
The British government has unveiled its first set of sanctions against Israeli companies linked to illegal West Bank settlements, after announcing comprehensive sanctions in September.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the sanctions on Tuesday, shortly before tenders for the E1 settlement bloc - which would effectively split the occupied West Bank in two - are scheduled to be allocated by the Israeli government.
The sanctions are targeting eight Israeli construction, property development and architectural business firms.
The UK is also sanctioning Tsav9, an Israeli group involved in stopping aid trucks from entering Gaza, which the United States also sanctioned in 2024.
The Foreign Office described Tsaz9 as "an Israeli activist movement whose stated mission has been to stop humanitarian aid entering the Gaza Strip, and which has organised and carried out blockades of crossings, ports and roads used by humanitarian aid convoys bound for Gaza".
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution."
The foreign secretary added: "And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable."
Miliband also said the UK was "committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike".
The Foreign Office has published a list of the Israeli companies sanctioned on Tuesday.
Sanctions rollout could take nine months
Chris Doyle, the director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding, said: "This is a welcome first step under the new UK sanctions regime including on construction companies but also Tsav which blocks aid into Gaza."
However, he argues that the measures fail to address the role of the Israeli state itself in settlement expansion and restrictions on humanitarian aid entering Gaza.
"The greatest flaw is that it is the Israeli government that builds the settlements and it is the Israeli government that restricts life-saving aid into Gaza," he added.
Implementing the full sanctions announced in September could take up to nine months, according to government sources.
Senior UK government figures privately told Middle East Eye last month that even if Benjamin Netanyahu is no longer Israel's prime minister, they intend to implement comprehensive sanctions, including against companies providing construction and real estate services for settlement expansion.
But within the Foreign Office, MEE understands, some officials have been pushing for the sanctions to target Israeli companies complicit in the illegal settlements but not British companies that are complicit.
Officials have also argued that companies that operate mostly within Israel itself, as well as in occupied Palestinian territory, should not be affected by the sanctions.
If implemented fully, the new sanctions would require British banks, pension funds and asset managers to divest from companies operating in settlements.
They would also stop financial institutions from providing mortgages, insurance and other services that support settlement activity.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
Infantino’s FIFA challenger Diallo claims to have support beyond Europe
French football chief Philippe Diallo says he has received ‘spontaneous signs of strong support’ against Infantino.
French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo says he has the backing of countries beyond Europe in his bid to depose Gianni Infantino in the upcoming FIFA presidential election.
“To beat him you need 106 votes, which is a majority,” Diallo said on Tuesday following his nomination as the European governing body UEFA’s representative.
“It is now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents, but already since yesterday I have received spontaneous signs of strong support which will be revealed in the coming days.”
Diallo was speaking in Paris the day after accepting an invitation from UEFA to stand against Infantino in the election to be held next March.
UEFA, which has 55 member associations, said that European nations had “unanimously pledged their full support” to Diallo, ahead of Wednesday’s deadline for candidates to declare themselves.
Under its Slovenian president Aleksander Ceferin, UEFA has led the opposition to Infantino since his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors was revealed in July.
Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of widespread uproar, but UEFA has since gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the current FIFA president in Switzerland.
Diallo announced in September that the French Football Federation (FFF) was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election, following similar announcements from other European associations. At the time he said that “the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed”.
‘Open governance’
“There can no longer be a type of single-handed governance where the biggest issues in football are decided behind the scenes, without any transparency and without anyone being consulted, without going through the executive committee,” Diallo, 63, said on Tuesday.
“My vision will be one of open, collegiate governance, in which the different bodies really play their part.”
Diallo, the 63-year-old son of a Senegalese boxing champion, has been president of the FFF since January 2023.
UEFA had been struggling to find a credible candidate to stand against Infantino in the election, which will take place at the FIFA Congress on March 18 next year in the Moroccan capital, Rabat.
Arsene Wenger, the French former Arsenal manager and FIFA’s current chief of global football development, had at one point been seen as a potential candidate who could get Europe’s backing, but he will not stand.
FIFA has a total of 211 member associations, with each having one vote in the presidential election. A majority is needed for a candidate to win.
