How Nvidia’s CEO Flirted With Oblivion
A tech titan’s dopey affair with a suspected Chinese agent could upend the economy.
Will the AI boom that currently powers the stock market—and pretty much the whole economy—be brought low by one tech exec’s inability to keep it in his pants? Nervous investors sent Nvidia’s stock skittering downward after hours Wednesday in the wake of reports that the already scandal-infected company CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an executive who reports to him—and that Nvidia’s board was about to send him packing. Huang wound up sparing them the trouble by announcing his resignation Thursday.
This was all, of course, on top of his recent admission that he’d had an affair with a Chinese executive at the tech firm Megaspeed with the same last name who the US government says is a Chinese spy. Many observers thought that Huang would somehow survive the revelation of the Chinese spy affair, but evidently two affairs is one too many to overlook.
A CEO having a fling with a subordinate is an egregious HR nightmare, to be sure, but it was the affair with apparent Chinese Ministry of State Security employee Alice Huang that raised actual geopolitical concerns. Had the Nvidia CEO (knowingly or unknowingly) passed along information to her or lobbied for an easing of restrictions on plans to export chips to China at least in part on her behalf? Was he so gullible that he didn’t realize she was a spy? Or could he have known, and thus committed some light (or possibly heavy) treason?
But the whole Huang fiasco looks like it could be far more than a sex scandal with a side of espionage. Some company critics are suggesting that Nvidia’s “China problem” goes well beyond Huang’s bad spy romance. We know that Nvidia sold some $4.6 billion worth of chips to a Megaspeed subsidiary, ostensibly intended for a Malaysian data center. But Culper Research, a small short-selling shop that produced an explosive report on Nvidia back in May, says that this is just the tip of the iceberg: Culper estimated that at least 20 percent of the company’s compute revenue in the 2026 fiscal year may have come from illicit sales of its most advanced chips to a network of sketchy companies in Southeast Asia that have in some instances diverted the chips to China, contravening the US export ban.
According to Culper, “Numerous experts told us that Nvidia has long possessed the means to detect diversions”—including post-sale technical tests of server IP addresses and latency time, which could prove that the chips were physically in China. The implication is clear: Either Nvidia knew about the diversions and did nothing, or it didn’t even bother to check, almost certainly because company leaders didn’t want to know. (Culper Research acknowledged in its report that it was shorting Nvidia stock, which means that it benefits if it goes down.)
Ed Zitron, a tech muckraker and AI-boom skeptic contends, based on Culper’s research and his own, that “Nvidia is an untrustworthy company inflating its revenues with deals that range from dodgy to outright illegal.”
Culper’s broad-ranging accusations haven’t exactly been at the center of the media coverage of the scandal. A Wednesday New York Times profile of the man behind Culper mentioned them only glancingly, but you can rest assured that reporters at the Times and elsewhere are hard at work trying to corroborate the Culper research—and so are congressional investigators. In other words, as big as the Nvidia scandal is now, it could get a lot bigger.
And of course there’s the not-inconsiderable political angle. President Donald Trump was first informed of Huang’s affair with a spy about a year ago, and was reminded again by Marco Rubio just prior to a trip Trump took to Beijing back in May. Trump was evidently so unbothered by the fact that the CEO running the firm that provides the essential infrastructure for the AI boom, whose most powerful chips are so cutting-edge that it is forbidden to sell them to China, might be compromised by Chinese intelligence that he went ahead and invited Huang on his trip. As the Times put it, in its deadpan prose, “Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market.” (Trump also harbors his own conflict of interest, having brokered a deal for the United States to share between 15 and 25 percent of Nvidia’s revenues derived from China sales.)
Trump continues to insist that he knew nothing of any of this until “not too long ago.” As far as he’s concerned, Huang is “an amazing guy” who, as far as Trump knows, hasn’t “done anything wrong.” He went on to offer the perplexing explanation that Huang “dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.” On Sunday, after Huang had publicly confessed to having an affair, Trump assured reporters that the CEO was “an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
It’s unlikely that Huang has even one convincing explanation for his actions. But what Huang did have was a crisis PR firm—run by Risa Heller, who famously also represented former (and greatly disgraced) Democratic Representative Anthony Weiner, and which he hired around the time the Times first raised questions about his association with Alice Huang in an article more than a year ago. Presumably, Huang (Jensen, that is) thought that he was about to be enveloped in a scandal of his own making. The Times article, titled “A Mystery C.E.O. and Billions in Sales: Is China Buying Banned Nvidia Chips?,”not only featured several photos of Huang and Huang, er, networking in Taipei; it also made a pretty convincing case, if an implicit one, that Nvidia should have known that Megaspeed was not exactly on the up-and-up. The article closed with a memorable vignette, noting that when a Times reporter visited the headquarters of Megaspeed’s subsidiary Speedmatrix in a Malaysian mall, “three employees inside did not answer despite repeated knocks. A woman eventually emerged for lunch and identified herself as an administrator. She said she had no contact with her bosses. When asked what the company did, she said, ‘It’s not clear.’ ”
You might have thought that this report, which sketched out many of the basic elements of the scandal that now saturates the financial media, would have been a huge deal at the time. But the world only really stood up and took notice when we learned last week that Huang was literally fucking someone who seems to be a Chinese spy.
But the scandal’s salacious aspects aren’t the key issue here, largely because of who Jensen Huang is. He wasn’t just any CEO, just as Nvidia isn’t just any company. Huang was the de facto “key man” of the second-biggest company in the world by market cap, after Apple. Many tech industry observers regarded him as an indispensable figure in the rolling AI boom, and he apparently concurred, having made no effort to groom a successor. Oops.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
As for the $4.2 trillion company he cofounded, it isn’t just a supplier of the chips that make the AI boom possible; it’s widely considered the “central bank of AI.” Its outsize market valuation has left it deeply entangled in a web of circular finance with companies ranging from tech giants like Meta and OpenAI to smaller companies like the cloud-computing rentier CoreWeave. Nvidia will often invest billions of dollars in companies that in turn buy billions of dollars worth of chips from it. It’s all a bit reminiscent of writer Brandy Jensen’s definition of “modern friendship [as] just sending the same $20 back and forth via venmo, forever.” The Economist, noting that Nvidia pledged more than $70 billion in investments in start-ups over three years and offered $300 billion in financial support to customers, warns that “the more of this boom they finance, the more of any bust they will have to bear.”
And the more of this boom they finance, the more likely that a scandal like the one they now face could trigger an AI market crash that could quickly spread to other stocks and take down the economy itself. As Charlie Warzel of The Atlantic notes, “Nvidia has much of the financial system in a hostage situation. Huang is too big to fail.” And now he has.
But Nvidia isn’t the only company that is, as Warzel and Matteo Wong put it in an Atlantic essay last year, “load-bearing” for the economy. So are the other giant firms at the top of America’s corporate heap, many of which have become monstrously large in recent years. Concentration of economic power has increased dramatically. At the end of 2015, the top 10 firms in the S&P 500 represented roughly 19 percent of the market cap of the total index, according to RBC Wealth Management; by the end of last year the top 10 represented nearly 41 percent, a record. (My own back-of- the-envelope calculations suggest the number is a few percentage points higher today.)
Meanwhile, the diversity of these top firms has decreased as the AI boom has inflated the top tech firms and pushed older stalwarts like GE and Johnson and Johnson off the list. Currently, after Apple and Nvidia, the next five-largest US companies by market cap are all tech firms, with most of them, including Alphabet (the parent company of Google), Microsoft and Meta, heavily invested in AI—and all are large customers of Nvidia. If Nvidia falls, so will they, and we’ll all suffer the collateral damage. Hey ChatGPT, are we all screwed?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New York auction houses hope single-owner collections will fuel $2.4bn week of sales
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
New York’s major auction houses are heading into the November marquee sales next week with a sustained sense of confidence, as the global art market continues to show signs of recovery and a set of significant single-owner collections comes on the market. Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips and Bonhams expect to bring in at least $2.04bn collectively from their auctions in the Big Apple this month, with sales potentially exceeding $2.4bn, slightly above last year’s estimates for the period.
The confident estimates for this month’s top lots—and strong results for New York’s May sales—resonate with an ArtTactic report released earlier this year, which found the top auction houses made strong recoveries during the first half of 2026. Global auction sales were up 70% year on year at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips in the first six months of the year, thanks in part to the enduring appeal of single-owner collections and major estates.
That consignment strategy will be on full display at New York’s blockbuster auctions next week. Single-owner collections allow the houses to rebrand regular seasonal auctions as can’t-miss, once-in-a-lifetime events, and craft marketing campaigns around not just the works on sale but also the legacies of the collectors.
Sotheby’s boasts the highest collective estimate of the auction houses, projecting more than $1.1bn, which would be a house record for a marquee sale season. Around 40% of that total is attributed to the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, a fully guaranteed group of 12 Impressionist, Post-Impressionist and Fauvist paintings expected to sell for around $450m, making it the highest-value single-owner collection on offer this season across the city.
The collection was assembled by the Argentine sugar magnate Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his wife, María Elena “Nelly” Arrieta de Blaquier. Blaquier faced charges relating to the kidnapping of suspected left-wing activists during Argentina's 1976-83 military dictatorship. He denied the allegations and died in 2023 without standing trial. The 12 paintings have been consigned by the couple’s five children; the auction on 18 November will immediately be followed by Sotheby’s multiple-owner evening sale of Modern art.
“The market is very much moved by these collections,” says Allegra Bettini, Sotheby’s head of Modern evening auction. “Collectors today like to understand a narrative and see where works are coming from to understand the taste of how they all hung together.”
When the works in the Blaquier-Arrieta hoard were acquired, mostly in the 1960s and 70s in Europe, collectors could still purchase museum-quality works by Modern masters from commercial art galleries. That is no longer the case, Sotheby’s specialists say, even with a seven-figure budget. The Blaquier-Arrieta family rarely, if ever, loaned works for public display. Until Sotheby’s put them on view in its galleries at the Breuer Building on the Upper East Side, few of the 12 consigned works had been on public exhibit or offered on the market in decades.
The trove’s headline lot is Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (1890), one of the final works the artist painted in Auvers-sur-Oise in the months before his death. It carries a staggering estimate of around $180m and, because it has been guaranteed, is sure to exceed the current auction record for a Van Gogh of $117m (including fees), set by Orchard with Cypresses (1888) at the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York in 2022.
“It’s hard to not want to just touch and feel these brushstrokes because it is so alive,” Bettini says, gesturing to the leaves of the trees in the painting. “There's an intensity to it that really brings us into this landscape with the artist.”
Another possible recordbreaker is Arlequin (1888–90) by Paul Cezanne, which is estimated to sell in the region of $120m. The late harlequin painting is the only example from Cezanne’s series still in private hands, according to Sotheby’s. The current auction record for a Cezanne work, also set during the Paul Allen sales at Christie’s, is $137.79m.
Other standout works from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection include paintings by Camille Pissarro, Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Sotheby’s will also offer works from the collections of oil tycoon Armand Hammer, Seattle property developer Richard Hedreen and his wife Elizabeth Hedreen, and cable television pioneer Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth Baum.
In Midtown at Christie’s, the leading lot of the season is Wassily Kandinsky's Betonte Ecken (1922-23), from the artist’s Bauhaus period. Once part of the Guggenheim collection, it was purchased by its current owners—reportedly the billionaire, art-dealing Nahmad family—at Sotheby’s in 1986. It is estimated to sell for between $60m and $80m during the 20th-century evening sale on 17 November.
With the same estimate and on offer during the same sale, Gustav Klimt’s landscape Litzlbergkeller (1915-16) was once part of the collection gathered by Serge Sabarsky, the late art dealer who co-founded the Neue Galerie in New York (the beloved Austrian restaurant on the museum’s ground floor is named for him). Leading the 21st century evening sale is an untitled 1983 work by Jean-Michel Basquiat that references a drawing on paper by Leonardo da Vinci and is estimated to sell for between $30m and $50m.
Christie’s is also offering a wide variety of works from the holdings of well-known collectors, among them the music executive Clive Davis, the billionaire businessman William Koch, and more works belonging to the late Museum of Modern Art trustee Agnes Gund that will benefit her foundation. Also on offer is a group of seven works including Old Master, Modernist and post-war artists understood to have been consigned by Jeff Koons. Altogether, the auction house expects to take in between $823m and $1.1bn during its November sales in New York.
Despite recent stock market volatility following the “blue tsunami” during the US midterm elections earlier this month and concerns over a Democrat-controlled Congress’s regulation of artificial intelligence and datacentre development—heightened by recent revelations about chipmaker Nvidia’s president Jensen Huang being embroiled in a spy scandal—stocks show early signs of stabilising. Christie’s specialists are similarly optimistic ahead of the November auctions.
While fluctuations in the stock markets can influence the art market over the longer term, the immediate impact on high-end auctions tends to be limited. Particularly for evening auctions, where lots are estimated to sell for seven-, eight- and nine-figure sums, potential buyers are often wealthy enough to be insulated from the day-to-day fluctuations of the stock market.
“The art’s quality is going to supersede any day in the market. People aren’t day-trading Picassos,” says Kat Widing, Christie’s senior vice president, senior specialist in post-war and contemporary art, and head of the 21st-century evening sale.
Collectors are “looking at these works over months, and they’re thinking through these major purchases”, she adds. “These would be additions to major collections that are quite significant. With those two things in mind, I’m still very optimistic.”
Phillips expects to bring in between $80.4m and 128.7m in New York this month, with its auctions led by Amedeo Modigliani’s limestone sculpture Tête (1911-12), estimated to sell for between $28m and $35m after having been in the same private collection for more than 50 years.
Bonhams estimates it will sell at least $40m worth of art in November in New York, with most of that total coming from a collection of five fresh-to-market Constantin Brâncuși bronzes that were held in the same private collection for decades after being acquired from the artist’s estate. Collectively, they are expected to fetch $25m.

Big-box retailers jack up the price of goods between the time you set foot in the parking lot to when you get to the shopping aisle. Airline companies mine your personal data so they can squeeze as much fare money from you as possible. A grocery delivery app used what they called "price rounding" to arbitrarily increase the cost of a box of crackers by 23 percent. For-hire vehicle apps scrape your phones for reasons why you'd pay an extra $10 or $20 for a late-night ride home.
This kind of rotten, insidious, algorithm-boosted surveillance capitalism has become routine across most industries.
On Thursday, the City Council is expected to vote on a bill that aims to ban the practice in New York City.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Eileen Kinsella
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
This past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in New Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.
The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.
“What happened this July was really special,” says George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.
According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.
“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke says. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”
According to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker says. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”
Things moved quickly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director says.
After the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.
“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree says, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.
Baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker says, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.
“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker says, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Never Let Trump’s Elite Enablers Forget What They’ve Done
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Gregg Gonsalves
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Never Let Trump’s Elite Enablers Forget What They’ve Done
Universities, scientists, law firms, and many other powerful institutions are about to start pretending they never rolled over for the president. But we know better.
Just before sunrise on the day after the midterm elections last week, progressive journalist Walker Bragman posted this: “Many people, institutions, and companies sacrificed their integrity because they thought Trump’s power grab was inevitably going to succeed and he’d be the American Orban. Don’t forget their names.”
Bragman is right. One of the most remarkable, and despicable, things about the last two years is how many so institutions—the law firms, the tech companies, the universities, the august scientific and professional societies—swiftly, completely, and indeed eagerly “obeyed in advance.” Meanwhile, ordinary Americans with much less money and power were left to both shoulder the burden of the attacks from the Trump administration and lead the resistance to those attacks.
If the midterms showed us the resolve and determination of the American people, the preceding two years demonstrated the fecklessness, cowardice, and selfishness of American elites—many of whom would frankly do anything to remain “on top,” even if it meant bowing down to fascists. These folks are a portrait of “upper-middle‐class decadence” straight out of Bertolucci’s The Conformist. They are a type that always rises up under authoritarianism— not so much true believers as true opportunists—and they always survive, no matter whom they step on in their rush for the exits when things go badly.
I’ve written many times about these acts of collaboration, large and small, over the past two years. But in the wake of the drubbing that the Republicans took last week, it’s worth reviving the greatest hits of appeasement, now that these truly bad choices made by so many are running up against the sunshine of a new day.
As a university scientist, watching the decay of American science, public health, and higher education up close has been painful. The entire infrastructure of these sectors is so damaged and compromised that, even with a new Congress and potentially a Democrat in the White House in 2028, we will be digging out of this mess for decades to come.
But the collaborators who helped create this crisis engender a whole set of other feelings: scorn, disgust, anger. Now that Trump is headed toward political oblivion, get ready for them to tell us how they were always against this, trying to do their part, to ingratiate and rehabilitate themselves with the rest of us—and don’t believe a word of it.
When I think back to November 2024, I still remember my shock when two political scientists at Princeton with no expertise or experience in biomedical research, Frances Lee and Stephen Macedo, penned an over-the-top encomium pushing for Jay Bhattacharya to run the National Institutes of Health, claiming he would bring: “a strong dose of fresh thinking and institutional reform from experts prepared to challenge the reigning consensus and renew our commitment to the basic values of science and liberalism.” Ahem. No. Now, as the NIH sits as a smoking husk of its former self, I wonder if they have even an ounce of buyer’s remorse. Not likely. And even within public health, we had people making craven pronouncements to keep themselves in the story. “I think @MartyMakary at FDA, @DrOz at CMS and @DrJBhattacharya at NIH are all pretty reasonable,” tweeted former dean of the Brown University School of Public Health Ashish Jha weeks after Trump’s reelection. Ahem. No. Again.
Then, I think of people who cozied up to MAHA influencers as if they were tribunes of the people. Some were just making a buck with their Substacks and podcasts by blaming public health. Outlets like Why Should I Trust You propped up purveyors of vaccine misinformation like RFK Jr.’s bestie Del Bigtree and gave a platform to people like Bret Weinstein who have fantasized about hanging public health officials. As writer and podcaster Michael Hobbes snarkily said:
The argument is always the same: rather than judge MAHA supporters on what they do, we should judge them on what they say. This is dangerously uninformed about how conspiracy movements work…. the second MAHA took power it started gutting basic science, promoting quack treatments and loosening health regulations. *This* is what the movement is. Yet it’s up to critics not to conclude or predict anything from these actions and bend over backward to find common cause.… It’s not the anti-science movement’s fault that public opinion has shifted against public health, it’s the public health authorities they’re constantly lying about!
Others took bad-faith MAHA arguments at their word, and became credulous to a fault, which sent them into the embrace of the indefensible. Despite wanting to maintain that MAHA wasn’t all bad, they elided the fact that the single most reliable indicator of supporting the MAHA movement is political affiliation, and identification with the MAGA movement most of all.
Then, think about the champions of free speech and expression on university campuses—as long as that speech doesn’t involve discussions of race, gender, or sexuality, and anything they might consider “woke.” These are the denizens of the heterodox academy, the good ol’ boys touting viewpoint diversity for me, not for thee. I remember one academic at Harvard writing to me after the abrupt removal of Mary Bassett, the university’s director of the FXB Center for Human Rights. He wondered where economist Larry Summers, psychologist Steven Pinker, and law professor Alan Dershowitz and the Harvard Council on Academic Freedom had disappeared to during this show trial for a physician who had devoted her life to the improvement of health for the most vulnerable, run the health departments in New York City and New York State, and worked for the Rockefeller and Doris Duke Foundations over a long, distinguished career. Not a peep. Because, of course, under the guise of championing fundamental rights, they were simply protecting their own, not others they considered expendable. It made them little different from the Trump administration officials attacking universities around diversity, equity, and inclusion, yet no one called them out as they used their seniority in academia as a shield for their behavior.
Finally, here at Yale, where I teach, students, faculty, alumni, and staff are locked in a battle with an administration and set of trustees who have been absolutely unwilling to talk about the decay of the rights to free speech and assembly on campus, the erosion of academic freedom, and the long game of footsie they’ve been playing with the Trump Department of Justice over admissions policies.
Yale decided at the start of the Trump administration that appeasement was the play to make. The university clamped down on protests; issued a self-flagellating report on trust that mirrored conservative critiques of higher education, which was praised by none other than Secretary of Education Linda McMahon; took down resources on DEI and anti-racism from its website devoted to a five-year campaign on Belonging at Yale; and changed the names of DEI and disability offices to ones that were more palatable in the political climate of the day.
While the president of the university and the trustees stonewall their own community, they constantly maintain the need for open dialogue on difficult topics on campus. It is a doublespeak that is just shocking to watch and reflects an unvarnished disdain for everyone here. Like the good old boys at Harvard, Yale leaders see everyone but themselves and big-name donors as incidental to their mission and the success of the university. Students, faculty, alumni, and staff are treated as a set of irritants, as a recent hot-mic episode with the president and the dean of Yale College exposed.
So what are we supposed to do now? The first thing is: write it down. We’ll soon be awash in revisionist history, or rather, as the historian Henry Rousso calls it, “historical negationism,” where the past is deliberately distorted for contemporary ends. So again: Just keep the receipts. They are the primary sources for truth-telling. No detail is too small. And as Bragman says: Don’t forget.
Long after Trump is history, you’ll run into people who will be all too happy not to have tales of their capitulation restated, rehearsed again and again. It’s what they depend on, so they can slip into new roles, without any consequences or accountability. And yes, the country will move on; it’s a national pastime to sweep things under the rug.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
But the election last week was about more than science, public health, and higher ed, the arenas in which I spend most of my time. While it may have been “the affordability election,” it also showed that the pillars on which Trump’s political empire rests—like democratic backsliding, white supremacy, and Christian nationalism—can be toppled. As conservative New York Times columnist David French, said, it was the Ozymandias election too, and for all his inflated aspirations, Trump’s legacy is dust.
Repairing science, public health, and higher education requires that we make this so, as so much of the motivation for what Trump has done to our fields is tied straight to these noxious underpinnings of his movement. It thus points us to a more fundamental mission tied to the future of a fair, multiracial democracy in America. It connects scientists, clinicians, and academics to those fighting for democracy in the US. It calls us towards the need for what my Yale colleague and fellow Nation correspondent the Rev. Dr. William J. Barber II has called a Third Reconstruction in America, and what he has called a moral policy agenda for this country.
As I watched election returns in my hotel room in San Antonio, Texas, last week, tears streamed down my face, from relief and from joy. I have no doubt that the fight has only begun and that difficult times are still ahead, but the size and scope of the rout shows that something else is possible. Even in places that seemed locked into the past, from Texas to Mississippi, from Kansas to Georgia, change is afoot. We have to do our part to keep it going, not simply for science, public health, and education’s sake but for our shared humanity and the future of this planet.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Women finally start to get pride of place with central London sculptures
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Louisa Buck
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
London bristles with sculptures of men. Only 4% of public monuments in the city are devoted to named women, according to the charity Art UK. It says something about the national psyche that there are twice as many animal statues in the city as there are sculptures devoted to specific women. But right now a pair of radical new works depicting and made by women—Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue in Trafalgar Square, and Nicole Eisenman’s Stack outside the Royal Academy of Arts (RA) on Piccadilly—are making their presence powerfully felt in two of the most male-dominated locations in the capital.
In Trafalgar Square, surrounded by depictions of monarchs and militia and across from Admiral Nelson atop his 51m-high column, Self’s Lady in Blue painted bronze cuts a distinctive dash on the empty plinth to the northwest of the square that, since 1999, has hosted a programme of contemporary sculpture commissions. Head held aloft with her vivid blue dress clinging to her ample curves, she strides forth in high heels, exuding purposeful confidence and optimism. As with all Fourth Plinth sculptures, this impressive female will be in situ for two years, before going to a permanent home in Fornebu in Norway.
“She’s not an idol to venerate or a historic figure to commemorate, she’s an everyday young metropolitan woman much like those who use the square every day,” Self declared at the work’s unveiling, adding: “Lady in Blue is not static, she’s in motion… and I hope she inspires all who see her to find the optimism to move forward in community with all those around them.” In this spirit, Self sees her sculpture as an attempt to redress both racial and gender imbalance in public art whether in her native US, the UK or Norway. “In most cities there’s an underrepresentation of sculptures that depict women, and especially women of colour, so I think that it is important to add more images and visual representation,” she said.
Meanwhile, a few streets away outside the RA, which in 258 years has shown only two living women in its main galleries, New York-based Eisenman has erected Stack, a towering work at over 8m tall. This totem of figures and objects made from an assortment of materials, including bronze, oak, brass, steel, nylon, acrylic resin and tin, is currently having a friendly face-off with Alfred Drury’s grandiose bronze sculpture of Joshua Reynolds, the RA’s first president, who brandishes his paintbrush and easel just outside the main entrance. In 2021 Eisenman got to the shortlist for Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth and now with Stack, she has created her own column, impressive in its scale and magnitude, but also irreverently anti-monumental.
Eisenman’s column
At its base hunches a craggy, androgynous figure shod in Birkenstocks and with a wooden barrel strapped to its back. A stand-in for the artist, perhaps, abject and emphatically earthbound, clutching not a paintbrush but an empty wine glass. On top of the barrel, rising out of a puddle of what looks like gooey melted cheese is a giant potato, over which lolls a rusty leonine cat modelled on Edie, Eisenman’s studio companion. Rather than a posturing war hero, Stack is topped off by the amiably smiling seated figure of the late artist Phyllida Barlow, rendered in gleaming sky-blue aluminium and jauntily balancing a vase of flowers on her head.
Barlow, who died unexpectedly in 2023, was a Royal Academician. Given where this work is situated, it is hard not to see Stack as a memorial to this much loved and greatly mourned artist. Eisenman is a huge admirer of Barlow, whose colossally ambitious but always defiantly anti-hubristic sculpture she first encountered when they were both in the Carnegie International in 2013. They subsequently became friends to the extent that an apparently amused Barlow went to Eisenman’s New York studio in 2022 to be 3D-printed for this work—“She was really good humoured about it,” Eisenman recalled in a recent talk at the Royal Institution. But while undoubtedly honouring Barlow, Stack is also more than a tribute to one person.
Eisenman is reluctant to offer specific interpretations but in her talk she revealed that the work was conceived with London in mind, declaring: “It’s amazing to me that it is at the RA. I hope it can stay in London.” She also stated that Stack emerged during the pandemic and forms a personal testament to when, as she put it, “life got pared down to the basics: food, wine, art, my cat”.
In strikingly different ways but with similar underlying intent, Stack and Lady in Blue offer alternative monuments to aspects of all our lives that rarely get acknowledged, and most notably the power of great women of all ages and from all origins. May we see more of their kind in all our cities.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Unpardonable Malpractice of Pete Hegseth
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Michael T. Klare
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Unpardonable Malpractice of Pete Hegseth
Yes, the defense secretary has committed impeachable offenses. But he’s also just really, really, really bad at his job.
The offenses cited by Representative Thomas Massie (R-KY) in commencing impeachment proceedings against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth—that he initiated and sustained the war with Iran without required congressional approval, conducted military operations in Yemen and the Caribbean without such approval, and eroded protections for civilians trapped in overseas war zones—are all valid and fully justify his removal from office in accordance with constitutional precepts. But however worthy, they fail to capture his essential, unpardonable offense: strategic malpractice when commanding troops in battle.
Hegseth himself has been very outspoken about the need to cleanse the armed services of incompetent generals and admirals (many of whom, he claims, received their promotions as the result of some sort of affirmative action process) and to retain only those able to fight and win. “The previous administration wanted politically correct generals,” he told an assembly of junior officers on September 30. “We only want the top performing generals. It’s not just pass or fail…. The best move on, the worst do not.”
Secretary Hegseth wants us (and every member of Congress) to believe that he ranks among the successful generals and so should be retained. After berating Massie (“a disgruntled and defeated congressman”) and others during his unapologetic Pentagon press conference on November 10, Hegseth sought to defend his record as the ultimate commander of US forces. “By every measure,” he said of the war against Iran, “we achieved a historic military victory.”
But this is sheer fabrication. Were Hegseth to hold himself to the same high standards he supposedly set for his generals, he would have to say: “By every measure, we achieved a total fiasco in Iran,” and hand in his resignation.
To fully appreciate the magnitude of Hegseth’s incompetence, let’s recall the tasks he was assigned when ordered by President Trump to commence hostilities against Iran on February 28. As indicated by Trump in a prerecorded video address that morning, Hegseth was given four overriding objectives: (1) to eliminate, forever, Iran’s ability to construct a nuclear weapon; (2) to eliminate Iran’s ability to manufacture and launch long-range ballistic missiles; (3) to eliminate Iran’s ability to project power in the region, whether with its own military or via proxy forces like Hezbollah and the Houthi rebels; and (4) to eliminate the Iran problem altogether, by killing off Iran’s top leadership and igniting a popular rebellion.
Hegseth set out to achieve these goals with unrestrained vigor. The US military alone struck 13,000 targets in Iran during the first 38 days of fighting, and its Israeli partners struck many thousands more. From the administration’s perspective, it was a total win. In a press statement released on April 8, following the announcement of a ceasefire (that was to prove temporary), the White House declared that “the greatest fighting force the world has ever known has met those objectives with overwhelming strength and lethal precision.”
Among the war’s ostensible accomplishments: “Iran’s ballistic missile arsenal and production capacity has been razed…eliminating its ability to project power.” Also, “Iran can no longer arm terrorist proxies.” And, although the regime was still clinging to power: “What’s left of [it] is desperate, dejected, and in denial.”
For Hegseth, this was a “decisive military victory.”
But, in fact, it wasn’t: Not one of Trump’s stated objectives was achieved by Hegseth and the forces under his command. Not one.
To begin with, the Iranian regime has remained intact and (so far as can be determined from afar) remains as entrenched as ever, with no signs of an imminent popular rebellion.
Although the Iranians have made no visible move to reconstitute their uranium enrichment program (a prerequisite for manufacturing a nuclear bomb), they have demonstrated no inclination to surrender their existing stockpiles of highly enriched uranium or to renounce their enrichment efforts entirely.
And Iran’s regional clout—now buttressed by its apparent capacity to disrupt the Persian Gulf oil flow at will—appears enhanced, not diminished.
Most significantly, Iran’s ability to project power with missiles and long-range drones remains robust, as demonstrated by repeated strikes on US bases in the region. As if to prove this point, the Iranians struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 17, killing three US Army service members and destroying or damaging vital military equipment.
The Iranians have also continued to strike tankers attempting to traverse the strategic Strait of Hormuz without their approval, sharply constricting the world’s oil trade and keeping diesel and gasoline prices high.
From any perspective, then, the Hegseth-run war on Iran has been a total fiasco, failing to achieve a single one of its stated objectives. For these reasons alone, the self-styled “secretary of war” should resign. But the war was more than a failure: It entailed a massive strategic disaster, one whose vast dimensions are only beginning to be calculated.
The Strategic Calculus
How do you measure a strategic disaster? We begin, properly, with an intelligence failure, followed by military miscalculation and geopolitical retreat—all adding up to an astonishing contraction of America’s global clout.
Let’s start with intelligence failure, the origin of so much of the sorrow to come. Hegseth and his top lieutenants began with the assumptions that (a) the Iranian military was no match for the technologically superior US military, and (b) the Iranian regime was fragile and would be swept away once its top leaders were killed. Neither assumption has proved even remotely accurate: The Iranian military has demonstrated a remarkable degree of resilience under fire, able to inflict far more damage on US forces than was ever thought possible; and the regime has proved equally resilient, able to reconstitute itself after the loss of its top leadership on the first day of fighting.
Some of this leadership myopia can be attributed to Trump’s ebullience after the successful January 3 US seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in Caracas, and to the overly optimistic assessment of the regime’s fragility given to Trump on February 11 by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a pivotal White House meeting. From the accounts by Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman of The New York Times, we know that Vice President JD Vance and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, warned of possible risks in starting a war with Iran, but that Hegseth assured the president of a rapid US victory. With this assurance, Trump took the plunge.
But this is only part of the story. Hegseth was clearly so blinded by his faith in “the greatest fighting force the world has ever known” that he failed to consider the potential strengths of his adversary—the very first responsibility of a capable commander. The Iranians may have possessed a third-rate navy and air force, but they had also developed a substantial missile- and drone-production capacity and had hardened their launch facilities against possible attack. More importantly, the Iranians had clearly studied US military tactics and prepared for Hegseth’s air and missile bombardment by decentralizing their command and combat capabilities around the country, allowing them to absorb a massive US-Israeli assault and still conduct punishing retaliatory strikes.
By predicting a swift US military victory, moreover, Hegseth saw no need to account for the possible consequences of Iranian retaliatory strikes against Persian Gulf oil shipping. Why worry about oil tankers’ safety if the war would be over in a matter of weeks? Evidently, no one in Hegseth’s inner circle foresaw the possibility of recurring Iranian drone strikes on vital ships and oil infrastructure, depriving the world of approximately one-fifth of its daily petroleum supply and sparking economic hardship around the world.
Surely, those responsible for such a mammoth intelligence failure should be removed from their posts—including those at the very top.
From intelligence failure we move to military miscalculation, another lethal command deficiency. If, like Hegseth, you believe you command the greatest fighting force that ever was, you might be forgiven for a touch of overconfidence when going into battle against a demonstrably weaker power. But when your hubris endangers the lives of your soldiers and their ability to fight, you are unfit to lead.
Most egregious, of course, is Hegseth’s failure to learn from Ukraine about the devastating impact of one-way attack drones on contemporary combat. Anyone who has followed the Ukrainian conflict—and this should have included every senior US military official—knows that drone warfare has transformed the battlefield, placing any unprotected asset at extreme risk of being targeted and attacked by long-range assault weapons, like the Iranian Shahed-136 drones employed by Russia in great numbers.
Yet Hegseth deployed tens of thousands of US soldiers, along with some of America’s most advanced military systems, at bases in the Gulf area within easy range of Iran’s own fleet of Shahed drones. Yes, those troops and weapons were protected by America’s advanced interceptors, such as Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles—but never in sufficient quantities to knock down all of the drones and missiles pitted against them. The unsurprising result: 18 US lives lost, over 800 wounded, and billions of dollars in damage to weapons and equipment.
And then there is the critical issue of interceptor use. To defend US facilities in the Gulf (along with the energy assets of US allies in the region), the Pentagon fired off a substantial share of its available supply of Patriot and THAAD air-defense missiles, leaving US bases elsewhere at greater risk of potential attack. According to a report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Republican-leaning Washington think tank, the US fired between 1,000 and 1,400 Patriot interceptors during the first weeks of the war, representing about half of the total US inventory at that time; it also expended 190–290 THAAD missiles, or two-thirds to three-quarters of its prewar inventory.
To stem the losses at US bases in the Middle East, Hegseth reportedly ordered US commanders in Europe and Asia to ship scarce Patriot and THAAD batteries from their areas of responsibility to the Gulf, substantially weakening US air and missile defenses in other likely hot spots.
Replacing all those expended missiles and bolstering US air defenses around the world will cost this country tens of billions of dollars and take years to accomplish, Pentagon officials acknowledge.
Add all of this up, and the outcome includes what should be termed geopolitical retreat, or reduced US political clout in the Gulf and elsewhere. As Trump and Hegseth made clear in the opening days of the war, a major US objective was to demonstrate that America’s global reach and power were greater than ever. “[The Iranian] regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States Armed Forces,” Trump declared on February 28. A victory there, coming on top of the seemingly cost-free intervention in Venezuela, would again demonstrate Washington’s capacity to project power and overcome adversaries worldwide. But the Iran venture failed, severely damaging US credibility.

It will take a long time to calculate all the consequences of this geopolitical setback, but we can begin with Washington’s apparent failure to eliminate all Iranian threats to the untrammeled flow of Persian Gulf oil. Ever since the world economy became dependent on the Gulf’s oil output, in the early Cold War era, protection of the Gulf oil flow has been viewed in Washington as a vital US interest. Following the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, President Jimmy Carter told Congress in 1980 that Soviet forces were now “close to the Straits of Hormuz, [thereby posing] a grave threat to the free movement of Middle East oil.” Any attempt by Moscow or some other power to block that flow, he asserted, “will be regarded as an assault on the vital interests of the United States of America, and such an assault will be repelled by any means necessary, including military force.”
In accordance with this edict, Carter established the US Central Command (currently responsible for the fighting with Iran) and installed a permanent US military presence in the region. His successors, beginning with Ronald Reagan and continuing with the two Presidents Bush, have cited this so-called Carter Doctrine to justify repeated US military intervention in the Gulf. Over time, the US role in safeguarding “the free movement of Middle East oil” has become a defining feature of America’s global dominance, along with the US military presence in Europe, Japan, and South Korea. But the Iranians have demonstrated an invincible capacity to disrupt that flow, throwing into question a core component of America’s claim to global hegemony.
The US failure to subdue Iran has also undermined America’s dominant status in the other major foci of its hegemonic sway, Europe and Asia. Not only has Iran demonstrated that a medium-sized power can, under the right circumstances, hold a much more powerful force at bay—a feat no doubt being closely studied by Russia and China—but also, by eliciting such a wanton expenditure of advanced US munitions, it has actually left the US less well-equipped to counter those rivals in any future conflicts. According to that same CSIS study on US missile use, the Pentagon consumed a large share of its offensive strike weapons during the opening weeks of the war, including approximately one-third of its prewar inventory of Tomahawk cruise missiles and one-fourth of its Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles.
No doubt there will be other negative consequences from this geopolitical retreat, some possibly of equal concern, but we already know enough to conclude that Hegseth’s combat malpractice has resulted in a severe strategic debacle.
This, combined with his intelligence failures and combat miscalculations, would, in other countries and at other times, result in his forcible removal from office. With this not in the immediate offing, despite calls for his impeachment by prominent Democrats and Republicans in Congress, Hegseth should pay homage to the martial ideals he holds so dear, take personal responsibility for the debacle, and resign.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘Hurry, hurry, get your tickets now!’ The last of the great Australian showmen – photo essay
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Words by Tereasa Trevor and photographs by Liz Ham
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
My uncle Teddy Trevor remembers Casey Nelson, a fellow showman, spruiking his double-jointed horse to sideshow punters in the 1960s. The horse, Nelson warned, was “showing here for the last time”. “Too late, too late will be the cry, when Happy Harry has passed you by,” he called. The act continued for another two decades.
I’ve been hearing stories like this my whole life. Ted laughs at Casey’s line as he pours another cup of tea and passes the biscuits at the kitchen table of the family home in Brisbane. At 91, after a lifetime in Australia’s travelling shows, he has no desire to quit the showgrounds yet. While their mid-century heyday may have passed, these grounds are still the lifeblood of his friendships and family.
Ted feels blessed, he says, to belong to two great show families: the Trevors, circus people on his father’s side, and the Fosters, sideshow people on his mother’s. Born on the showgrounds in 1935, he comes from more than eight generations of show folk.
Ted’s grandmother Cora Trevor performed an iron-jaw act, hanging upside-down and spinning grown men by her teeth, including her 14-stone (88kg) acrobat father. My great-grandmother Alice Foster, known as LuLu, arrived in Australia in 1913. She was a widow with six sons and a daughter. Lulu kept her whole family fed while running a dancing duck as a sideshow act.
Uncle Teddy’s own entry into work coincided with the second world war, which brought the showgrounds to a halt. He started his career selling fabric door to door from my grandmother’s vardo caravan. As a young man in the 1950s, he worked with my uncle Frank Foster, promoting Slim Dusty’s tent show on the sideshow alley. Those days were hectic. “You start at nine in the morning, you don’t finish till after 11 at night, and you do a show every 20 minutes,” Ted tells me.
“The show was a big event for the town,” Ted says – the biggest day of the year for some places. The men wore suits, hats and ties, the women their best dresses. “Now they go in a pair of shorts and thongs,” he says.
Teddy says the atmosphere of the sideshow was what everyone came to the show for. He can still recite the lines they used to entice the crowds: “The Slim Dusty show is just about to start! Australia’s top country-and-western recording star, the only Australian to top the hit parade in England, our only gold record-holder, is on this next big program. Hurry boys, hurry girls, get your tickets now! The cowboys, the cowgirls, the knife-throwers, the jugglers, you’ll see and meet them all on the inside.”
Uncle Teddy says that between the advent of TV, RSL clubs offering sideshow talent a new touring strategy, and state-based showground permits hindering showpeople from pivoting beyond the scope of their trade (for example, a clown joint can only do clown business), the landscape of the showgrounds drastically changed in the early 1970s.
Performers could sing half a dozen songs at an RSL, Ted tells me, “for what three or four days and hundreds of songs paid them on a sideshow”.
Participator numbers also declined, while costs climbed, he says. The big rides came in, worth millions. “The showgrounds are saturated with equipment now,” he says. “There’s no more ground available, so there’s no permits for the young showman.”
The cost escalated, too. “They’re charging $12 for a game on the clown joint. It’s all ridiculous,” he says. In Ted’s day, it used to be “only four bob [40 cents] to go and see the show”. Some shows were three shillings, and a shilling for a child. As he puts it: “The money was sort of nothing.”
In the last couple of years, I had seen Uncle Teddy posting diary-like entries on Facebook, sharing his memories along with photographs It led me to ask him some more questions.
Uncle Teddy often says: “I’m sorry you were born a bit late to see the action.” It’s clear he thinks I’d have loved it. He describes the camaraderie of the sideshow community, with everyone pitching in when they were needed. “Everyone’s got to do their own thing,” he says. “The stars have got to get out in the middle of the night and knock pegs in if a storm’s coming up.”
“I always loved the showgrounds because of the people,” Ted says.
 
My cousins still travel the showground runs, working joints, food trucks and rides. The skills of a modern showman are totally different from the past.
“Today you buy a $2m ride and you don’t have to be a showman,” he says. “People either like the ride or they don’t. It’s just got to be a spectacular ride, a thrill ride, and they’ll queue up and go on it … it’s a different ballgame.[Showpeople] don’t have to get up and tell a tale. They just say, ‘Next ride, hurry now, get your tickets for the next big ride,’ and that’s it.”
These days, Uncle Teddy visits his friends and family at the Beenleigh or Brisbane shows, and chats on the phone to his friends across Australia. “You get friends in different towns. You meet their kids, and when you get old, you meet their grandchildren, and they all become like family.”
I take my own child to the Royal Easter Show when it’s on in Sydney, and the moment I spot a laughing-clown joint, I half expect to see Uncle Teddy come around the corner, his eyes sparkling, a joke on his lips and coins jingling in his waist pouch. I tell them the stories Ted told me, alive with dancing ducks and my iron-jawed great-grandmother. Their eyes widen the way mine did at Ted’s kitchen table, and the show rolls on to another generation.

https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.title: Mayor’s Office Backs Two New Hell’s Kitchen Tenant Unions, As Residents Push for Repairs
https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/mayors-office-bac.text:
Share This Article
Tenants organizing across 31 Manhattan buildings in foreclosure are the latest to see support from Mamdani’s newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants.
Since January, the newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants has made it its business to support tenant unions across the city.
Now, city-employed tenant leaders are working with two new tenant unions in Hell’s Kitchen, where residents are asking for help in securing repairs and stewarding their troubled rent stabilized properties through a potential future sale.
The majority of tenants in the impacted buildings have come out in support of the union effort—a milestone, organizers say, that helps them get the attention of both their landlords and the city—and could represent another chance for the Mamdani administration to steer distressed affordable housing into the hands of tenants’ preferred buyer.
One of the unions represents tenants in 31 buildings owned by Arthur Haruvi and Peter Hungerford, which launched on Saturday, where tenants stood with city leaders outside 408 W. 56th St., where they say cooking gas has been out for 722 days. The residents are demanding repairs and a seat at the table when it comes to the future of their dilapidated buildings, now in foreclosure and bankruptcy.
“The two years without cooking gas has had a big toll. My family, and especially myself, like to cook during the holidays. We can’t cook Thanksgiving and Christmas meals on a hot plate,” said Luis Pelaez, who has lived in the building for 34 years.
There are 357 open housing code violations across the 478 units facing foreclosure, according to analysis by Housing Conservation Coordinators.
Tenants say that Peter Hungerford has responded to their request to meet, and they hope to go to the bargaining table in the coming weeks. Hungerford did not respond to City Limits’ requests for comment.
On Saturday, tenants of landlord David Ohebshalom will launch their own tenant union for nine buildings (including both rent stabilized and market rate units) on West 47th Street, alongside the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants head Cea Weaver.
Ohebshalom’s brother Daniel has made headlines before: he did jail time in 2024 for failing to comply with court orders to repair hazardous conditions at two buildings in Washington Heights.
Can tenants influence a sale?
Third time’s the charm?
Since January, the newly reinvigorated Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants has tried to influence the sale of two major portfolios of rent stabilized housing in New York. But each time, efforts to steer the buildings to preferred buyers have stumbled.
Early this year, officials intervened too late to stop the bankruptcy sale of 5,000 units from prior owner Pinnacle to private landlord Summit. And in July, housing officials backed the bid of preservation group Spatial Equity to buy 850 units in East Harlem, only to see their offers turned down and the portfolio go up for foreclosure auction this week.
Tenants in the Haruvi-Hungerford buildings say that their immediate concerns are securing repairs and maintenance, including restoring cooking gas and addressing pests. Some of the buildings are also included in a class action suit by Housing Rights Initiative against Peter Hungerford’s PH Realty Capital, which accuses the company of overcharging tenants in 18 buildings by $15 million.
But residents know they face a precarious position with their buildings in foreclosure. “If our buildings go up for sale we need a say in who buys them and the terms of that purchase,” said Joseph Di Salle, a resident at 450 57th St.
Tenants and their allies in city government have limited control over what ends up happening to their buildings in such scenarios. But some have credited the work of unions with pushing new landlords into concessions, like when Summit real estate forgave back rent for former Pinnacle tenants shortly after taking over.
The mayor’s housing plan includes some measures that can help tenants assert more control over their buildings when they go up for sale. Tuesday, he signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act into law, a measure that would give some city-approved buyers first dibs on distressed rental properties before they hit the wider market.
Those attempts to influence ownership, and the city’s overt support for tenant unions, has rubbed some property owners the wrong way, saying it “vilifies” them. And at least one developer that the administration championed recently, in the sale of three debt-riddled rent stabilized Crown Heights buildings, has a less than stellar maintenance record of its own, The City Reporter reported Tuesday.
But others see a clear role for City Hall to play.
With the Hell’s Kitchen buildings, Charlie Dulik of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants said that the city could coordinate code enforcement, come to the bargaining table with tenants, or liaise with the landlord for the Haruvi-Hungerford tenant union.
The tenants have not, as of yet, asked for support in steering their homes to a preferred buyer. If they asked, “we would absolutely talk about it and see what we can do,” said Dulik.
To get traction, get the majority of tenants on board
The Hungerford-Haruvi buildings fit the profile for the kind of properties most likely to get City Hall’s attention. The portfolio is vast, mostly rent stabilized, and connected to a former member of the city’s worst landlord list. It also has a tenants union.
And its members on Saturday, wearing freshly pressed royal blue T-shirts, said that a majority of tenants across 10 Hell’s Kitchen buildings in the Haruvi-Hungerford portfolio had signed on with the union.
Ten blocks south, the West 47th St. Tenants Union also declared that it has the majority support of tenants in nine buildings between 8th and 9th avenues, and are calling on their landlord Ohebshalom and his management company to address rat, mouse, and pest infestations, as well as ongoing maintenance needs.
The 50 percent threshold—getting at least half of a building or buildings’ tenants on board with the union—is key, tenant leaders said, indicating that they will have significant bargaining power.
“Supporting tenant unions and majority tenant unions is incredibly important,” said Dulik, wearing a freshly screenprinted Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants jacket.
Getting to a majority of tenants has become standard practice in the field, advocates say, in part to a growing national tenant movement. The Mamdani administration has been exploring ways to give tenant unions official legal status and recognition and allow them to sue, similar to how the National Labor Relations Board recognizes labor unions.
“There’s going to be more of an emphasis on majority unions for sure, but there’s also going to be an emphasis on portfolio-wide organizing because that’s when you can make the most changes,” said K Agbebiyi, director of communications at Housing Justice for All.
Hell’s Kitchen is one of the city’s most expensive neighborhoods, with smaller walk up buildings nestled between luxury towers.
“Neighborhood tenant unions and community-based organizations are anchors for neighborhood stability,” said Alejandro Coriat, director of borough organizing for Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal. “It is what kept Hell’s Kitchen, some parts of Chelsea, and some parts of the Upper West Side affordable for working class people for a very long time.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.title: Oklahoma Drops Murder Charge Against Richard Glossip, Avoiding Third Trial
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.author: Liliana Segura, Jordan Smith
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/rich.text:
Less than a month before he was scheduled to stand trial a third time, accused of a murder he has always sworn he did not commit, Richard Glossip on Thursday agreed to plead guilty to a lesser charge, a final step toward bringing his three-decade legal saga to an end.
Glossip, 63, was twice convicted and sentenced to death for the 1997 murder of his boss Barry Van Treese inside Room 102 of the rundown motel the Van Treese family owned on the outskirts of Oklahoma City. A 19-year-old maintenance man named Justin Sneed admitted to killing Van Treese, but he insisted Glossip put him up to it. Sneed, who is currently serving a life sentence, escaped the death penalty by becoming the star witness against Glossip.
During a brief hearing that was originally scheduled to address pretrial matters, Oklahoma County Court Judge Natalie Mai instead accepted a plea from Glossip to accessory after the fact and dismissed the murder charge against him. With members of Van Treese’s family looking on from their seats in the jury box, Glossip stood to answer a series of routine questions to confirm that his plea was voluntary. Mai did not ask any specific questions about the crime itself.
Under Oklahoma law in place at the time of the killing, the maximum punishment for accessory after the fact was 45 years. Taking into consideration the decades Glossip spent on death row and credits earned for good behavior, Glossip’s attorneys say he would have been eligible for full release in 2016 and should serve no more time behind bars. But defense lawyers did not reach an agreement with the state as to a proposed sentence. In a statement released after the hearing, Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who once expressed deep concerns about the state’s case against Glossip, made clear that his office will be seeking additional prison time.
Ultimately it will be up to Mai to decide if Glossip should be sentenced to time served or if any additional punishment is warranted.
The contours of Glossip’s plea are remarkably similar to a behind-the-scenes agreement made in 2023 between Drummond and Glossip’s lead attorney Don Knight. At the time, Drummond told Knight that if a court were to overturn Glossip’s conviction, he would resolve the case by accepting a plea to accessory after the fact in exchange for time served – and a promise that Glossip would not sue Oklahoma for anything related to his arrest and incarceration.
But after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Glossip’s conviction in 2025, finding that it was rooted in false testimony and prosecutorial misconduct, Drummond, who by then was running for governor, did an abrupt about-face, announcing he would once again prosecute Glossip for first degree murder.
In the year and a half since then, it has become glaringly apparent that prosecutors from Drummond’s office are grossly ill-equipped to take Glossip’s case to trial. Since his original trial in 1998, the state has lost or destroyed evidence, numerous witnesses have died, and prosecutors have conceded that their own star witness — who has sought to recant his testimony multiple times — can’t actually be expected to remember what happened the night of the killing.
“For 30 years, Richard Glossip has maintained his innocence,” Knight said in a statement after the hearing. “After nearly executing him 9 times, the State of Oklahoma has now dismissed the murder charge against him. This morning, to finally put this matter to rest, Rich pleaded guilty to being an accessory after the fact. We believe Rich has more than paid his debt to society.”
Glossip had originally been charged as an accessory after the fact for initially failing to give police information about the killing. The night Van Treese was killed, Glossip said, Sneed woke him up around 4 a.m. by knocking on the wall of his apartment, which was adjacent to the motel’s office. Standing outside with a black eye, Sneed told Glossip he had chased off some drunks who had broken a window in one of the motel rooms. According to Glossip, he asked Sneed about his black eye, and Sneed flippantly replied, “I killed Barry.”
According to Glossip, it wasn’t until the next morning, when Van Treese was missing, that he realized Sneed might have been serious. Still, Glossip didn’t tell the cops right away; he said his girlfriend suggested waiting until they figured out what was going on.
But Sneed told police Glossip was the mastermind behind the plot to kill Van Treese, and, with no other evidence tying Glossip to the crime, Sneed’s statement became the basis of the state’s case. At Glossip’s 1998 trial, prosecutors said that he had taken advantage of the younger, more vulnerable Sneed, offering him money to kill their boss so that Glossip could take over the motel. “Glossip encouraged, aided and abetted and sent Mr. Sneed off to do his dirty work,” then-prosecutor Fern Smith told the jury.
But this story began falling apart not long after Glossip arrived on death row. A video of Sneed’s police interrogation cast serious doubt on the state’s version of events, revealing coercive questioning by Oklahoma City detectives who pressured Sneed into implicating Glossip.
Glossip’s defense failed to present the tape to the jury, which led an Oklahoma court to overturn Glossip’s first conviction based on ineffective assistance of counsel. Although a second jury convicted him and sent him to die in 2004, doubts over Glossip’s guilt continued to grow.
Glossip subsequently came close to execution many times and may well have been executed if Drummond hadn’t intervened upon taking office in 2023. He ordered an independent investigation into the case, which concluded that rampant prosecutorial misconduct had infected Glossip’s conviction. Drummond asked the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals to overturn the case. When that failed, joined Glossip in asking the Supreme Court to intervene, arguing that Sneed – whom the state has described as its “indispensable witness” – had lied on the witness stand.
Drummond’s concessions about the flaws in the state’s case and his unprecedented advocacy on Glossip’s behalf made his announcement in June 2025 that he would seek to retry Glossip for murder all the more shocking. According to Glossip’s lawyers, the decision also betrayed the long-standing agreement with Drummond to resolve the case and set Glossip free.
After that, Drummond essentially washed his hands of the case to focus on his ultimately failed attempt to become Oklahoma’s next governor, handing off prosecutorial duties to other lawyers in his office. Prosecutors declared that they intended to use the same discredited evidence to try Glossip a third time and spent months fighting to keep him in jail. Despite those efforts, Mai ordered Glossip’s release.
With a December 2026 trial date looming, tensions between the two sides have ratcheted up. Glossip’s lawyers have complained about prosecutors failing to turn over evidence as required under the law. Prosecutors have tried to limit what the defense can present to jurors at trial regarding the history of the case – including asking Mai to bar any mention of Drummond’s previous advocacy on Glossip’s behalf.
Glossip’s sentencing hearing is scheduled for December 17.
Since his release, Glossip has “been living a peaceful and law-abiding life,” Knight said in his statement. “We look forward to an opportunity to show why returning him to custody would not serve the interests of justice, and to ending this nightmare for Rich and all concerned.”
After the hearing, Glossip and his wife, Lea, stood with Knight to address reporters. Glossip thanked Knight and Lea for their support. “It was a hard day,” Lea told The Intercept, “but Richard and I are both people of faith.” She expressed that “today marks a meaningful step toward finally bringing this case to an end. We are both deeply grateful for the tireless efforts of his legal team.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
