https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Before Scott Colom, There Was Hiram Revels
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Eric Foner
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Before Scott Colom, There Was Hiram Revels
As Mississippi sends its first Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction, historian Eric Foner profiles the man who went first.
When Scott Colom is sworn in this January, he will be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Blanche K. Bruce left office in 1881.
The first was Hiram Revels, whose election by the Mississippi legislature in 1870 made him the first African American to serve in Congress. In February 2020, at a ceremony marking the 150th anniversary of that election, held in the same Old Capitol chamber in Jackson where legislators chose Revels, the historian Eric Foner gave the keynote address.
Foner is a longtime contributor to The Nation, a member of its editorial board, and the author of Reconstruction: America’s Unfinished Revolution, 1863–1877, along with many other books. His remarks, lightly edited, follow.
It’s a great pleasure to be here for this historic evening and to celebrate the election of Hiram Revels to the US Senate.
Everybody in the United States probably knows that in our two centuries or so of existence, Barack Obama has been the only African American president. Less familiar is the fact that of the approximately 2,000 men and women who have served in the US Senate since 1789, only 10 have been Black. Ten out of 2,000, or one-half of 1 percent, is a considerably worse ratio than one president out of 45. Of those 10, two—Hiram Revels and then Blanche K. Bruce—were elected from Mississippi during Reconstruction, the era that followed the Civil War. These numbers offer a stark reminder of the almost insurmountable barriers that have kept African Americans from the highest offices in this land, and they also remind us how unique a moment Reconstruction was in the history of American democracy.
This month, February 2020, appropriately Black History Month, marks the 150th anniversary of two momentous events. On February 3, 1870, Iowa became the 28th state to ratify the 15th Amendment, which prohibited denial of voting rights because of race, making the 15th Amendment part of the Constitution. Three weeks later, on February 25, Hiram Revels became the first African American to take a seat in Congress—either house. Later that year, Joseph Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black member of the House of Representatives.
Revels was elected to fill an unexpired term that had been vacant since Mississippi’s secession from the Union in 1861. He served for only one year. No senator could be expected to accomplish a great deal in one year as a freshman senator. “We could have wished for more activity in a virgin field for Negro talent,” commented Frederick Douglass’s newspaper, the New National Era, when Revels’s term concluded, “but on the whole we are content. The precedent itself was something…. by the blacks he was hailed with joy as the harbinger of a better time and a brighter period for the black man and the nation.” As this observation suggests, Revels accomplished more as a symbol than as a legislator.
One indication of his impact on public consciousness lies in the wide circulation of his pictorial image. These years saw the production of numerous lithographs celebrating the overthrow of slavery and the achievement by African Americans of equal civil and political rights. They generally depicted scenes of slavery and freedom, along with likenesses of Abraham Lincoln and prominent Black leaders—Revels almost always among them. In addition, an engraving of a portrait of Revels by the German-born artist Theodore Kaufmann was widely sold during and after Reconstruction, especially to Black families. Frederick Douglass noted that African Americans “so often see ourselves described and painted as monkeys that we think it is a great piece of fortune to find an exception to this rule.” The dignified portrait of Revels was on the wall of many, many Black families in this post–Civil War era.
Revels’s election to the Senate would have been inconceivable without the advent in 1867 of what historians called Radical Reconstruction, when Congress required the former Confederate states, with the exception of Tennessee, to extend the right to vote to Black men. At that time, most Northern states, as well as the border slave states that had remained in the Union, still limited voting to whites. In fact, it’s ironic that African American men in the South, the vast majority of them recently emancipated slaves, won the right to vote three years before most of those in the rest of the country.
Black male suffrage in the South led directly to the election of the country’s first Black political officials. During Reconstruction, some 2,000 African American men, by my estimate, occupied public offices, ranging from Mississippi’s two US senators to 14 members of the House of Representatives, hundreds elected to state constitutional conventions and legislatures, and numerous sheriffs, city councilmen, magistrates, and many others. This was a remarkable experiment in biracial democracy, something virtually without precedent in world history up to that point, and it aroused intense opposition from adherents of white supremacy. It was met with violent assaults on Black voters and officials by the Ku Klux Klan and similar organizations. Democrats—then the party of white nationalism, to use a modern phrase—also launched a highly organized campaign of vilification (fake news, we would call it today) portraying Black voters as incapable of participating intelligently in political life, and Black officials as ignorant, corrupt, and unfit for public service.
At the beginning of the 20th century, as the rights Blacks had acquired in Reconstruction were being systematically stripped away, this political propaganda was given scholarly legitimacy by the nation’s historians. Indeed, Reconstruction stands as a prime example of what we might call the politics of history. I don’t mean whether the historian is a Democrat or Republican. What I’m talking about is the way in which historical interpretation both reflects and helps to shape the politics of the time in which the historian is writing.
For most of the 20th century, what we call the Dunning school—after my long-ago predecessor William Dunning, who taught Civil War history at Columbia University—dominated historical writing and popular thinking on Reconstruction. In that view, Reconstruction marked the lowest point in the saga of American democracy. It was a time of corruption and misgovernment. This portrait reached a broad public in the film Birth of a Nation, which had its premiere in Woodrow Wilson’s White House. One crucial scene in that film vividly demonstrates the so-called incapacity of Black legislators: They sit with bare feet propped on their desks, swigging whiskey, munching on chicken bones, and lasciviously eyeing white women in the galleries.
As late as 1947, the University of Georgia historian E. Merton Coulter, a former president of the Southern Historical Association, described Black officeholding in Reconstruction as, quote, “the most spectacular and exotic development in government in the history of white civilization, the longest to be remembered, shuddered at, and execrated.”
The Dunning school has long since been repudiated by professional historians, although its outlook survives to this day in some corners of popular historical consciousness. But it enjoyed a remarkable longevity, which can be explained by the fact that it harmonized with the racial system of the United States from around 1900 until the civil rights era of the 1960s, because the political lesson of this interpretation of history was very clear: It was a mistake to give Black people the right to vote and hold office; therefore, the white South was correct—legitimated—when it later took those rights away. As Gunnar Myrdal noted in his influential 1944 book An American Dilemma, when confronted with demands for change in the racial system, white Southerners, quote, “will regularly bring forward the horrors of the Reconstruction governments.” That was the trump card if you said that African Americans should enjoy the same rights as anybody else in the South.
When the civil rights revolution took place, the pillars of this old interpretation, especially its overt racism, fell to the ground, and Reconstruction was completely reinterpreted. Today, most historians see it as a noble, if ultimately unsuccessful, effort to establish for the first time in American history an interracial democracy—a precursor of the modern civil rights movement, which was sometimes called the Second Reconstruction. If the era was tragic, we now think, it was not because it was attempted but because it failed, and thus left to subsequent generations the difficult problem of racial justice. Yet far too many Americans still know little or nothing about this transformative period in our history.
So Hiram Revels is worth remembering today both as a pioneer of Black officeholding and as a refutation of outdated stereotypes. Modern research has established that, far from being ignorant and impoverished field hands, as portrayed by the Dunning school, the majority of Black officeholders in Reconstruction owned property, had access to education before or immediately after the Civil War, and many had been free before the war. Some were indeed corrupt, but no more so than white politicians of both parties in an era dubbed by Mark Twain the Gilded Age because of its less than exacting standard of political rectitude.
Of course, Black Reconstruction officials were almost all men of modest means. They stood in sharp contrast to the wealthy lawyers and plantation owners who dominated Southern government before the Civil War. In fact, the emergence of these men like Revels offers living proof of what Thomas Paine, writing about the American Revolution, described as “all the extent and capacity of ordinary people, invisible in normal times, that never fails to appear in revolutions.”
Rather than an ignorant former slave unfit for office, Hiram Revels, for one, was well educated, widely traveled, and fully prepared for legislative responsibilities. But it’s inconceivable that Revels and others like him could have been elevated to public office without the transformative events of the 1860s: the Civil War, emancipation, the rewriting of the Constitution, and the advent of biracial democracy in the South. To understand how this happened requires a very brief look at the unfolding of Reconstruction.
Before the Civil War, slavery powerfully shaped the boundaries of the American body politic. Only a handful of—maybe less than five—Black officials existed anywhere in the country, a few justices of the peace in Northern communities with strong abolitionist sentiments. On the eve of the Civil War, no person, free or slave, could be a citizen of the United States. That was what the Supreme Court decided in 1857 in the infamous Dred Scott decision.
The only ones before the war who advocated a nonracial definition of American nationality were the abolitionists, white and Black. They not only fought against slavery but also for equal rights for free Black Americans. Black political gatherings before the Civil War consciously chose to call themselves conventions of colored citizens. They were claiming a citizenship that the nation denied them. They put forward a definition of citizenship based on birthright—being born in the country—severed from the concept of race.
This is what came about during Reconstruction, with the ratification in December 1865 of the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, which irrevocably abolished slavery. “The one question of the age,” one congressman declared, “was settled.” But if it resolved the fate of slavery, abolition opened a host of other issues. Was the racial inequality inseparable from slavery also being abolished? What would be the status of the former slaves, and who would determine it? What did it mean to be a free person in postwar America? These were the questions on which the politics of Reconstruction persistently turned.
White Southerners had their own answers, as became clear when Abraham Lincoln was assassinated and Andrew Johnson became president. Once lionized in the Dunning school as a heroic defender of the Constitution against vindictive Radical Republicans, Johnson today has a strong claim to being considered the worst president in American history. There are other claimants, but he is a—he is a contender, let’s put it that way.
Johnson lacked all of Lincoln’s qualities of greatness. He was deeply racist, unwilling to ever change his mind, had no sense of Northern public opinion, and lacked the ability to work with Congress. Johnson set up new governments in the South in the months after the Civil War, controlled entirely by white men. These governments, including that of Mississippi, enacted a series of laws called the Black Codes to define the freedom African Americans now enjoyed. These laws gave Blacks virtually no civil or political rights. They required all adult Black men, at the beginning of each year, to sign a labor contract to go to work for a white employer or be deemed a vagrant and sold to someone who would pay his fine.
The Black Codes alarmed the Republican Party, which controlled Congress, into thinking that the South was trying to restore slavery in all but name. Most Republicans agreed that the 13th Amendment, which freed all the slaves, empowered Congress to ensure, as one senator put it, that “the man made free by the Constitution is a free man.” Indeed, Congress soon passed one of the most important laws in American history, the Civil Rights Act of 1866, the first law to declare who is a free citizen of the United States and what rights they are to enjoy.
The Civil Rights Act declared that all persons born in the United States—except Native Americans, who were still considered members of their tribal sovereignty—all other persons born in the country are American citizens. This is the principle of birthright citizenship, a statement that anyone can be a loyal American. Race, religion, national origin do not matter, nor does the legal status of one’s parents. It severs citizenship from race, as the abolitionists had long demanded.
The Civil Rights Act went on to declare that all these citizens must enjoy basic legal equality. States cannot pass one set of laws for Black people—as, indeed, they have just done—and another set for whites. The law guarantees equality of civil rights, specifically the right to sign contracts, own property, testify in court, sue and be sued. These are the rights of free labor, necessary to compete in the economic marketplace.
Andrew Johnson vetoed the civil rights bill, and it became the first important law in American history enacted over a veto. Johnson’s veto message denounced the law for what today is called reverse discrimination. This is Johnson on the civil rights bill: “The distinction of race and color is by the bill made to operate in favor of the colored and against the white race.” But of course, a law a law can always be repealed. So very soon, Congress put these principles and others into the 14th Amendment, the most important change in our Constitution since the Bill of Rights.
Among other things, the amendment tried to address an ironic consequence of abolition. The end of slavery also ended the three-fifths clause of the Constitution. Under that, the white—the free population and three-fifths of the slaves were counted in apportioning members of Congress among the states. Now, with all free, the entire Black population—five-fifths—would be counted, giving the Southern states enhanced representation in the House of Representatives. Radical Republicans in Congress insisted that the only way to guarantee that Southern congressmen fully respected Black freedom was to give the right to vote to African American men.
But Black suffrage still remained highly controversial, and the more moderate majority in Congress believed the Northern public would not embrace such a departure from the long tradition of state control of voting qualifications. The result was a complicated compromise: a section, which has never been enforced, that deprives states of part of their representation in the House if they denied the right to vote to any group of male citizens. Thus Mississippi, whose population then was a little over 50 percent Black, would lose half its congressmen if it continued to deny Black men the right to vote. But, as I say, it was never enforced.
This section also raised an outcry among the era’s feminist movement, because for the first time it introduced the word “male” into the Constitution. Unlike men, there was no penalty if states denied women, Black or white, the right to vote, as all of them, of course, did at that time.
But the heart of the 14th Amendment is the first section. This constitutionalizes the principle of birthright citizenship and goes on to bar states from abridging the privileges or immunities of citizens or denying to any person—citizen or immigrant—the equal protection of the law. The 14th Amendment introduces a commitment to equality into the Constitution for the first time, and the language is race-neutral, which has had enormous consequences in our own time. In recent decades, the courts have used this amendment to expand the legal rights of numerous groups of Americans, most recently gay men and women seeking to marry. All in all, to borrow a phrase from the editor George William Curtis at the time, the 14th Amendment changed the constitution for white men into a constitution for mankind.
Encouraged by President Johnson, the all-white governments he had established in the South, except for Tennessee, refused by overwhelming margins to ratify the 14th Amendment. The vote in the Mississippi legislature, probably in this very room, was 115 to 0. Clearly, the principle of equal rights regardless of race was not easy to accept. After winning a sweeping victory in the congressional elections of 1866, Northern Republicans decided that the only way to secure both ratification of the 14th Amendment and what they called loyal government in the South was to replace the Johnson regimes which one with ones in which African Americans enjoyed the right to vote and hold office. Thus began Radical Reconstruction.
Black voters celebrated the winning of the right to vote—at least for men—as recognition that they were now full members of the American body politic. They flocked to the polls in remarkable numbers. In Southern elections in 1867 and 1868, over 80 percent of those eligible to vote cast ballots, a far higher percentage than we experienced in elections today.
Along with white allies, Black voters elected biracial constitutional conventions, which drew up new documents for the Southern states based on political equality. The 15th Amendment, as I noted, soon followed, its ratification sweeping away the laws of the 17 states that still limited voting to white men. Republicans, Black and white, celebrated the 15th Amendment as the triumphant conclusion of what the party leader Carl Schurz called the “constitutional revolution” of Reconstruction.
At a gathering here in Jackson, James Lynch, Mississippi’s newly elected African American secretary of state—a predecessor of Congressman Espy, who I think was secretary of state here also a while ago—James Lynch described the amendment as both an embodiment of the ideals of the Declaration of Independence and part of the worldwide spread of democracy. “Nothing in all history,” exclaimed the veteran abolitionist editor William Lloyd Garrison, “equaled this wonderful, quiet, sudden transformation of 4 million human beings from the auction block to the ballot box.”
Hiram Revels’s life and his brief career in the US Senate reflected this constitutional revolution. Born free in Fayetteville, North Carolina, in 1827, Revels was descended from ancestors as diverse as America itself. They included Native Americans, whites, and Blacks. However, Revels enjoyed opportunities, especially extensive access to education, unavailable to most African Americans before the Civil War. His forebears, he wrote in a brief autobiographical essay, “had been free as far back as my knowledge extends.” He recalled that two fine colored schools existed in Fayetteville, and one of them he attended as a youth. In 1844, Revels moved to Indiana, where he received further education as the only Black student in a Quaker seminary. He went to attend another seminary in Ohio, a school in Baltimore, and at a time when only a tiny number of Americans of any race attended college, he studied for a year at Knox College in Illinois.
Even in a society known for its migratory population, Revels before the Civil War was unusually well traveled. Ordained a minister in the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1845, he preached as an itinerant missionary in Indiana, Illinois, and Kansas. He even ventured into the Upper South slave states of Kentucky, Tennessee, and Missouri, hoping to bring religious instruction to slaves. His presence there sparked what he later described as “a great deal of opposition.” At one point, he was jailed for “preaching the gospel to Negroes.” Revels later claimed not to have said anything that might incite enslaved men and women to run away, but he added that when in the free states, “I always assisted the fugitive slave.”
When the Civil War broke out, Revels was working in Baltimore as an AME minister and principal of a high school for Black students. In 1863, he moved to St. Louis, where he founded a school for freed slaves and, according to some accounts, helped to organize Missouri’s first regiment of Black Union soldiers. He appears to have come to Mississippi in 1864. He threw himself into educating the freedmen and women, and in 1868 became pastor of an AME church in Natchez.
Revels’s political career began in 1868, when Union Gen. Adelbert Ames, the state’s provisional governor, appointed him to the Natchez Board of Aldermen. Revels was soon elected here to the state Senate. Before the ratification of the 17th Amendment in 1913, US senators were elected by the state legislatures, not by popular vote. With a large Republican majority, which included almost three dozen Black members, Mississippi’s lawmakers chose Governor Ames to fill one Senate seat, which was a full term, and Revels to fill the shorter term, which, as I said, expired in one year. His election came as something of a surprise, as Revels was little known in Republican Party circles outside Natchez.
John R. Lynch, later a Black congressman from Mississippi, claimed that the invocation Revels delivered at the opening of the legislative session, which he called “one of the most impressive and eloquent prayers ever delivered in the Senate chamber,” made Revels a candidate for the US Senate seat. But it’s also true that as a presiding elder of the Methodist Episcopal Church, which he had recently left the AME to join, Revels was well known in Mississippi’s Black community. In any event, the Black members of the legislature pressed for the elevation of one of their own to the Senate. The assertiveness of Blacks—of Mississippi’s Black political leadership continued throughout Reconstruction, to the chagrin of many white Republicans.
Revels arrived in Washington in February 1870. He received an enthusiastic welcome from the city’s Black community, complete with dinners in his honor, including one attended by President Grant and the members of his cabinet. The Senate’s small contingent of Democrats challenged Revels’s right to take his seat. The Constitution requires a senator to have been a citizen for at least nine years, but Black citizenship, Democrats insisted, had only been established by the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868. Before then, they said, the Dred Scott decision, which limited citizenship to whites, was the law of the land. Thus, they said, Revels fell several years short of eligibility.
This debate, which also played out in the nation’s press, took on a starkly racist tone. The New York World, the nation’s leading Democratic paper, described Revels as, quote, “a lineal descendant” of an orangutan. Senator Garrett Davis of Kentucky claimed that Dred Scott had been correctly decided and indeed was still the law of the land. The Republican leader Senator Jacob Howard of Michigan declared himself nauseated by the overtly racist language and that anyone in 1870 could still invoke Dred Scott. Republicans insisted that the Reconstruction Amendments—13, 14, and 15—not to mention Union victory in the Civil War, had nullified central parts of the prewar legal order rooted in slavery, the disqualification of Blacks from citizenship among them. On February 25, 1870, by a vote of 48 to eight, entirely along party lines, the Senate voted to seat Hiram Revels.
During his year in the Senate, Revels later insisted, “I did all I could for the benefit of my needy and much imposed-upon people.” He spoke vigorously for the reinstatement of Black legislators who had been illegally expelled from Georgia’s General Assembly. He persuaded Secretary of War William Belknap to arrange for Black mechanics to be hired for the first time at the Baltimore Navy Yard. When a bill to establish a free public school system in the nation’s capital came before the Senate, Revels strenuously opposed an amendment that deleted a clause banning distinctions on account of race in school admissions. In other words, he opposed allowing the schools to become racially segregated. He spoke eloquently of the discrimination faced by Blacks on railroads, streetcars, and steamboats, discrimination he and his family had experienced while traveling in Kansas before the war, when they were ordered to leave the first-class railroad car. Revels condemned, quote, “the prejudice in this country to color,” emphasizing that Blacks had done nothing to deserve it. “I sometimes fear that it is on the increase,” he added. “We must admit that it is wrong.” But the amendment passed, and the District of Columbia’s school system remained segregated until the mid-1950s.
When Revels was elected, a Mississippi Democratic newspaper called the result “a good omen,” as he belonged to the moderate wing of the Republican Party. And in fact, on the spectrum of Reconstruction politics, Revels was one of the more conservative Mississippi Black Republicans. Like any senator, he introduced bills to benefit local constituents, including one calling for federal aid to rebuild Mississippi River levees damaged during the war and another to help support the construction of a railroad in Mississippi. But these did not pass.
Only one of his measures became law: a bill restoring the civil and political rights of former Confederate Army officer Arthur E. Reynolds, so that he could be appointed to a judgeship by Mississippi’s governor, James L. Alcorn. Revels told the Senate that while violence was common in other states, Blacks and whites in Mississippi were getting along harmoniously—a statement that led to criticism from fellow Republicans in Mississippi, where the Klan had already made its appearance and was committing outrages.
During his brief career in the Senate, Revels was in great demand as a public speaker. In the summer and fall of 1870, he embarked on an ambitious lecturing tour. Many of his speeches celebrated the ratification of the 15th Amendment. Except in Philadelphia, where the Academy of Music refused to allow him to speak in its hall, he drew large and appreciative audiences. When Revels lectured in Boston, the abolitionist Wendell Phillips said he could hardly believe that a thousand men had come to hear “a senator from that race which has been so long victimized.” The speaking tour proved to be quite successful, and on October 1, 1870, Revels sent his wife a check for $3,000—an enormous sum at that time—to help the family purchase a plantation.
After Revels’s term expired, Governor Alcorn appointed him to head a new college for Black students named for the governor. Alcorn State was the nation’s first Black land-grant institution. A prominent planter, Alcorn had hoped to lead what he called a “harnessed revolution,” in which Black civil and political rights would be respected by prominent whites like himself, but effective political power would remain in white hands. Revels sided with Alcorn against a more radical wing of the party headed by Adelbert Ames, the ex-governor. Few Black leaders or voters followed his example. With overwhelming Black support, Ames was elected governor in 1873. Shortly thereafter, Revels resigned from his university presidency after Ames indicated a desire to replace him because of his close ties with ex-governor Alcorn.
Revels, virtually alone among Mississippi’s Black leaders, supported the Democratic campaign that overthrew Reconstruction in the state in 1875. Immediately after the election, he wrote a letter to President Grant criticizing Northerners who had taken leadership positions in the Republican Party, known by their opponents as carpetbaggers. Despite the abundance of evidence that Democratic political terrorism was largely responsible for the end of Reconstruction in Mississippi, Revels told a Senate investigating committee that he himself had no knowledge of acts of violence against Black voters. After what Democrats called the “redemption” of Mississippi, Revels was reappointed president of Alcorn State. He retired in 1882.
As the harsh reality of Jim Crow replaced the optimistic vision of the future embodied in Reconstruction, Revels seemed to become more and more conservative. He was always more of a churchman and an educator than a politician. He had long believed that the descendants of slavery, through no fault of their own, needed guidance from well-disposed whites. In 1876, Revels published a protest in a religious newspaper against the Methodist Episcopal Church’s plans to hold racially segregated annual conferences in the South. He warned that such a policy would damage the self-esteem of Black clergymen and deprive the, quote, “unavoidably poor and ignorant colored people” of white religious instruction.
In 1890, in this room here, I think, Mississippi’s constitutional convention stripped the state’s Black population of the right to vote through ostensibly race-neutral requirements, such as payment of a poll tax and the ability to provide a reasonable interpretation of the state Constitution. This so-called understanding clause left the right to vote in the hands of local registrars, generally low-level Democratic Party functionaries. For good measure, the convention called for the repeal of the 15th Amendment. Some Black Mississippians challenged these provisions in federal court, but the Supreme Court did not heed their pleas.
Revels’s response reflected his more moderate style of political leadership. He called on African Americans to seek the confidence, respect, and protection of white citizens who have the influence and power to protect them, winning this respect by their industry. This was essentially the message Booker T. Washington would articulate five years later in his celebrated speech at the Atlanta Cotton States Exposition. So Revels, I think, represents that strand of Black political thought from the Reconstruction era up through the era of Booker T. Washington.
In his last years, Revels served as pastor of churches in Vicksburg and Holly Springs and taught school in Claiborne County. He died in 1901. Two weeks after his death, George H. White of North Carolina, the last Black congressman of the long post–Civil War era, gave his farewell address to the House of Representatives. “This is perhaps the Negro’s temporary farewell to Congress,” said Congressman White, “but let me say, Phoenix-like he will rise up some day and come again.”
But the reemergence of Black members of Congress did not take place for quite a while. Until Oscar De Priest’s election to represent a Chicago district 28 years later, Congress remained completely white. Not until 1973, when Barbara Jordan and Andrew Young took their seats, did a former Confederate state send another African American to the House of Representatives. As for the Senate, Blanche K. Bruce served one term after being elected from Mississippi in 1874. Not until nearly a century passed, in 1967, would the Senate welcome its next Black member, Edward Brooke of Massachusetts.
Today, the House of Representatives includes 54 Black members, including two nonvoting delegates. No fewer than 22 of them represent states of the old Confederacy. As for the Senate, Carol Moseley Braun, elected from Illinois in 1992, was the next after Brooke. Barack Obama and Roland Burris later succeeded her in that same Illinois seat, and William Cowan of Massachusetts served very briefly. Today, for the first time in American history, the Senate has three African American members: Cory Booker of New Jersey, Kamala Harris of California, and Tim Scott of South Carolina. Scott is the first African American senator since Revels and Bruce from a state that seceded from the Union and experienced Reconstruction. Perhaps there will be another one soon.
Revels’s career exemplifies important features of the Reconstruction era. Then as now, the Black church and school were springboards to political careers. As with him, after farmer, minister was the most common occupation of Black Reconstruction officials, with educator not far behind. Like Revels, many Black leaders had a connection with the Union military during the Civil War.

While the Reconstruction Republican Party achieved a remarkable degree of racial cooperation, the Black-white alliance—and relations between African Americans, Northerners, and Southern whites—was frequently fraught with tension, as in Mississippi. Like many other Black Republican officeholders, Revels had descendants who went on to distinction in other fields. His daughter Susie Revels Cayton edited a newspaper for many years in Seattle, Washington. She had two sons: the sociologist Horace R. Cayton Jr., the co-author of a classic study of African American life in Chicago, Black Metropolis, and Revels Cayton, a very important West Coast labor leader.
Revels’s career also suggests that, even after the passage of a century and a half, Reconstruction remains part of our lives today—or, to put it another way, key issues of that era remain unresolved. Who should have the right to vote? As in the late 19th century, state voter-suppression laws today have denied thousands of Americans the right to cast a ballot.
And I should say that, since that is the case, the second section of the 14th Amendment ought to be enforced, taking away members of Congress for those states which are denying so many citizens the right to vote. As in the late 19th century, who is entitled to citizenship remains highly contested. It’s fought out every day on our country’s borders. Indeed, last year President Trump claimed the right to abrogate the first section of the 14th Amendment by executive order, with regard to American-born children of undocumented immigrants. The public campaign a few years ago to deny the citizenship of President Obama is reminiscent of the efforts in 1870 to prevent Hiram Revels from taking his Senate seat because he was supposedly not a citizen. And in the oft-encountered idea that expanding the rights of non-whites somehow punishes the white majority, the ghost of Andrew Johnson still haunts our discussions of race.
The greatest lesson of Reconstruction is that rights, even when inscribed in the Constitution, can never be taken for granted. If the election of Revels and hundreds like him seemed to augur a permanent change in our democracy, the subsequent abrogation of those rights in the South, with the acquiescence of the rest of the nation, reminds us that, to alter a celebrated observation of Martin Luther King Jr., the arc of the moral universe does not always bend toward justice.
Today, we live at a time in some ways like the 1890s, when, as Frederick Douglass complained, “principles which we all thought to have been firmly and permanently settled have been boldly assaulted and overthrown.” But despite the many disappointments that followed, the anniversary of the seating of Hiram Revels remains worthy of celebration as part of the long effort to purge this nation of the legacy of slavery. And, properly remembered, Reconstruction remains an inspiration to those striving to make this a more equal, more just society.

The Trump administration quietly broadened its crackdown on campus pro-Palestine protests over the summer, moving to ensnare one of the largest unions in the country in a case revolving around alleged incidents of vandalism.
The national headquarters of the American Federation of Teachers, or AFT, received a grand jury subpoena in August as part of an ongoing federal investigation into protests at the University of Michigan. Twelve pro-Palestine activists have been charged with felonies in the case.
The subpoena against the AFT, which has not been previously reported and was obtained by The Intercept, shows the administration casting a wider net in its investigation into student protesters than was previously known.
The Graduate Employees’ Organization, or GEO, an AFT local at the university, also received a notice to provide information and testimony to a grand jury around the same time, according to a copy of the previously unreported subpoena obtained by The Intercept.
The effort to draw a powerful, liberal union into a case that revolves around spray-painting charges represents a dramatic escalation in Donald Trump’s war on the left.
“They’re using this language around conspiracy and trying to draw in all of these different organizations that are taking stances against fascism, against the government, and anything that’s counter to their ideology,” said Natalie Chen, who serves as GEO’s communications director. “This is perhaps another ‘in’ for them to broaden their attack
on labor.”
Subpoenas to Crush Dissent
As pro-Palestine protests swept campuses across the country in 2024 and widespread demonstration broke out against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this year, the Trump administration has sought to paint left-of-center protest, nonprofit work, and labor organizing as a nefarious far-left conspiracy, even labeling some activists and groups as terrorists.
Critics of the administration’s crackdown on Palestine solidarity and protests against ICE see moves like the ones against AFT and GEO as part of an effort to silence dissent.
“Historically, federal grand jury subpoenas have been used against social movements and political dissent to gather information, to isolate individuals, and of course to try and prosecute people,” said Xavier de Janon, executive director of the National Lawyers Guild. “What is different in politicized cases is the extent of people and places that get subpoenaed, which many people see clearly goes way beyond what they’re supposedly trying to prosecute.”
Activists at the University of Michigan said the effort to extract information about students from the union was an attempt to further target pro-Palestine protesters and their relationships with labor organizers.
The grand jury subpoenas came as part of a case that has seen a dozen protesters become caught up in serious federal charges against the students, dubbed “the Michigan 12.” They allege that protesters committed illegal acts like vandalism as part of a pressure campaign seeking to push university officials to divest school holdings tied to the Israeli genocide in Palestine.
The subpoenas against the GEO and AFT were requested by federal prosecutor Margaret Smith with assistance from FBI agent Kara Phipps — two federal officials deeply enmeshed in the investigation into the Michigan 12. (The Department of Justice declined to comment for this story.)
GEO Under Fire
The subpoenas were issued as the GEO was already reeling after its president, Hiab Teshome, was charged with felony embezzlement by local prosecutors working in conjunction with the University of Michigan Police Department.
Authorities alleged that Teshome, who was a bargaining team member in the middle of intense contract negotiations between the union and the school, misused organizational funds to purchase laptops for a campus club.
In a statement, the GEO called the charges meritless and characterized them as an attempt to limit protected union activity. Teshome was later cleared of any wrongdoing by the university’s student government, and the charges against her were thrown out by a judge.
Federal prosecutors issued the subpoenas the same day the charges against Teshome were dismissed, leaving activists little time to regroup.
Although GEO is not mentioned in the federal indictment against protesters, the AFT chapter is a prominent member of the Tahrir coalition, a pro-Palestine student collective that is referenced repeatedly in federal filings and characterized by prosecutors as having ties with defendants.
Broad in Scope
The scope of the information requested of the unions by the federal government is broad. GEO and AFT are being compelled, according to the subpoenas, to surrender information including complete membership rolls, payroll records on officers, reimbursement policies, audit reports, and all transcribed minutes on membership and executive board meetings of the University of Michigan local since January 2023.
The American Federation of Teachers has more than 1.7 million members and more than 3,000 local chapters.
After receiving the subpoena, GEO immediately obtained attorneys and filed a motion to quash the order. The national office of the AFT, however, has not publicly acknowledged receiving the directive or stated whether it intends to comply. (AFT did not respond to requests for comment about the subpoenas, including whether the union would be complying.)
Teshome, the GEO president, believes that the subpoena against the AFT may be an attempt by the federal government to circumvent the local union and force the national organization to comply.
“GEO has taken the stance that we will do everything in our power to protect the data and the information of our membership,” Teshome said. “I think that this is a strategy that the federal government is using in order to try to actually receive the information that they are trying to get by usurping us as a local union and going instead to AFT national.”
Additionally, Teshome likened the GEO’s case to similar surveillance activities conducted by federal agents against trade unionists in Minnesota as part of the Trump White House’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, a presidential directive that attempts to criminalize leftist political organizations.
“All of the repression we are seeing across the country is the federal government’s attack on anyone who has political thought,” Teshome said. “Michigan is no different than all of these other cases in that we are one of the testing grounds for NSPM-7 and how much oppression can be applied through the federal government in order to demobilize and disorganize.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.title: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.author: Ben Berke, John Moritz, Anastasia Lennon
https://www.propublica.org/article/offsh.text:
On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.
Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea.
He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast.
Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke.
The company never came.
A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind development.
In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out.
Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be recouped.
ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s efforts.
Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal views.
But last year, the administration temporarily forced five projects to stop construction, further clouding the horizon. Courts allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat. Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind, which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England homes at maximum capacity.
The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, the administration is paying other wind developers billions of dollars to sell back their leases and walk away.
At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that would accelerate U.S. energy development. When a reporter pointed out that the bill includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause wind turbines are a major loser.”
The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”
Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind farms.
As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed new contracts servicing the wind industry.
In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300 million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry.
Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working on construction sites offshore.
“I think the future just looked limitless,” said New London Mayor Michael Passero.
Before wind, Passero said that officials tried for years to attract different industries to the pier, which is overshadowed by larger port facilities in New York and Boston. It was often used to import and store large piles of road salt.
The most recent wind project based at the pier is scheduled to finish work next year. Port officials have yet to find a tenant to occupy the space.
“They’ll be back to the old days of trying to lure cargo here,” Passero said.
Amid Trump’s war on wind, a frontline of union and nonunion workers watches opportunity disappear. One project alone, Vineyard Wind, directly employed a total of more than 3,700 full- and part-time workers — most of them from Massachusetts — over eight years of development and construction, according to the developer.
During peak construction activity, as many as 300 union members worked onshore in southeastern Massachusetts for the project, the first large offshore wind farm fully permitted by the federal government. The wind farm was completed this year.
Longshoreman Onix Vazquez, 34, worked full-time tying up barges and moving turbine components on and off New Bedford’s wind pier. He grew up a few blocks away and said he had struggled to find lucrative work until Vineyard Wind began hiring from his union.
Vazquez’s hourly wage of $50 was nearly double what he previously earned unloading occasional shipments of tangerines and juice concentrate. It allowed him and other members of his historically Black union to make down payments on houses, pay off medical bills and for the first time take their families on out-of-state vacations.
“Most of us have to get other jobs for now or collect unemployment,” said Kevin Rose, president of New Bedford’s longshoremen union, which put about two dozen members to work on the project.
The union had been planning to rebuild its nearby meeting hall, which was demolished a decade earlier when work grew scarce. But the next developer to lease New Bedford’s wind pier has delayed its project indefinitely. The union members have put the plans for their new hall on hold.
Vazquez said he now works a seasonal job in the cranberry industry for much lower pay.
“They don’t see that it affects us, the ones that work the projects,” he said.
In response to questions about the impact of the administration’s actions on American offshore wind workers, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of the Interior repeated criticisms of offshore wind as an expensive and unreliable source of energy.
“The reality is that the Biden administration lured companies into these projects with the promise of millions of taxpayer dollars in subsidies to make these offshore wind projects viable,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The view is more nuanced on the ground. New Bedford’s fishing industry is generally critical of wind farm development because fishermen worry about disruption to fishing grounds.
But fishing catch limits keep boats tied to docks for much of the year. Work for wind farms gets them out to sea and helps pay the bills.
Over the past few years of construction, Vineyard Wind paid about $11 million to 55 fishing vessels from New England and an estimated 60 to 70 fishermen, according to the developer. (The figure also covers fuel.) The fishermen look out for protected species, guard exposed underwater cable as it’s being laid and log information for the developer.
Some fishermen say they will work in offshore wind for as long as they can.
“The scallop boats need the extra revenue,” said Patrick Walsh, 37, a fifth-generation fisherman who plans to rejoin his father’s fishing business when wind work wraps up. “The worst thing for a boat is to sit. Those boats are made to work.”
Wind farm work made it possible for him to buy his first house, he said.
“Fishing would pay bills, and wind was going in the bank.”

https://inthesetimes.com/article/massage.title: Seattle’s Massage Workers Demand Safety and Solidarity—Not Stigma
https://inthesetimes.com/article/massage.author: Kim Kelly
https://inthesetimes.com/article/massage.text:
SEATTLE—On September 7, 1885, three Chinese hop pickers were shot dead in their camp outside Seattle. That night, their attackers snuck up to the tent of sleeping laborers and opened fire. Three died and three more were wounded, yet their assailants were never convicted or punished for their bloody crimes.
The attack marked the beginning of a years-long campaign of harassment and violence toward Chinese immigrant workers in what was then called Washington Territory.
Two months after the Squak Valley murders, a white mob, led by the town’s elected leaders, descended upon Tacoma’s then-thriving Chinatown neighborhood, drove out 700 of its inhabitants and burned the entire district to the ground. This pattern of white supremacist, anti-Chinese violence was repeated across the Northwest, including in Seattle, where more than 200 Chinese residents were expelled at gunpoint in 1886.
“It was not looked at with shame, but with pride by the anti-Chinese vigilantes and the state — so much so that it had a name: the Tacoma method,” said J.M. Wong, a member of the Massage Parlor Organizing Project (MPOP), during a press conference in late May.
Ahead of the summer 2026 World Cup, police raided more than 50 Asian massage parlors in the Seattle area, costing workers their jobs and homes. The workers and their advocates at MPOP responded by demanding an end to the raids and emphasizing the need for a state licensing path that recognizes their cultural expertise.
The press conference, held outside the Wing Luke Museum of Asian Pacific American Experience in Seattle, was part of MPOP’s ongoing Safety Not Stigma campaign. “Anti-Asian stigmatization and racism is still here with us today,” Wong said. “Today’s model chases after immigrant women and workers in the name of stamping out trafficking and rescuing the very people they want to silence and exclude from the city’s future.”
The raids came as Seattle prepared to host six World Cup matches in June and July — and news of increasingly violent ICE raids on immigrant communities continued to spread throughout the country. Police and fire departments in King and Pierce counties raided the parlors as part of a “cross-agency anti-trafficking initiative”; but in the eyes of these workers, and their advocates, they weren’t being “saved”; they were being punished.
“Police and fire tell us in the media that these women were victims who needed to be rescued,” Wong said. “But this is not what we heard from the workers who were in distress outside their places of work, afraid to get their belongings.”
As a result of the raids, many workers lost their livelihoods and their housing in one fell swoop.
In response to the raids, MPOP and its allies in the Asian Pacific American Labor Alliance (APALA) publicly called for a moratorium on anti-Asian police raids of King County massage parlors. The Martin Luther King, Jr. County Labor Council — the county’s central labor organization — passed a historic resolution in support of the workers.
The vote marked “the first time a resolution has passed supporting an active campaign pushed by Asian massage workers (Safety Not Stigma), instead of memorializing those lost to police or white supremacist violence,” according to an MPOP press release.
The increased frequency of police and ICE raids and the dramatic uptick in anti-immigrant rhetoric from the political class have contrived to make these workers’ jobs even harder. Many immigrant massage workers, especially those who speak little or no English, struggle with the licensing process. Applicants must complete 625 hours of training at a state board approved massage school, for which tuition varies wildly, and in many said schools, training materials are only offered in English or Spanish. MPOP says workers regularly spend thousands of dollars and months of training at schools whose programs turn out not to qualify for licensure, forcing them to start over. “Some of us have experienced this multiple times,” said an MPOP speaker at the press conference. Fraud in the massage-school industry is well documented: A 2021 USA Today investigation identified two dozen schools with alleged ties to fraud or prostitution, including operators accused of selling fake credentials. In 2012, lawmakers removed language accommodations from the state’s massage and reflexology licensing framework that would have provided alternatives for non-English speakers.
Since the licensing framework only recognizes state-approved institutions, it fails to account for previous work experience or training acquired in traditional Chinese medicine and other cultural practices. MPOP is calling on the city and state to create an alternative licensing pathway for Asian massage workers by establishing a “cultural bodywork” category. “The industry is so stigmatized by the government officials that they just deem all the professional work you do, especially the Chinese medicine part, not proper massage,” Sally told me in Mandarin, while an MPOP staffer translated. She’s a Chinese-born massage worker who has lived and worked in Seattle’s Pike Place neighborhood since 2013. In her view, the current licensing system only accepts “Westernized medical massage.”
It’s a catch-22: It’s extremely difficult to acquire a license, but without one, workers are at risk of arrest, and those with complex immigration statuses are in further danger of detainment or deportation. This climate of fear has also emboldened bad actors to take advantage of these vulnerable workers: Some customers have threatened to report workers to the police or ICE to avoid paying, have sexually harassed workers or even robbed them. “Because workers fear arrest and deportation,” said an MPOP spokesperson, “they will not call the police or report incidents of violence or exploitation within their workplace.” Trapped in a vicious cycle by the current system, there is little workers can do right now to defend themselves. But they’re trying to change that.
Sally (who asked to use a pseudonym for her safety and privacy) originally moved to the Seattle area in 2011 with her American husband, leaving behind a career managing a shopping mall in her home province, Sichuan. When he died of cancer in 2013, she scrambled to find whatever work she could. A friend recommended she look into the massage business. “I actually didn’t do massage back in China; in China I was the one receiving the massage!” she said. “But at the time I did feel like, Oh, this is so relaxing for me, this is a helpful kind of work.”
Over the next fifteen years, Sally learned from coworkers in the massage field, perfected her technique and now sees herself as almost a mother to many of her customers. She listens to their problems, checks in on their health and recommends exercises for them to do at home. “We provide services for both really rich engineers and also the low-income customers who really need the massage to relieve their muscle pain,” she said. “I have a lot of customers who are doing heavy lifting work, and they can’t afford really expensive medical massages or don’t have health insurance in that way. … This is really important care labor.”
Now Sally is fighting alongside MPOP to break down barriers preventing other immigrants from safely working in the industry and to end the stigma against Asian massage workers. She is especially disappointed in the lack of respect she feels she and her coworkers receive from the government, the media and those who want to “rescue” them. Her stern recommendation for them: “If you really want to talk about trafficking, go listen to the real workers who are in this industry, instead of believing some biased news.” That’s what MPOP and APALA are doing, and that’s why massage workers like Sally are involved in their collective push for reform. MPOP was formed in the wake of the 2018 police raids on Asian massage parlors in the Chinatown-International District in Seattle. It has since grown into a powerful resource for legislative and community organizing. Its members are Asian immigrant workers who are often excluded by the dominant labor movement and criminalized under existing laws.
In a region with such a deep and ugly history of anti-Asian violence, righting these historic wrongs will take action, not just words. “Once again, we see this region’s legislators, industry bodies, neighborhood groups, the city, and the country’s police and safety systems attack the most vulnerable Chinese workers in our communities under the guise of stamping out social ills and bad business that undercut struggling professionals,” J.M. Wong said during the May press conference. Since lawmakers and the powers that be have continually failed them in favor of top-down “anti-trafficking” initiatives, these workers are determined to make it happen for themselves.
“The government doesn’t listen to us migrant workers,” said a Seattle massage worker who spoke during the press conference. “They speak for us and make laws based on stereotypes and biased views of Asian women. What is truly good for us? We need to be able to report wage theft and violence without fear of being criminalized or deported. We need translators, lawyers, doctors and affordable housing. If police raids and shop searches only make us poor and more silent, then they are not helping us.”
Safety, not stigma, is both the demand and the goal. Massage workers “are really a part of this society,” Sally said. “We’re contributing, we’re also taxpayers, so just give us enough respect and value our work.”
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
Kim Kelly is a freelance journalist and author based in Philadelphia, PA. She is a labor writer for In These Times and regularly contributes to many other publications. Her first book, FIGHT LIKE HELL: The Untold History of American Labor, and the young readers edition, Fight to Win! Heroes of American Labor, are both available from One Signal/Simon & Schuster. https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Exhibition explores how the fisherman-turned-artist Alfred Wallis inspired leading British artists
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Maev Kennedy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Pallant House Gallery in Chichester, southern England, does not own any paintings by the self-taught Cornish artist Alfred Wallis (1855-1942). But it does own many works by the early 20th-century artists who were heavily influenced by the former fisherman and rag-and-bone merchant, who first took up painting with pots of house paint and sheets of cardboard as a lonely widower aged 70.
Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist gathers together works by Wallis and by artists who visited, lived in or worked in St Ives, including Barbara Hepworth, Peter Lanyon, Margaret Mellis, Adrian Stokes, John Wells, Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, Ben and Winifred Nicholson and Christopher Wood. It was Ben Nicholson and Wood who first befriended Wallis in 1928 when they peered in astonishment into his tiny dark cottage stuffed with paintings.
Many of the Wallis paintings—of tilted houses and harbours, ships and stormy seas, under lowering grey skies—originally acquired as gifts or bought for a few shillings, are now being borrowed from private collections and museums including the Tate, Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge and Aberdeen Art Gallery. A private collector is loaning a unique collaborative work: a half-finished view of a Brittany quayside by Christopher Wood, which Wood gave to Wallis who then completed it.
A record price of £184,000 was set at a Christie’s auction last year for a work by Wallis, who once said to a buyer: “gimme what you like for ’em”. Ben Nicholson, barely earning himself and with a young family, bought his first Wallis painting for half a crown; Wallis once sent a bundle of paintings to the collector and curator Jim Ede for ten shillings. When the artist died in 1942, a roll of uncashed postal orders was found on his mantelpiece. He was only saved from a pauper’s grave by the St Ives artists.
The exhibition is curated by James Scott, an orthopaedic surgeon, who first discovered Wallis when, as a bored medical student, he spent days in Sotheby’s auction rooms, watching sales and afterwards tracing the buyers out of curiosity.
Scott insists there was neither condescension nor exploitation in the relationship between Wallis and Nicholson and the other art school educated artists. Hepworth wrote that Wallis never knew “how much we all learnt from him”.
The St Ives artists “discovered him when they were looking for a new direction, experimenting with a restricted palette and flattened picture plane,” Scott says, “and they found he was already doing it and doing it better.” Wallis learned nothing from them, continuing his own unmistakable style until weeks before his death.
Scott treasures two works by Wallis. “I’ve often thought maybe the time has come to sell them, and then I come downstairs and see them on the wall and think no, I can’t, I love them more and more.”
• Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist, Pallant House Gallery, Chichester, 21 November-2 May 2027; Penlee House, Penzance, 15 May 2027-9 October 2027

Who Will Lead the New Congress? Van Hollen vs. Schumer
Can the bluenami clean its own house?
A stunning realigning election. Previously unimaginable Democratic majorities in both the House and Senate. Stark repudiation of Trump and his Republican enablers and a loud demand for dramatic change. Every swath of voters moved left. Economic populism drove the debate. Democrats won across the country. Hell, Texas went blue top to bottom. And Mississippi, goddamn.
Donald Trump is visibly discombobulated by the rout. But beneath him, MAGA is girding for war. The loathsome Stephen Miller has been named chief of staff. Russell Vought is arming OMB to control the power of the purse. House Republicans chose the MAGA zealot Jim Jordan as their leader. Their gloves are off.
So, who will lead the newly empowered Democrats for the next two years? Who can galvanize the new majorities, lay out a bold vision, champion aggressive reforms, and drive the battle against Trump and the MAGA remnants?
Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries?
Really? It is hard to conjure up a pair less suited for the time. Both are cautious and compromised, more comfortable plotting tactical retreats than launching full-force offensives. Both are wooden speakers. Both are too close to Wall Street, to Big Tech, to Israel and AIPAC. Both are practitioners of small-bore, big-money politics, not populist insurgencies.
In revealing ways, both have already failed the moment. As House Democratic leader, Jeffries could have crystallized the insurgency. The head of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, Greg Casar, presented it to him on a plate. Last April, the CPC put out a 10-point affordability agenda of popular reforms that could unite Democrats. Jeffries could have imitated Newt Gingrich when he led Republicans to capture Congress for the first time in 40 years against Bill Clinton. Put out a clear platform, line up 300 candidates to commit to passing it in the first 100 days. Democrats would now be armed with a clear mandate to move from the get-go, so they wouldn’t end up enmeshed in investigating Trump’s crimes while they cast about for positive reforms. Jeffries chose to set up “working groups” instead.
Then this week, in the lame-duck session, Jeffries demonstrated that his competence may be as questionable as his charisma. He inexplicably failed to mobilize all Democrats to show up and vote on the Hegseth impeachment resolution, giving MAGA a cheap win. A missed opportunity and a failure of basic responsibility—hardly an auspicious start.
Schumer boasts that he gave Democrats their message of “costs, corruption and chaos,” and defines that as his charge as Senate majority leader. But a message is not an agenda; alliteration is not a plan. In fact, the election victory was launched by popular mobilizations—No Kings, anti-ICE, anti-AI—and framed by the populism of the Bernie Sanders–AOC anti-oligarchy tour. With voters squeezed by Trump’s wars and rising prices, appalled by brazen corruption and big money, revolting against AI and Big Tech’s swagger, and young voters particularly appalled by the Gaza horrors, Schumer’s record lines up too often on the wrong side of the barricades.
Even as Jeffries and Schumer basked in the victory, a revolt against their ascension was brewing. Indivisible and other organizers of the No Kings demonstrations inundated congressional offices with calls for new leadership. A Change.org petition against Jeffries has garnered over a million signatures since its launch in September. The International Association of Machinists (IAM) called for Schumer to step aside. But in both the House and Senate, the deck is stacked against change.
Jeffries
Of the two, Jeffries is the more structurally vulnerable and the more politically secure. To be elected speaker of the House requires a majority vote of the entire House. Despite the remarkable Democratic Party margin, the active base of the 110-plus members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus could in theory join the unified Republican opposition to block his candidacy.
But there is no alternative candidate—and Democrats will choose their leader and candidate for speaker next Tuesday. Few Democrats will want to usher in a new era by defeating their own candidate for speaker.
Also, Jeffries would be the first African American speaker of the House, a milestone that many will be reluctant to oppose, particularly in the face of Trump’s race-baiting politics. Add to that the support any Democratic leader garners by raising funds for candidates and the power the leader has to punish insurgents by denying them prized committee assignments, threatening them with ostracism and more—and Jeffries’s election is assured. Even a former vocal opponent, Representative-elect Will Lawrence, cofounder of the Sunrise Movement and former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, now plans to vote for Jeffries. The CPC’s leadership is focused on defining reform priorities, not on leading a coup attempt.
Schumer
Schumer, in contrast, is more structurally secure and more politically vulnerable. He only must win a majority of the Democratic caucus to become Senate majority leader. Most of the caucus are incumbents who weren’t even up for reelection this year.
Schumer confidently predicted victory: “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” claiming he had the votes in hand. Turns out that may be only another indication of how removed he is from the moment.
From Maine to Texas, the newly elected senators—El-Sayed of Michigan, Talarico of Texas, Hamilton of Kansas, Andrews of South Carolina, Stratton of Illinois, Pappas of New Hampshire, Flanagan of Minnesota, and Jackson of Maine—declared they were not ready to commit to Schumer.

Then, in a stunning press conference, Bernie Sanders, the populist independent who caucuses with Democrats, joined with Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin, an ambitious centrist Democrat, to announce that they wanted a full debate before a leader was chosen. Sanders said it was “time for a change,” and that he was a “no” on Schumer. Slotkin called for a debate, saying that this wasn’t about left or right, but a choice between “team fight vs. team flight,” intimating that Schumer was on the wrong team. “You can’t lead people,” she said, “if you can’t lay out where you’re going.”
Then, after canvassing many members, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced he would run for majority leader. The election, he declared, “wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption, and his wars and his cruelty.” It was also a call to “take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people.… The call was to reject…business as usual, and to do that, I think we need new leadership.”
Van Hollen, a respected progressive, earned acclaim for his courageous opposition to ICE and its criminal wilding, and his demand that the US stop arming and abetting Israel’s military, given the horrors in Gaza. Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected senator from Michigan, immediately voiced their support for Van Hollen.
Although even Van Hollen recognizes that Schumer at this point is still the odds-on favorite, a serious challenge is assured. Whatever the outcome, the contest will have important effects. Van Hollen will drive commitments from the caucus on bold reforms. Both party posts beneath Schumer in the Senate—the party whip and the chair of the steering and policy committee—are open. Long-overdue changes in caucus planning, coordination, and communication strategy might also open new positions. Van Hollen’s challenge will open the way for new leaders from the younger generation to emerge.
The press tends to dismiss the leadership fights as either destructive or a distraction. In fact, this is a direct product of the transformative election. A new generation of economic populists has been elected. They don’t outnumber the centrists yet, but the incumbents have been put on notice. If real change is to come, activists must continue to ratchet up pressure on legislators. The challenge to Schumer lays down a marker: Business as usual will no longer be acceptable.
