https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-a.title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-a.author: Corey G. Johnson, Brandon Roberts
https://www.propublica.org/article/hhs-a.text:
A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”
Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.
In a letter to the department’s inspector general, the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.
Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why.
In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.
At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures.
Read More
It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025.
Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.
The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.
“Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote.
The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds.
ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson. The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies.
Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency. 
The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said.
Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.
HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote. President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term.
ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”
Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses.
Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database, a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Democrats Should Not Give an Inch to the Lame-Duck Congress
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Should Not Give an Inch to the Lame-Duck Congress
In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent makes the case for Democrats to block Trump’s attempt at judiciary-stuffing. Plus, boycott Harry Potter!
Donald Trump and the Republican Congress have confirmed 57 new federal judges over the last two years. Now, with Republicans on the way out, Trump is demanding that Congress confirm another 25 judges during the lame-duck session.
That’s a tough ask. Confirming judges takes a lot of Senate time and resources, both of which the Republicans might prefer to use for whatever other fell priorities Republicans may have before they are removed from power. It’s also worth remembering that the government runs out of funding (again) on December 11, and figuring out how to avoid (another) government shutdown should probably take priority for Republicans over confirming lame-duck judges.
Adding to the challenge is the question of whether Democratic minority leader Chuck Schumer will be in a deal-making mood when it comes to judges. On the one hand, Schumer allowed a number of Republican-aligned judges to be confirmed at the end of Joe Biden’s term in order to give Biden the “record” for the largest number of judges appointed in one presidential term. On the other hand, Schumer is facing increasingly loud questions about his leadership, and his ascension to majority leader is far from assured. If Chuck caves now—on the budget, on judges, on anything—the calls for his head will only get louder. I don’t think it’s in Schumer’s best interest to help Trump confirm 25 judges in the lame duck and then turn around and ask Democrats to give him the gavel in the new Congress.
Of course, outgoing Senate majority leader John Thune doesn’t need the Democrats to confirm a slate of new judges. He has the votes in his own caucus to do this, assuming retiring or defeated Republican senators are willing to give Trump a parting gift even though he’s ruined their careers.
But I do think if Republicans confirm 25 new federal judges in the lame-duck session, that becomes another data point to convince Democrats to confirm no new federal judges for the last two years of Trump’s term.
Now is the time for judicial hardball, and I hope Democrats get this memo.
The Bad and the Ugly
- Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 3,000 votes in their Mississippi Senate race. Hyde-Smith conceded, saving us all from a weeks-long court battle to confirm her defeat. My mother is a Black woman who was born in Clarksdale, Mississippi, in 1950. Watching her react to a Black person being elected as senator from her home state for the first time in 145 years has been one of the joys of my life.
- In Alaska, Senate candidate Mary Peltola now has more votes than both Dan Sullivans combined, further obviating the Department of Justice’s antidemocratic lawsuit aimed at overturning the election, and making even more of a mockery of Trump’s wild claims that all of one Dan Sullivan’s votes should be given to the other. Peltola still hasn’t quite breached the 50 percent barrier, which is the point at which the state shuts down the ranked-choice voting process, but there are still more votes to count.
- Remember when Trump said he would accept the results of the election after his party got walloped? Yeah, that didn’t last a week. On Monday, Trump asked on Truth Social, “Does anybody really believe this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote.” An authoritarian goon does not change his spots so easily, and everybody who thought he did deserves another time-out in the dunce chair.
- The Kennedy family joined the lawsuit to block Trump’s arch, saying that the monstrosity would disturb and diminish John F. Kennedy’s gravesite at Arlington. I have watched enough movies to know that you should never disturb the ancestral burial grounds if you can possibly avoid it.
- Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. At the sentencing hearing, Justice Joel Bennathan said, “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.” I don’t have a joke here. This is just a perfect and true statement.
Inspired Takes
- Not gonna lie, I have enjoyed the Pope Leo experience. In The Nation, Victor Gaetan writes about how Pope Leo has gone to war—against war. Specifically, Pete Hegseth’s wars.
- In The New Republic, Perry Bacon makes the point that the “groups” that centrists and Democratic consultants maligned over the past few years are the reason Democrats won the midterms.
- Jamelle Bouie has a great article on the new “Southern Strategy” that helped the Democrats win in the South. Maybe next time the Democratic Party could actually invest in that strategy and give these candidates some money.
Worst Argument of the Week
OK, I think I understand what happened with the Pete Hegseth “impeachment” situation, and I think there‘s a lot of confusion out there that’s causing Democrats to get criticized unnecessarily. TLDR: This wasn’t the real Hegseth impeachment effort. The real one will be coming in the next Congress.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Here’s what happened. Representative Thomas Massie submitted articles of impeachment for Pete Hegseth on eight charges (mostly relating to the war in Iran and the extrajudicial killings Hegseth has overseen). Massie is a Republican from Kentucky who has been vocal about the Epstein files—so vocal that Trump backed Massie’s primary challenger, Ed Gallrein, who defeated Massie in the primary and won Massie’s seat last Tuesday. Massie is on his way out, and the impeachment articles were a parting gift to an administration he hates.
Trying to impeach Hegseth now, in the lame-duck Congress, was a stunt. And a stupid one.
In any event, there was a procedural vote this week on whether to send the articles of impeachment to the full House (which is still controlled by Republicans) or leave it with the House Judiciary Committee (which is still controlled by Republicans). The option to send it to the full House (which is what Democrats ostensibly wanted) was defeated 211–204, with only Massie breaking party ranks and joining Democrats in the losing effort. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans “missed” the vote. Many people have pointed out that if the 11 Democrats had shown up, the measure would have passed (many of these people skip over the fact that if the seven Republicans had shown up to counter the Democrats, the measure would have failed). Since the Democrats have a history of snatching defeat from the jaws of victory, a firestorm over weak Democratic leadership erupted online.
Here’s the thing that I think is important to remember: Hegseth was never going to be impeached by this Republican-controlled Congress, and there were two legitimate dangers in trying to force it:
- No investigation
- Double jeopardy
There is a lot of potential evidence that Pete Hegseth has committed high crimes and misdemeanors, but Massie, acting on his own, was not in a position to provide any of it. Hegseth needs to be investigated by the House Judiciary Committee; that will not happen as long as Republicans control Congress. But I will bet all the money in my grabbable area that he will be investigated, once Representative Jamie Raskin is in charge of the Judiciary Committee. Impeaching him now, without that investigation, looks like a political stunt spearheaded by a bitter politician because it is. After Raskin gets ahold of the gavel, it will look a lot different.
And that might matter, legally speaking, because we might get only one shot at this. Look, I don’t believe that “double jeopardy”—the prohibition against prosecuting somebody twice for the same crime—should apply to impeachment proceedings. But, as I must regularly remind people, I don’t happen to have a seat on the Supreme Court. If you impeach Hegseth now, and he gets acquitted, can you impeach him six months from now for the same crimes? I think so. But I don’t know so. And I don’t want to give John Roberts, Clarence Thomas, and Samuel Alito an opportunity to answer that question for me.
Is it a bad look for 11 Democrats to “miss” a vote on impeachment so soon after the midterms? Sure. The optics are not good. The communication from the Democratic leadership on what really happened is worse. But by the same token, the “optics” around doing a rushed impeachment—a rushed impeachment that is destined to fail in front of a Republican-controlled House—are arguably worse.
If I were in the leadership chair (and I’ll note that’s yet another job I don’t have), I’d have told all my members to opt out of Massie’s vainglorious charade.
Democrats will impeach Pete Hegseth when they have their ducks in a row. They don’t need a Republican who has been booted out of Congress to lead the charge.
What I Wrote
Soo… I have the cover story in the December issue of the magazine. You can read it online here. It’s about how Democratic presidential hopefuls should campaign on court reform in 2028, and what will happen to their entire agenda if they do not.
I also wrote about how Texas has a new Democratic attorney general who will become the regulator of first resort of Elon Musk and his companies.
In News Unrelated to the Current Chaos
I’m not going to watch the new HBO Harry Potter series. I’m not going to watch it because the creator of Harry Potter, J.K. Rowling, is a drooling transphobic bigot.
There are a lot of artists and creators who are problematic in some obvious and heinous way. Rowling has committed no crime, but where she stands out to me is that she’s made being a bigoted scumbag her entire personality. It’s not that she’s said a few anti-trans things, here or there. It’s that she’s happily become the face of the anti-trans movement in the UK. It’s that she uses her money and power and influence to fund anti-trans organizations that try to erase trans people from public life. She works, tirelessly it would seem, to menace trans people and manipulate the laws against them. When you support a J.K. Rowling project, you are directly supporting her financial efforts to hurt trans people. Why would you do that?
And here’s the thing about boycotting Rowling media products: It’s easy. There are so many evil people in the world whose products have been integrated into our lives in ways that make it almost impossible to excise them. I hate Jeff Bezos, for example, but pretending Amazon and The Washington Post don’t exist is really hard. I don’t support the actions of the Saudi Arabian government, but it has major investment stakes in Uber and the company that makes football video games. And, speaking of football, I believe I’ve already discussed my ongoing issues with loving a sport that is based on my favorite athletes’ getting repeatedly concussed into early oblivion.
But Harry Potter? A Harry Potter television show? I can cut Harry freaking Potter out of my life with almost no downside. If the question is, “Watch a television show or stand with transgender people?,” it’s the easiest call in my otherwise complicated journey of trying to be a moral person in an immoral world.
“What’s on HBO tonight, honey?”
“Transphobus Maximus!”
“Umm… what else is on HBO?”
“Well, John Oliver comes on in about an hour.”
“Cool, let’s watch LITERALLY ANYTHING ELSE until then.”
It’s not hard. Just don’t watch Harry Potter and let trans people live their best lives.

F and G trains have ground to a near halt the MTA said Friday evening, resulting in delays throughout the transit system.
Signal issues were once again the culprit according to city and state officials, this time during the Friday night rush. Passengers were spilling out onto the streets at stations along the two lines in Brooklyn.
At 7:30 p.m. the MTA reported there was no F service between Brooklyn and Manhattan and no G service between Church Avenue and Bedford-Nostrand Avenues.
The stoppage followed delays on the 4 and 5 trains earlier in the day after officials said a passenger was struck.
The subway delays also came as the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the nation amid a communications meltdown at the federal level.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: The late Los Angeles artist Betye Saar receives heartfelt send-off at the Getty Center
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Jori Finkel
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
When a major artist dies, the tributes that come pouring in often gloss over personal shortcomings, whether the failure to complete educational degrees or the abandonment of wives and children. But the memorial to Betye Saar this week at the Getty Center did just the opposite, setting into relief how powerfully she managed to balance—even integrate—acts of mothering and artmaking. (She also managed to earn her bachelor’s degree at the University of California, Los Angeles in 1949, a time when there were few Black students.)
Earlier this week the Getty filled its largest, 450-seat auditorium with fellow artists, curators, friends and family members of the artist, who died last July only four days short of her 100th birthday. The tone was sombre and celebratory, ending with her brother-in-law Bennie Maupin on saxophone and the band Bayou Bump leading a procession, as Saar had wanted.
One of the most powerful tributes came from her eldest nephew, Channing Johnson, who described her as a “true” if untraditional matriarch. “She was as impactful and skilful as a family matriarch as she was a gifted artist. She gathered us together whether it was in a back yard or public park. She kept our family history in the forefront of our minds and in the public eye—you can literally see our family in her artwork,” he said, referring to assemblages where she incorporated family snapshots or memorabilia.
Johnson also celebrated Saar’s sense of humour and adventure, noting that she learned to belly dance early on and showed off her dance moves in June when she was honoured by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) at its Party in the Garden gala.
His tribute followed one by MoMA director Christophe Cherix, who recalled Saar’s studio in Laurel Canyon being “unlike any other studio I had ever seen…overflowing with treasures, almost archaeological, with objects patiently waiting sometimes years or even decades to be gathered, recognised [and] assembled into works of art”.
Saar’s longtime home and studio in Laurel Canyon is where she developed her deeply spiritualist, Black-centred, female-empowered vision through printmaking and assemblage, most famously using a windowpane to organise the esoteric, celestial images that make up the 1969 work Black Girl’s Window. It is also where she raised her three daughters: the sculptor Alison Saar, the mixed media artist Lezley Saar and the writer Tracye Saar. Early on they liked to pretend the wheel of their mother’s printing press was the helm of a pirate ship, and they have said in interviews they are happy they survived without losing a finger or hand.
The veteran Los Angeles collector Joy Simmons, who recalled bringing her week-old daughter Naima to a Saar opening at the Jan Baum gallery in 1981 (“I was not going to miss this opportunity to celebrate a Black woman opening up at a white woman’s gallery”), described the Saar creative lineage, which extends to grandchildren who work in the arts today.
“To Alison, Lezley, Tracye and the whole family: I’ve watched three generations of Saar women make this city’s art history something special. Betye’s work belongs to museums now,” Simmons said, “but I know her proudest moment and her proudest accomplishment is all of you.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/interview-bo.title: Organizing for Tenant and Political Power in Montana
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/interview-bo.author: Benjamin Finegan, Willem Morris
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/interview-bo.text:
Organizing for Tenant and Political Power in Montana
We spoke to a Montana tenant union leader about organizing renters in the state and the midterms victory of Sam Forstag, a smoke jumper, a union leader, and the first elected House Democrat in Montana in three decades.
- Interview by
- Willem Morris
Sam Forstag, a smoke jumper and union leader, flipped western Montana’s US House seat blue in last week’s midterm elections. He is the first Democrat from Minnesota elected to the US House in more than thirty years, having run on a grassroots progressive campaign that brought together labor unions, environmental organizations, indigenous groups, and tenant unions.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez played a significant role in Forstag’s upset victory in the Democratic primary. She endorsed Forstag when he was trailing by 20 points and traveled to Missoula for a get-out-the-vote rally. Missoula County carried Forstag to a narrow primary victory, with Democratic primary turnout increasing 23 percent from 2024.
Bozeman Tenants United (BTU) endorsed Forstag for the general election and campaigned for him in Gallatin County, which had the highest increase in Democratic votes between the primary and general election. The county has recently become a destination for wealthy transplants, driving up housing costs. Since the start of the pandemic, the median home price in Bozeman has nearly doubled to over $700,000.
BTU was formed in 2022 and was a cofounding organization in the national Tenant Union Federation in 2024. Benjamin Finegan was a cofounder of BTU and currently serves as president. Jacobin contributor Willem Morris spoke to Finegan about Forstag’s win and how to organize tenants in Montana.
- Willem Morris Who is Sam Forstag, and why did Bozeman Tenants United (BTU) endorse him in his race for the US House of Representatives in Montana’s 1st congressional district?
- Benjamin Finegan This May, Sam Forstag drove two hundred miles from Missoula to Bozeman to join the picket lines of BTU members on a rent strike at two major mobile home parks, the first major rent strike in Montana in fifty years. Sam really went out of his way to support the strike. He used his social media platforms to rally public support for the strike and raised money for our strike fund. Forstag also committed to a co-governance pledge with BTU. He committed to consulting tenants on policy, maintaining ongoing engagement with the union, and working to hold landlords accountable. That’s who Sam Forstag is. He knows what it’s like to have to choose between gas or groceries in order to pay the rent. He’s also someone who has proven that he will stand with working Montanans against multimillionaires and billionaires. BTU is an independent group of tenants with many different political backgrounds. We have been very selective with our endorsements, avoiding establishment picks from both parties, and have focused mostly on local races. Our decision to endorse Sam was the first time we have endorsed a federal candidate. The vote was nearly unanimous, with enthusiastic support across political differences. Our members remembered that Sam was willing to stick his neck out and fight for tenants during their strike at such a high-risk and high-profile moment.
- Willem Morris Missoula carried Forstag to victory in the primary. Your home in Gallatin County made a significant difference in the general election. Who are these voters in Gallatin County?
- Benjamin Finegan Gallatin County is home to Montana State University in Bozeman. It’s also home to the thousands of workers who staff nearby playgrounds for the ultrarich, Big Sky and the Yellowstone Club. The wealthiest people in the world pay $500,000 to join the Yellowstone Club. Working people serve as their landscapers, cooks, and maids. BTU’s membership comes from these two main groups: students and young professionals centered around the university, and families renting apartments and mobile home parks, many of whom work in the service industry or live on fixed retirement incomes.
- Willem Morris BTU formally endorsed Forstag in September. How did BTU contribute to his race in Bozeman?
- Benjamin Finegan BTU organized our members to vote in large numbers for Sam Forstag, and we led mass canvasses in Bozeman. The majority of tenants that struck the trailer parks this summer voted for Sam. This includes folks who I know are more conservative and have historically voted Republican. One of our members is an older retired veteran who went on strike; he told me, “We are getting chiseled, we are getting gouged, we are being sheared like sheep.” He has voted Republican but was one of the folks that voted for our union to endorse Sam in the election. The solidarity that Sam showed us during the strike ultimately meant a whole lot more to our members than the party label. After our endorsement vote, folks hit the doors to get their neighbors committed to vote for Sam. The union is generally pretty trusted by tenants in our city, even if they’re not members. We have a reputation for fighting for tenants and against landlords. Last year, we won a law for tenants to have the right to counsel before eviction, which got city-funded legal representation for tenants. We have organized to enforce that law. So when we knocked doors, we were able to say: “We’re with the tenant union. We won this law called right to counsel, and you can call this number if you ever are in trouble with your landlord. And we’re trying to get this candidate elected who is willing to fight alongside us, Sam Forstag. We trust him, and you can trust him too.”
- Willem Morris Forstag’s support extended well beyond Missoula and Bozeman. He dominated in Butte, Anaconda, and Glacier County. These three areas are traditional Democratic strongholds where MAGA had made inroads over the last decade. The largest shift for Forstag compared to 2024 was in Butte. Why was Forstag able to succeed in these three counties?
- Benjamin Finegan The AFL-CIO threw down for Sam Forstag. They led impressive turnout operations across the state. Sam comes from the labor movement, and unions organized to send one of their own to Congress. Butte and Anaconda, two old union mining towns, are almost legendary places in our state’s labor history. Sam Forstag ran almost 20 points better than Kamala Harris in these two places. Native American voters were very significant for Sam too. Prominent Native leaders supported Sam, and the Blackfeet Nation and Reservation turned out for Sam in Glacier County. Public lands advocates are always important in every Montana election too. These are the forces that came together and were able to lead Sam to such an important victory.
- Willem Morris What else has BTU been organizing around this year?
- Benjamin Finegan Our bread and butter is organizing tenants to fight and win the changes we need from their landlords and from the government: getting members talking to their neighbors in apartment buildings or mobile home parks; developing leaders; deciding on demands; and taking action together. Our membership needs to be able to stay in their homes, regardless of who wins an election. BTU is also one of the five founding locals of the national Tenant Union Federation (TUF). We came together with tenant unions from the South Side of Chicago, Connecticut, Kentucky, and Kansas City, Missouri, to form TUF. In the last few months, TUF ran a three-month intensive training on tenant union organizing. We trained nearly a thousand tenant unionists from over 130 cities in forty states who learned how to organize tenant unions and fight for their homes. This training series has already been getting results around the country and leading to brand new tenant unions in places like Colorado, Idaho, New York, and in the South, and winning collectively bargained leases, repairs, and rent reductions.
- Willem Morris Four years ago in Jacobin, I tried to think about how environmental, labor, and indigenous movements could start to rebuild the Left in Montana. I left out tenants. What does this election show about the potential power of organized tenants?
- Benjamin Finegan Tenant unions and tenant voters were a significant force in the midterms. And tenants are going to be decisive in 2028 and every election going forward. Tenants make up nearly one-third of all Americans. We are facing higher rents for worse conditions and have less and less control over one of our most fundamental needs. Tenants want the government to take action on capping the rent, and I believe this will continue to mobilize more and more people to the ballot box. I’ll also say that many tenants are poor and working-class people who live off a fixed income or work jobs not typically covered by labor unions. And even for tenants who are fortunate to have a labor union, rent increases can outpace wage increases. Organizing at our homes in addition to the workplace is necessary to have a stable, dignified life. As more tenants unionize across Montana and around the country and control our rent, we will wield more power in the economy too. Last, when tenants unionize their apartment building or mobile home park, they experience collective power together, often for the first time. The experience serves as a training ground for democracy for regular people. It shows them how to negotiate and how to make decisions together. It teaches people that taking risks and exercising power collectively can get results. And they take those lessons to other parts of their life. One of our members is a woman in her seventies who works at a nursing home, and she was elected by her neighbors to sit on the bargaining team for her union. We forced a representative from the corporation that owned their building to come to negotiate. During negotiations, I could see her literally shaking as she talked to this landlord representative demanding that they fix parking lot lights outside her building. Afterward, she told us: “I’ve never felt stronger in my entire life.”

https://gothamist.com/news/faa-meltdown-.title: FAA meltdown strands NJ Gov. Sherrill at Dem conference in Denver
https://gothamist.com/news/faa-meltdown-.author: Ryan Kost, Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/faa-meltdown-.text:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill is among the thousands of travelers stranded after an air traffic control breakdown that grounded all flights nationwide for more than five hours Friday.
Sherrill left New Jersey late Thursday and was expected to return Friday evening, a spokesperson said. She’s now expected back sometime Saturday morning.
The governor was among a number of prominent Democrats who went to Denver to attend the “What’s Next” conference, a meeting about the future of the party. U.S. Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey, who ran for president in 2020 and is seen as a possible 2028 contender, was also at the conference.
The Federal Aviation Administration stopped all flights Friday afternoon, citing a “temporary telecommunications outage.” It lifted the nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m., but not before the stoppage had resulted in more than 7,500 canceled flights and more than 25,000 delays, according to FlightAware.
The region’s airports, including Newark Liberty, will likely see longer delays than the rest of the country as flights resume. Dartmouth engineering professor Vikrant Vaze told Gothamist that’s because the area has heavy demand, limited runways and crowded airspace.
More than a thousand flights at Newark, JFK and Laguardia were canceled as of Saturday morning and passengers were still facing long delays, according to FlightAware, a national flight tracking site.
Lt. Gov. Shirley Emehelu, who was only just appointed on Monday, has been serving as acting governor while Sherrill is away. Emehelu replaced Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September, after an investigation substantiated a sexual harassment complaint against him and other allegations surfaced that he had made women on his staff uncomfortable.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘None of them had ever seen an eclipse in real life’: Maurice Bakley’s best phone picture
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Grace Holliday
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Maurice Bakley was chaperoning an eclipse watch party at his son’s elementary school in Arlington, Virginia, when he took this photograph. As he had arrived early to fit his iPhone to a tripod to capture a time-lapse of the event (with the help of a monocular and a solar filter), he reached for his iPad for this shot.
“The boys in the photo, one of whom is my son, are part of a tight group of friends. They’ve known each other since kindergarten through their bilingual Spanish immersion school,” Bakley says. “They were eight and nine years old at the time, and none of them had ever seen an eclipse in real life.”
As the kids were sitting cross-legged on the ground, Bakley made sure to get down to their level for this shot. “A top-down angle wouldn’t have conveyed the same intimacy,” he says. “I approach mobile photography in the same way that I used to approach SLR photography, which includes being intentional in both the capture and the edit.”
When editing, Bakley applied a film-like colour grading, and a touch of blur to the background to focus attention on the boys. He also opted for a square crop. “I don’t crop in that way often,” he says, “but it suited this composition, lending a more timeless, nostalgic feeling.”

https://www.newyorker.com/culture/critic.title: “Avedon” Shows the Scars, Just Not the Photographer’s Own
https://www.newyorker.com/culture/critic.author: Naomi Fry
https://www.newyorker.com/culture/critic.text:
In an archival clip from the nineteen-seventies, an interviewer asks Richard Avedon, the legendary photographer, about his portraits. The photos, the interviewer notes—which are often oversized, shot in stark black-and-white, with their subjects set against a blank, solid background—aren’t captioned with any identifying details. “It isn’t really important where they were photographed, or that one [person] is an author and the other is a politician,” Avedon says. “What interests me about the people I photograph is that they are connected by something else.” When pressed to name what that thing is, he pauses, then laughs, a little sheepishly. “You don’t want me to say the human condition, do you?” he responds.
As I watched this exchange, which is featured in “Avedon,” the new Netflix documentary directed by Ron Howard, it struck me that the photographer was being both honest and, perhaps, a little slippery about his work and its meaning. As one of the greatest portraitists of the twentieth century, up until his death, in 2004, Avedon was, indeed, omnivorous in his choice of subjects. He took pictures not just of authors and politicians but of actors, artists, activists, and socialites. He was also a top fashion photographer who, despite “making a lot of money shooting beautiful, elegant models,” as the art director Greg Wakabayashi puts it in the documentary, “could not stay away from the events of the time.” He became a committed chronicler of the marginal and the controversial, capturing Vietnamese napalm victims and residents of mental institutions, Texan oil-field workers and Oklahoma drifters.
I’m not sure whether it’s the case that, as the photographer claims, it didn’t matter who his subjects were. (It certainly mattered a great deal to many of them; getting shot by Avedon, the John Singer Sargent of his time, must have felt like a moment of professional and social wish-fulfillment.) But it’s true that these distinctions—between the famous and the anonymous, between the powerful and the powerless—became blurred once the picture was made. What mattered, then, and what ended up uniting Avedon’s subjects, wasn’t really the human condition, but the fact that, once photographed, they became Avedons, which is to say, stars. Caught in his lens, his protagonists became worthy of being looked at. They were made into celebrities, whether they were actual celebrities or not.
Richard Avedon, known as Dick, was a child of the Depression. He was born in New York City in the early nineteen-twenties; his father, a Russian Jewish dress-shop owner, lost his department store, Avedon’s Fifth Avenue, after the crash. As a student, Avedon was an underachiever, whose lacklustre academic performance belied his intense ambition. He enlisted in the U.S. Merchant Marine during the Second World War, and was tasked with taking photographs of new cadets for their I.D.s—shooting “a hundred thousand baffled faces,” all posed, in what would foretell his later work, in front of a plain background. After his discharge, in 1944, he set out to become a professional photographer, and went to study at the New School under Alexey Brodovitch, the influential former art director of Harper’s Bazaar. Brodovitch ended up hiring the young, charismatic Avedon at the magazine, not for his pictures but “because of his personality,” Brodovitch said. At Bazaar, Avedon swiftly rose through the ranks, working with the editors Carmel Snow and Diana Vreeland to capture the postwar fashion landscape. Sent to Paris to shoot Dior’s New Look, he was a naïf. “I knew nothing about the world I was sent to photograph, except what I had learned from Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers movies,” he says in another old interview included in the documentary.
Quickly, however, he understood that, much like his childhood’s song-and-dance classics, photography was about creating a fantasy rather than capturing objective reality. (“Nobody cries in a Dior hat, Dick,” Snow admonished him, after Avedon shot a weeping model.) He learned, in his words, “how the world worked, how society worked, how money worked.” And he learned fast. He returned to Paris each season, pulling models out of the studio and shooting them in effervescent movement. But this apparent spontaneity never disturbed the photographs’ creation of what my colleague Vince Aletti recently called “Paris as a film set . . . where the women are beautiful and in love and even the bystanders are charmed.” Avedon developed such a recognizable style that, a little more than a decade hence, Astaire himself came to play a character that was based on him: Dick Avery, the fashion-photographer protagonist of Stanley Donen’s 1957 film “Funny Face.” In a remarkably short time, the photographer had become part of the romantic fantasy that he’d only so recently begun to create. With his signature heavy-framed glasses and leonine head of hair, his good watch and casually expensive clothes, Avedon had become Avedon.
There were deep-seated reasons for the photographer’s attraction to fantasy. For one, his family was troubled—his beautiful younger sister, Louise, who was an early muse of his, was mentally ill—but this darkness remained private, hidden under a pretty surface. “With skin like that, you don’t have to open your mouth,” Avedon’s mother used to tell her, and this focus on appearance rather than truth was practiced by the family more generally: cute dogs, for instance, were often borrowed and posed with in family photos, to give the Avedons a homier, happier sheen. As my colleague Hilton Als notes in the film, these were “real people—his family—living in a fiction. . . . The smoke-and-mirrors aspect of it was a tension that [Avedon] lived with as an artist.”
Howard’s film largely skims over some of the knottier aspects of Avedon’s life. His tortured bisexuality is entirely evaded, and his two unhappy marriages are only briefly addressed, as is his clearly difficult temperament. (At one moment, the model Beverly Johnson refers to him, diplomatically, as “high-strung,” and we see the briefest archival clip in which he snaps at a visitor on set.) When it comes to the actual photographs, however, the documentary’s cagy references to the shadowy underside of Avedon’s life begin to make a kind of sense, because his pictures, too, were conflicted about addressing that darkness. How does one treat blemishes and scars? In Avedon’s world, they were handled with a vise grip, making his pictures studies in utter control.
Avedon’s images—spare, sharply articulated, perfectly composed—do show their subjects’ rough edges. We see a pensive Marilyn Monroe looking a bit deflated, her sparkly halter top slack, as if drooping under the glamorous weight of its own sequins; a Texan teen-ager, a gutted snake held aloft between his two hands, his light apron stained with the reptile’s blood; Nancy Reagan’s gnarled, mottled fingers gripping her husband’s, giving the lie to her smooth, lifted face. And yet each of these disturbing elements, when thrown into crisp black-and-white relief, becomes iconic, larger than life. For a portrait of Andy Warhol, taken in 1969, the year after the attempt on the artist’s life by Valerie Solanas, Avedon photographed his bare torso, crisscrossed with scars whose geometric mapping parallels the lines of the leather jacket he’s wearing. But, while Warhol’s faceless form presents a shocking vision of injury and hurt, there’s also something almost sexy about it, its ruthless presentation a kind of dare: look at me, lifting up my shirt to show you.
Avedon, whose career spanned sixty years, from 1944 to 2004, was a man of his time. The quintessential twentieth-century photographer, he hopped between the commercial, artistic, and reportorial with an ease enabled by his era’s robust publishing landscape. As Tina Brown says at one point in the documentary, “Dick was a great magazine man.” (Brown, a onetime editor of The New Yorker, made Avedon the magazine’s first and, for a long time, only staff photographer, in 1992.) The ample production budgets and the wealth of print pages at the time allowed for the creation of a figure like Avedon, whose images had the aura of the outsized even when they were experienced in letter format. In our current, hyper-dispensable age of Instagram, in which images are scrolled past and immediately forgotten all day, every day, a figure like Avedon seems as if he belongs to an entirely different planet. As I watched the documentary, I kept thinking of a paraphrase of the well-known words of Gloria Swanson’s Norma Desmond in Billy Wilder’s 1950 film, “Sunset Boulevard.” Avedon and his work have remained big. It’s the pictures that got small. ♦

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: My Journey Through San Francisco’s Internet Archive
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Kim Hew-Low
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
My Journey Through San Francisco’s Internet Archive
To most people, the archive is just a portal on their computer. But it’s also a physical space made by a person who has never cared more about the preservation of digital history.
I was in San Francisco late this summer, against my will. My husband has family there, and when we visit, we stay at the townhouse in Inner Richmond where his mother, her mother, and her mother before her all grew up. His great-great-grandmother, Carolina, sailed from Genoa to New York in early 1889, and, for whatever reason, continued west—perhaps to farm or to reunite with relatives, though the family only speculates, since the details went unrecorded.
But evidence of her existence is sprinkled all over the townhouse. I am told by my mother-in-law that the interior looks the same as always: the parquet floors and pink-tiled bathroom are a portal to Carolina’s time. There is a metal chute in the kitchen for disposing of gas-stove matches, and a fold-out booth in the hall where you can sit to make telephone calls. We use a plastic lighter these days, and the landline is disconnected, but my mother-in-law ensures that the chute and the booth remain. She lives in Michigan now and becomes more wistful in San Francisco, as if everything there is asking her to remember a time before. In the morning, she asks us over coffee if we heard the foghorns last night: As a child, she had kept her windows open to hear them boom out as she fell asleep.
I love staying there, in that apartment. But I do not love staying in that city. People say that, because I’m Australian, I should like the eucalyptus and the swell from the Pacific. But there are the Teslas and the Waymos and the coolers with blinking faces delivering food that was probably 3D-printed in an automated ghost kitchen. I saw a billboard walking down Geary for a start-up that said “THAT’S SO AGENTIC.” Their CEO had recently posted a selfie with Benjamin Netanyahu on X, while opining about how artificial intelligence is enhancing Israel’s defense forces.
Near the billboard were clusters of people milling about the Safeway parking lot, people in vans with the engines running, and people counting change at the Chinese butcher. I wondered what they thought about being “agentic,” or about self-driving cars and coolers with pixelated heart eyes. I wondered, in other words, how a handful of nerds had terraformed the city, and what their despotic ambitions mean for everyone else. I can ignore that thinking more easily once I am out of San Francisco; it helps to live in a place like Brooklyn, and to work with people who are obsessed with books—people who, I imagine, would also treasure match chutes and telephone booths.
And yet: Just the other day I was chatting with my neighbor, who happened to share that they worked as a programmer at an AI start-up called “Writer.” I did not care to reciprocate what I do for work in response. As we spoke, the precious binary I had constructed between San Francisco and New York began to fray. I had to acknowledge what I already knew: Geographical distance from Silicon Valley is increasingly irrelevant as its political economy widens. But if there are AI people in Brooklyn, there must be people who still read and write books in San Francisco, too, I thought. Which is why I decided, when I was there, to visit the Internet Archive.
The Internet Archive, a digital library website, began 30 years ago in San Francisco. But in other, less obvious ways, it does not belong to its city of origin. A portion of its servers are housed in a Greek Revival building, formerly a Christian Science church, whose crowning acroteria break with the rows of pastel townhouses. The site was chosen as Archive headquarters for its vast Corinthian columns, which lend it a resemblance to the Library of Alexandria: fated real estate for a nonprofit striving for “Universal Access to All Knowledge,” which its founder, Brewster Kahle, calls “Alexandria 2.0.” When I enter through the iron doors for a tour one Friday afternoon, Kahle welcomes me in belted khakis and thick-soled tennis shoes. He is a bespectacled, ruddy-faced figure, whose general vigor—and frizzy tonsure of gray hair—suggests that he has been electrocuted in a minor, even pleasant way. He remarks, while rising to his tiptoes, that our group is filling out the foyer.
I have technically visited the Archive several times before. On my laptop, I frequently use the Wayback Machine in the process of my research to view old websites and books and magazines. A good portion of the group here, I learn, has also visited the Archive online. So why have all of us pilgrimaged here—some of us for the second time—in real life? Kahle begins the tour by playing an obsolete record on a gramophone; then he shows us, across the foyer, a 1980s arcade game called Prince of Persia. I find myself, improbably, next to a family from Australia, who tell me they planned their visit around a week-long computer programming conference. “What a name,” says their mother, “Brewster Kahle. It’s almost mythical, don’t you think?”
Kahle summons us, like disciples, to ascend to the building’s former nave: a grand rotunda that slopes toward an altar bathed in stained-glass-filtered light. I slot into a pew behind some incoming Berkeley freshmen, who are taking a summer English class titled “Language, Culture, and the Media.” Their teacher has assigned them a list of media-literacy terms to consider: things like “bias” and “deepfakes” and “truth” and further down the page, “power and control.” Kahle walks up to the altar to introduce the Wayback Machine, a software robot that crawls the Internet taking snapshots of what it finds for posterity. Some of its 1 trillion archived Web pages are stored on the servers arranged behind us, black towers that flicker blue whenever someone, from anywhere in the world, is accessing those archives from their device. Kahle loads the machine from his computer and projects his view on a screen that spans the altar. It lights up with scrollable thumbnails—a small sample of the million archived webpages—from which he chooses, at random, the homepage for a wildcat conservation organization in the Netherlands.
Kahle shares that he named the Wayback Machine after a segment of Rocky and Bullwinkle that he watched while growing up in Scarsdale in the early 1960s. In “Peabody’s Improbable History,” Mr. Peabody, a polymath Harvard graduate—and, it bears clarifying, a bowtie-wearing beagle—introduces his human, Sherman, to a gizmo-laden portal. “Open the door and there we are—or were, really,” he explains, walking on all fours through the WABAC Machine into an Ancient Grecian agora. At the Archive, our own Peabody scrolls back in time on his computer, raising bygone versions of the leopard conservation homepage: a streamlined menu followed by a photo of a leopard followed by blocks of black text on a solid white screen. “Here we are,” he says, “a good 1990s look,” as if we followed him through the portal. “The idea is to help people see what the world really looked like in the past.”
In the 1990s, Kahle was in the midst of moving from Cambridge, Massachusetts, to Menlo Park. He had studied at MIT and was working at Thinking Machines Corporation, where he spent the ’80s devising a system to connect their supercomputers to one another in an “interconnected network”—literally an early version of the Internet. With Wide Area Information Servers, or WAIS, you could search through text that was indexed on that network, and receive a list of documents ranked according to how they matched. By the end of that decade, Kahle was looking to California, with intentions to take his system to the market.
Then Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist, came along with a protocol called the World Wide Web. The Web supplanted WAIS partly because of its streamlined design, which enabled the routine ease with which we continue to browse: URLs offer users a standardized language for describing where files live, and when you visit a file’s address, embedded hyperlinks lead you to others. It’s a system that prevails for good reasons, though it made some real trade-offs, too. WAIS, which became obsolete, was underpinned by a time axis: this enabled “version control,” which recalled past versions of a page. Berners-Lee had at one point considered something similar for his Web. It was ultimately not a priority, as users seemed more excited to access up-to-date information.
Berners-Lee and other scientists have grown more concerned about digital transience, or the way that things on the Internet frequently disappear for good. But Kahle belongs to a group for whom that has always been a priority. He started the Archive from his attic in 1996, a year before Terry Kuny, an information and communication specialist, published an academic article on the possibility of a “digital dark age”—the idea that a lack of information could seriously compromise the historical record. By and large, however, most people were just acquainting themselves with the Internet rather than thinking of how to preserve it, and were thrilled with the prospect of life online as we know it: a place that pulses along in the present without much regard for the past.
Kahle describes these conditions as akin to “standing on shifting sand.” At the altar, he points to the shelves that once displayed numbers of hymns: 314, 404, and 451, for the kind of congregation that gathers these days. Most of our group gets 314: pi. Fewer of us get 404: the code for link rot, which is when a web page no longer lives at the address that is linked in a URL. Kahle says that the lifespan of a Web page is, on average, 100 days. But the fact of its expiration is only stated when the cause of death is rot, which produces the explicit, if enigmatic message “Page Not Found.” It is far more common, instead, for a page to be simply overwritten, which bears no similar indication that the original page is lost. In these cases, the grain of sand is buried, disappearing permanently without a trace.
As someone who has plastered images of their life all over MySpace and Facebook and Instagram, this comes as a surprising and in some ways welcome fact: Nothing on the web lasts forever—not braces or ex-boyfriends or overpenciled eyebrows. Though I am privy, too, to the ways in which this generates other problems. I edited at The Believer shortly after it had been sold, first to an Internet marketing company, then back to the publisher McSweeney’s: Its online archive contained the essays that lit up my interest, as a teen, in magazines, but during my time on staff were replaced by listicles of sex toys (the marketing company kept contractual rights to the domain). Web pages are, in this way, frequent collateral to commerce. Mountains of data were lost when MySpace, Friendster, and Tumblr reconfigured. I only grasped the implications, however, as magazines moved from print to online, and parts of Hairpin, Catapult, Gawker, and Curbed went dark. These do not include the conscious deletions made at Buzzfeed in 2014, when four thousand older posts were judged to conflict with new editorial standards.
No one from our tour group correctly guesses 451: the specific kind of rot that occurs when a page is removed for legal reasons. Downstairs, where the tour concludes over tubs of ice cream from Mitchell’s, I find Kahle savoring a cone of his favorite Macapuno. I introduce myself as a reporter from New York. “Fuck The New York Times!” he blurts out.“Sorry, I mean, I love journalists. But seriously, fuck those guys.”
The outburst seems to reveal the cumulative stress that various media and publishing conglomerates have wrought for the Archive in recent years: it was brought to court for alleged copyright violations, first by Hachette in 2020, then by UMG Recordings last year. The Archive settled with UMG but lost to Hachette in a costly appeal that threatened to bankrupt the organization. Now, news outlets like the Times—and the Financial Times and The Guardian—have limited the Archive from accessing their content. They have argued that the Wayback Machine allows their archive to be mined for LLM training. But Kahle refuses to take this on face value. “Copyright is about fair pay,” he says. “But they don’t care about paying their people. They only care about paying themselves.” Last year, to his point, Reddit gave the familiar reasons when it decided to limit the Wayback Machine from crawling its web pages—all while licensing that content to Google, as data sets, for tens of millions of dollars.
But undermining the Archive at this moment might be especially debilitating to the historical record. While it is typical for new governments to make changes to federal websites, the scope and pace of deleted government data has been unprecedented under Trump. In his first week back in office, more than eight thousand web pages vanished: guidelines for overdose prevention; statistics on hate crimes; research on experimental medicines and vaccines. Analysts observed that the deletions may have been triggered by certain terms: this might account for the wholesale purge of pages about the Enola Gay, the aircraft that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima in WWII. The Wayback Machine was able to catalog most of these otherwise defunct details; it remains the only place where the public can access a detailed timeline of January 6, produced by the Congressional Committee that reviewed the attack on the Capitol.
This is compounded by the ease with which the government has deputized Big Tech. Shortly after the United States sanctioned three Palestinian human rights groups last year, YouTube deleted the accounts that belonged to them, adding to censorship by Meta of thousands of posts of the atrocities in Gaza. Meta was later found to have also complied with the Israeli government, which requested that it censor posts that opposed its involvement in the conflict in Iran. Domestically, Google Maps has deleted reviews of ICE detention centers. Every day provides more reasons, in Kahle’s mind, for news outlets to work with the Wayback Machine: Restricting the public record further undercuts their own goal to distribute information. He reminds me that 451 is also the number of degrees, in Fahrenheit, at which paper is said to ignite automatically—made famous by the Ray Bradbury novel about a government that burns books.
At the end of Fahrenheit 451, a group of exiled “Book People” make their return to a bombed-out city. They are led by a former government fireman. When he makes a fire at their campsite for the night, he considers how those flames will be used for warmth instead of destruction. I had walked into the Archive with a narrow idea of who constitutes “Book People.” As it turns out, many technologists study the Internet because they were captivated, first, by books. Right before the Internet Archive was founded, about an hour away at Stanford, two doctoral students in computer science dreamed of a digital library project. Larry Page and Sergey Brin later founded the company Google. In 2002 they started scanning books under the codename Project Ocean.
Kahle was a vocal opponent of this project, which we know now as Google Books—in short because it was billed as a library while largely privatizing potential public resources. I realize, after we talk, that I cannot simply look for people in this new era of technology who work with books: Sometimes people with books still want to burn libraries down (or in Anthropic’s case, shred them en masse with hydraulic guillotines). The “Book People” I am looking for are preoccupied specifically with libraries, which is another way of saying that they are devoted to the past and to the public—to ensuring that everyone can access the archive. I assumed that most of these “Book People” worked in publishing or media and lived in New York. But I learn in San Francisco that they might look different to how I’d imagined them: They might be engineers or even programmers, more fluent in code than in Classics, but just as committed to the project of preserving history.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Jack Cushman, for example, taught himself programming at 13. (He bought C Programming for Dummies and a computer from Sears on an installment plan.) But he has worked for over a decade at the Berkman Klein Center at Harvard, one of several library institutes that works in tandem with the Internet Archive.
I initially came to Cushman through the Public Data Project, which he established just over a year ago to catalog disappearing government data. Cushman formerly worked as a lawyer, which he went to school for in 2005, driven in part by what was happening at Google Books. “It started to seem like law as much as code controlled what was possible in the world,” he told me over the phone. “They were like: We have all the books of the world and we can’t show them to you because that would be against the law. I remember thinking that was not how that was supposed to go.” A decade later, in 2016, Cushman’s instincts were confirmed: Google won a copyright legal battle in which the courts upheld their right to scan millions of books.
After working for a time in appellate courts—the branch of law that depends, in particular, on referencing what came before—Cushman went to work in libraries, where he continues to use technology for preserving public knowledge. I expected that most of our call would be devoted to the Public Data Project—how much data is missing, and what kind. But Cushman instead gently steers me to think beyond the scope of those deletions. He tells me that the problem goes beyond one administration; It is that we have built, both through code and through the courts, a highly privatized Internet, which conflicts with the very notion of a functional public memory, one that enables future generations to retrieve the information they need.
If the architects of the Internet dreamed of a network of interconnected servers, then “Book People,” like Cushman, are dreaming up a network of interconnected archives: where institutions all over the world work to preserve some slice of history, such that the endangerment of one could be protected by the others. The design problem, in his mind, is not technological in nature. It is how to get working people the resources to continue library work, broadly defined. “It’s not about what kind of hard drive we need to buy for storage,” he says. “It’s about what people need so that they can keep these institutions going.” Berkman Klein is university-funded, and independent donors have enabled Internet Archives to open in Canada and Amsterdam. But the private sector, historically backed by the courts—and in collusion with the Trump administration—requires that funding, and protection from litigation, is pursued through multiple governmental channels. (Places like France and Sweden have already sponsored library projects.)
Cushman thinks that we should start looking in places like these to house more archives, where governments are resilient and interested in thinking, not unlike my mother-in-law, about how to preserve the past and pass it down the generations. Though he also thinks the United States should act as a cautionary tale, a reminder about what can happen when administrations change. A truly resilient network of libraries relies on more than one place or a single group of people: beyond San Francisco or New York or even a handful of countries alone. “Of course. there are other places that won’t feel like natural homes,” he says. “But I think it’s still important for us to keep trying, to keep looking everywhere.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/14/reli.title: Will Senate Religious Freedom Bill Actually Protect Land Sales for Israeli Settlements?
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/14/reli.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/14/reli.text:
A proposed “buffer zone” around religious facilities across the country — touted as protecting the right to worship — is alarming free-speech advocates who say the Trump administration could use it to crack down on protests.
The new bill, a national version of a controversial law passed in smaller jurisdictions, could hamper demonstrations against illegal sales of land in the West Bank to Jewish settlers that occur inside U.S. synagogues, the advocates say.
The bipartisan legislation could face another layer of opposition from a surprise corner, however, in the form of reproductive rights groups worried it would undermine an existing law that protects abortion clinics.
Called the Right to Worship Act, the bill cosponsored by Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., will be the subject of a Tuesday hearing in the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The bill has drawn backing from Christian, Jewish, and minority religious leaders who say it could be used to prevent hate crimes. Major Muslim groups, however, have been notably absent from supporter lists.
That isn’t just because Cruz regularly demonizes Muslims. Muslim leaders also worry that while in theory the law would be used to promote religious freedom, in practice it would be used to punish non-violent, pro-Palestine protesters, said Dahlia Taha, the director of the First Amendment Center at the Muslim Public Affairs Council.
“Protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other Constitutional rights,” she said. “We believe that this can have very detrimental and long-term impacts. And under this administration, specifically, we’re concerned about those long-term implications.”
Slotkin and Cruz’s offices did not respond to requests for comment.
Land Sales as “Religious Services”?
Under the bill, the Department of Justice could seek civil fines or injunctions against anyone who engages in a “course of conduct” that disrupts religious services, or disrupts access to them, within 100 feet of a church, mosque, synagogue, or other religious facility. Worshippers and state attorneys general could also file lawsuits.
Numerous states have already passed similar legislation creating “buffer zones” around religious buildings. In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani vetoed a buffer zone for protests near schools and colleges, while allowing another one for religious institutions to pass.
Supporters of the federal bill argue that it is needed to protect worshippers from harassment or worse.
“Attacks on synagogues, mosques, churches, and other houses of worship are unfortunately on the rise in Michigan, and across the country,” Slotkin said in an August press release. “No one should ever fear going to their house of worship. Period.”
The law’s authors tout it as a narrowly tailored guardrail, but critics say that the “course of conduct” subject to fines and lawsuits is so ill-defined that the Trump administration could use it to target peaceful protesters.
One of critics’ top fears is the “religious services” protected by the law could be defined to include real-estate pitches for land illegally seized from Palestinian people in the West Bank. In a press release, the Anti-Defamation League cited two West bank land-sale protests in New York City as examples of the need for the legislation, along with the March ramming attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan.
When it comes to violent attacks, argued Eli Williams-Szenes, the director of advocacy and political affairs at the progressive Jewish group Bend the Arc, synagogues are better protected by an existing federal law called the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act. The FACE Act makes a federal crime out of force, threats, or physical obstruction near both religious institutions and abortion clinics.
“There is no relationship between this legislation and the prevention of violent acts at synagogues, mosques, or churches,” Williams-Szenes said of the new bill. “The idea that telling someone that if they wave a pamphlet 97 feet from the entrance to a synagogue, they’ll get a $10,000 fine would be the reason that someone didn’t try to drive a car into Temple Israel is crazy.”
Abortion Rights Angle
The Right to Worship Act faces long odds in the final weeks of the Republican-controlled Congress. Still, Williams-Szenes said he is concerned that even a hearing could set the stage for eventual passage.
Abortion rights groups are also worried. They fear that if the Right to Worship Act passes, Republicans will be inclined to repeal or weaken the FACE Act because of its protections for abortion clinics.
One of President Donald Trump’s first actions upon taking office last year was to pardon anti-abortion rights protesters convicted of blockading a clinic under the FACE Act.
“The Right to Worship Act is a wolf in sheep’s clothing,” Kelsey Ryland, a policy counsel at the National Abortion Federation, said in a statement. “The impact of this policy could become a backdoor FACE Act repeal, weakening enforcement against violent disruptors at abortion clinics.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
