https://jacobin.com/2026/11/farc-colombi.title: Inside Colombia’s FARC, as Victory Gave Way to Survival
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/farc-colombi.author: Oliver Dodd
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/farc-colombi.text:
Inside Colombia’s FARC, as Victory Gave Way to Survival
Tanja Nijmeijer’s memoir tells of how Colombia’s FARC was forced into a long and painful retreat. Her account of its political setbacks suggests that power doesn’t always flow from the barrel of a gun.
In the early hours of September 23, 2010, Tanja Nijmeijer was awakened by a bomb in a FARC guerrilla camp in the Colombian jungle. The strike landed on her commander’s bunker, followed by screams from her comrades. Moments later, dozens of aircraft roared above and launched another wave of bombs. Nijmeijer grabbed her rifle and dived into her foxhole. As the ground shook around her, she closed her eyes, tensed her body and thought: Aquí fue — this is it.
Seven years earlier, when the Dutch internationalist had first entered the jungle to join the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia (FARC), the war looked very different. She remembers it as “the calm before the storm,” with abundant supplies, comparatively large and settled camps, and a degree of security.
Nijmeijer’s autobiography, Into the Jungle, recently published by Pluto Press, traces her trajectory from guerrilla warfare to the negotiations that produced the 2016 peace agreement and the troubled transition that followed. Yet what makes the memoir especially politically revealing is that Nijmeijer joined the FARC at almost exactly the moment when the war started to change so decisively against it.
Stark Disparities
Initially traveling to Colombia in order to teach English to the children of the rich, Nijmeijer quickly encountered the extreme inequalities dividing Colombia. She witnessed gated communities, stark disparities separating the northern part of capital Bogotá from the south, and the concentration of wealth and power among an elite while poorer neighborhoods suffered neglect and repression.
Nijmeijer came into contact with FARC militants through her work and began to question the dominant image of the guerrillas as little more than “narco-terrorists.” Instead she encountered people prepared to sacrifice their lives in pursuit of a revolutionary project. Gradually developing a socialist outlook, she began to recognize that the ruling class was blocking any prospects of meaningful, peaceful change. She increasingly regarded armed struggle as not only legitimate but necessary and was convinced that the guerrillas could “take power and plant the seed for a new world.”
Although it was not apparent then, when Nijmeijer went into the jungle, the FARC’s decline was already underway. Right-winger Álvaro Uribe won the presidential election in 2002 on the back of mounting hostility to the FARC following the collapse of the 1999–2002 peace process. Harnessing hegemonic narratives that portrayed the FARC as having acted in bad faith and merely exploited the peace process as an opportunity to expand, Uribe promised a “military solution,” relying on massive US support through Plan Colombia to modernize the armed forces.
By late 2003, seven months after Nijeimer went into the jungle, the counterinsurgency offensive organized through Plan Patriota had reached Sumapaz, where military operations targeted guerrilla fronts in a region central to the FARC’s strategic plan for surrounding Bogotá. Areas over which the FARC had historically enjoyed complete control were now being contested.
The guerrillas later discovered evidence of around sixty helicopter landing sites, army surveillance of guerrilla roads and infrastructure, and reconnaissance teams operating inside jungle territories that the insurgents had assumed were impenetrable.
The state’s expanding war chest enabled significant increases in military personnel, specialized mountain battalions, and airpower. This was supported by satellite imagery and geospatial intelligence, communications interception, and other technologies challenging the guerrillas’ traditional reliance on rugged terrain as a form of defensive protection.
The military’s expanding reach is already evident earlier in Nijmeijer’s account, when she describes the penetration of her units by infiltrators who pulled various stunts as part of a tactic to undermine morale — unlocking weapons, defecating in huts, and cutting up the guerrillas’ rubber boots. The result was that “nobody trusted anybody else.”
Whereas in the past, counterinsurgency campaigns were temporary, with troops eventually withdrawing due to budget cuts and other constraints, now the Colombian army established a permanent offensive presence and pursued the guerrillas into rearguard zones and jungles, closing in on commanders once thought invulnerable.
The shifting conditions led the FARC’s leading military commander, Mono Jojoy, to declare before a crowd of five hundred guerrillas, “Thanks to President Álvaro Uribe Vélez, we are going to learn how to live as guerrilla fighters again! We must go back to basics.”
Improvements in airpower gave the state forces a decisive advantage. Vehicles disappeared, supplies and comforts were reduced, marches replaced a comparatively settled life, and concentration gave way to greater mobility and dispersion. “Our days of easy living,” as Nijmeijer puts it, “were over.”
For the FARC, going back to basics meant adopting an increasingly defensive posture: land mines, often described as a “weapon of the weak,” became an especially useful tool for slowing the encroachments of army patrols. However, they also caused civilian casualties and left the FARC exposed to criticism for disregarding human rights.
To reduce the risk of interception when communicating with urban militants, the guerrillas began sending encrypted messages via satellite internet. But this wasn’t a comprehensive solution. Air surveillance, increased extensively under Plan Colombia, could still intercept such communications. They had to switch off the equipment whenever an approaching plane was suspected, but the introduction of small, largely undetectable drones enabling real-time surveillance in 2006 made it harder to know when they were being watched.
The transition to a more defensive mode of operating affected daily life. Camps were built with deep foxholes; smoking and flashlights were prohibited after dark; vines were strung along paths so fighters could navigate without light; fireflies were used as improvised illumination. The nightly hour of cultural activities, essential for political education and boosting morale, became a thing of the past in Nijmeijer’s units. Meanwhile, massed forces of guerrillas were restricted — a setback from the FARC’s war of movement strategy at the end of the 1990s, in which large concentrations of troops overwhelmed military bases.
Isolation
True, this was a form of adaptation. Yet adaptation increasingly meant preserving the guerrilla organization under adverse conditions rather than recreating the offensive possibilities of the previous decade. Nijmeijer recounts, “The war changed, and it changed in the army’s favor.”
The psychological impact is described in a way that military histories and government documents rarely capture. Nijmeijer recalls the “pure terror” as bombs drop around her, with nowhere to run for safety, and no visible opponent to shoot at, only the hope that the jungle canopy might offer some protection.
Having to be constantly on the move, often in treacherous terrain, had its physical costs. Long marches left the guerrillas hungry and low on calories, and illness and fatigue, inevitable in such conditions, spread and grew more difficult to overcome. The army had repeatedly blocked Mono Jojoy’s attempts to meet up with Manuel Marulanda, the FARC’s founder and long-standing leader. Nijmeijer describes the resulting two-month march through particularly arduous territory on inadequate rations, which left her body aching so badly that she could barely manage to endure the night watch.
The psychological and physical impact had broader organizational repercussions. Demoralization deepened, and desertion rates increased, which the counterinsurgents exploited to the full. One guerrilla defector recorded the coordinates of Raúl Reyes’s location while sitting on the FARC leader’s bed. Iván Ríos, then the youngest member of the FARC’s secretariat, who had decided to remain with a guerrilla front to tackle problems of indiscipline and disorganization, turned up dead alongside his girlfriend — killed by his own head of security, who hoped to collect a lucrative bounty. Even people imagined to be staunchly politically committed ended up deserting and providing crucial intelligence.
As my own interviews with various former FARC leaders confirm, from around 2007, the counterinsurgents took the FARC by surprise, systematically hiding tiny GPS trackers in items that the guerrillas relied upon to survive. They identified stores in guerrilla areas and forced merchants to cooperate and even pressured family members and the children of guerrillas, as revealed in an interview with a retired strategic intelligence analyst in the Colombian navy. The trackers guided precision strikes on guerrilla camps, such as in the case of Mono Jojoy, whose boot concealed a GPS tracker.
Nijmeijer reflects that “if I had to pinpoint a moment when I began to see we wouldn’t take power by military means, it would be some time before Mono’s death in 2010.”
Yet her growing recognition that the FARC could no longer take power militarily was also linked to the organization’s broader political isolation.
As many former FARC commanders have admitted, kidnapping and extortion, justified by the organization as “revolutionary taxation,” inflicted enormous political costs and enabled the ruling classes to paint it as a group of terrorists and bandits, especially in urban areas where most people were based.
The FARC’s communications strategy — deemed a complete failure by Nijmeijer — also left it politically vulnerable. The state had dedicated task forces whose entire purpose was to undermine the FARC’s claim to political legitimacy. According to Nijmeijer, FARC leader Manuel Marulanda had decided “there was no good reason to respond to falsehoods the state made up.”
Given that the FARC was overwhelmingly rooted in the countryside, and the country was increasingly organized around the big cities, political communication was fundamental. Yet Nijmeijer recounts how long the FARC ignored this issue.
Nijmeijer concludes that while the conflict had no straightforward military victor, the FARC “certainly lost the ideological battle.”
Negotiations
The FARC’s strategy had always theoretically left open the possibility of negotiations alongside the more ambitious goal of taking power through a popular insurrection.
But as the FARC faced military blows and narrowing strategic possibilities, the idea of a negotiated settlement gained prominence.
In November 2011, the FARC’s supreme leader — Alfonso Cano — was assassinated by the counterinsurgents, the first time this had occurred in the organization’s half-century history, a moment Nijmeijer remembers as a “heavy blow” that left even the more radical commanders Iván Márquez and Jesús Santrich sitting in stunned silence, repeating, “We have to go on, anyhow.”
While the FARC was capable of sustaining the war over many more years, its influence had been significantly weakened. Key figures, including Nijmeijer, no longer realistically envisaged taking power through a popular insurrection and the point of war, they saw, was to win it, not simply endure it.
Unable to foresee victory or a realistic possibility of retaking the strategic initiative nationally, the FARC turned to negotiations from a position of relative weakness. The state only agreed to talks on the condition that changes to its fundamental economic model were off the cards — thus leaving intact the exploitative social relations that sustained the conflict.
Ultimately, from the perspective of a former guerrilla fighter who experienced firsthand the FARC’s military reversal, the book reveals that political power does not necessarily grow from the barrel of a gun. To be sure, the FARC became one of Latin America’s most powerful communist organizations, with many thousands of guerrillas, control over territory, and access to an enormous war chest. And yet, this capacity to sustain an insurgency did not translate into nationwide appeal or a credible strategy for taking power.

https://gothamist.com/news/expansion-pro.title: Expansion proposal for Brooklyn plants fuels data center fears
https://gothamist.com/news/expansion-pro.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/expansion-pro.text:
The owner of a pair of floating power plants near Sunset Park, Brooklyn wants to expand the facilities, prompting protests from environmentalists who fear they could be used one day to power data centers.
The Gowanus Generation Station and nearby Narrows Generation Station are peaker facilities that are only activated during periods of peak demand. Such plants produce a disproportionate amount of pollution. But environmentalists' goal of closing the peakers has run into the reality of the downstate grid, which is under strain and largely dependent on fossil fuels since the closure of the Indian Point nuclear facility.
The owner of the plants, AlphaGen, submitted an expansion plan to Con Edison earlier this year, stating that it expects the company's operating permit will be extended past 2029. Alarm over that proposal grew in recent weeks when a company that owns, invests in and operates data centers, DigitalBridge Group, bought AlphaGen’s parent company for more than $1 billion.
“Sunset Park is not a dumping ground for dangerous energy projects,” said State Senator Andrew Gounardes, who joined a protest Thursday over the expansion plans. “Big Tech has the resources to invest in clean energy and help lower our utility costs, but instead, they’re doubling down on polluting a community that has already carried the burden of projects like this for decades. We demand investments that move us forward and we won’t stop fighting until we get them.”
AlphaGen’s expansion proposal “recognizes the realities of current power technology and the need to balance reliability with sustainability,” Curt Morgan, CEO of AlphaGen said in a press release. He added that the plan is intended “to start a conversation about supporting cleaner technology as a bridge to a zero-emissions future.”
But environmental activists who rallied near the Gowanus Generation Station said there is no conversation to be had. They want the peakers shut down entirely.
“ We can't let big tech get a wish list of gas plants, and we can't let them throw Sunset Park residents under the bus just so that they can continue to pad their profits,” said Santosh Nandabalan, organizing director at New York Communities for Change.
The Gowanus Generating Station is a floating 260-megawatt natural gas power plant on barges in New York Harbor. The facility houses 32 turbines on four floating platforms.
The nearby Narrows plant is a 322-megawatt floating peaker plant that consists of 16 turbines on two barges.
AlphaGen wrote it wants to replace the units on all six barges with three new power barges that will deliver a total of 819 megawatts. The company said it will reduce emissions by more than 50% through the upgrade.
"New York City's electric grid is facing a growing reliability gap as older infrastructure retires and demand continues to rise," Morgan said in a statement.
Under the 2025 Peaker Rule, both Brooklyn plants were scheduled for closure by last July. But the state grid operator determined that the plants needed to remain open until May 2029 for grid reliability, citing surging demand from electrification and heat waves.
According to the federal government’s accountability office, peaker plants produce 1.6 times more sulfur dioxide, high levels of nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter than baseload plants that run continuously. Rapidly activating the peakers during times of maximum demand results in less efficiency and more pollution.
AlphaGen spokesperson Aaron Gruen said in a statement that its proposal had no connection to data centers and that it had yet to submit a formal plan to a state regulator.
“New York’s grid operator has found that New York City needs new, dispatchable power by the mid-2030s to replace aging plants and maintain reliable service as electrification of buildings and vehicles increase electric demand,” Gruen said. “The Gowanus proposal would replace 1970s-era units with more efficient, lower-emitting turbines, and if it moves forward, AlphaGen will work alongside the state, the city and our neighbors in the Sunset Park community.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-speciali.title: NYC's specialized high school test stalled by technical problems, DOE says
https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-speciali.author: Christian Santana
https://gothamist.com/news/nycs-speciali.text:
A number of students were unable to access and finish the Specialized High School Admissions Test on Saturday due to a technical issue, city officials said.
In a statement, the New York City Department of Education said it would reschedule the test after the test's vendor, Pearson, reported technical problems.
"I understand and share the frustration of our students and families," Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said in a statement. "I have spoken with the vendor and shared this frustration, and they have assured me the issue has been corrected."
The department said testing will continue as planned on Nov. 15. It did not elaborate on the nature of the issue or how many students were affected, and Pearson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday.
School officials said students who were unable to finish the test would be automatically rescheduled, and that families would receive follow-up information by the end of the day on Monday.
Testing on a new date will not affect any student's score or consideration for admission to a specialized high school, according to the department. Students who finished and submitted a test on Saturday are also eligible to retake the test if they choose, the department said.
In a joint statement on Saturday, a group of city and state lawmakers demanded a thorough and transparent investigation into the issue.
“The DOE may point to its testing contractor, Pearson, but accountability cannot be outsourced,” read the statement from Councilmember Susan Zhuang, Assemblymember William Colton, state Sen.-elect Larry He, and Assemblymembers-elect Joyce Xie and Joey Saban. “The DOE selected the vendor, oversees the process, and is ultimately responsible for ensuring that every student receives a fair and reliable opportunity to take this examination.”
“Under mayoral control, the buck stops with City Hall and DOE leadership,” the statement read.
The SHSAT is administered to eighth and ninth graders in New York City and is used to determine admission to eight of the city’s nine specialized high schools.

Hello!
As the lords of chaos (see Monireh’s cartoon here above) continue to wreak havoc, we use the tools at our disposal (pen and paper, or tablet) to keep the chaos at bay.
In this newsletter we share the comic about humor and democracy we’ve been working on for the past couple of months. We also have an upcoming webinar and we show cartoons from the frontlines in Ukraine. Ukrainian cartoonist Ruslan Pikhota serves in the Ukrainian army, and captures the reality of war with pencil on paper as he fights for freedom. And, as our regular feature, we share the most popular cartoons of the month.
You can check out our other, daily newsletter, (featuring our daily editor’s choice) here:
Comic: Humour and Democracy
As some of you might know, Cartoon Movement is a consortium partner in Horizon Europe project DELIAH (Democratic Literacy and Humour). In addition to researching humour, part of DELIAH’s mission is to raise awareness about the role of humour in our democracies. We try to do this in various ways: by writing about it, by giving workshops and now also by making a comic about it.
Over the last few months, we have worked with the renowned cartoonist Pedro X. Molina to create a four-page comic that explains what we currently know about how humour works in a democracy.
Depending on your device, you can choose to read the mobile version or the desktop version.
We also have the comic available as a PDF and a slideshow. All formats of the comic are freely available to download and use, provided DELIAH and the artist Pedro X. Molina are credited when the comic is published.
Cartoons from the front lines
Ruslan Pikhota is a Ukrainian frontline cartoonist and an active-duty officer in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Before the full-scale invasion, he spent 15 years working in children’s publishing in Kharkiv. He volunteered in February 2022, served as an infantryman on the Donetsk and Kharkiv fronts, and was wounded near Bakhmut. He now serves with an unmanned systems unit.
Since the spring of 2022, he has created more than 550 drawings in trenches, dugouts, ruined buildings, and between military duties. We asked him to select what he considers to be his ten most telling drawings made at the front lines.

https://gothamist.com/news/some-in-ny-fr.title: Some in NY fret about being hit by the AI bus. Others are trying to board it.
https://gothamist.com/news/some-in-ny-fr.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/some-in-ny-fr.text:
In a conference room in Manhattan on a recent afternoon, a speaker named Claira spoke to a captive audience about the benefits of using an artificial intelligence agent as a personal assistant.
Claira would know — she herself is one.
The bot, appearing on a large screen, had caramel-color skin and bouncy, curly hair, and is the first ever Afro-Latina, multilingual virtual assistant to hit the market, according to Abran Maldonado, who helped invent her.
Claira was designed, Maldonado said, to bring a multicultural perspective to the AI space, which too often leaves Black and brown voices out of the mix.
Maldonado has showcased Claira across the globe, but in this case relied on the bot to help keynote last week's Latino AI Summit, in front of dozens of attendees who were mostly Latino and Black.
“It’s about visibility,” Claira told Gothamist in an interview. “When people see an Afro-Latina AI, it challenges the idea of who belongs in tech and opens the door for inclusive innovation.”
The Latino AI Summit, the in-person iteration of a forum that also has been featured online, is one of several efforts cropping up in the city designed to empower Black and brown people to get jobs in the AI world, hear from experts about how AI is changing the workforce, and build personalized tools that people can apply to their daily lives or jobs.
Other organizations are pushing similar initiatives, also with an eye toward reaching those often on the sidelines of the tech landscape, an arena at the center of attention, with the upcoming initial public offering of AI giant Anthropic set for Wednesday and expected to value the company at more than $1 trillion.
The Knowledge House in the Bronx provides coding and design training for underserved young people interested in the burgeoning AI economy. For adults, the Rev. Al Sharpton’s AI Fluency Initiative teaches people without tech experience the basics of AI. There, the mission is simple: It's to "close the digital divide and put the power of these tools in the hands of the people," the group states on its website.
The imperative is crystal clear to Michal Tapia, the cofounder of the Latino AI summit, which was held at Civic Hall and Berkeley College in Midtown. AI will play a major role in our future, whether people like it or not, she said.
The key now, she said, is making sure that people of all ethnicities and backgrounds are involved in the builders’ room.
“AI is happening, and it's either we get on the train, or we get left behind,” Tapia said.
A mixed view of the future
Early research on the impact of AI on Black and brown communities is a mixed bag.
A disproportionate number of Black workers hold jobs that are likely to be automated by AI, including in transportation, production and administration roles, according to a report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility.
And Black workers may already be feeling the squeeze. In a 2025 report from Jobs for the Future, a national nonprofit that influences education and workforce systems, found that 67% of Black survey respondents said they feel like AI is already impacting their jobs, compared to 57% of white survey respondents.
The report also found that more Black respondents said they feel like they need to gain new skills due to the impact of AI on their work than the overall sample of people surveyed. More than half of Black respondents in the same survey said they already use AI tools daily or weekly, compared to about 40% of all respondents.
Latinos, likewise, are underrepresented in the tech space. About 19% of the U.S. workforce is Latino, according to a report from the Kapor Foundation, which publishes research on racial equity and technology issues. But Latinos fill just 3% of board seats, 5% of executive leadership roles, and 6% of technical roles across the country’s largest tech companies, according to the same report.
To stay in the game, Maldonado said in an interview, it’s essential for all jobseekers to market themselves as AI-literate.
No matter what field you’re in, your resume should change, Maldonado said. The section that used to list skills in programs like Microsoft Office and the Adobe Suite, now should list proficiency in AI tools like Claude, Codex and Google AI Studio.
And instead of updating a resume every couple of years, jobseekers should update it once a month — that’s how fast the relevant AI tools change, he said.
But even ChatGPT, an AI chatbot, is becoming antiquated, he said. Baseline prerequisites for jobs of the future will include things like knowing how to use Claude projects, an AI work space and Cowork, a tool that helps people complete tasks. And ultimately, he added, administrative tasks should be delegated to an AI agent.
The best thing a person can do to prepare themselves for the changing workforce, Maldonado said, is to always be learning.
“Putting our heads in the sand is not the move,” he said. “ You have to tinker. You have to try these things out.”
Schools will also have to meet the moment, experts say — and some already are. Alpha School, for example, are K-12 schools with programs across the country that provide kids training on AI tools.
“ Kids are scoring through the roof ... the level of fluency and literacy that they have,” Maldonado said.
These curriculums need to be available in all schools, not just those that are predominantly white or wealthy, tech experts argue. Taylor Shead, founder of a company that develops AI-driven education, in the Jobs for the Future report, emphasized “prevention over intervention.”
“Equity and access mean meeting people where they are—going to the systems Black learners and workers are in,” she wrote in the report.
Kara Emery, the director of data science at the AI Hub of NYU’s McSilver Institute for Poverty Policy and Research, said time will tell how these things shake out.
“A lot of these projections of what AI will potentially impact are just that,” Emery said. “Projections on the future of what this technology might be able to do.”
The fear, said Emery, is that AI could make the already staggering racial income inequalities worse. But, Emery emphasized, people have a say in how things unfold.
There are “preparations and things that can be done now to try to protect against what could be a continuation of this wealth gap,” she said.
‘We are rapidly losing our jobs’
Summit attendee Fradely Delacruz, a computational scientist student and a professional data architect, said she is already feeling the economy change beneath her feet.
“Women of color specifically, we are rapidly losing our jobs in the STEM space and the research and development space,” Delacruz said. We’re “losing our jobs in huge amounts.”
Delacruz said she doesn’t entirely blame AI, which she feels is only exacerbating existing social systems and prejudice.
But, she said, half the battle is making sure all people have access to resources and information about what technology is up and coming and how it’s being designed.
“ When AI came, it kind of felt like there was other people who knew about it before we did,” Delacruz said. “By the time we're catching on, we're like, ‘Oh, we're not even part of the conversation.’ I think it's really important to position ourselves in community as innovators.”
Emery said she is seeing Black and brown New Yorkers rising to the occasion.
“ These communities aren't just sitting on the sidelines waiting for these things to have a negative impact,” Emery said. “They really have the agency.”
Not everyone is quite as optimistic.
David Gabeau, who created an online interface of AI companies in New York, is an AI entrepreneur who worked at tech-driven companies like Snapchat and Lyft before eventually starting his own company, which he has since retired.
Gabeau, who is Black, said that his race was one of the reasons he was inspired to work in tech. He said he felt like the social media he consumed growing up was based on Black culture, and he wanted to contribute to the technology’s design.
But after years of working in the space, he now fears that AI is only broadening social inequities across racial lines.
“People [working in AI] are going to get so, so so wealthy,” Gabeau said.
It’s my biggest fear, he continued, that “there will be no forcing function to spread the wealth, and that it will massively and drastically create a divide between the have and have nots.”
After spending 10 years in New York, Gabeau recently moved to San Francisco to get closer to the epicenter of AI.
There, he said, he recently spent an afternoon wearing a 4 pound headset that scanned his brain while he watched videos and answered questions. The effort was for a company that is working on using AI to develop a tool that’s akin to telepathy: the tool converts your thoughts into text without the need to type.
Gabeau said he was paid about $50 for his troubles, although he participated for the sake of his own curiosity. But the experience was an eye opener, Gabeau said. The other people in the room, many of whom were Black and brown, seemed to be there because they needed the money.
“These people's thoughts are gonna have helped create and train the AIs,” Gabeau said. “And they're definitely not gonna receive the benefits of this company getting very big.”
“It was a little predatory,” he added.
But Emery, the NYU researcher, said that sometimes the most outsize fears about AI come from within the tech industry itself. We should be wary, she said, of taking the promises of these companies’ success at face value.
“ This narrative of the inevitability of what these technologies will become is something that's often pushed by those who are currently in the big companies building them now,” Emery said.
She said the right combination of policy, education and a diversity of innovators working behind the scenes is key to preventing existing inequalities from worsening.
And Delacruz, one of the students who attended the summit, said she’s eager to put her skills to use. But at this point, she said she still feels unseen.
“They don't see the scientists and the researchers that are Black and brown and Latinos and Afro-Latinos. They don't know we exist, but we're here,” Delacruz said. “Well, let's look at the people who are professionals and let's collaborate.

https://www.propublica.org/article/alaba.title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
https://www.propublica.org/article/alaba.author: Amy Yurkanin
https://www.propublica.org/article/alaba.text:
Reporting Highlights
- A Brutal Attack: A rookie cop in rural Alabama told his colleague he had hit his pregnant wife in the stomach and choked her before she started to miscarry.
- Laws for the Unborn: Under Alabama law, fetuses have equal protections. But those laws are limited in how they punish people who abuse their pregnant partners.
- Unequal Outcomes: Women accused of drug use during pregnancy face far more legal scrutiny, even when their babies are healthy.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital.
Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help.
The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.
When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container.
“They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said.
Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family.
“Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.”
Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground.
“I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.”
According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.”
In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences.
The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder.
But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell.
His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.
In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison.
A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.
Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court.
“During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”
As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said.
Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital.
“If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email.
Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion.
“Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.”
Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.
“I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.
She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him.
About a week before she went to the authorities, she got a text from her husband asking if she’d give him one more chance. “I can’t give you your baby back,” he wrote. “That’s something I’m always going to live with knowing I did that.”
Asked about the text, Robert wrote to ProPublica, “I was referring to having to pull my kid out a toilet I couldn’t believe I had to do that. It was painful emotionally.”
Robert had started working as an officer at the Headland Police Department about four months earlier. Brittany worried the other officers would side with her husband, but she quashed her fears and reached out on social media to several of them anyway. She said Robert went into her account and deleted the messages she’d sent. But it was too late.
Knight, one of the officers she messaged, confronted Robert, who admitted that he had hit Brittany in the stomach before the miscarriage, the officer later told the Dothan police. Robert furiously messaged Brittany.
“If you want me to go to jail keep accusing me of it,” he wrote. “Just know I love you and it will never happen again but I think I’m getting fired.”
Domestic abuse is a leading killer of pregnant women. And for every fatal case, there are an estimated 70 nonfatal ones. Researchers have found that almost 13% of women surveyed experienced domestic violence during pregnancy.
Nonfatal cases usually go unreported, according to Maeve Wallace, an expert on domestic violence at the University of Arizona. The same goes for miscarriages, which often happen at home and may leave no medical record. That can make it difficult to determine how often abuse causes miscarriage, she said.
Brittany said her relationship with Robert had been turbulent from the start. She was still in high school when they started dating, and she uprooted her life to relocate to his hometown of Dothan. She said he started physically hurting her months into the relationship and that it escalated after the move. Brittany found herself isolated in Alabama, where life revolved almost entirely around her husband, two young children and the couple’s car-detailing business.
“Robert would also hurt me if things weren’t done perfectly or if any issues happened,” Brittany wrote.
Unlike many other victims of domestic violence, she hounded the police and prosecutors to take her case seriously after the miscarriage.
Cases against abusers accused of causing pregnancy loss can be tricky to prove, often requiring evidence that the abuser intentionally struck the victim in the stomach and testimony from a forensic pathologist linking the violence to the pregnancy loss. In one strange turn, a grand jury in a city outside of Birmingham indicted a woman for starting a fight that led to her being shot in the stomach and suffering a miscarriage.
It’s easier and more common to pursue charges against defendants when they are accused of killing both a pregnant woman and her fetus.
Laws don’t provide an easy path for punishing abusers of pregnant women, especially when the baby survives, according to law professor Mary Ziegler, who teaches at the University of California, Davis. But laws do make prosecution of pregnant women who use drugs astonishingly easy. Those cases come to light almost automatically — and there is little opportunity to challenge them. Hospitals frequently administer drug tests to pregnant women and notify child protective services of positive results. Those agencies often turn over that information to police in Alabama, where drug use is not grounds just for a child welfare investigation but for a felony charge.
The women are prosecuted under Alabama’s chemical endangerment law, which makes it illegal to expose children to drugs. Although the 2006 law initially was designed to address the dangers of home-based meth labs, prosecutors almost immediately began using it against pregnant women.
ProPublica identified more than 40 pregnant women arrested in Houston County since 2009 on chemical endangerment charges after testing positive for drugs. An analysis of court data also found that the county prosecuted women for chemical endangerment at one of the highest rates in the state, though the data doesn’t specify whether the cases involved pregnancies.
In one case, a 24-year-old whose newborn tested positive for methadone and marijuana received a five-year prison sentence in 2009. Another woman, who’d been convicted for exposing her fetus to THC in 2013, had her probation revoked for possessing synthetic marijuana and spent about nine months in prison.
Pat Jones, who was Houston County’s district attorney at the time of these cases, did not respond to a request for comment.
According to Ziegler, there is a pronounced unevenness in who gets punished under statutes that protect fetuses.
“The versions of personhood that are enshrined in our laws have tended to focus on the conduct of women,” she said.
Courtney Haney grew up in Dothan but left at age 18 to join a high-pressure sales crew that traveled across the country, selling boxes of frozen meat door-to-door. The work was stressful, and it attracted misfits and risk-takers. Several of her colleagues used drugs, but Haney became pregnant unexpectedly and stayed clean.
Her daughter was born healthy, arriving exactly on her due date. But soon, cracks appeared in her relationship with the father, and he split, taking the baby with him. When her colleagues moved on to other cities, Haney remained in Denver to look for her child. She had no family there and no friends. Her despair became overwhelming. She turned to drugs and became homeless, eventually losing custody.
Almost a year later, Haney found out she was pregnant again and returned to Dothan in 2020 with a full-blown addiction to heroin. She went to the hospital with contractions the week before she gave birth and knew she would test positive for drugs. She also said no one offered her options for drug treatment, even after she asked for help. Instead, hospital staff stabilized and discharged her. She kept using until she returned to give birth, when she was drug-tested again.
“I was holding my daughter in my hands and the police walked in,” Haney said.
They asked her questions, and she hoped they might show mercy and allow her to go home with her child. After they told her she might be charged with a felony for exposing her fetus to drugs, she burst into tears.
“I answered honestly, thinking that if I’ve answered honestly they wouldn’t press charges,” she said. “And that was pointless.”
She was arrested for chemical endangerment three months later.
For women struggling with addiction during pregnancy, a chemical endangerment arrest can initiate a cycle of devastating court fees, imprisonment on probation violations and even additional charges. And the separation from their newborns and other children can drive them deeper into addiction. Unlike in many other counties, Houston County does not offer a drug court program, which allows defendants to get substance-abuse treatment instead of prison time and avoid a felony on their record.
A woman who was about seven months’ pregnant was arrested in Houston County the very same day as Robert Maddox, in 2022. She was briefly jailed for violating probation stemming from a past chemical endangerment conviction. She then faced additional felony charges when, weeks later, she tested positive for cocaine at the hospital where she gave birth. She later received a five-year sentence and wound up at Tutwiler Prison for Women.
Her release date is right before Christmas in 2028.
Haney had no felony convictions, but a sentencing report recommended against straight probation due to charges in other states that had been dismissed. Ultimately, the Houston County district attorney’s office offered a plea deal for a lesser charge and just over a year of probation.
Haney struggled to abide by the conditions of her sentence. She did not complete court-ordered drug treatment and failed to report to her probation officer several times. As a result, she was jailed for a total of four months.
Many of the other women jailed with her also had been arrested on charges of chemical endangerment as a result of failing drug tests during childbirth.
“Whenever I went to jail, that’s where I met most of them,” Haney said. “There’s a whole lot of them in Houston County.”
Haney became pregnant two more times while she was addicted. For her third child, she traveled to nearby Georgia to give birth, and then to Florida for her fourth. Neither state arrests women for prenatal drug use at the same high rate as Alabama.
Xaviera Smith, a former nurse and mother of three from Tennessee, said she knew she would be arrested before she even gave birth in Houston County to her youngest son in 2018. Smith couldn’t deny the results of the drug test that had been administered while she was in labor. She had been battling a meth addiction for years.
She said that, fortunately, her baby was born healthy and did not need to go to the neonatal intensive care unit for drug withdrawal.
Smith had a court-appointed attorney who negotiated a deal on her chemical endangerment charge. She was sentenced to 10 years but could avoid prison by serving time through the local work-release program.
“I just went to court and took what they gave me,” Smith said. ”There’s nothing I really could do.”
After violating the terms of work release, she ended up in prison for nearly a year.
Brittany Maddox believed the case against her husband was a straightforward one. She felt there was solid evidence that the abuse caused her miscarriage. But the effort proved to be harder than she anticipated.
A few months after his arrest, the grand jury declined to indict him for murder, opting instead for a lesser charge of manslaughter.
The indictment alleged that Robert had “recklessly” caused the death of his wife’s fetus by “punching her in the stomach with a closed fist.” The maximum punishment would be 20 years in prison.
As Robert waited for his day in court, he asked the judge to relax some of the conditions of his bond. He had lost his job with the Headland police because of his wife’s claims of abuse and had started washing cars again. He wanted the court to remove the ankle monitor so he could more easily travel to work in Florida, which is near Dothan.
From her home out of state, Brittany had been calling the district attorney’s office once or twice a month to ensure authorities kept an eye on her estranged husband’s whereabouts. She was shocked to learn of his out-of-state travel request — not from prosecutors but from a news story. For the first time since his arrest, she felt unsafe.
A judge denied his motion to remove the ankle monitor but granted his request to commute to north Florida.
Brittany stayed in touch with prosecutors and began to mentally prepare for trial. She said that as months stretched into years, the conversations with them began to shift. They asked her how she felt about a plea deal, and she said she would be open to it, as long as the charge related to her miscarriage wasn’t dropped completely.
“I told them I could push through a trial emotionally,” Brittany wrote.
Finally, almost four years after Robert was arrested, his attorney brokered a plea deal with prosecutors. He would plead guilty to domestic violence, and the prosecution would recommend the manslaughter charge be dismissed.
Goodman, the district attorney, told ProPublica that he would not have been able to prove at trial that Robert committed manslaughter. “There was never any evidence that tied the actions of the defendant to the death of the baby,” he said, adding that “no expert could tie a causal connection.”
He also said he explained to Brittany that “we would not have moved forward on the manslaughter case” had he been in office when his predecessor chose to seek an indictment against Robert.
Brittany said if Goodman believed the charge should be dropped, he should have done it sooner, instead of having her spend years preparing for trial.
“The charge being dropped four years after he was arrested as part of a plea deal makes no sense to me,” she said. “That wrecked me in a lot of ways, more than the times I laid in bed for days after he hurt me.”
On May 18, 2026, Robert appeared before a judge in a Houston County courtroom. Brittany attended the hearing as well. She had traveled to Alabama for all of the hearings, even though she still feared being in the same room with Robert.
After all that waiting, the sentencing felt surprisingly short to her. When the judge moved to dismiss the most serious charge, he didn’t say the word manslaughter or mention the miscarriage. Brittany said she tried to ask questions about the deal, but she wasn’t sworn in, and the judge quickly moved on.
“The victim and the defendant were in a verbal dispute whereas the defendant was alleged to throw the victim down and choke her,” the judge said. “The state alleges that this occurred in front of their minor children as well.”
The judge went on to say that the presence of the children might have increased Robert’s punishment to a minimum six months’ imprisonment. But because he was a first-time offender, that minimum didn’t apply.
The judge sentenced him to five years’ probation and fined him about $3,000, which he could pay off at $50 a month. Then the judge added one more thing: anger management classes, to be completed through the court referral office.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-fatally-.title: NYPD fatally shoots driver on Belt Parkway following suspected kidnapping
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-fatally-.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-fatally-.text:
Police shot and killed a man in Brooklyn on Saturday night after responding to reports of a woman trapped and screaming for help from inside a van in Coney Island.
The driver of the van, Omatoyo Neverson, was shot on the Belt Parkway following a police chase. Neverson, 26, was taken to a nearby hospital, where he was declared dead.
The woman was able to flee the vehicle and was unharmed, police said.
“ She has confirmed that she was in the van and was screaming and exited the vehicle before the police officers first arrived,” Assistant Chief Charles Minch, the commander of the NYPD’s Patrol Borough Brooklyn South, said at a press conference.
The incident began at 7:20 p.m., when two people called 911 to report a possible kidnapping in Coney Island at West 22nd Street and Surf Avenue around 7:20 p.m., Minch said.
“ The male caller said that he saw a white van and further stated, ‘There's a girl kicking and screaming in there,’” Minch said. “The female caller stated that she heard the girl saying, ‘Let me go,’ multiple times.”
The callers, while on the phone with 911, saw two uniformed cops and told them about the van. Minch said when those officers approached the vehicle, it took off at high speed down the sidewalk.
The van entered the Belt Parkway, heading east, but was slowed by heavy traffic, Minch said. Officers approached the vehicle and ordered Neverson out, and then broke the front passenger side window when he refused.
“The driver began to drive forwards and backwards, ramming both police and occupied civilian vehicles indiscriminately,” Minch said.
Minch said police then tried to use a taser and pepper spray against the driver, but neither was “effective, and the driver continued to ram nearby vehicles.”
Multiple officers then shot Neverson, Minch said. It is unclear how many officers fired, or how many shots were fired.
The officers pulled Neverson from the van and performed CPR while they waited for an ambulance, Minch said. Neverson was taken to NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn, formerly Lutheran Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.
He had a known history of aggression towards the woman, Minch said.
“ The driver of the vehicle was wanted for an unlawful imprisonment last month and also a domestic assault earlier this month,” Minch said. “The victim in both cases was the female who had been in the white van.”
Investigations are ongoing into both the suspected kidnapping and the fatal police shooting. Minch said the shooting was recorded on police body cameras.
This story has been updated.

Launching as part of the new Powerhouse Museum Parramatta, the two-storey art and design exhibition The Mall examines the history, evolution and cultural significance of the shopping mall. The ‘My Mall’ series of 100 new photographic works by Jo Duck and Bahram Mia, commissioned by the Powerhouse for the exhibition, documents the intersection of private retail and public space in the malls and shopping strips of western Sydney
