https://jacobin.com/2026/11/south-africa.title: South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/south-africa.author: Zwelinzima Vavi
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/south-africa.text:
South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
The African National Congress is losing its working-class base. The beneficiaries: parties of the Right. South Africa’s local elections expose the fallout of three decades of economic failure — and the need to rebuild working-class power.
While the global left celebrates the recent successes of the Workers’ Party in Brazil and the Democratic Socialists of America in the United States, the African National Congress (ANC) has suffered a historic collapse in South Africa’s November 4 local government elections. After three decades of mass unemployment, deepening inequality, corruption, and economic policies that have failed the working class, the former liberation movement is losing its political authority. The principal beneficiaries of the ANC’s electoral rout are parties of the Right, including an increasingly powerful far right that has built its project around aggressive and often violent xenophobia.
With more than 70 percent of votes counted, the ANC’s national share of the vote fell to around 32 percent. The ANC is not expected to retain an outright majority in any major city, and the center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), historically the principal party of the white liberal establishment, is making substantial gains and is projected to become the largest party in most of South Africa’s big cities. Former President Jacob Zuma’s Zulu nationalist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) is on track to be the largest party in Durban. The far-right ActionSA has made a strong showing in Johannesburg and Pretoria and is likely to be the second-largest party in Pretoria, with the ANC in third place.
The central question is not only why the ANC has lost so much support. It is why the suffering and anger of the working class have failed to produce a powerful democratic socialist alternative, and why the Right has been so successful in presenting itself as the answer to a crisis created by the existing economic and political order.
The ANC’s Historic Failure
The defeat of apartheid was an extraordinary achievement. We won universal suffrage, democratic institutions, constitutional rights, and legal protections for workers. Those victories were won through generations of sacrifice and collective struggle, and they must be defended. But political apartheid was defeated while the economic structures inherited from apartheid remained largely intact.
The liberation movement historically brought together different classes and social groups united against racial oppression. That unity was indispensable to apartheid’s defeat. But national identity does not abolish class contradictions. Instead of using democracy to transform the ownership and control of the economy in the interests of the majority, the ANC increasingly became an instrument through which a new elite could enter and benefit from the existing economic order.
The ownership and control of the commanding heights of the economy were never fundamentally transformed. Land ownership remained extraordinarily unequal. The former Bantustans, created as reservoirs of cheap African labor, were never provided with the productive economic foundations needed to overcome their inherited poverty.
Over time, the ANC came to treat the advancement of an emerging black capitalist class as evidence of economic transformation. A narrow layer of businesspeople accumulated wealth, in some cases extraordinary wealth, through access to political power, state contracts, and opportunities created by the Black Economic Empowerment policy, while the overwhelming majority remained excluded from meaningful economic power.
The ANC’s adoption of neoliberal economic policies in the 1990s deepened this problem. The language of economic liberation gave way to investor confidence, competitiveness, and market reform. Brutal austerity, liberalization, and dependence on private investment displaced the redistributive ambitions of the liberation struggle.
We were repeatedly told that economic growth would eventually deliver employment and redistribution. We were also told that redistribution must wait for economic growth and the development of the productive forces. But if redistribution had to wait while productive capacity developed, why did South Africa simultaneously deindustrialize?
We have become what I have described as a “warehouse economy.” We export raw materials and insufficiently processed mineral wealth, allow other countries to manufacture finished products, then import those products for domestic consumption. We export jobs embedded in raw materials and import unemployment embedded in finished goods.
Factories have closed while warehouses have remained open. South Africa continues to extract enormous mineral wealth without developing the productive industries capable of turning that wealth into decent employment on the scale required.
It is a very painful fact that, after decades of mass unemployment and deindustrialization, the poor are now poorer and more numerous than under apartheid. In the second quarter of 2026, South Africa’s official unemployment rate stood at 33.6 percent. Including people who want work but have stopped actively searching, the rate was 43.8 percent. Among young people age fifteen to twenty-four who were in the labor force, unemployment reached 62.8 percent.
This crisis has meant the destruction of hope for millions of people. It has also been accompanied by the weakening of the organized working class. Mass unemployment undermines bargaining power, makes workers afraid to exercise their rights, and encourages casualization and precarious employment. A worker who knows that thousands of unemployed people are desperate for a job is in a much weaker position to resist exploitation.
The crisis has also fragmented the working class itself. Millions of people are unemployed, casually employed, working in the informal economy, or moving between different forms of insecure work. Traditional trade unions organize only a section of this wider class.
The working class cannot be reduced to people fortunate enough to receive a regular pay slip. The unemployed, precarious workers, labor-broker workers, informal workers, women carrying the burden of unpaid care, and young people who have never had secure employment must all be part of the social movement capable of transforming South Africa.
At the same time, the combination of austerity and extreme corruption has resulted in the decay of the state and the collapse of public services. Municipalities have become centers of patronage, political competition over tenders, and the accumulation of private wealth. Water systems collapse, roads deteriorate, sewage flows through communities, and public transport becomes increasingly unreliable. It has become normal for even middle-class areas to go for weeks or even months without water, while the poor live among stinking piles of uncollected refuse.
The crisis is also visible in the ANC’s conception of the state. A developmental state cannot simply outsource development and then claim the credit. It requires public institutions with the capacity to plan, build, maintain infrastructure, and provide services directly.
South Africa has developed a system in which government contracts out essential functions while state capacity deteriorates. The result is an expanding network of contractors, consultants, and intermediaries whose accumulation depends on public expenditure, while the institutions responsible for serving the people become weaker.
The tragic reality is that the ANC’s neoliberal policies have not simply failed to resolve the economic crisis. They have also undermined the credibility of the very idea of democratic transformation, opening the door to right-wing demagoguery.
Corruption and the Destruction of Political Authority
Economic failure has been compounded by the degeneration of political leadership. The ANC once insisted that leadership required exceptional qualities: political understanding, integrity, discipline, courage, humility, service, and sacrifice. Its own document, “Through the Eye of the Needle,” expressed the idea that leadership should be earned through commitment to the people rather than acquired through personal ambition.
Today the competition for leadership largely revolves around factions, access to resources, control of organizational structures, and the distribution of positions. Political office has become a route to private accumulation.
This cannot be understood merely as a series of individual moral failures. It is connected to a political culture in which access to the state and public wealth becomes a route to private economic advancement. Where the public sector is treated as a source of tenders and contracts rather than an instrument for meeting social needs, the distinction between political leadership and business accumulation becomes blurred. The result is a profound loss of moral authority.
When working people see leaders acquiring enormous wealth while unemployment rises, schools deteriorate, hospitals struggle, and the water supply fails, they inevitably begin to lose confidence in the institutions that claim to represent them. The ANC’s electoral collapse is therefore not mysterious. It is the political expression of a much deeper social, economic, and organizational failure.
At the same time, trade unions have been divided, and some have become very corrupt, as corrupt as the ANC. The capacity of unions and community organizations to develop working-class leaders has weakened. Organizations have often concentrated on internal contests or debates between established political figures instead of building the democratic power of ordinary people. Political education, once central to the union movement, has declined. With the exception of Abahlali baseMjondolo, the two-hundred-thousand-strong movement of the urban poor, community organizations have lost much of their former strength, with many collapsing completely.
The Right Advances
A rapidly growing Right has been very successful in redirecting legitimate popular anger away from those responsible for generalized social suffering and toward African and Asian migrants. Fascist organisations such as Operation Dudula and March and March have built movements around violent hostility toward African migrants. In communities devastated by unemployment, crime, and failing services, they offer a simple explanation: foreigners are responsible for the crisis. Political parties have increasingly adopted the same language. Like many centrist parties elsewhere in the world, the ANC made a profound error of political judgment in indulging organized xenophobia rather than opposing it.
The two parties that have surged forward in these elections, ActionSA and the MKP, have both actively supported the xenophobic street thuggery that forced up to 150,000 migrants, including refugees and other documented migrants, from the country in a matter of months.
This right-wing mobilization, which includes fascist elements, does not only target migrants. It increasingly argues that South Africa has too many rights, that the Constitution should be changed to do away with some of these rights, and that strong leaders should be freed from democratic constraints.
The result is a political paradox. South Africa faces one of the most severe crises of unemployment and inequality anywhere in the world, yet the electoral beneficiaries of popular anger are largely forces advocating policies that will deepen inequality as they redirect anger toward vulnerable minorities.
Renewing the Left
The Left is also in crisis. For decades, the South African Communist Party (SACP) presented itself as the socialist component of the ANC-led alliance. Yet it remained politically committed to governments that implemented austerity, privatization, and other neoliberal policies. Its leaders participated in those governments while continuing to speak in the language of socialism and working-class liberation. The contradiction between revolutionary language and participation in the administration of neoliberal capitalism became increasingly difficult to ignore.
This contradiction has never been satisfactorily resolved. Earlier this year, the SACP proposed convening a “Conference of the Left,” inviting organizations including the ANC and Zuma’s MKP, which had been on the streets with the xenophobic mobs. How could a conference claim to unite the Left while including a governing party responsible for decades of neoliberal economic policy and a political formation associated with state capture, ethnic chauvinism, and xenophobia? The independent South African Federation of Trade Unions (SAFTU) considered the invitation carefully and decided not to participate. Other progressive organizations, such as Abahlali baseMjondolo, took similar positions.
Working-class unity is indispensable, but it must be based on principles and a shared program. A Left that abandons its defining commitments in pursuit of alliances with corrupt or reactionary organizations will not resolve the present crisis. It will only deepen it.
Rebuilding Independent Working-Class Power
The answer cannot be to demand that workers and the poor continue supporting political organizations that have repeatedly failed them. Nor can we respond to the advance of the Right with moral denunciations while leaving the underlying conditions of life unchanged.
South Africa needs a new working-class political project rooted in a credible program of economic transformation. But no program, however coherent, will succeed without organized social power. A genuine working-class political alternative must emerge from renewed organization, political education, democratic debate, and collective struggle.
The principles of such a movement cannot be negotiable. It must be independent of employers and the capitalist state, committed to socialism and worker democracy, and resolutely opposed to racism, xenophobia, sexism, patriarchy, and ethnic chauvinism. It must be internationalist in its outlook and rooted in the everyday struggles of workers and poor communities.
Rebuilding working-class power also requires reconnecting workplace struggles with those of communities. Water is a workers’ issue. Electricity is a workers’ issue. Public transport, housing, health care, education, gender-based violence, and the climate crisis are all workers’ issues.
The struggles of an employed factory worker cannot be separated from those of an unemployed young person, a mother trying to feed her children, a shack dweller fighting for water, or a community resisting the destruction of its environment.
The organizations capable of creating a new political alternative will have to emerge from these connected struggles.
South Africa’s democratic transition was a great victory for popular movements across the world. The possibility that its political future could now be shaped increasingly by xenophobic and authoritarian forces should concern everyone committed to democracy, equality, and international solidarity.

https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-big.title: New York's biggest trash dump is releasing even more methane than thought
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-big.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/new-yorks-big.text:
New York’s largest landfill is pumping a lot of methane into the atmosphere — as much as 90 times the federal limit.
The Seneca Meadows landfill, located in the Finger Lakes region 275 miles from Midtown Manhattan, is leaking copious amounts of methane despite repeated repairs and persistent warnings from state regulators, a new report by the advocacy group Full Circle Future revealed on Thursday.
The analysis was based on documents obtained from the state Department of Environmental Conservation and self-reporting from 16 landfills across New York. It found that six sites, including Seneca, surpassed federal limits.
“I certainly knew that the methane emissions were a big problem, but that is an enormous problem,” New York State Assemblymember Emily Gallagher, who chairs the state’s Solid Waste Management Legislative Committee, said in response to the report’s findings.
In a statement, Department of Environmental Conservation spokesperson Andrea Pedrick-Bird said landfill operators are required to “take appropriate measures and conduct re-monitoring” to ensure any methane leaks or excessive emissions are resolved.
The Full Circle Future analysis concludes that DEC’s process isn’t effectively managing methane emissions. The study notes recurrences of leaks in the same spots.
Methane is a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential that is around 80 times more potent than carbon, according to the EPA. Exposure to the gas is also harmful to humans, contributing to respiratory-related deaths.
Seneca Meadows, New York’s largest active landfill, is the state’s biggest source of methane, according to aerial estimates published in a peer-reviewed science journal, Copernicus.
First opened in 1983 near Seneca Falls — the birthplace of the women’s rights movement — the 400-acres landfill is almost as tall as the Statue of Liberty. About 6% of its annual refuse, or 75,000 tons, comes from commercial sources in New York City, according to DEC’s most recent records.
The site is close to full capacity and was originally set to close at the end of last year. But its owner, Texas-based Waste Connections, has applied to increase the size of the landfill and continue operating through 2040.
Locals have strongly opposed the expansion.
“If you could imagine sticking your head into a dumpster in the middle of an alleyway in New York City on a hot, humid July day, it is like someone sucker punched you in the face,” said Mark Pitifer, an employee at Waterloo Container, a nearby business.
The landfill’s owners, Texas-based Waste Connections, did not return requests for comment.
Federal law requires landfill operators to self-report methane releases. But, according to Full Circle Future, it’s a law with no teeth.
“The most shocking thing for me is that all of this is actually within federal regulation,” said Kimenthrie Finlay, Full Circle’s Director of Research and Analytics and a coauthor of the report. "Most of the federal actions don't really require too much.”
Between February 2024 and June 2025, the Department of Environmental Conservation recorded discharges at the same locations six times. According to DEC correspondence, Waste Connection was told to fix the leak and retest the spot within 120 days.
“These quick patches and fixes don't really stay in place,” Finlay said. “In several instances these fixes didn't work and that same spot kept recurring.”
Finlay said the group’s analysis is likely an underestimate since as much as one-third of the Seneca landfill is not monitored, according to the mapping of testing areas.
Those calling for Seneca to be shut down said that the report is further proof that the pollution outweighs any benefits.
“The only way that we can start to recover from this heinous mountain of trash is to close it right away, cap it, and start dealing with the problem, not consider letting it grow,” said Yvonne Taylor, cofounder of local advocacy group Seneca Lake Guardian. “We need to close this thing. And if we need any more signals, this is it. Time is now. Do it. Close it.”
Seneca Meadows has been running on an expired permit for nearly one year, but continues to operate legally. An administrative loophole allows the facility to continue accepting trash while its expansion application is under review. The site is nearly at full capacity under its original limits.
More than 11,000 surrounding residents are exposed to the emissions from the landfill.
The DEC is hosting a public hearing on Nov. 16 on a statewide management plan that aims to greatly reduce dependence on landfills.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Rugby centre Henry Slade and his father look back: ‘I’d seen my dad live with diabetes, so my diagnosis wasn’t as upsetting as it might have been’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Harriet Gibsone
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Born in Plymouth, Devon, in 1993, Henry Slade is a centre for Exeter Chiefs and England. He came up through the Exeter Chiefs academy, making his senior debut for the club in 2012, and has since earned more than 75 caps for England. He lifted the Champions Cup and won the Premiership title and the Six Nations in successive weekends in 2020. At 18, he was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes – a condition his father, John, also lives with – and he has since launched the Tackle Diabetes campaign, in partnership with the pharmaceutical company Sanofi, to raise awareness of the signs and symptoms of the disease and the value of early detection. He lives near Exeter with his wife and three daughters. For more information about early detection, visit testfortype1.com
Henry (on left)
This was taken after my first game for England’s under-18s. Wearing the shirt was a cool moment, but I was feeling knackered and giving a nervous smile. I was a bit of a shy kid back then.
A few months later, I was diagnosed with diabetes. I was 18 and doing my A-levels. There was no real sign – I was healthy and didn’t have any of the typical symptoms, such as losing loads of weight, frequent urination or being thirsty. I just woke up and felt really bad one day. Actually, it was the only day I ever had off school – Mum and Dad never used to let me have a sick day as they needed to go to work. My mate was ill, too, but I didn’t realise he’d been admitted to hospital with diabetic ketoacidosis. He was back at school the next week and told us he’d been diagnosed with diabetes – he’d brought in a finger-prick test we could all try. I did mine and my blood glucose levels were high. I had another test at the GP that confirmed the diagnosis. It was a shock, but I was lucky we detected it early.
I’d grown up seeing my dad live with diabetes, so my diagnosis wasn’t as upsetting as it might be for other people. Throughout my childhood, I’d always seen Dad do triathlons and windsurfing. There were definite challenges, though – I was a teenager and had started going out and drinking with mates, and I was also a sportsman. It took a lot of getting used to, constantly thinking about what food and drink I was putting in my body so I could get my blood glucose levels right. Has it inhibited me in a game? I’ve only needed to eat a load of Jelly Babies to avoid a hypo (low blood sugar) before playing a few times. If anything, I like to focus on the positive side to type 1 diabetes: it’s made me so resilient and very conscious of my body and what it needs.
As a child, I did certain things to feel OK – small rituals to make sure my friends and family were safe. I now know that was obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). I’m a bit better now, but some rituals I can’t quite kick. Like, if I pick something up, I need to put my little finger down first, and there’s a certain way I like to turn off a light switch. In a strange way, OCD and type 1 diabetes aren’t a bad combination – both need controlling 24/7, and the hypervigilance that comes with OCD has actually made me very good at managing my levels. At the minute, I’m obsessed with my glucose data, which is obviously important because it’s my health – but it’s also occasionally annoying.
Throughout it all, it’s been so reassuring to have Dad next to me, someone who understands completely. Dad’s very particular. He knows what he likes, and what he doesn’t. He is strong-willed, but I haven’t argued with him since I was a teenager. We’d have some small fallouts, and some louder ones. Mainly about going to parties. The day I passed my driving test, my mate was having a party in Cornwall and I wanted to drive my friends to it. Dad said no – he didn’t want me to be responsible for four other boys in the car the day I passed. He knew I would be too excited to drive properly. I was angry at the time, but now I’m a dad I’d do the exact same thing.
I’ve probably played 280 times for Chiefs and I reckon Dad’s missed about five games in total. I’m very grateful for everything he has done for me. Along with Mum, he’s given up a lot. They sent us to private school when finances were tight. He gave me every opportunity, but never pushed me to do anything I didn’t want to. He told me anything was possible and has been there every step of the way.
John
I was extremely proud of Henry that day he played for England’s under-18s. I never expected my own child would play at that level. I’d always thought, “Wouldn’t it be great if I could be Jonny Wilkinson’s dad?” That’s why I am smiling from inside out.
When Henry got diagnosed with diabetes, my first thought was, “This is my fault.” I worried he’d inherited it from my genes. It was a little bit traumatic for me to process what had happened, but since then I’ve learned there is a one in 300 chance of developing type 1 diabetes for anyone. If there’s a close family member, then it’s one in 20.
Henry was nine months old when I was diagnosed. One of my biggest fears was that I wouldn’t be able to see him grow older. My eyesight had changed and I was worried I was going blind. That was a heavy time.
As Henry got older, he became a determined kid – very focused. He didn’t like to lose. It’s a competitive spirit that my wife and I have. Henry and I are both quiet, compared with Henry’s mum, who can talk for England. He and I aren’t the loudest in the room, but we have to win.
Even though I could see Henry had a tremendous talent, I was never a pushy parent. You do see mums or dads giving their kid £10 or a Mars bar for scoring a try, but I never did that. Instead, I encouraged him to acknowledge the commitment we were making. At the start of the season, I would hold the chequebook in front of me and say, “Right, I’m going to write this – if you want to drop out halfway through the season, forget it. It’s paid for.” That was the only push – that we were financially locked in for that year. I was also often loud on the touchline. Once, I got sent off by a school in Devon for cheering our side too enthusiastically. What did I shout? Nothing bad, I just loudly encouraged them, as the opposite side was cheating.
Diabetes has definitely bonded us. Henry teaches me, really, because he’s so well controlled. I am 33 years into it now, so my symptoms are very faint, although I did fall asleep after bathing Henry’s daughter a few years ago. I took her into the bedroom to dry her and was just about to put her nappy on when I fell asleep on the floor. I’d been out for 10 minutes. She shouted, “Dada’s asleep!” Thankfully, someone else was at home to take over.
Before every game, I text Henry, saying “best of luck”. I send him some heart emojis and tell him how proud I am. I don’t tend to say it to his face much, as the written word is easier. But I hope he knows that what he has achieved is beyond my wildest dreams.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-yamaz.title: A Childlike Devotion Runs Through Godzilla Minus Zero
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-yamaz.author: Eileen Jones
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-yamaz.text:
A Childlike Devotion Runs Through Godzilla Minus Zero
It’s heartwarming the way Takeshi Yamazaki has been able to channel his childhood commitment to that ultimate destructive monster, Godzilla, into Godzilla Minus Zero.
There’s a familiar but always thrilling moment in Godzilla Minus Zero when Godzilla is fighting the newer, faster, entirely more visually glamorous monster King Ghidorah — an immense three-headed, golden-ray-shooting dragon that seems set on destroying the human race — and Godzilla is losing. In fact, it seems Godzilla is beaten and dying.
But then Godzilla goes deep and dredges up the last of his prehistoric mojo and comes back to win the brutal kaiju battle. Godzilla the destroyer from the sea becomes Godzilla the hero and savior of the Japanese protagonists watching in wide-eyed terror. All the viewer’s childhood love of Godzilla, who lumbers around on big, squat feet like a crude, clumsy dinosaur based on some devoted but impractical kid’s drawing, surges to the fore.
Writer-director-CGI effects master Takeshi Yamazaki seems highly motivated by such lingering childhood feelings. He cautions us in interviews, in a caringly paternal sort of way, to remember that though Godzilla fights King Ghidorah, it’s not because he sides with human beings: “He can’t become humanity’s friend.”
Oh, we know. But many small children aren’t entirely on the side of humans either. Personally, I was all for the animals as a kid and relentlessly pretended to be an animal for years before the US educational system crushed it out of me. And most little children are united, at least for a few years, in a love of dinosaurs that borders on obsession. Though I’ve known a few kids who loved and identified with cars and trucks and industrial vehicles more than adult people.
Yamazaki seems to understand all that. He says he opted to revive King Ghidorah and have him wreak havoc on Yamazaki’s own hometown of Matsumoto in the first scene of destruction in Godzilla Minus Zero, then fight the climactic epic battle with Godzilla because, fifty-five years ago, he was a seven-year-old kid in Matsumoto eagerly awaiting a revival screening of the Godzilla movie sequel Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster from 1964. The promotional flyer specifically promised, “King Ghidorah attacks Matsumoto!”
But he was terribly disappointed when “the monster finally appeared [and] all he did was clip the roof tiles of the city’s castle before flying off.”
Yamazaki said, “I was so frustrated, so heartbroken. . . . I held a grudge for years.”
But ultimately, it’s heartwarming the way Yamazaki has been able to channel his childhood commitment and frustration into making the gorgeous and emotionally compelling Godzilla Minus One, released in 2023 and Godzilla Minus Zero, currently playing in theaters. It goes a long way toward explaining the immense critical and popular appeal of both.
Yamazaki was stunned by the global success of the first film, which he claimed he never expected to get such a warm reception beyond Japan. Its embrace by mass audiences in the United States was especially surprising, since we’re notorious for refusing to see “foreign films” requiring us to read subtitles. But a grand exception is made in the case of Yamazaki’s Godzilla films.
And Yamazaki isn’t conciliating American feelings either. Given the subject matter, it wouldn’t make any sense.
In Godzilla Minus Zero, the characters representing the US military brass in post–World War II Japan are all sinister, arrogant conquerors clearly up to no good, always plotting ways to harness additional power and further subjugate the Japanese. Even the lowly GIs stationed in Tokyo are portrayed as a disturbing alien presence — jittery, full of directionless aggressivity, vaguely looking for trouble. One American soldier chews gum with a manic ferocity.
The satirical portrayal of this platoon looks a lot like British filmmakers Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger’s 1946 take on American GIs in A Matter of Life and Death, and Powell and Pressburger were being conciliatory to the United States in a “hands-across-the-pond” manner. Their GI Joes, killed near the end of World War II, arrive in heaven all hopped up on a similarly strange, angsty energy and immediately scramble over to a suddenly revealed vending machine stocked with Coca-Cola.
Set in 1949, Godzilla Minus Zero has no humor of that kind. It’s a somber film entirely preoccupied with the relentless calamities besetting Japan: World War II, the US nuclear bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, living in postwar poverty and wreckage, the Godzilla attacks in Godzilla Minus One, and the King Ghidorah attacks in Godzilla Minus Zero. The character of Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), the elderly biologist who found the charred bodies of his family in the aftermath of the bombing of Hiroshima, miraculously comes through all the mayhem, exclaiming bitterly, “And again, I survive!”
He joins forces to face the King Ghidorah threat with Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), director of the government’s Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, who has to put together the reluctant team that will fight this new monster. Former kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who flew the mission that apparently destroyed Godzilla in the previous film, is hoping — in vain — to avoid having to go up against King Ghidorah. Kōichi has married Noriko Ōishi (Minami Hamabe), a survivor of a previous Godzilla attacks, and together they’ve adopted war orphan Akiko (Sae Nagatani). The investment in their new family gives them a great stake in escaping any further life-threatening calamities.
Director Yamazaki particularly wanted a woman represented among the experts on the disaster team, so he created the character of Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a meteorologist with a useful theory about King Ghidorah’s attraction to lightning storms.
Godzilla Minus Zero has that typical sequel effect of moving away from a streamlined narrative toward a complicated one involving more monsters, more characters, more plotlines, more everything. There are promising story developments that aren’t fully explored and are presumably there as starter plotlines for sequels, such as the way living “Godzilla cells” are affecting humans, with a handful of scientific subjects who’ve survived contact with Godzilla but are now manifesting mutations. Noriko wears an eyepatch to cover her one reptilian yellow eye, and she also has Godzilla scales and spikes beginning to grow on one shoulder-blade, hidden by her clothing.
Still, the film maintains that basic rhythm also remembered from childhood when watching old Godzilla films: big action scenes full of exciting destruction and terror interspersed with far duller but somehow reassuring meeting scenes when characters representing science, government, the military, and the model family unit regroup to try Plan B, Plan C, and so on. Yamazaki hasn’t come to challenge the genre conventions but to fulfill them and render them more beautiful.
He makes vast CGI action sequences as sensational as it’s possible to make them, and it seems churlish to complain that, though generally magnificent, it’s still so much goddamn wearying CGI. It’s a generational viewership problem, really. I don’t think young people miss the sense of imprinting off of physical reality that once defined the film medium.
But the figure of Godzilla has such lasting, surefire appeal, it’s hard to quell the basic moviegoer longing to see him again. As Yamazaki put it about his own lifelong obsession,
As a kid, it was just: monster, cool, scary, amazing. Making these films now, I understand how much anxiety Japanese audiences were carrying when the first film came out in 1954, and how the monster’s shape matched that fear exactly. . . . Godzilla was never just a cool monster that wrecks things; he’s always carried the weight of the nuclear question, of war. The more I make these films, the more I feel that weight, and I think it’s exactly why people are still drawn to him.
Godzilla brings his fear-shaped silhouette into contemporary times as we’re “drifting toward conflict” on a global scale, in Yamazaki’s view. He meant the sequel to be weightier and more complex: “It’s entertainment, but I wanted it to leave something heavy behind, too.”
Yamazaki’s ability to unite fond nostalgia for Godzilla movies past, reaching back to childhood, with intensified modern angst forged in twentieth-century horrors that only grow over time, creates a riveting emotional combination. The third sequel is guaranteed, but it’s easy to imagine Yamazaki’s Godzilla movies maintaining their global appeal for as long as we’ve got a habitable globe to stand on.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/capitalism-w.title: Under Capitalism, Even Kids’ Playtime Is Alienated
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/capitalism-w.author: Evelina Johansson Wilén
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/capitalism-w.text:
Under Capitalism, Even Kids’ Playtime Is Alienated
Capitalism turns children’s play into preparation for work, but it cannot fully contain what play makes possible. In her new book, Susan Ferguson explores how the openness and pleasure of play can help us imagine other ways of being together.
A central concern of feminist Marxist theory and practice has been how to understand the relationship between paid and unpaid labor. Marxist feminists have drawn on Karl Marx’s observation that capital leaves workers to ensure their own reproduction, a process that depends on their instinct for self-preservation. They have shown how capitalist accumulation depends on reproductive labor, work that has fallen primarily to women. But what, exactly, is being reproduced? Workers must replenish their strength so that they can work again the next day; importantly, reproduction also encompasses bearing children and creating future labor power.
But it does not stop there of course: children must then be shaped into capable workers, a process that does not happen by itself and in which social reproduction is by no means simply left to the workers themselves. For anyone who has attended school, and perhaps even more so for those of us — myself included — who are now experiencing school all over again through our children’s education, it is more than apparent that school is, in many ways, an institution designed to socialize children into their future roles as wage workers.
As E. P. Thompson writes in Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism, schooling can be understood as an acclimatization to the factory’s temporal discipline. Today, however, this involves more than the straightforward discipline Thompson identified. It also entails producing flexible, self-directed learners who can seamlessly retrain and acquire new skills in an ever-changing and volatile labor market.
Playtime for Future Workers
Despite this recognition of the importance of shaping working-class children in particular ways, children, and their role and position within capitalism, have remained marginal concerns within Marxist theory, as well as within feminist social reproduction theory. Perhaps this is precisely because children are not regarded as workers: neither productive nor reproductive. In her new book, Child’s Play: Childhood in and Against Capitalism, Susan Ferguson turns her attention to children, challenging the idea that they do not participate in reproductive activities. Ferguson argues that children are constantly involved in processes of creating and sustaining life, but primarily through play rather than through reproductive labor in any conventional sense.
While Marxism has shown limited interest in children’s creative and life-sustaining activities, Ferguson argues that capitalism has a contradictory relationship with children, and particularly with children’s play. On one hand, the ideal of childhood as a sacred time for play, exploration, and curiosity emerged under capitalism and has since become firmly established. On the other, the regulation of children’s play, along with models from developmental psychology for determining whether play is age-appropriate, has become increasingly pronounced. Under capitalism, not only schooling but play itself becomes a preparation for the future. In this way, play acquires a kind of constructive dimension, with a clearly defined purpose, rather than being something free and open-ended, with no explicit goal beyond the sheer satisfaction that play itself provides. Learning to play properly becomes part of learning to work. In this sense, we are dealing with a form of alienated play.
Beyond learning to play properly, it is also important to learn how to stop playing: to make the transition from being a “player” to being a “worker.” Children who deviate from the expected developmental trajectory, or who fail to acquire certain abilities according to an imagined timeline, quickly become targets of intervention. It is partly against this backdrop that we can understand the dramatic increase in ADHD diagnoses and other neurodevelopmental diagnoses that we are witnessing around the world. Children who cannot seamlessly adapt to the routines of school, whose minds wander during lessons, who are too lively or struggle to sit still, children who want to play rather than work, become problems to be solved, sooner rather than later.
The Power of Play
But what problem is solved by these interventions? Rates of depression and burnout are particularly high among women aged forty to fifty who work in health and social care. Women experiencing these problems are often medicated them rather than offered changes to their working conditions — changes that would require a redistribution of economic resources.
Following a similar logic, instead of creating a school system that does not systematically produce failure, children are increasingly medicated so that they can cope with school. More than one in ten boys aged ten to seventeen in Sweden has an ADHD diagnosis. Surely this should prompt us to reconsider what counts as normal, and to place the school system that sustains this state of affairs under scrutiny, rather than focusing on how individual children can be helped to integrate into this abnormal normality?
But Ferguson’s book is not only about how play has become subject to capitalist control; it is also about how children’s play can be understood as a site of resistance to capitalist logic. Although children’s games can, of course, be cruel, exclusionary, and governed by clear norms, Ferguson nevertheless sees the possibility of something transformative in children’s play. She describes this as “the embodied capacities of imagining and acting on and in the world in ways that fulfill our needs while nurturing human connections to the self, others and our environments.” Just as play can be utopian in its creation of new worlds, political organizing can also adopt a playful — that is, open-ended — attitude toward what might become possible. This does not mean that we can play capitalism to pieces, but that we can resist capitalism’s attempts to instrumentalize our creative impulses.
Despite attempts to curb children’s play, whether through direct intervention or by restricting it to specific times, the games children play cannot be understood as exclusively capitalist or alienated activities. Rather, they can be seen as practices grounded in the sheer pleasure of playing, in the possibility of exploring, imagining and creating together without the activity necessarily having to lead to anything beyond itself. In this sense, play holds the potential to elude the capitalist logic that seeks to make every activity productive, measurable, and purposeful. Perhaps it is precisely in this openness, in the unpredictability of play and its capacity to imagine other ways of being together, that its political potential lies. Remember that you were once a child.

France’s “Hot Autumn” Is Boosting the Left
High school students in France’s working-class suburbs sparked a revolt that now includes workers, unions, and a new generation of yellow vests. Stathis Kouvelakis explains why it could reshape France’s 2027 presidential election and the European left.
- Interview by
- Jacobin
Since mid-September, a wave of protest has swept across France. High school students in working-class banlieues (suburbs) and the overseas territories started it by occupying their schools. University students, teachers, trade unionists, and a new generation of yellow vests (gilets jaunes) soon joined them. On November 5, about 1.6 million people took to the streets in two hundred cities.
Emmanuel Macron’s government has answered with the harshest crackdown in half a century. Police have arrested more than ten thousand people, most of them teenagers. A new “Rioters Pay” bill would punish protesters for acts they did not personally commit. Meanwhile, the far right is stoking a racist backlash, and, on October 23, a far-right gunman killed a young man in Trappes.
Stathis Kouvelakis has lived in France for more than four decades and has seen nearly every youth revolt there since the 1980s. In a wide-ranging interview with the editorial board of Jacobin Greece, he explains what makes this movement new, and why its young protesters are rallying around the idea of a “New France.” He also discusses the role of Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise (LFI) and why the uprising could reshape next year’s presidential election and the European left.
- Jacobin How would you assess the state of the movement after October 17 and the government’s response?
- Stathis Kouvelakis Let me clarify, first of all, that the movement did not begin on October 17 but at least a month earlier, with the mobilization of school students. In the initial phase, it gradually spread to universities, parents, and teachers, and subsequently to the militant wing of the trade unions. What we saw on October 17 was a shift in the composition and a further expansion of the mobilization, with the rapid entry of virtually the entire trade union movement, of young workers, and of the new yellow vests. October 17 marks a turning point, because on that day the mobilization took on the characteristics of a popular uprising. We saw attacks on public buildings, the looting of three thousand shops, and a section of demonstrators — a minority, but by no means negligible — determined to clash with the police. The media, as usual, gave these acts of violence from below enormous and disproportionate coverage. But we must first and foremost see them as a response to the violence from above. On the one hand, they are a reaction to police repression unprecedented in over fifty years. On the other hand, they externalize the systemic violence that a section of society endures daily — marginalized young people in multiracial working-class suburbs endure it to a particularly acute degree. To grasp the extent of the repression, let us look at some figures. In less than a month, and before October 17, the police arrested eight thousand people — more than in the first six months of the yellow vests’ protests (2018–19). Eighty-five percent of those arrested were under eighteen; 2,700 are facing prosecution, and the courts have handed down 2,300 “alternative sentences.” On October 17, police arrested 2,700 more people, prosecutors brought around a thousand before the courts, and judges have already sentenced 217 to prison. These are staggering figures. Added to this is the brutality with which the police dealt with the students’ actions from the very outset. The government’s line was that this was not a social movement with specific demands but “riots” (“violences urbaines”), mere instances of “disturbance of public order” to which the only appropriate response is repression. The result was those unbelievable scenes of police violence both outside and inside schools, and on the streets of cities across the country. The situation is similar to that of the extremely violent crackdown on the yellow vests in 2018–19, except that now the main target is young people age fourteen to eighteen. So far, police grenades have torn off the hands of at least three people, and five have lost eyes to “rubber bullets” that police fired from defensive ball launchers (LBDs). Dozens, perhaps hundreds, of others have suffered irreversible physical injuries. On October 3, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez declared on television that he had given the police “no instructions to exercise restraint.” He emphasized that the security forces “will make use of the full range of weapons at their disposal,” meaning the lethal grenades and LBDs.
- Jacobin How did Emmanuel Macron and the government react to the unrest on October 17? Are they stepping up repression, backtracking, or remaining unyielding, believing that the movement will fizzle out?
- Stathis Kouvelakis The sheer scale of the mobilization and the violent clashes that followed came as a shock to the government. It had clearly underestimated the scale of the demonstrations (550,000 according to police figures, 800,000 according to the trade unions) and had consequently deployed relatively limited police forces. According to numerous accounts, while they made extensive use of force against the demonstrators, these forces remained passive or kept their distance from the areas where looting was taking place. In any case, police brutality backfired on the government. The brutality of the crackdown helped radicalize and expand the mobilization, undermining the government’s narrative within families and more broadly across society. On the other hand, however, the continuous escalation of repression that we have been witnessing for a decade now is accustoming a section of French society to the indiscriminate use of state violence. It fuels demands for restoring “law and order” by any means. The far right exploits these demands for political gain, particularly when the situation itself appears to be spiraling out of the state’s control. This crackdown, however, failed to break the movement. The authorities banned demonstrations in forty towns and cities and imposed daily curfews in many central areas. Despite this, on October 24, the rallies and demonstrations matched the scale of the previous Saturday (420,000 according to official figures, 800,000 according to the trade unions). In many cities, and particularly in Paris, the marches were even larger than the previous week. And this was during school and university holidays, with the army guarding public buildings and special anti-terrorist units patrolling the streets. For October 31, Macron stated that the authorities would only permit demonstrations in the “outskirts” of cities, far not only from their centers but also from the urban fabric itself. This provocative stance and repressive headlong rush are signs of weakness on the part of a faltering state authority that sees the ground slipping from under its feet.
- Jacobin We see school students at the forefront of the movement. This is a new phenomenon — how do you explain it?
- Stathis Kouvelakis It is not unusual in the French context for students to spark a wider mobilization. In a sense, the degree of convergence between the youth and the workers’ movement is the key to the major uprisings that periodically shake French society and to the radicalism that characterizes them. What is new is that it is now high schools rather than universities that are at the forefront. A second innovation of this movement is that it originates in deprived areas rather than, as is usually the case, in high schools in city centers. This means that at the forefront are students from working-class backgrounds and the multiracial banlieues, where a large proportion of the population originates from postcolonial immigration. It is no coincidence that the first school occupations took place in high schools in France’s overseas territories (Mayotte, the Antilles, French Guiana), where the situation remains strongly colonial. We therefore have a dual dimension: class and race. Both directly affect a youth that experiences firsthand the consequences of the neoliberal steamroller and the structural racism that permeates state institutions, the labor market, and social relations more generally. We can say that this movement has, from the outset, been deeply anti-racist and has a clear perception of the interconnection between racism and class inequality. This is also the key to understanding the third innovation of this student movement: its level of politicization and radicalism. Let me share a personal testimony here. From the early 1980s, when I began my studies in France, I took part in or observed at close quarters almost all the youth protests. The scene I witnessed on October 6, during the first major march with widespread participation, was unprecedented. What struck me most was the ability of the school students to link their material demands for better study conditions with the broader issues of the day. Alongside material demands concerning study conditions (shortage of teaching staff, deteriorating buildings, a competitive admissions process for higher education), this youth puts forward opposition to racism, war, genocide, police violence, and the logic of profit. Everywhere there were Palestinian flags and scarves, slogans against the far right and police violence, and a rejection of the militarism encroaching on schools — all this in a combative atmosphere. I heard thousands of schoolboys and schoolgirls, who were clearly not members of any left-wing organization, chanting rhythmically “jeunesse déterminée et révolutionnaire” [“We’re a determined and revolutionary youth”]. Such a thing was unthinkable not only for my own generation, which grew up in the bleak 1980s (especially bleak in France) but also for those that followed. The explanation lies in the overall nature of youth politicization internationally and in the particular significance that communities originating from postcolonial immigration hold for these generations. This is why Palestine occupies such a central position. It is not simply a matter of solidarity with a distant cause, however important that may be. In the oppression the Palestinians suffer, this youth recognizes the racism that it confronts itself. And the unyielding resistance of the Palestinian people is a source of inspiration for their own resistance and way of life.
- Jacobin What other forces have joined the school student movement?
- Stathis Kouvelakis The qualitative leap took place on October 17. Two factors played a decisive role here. The first was the call from the new yellow vests, which began circulating on social media in early September, even before the school occupations broke out. Unlike last year’s failed “Bloquons tout!” (“Let’s block everything!”) call, this one had strong organization and above all deep social roots. We know from related reports that the initiative came from young people, mainly non-white men from the working-class suburbs of major cities — a group very different from the “historic” yellow vests. Nor, for that matter, was the choice of date a coincidence. It falls, of course, on a Saturday, just like the days of action during the 2018–19 yellow vests movement. But it also coincides with the anniversary of October 17, 1961, when, during the Algerian War, the police fired into a protest march by Algerians in central Paris, killing dozens and throwing the bodies into the Seine. The parallel with the 2018–19 movement lies in the grassroots way the action spread and in its repertoire: rallies and marches scattered across the city that organizers did not declare to the authorities. It also lies in the demands, which focus on the cost of living. Gas prices are extremely high, which places an overwhelming burden on the working classes, who generally live some distance from their workplace. The cost of living is, of course, a broader issue, as real wages have stagnated, and the quality and accessibility of public services have plummeted. In the run-up to October 17, the student movement and the brutal police repression it faced had created a confrontational atmosphere. In that climate, the call met with a remarkable response from young workers, particularly those in precarious employment and in multiethnic suburbs, but also among sections of the working class outside the scope of trade unions. Despite initial reservations, it ultimately mobilized a minority but significant section of the “original” yellow vests. We can say that the experience of that movement is now part of the shared code of social movements in France. We even saw schoolboys and schoolgirls wearing these yellow vests at the roadblocks students set up during school occupations and, to a lesser extent, at the marches. The second factor is the involvement of the trade union movement. The most militant sections had already joined the fray earlier in October, protecting and supporting the school occupations and marches. These were mainly local branches of the General Confederation of Labor (CGT) and Solidaires, and in some places Force Ouvrière. In Toulouse and elsewhere, we also saw school and university students heading to workplaces and calling on workers to take to the streets. On October 17, trade union participation became widespread, drawing in even the extremely moderate French Democratic Confederation of Labor (CFDT). We could say that there is now a powerful popular bloc on the streets opposing “Macron and his world” — that is, the neoliberal steamroller and the growing state authoritarianism. This is the moment when all the separate movements of the last decade finally crystallized and converged. Its driving force is the youth as the bearer of a qualitatively new political consciousness.
- Jacobin La France Insoumise (LFI) is supporting the protests and is once again in the firing line of the government, the far right, and the media who say it is instigating them. How do you assess the role of LFI at this stage?
- Stathis Kouvelakis Indeed, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu stated on October 1 that behind the student occupations lie “LFI and its proxies from the ultraleft (ultragauche).” Lecornu chose these words on purpose: “proxies” is the term the media and mainstream discourse use for Hamas and Hezbollah, which they regard as proxies of Iran. And the term ultragauche refers not so much to organizations of the extra-parliamentary left as to the constellation of anarchists and autonomist groups — that is, groups or individuals operating outside the institutional, and sometimes even outside the legal, framework. This vocabulary reveals the mindset of those in power, who view a mobilized society in warlike terms. For years, the ruling extreme center and the far right have targeted LFI, often with the complicity of sectors of the “soft left.” The reason is that LFI is the only significant political force that breaks the consensus on critical issues such as support for the genocidal Zionist state, police violence, Islamophobia and structural racism, and alignment with US and Western imperialism. It is essentially the only genuine opposition to the current order. For LFI, supporting the mobilization is a matter of course. It means something very concrete and practical: mass participation in the marches and protection of the occupied schools and marches by LFI’s grassroots as well as by its deputies and mayors. The iconic figure is Bally Bagayoko, the charismatic newly elected mayor of Saint-Denis. He stands in solidarity with the occupied high schools in his city, and police have repeatedly beaten him when he tried to shield the students from their attacks. Within the movement, at the marches and at the roadblocks set up by the students occupying schools, LFI is like a fish in water. The mainstream media are speechless every time they see young people and, more broadly, the crowds in the streets enthusiastically cheering the seventy-five-year-old Jean-Luc Mélenchon. It is not simply because of his position on this particular issue. LFI is the only organization that has articulated the issues we now see stirring up those who take to the streets. To put it another way, what we are seeing is a dialectical relationship between the movements and LFI. To borrow a fine phrase from Houria Bouteldja, we should see LFI as our “war booty,” the fruit of our struggles of recent decades. As for the other sectors of the Left, they are of little concern to society. The only exception, in a sense, is the candidate of the Socialist Party and its allies, Raphaël Glucksmann, who represents the most right-wing, warmongering, and pro-US element within this part of the political spectrum. At every public appearance, people boo him, particularly young people, and he conspicuously stays away from any demonstrations. In his latest statements, he has endorsed the government’s so-called concessions. In essence, he is nothing more than a variant of Macron. I should also point out that Macron does not even have a working majority in the National Assembly. The successive governments he appoints survive solely thanks to the Socialists, who refuse to support the motions of no confidence that LFI, the Greens, and the Communists have introduced.
- Jacobin What is this “New France” that LFI speaks of? Has a new, multiracial subject of struggle and demands come to the fore?
- Stathis Kouvelakis “New France” is both a statement and an interpellation, or a call to action if you prefer. At first sight, it refers to the profound changes that French society has undergone in recent decades. The first is the end of the traditional countryside, and with it of the peasantry as a significant social group. The second is the internal migration that followed and continues to this day, albeit in a different form. Today one in two inhabitants of the country lives in a different area from that of their birthplace. But of course, “New France” refers above all to people with migrant origins, the overwhelming majority of whom are now French nationals. If we go back three generations, one third of the population has at least one non-French ancestor. France is a country with a tradition of immigration dating back to the very beginnings of the Industrial Revolution and even more so since the late nineteenth century. From the 1960s onward, however, the origin of this immigration shifted from Southern and Eastern Europe to the Global South, and in particular to the former French colonies of North and sub-Saharan Africa. Today, 20 percent of those under the age of eighteen are descendants of immigrants, and 84 percent of them are of non-European origin. However, as we know, this section of the population, despite being French citizens, faces persistent racist discrimination, which has intensified in recent years and taken the form of escalating Islamophobia. Many laws create an atmosphere of permanent suspicion against Muslims and deprive them of any form of independent organization. Furthermore, until recently, the French left — with the partial exception of the trade unions — had stubbornly refused to recognize this group as an integral part of its social base. It did so even though it constitutes the “hard core” of the working class. LFI recognizes racism not as an individual moral failing but as a mechanism of domination and exploitation that permeates all social relations. It speaks openly about the racist nature of police violence, of the labor market, and of an entire body of legislation that targets Muslims. In doing so, it turns a new page in the history of the French — and perhaps the European — left and its relationship with the working classes. One immediate result is the overwhelming share of the vote it is securing in the multiethnic working-class districts of the major cities, in the region of 60 to 70 percent. According to estimates, 70 percent of Muslims voted for Mélenchon in the first round of the 2022 presidential elections, and this figure is likely to be even higher in the next elections. Since the beginning of last year, New France has taken center stage in the discourse of Mélenchon and LFI. They now couple this observation with a call: those whom racism targets are not (merely) victims. They are, first and foremost, political subjects whom LFI calls on to take part in — and indeed to be at the forefront of — the struggle for social upheaval. At the impressive rally on June 7 in Saint-Denis (26,000 people), which launched LFI’s election campaign, the colorful — and largely youthful — crowd spontaneously chanted “New France,” waving French flags. The rally ended, as usual, first with the Marseillaise and then, at the crowd’s initiative, with the Internationale. However, New France’s “baptism by fire” in mass action was undoubtedly this current movement. On the streets, and particularly in the student blocs and in front of the occupied high schools, the French flag was emphatically present, often alongside the Palestinian flag or those of other countries where Gen Z is rising up. Strong references to the French Revolution and its symbols accompany the tricolor. In the face of the far right’s racism and chauvinism, young people are putting forward a different France — one that reflects its people and their revolutionary traditions. It reflects the people as they are and as they constantly remake themselves through their struggles. The current situation marks the convergence of the political force of New France with a mass movement that is rallying an emerging popular bloc with majority support and a radical left-wing orientation. This is a historic moment, the moment when a new conception of the nation is emerging through the very action of the subordinate classes. In my view, far from contradicting a class-based hegemonic politics, New France paves the way for its reconstruction. The reason is simple: it is the only proposal capable of shattering racial divisions within the French working and popular classes. Only it can open up the possibility of uniting them into a new “historical bloc” — a force capable of leading society and giving it a radically new direction. It is also clear that this is the antithesis of nationalism and nostalgia for colonialism. As for LFI, its core position is that New France means a “de-Westernized” (“désoccidentalisée”) France. That France would have an independent foreign policy, breaking with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the imperialist framework and forging an alliance with the progressive forces of the Global South. It also means coming to terms with France’s colonial past and immediately recognizing the right to full self-determination of the people of Kanaky/New Caledonia. The New France project embodies the “internationalist patriotism” of Houria Bouteldja, a prominent figure in the de-colonial, anti-racist, and anti-imperialist movement in France.
- Jacobin How is the uprising affecting the wider political landscape?
- Stathis Kouvelakis It is still too early to have a clear picture, but a reasonable assessment is that such a development will intensify the existing social and political polarization. LFI is emerging as the natural political representative of the popular movement bloc, but on the other hand we are also seeing the formation of a “law and order” bloc, with Marine Le Pen’s National Rally as its main component. Two Frances are heading toward a frontal clash. The far right and its supporters, whose influence objectively extends into sections of the extreme center, are railing against the “unrest.” They blame it on “Arabs,” “blacks,” and “Islamo-leftists” — that is, the supposed unholy alliance between Islamists and LFI. The incidents that took place on October 17, and in particular the looting, provided ammunition for far-right rhetoric to denounce the actions of the “barbarians” — that is, the non-white youth of the working-class suburbs. The tragic culmination of this line of reasoning was the deadly attack on October 23 in Trappes, a working-class suburb on the outskirts of Paris. A thirty-nine-year-old fascist, driving around in his car, began shooting at non-white passersby who had the misfortune to be in his path. He killed a young man and seriously injured seven others, including an eleven-year-old girl. The perpetrator, who kept a copy of Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf at his home, stated that he had targeted “black people, Arabs, and Muslims” to “take revenge for the shopkeepers who lost their livelihoods on October 17.” An initial response to the far-right escalation came in recent days, when mayors and local organizations initiated a series of rallies and marches in working-class suburbs. But the most effective response is a mass presence on the streets in the coming days and, on a political level, the hegemonic momentum that the call for a New France has generated.
- Jacobin What do you think is now at stake for LFI?
- Stathis Kouvelakis LFI has so far succeeded in forging an organic relationship with the movement in terms of its agenda, its central narrative, and the participation of its grassroots. The challenge now is to offer a perspective that goes beyond the immediate task of the day, namely the mass mobilization for Mélenchon’s victory in next year’s presidential election. Here, however, lurks a difficulty. LFI is not a traditional party but a “movement.” In practice, this means there are no formal members; an online registration is sufficient to join a local “action group,” which enjoys a great deal of autonomy in practical matters. The organizational structure remains very loose, although for the past three years LFI has put coordinating structures in place at a regional level. This porous structure facilitates communication with the movements and respects their autonomy. However, it does not allow for coordinated intervention within them. Everything relies on the initiative of the grassroots, which naturally varies from place to place. It is, of course, entirely reasonable and correct to avoid the well-known pretension of “leading” movements by self-appointed “vanguards” and bureaucratic apparatuses. On the other hand, however, this does not help overcome the barrier that social movements have come up against throughout the recent historical period, and not only in France. That barrier is the challenge of forming a structure that gives them durability, cohesion, and the capacity for strategic autonomy. The question that arises is: How can we combine the autonomy of movements with the necessary, distinct intervention of political actors? The problem is by no means new. Nevertheless, it remains one of the most critical issues that not only LFI but also the radical left internationally must resolve — bearing in mind that every approach so far has failed.
- Jacobin What are the prospects for the uprising from here, and what are the next key dates?
- Stathis Kouvelakis November 5 was a milestone for the movement. About 1.6 million people took to the streets in two hundred cities across the country. The strike had a significant impact in some sectors, such as education, the civil service, the railways, and oil refineries. However, it did not grow into an all-out strike. The demonstrations were particularly impressive and joyful, bringing together young people and workers from various sectors. There is now a sense that a more cohesive popular bloc is emerging, carrying a novel and creative protest culture with its own music, scenography, and slogans. The government has responded with a simulacrum of negotiations on the one hand and a new escalation of repression on the other. It has offered some insignificant concessions, such as a €25 rise in the minimum wage and a minor modification of the admissions procedure for higher education. The only success the government can claim on that front is that it has split the union movement. The more moderate confederations, such as the CFDT and Force Ouvrière, have refused to call for further action. But the CGT, the teachers’ union Unitary Union Federation (FSU), and other important unions such as Solidaires and the National Union of Autonomous Trade Unions (UNSA) have called for a new day of street protests and strikes on November 17. The real purpose of those concessions is to cover up the hardening of police repression and of the legislation on street demonstrations. Since the schools reopened, police have intervened to prevent any form of occupation. The authorities are also asking principals to provide lists of students involved in the movement. University authorities have kept campuses affected by protests closed, some since late September, drastically reducing the possibilities for organizing mass action there. The government has also introduced a “Rioters Pay” bill in parliament. It would hold individuals liable for acts they did not personally commit, provided they “knowingly” took part in a gathering where acts of violence or property damage took place. The penalties are heavy: up to three years in prison and a €45,000 fine. Furthermore, the bill would allow the state to seize benefits that families of children involved in these actions receive and to expel foreign nationals whom courts find guilty of those offenses. The Senate has already approved the bill, and the National Assembly will now debate it. If parliament adopts it, the bill would “enshrine in law France’s shift toward authoritarianism,” as a petition launched by several well-known public figures puts it.
- Jacobin At a more strategic level, what is the movement’s political perspective?
- Stathis Kouvelakis What is really exceptional about this movement is that it is happening only months before next year’s presidential election, certainly the most decisive in half a century. The radical left, and LFI in particular, should see this as a gift from heaven. As historical experience suggests, only major social mobilizations can overturn the balance of political forces, both in society and at the ballot box. We should see the impressive momentum of Mélenchon’s campaign as the result of the movements of recent years, and the current movement will no doubt expand it even further. There is now a sense that a Mélenchon victory next year is a real possibility, albeit far from a certainty. In the streets and in everyday conversations among ordinary people, within families and groups of friends, one can feel this novel optimism. If Mélenchon wins, it will be a political earthquake of continental, even global, magnitude. But he will immediately have to confront an extremely hostile environment, both at home and internationally. The dominant classes have extremely powerful weapons at their disposal to strangle a government of the radical left. We have seen this happen many times in the past, in Europe and Latin America, and more recently in Greece in 2015. To survive this ordeal, the Left needs a confrontational line that mobilizes its own social base. The current situation in France provides these elements: broad sectors of society with an experience of mass action and a political force with a radical program and a real chance of electoral success. LFI calls this strategy a “citizens’ revolution.” I would prefer the term “democratic road to socialism,” which the late Nicos Poulantzas theorized. But the substance, I think, is quite similar: the articulation of a struggle within the state with mass movements that develop autonomously and push a left-wing government in a more radical direction. Once again, France appears as the laboratory for the European left. It is the only country where a force of the radical left can defeat the far right. It is also the only country, for the moment, that can initiate a process of social change capable of shifting the international balance of forces and opening up new possibilities for the Left worldwide.
