https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: Coffee lovers and matcha girlies, rejoice! There’s an abundance of Advent calendars just for you
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Marian Bull
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
The holiday season can be exhausting: shopping, hosting, plotting out an elaborate popcorn garland for your annual holiday party, etc. This means that caffeine is really ready for its moment to shine. Enter the caffeinated Advent calendar. This year, there’s a bevy of Advent calendar options for coffee and tea aficionados alike, from the K-cup devotees to the single-origin matcha obsessives. I’ve tried a bunch of them – and have the energy levels to prove it. Here are the best of the year.
Great espresso, without the machine:
Cometeer Advent Calendar
The Cometeer people have pulled off a magic trick: making delicious espresso accessible to the bleary-eyed, just-woken-up person without any fancy equipment. Their (recyclable!) pods arrive frozen, and all you need to do is add hot water, or stir them into a glass of cold milk; they dissolve surprisingly quickly, and taste like a $7 latte from your local shop. Their sleek Advent calendar offers 24 pods, each of them different and many of them limited edition – like First Person Coffee’s ‘Tis the Season Blend on day one – all from roasters across the country. And if you sign up for a refill subscription, you will get $30 off. If you want to encourage your younger brother to upgrade his instant espresso addiction, this is an easy upgrade.
A tea for every mood, part one:
Stash Tea Advent Calendar
If you’re looking to give someone 24 cups of very cozy tea this winter, Stash has you covered. Their sturdy, open-book-shaped Advent calendar reveals a mix of flavored black, green and herbal teas. Wake up with a cup of Christmas Shortbread black tea, sip some (green) Tropical Snowflake during your afternoon slump and turn down with some Blueberry Joy before bed, depending on the day. I loved that these felt boldly flavored without too much artificial edge.
A tea for every mood, part two (and three):
Tea Forté Warming Joy Advent Calendar
Listen, I know that the paper teabags are slightly better for the environment, but I just love the way that the sturdy Tea Forté teabags have a little, bendable leaf at their triangle tip, which can easily latch over your mug’s edge – reminiscent of a Christmas tree, which is festive and appropriate. There are two types of calendars to choose from: because not every tea freak likes (or wants) caffeine, Tea Forté also offers an herbal-only calendar, which is all caffeine-free in addition to their “regular” assorted option. (I’ve gifted the herbal set to a fellow tea-head in the past, to great success.) I particularly loved the Spiced Herbal Mate and Ginger Lemongrass.
A merry Podmas:
Keurig 24 Cups of Cheer Advent Calendar
Perhaps you have a parent, a co-worker or a cousin who is in a co-dependent relationship with their Keurig machine? (Trick question: we all have one.) Here is a no-fail gift for that person (or those millions of people). This box holds 24 pods of various flavors and roasts, all of them meant to evoke a bit of holiday cheer, from Cinnamon Sugar Cookie to a Donut Shop classic roast.
Matcha madness:
The Roasters’ Pack Matcha Advent Calendar
I am a matcha girlie. There is simply nothing like grabbing an iced matcha latte with a friend while walking around your neighborhood, sipping on the verdant, milky, potentially sweetened caffeinated beverage. So really, this is the Advent calendar you should get for me, or for the matcha girlie (gender-neutral) in your life. The Roasters’ Pack, which also sells two coffee calendars, has put together a sampler of matchas from brands across Japan, some of which are exclusive to the Advent calendar. I loved sipping through these various matchas, which range from smooth and savory to vegetal and bright. (The Ikkyu, on day four, was a standout for me for its crisp, pronounced grassiness – that hint of springtime really picked me up post-daylight savings.)
Pourover party:
Pirates of Coffee Advent Calendar
Finally, we have an Advent calendar for the true coffee nerd in your life. Pirates of Coffee, based in Ontario, has collected (and roasted) single-origin beans from around the world, from Ethiopia to Laos. I was struck by the variety of their selection and, of course, the quality of their beans, which work equally well in a pour-over or a shot of espresso. Plus, I love that they really leaned into the brand name: the box opens up like a treasure chest – or maybe a treasure bureau, really – that makes for a gorgeous gift. Each bag holds 20g of coffee, enough for a perfect pour-over coffee or a shot of espresso. Dealer’s choice.

https://gothamist.com/news/a-dj-survived.title: A DJ survived the Brooklyn building collapse: His prized record collection did not
https://gothamist.com/news/a-dj-survived.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/a-dj-survived.text:
In the days after last week's deadly building collapse in Brooklyn, TV cameras and photographers captured hundreds of vinyl records scattered in the rubble.
Most, if not all of them, belonged to one man: Omari Jack, an immigrant from Saint Vincent and the Grenadines who has spent 30 years collecting reggae records and performing vinyl DJ sets under the name Roots Outernational at venues like E-K’s Hideaway in East Flatbush.
Jack said he had lived on the top floor of 1321 Flatbush Avenue for around five years. Jack wasn't home when his building crumbled into a neighboring, vacant lot last Wednesday afternoon, killing eight people, including two children, and injuring 18 others. But he lost a lot of his life's work.
His apartment was home to thousands of records, a collection he estimates to have been worth upwards of $100,000.
“I lost tons of records,” he said. “ I literally had one of the rooms as a music room,” Jack said – a space he called his “headquarters.”
“ I had vinyl in my bedroom closet. I had vinyl scattered in the kitchen area,” he said.
In the days since he lost his home, Jack has seen videos of rescue workers carrying some of his record boxes out of the rubble. But he doesn’t know where any of his belongings were sent — or if they were saved at all.
“ Nobody has contacted me from the city for, like, ‘We found some stuff that is still usable.’ I didn't hear anything like that,” Jack said. “And I don't know who to reach out to either.”
Neither City Hall nor FDNY immediately responded to requests for comment on Sunday afternoon.
'I was hoping it ain’t my building'
When Jack left his apartment Wednesday morning, he said his mind was on an upcoming set he was scheduled to do on Friday night for Global Medz Radio.
“ I left everything in my bedroom organized for the radio show,” Jack said. “I have my boxes ready. I have everything all done. I took out the clothes that I was going to wear at the show.”
Jack was at work when it happened. He said he got a call and rushed home.
“I was hoping it ain't my building,” he said. “ It's rough, man. You know, you, you go to work, you come home and you lose everything.”
He didn’t know any of his neighbors very well. He said that construction in the neighboring lot, where developers were planning to build a nine-story complex, meant his apartment rumbled all the time. “Almost every day, man,” he said.
He’d had his laptop with him that day, along with a hard drive with six terabytes of music on it. Some of his records were being stored with a friend on Long Island.
But everything else — his rare recordings of concerts dating back to the 70s, his books on musicians like Bob Marley and Dennis Brown, his CDs and cassette tapes, his favorite poster of the reggae artist Garnet Silk — was lost when the building went down.
Jack said his sets, which take him from New York to Canada, Barbados and back home in St. Vincent, include records from reggae legends like Johnny Clarke, Garnet Silk, Jacob Miller, Prince Lincoln Thompson and Barry Brown.
One bright spot, he said, was he'd spent much of the week before the collapse backing up the digital version of his collection.
“ Every single day I was just backing up stuff. I don't know if it's intuition was telling me to do this. But I was doing it every day for the past week,” Jack said.
Jack is still living in the hotel that the city placed him in after his home was reduced to rubble. He said he's not sure when he’ll DJ again, and he’s not sure he’ll ever come close to rebuilding what he had.
“ I'm not going to focus on that right now because there's other things to do. It's not possible for me to go back to how I was in terms of all the music I lost,” Jack said. “When the time is right I might collect a little stuff, but that's not my priority.”
For now, Jack is focused on getting his life back together.
A fundraiser show for Jack will be held at E-K’s Hideaway on November 28. And a GoFundMe to help Jack recover from the collapse has been launched by his friend Kelly Uman, a fellow collector and DJ who lives in Montreal.
Uman said Jack, like a lot of collectors, didn't have insurance.
“ It's this really hard thing to document and pinpoint. It's not quite as easy to appraise as, like, jewelry,” Uman said. “It definitely is nuanced, and I've yet to hear of anybody who lost their collection get fully reimbursed.”
She added: "He has to start from zero."
Liam Quigley contributed reporting.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-man.title: NYPD says man murdered his elderly aunt at their Bronx home
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-man.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-says-man.text:
A 35-year-old man was arrested and charged with murder Sunday after police say his aunt was found beaten to death in the Bronx home the two shared.
Police said officers responded to a call about an assault in progress at 754 Manida Street just after midnight Saturday morning.
When police arrived they found 75-year-old Carmen Nunez unconscious and unresponsive, according to the NYPD. EMS rushed her to Lincoln Hospital, where she was pronounced dead, officials said.
Officers took Joshua Nunez into custody at the scene on Saturday, and charged him with murder, manslaughter, and assault on Sunday morning.
Records show they both lived at the Bronx address where the assault was reported, but police did not provide information about what prompted the attack, or if anyone else was present.
Nunez's attorney information was not immediately available.
There have been three murders in the precinct, which includes Hunts Point and Longwood, so far this year; the same rate as 2025, according to NYPD data. Felony assaults in the precinct have declined by roughly 10% so far this year over last.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Lotus L. Kang wins Canada’s top art prize, the Sobey Art Award
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Hadani Ditmars
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation named the artist Lotus L. Kang asthe winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award during a ceremony on Saturday (14 November). The Toronto-born, New York-based photographer, sculptor and installation artist won the 23rd edition of the annual award, the most high-profile and lucrative prize devoted to Canadian contemporary artists, and will receive C$100,000 ($70,000).
The other five shortlisted artists—Melaw Nakehk'o (from the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Québec) and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic)—will each receive C$25,000 ($17,500), while the 24 longlisted artists each received C$10,000 ($7,000), bringing the total value of the award to C$465,000 ($325,800).
In a statement, Jonathan Shaughnessy, the chair of the jury for this year’s Sobey Art Award, praised Kang for “the commitment and rigour demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade”. He continued: “Through installations using unfixed photographic film, cast and found objects, and fabricated armatures, her practice resists the stabilising impulses traditionally associated with photography. Reoccurring motifs including lotus root, flowers, soju bottles, birds, anchovies, are not fixed objects, but repositories of place, longing and desire.”
Kang, a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2024 whose work was included in the 2024 Whitney Biennial and the 2025 Shanghai Biennale, works across sculpture, photography and site-responsive installation. Her materially dense, non-linear installations explore the liminal space between industrial and architectural forms, familial and social histories, as well as poetry and non-human figures. One of her celebrated installation works, Mother (2020), comprised dozens of metal mixing bowls filled with scattered abstract clay, rubber and stone sculptures as well as aluminium casts of fruit and anchovies. Her critically acclaimed solo exhibition at 52 Walker in New York last year featured several greenhouse installations as well as one made of strips of film extended around a spinning rotary dryer.
“It is an honour to be recognised by this prize,” Kang said in a statement. “I am grateful to those I love, those who love me and those who have supported me; you keep me going. The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing. Art is essential to life, progress and love.”
During the ceremony, Kang told those assembled at the NGC and those watching via livestream: “I just want to congratulate the other artists. It’s an honour to be nominated alongside you. Shane, Melaw, Caroline, Audie, Samuel. It is really inspiring to be showing alongside you, and who knows what would have happened, and I’m just glad we’ll all keep making art, because it’s really the best thing. So, thank you so much.’’
Rob Sobey, the chair of the Sobey Art Foundation, offered his “heartfelt congratulations” to Kang and added: “We also celebrate tonight all 29 artists on this year’s longlist and shortlist for their creativity and vision. We are proud to champion their work and grateful to the National Gallery of Canada for helping bring these remarkable artistic voices to audiences at home and around the world.”
Selected by an independent jury of curators and cultural leaders, Kang was chosen following a rigorous review process. The jury, who evaluated the artists’ practices, achievements, and contributions to contemporary art in Canada included Kimberly Phillips, the director of the Marianne and Edward Gibson Art Museum at Simon Fraser University, representing the Pacific region;Daisy Desrosiers, a curator at large for North America at Tate, representing the Quebec region;and Helen Nisbet, the director of Glasgow International, serving as international juror.
Works by all six shortlisted artists are currently featured in the 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition at the NGC in Ottawa (until 3 January 2027).
The late Frank H. Sobey, an enthusiastic collector of Canadian art, established the Sobey Art Foundation in 1981 and the Sobey Art Award was launched in 2002. Five years ago, the award’s criteria were amended from a prize devoted to “emerging artists” under 40 to recognising artists of any age who are at a “critical juncture” in their careers. Past winners have included Brian Jungen (in 2002), Annie Pootoogook (2006), Abbas Akhavan (2015), Laakkuluk Williamson Bathory (2021) and Nico Williams (2024).

https://gothamist.com/news/how-one-brook.title: How one Brooklyn cat avoided the building collapse and was rejoined with his human
https://gothamist.com/news/how-one-brook.author: Catalina Gonella
https://gothamist.com/news/how-one-brook.text:
When 13-year-old Zariah Coleman came back to the apartment she shared with her mom, one entire wall had been shorn off, leaving the wreckage of a deadly building collapse exposed outside.
But what scared her the most, was that she couldn’t find her cat Isaac.
“The first thing I thought about was my cat,” she said during a press conference last week that quickly went viral. “They said they went inside the house to try to find him but I don’t think they really did… he’s hiding from them and I think he’s scared.”
Among the many who watched videos of her tearful plea was Will Zweigart, executive director of local cat rescue non-profit Flatbush CatsHe said he had to do something.
Zweigart went to the site the next day, but rescuing Isaac would be more complicated than just showing up and looking around.
The disaster killed 8 people and injured close to 20 others in one of the worst residential building collapses in New York City over the last 90 years. City agencies and law enforcement had the entire area cordoned off for safety as well as the ongoing investigations into the cause of the collapse.
For two days, Zweigart worked with cat lovers within the city government, including Allie Taylor, the director of the Mayor's Office of Animal Welfare, to get the safety clearance needed to enter the site.
“ We had to go through more city agencies than I can count,” Zweigart said.
Finally, on Sunday, the Department of Buildings granted him approval, and First Deputy Commissioner Yegal Shamash, the department's senior-most engineer, escorted Zweigart into Coleman’s apartment. Hers is one of the apartments with its interior now exposed, missing an entire side wall where its neighboring building once stood.
Armed with a glasses, hard hat, trap, carrier, bait, lights and, towels (for claws), Zweigart made his way inside. One video shows the precarious steps, covered in debris, that he had to make his way up to Coleman’s home.
“ I circled the entire space three times and I saw no cat,” he said. “All the regular places you might look on a hide and seek… Under the sink, under the couch,, in the bathroom, in the closets, underneath clothes, no cat.”
But he decided to check one more time, dreading having to tell Coleman, who was waiting outside, that he hadn’t found Isaac. It was in that last sweep of the kitchen, when he looked in the cabinet under the sink, that he heard “a little meow.”
“ Hearing that meow was a relief, but also even more special because I knew that he knew that we were here, and he knew that we were gonna help even though it was scary,” he said. “That's my favorite sound that I've heard in a while.”
Isaac was scared, and it took some work to get him into the carrier — clearing everything from the cabinet and nudging him into it, Zweigart said. But he was finally safe, and on his way to reunite with Coleman.
In a heartwarming video of their reunion, a smiling Coleman greets Isaac still inside the carrier, reaching her fingers through the holes in it. Isaac meanwhile, meows repeatedly.
“Isaac! Isaac! Isaac! Hi!,” she says. “Aw, he looks so stressed out… Isaac, it's ok!”
It was an outcome people all over the city, and even across the world were waiting for after seeing Coleman speak at the press conference Friday.
“ I think the internet was looking for a little bright spot, because I've had people from Australia — you can't get any further away — I've had people from the farthest reaches of the world asking about this cat, 'What's the latest?' [and] celebrating in the last couple hours,” Zweigart said in an interview Sunday.
Taylor, with the Mayor’s Animal Welfare Office, waited with Coleman while Zweigart searched and said the rescue took about half an hour but “felt like forever.” Isaac was taken to Flatbush Cats’ clinic for evaluation through Sunday night, Zweigart said.
“Seeing how incredibly relieved Zariah and her mom are was really moving,” Taylor said, adding that Isaac is an approved emotional support animal. “It's incredibly important that they have their pet during one of the most traumatic experiences of their lives.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.author: Robert Faturechi, Nick McMillan
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.text:
When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.
The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.
Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:
Its own leaders.
The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.
Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses.
The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.
Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.
But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.
“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.”
The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.
Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries.
Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.
That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.
The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year.
The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president, asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.”
Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event.
Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.
“The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference. “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.”
In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs.
Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx, have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. The companies are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them.
A series of lawsuits are attempting to force companies that sell directly to consumers to share some of their refunds. Dozens of firms have been sued, including big-box stores Walmart and Target and apparel companies such as Nike and Lululemon. Apparel and leather costs were some of the hardest hit by Trump’s tariffs. Legal analysts have cast doubt on whether these lawsuits will succeed, though some trade experts have speculated that businesses that used the tariffs as cover to raise prices more than they needed to might settle to avoid embarrassing disclosures.
One of the companies facing a lawsuit is Stanley Black & Decker, the toolmaker that ProPublica found was using some of its refund on bonuses. The named plaintiff is a Wisconsin resident who bought a handheld blower, an impact wrench, a hedge trimmer and other tools from the company last year, but the lawsuit seeks to represent thousands of other customers as well.
“Unless restrained by this Court,” the complaint reads, the company “stands to recover the same tariff payments twice — once from consumers through tariff-inflated prices and again from the federal government through tariff refunds.”
On multiple occasions, the company has acknowledged publicly that it was raising prices because of the tariffs.
The month before the November 2024 election, as Trump was campaigning on dramatic new tariffs, the toolmaker’s then-CEO, Donald Allan Jr., told shareholders that Stanley Black & Decker was preparing for the possibility. “Obviously, coming out of the gate, there would be price increases associated with tariffs that we put into the market,” he said during an earnings call. Then, a few months after Trump unveiled his tariffs, Allan said his team was “remaining focused on executing our robust plan designed to mitigate tariffs” that he said included “targeted pricing actions to improve our gross margin.” Later that year, his successor as chief executive, Chris Nelson, described more price hikes: “We are implementing a second price increase during the fourth quarter to maintain our innovation and brand investments, given the pressures resulting from tariff-related cost increases.”
In its more recent disclosures, the company has been vague about how much of its refund was going to executives, simply saying that some of that gain “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation.” “Incentive compensation” is a term the toolmaker uses to describe bonuses.
The company has not responded to the allegations in the lawsuit brought by the Wisconsin resident and did not answer ProPublica’s questions about who is getting paid the bonuses, how much they’re worth and whether customers should be reimbursed.
Securities experts who reviewed the disclosures for ProPublica said it appeared the windfall boosted the company’s profits, which factor into formulas that help determine bonus pay for executives and other employees.
“It wasn’t the executive that triggered that extra profit, so why should their compensation go up?” Germain, the corporate law professor said. “This is one of many examples where these formulas don’t do what they should do.”
The company’s leaders, securities experts said, could have given money back to consumers or lowered prices. Retail giant Burlington Stores, formerly known as Burlington Coat Factory, appears to have done just that.
CEO Michael O’Sullivan recently said the company got $55 million in tariff refunds and “rather than taking a one-time boost to earnings” the company plans “to deliver even sharper values to our shoppers,”
“Over the last few years, the rising cost of living has made life difficult for many customers,” O’Sullivan said, adding that the coming discounts meant investors should expect the “direct impact of tariff refunds to be neutral.”
A company spokesperson confirmed to ProPublica that none of its tariff refund will be going to bonuses.
Not so for other companies.
Acushnet, the Massachusetts golf equipment company that includes the brand Titleist, disclosed an “incentive compensation expense of approximately $12.0 million” out of its refund. Acushnet declined to respond to questions from ProPublica.
TJX, the Massachusetts parent company of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, said it got back $331 million, but as a result, it “accrued incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible Associates globally.”
The company declined to answer questions from ProPublica about how far down the chain of command the bonuses would go and how much of them would be reserved for top managers. “Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” a spokesperson said. The company also declined to say whether it would lower prices or pay back customers with the rest of its refund, saying only that “the remaining amount will be used to support our future growth.”
ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such information.
Nick Guest, an accounting professor at Cornell University who has studied executive compensation, said the argument for granting leaders bonuses based on the tariff refunds could go both ways.
“If they were penalized for something out of their control,” he said, referring to earnings hits caused by Trump’s tariffs last year, rewarding them now “seems reasonable.”
“But you could say the same thing about customers. If they were penalized, then is it reasonable that they’re not getting rewarded now?” Guest asked. The companies, he said, are “not obligated to give refunds or reduce prices, but doing so could certainly build goodwill with customers.”

The Hochul administration robbed the MTA of $200 million in bus operating funds in a secret maneuver to shore up the first budget put forward earlier this year by the Mamdani administration, a bombshell report from an Albany watchdog group shows.
As part of a budget deal that closed a $4-billion city budget gap, Gov. Hochul allowed Mayor Mamdani to reduce the city’s annual payment to the MTA’s bus division by $200 million — money that Hochul initially said she would cover from the state’s massive budget, but ended up being covered by the transit agency itself, according to the report from Reinvent Albany.
“The MTA is not the piggybank of the state and the city whenever they need to find money to pay for some other priority,” said Rachael Fauss, Reinvent Albany’s senior policy analyst, who wrote the report. “[These] funds are supposed to be dedicated and safe for the MTA. The MTA Bus aid in this case is supposed to be protected under a 2004 agreement between New York City and the MTA. Transit riders are the ones who get hurt, who are too often asked to pick up the bill to balance the budget.”
The raid became clear over many months and in ways that could easily elude sharp-eyed observers — even those who, as Robert Caro once said, turn every page.
For instance, on May 12, Hochul and Mamdani announced an agreement on “$4 billion in gap-closing support” from the state to the city. At the time, neither lawmaker specifically cited that $200 million of the city’s regular payment to the MTA would be forgiven or deferred as part of the package.
“Indeed,” as Reinvent Albany’s report put it, “the announcement made it sound like the $4 billion was ‘new state assistance’ to the city.”
And the city’s May 2026 Financial Plan Reconciliation – which reflects changes to the budget after the Hochul-Mamdani pact – shows the $200 million savings for the city as “State Aid for MTA” (see the screenshot below):
Throughout the spring, everyone — including the city and state comptrollers — asserted that the state would indeed pay the city’s $200-million contribution to MTA Bus.
A similar report a month later by state Comptroller Tom DiNapoli also said the $200 million reflected “city-funded MTA-related costs” that would now be picked by “by the state.”
By late June, however, the fiscal watchdogs figured out that they’d been had.
“The [budget] reflects a corresponding one-time reduction in the expected city subsidy reimbursement, which will be covered by MTA resources,” the document states. “Despite the reduction in city reimbursement, the MTA Plan continues to provide the resources necessary to maintain current bus service levels for customers.”
Advocates are not convinced. First, Reinvent Albany pointed out that the plan itself shows that predicted deficits have worsened, despite the 4-percent fare and toll increases in 2027:
Second, the raid undermines public trust.
“Raiding public transit funds or trying to balance the city budget on riders’ backs makes New York less affordable and erodes trust in our government,” said Danny Pearlstein, the spokesperson for Riders Alliance, which has supported regular fare hikes. “MTA enforcement agents recently got so aggressive that they assaulted bus rider Kyle Taylor over a $3 fare, so it’s pretty clear our transit system needs the missing $200 million and the governor should make it whole. Raising fares while raiding funds is not the policy New Yorkers expect from our transit champions in public office.”
Fauss added that those “champions” may appear that way in public, or to some reporters, but this particular shell game suggests a different portrait is in order.
“The MTA is getting $200 million less than it is supposed to from New York City — all while the governor could claim credit for helping the city to balance its budget,” she said. “Furthermore, none of this was written down in the state budget agreement. We had to dig through the financial records to even figure out what happened here.”
The $200-million MTA loss more or less wipes out the revenue it anticipated from next year’s fare and toll hike, Reinvent Albany added, which will make it harder for Mayor Mamdani to realize his signature campaign promise of buses that are both fast and free:
Streetsblog reached out to City Hall and the governor’s office for comment on Friday. We will update this story if we hear back.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.title: The Year of the Pro-Palestine Super PAC
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.author: Akela Lacy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.text:
The recent midterm election cycle marked by historic levels of pro-Israel spending saw an emerging trend that aimed to counter their influence: a new crop of pro-Palestine PACs.
Led by American Priorities PAC, which formed in January as part of an effort by donors, including supporters of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who opposed U.S. military support for Israel, a cadre of pro-Palestine organizations spent more than $14.4 million on races this cycle. Almost all of their candidates won.
“In the midst of the genocide, we felt compelled to push every lever and engage in every way possible to push candidates and the [Democratic] party to catch up to its base,” said Margaret DeReus, who leads the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project and the Peace, Accountability, and Leadership political action committee, or PAL PAC. Both groups spent on pro-Palestine ads for the first time this cycle.
As DeReus and other leaders of the emergent pro-Palestine lobby told The Intercept, voters, especially Democratic ones, have become increasingly disillusioned with Israel and frustrated with politicians who support unchecked military aid to the country. “I don’t think there is an issue that I can think of where the party position, the mainstream party position, is so out of step with the base,” DeReus said.
The new pro-Palestine spending is a drop in the bucket compared to the more than $84 million the pro-Israel lobby poured into elections this cycle. AIPAC’s super PAC outspent pro-Palestine groups almost 6 to 1 — and that doesn’t include the more than $50 million AIPAC funneled directly to candidates. The pro-Palestine side may never match their opponents dollar for dollar.
“The point is, nobody has to outspend AIPAC,” said Beth Miller, political director at the advocacy group Jewish Voice for Peace Action. Her group doesn’t spend directly on elections and instead focuses on mobilizing anti-Zionist Jewish voters. “AIPAC is spending this much money because the message they are trying to force down voters’ throats is unpopular.”
The pro-Israel lobby long dominated the discourse on Israel policy before its flagship group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, started spending directly on elections for the first time in the 2022 cycle. But as AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups find their brand growing increasingly toxic amid public outcry over U.S. military support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, pro-Palestine money is shifting the terrain when it comes to election spending.
Simply put, Miller said, “Their message goes further because it’s popular.”
Whether the spending is for or against the pro-Israel lobby, it’s rare to see political ads that directly address U.S. policy toward Israel. For one thing, the topic can be controversial — even if the controversy is manufactured.
When Rebellion PAC, a committee founded to back the 2020 congressional campaign of left-wing commentator Cenk Uygur, ran an ad supporting Abdul El-Sayed and connecting high grocery prices to U.S. support for Israel, the fallout threatened to upend the Michigan Senate race. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., called the ad antisemitic and took it as an opportunity to air her grievances with her former primary opponent, eventually switching her endorsement to Republican Mike Rogers. The PAC originally ran a version of the ad during Uygur’s short-lived 2024 presidential bid.
Voters didn’t seem to be swayed by the controversy, and El-Sayed beat Rogers by a comfortable 7 percentage points. “The drama comes from a handful of elected officials and an establishment that, at best, takes an outdated view of how Israel and AIPAC operate,” said Greg Krieg, spokesperson for American Priorities, which was not affiliated with the Rebellion PAC ad but did produce other ad spots that criticized the U.S. relationship with Israel.
“Not every ad we ran was about Israel, obviously, but the topic came up often because it united Democrats across the party’s ideological spectrum,” Krieg said. “This is not a controversial issue at a grassroots level.”
That new, vocally pro-Palestine PACs are backing successful candidates alongside veteran left organizations is a sign of health for a nascent effort, Miller said.
The midterms were “a test case of: Will this message resonate with voters? And the answer overwhelmingly was yes,” Miller said. “This is a sign of the increasing power and mobilization of the Palestinian rights movement in the political and electoral space.”
Groups like American Priorities and PAL PAC often endorsed the same candidates as progressive bench-builders like Justice Democrats and the Working Families Party. In some cases, the Palestine solidarity movement seemed to breathe a much-needed new life into the electoral left.
The pro-Israel lobby doled out bruising defeats last cycle, after making a promise to unleash its full arsenal to oust critics of Israel from Congress. AIPAC’s super PAC spent more than $25 million to unseat then-Reps. Cori Bush, D-Mo., and Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y. — a quarter of the $100 million it spent on primaries in 2024.
Reeling from those losses, progressive and Democratic strategists went back to the drawing board. Alone, they could never hope to have the same infrastructure or wield the same influence as a group like AIPAC. But together, they could more effectively pool their resources to tap into public opinion shifting further each year in their favor.
One of the new pro-Palestine groups, American Priorities, was born out of a desire to leverage that shifting public opinion against U.S. support for Israel into electoral wins. As the first truly pro-Palestine super PAC, the group spent $8.15 million backing 15 candidates this cycle, 13 of whom won. (The group also considered spending for Angie Nixon, a Florida democratic socialist who narrowly lost her bid for U.S. Senate, but ended up putting the money into another race.)
Twelve of the 20 candidates backed by PAL PAC won their races, including El-Sayed and Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, Adam Hamawy in New Jersey, Melat Kiros in Colorado, and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania.
The growing networks allowed groups like Justice Democrats to get involved in more races. It came back from its losses and had its most successful cycle yet, electing eight of the 15 candidates it endorsed, four of whom unseated Democratic incumbents. The group spent $5.5 million in total this cycle, including $4.6 million on ads across all its races. And it went much further: Last cycle, Justice Democrats spent a combined $3.3 million alone backing Bush and Bowman before they lost.
Together, IMEU Policy Project and PAL PAC spent $2.15 million on ads and bundling for candidates. “We ran on proud anti-genocide and pro-freedom platforms,” DeReus said. “We knew that this was a cycle where that platform could win, and we wanted to be a part of making that happen.”
Meanwhile, AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups saw diminishing returns on election spending this cycle, as they battled waning public opinion and increasingly concealed their spending in races.
“Their names often tell you very little about who’s behind them or what they’re actually trying to do — and their ads almost never mention Israel,” Krieg said. “Everybody is looking at the same polling. We have voters who agree with us, so we’re willing to say plainly what we stand for and put our names on it. When you’re pushing a position that voters don’t support, you’re naturally going to be a lot less transparent about what you’re doing.”
The general public had a greater knowledge of AIPAC’s brand and its role in maintaining a pro-Israel U.S. policy this time around, said Justice Democrats spokesperson Usamah Andrabi. This cycle also saw more candidates willing to translate public agitation against U.S. support for Israel into campaigns, he said, pointing to other efforts he said helped voters understand AIPAC’s role in elections from groups like TrackAIPAC.
“Voters’ awareness and opposition to Israel’s genocide and apartheid was raised so much higher due to grassroots movements and groups that organized against it,” Andrabi said. “We were able to — across every single one of our campaigns — talk about AIPAC as AIPAC, and talk about the genocide as something we wanted to end, and connect the dots for people.”
It’s a stark contrast to 2024, when Justice Democrats met with candidates whose top concerns were avoiding AIPAC’s wrath, Andrabi said. “Even then, in 2024, we were telling these campaigns, ‘Look, there’s no going under, around, behind, over AIPAC. The only way to defeat this lobby is to go right through them,” he said. “The political courage amongst a lot of Democratic candidates and a lot of people within the Democratic Party was just not there in 2024.”
As the 2028 presidential race begins to take shape, the same pro-Palestine groups are preparing to push candidates to meet voters where they are on Israel policy.
“Particularly with Abdul’s victory in Michigan, that win capped off a year that has really proved that Palestinian rights is an asset, not just in safe blue districts, but in the most critical of swing states,” DeReus said. Even President Donald Trump knows how much of a liability being pro-Israel has become, she added, pointing to his late-breaking claim on Election Day that the U.S. would end military support to Israel.
Potential Democratic contenders in 2028 would do well to take that lesson to heart, DeReus said, as groups like hers gear up to push candidates to support an arms embargo, sanction Israel, and recognize the genocide. She said the group hopes to see someone like Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., enter the race, but that it would also support Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., should she decide to run.
In DeReus’s view, “2024 was the last presidential election we will see where Palestinian rights were disregarded.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: What Are Your Odds of Winning New York’s Affordable Housing Lottery?
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado, Kennedy Sessions, Rachel Holliday Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Good news: You almost certainly have better odds of winning the New York City affordable housing lottery than of getting audited — a 1 in 1,101 chance — or getting bitten by a city dog, a 1 in 2,222 chance.
And you’ve got way better odds of winning a lottery apartment than nabbing one of those Knicks-themed wastebaskets the Sanitation Department gave out in June. Just five people snagged one, out of 125,000 who applied, putting the odds at 1 in 25,000.
Meanwhile, the chances of winning New York City’s coveted and frustrating affordable housing lottery for any one application have been 1 in 510, according to The City Reporter’s analysis of a two-year span using public data. In that time period, the city received 10,250,872 applications and, of that pool, 20,200 households ultimately signed a lease for an affordable, rent-stabilized lottery apartment.
In real world terms, the odds look like this: If everyone in five full subway cars — which carry about 100 people each — applied to Housing Connect, just one straphanger would have won an apartment in the group.
“It’s crazy,” said Brad Greenburg, executive director of the NYU Furman Center, a real estate think tank. “A lot of people apply for more than one [lottery], so it’s not like one person has a 1 in 510 chance necessarily of getting a unit — they might have a much better chance than that.”
The housing lottery is not the only way to find an affordable apartment in New York City, but it is the most accessible option for New Yorkers who are not eligible for, unable to access or don’t want to use other forms of taxpayer-funded housing help, such as rental vouchers or traditional public housing.
In an opaque and complicated system that garners millions of applications a year from New Yorkers desperate to find a stable and affordable place to live, 1 in 510 are the rough odds. (Read our methodology on how we calculated the odds and why we are confident in our findings.)
But the devil’s in the details, and an applicant’s chances can climb or fall steeply based on factors like household income and where they apply.
Frustratingly for those who need affordable housing the most, your chances of winning a lottery apartment were better if you earned more money, according to lottery data compiled between January 2022 and October 2024 and by law submitted by the Department of Housing Preservation and Development to the City Council.
This trend was also true when our newsroom first analyzed housing lottery data in 2020.
Generally, the lower the monthly cost of an apartment, the lower the income of the household that is eligible to rent it, and the greater the number of people who apply to live there. The households with the worst odds of all, in the “low income” category — which at the time of the data analyzed was between roughly $78,000 and $124,240 for a family of four — had a roughly 1 in 639 chance of winning, meaning there were 639 applications for every one apartment available in that group.
But in the higher income categories, dubbed “moderate” and “middle” income, the chances were almost twice as good: 1 in 325 and 1 in 398, respectively. Across those two categories, the incomes for applicants spanned about $124,240 to $256,245 for a family of four, depending on the size of the household.
At the same time, of the 20,200 signed leases in the two years analyzed, the majority were awarded to people who were listed in the lowest economic income groups.
Roughly 30% or just under 6,000 applicants who signed leases were in the extremely low income category. Those tenants earned $32,610 for a single person or $46,590 for a family of four.
MORE: What is Area Median Income? The Magic Number Behind Affordable Housing Math in NYC
Applicants considered very low income made up roughly a third of the overall leases. These applicants typically made up to $54,350 for a single person or $77,650 for a family of four. And nearly 24% or 4,735 applicants who categorized as low income won a housing lottery. They made up to $86,960 for a single person or $124,240 for a family of four.
That means that the majority of housing lottery leases were awarded to New Yorkers who make less than about $90,000.
Amira Willingham, who works in e-commerce marketing, felt like she beat the odds in early 2024 when she moved into a Chelsea studio she’d applied to the year before. She was in the low income category, the group with the lowest odds, according to The City Reporter’s analysis. It took years of trying before her number hit.
“As soon as the clock struck on my 18th birthday, I started applying,” the now 25-year-old said. “I was ready to move to any borough, any apartment size.”
Five years passed without luck, but then in 2023 she got a call back for the Chelsea studio. The rent was $1,329.
“There’s literally no world in which I’d be able to live alone for the rent I have,” Willingham said. She previously paid about the same to live with three roommates, and her current building has a rooftop pool, a gym and outdoor terraces.
More Choice for the Wealthiest
Among the lottery applicants earning the most, the odds of winning were the best.
That’s because there are relatively more apartments available for higher-income applicants, fewer of those applicants competing for the units and more choice for those applicants in the form of traditional, market-rate apartments.
“If you’re a renter of that [higher] income you would have market options in a range of neighborhoods,” said Rachel Fee, executive director of the New York Housing Conference, an affordable housing policy nonprofit. “If you’re below 80% [Area Median Income], you’re really priced out of most available housing in New York City.”
Patrick Boyle, senior policy director at Enterprise Community Partners, a nonprofit that helps arrange affordable housing financing, said the numbers speak to a staggering amount of demand, even when the odds at one income tier appear better than another.
“One in 325 is still pretty long odds,” he said. “Those numbers just highlight that there’s tremendous demand across all income brackets.”
Sometimes, applicants in the higher-income groups make a decision unthinkable to many New Yorkers: They win the housing lottery, then turn it down. Across all income groups, roughly 2,698 applicants rejected a unit, according to the data — most of them by residents in the low income category.
Shay O’Reilly, a nonprofit worker, was one of them. Several years ago, he won a two-bedroom lottery apartment in Flatbush but ultimately said no, in large part because at the time the $2,400 rent was higher than rent-stabilized places on the open market.
“We decided not to go for it just because we were like, ‘We can probably find something that’s cheaper,’ and we did,” O’Reilly said. “In 2020, we ended up moving into a two-bedroom, much closer to Prospect Park.”
The rent at the time for that place, he said, was $2,000.
Preferences in the Lottery
In spite of the hurdles and the cumbersome process to get approved, when applications to the housing lottery are selected, it’s random.
“There is no favoritism. I keep hearing, ‘You got to know somebody who knows somebody,’ or ‘Pay something under the table’ — all kinds of nonsense. But that’s not true. It really isn’t,” said Charmaine Marizan, affordable housing marketing and leasing manager at Fifth Avenue Committee. “It’s a very stringent, fair, highly supervised process by the city of New York.”
But there are factors that add weight to certain applicants within the random lottery, and those built-in preferences influence the odds.
Lotteries often include preferences for certain groups, including city employees, people with disabilities and public housing residents. Of the more than 2 million municipal employee applicants, 3,730 signed leases, giving them an overall chance of 1 in 564.
For NYCHA residents, the odds are some of the highest out of subcategories. Of the 44,702 NYCHA residents who applied to the lottery, no more than 255 households signed a lease. Those odds are roughly 1 in 182.
Across racial groups, the applicants who identified themselves as Pacific Islanders had the best odds: 1 in 444. Meanwhile, the odds for Hispanic residents were roughly 1 in 591; for Black New Yorkers, it was 1 in 524; while white New Yorkers saw odds of 1 in 481. Asian New Yorkers’ odds were 1 in 467 and Native Americans’ odds were 1 in 570.
Some applicants chose not to disclose their race. Their odds were 1 in 568.
The lottery also has a special boost for applicants from the community district where the apartments are located. That last rule, known as “community preference,” used to set aside half of all lottery apartments for locals, but since the settlement of a federal lawsuit challenging the practice, the preference set-aside has dropped dramatically.
Community preference gives an applicant a much better shot at signing a lease. The City Reporter’s analysis found that, with community preference in the time period analyzed, an applicant’s odds are about 1 in 53, whereas without community preference, the odds are 1 in 1,051.
Speaking of location, there are huge variations among neighborhoods as to where there are affordable apartments.
Part of this has to do with where developers are building apartments. Neighborhoods where land-use rules have changed to accommodate more housing may see a boom of buildings that contain affordable apartments, especially if the developers take advantage of tax credits that require them.
For example, the community districts that include Long Island City, Williamsburg and Greenpoint Downtown Brooklyn, East New York and the South Bronx were home to the greatest number of affordable apartments since 2020, according to an analysis of HPD advertised lottery data.
“That’s where all of the affordable housing is being built, and then places like Bay Ridge have not historically produced very many income-restricted units, if any,” Greenburg said.
The community districts containing Staten Island’s Mid-Island and South Shore; Laurelton, Rosedale and Queens Village; Bay Ridge, and Howard Beach and South Ozone Park offered the least amount of affordable housing through the lottery.
Lower Incomes, Greater Demand, Less Inventory
The levels of affordability of the housing that appears on Housing Connect shape who can apply in the first place. There were more apartments geared towards families making more money in a six year period, the analysis of advertised lottery data shows.
From July 2020 to November 2, 2026, just 4% of the 56,271 advertised apartments available on Housing Connect were designated for extremely low-income households. Meanwhile, advertised lotteries for middle-income households made up 39%.
Those numbers didn’t surprise Jumelia Abrahamson, director of programs at University Neighborhood Housing Program, which has helped applicants successfully navigate the affordable housing lottery. The clientele of the organization, which is located in the Northwest Bronx, is typically extremely low income, making under $25,000 per household.
“One of the biggest complaints we continue to hear: most of what’s available on Housing Connect is not available for me,” Abrahamson said. “We’re working with people that are at the bottom of the [income] column.”
That means there is great demand for inventory built for households on the lower end of the income spectrum.
Take one lottery for 45 affordable apartments in Park Slope, Brooklyn. The new building was located on bustling Fifth Avenue and close to the Barclays Center, and its affordable apartments had rent set between $654 for a studio and $2,872 for a two-bedroom. (That is, geared toward very low-income to moderate-income households.)
More than 100,000 applicants entered the lottery — most in the first two weeks of the 60-day application period, which closed in December 2025.
“I’ve been doing this a long time, and I’ve never seen those numbers that fast. I was amazed,” said Marizan, of the Fifth Avenue Committee, which oversaw the lottery.
While only qualified applicants — those whose household size and income match the requirements — should apply, the process of whittling down from the full applicant pool to the people who are verified as eligible to then sign leases can be complicated.
All the information an applicant includes in their application must be manually confirmed when and if an applicant’s number is picked in the lottery.
That process is onerous, time-consuming and frustrating for both the potential tenant and the lottery specialists trying to match apartments with people, as The City Reporter detailed in our guide on what happens when you go through the lottery.
Lots of people get that first call back, but very few actually sign a lease. In the case of the Park Slope building, Marizan’s team looked at 500 applicants within different categories. All 45 households they selected signed leases.
When It Works
Other reasons for missing out on an apartment can be maddeningly slight: A missing document, or income just over or under the limit.
That’s what happened to Dutch de Carvalho, an arts educator, professional dancer and content creator who had been applying to the housing lottery for years; at one point, he counted filling out 196 applications. When he finally got a call back for an apartment, he waited for months to be told he was $400 short on income — and ineligible.
“I got rejected at the last minute,” he said.
But later that year when the native Manhattanite got a different call back for another lottery apartment — after five months of paperwork — he signed a lease and moved in.
“It’s really life changing,” he said. “I’m not worried every month about if I can pay my rent. I’m able to help out my family.”
When he shared the news about the apartment on his feed it went super-viral. His first video drew 1.1 million views; a subsequent apartment tour has drawn 9.8 million.
“People who live in our city are desperate for affordable housing and our city government does not make it easy to understand the affordable housing process,” de Carvalho told The City Reporter. “I think when people are able to hear first-hand accounts of what it is like to apply, the steps involved, etc. and actually see someone receive a unit, it’s going to spark interest.”
Content about the lottery, including tips, tricks and advice from those who won, has an avid audience. The Reddit community for discussing it, r/nychousinglottery, has 25,000 visitors a week. The hashtag #nychousinglottery on TikTok has more than 20 million views.
In Chelsea, as thrilled at Willingham is with her affordable studio, she thinks maybe she can hit the lottery twice. She’s continued applying to other Housing Connect apartments in the hopes of leveling up: her sights are on a one-bedroom in Brooklyn.
“It doesn’t always work for everybody,” she said, “but when it works, it really works.”
Additional reporting by Haidee Chu.

Black People Have Every Reason to Doubt Official Narratives About a Recent Spate of Hangings
Prematurely ascribing deaths to suicide does away with questions that deserve real answers.
Since September 2025, at least 10 Black people have been found hanged in public outdoor spaces across the country. Among the first institutions to sound the alarm was the Legal Defense Fund, an outgrowth of the NAACP, an organization founded nearly 120 years ago to resist anti-Black violence, particularly lynchings. Citing “the well-documented legacy of racial terror against Black people in the United States,” the group sent letters to Congress and the United Nations in August calling for “a rigorous inquiry to ensure that our past history of widespread targeted Black killings is not recurring.” The following month, Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts and 59 other House Democrats wrote to the Justice Department and the FBI demanding a “comprehensive federal investigation into every hanging death of a Black individual.” Also in September, the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s 55th annual conference convened a panel discussion titled “Stop the Lynchings.”
I do not pretend to know that every Black person found hanged over roughly the last year was the victim of a lynching. As the civil rights lawyers, forensics experts, and mental-health scholars on the CBCF panel emphasized, Black American suicide rates have increased 53 percent over just the last decade; for Black adolescents, the rates skyrocketed 144 percent between 2007 and 2020. In some of these cases, authorities have offered evidence that rules out foul play or suggests that the death wasn’t motivated by racial hatred. A publicly unidentified Black man found hanged this September in Maryland was reportedly shown on security footage carrying a rope. After Tasia Fortune was found hanging in Mississippi, three Black men were charged with murder, and police concluded that the scene was “staged” postmortem to look like a lynching. But clearance statistics prove that police put in less work to solve homicides, or any violent crime, when the victims are Black. Prematurely ascribing deaths to suicide—as too many families contend the police have in these cases—does away with the pesky questions that deserve real answers.
As in the case of Juliana Nzita, a 16-year-old found hanged from a tree in May at a North Carolina church she did not attend, whose death was ruled a suicide within three days. A Charlotte Observer investigation found that police hadn’t ordered an autopsy, recovered her cell phone, or interviewed the man who found her body. The aunt of Justice “Kai” James, found hanging in Albany, Georgia, told the local outlet WALB that police claimed surveillance footage existed but then refused to let her see it. When the Atlanta Black Star asked a Michigan State Police officer why Jerard “Jay” Jackson’s death in Roxbury, Michigan, was ruled a suicide, he stated, “It looked like that, so that’s why I said it appeared to be a suicide.”
Yet as these cases have gained attention, a familiar strain of disparaging commentary has followed. Syndicated columnist Rich Lowry called questions about whether the hangings might be lynchings symptomatic of a “profound and disturbing racial paranoia.” More than one outlet mocked Pressley’s description of the deaths as a “national crisis.” In the National Review, Black conservative writer Wilfred Reilly pronounced fears of resurgent racial terror a “fake lynching scandal.” In seeking to understand the causes of these deaths, it is certainly fair to think critically. But the notion that Black folks’ distrust of law enforcement and other government officials is a kind of hysteria—instead of a logical response to US history—is a familiar way of waving off Black pain to avoid reckoning with its underlying causes.
There were nearly 6,500 extrajudicial lynchings between the end of the Civil War and 1950, according to the Equal Justice Initiative. The law didn’t simply fail Black Americans; the institutions supposedly tasked with enforcing it regularly abetted, covered up, or sanctioned bloody violence against them. Sheriffs and deputies facilitated or even participated directly in the violence, and coroners, prosecutors, juries, and politicians helped the perpetrators avoid punishment. Though the heyday of white racial terror arguably ended with the demise of Jim Crow, the federal government only passed the Emmett Till Anti-Lynching Act in 2022—after 200 similar bills had failed.
In its 1951 petition to the UN, the Civil Rights Congress wrote that lynchings were intended as “a powerful source of constant terror…to the whole Negro people.” That terror created trauma that was passed down through generations. Reilly snarks at the idea that “simply seeing a picture of a rope tied in a hangman’s knot can allegedly invoke this pain,” as if Black folks don’t deserve to still be hurt by the imagery of racial terror. Such dismissiveness is galling in a country where Black life has been so indelibly shaped by lynching. Many members of Black communities in the North and West can trace their family’s Southern origins back along the railroad lines that carried 6 million Black refugees away from Jim Crow racial terror. Places that once had the most lynchings now have the lowest Black voter registration and Black economic mobility, as well as the highest numbers of Black folks imprisoned or shot dead by police. Montgomery, Alabama, is home to an entire museum devoted to lynching and the scars it has left on this country.
After police declared the 2018 hanging death of Willie Andrew Jones Jr. a suicide, the civil rights lawyer Jill Collen Jefferson conducted her own investigation, turning up evidence the police had missed. Those findings helped Jones’s family win an $11 million wrongful-death settlement. In February, Jefferson’s human-rights nonprofit, Julian, released a study cataloging more than 70 deaths of Black people between 2000 and 2025 that she describes as “modern-day lynchings” by hanging or other violent means.
The history of racial terror does not answer what happened in any of the cases now under scrutiny. But it does explain why Black people’s fears are rational, their questions justified, and why “Just trust the authorities” is an absurd demand to make of them.
