https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-annou.title: Mamdani announces plan to disband NYPD’s Strategic Response Group
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-annou.author: David Giambusso
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-annou.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he is disbanding the heavily criticized NYPD unit that responds to protests in the city.
Mamdani announced Monday that the NYPD's Strategic Response Group would be formally disbanded and its core functions split into new and existing divisions. The mayor pledged to shut the group down during his 2025 campaign.
The unit was created in 2015 and was tasked with managing counter-terrorism as well as crowd control — two functions critics have said call for starkly different approaches. The group has drawn numerous lawsuits and accusations of police brutality since it was created.
Mamdani said he would create a new unit specially designed to maintain peaceful public demonstrations.
“New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat,” he said in a statement. “We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation.”
The SRG became a symbol of police aggression in June 2020, during chaotic citywide protests in the wake of George Floyd’s murder by a Minneapolis police officer. Officers from the group were criticized for “kettling in” protesters, using pepper spray and truncheons, beating demonstrators and other aggressive tactics. The police response at the time led to a battery of lawsuits and historic payouts by city taxpayers to those harmed by the NYPD.
Now, protest response and crowd control will be handled by a new team focused on de-escalation, civilian coordination and peaceful assembly, the mayor’s office said.
That new unit will be called the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division and will exist within the mayor's Office of Community Safety. It will “plan for and respond to protests,” the mayor’s office said.
The group will work with FAST, a team of 30 uniformed officers within the NYPD’s Community Affairs Bureau who specialize in communication and crowd de-escalation, according to information provided by City Hall.
Groups like the New York Civil Liberties Union have criticized the NYPD for bringing heavily armored vehicles and weaponry to peaceful protests. Now, instead, a Patrol Support Division comprised of closely vetted and trained officers will be on hand to assist other teams. It will only be called on in dangerous situations, the mayor's office said.
Some of the practices that have drawn the most criticism from protesters and civil libertarians will no longer be allowed, city officials announced. The mayor’s office and the NYPD will formalize a ban on kettling, and prohibit the use of long guns, pepper spray and tear gas during “First Amendment activities.”
The SRG’s counterterrorism functions will be put under the control of the NYPD’s Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau, the city said.
Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement that she endorsed the changes.
“I believe strongly that the NYPD must always be willing to examine how we operate and make improvements,” she said. “I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD's ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Seven shows to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Razmig Bedirian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Reem Al Mubarak: What We Left in the Sandbox
Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027
In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.
The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.
Shaikha Al Mazrou
Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027
In 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.
She receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside new commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.
All Manner of Experiments
NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027
In 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Said established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.
All Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.
The exhibition at the New York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Said’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.
A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.
Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean
Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027
The Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.
This investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).
Serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.
Vantage Point 13
Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November
The 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.
Sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.
The other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu shows life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.
Artist’s Rooms: Walid Siti; Shezad Dawood; Lulua Alyahya; Afrah Shafiq; Bani Abidi
Jameel Arts Centre, Dubai
The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.
One room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.
Bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.
Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.
New Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.
Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.
The sky held it, the earth remembered
Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December
The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.
In Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.
The work—a new iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—shows how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.
Devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.
In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.author: Heather Cherone
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.text:
Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess.
The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble.
The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund.
Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole.
Pension Holiday Snowballs Into Peril
In 2000, the city’s pensions were 85% funded, which meant the funds could easily pay benefits to employees as they retired, records show. But a series of decisions in both Chicago and the Illinois capital of Springfield unraveled that strong position, leading to the current mountain of $36.4 billion in pension debt.
First, the twin blows of the “dot-com” bubble bursting in 2000 and the Great Recession in 2007 wiped out nearly $16 billion from those funds.
Around the same time came a self-inflicted blow. In 2005, the state legislature, at the request of then Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, passed legislation allowing the city to contribute less every year than what was actually needed to pay retirees.
As a result, in 2006 and 2007, Daley was able to stop making annual contributions to four pension funds for police officers, firefighters, laborers and municipal employees. He received near-unanimous support from the Chicago City Council. Daley, who was mayor from 1989 through 2011, declined to comment for this story.
Daley’s “pension holiday” meant the city could balance its budget without a politically perilous property tax hike. But that maneuver laid the foundation of the current pension crisis facing the city.
In 2010, having seen the financial fallout from the pension legislation, state legislators passed a law that banned city officials from taking another pension holiday by setting a firm schedule for the city to pay back its skipped payments — no excuses allowed.
Two of Chicago’s pension funds must be funded at a 90% level by 2055, with the other two hitting that mark by 2058, according to state law. This requirement caused a spike in the city’s annual payments.
Trying to ease Chicago’s snowballing pension burdens, lawmakers passed a new measure reducing the retirement benefits offered to state employees who began work on or after January 1, 2011.
But that revised law touched off a new set of problems. The well-intentioned effort to reduce costs actually reduced pension benefits too drastically. Under federal law, public sector pension funds must pay workers no less than what they would have earned if they paid into Social Security.
In 2021 and 2025, lawmakers agreed to change the law and ensure that first responders — police and firefighters — in Illinois are paid at least the minimum required by law.
Fixing those funds will cost Chicago an additional $11 billion to get to the 90% funded level required by state law over the next three decades, according to city projections. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the legislation over the objections of city officials.
Long-Term Lease, Long-Lasting Regrets
Facing big deficits in 2008 in the wake of the Great Recession, Daley and the City Council found what they thought was a creative solution to the city’s financial woes.
They would lease the city’s parking meters to a conglomerate of investment funds for 75 years in return for $1.5 billion up front. That massive influx of cash meant no one had to make any hard decisions to fill the city’s budget gap and avoid a politically unpopular property tax increase.
But the deal ended up a loser both politically and financially.
The new owners of the meters immediately jacked up the cost to park, infuriating residents. In a matter of months, members of the City Council began regretting their votes, and Daley announced he would not run for reelection.
By 2025, the city’s meters generated $2.2 billion in revenue for the investors, with another 58 years still left on the lease.
The city considered buying the parking meters back this year, but Mayor Brandon Johnson told reporters “the final purchase price was far too high.” The city would have had to borrow billions to finance the $3.2 billion purchase.
Elected officials across the political spectrum agree that the city would have been much better off raising property taxes instead of leasing the parking meters in 2008.
But even as the gap between the city’s revenues and its expenses continues to widen, property tax hikes remain the third rail of Chicago politics.
Chicagoans’ property taxes last jumped in 2021, when former Mayor Lori Lightfoot raised them by $93.9 million and passed a budget that automatically hiked property taxes to keep pace with inflation.
Johnson campaigned against those automatic property tax increases, forcing Lightfoot to drop a proposal to hike taxes by $42.7 million in 2023, just months before she lost her bid for reelection.
The automatic property tax hike was eliminated, even though it could have prevented the city’s credit rating from being downgraded repeatedly and significantly reduced the annual budget gaps.
In a postscript to the parking meter debacle, Chicago Parking Meters LLC sold the meters contract earlier this year to an investment firm, triggering a one-time payment to the city of $75 million. The City Council and Johnson then battled over how best to use that money for pension costs, creating a temporary hole in the 2027 city budget.
The Financial Toll of Police Misconduct
The 2014 police murder of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald changed nearly every aspect of City Hall politics around policing. Despite decades of scandals, misconduct and brutality, the Police Department had managed to fend off reform. But that ended with McDonald’s death, even as city leaders continued to fear a backlash from residents concerned about crime rates and a politically powerful police union.
After a massive outcry greeted footage of McDonald getting shot 16 times while he walked away from officers, the federal government launched a probe that in 2017 found ample evidence that the department routinely violated the constitutional rights of Black and Latino Chicagoans.
In 2019, the Chicago Police Department agreed — under the oversight of a federal judge — to change the way officers are trained, supervised and disciplined. In taking so long to address a pernicious problem, a succession of city leaders set up Chicago for a huge financial hit.
The true scope of police misconduct and what it will cost the city is only now becoming clear.
From 2019 to 2025, as the city scrambled to fill budget holes, it agreed to pay nearly $730 million to resolve lawsuits alleging officers committed a wide range of misconduct, according to a WTTW News analysis of city records. The most expensive cases involve wrongful convictions that sent Chicagoans now declared innocent to prison for decades, as well as botched raids and police pursuits that violated CPD policy and led to injuries, according to that analysis.
In 2026 alone, Chicago has spent more than $277 million to resolve lawsuits alleging police misconduct, records show. That includes nearly $100 million to resolve 90 lawsuits filed by people who allege they were wrongfully implicated based on evidence gathered by former Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was convicted in 2013 of taking bribes. He has denied wrongdoing.
Johnson has urged the City Council to borrow an additional $481 million to cover the costs of resolving more lawsuits, with $260.8 million earmarked for 17 people wrongfully convicted based on evidence developed by former Chicago police Detective Reynaldo Guevara. A judge determined Guevara told “bald-faced lies” while under oath in 2017, a fact that will be presented to any jury asked to determine whether the city should be held accountable for claims of misconduct. He has repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right not to incriminate himself when pressed to testify in civil cases.
Another 25 lawsuits naming Guevara remain pending.
Guevara is now one of the most notorious members of the Chicago Police Department, costing taxpayers more than any other officer, including former Cmdr. Jon Burge, who tortured and beat more than 100 Black men from the 1970s to the 1990s, city officials have acknowledged.
Records show that Guevara, who retired from CPD in 2005 and lives in Texas, collects an annual payout of $91,000 from the city’s depleted police pension fund.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/h.title: Highway or the Highway: Brooklynites Slam BQE Bypass Proposal
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/h.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/h.text:
Mayor Mamdani should not simply rebuild the ailing Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, and saddle future generations with its inevitable and costly upkeep, but instead explore options to transition away from the roadway’s truck-first approach, Brooklynites said at a public meeting on Thursday night.
The Department of Transportation has begun gathering feedback for a required environmental review of its $4 billion proposal to rehab what it calls BQE Central, a deteriorating section of the highway between Atlantic Avenue and Sands Street, over the next decade. The agency wants to construct a temporary bypass that involves a dramatic flyover above the Brooklyn Bridge’s approach in Dumbo.
Residents and advocates called on the Mamdani administration to broaden its scope, not double down on the Robert Moses infrastructure. “You are asking New Yorkers to spend $4 billion to end up in 2040 with the same 1954, racist highway that Robert Moses built,” said Red Hook resident Victoria Hagman Alexander at the virtual feedback session with the agency. “Your scope studies two options: build it or don’t. And that’s not a choice for communities. And it’s a choice that we’ve rejected multiple times.”
According to DOT’s Oct. 2 draft scope of work for the environmental review, the agency will study the impacts of building a bypass versus not rebuilding the BQE — an approach the leader of the influential Brooklyn Heights Association described as “far too narrowly defined.” 
“The purpose and scope have to include the goal of moving people and freight much more efficiently and much more sustainably throughout our borough, and preferably not in thousands of cars carrying one person at a time, as we see now on the BQE,” said the BHA’s executive director, Lara Birnback. In 2018, the BHA successfully rallied against former mayor Bill de Blasio’s proposal to erect a six-lane temporary highway atop the Brooklyn Heights promenade.
Construction is set to begin in 2030 and last 10 years, and the rebuild will extend the BQE’s lifespan until 2080. Mamdani’s DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn has argued that the city needs to renovate the BQE to facilitate the movement of its daily 130,000 motorists, including 13,000 trucks, and that the agency has run out of time to consider larger overhauls to reduce the city’s dependence on the highway.
New York City maintains an unusually heavy reliance on trucks: Nearly 90 percent of all goods move through the city on big rigs, compared to a national average of 70 percent. The city could instead spend its finite time on pivoting to alternative methods of moving freight, such as Blue Highways, good-old-fashioned rail or smaller vehicles like cargo bikes.
“This draft scope of work asks us in the community and beyond — all of us adjacent to the BQE — to endure at least a decade and likely more of highly disruptive construction, just to end up with the exact same loathed and discredited infrastructure that we’ve already endured for 70 years. We have to do better,” Birnback said.
The mayor’s proposed bypass highway will run next to the triple-cantilever level with the upper roadway, and sit within feet of adjacent residential buildings like 360 Furman Street, said a representative for the building’s roughly 1,200 residents. 
“The proposed bypass highway would come within four feet of our façade,” said Diane Genova. “A decade is not temporary for the people who have to live next to it.”
The city should look at construction approaches that don’t create an entirely new highway, such as a lane-by-lane rebuild with a traffic reduction plan, Genova said. In 2021, following recommendations by an expert panel, de Blasio reduced the triple-cantilever’s six lanes to just four. The intervention cut cut the number of daily vehicles on the bridge by 15 percent.
Transportation officials must also finally fix the chaotic Atlantic Avenue interchange by closing the Queens-bound on-ramp and removing the dangerous pedestrians crossings to and from the waterfront, said a representative for an area business group. De Blasio’s expert panel emphasized the same recommendation in its six-year-old report, to avoid creating exactly the kind of spillover traffic that now plagues adjacent neighborhoods. But neither subsequent mayor followed through and DOT now plans to rebuild it.
“The ramp truly just should be closed. For years, this has invited and incentivized cut-through traffic into our neighborhoods,” said Layla Passman, director of special projects at the Atlantic Ave BID. 
DOT has shied away from decommissioning the structure, saying that its retirement would dump car and truck traffic onto residential streets — but that has already happened amid the agency’s inaction.
Agency officials have said closing a ramp would trigger federal reviews, which could delay the project, but former commissioner Hank Gutman recently countered that the city could temporarily shutter it without an intervention by Uncle Sam, as he did under de Blasio with an off-ramp at Cadman Plaza to shore up the triple cantilever’s retaining wall.
But the winds in Washington, D.C., have shifted with the flipping of both houses of Congress to Democratic control in the election last week, and the city should use that political leverage to think bolder, said another resident.
“When this project was conceived… there was no expectation that the extent of the blue wave that we experienced last week,” said Bill Stein of the Fulton Ferry Landing Association. “So there’s going to be fresh air, let’s say, in Washington come January, and hopefully even fresher air by November ’28.”
Preserving the Atlantic Avenue interchange has encouraged motorists to cut through residential streets between Hamilton Avenue and the Atlantic on-ramp to avoid traffic on the trench section slicing through Cobble Hill and Carroll Gardens. This led some frustrated residents to ask DOT to re-widen the cantilever to three lanes, even though doing so would encourage even more traffic.
“Having the pinch at the cantilever of two lanes has been disastrous on Columbia Street, Hicks Street. The traffic has been increased. The pedestrian safety has been decreased,” said Michelle Ocampo at the hearing. “The BQE has to be expanded to three lanes, supporting all structure implementation to make that happen.”
Another public speaker argued for the exact opposite: the city should simply shut down the highway and commerce would survive. “I think there’s a way for businesses to thrive and and take cars off the cantilever,” said Wendy Hoopes. “I personally don’t drive on it, it’s not safe. I think it should be left for pedestrians and bicyclists alone, and I don’t see how building temporary highways makes any sense when they’re four feet from where people are living.”
“We’re talking about [a] long construction period for a 40-year end frame,” Hoopes added. “You want to break up a lot of people’s lives and neighborhood to have a 40-year fix. That is not sensible, and there’s got to be a better way.”
DOT will draft an environmental impact statement over the next year, before preparing a final EIS in 2028. The city also plans to commence the city’s uniform land use review procedure, or ULURP, the same year. That will require sign-off from the City Council along with separate state approval to alienate several pieces of parkland along the project to make way for construction.
An agency spokesperson reiterated that the city has run out of time and that the deadline to repair the triple cantilever was “more immediate.”
“For too long, the BQE debate has been governed by politics. Today, it is governed by physics,” said Will Livingston in a statement. “While the triple cantilever is safe today, our latest engineering work tells us something we cannot ignore: the window to act is more immediate, and we are running out of time.”
The rep added that shoring up the triple-cantilever “does not preclude future work” to rethink the larger BQE, the majority of which is controlled by New York State. “We are out of options and must pivot towards the shortest-term rehabilitation plan needed to keep the structure safe and stable,” he said.
DOT is accepting public comment through Jan. 11 via this contact form, by emailing BQECentral@dot.nyc.gov, or sending snail mail to:
NYC Department of Transportation
Division of Bridges – BQE Central Project Team
Attention: Albert Silvestri
55 Water Street, 5th Floor
New York, NY 10041

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: How To Apply for the NYC Housing Lottery
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Want to secure an affordable, rent-stabilized apartment through New York City’s housing lottery? Step right up and try your luck!
As The City Reporter has shown, your chances of winning a subsidized apartment through the affordable lottery are a long shot, but not unheard of. In recent years, there has been one apartment available through the lottery for every 510 applications.
Those lucky New Yorkers have a fabled, enviable opportunity: Moving into (typically) brand-new buildings with stabilized rent that’s likely cheaper than the market.
But even when your number comes up in the lottery, there are a lot of hoops to jump through before you secure a lease. We spoke to leasing agents, city officials and some winners to find out the inside scoop on the lottery.
Here’s our guide for locals on how to access those opportunities, tips to navigate the process and how you can prepare — with insight from people who won the lottery and professionals who screen applicants for lottery apartments.
I’m Ready to Apply! Where Do I Start?
You can sign up for and apply to housing lotteries on Housing Connect, a web-based system run through the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development that lists and manages all available subsidized apartments.
Think of Housing Connect as the portal through which you enter lotteries for individual buildings.
First, create a profile.
You’ll include details about all sources of income, including from jobs, government assistance, investments or workers’ compensation, as well as the value of your assets in bank and investment accounts. You must include this income information for the people you’d live with.
You’ll also indicate your current residence, whether it’s a rental, NYCHA building or a homeless shelter, and whether anyone you’re applying with receives rental assistance.
The information must be provided on the profile for each member of your household — that is, the people you’ll live with in that lottery apartment, not necessarily your current household.
Make sure this information is complete, or else you won’t be able to submit an application.
You can also include details about your preferences, such as interest in a ramp or elevator, number of bedrooms and a pet-friendly policy.
One thing to keep in mind: “Anything you put on your profile, you will have to prove that it’s true,” said Wout Stienaers, a founder of Homey, a paid service that helps people apply to the housing lottery. “Don’t lie about anything.”
For instance, Stienaers said applicants might be tempted to say they have a disability because there are apartments set aside for those who do (more on that later). But you’d be asked to provide proof of that disability, like a letter from a doctor.
You can get free help to apply for the housing lottery through HPD’s Housing Ambassador Program.
I Made a Profile on Housing Connect. Now What?
Once you’ve made a profile, check buildings for which you’re eligible and click “Apply Now.” You’ll know if you’re eligible if your household income falls within a range based on the number of people you’ll be living with. (How is that income range determined? Read our guide on that here.)
Keep the information about your household and income updated as you go along. For example: If you or your partner get a raise or lose a job, make sure to log that information. If you become a parent, add your child as a member of your household!
One caveat: don’t change your household size after you apply to a lottery.
“If a household is a single mom and a teenager, and then they find out they only qualify for a studio, they can’t then add the grandmother with Social Security income to see if they qualify for another unit,” said Christine Wendell, CEO of Pront Housing, an affordable housing leasing company. “If they try to do that, they will be rejected, so they should just pick their household size, and stick with it.”
MORE: What Is ‘Affordable Housing’ in New York, and What Are My Options?
Make sure to check back on Housing Connect frequently, as new opportunities come online often.
Application periods for each building are open for two months. It doesn’t matter when you submit your application within that period, as long as you apply before the lottery closes.
“No matter at what point in time you submit your application, you have the same chance to win as everybody else,” Stienaers said.
Don’t be shy about throwing your hat in the ring! You can apply to as many lotteries as you’re eligible for.
“You can apply to an unlimited number of buildings,” Wendell said. “Just statistically speaking, you will have a greater chance of getting an affordable housing unit if you apply to a lot of buildings, which everyone is completely allowed to do.”
How Can I know if I’m Eligible?
To be eligible for affordable housing through Housing Connect, your household income must fall within a specific band. Your household’s assets must also fall under a certain amount.
The asset limits vary based on building and requirements. That means if you have a lot of savings or holdings in a stock portfolio, you may not be eligible for the lottery, even if your income falls within the bands.
Can I Apply With a Voucher or Rental Subsidy?
Yes! If you get rental assistance through programs including Section 8, CityFHEPS or Medicaid Waiver, you’re good, and then you’re not subject to minimum income requirements. But the amount of rent of the apartment you’re applying to must be within the limits of what your voucher covers.
“If you have a voucher, you should apply for everything because your income isn’t your limiting factor anymore,” said Michelle de la Uz, executive director at the nonprofit Fifth Avenue Committee. “It’s basically whatever your voucher is approved for.”
That means as a voucher-holder, you may be eligible to apply for more housing lotteries than you think. Even if you don’t make enough money, you can apply for apartments based on the amount of rent — as long as it’s no more than what your voucher is worth.
Can People Apply to the Lottery if They Don’t Live in New York City?
Yes, they technically can, but applicants who are New York City residents get priority.
“While any and everybody can apply for Housing Connect lotteries, it first focuses on folks that reside within the five boroughs of New York City before it can move someone that does not reside in New York City into one of its apartments,” said Shaheem Taylor, a marketing outreach coordinator at HPD, in a webinar.
It’s very rare for outside applicants to secure an apartment through a lottery. A New York City resident who applies to the lottery is over 10 times more likely to sign a lease for an affordable apartment than someone who lives outside the city, according to an analysis of HPD data by The City Reporter.
MORE: What Are Your Odds of Winning NYC’s Affordable Housing Lottery?
Having set his sights on someday moving back to his birthplace of New York City, Grayson Sparrow applied to housing lotteries from his home in Virginia. He lucked out when he moved back to the city in April 2024 and was asked to submit his documents for a housing lottery building in East New York just three months later.
“I’d been applying just in the event if I move back someday and maybe it lines up with something,” Sparrow, 30, said. “My info went in and by the time they pulled it, I had New York residency.”
Can I Apply to the Lottery for a Rental Apartment if I Own Property?
If you or a member of your household own property within 100 miles of New York City, then you can’t apply through the lottery. (And you can’t try for an affordable homeownership lottery if you own, or ever owned, property anywhere.)
Can I Apply for One Lottery Multiple Times?
No! One entry per household.
Your household means all the people who will live in the apartment you’ll be applying to. Only one member of the household should apply for the lottery. And you can’t apply for the same lottery twice, even if, for example, you’re applying with a roommate and then on your own.
If more than one member of a household applies to the lottery, the application is automatically disqualified.
Christina Harsch, director of leasing and compliance at Wavecrest Management, recommends keeping track of what you’re applying to and the information you’re sending in, if you get your number called.
“Keep a journal of what you’re applying to and when you apply, keep copies of the [Housing Connect] ad if you can and even copies of applications so you remember what you’re doing,” she said.
That way, you know your household only applies to one lottery and you can follow up with the agents if need be.
Need more help? Connect with a housing ambassador to get assistance preparing for and applying to the housing lottery.
What Else Might Improve My Chances of Being Selected?
If you work for the city government, are a military veteran or live in the same neighborhood as the building you’re applying for, you might get a boost in the lottery. That’s because a percentage of the available apartments are set aside for people who fall under specific categories. In all new buildings, 5% of apartments are for households where a member has a mobility disability and 2% for households where a member has a hearing or vision disability.
In addition, 10% of apartments are set aside for city employees and military veterans, and 20% for residents of the community district where the building is located. Some projects offer preferences for seniors or formerly homeless individuals, as well.
OK I Entered a Lottery! How Long Will It Take Before I Hear Back?
Once you apply, you get assigned a random number called a log number. The lower it is, the better chance you have of being contacted for the development.
And then it could be weeks, months or years before you hear back if your number has been selected. Some people never hear back, even if they are eligible! Others don’t hear anything for a long time, but all of a sudden, will be notified their number was chosen for multiple buildings.
Pro tip: Make sure to stay on top of your Housing Connect account so you don’t miss any notifications. Taylor, of HPD, recommends applicants check their Housing Connect account three times a week.
Jumelia Abrahamson, director of programs at University Neighborhood Housing Program, said she tells people to log into Housing Connect “as often as you’re logging into your social media.”
She also tells applicants to check their email on a daily basis.
“Leasing agents are not calling, they’re not texting, and if these communications are going into the junk mail or if people don’t check their emails on a daily basis, they’re missing a lot of communication,” she said.
(If you applied on paper, you can choose whether to get notifications via email or in your actual mailbox — but ideally, you’ve applied through Housing Connect! Otherwise, it can be a slower process.)
What’s the Status of My Lottery Application?
Housing Connect will indicate where your application is in the process. Here’s what those statuses mean, according to experts:
- Pending just means you submitted your application. Nothing else!
- Action required means there is a request for documentation, indicating you moved to the next stage in the process — your log number was pulled — and you need to respond to a request from the lottery administrators. (If you happen to be rejected, that will also appear under “action required.”)
- In process could mean one of two things: either that you submitted your documents and they are under review, or you missed the window to submit the documents.
- Completed indicates the end stage of the application process. It can mean that you signed a lease and received your keys. Or it could mean there are no more apartments available in a development. Or it could mean you were rejected in the process and did not appeal the rejection within the required timeline.
My Number Got Picked! Now What?
Once you’re notified your number was called in a lottery, get ready for a long road. This is where the process can get tricky, as you must provide a pile of paperwork to verify your eligibility, including identifications and proof of income. You have 10 business days to submit those documents.
And if the leasing agent requests more documents beyond what was in your original application, an applicant has five business days to respond.
“Five days is really not a long time if you’re not checking, and once that five days is gone, your place in line has been passed by,” said Charmaine Marizan, the affordable housing marketing and leasing manager at Fifth Avenue Committee. “If you don’t get back quickly, there’s a bunch of people who need it.”
It’s good to get as many of your documents in order as you can before you’re selected, experts say. Keep a digital file of PDFs of important information so you can send it off quickly if your number is called. Here is a list of the documents you may need to provide.
In sum, you must provide IDs — such as IDNYC, drivers’ license, or state ID card — for all members of the household, plus birth certificates for minors.
You’ll need to show all sources of income so the agent can verify you qualify within the income bands. That includes interest from assets, student loans, child support payments and even regular checks or Venmo payments from family members or others. Applicants employed by jobs must submit a month of pay stubs, and self-employed applicants must provide tax returns.
If you get benefits through SNAP, TANF or Social Security, you can simply submit the income determination you got through those programs.
You’ll also have to show your assets, if you have more than $51,600 saved and in investment accounts. That means providing bank account and retirement account statements, among other records. If you have less than that $51,600 in assets, you can just self-certify that that’s the case — no need to prove it.
Once it’s confirmed that you’re eligible for an apartment — and there’s a vacancy available — you can either show you’ve paid rent for the past year, or you can opt for a credit check.
There’s no application fee, but you might be charged $20 for a background or credit check.
You might have a back-and-forth with the listing agent who represents the development. They may ask for more information or clarification. You can also ask them questions.
Amira Willingham, 25, who won her Chelsea studio through the lottery, said the agent asked her about specific transactions on her bank account.
“I had to explain to them every transaction,” she said. “I bought a lot online so I had lots of receipts to show.”
On one occasion, Willingham had to get a copy of a friend’s bank statement with everything blacked out except a transaction showing Willingham sending the friend money for a dinner.
“There’s no privacy in the process,” Willingham said. “I wish I had known to have a folder of everything I’d ever done put together and up to date.”
When she wasn’t sure about how to move forward, Willingham turned to an online forum she found helpful to chat with others navigating the process.
Dan B., a musician who lives in a Greenpoint apartment he won through the lottery, advised following up with the agent to get clarity on requirements and to check in for updates: “You really have to advocate for yourself because no one’s going to care more about you getting it than yourself.”
And when you advocate for yourself, it’s good to stick to email when contacting agents in order to maintain a record, said Mildred Flores, director of affordable housing marketing and compliance at Settlement Housing Fund.
“Everybody’s going to do things differently. There are some marketing agents that terminate applications as quickly as they can, and then there are others that you know will work with applicants,” Flores said.
She said she typically tells applicants to wait to contact agents for a status update until 30 days have passed since the start of tenant selection. Have patience, she cautioned, as agents often are working to lease up multiple buildings at a time and handling hundreds of applications.
For those who inquire, Flores said she will give applicants a sense of their chances and the timeline based on their log numbers — again, the random number assigned to you when you enter a lottery.
I Got Turned Down. What Can I Do?
You can appeal the decision. Within five days of the decision, write to the agent to say why you think you should not have been rejected, or why you think you should still be moving forward, and send in supporting documents.
“An applicant can appeal at any part in the process, except during the initial qualification period,” Flores said. If an applicant successfully appeals, they will not lose their place in the queue.
HPD is not involved in this process — it’s the agents associated with the building who handle the appeals.
Often, applicants face rejection because they don’t meet income or household eligibility requirements, because a single household submitted more than one application for a building or because there was insufficient information provided to the leasing agent.
Willingham said she appealed at least three times during the process when agents disqualified her based on insufficient information or not providing the right documentations.
“I had to kind of be a Karen about it,” she said. “This is one of the only paths to affordable housing in the city. Doing anything you can to fight to get it is really important.”
I Got Approved. What’s Next?
You’ll likely take a tour of the apartment — or multiple open apartments in one new complex — and if you like what you see, you can decide to move forward. You’ll have 30 days to accept a lease offer or complete a purchase, if it’s a lottery homeownership opportunity.
You’ll have to pay the first month’s rent and a security deposit (equal to a month’s rent) upfront, so make sure you have savings!
You’ll also have to figure out how to get out of your current lease, sometimes with limited notice. That requires negotiating with your landlord.
How Long Will This Whole Process Take?
It can vary a ton! The answer has to do with how fast you as the applicant are able to mobilize, and what kind of obstacles may pop up in the screening process.
Between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026, the median time it took for an applicant to get approved for an apartment after the lottery ended was 136 days (about 4.5 months).
For Sparrow, who had applied to the housing lottery from outside New York, a year passed between when he applied for the building and when leasing agents reached out to ask for documents. Three months after that, he signed the lease for his affordable apartment.
“It is a little surprising how my process was seamless,” he said. “I’ve seen other people where they get asked for documents and it takes months for them to move into the apartment.”
WIllingham, on the other hand, applied for her building’s lottery in February of one year, received a request for documents by November, and moved in the following March.
What Happens if My Life Changes Between When I Get a Call for the Lottery?
That can happen — and it’s why you should keep your Housing Connect profile updated.
If your life changes between when you apply for a lottery and your number gets picked, you get screened for your current situation. Maybe you got married and had a family, or maybe you got promoted. Either way, you may or may not qualify for the apartment any more. The agent will work with you to figure it out.
But be careful! You don’t want your situation to change during the screening process. Marizan, for instance, cautions against earning too much overtime, which can alter your income.
“If you’re currently in the screening process and you’re due a promotion, hold back on it,” she said. “You cannot be over-income by a penny.”
Any Other Way to Secure Affordable Housing?
Yup: look for apartments that people won through the lottery but are now vacant.They’re called re-rentals (or re-sales, for homeownership). These kinds of apartments don’t go through the lottery — at least until April 30, 2027. That means you can apply for these affordable apartments almost like any other apartment — essentially, first-come, first-served. You can find listings here and here, or on the sites of individual property management companies. StreetEasy, Zillow and other listings sites may also feature vacant affordable housing re-rentals.
Harsch, of Wavecrest Management, suggested reaching out to affordable management companies by cold-calling or emailing to ask about their re-rental stock. (She mentioned even if there’s nothing to offer, she may add people who get in touch to a mailing list and send them info about new housing opportunities.)
If you apply for a re-rental opportunity, you still must be eligible for the apartment based on your income and household size — details that the leasing agent will need to verify. So it takes time! And they may add you to a wait list that they’ll pull from if another applicant doesn’t work out.

https://gothamist.com/news/meet-the-syra.title: Meet the Syracuse tile guy with a monopoly on NYC subway mosaics
https://gothamist.com/news/meet-the-syra.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/meet-the-syra.text:
When the colorful, intricate tile mosaics featuring the names of subway stations like Columbus Circle or Cortlandt Street need to be replaced, the MTA relies on just one man to get the job done.
He lives 250 miles north of the city in Syracuse. He’s 73 years old. And he wishes the MTA would understand you can’t rush art.
“They'll say, ‘Oh, don't you have that just laying around? Can't you put it together?’ And I go ‘No,’” said Robert Shenfeld, who has a monopoly on restoring the MTA’s century-old tile mosaics. “Every station was done differently, and that was done for a reason, so that people would know their stop.”
MTA officials acknowledged Shenfeld doesn’t always work on their preferred timeline. But they said they have no other choice.
“Sometimes there's a tension between getting the work done faster and cheaper, as we're always intending to do, and ensuring that it's done well and better,” said MTA head of construction Jamie Torres-Springer.
Shenfeld says his ceramic studio is the only one on the planet capable of recreating the intricate tile designs that are a signature of the sprawling mass transit system. His workshop — tucked down a gravel road next to a motel and an open field — is filled with a team of artists who are the masters of the city’s subway tiles.
He’s recreated mosaics at 50 subway stations, including the recently renovated Borough Hall in Brooklyn, his biggest project ever. His ongoing mosaic projects include 14th Street Union Square, Jamaica-Van Wyck in Queens and Parkchester in the Bronx.
Shenfeld previously worked as a school art teacher, but in 2008 he bought the tile-making equipment from a woman in New Jersey who previously oversaw the MTA’s mosaic restoration work.
“In order to do mosaics with the MTA, you have to have done mosaics with the MTA,” he said. “So the only way for me to do it was to buy the company that was making them.”
His team painstakingly replicates the exact colors and designs of mosaics the MTA needs replaced. The work is so detailed and labor intensive that Shenfeld’s team regularly blows deadlines imposed by the transit agency. But Shenfeld notes you can’t rush perfection. And the MTA has little recourse because of the Syracuse studio’s monopoly.
Shenfeld’s replacement of the mosaics at Borough Hall weren’t ready by the time the MTA cut the ribbon on the overhauled station earlier this year, so crews put up a poster until the mosaic was ready to be installed a month later.
“A lot of ceramic artists do mosaic, but having the equipment, the knowledge of how that goes together and the knowledge of the color range, I'm probably the only one I know in the country or maybe the world that can do it,” he said.
During a recent visit to Shenfeld’s studio, it was clear why the work takes so long.
The space is filled with artists — most of them who work part-time — working on thousands of tiles, many of which are as small as a postage stamp. A top priority of the group is to replicate the exact color and designs of original subway mosaics. Shenfeld said he had to do more than 300 color tests to match the 60 different colors on the Borough Hall mosaic.
“The original glazes were lead-based, so we can't use that,” he said. “So we do things that are close to that.”
Some minerals used in the glazes are harder to come by these days, like lithium, which creates a matte surface on the tiles. It used to cost $10 dollars a pound, but now goes for $200 a pound because it’s in high demand for rechargeable batteries.
”Silica, that's another one, the prices have skyrocketed,” Shenfeld said.
Shenfeld’s team mixes and matches minerals, and then fires them in kilns.
John Das, one of Shenfeld’s longtime employees, did most of the work matching the colors on the Borough Hall mosaic. He said the MTA didn’t make the job easy.
“They didn't send us the nice and clean picture,” Das said.
He used a computer to recreate how the sign likely looked when it was new — in 1908. It took two years to complete, but his two brothers, wife and brother-in-law all helped.
Das, 39, arrived in Syracuse in 2008 as part of a resettlement of 60,000 Nepalis to the U.S. who’d been kicked out of Bhutan. Shenfeld hired him three years later.
The actual process for making ceramic tiles hasn’t changed much since the MTA first installed mosaics a century ago. Shenfeld has six kilns, and a “Breaking Bad”-style lab full of bottles of various shapes filled with color powders.
Shenfeld said the prospect of his retirement has been a source of consternation with MTA officials.
He recalled telling NYC Transit president Demetrius Crichlow, “You know I’m 73, I might retire, but I don't think so. What would you do? And he goes, ‘You're not retiring.’”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Nomad art and design fair lands at Abu Dhabi’s Modernist former airport terminal
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Aimee Dawson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.
“Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” says the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”
This year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.
Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.
Bellavance‑Lecompte says that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.
Another important development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something new can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte says.
For Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte says. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year showed us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.
• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November

A delivery worker in Sunset Park on an illegal e-bike. Photo: Sophia Lebowitz
The City Council has slowed passage of a large package of bills to regulate e-bikes amid pushback from the city chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America as Mayor Mamdani’s political base moves into the politically charged policy area to urge legislators to slow down.
Last week, bills that were part of Speaker Julie Menin’s mega-hearing in September were pushed back until December at the earliest, giving members more time to modify their proposals, multiple Council sources confirmed.
The delay came amid pushback from the DSA’s Transit Working Group, which says it wants any Council reform to more meaningfully reflect the needs of, and protections for, the city’s delivery worker advocacy groups.
“Legislating is sometimes frustratingly slow, but it’s that way for a reason,” said Alex Morano, the working group’s co-chair. “The Council needs to make sure they listen to the deliveristas when they do this they can’t just move on their own.”
The DSA targeted only a few of the 23 bills that Menin (D-Upper East Side) is considering, specifically the ones that would be the most consequential for the city’s delivery workers, who mostly use e-bikes to work as independent contractors for apps like Uber Eats, Doordash, Instacart and Grubhub.
One of the bills, for example, would ban the use of the Class 3 e-bikes preferred by delivery workers and empower the NYPD to randomly stop members of this large, mostly immigrant workforce for suspicion of using the banned bikes, which look identical to other electric bikes and differ only in top speed. (The ban on Class 3 bikes, which are only legal in New York City, is sponsored by Council Member Crystal Hudson, D-Fort Greene.)
“Even if they weren’t using a Class 3, [a delivery worker] could be stopped under the premise that the police thought they were [and it would increase] interactions with police,” said Morano. “It’s not going to help anyone to just change the law, issue a bunch of summonses to people and take their bikes. The Council needs to understand that it’s a nuanced issue and take a slower approach to legislating.”
The DSA has common ground with Los Deliveristas Unidos, which advocates for better working conditions for these app-workers and has previously raised similar concerns that the Council’s package blames the 80,000-strong workforce rather than improves working conditions for it.
“We are deeply concerned that the City Council’s street safety and micromobility package … fails to address the real needs of working-class bike riders and instead scapegoats Deliveristas,” said the group’s executive director, Ligia Guallpa, adding that it is “deeply misguided” to prioritize “enforcement and bans on legal devices over safe bike infrastructure.”
A second bill, Intro 224, also sponsored by Hudson, would target sellers of Class 3 bikes. That bill has the support of both organizations because it would ban the future sale and rental of Class 3 e-bikes.
But Hudson said her two bills work together to wean delivery workers from Class 3 e-bikes. The bill to ban their use would not go into effect for three years to give workers time to switch to different rides. She said she is committed to continue working with the deliveristas on both bills.
A third bill, Intro 985 from Council Member Shaun Abreu (D-Morningside Heights) would establish a trade-in program for the soon-to-be illegal Class 3 bikes. As is, the bill would force the city to operate a trade-in program that gave new bikes or vouchers to purchase new bikes to 10,000 delivery workers. The DOT allowed 400 workers to trade in their uncertified e-bikes in 2025 for new, fire-safe ones as part of a City Council mandated pilot program. The program cost $2 million for a fraction of the trade-ins that the new bill would mandate.
The deliverista group, and the DSA, want to make sure that any new regulation is coupled with worker protection. The city is currently fighting a lawsuit from some major app companies over a law that would protect workers from being fired, or “deactivated,” without cause. Until that lawsuit is settled, and the protections are in place, the Council shouldn’t be legislating more rules that the apps could use as an excuse to deactivate accounts, Morano said.
“Why are we trying to pass bills when there’s litigation happening that’s relevant to the laws we’re passing?” he said.
The Council is poised to pass its bill package in the coming months, a spokesperson said, adding that the governing body has been in conversation with a wide range of stakeholders, including Los Deliveristas Unidos.
Hudson said she expects to meet with the administration, the Speaker, and the workers to continue fine tuning the consequential bill package before it comes to a vote.
“I have already requested a meeting with the Administration, Speaker’s Office, bill sponsors, and representatives from the delivery worker community to discuss these proposals and work through remaining concerns. I am hopeful that the package will only move once this meeting happens,” she said.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/m.text:
Jimmy and the Jaywalkers' "Criminal Mischief" — live and unplugged.
I want my GershTV.
As Streetsblog Editor-in-Chief Gersh Kuntzman nears the end of his tenure atop this esteemed publication, we felt it was time to bring his license plate-correcting hit “Criminal Mischief” (1,277 plays on Spotify) to the small screen.
That’s right: The saga of Adam White — the attorney whose arrest and criminal mischief charge for fixing an obstructed license plate inspired Gersh to make hundreds of short videos of himself doing the same — is now a music video:
Gersh came to Streetsblog in 2018, 12 years into our existence and many decades into his own career in the news business. Under Gersh, we’ve seen massive readership growth, expanded our staff from four to 11, built a cutting-edge video journalism program and won several awards including a Polk, which is basically the Golden Globes of journalism.
Gersh’s knack for drawing the public’s attention has served Streetsblog throughout his time here, and will continue to serve us as he transitions into a senior editor role. His “Criminal Mischief” series exemplified how he turned Streetsblog’s righteous anger at government indifference to the streetscape into entertainment. The crusade earned the attention of The Daily Show, Inside Edition, the New Yorker and This American Life (to name a few).
Gersh likens his stepping down to George Washington declining to serve a third term so a new generation could lead. And like Washington, he hopes the institution he helped build can continue and thrive for centuries.
But we need your help to make that happen. We hope you’ll consider making a donation.
Streetsblog has no paywalls — our articles, videos and newsletters are all free — but we’re still a non-profit that relies on our readers and supporters to pay our salaries, provide our employees healthcare and continue to produce high quality, high impact journalism.
Use the widget below to support Streetsblog!

Mayor Mamdani celebrated the completion of the McGuinness Boulevard protected bike lane on Friday. (The City Reporter)
Gov. Hochul called on her congestion pricing foe U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to resign after Friday’s nationwide airport ground stop. (Gothamist)
FDNY fined lithium-ion charging and swapping company PopWheels for using unapproved charging cabinets after a seemingly unrelated “thermal event” knocked out 433 of the company’s batteries in August. (NY Post)
Watch The War on Cars podcast host Doug Gordon break down the lies and falsehoods spread by Brooklyn bus lane opponents. (Brooklyn Spoke via Instagram)
NYPD officers shot and killed a man on the Belt Parkway “following a suspected kidnapping.” (Gothamist)
An NYPD sergeant died in a one-vehicle crash last week where he struck a guardrail and overturned his Jeep at 3 a.m. on the Long Island Expressway (Daily News)
Long Islanders aren’t buying U.S. Rep. Laura Gillen’s “traffic” excuse for missing last week’s Pete Hegseth impeachment vote. (NY Post)
New York City is the best place to live car-free, according to a new study. (NY Times)
Brooklyn Community Board 1 wants parking meters to improve safety Wallabout Street. (Williamsburg 365)
The MTA wants to use AI cameras to detect trespassers on subway tracks. (Gothamist)
Mamdani is either getting rid of or rebranding the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group, depending on who you ask. (Politico, NY Post)
