https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.title: ICE Shot Pepper Spray Into a Car in a Traffic Stop, Then Broke a Detainee’s Collarbone
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.text:
Jose Rosito Roca Estrada and his friends were on their way to work in a van on June 27, when a car in front of them slammed on its brakes, forcing them to crash into it and ricochet backward on the busy highway.
Three more cars surrounded theirs, and an estimated 10 to 12 officers poured out. The agents screamed at the men to get out of the vehicle despite traffic whipping by, Roca Estrada and fellow passenger Elvis Manuel Mejia told The Intercept. The stalemate ended with the sound of shattering glass and an asphyxiating cloud of chemicals flooding the car.
According to a new federal lawsuit and photos from the scene shared with The Intercept, federal agents smashed the car’s back windows and “sprayed the occupants with pepper spray through the lowered side windows.”
Officers then dragged a scared and temporarily blinded Roca Estrada from the car. “I was afraid they might be robbing me,” 24-year-old Roca Estrada told The Intercept through a translator. “They did not identify themselves. I was worried they were kidnapping me because they were asking very personal questions.”
The June attack is one of six stories described in a lawsuit brought by several groups — including the American Civil Liberties Union of Virginia, the Washington Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, the Legal Aid Justice Center, and multiple law firms — alleging widespread “unlawful and dangerous” warrantless arrests by immigration officials in Virginia.
On behalf of Roca Estrada and other plaintiffs, the groups are suing the Department of Homeland Security, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Acting Director of ICE David Venturella, and ICE D.C. Field Office Director Robert Guadian. They’re asking the court in the Eastern District of Virginia to force DHS to comply with congressional limits on warrantless immigration arrests and prohibit the agency from making immigration arrests without legally required individual assessments.
“They have a mandate from the Trump administration … to get creative and make arrests, however they see fit,” said Sophia Gregg, an immigrants’ rights attorney at the ACLU of Virginia. “The agents are ill-trained, and even when they do violate the law, there are no consequences.”
Roca Estrada said that the officers demanded to search his pockets, and when he declined, an agent threw him to the ground headfirst and dug his knees into his upper back. He remembered screaming as pain began to radiate through his collarbone. An X-ray reviewed by The Intercept would later confirm it was broken.
According to Roca Estrada and the lawsuit, officers began to punch and hit him in the back, eventually twisting his arm to place him in handcuffs and into the vehicle. Roca Estrada said that nurses who examined him after the alleged assault told him that blood had filled his lungs, and the lawsuit notes he was diagnosed with a broken clavicle and a lung injury. At no point, the lawsuit alleges, did officers ask the necessary questions to determine whether Roca Estrada was deportable or whether he was a flight risk.
Immigration officers are only supposed to make warrantless immigration arrests if they have determined “probable cause” to believe a person is unlawfully present likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. But in an effort to meet the Trump administration’s nationwide quota of 3,000 immigration arrests per day, the lawsuit alleges, the Department of Homeland Security has chosen to pursue an unlawful policy and practice of “arrest-first, investigate-later” — leaving a trail of traumatized victims who should have never been arrested in the first place.
In the first year of the Trump administration, immigration arrests drastically increased in Virginia. According to the lawsuit, in 2025, ICE made “970 arrests each month in Virginia and Washington, D.C. — nearly five times the average monthly arrest volume in 2024.”
Reached by The Intercept, a DHS spokesperson said that agency had “arrested Jose Rosito Roca Estrada, an illegal alien from Guatemala,” using Roca Estrada’s full name even though The Intercept had not provided it, but denied that its officers “fractured a detainee’s collarbone.” The spokesperson did not deny that officials had deployed chemical weapons, saying, “staff relied on their training to gain compliance.”
“Claims that agents did not properly identify themselves are FALSE. When our heroic law enforcement officers conduct operations, they clearly identify themselves as law enforcement,” wrote the spokesperson. “At NO time were any of the detainees thrown to the ground during the arrest. Allegations that our officers fractured a detainee’s collarbone during the arrest are FALSE.”
Six weeks after Roca Estrada’s arrest, 18-year-old Britney Ramirez Corona was home caring for her 4-year-old sister in Norfolk, Virginia, when she found out ICE had detained her fiancé, his brother, and his brother-in-law.
It was another traffic stop, and Ramirez Corona, a U.S. citizen and recent high school graduate, had to go pick up their abandoned car. There, according to the lawsuit, an ICE officer demanded her identification, refused to let her get her wallet, and accused her of lying about who owned the vehicle. They handcuffed and pinned her, the lawsuit alleges — leaving her little sister to cry and wander into a busy road.
Eventually, ICE allowed another sister, 15, to come pick up the 4-year-old, then took Ramirez Corona into custody. She sat in “handcuffs, ankle shackles and a waist chain” for hours, according to the lawsuit, until her 15-year-old sister was able to bring her birth certificate — showing she was a natural-born U.S. citizen.
The lawsuit argues that Ramirez Corona’s arrest exemplifies an out-of-control trend of warrantless and often nonsensical arrests. Stephen Miller, then homeland security adviser and now the White House chief of staff, directed agents to “just go out there and arrest,” and the department seems to have complied.
“More than half of all the people ICE arrested in July 2026 did not have a criminal record,” the plaintiffs note. “And more than 500 people detained by ICE since January 2025 are U.S. citizens — another likely undercount — like Ms. Ramirez Corona.”
The same month that Roca Estrada says that federal agents temporarily blinded him, broke his collarbone, and beat him until his lungs filled with blood, Congress approved another $72 billion in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Immigrant advocacy groups warned ahead of the funding vote that additional money for ICE and President Donald Trump’s brutal immigration crackdown would mean more people would suffer a fate like Roca Estrada’s — or worse. The next month, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, both in their cars.
Physicians for Human Rights and the UC Berkeley Human Rights Center documented over 412 incidents of misuse of force by law enforcement agents at immigration protests from June 2025 to May 2026, including the use of chemical irritants like pepper balls and pepper spray — the same family of weapons Roca Estrada and Mejia suspect was set off in their car.
In ICE custody, 52 people have died during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, according to Human Rights Watch, while use-of-force by guards remains largely unknown.
“We have received many more reports of violent use of force against people,” said Jeff Migliozzi, the communications director for Freedom for Immigrants, which runs the National Immigration Detention Hotline, referencing hotline numbers from June and July. “The overwhelming forces of intimidation and fear and retaliation, the M.O. of ICE has not changed. But certainly, as more people are detained, there’s more incidents [of violence].”
The DHS spokesperson claimed that Roca Estrada and everyone arrested along with him were offered medical care but declined, adding that “one of the detainees indicated that he had a prior shoulder injury.”
Roca Estrada tells a very different story.
He says he spent the next month tossed between detention centers in Virginia and West Virginia. Because he was not given a sling, Roca Estrada fashioned one for his broken collarbone out of bedsheets. He said he largely went without medical care despite agonizing pain that prevented him from laying down at night.
Roca Estrada said it got so bad he nearly fainted, at which point he was taken to a hospital.
“After medical personnel offered to document his injuries and consult a forensic physician, officers abruptly removed him from the hospital and returned him to detention,” the lawsuit alleges. “For weeks thereafter, Defendants failed to provide the promised follow-up care.”
According to the lawsuit, none of this should have happened because Roca Estrada never should have been detained in the first place.
The suit alleges that immigration officers never asked the 24-year-old “about his immigration history, whether he possessed lawful status, where he worked, how long he had lived in Virginia, whom he lived with, whether he had family or community ties in the United States, or similar questions to assess whether he was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”
Other stories in the lawsuit follow a similar pattern. Catarina Rebeca Us Lopez, a 24-year-old woman from Guatemala, was detained in Centreville, Virginia, during a traffic stop around 6:00 a.m. with her husband. She alleges that masked officers blocked her car at a traffic light and forced her and her husband from the vehicle.
The officers falsely claimed that her husband had a deportation order, according to the lawsuit. But when her husband asked questions about the stop, Us Lopez alleges an agent pepper-sprayed him in the face and threatened to draw their weapons.
According to Us Lopez, officers did not “inquire about her immigration status, ask where she lived, inquire about her family, ask about her ties to the community, or otherwise conduct any individualized investigation concerning whether she was lawfully present in the United States or likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”
Instead, she claims that officers ignored her as she explained that she had work authorization and did not have a deportation order in place, and allegedly mocked her requests for answers and legal assistance.
For Roca Estrada, his physical injuries and trauma left him unable to work for a month. While he was detained, he also lost his apartment and had his personal belongings sent back to Guatemala without his consent, according to the lawsuit.
“The way that I was arrested … and the immense pain that I had to go through during this whole experience,” said Roca Estrada. “What happened to me was not just.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

Inside the Epic Battle Over Control of a CA Grocery Union
For over 40 years, one family has controlled (and reaped the spoils from) a 23,000-member California union. Rank-and-file workers are trying to change that — and say they are facing surveillance, intimidation, and interference from their own union’s staff.
Eric Marcuz is one of the most naturally gifted rank-and-file organizers I have ever met. Overflowing with passion for his union, love for his coworkers, and C4 Energy drinks, he has been spending what little time he has outside of working full time as a dairy clerk at a Safeway grocery store in Redding, California, driving for hours to visit grocery stores across the state and talk with his fellow union members.
Marcuz is running for president of United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 8–Golden State as part of the At What Cost slate, a group of seven rank-and-file grocery workers who are committed to giving their coworkers something that should be taken for granted: an opportunity to choose who leads their union. Standing in their way are staff supporters of Jacques Loveall, the local’s longtime president, whose family has maintained tight control over the union for more than four decades.
Loveall inherited the presidency from his father, Jack, in 2004, through an appointment by the union’s executive board. Neither father nor son ever faced a contested election for the presidency, and the union’s top officers and executive board have been filled through appointments rather than competitive elections. The Lovealls seem straight out of central casting for a Hollywood depiction of out-of-touch, self-serving business unionists, complete with exorbitant salaries, palatial offices, a private jet, and even a bronze bust of the family patriarch.
The At What Cost slate is fighting to introduce real democracy into their union. To do that, they must first collect hundreds of signatures from their fellow union members scattered across California. They have until November 17 to collect and deliver the required number of signatures. If they are successful, ballots will be mailed on November 21 and counted on December 7. The reformers have only the next few weeks during one of the grocery industry’s busiest times of year to campaign — if the union’s staff and leadership don’t stop them.
The UFCW is one of the largest private sector unions in North America, representing more than a million workers, primarily in grocery stores, retail, meatpacking, and food processing. These are some of the lowest-paid and most exploited workers in the labor movement, but also some of the most indispensable to daily life, as the COVID-19 pandemic made painfully clear. Nearly everyone comes face-to-face with a grocery worker every week. This gives grocery workers a strategically important position in an increasingly concentrated industry where powerful corporations squeeze workers through understaffing, speedup, and automation while consumers struggle with rising grocery bills.
Fights for democracy within megalocals — often the combination of multiple small union locals to create huge bodies that are difficult for rank-and-file workers to have real democratic say in, like UFCW Local 8 — have the potential to connect the fight for better wages and working conditions at companies like Albertsons, Kroger, Vons, Save Mart, and Safeway to the broader working-class struggle against runaway inequality. The stakes of this local election extend far beyond who will run the union. It raises the question of what kind of power tens of thousands of grocery workers could exercise if they were organized and mobilized to fight together.
Which is why, after donating to their campaign, I traveled to California to spend a few days observing Marcuz and other slate members as they crisscrossed the state gathering signatures, visiting nearly twenty grocery stores in multiple towns and speaking with dozens of unionized grocery workers. I heard firsthand how grocery workers are being crushed by the rising cost of living and stagnating wages, how excited many are at the possibility of new union leadership, and how terrified some of them are of the union’s current leaders and staff.
Dozens of workers described how union staff have been openly sharing their plans to harass and intimidate the At What Cost slate members as they try to gather signatures. Staff are also following behind At What Cost slate members and pressuring the workers they have spoken with into withdrawing their signatures to get them on the ballot, using a special form the staff have made specifically for this purpose.
One grocery worker, who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation, described how union staff were openly discussing efforts to prevent Marcuz from qualifying for the ballot. Staff explained that if Marcuz failed to collect the required 443 signatures, there would be no contested election and Jacques Loveall would remain president. Staff were out doing everything they could to keep him from reaching that threshold.
One produce clerk who has been a union member for over thirty years described Local 8’s well-known use of intimidation tactics to crush union democracy as “Jim Crow unionism.” He refused to sign Marcuz’s petition because he didn’t want “to end up in a ditch” for crossing staff.
The heavy-handed intimidation tactics I’ve seen here are clearly having the intended effect on some union members. But for others, watching their own union’s staff try to stop a fellow worker from running for office has backfired. Ryan Crahm, a longtime Save Mart employee, said he wasn’t going to get involved until he saw four union staff representatives swarm Marcuz in his store.
“It was straight up intimidation, and it made me pissed,” said Crahm. “I want to ask Jacques Loveall why he is so afraid to have someone run against him. And I want to know why it is that we never saw any staff reps before, but now that there might be an election, they’re in our stores all the time.”
At What Cost
Donning a baseball cap and a backpack filled with petitions, flyers, stickers, and homemade bandanas, the forty-three-year-old Marcuz is excited, urgent, and confident. Visiting store after store from 5 in the morning to 11 at night, he takes his time, listening, asking questions, and sharing his own experiences. His approach to petitioning resembles deep canvassing — a patient, open, and story-driven approach to sharing experiences while engaging with workers during a union drive or voters during an election campaign shown to be effective at winning hearts and changing minds — more than typical rapid-fire signature gathering. Few of his conversations run less than twenty minutes, and they typically cover a range of topics.
Workers repeatedly open up to Marcuz about their frustration with the union contract’s pay scale and how the basic building blocks of the good life — home ownership, a reliable vehicle, vacations — feel increasingly out of reach. California fast food workers have a $20 minimum wage, but under Local 8’s contract, it takes members working full time about five years to reach that hourly rate. Since many grocery workers struggle to get full-time hours, it takes many of them seven or eight years, even in the delis and in-store Starbucks franchises, to earn what they could be making on their first day working at a neighboring In-N-Out Burger.
Members also described unpredictable schedules, chronic understaffing, and the chaos caused by new artificial-intelligence-assisted inventory systems. Many were frustrated not only by the erosion of their contracts but also by how little say they had in negotiating them. There are no elected bargaining teams, and contracts are negotiated exclusively by the president and other appointed leaders and staff.
Members, including several stewards, repeatedly complained about union staff who are rarely in the stores, don’t return phone calls, can’t answer questions about the contract, and are seemingly never around when members need them. The local’s website doesn’t provide information on the twenty-plus appointed vice presidents who allegedly represent members, or which staff representatives service their stores and how to contact them. The local also refuses to provide members with digital copies of their contracts.
Remarkably, despite talking to dozens of union members, including more than a few who had worked in these stores for decades, I couldn’t find a single Local 8 member who had actually met Jacques Loveall. If the union was primarily known for anything, it is for its absence.
“My mind was blown by how little visibility we had into our contracts, union negotiations, and the leadership’s decision making,” said Marcuz. “I started driving down to the union meetings in Sacramento. They’re two and a half hours from my house and held once a quarter at 8 at night. I went to my first meeting, and it literally lasted five minutes. I was the only member there.”
Marcuz says he spoke up at a different meeting and asked whether, given the vast jurisdiction the local covers, quarterly meetings could rotate between different cities across the state to encourage more members to attend. He says the staff laughed him out of the room.
So Marcuz started a petition, collecting three hundred signatures from grocery workers in his area demanding that the meetings at least be live streamed over Zoom so members could listen in. This time, he says, staff angrily shouted him out of the room.
“Every time we tried to get involved, to make our union more responsive to the membership, we got smacked down. And once we start losing faith in our own union, we are on the road to no longer having one,” said Marcuz.
The At What Cost slate is proposing sweeping changes in how the union functions. They want elected bargaining teams, open negotiations that members can attend, local meetings that encourage member participation, a $20 minimum wage in grocery, and aggressive contract campaigns backed by leadership that isn’t afraid to strike over ambitious demands.
Marcuz and his small rebel army want to elect new officers, win better contracts, and fundamentally change who is exercising power inside their union, transforming members from mere spectators into active participants in the fight to better their working conditions and lives.
Not a Union, but a Family Business
The Loveall family has held tight control over UFCW Local 8–Golden State and its predecessor, UFCW Local 588, for more than four decades. Jack Loveall was first appointed president of the union in 1984 and ran it continuously until he retired in 2004, when his son Jacques was appointed by the union’s executive board to succeed him. At the time he retired, Jack Loveall was one of the highest-paid union officials in the country, making over $1 million a year in today’s money. The local owned a twin-engine business jet and had two pilots on staff to shuttle Loveall around the state. He oversaw the construction of a new union headquarters in Roseville, near his personal residence, which featured an 1,100-square-foot presidential office, the size of a modest house, complete with a sauna and marble wet bar.
The local also paid $28,000 a year to cover the cost of Loveall’s membership in an exclusive Roseville country club, an expense the union president justified to the press by stressing that it was a place to talk business with employers. During his final year in office, there were seven Loveall family members on staff, comprising a quarter of the union’s payroll.
Loveall built his empire through a series of mergers that expanded the union’s membership and assets while consolidating his control over its leadership. According to a 2004 investigation by the Contra Costa Times, critics accused Loveall of securing mergers by rewarding the officers of absorbed locals with lucrative positions in his administration.
When Local 498, a Sacramento meatcutters’ union with 1,600 members and $2.3 million in assets, merged into Local 588, its former president saw his annual pay jump from roughly $12,500 to $85,000, while its former treasurer’s pay increased from less than $11,000 to nearly $76,000. The mergers helped Loveall build an increasingly loyal staff and executive board, with well-paid positions that extended to the relatives of some officers.
But Loveall wasn’t always successful. Members of Local 1179 put a halt to a proposed merger with Local 588 by organizing an opposition campaign centered on Loveall’s pay and perks, arguing their dues would be better spent if their local remained independent rather than contributing to Loveall’s lavish lifestyle.
Responding to these criticisms, Loveall told the press, “Just because we run a union doesn’t mean we’re supposed to be paupers” and said that “my members don’t want me driving around in a stagecoach or working in some shithouse office.” The elder Loveall also bragged about how tightly he controlled the union membership, saying that members were “ready to do what I tell them to do.”
Jacques Loveall took over the top spot in 2004 but kept his father on the payroll earning more than $70,000 a year as a consultant, on top of his pension, until the elder Loveall died in 2020. Jacques is also chair of the Loveall Foundation for Children, a nonprofit founded in honor of his father and described on their website as being founded and run by “the staff, family and friends of UFCW 8–Golden State.” The union has financially supported the nonprofit for years, including $25,000 in 2025 alone, and at least one major collective bargaining agreement negotiated by Loveall obligates the employer to contribute three cents for every hour employees work directly to the Loveall Foundation.
The salary of the president is set by the union’s top officers and vice presidents, all of whom were appointed over time by other top officers and vice presidents as vacancies arose. At no point over the past four decades have any of the Local’s top officers or the twenty-plus vice presidents actually been elected by union’s membership.
Discussing this reality with other union members, Marcuz is blunt: “Our local hasn’t been acting like a union. It’s been run like a family business.”
A Long History of Schemes and Intimidation
There have been past attempts by union members to challenge the Lovealls’ tight control over the union. But those who have tried have repeatedly encountered a familiar combination of intimidation, interference, and mergers that postponed or eliminated the possibility of a contested election.
Union activists in UFCW Local 1179 who were active in the effort to block the proposed merger with Local 588 reportedly experienced aggressive intimidation and surveillance from Loveall’s associates. According to an investigation by the Contra Costa Times, union staff began following reform activist Michael Ross-Smith, staking out his home and trailing him in union vehicles. In June 1994, three Local 588 business agents following Ross-Smith rear-ended his car in Walnut Creek, an incident documented in a police traffic collision report.
A union representative acknowledged to the press that staff had been following Ross-Smith but defended the practice as a legitimate effort to investigate Loveall’s political opponents.
In 1997, Raley’s grocery clerk Jack Nordby attempted to challenge Jack Loveall for the presidency. Nordby wanted to cut the excessive salaries of union officers and open contract negotiations to the membership. Following his announced run for office, Nordby alleges that union representatives followed him and his family, harassed him while he collected nomination signatures, and pressured workers into withdrawing their signatures from his petition. So many signatures were withdrawn that Nordby failed to qualify for the ballot.
Another reformer, Lorna Greenlee, described similar intimidation. Greenlee said two union representatives confronted her while she collected signatures, then berated her for hours. She and her daughter also reported seeing union representatives watching their home. Although Greenlee said she had nearly collected enough signatures to run against Loveall, she eventually withdrew out of fear.
The Lovealls have also benefited from mergers that postponed contested elections. In 2006, another reform slate, led by longtime meatcutter Doug Slaydon, was preparing to challenge Jacques Loveall. But before members could vote, Local 588 merged with Local 1288 to create UFCW Local 8–Golden State, postponing the election until 2008. Slaydon, who was fired from Safeway shortly after his attempted run for local union office, believed the merger was designed to prevent his challenge.
Nearly two decades later, the same maneuvers again threatened to derail the current election. In October, Local 8 members received an election notice announcing that ballots would be mailed in November. But buried in the notice was a provision stating that the election would be canceled if the local completed a merger with an organization called Staffing Agencies Federated Employees (SAFE).
None of the rank-and-file members of the At What Cost slate had ever heard of SAFE. The organization claimed to represent thousands of workers, but there was no evidence of where those workers were organized or what contracts SAFE had negotiated. What they did find were more connections to Loveall: a family member was listed as SAFE’s president on its initial federal filing just eight months before the election.
The At What Cost slate, working with the UFCW reform organization Essential Workers for Democracy, on which Marcuz serves on the organizing committee, challenged the proposed merger and called for a Department of Labor investigation. After a federal investigator began asking questions, Local 8 announced that the merger had been postponed indefinitely, five days after it was announced.
The election was back on. But that doesn’t mean the rank-and-file reformers would be allowed to campaign without interference.
Fear and Intimidation on the Campaign Trail
On November 2, Marcuz drove to the union’s headquarters in Roseville to pick up the nomination petitions that he and his slate needed to start collecting the hundreds of signatures required to qualify for the ballot. From there, he headed south toward Fresno to begin collecting signatures from grocery workers.
But shortly after leaving the union headquarters, where a bronze bust of Jack Loveall stands in the central hallway, Marcuz noticed a black pickup truck following him. When he stopped for gas, the truck stopped too. He recognized the driver as Jeff Berns, a senior Local 8 staff representative whose brother, Mark Berns, was appointed by Jaques Loveall to chair the election.
Multiple members of the Berns family have been on the local’s payroll going back decades. Mark Berns is currently the highest paid nonofficer staff member at the local, earning more than most of the vice presidents. He has repeatedly served as the local’s election chair, including in 2009, when the Department of Labor found that Local 8 had violated federal labor law by burying an election notice inside a union newsletter, mailed just a week after another issue with a nearly identical cover. The notice was so inconspicuous that members could easily have mistaken the second mailing for a duplicate and thrown it away without realizing an election was approaching.
Despite finding that the local had violated federal labor law, because investigators couldn’t identify any member who said they would have run for office against Loveall, the department concluded that the violation had not affected the election’s outcome and took no further action.
According to Marcuz, Jeff Berns told him that he intended to follow him throughout the day to make sure workers heard the Loveall team’s side of the election. And that’s exactly what he did. Berns followed Marcuz to a Save Mart in Fresno, where Marcuz and fellow slate member Mike Romero say three union representatives, including longtime Vice President John Micheletti, confronted them and interfered with their attempts to collect signatures. According to Marcuz, Berns threatened to invalidate every signature his slate collected.
This behavior continued as Marcuz left Fresno and traveled to meet Silas Saldivar, a twenty-six-year UFCW member and head clerk, at the Safeway where he worked in Modesto. Marcuz became so concerned for his safety that he called Saldivar, and they agreed to instead meet at Saldivar’s house.
I traveled with Marcuz to the Safeway in Modesto, where Saldivar recounted the story to me.
“I walked outside into my driveway to meet Eric and saw Jeff Berns pull up in front of my house in his truck. John Micheletti parked in front of my neighbor’s house and then got out of his car and started walking toward us. I looked at Eric and said, ‘Dude, is this guy serious right now?’ Those two guys sat outside and watched my house for over an hour,” said Saldivar. “I didn’t feel safe. I still don’t, honestly.”
While Saldivar was recounting this story to me, two union staff showed up at his Safeway. They kept their distance but made it clear that they were watching us. One pulled out his phone and began recording us.
Marcuz estimated that he had been followed for seven hours and roughly three hundred miles on November 2. The following morning, he filed a police report alleging stalking and harassment.
The intimidation hasn’t been limited to Marcuz and the other candidates. Less than a week later, Mike Denham, a Local 8 staff representative, showed up at the Perfect Union cannabis dispensary in Shasta Lake, California, where Marcuz had recently visited and received overwhelming support from members. Many workers were frustrated that they had never seen a copy of their union contract and couldn’t get one from the local. One supporter had asked Marcuz to leave a nomination petition so workers on other shifts could sign it, planning to return it to him later.
According to multiple workers who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from their union, Denham, the union staffer assigned to the dispensary, subsequently arrived and demanded that they either destroy the petition or turn it over to him so he could destroy it himself.
According to several members, Denham repeatedly insisted that Marcuz had acted “illegally” by leaving the petition with workers at the store. When workers refused to turn it over, Denham eventually left in frustration.
“It’s absolutely insane that our own union staff would come into our workplace to intimidate us to stop us from participating in our own union,” one worker told me.
Federal labor law guarantees the right of union members to participate in democratic elections. The conduct of Local 8’s leadership and staff could have legal consequences.
“The quantity and variety of the efforts by Loveall’s team are not only shocking, but likely unlawful, and could lead to the Department of Labor having to step in and rerun the election,” said Will Bloom, law professor at City University of New York and board member of the Association for Union Democracy.
Discouraging Participation Is Anti-Union
At a Vons grocery store in Fresno, multiple workers confessed to us that their union staff representative, Justin Putney, aggressively pressured them to sign the Loveall slate’s nomination petition. Workers told me Putney had forcefully instructed them to call him if Marcuz or anyone else from the At What Cost slate showed up so that he could come down and run them out of the store. It wasn’t long before that happened.
Members working in the Starbucks kiosk were signing Marcuz’s petition when Putney came running up. “There he is,” Putney announced. “I wish I could say it was nice to meet you, but it isn’t.”
Putney proceeded to lecture Marcuz about how “there is a right way and a wrong way to do things.” Putney, he said, had done things the right way. He had worked his way up through the union, starting as a steward before being appointed to a member advisory committee, then the executive board, and finally landing a position on staff.
Putney failed to mention that his father is also a longtime paid executive board member in the union — a point Marcuz raised and Putney didn’t dispute. According to Putney, Marcuz, by contrast, was doing it wrong. “You’re like someone who has been playing rec league soccer saying he wants to jump into the big leagues and play professional soccer.”
Marcuz responded that he believed democracy was the right way for members to decide who should lead their union.
“And I don’t think you should have the right to run for a job that you have no qualifications for,” Putney shot back.
Marcuz challenged Putney over the union’s bargaining record. “Our last contract was horrible,” Marcuz said. “It only provided a dollar raise for topped-out, high-seniority clerks. Nobody else got anything. We are barely able to survive on our wages. I can’t afford a house for my family. I can’t buy a truck. We can’t afford to shop in the stores where we work.”
“You can’t show me anywhere in the country where grocery workers have a better contract,” Putney insisted.
“Any contract that the membership fights for and wins together is better than one that is delivered from on high without our involvement,” Marcuz replied. “Members should be in the room when negotiating is happening. We should own the outcome.”
I introduced myself as a journalist following Marcuz’s campaign and asked Putney why he had rushed down to the store to confront him.
“He is a threat to the future of our members,” Putney told me. “It’s my job to protect the membership, and he represents a threat to that.”
I asked whether he thought it was appropriate for union staff to confront members who were exercising their democratic rights, and whether he had been instructing workers to alert him whenever Marcuz showed up so he could interfere with his campaigning.
“Yes,” Putney acknowledged.
Marcuz was incredulous. “How am I supposed to exercise my rights if everywhere I go I’m being accosted by people on the union’s payroll?” he asked. “I have a right to speak with members, and you’re showing up here just to stop that from happening.”
Putney maintained that he was simply encouraging workers to be cautious about what they signed. Marcuz wasn’t buying it.
“Discouraging people from participating in the democratic process of a union election is anti-union. This process should strengthen us as a union, because it should cause the incumbent union leadership to state and defend their platform. We should debate our visions and what we are fighting for, and the members should get to vote on the best ideas,” said Marcuz.
“But that is not what is happening. What’s happening is that I’m being followed, my conversations are being interrupted, and I’m being harassed by staff who have no honest interest in what I have to say and are only trying to stop others from hearing what I have to say. Let’s be honest. Your goal is to make sure that we don’t have a choice.”
Putney denied the accusation, but Marcuz continued.
“You tried to merge with a fake union that doesn’t really exist and that Jacques Loveall put his cousin in charge of. Staff followed me three hundred miles and sat in front of a member’s house for over an hour to try to intimidate me from participating. You have encouraged people in this store to report to you that I’m here so that you can come here and interfere with my campaigning,” he said. “None of these actions are to prove to the membership that your vision for our union is better. All of those actions are to prevent democracy in our union.”
As the exchange continued, a crowd of grocery workers were gathering to listen. Eventually, a distraught-looking manager approached Putney and asked to speak with him privately. Marcuz took that as his cue. We left the store so he could continue gathering signatures, hoping that he wouldn’t be followed.
“Solidarity Works”
Loveall and the executive board members supporting him are running together on the “Solidarity Works Team” slate. And their materials look deceptively similar to official communications from the union. “Solidarity Works” has been Local 8’s slogan for at least fifteen years, appearing regularly in union communications, especially those concerning contract negotiations. Loveall himself has described it “as the motto of UFCW 8–Golden State.”
A recent Solidarity Works Team mailer sent to every Local 8 union member’s personal address is virtually indistinguishable from an ordinary union communication. For one, the return address on the mailers is the union headquarters. For another, it features Loveall’s photograph and title as union president, invokes the local’s record of bargaining victories, and describes the Solidarity Works Team as a “network of member contacts” that lays “the groundwork for the solidarity, communication, and mobilization that will be needed when bargaining begins.”
A QR code on the mailer links to the Solidarity Works Team website, where members are encouraged to join the team by providing their contact information. What the mailer and website don’t mention is that the Solidarity Works Team is running for reelection. There is no information on any of the slate’s candidates other than Loveall, and the word “election” doesn’t appear anywhere on the mailer or the slate’s website.
The website is carefully crafted to lead members to believe they are signing up as part of the process of preparing for contract bargaining, not agreeing to receive information to vote in support of the current leadership in an election that isn’t mentioned anywhere.
While out visiting stores, multiple grocery workers told me that the union staff representatives had asked them to update their contact information to prepare for upcoming negotiations. The representatives handed workers their phones and had them fill out a sign-up page, only for the workers to later discover it was to receive messages from the Solidarity Works Team slate. Those members subsequently received text messages notifying them that “petition signing is under way” and warning, “Reminder: DO NOT sign anything for anyone you don’t know. Solidarity Works!”
The Loveall slate’s materials also issue stark warnings about “anti-union campaigns” and “attempts to weaken your bargaining power and possibly your benefits package.” In a video posted on the slate’s website, staff warn: “Be very careful with your signatures. Do not sign petitions. Do not sign cards. Do not trust the word of people who say they are with our union that you are not familiar with. Again, you should not be signing anything for anyone you do not know.”
Anyone who has organized a union will recognize these talking points. They’re the same warnings employers routinely deploy during union-busting campaigns: beware of outsiders, don’t trust anyone asking for your signature, don’t believe their promises, and don’t risk the wages and benefits you already have. Only this time, these warnings aren’t coming from an employer but from the union’s own leadership.
Jacques Lovall did not respond to an interview request for this story.
“We Are at War”
At a Safeway in Lincoln, a suburb outside Sacramento, I meet Mary MacDonnell, who has worked in the grocery industry for over thirty years and supports the At What Cost slate. The night before we met, John Micheletti arrived at her store and began badgering her and others to sign the Solidarity Works Team slate’s petition. Micheletti loudly announced to a group of members gathered near her that “we are at war. The union is under attack. That is why I am here.”
MacDonnell has just finished her shift, and Marcuz and I are sitting on the bench outside the front entrance of the grocery store talking with her. She is emphatic that her union should be an organization of workers, run by workers, to fight for workers. That can’t happen if the union’s leadership is completely insulated from the membership and the staff and executive board are packed with relatives and appointed loyalists.
She says she was drawn to the At What Cost slate because they practiced what they preached. The slate is encouraging members to talk and listen to each other, to build relationships, to be courageous and more ambitious, and to see greater member involvement as a source of strength for the union, not a threat to be mocked or ham-fistedly suppressed.
As we are talking, one of the Loveall slate supporters from the night before arrives. He posts up with his back against the brick wall on the other side of the store’s entrance, conspicuously watching us.
“This has been hella intimidating,” MacDonnell sighs as she eyes the man. But then her resolve seems to harden. “I respect Eric, but at the end of the day, this is bigger than any particular candidate. I want a choice. And I’m just not going to allow them to take that away from us.”

https://hyperallergic.com/what-mary-love.author: Stephanie Wambugu
https://hyperallergic.com/what-mary-love.text:
What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind
"Requiem" is a fitting self-elegy for the painter, precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.
Upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful.
The work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them.
The result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows.
Though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous through the hands of a master craftsman.
During this formative and fruitful period between the 1970s and 1990s, when her visual language and iconoclastic artistic sensibility crystallized, O’Neal was also coming into her own as an artist. She was a groundbreaking student, becoming the first Black woman to receive an MFA from Columbia University in 1969, and in 1985, she became the first African American professor to receive tenure in UC Berkeley’s Department of Art Practice.
The back room offers a rich sketch of the painter’s life as it intersected with both world history and art history. Born in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1942, Jim Crow was fully in place in the American South during the artist’s childhood. She attended Howard University in 1960 alongside David Driskell and Lois Mailou Jones, dated the activist Stokely Carmichael, and was an activist in her own right.
The archival materials reveal the cultural and political concerns of O’Neal’s time. It’s all the more remarkable that she navigated these constraints while retaining the verve and genuine, delightful strangeness these paintings must have necessitated. “Untitled” (n.d.) gets at the humor and irreverence of O’Neal’s style. An Uncle Sam-like figure, half-covered in chalky white paint, evokes a satirical Ralph Bakshi cartoon, with many identifying features erased. It has a winking quality. Though political in nature, it foregrounds O’Neal’s formal concerns, which circle mainly around the possibilities of certain pigments (like the enveloping darkness of lampblack contrasted with punchy neons) and the permeable boundary between abstraction and figuration. It is this formal rigor that made O’Neal trailblazing in more ways than one –– both as a Black American shattering institutional barriers and as a woman painter making important interventions into the inherited, lionized artistic movements of the Color Field, Abstract Expressionism, and Minimalism.
“Race Woman Series #7” (1992–93) dramatizes the tension between the structural or compositional and the political, suggesting that it was an enduring preoccupation for the artist. A dazed face vaguely springs up from a prominent green being, which could just be read as an indecipherable scrawl, while a white specter at the top of the canvas drips over it. O’Neal’s use of color is frenetic and instinctive, resulting in a painting that is too varied to slot into a clear interpretation. Like the Klannish chiaroscuro of Norman Lewis’ “Alabama” (1960), the legibility of “Race Woman Series #7” relies on the light its instructive title sheds on it.
But unlike Lewis, when we search for correlation between O’Neal’s caption and the canvas, we are pulled deeper into her self-reflexive, numinous and unrepeatable idiom, which makes its own intuitive sense and, anyway, seeks to go beyond sense-making into the terrain of near-mystical experience.
Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem continues at Boesky Gallery (509 West 24th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan) through December 19. The exhibition is organized by the gallery.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-public-sc.title: NYC public school enrollment drops yet again, even as some schools overflow
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-public-sc.author: Jessica Gould
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-public-sc.text:
New York City’s public school enrollment declined once again this fall, a trend that’s already added pressure to school budgets, and accelerated calls for closures and mergers that can be divisive in local communities.
As of this month, 863,100 kids were enrolled in the city’s public schools, including the city's 2K, 3K and 4K programs, according to a preliminary count released by the Mamdani administration on Monday.
That’s a 2.6% decline from last year and part of a downward trend that has continued for more than a decade. The exception to that was in 2023, when public schools saw an influx of migrant students.
According to city data, the school system has lost roughly 200,000 students over the past ten years, even as it has expanded public early childhood programs.
Experts have said the decline is driven by lower birth rates and families with children leaving the city. The decline is not unique to New York City: dwindling public school enrollment is affecting school districts and upending education budgets across the country.
Some of the steepest enrollment declines have been concentrated around central Brooklyn, the Bronx and Washington Heights, according to a report the city comptroller released last month. Schools chancellor Kamar Samuels has said 30,000 students attend small or underenrolled schools.
But enrollment is not declining evenly across the nation’s largest school system. Highly sought-after schools in parts of Manhattan and Brooklyn are exploring additions to accommodate students, even as schools in adjacent neighborhoods see their rosters shrink.
Samuels has called the enrollment decline one of the system’s biggest challenges. Over the summer, he convened working groups in five districts across the city to develop community-driven solutions to the intertwined issues of declining enrollment, class size, and segregation.
“We have to figure out what is the thing that we are going to do on behalf of our most marginalized young people, oftentimes, but on behalf of every single child in your district,” Samuels said at the time.
Samuels has said he expects to form similar working groups throughout the city.
Small schools are expensive because they still need enough administrators and teachers to oversee and instruct students. At the same time, many small schools can’t afford art programs, advanced courses or extracurriculars, putting their students at an educational disadvantage.
Ana Champeny, vice president for research at the Citizens Budget Commission, said the enrollment decline shows a “worrisome trend leading to schools that are too small to be efficient or effective, underutilized buildings, and ultimately, funding inequities between schools.”
Champeny said the city should end its practice of funding schools based on previous enrollment levels – known as “hold harmless” – that’s been in place most years since the Covid pandemic, and that more mergers and closures have to be on the table.
But past efforts to merge and close schools have been explosive, and decreasing funding for schools can cause a political backlash.
Mamdani administration officials did not respond to questions about whether there would be funding cuts related to declining enrollment this year.
City Hall spokesperson Penelope Birnbaum said the enrollment numbers underscore the need to address the city’s affordability crisis, and emphasized the investments made in free childcare, including 2K.
“With this enrollment data, we’re seeing the implications of the affordability crisis in real time – birth rates are down, immigration has slowed, and New Yorkers are leaving the city they love,” said Birnbaum. “We’ve taken major steps towards building a city that is affordable and livable, including through the launch of 2-K this fall, but this data is proof that we cannot stop or slow down.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/mayor-disbanding.title: The Mayor Is Disbanding the SRG—But What Exactly Does That Mean?
https://hellgatenyc.com/mayor-disbanding.author: Nick Pinto
https://hellgatenyc.com/mayor-disbanding.text:
Following through on a longstanding campaign promise, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday morning that he is disbanding the NYPD's Strategic Response Group, a controversial unit established in 2015 to combat terrorism, whose mission soon expanded to include the policing and, as alleged in numerous civil rights lawsuits, the suppression of constitutionally protected protests.
The mayor released a statement along with his police commissioner, Jessica Tisch. "I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD's ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat," Tisch's statement read in part. "These changes will make us a stronger, more effective department."
What does the announcement actually mean?

Welcome to City Limits’ NYC Housing Calendar, a weekly feature where we round up the latest housing and land use-related events and hearings, as well as affordable housing lotteries that are ending soon.
Know of an event we should include in next week’s calendar? Email us.
Upcoming housing and land use-related events:

More here.

- Tuesday, Nov. 17 at 10 a.m.: The Department of City Planning will hold a public hearing to on new proposed rules to how the city assigns and verifies street addresses. More here.
- Tuesday, Nov. 17, 10 a.m to 2 p.m.: Manhattan State Sen. Liz Krueger’s office will offer assistance to constituents applying for the city’s rent freeze programs for seniors and renters with disabilities (SCRIE and DRIE). More here.
- Tuesday, Nov. 17 at 11 a.m.: The NYC Council’s committees on Finance and Housing and Buildings will hold an oversight hearing on increasing homeownership opportunities in the city. More here.

The Commission will hold public hearings for: 5801 Amboy Road Commercial Overlay, 1584 Flatbush Avenue Rezoning, and 240 Nassau Street. More here.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, and the Shanghai Museum on November 16 signed a Memorandum of Understanding cementing the two institutions’ commitment to collaboration via exhibitions, research initiatives, and curatorial exchange. Met director and CEO Max Hollein and Shanghai Museum director Chu Xiaobo signed the document at People’s Square, at the Shanghai institution.
The MoU extends a partnership begun between the two museums in 1980, when the Shanghai Museum took part in the Met’s exhibition “The Great Bronze Age of China.” Since then, the institutions have exchanged loans for a variety of exhibitions; their first cooperatively organized exhibition, “Recasting the Past: The Art of Chinese Bronzes, 1100–1900,” took place last year at both venues.
“The friendship between the two institutions, spanning more than four decades, is built on a shared passion for art and cultural heritage and mutual trust,” said Chu in a statement. “The MoU will further strengthen cooperation in collections, exhibition planning and scholarship, enabling Chinese audiences to experience artistic treasures from around the world while introducing more international visitors to the rich Chinese civilization. The partnership will help foster dialogue and mutual understanding between different cultures.”
“Our collaboration with the Shanghai Museum is rooted in a shared belief in the power of art to foster understanding between cultures,” said Hollein in a statement, noting that he had been impressed by Chu’s leadership of the institution. “This agreement reflects the Met’s deep commitment to extending the reach of our collection and cultivating meaningful connections with global audiences. Such rigorous scholarship and international cooperation are central to the museum’s mission, and we are excited to bring our longstanding institutional friendship to a new level.”
The announcement of the collaboration comes two days before the Shanghai Museum opening of “Jewelry: The Body Transformed, Treasures from the Metropolitan Museum of Art,” a traveling exhibition for which the Shanghai Museum provided objects in addition to those from the Met collection. Later this year, the Met will loan five works for a show at Shanghai Museum titled “Sonorous Silence: The Painting and Calligraphy of Bada Shanren on the 400th Anniversary of His Birth.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Democrats Finally Ran as Economic Populists—Thanks to Newcomers
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jared Abbott, Frederick DeVeaux
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Finally Ran as Economic Populists—Thanks to Newcomers
We analyzed 16 years of Democratic campaigns. The 2026 surge in attacks on billionaires and corruption came from newcomers, not party leaders, and they’re about to remake the caucus.
Ten years after Bernie Sanders’s first presidential run, the left’s argument that economic populism is the way to win back working-class voters has gone mainstream. Within days of the November 3 midterms, a consensus had formed that economic populism was why Democrats won. “The simplest summary,” the New York Times editorial board wrote on November 9, “is that they ran as economic populists and cultural moderates.” The board granted that Trump’s unpopularity was “the main engine” of Democrats’ victories, but in the Times’ telling it was the populist message that allowed Democrats in places like Kansas and Texas to “persuade many voters who previously considered their party unacceptable,” which made their campaigns “a road map” for Democrats.
Along similar lines, Data for Progress titled its postelection memo “How Democrats Rode Economic Populism to Landslide Victory,” concluding that “candidates who ran on bold, economic populist agendas won competitive races.” Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote in Time that Democrats won as “populist economic fighters” who called out the corrupt politicians and corporate interests that had rigged the system.
At the Center for Working-Class Politics, we have spent years urging Democrats to make exactly this turn toward economic populism, ideally delivered by working-class candidates. Economic populism starts with basic economic concerns like affordability, but it does not stop there. It also speaks to the sense that government serves a wealthy few rather than ordinary people. By blaming economic elites and the politicians who serve them, economic populism connects pocketbook concerns with anger about corruption and political unresponsiveness, and promises to take them on.
A 2021 survey we conducted found that economically populist messages did better with working-class voters than the Democratic establishment’s usual fare, and a 2023 follow-up found that “economic populism can help progressives win more working-class voters,” including in Trump country. After the 2024 election, we argued that Kamala Harris had turned away from economic populism to her peril. Last fall, our survey of voters in four Rust Belt states found that economic populism had broad appeal, especially when it named corporate greed and mass layoffs. And this year, an enormous survey experiment we conducted found that Democrats who placed themselves on the side of working people and took on corporate and political elites won more working-class support than Democrats who stuck to more traditional Democratic messaging.
But is it really true that Democrats of all stripes at last took our advice and turned to economic populism in 2026? And if they did, was it incumbents who changed their tune, or a new wave of challengers committed to a break with the party’s past messaging failures? To find out, we measured the populist content of Democratic campaigns going back to 2010.
What we found runs against much of the postelection conventional wisdom. Democrats really did run as economic populists in 2026, a major shift from previous years. But that shift came largely from a new class of candidates, not from incumbents or party leaders like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, whom the Washington Monthly’s Bill Scher credited with “colossal midterm victories.”
Still, it is much harder to say how much economic populism helped Democrats win in a year when all Democratic candidates rode the same wave. Candidates who ran more populist campaigns do not appear to have performed better than those who ran less populist ones. If economic populism mattered electorally, beyond what might mostly have been a national backlash against Trump, it may have worked by shifting the party’s brand as a whole rather than by boosting individual candidates. What is clear is that the candidates driving this populist shift were disproportionately newcomers, including many who won and will now pull the Democratic caucus in a direction that sounds much more like Bernie Sanders than like Chuck Schumer.
Democrats Turned Up the Economic Populist Dial Dramatically in 2026
To see just how differently Democrats campaigned in 2026 compared with past cycles, we scraped and analyzed the campaign websites of more than 6,000 Democratic candidates who ran for Congress between 2010 and 2026. Campaign websites are one place where nearly every candidate lays out what they stand for in their own words, which lets us compare the whole field of Democratic candidates from one cycle to the next.
The chart below shows a striking shift from 2024 to 2026. The share of Democrats who mentioned billionaires more than tripled, from 12 percent to 40 percent. Mentions of corruption rose from 18 to 39 percent, corporate PACs from 10 to 25 percent, monopolies from 6 to 19 percent, and working people and families from 43 to 68 percent. Democrats also talked much more about affordability, tariffs, Medicaid, and other economic issues, while abortion, climate change, and several cultural issues appeared less often.
But more talk about the economy does not necessarily mean more economic populism. Economic populist messages also blame economic elites for making ordinary people’s lives harder. So we built a model to identify anti-elite sentences that specifically blamed economic elites, rather than simply attacking Trump or Republicans.
That measure shows an even clearer break in 2026, as well as which candidates drove the surge in economic populism. Among Democrats who won House and Senate seats, newcomers used about 93 anti-elite sentences per 1,000 sentences on their campaign websites, compared with about 36 for incumbents. Incumbents changed relatively little. The big jump came almost entirely from candidates who were not already in office.
Breaking the pattern down by issue tells the same story. Among Democrats elected in 2026, newcomers were much more likely than incumbents to talk about billionaires, corruption, working people, large corporations, corporate PACs, monopolies, wealthy donors, and corporate greed. This difference appears on almost every economic populist theme we measured.
The sharpest populist shift came from newcomers. Sitting Democrats did not suddenly remake themselves in the image of Sanders. Instead, a new class of Democrats brought a much more anti-elite message with them and will now make up a substantial part of the Democratic congressional caucus.
To be clear, campaign websites do not capture everything candidates do or say, and candidates may strategically emphasize certain issues or types of language on websites that they wouldn’t foreground in higher-stakes settings like paid media. So we also collected a much broader set of campaign materials for the 56 Democrats in the most competitive House and Senate races, including ads, debates, press releases, and social-media posts.
In that fuller record, anti-elite rhetoric was widespread: Virtually every candidate used economic populist language at least to some degree; 43 percent of the roughly 400 ads we analyzed attacked economic elites specifically, and at least 44 of the 56 candidates ran at least one ad attacking elites of one kind or another. The populist turn was broader than the website data alone suggest. But the websites still show who leaned into it most heavily and made it central to their campaigns: overwhelmingly, the newcomers.
The Most Populist Candidates Did No Better Than Other Democrats
A thornier question, however, is whether individual candidates were rewarded for leaning furthest into economic populism. Much of the postelection commentary assumes they were. The Times editorial board held up candidates like Josh Turek, who won Iowa’s open Senate seat as a self-described “common-sense prairie populist,” and Bobby Pulido, who flipped Texas’s 15th Congressional District after telling voters that “the people in office have sold us out,” as models for the party. Data for Progress went further, concluding in its postelection memo that candidates with bold economic populist agendas had won competitive races.
That is a much harder claim to test. Congressional races differ in all kinds of ways, and in 2026 Democrats everywhere benefited from the same national swing. So we cannot cleanly say how much any one message caused a candidate to do better. But we can ask a simpler question: Did the Democrats who leaned hardest into economic populism clearly outperform those who leaned into it less?
Our own research gave us reason to expect a mixed answer. In the large survey experiment we fielded this year, Democrats who put themselves on the side of ordinary people did better with working-class voters than Democrats who used conventional, technocratic language. But once they had done that, adding sharper attacks on economic elites barely pushed voters’ support up any further.
We see something similar in the election results. We sorted nearly all Democratic House and Senate nominees into thirds based on how much of their campaign website attacked economic elites. If turning up the populist dial gave candidates an extra boost, the most populist third should have gained more ground over Harris’s 2024 margin than the least populist third. They did not. All three groups ran about 14 to 15 points ahead of Harris, almost exactly the same improvement. Adjusting for incumbency gives the same result.
In the chart below, we also highlight candidates with working-class backgrounds, shown in green. Democrats elected more working-class candidates in 2026 than in any recent cycle, and our past research finds that working-class voters tend to prefer candidates with working-class backgrounds because they see them as more likely to understand voters’ everyday problems. But here too, there is no obvious electoral bonus. Working-class candidates, while running more economic populist campaigns than the typical Democrat, performed neither better nor worse than expected.
We then looked more closely at the 56 most competitive House and Senate races, where we had much richer data. Here we could also compare each result with what a typical Democrat would have been expected to do in the same race, given the district, incumbency, and the national political environment.
Again, there was essentially no relationship between how populist a candidate sounded and how far they ran ahead of or behind expectations. Our sentence-level measures of anti-elite rhetoric told the same story. Some of the biggest over-performers, including Henry Cuellar in South Texas, were among the least populist candidates in the group, while some of the most populist ran behind expectations.
None of this shows that economic populism hurt Democrats, or even that it did not help them. The comparisons are too noisy for that. But they do show that the candidates who leaned into economic populism most heavily did not clearly separate themselves from the rest of the Democratic field. Whatever economic populism did for Democrats in 2026, it does not look like individual candidates could simply ratchet up their economic populist messaging to win more votes.
Voters Knew Which Candidates Were Working-Class Populists, but Partisanship Drove Their Support
If voters had never noticed which candidates were running as economic populists, it would be no surprise that the populists did no better than other candidates. But our tracker surveys show that many voters did notice.
To see this up close, we tracked four races through the fall with The Nation and the polling firm Nira Data, interviewing likely voters each month from August through October. Dan Osborn, an independent running for Senate in Nebraska, Brian Poindexter in Ohio, Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania, and Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin were chosen because each candidate paired a working-class biography with a campaign built around economic populism. We asked voters whether each candidate was more or less on the side of working people, and of corporations and the wealthy, than most Democrats, and what kind of work they had done before politics.
We found that the candidates’ populist messages and their working-class biographies both registered with the electorate: Voters were much more likely to say each candidate was more on the side of working people than most Democrats and less on the side of corporations and the wealthy.
Many voters also recognized the candidates’ working-class backgrounds, though far from all did. In Nebraska, 58 percent said Osborn had done working-class work before politics, compared with 7 percent for Republican Pete Ricketts, and Brooks and Poindexter opened smaller but still sizable gaps over their opponents. The exception was Wisconsin, where Republican Derrick Van Orden, a retired Navy SEAL, was about as likely as Cooke to be seen as working class.
Yet when we asked voters in their own words what they liked or disliked about these candidates, few talked about economic populism or working-class backgrounds. Across the four races, 35 percent mentioned the candidate’s party, Trump, or the Republican opponent, compared with 18 percent who mentioned the candidate’s background or economic populist messaging.
So these candidates’ economic populist messaging did reach voters; many saw these candidates as more pro-worker, less corporate, and more working-class than the typical Democrat. But those perceptions rarely seemed to be the driving force behind voters’ support for candidates. Party labels, Trump, and the candidates’ Republican opponents mattered more.
These results fit a broader story about the election. Trump was deeply unpopular, and much of the Democratic wave was plainly a backlash against him and the Republican Party. CNN’s postelection analysis found that more than three-quarters of voters who backed Harris in 2024 said they used their House vote to express opposition to Trump, while only about a third of Trump’s own 2024 voters said they used their 2026 vote to show support for the president.
When the national political environment is so strongly tilted against the party in power, there is less room for differences between individual Democratic candidates to matter. So the fact that the most populist candidates did not clearly outperform the rest does not mean economic populism was irrelevant. It may simply mean that, in 2026, voters were responding more to the parties as a whole than to which Democrats leaned the hardest into economic populist messaging.
Economic Populism Won Inside the Democratic Party
While it is hard to say how much economic populism helped Democrats win in 2026, it clearly changed the Democratic Party itself.

Voters seem to have noticed the shift at the party level. In Data for Progress’s survey of likely voters in the last days of the campaign, the populist lines Democrats used reached far more voters than their moderate ones, and they did so across party lines.
Seventy-eight percent said they had heard Democratic candidates say billionaires and the wealthy should pay more in taxes, and 71 percent had heard them say big corporations were raising prices to boost their profits. Fewer than half had heard Democrats call for an all-of-the-above energy policy (49 percent) or talk about securing the border (42 percent), and only 37 percent remembered hearing Democratic candidates promise to work with Republicans.
And the messaging shift voters heard showed up in whom Democrats sent to Congress. The chart below compares the Democrats serving in Congress after the 2016 and 2026 elections. In 2016, only about 10 percent had mentioned billionaires in their campaigns. Sanders was one of them. By 2026, that share had tripled to 33 percent, with newcomers accounting for much of the growth. Attacking billionaires and corporate power once marked a Democrat as a Sanders insurgent. In 2026, it was something Roy Cooper’s, Chris Pappas’s, and Josh Turek’s campaigns had in common with Dan Osborn’s.
Moving economic populism to the center of the Democratic Party did not happen by accident. Sanders and the movement around him spent years pushing Democrats toward economic populism, as did researchers and organizations like ours. The evidence from 2026 suggests that this effort succeeded in changing how much of the party talks and how Democrats are perceived by voters.
The Sanders wing is no longer a lonely corner of the Democratic Party. It is growing. Many of its newest candidates are winning, and its language is increasingly the party’s language. The next question is what Democrats do with that victory.
