https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Quel head trip! Failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film rock Paris Photo – review
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Charlotte Jansen
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist.
This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue. The strongest thread running through Paris Photo is the uncertainty and instability of photography: as evidence that collapses into fiction and performance.
Lara Tabet’s Vitreous Body, developed with curator Yasmine Chemali, was among the fair’s most conceptually adventurous projects. Tabet, who trained as a medical biologist, collected water samples from canals, natural sources and waterways around Marseille, then mixed them with photographic film. The bacteria in the samples eat away at the film and transform it into brightly coloured abstract compositions, portraits of the city of sorts, a way of representing the landscape through microorganisms invisible to the naked eye. The works on agar bioplastics are the most interesting – the bacteria continue actively to transform the material, so that the work will continue to be alive, and changing. They are both beautiful and disquieting. Nature is not just depicted, but a collaborator in the image.
A different but equally intriguing interrogation of representation came from the young Colombian artist Felipe Romero Beltrán, who has frequently collaborated with African migrants in Europe, especially dancers. In his carefully constructed black-and-white photographs, his collaborators re-enact the positions used by police to subdue someone they’re arresting; yet without the uniforms or weapons, the aggression and hostility, the hierarchy and power, the choreographed movements become surprisingly tender and soft, institutional control becomes intimacy. The bodies carry the narrative without directly showing the violence those same bodies are regularly subjected to by the state.
Kourtney Roy showed works from her Failed Postcards series, taking another kind of vernacular visual language, travel photography, and turning it into something more ambiguous, strange and at times hilarious – saturated colours, theatrical poses and awkward fails, as she constructs scenarios in front of the kind of picturesque views tourists are prone to photograph. Beneath these polished shiny pictures, there’s also a darker rumination on the way experience is commodified.
Silina Syan brings a different understanding of the relationship between image and place. Her Made in Bangladesh series is rooted in Bidyakut, her father’s village in Bangladesh, and the architectural transformations that result from migration. The elaborate mansions financed by family members living abroad stand in striking contrast to the surrounding vernacular architecture; these buildings become visual markers of economic aspiration, family obligation and belonging. Some of her photographs are encased in their own architecture, carved wooden frames or sculptural elements framing the image. The architecture becomes a portrait of people who are absent.
One of the fair’s big draws was the chance to see Ponte City by Patrick Waterhouse and Mikhael Subotzky. Developed over 15 years, the project examines Johannesburg’s famous 54-storey residential tower through an extraordinary accumulation of photographs, documents, objects and residents’ stories. A new addition is their Ponte City book box presentation, which turned this archive into a modular installation of mobile towers, books, images and archival material. Photographs of doors, windows and television screens become fragments of a collective portrait of the tower, revealing the complexity of a building that embodies South Africa’s contested social and architectural history. It raises questions about the ethics of documenting a community, about how to preserve residents and honour their lives without reducing them to an art object. It’s a richly layered and absorbing story – enough to make you forget you’re at a fair.
Ultimately, Paris Photo 2026 was at its most convincing when it moved beyond the familiar. The bicentennial resulted in a load of nostalgic booths, not only at the fair but at institutions across the city, but does anyone really care about the anniversary? The best bits were about photography’s future – its capacity to be porous, to absorb other references and disciplines, to challenge reality as we know it. Two hundred years after its invention, photography’s most interesting question may no longer be what it can show us, but what it can make visible that we have previously been unable, or unwilling, to see.

https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.title: Deze impact had Apache in oktober
https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.author: Redactie Apache
https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.text:
Van Reynders in steeds nauwere schoentjes tot privérusthuizen die subsidies wegsluizen. Onderzoeken van Apache rolden in oktober over de tongen. Zo woog Apache de voorbije maand op het debat en het beleid.
- Het op een schandaal zonder weerga afstevenende fraudeonderzoek naar Didier Reynders – met nu ook smoking gun-bewijzen dat de ex-Eurocommissaris zaken waarin zijn naam viel in de doofpot liet stoppen – waarbij een “geklasseerde” zaak uit 2014 heropend werd na onthullingen van Apache.
- De financiële doorlichting die uitwees dat drie op de tien private rusthuizen in Vlaanderen en Brussel niet kunnen uitleggen waar hun zorgsubsidies naartoe gaan. Die kwam er nadat Apache in 2020 beschreef hoe private zorggroepen dat geld met slinkse truken wegsluizen naar hun aandeelhouders.
- De zogezegd “onaanraakbare” bevroren Russische miljarden bij Euroclear die dan toch al bleken te zijn aangesproken, niet om Oekraïne te steunen maar om Europese investeerders wiens geld vastzit in Rusland te compenseren. Een onthulling waarmee Apache ook in Kyiv de krant haalde.
Het zijn maar drie van de meer in het oog springende vormen van impact die Apache in oktober had. Ze illustreren hoe onze journalistiek niet alleen bewustzijn creëert, maar ook het beleid achter de veren zit en het gerecht een handje toesteekt.
Wegen op het beleid
Wegen op het debat én het beleid: dat probeerden we in oktober ook te doen met stevige argumenten voor een stop op het bouwen van datacenters, of om de kerncentrales niet holderdebolder te nationaliseren. Maar ook met een gouden tip voor de regering-De Wever over 15 miljard euro die zomaar voor het oprapen ligt. En met harde cijfers over beroepsziekten veroorzaakt door pesticiden – waarvan België er in tegenstelling tot meerdere buurlanden niet één erkent.
Weg van Amerikaanse big tech
De impact van datacenters en big tech onder de loep nemen, dat kun je moeilijk zonder conclusies te trekken over je eigen technologiegebruik. Daarom ruilde Apache de diensten van een Amerikaanse bigtechreus in voor Europese opensource-oplossingen, voor onze digitale werkplek, onze cloudopslag en onze redactionele chat. Dat vergde enig aanpassingsvermogen en had een zekere impact op de geoliede machine die we doorgaans zijn, maar daar heb jij als lezer hopelijk niets van gemerkt. Niettemin kunnen we iedereen aanraden om zelf de switch te maken – ook de Vlaamse overheid.
Klacht ongegrond, toch op kosten gejaagd
Impact van het minder leuke soort creëert onze journalistiek helaas ook van tijd tot tijd. Zoals voor de rechtbank of de Raad voor de Journalistiek gedaagd worden. En ook als zo’n klacht ongegrond wordt verklaard – omdat je aan niets schuldig bent behalve aan waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving – word je op kosten gejaagd. Ook daarom is journalistiek zoals die van Apache niet goedkoop, en de steun van onze leden onbetaalbaar.
Meer directe en indirecte impact van ons werk, maar ook kanttekeningen van onze redactie bij de dagelijkse actualiteit, vind je voortaan in de nieuwe rubriek Opgepikt.
Niets van het bovenstaande hadden we kunnen uitzoeken of onder de aandacht brengen zonder financiële steun van onze betalende leden.
Ben jij nog niet aangesloten bij Apache? Neem dan vandaag nog een betalend lidmaatschap, en geef ons meer middelen om te schrijven wat iedereen moet weten. Om kritische vragen te blijven stellen – hoe hardnekkig sommige politici ze ook negeren.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the 'turbulence and violence of our times'
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Razmig Bedirian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.
Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.
Curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.
Organic process
“The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik says. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”
With Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.
The Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.
Complementary projects
“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik says. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”
These themes, Malik says, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.
Through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.
Reconstruction from ruin
With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.
The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.
“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik says. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”
The Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.
The Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.
Post-conflict narratives
Finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.
“We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik says. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”
All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik says, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.
“I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik says. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”
• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Future of NYC Teen Therapy Service Uncertain Amid ‘Independent Evaluation’
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Trenton Daniel, Healthbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Healthbeat. Sign up for their public health newsletters at healthbeat.org/newsletters.
One of New York City’s more high-profile efforts to tackle the youth mental health crisis after the pandemic appears to be in limbo, and Health Department officials refuse to say whether they plan to renew a service that has drawn scrutiny.
Teenspace launched under former Mayor Eric Adams in November 2023 to provide local teens with free therapists by text, phone or video chat. The Department of Health and Mental Hygiene signed a three-year contract for $26 million with the platform.
Roughly 52,000 teens had signed up for Teenspace as of April 2026, Health Department officials told Chalkbeat. About 80% of the registered users were students of color in the first two years of the program, they added. Teletherapy services such as Teenspace are hailed as an innovative way to help teens confront stress, anxiety, and depression in a way that feels comfortable for them: by texting. For some New York City teens, the platform was their first encounter with a therapist.
The Teenspace website says the program will run through November 2026.
The contract with Talkspace, the New York-based company that oversees Teenspace, was scheduled to end in September but was amended to add two years, according to the city contract portal.
Parent advocates have long raised concerns that health officials haven’t done enough to protect teens’ privacy on the Teenspace platform. They alleged that Teenspace collects user data and shares it with third parties for marketing purposes without their knowledge. The Health Department says that after advocates raised privacy concerns in 2024, it worked with Talkspace to create a privacy policy specific to Teenspace.
“They really should have been doing their due diligence,” said Shannon Edwards, a digital marketing consultant and founder of an online platform called AI for Families. “The work should have been done. It should have been understood.”
Neither the New York City Department nor Talkspace would answer questions about the contract. Rachel Vick, a Health Department spokesperson, said the agency “is in the process of an independent evaluation to review the demonstration project and its outcomes. NYC Teenspace will continue to serve clients while that process continues.”
Talkspace spokesperson Alana Morales referred questions to the Health Department.
One of the program’s biggest champions was then-New York City Department of Education Chancellor David Banks. In a recent interview with Chalkbeat, Banks said he wasn’t paying attention to the initiative. “I don’t know where it really went. I don’t know how impactful it is now.”
Though youth well-being has remained a major concern among mental health professionals since the pandemic, there are signs suggesting improvement. In September, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced that it had seen gains concerning youth mental health and suicide risk factors. Among such risk indicators: Persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness had improved from 33% to 40% from 2023 to 2025.
Public Records Show Advocates Compelled Health Department Officials To Respond
After the contract was inked three years ago, privacy advocates sent Adams, Banks, and the health commissioner a letter expressing their “deep concerns” about Teenspace sharing users’ personal information with third parties.
Leonie Haimson, a critic of education technology who has long raised concerns over privacy issues, said it took advocates nearly a year of fighting to get the Health Department to improve the platform’s privacy policy. Public records she obtained and shared with Healthbeat showed that Health Department officials and Talkspace executives, including its CEO and a lawyer, were looking into the group’s inquiries about the use of trackers to monitor user data. Talkspace said it agreed to remove the trackers from the Teenspace website “as well as trackers not necessary for website operations or security,” records from December 2024 show.
In an email that same month to the Health Department, a Talkspace lawyer wrote that the company had taken measures “above and beyond what is normally required by even the more stringent public privacy standards.” He also noted the company hired an outside privacy law firm and “an outside pixel expert firm to independently and objectively scrutinize our privacy practices, policies and pixel usage, which was a material expense undertaken to help New York City DOH/DOE gain clarity on all of our practices.” In response, Talkspace revised its Teenspace privacy policy.
The advocates were irritated that the Health Department hadn’t taken a closer look at the Teenspace privacy protections before the contract was awarded.
“I just don’t think New York City is doing the job that it should be doing to really safeguard the privacy of children and teens in New York City,” Haimson said
Privacy concerns have continued to dog Teenspace.
At a City Council oversight hearing in April, Councilmember Rita Joseph (D-Brooklyn) wanted to know if any of the Teenspace data collected were being “shared or sold” with third parties.
“The data is protected,” Marnie Davidoff, an assistant commissioner with the Health Department, said. “The data that is used is only for service provision. There is no other allowable use of the data.”
The Health Department says it had privacy protections in place before parent advocates raised their concerns and had protected student data by including several contract stipulations. Among them: keeping client data confidential during and after the completion of the city’s contract, prohibiting the use of data for any purpose other than providing mental services, and requiring data to be destroyed after 30 days if the user did not start therapy.
Chalkbeat Senior Reporter Alex Zimmerman contributed to this story.
Trenton Daniel is a reporter covering public health in New York for Healthbeat. Contact Trenton at tdaniel@healthbeat.org or on the messaging app Signal at trentondaniel.88.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/shaikh-econo.title: Anwar Shaikh Gave Us an Emancipatory Economics
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/shaikh-econo.author: Clara E. Mattei
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/shaikh-econo.text:
Anwar Shaikh Gave Us an Emancipatory Economics
Anwar Shaikh, who died in October at 80, showed how capitalism really works: profit drives it, competition is a war, and crisis is the norm. Economist Clara Mattei argues that his work remains a guide to changing the world.
Writing about someone who has changed your life and to whom you owe so much is much more difficult than I would have thought. It is impossible to feel capable of delivering even a fraction of what it would take to fully honor the human and intellectual memory of Anwar Shaikh.
I met Anwar at a moment of great intellectual insecurity for myself that he helped me overcome. Now, in front of this blank page, that insecurity is back. At the same time, this state of mind allows me to fully reconnect with the memories of our first encounters and the development of a mentorship and friendship that has deeply shaped me as a scholar and as a person.
Grounding Theory in Historical Analysis
It was 2015, and I was struggling to pursue the research for my economics PhD in Pisa, Italy. It had been a tough couple of years: after a five-year university degree in philosophy and history, the doctoral program had thrown me into hardcore economics courses. There were intense examinations in mathematics, econometrics, statistics, microeconomics, and game theory, which I had survived by studying nonstop and memorizing formulas that I would obsess over at night, half awake, half in my dreams. After so many examinations and so much peer pressure, it took me a while to find a subject I could feel passionate about.
Economics, as my course textbooks presented it, was a dry, abstract discipline, all about technique and not much about intellectual stimulation. I felt demotivated and especially out of place. Was I ever going to be fit for this?
I cared deeply about social justice and critique of the system — I read Karl Marx’s Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts and Karl Polanyi’s The Great Transformation — but none of it seemed to fit the current canon of scientificity. My supervisor, Giovanni Dosi, suggested I work on austerity, and I agreed, but I could not find an approach that was not so deeply economistic, focused only on debt and growth.
Finally, while desperately roaming the library, I found an article on Fascist economics in 1920s Italy. I realized its deep affinity with contemporary economic policies in Europe, especially Italy. That day, I had a moment of awakening and decided to embark on archival research to trace the genesis of these policies in the thought of the economists who were advising Benito Mussolini.
The research was challenging. I adhered to no specific methodological framework. To make sense of things, I realized I had to surpass the narrow limits of what history of economic thought, economic history, or economics meant for the profession.
In my scholarly journey, I had found supportive mentors — Nicola Giocoli, Alessandro Nuvolari, and George Peden, for example — but there was clearly not much space for me in Italian academia, especially within economics. I was not doing enough of what economics was supposed to look like, but to maintain my motivation, I could not conform.
This is when an email from Anwar changed my life forever. It read: “Dear Clara, I could not stop reading your paper once I started! It is excellent, and I hope you continue to pursue the parallels between the post-WWI rationale for austerity and the subsequent reincarnations in the 1980s and again now. Congratulations on a fine piece of work.” I remember gasping with happiness and a sense of recognition that I had never felt before. Really? A scholar like Anwar was taking my research seriously? And in an economics department?
In his role as chair of the Economics Department at the New School for Social Research, Anwar was responding to an exploratory email I had sent just a week earlier, inquiring about a visiting scholar position. I had only recently discovered the existence of a department where Marxian economics was part of the canon, where economics seemed to be about substance as well as technique. In that email, I had attached a chapter of my dissertation, but I had no expectation whatsoever that Anwar was going to open the file.
But he did, and from then on he would continue to make clear the importance of understanding the history of economic thought as integral to the analysis of capitalism itself. He wrote again inviting me both as a visiting scholar and to give a talk on my work to the department. That email exchange was a real turning point in my life’s journey.
When I arrived in New York City in September 2015, I went to Anwar’s office hours. His wisdom and generosity were traits that struck me immediately. He was not teaching that semester, but I would stop by his office to get his feedback on some ideas.
The week before my scheduled department talk, he told me: “You know, we are hiring, and you should apply.” The message was implicit: take this talk as an opportunity to showcase your work. At that point, I was exhilarated. The amount of adrenaline I felt leading up to that 4 p.m. Tuesday seminar was something I would never experience again.
Anwar fought hard for the department to hire me. I only learned this after I had begun working as an assistant professor of economics at the New School. He believed in me so strongly. I still have a hard time understanding why and have never felt worthy of such high esteem.
My dear colleague Ying Chen, whom the department hired at the same time as me, and I were both so lucky to have his support. We will miss those lunches, sharing different varieties of spicy Chinese food over conversations both fun and serious.
A Life’s Mission
In the summer of 2016, right before I moved to New York to start teaching, I helped organize a couple of stops for Anwar’s book launch in Italy. The stops were at the International University College of Turin and at my alma mater, the Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies in Pisa. Anwar had just published his masterpiece, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises.
There is one conversation with him I will remember forever: We were sitting at a café on the Po River, and he started telling me about the commitment and devotion it had taken him to produce his book. It had taken him over thirty years to completely reset the foundations of economics and the study of capitalism. He told me that escaping the traps of dominant economic theory was a sacrosanct mission to change the world, that deep study carried enormous transformational weight, and that it required sacrificing a lot of worldly distractions.
He emphasized that he had supported me so strongly because he had seen potential in my research and in my devotion to it. He believed I could make a critical contribution to the study of capitalism and the political dimensions of economics. The connection between so-called pure economics and fascism that I was unveiling was for him key to unsettling some accepted truths about our economic system.
It was then that I promised him I would persevere. And in times of demotivation, his words are always there to motivate me.
I spent another six years developing my book, The Capital Order. I always wondered whether the final result lived up to his expectations, but luckily, he did seem proud.
It was really thanks to Anwar’s influence and mentorship that I was able to give a sturdy theoretical foundation to the archival research, tracing its roots in the deep tendencies of our economic system. I also wanted the archival research to bolster the systemic analysis, especially of the deeply political forces that shape our economy. More generally, the book is the product of the intellectual milieu of the department Anwar introduced me to. The intellectual stimulation and methodological insights I received, including from colleagues like Duncan Foley, completely transformed it.
I remember the long conversations on the phone with Anwar during the COVID-19 lockdown, in which he meticulously commented on my interpretation of Ralph Hawtrey’s theory of inflation and explained how best to measure rates of exploitation and profit. His comments, often critical, were not easily digestible, and I would take them bit by bit and dissect them with Aditya Singh, my loyal research assistant, who was also Anwar’s student.
Neither the Perfect Nor the Imperfect but the Real
What Anwar has gifted us all is his formidable lens through which to interpret capitalism and challenge the mainstream. He offered a lucidity about the systemic tendencies of our economic system and a holistic approach that, as many, including Vivek Chibber, have already stated, bears comparison with that of Karl Marx himself.
In my years working at the New School, I attended two of Anwar’s graduate courses. I experienced firsthand how he was able to translate the titanic amount of knowledge in his book into effective pedagogical tools.
His story of the chicken pot pie, for example, embodies his capacity to convey the nature of capitalism in an intuitive and lasting way. Once Mary sold her chicken pot pie hobby to a business, it did not matter what was in the pies, which became full of hormone-treated chicken; what mattered was their price. With an image that stuck, Anwar explained the fundamental logic of value as being completely detached from use value, from those qualities that made the chicken pot pie so good.
Anwar delivered, like no one else, the antibodies against bourgeois economics, against those “theories” that only help hide rather than explain. In his book, as in his classes, students learned to wear different lenses through which to look at the economic world. They came to understand the slick capacity of the “perfectionist” and “imperfectionist” approaches to idealize markets, competition, and progress.
Shifting from one framework to another, examining their explanations of inflation, profits, and unemployment and their policy implications, Anwar was able to deliver a scathing critique of both neoclassical (perfectionist) and Keynesian (imperfectionist) economics. He tore down the edifice not just of neoclassical economics but also of its supposed Keynesian alternative with grace and precision. He unmasked how they shared much more than one would think, especially a common backbone of idealization and an urge to get back to perfection, which Keynesians thought state intervention could achieve.
As he put it in his brilliant interview with the Institute for New Economic Thinking: “The notion of imperfection is a dual of perfection; you can’t speak of imperfection unless you are implicitly paying allegiance to perfection, and I do not want to be trapped in that space.” He also recalled something I had felt deeply myself: “When I started as a graduate student, I was surprised to discover that the representation of the world was an idealized fictitious form that makes no sense to me, and that as an economist you had to accept that, then spend your time showing how the world is imperfect.”
That is why his blackboard did not have just these two possibilities: next to the perfectionist and the imperfectionist, there was a third column that had vastly more explanatory power. Anwar was not content with merely modifying the existing framework but spent thirty years rebuilding the foundations of economics from scratch. What he built was revelatory. And it had to start from real observation, from confronting the naked reality of capitalism.
Real economics, he liked to call it: an approach that vindicated and expanded, both theoretically and empirically, the most important intuitions of Adam Smith’s, David Ricardo’s, and especially Marx’s analysis, without calling it Marxist. In this, Anwar was adamant and would not accept compromises. He thought it important to get out of the niche, to avoid the self-sectarianism typical of heterodox economists.
As a matter of fact, he disliked the term “heterodox” for exactly that same reason: identifying yourself as an antithesis to the orthodoxy weakens the capacity of real economics to stand on its own feet and gain hegemony. As he wrote in the introduction to his book: “Its object of investigation is neither the perfect nor the imperfect but the real.”
Profit as the Engine
Anwar’s whole economic edifice rested on one crucial intuition that, paradoxically, the perfectionist and imperfectionist paradigms had disregarded: profit drives all the system’s dynamics; it is the engine of the whole economic system.
The incessant quest for profits drives investment and economic growth. Profit shapes supply (firms produce with the goal of making a profit) and aggregate demand (purchases of inputs, plant, and equipment, and the hiring of workers and their capacity to consume). As he put it concisely in the slides he shared with me: “The profit motive always remains central, and its dominance creates the force field that shapes and channels microeconomic and macroeconomic outcomes. This is the proper meaning of the invisible hand.”
He reappropriated the meaning of Smith’s invisible hand not as a metaphysical myth of the eternal efficiency of the market but as the expression of those profit imperatives that operated through real competition. Through the lens of the profit motive, Anwar drew a few fundamental intuitions.
First, class struggle is at the heart of the system, and technological dynamism is one of its expressions. Modern economic analysis reduces capital to durable wealth and understands profit as a reward for abstinence and entrepreneurial search. Against this, Anwar reminded us that capital had nothing to do with the qualities of the commodity. Instead, it had everything to do with capitalism’s specific historical process — potentially infinite accumulation — and the class strugglethat grounds it.
Indeed, profit mirrors surplus labor, and as he says, the existence of surplus labor is a “social outcome.” He writes: “Surplus product only arises when the length of the working day exceeds the working time to reproduce the standard of living of the employed worker, that is, only when surplus labor is performed.” Technological progress is no proof of the fairy tale that capitalism exists to maximize consumer satisfaction with ever better commodities. To the contrary, firms invest in new technology to squeeze more surplus out of their workers and to cut costs below their rivals’. In real competition, firms that fail to do so don’t survive.
Second, the real rests on a conflictual structure, precisely the one that neoclassical economists seek to erase in favor of a harmonious scheme that persuades us to believe we live in the best of all possible worlds. Far from the “ballet” of perfect competition, it is a war of all against all.
The business literature showcased extremely well how the profit motive played out through real competition. In Anwar’s words, “Firms set prices; they try to survive; some win; some don’t; they use tools to attack each other. Roughly 70 percent of firms die within the first three years.”
As Chibber has pointedly discussed, this theory led Anwar to deconstruct traditional leftist understandings of the dysfunctions of capitalism. Capitalism’s violent outcomes do not stem from monopoly power “corrupting” competition; they arise precisely out of a system working as it should, driven solely by the quest for profit.
Third, crisis is the norm under capitalism, an expression of crucial recurrent patterns or “gravitational tendencies” that emerge out of the very dominance of the profit motive itself. As Anwar put it, “The history of market systems reveals recurrent patterns of booms and busts over centuries, emanating precisely from the developed world.” These include the great depressions of the 1840s, the Long Depression of 1873–1896, the Great Depression of the 1930s, the stagflation crises of the 1970s, and the great global crises of the 2010s. In this long-run perspective, excessive financialization was merely the trigger of the 2008 crash; its underlying cause was a crisis of profitability.
Anwar’s real economic framework can also explain other devastating features of our economic system, including the structural economic plunder of the Global South and permanent warfare as a stimulus to profitability that does not risk subordinating the profit motive to social goals. Such subordination is correctly seen as a threat to the capitalist order and labeled “socialistic.” My work on austerity’s structural role in managing capitalism — by repressing wages and preserving the social relations underpinning profitability — is charged by this theoretical insight. Indeed, it underscores how capitalist governments must find the “right” stimulus policies — those that do not challenge market dependence or the command of private investment.
Turbulent Gravitation
These observations are important to avoid easy misunderstandings. Anwar was not a determinist. The patterns he discovered were important to guide systemic knowledge but did not eliminate agency.
Rather, Anwar developed a multidimensional structure of influence that is at once hierarchical and deeply historical. This is the significance of turbulent gravitation: a relatively small set of operative principles can explain a great variety of economic phenomena, without reducing the dynamics of capitalism to mechanical laws. There are observable patterns in the system — but humans can organize and change the system through political action.
This is the deeply historical and political approach that runs through Anwar’s analysis. He repudiated the bourgeois distinction between, on the one hand, “ahistorical laws” and, on the other, the “contingencies” of history. One must understand that classes, through their historical agency, create the very imperatives upon which they act, even as those imperatives bind them.
This is particularly important when it comes to the “gain-seeking behavior” that defines capitalism as a particular social form. The imperatives of profitability are not simply external laws bearing down on historical actors, nor are they merely the outcome of individual choices. Class relations and competition produce them historically, even as they confront those actors as real constraints that shape their actions. The beauty of Anwar’s economic analysis is that he could identify the underlying regularities of capitalism without abstracting them from the historical relations of class and agency through which actors continually reproduce them.
This also speaks to Anwar’s particular relationship to empirical data. He was emphatically empirical, but not a positivist. His argument was that classical assumptions are consistent with empirical reality.
He understood that data are never innocent. Data are not simply a collection of preexisting facts waiting for an observer. As he writes, “Theory intervenes not merely in the interpretation of events but in their very representation (and occasionally in their suppression, as we know only too well).”
His example of unemployment is particularly telling: the official definition counts someone as employed if they did any work at all for pay or profit. Such a definition masks a much bleaker picture of the realities of unemployment and underemployment as structural features of the system.
Anwar’s historical proclivity, expressed in his attention to social relations, is particularly clear in his passion for Michał Kalecki’s famous 1943 article, “Political Aspects of Full Employment,” which we discussed at length on many occasions. He thought this was one of the most important pieces of political economy ever written, as it clearly stressed one of the strongest Marxian intuitions: capital not only produces unemployment — it fundamentally depends on it.
Keynesian economics, with its utopian delirium of ignoring exploitation, had depoliticized the economy. It failed to realize that its goal — full employment — was technically possible, but that only a fascist dictatorship could achieve it without undermining capitalism. Indeed, only under fascism can you forgo the impersonal discipline of unemployment because political discipline is firmly in place.
I draw heavily on these conversations in my most recent book, Escape From Capitalism. Anwar reviewed it in detail and wrote a final blurb for it: “A book for the times. Mattei takes aim at the notion that the forces which regulate market and social outcomes are socially neutral. Mattei argues that we need to reject this framework, to ‘politicize our lives to participate in the transformation of the material and social reality around us’ at the local and global level.”
Anwar’s approach deeply inspired the book, and I try to bring it to life for a broader, nonacademic audience. I carry forward his conviction that economics is a social science and therefore a historical and political science.
I especially carry forward what I understand to be the fundamental Shaikhian spirit: it is only by explaining how capitalism really works that we can sharpen our tools to overcome it. Indeed, Anwar’s work has inspired generations of young people and won international acclaim.
“Don’t Give It Up”
Anwar was extremely supportive of my embarking on the journey to the University of Tulsa. He gave a brilliant opening lecture at the inaugural conference of the Center for Heterodox Economics there, which I had organized. He remained deeply supportive throughout the turbulent times at the university and when I began setting up the independent Forum for Real Economic Emancipation (FREE).
I helped organize a wonderful retirement celebration for Anwar, which produced a special issue on his work in The New School Economic Review. Afterward Anwar enjoyed his new home at the lake in Amherst, writing, fishing, cooking, and visiting friends like Robert Pollin.
We spoke on the phone often. Anwar had helped create the intellectual ethos of the New School for Social Research Economics Department and had opposed academic hierarchies all his life. He was appalled at the administration’s attacks, like firing tenured and untenured faculty members and blocking PhD admissions, which were effectively dismantling the department.
His recorded words at the retirement party ring true to all of us:
The important thing about democracy is that you have a voice. It does not mean you have to agree with me. You have to have a voice, and you constantly need to protect it, and you have to act on it. Look around you — no department anywhere has this kind of voice. So don’t give it up. No matter what they do. They are going to try to make you give it up. Don’t give it up. Go and strike if you have to. Close the place down.
Carrying the Work Forward
Iremember the shock of that phone call in which he told me he had cancer. I pretended it wasn’t real: his voice was so combative that it seemed impossible that anything could beat him. To the very end, as he heroically fought his devastating illness, he remained focused on his scholarship and on the possibility of delivering an abbreviated version of his masterpiece, updated with new empirical data.
Anwar’s archives at Bard College reveal letters that Joan Robinson and Nicholas Kaldor wrote to him in the 1970s, already recognizing the power of his work. Fortunately, Anwar leaves behind a considerable number of students, now spread across the world. A recent piece by Nikos Chatzarakis perfectly exemplifies their power to speak of his breakthroughs. As his former student Juan Santarcángelo, now a professor in Argentina, has forcefully put it, “Anwar will never truly die; he will live on in each of us and in those who were lucky enough to know him.”
It is our task to carry his paradigm forward, advance it, and spread it widely, publishing and making his work available in many different forms. This is something to which I intend to devote considerable energy in the coming years.
Anwar was one of the most powerful thinkers of our time. His legacy finds an especially important place in this historical moment, when the violence of capitalism is rampant and the thirst for radical political change so strong. The massive archive that his youngest student, Nicholas Anderson, has digitized, now held at Bard College, is a treasure that we need to cultivate and explore in detail.
It is Anwar’s real economics, and its potential for full emancipation, that we need to keep alive as a guide to collective action and the possibility of change. This is what we are trying to do at FREE, an assembly-based project for empowering education and concrete postcapitalist alternatives that is spreading globally. I hope many more people will join us in this collective endeavor for a humane, profit-liberated future.

https://hyperallergic.com/latinx-artists.title: Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries
https://hyperallergic.com/latinx-artists.author: Arlene Dávila
https://hyperallergic.com/latinx-artists.text:
Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries
Without guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.
Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry: Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.
Over the past several years, I have documented the work of Latinx creatives across public art, fashion, and independent filmmaking, and I believe we have every reason to feel unabashedly optimistic. Across these fields, artists are choosing to create work that is deeply rooted in their communities, drawing directly from vernacular traditions, oral histories, and family memories that were once pushed to the margins. They are using culture to reclaim heritage and reframe the narrative. This marks a distinct departure from older paradigms, where artists were taught — or forced — to believe that conforming to mainstream, assimilationist models was the only path to success. While they recognize there are no guarantees of commercial or institutional rewards, their work stems from a shared conviction: We have rich cultures to offer, and we will tell our stories by any means necessary.
Sometimes, their methods involve elevating vernacular and popular culture to expand traditional aesthetic repertoires. We see this in contemporary fashion with designers like Willy Chavarria and Raul Lopez (Luar), who draw from working-class aesthetics, immigrant youth, and urban street culture. Most importantly, these designers openly credit their sources of inspiration, making clear that Mexican-American communities and neighborhoods and Black and Brown queer nightlife are fashion-forward in and of themselves. They frequently use street-cast Black and Brown models to communicate a richer, more inclusive vision beyond traditional, Eurocentric runways.
In other cases, artists reassess their communities' histories to directly challenge historical marginalization, as seen in the work of Gina Gwen Palacios in Brownsville, Texas. As SpaceX expands across the region, treating the land as empty of people and culture and ripe for corporate speculation, Palacios centers the rich legacy of Mexican-American communities and their direct links to the present. Through paintings that highlight her family’s legacy as fieldworkers alongside the underrepresented landscape of South Texas, Palacios elevates everyday elements such as nopales and mesquite trees to tell stories of migration, hard labor, and policing.
Against the settler-colonial myths propagated by SpaceX pundits, artist-led projects in the area, such as Boca Chica, Corazón Grande, have focused on crowdsourcing archival materials from residents to uplift their deep roots in the region. This effort reaffirms Boca Chica Beach’s identity as "the people’s beach," directly challenging claims that Brownsville and Rio Grande Valley communities are devoid of people and value, and merely sites for space launches, by centering residents' memories and their continued symbolic and living ties to the land.
The political significance of these types of projects cannot be overstated. While Guadalupe Rosales's landmark archival initiative Veteranas and Rucas has garnered considerable recognition in art circles, similar crowdsourced, post-custodial digital archives are emerging across Latinx communities nationwide. Examples include Nuevayorkinos, Documenting the Nameplate, Rhizomes: Mexican American Art Since 1848, and, of course, Boca Chica, Corazón Grande. By inviting community contributions, these platforms deliver the empowering message that everyone's history is inherently worthy of analysis and documentation.
This spirit is also evident in New York City’s public art, where artists are Latinizing the cityscape through projects that draw on marginalized elements of history, such as Afro-Indigenous heritage and the city’s Latinx and multicultural history, challenging the erasure of their presence across the city’s memorial and monument landscape. Melissa Calderón, the first Latina to create a permanent public monument in the city, paid homage to Roberto Clemente with “Para Roberto” (2019), the first monument of its kind in the Bronx. Maria Magdalena Campos Pons’s “Procession of Angels for Radical Love and Unity” (2024) reframed New York City’s history from the perspective of its Black and brown residents in a performance filled with Orisha Santeria references. That same year, Edra Soto’s “Graft” (2024–25) took over the Doris C. Freedman Plaza in Central Park, inaugurating a sculptural installation drawing on Caribbean and Puerto Rican vernacular architecture. Think also of David Rios’s “Get Carried Away, You have the Right” (2023), drawing on Afro-Taino futuristic images in his installation at Amtrak, and Shellyne Rodriguez’s “Phoenix Ladder: Monument to the People of the Bronx” (2025), a reproduction of a Bronx building evoking the borough’s strength and rebuilding after the 1970s fires.
It is true that many of these artists remain marginalized, navigating a chronic lack of opportunities and resources. Consider the last time you saw a film by award-winning independent Latinx directors like Cecilia Aldarondo or Diana Peralta on a mainstream streaming home screen or in a theater. Yet when we look at the work itself — its courage, its artistry, and its local impact — the movement is undeniably transformative. It demonstrates that Latinx communities are resilient and that art and culture are powerful tools of empowerment and continuity.
This realization is vital not just for us, but for society at large. Appreciating Latinx art offers a clear path beyond the polarized, distorted representations that have dominated public discourse for so long. The narratives Latinx artists uplift are the very ones everyone must champion as we navigate the rapid rise of AI technology and the growth of violent capitalism. Artists in the Rio Grande Valley, for example, are fiercely defending the intrinsic value of their environment and history, reminding us that community and culture are ultimately priceless. Others are also confronting traditional histories and value hierarchies within creative industries while redefining what is considered fashionable, memorable, and significant.
Most importantly, artists’ visions have the potential to generate change in all of us. This work actively transforms the lives of future generations: raised with powerful models of resistance against dehumanization and persecution, their imaginations will remain free.
Arlene Dávila's new book, Visualizing Latinx: Creative Practices in Fashion, Film, and Beyond (2026), is now out through Duke University Press.

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-falls-fur.title: MTA falls further behind on $2B in upgrades to NYC subway signals, consultant finds
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-falls-fur.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-falls-fur.text:
The MTA has fallen further behind schedule on a massive effort to upgrade aging signal technology that guides trains on some of the city’s busiest subway lines, according to a report published Monday by a consultant for the transit agency.
The signals will replace 1930s-era technology with new systems designed to allow trains to run faster and closer together. The agency’s consultant last year found the signal upgrades had faced months of delays, and the new report found that unanticipated infrastructure repairs and software issues have pushed the installation back even more.
The report stated the upgrades to signals on the A, C and E lines running along Eighth Avenue were running 15 months behind schedule and wouldn’t be completed until January 2029. The consultant reported another eight months of delays in the project to add new signals on the F and E lines in eastern Queens, which is also expected to wrap in January 2029. And the effort to upgrade the signals on the G line, which has caused regular service disruptions for riders, is delayed another 14 months and a final determination for a complete date is still being considered, the report found.
The consultant noted the new signal technology was expected to be operational months before each project wraps. The construction timelines published in the report also include other technical work.
MTA officials last year blamed delays in signal upgrades on contractors the agency hired and a lack of engineering expertise in the field of signal work. The agency earlier this year said the delays in the G line work were in part due to leaks that workers found in the Greenpoint Tube under Newtown Creek, which took a year to repair.
MTA construction chief Jamie Torres-Springer said Monday that riders were already seeing benefits from the disruptions to G train service, noting the agency has added new elevators and modern subway cars to the line.
“I just want to be clear that as we’re doing this work, the benefits to riders accrue incrementally even before we get to turning on the CBTC program and it’s a good new story in that way,” Torres-Springer said.
He said the delays to the Eighth Avenue project were “primarily due to software issues” and the "unavailability" of time to test the technology on subway tracks.
Dr. Nabil Ghaly, a signal technology expert who issued the report for the MTA consultant at the agency’s committee meeting, said it was difficult to upgrade New York City’s subway signals because the system runs around the clock.
“The [independent engineering consultant] recognizes that implementing [communications-based train control] on an existing transit system that operates 24/7 presents operational, technical and physical complexities,” Ghaly said.
The consultant estimated the combined cost of the three delayed signal projects at more than $2 billion. The MTA earlier this month also started work on another $2 billion project to upgrade the signals on the Fulton-Liberty line, where the A and C trains run in Brooklyn and Queens.
Modern signals are already operational on the entire lengths of the L and 7 lines. The MTA also completed an upgrade to the signals on the F line in Brooklyn last year.
Officials said they plan to release a new report on Wednesday that lays out the MTA’s vision of implementing the new signal technology on every subway line.

https://citylimits.org/new-federal-rule-.title: New Federal Rule Threatens Housing for Thousands of NYC Families With Mixed Immigration Status
https://citylimits.org/new-federal-rule-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/new-federal-rule-.text:
Share This Article
Advocates say they intend to fight implementation of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule, which they say could force some 2,500 New York households to give up their federal housing assistance or separate from family.
On Nov. 10, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) issued a final rule requiring households in federally funded public housing to verify citizenship, potentially affecting thousands of families with mixed immigration statuses.
The new rule, which was proposed earlier this year and would go into effect on Dec. 14, tightens eligibility requirements for federal rental assistance for immigrants especially.
Currently, undocumented immigrants are not eligible for federal housing subsidies. But they are allowed to live in federally subsidized properties—like New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) buildings—with other qualifying family members in what’s called “mixed-status” households.
Those households pay a higher percentage of the rent to account for the ineligible family member, receiving what’s known as “a prorated rate.”
Under the new rule, every member of a household that receives federal rental assistance—including those with Section 8 vouchers, or who live in Section 9 public housing—will be required to provide proof of their citizenship or an immigration status that’s eligible for federal subsidies, as outlined in federal regulations called Section 214.
Even immigrants who are in the United States legally could be at risk under that requirement, experts said.
“People can be in the United States lawfully, but they are not necessarily eligible for rental assistance under Section 214,” explained Lucy Newman, the supervising attorney of Legal Aid Society’s public housing unit, adding, “that’s a really significant part of this.”
Immigration statuses that are eligible for federal housing assistance include green card holders, asylees or refugees, survivors of human trafficking, self petitioners under the Violence Against Women Act, immigrants admitted for lawful temporary assistance, amongst others.
Non-eligible immigration statuses include U visa holders, DACA recipients, TPS holders, and undocumented immigrants.
Newman explained that on average, three out of four members of New York City’s mixed-status households have an immigration status that’s eligible for federal assistance, and warns that the new rule could trigger those eligible members to move, or force them to separate from loved ones.
A coalition of 22 state attorneys general, including New York’s, wrote a letter to HUD Secretary Scott Turner in April opposing the rule change, which would impact 2,500 mixed-status households in New York.
“We and other activists are working on delaying or stopping the implementation of this, including considering legal action,” Newman said.
Public comments submitted in opposition of the rule argued that it’s unnecessary because non-eligible household members don’t receive federal subsidies, and that it would displace households without freeing up assistance for others.
“It is actually more expensive to fund fully eligible households, because the subsidy has to cover all of the people in that household,” Newman explained. “If this rule goes into effect, the overall situation is they end up helping fewer people because the program will cost more.”
According to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan policy group, nearly 80,000 people in 20,000 households nationwide could be at risk of losing their homes; 96 percent are people of color, including 86 percent who are Latino.
After California and Texas, New York State has the third-highest number of mixed-status households in public housing.
NYCHA, which administers a Section 8 program as well Section 9 public housing developments, did not immediately reply to a request for comment about the rule change. The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development, which also administers Section 8 locally, referred questions to the mayor’s office.
In a statement to City Limits, Mayor Zohran Mamdani expressed his opposition to the rule, while reassuring New Yorkers receiving federal housing assistance that last week’s announcement will not result in an immediate change to their subsidy.
“In New York City, we believe everyone deserves a safe, affordable place to call home, regardless of where they were born or their immigration status,” Mamdani said. “The City is evaluating every available option to defend New Yorkers and protect their access to housing. Because no one should live in fear of losing their home because of where they come from.”
The Division of Housing and Community Renewal (DHCR), which is part of the New York State Homes and Community Renewal and oversees some Section 8 programs, said it will “continue to analyze the potential impact of these proposed changes.”
In an interview with FOX, HUD Secretary Turner referred to the rule as closing a “decades-old loophole.”
“We are ending the subsidization of Biden’s open borders, upholding the rule of law, closing the decades-old ‘mixed status roommate’ loophole, and safeguarding American taxpayers’ dollars,” a HUD spokesperson said in a statement to City Limits, saying the change will free up $218 million in subsidies for “fully eligible American households.”*
But housing advocates note that no subsidies are currently offered to people who are not eligible for the program.
“Mixed-status families subsidize HUD housing for everyone else,” said Marie Claire Tran-Leung, director of the Evictions Initiative Project and managing attorney at the National Housing Law Project.
“If these families are forced to leave, there will be less funding available for HUD-assisted housing, which reduces the housing supply and worsens the housing crisis for everyone,” Tran-Leung added. “This is especially important in a place like New York, where there is definitely a shortage of housing, and especially a shortage of affordable housing.”
Still, she and other housing advocates are urging people to be patient and remain calm.
“There is a danger of families self-evicting right now, even though they have the right to stay where they are,” Tran-Leung emphasized. “They don’t yet have to leave until this rule goes into effect, and advocates are trying to think or trying to push different avenues for potentially blocking or delaying that effective date.”
Housing attorneys explained that after Dec. 14, should the rule take effect, tenants would have 90 days to prove their eligible immigration status. Even if a housing authority decides that someone doesn’t qualify, advocates emphasized, residents still have due process rights.
“That’s another thing we want to stress: there is supposed to be a process that happens, so it should not be just something that happens overnight,” Tran-Leung explained.
Advocates linked the rule change to the Trump administration’s aggressive crackdown on immigration. HUD attempted to advance a similar policy in 2019, during President Donald Trump’s first term, but President Joe Biden later withdrew it.
“What we see is Trump and HUD exploiting economic crises to destroy the federal housing programs by sowing division and scapegoating immigrants,” Tran-Leung said.
Another implication of the rule, Newman explained, is less stability for immigrant New Yorkers who are on the brink of obtaining legal status.
“We’ve had clients who over the span of 18 months are now green card holders,” she said. “There are many people who are living in those households who may be able to adjust to an eligible immigration status in the near future.”
For now, however, Newman said, “people need to know that until it goes into effect, nothing has changed. They should not move, or evict out of fear.”
*This story was updated after initial publication to include comment from HUD.

Forty-five percent of respondents to a survey conducted by the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation and Critical Minded in 2026 felt that current business models are unsustainable without “profound changes” to the funding landscape for arts and culture content. “Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent arts and culture publications across 34 states and the District of Columbia about the financial and free-speech pressures they have faced over the past two years, how they address these pressures, and whether their strategies are sustainable. The results are dire. Nearly 65 percent of respondents indicated that financial support primarily comes from foundation and philanthropic grants, yet more than 40 percent reported a decrease in this category. These grants frequently determine whether publications are able to offer a standard of minimum pay for contributors, which in turn affects a publication’s ability to attract such funding. Publications with annual budgets under $49,000 saw an 83 percent decrease in funding through grants, a likely result of foundations preferring to award money to organizations with nonprofit status. 
One respondent said, “Without nonprofit status, which is difficult and time-consuming for an independent, volunteer-run publication to get, it is near impossible now for us to get grants from state agencies or foundations.” The report also identified a correlation between financial precarity and a publication’s experience with censorship, particularly in the South. “Outlets covering marginalized communities also described how rollbacks to funding for diversity, equity, and inclusion programs have resulted in reductions, further exacerbating longstanding inequities in which cultures are disseminated and discussed,” the report details. 
Overall, the report determined that arts journalism is not supported with the same consistency and resources as other forms of journalism, and yet it is equally vital. “Art in all its forms reflects our experiences of increasingly complicated and challenging times,” the report notes, “and arts journalism helps us understand, document, and share those experiences. It also serves as a platform for the exchange of opinions, arguments, and ideas that can lead to new ways of interacting, understanding, and existing together.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Sean Duffy and the Perils of Trump's Made-for-TV Cabinet
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Sean Duffy and the Perils of Trump’s Made-for-TV Cabinet
The secretary of transportation was a reality-TV “star” and a Fox Business cable host. But when the American aviation system was grounded, he lost it.
Twenty years ago, Sean Duffy was a washed-up reality-TV personality competing in lumberjack contests and making ends meet as a small-town district attorney in northern Wisconsin. Then, the 2010 Tea Party election wave swept him into Congress. But Duffy wasn’t exactly satisfied with the new gig. He grumbled about the pay—$174,000 annually—and, in 2019, he quit to become a lobbyist and the cohost of a cable show on the Fox Business channel.
This turned out to be an unexpectedly shrewd choice. Duffy was glib, good-looking, and on cable news, and that was enough to convince Donald Trump—who, as we all know, thinks that being glib, good-looking, and on cable news automatically qualifies you to run essential sections of the federal government—to nominate the Wisconsinite as the nation’s 20th secretary of transportation. Unfortunately, like so many of the score of Fox hosts who have gotten Trump administration gigs as cabinet secretaries, czars, ambassadors, and Justice Department hangers-on, Duffy was woefully unprepared to do the job.
That was abundantly clear last Friday, when Duffy was called upon to explain the FAA’s decision to bring the nation’s aviation system to a halt. In the same week that another Fox alum, “War Secretary” Pete Hegseth, narrowly escaped impeachment, Duffy was thrust into the limelight as a bumbling sidekick for Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, himself a former mixed martial arts prizefighter. At a moment of national anxiety, Duffy defaulted to the talking-head formula, which imagines that any crisis—no matter how serious—can be addressed with a word salad of implication, insinuation and invective.
Duffy’s performance was so miserable that it provoked an immediate demand for his removal from New York Governor Kathy Hochul, who called to mind the cabinet secretary’s former career as a “star” of MTV’s The Real World: Boston and his recently launched reality travel series The Great American Road Trip. “Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency,” said Hochul, adding, “From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch.” Richard Clarke, a former counterterrorism official in Republican administrations, labeled Duffy and Mullin’s double act “perhaps the worst crisis communications press conference I’ve ever seen.”
Facing questions about whether the grounding of 14,000 flights and the disruption of travel plans for millions of Americans might have resulted from software problems, cyberattacks, or rogue AI agents, Mullin mused about how “you just can’t rule out anything at this point” and complimented his absent boss. “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” he declared. “He puts leaders in place, and he allows them to lead.”
That pronouncement provoked major head-scratching when Mullin turned the microphone over to Duffy, whose performance reminded everyone that “the leadership of President Trump” involves installing Fox hosts in positions where they inevitably get in over their talking heads. In no time, they are mismanaging wars and national emergencies with the sort of deer-in-the-headlights desperation that inspires confusion rather than confidence.
On Friday, and then again in a follow-up press conference on Saturday, Duffy made excuses, muddled explanations, and griped about how he didn’t have enough money to do his job—even though he’s a Republican cabinet member in a Republican administration with perhaps the most subservient Republican Congress in US history at his disposal.
On this weekend’s Saturday Night Live, “Weekend Update” anchor Colin Jost reflected on how “the FAA suddenly and mysteriously grounded all US flights yesterday” and then—barely containing his laughter—explained, “The scary thing by far about all these flights getting grounded was the messaging from the normally dependable Trump administration. First, they said it was a telecommunications outage as of now. Why add ‘as of now’? No one wants to hear, ‘Your child is safe—as of now.’ Then Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the whole situation was the result of a contractor upgrading copper wire to fiber optic cable. So, one guy switched out one wire and took out all planes? I think that’s literally a scene from the movie Airplane!”
Just as jarring was Duffy’s wild-eyed ranting about how Congress was not providing sufficient funding to upgrade communications systems and airports. During the Friday night press briefing, Duffy repeatedly demanded $50 billion in new money—even though he had a hard time explaining precisely what he’d done with the $12.5 billion his department got last year for air traffic control improvements, and even though Duffy had been asking just a day earlier for a mere $30.1 billion for aviation upgrades.
Instead of making a compelling case for necessary infrastructure investment, Duffy appeared to be grabbing numbers out of the sky. CNN headlined a report: “Messaging failures worsened the air traffic freeze and sowed distrust in government.” When Duffy attempted to hold another briefing on Saturday, microphone feedback created such a mess that the Irish Star newspaper declared, “Sean Duffy forced to halt ‘clown show’ press conference due to technical glitch.”
On a more serious note, newly elected US Representative Fred Wellman (D-MO) announced, “I’m calling for a full investigation of this failure and the resignation of Secretary Duffy. We will find out the damage that his incompetent leadership has done to our air traffic system. Instead of filming reality TV shows he should have been ensuring the safety of Americans.”
The calls for accountability will keep coming. No one seriously doubts that America has underfunded infrastructure projects that must be addressed—on the ground and in the air. But everyone who is serious about these issues is entertaining fresh doubts about whether Sean Duffy’s TV experience has prepared him for this reality.
