https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.title: ‘Aboriginal people were the backbone of this state’: rediscovered photographs reveal life inside the 1946 Pilbara strike camps
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.author: Rosamund Brennan
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text:
Troy Eaton lives in Pippingarra, near Port Hedland, where the Pilbara’s multibillion-dollar mining industry looms large. “It’s a mecca of mining,” says the Nyamal man. But his family’s mining history stretches back long before the arrival of today’s resources giants.
In September, Eaton took the long drive from Pippingarra to Perth to see some of those early pioneers: his ancestors, who established their own mining ventures in the Pilbara some 80 years ago.
On the walls of Lawrence Wilson Art Gallery at the University of Western Australia (UWA), he saw colour photographs of women sifting minerals with shallow tin yandies, and men wielding picks and shovels beneath vast blue skies. Among them were his grandmother, Kakaya Lucy Mitchell, his great-grandmother and other relatives, captured in photographs he had never seen. “It’s a bit emotional … just reminiscing on what it was like in their time,” he says.
“They look healthy. They look happy. There was a sense of pride looking at it, because they was doing something that they could never believe, most probably in their lifetime – taking control of their own destiny.”
The photographs feature in Strike Camps: The Photographs of John Wilson, an exhibition documenting the independent mining communities established after the 1946 Pilbara strike, when about 800 Aboriginal workers walked off pastoral stations over appalling conditions and meagre wages. Many were paid only in rations of tea, flour, sugar and tobacco.
The walk-off soon became more than a labour dispute. Hundreds of workers established camps near Port Hedland and Marble Bar, building spinifex shelters and setting up schools. Over the following years, they supported themselves by mining tin, beryl and other minerals, as well as pearl shelling and collecting buffel grass seed.
The camps offered them a measure of freedom from pastoralists’ control and the chance to raise families on their own terms. In 1952, their mining company, Northern Development and Mining, produced minerals worth £70,000.
The anthropologist John Wilson photographed the camps in the late 1950s and early 1960s, conducting fieldwork alongside his wife and fellow anthropologist, Katrin. Both have since died, and this year their daughter Bu unearthed a cache of slides beneath a wardrobe in the family’s Fremantle home, helping reunite an archive of some 350 colour images.
The UWA art historian Darren Jorgensen, who co-curated the exhibition, had spent years searching for Wilson’s photographs. They form what he calls “the most substantial collection of pictures” of the camps, documenting Aboriginal self-determination 20 years before the Gurindji walk-off at Wave Hill, the 1966 strike that became a turning point in Australia’s land rights movement.
Jorgensen believes the Pilbara strike remains less well known partly because it lacked a defining image, unlike Wave Hill’s famous photograph of Gough Whitlam pouring soil into Vincent Lingiari’s hand. Yet the communities Wilson photographed had achieved something remarkable: at a time when Aboriginal people in Western Australia were still denied the vote and subjected to discriminatory laws, “they were making international mining deals and shipping off barrels of columbite to Singapore”, he says.
Alongside 35 photographs, the exhibition features two short films that use generative AI to animate scenes of work and everyday life in the Pilbara camps. Created by the exhibition co-curator and UWA fine arts head, Vladimir Todorović, the films were developed in consultation with descendants of the strikers.
The strike itself was carefully orchestrated. As early as March 1945, more than a year before the walk-off, Nyamal organiser Clancy McKenna and Nyangumarta lawman Dooley Binbin travelled between remote pastoral stations, distributing makeshift calendars drawn on food packaging, including jam-tin labels, so workers could count down to the planned walk-off on 1 May. With the help of white prospector Don McLeod, they coordinated a strike that spread across more than 20 stations and some 10,000 sq km. Both Aboriginal leaders were jailed, but the strike gathered strength.
The walk-off lasted three years, making it the longest recorded strike in Australian history. But the workers’ right to remain in their camps was contested. In 1949, when authorities ordered families to dismantle their homes at Twelve Mile near Port Hedland, the strikers protested in writing, warning that the closure could reignite the dispute. The government subsequently withdrew the order. The strike ended that year with improved pay and conditions at two stations but unfulfilled promises of wider reform. Some returned to work on sheep and cattle stations; others stayed in the communities they had built, which endured for decades.
Eaton’s grandfather Putangaja Ernie Mitchell became a key leader, coordinating mining operations and negotiating with government officials. Mitchell’s daughter Doris, who also attended the exhibition opening, remembers growing up in the camps, where children sifted ore and traded tins of minerals for lollies. Welfare authorities once labelled her a “neglected child”. “But I wasn’t neglected,” she says. “As children, we grew up with many parents.”
Yet even within the mining cooperatives, control remained contested. In 1959, Mitchell and fellow leader Peter Kangkushot Coppin broke with McLeod amid disagreements over how earnings were used, with workers receiving rations rather than cash. Wilson photographed a meeting as the movement split. “They didn’t get any money in their hands,” Doris recalls.
Mitchell and Coppin continued the mining cooperative known as Pindan, while McLeod’s supporters formed another, Nomads. Both groups went on to establish pastoral enterprises: Pindan’s successors at Yandeyarra and Nomads at Strelley, where an independent Aboriginal school established in 1976 still operates today.
One of the last surviving strikers, Nyamal elder Captain Mudjawariny Wilson, is now in his 90s and living in aged care in Roebourne. His daughter Ursula, an exhibition co-curator, brought him to Perth for the exhibition’s opening, where he recognised himself working as a young man in the photographs. “When I first looked at the pictures, I stood there and had tears in my eyes,” Ursula recalls.
For Eaton, the photographs tell a story too often overlooked. “We always hear doom and gloom stories, but we don’t hear any great stories like this,” he says. This year, he notes, Rio Tinto celebrated 60 years of Pilbara operations; his ancestors were mining there decades earlier. “Aboriginal people were actually the backbone of this state.”
Eighty years after the strike began, Eaton is working to establish an Aboriginal-owned mining venture in the Pilbara, pursuing the same independence his grandfather’s generation fought for.
“I need to finish that journey,” he says. “Because my grandfather and those guys started it back then, right? And that journey continues to this day.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: 'It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person': Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.
It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.
“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she says. “Not
many gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.
Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali says. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”
Informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she says.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.
Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.
Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”
As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”
The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?
Shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.
And the most recent?
A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.
If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?
I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.
Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?
My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.
What do you recommend doing outside the fair?
November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.
What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?
Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.
What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?
The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.
• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Administration Touts Compliance With Class Size Law as ‘Huge Step Forward’
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Michael Elsen-Rooney, Chalkbeat, Alex Zimmerman, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
New York City public schools not only met the state-mandated targets to shrink classes, they surpassed the goal, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Friday.
Nearly three-quarters of classes across New York City’s public schools are capped at 20 to 25 students, depending on the grade.
The city cleared the state’s benchmark for two reasons. First, state lawmakers moved the goal post when they agreed in June to give the city more time to comply with the law, requiring 70% of classes meet the caps this school year instead of the original target of 80%.
Additionally, the city made a change in which classes it counted toward class-size compliance. Officials added to the calculation for the first time “cluster” classes in elementary schools — courses like science, art, physical education and music that are not taught by students’ typical classroom teacher. Without counting cluster classes, 69.5% of classes would have met the caps, schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said, just shy of the new requirement.
Unlike last year, city officials are no longer exempting any classes from the size limits, after agreeing with the teachers union to pay a financial bonus of up to $8,500 to certain teachers whose classes were excused from the requirements.
All classes must meet the class size mandates by the 2029-30 school year.
Granting the city a two-year extension to meet the mandates came after months of lobbying from Mamdani, who maintains a close relationship with Gov. Kathy Hochul and was desperate to cut spending amid a budget deficit. State legislative leaders said they were satisfied with Mamdani’s plans to recruit new teachers and build additional space for the most crowded schools.
Samuels said the improving class size compliance rates are a “huge, huge step forward” during a visit Friday to Brooklyn’s M.S. 582, which received funding to hire four additional teachers. “Simply put: More attention for our kids, more one-on-one time from their teachers.”
Counting Art, Gym and Music Classes Gave NYC’s Compliance Rate a Crucial Boost
The city did not previously count elementary school cluster classes because the Education Department didn’t have the ability to track those classes’ sizes, officials said. But this year, the city updated its reporting capabilities to count those courses, which turned out to be a big boon to the city’s overall compliance rate.
Physical education and “performing group” courses like band and dance are capped at 40 students. Nearly 100% of those classes are under their caps, according to the new city data.
City officials said they also started counting middle and high school “exam prep” courses for the first time, but didn’t immediately explain what qualifies as an exam prep course or provide a breakdown of what percentage met the state requirements.
Including those new courses pushed the city’s compliance rate up to 73%.
New Hires, Declining Enrollment and Union Penalties Helped Shrink Classes
City officials credited a $244 million investment last spring that helped schools hire some 1,900 teachers to reduce class sizes. The year before, the city shelled out roughly $400 million to help schools hire an additional 3,700.
Despite the extra investment, the city’s overall teacher headcount actually went down slightly compared to last year, from about 69,900 to 69,400. (That’s still about 5,000 more teachers than the city had two years ago.)
At M.S. 582, the funding helped the school significantly reduce class sizes, in some cases cutting them to 20 students down from about 30, said Principal Jeffrey Merced. The math class Samuels toured included 15 students, though a few were absent.
The hiring has been a boon for the school, Merced noted, allowing more opportunities for small group instruction. There are other benefits, too. A new cluster teacher, hired with extra class size funding, is offering photography lessons. Several students with professional cameras trailed Samuels through the school on Friday.
“What really helped us was the manpower,” Merced said.
For now, the Education Department is picking up the tab for new hires, but Merced is “very worried” the costs will one day have to come out of his own budget. His school’s enrollment ticked up this year, which brings additional money, and he hopes the school will have enough resources to maintain its staffing levels in the future.
Declining enrollment has likely also helped the city shrink classes. Officials did not immediately share enrollment figures for this school year, but city projections anticipated a 20,000-student drop this year, according to a Chalkbeat analysis of the data. (The enrollment projections don’t include students in prekindergarten programs, or District 75 schools for students with complex disabilities.)
Union officials believe that imposing a financial penalty for exemptions from the law — the bonus of $8,500 for teachers whose classes were excused from the state caps — helped coax the city to meet the mandate. Principals are also eligible for pay bumps of up to $10,000 for bringing class sizes into compliance, though Samuels did not say how many will receive them.
Officials said they offered no exemptions this year, down from 10,000 the year before, which helped schools meet the state’s 60% requirement last year.
The pay bonus remains in place for next year, when the city will have to hit 80% compliance, union officials said.
Broad Progress Across the City, but Nearly 500 Schools Still Lack Space
The progress on class sizes stretched across almost the entire city, with 31 of the 32 geographic districts increasing their percentage of classes under the caps.
There was one notable exception: Brooklyn’s District 13 dropped from 78% of classes under the caps last year to just 59% this year. Education Department officials didn’t immediately respond to questions about what led to the surge in class sizes in that district, which spans from Brooklyn Heights to Prospect Heights, Fort Greene and parts of Bedford-Stuyvesant.
Districts’ class sizes varied widely, from a high of 92% of classes under the caps in District 32 in Bushwick, Brooklyn, to a low of 56% in District 26 in northeast Queens.
At the poorest city schools, an average of 90% of classes were under the caps, while 57% of classes were under the caps at the wealthiest schools. Education officials and experts have repeatedly raised equity concerns, as high-need schools stand to benefit least from the new investments in smaller classes.
There are still nearly 500 schools that city officials say do not have enough space to bring all their classes under the caps.
Michael Elsen-Rooney is a reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Michael at melsen-rooney@chalkbeat.org.
Alex Zimmerman is a senior reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Alex at azimmerman@chalkbeat.org.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/flavio-bolso.title: The Scandal of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Escape Won’t Fade Away
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/flavio-bolso.author: Felipe Antunes de Oliveira
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/flavio-bolso.text:
The Scandal of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Escape Won’t Fade Away
Shortly after losing the Brazilian presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro fled the country with help from a Trump operative and a former Mossad agent. The newly elected US Congress needs to investigate Washington’s role in this shady exfiltration job.
To exfiltrate means “to smuggle [an intelligence agent, soldier, etc.] out of an area under enemy control.” The term belongs to military jargon, rather than to political commentary. Nevertheless, the Brazilian media has been using it to describe the sudden removal of former presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro from Brazil’s territory a couple of days after he lost the second round of this year’s presidential elections.
José Roberto de Toledo, a veteran journalist, was probably the first to use the word “exfiltration” in relation to Flávio Bolsonaro, in his influential weekly podcast. The circumstances of Bolsonaro’s escape seem to come directly out of a spy film. Smuggled in the middle of the night across the border with the active participation of a former Mossad agent and US government officials, he reappeared in Florida and pledged to take the details of his escape to his grave.
An exfiltration is not an act of political sympathy. It is an extremely risky operation to preserve an asset from being captured by the enemy. On the one hand, the exfiltrated asset enjoys safety when he finally reaches his destination; on the other, the exfiltration makes all masks fall, and the fugitive’s true allegiances become transparent.
For that reason, if Flávio Bolsonaro was indeed exfiltrated to the United States, this episode should figure side by side with the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro as a blatant example of US neo-imperialism in Latin America. The political and legal responsibilities for this case cannot be brushed under the carpet of history and will certainly come back to haunt Brazil-US relations for decades to come.
A Very Suspicious Escape
The details of Flávio Bolsonaro’s escape from Brazil are not entirely known. So far, The New York Times has reported that Jason Miller, a White House operative, arranged the luxury private jet that Bolsonaro and his family used (at the cost of almost one million reais, paid for by an American corporate account).
The party crossed the border with Argentina through means that are not yet entirely clear, most likely by land, on the night of Tuesday, October 27, near Foz do Iguaçu. Brazil’s top Sunday night TV news show, Fantástico, revealed that a former Israeli intelligence operative accompanied the fleeing Bolsonaro family. From the Argentinian border location of Puerto Iguazú, the disgraced former presidential candidate took a private jet to the United States, stopping in Ecuador for refueling and avoiding Brazilian airspace.
Arriving in the US, Flávio Bolsonaro landed at the infamous Miami–Opa Locka Executive Airport, used six decades earlier to prepare for the US-supported Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba, one of the worst historical examples of direct US imperial aggression in Latin America. Upon arrival, despite presenting his canceled diplomatic passport, Bolsonaro received “parole status” and was escorted by a motorcade to an undisclosed location.
Who Takes Responsibility?
Donald Trump’s secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was quick to deflect responsibility. “We didn’t facilitate anything,”claimed Rubio in a press conference on the sidelines of a G20 meeting a few days after the fact. He knew that confessing the exfiltration would mean exposing the State Department to serious internal and international reckoning.
Flávio Bolsonaro himself told The New York Times he would take the details of his fleeing “to the grave.” In an open letterreleased after his arrival in the United States, he compared himself to figures like José Martí and Charles de Gaulle and denounced the election result. He also thanked Argentine President Javier Milei “for his courage, sense of justice, and legality” and expressed his gratitude to Trump “and the wonderful American people” for hosting him.
By fleeing Brazilian justice, Flávio Bolsonaro has secured protection, at least for now, from having to answer for his alleged crimes in two different investigations. More important, as long as he is safe in the United States, it becomes more difficult for Brazilian investigators to prove the precise nature of his ties to Washington.
He is not the first person to have claimed US protection in suspicious circumstances. His younger brother Eduardo has been agitating from Texas for the Trump administration to impose sanctions against his own country, while the former head of the Brazilian intelligence agency under Jair Bolsonaro is also on US soil, having dodged immigration enforcement under very mysterious circumstances.
However, Trump and Rubio cannot shield Flávio Bolsonaro from justice and history indefinitely. It took decades for Washington’s involvement in military coups across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s to be proven with overwhelming evidence. A comprehensive apology is yet to materialize.
Hopefully, we will not need to wait that long this time. A newly elected Democratic-controlled Congress should hold US officials accountable for any interference in the Brazilian democratic process. It should clarify whether US taxpayers’ money was used to facilitate Bolsonaro’s escape from justice and whether he promised his eventual US handlers any specific information or advantages, beyond his public pledges to give the US preferred access to Brazilian rare earths.
In due course, Flávio Bolsonaro must be extradited, and cables and intelligence documents pertaining to this case should be declassified, so that the Brazilian and American people can finally learn what really happened on the night of October 27.

https://hyperallergic.com/what-does-frid.title: What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?
https://hyperallergic.com/what-does-frid.author: Eileen G’Sell
https://hyperallergic.com/what-does-frid.text:
What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?
A new documentary poses this question across socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history.
These days, Frida Kahlo isn’t free. She is the plastic cosmetic bag in an Ulta carousel. She is a throw pillow in a World Market bin. Her name and image might be the most commodified of the 20th century, so ubiquitous that she feels emptied of meaning. Or is she?
Relying primarily on the testimony of Mexican voices, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, a new documentary by Trisha Ziff, poses this question across a colorful spectrum of socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history. “I learned about Communism from Frida’s bookshelf,” shares actress and activist Ofelia Medina, who visited Kahlo’s home on a sixth-grade field trip.
“Frida gave me strength, she gave me a life and a job,” explains Juana López Sánchez, an Indigenous artisan whose livelihood is selling hand-crafted Frida dolls in Mexico City.

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-will-test.title: MTA will test body-worn cameras on bus fare enforcement teams
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-will-test.author: Stephen Nessen
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-will-test.text:
The MTA will begin testing body-worn cameras on its bus fare inspector teams, officials said Monday, one month after agents were caught on video slamming a rider to the ground who was suspected of not paying $3 to ride the bus.
New York City Transit President Demetrius Crichlow said members of the so-called EAGLE team will also be retrained on de-escalation and emotional intelligence. The body-worn cameras will begin as a pilot program. New uniforms will be issued to team members, and the MTA is also creating a dedicated fare inspector customer incident hotline to report bad interactions.
Last month, members of the EAGLE team stopped the dean of a Brooklyn public school, Kyle Taylor, who said he paid his fare using a paper bus transfer. Video captured the fare enforcement agents wrestling him to the ground. Taylor appeared at a news conference a week later with his arm in a sling, saying he couldn't return to work and was still in pain.
“ It is not what we expect of them, nor what they have been delivering to date,” Crichlow said Monday. “It's a shame again that we have to address it, but this is not indicative of the level of performance or customer service that we give to our customers.”
Crichlow added that the agents involved in that incident could be fired.
“Charges will be drafted against select individuals and those charges could end up in discipline up to and including termination,” Crichlow said. “These actions are not what we expect or have come to expect from our fare inspectors.”
The EAGLE teams have been off the streets since late October, when MTA Chair Janno Lieber said he’d recently learned of a second confrontation between the fare enforcers and a rider.
The MTA reports that it loses $300 million a year to fare evasion on buses, where nearly half of all riders don’t pay. The NYPD has said it has no plans to assist the MTA with bus fare enforcement.
“This is a step in the right direction. However, these so-called EAGLE team members need to be held to the full extent of the law, meaning criminal charges should be brought on these individuals for using excessive force on a passenger,” Rev. Kevin McCall, a civil rights activist who has been speaking on behalf of Taylor. “The MTA has a duty, so I hope after they bring charges internally, they refer to the case to the DA for criminal charges.”
The Riders Alliance advocacy group, which supports Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s goal of making the buses free, said fare enforcement is not the answer.
“Putting a more gentle squeeze on riders isn't going to fix the bus or raise the several hundred million dollars in lost revenue we need for better operations and maintenance,” Danny Pearlstine with the advocacy group Riders Alliance said. “The governor and mayor need to find sufficient, reliable funding to deliver the bus service New Yorkers deserve.”

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) and the Sobey Art Foundation have named Lotus L. Kang, known for a practice combining photography, sculpture, and site-responsive installation, as the winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award. Presented annually, the honor is widely regarded as Canada’s most prestigious contemporary art prize. It is also one of the world’s largest, awarding C$100,000 (about $70,000) to its winner.
Frequently deploying film and photographic paper as sculptural components, Kang draws from poetry to create dense installations exploring themes of body, history, and identity. She participated in the 2025 Shanghai Biennale and the 2024 Whitney Biennial and was a 2024 Guggenheim Fellowship recipient.
“In selecting Lotus L. Kang, the jury recognizes the commitment and rigor demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade,” said jury chair Jonathan Shaughnessy, director of curatorial initiatives at the NGC, in a statement. “Through installations using unfixed photographic film, cast and found objects, and fabricated armatures, her practice resists the stabilizing impulses traditionally associated with photography. Reoccurring motifs including lotus root, flowers, soju bottles, birds, anchovies, are not fixed objects, but repositories of place, longing, and desire. We celebrate the increasingly global reach of Kang’s poetic and beautiful work, which presents an active reflection on our contemporary moment.”
The Toronto-born Kang represented Ontario as one of six finalists for the prize. Runners-up Melaw Nakehk’o (representing the Circumpolar region), Samuel Roy-Bois (Pacific), Audie Murray (Prairies), Caroline Monnet (Quebec), and Shane Perley-Dutcher (Atlantic) will each receive $C25,000, while the twenty-four longlisted artists will be awarded $C10,000 apiece.
“The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing,” said Kang in a statement. “Art is essential to life, progress and love.”
Kang’s work and that of the other shortlisted artists is on view through January 3, 2027, at the NGC.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum extend loan of Asante regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Ghana
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gareth Harris
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Asante regalia gold objects on loan from the British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) will remain on show in Kumasi, Ghana until 2030 following the extension of loan agreements by the two UK museums. The British Museum has loaned 15 objects while the V&A lent 17 pieces, almost all of which were looted during military operations in the late 19th century.
The British Museum and the V&A signed a loan agreement in 2024 with Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the 16th Asantehene (King of the Asante), to return the gold regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, the historic capital of what was then the Asante (Ashanti) empire. The loans will be renewed for a further three years at the end of the current term in April 2027. The two UK museums are legally unable to deaccession so the objects are being returned as long-term loans.
“The rollover of the loan agreement was always likely and from both the British Museum’s and Manhyia Palace Museum’s point of view, this has been a successful partnership with increased visitors, training and expansion at Manhyia. There is nonetheless enduring frustration from many in Ghana, both in Asante and beyond, that this is only a loan,” says Barnaby Phillips, author of The African Kingdom of Gold: Britain and the Asante Treasure.
The loan renewal announcement followed a recent visit to Kumasi by Nicholas Cullinan, the director of the British Museum, following an invitation by the Asantehene.
The gold regalia associated with the Asante royal court is on display in the Manhyia Palace Museum's Homecoming exhibition. Items shown include a small gold ornament in the form of a lute-harp (sankuo), one of the cast gold objects presented in 1817 to British diplomat Thomas Bowdich during his trip to Kumasi.
“The British Museum has about 220 pieces of Asante gold regalia and the Manhyia Palace Museum has been involved in the selection of objects [for loan]. There has been considerable input regarding what goes back to Ghana,” adds Phillips.
The idea of a loans deal, first discussed in the 1970s, was revived when the Asantehene visited London in May 2023 to attend the coronation of King Charles III.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trujillo-dic.title: The Dominican Government Uses Zionism to Whitewash Trujillo
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trujillo-dic.author: Simón Rodríguez
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/trujillo-dic.text:
The Dominican Government Uses Zionism to Whitewash Trujillo
The Trujillo dictatorship was obsessed with “whitening” the Dominican Republic. But despite its record suppressing Afro-descendants, today’s Dominican government paints Trujillo as a fighter against discrimination because of his solidarity with Israel.
On August 24, the Dominican government announced its adherence to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) definition of antisemitism. President Luis Abinader, a businessman of Lebanese descent, made the announcement at the opening ceremony of the Sixth Latin American Forum Against Antisemitism,held in Santo Domingo by the US-based Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM). Abinader also promised to invest 50 million pesos (approximately US$852,000) in the construction of a Jewish museum in Sosúa, in the north of the country, where 747 European Jewish refugees settled during the 1940s.
The foreign ministry statement announcing Abinader’s decision included a defense of the Trujillo dictatorship (1930–1961) as a supposed opponent of discrimination, hatred, and religious intolerance. Rafael Trujillo, whose dictatorship was fanatically racist, perpetrated a genocide against the Haitian population along the Dominican border between late 1937 and early 1938 and was obsessed with “whitening” the Dominican Republic, whose overwhelming majority was and continues to be of African descent. The government’s invocation of Trujillo’s legacy is key to understanding its real motivation in pledging allegiance to the IHRA definition of antisemitism.
The Dominican government is an unconditional ally of Israel’s apartheid regime. One of its first measures upon coming to power was a statement in 2020 in favor of establishing the Dominican embassy in Jerusalem. In 2023, the Santo Domingo International Book Fair had the Israeli embassy as guest of honor. An agreement with Mekorot, Israel’s state-owned water company, to design a national water management plan was signed, and there is also Israeli cooperation with the Dominican office for the technification of irrigation. President Abinader has drawn inspiration from the Israeli wall system that encloses Gaza and Palestinian communities in the West Bank for his own border wall with Haiti, and he has relied on the purchase of Israeli weapons to drive the largest arms buildup in the country since the Trujillo dictatorship. The government also relies on Israeli technologies for internal repression, having used Pegasus spyware against a journalist who was investigating corruption.
The current Dominican government’s claim to oppose discrimination runs counter to all evidence. It has refused to introduce legislation against hate crimes and incitement to racial or religious hatred. The Penal Code, which took effect in August 2026, defines the crime of discrimination but effectively eliminates any penalty for discriminatory actions justified on religious grounds or in which the legitimate exercise of a legal authority is invoked, which amounts to the legalization of discrimination. The 1943 law banning the Vodou religion, enacted by Trujillo, remains in effect and is used to persecute Afro-Dominicans and Haitians. Meanwhile, a 1962 law prohibiting the glorification of Trujillo and Trujilloism is not enforced. Neofascist paramilitary groups that praise Trujillo, Benito Mussolini, and Adolf Hitler operate openly and collaborate with the police to repress the Left and Haitian communities.
In this context, Abinader, like Trujillo, claims to oppose antisemitism in order to whitewash and further his own racist agenda.
In Service of Genocide
CAM, which promoted the Dominican adoption of the IHRA working definition of antisemitism, is linked to the Israeli foreign ministry. Both its CEO, Sacha Roytman-Dratwa, and its editor in chief, Barney Breen-Portnoy, have worked in communications for the Israel Defense Forces. Senior Israeli officials, such as the country’s current president, Isaac Herzog, have served on its advisory board. The organization has promoted the criminalization of the slogan “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free,” following the example of the Austrian government in 2023. The Jewish Council of Australia has considered CAM’s summits on antisemitism to be part of an effort to silence criticism of Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people by equating it with antisemitism.
In its statements, CAM has defended Israel’s military actions in Gaza, describing them as an exercise in self-defense. Conversely, the International Association of Genocide Scholars has described Israel’s actions and policies in Gaza as crimes against humanity and war crimes and has stated that they meet the legal definition of genocide.
Among the organizations that initially affiliated with CAM was the Clarion Project, an anti-Islam lobby that has been classified by the Southern Poverty Law Center as a hate group.
For the Dominican government, hosting a CAM event and adhering to the IHRA definition serves four main purposes: it reaffirms its political subservience to US foreign policy, contributes to whitewashing the image of its ally Israel, portrays the Dominican regime as opposed to discrimination, and attempts to rewrite history to present the Trujillo dictatorship as the initiator of an alleged antidiscrimination policy upheld today by Abinader. There is indeed continuity between the Trujillo dictatorship and the current regime, but in a different sense.
One Hand Washes the Other
The statement from the Dominican foreign ministry announcing the adoption of the IHRA definition of antisemitism asserts that “the Dominican Republic underscores its ongoing commitment to the fight against all forms of hatred, discrimination, and religious intolerance, a position it has consistently maintained since 1938, when the Dominican state was the only one to offer asylum in Sosúa to a significant number of Jewish refugees.” The Dominican government goes on to urge all governments to take measures to “prevent hatred, intolerance, and discrimination in all their manifestations.” These are curious statements in light of Dominican history, not least the last six years of rule by Abinader’s right-wing Modern Revolutionary Party.
That the Dominican government considers itself the heir to the Trujillo legacy is an important admission. President Abinader, named in the Pandora Papers leaks for having offshore accounts, has also admitted to sharing the ideas of dictator Joaquín Balaguer, who ruled the country with an iron fist from 1966 to 1978 and before that was one of the main ideologues and officials of the Trujillo regime. Since 2021, Abinader has been enforcing an undeclared state of exception to carry out mass deportations of Haitians, including the systematic use of arbitrary detentions based on racial profiling, raids without warrants, and militarization of hospitals and their use as immigration detention centers, as well as widespread violence by migration agents, including murders, torture, forced disappearances, and sexual violence.

https://gothamist.com/news/chase-bank-of.title: Chase, Bank of America and other major banks report online banking outages
https://gothamist.com/news/chase-bank-of.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/chase-bank-of.text:
Thousands of customers of major banks across the country reported difficulty accessing their online banking accounts Monday.
Customers of Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and users of payment service Zelle reported technical difficulties, according to Downdetector, which tracks service disruptions.
Users reported being unable to log into their accounts, check balances and transfer money.
Chase confirmed it was experiencing a technical issue that was delaying some transactions, but said customers still had access to their accounts and funds. A spokesperson said the problem was not related to a cyberattack.
It's the latest technology meltdown to affect the nation after flights were grounded for hours at U.S. airports Friday afternoon because of a "temporary telecommunications meltdown."
The flights were grounded just one day after millions were unable to access their Microsoft Outlook emails because of a worldwide outage.
A spokesperson for U.S. Bank said its customers “are not directly impacted” but that clients may still have issues because of the outage.
“However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” U.S. Bank spokesperson Jeffrey D. Shelman said.
A Zelle spokesperson also directed Gothamist to other banking institutions and said its site isn't down either.
“Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds,” Zelle spokesperson Eric Blankenbaker said. “An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers.”
Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo did not immediately respond to Gothamist's requests for comment.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Chuck Schumer Is Yesterday’s Man
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Chuck Schumer Is Yesterday’s Man
The Senate Democratic leader just keeps showing why he needs to be replaced.
If you want to ruin a boisterous celebration, just hand over a microphone to Chuck Schumer. The Senate Democratic leader is the ultimate buzzkill, adept at deploying a droning voice that can turn giddy jubilation into existential dread.
November 3 was one of the happiest nights Democrats have known in decades, as the sheer size of the party’s victory in the midterm elections became apparent. After a decade of Trump dominating public life as standard-bearer of the Republican Party, here at last was proof that the public, even in red states such as Texas and South Carolina, were fed up. Beaten down as they were by frustration at the GOP pushing a hard-right agenda, Democrats could finally entertain the hopes of a better future.
But the brief remarks Schumer delivered that night were a reminder that Trump and the Republicans were only part of the problem the country faces. There’s also the disheartening fact that the Democrats are led by political dinosaurs who have no understanding of the urgency of the current moment.
Schumer is now facing a challenge for the post of Senate majority leader from Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen. Schumer’s election night speech offers clear evidence as to why Van Hollen deserves to win.
Schumer started with a question: “How did he win?” His answer: “First and foremost, we focused on American families and their pain and their needs, their suffering. They are not having a good life, and they are worried about the future for themselves and their children.” Schumer summed up the election as being about three issues: costs, chaos, and corruption.
What’s notable among this vague litany of complaints are all the issues left out that produced heated debate and no shortage of voter anger: the Iran War and its role in destabilizing the world economy, US support of Israel as a factor in the war, the rise of AI and data centers, and the outsize roles of tech plutocrats like Elon Musk in corrupting the political system.
Schumer expressed surprise that the Republicans “embraced Trump” and “followed Trump over the cliff as some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous but much of the time he implemented things that raised their costs.” For most people, talking about “extraneous things” would not make the list of Trump’s thousand worst offenses, so it was puzzling why Schumer felt it necessary to highlight in a short victory speech.
Schumer ended his peroration with a puzzling metaphor: “The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.” As commentators such as Jon Stewart and Sam Seder pointed out, these words were more likely to generate confusion than inspiration. What exactly is the “red brick wall”? Further, walls are usually reduced to rubble, not a pile of bricks. If the bricks still exist, then the red wall can be rebuilt.
Seder rightly noted the absurdity of Schumer’s amazement at congressional Republicans’ loyalty to Trump, given that anyone who has been sentient for the last decade should have noticed that Trump easily won the GOP presidential nomination three times in a row and turned the party into his personal cult. There are few facts more obvious in American public life than that the Republican Party is completely subservient to Trump. But it’s a fact that Schumer still has a hard time accepting or acknowledging.
Partly, this is because Schumer is deeply committed to ancien régime restoration. He still seems to see Trump as a regrettable anomaly who will one day disappear and allow those most mythical creatures, the “reasonable Republicans,” to return. In this worldview, Democrats such as Schumer have to keep signaling they are ready to work with Republicans in order to hasten the return of normal politics. This is why Schumer can only talk about politics in the most abstract of terms (costs, chaos, and corruption) rather than specifying real areas of disagreement.
Schumer has been quite candid about this strategy. In March 2025, he caved in to Republicans during budget negotiations, making concessions that angered his fellow Democrats. Explaining his thinking in an interview with The New York Times, Schumer said his goal was to wait till Trump’s approval ratings have dropped below 40 percent:
And when he went below 40 percent in the polls, the Republican legislators started working with us. He was at 51. He’s now at 48. We’re gonna keep at it until he goes below 40. Look, I talk to a lot of these Republican legislators. I’ve worked with them. Some of them are Trump devotees. But many of them don’t like him, don’t respect him and worry about what he’s doing to our country. Right now he’s so popular they can’t resist him. I mean, so many of them came to me and said: “I don’t think Hegseth should be defense secretary or R.F.K. should be H.H.S. But Trump wants him. He won.” The Republicans would like to have some freedom from Trump, but they won’t until we bring him down in popularity. That happened with Bush in 2005. It happened with Trump in 2017. When it happens, I am hopeful that our Republican colleagues will resume working with us. And I talk to them. One of the places is in the gym. When you’re on that bike in your shorts, panting away next to a Republican, a lot of the inhibitions come off.
This theory of latent Republican moderation rests on nothing more than locker-room conviviality—hardly the basis for a meaningful political agenda. We will now have an empirical test to see if Schumer’s theory is correct. Trump’s approval ratings went below 40 percent in April and have generally stayed well under that threshold. The Republicans suffered a wipeout in the midterms. Yet there is no evidence that the GOP is moderating. In the wake of the midterm trouncing, House Republicans picked Jim Jordan, a hard-right Trump loyalist, as their new leader. The House held a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who brought the motion to the floor, was the only Republican to vote for it. That near-total GOP opposition, and the fact that 11 Democrats failed to show up for the vote, was enough to kill the effort. Massie himself had been defeated earlier this year in the Republican primary and is leaving Congress.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Like many centrists, Schumer fashions himself as a realist. In truth, he’s a fantasist whose theory of politics rests on a world that no longer exists, if it ever did.
Beyond his fetishization of bipartisanship, Schumer’s substantive political commitments are also out of tune with the current urgent moment in politics. In an interview with The Nation, Senator Bernie Sanders listed three areas where Schumer is out of touch: Israel/Palestine, taxing the wealthy, and AI. Sanders described Schumer as someone who “a guy who wants to tinker around the edges” rather than fight for systematic change. In other words, Schumer is yesterday’s man, which is reason enough to support Chris Van Hollen as a replacement.
