https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Show of every Jan van Eyck portrait reveals many new sides to his works
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
There is a lot we do not know for certain about Jan van Eyck, including where and when he was born. What we do know is that his career—from the early 1420s until his death in 1441—helped launch the Early Netherlandish school, influencing the use of oil paint far beyond his native Low Countries and instilling a new and arguably everlasting value of verisimilitude in Western art.
But we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait. The bijoux blockbuster show will give scholars a unique opportunity to compare scattered works of singular importance. Van Eyck: The Portraits—with a checklist that expands all the way to 13 through the addition of three works on paper by his followers—is built around some remarkable pairings.
Fresh from a conservation treatment completed in 2024, the National Gallery’s own Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) (1433) will meet up with Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439), the artist’s wife, on loan from Bruges, where Van Eyck had his workshop when he was the court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.
The National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434), Van Eyck’s enigmatic view of an elegantly dressed couple in an impressive reception room, will be shown for the first time with its related work from the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin clearly showing the same man, Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) (around 1435-38).
Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum is loaning Portrait of an Elderly Man (A Scholar?) (around 1438). It will be shown with the preparatory drawing from Dresden, in goldpoint and silverpoint on prepared paper, with its revealing notes on how to colour the painting itself.
Van Eyck’s devotional portraits, such as those in his groundbreaking Ghent Altarpiece and the Musée du Louvre’s recently treated Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (around 1435), are outside the scope of the National Gallery exhibition.
Some of the portraits have reverse imagery of fictive marble, and the museum is placing them in cases so visitors can view both sides. “We’re really excited to be able to show people how amazing the reverse is,” says Nicholas Flory, who is curating the show along with Emma Capron, the museum’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting. Flory says the elaborate reverses suggest that “these objects were not designed for a single kind of specific space or to be flat against the wall”, but rather “to be interacted with”.
Newness abounds in the show. The Arnolfini Portrait had long had an ornate Gothic Revival frame until it was replaced in 2024 by a 15th-century gilded frame. Meanwhile, the Berlin work, showing its male figure in distinctive red chaperon headgear, completed a conservation treatment in 2023 that removed distorting yellow varnish. The result of that treatment, says Stephan Kemperdick, the curator of Netherlandish paintings before 1600 at the Gemäldegalerie, has been to “make the palette cooler”. Before, he says, the chaperon was “fire-engine red”, and the man’s face looked “suntanned”, whereas now, he says, the face is “pinkish or whiteish—a feature that distinguished people from the better classes in the 15th century”.
The London exhibition, which Kemperdick calls a “once-in-a-lifetime” event, is a culmination of sorts. Several Van Eyck works, including the Ghent Altarpiece, have undergone recent treatments, which Flory says has been “an impetus in Van Eyck scholarship”, and the National Gallery show reflects new research into Van Eyck’s technique, his original frames and inscriptions. Recent analysis of the National Gallery’s self-portrait, examined during its recent treatment, revealed how Van Eyck modulated the blueness of the background in the lower-right corner to “throw the sitter’s shoulder forward”, Flory says, creating a 3D effect.
Arnolfini not Arnolfini?
Just out of view of the show itself, lurking in Kemperdick’s catalogue essay, is a possible bombshell: that the couple shown in the Arnolfini Portrait are not the titular Italian merchant and his wife at all, but rather Van Eyck and his wife. This would also mean that the Gemäldegalerie’s Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) is also a self-portrait.
The Arnolfini Portrait is among the gallery’s most popular works, and the minuscule size of the show is in marked contrast with the likely museumgoer interest. However, Flory says the diminutive roster is, in fact, the big attraction.
“There was the possibility to expand it beyond Van Eyck and show his work in the context of his contemporaries,” Flory says. “But because he is such a monumental figure in the history of Western painting, and his portraits are so special, we really wanted to focus the exhibition on just Van Eyck himself.” Luckily, he adds, the remarkable loans, which have involved several museums sending some of their most precious works, mean “we got everything we were hoping for”.
• Jan van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/will-lawrenc.title: Heading to Congress, Will Lawrence Still Has Some Questions
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/will-lawrenc.author: Liza Featherstone
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/will-lawrenc.text:
Heading to Congress, Will Lawrence Still Has Some Questions
The election of left-wing environmental activist Will Lawrence to Congress from Michigan offers hope for American democracy. But in a conversation with Jacobin, the congressman-elect is sober about just how much our system can change.
Will Lawrence has been part of every anti-oligarchic organizing effort that has mattered over the last two decades: Barack Obama–era climate activism, Occupy Wall Street, Sunrise Movement, housing justice, the Bernie Sanders campaigns, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), and resistance to artificial intelligence data centers. Before the recent midterm election, the thirty-six-year-old East Lansing, Michigan native was exactly the sort of candidate who, according to conventional wisdom, could maybe beat establishment Democrats in liberal blue districts but would lack traction against the Right in a general election.
Yet on Election Day, Lawrence proved that conventional wisdom wrong. He flipped a Republican seat in Mid Michigan and is now headed to Congress.
Lawrence is not the only one showing that an anti-oligarchy, pro-working-class politics can succeed in purple and red America. From Maine to Montana, Bernie Sanders–style politics beat Trumpism across the nation. In Washington, DC’s incoming Congress, Lawrence, reached by phone while walking through the tunnels of Capitol Hill, joins numerous “regular people, many of whom are complete outsiders,” newly taking their place in Congress.
They’re not just “regular” in the sense of not being billionaires. They’re also not career politicians. They “owe nothing to anybody” in power, Lawrence emphasizes, and they “have a mandate to root out corruption, get money out of politics, deliver economic security for their constituents, stop stupid wars, and stabilize the climate.”
But Lawrence has serious questions about what’s possible in this moment.
“We can undo everything that Trump has done,” he vows. “We can undo the Big Beautiful Bill. We can restore SNAP [the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program], Medicaid, and the ACA. We can take action to lower prices in certain sectors,” he says:
And yet, economic volatility will continue. People will continue to feel that the future is looking worse. And we’ll still be stuck with the questions of, “What is America’s global role in the twenty-first century? How do we deal with the billionaires, the oligarchs, at the commanding heights of the economy?”
He pauses, aware that he’s brought down the mood. I feel a bit superficial bringing us back to the elections, asking how he won his congressional seat, but it turns out not to be a change of subject or tone. Lawrence’s refusal of sunny platitudes continues.
“Acknowledging the despair and disillusionment that people feel as rational and legitimate, and then drawing on those who have come before, to remember that people have dealt with adversity, uncertainty, and volatility and have fought back against the powerful of their time to win the rights and freedoms and quality of life that we have until recently enjoyed,” is crucial, he says. “The social compact of the New Deal era was fought for and won with blood.”
Lawrence’s parents, like my own, worked at Michigan State University, and I’ve spent a lot of time in his hometown, a land grant university town bordered by flat cornfields on one side and Lansing, the state capitol, on the other. I’m not surprised his bleak honesty and capacious politics could draw Michiganders together.
Lawrence unseated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, a Trumper who staunchly supported the war in Iran and opposed extending the Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax credits at the beginning of this year. The district backed Donald Trump in 2024 but has flipped so often that it is regarded as a bellwether for the presidential election.
“There are a lot of bad people,” Lawrence continues,
and a lot of reasons to feel disillusioned when bad people manipulate their way into having a lot of power. And yet we have it inside of us to become the better versions of ourselves, to build a better version of our society. [The campaign] was all about that: giving people a reason for hope, creating space for community, for people to make friends and get to know each other, challenge each other, challenge themselves to take action and to take responsibility.
“And it did,” he allows, passing the hopium pipe for just a second, “make me feel more optimistic about democracy. There is some juice left.”
Lawrence isn’t calling himself a socialist these days. He let his DSA membership lapse, which he announced during the campaign, wanting to focus, he told CNN at the time, on uniting the district. He said that he wanted his constituents to feel he represented and was listening to them, rather than any specific organization.
Whether he was wearing his green-and-white Spartans hat at the tailgating parties on Michigan State’s massive campus, where the student vote shapes elections more than it does anywhere else in the nation; or canvassing or conducting town halls across the district, in small cities and towns like Grand Ledge and Brighton — this approach clearly resonated, winning over independent voters and even Republicans.
“The more I continued with the campaign,” he tells Jacobin, “the more I just chafed at some of the attempts to label me as ‘socialist,’ ‘communist,’ or whatever, in a way that was about making people fear me.” So he decided, “Let’s just focus on the values and the issues. When we start there, there’s tons of common ground.”
As he points out, he’s not alone among the incoming left wing of the party in taking this approach. While the new Congress includes New York City socialists Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, it also includes Lawrence’s fellow Michigander, incoming Senator Abdul El-Sayed, who beat a Republican with a Bernie Sanders platform and no “socialist” label; or Troy Jackson in Maine, who did the same.
“With this incoming freshman class that is large and historic,” Lawrence says, “people identify themselves in a variety of ways: progressive, moderate, none of the above. But everybody campaigned on the same issues. And they feel a mandate to deliver change.”
It has been striking to see the continuity, across the country, of Sanders-style issues in the winning candidates’ platforms: Medicare for All, taxing the rich, childcare, defunding the war machine, a moratorium on AI data centers. It is a mandate against billionaires and for the common good. And, Lawrence suggests, there may be a variety of ways to express that:
For the self-identified Left, my push is not to get too hung up on labels or making assumptions about others based on their labels. . . . The project of reconstituting the social and political compact for the twenty-first century has to be based in the bid for a supermajority of the people of this country. And there is no supermajority of this country who currently identifies with any common label. So, we have to be willing to listen beyond that and then find new symbols and perhaps new labels that allow us to establish that majority.
Lawrence feels strongly about changing the direction of foreign policy, and this incoming class has a mandate to do that, probably for the first time this century. But he’s very worried about whether it can be done — and not for the reasons I’m expecting, like the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and defense lobbyists.
“For me, this is one of the lessons of Joe Biden’s administration, which I do really believe tried to do something good for the American working class and wanted to deliver on economic security,” yet was “so militarist and hawkish.” He points to the administration’s position on Israel and Palestine: “It completely undid the coalition that Bernie and Biden supporters had painstakingly built together for the sake of building a united front to defeat Trump.”
Lawrence is worried about whether, in America, we can have peacetime social democracy. “Social democracy without a Cold War posture is unproven,” he says. “Social democracy was forged in the context of the Cold War. And in the attempt to reforge a social democracy [today], there will be those, like in the Biden administration, who believe that a new Cold War is a natural part of that project.”
He’s right: During the Cold War, workers’ material gains — including civil rights for black Americans — could often be framed as part of an anti-communist argument that capitalism could deliver a better life for the working class than communism. And a state of permanent war readiness fueled the economy, bringing billions of federal dollars into defense spending and creating millions of good jobs.
Lawrence worries that many Democrats still can’t separate militarism and social democracy, that they believe that ongoing war can “clarify the resolve and the sense of national purpose, but also that it’s the only way that we can have an economy which is prosperous, with a broad-based growth that includes a strong deal for the working class.” That won’t cut it today, he says: “I don’t believe that that will work for the twenty-first century, because the conditions of the political economy are different. It’s not 1946 anymore. And we’re not going to recreate the economic conditions that existed then. So we have to find a different way.”
One of the fights that politically shaped Lawrence, a Sunrise activist, was the campaign for the Green New Deal during the Biden administration; it seems possible that an energy transition off fossil fuels could contain the seeds of that “different way.” Maybe in Congress, Lawrence can help bring those ideas back to political life.
Maybe. But he’s certainly not overpromising. It’s jarring to talk to a politician who has thought so deeply about the perils and limitations of our moment and speaks so frankly about them. Not only does Lawrence not think perpetual geopolitical conflict can deliver for Americans. (Americans, squeezed by gas prices during the war in Iran, seem to agree.) “I really don’t want to see World War III. It’s as likely as not that that’s where things are headed,” he warns. “Preventing that is one of my main missions.”

https://gothamist.com/news/3-people-shot.title: 2 Co-op City peace officers shot during Bronx wellness check, officials say
https://gothamist.com/news/3-people-shot.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/3-people-shot.text:
Two Co-op City peace officers were shot during a wellness check at a Bronx apartment building Monday morning, officials said. The 56-year-old man who police said opened fire on the officers was later found dead from what authorities described as a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
The officers were responding to a wellness check request forwarded by the NYPD when the man fired four shots from inside his apartment on the 25th floor, according to Andre Waring, chief of the Co-op City Department of Public Safety. Both officers were hospitalized with injuries police described as not life-threatening.
“As they were going into the apartment, he just started shooting,” Waring told Gothamist.
The shooting happened in the hallway outside the apartment, Waring said.
NYPD Emergency Service Unit officers later entered the apartment and found the man with a self-inflicted gunshot wound, police officials said.
One officer was grazed by gunfire and was recovering, while the other, a female officer, was still in surgery Monday afternoon, Waring said. He said it was not yet clear whether she had been shot twice.
Waring said his department had no previous problems with the man and did not know why the wellness check had been requested.
Co-op City, a 15,000-unit development, is a self-governed, private residential housing cooperative with its own Department of Public Safety.
According to the department, its officers are state-certified peace officers who are authorized to carry firearms and make arrests.
This is a developing story and has been updated based on new information from police.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842. A few key facts about the dual portrait, showing a youngish man and his idealised wife, could be gleaned just by looking at the work’s prominent Latin inscription, which translates as “Jan van Eyck was here 1434”. Over the years, just about everything else associated with the painting, from its mysterious room to the obscure occasion, has been open to debate, other than the surname of the man—Arnolfini, connected to an extended family of wealthy merchants from Lucca active in 15th-century Bruges, where Van Eyck had his studio.
Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.
Kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely new one. In the late 1840s, the National Gallery’s future first director Charles Eastlake contended that the artist’s inscription, which he thought could be translated as “Jan van Eyck was this [one]”, meant that the painting was also a dual portrait of the artist and his wife. But in the early 1860s, the British art historian W. H. James Weale interpreted a reference in a 16th-century inventory to a certain “hernoul le fin” in the painting, which he regarded as the French version of the Italian surname Arnolfini. The connection between the couple and that family was thus set in stone, though scholars disagree, often vehemently, about which particular member of the Arnolfini clan is shown.
Kemperdick has revisited the inscription, which is unusually large and conspicuously places the artist’s name next to the male figure’s head. He argues this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man. He has also reconsidered the association between the “hernoul le fin” reference and the surname Arnolfini. Citing the early-modern categorisation of the late-medieval work as not a portrait at all, but rather a lewd genre painting, Kemperdick suggests that “hernoul le fin” is not the correct surname of the sitter, but a subsequent and mocking moniker used by later generations to misidentify the man as a “a deceived cheat”. Kemperdick also suggests that a reference to St Margaret in the bedstead statue near the woman’s head serves to identify her as Van Eyck’s wife.
Multiple Arnolfini portraits
Kemperdick is the curator of German, Netherlandish and French Paintings before 1600 at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which is noted for its Early Netherlandish holdings and has in its own collection a Van Eyck portrait (around 1435-38) of the very same man who appears in the National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait. The two will be shown together in the London exhibition.
Nicholas Flory, the co-curator of Van Eyck: The Portraits along with Emma Capron, the National Gallery’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting, says that he and Capron find Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative”, citing, among other reasons, that the woman in the Bruges portrait, whom we know to be Margaret based on the inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.
Other leading Van Eyck scholars also have their doubts. The German art historian Till-Holger Borchert—now the director of the Suermondt-
Ludwig-Museum in Aachen and the former director of Musea Brugge in Bruges—is familiar with Kemperdick’s theory. “I’m not entirely sure I can concur,” he says. He thinks the early-16th-century inventory reference—associated with the painting’s owner at the time, Margaret of Austria, the governor of the Habsburg Netherlands—is a near iron-clad reference to the Arnolfinis. The Ghent University art historian Maximiliaan Martens, who has been involved in the lengthy restoration of Van Eyck’s Ghent Altarpiece, also “doesn’t see any reason to doubt” that the inventory reference is to the Arnolfinis.
The implications of Kemperdick’s theory are far-reaching. Another Van Eyck portrait at the National Gallery, from 1433, showing a much older man than the figure in the Arnolfini Portrait, is now tentatively identified by the London museum as a self-portrait. This, however, cannot be the case if Kemperdick’s theory is correct.
The exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits will label the Berlin work with its previous and longstanding reference to the Arnolfinis, while the Gemäldegalerie, under Kemperick’s guidance, has recently renamed it Portrait of a Man with a Red Chaperon. And the debate about the couple promises to continue long after the show closes in April.
“I have thought for 30 years about this,” Martens says of the figures in the Arnolfini Portrait. He says he is still not sure if the man is Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (who was apparently not married at the time the painting was made) or his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini (whose wife had died before the painting was made).
Other aspects of the dual portrait that scholars continue to debate include whether the heavy-bellied woman is actually pregnant (Kemperdick and Martens think that may be possible, while Flory and Capron think she is just gathering up her heavy skirts), and whether the room itself is a real space or an imagined one (imagined, say Flory and Capron; real, says Martens).
Beyond who made it and when, the Arnolfini Portrait remains a mystery, which is in keeping for an artist whose date and place of birth, among other foundational knowledge, is also speculation. Asked to comment on the enigma associated with the Arnolfini Portrait, Borchert says: “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-the-freedo.title: NY, the 'Freedom Summer' murders and an improbable election win in Mississippi
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-the-freedo.author: Amanda Rozon
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-the-freedo.text:
In 1964, a 20-year-old student from New York City was murdered in Neshoba County, Mississippi, along with two other civil rights workers.
Andrew Goodman was there trying to help Black Mississippians register to vote. A member of the Ku Klux Klan was eventually found guilty of directing the killing of Goodman, James Earl Chaney, who was from Mississippi, and Michael Schwerner, who was from Pelham, New York.
Now, 62 years after the deaths, Mississippians have elected their first Black senator in 150 years. Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in a closely contested race.
David Goodman, a New Jersey resident and the brother of Andrew Goodman, serves on the board of the Andrew Goodman Foundation.
He spoke with Morning Edition host Michael Hill in the aftermath of Colom’s victory.
Here is a transcript of their conversation, which has been edited for length and clarity:
Michael Hill: David, good morning, and welcome to Morning Edition.
David Goodman: Good morning, Michael. Thank you so much for inviting me. I really appreciate it.
Tell us briefly how your brother Andrew, who you called Andy, came to join what's known as Freedom Summer in the 1960s, and how it eventually led to his murder.
We lived in New York City, and we were brought up by our parents to believe in this concept of fairness. I gotta tell you a funny story, because it sort of set the pace. My mother would take me to the butcher. And this is before big supermarkets. You had to buy your meat fresh. She said during one trip, “Watch so-and-so." They had 10 butchers behind the counter, and I did, and she's looking at him, and he's looking at her. And l asked, "What's this about, mom?" She said, "Well, he had his thumb on the scale and was cheating us, right?” So that became kind of a password in our family, and many families take it to mean being cheated. And, my brother — we all had that kind of sense of fairness. Things should be fair, and you shouldn't be cheated, and you shouldn't cheat anybody else.
And in the spring of 1964, I was about to graduate high school. He was three years older than me. And he announces to the family, "I'm going to Mississippi." And I don't even know where Mississippi was, and I said, "Why?" He said, "Well," he heard that African Americans weren't allowed to vote by the white power structure in Mississippi. I didn't know what that meant. And then he says, "You know, the ‘thumb-on-the-scale thing.’" I said, "Oh, not fair." And he said it that way. He said, "It's just not fair." And then he said something that was strange. He said, "And I wanna do something about it." And that was just his nature. He was really a big proponent of living a fair life. It almost sounds naive. I don't think we really realized the danger, but this is how we were brought up. So he went to Mississippi and joined the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. John Lewis was the national chair at the age of 24, and Andrew got murdered being fair. That's what happened.
What do you think of the election of Sen.-elect Colom? And do you see a nexus, a link to Andrew's advocacy some six decades ago?
Absolutely. We have 50 states in the union, and none of them are perfect. Specifically in Mississippi, this had a more than a rough justice kind of feel to it. Mr. Colom is a shrewd guy — a prosecutor and lawyer, and he had his eyes out for things that were unfair, and he turned on enough voters to see some folks had their thumb on the scale. And he said something about it, and he worked hard and took a big risk, and he won. The people of Mississippi have spoken.
But as I say that, I wanna make something really clear. You know, we're New Jersey residents. Mississippi isn't the only state where powerful people have their thumb on the scale. I mean, in New Jersey recently, we put a Democratic senator in jail for stealing from us, right? And we have to keep in mind that Mississippi is just one of 50 states, and we all have a responsibility to keep our eyes on the prize, and when we see something wrong, do something about it. That's why we, my parents, formed the Andrew Goodman Foundation.
As the civil rights movement came under attack in Congress in the 1960s, your brother Andrew said, “the senators could not persist in this polite debate over the future dignity of a human race if the white northerners were not so shockingly apathetic.” Does what he said still apply today?
Oh, absolutely. This is the exact point I'm making. Every state has some people who have their thumbs on the scale of justice. And we the people, we have to watch that. He wrote a paper that I think you're quoting from, that if you're in New York and you don't say anything about something bad going on in Montana or Maine or Mississippi, it's hurting you in New York even though you may not know it. We're all part of the same country. You know, Sen.-elect Colom is going to the U.S. Senate, and he votes on stuff that affects us in New Jersey, and vice versa. We're all in one country, and if someone has their thumbs on the scale of justice in New Jersey or Mississippi or Montana, it hurts all the other states.
So what he was saying was we all gotta pay attention, which is what we do at the Andrew Goodman Foundation today, whose mission is making young voices and votes a powerful force in democracy, and you do that by voting. And if you don't like what someone is doing who is in power, you fire him, vote him out, and you vote somebody else in. And that's what my brother meant in what he wrote, "New York, pay attention. New Jersey, pay attention. Mississippi, pay attention, and get rid of the people who got their thumb on the scale, and put in people who are gonna represent us."
Our guest has been David Goodman, brother of Andrew Goodman, a New York City student who in 1964 was murdered helping Black Mississippians register to vote. David, what an honor.
Thank you so much.

https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.title: Man charged with murder in shooting at NJ vigil that left 1 dead, 4 injured
https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/man-charged-w.text:
A New Jersey man is facing murder charges in connection with a shooting at a candlelight vigil in Elizabeth last month that left one person dead and four others injured, prosecutors announced Monday.
Travon Holmes, 29, is charged with first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit murder and four counts of attempted murder, according to the Union County Prosecutor's Office.
The shooting happened around 9:30 p.m. on Oct. 26 during a candlelight vigil at the intersection of Elmwood Place and Irvington Avenue in Elizabeth, authorities said.
Five people were shot, including 26-year-old Steve Scott of Edison, who was pronounced dead at the scene. The four other victims were taken to a local hospital for treatment, officials said.
Holmes was arrested Friday, Nov. 13, in Elizabeth and is being held at the Essex County Jail, prosecutors said.
The investigation remains ongoing. Attorney information for Holmes was not immediately available to Gothamist.

After leading South London Gallery (SLG) since 2001, Margot Heller will step down as its director in May 2027 to work as an independent curator and adviser. Heller offered the following statement in a press release: “The South London Gallery has been a huge part of my life and I believe passionately in its importance. After twenty-five years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career.”
Heller previously worked as a curator, before serving as director of the Southampton City Art Gallery between 1989 and 1996. She then became Director of Exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery in 1996 and also worked as freelance curator before joining SLG.
During her tenure at SLG, Heller tripled the gallery’s footprint, refurbishing and adding a neighboring house and fire station to the institution’s complex. She also facilitated the development of a publicly accessible garden in the gallery, designed by Mexican artist Gabriel Orozco.
Heller also curated solo shows by major artists at SLG, including those by Superflex (2009), Tatiana Trouvé (2010), Rashid Johnson (2012), Lawrence Weiner (2014), Thomas Hirschhorn (2015, Katharina Grosse (2017), and Haegue Yang (2019), among many others.
Her time at the gallery also saw SLG set up its Communities and Learning programme, and support emerging artists through its Post Graduate Artist in Residence Programme for 12 years. “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own,” said artist and SLG board member, Alvaro Barrington, in a statement.
Heller also helmed SLG’s leadership of the pioneering Louis Vuitton Young Arts Project (2010) which marked a collaboration between Tate, Whitechapel Gallery, the Royal Academy, and Hayward Gallery. Before Heller departs, she will curate the first solo show by Dutch artist Mark Manders at a London institution. The exhibition will be on view at SLG from 23 September 2027 to 9 January 2028.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/s.title: Signal Problems: MTA Reports Delays On Multiple CBTC Upgrade Projects Amid Data Center Threat
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/s.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/16/s.text:
Signal work is not getting done any faster these days. Photo: Marc A. Hermann/MTA
It’s all red signals ahead.
New York’s efforts to upgrade signals on five subway lines are months behind schedule, MTA officials revealed on Monday, with none of the new signals set to come online until 2028 at the earliest — as data centers pose a looming threat to the agency’s efforts to complete the projects with less money.
With the exception of the recently commenced A/C signal upgrades between Downtown Brooklyn and Ozone Park, each of the MTA’s individual signal upgrade projects is now running late:
The Fulton Street-Liberty Avenue project, which upgrades the signals alone the A, C and E lines between 59th Street and High Street, was scheduled to come online in the first quarter of 2027 and now won’t do so until the fourth quarter of 2027.
The Queens Boulevard Line East project, which upgrades signals on the F train between Union Turnpike and 179th Street, was scheduled to come online in the second quarter of 2027 and now won’t be in service until the second quarter of 2028.
The Crosstown project, which upgrades signals on the G and F trains between Court Square and Church Avenue, was scheduled to come online in 2027 on the north piece of the line and 2028 on the south piece, and now won’t be online on either line until 2028.
The problems plaguing the communications-based train control upgrades vary by project, but mostly relate to software issues, train compatibility issues and design plans for how to safely change signals over from the old system to modern computerized signals, according to the MTA executives in charge of the upgrades.
This is most apparent on the Eighth Avenue project. An MTA executive said it was all ready to go, but that the agency found that the track geometry it fed into the computer that controls the train under CBTC was not accurate.
“We can see some issues in some of the testing,” said Mark Roche, the deputy chief development officer at MTA told the Capital Committee. “We can see there’s one silly thing that happened in the project that we have to correct. As the trains run down the system they’re telling us, ‘This curve is a bit bigger than you told us, this hill is steeper than you told us.’ The accuracy of the survey that we gave the computer is now telling us back [that] there’s something a bit strange here.”
Switching trains over to being controlled by computerized signals without accurate track geometry could lead to the same problems that snarled the Queens Boulevard West line in 2022, when the agency activated CBTC and experienced up to 20 signal malfunctions per day on the line.
“We could turn this system on now, it’s ready to go,” Roche said. “But you’d have lots of problems so we’re not gonna turn it on. On the QBL West we probably turned it on too soon, we’re not going to do that again.”
The MTA is running into problems with maintaining the existing signal system on the easternmost portion of the Queens Boulevard line. The agency chose to the legacy signals in place when it designed the new system. Its leaders found it difficult to ensure that an interlocking using CBTC software can respond quickly enough to provide safe and reliable service.
On the Crosstown line, Roche said the agency found a combination of physical work issues and planning issues. The MTA discovered much more serious tunnel damage and leaks, which took the agency a year to fix as it got to work installing new signals.
“State of good repair and discovering state of good repair problems on these projects is a major issue to make these happen quickly,” he said. “We’re finding too many things wrong with the system.”
But the agency also seems to have bitten off more than it can chew with its plans for the project. Roche told the committee that the contractor performing the work for the agency originally pitched the MTA on doing a “cutover” — the term for when a subway system moves from its legacy signals to modern signals all at once, instead of in phases as is usually done.
Despite agreeing to that, the MTA later determined that the idea wouldn’t work, and now has to work with the contractor on a phased cutover plan while the signals are being installed.
“One of those ideas was we could cut this project over in one go,” he said. “On the first day it’s non-CBTC, on the second day it’s CBTC. We’ve not been able to prove that’s a good idea. So we’ve slowed down the project. We’ve worked with [the contractor] to say hold on, let’s cut this over in five or six pieces, let’s spend a little more time.”
The MTA had some good news, too. Its leadership said that the physical work of ripping up tunnels and installing new track has gone according to plan. “The civil work, the track, switch, infrastructure — that is very much going on schedule,” said MTA Construction and Development President Jamie Torres-Springer. “The stuff that disrupts our customers, we are managing those very effectively.”
Roche also pointed out that the MTA has cut the cost of signal upgrade projects on a per-mile basis by about 33 percent, when looking at the Crosstown and Fulton-Liberty projects compared to the per-mile cost for the 7 train, QBL West, Culver, Eighth Avenue and QBL East projects.
There is a touch of grey in that silver lining though, as Roche said that everyone’s favorite boogeyman, data centers, are threatening to drive up the prices for CBTC upgrades. “We are seeing a massive competition with data centers,” said Roche. “The cables, the equipment is getting more expensive. We have a huge competition on the market with data centers.”
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.

https://hyperallergic.com/why-is-the-whi.title: Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?
https://hyperallergic.com/why-is-the-whi.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/why-is-the-whi.text:
Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?
“Yellow River” (1958) was deaccessioned and will be auctioned at Christie's just three years after it was gifted to the museum in 2023.
Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million.
The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy. In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections.
A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”
The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.
“Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the artist's shift from cacophonous urban compositions to more airy landscapes, designating the freeway as a conduit connecting New York City to the Hudson River Valley and Long Island's South Fork. In vibrant warm yellow, earthy brown tones, and stretches of deep blue, de Kooning's decisive gestures direct viewers across overlapping paths and visual rest stops throughout the canvas.
“I love to be on those highways,” de Kooning said to British critic and curator David Sylvester about the expansive roads during a BBC interview in 1960. “And they are really not very pretty, but the big embankments and the shoulders of the roads and the curves are flawless.”
“Yellow River” hung at the foot of Solinger's bed for some time, serving as a testament to Solinger's fascination with the artist. His wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, took ownership of the work after Solinger passed in 1996, and in 2011, she designated the work as a promised gift to the Whitney in honor of her late husband. It officially entered the Whitney's holdings in 2023, the same year that the museum deaccessioned seven works, including an Edward Hopper landscape, and sent them to auction to benefit the collection.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/inte.title: The Intercept Sues U.S. Military Over Iran Casualty Tally and Blacklist of Journalists
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/inte.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/inte.text:
The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon in a pair of lawsuits demanding the release of documents related to the number of U.S. casualties in its war on Iran and the Department of Defense’s secretive blacklist of journalists.
One lawsuit, filed on Friday, responds to the department’s “repeated, unexplained changes” to its publicly available tracker showing U.S. service members killed or injured in the conflict with Iran — including a failure to acknowledge one soldier’s death for the six months after he died — that were documented by Intercept reporter Nick Turse. The shifting figures led one defense official to call the undercount a “casualty cover-up.”
In August, Turse requested from the Pentagon, through the Freedom of Information Act, casualty-related records and briefing materials presented to Defense Secretary Hegseth and his chief of staff, directives and guidance on casualties, as well as communications related to casualties between Hegseth and his staff of advisers. A later request filed by The Intercept in September sought the financial costs of the Iran war since its start in February. In all cases, the government stopped responding to The Intercept and has failed to provide any documents.
A second lawsuit against Hegseth’s DoD, filed on Monday, follows a July conversation with The Intercept in which a spokesperson for U.S. Central Command admitted the military post keeps a blacklist of media members. While reporting on the shifting U.S. soldier casualty figures, the CENTCOM spokesperson, Richard Allee, threatened Turse that he would be “put on a list of people to disregard” for calling the command too often.
CENTCOM later denied the existence of such a list. But Turse spoke with an unnamed U.S. official who confirmed that “Hegseth’s office had a standing order not to engage with [Turse] and would deny it if challenged.” During the first Trump administration, Turse had been placed on a separate blacklist kept by U.S. Africa Command, also within the Pentagon, after he reported on the torture of prisoners at a remote military base in Cameroon used by the U.S. for drone surveillance.
Turse has since filed a public records request seeking a copy of any “lists of journalists that CENTCOM discriminates against or disregards.” The Freedom of the Press Foundation also filed a request for communications and guidance related to the blacklist, as well as any records related to the command’s response to Turse’s article on the matter, published in August. The government has yet to provide any such information to The Intercept or Freedom of the Press Foundation.
“The military doesn’t get to decide which reporters it speaks to or ignores, especially when it’s engaged in legally questionable military actions and the human cost is at its highest. It’s not just the journalists who are harmed when the Pentagon behaves this way — the public and Congress are each denied critical information about what the military is doing in our name and with our taxes,” said Lauren Harper, Daniel Ellsberg chair on government secrecy, who filed FOIA requests for the blacklist on behalf of FPF. “If the Defense Department refuses to answer basic questions about how it engages with journalists, we’ll use the Freedom of Information Act to compel them in court.
The Intercept’s Turse called the Pentagon’s journalist blacklist “fundamentally un-American” and a way to avoid accounting for the real human toll of the ongoing war.
“Central Command wants to keep the sordid details of its wars — from civilian casualties in Iran and Yemen to U.S. military casualties across the Middle East — under wraps,” he said. “They need to come clean to the American people. We have to hold them accountable.”
Hegseth’s Department of Defense has long been hostile toward members of the media. In February 2025, days after Hegseth assumed office, the department forced out outlets such as NBC News, NPR, the New York Times, Politico, CNN, and the Washington Post from their Pentagon press desks. That October, Hegseth issued a new requirement in which journalists could only gain access to the Pentagon if they pledged to only report on information from government employees pre-approved by the Defense Department. This prompted most media outlets, except for the right-wing MAGA-friendly One America News Network, to surrender their press passes.
Trump has also targeted specific media outlets and individual journalists by barring them from the White House or Air Force One, though a federal court judge has since paused the bans, cautioning against possible violations of the First Amendment.
The Intercept and FPF’s lawsuits arrive days after Hegseth narrowly survived an impeachment attempt over his handling of the Iran war. The effort, led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and backed by Democrats, failed to garner enough votes to impeach Hegseth.
In addition to the war on Iran, incoming Democratic members of Congress, along with human rights groups, seek to hold Hegseth accountable for his bloody airstrike campaign on boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, in which the U.S. has killed more than 240 civilians, and his overseeing of the U.S. invasion of Venezuela.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://citylimits.org/nueva-norma-feder.text:

Los defensores de la vivienda afirman que tienen la intención de oponerse a la aplicación de la normativa del Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano de Estados Unidos (HUD por sus siglas en inglés), que, según ellos, podría obligar a unos 2.500 hogares neoyorquinos a renunciar a las ayudas federales para la vivienda o a separarse de sus familias.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 16 de noviembre. Traducido por Daniel Parra. Read the English version here.
El 10 de noviembre, el Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano de los Estados Unidos (HUD por sus siglas en inglés) publicó una norma que exige a los hogares que residen en viviendas públicas financiadas con fondos federales que acrediten su ciudadanía, lo que podría afectar a miles de familias con situaciones migratorias mixtas.
La nueva norma, que se propuso a principios de este año y entraría en vigor el 14 de diciembre, endurece los requisitos de acceso a las ayudas federales para el alquiler, especialmente para los inmigrantes.
Actualmente, los inmigrantes indocumentados no pueden optar a las ayudas federales para la vivienda. Sin embargo, se les permite vivir en viviendas subvencionadas con fondos federales —como los edificios de la Autoridad de Vivienda de la Ciudad de Nueva York (NYCHA por sus siglas en inglés)— junto con otros miembros de la familia que cumplan los requisitos, en lo que se denomina hogares de “estatus mixto”.
Estos hogares pagan un porcentaje más alto del alquiler para compensar la presencia del miembro de la familia que no cumple los requisitos, y reciben lo que se conoce como “una tarifa prorrateada” (prorated assistance).
Según la nueva normativa, todos los miembros de un hogar que reciba ayudas federales para el alquiler —incluidos aquellos con vales de la Sección 8 o que vivan en viviendas públicas de la Sección 9— deberán probar su ciudadanía o un estatus migratorio que les dé derecho a recibir subvenciones federales, tal y como se establece en la normativa federal denominada Sección 214.
Incluso los inmigrantes que se encuentran legalmente en Estados Unidos podrían verse afectados por ese requisito, según los expertos.
“Las personas pueden estar en Estados Unidos de forma legal, pero no por ello tienen necesariamente derecho a la ayuda para el alquiler en virtud de la Sección 214”, explicó Lucy Newman, abogada supervisora de la unidad de vivienda pública de Legal Aid Society, y añadió: “esa es una parte realmente importante de todo esto”.
Entre los estatus migratorios que dan derecho a recibir ayudas federales para la vivienda se incluyen los residentes permanentes, asilados o refugiados, supervivientes de la trata de personas, solicitantes en virtud de la Ley contra la Violencia hacia las Mujeres e inmigrantes admitidos para recibir asistencia temporal legal, entre otros.
Entre los estatus migratorios que no dan derecho a estas ayudas se incluyen los titulares de visas U, beneficiarios del programa DACA, TPS e inmigrantes indocumentados.
Newman explicó que en promedio tres de cada cuatro miembros de los hogares de estatus mixto de la ciudad de Nueva York tienen un estatus migratorio que les da derecho a recibir ayuda federal, y advirtió que la nueva norma podría provocar que esos miembros con derecho a la ayuda se muden o les obligue a separarse de sus seres queridos.
Una coalición de 22 fiscales generales estatales, entre ellos el de Nueva York, envió en abril una carta al secretario del HUD, Scott Turner, oponiéndose al cambio normativo que afectaría a 2.500 hogares con estatus mixto en Nueva York.
“Nosotros y otros activistas estamos trabajando para retrasar o detener la aplicación de esta medida, lo que incluye plantearnos emprender acciones legales”, afirmó Newman.
Los comentarios públicos presentados en contra de la norma argumentaban que es innecesaria porque los miembros del hogar que no cumplen los requisitos no reciben subsidios federales, y que desplazaría a algunos hogares sin liberar ayudas para otros.
“En realidad, resulta más caro financiar a los hogares que cumplen todos los requisitos, ya que la ayuda tiene que cubrir a todas las personas de ese hogar”, explicó Newman. “Si esta norma entra en vigor, la situación general será que se acabará ayudando a menos personas porque el programa costará más”.
“En realidad, resulta más caro subvencionar a los hogares que cumplen todos los requisitos, ya que la ayuda tiene que cubrir a todas las personas de ese hogar”, explicó Newman. “Si esta norma entra en vigor, la situación general es que acabarán ayudando a menos personas porque el programa costará más”.
Según el Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, un grupo de análisis político no partidista, casi 80,000 personas de 20,000 hogares de todo el país podrían correr el riesgo de perder sus viviendas; el 96 por ciento son personas de color, de las cuales el 86 por ciento son latinas.
Después de California y Texas, el estado de Nueva York es el tercero con mayor número de hogares de estatus mixto en viviendas públicas.
NYCHA, que gestiona un programa de la Sección 8, así como conjuntos de vivienda pública de la Sección 9, no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios sobre el cambio normativo. El Departamento de Conservación y Desarrollo de la Vivienda de la ciudad, que también gestiona la Sección 8 a nivel local, remitió las preguntas a la oficina del alcalde.
En una declaración a City Limits, el alcalde Zohran Mamdani expresó su oposición a la norma, al tiempo que tranquilizó a los neoyorquinos que reciben ayudas federales para la vivienda asegurándoles que el anuncio de la semana pasada no supondrá un cambio inmediato en su subsidio.
“En la ciudad de Nueva York, creemos que todo el mundo merece un lugar seguro y asequible al que llamar hogar, independientemente de dónde haya nacido o de su situación migratoria”, afirmó Mamdani. “La ciudad está evaluando todas las opciones disponibles para defender a los neoyorquinos y proteger su acceso a la vivienda. Porque nadie debería vivir con el miedo de perder su hogar por el lugar de donde proviene”.
La División de Vivienda y Renovación Comunitaria del estado de Nueva York (DHCR por sus siglas en inglés), que forma parte del Departamento de Vivienda y Renovación Comunitaria de Nueva York y supervisa algunos programas de la Sección 8, afirmó que “seguirá analizando el posible impacto de estos cambios propuestos”.
En una entrevista con FOX, el secretario del HUD, Turner, se refirió a la norma como el cierre de una “brecha legal que llevaba décadas existiendo”.
“Estamos poniendo fin a las subvenciones destinadas a las fronteras abiertas de Biden, defendiendo el estado de derecho, cerrando la brecha legal de décadas de antigüedad relativa a los ‘compañeros de piso con estatus mixto’ y protegiendo el dinero de los contribuyentes estadounidenses”, declaró un portavoz del HUD en un comunicado a City Limits, señalando que el cambio liberará $218 millones en subvenciones para “hogares estadounidenses que cumplan todos los requisitos”.
Sin embargo, los defensores de la vivienda señalan que, en la actualidad, no se ofrecen ayudas a las personas que no cumplen los requisitos para acceder al programa.
“Las familias con estatus mixto subvencionan las viviendas del HUD para el resto de personas”, afirmó Marie Claire Tran-Leung, directora del Proyecto de Iniciativa contra los Desahucios y abogada responsable del Proyecto Nacional de Derecho de la Vivienda.
«Si estas familias se ven obligadas a marcharse, habrá menos fondos disponibles para las viviendas subvencionadas por el HUD, lo que reducirá la oferta de viviendas y agravará la crisis de la vivienda para todos”, añadió Tran-Leung. “Esto es especialmente importante en un lugar como Nueva York, donde existe sin duda una escasez de viviendas y, sobre todo, una escasez de viviendas asequibles”.
No obstante, tanto ella como otros defensores de la vivienda instan a la gente a tener paciencia y a mantener la calma.
“Existe el riesgo de que las familias se autoexpulsen en este momento, a pesar de que tienen derecho a quedarse donde están”, subrayó Tran-Leung. “Aún no tienen que marcharse hasta que esta norma entre en vigor, y los defensores están tratando de idear o impulsar diferentes vías para bloquear o retrasar esa fecha de entrada en vigor”.
Los abogados en vivienda explicaron que, a partir del 14 de diciembre, en caso de que la norma entre en vigor, los inquilinos dispondrían de 90 días para demostrar su situación migratoria. Incluso si una autoridad de vivienda decide que alguien no cumple los requisitos, subrayaron los defensores, los residentes siguen teniendo derecho a un debido proceso con las garantías debidas.
“Eso es otra cosa que queremos destacar: se supone que debe haber un proceso, por lo que no debería ser algo que ocurra de la noche a la mañana”, explicó Tran-Leung.
Los defensores relacionaron el cambio normativo con la agresiva campaña de la administración Trump contra la inmigración. El HUD intentó impulsar una política similar en 2019, durante el primer mandato del presidente Donald Trump, pero el presidente Joe Biden la retiró posteriormente.
“Lo que vemos es cómo Trump y el HUD se aprovechan de las crisis económicas para destruir los programas federales de vivienda, sembrando la división y convirtiendo a los inmigrantes en chivos expiatorios”, afirmó Tran-Leung.
Otra consecuencia de la norma, explicó Newman, es una menor estabilidad para los inmigrantes que están a punto de obtener la regularización.
“Hemos tenido clientes que, tras un periodo de 18 meses, ahora son titulares de la tarjeta verde”, señaló. “Hay muchas personas que viven en esos hogares y que podrían regularizar su situación migratoria en un futuro próximo”.
Por ahora, sin embargo, según Newman, “la gente debe saber que, hasta que entre en vigor, nada ha cambiado. No deben mudarse ni ser desahuciados por miedo”.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.title: Big Tech’s Millions Backfired in the Midterms
https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.author: Maegan Llerena and Theo Oshiro
https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.text:
Big Tech’s Millions Backfired in the Midterms
Big Tech companies and their executives poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the midterm elections to both Democrats and Republicans—and, in large part, they lost.
Maegan Llerena and Theo Oshiro
Big Tech billionaires tried to buy our elections — but the millions of dollars in political contributions they made largely backfired. In a number of high-stakes races, rejecting Big Tech money helped deliver wins to candidates that ran on an anti-Big Tech platform. Why? In the recent midterms we witnessed a popular uprising that cut across traditional political fault lines to build new political power that overcame Big Tech’s millions.
We’ve had a first hand look at how voters are coming together to reject Big Tech’s undue influence. At Make the Road Action, we knocked on hundreds of thousands of doors and have organized in some of the communities where popular rejection of Big Tech is at its highest — Lehigh Valley, PA, Lansing, Michigan and Reno, Nevada, to name a few. On the doors, we saw that voters — across party lines and demographic differences — consistently shared concern over skyrocketing utility bills, fears around job replacement, and the role of Big Tech surveillance firms in ICE enforcement.
For example, in Northeastern Pennsylvania, which is quickly becoming one of the epicenters of the data center boom, working class Latino voters in Reading and Hazleton — once strongholds for President Doanld Trump — expressed increasing concern about spikes in utility costs and the rise of data centers. More than 77% of voters we surveyed in the area told us they were worried about the growth of data centers, especially as it impacted their electric bills. Nationally, the Wall Street Journal reported that 56% of the voters they polled cited data centers as a key issue in determining who to vote for in Congress. Pennsylvania Republican Reps. Ryan MacKenzie and Rob Bresnahan — both of whom took large sums from Big Tech executives — lost re-election, in part due to their pro-data center, pro-AI stances.
Rejection of data centers and a broad based fight around AI also powered Will Lawrence’s long shot win in the deep purple 7th congressional district in Michigan. Voters we spoke with were deeply skeptical of his opponent, sitting Rep. Tom Barrett, a Republican who took substantial campaign contributions from Big Tech executives and voted to stop states from regulating AI. Lawrence flipped the seat on an AI accountability platform that spoke to the pocketbook concerns of voters as well as the more pervasive fears of AI job replacement and safety.
In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, the top recipient of Palantir donations in Congress, lost her race, as did Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina, who lost despite substantial support from data center companies. Democrats that cozied up to Big Tech also lost: Jimmy Gomez, a California pro-tech Democrat lost to a progressive in an “AI proxy battle.”Our analysis shows that about half of all incumbents that took money from Palantir Technologies lost their races this year — six out of the top eight recipients of money from Palantir executives lost. And in a shocking twist, one of the largest AI Super PACs, Leading the Future, run by Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale and OpenAI CEO Greg Brockman, pulled back their investments just weeks before the midterms because of concern their support would hurt, not boost, candidates. 
Across the country, voters came out to demand a say in what happens in their neighborhoods and towns, and an America they can afford, where rights are respected, kids are safe, and local economies are thriving. Where technology makes life better, not worse. And where elected officials are not in the pockets of corporate giants.
As Democrats take back control of Congress, now is the time to set a vision and comprehensive plan for AI in our country. We are at a critical juncture. Democrats must use their investigatory powers to bring AI CEOs before Congress to demand answers on safety breaches, out of control surveillance, and the impact of AI on workers and families. 
Now is the time to advance a vision for AI safety and regulation that includes public oversight and real public enforcement, a jobs guarantee for workers who fear being left behind by automation, and a plan to tax AI companies so that working people can share in the increased productivity. 
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.

https://gothamist.com/news/united-airlin.title: United Airlines says system outage affecting departing flights is resolved
https://gothamist.com/news/united-airlin.author: Phil Corso
https://gothamist.com/news/united-airlin.text:
United Airlines said it has resolved a widespread technology outage that affected some departing flights Monday evening.
The airline acknowledged the outage in a post on X shortly before 5 p.m.
"We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," the first post said.
In an update shortly after 6 p.m., it said the issue had been resolved but did not say what caused it or how many flights were affected.
The outage comes just three days after a nationwide ground stop caused thousands of flight cancellations and delays, including at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark airports. Federal officials attributed that disruption to a telecommunications failure.
It also comes as customers of several major banks reported trouble accessing their online accounts Monday. There is no indication the outages are connected.
United advised passengers to check their flight status through its app or website.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

The heirs of a former owner of Vincent Van Gogh‘s Châtaigniers en fleurs, 1890, have called for its withdrawal from an upcoming auction at Sotheby’s in New York. As per the New York Times, the heirs allege that the painting was sold under duress due to persecution by the Nazis.
The painting is set to be the centerpiece of twelve pieces on auction from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection on November 18. That upcoming sale is expected to total $450 million, and Sotheby’s has already guaranteed the sale of the Van Gogh painting. With an estimated value of $180 million, Châtaigniers en Fleurs could surpass Van Gogh’s current auction record of $117.2 million, set in 2022.
The Sotheby’s catalog states that the painting was acquired by Hungarian-born German-Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer in 1909. Sometime in 1932 or 1933, Fischer’s family deposited the painting with dealer Walter Feilchenfeldt at the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer, prior to fleeing Nazi persecution in Berlin.
The painting was sold by Feilchenfeldt in 1936—this sale is the subject of the withdrawal request that Gunnar Schnabel, the lawyer for Fischer’s heirs, sent to Sotheby’s. As per the New York Times, Schnabel’s research found that the Fischers had to pay the “Reich flight tax” for those who emigrated, and there were restrictions on what they could take with them when they left. In his letter to Sotheby’s on November 12, Schnabel asked for proof that the family “would have wanted to carry out the sale even without Nazi rule.”
Speaking to the New York Times, Sotheby’s said its “research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress,” but they “are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution” with the family.
Sotheby’s confirmed to ARTnews that the painting sold for 68,000 Swiss francs ($22,000), after reviewing the archives of Paul Cassirer. Luke Nikas, a lawyer for Sotheby’s, told ARTnews that the sale was made outside Nazi control in Amsterdam, and the price was fair for the time. The auction house did not reveal whether the painting would still be up for sale.

Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi
The award-winning journalist and artist talks about her first book. Plus, Carolina A. Miranda on two new Guadalupe Rosales tomes out this fall.
Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.
The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)
Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015, among other instances of artwashing. They penned a joint review of Italian curator and organizer Marco Baravalle’s book The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism, a toolkit for seeing through the mainstream art world’s undermining of political movements and building sustainable alternatives.
Critic Carolina A. Miranda, meanwhile, takes up two new books by East Los Angeles artist Guadalupe Rosales, who came up in a community of Chicano kids raised in the 1990s amid uprisings and political action. Miranda writes that the anthology Rosales edited, as well as her blended memoir and photo book, perfectly encapsulate “the ways she engages the stories of others even as she tells her own.” A wise observation to carry with us as we face the week ahead; more of the latest in art book reviews and news below.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
