https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Lights Out: Broken NYC Streetlights Surge As Repair Times Get Longer, Data Shows
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Jose Martinez, Kennedy Sessions
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
New York City is taking longer to fix broken streetlights, with the average time to complete repairs hitting its lowest rate on record, city data reveals.
An analysis by The City Reporter of Department of Transportation data found the number of 311 complaints for out-of-service streetlights has surged to 27,609 so far this year — a 6% increase from 2025 and 23% increase from 2024. The outages are causing safety concerns among residents and elected officials, who point to the risk of traffic crashes, crime and trips and falls in the dark, especially as the sun sets earlier during this time of year.
Some streetlights have been out for months, and several New Yorkers said their requests for service from the city have often dragged out or gotten no response.
“The setting, when you come out [of] the train station, it’s almost like a horror flick,” said commuter Jonny Pastrana on Wednesday night at Flatbush and Ocean avenues in Brooklyn, where a light pole across from the Prospect Park subway stop had long been out. “The lights is off. ‘Thriller’ video, yeah, that’s what it feels like.”
The Mamdani administration is aware of the problem, stating in the latest Mayor’s Management Report that last fiscal year, DOT took action to fix broken streetlights within 10 days just 76% of the time — the lowest rate ever and the first time it had sunk below 90% in almost 20 years. The report cited a combination of “increased demand and repair complexity” for the growing delays.
The city’s 311 system has received nearly 180,000 complaints for broken streetlights since 2021, DOT data shows. Out of the five boroughs, Brooklyn and The Bronx topped the list, with 43,150 and 41,689 complaints, respectively.
The intersection of Flatbush and Ocean avenues, where Pastrana was walking, has rung up the most streetlight repair requests out of any spot in the city during that period, with 295. The Ed Koch Queensboro Bridge followed with 208, while 195 complaints were logged from Riverside Drive and West 116th Street in Manhattan.
While the number of broken streetlight complaints so far in 2026 is down 31% from the five-year high of more than 40,000 in 2022, DOT spokesperson Vin Barone acknowledged the most recent winter factored heavily into the repairs backlog.
“Well-lit streets are essential to the safety and comfort of New Yorkers and they deserve nothing less,” he said. “This winter’s historic snowstorms and freezing temperatures took a toll on our aging street lighting infrastructure — some of which dates back to the early 20th century.”
‘It’s Like Pitch Black’
Bay Ridge resident Dimitri Kontakos said one streetlight on his 81st Street block between Fourth and Fifth avenues remained out of commission after a January snowstorm until crews removed the light earlier this month.
He compared the drawn-out response to “pulling teeth.”
“At night, it’s like pitch black,” Kontakos said. “I get that they’re busy and I understand it’s not going to happen the next day, but it’s frustrating for sure.”
Brendan Bolger, 80, said he and neighbors on Dahlgren Place in Bay Ridge have repeatedly contacted 311 about two streetlights that have been out for months, leaving him to feel “a little leery.”
“They said there were major problems with the light further down the block, that it’s a lot more work than just changing the bulb,” he said.
The Mayor’s Management Report, essentially a report card for city agencies, said streetlight repairs “vary by case.”
“Some repairs are straightforward, such as replacing a luminaire or changing a fuse, while more complex cases may involve electrical issues at the base of a pole, foundation work, utility obstructions or ConEd coordination to restore power,” it said.
In a statement, Con Edison said it works with the city to “get streetlights back in service as soon as possible, as we have a shared commitment to public safety.”
‘Bread-and-Butter’ Constituent Services
DOT’s Barone said the city has committed to replacing all LED lights citywide as part of its Vision Zero plan to eliminate traffic deaths. The Mamdani administration is also aiming to develop a connected streetlight network in the coming years to automatically detect outages and speed up repairs while improving visibility in high-risk locations, including beneath elevated trains and highways.
State Sen. Andrew Gounardes said he and City Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso — both Democrats who represent Bay Ridge and parts of Dyker Heights — have asked DOT to conduct a “thorough review” of the streetlight repair backlog because of what they said were more than 130 inoperable lights in Brooklyn Community Board 10 as of the end of October.
“Those are typically very easy things to solve. It’s like a bread-and-butter constituent service case,” Gounardes said. “Someone calls in, ‘This is a problem, here’s my 311 number, can you help me figure it out.’ We do — usually, it’s pretty routine.”
At Flatbush and Ocean avenues, Fox White said the broken lights add to the stress of crossing a “gnarly intersection.”
“This area in general is just kind of dark,” White said. “I don’t notice the streetlights in particular, but it does make the area kind of gnarly.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: A Rogue DA in No-Man’s Land
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: J.C. Hallman
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
A Rogue DA in No-Man’s Land
A strange case of prosecutorial misconduct during a murder investigation in the Oklahoma panhandle.
In January 2025, I accepted an odd freelance assignment. A Florida-based trucker had received an unusual speeding citation while traveling through the panhandle of Oklahoma, which she had offered as a tip to numerous local media outlets. My mission was to investigate the trucker’s claim that the ticket represented nefarious goings-on in the part of the state known as No Man’s Land, owing to its 40-year-stint as stateless territory in the 19th century.
The trucker turned out to be right. Years before, the local district attorney’s office had assigned its drug task force the ancillary duty of writing deferred-prosecution-agreement (DPA) tickets to truckers. The task force was a kind of 20th-century posse, run by the DA and fueled by civil-asset-forfeiture laws, which amounted to the legal robbery of drugs and money by law enforcement. A DPA is a reverse bribe: If truckers caught in speed traps agree to pay a hefty fine directly to the DA, the charges go away. In theory, drug task forces seize sums of money that implicate criminal organizations. Speeding tickets seemed like peanuts. But the trucker I spoke with was asked to pay $360 for a violation that carried a $160 fine—going 11 to 15 miles per hour over the speed limit of 45. Because of the load she was carrying, she told me, she was driving well below even that.
There was a bigger problem with this arrangement than the fuzzy math: DPAs for holders of commercial driver’s licenses are prohibited under federal law. In short, the tickets weren’t shady-but-legal asset forfeitures but actually illegal shakedowns, and who knew how many of them had been written? I traveled to the panhandle to interview the head of the local drug task force, a man who had once been indicted on an embezzlement charge after being accused of staging a fake robbery to explain the mysterious disappearance of $2,600 from a separate drug-task-force office in Ardmore, in southern Oklahoma. Eventually, I learned that over a period of six years, the panhandle drug task force had written approximately 6,000 DPAs, sending more than $2 million straight into the coffers of the DA’s office.
I had my story. But something strange happened as I began to write it: The head of the task force called me to say that the DA of Texas County, George “Buddy” Leach, had canceled the ticketing program outright. The executive director of the local journalism outlet that had assigned the piece to me said it might have been the first time in his 35 years that something had changed before he published an article.
The reversal was curious, and there was only one hint as to why it had happened: The head of the task force told me they had canceled the ticketing scheme because they were concerned that negative publicity would affect Leach’s ability to prosecute a high-profile murder case.
The sudden collapse of a lucrative ticketing scheme operated by a sketchy law-enforcement outfit that had more in common with the Wild West than the modern world led my investigation to unexpected places: to cattle ranches far from Oklahoma, to the highest offices of state criminal justice, and to the remnants of a violent anti-government cult born in a nether region of the country that not long ago wasn’t part of the country at all.
In April 2024, five members of a small, cultish anti-government prayer group known as God’s Misfits were arrested over the deaths of two Kansas women. Little is known about the origin or beliefs of God’s Misfits, apart from their adherence to a vague Christian ideology and that the group, consisting of a handful of members, met weekly at a private home. In 2023, one of the members who would be accused of the murders filed a manifesto-like document in a court proceeding that lashed out at the United Nations, vaccines, government regulation, and genetically modified foods.
The killings followed a fierce custody dispute and wild accusations of child sexual abuse against one of the women who were murdered. As subsequently reported by outlets ranging from The Washington Post to the BBC, the crimes came to light when the 16-year-old daughter of Cora Twombly, one of the alleged killers, contacted the police. Grisly details emerged: Twombly had forced her daughter, CW, to clean blood from a vehicle used in the crime and had once put CW, then 15, in a bulletproof vest in anticipation of a shootout that never happened.
The publication of my article about the ticketing scheme triggered a flood of tips about corruption in the Texas County DA’s office. I received too many e-mails to keep track of, and there didn’t seem to be any reason to pay special attention to the story known as the God’s Misfits Murders—or, more simply, the Kansas Moms Killings. Then I was contacted by national media outlets that were planning to cover the murders. I agreed to an interview because many of the people I had written about—Leach and the head of the drug task force—also appeared in the God’s Misfits story. But for almost a year, I remained oblivious to the details of the murders. There were plenty of other stories of corruption to keep me occupied, most prominently a car crash that involved one of the agents of the drug task force and resulted in the death of a young Guatemalan girl and her grandfather.
In the summer of 2025, I was introduced to Lisa and Coby White, CW’s stepmother and biological father. The Whites, who were themselves witnesses in the God’s Misfits case, had been awarded full custody of CW after arrests were made in April and May 2024.
The Whites told me something troubling. They had evidence, they said, that Leach, in violation of a standing protective order, had been facilitating contact between CW, whom he described as the case’s key witness, and her mother, Cora, whom he had accused of murder.
This was puzzling. I described the evidence that the Whites had told me about to an attorney I called, who was incredulous.
“Why would he want to tank his own case?” the lawyer said.
It wasn’t the first time I had stumbled across prosecutorial misconduct in Oklahoma. In 2024, I pitched an article dissecting the oral arguments in the Supreme Court case Glossip v. Oklahoma, which hinged on exculpatory evidence that state prosecutors had withheld. Glossip was an infamous death-penalty case that had attracted the attention of the likes of Dr. Phil, Sister Helen Prejean, and Kim Kardashian.
The prosecutors were caught dead to rights. Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond publicly admitted that the state had erred, and he refused to defend a decision by the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals to uphold Richard Glossip’s conviction. The Supreme Court was forced to recruit a ringer to defend an indefensible position. Predictably, the court ruled that Glossip deserved a new trial and that the OCCA should have no further say in the matter. “Because ample evidence supports the attorney general’s confession of error in this Court, there also is no need to remand for further evidentiary proceedings at the OCCA,” the 5–3 decision read. (A new trial is scheduled to begin on December 7.)
I admired the stance that Drummond took on the Glossip case; it was a far cry from the prosecutorial misconduct that appeared to be characteristic of the Oklahoma legal system. This was particularly true in No Man’s Land, where the stories of corruption I investigated through 2025 peeled back the curtain on a culture of legal impunity that Oklahoma media had tended to ignore. As I’d heard it said around the newsroom, “No one cares what happens in the panhandle.”
I communicated with Lisa and Coby White for months, hoping to gain access to the evidence they said they had, but they were hesitant. On the one hand, they knew that Leach was doing something wrong and that he was complicating their efforts to protect CW. On the other hand, they worried that their evidence might provide ammunition to defense attorneys.
Months later, they decided to trust the system rather than share evidence with a journalist. A live meeting wasn’t possible: The Whites were ranchers and lived at a significant distance from Oklahoma. It was calving season; births and the needs of newly born calves precluded a more than 10-hour drive to Oklahoma City. So they authorized me to approach Drummond’s office on their behalf and inform the authorities that they had evidence. In March 2026, a Zoom meeting was set up with the head of the AG’s criminal division, Jimmy Harmon, with a specific purpose: The Whites would describe, but not share, their evidence. If that information was found to be compelling, a subsequent in-person visit would be arranged.
During their meeting, the Whites counted off a string of uncomfortable revelations. Leach had admitted that he had deep personal ties to Cora Twombly’s family. He had initiated contact between Twombly and CW, in violation of the standing court order. He had shown little concern when Twombly, roughly eight months after she was arrested and while in jail, had established and funded a bank account for her daughter. The Whites reported alarming statements that Leach had made in their presence about the family of one of the victims, and they recalled discovering a handwritten note in which Twombly had informally addressed him as “Buddy.”
The Whites told Harmon that they and their attorneys had been left scratching their heads at Leach’s behavior. Consistent with the Oklahoma habit of ignoring corruption in the panhandle, Harmon shrugged off most of what they said, but he agreed to talk to Leach.
A month later, Leach attacked me and the whites in a panicky blog post on the DA office’s official website that would soon elicit a public rebuke from a panhandle judge. The April 14 post was an attempt to control two separate stories: both the fatal car crash that I had been investigating, and what the Whites had told Harmon about Leach’s communication with CW. The post severely mischaracterized the Zoom call and distorted basic facts of the God’s Misfits case.
“The stepmother, Lisa White, told [a] reporter that a no-contact order exists between Twombly and her daughter,” Leach wrote. “I am not aware of any such order.”
“He was in the courtroom when it was ordered,” Lisa told me, scoffing. “He knows.”
Court documents back her up, verifying that a protective order exists. Issued five days after the murders, the emergency order stated, “Petitioner/Mother, Cora White [Twombly] shall have no contact, electronic, physical or through third parties with the minor child until further Order of this Court”; just over three weeks later, the prohibition was extended.
There was no reasonable explanation for Leach’s claim that he was unaware of the order. In fact, the Whites’ first interaction with Leach, they said, came on the day the order was put in place. Leach had organized an entourage of eight officers to carry out one of the order’s few provisions: that CW be able to retrieve personal belongings from her home.
But whatever confidence the Whites might have had in Leach crumbled as Cora Twombly’s mother, Evalyn Moore, attempted to relay messages between her daughter and granddaughter.
Public-records requests unearthed letters from Moore to CW and text conversations in which Moore conveyed messages from Twombly to her daughter, disparaging Coby and Lisa White. But the problems had begun well before then, Coby said. The Whites did not initially object to the contact between CW and her grandmother, but as it became clear that Moore was discussing the case and sharing messages from CW’s mother, the Whites turned to Leach to find out whether these contacts were in violation of the protective order—the one he would claim to know nothing about.
When the Whites returned to the panhandle in December 2024, a bombshell dropped in the form of added detail about the extent of Leach’s connection to Cora Twombly: His own parents had been close friends with Twombly’s grandparents—Evalyn Moore’s parents—in Boise City.
Leach himself had described the two families as “close,” Lisa said.
During the Whites’ visit, Leach conducted a private interview with CW, who is still a minor. The Whites recounted to me what CW had told them of the more than two-hour exchange: A small portion of the conversation was dedicated to CW’s potential testimony, but most of it was about Cora Twombly and Evalyn Moore. Leach praised Twombly, telling the Whites that she was a good mom who had gotten mixed up with the wrong people.
The Whites told Leach that in the months since the murders, they had become acquainted with the family of one of the victims, Veronica Butler. Leach could not forbid contact with Butler’s family, but he expressed his preference for the family of the other victim, Jilian Kelley, because they were “good people.” He went on to malign Butler’s family. “He told us to stay very far away from them,” Lisa told me, “because they were trailer-park trash basking in their 15 minutes of fame.”
Studies on prosecutors gaming the system to secure convictions, as in the Glossip case, are far more common than studies on prosecutors going light on defendants because of personal conflicts of interest. A 2024 report on prosecutorial misconduct in Oklahoma from the Oklahoma Appleseed Center for Law & Justice in Tulsa focused on Brady violations, in which prosecutors fail to turn over evidence favorable to defendants. The report’s authors lamented a lack of prosecutorial oversight in Oklahoma, writing, “The citizens of Oklahoma have largely been asked to ignore and bypass the gross misconduct and indefensible administration of our criminal justice system for decades.”
In a 2017 Boston College Law Review article that did look at prosecutors compromised by conflicts of interest, the authors argued that prosecutors may make poor legal decisions because of political or pecuniary interests—that is, running for office or seeking fame through book sales—but they struggled to articulate a concrete solution. Even in states where an attorney general or governor is empowered to remove a district attorney—in Oklahoma, DAs do not serve at the pleasure of the AG or governor—the authors did not see removal as a viable solution. “Other executive officials are not better situated than the prosecutor who has declined to recuse himself,” they wrote. “The other officials are probably less knowledgeable about the relevant facts.”
In the God’s Misfits case, the evidence of improper contact was voluminous. Four months after the killings, Evalyn Moore had begun telling her granddaughter that the problem was not CW’s mother, arrested for murder, but her father and stepmother. “But your DAD has custody and it’s his word,” Moore wrote. “Him and Lisa are the only people in the World who wants to keep us apart!”
On Facebook Messenger, Moore relayed messages to CW that Twombly had sent to Moore from prison, claiming to speak on Leach’s authority.
November 28, 2024: “Mom says she loves you and is thinking of you.”
December 3, 2024: “Your mom talked to Judge [sic] Leach about your situation…. He is going to visit with you when you are in Guymon.”
December 8, 2024: “When Judge Leach talks to you, you have to tell him how bad things are…. The DA has no problem with you talking to me. That is what he told your mom.”
The Whites recalled a remark from one of the DA’s office staff during the December 2024 visit, claiming that Evalyn Moore was in the DA’s office frequently and appeared to have direct access to Leach. When I reached her by telephone, Moore admitted that Leach’s mother had worked as her accountant. Confronted with evidence of her text exchanges with CW, she quickly ended the call. “I don’t want anything,” Moore said. “I don’t want to talk to you.”
Leach’s April 14 blog post had taken particular note of a birthday card that Twombly had sent to CW in early 2026.
“Actually, that was the second birthday card,” Lisa said.
The blog post claimed that Leach and the Whites had reached an agreement: His office would review correspondence from Twombly and forward it to the Whites, if appropriate. “Absolutely not,” Coby said. “There is no communication that we had with Leach that could have been interpreted in this way.”
I drove 10 hours to visit the Whites and examine a one-line missive on Leach’s letterhead instructing them to deliver a birthday card to CW. “Under no circumstances would that be appropriate,” Lisa said. A year later, another card arrived. This time, tucked inside, there was a notably casual message from Twombly to Leach: “Buddy, per your request, I am sending this card for [CW] to you for your approval.”
In the weeks leading up to the announcement of her plea deal—only one of the five God’s Misfits defendants has been sentenced; two, including Twombly, have entered into plea agreements; trials for the other two are scheduled for 2027—Twombly and her mother established a bank account for CW, ostensibly to give her access to funds associated with cows owned under CW’s name. It was an unusual amount of money for a teenager, Lisa said, but Leach had dismissed any concerns: “He said, ‘Oh, isn’t that kind of her to think of her daughter?’”
The Whites’ attorneys—the couple had spent more than $30,000 on lawyers’ fees, even though they were just witnesses—saw the bank account differently. “They were like, ‘This cannot happen! It’s witness tampering. She’s buying a witness,’” Lisa said.
But there was an even more shocking statement in Leach’s imperious blog post: He claimed that Lisa had told a reporter—me—that his office intended to force CW to testify in the upcoming trials in violation of Twombly’s plea agreement. “Never said that to anybody,” Coby said.
“Why would he put us on the witness list and then throw us under the bus?” Lisa said.
Conflicts of interest aside, Leach was strongly rebuked on July 30 by Texas County District Court Judge Jon Parsley over his April 14 blog post. The post was cited in a June 19 motion from Tad Cullum, one of the God’s Misfits defendants, whose capital-murder case is set to go to trial early next year. Cullum argued that Leach had violated a 2024 gag order.
“The Court finds that the statements to media and blog post by the state did violate the express terms of the order,” Parsley said in his ruling. “The Court reprimanded the State and Ordered that they re-read the [gag order].”
Leach’s blog post remains publicly available. Leach did not respond to an interview request, and the offices of the Oklahoma attorney general and the State Bureau of Investigation refused my requests for comment.
But Leach’s actions are neither an isolated nor an atypical case. Nationwide studies reveal that prosecutorial misconduct is as difficult to define as it is to investigate and punish. A 2023 survey of judges found broad agreement on the most egregious forms of illegal or unethical prosecutorial behavior, but a frustrating lack of consensus on what other behaviors should result in investigation and possible sanction.
“Why is it that prosecutors are seldom disciplined, often in the face of ample evidence?” the survey’s authors wrote. “One reason may be that judges and others within the system do not agree on what acts of prosecutorial discretion constitute willful or intentional forms of misconduct.”
Furthermore, a number of the judges who responded to the survey suggested that whatever flaws the system may have should be addressed by the system itself. “In my opinion,” one judge said, “often the response to bad prosecutors needs to come from voters, the defense team, and the bench.”
Cora Twombly’s plea agreement was for a life sentence with a possibility of parole after 30 years for each of the two murders, with one of the sentences suspended depending on her good behavior.
“It’s a sweet deal,” Lisa White said. She believed that Leach had put his thumb on the scale to secure Twombly a better sentence than the others—such as Cullum, who’s facing the death penalty for the same crime. Under Oklahoma’s 85 percent rule, which requires the perpetrators of serious crimes to serve at least 85 percent of their sentence, Twombly could be released after serving 25.5 years.
“There’s consequences that need to be paid,” Coby White said. “She’ll be 70-some years old when she gets out.”
But Lisa questioned whether the punishment matched the crime. “I don’t know,” she said. “Does only one of the murders matter?”

https://taz.de/Leipzigs-neue-Flaniermeil.title: Leipzigs neue Flaniermeile: Assimilation, Digga
https://taz.de/Leipzigs-neue-Flaniermeil.author: Jona Rausch
https://taz.de/Leipzigs-neue-Flaniermeil.text:
Leipzigs neue Flaniermeile: Assimilation, Digga
Der Parkbogen Ost soll für Leipzig sein, was die High Line für New York ist: ein hipper Ort, wo einmal Gleise waren. Nicht alle fühlen sich da wohl.
W o früher eine verlassene Bahntrasse lag und man Kleeblätter zwischen Schienen sammelte, rollen jetzt Kinderwagen und Gravelbikes über asphaltierten Boden. Neben in Kästen eingepflanzten Birken und hellen Holzbänken überall traut man sich kaum, sein Sterni mit einem Feuerzeug zu öffnen. Um es mit den Worten meiner Mutter zu sagen: Scheiße, ist der glatt, scheiße, sieht das gemacht aus. Scheiße, warum hat nichts hier Persönlichkeit?
Diese kluge Frau kommt mich an dem Wochenende besuchen, an dem der Parkbogen Ost gerade eröffnet worden ist, so nennt sich die aufgemöbelte Trasse. An der Haltestelle Annenstraße gehen wir die Treppe hoch. Oben angekommen, keucht sie, dann zieht sie an ihrer Vape. Begeistert ist sie von dem Projekt nicht und das sagt sie auch: Dieser Ort ist zum Kotzen! Ich, als Queen of Assimilation, schäme mich für ihre laute Stimme, denke: Uff, Mama, das ist peinlich. Red leiser, bitte.
Den Parkbogen entlang kommen uns vor allem Jack-Wolfskin-Jacken entgegen, oder Rentner. Rentnerlifestyle finden viele meiner Freund:innen gerade richtig geil, zu Hause sitzen und stricken. Blöd nur, dass zu diesem Lifestyle auch Einsamkeit gehört.
Das merkt man, weil meine Mutter innerhalb von zwei Minuten eine ganze Lebensgeschichte erzählt bekommt, es geht um den besten Bäcker und die tote Frau. Meine Mutter wird zugelabert, wahrscheinlich, weil sie sich in ihr wieder erkennen: Sie steckt in einem Körper, der gezeichnet ist durch drei Jobs, Erschöpfung, chronische Krankheit. Ein Körper, der unangepasst ist und so zeigt, dass hier gar nichts okay ist.
Der Verschleiß des Körpers durch Arbeit und Einsamkeit, man erkennt sich irgendwie. Oder man startet den ausweglosen Versuch der Anpassung, gibt sein weniges Geld für teure Kleidung aus und senkt die Stimme. Bloß nicht auffallen. Ich schlucke, schaue mich um. Glaube, Blicke zu spüren. Mama, bitte rede leiser.
Dabei komme ich von: Kaffeepulver, aufgelöst in heißem Wasser, Schinken-Käse-Croissants jeden Freitag, Wandtattoos, auf denen „Lebe, Liebe, Lache“ steht. Ich komme von: Mama pennt im Wohnzimmer, damit ich und meine Schwester ein eigenes Zimmer haben können. Ich komme von: Antifa-Punksongs auf maximaler Lautstärke auf dem Nachhauseweg hören, damit jeder weiß, wie scheiße ich Deutschland finde. Ich war mal lauter und jetzt:
Jack-Wolfskin-Jacken schauen genervt
Lebe. Liebe. Lache. Leipzig Ost. Die Leute um mich herum tragen Sprüche-T-Shirts nur ironisch, würden aber jeden Mann peinlich finden, der „Es läuft. Zwar bergab und rückwärts, aber es läuft“ trägt. Digga. Ich würde niemals mehr laut Musik über eine Musikbox hören – freue mich aber, dass es hier passiert. Jack-Wolfskin-Jacken schauen genervt, ich rieche frischen Lack.
Menschen, die die Codes sprengen, machen die Machtverhältnisse eines Raumes sichtbar. Wer darf den öffentlichen Raum mitgestalten und für wen? Wer hat diesen Ort vorher viel benutzt und wofür? Das ist ja auch unser Raum, der muss nicht aussehen wie von Ikea.
Etwas entfernt von uns steht das Team von Sachsenfernsehen und versucht, Passant:innen abzugreifen. Vorzugsweise Patagonia-Fleecejacken, aber ganz sicher nicht meine Mutter. Wir sitzen da und vapen.
Es ist Mittag und es ist November und es ist Sachsen, und als wäre das nicht schlimm genug, schauen wir einem jungen Mann dabei zu, wie er in die Kamera was von Neoliberalismus und Viertelaufwertung schwafelt. Ich stupse meine Mutter von der Seite an: Du solltest lauter reden, sonst checkt der da hinten nicht, was Verdrängung bedeutet.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: South London Gallery director Margot Heller to leave role after 25 years
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Joe Ware
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, will step down from her position in May 2027 after more than 25 years. Over this time the institution’s physical footprint has more than tripled and visitor numbers increased tenfold, according to a gallery statement.
Heller, who joined SLG in 2001, plans to become an independent curator and adviser. She will retain a connection with the gallery, curating the Dutch artist’s Mark Manders’s first solo exhibition at a London institution, opening at SLG on 23 September 2027.
“After 25 years at the helm, I feel it’s time for new adventures in my career,” Heller said in a statement.
“From the day I took up the role, I saw an opportunity to build an institution that could be internationally acclaimed for its contemporary art programme, and deeply embedded in its local community. I have stayed true to that vision ever since.”
Serge Ramin, the chair of the gallery’s trustees, described Heller as “a visionary curator and cultural leader”, adding: “She leaves a museum that is artistically ambitious, rooted in its community and physically transformed.”
Heller’s tenure encompassed two major building projects with 6a architects: the conversion of a neighbouring house and construction of an education studio in 2010, followed by the opening of the former Peckham Road Fire Station in 2018.
The fire station was donated in 2014 by the artist Raqib Shaw, whose identity was initially withheld. Its conversion cost £4m. Heller told The Art Newspaper in 2018 that the gallery had not been actively seeking to expand when the building was offered.
A garden designed by Gabriel Orozco opened in 2016, while Art Block, the gallery’s free space for children and young people on the neighbouring Sceaux Gardens estate, opened at its current site in 2017.
The artist and SLG trustee Alvaro Barrington said: “In Margot’s time at the South London Gallery she has created pivotal moments in many artists’ careers, including my own.”
He added: “Her commissioning of the Orozco Garden should be considered one of the most important architectural interventions in the UK.”
Exhibitions Heller has worked on during her tenure include solo presentations by Steve McQueen, Rashid Johnson, Oscar Murillo, Michael Armitage and Christina Quarles. The gallery was a joint winner of Art Fund’s Museum of the Year award in 2020.
Before joining the SLG, Heller worked at Southampton City Art Gallery, becoming its director, and as director of exhibitions at Anthony d’Offay Gallery. She was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2014.
The gallery became an independent charity in 2003, having previously been managed by Southwark Council.
Joy Gregory, an artist and SLG trustee, said of Heller in a statement: “As a local resident and artist, I am enormously grateful for the extraordinary legacy she leaves behind and excited to see what she does next.”

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-b.title: NYC Council bill pits Amazon against Teamsters union in fight over delivery workers
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-b.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-council-b.text:
In the shadow of StuyTown, Gabrielly Sierra-Moreno adjusted her blue, Amazon-branded vest and lifted a box half her size. As she hauled the Amazon packages from a truck with the Prime logo to a push cart destined for the apartment buildings, she weaved around a dozen other workers wearing similar outfits.
“ Since I'm very tiny, it's kind of hard for me,” said Sierra-Moreno, cracking a grin. "But I’m able to manage it. I'm starting to get a little muscle.”
Despite the ubiquitous Amazon branding, Sierra-Moreno, 21, and her colleagues don’t actually work for the online retail giant. They’re employees of Brimela Routes Corp, one of more than 40 delivery service providers bringing Amazon packages to New Yorkers’ doorsteps.
That arrangement — where workers like Sierra-Moreno deliver Amazon packages without officially working for the $2.8 trillion e-commerce giant — is the subject of a major battle pitting City Hall against Amazon and its contractors. The Delivery Protection Act would ban these third-party arrangements and force companies like Amazon to hire its delivery workers directly. A majority of the City Council supports the bill and Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he’ll sign it if it passes.
Supporters of the bill, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, the powerful transport union with about 1.3 million active members, argue the current structure shields Amazon from liability, leads to lax safety standards and dilutes the power of unionized workers.
Amazon, alongside business groups and the National Urban League, say the measure would decimate a network of small businesses, about a quarter of which are owned by Black or Hispanic entrepreneurs. Amazon has already spent millions of dollars lobbying against the proposal.
“There's people today that I employ that will be overlooked if this bill passes through,” said Julissa Alvarez, the owner of Brimela Routes Corp. “ Amazon is not going to be forced to hire my employees. They’re going to have to go through the whole pipeline process, which is going to be devastating for many of our employees.”
Sierra-Moreno said she likes that she knows her boss personally and that they can communicate in Spanish. She said her schedule is flexible and she has easy access to paid time off. “ I wouldn't want them to get shut down,” she said.
But workers for other delivery service providers, or DSPs, feel differently. They allege their employers often cut corners to save money, like deferring maintenance on their vehicle fleet and renting out budget vans.
“ Nine times out of 10, there's something wrong with my van,” said LeAnn Rivera, a driver for Excell Logistics, which operates out of Amazon’s DBK1 warehouse in Woodside, Queens.
Rivera said she recently had a van that kept rolling even after she pulled the emergency brake to park.
Samuel Mangual, another Excell Logistics driver at DBK1, said he’s also dealt with faulty brakes and other issues that can force him to abandon his route.
“I've been on a road where my van door didn't close,” he said. “So now I'm sitting in a van where I can't make the rest of the deliveries because I'm afraid someone might be able to steal it, along with my belongings.”
Some drivers said the contractor model allows both Amazon and the third-party companies to evade responsibility.
“Right now, if any accident happens to one of us drivers, Amazon claims the DSP is responsible,” said José Huerta, a driver with Fast Track Delivery Inc. and union organizer with the Teamsters. “The DSP, on the other hand, says no, that it’s Amazon that’s responsible. In other words, they just blame each other.”
Excell Logistics did not respond to a request for comment. A representative for Fast Track Delivery denied their vans were unsafe. “Vehicles identified with safety-related defects are grounded and removed from service until the necessary repairs are completed and the vehicle is cleared to return to operation,” said Amar Patel, the company’s president.
Many of the workers say that drivers delivering Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans should be able to make direct demands of the e-retail giant.
In December, Teamsters Local 804 organized with over 200 drivers at Amazon’s Queens warehouse to demand better safety standards and higher pay in a union contract.
Drivers, who typically work 10-hour shifts delivering up to 230 packages a day, say they’d like to see an increase in their average pay of $24 an hour and better protections from layoffs.
“Why do I have their uniform if I’m not their employee,” Huerta said.
Amazon is spending millions of dollars to oppose the bill. The online investigative site New York Focus reported Amazon has spent an unprecedented amount of company money on a lobbying effort, pouring millions into a group called the Five Borough Jobs Campaign. City data shows the Five Borough Jobs Campaign has spent over $8 million dollars lobbying against the bill this year.
In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the company is “committed to the local small business partners who work with us every day to provide fast, reliable delivery for New Yorkers.”
The legislation as written would “undermine that commitment – threatening the small businesses that deliver to customers, putting the jobs of more than 5,000 of their employees at risk, and forcing us to consider relocating delivery operations outside of the city,” Nantel said.
Marc Morial, the president of the National Urban League, the historic civil rights organization headquartered in New York City, said the third-party delivery companies are being treated unfairly as “a political football.”
“ They've taken out loans, they've taken out debt to build these businesses, and they're going to be wiped out,” Morial said. “Where are the reparations for the small business owners, the Black-owned business owners, the Latino-owned business owners that are going to be eliminated because of this bill?”
Amazon is a “diamond partner” of the National Urban League, meaning they’ve given the organization more than $1 million. A spokesperson for the organization said financial contributions do not influence their policy positions.
The council bill, championed by Queens Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, currently has 35 co-sponsors, well past a majority.
Council Speaker Julie Menin said her office was working “around the clock” to get the bill to the finish line. At a press conference last week Menin said her staff was working on some changes to address legal concerns.
“To be clear, we are going to be regulating Amazon,” Menin said. “We will be the first city in the country to regulate Amazon in a very significant way.”
Orin Starn, an anthropology professor at Duke University who did fieldwork as an employee at an Amazon warehouse until he was fired, said that if the bill passes, it will likely be seen as a model for other cities.
“That makes something like a giant city [taking] action at the municipal level to try to hold Amazon to account so important,” he said.
Alvarez, the owner of Brimela Routes Corp, said she’d be supportive of reforms that mandate better oversight and benefits but don’t blow up the entire system of third-party contractors. She said she feels swept up in a crusade that the mayor and city councilmembers are waging against big companies like Amazon.
“ What about me? I am also one of your constituents,” she said. “Are you trying to kill my business, my family, my dreams, my opportunity to help the community?”

https://www.propublica.org/article/publi.title: Democrats in Washington Move to Ban Data Centers on Public Lands
https://www.propublica.org/article/publi.author: Mark Olalde
https://www.propublica.org/article/publi.text:
A dozen Democrats in Congress are calling for limiting or banning the construction of data centers on public lands. The moves follow reporting from ProPublica that revealed Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who leads the White House’s artificial intelligence push, has tens of millions of dollars invested in AI companies.
“Our public lands aren’t a piggy bank for Trump’s powerful friends,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said in a social media post that pointed to ProPublica’s reporting. Her office told the news organization that the senator, who serves on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, is working on legislation to regulate data centers on public lands and will use the panel’s oversight authority to address concerns about transparency surrounding them.
Burgum was asked about ProPublica’s reporting at a recent event hosted by the conservative website Daily Caller. He said that his financial reporting and ethics were “clean as a whistle,” and that he invested in software companies before they turned to AI. “I don’t even know all the names of the companies that are in the portfolio,” he said of his vast wealth.
ProPublica found that hundreds of President Donald Trump’s political appointees in the executive branch, or their spouses, held stocks, owned equity or had other financial ties to AI companies and data center developers. Other offices, including the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture, defended their political leadership, saying the appointees followed lawyers’ guidance and had not violated ethics rules.
Our reporting also found that a U.S. Geological Survey study released earlier this year identified an area of U.S. Department of the Interior land nearly the size of Montana that might be suitable for data centers.
Several members of Congress pledged to float legislation to ban data center development on this land.
“These lands are treasured and must be protected for future generations to benefit from and enjoy,” Rep. Maxine Dexter of Oregon said in a statement. In mid-November, she filed the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban data center construction on land managed by the Interior Department and the Forest Service.
Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan in July filed the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, which would also prohibit their build-out on federally managed land. The measure was dead on arrival in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives.
“I’m going to continue building the coalition for our bill, and at the same time, I’m going to push the Oversight Committee to investigate the outrageous corruption of the Trump Administration,” she told ProPublica in a statement.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the pushback from Democrats in Congress.
Also speaking up were Rep. Jared Huffman of California and Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, who serve as the ranking members of the natural resources committees in their respective chambers. Huffman and Heinrich are in line to take up the gavel in those committees in January when Democrats retake the majority.
“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Public lands belong in public hands.”
Heinrich is pushing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a generational overhaul of the legislation governing how federal agencies permit major developments. Republicans in Congress and the White House support the swift passage of the bill, as do some Democrats. The more environmentally minded members of the Democratic caucus, however, are calling on Heinrich to slow down and force a better deal once Congress reconvenes next year with Democratic majorities.
Environmental policy experts agree that permitting reform is desperately needed to address climate change by allowing the faster build-out of renewable electricity generation and transmission lines. But green groups including the Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council and League of Conservation Voters oppose the bill because it would likely also lead to more fossil fuel projects while limiting input on projects from Native American tribes.
The legislation presents a mixed bag for data centers. A spokesperson for Heinrich defended the permitting reform bill, pointing out that it would require data center companies to bear their own costs for connecting to and upgrading the electrical grid. But the legislation would also streamline approval of natural gas-fired power plants, which power many data centers. The bill would make it more difficult to take away a permit after it’s issued.
Meanwhile, the Interior Department released a five-year strategic plan last week that includes a proposal to sell off public lands or pursue “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges and direct transfer of lands.” It is unclear whether the department intends to offer to sell to companies or only to local, state and tribal governments. Researchers who study natural resources policy told ProPublica that the country’s foundational land management law lays out steps that must be followed to dispose of federal land, steps that will be difficult for the Trump administration to legally navigate.
Still, with permits for data centers pending before the Interior Department, the release of the strategic plan sparked fear that developers might try to buy federal land. Jayson O’Neill, spokesperson for conservation group Save Our Parks, said the plan was another attempt by Burgum to “sell off what’s left to AI data center developers and his extractive resource buddies.”
The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment on its proposal to sell federal land.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Who Decides What Matters? The Jensen Huangs of the World or the American People?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Stephen Crowley
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Who Decides What Matters? The Jensen Huangs of the World or the American People?
Why we need greater democratic control over how society’s vast wealth is invested.
Two seemingly unrelated scandals captured the country’s attention last week: Jensen Huang’s downfall as CEO of Nvidia following an alleged honey trap, and a technical glitch that led to the sudden grounding of all flights in the United States. The impacts of both scandals are stunning on their own, but their juxtaposition—of cutting-edge technology against technological obsolescence—underscores a profound imbalance at the heart of our capitalist economy.
There is much to unpack in the Nvidia scandal beyond the sex and espionage: a single individual, a centibillionaire, running a multitrillion-dollar enterprise as if it were a small business, yet one that is at the center of an AI bubble whose bursting could reverberate throughout the global economy. Nvidia’s monopolistic control over a vital technology places it at the very core of the promised AI revolution. Where will that technological revolution lead? Will AI cure cancer or lead to human extinction? The possibilities appear endless. As the acronym has it: FAFO.
Meanwhile, in the skies, actual lives are already at stake, with over 3 million people flying in and out of US airports every day. No tech revolution here: These lives rely on copper wires and (only recently retired) floppy disks, technology said to hark back to the 1980s. The risk here is not hypothetical. Besides the numerous near misses, 67 lives were lost last year in the nation’s capital when a passenger plane collided with a military helicopter.
Avoid the distraction of Trump’s incompetent appointees’ failing to reassure us about the safety of air travel, or the partisan recriminations over funding for the FAA in Washington. Both miss a larger point: Who ultimately decides what matters most?
If one were searching for a succinct definition of capitalism, two words might suffice: “Capital decides.” Capital decides where investment should flow and what is considered “valuable,” as capital inevitably seeks to amass yet more capital.
The alternative is greater democratic control over how society’s vast wealth is invested, shifting it toward the values that the public holds dear.
As I write this in Washington, DC, I hear planes taking off from that same airport where those 67 lives were lost. That airport is named, ironically enough, for Ronald Reagan, the president who fired striking air traffic controllers in 1981. The air traffic controllers then were demanding not only better pay but also an end to outdated equipment, chronic understaffing, overlong hours, and workplace stress.
The crushing of that strike decimated America’s labor movement—one of the few checks on the power of capital—and ushered in the era of neoliberalism, freeing markets from government regulation so they could invest wherever the profits are greatest. Hence the world we live in now.
How different would our world look if people could vote on how trillions are invested?
Should they go to data centers? Based on the midterm elections, the votes on that score are already in. Or should investment go to ensuring safety in the air? How about healthcare for all? Or perhaps retiring some of the $1.7 trillion in student loan debt? As we imagine the possibilities, there will be inevitable limits and trade-offs. But let the deliberations begin.
Then again, we can continue to trust the brilliance of people like Jensen Huang to make those decisions for us. Will AI lead to a bright new economic future for all or a job apocalypse? Let’s FAFO!

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/t.title: Tuesday’s Headlines: Slow Motion on Super Speeders Edition
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/t.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/t.text:
How excited were we all earlier this year when Gov. Hochul and the state legislature passed a law allowing New York City to finally rein in the worst of the worst super-speeders?
We were very excited because the law would finally marry the city’s speed-enforcement camera system to real accountability: the city could order the installation of speed-limiting devices inside cars whose drivers got more than 15 school-zone speed-camera tickets in one year.
We’ve heard virtually nothing from the Mamdani administration on its plans to implement the law, but the City Council took a step forward last month when Council Member Kayla Santosuosso (D-Bay Ridge) introduced an actual bill to require the mayor to create and launch such an enforcement regime by the end of May 2027.
As loudly as that clock is ticking inside my head, it appears to be a lullaby for everyone else in town. Every day, I refresh the list of supporters of Santosuosso’s bill, and every day, I’m disappointed by how few members of the supposedly safety-conscious Council have signed on, and by how little urgency Speaker Julie Menin is exhibiting. I’m not panicking yet, but the bill is stuck at just 19 of 51 Council members, so I’d thought I’d use one of those hyperlinked sentences to remind our esteemed lawmakers whathappenswhenspeedingdriversarenotreinedin: theykillus.
The Department of Transportation has also pointed out that drivers with 16 speed-camera tickets are twice as likely to be involved in a crash to begin with. Once they get to 20 such tickets, they’re four times as likely. Thirty tickets? Fifty times as likely.
You get the idea. But does the City Council? Pass Intro 1153 now.
In other news:
If only more judges understood the Department of Transportation’s authority to make roadways safer — but Brooklyn Judge Inga O’Neale did by tossing a lawsuit by a random NIMBY against bike lanes on Brooklyn and Kingston avenues. (Reddit)
A hit-and-run driver hit someone in Brooklyn — and the cops said he was just “lying in the roadway.” Really? Sounds like the only thing lying is that preliminary report. (NYDN)
We always refer to The New York Post as our favorite tabloid, despite all the problems we have with its suburban, windshield perspective on the streetscape, but we do have to give at hat tip to former Mayor Bill de Blasio and Gov. Hochul for their appropriately critical, yet honest, best wishes in this Post birthday video.
Meet a real New York City hero: Lord of Bench. (Jacobin)
Our Open Plans colleague Jackson Chabot celebrated the victory of the mayor’s “government efficiency” ballot referenda with WNYC.
And the Post and Streetsblog covered Gov. Hochul’s “raid” on the MTA. (Our graphic was better.)
Following up on our own coverage of the cost of owning a car, Hunters Point Ledger did a nice visualization: The cost of owning a car for one year is the same as nearly 6,000 subway rides, or daily subway or bus commutes all year long for 12 people (more if they only have to go into work four days a week).
A part of the long-closed East River Esplanade will reopen this week. (Patch)
Meet the perfect location for a sandwich shop, which I’m happy to open and operate if I can get some backers. (West Side Rag)
Food for thought: Queens BP Donovan Richards wants to close fast-food restaurants for housing. (Queens Eagle)
And, finally, in case you missed it, “Saturday Night Live” took on the horse carriage “issue.” It’s not a perfect sketch, but it’s a reminder that the only time I wish I was working at SNL instead of at Streetsblog is when the entire cast breaks out in Broadway show tune parodies when debating the transportation issues of the day:
Tabloid legend Gersh Kuntzman has been with New York newspapers since 1989, including stints at the New York Daily News, the Post, the Brooklyn Paper and even a cup of coffee with the Times. He's also the writer and producer of "Murder at the Food Coop," which was a hit at the NYC Fringe Festival in 2016, and “SUV: The Musical” in 2007. He also writes the Cycle of Rage column, which is archived here.
