https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Catherine Hickley
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.
In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.
“Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.
But now, Brinkmann says his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.
Long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.
Elgin Marbles row makes ripples
Greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.
“The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on new findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”
The east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann says, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.
The rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”
The most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.
“He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann says. “That was our basis.”
Although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.
“It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann says. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”
They discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”
None of these reliefs showed the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.
The team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann says. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.
This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann says. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.
“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann says. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.
Brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.
It is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann says. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.
• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027

https://gothamist.com/news/a-new-day-arr.title: A new day arrives on Brooklyn's Flatbush Avenue as redesign gives bus riders priority
https://gothamist.com/news/a-new-day-arr.author: Carol Chen, Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/a-new-day-arr.text:
City officials on Tuesday unveiled an overhaul to a stretch of Flatbush Avenue designed to speed up commutes for tens of thousands of bus riders.
The redesign revolves around two new bus lanes in the center of the road between Grand Army Plaza and Livingston Street, where passenger cars are now banned 24 hours a day. Six concrete bus boarding islands were installed to make it easier for riders to board. The changes pushed most car traffic into a single lane in each direction.
Crews also added 36 new bike racks to the street, as well as fresh bus shelters, benches and leaning bars at every single bus boarding island, according to the city transportation department. The changes removed 41 parking spaces, but also added new loading zones for trucks and deliveries on side streets.
The city transportation department also said the new bus lanes will speed up commutes on the B41, which previously averaged 4 mph along the corridor. City officials claimed the upgrades would help 120,000 daily riders, which also includes those who use the nearby B67, B45 and B103 routes.
The redesign is the most ambitious bus lane project the city transportation department has completed since Mayor Zohran Mamdani took office at the start of the year.
“Flatbush Avenue is the foundation for the future of bus service in New York City … Bus riders are tired of waiting — waiting for the bus that never comes, waiting for the bus to crawl through traffic and waiting for government to care about their precious time,” Mamdani said in a statement.
The changes cover only about a mile of Flatbush Avenue, but officials plan to eventually implement similar redesigns that give buses priority all the way to Kings Plaza. The transportation department is also mulling an overhaul to Grand Army Plaza to make the traffic circle more hospitable to pedestrians.
The new bus lanes prohibit regular vehicle traffic but allow emergency and paratransit vehicles to use them.
Bus riders on the B41 bus said they already noticed a slight improvement in their commutes
Monica O’Neill, 30, who rides the route every other day to get to work, said “traffic goes a little bit faster than usual” since the buses no longer have to stop in front of restaurants and shops.
Some locals were still getting used to the new street design, having never seen a bus island where riders wait to board in between lanes of traffic instead of the sidewalk.
Nadine Barry, 45, worried that cars would crash into the boarding islands.
“I think pedestrians…are the first priority,” she said. “Because living in New York, New York is always congested.”
Workers at Antonio’s Pizza on Flatbush Avenue were up in arms about the bus lane, claiming it’s already pushed customers away from the slice shop.
“This place used to be full around 12 o’clock with all the construction guys, plumbing guys,” said Arlind Kirkuti, 20, who’s worked at the shop for five years. “Now they can’t even find parking, so they don’t even stop by no more.”
Sy Hannan, who runs a painting business in the area, said he might have to charge more for jobs in the area because it takes longer to find parking and haul his equipment to the location.
“If I had to work for one of these people, I'd have to park several blocks away and haul my gear, and that costs the client more,” Hannan said.

https://www.propublica.org/article/faith.title: I Photographed Her Parents as They Were Sentenced for Her Twin’s Death. Years Later, I Photographed Her Life.
https://www.propublica.org/article/faith.author: Beth Nakamura
https://www.propublica.org/article/faith.text:
About eight years ago, I was assigned to photograph the sentencing of Travis and Sarah Mitchell, a couple with deep roots in an insular faith-healing sect outside of Portland, Oregon.
The Mitchells, as members of the Followers of Christ, adhere to a doctrine that forbids medical care. Instead, followers rely on healing through faith. So when Sarah Mitchell gave birth prematurely to twins in 2017 — and both gasped for breath in their first hours — the couple didn’t rush them to an emergency room. Instead, they turned to prayer.
One twin, Ginnifer, lived for four hours, each one a struggle. The family eventually sought medical care for her surviving twin sister, Evelyn, but only after the county’s deputy medical examiner arrived at the location of the home birth and learned, though not right away, of Evelyn’s existence. Even then, he had to seek help from police, who arrived at the Oregon City home and told reluctant family members to take the struggling infant to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.
The Mitchells pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide in the death of their infant daughter, Ginnifer, and to criminal mistreatment for failing to seek medical care for her surviving twin, Evelyn. The couple’s lawyer told the judge that the Mitchells grieved the loss of Ginnifer and loved Evelyn. “Travis and Sarah are utterly sincere, decent and caring human beings,” he told the judge. (The Mitchells and their lawyer did not respond to ProPublica and The Oregonian’s recent requests to be interviewed.)
Today, my memory of the sentencing is more montage than detail. But I remember the crowded gallery, the couple in black-and-white-striped prison clothing, and their prison sentence of more than six years. Evelyn, who within days of her birth had been placed in the custody of Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, another couple in the Followers of Christ, wasn’t present. She remained in the couple’s permanent care.
The Mitchells went off to prison, and I went on with my life.
Such is the grinding rhythm of the daily news cycle. So often I see people on their worst day — and then never again. Stories don’t really end, of course, but my role as a photojournalist is limited. I’m an observer rather than a participant, seeing mostly slivers of the human experience that offer only a window into the whole. It’s rare that I get to see what happens next.
Never would I have dreamed that the surviving baby in this case, Evelyn, would be someone I’d later come to know and care about through my work. But that’s precisely what happened eight years after that courtroom scene played out, when I began documenting the lives of Evelyn and her parents, the Phillipses. (In a legal filing in an ongoing case relating to Evelyn’s custody, the Mitchells criticized the Phillipses for allowing her to participate in our coverage.) The resulting story, a collaboration between ProPublica and The Oregonian, is one of several recently published about faith healing and the Followers of Christ church. It intimately explores the Phillipses’ journey out of the sect and illustrates how changes in Oregon state law — in contrast to neighboring Idaho, where the Followers have a handful of churches — have led to a reduction in child deaths.
To spend time around 9-year-old Evelyn is to behold a luminous, magnetic force of nature. It’s impossible to imagine this same girl as a premature baby so small that the only items that fit her were doll clothes purchased from the supermarket toy aisle.
Series Timeline
For months, as I documented Evelyn’s life — from her baptism to her home life to doctors’ appointments — my journalism colleagues worked on their own pieces of our project. Teresa Mahoney, video editor at The Oregonian, produced a video introduction to the story that included a sequence of footage recorded by body cameras worn by police officers who stood outside Evelyn’s grandparents’ house that night, at first nudging, then ordering, Evelyn’s family to get her to the hospital. Each time I viewed it, as I watched the officers politely letting time slip away, I’d need to regulate my own breathing as I imagined Evelyn on the other side of that door, struggling to breathe herself.
I hope that reporter Noelle Crombie’s words, Teresa’s video and my photographs allow readers to see not only the journey of the couple who are raising Evelyn as their own but also the surviving — indeed, thriving — twin I came to know. That Evelyn is alive at all is, depending on your worldview, a miracle.
My work is all about observing and capturing moments, about freezing time. Here, I was witnessing the unfolding of time. I got to see what happened next.

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Critical Condition: What Are We Doing About Nuclear War?
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Matt Bivens
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Critical Condition: What Are We Doing About Nuclear War?
Doctors are calling for verifiable, deadline-driven agreement to eliminate all nuclear weapons. The flourishing—and even the survival—of the human species is at stake.
What will it take to get us all to think in a new way?
Someone (the artistic wife of a Manhattan Project scientist, actually) came up with the idea for a clock, its hands ticking ever closer to that sinister midnight. Dentists collected more than 320,000 baby teeth to show how radioactive strontium-90 accumulated in the mouths of our children after all of the hydrogen bomb tests.
Moviemakers offered dramatizations. Think of actor John Lithgow in the closing moments of The Day After, broadcasting via shortwave radio from postapocalyptic Kansas City: “Hello? Is anybody there? Anybody at all?” Or actor Slim Pickens straddling a missile like a mechanical bull, waving his cowboy hat and whooping as he rides a nuke down to blow us all up.
Our most famous thinkers tried logic and eloquence. Physicist Albert Einstein, mathematician Bertrand Russell, chemist Linus Pauling, and other great minds begged us in a famous and beautiful letter: “Remember your humanity, and forget the rest.” It’s been an exhortation cited ever since, blazoned across T-shirts and saluted by a Nobel Prize. The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., another giant of American moral life, repeatedly pointed out that the civil rights movement couldn’t succeed if the world were annihilated by nuclear war. “It is a wonderful thing to work to integrate lunch counters, public accommodations, and schools,” King observed. “But it would be rather absurd to work to get schools and lunch counters integrated and not be concerned with the survival of a world in which to integrate.”
Others buttressed logic and eloquence by sharing tragic personal experience. The child survivors of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings, now all quite elderly, travel the world to testify about a horrible tragedy from the quaint old days, back when the world knew of only two small (15-kiloton) nuclear weapons. It can be startling to remember this: These weapons have only been around for less than a single human lifespan. We have very little actual experience with them.
More than 1 million people gathered in New York’s Central Park in 1982 to insist something be done, in the largest political demonstration in American history. Catholic popes repeatedly called for nuclear disarmament. Nuns and priests went to jail, often for years, for the crime of sneaking onto military bases and hammering symbolically upon the ICBMs there, as per Isaiah 2:4: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.”
In fact, every major religion has condemned nuclear weapons. Of course they have; these weapons are utterly immoral.
Monks in traditional Buddhist robes once walked 1,600 miles across America to make this point, carrying burning embers lit by a fire associated with the Hiroshima bombing.
Quakers in the 1950s sailed into closed military zones to disrupt nuclear tests, and the Golden Rule Peace Boat sails again today for nuclear disarmament, thanks to a salvage and restoration by Veterans for Peace.
Muslim leaders who have publicly opposed nuclear weapons on moral grounds include Iran’s Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed at age 86 by the Trump administration. Khamenei was killed—alongside his daughter, his toddler granddaughter, and other family members—at the opening of a war the White House says is about preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
How many ways can a message be shared?
Dramatic clocks, heroic sailboats, radioactive baby teeth, nuns going to jail for hammering on a missile, Buddhist monks walking hundreds of miles across America with fire from Hiroshima, the wisdom of Einstein and King and the child survivors of Nagasaki, a million people crowded into Central Park… How many different ways can the great danger to human survival be risen up against, revealed, explained?
To the long list of those efforts we can now add an editorial published this week simultaneously in more than 100 medical journals around the world, ranging from The Lancet and the British Medical Journal of the United Kingdom to the Nigerian Journal of Paediatrics and the Medical Journal of Australia. (Disclosure: I am one of the coauthors.)
From Switzerland to Nepal and from Croatia to Colombia, across general journals and specialty journals, the world’s physicians (and medical students, dentists, nurses, and even veterinarians) will share the same message with one another.
It will be published by and for the geriatricians of Germany in Zeitschrift für Gerontologie und Geriatrie; by and for the doctors of North Africa in La Tunisie Médicale; and by and for the medical educators of Central America in Revista Médica Hondureña. It will be offered in the British Journal of Cancer, the African Journal of Reproductive Health, the International Nursing Review, the Philippine Journal of Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery, and many other niche publications. Along the way, it has been actively supported by national medical societies, including those of France, Norway, Denmark, and others.
And it will be read. We know this from the two prior times (in 2023 and 2025) that International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War has pulled off this feat of a simultaneous worldwide medical journal publication.
“As a project, this is not merely a broad communications effort, it is a real game-changer,” says editorial coauthor Chris Zielinski, a past president of the World Association of Medical Editors. “Normally, medical journals go to great lengths to ensure that the material they publish has not appeared in any other medical journals. The fear of plagiarism is extreme.”
But species-level threats to humanity have motivated scientific journal editors around the world to set aside business as usual. (There have also been simultaneous worldwide editorials in 2021, 2022, and 2023 about the dangers of climate change.)
“The international network has been used to raise information literacy in a way which is both refreshingly new, and yet extremely traditional,” Zielinski says. “There has never been anything remotely like it in the health sector—or, for that matter, in any other sector.”
Will it matter? Will it help?
It’s certainly not more eloquent than Russell-Einstein or Martin Luther King. Or the author Jonathan Schell, a former peace correspondent for The Nation, who in The Fate of the Earth warned how easy it is to slip into denial about the nuclear bomb—that “while it relentlessly came to threaten the existence of everything, it physically touched nothing, and thus left people free not to think about it.”
It was not unless one lifted one’s gaze from all the allegedly normal events occurring before one’s eyes and looked at the executioner’s sword hanging over everyone’s head that the normality was revealed as a sort of mass insanity. This was an insanity that consisted not in screaming and making a commotion but precisely in not doing these things in the face of overwhelming danger, as though everyone had been sedated.
Passengers on a ship who are eating, sunning themselves, playing shuffleboard, and engaging in all the usual shipboard activities appear perfectly normal as long as their ship is sailing safely in quiet seas, but these same passengers doing these same things appear deranged if in full view of them all their ship is caught in a vortex that may shortly drag it and them to destruction. Then their placidity has the appearance of an unnatural loss of normal human responses—of a pathetic and sickening acquiescence in their own slaughter.
No editorial published simultaneously in Farm Animal Health and Nutrition, the European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, and Supportive Care in Cancer is going to rival that kind of passionate prose.
All we can do is lay out the scientific facts.
§ Nine nations hold more than 12,000 nuclear weapons—most of them so massive that a Hiroshima A-bomb is tiny in comparison (and in fact, a Hiroshima-sized bomb often literally acts as the blasting cap to detonate the larger bomb).
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
§ There are enough nuclear bombs to torch the cities, wreck the climate, and kill every human being many, many times over. (In fact, as recounted in The Nation not long ago, a “minor” nuclear war between far-off India and Pakistan would so disrupt world agriculture that, over the next two years, it could kill two out of three Americans. From hunger!)
§ Yet the plan is to keep these weapons on hair-trigger alert—ready for accidental or intentional launch in a matter of minutes—and to sink billions of dollars into building more.
§ All of the US-Russian arms control agreements have been rescinded or have expired. As the US, Russian, and Chinese presidents meet this week in China, Donald Trump says he wants to talk about a major new arms control agreement involving all three nations. But expectations for success are exceedingly low.
§ The majority—the majority!—of the world’s nations have voted emphatically to do away with these ridiculous and morally offensive explosive devices. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons was passed easily by the United Nations and has been gathering ratification by national parliaments around the planet. That said, the ban treaty has been ignored by many nations, including every nuclear-armed nation: America, Russia, China, Israel, North Korea, Britain, France, India, and Pakistan.
Hello? Is anybody there? Anybody at all?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: MCA Chicago receives gift of 65 works, most of them by women and artists of colour
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ruth Lopez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.
The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.
Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.
For Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.
The Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and currently serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.
The current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.
“In some cases, we are adding an entirely new collection,” Grynsztejn says, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”
The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.
During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.
Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she says. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: What Gavin Newsom’s Commutations Mean for the Future of the Death Penalty
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Victoria Law
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
What Gavin Newsom’s Commutations Mean for the Future of the Death Penalty
Officials in some states continue to seek the death penalty while others, like Newsom, have vowed to bring the sentences to a halt.
June Oceans was returning to her dorm from a tutoring session when she learned she was no longer sentenced to execution.
“Congrats, did you hear?” the other woman asked. Oceans had no idea what she was talking about.
Her friend had been listening to the news at her prison job and heard that California Governor Gavin Newsom had commuted the sentences of every single person sentenced to death in the state.
“I was shocked,” Oceans, who had been sentenced to death in 1994, told The Nation. Watching the news later, she was filled with excitement. But it was a cautious excitement. “I needed to know some details before I could feel relief,” she added.
On November 5, two days after Election Day, Newsom commuted the sentences of the 548 people on death row to life without parole. Newsom’s action is the largest death sentence commutation in recent US history.
California has more people on death row than any other state. Its last execution was in 2006. In 2019, Newsom issued a moratorium on executions, stating that the death penalty is “unfair, unjust, wasteful, protracted and does not make our state safer.”
“I will not oversee execution of any person while Governor,” he stated in that executive order.
“Newsom’s decision is huge,” Sandra Babcock, founder of the Cornell Center on the Death Penalty Worldwide, told The Nation. “California was the behemoth of the death penalty because of the sheer number of people on death row.”
Under California law, the governor can unilaterally grant clemency to people with one felony conviction, which is 166 people on death row. The only requirement is notifying prosecutors and victims’ families.
For the other 382 people, who have a felony conviction unrelated to their death penalty case, they must wait for the California Supreme Court to rule on the governor’s mass clemency. “The court is not reviewing cases one by one,” clarified Natasha Minsker, director of the California Anti-Death Penalty Coalition, which had called on Newsom to grant this mass commutation. “The issue has been presented to the court as: Can the governor commute all death sentences because they are death sentences? Can he choose life over death in all cases at once? And that’s the question they’re going to answer.”
If the court does not approve the commutations before Newsom leaves office in January, they would expire, leaving the death sentences in place. But, notes Minsker, final briefs are due December 4, signaling that the court intends to resolve the issue before Newsom leaves office.
Before Newsom, the largest mass commutation happened in 2003 when the then–governor of Illinois, George Ryan, nullified death sentences for 167 people shortly before leaving office.
Newsom’s action doesn’t abolish the death penalty in the state. Only voters can do that via a ballot referendum, and they failed to do so in 2012 and again in 2016. Incoming Governor Xavier Becerra has vowed to continue the moratorium on executions.
Nonetheless, some prosecutors have pledged to continue seeking the death penalty. “I’m going to continue to seek it when appropriate,” Michael Hestrin, the Riverside County district attorney, told The New York Times. His county has sent more people to death row than any other in recent years, and its prosecutors are currently seeking capital punishment in 20 cases. In Kern County, 179 miles north, prosecutors are seeking the death penalty in 13 cases.
They are in the minority. Across California’s 58 counties, only 12 continue to pursue death sentences. “In California, the death penalty is dying on the vine,” said Minsker. “The vast majority of prosecutors understand this is a false promise and a waste of public safety resources.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
It seems to be dying nationwide as well. In 1991, a Gallup poll found that 76 percent of US adults were in favor of the death penalty. The next year, Bill Clinton made a point of leaving the presidential campaign trail to attend the execution of Ricky Rector, a man with mental disabilities so pronounced that he saved the dessert from his last meal “for later.” Two years later, in 1994, approval of the death penalty rose to 80 percent. Support has been waning ever since thanks to decades of organizing against the death penalty by advocates and family members of those behind bars. This past October, a Gallup poll conducted in the weeks after Christa Pike’s horrifically botched execution in Tennessee found that 49 percent of US adults were in favor, the first time approval has dipped below 50 percent since 1971.
Still, on the same day as Newsom’s announcement, Florida, Alabama and Indiana each executed a person via lethal injection. But, noted Babcock, only a small percentage of jurisdictions within death penalty states still seek executions. In Texas, for instance, only two of its 254 counties pursued a new death sentence in 2025.
“Newsom’s decision to commute death sentences is an incredibly important act of moral courage and leadership,” said Minsker. “He is showing leaders that we can have safety without sacrificing our shared humanity.”
Noting that California holds one-quarter of all death sentences in the country, she added, “For Governor Newsom to commute one-quarter of the death sentences, the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere, it’s the most significant blow to the death penalty in decades.”
She hopes that his action will push other governors to follow suit, such as Ohio’s Mike Dewine, who has publicly called for an end to the death penalty, or incoming Governor Amy Acton, who has vowed to continue Dewine’s moratorium.
Not only does Newsom’s action clear the way for them to do the same, but the sheer size of California’s death row means that mass commutations elsewhere will seem less extreme. For Ohio, that would mean 112 sentences, or for Pennsylvania that would mean 103 sentences, said Babcock, noting that any other mass commutation would be much smaller.
Oceans turns 58 next month. She was 25 years old when she was sentenced to death. During her years on death row, she was incarcerated in a men’s prison before her transition. There, she watched some of her peers, including those who mentored her, be taken away for execution.
“Shakespeare wrote, ‘When sorrows come, they come not by single spies, but in battalions,’” Oceans, now at the Central California Women’s Facility, reflected. “It’s a difficult situation to be isolated and realize that every good inspiration [including the men who befriended and mentored her] you ever had is no longer here. And then you have to wrestle with the reality that that is the exact process they [the state] intend[s] to exercise on me.”
For over a decade, Oceans was left in legal limbo after voters passed Proposition 66 in 2016. Intended to speed up legal proceedings before execution, it did the opposite: The new law required that state habeas cases (in which people who are incarcerated can challenge their sentence of execution) begin at the lower courts but did not provide a method to pay for counsel, leaving Oceans and many others without representation.
“Now everything seems bright,” she said.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Fossil-fuel industry accused of violating Colorado law over not disclosing drilling chemicals
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Tom Perkins
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it uses in drilling, a new analysis by the FracTracker Alliance nonprofit alleges, and state records show it has used illegal or dangerous compounds while fracking.
Drilling chemicals can include xylene, toluene, benzene, Pfas, and other dangerous toxicants, industry records and literature from other regions show. A first-in-the-nation 2022 Colorado law requires fossil-fuel operators and their suppliers to make public all chemicals used in “downhole oil and gas production”. But regulators have exempted compounds used in drilling, claiming that drilling is not part of production.
FracTracker contends this exemption contradicts the widely held definition of production, including that implied in Colorado’s regulatory literature.
Legislators who authored the law, public health groups, and industry all use definitions of “production” that includes drilling, FracTracker states, and it notes the law requires “disclosure of all chemicals used underground or ‘downhole’ in oil and gas wells.”
Meanwhile, at least five chemicals that were reported for use in fracking are prohibited by Colorado law, FracTracker alleges. It also found fossil-fuel companies reported using at least three highly toxic chemicals that raise serious safety questions.
About 43,000 people live within a mile of the state’s wells, and many within a few hundred feet. Regulators are flying blind on what the sum impact of the chemicals may be, the authors allege.
“This is a public health crisis and it should be treated as such,” Shannon Smith, FracTracker’s executive director and report co-author, told the Guardian. FracTacker is a nonprofit that investigates and monitors public health threats created by the fossil-fuel industry, and advocates for protections. It began in Pennsylvania in 2010, but now organizes nationally.
Fracking operators and their suppliers are supposed to disclose all downhole chemical ingredients to the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC) regulatory agency within 150 days. The agency then must post the chemicals on its website.
ECMC literature implies the agency considers drilling as part of oil and gas production. In a statement, an ECMC spokesperson said the agency is “aware of differing views regarding the scope and implementation of the chemical disclosure requirements”.
“We are applying the law and Commission rules under the current statutory and regulatory framework while continuing to work with stakeholders to clarify these issues and support consistent, appropriate implementation,” the spokesperson said.
Halliburton, Chevron and Occidental Petroleum are among the state’s top fossil-fuel producers.
In a statement, a Chevron spokesperson said the company “is committed to safe and responsible operations in Colorado”.
“We take chemical-disclosure requirements seriously and remain focused on meeting our obligations and maintaining transparent, responsible operating practices,” the spokesperson added.
In order to drill wells and extract minerals, fossil-fuel operators pump huge volumes of pressurized liquid into the earth to fracture – or “frack” – bedrock, stimulating the release of trapped oil and gas. These fluids are mostly water and sand by volume, but they also contain industrial chemicals, including biocides, surfactants, and lubricants.
Hundreds of studies have pointed to health risks for those in fracking regions. Toxic chemicals such as formaldehyde, Pfas, and benzene have been widely detected or reported in fracking fluids. These and other chemicals used – or thought to be used – in production are linked to issues like cancer, hormone disruption, and neurological damage.
Gas companies reported as many as 11 spills per week in 2018, and people are exposed to the chemicals through multiple pathways, including groundwater, above ground spills, wastewater seepage into drinking water supplies, and air emissions.
The ECMC has told FracTracker that it does not consider drilling to be part of the fracking and production said Dusty Horwitt, a senior research and policy consultant with the group who co-authored the report.
“That was news to us, and it is not consistent with The American Petroleum Institute definition of what oil and gas production is,” Horwitt added. API literature shows oil and gas production includes “drilling, extraction, and recovery of oil from underground”.
Colorado state representative Meg Froelich, who co-wrote the 2022 legislation, said she intended for drilling chemicals to be disclosed. The legislation is called “Concerning enhanced oversight of the chemicals used in oil and gas production.” Production includes drilling, Froelich said.
She accused the ECMC of “word-parsing” and added that she is “mad about their stalling”.
“The law covers everything that goes downhole because everything that goes downhole has the potential to affect neighbors,” Froelich told the Guardian.
The ECMC until recent years has largely worked to promote the fossil-fuel industry, and only since Democrats took over the state government has it shifted to also protect public health, but the shift has come in “fits and starts”, Froelich said.
State records show that wells covered by law operated without drilling chemical disclosure for at least a collective 843,369 days from the rules’ implementation to May 16, when the analysis was conducted.
The law also requires fossil-fuel companies to provide schools, first responders, and other community institutions with lists of chemicals it uses, but it has failed to do that, advocates say.
The report comes after a previous analysis reported on by the Guardian found Colorado fossil-fuel companies pumped at least 30m lbs of secret chemicals into the ground over an 18-month period without making legally required disclosures. Out of over 1,100 fracked sites across the state, companies did not disclose 675, or about 60%.
Since then, the compliance rate is closer to 100% – except for the drilling chemicals, advocates say.
The report raises questions about which chemicals are being used for drilling. A recent law banned any use of Pfas at oil and gas sites, and industry literature and peer-reviewed research suggests that Pfas are a common drilling chemical. Horwitt told the Guardian he fears the chemicals may be used in Colorado.
“Publications, including those issued by major oil and gas-producing nations Canada and Norway, report that PFAS is used for multiple purposes in oil and gas production including drilling and enhanced oil recovery,” FracTracker states. The lack of drilling chemical disclosure in Colorado “creates uncertainty about whether companies are complying with the PFAS ban”, the report added.
Meanwhile, records from Ohio show the frequent use of xylene, the report states. The chemical can cause headaches, dizziness, confusion, loss of muscle coordination, and in high doses, death.
FracTracker also points to five chemicals that were disclosed as being used for fracking on some well pads despite state rules prohibiting their use in fracking: 1-butanol, 2-butoxyethanol, 1,4-dioxane, N,N-dimethylformamide and BMPA. Some of these compounds are linked to cancer, liver disease, and harm to developing children.
In its statement, the ECMC said it has “issued notices of alleged violation when prohibited substances are identified, including cases involving 1-butanol, 2-butoxyethanol and 1,4-dioxane”.
Among potentially harmful chemicals that are permitted are acrylamide, ethylene oxide, and methanol. FracTracker noted that those were among the chemicals disclosed as being used in a well in Galeton that sprayed a geyser of gas and at least 3.7m gallons of fluid for over four days in April 2025.
Living near wells has well-established links to leukemia, birth abnormalities and other serious health problems. Residents in July reported to the Guardian that they are plagued by loud noise, acrid air emissions, headaches, nosebleeds, and respiratory issues.

https://taz.de/Umfrage-und-Studie-zu-Dis.title: Umfrage und Studie zu Diskriminierung: Viele psychisch Kranke sehen sich im Job benachteiligt
https://taz.de/Umfrage-und-Studie-zu-Dis.text:
Umfrage und Studie zu Diskriminierung: Viele psychisch Kranke sehen sich im Job benachteiligt
Mobbing statt Beförderung? Wer eine psychische Erkrankung hat, ist auf der Arbeit oft mit besonderen Schwierigkeiten konfrontiert.
epd | Viele Menschen mit psychischen Erkrankungen sehen sich im Arbeitsleben benachteiligt. Rund 40 Prozent der Betroffenen gaben an, dass sie bereits eine solche Diskriminierung erlebt hätten, heißt es in einer am Dienstag vorgestellten Umfrage im Auftrag der Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes. Konkret wurden unter anderem eine schlechtere Leistungsbewertung als bei anderen Mitarbeitenden und ein respektloser Umgang beklagt.
Von den rund 8.000 Befragten berichteten den Angaben zufolge gut 27 Prozent von einer aktuellen oder früheren psychischen Erkrankung. Unter den Betroffenen mit einer Angst- oder Zwangsstörung sprachen demnach 45 Prozent von Diskriminierungserfahrungen, bei Menschen mit Depressionen waren es 42 Prozent und bei Menschen mit einer Suchterkrankung 37 Prozent.
Verunsicherung und Rückzug als Folgen
Bei der Frage, wie die Diskriminierung aussah, wurde am häufigsten (47 Prozent) eine schlechtere Bewertung der Leistung als bei anderen genannt. 45 Prozent gaben an, sie seien respektlos oder unangemessen behandelt worden. Berichtet wurde beispielsweise auch von Mobbing oder davon, bei einer Beförderung, Gehaltssteigerung oder Entfristung übergangen worden zu sein. Als Folge der Diskriminierung erklärten 52 Prozent der Betroffenen, sie seien verunsichert gewesen und hätten sich zurückgezogen.
„Wir brauchen mehr Wissen über psychische Erkrankungen, eine klare Haltung gegen Diskriminierung und eine Unternehmenskultur, in der niemand seine Erkrankung verstecken muss, um beruflich bestehen zu können“, folgerte die Antidiskriminierungsbeauftragte des Bundes, Ferda Ataman. Niemand solle Angst haben müssen, im Job über eine psychische Erkrankung zu sprechen.
Online-Umfrage und qualitative Studie
Für die Erhebung wurden im Frühjahr 8.004 Menschen zwischen 18 und 66 Jahren online befragt, die erwerbstätig sind oder waren. Die Umfrage wurde den Angaben zufolge durch eine qualitative Studie mit Einzelinterviews und Gesprächen in Fokusgruppen ergänzt.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Scott Reyburn
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?
“It’s important to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.
The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 currently stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.
On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.
Of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).
The mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.
That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.
The disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?
Luxury playground?
“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” said Andrew Terner, a New York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.
The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.
But maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.
Tax breaks
Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.
The ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.
Today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.
Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?
Young people priced out
Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?
The following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” says Magnus Resch, a New York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.)
“It is important for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”
The main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always
Sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.
In the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.
Collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.
After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Want to Upend “Citizens United”?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Moore
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Want to Upend Citizens United?
Check out the Montana Plan.
Want to Upend “Citizens United”?
Check out the Montana Plan.
On November 3, two-thirds of Montana voters approved a measure that strips corporations of the power to spend money on elections, striking a blow against corporate political cash in a state that went for Donald Trump by 20 points in 2024.
Initiative 194, known as the “Montana Plan,” is a first-of-its-kind ballot measure that rewrites state law so that “artificial persons”—such as corporations, nonprofits, unions, and trade associations—are no longer allowed to spend on candidates, PACs, or ballot measures. Advocates hail the plan as a novel legal strategy to bar corporate and dark money from influencing elections, and say that versions are being pursued in more than 30 states.
The measure passed by 66 to 34 percent, making Montana the second state, after Hawaii, to use its power over corporate charters to sidestep the US Supreme Court’s 2010 decision in Citizens United v. FEC. The ruling, which held that the First Amendment prohibits the government from restricting independent political spending by corporations and unions, relied on the claim that spending not coordinated with a candidate cannot corrupt; now candidates are permitted by the Federal Election Commission to raise money for their allied super PACs, and in practice frequently coordinate with them. Over 465,000 Montana voters voted on the initiative, which was greeted with a lawsuit from the Montana Republican Party and conservative groups on election night, before the race was called.
The initiative’s approval came as the 2026 elections smashed spending records. AdImpact tallied $11.9 billion in media spending nationwide, making this the most expensive election on record for political advertising. Outside spending on federal races, by groups like super PACs that pay for things like ads and mailers, was projected by OpenSecrets to reach $3.9 billion, a record for a midterm. The nonprofit also calculated that dark money flowing into federal races surpassed $1.5 billion, more than in the 2024 presidential cycle.
Voters this year noticed. An AP poll of midterm voters found that government corruption was the factor most mentioned in the survey as “crucial” in their choice for Congress, followed by the cost of living. More than half of midterm voters pointed to corruption as a main concern in the poll, conducted by the nonpartisan SSRS.
The Montana Plan redefines the powers the state grants to artificial persons, like corporations and nonprofits, to no longer include spending in elections—harnessing the legal distinction between constitutional rights and charter powers that are issued by states. Rather than restricting corporate speech rights, which Citizens United protects, the statutory Initiative 194 changes Montana’s code so that the state no longer grants artificial persons the power to spend on politics. Corporations and covered entities would no longer be allowed to contribute to any candidate, political party, or political committee in an election in Montana, including state and local ballot initiatives. Backers say that corporations remain free to advocate for candidates without giving money.
The measure applies to companies chartered in the state as well as out-of-state companies and nonprofits, so a Delaware corporation or a Washington, DC, nonprofit will be barred from unloading cash in a Montana election. Political committees, including super PACs, can still spend in the state, and individuals can still give to them—but corporations, nonprofits, and other artificial persons can no longer contribute to those committees. The new law does not apply to individuals, government bodies, or the distribution of news or commentary, unless the outlet is controlled by a party, PAC, or candidate.
A company, nonprofit, union, or other group found to be in violation would forfeit its charter privileges, including limited liability, and would be required to pay back its spending, regardless of whether it won or lost in the contest. The legal theory behind the plan, dubbed the Corporate Power Reset, was developed by Tom Moore, senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, who compiled a tracker of ballot initiatives and state bills introduced or being considered. Montana supporters say that once the law is in effect, disclosures listing the donors behind spending groups in the state will be names of real people, not corporations or dark-money groups.
The law is set to take effect on January 1, 2027, and legal challenges are underway that could be bound for the US Supreme Court, where the case would pit long-standing legal precedent for states’ authority to define corporate powers against the ruling in Citizens United. The Montana lawsuit, filed by the Institute for Free Speech on behalf of the state GOP and conservative groups, argues that the law violates the First Amendment by barring them from spending to communicate about candidates and ballot measures.
The nonprofit behind the initiative, the Transparent Election Initiative (TEI), says it anticipated the legal challenge and is prepared to defend the plan while helping other states advance their own versions.
“What I’ve been saying to folks for two years now is, there is a solution,” said Jeff Mangan, a former state legislator and Montana commissioner of political practices who is TEI’s founder and president, of the flood of corporate and dark money in elections.
“I started at the beginning of 2025, doing a listening session across the state, just asking folks about how they felt about money in politics, and if they’re ready for a change,” Mangan said. “I always led with the same question: Do you believe there’s too much money in politics? Everyone said yes.”
Since Citizens United, he said, people had been told that “there’s nothing you can do unless you have an amendment to the Constitution or the Supreme Court overturns it.” When he outlined the plan building on the state’s authority over corporations “to change the way corporations spend in elections, which will affect dark money and the amount of money going into our politics,” he said, “people got excited about it and wanted to collect signatures.”
TEI’s all-volunteer signature drive collected more than 50,000 signatures from all 56 Montana counties, above the 30,121 valid signatures required, with more than 600 volunteers helping the initiative qualify for the ballot. Mangan said TEI aimed to show the measure could make the ballot without the paid signature gatherers that have become commonplace for campaigns.
He pointed to the surge of corporate money this cycle. “The amount of money this year alone is staggering,” he said. Public Citizen recently found that 40 percent of the $1.8 billion that corporations have spent since the Citizens United ruling came in the 2026 midterms. The scale of the spending was inescapable, Mangan said, in recent Montana races like the 2024 Senate contest between Democrat Jon Tester and now-Senator Tim Sheehy, which set a national record for per-voter spending. He points out that billionaires are free to form PACs, just with their names attached. “They choose to spend anonymously through C4s or keep it dark for a reason,” he said, referring to 501(c)4 nonprofits.
A 2018 documentary about secret spending in Montana politics, Dark Money, was a regular feature of the signature drive. TEI showed the movie about a dozen times around the state, Mangan said, including a screening in Helena with remarks from the filmmaker, Kimberly Reed, who is from there.
Volunteers from other groups joined to put the Montana Plan in front of voters. The League of Women Voters of Montana’s members gathered signatures and hosted voter education events around the state, said Bonnie Lorenzen, the group’s president.
“The League of Women Voters of Montana chose early on to endorse the Montana Plan because it aligned perfectly with the League’s goal to ensure that our government serves the people, not wealthy special interests,” Lorenzen told The Nation. “We believe this is best attained by promoting transparency in government and eliminating dark money, which is what the Montana Plan aims to do.”
Popular

“Our elected officials need to be responsive to their constituents who elect them, not to corporate entities financing their campaigns,” Lorenzen said.
Former Republican governor Marc Racicot endorsed the Montana Plan, calling it “a brilliant idea,” along with Tester and Gary Buchanan, a former independent candidate for Congress. Groups applauding the plan included the cross-partisan Issue One, Free Speech for People, and Craig Holman, government affairs lobbyist for Public Citizen. Opposition to the ballot initiative came from groups including the Montana Chamber of Commerce, the Montana Mining Association, and the Montana Petroleum Association, as well as the state GOP. In April, the Montana Supreme Court unanimously dismissed a challenge from business groups that would have barred I-194 from the ballot, ruling that citizens have a right to go through the initiative process.
In May, Hawaii became the first state to enact a law based on the Corporate Power Reset framework, when Act 11, passed with near-unanimous support in the state House and Senate, was signed by Governor Josh Green. The law takes effect July 1, 2027, though it faces two federal lawsuits: one from the free-market think tank Grassroot Institute of Hawaii, and a second from the massive dark-money lobby the US Chamber of Commerce.
Bills based on the Corporate Power Reset were introduced in nearly 20 states this year, after New York was the first to introduce the legislation in late 2025. The New York Assembly bill was sponsored by Assemblyman Micah Lasher, now a US representative-elect, and the Senate bill by Senator Kristen Gonzalez; both bills were left in committee.
“We’ve always said it has to be a local solution, it has to be a state-by-state solution,” Mangan said of others seeking to pass the plan, whether through ballot initiatives or state legislatures. The measure’s spread across the map, he said, shows it has been “embraced by folks across the political spectrum.” After the plan’s resounding passage in Montana, he sees people thinking, “Oh, we can actually do something, rather than just saying we can do something.”
