https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.
The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.
The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.
The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.
“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, said during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”
Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she said. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”
Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.
A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.
More than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-aslan.title: Do Peasants Hold the Key to Humanity’s Future?
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-aslan.author: Daniel Colligan
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-aslan.text:
Do Peasants Hold the Key to Humanity’s Future?
A new book attempts to revive interest in peasants by casting them as humanity’s last defenders against ecological catastrophe. But this perspective misconceives the peasantry’s relationships to both nature and economic development.
In 1966, the sociologist Teodor Shanin boldly asserted that “peasants are the majority of mankind.” This declaration coincided with the beginning of a decades-long increase in academic focus on the peasantry, which, in addition to its demographic weight, was the driving force of some of the most important political movements of the twentieth century. Classic works such as anthropologist Eric Wolf’s 1969 Peasant Wars of the Twentieth Century chronicled the various ways in which subsistence farmers asserted themselves on the world stage.
In the sixty years since Shanin made that declaration, the situation of world agriculture has changed dramatically. On large farms, highly mechanized operations have raised productivity and output to unprecedented levels. Smallholder agriculture has been transformed by the adoption of Green Revolution technologies such as synthetic fertilizer, high-yielding crop varieties, and pesticides. A continuous flow of migrants exiting agriculture has swelled the urban areas of both rich and poor countries alike.
The epic overhaul of the global countryside has caused the peasantry to recede as an object of interest. Historian Eric Hobsbawm’s assessment that the twentieth century witnessed the “death of the peasantry” is often taken as a final judgment on the peasantry’s political relevance. That epitaph was reiterated two years ago in the most recent work on (European) peasants targeted at a general audience.
A new book attempts to counter this conventional wisdom on the peasantry by arguing that reports of the peasantry’s death have been greatly exaggerated. Maryam Aslany’s Peasants: Makers of the Modern World insists that there are actually more peasants living now than at any point in history: two billion who produce a third of the world’s food. Drawing on her fieldwork in India, Cambodia, Peru, and Ghana, Aslany attempts to “restore to the countryside the visibility it demands.”
And the visibility it demands is, in her view, superlative. In an article previewing the arguments of the book, Aslany argues that the present crisis of the peasantry is “the most important story of the 21st century.”
Aslany believes peasants to be a supremely important topic, because she thinks these agriculturalists are humanity’s final defense against total ecological ruin. Peasant cosmology’s sacral reverence for nature and peasants’ unique capability to steward natural resources, she claims, provide “our last protection against environmental collapse.” The peasantry’s eco-preserving essence is under continuous attack from urban-based and purportedly progressive forces that do not appreciate the indispensable role peasants play in environmental conservation. Humanity’s survival, then, depends on a global shift in agricultural policy toward supporting and strengthening the peasantry. This is all the more true, in her view, because intolerable urban conditions must lead to future repeasantization.
But Aslany’s revisionist perspective on the peasantry suffers from critical flaws. Her misleading historical account of global economic development confounds the role of both states and peasants in it. These distortions lead her to erroneously inflate the peasantry’s potential future importance. Ultimately, her peasant exceptionalism is unconvincing: it is highly doubtful that peasants possess a unique solution to the world’s environmental dilemmas.
What Is a Peasant?
Where does the two billion peasants figure come from? The source that Aslany cites for her claim regarding the existence of two billion peasants is her article, where she makes a slightly different claim — namely, that the rural populations of the three less-developed continents comprise two billion people: “By my calculations, as many as 2 billion people live in the countryside of Africa, Latin America and Asia, where small family farms dominate.” The article itself does not give any sense of how this particular statistic was derived, but two billion is in line with other estimates of the number of people involved in smallholder agriculture globally. Nevertheless, peasants, smallholder agriculturalists, and rural dwellers are overlapping but distinct categories whose differences should be preserved.
Defining peasants is a controversial endeavor. Aslany’s definition of a peasant — “a smallholder farmer who lives off the land . . . relies mainly on family labour, and farms both for subsistence and for the market” — blurs the distinction between farmers who primarily produce for exchange and those who are not fundamentally dependent on markets for their survival. This move allows her to to include a larger swath of people in her study, beyond only those rustics who raise crops and animals primarily for their own family’s consumption.
In fact, the cultivators Aslany studies are often highly dependent on markets, either on the input side, to purchase seed, fertilizer, and chemicals, sometimes via financial markets, and/or on the output side, through income generated by sale of their produce. They often cannot subsist on their own produce since they are husbanding nonstaple crops (e.g., coca, cocoa, or sugar).
Farming is not even the main income generator for some of the people Aslany profiles. One Cambodian farming couple’s income is overwhelmingly provided through the remittances generated by their children working in South Korean factories. Another farmer, this one in India, holds onto his land only though revenue earned from a transport business.
The point here is not to argue for one or another sociological definition of the peasantry or attempt the near-impossible task of precisely enumerating how many people fit any such definition worldwide. Rather, it is to note that a less expansive conception of what a peasant is would lead to an estimate of the peasantry’s size significantly lower than her marquee two billion figure.
Repeasantization?
Part of Aslany’s desire to stress the continuing importance of the peasantry derives from what she considers the failure of cities and industry to provide a tolerable existence for the future of humanity. The increase in world population over the next several decades will, she predicts, see many return from cities to rural areas and agricultural activities: “When all else fails, land is the only thing; in this sense, peasant cultivation must have a significant role to play in securing humanity’s future.”
Aslany tries to buttress this prediction by arguing against the veracity of two “compelling — if unexamined — stories about [the peasantry’s] demise.” The first is that peasant agriculture will decline in tandem with the progress of industry, and the second is that cities will absorb the peasants departing the countryside. Since these are precisely the processes that the world has witnessed over the past century, readers may be perplexed when encountering Aslany’s pushback on these claims.
Aslany attempts to rescue the first contention by writing that predictions of peasant agriculture’s demise was an “based on an extrapolation from the highly specific experience of north-western Europe” and “has still not happened.” But depeasantization is a phenomenon that has advanced far beyond the borders of the richest countries. For instance, taking as a sample the countries that Wolf profiles in Peasant Wars — Mexico, Russia, China, Vietnam, Algeria, and Cuba — the International Labour Organization reports the share of labor working in agriculture as under 10 percent in Algeria and Russia, under 20 percent in Cuba and Mexico, and, in China (22 percent) and Vietnam (25 percent), it is half of what it was mere decades ago. The countries Aslany visits in her book generally have higher labor shares in agriculture, but even they have come down rapidly in the twenty-first century: Cambodia’s, for instance, fell from 73 percent in the year 2000 to 33 percent in 2025.
On the second claim, Aslany recognizes that some formerly peasant countries like China have seen tremendous rural-to-urban migration. But, she insists, “China is exceptional: it cannot become the general condition.”
Again, the data intrudes on this perspective. United Nations figures show the Peasant Wars group with all non-Chinese countries at over 75 percent urbanization, with the exception of Vietnam, which has doubled its urbanization rate to 39 percent in the past generation. The countries Aslany visited, too, exhibit secular trends toward urbanization. In fact, of the three continents Aslany mentions as having significant rural populations, only in Africa is the rural population growing absolutely (although less rapidly than the urban population on the continent). Latin America’s and Asia’s rural populations have seen slight absolute declines over the twenty-first century.
It is therefore difficult not to be skeptical about Aslany’s predictions of saturated cities producing a demographic movement to the countryside; her statement that “even Europe is seeing traces of what some experts call ‘re-peasantization’” is baffling.
It is true that legitimate questions remain about how burgeoning urban populations in less-developed countries will be absorbed into the labor force, especially given that many of these countries are experiencing “premature deindustrialization.” However, outside of some massive crisis of urban life above and beyond what is currently being experienced in Global South cities, in all likelihood current trends of depeasantization and rural-to-urban migration will continue into the near future.
The State as Villain (Marx in Supporting Role)
The sense that peasants are currently facing an existential crisis (despite a somewhat contradictory insistence on their endurance) provides the motivating drama for Aslany’s book. Peasants themselves, Aslany avers, are not responsible for their endangerment. Rather, that is the fault of the states that have persecuted them over the last century: “Peasants are in crisis today not because they are somehow unsuited to modern conditions but because they have been hunted to the limits of possibility.” In this “class war between humanity’s urban and rural factions,” deliberate anti-peasant efforts by states have driven many peasants off of their land and threaten to eliminate the peasantry as a category in years to come.
The underlying reason that states have hit upon these anti-peasant policies, Aslany contends, is primarily ideological. Drawing on the English example, in which a vanquished peasantry coincided with rapid economic growth, the world’s technocrats adopted this experience as an ideal and, aided by British imperialism, exported it to the rest of the world. Thus, Aslany writes, “The world’s managers have believed their own urban fairy tale: that the peasantry no longer exists – or that it should, in the interests of ‘progress,’ cease to do so.”
Chief among the ideologists was Karl Marx, “who did the most to convert the dying peasant of bourgeois fantasy into scientific ‘fact.’” This peasant-averse ideology reached its most grotesque expression in various episodes of the twentieth century, when Marxist-influenced governments, through collectivization or otherwise, waged lethal mass campaigns against the peasantry.
This is a radical reinterpretation of the motives of state managers in the past centuries of global economic development, which completely neglects the more straightforward reasons that they pursued policies that did not prioritize peasant interests. State managers’ aspirations to increase economic prosperity derived primarily from the political pressures they faced both domestically and internationally.
Domestically, populations clamored for increasing living standards, and businesses demanded assistance in competing with foreign goods. Internationally, state managers wanted to avoid being dominated economically and/or militarily by rival states. Any successful historical example of rapid national economic development has required a transition of the labor force out of agriculture and into services and, especially, industry.
While not ignoring the suffering that peasants faced in historical episodes of persecution, it is also true that peasants themselves have found many reasons to voluntarily leave the country for the city. Urban wages are often higher than agricultural ones, and, for many, backbreaking labor in the fields is less preferable than employment in a factory or an office. Cities offer a more exciting cultural life and an escape from rural social conservatism and patriarchal family structures. Not every peasant who left their farm for the city over the past centuries was marched off at gunpoint by the state; migratory flows from countryside to city have existed both in times of acute crisis and in times of relative stability.
Therefore, it is misleading to portray depeasantization as a wholly top-down enterprise devised by sinister state bureaucrats drunk on Marxism or modernization theory. Many peasants have voluntarily chosen, for various reasons, to take their chances in the uncertain city rather than on the familiar farm.
The Thin Green Line
The book’s ultimate argument for the importance of the peasantry lies in peasants’ ecological sensibilities. “The fact that a substantial proportion of the world’s cultivable land is controlled by peasants,” Aslany writes, “protects us enormously against the final exhaustion of natural systems.” Peasants’ sacral veneration of their land and environment, Aslany argues, is actually superior as a form of conservation compared to more conventional legal approaches: “Over prolonged periods, the sacred offers a much stronger form of environmental protection than the law.” Peasant cosmology amounts to a kind of Thin Green Line preventing the world from tipping over into environmental catastrophe.
The balance sheet of the peasantry’s relation to the environment, however, is not exclusively on the side of conservation; peasants can play a very damaging ecological role. Smallholder agriculture requires land, which excludes the land from serving other purposes. The more small farms propagate, the more deforestation and biodiversity loss might result. On an individual level, too, small farmers are often compelled to adopt the latest potentially ecologically-damaging cultivation practices, whether it is synthetic fertilizer, pesticide and herbicide use, or others. In the extreme case, as Aslany documents in Ghana, small farmers might opt to despoil their plots with what is euphemistically called “artisanal and small-scale mining,” overwhelming a once-viable farm with toxic waste from gold extraction.
In truth, peasant agriculture is not inherently ecologically superior to other forms of agriculture — or, for that matter, other forms of economic activity. Agriculture undoubtedly has an important place in any plan for environmental sustainability. But comprehensive solutions to the climate crisis (to mention just one pressing ecological challenge) must go far beyond the areas where peasants purportedly have expertise. Transitioning to renewable energy sources, for instance, and decarbonizing industry and transit are necessary components of a climate strategy on which peasant cosmology will have very little bearing. All the more reason to abandon notions of peasant exceptionalism when thinking about how to achieve our ecological goals.
To the extent that Aslany has a political program in mind to address smallholder agriculture, she advocates placating the farmers who “would love a bit more capitalism in their lives” by deregulating state-sponsored commodity monopolies. But hers is not simply a laissez-faire program. Aslany also urges state support for “iron-clad protection for [peasant] land,” “forms of credit that are quite different from other kinds of businesses,” and “protection from excessive price fluctuations, or downward pressure applied by powerful buyers.” At base, the political program she outlines is one of subsidizing smallholder agriculture rather than an ecologically driven project per se. Perhaps this could be a small component part of a larger ecological strategy, but handouts to small agrarian businesses does not seem like a route to averting climate disaster.
Makers of a Previous World
Peasants raises pressing questions about agriculture, urbanization, migration, ecology, and economic development, particularly in the Global South. The stubbornly persistent absolute number of people involved in smallholder agriculture is certainly an important phenomenon that must be grappled with in both national and international contexts.
But such an assessment is not aided by mangling the history and present of the peasant predicament. Peasants have not left their land over the past few centuries exclusively because they were victims of state persecution. And states have not undertaken industrialization programs only or primarily out of ideological anti-peasant animus. Rather, peasant attraction to cities and new forms of employment provided reason enough for many to migrate. It seems highly unlikely that present trends of urbanization and deagrarianization will sharply reverse in the decades to come. Finally, peasants do not possess a privileged position when it comes to formulating a comprehensive solution to the planet’s environmental crises.
Peasants can be said to be “makers of the modern world” only in the sense that in the preceding epoch they provided the demographic foundation for agrarian empires. Today they account for an ever-dwindling share of the world’s population, a minority of global food production, and only really survive in the least developed countries. Extrapolating into the future, repeasantization on a significant scale looks far less likely than absolute peasant numbers dwindling further with the continuing advance of capitalism and falling fertility rates.
Karl Marx is often criticized, including by Aslany, for proclaiming that “The country that is more developed industrially only shows, to the less developed, the image of its own future.” However, insofar as this premonition is read as sketching the broad historical arc of depeasantization and urbanization, it hews closer to developments across the subsequent centuries than his critics might care to admit.

Le gouvernement se veut rassurant, mais la menace russe plane. Selon des informations révélées lundi 16 novembre par RFI et confirmées depuis, de petits groupes de militaires français sont présents sur le sol de l’Ukraine envahie par la Russie en février 2022 pour fournir des formations...

https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.title: They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them.
https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.author: Joe Rubin
https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Scant Scrutiny: After people died or were hospitalized soon after riding Six Flags’ X2 roller coaster, California regulators often did minimal or no inspection.
- Riders’ Responsibility: California regulators have regularly accepted Six Flags’ assertions that riders’ injuries could not be the fault of the X2.
- Insufficient Inspectors: A 2025 audit found that the state agency enforcing roller coaster safety had been short-staffed for years.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found.
A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided.
Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters.
Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph.
The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, CNN reported that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades.
Christopher’s is a third.
A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety.
But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents.
“How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.”
CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle.
Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”
Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said.
When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.”
Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain.
The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel.
That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4.
Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later.
It’s been a deadly year for Six Flags. In addition to the California incident, an Atlanta school worker died in October after riding one of the theme park’s “hypercoasters” at Six Flags Over Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily close nine attractions at six theme parks across North America.
Theme park rides are regulated by states, not the federal government. In 2000, the legislature gave CalOSHA, the agency responsible for worker safety in California, oversight of roller coasters. Millions of people flock to the state’s theme parks each year, and the move came after a series of high-profile accidents in the 1990s. Under the law, state officials were given new power to conduct annual inspections, and theme parks must report accidents that result in serious injury to the agency.
But ProPublica and L.A. Material found that officials in CalOSHA’s Amusement Ride and Tramway Unit have frequently determined that investigations are unnecessary when accidents happen on the X2.
In 16 instances involving people who wound up in the hospital after riding the X2 between 2009 and 2022, CalOSHA invoked identical or similar language after checking a box on accident reports that said state action was not called for. “At this time, this accident does not warrant an investigation,” said one typical form. “The condition which developed while the patron was riding does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride.” The report was filed in response to a woman who was hospitalized in 2016 with a head injury after riding the X2.
This also held true in cases where people lost their lives. When Hilda Farias suffered a massive brain hemorrhage after riding the X2 in October 2010, CalOSHA officials adopted similar language and conducted no inspection. The state regulator’s report did not even note that the 28-year-old mother of a 5-year-old had died, according to records obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material. Farias’ family sued the theme park, and the case settled in 2015.
When Hawley died in June 2022 after riding the X2, Magic Mountain initially told CalOSHA that the cause appeared to be heatstroke, according to a state report. The coroner later determined that Hawley, like Farias, had died of a massive brain hemorrhage. On that occasion, CalOSHA shut the ride down briefly while Six Flags conducted tests to measure the impact of g-forces on the rider and examined maintenance records. It ultimately determined that the ride was operating normally, according to a CalOSHA inspection obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material.
Christopher Gibson wore a Batman hoodie to school almost every day.
Diagnosed with autism when he was 5 or 6, Christopher was “high-functioning and verbal,” his mother told a sheriff’s detective. He had recently graduated high school and was headed to Colorado Mesa University to study theater.
As part of a family tradition, the teen’s mother let each of her five children pick the location of a celebratory senior trip. Chistopher wanted to ride roller coasters, and mother and son discussed a trip to Disneyland or Disney World. After some online research, Christopher chose Six Flags Magic Mountain, known for its thrill rides and DC Comics characters.
“He wanted to see Six Flags,” said Chadwick McGrady, an attorney representing the family in Christopher’s death. “The marketing worked.”
Magic Mountain sits about 35 miles north of downtown Los Angeles, in Valencia, the last notable stop before Interstate 5 climbs a steep stretch known as the Grapevine and drops down into the San Joaquin Valley. The park is aptly named: Roller coasters built into the mountainous terrain hurtle riders down hillsides and through trees, with disorienting turns taken at high velocity.
Christopher rode the X2 on June 2 and again on the morning of June 3. Soon after, reeling from a headache, he texted his mother from a park restroom: “I don’t think I can do any more today. My head is hurting me.”
They went back to the hotel. He had two days to recover before one of the big draws of the trip: DC Heroes and Villains Fest. Christopher “was a huge fan of DC Comics and was looking forward to meeting Batman on Friday, when DC Comics characters would be at the park,” sheriff’s detective Yoon Nam would later write in her report. Friday, June 5, was its opening day, and Christopher was determined not to miss it.
But on the morning of June 4, his head was still hurting him. He had taken refuge in the hotel room’s closet. His mother wasn’t unduly alarmed, because Christopher often retreated to dark spaces at home, a longstanding self-soothing ritual. She listened to the sound of his snoring — until at some point in the afternoon, the sound stopped.
In a statement released through her lawyer, Fascaldo said that her son “had so many dreams, and had his whole life ahead of him.”
After an autopsy, the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner found a large subdural hemorrhage. The cause of death: “blunt force head trauma.” The reason for the injuries was noted as a “history of theme park rides.”
Nam and the medical examiner spoke by phone with Fascaldo, Christopher’s mother, on June 6.
According to a source familiar with the investigation, Fascaldo was composed, recounting a precise chronology of the rides Christopher had ridden. Among them were Full Throttle and the Viper, and, at least twice, the X2.
Nam contacted CalOSHA. She knew that it was responsible for regulating the state’s roller coasters and wanted to make sure the agency was aware that the Magic Mountain rides could have contributed to Christopher’s death.
“I cannot attribute his death to his roller coaster ride experiences with 100% certainty,” Nam wrote in a July 2 email to Bobby Park, who runs the CalOSHA unit regulating roller coasters. “However, at this time, it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.”
The detective offered to help. “Please let me know if this case warrants additional follow-up by your office,” she wrote. “Feel free to call, text, or email with any questions or concerns.”
In the days after that unanswered email, more parkgoers suffered injuries after riding the X2.
On the evening of July 5, three days after the homicide detective sent her email, Pamela Guillen, 39, rode the coaster with her daughter.
When the car she was riding in trundled back into the station, Guillen’s daughter saw that her mother was “sitting with a vacant stare and her mouth open,” according to a lawsuit the family recently filed. Six Flags has not yet filed a response.
Guillen, who was visiting from Hawaii, managed to stumble off the ride, but a few minutes later park EMTs found her lying unconscious at the exit ramp. Two hours later, Gary Newman, the park’s vice president of maintenance, phoned CalOSHA to report the accident, relaying that a relative had said: “My cousin seemed out of it when she got off the ride so we took her to a bench and she went unconscious.”
The next morning, Scott Prather, a senior safety engineer with CalOSHA’s theme park unit, emailed his boss. According to a state official who has viewed the email, Guillen had been diagnosed with a brain bleed and was going into surgery. The email also said that the ride had been closed for inspection and g-force testing to ensure it was operating as intended.
Six Flags hired a firm that specialized in amusement park rides to conduct the test, according to a CalOSHA source familiar with the investigation.
State officials reviewed the results and authorized Magic Mountain to reopen the ride, the source said.
Then, on July 9, there was another incident, according to CalOSHA records reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. A woman from Nevada was visiting Magic Mountain with her family and others. They were roller coaster enthusiasts and had saved the X2 for their last ride of the day.
As soon as the ride started, the woman sensed something was wrong, according to an email she later sent to CalOSHA’s general inbox.
“The back of my head was repeatedly and forcefully slammed against the back of the seat,” she wrote in the email, which was reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. “I tried holding my head forward and tried pushing it back against the seat to stop the banging, neither worked.”
When the ride stopped, she wasn’t sure whether she could stand. She couldn’t turn her head from side to side. She had nausea, sensitivity to light and a headache that reached “approximately 9 out of 10.”
She wasn’t the only one. “Three of the eight people riding together experienced similar difficulty with their heads repeatedly striking the backs of their seats,” she wrote in August.
She also filed a formal complaint with Six Flags in July but has not received a response, she told ProPublica and L.A. Material.
Two days after the Nevada woman rode the X2, there was another, more serious injury.
Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, a healthy 25-year-old from Los Angeles, rode the X2 on the night of July 11.
According to a lawsuit her family filed in September against the park, Greer-Wilkinson came off the ride “confused and having difficulty walking.” She stumbled off and then lost consciousness. She has since had multiple emergency brain surgeries. The lawsuit says she “remains bedridden, ventilator dependent, unable to speak.” Six Flags has not responded to the lawsuit.
On July 12, the X2 was temporarily shut down. It has not reopened.
In the wake of the ride’s closure, many amusement park patrons are asking how regulators could have missed so many signs of danger.
California law requires CalOSHA to audit records related to every permanent ride each year, including reports of accidents. When amusement park patrons are seriously injured on rides, the theme park must notify regulators immediately.
And yet, again and again, records show, regulators accepted Six Flags’ assertions that the injuries people suffered were not the fault of the X2. ProPublica and L.A. Material reviewed the state’s reports on X2 riders who were taken to the hospital from 2009 to 2022. In more than two-thirds of the cases, or 17 out 23, CalOSHA checked “no” on the form that would determine whether an investigation was warranted.
In September 2022, less than three months after Hawley died, a 28-year-old woman passed out as she exited the ride and hit her head, according to Magic Mountain’s account of the accident in a report filed with the state Paramedics took her to Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital.
Two days after the woman’s injury, Park determined no investigation was necessary. Park wrote: “Patron has pre-existing TBI [traumatic brain injury], diabetes, and has not eaten or consumed anything throughout the day.”
The woman, who survived the incident, sued Six Flags, which denied fault. The case settled in 2025.
The pattern of regulators citing preexisting conditions or rider behavior went back years. In 2011, the state noted that a 21-year-old woman had “a history of panic attacks,” so no investigation of the ride was necessary after she complained of a head injury.
In 2016, a 49-year-old woman hit her head against the headrest and asked for an ambulance. CalOSHA noted that her condition “does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride,” adding that she “did not keep her head back” as riders are instructed.
Park declined to comment.
Some of the failures appear related to staffing shortages at CalOSHA. According to a 2025 staffing study by a Sacramento consulting firm commissioned by the state, audits of amusement park rides can be brief. The annual audit for a ride in X2’s class — a review meant to cover accident reports, training and maintenance reports and inspections — lasted an average of 3.7 hours.
The study also found that CalOSHA’s ride unit had been short-staffed for at least three years, with vacancies for its top job and two of four supervisor posts. There were “insufficient” supervisors for “thorough field supervision” and “inspection report review,” the report found.
Documents obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material show Park had voiced frustration about staffing for his division since at least 2019. In an email he sent last week to his supervisor and the state department that oversees CalOSHA, Park wrote: “We have done workload studies, classification studies, begged, pleaded, and warned of the impending doom, and we are still no further along than we were 11 years ago.”
He continued: “We have failed. I have tried to do this, but I cannot continue as the dwindling supply of tools has run out.”
Park had been the CalOSHA official who received the news of Christopher Gibson’s death from Nam, the homicide detective, in early July.
In late August, after the X2 had been closed for more than a month, the detective sent a follow-up email to Park about the teen’s death.
“I never heard back from you regarding my previous email,” Nam wrote. “I saw news about multiple injuries involving the X2 ride at the Six Flags. Is there anything else I need to do?”
Park finally wrote back: “Apologies, I thought we responded.”
Park told the detective that since Christopher had died in a hotel room, there was no way to confirm which roller coasters the teen had ridden and “it would be difficult to determine which ride to assign this to or if it even is associated with a ride.”
Still, a few weeks later, state officials ordered a more sophisticated g-force test of the ride, citing a series of injuries and a death over the summer. CalOSHA said in a statement that there are limits to commonly used ride testing. The standard test focuses on the torso and does not “necessarily establish the full range of movement or physical impacts experienced by an individual rider, including the potential effects on the head and neck,” the agency said. The order for new g-force testing didn’t mention anyone by name, but it did refer to an incident on June 3, the day Christopher left the park with a headache and eventually retreated to his hotel room’s closet, where he died.
The test results are pending.
Later in September, Six Flags announced the ride’s permanent shuttering without acknowledging the injuries or deaths connected with the roller coaster. “While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Magic Mountain president Brian Oerding said in a statement. “Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Two PhDs, Three Classes and One EBT Card: A CUNY Adjunct’s Struggle to Make Ends Meet
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Aisha Baiocchi
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
At 37, and with two PhDs, Juliana Nalerio relies on SNAP and Medicaid to get by while teaching as an adjunct professor at the City University of New York.
Nalerio is one of the 11,000 part-time faculty, some earning as little as $7,000 a course, who make the country’s biggest urban public university run.
She teaches one class in the History department at City College, and two English courses at Queens College. This semester, that’s 70 students across three classes. Between Harlem, Flushing and her home in Astoria, Nalerio spends eight hours each week on the commute alone.
GET THE CUNY SCOOP: Subscribe to our new weekly newsletter covering the City University of New York
“I keep telling myself that next year will be better, and if I keep teaching well, and trying to write, it will turn into something more stable,” she told The City Reporter.
In the last two decades, universities across the nation have become more reliant on non-tenure track part-time professors, mostly working on contracts that span less than a year. CUNY is no exception; in fact it is at least 10% ahead of the national average, with part-timers making up 52% of instructional staff.
Glenn Colby, a senior research officer with the American Association of University Professors said he’s observed a steady increase in contingent hires since the 2008 financial crisis, one that’s only continued through the COVID-19 pandemic and the Trump administration’s research budget cuts and attacks on universities.
“The driver of it all is institutions trying to deal with the uncertainty around finances, which is tied to student enrollment and state funding,” Colby said. “And as those issues fluctuate, institutions try to deal with it by saying, well, we’re gonna hire people on contingent appointments because we’re not certain about the future.”
The majority of adjuncts in the United States are highly educated and comparatively underpaid, according to a national study by the College and University Professional Association for Human Relations. Universities are most likely to use adjuncts to teach liberal arts, and nationally they are likely to hire women and minorities for adjunct positions at a much higher rate than full time.
“Adjunct faculty play an indispensable role at CUNY, enriching the educational experience of students through their teaching, expertise and dedication,” university press secretary Noah Gardy said in a statement. “Recognizing the vital role they play, our current labor contract with the PSC significantly increased compensation and continued investments in greater stability and access to health insurance.”
At CUNY, enrollment numbers are rising, but still haven’t passed pre-pandemic highs. Fundraising drives have been heralded as successful, but the university still has a massive $7 billion maintenance backlog as colleges endure floods, leaks and broken elevators.
Against that backdrop, adjunct professors make financial sense for cash-strapped universities. Part-time faculty can also include working professionals who bring on-the-ground experience into the classroom, a significant bonus for CUNY’s pre-professional programs and schools.
‘I Do Unpaid Labor’
But adjuncts like Nalerio may be left out by this model.
Last year, packing advanced degrees from Stanford University and the University of Salamanca in Spain, Nalerio made just $36,000. It is less than a third of what the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics says is the average annual income for someone with a doctorate.
According to the most recent Poverty Tracker report by the nonprofit advocacy group Robin Hood, Nalerio’s income puts her well within New York City’s “low income” range, experiencing similar material hardship to those living below the poverty line.
“My goal was never to make a lot of money. I spent a lot of time learning to teach, research and write. But now I’m presented with this problem: the work I’ve trained to do doesn’t line up with the reality of the work right now. So I can do unpaid labor, and hope it gets better, as I do, or leave it all together.”
While dividing her time between campuses in Flushing and Harlem might seem like a burden, this semester is actually easier than last semester, Nalerio says, because her classes in the two boroughs are stacked on different days. The Spring semester had her rushing from her morning Harlem course out to Flushing by the late afternoon, every Tuesday and Thursday, at the mercy of the 7 train and the weather.
Each of the three classes Nalerio teaches this semester is different, and she designs the coursework herself. She has an introductory women and gender studies class, a composition class for international students learning English, and a civilizations after 1500 class at City College, which she’s been teaching the longest.
Brutal University Math
The economics can be brutal. For each course, Nalerio is paid for three teaching hours, and one non-teaching hour, which includes time spent talking to students, grading, and course planning. According to this formula, Nalerio is working only 12 hours a week, with a full 28 hours left over to work other jobs and boost her income.
But that accounting is ludicrous, adjuncts say. Preparing course materials and grading student work takes far longer than an hour a week.
“If you have 70 students on two campuses it is literally impossible,” Nalerio said. She barely has time to eat between classes, much less find another part-time job.
Nalerio’s workload is determined by a union-negotiated contract: adjunct faculty can teach up to nine hours on one campus, and one additional section at another campus, which cannot exceed six hours. She teaches as many course hours as she can, always hoping to pick up more work to pay her bills — but is still working full-time while living on a part-time salary.
“My benefits are also dependent on my course load each semester,” she said, “but I don’t have time to keep track of the 75 students and the Tetris that they’re playing with my pay and my benefits and my life.”
Gardy, the spokesperson, said “CUNY adjunct pay remains highly competitive for a public university” and will be “nearly 75% above the national average” when a new contract goes into effect next summer.
Roommate Life
A full-time assistant professor at the City University teaching the same course load as Nalerio would earn a starting salary of at least $57,000, with generous health and retirement benefits.
Jasmine Bayron, a Hunter College adjunct with a PhD, said it isn’t uncommon for part-timers to struggle to find time for other jobs. Bayron has a number of side gigs, which she tries to set up a year in advance in case any of her courses falls through. Like Nalerio, she also has roommates.
“It’s kind of crazy to spend your entire life in school and then you can’t afford to live by yourself,” Bayron said.
MORE: Past Due – Why CUNY Adjuncts Can’t Get Paid On Time
Colby suggested universities underpay adjuncts because the job pool for contingent labor is so large and little attention is paid within higher education to working conditions for part-timers.
“It’s a challenge to get a full-time faculty position if you don’t have experience teaching and so one thing people do is say, ‘Well, I’ll do this so that I have it on my CV that I’m an experienced teacher.’ But then it becomes a permanent situation for a lot of people,” he said.
‘Their Education Matters’
Five years into adjuncting, Nalerio is still figuring out if it can be a permanent situation for her.
She started teaching at CUNY during her last semester at Stanford in 2022, and says she continued after receiving her PhD because she has New York roots and “drank the Kool Aid” of the university’s mission to serve working class students.
“These people are relying on me — they’re young people with lives,” Nalerio said. “Their education matters. It is an important step, and they’re really important. Serving them is a full-time job.”
Nalerio customizes courses to her students, this past week changing a lecture for her history course at Queens College to better include the large contingent of Latinos in the classroom and showing a documentary about white masculinity in her gender studies class after noticing the students seem disconnected from the original course material.
“I feel a sense of purpose doing it,” she said. “And I know I need more stability, but I love it, and I love the students.”
But Nalerio hasn’t found stability in years. Since coming to New York in 2022, she’s only been able to sublet since because her income is so low and inconsistent that she hasn’t qualified to rent an apartment in her own name.
MORE: ‘A Joke’ Missing State Aid Leaves CUNY Students Stressed
She can’t always afford to eat. She got a dog, for her mental health, and enrolled in SNAP to lift some of the stress off, but she’s still “just getting by.”
The CUPA-HR study found universities pay adjuncts the most in disciplines for which they use them the least, like engineering and architecture. Melissa Fuesting, the report’s co-author, pointed to high demand for graduates of engineering and other programs with direct career placement. A career path for liberal arts can be more difficult to find.
While representatives at CUNY’s Professional Staff Congress have suggested Nalerio apply for administrative jobs at the university, and she’s thought about leaving academia altogether, her heart is set on teaching. She loves ideas, her students, and the institution.
“It’s a one-sided affair,” she said. “Its very clear CUNY doesn’t love me back.”

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://taz.de/Album-The-Fork-and-Knife-.title: Album von Skepta: Er behandelt auch Klassenfragen
https://taz.de/Album-The-Fork-and-Knife-.author: Johann Voigt
https://taz.de/Album-The-Fork-and-Knife-.text:
Album von Skepta: Er behandelt auch Klassenfragen
Der Londoner Rapper Skepta reflektiert auf dem neuen Album „The Fork and Knife“ sein Älterwerden – und lässt die Jugend kreativ daran teilhaben.
„Oldhead“, „Unc“ und „Grandy“. Altern als Thema im Rap trägt viele oft respektlose Bezeichnungen. Die biologische Uhr ist frustrierend für die alte Garde und ermächtigend für die nachfolgenden Generationen. Wer will schon 50-Jährige als Speerspitze seiner Subkultur sehen, wenn man gerade dabei ist, gegen die Elterngeneration zu rebellieren? Und wie soll man beim Wettkampf um Coolness und Credibility mithalten, wenn die Haare grau und schütter werden und die Energie weniger?
„Kill your Idols“, man kennt’s. Gerade im HipHop werden die alten Helden einer nach dem anderen gekillt oder killen sich gleich selbst, siehe Kanye West und P. Diddy. Skepta aus London, der wichtigste Rapper Großbritanniens, einer der Innovatoren des Grime, weiß das natürlich alles, aber er begegnet diesem Prozess furchtlos.
Und so sieht seine Lage auch besser aus. Erkennbar am Verlauf einer langen Karriere und dem neuen Album „The Fork and Knife“, dessen Titel klingt wie der Name eines Pubs. Skepta ist inzwischen 44, alle britischen Rap-Generationen können sich auf ihn einigen.
Das Album
Skepta: „The Fork and Knife“ (Sony Music)
Das Beste, was Skepta in der Vergangenheit passieren konnte, war, dass er sich in den 2010ern an die Musikindustrie verkaufte, Pop sein wollte und krachend scheiterte. Sein Album „Doin It Again“ war ein grausames und seelenloses Pop-Rap-Konglomerat. Skepta, der mit der Musik von Londoner Piratenradios zwischen Dancefloor und Rap sozialisiert wurde und mit Grime eine kaputte, von Subbässen, 2-Step und doppelt beschleunigten Battle-Lyrics geprägte Musik voranbrachte, merkte es selber.
Radikale Entschuldigung
Der Künstler pausierte, atmete durch und veröffentlichte 2014 mit „That’s not me“ eine radikale Entschuldigung. Darin beerdigte Skepta seine Pop-Persona, „Put it all in the bin“, wie er es selbst formulierte. Und so inszenierte er auch gleich seine Wiederauferstehung.
Interessant ist, dass Skepta zwar mittlerweile auch bei der Fashion Week auftaucht, den Mercury Prize abstaubt, Hits produziert, dabei aber immer so handelt, als ginge es in irgendeiner Londoner Keller-Klitsche um alles! Underground ist bei Skepta habituell verankert. Das ist keine Behauptung. 2024 fragte er, vermutlich an sein eigenes Scheitern im Pop erinnert, wütend bei X: „Ist das Konzept einer organischen Underground-Szene tot?“
Wieder hatten sich die Vorzeichen geändert, wurden Idols gekillt und UK-Rap plötzlich dominiert von einer sehr digital orientierten Generation von Künstlern, die ihre Sounds wild zusammenmixt. Cloud Rap aus Schweden, Soundcloud-Nischen, UK-Bassmusik, alles in einen Topf und zehnmal püriert. Dass sich junge Künstler wie Fakemink und EsDeeKid von Skepta keine Absolution erteilen ließen, sondern einfach loslegten, kränkte den Alten womöglich. Dass die neue Grime-Generation um Leute wie Kido noch ein bisschen rabiater rappt als er, weckte den Konkurrenzkampf.
Und was macht Skepta? Er mischt sich beim in Großbritannien viel beachteten Freestyle-Format „Victory Lap“ unter einen Haufen Twentysomethings und rappt mit. Er beging also nicht den Fehler, alles Neue abzuwerten, sondern begann, mit der jungen Generation zusammenzuarbeiten. Ehre gerettet, Underground connected.
Alle hören genau zu
Womit wir bei Skeptas neuem Album sind, dessen Produktion sieben Jahre gedauert hat. Wahrscheinlich auch, weil darauf viele innere Konflikte ausgetragen werden: Credibility vs. Familienleben, Konkurrenzdenken vs. den Willen, es ruhiger angehen zu lassen. Oder anders gesagt: Was für ein Album will ich machen, wenn mir die komplette UK-Rapszene zuhört und die Eltern der Freund:innen meiner Kinder?
Mit „The Fork and Knife“ lotet er die Gemengelage detailgetreu aus. „Secrets of Patriarchy“ hinterfragt gleich am Anfang den Drang, sich beweisen zu wollen und Härte zu zeigen. Also auch patriarchale Muster, die er verinnerlicht hat und auf diesem Album reflektiert. Hier wird zwar gebattelt, aber hier werden weder Frauen degradiert, noch wird jemand abgestochen, wie es im Vorstellungswelten des UK-Rap in den letzten Jahren der Fall war, aber auch in den realen Gangwars der britischen Großstädte.
Skepta rollt in den Songs des Albums noch mal seine Geschichte auf, erzählt, wie er sich durchgebissen hat, von seinen Eltern, die aus Nigeria nach England migrierten und das Beste für ihn wollten. Von den Londoner Straßen, auf denen er Freunde an Drogen verlor und die Polizei ihn auf dem Kieker hatte. „The Fork and Knife“ verhandelt also Klassenfragen und erzählt zum Glück keine geschönte Aufsteigergeschichte, wie es sie im Rap so oft gab.
Skepta weiß, dass er Glück gehabt hat. Er weiß aber auch, dass er sehr gut in dem ist, was er macht. Und dass er die Möglichkeit hat, Leute mitzuziehen. Auch dafür steht dieses Album. Westafrikanische Musiker wie Asake treffen sich mit Skepta auf Afrohouse-Beats und die junge Grime-Garde wird auf dem knapp neunminütigen „Belly“ mit den Älteren vereint. Es geht um die Sache. Heißt: Rap in Verbindung mit Bass-Musik, Sounds aus Westafrika und den Nischen des Internets. Eine zeitlose Mischung. Alter – das spielt hier keine Rolle.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/m.title: Mayor Mamdani Mulls Motor Vehicles In Central Park
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/m.author: Sophia Lebowitz
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/17/m.text:
Prior versions of these "horseless" carriages (left) were really big compared to pedicabs. File art
He’s putting the electric carriage before the horse. Or, more accurately, after.
Having approved the end of horse carriage rides in Central Park, Mayor Mamdani now says he will study the feasibility of replacing those throwback rides with electric tourism vehicles — ostensibly restoring cars to the idyllic car-free roadway inside the world’s most famous park.
The news came as part of an announcement on Tuesday that outlined his administration’s plan to support horse-carriage workers, whose industry is being phased out by 2028. The announcement was thin on details, but said the administration would “commission a feasibility study examining electric carriages and electric pedal-assist bicycles as potential alternatives within Central Park, as well as electric carriages along the park’s perimeter.”
Advocates — especially those who had spent decades trying to get cars out of the park — were stunned.
“This is just crazy, it’s really sad to think that Mamdani would be supporting reintroducing motor vehicles into Central Park,” said Ken Coughlin, who led the fight. “I don’t want to have to spend another 26 years trying to get them out.”
And Upper West side Council Member Gale Brewer agreed, adding that the idea would “open the door to a whole new fleet of commercial electric vehicles.”
“The Central Park Conservancy, Transportation Alternatives, New Yorkers for Parks, the pedestrian safety community, and the overwhelming majority of New Yorkers who use the park every day are united against swapping one safety risk for another by introducing large electric vehicles into a park that is predominantly pedestrian,” she said.
After the mayor’s statement was released, the Central Park Conservancy also quickly warned that the cars would “return [the park] to a more dangerous past.”
“Adding heavy electric vehicles to Central Park that cater almost exclusively to tourists would come at the expense of the regular New Yorkers who run, walk, bike, and stroll through it — and who worked for decades to get cars out of the Park,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe the better solution is a reformed, well-regulated year-round pedicab fleet. There are bills before the City Council right now that would do just that.”
The idea to replace horse-drawn carriages with carriage-looking vehicles is not new. When the City Council voted to enact the horse carriage ban, Council Member Vickie Paladino (R-College Point) rallied in front of City Hall to push for the “timeless” carriage-like cars. Paladino even sent her Council colleagues a 10-page slide deck to convince them on the feasibility of deploying the Disney-esque cars.
“We envision bringing that same timeless appeal to Central Park through a fleet of 68 elegant, vintage-style electric [low-speed vehicles], operated by professionally trained drivers wearing tailored, period-inspired uniforms,” said Paladino’s presentation, which was first reported by Hell Gate.
Last month, Streetsblog reminded would-be Paladinos that a proposal to bring the electric cars to the park has been around since Bill de Blasio got elected in 2013 with some big help from well-financed horse carriage opponents.
At the time, those foes rolled out — literally — their vision for a post-horse world: an electric buggy that looked like a Model T on lasix:
Cars were banned from the Central Park Drive in 2018 after a long campaign by cyclists and street safety advocates. Coughlin, who led the charge then and still advocates for a safe park, said adding these electric carriages would be a “foot in the door” to let all vehicles back in.
This is a breaking story. We reached out to City Hall for comment and will update if we hear back.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.title: Extremwetterfolgen | Die unsichtbaren Opfer der Klimakrise
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.author: Joachim Wille
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Extremwetterfolgen
Die unsichtbaren Opfer der Klimakrise
Ein neuer Index von Germanwatch zeigt das Ausmaß der Wetterkatastrophen weltweit: über 916.000 Tote und Schäden von 4,7 Billionen Dollar in 30 Jahren.
Wenn ein Hurrikan Häuser zerstört oder eine Flut ganze Ortschaften verwüstet, gehen die Bilder um die Welt. Die tödlichste Wettergefahr bleibt dagegen oft unsichtbar: extreme Hitze. Allein im vergangenen Jahr wurden weltweit mehr als 24.000 Todesfälle durch Hitzewellen registriert. Das waren fast 70 Prozent aller erfassten Todesopfer durch Wetterextreme. Die tatsächliche Zahl dürfte noch um ein Vielfaches höher liegen, denn viele Todesfälle infolge extremer Temperaturen werden in der Katastrophenstatistik nicht erfasst.
Das ist eine zentrale Erkenntnis aus dem »Klima-Risiko-Index«, den die Umwelt- und Entwicklungsorganisation Germanwatch am Dienstag anlässlich des UN-Klimagipfels COP 31 im türkischen Antalya vorstellte. Von 1996 bis 2025 wurden demnach weltweit fast 10.000 schwere Wetterextreme registriert.
Sie kosteten mehr als 916.000 Menschen das Leben und verursachten direkte wirtschaftliche Schäden von inflationsbereinigt 4,7 Billionen US‑Dollar. Weltweit gezählt wurden rund 5,5 Milliarden Betroffene, also zum Beispiel Menschen, die durch Wetterextreme obdachlos wurden oder ihre Heimat verlassen mussten. 
Für 2025 verzeichnet Germanwatch weltweit 367 schwere Wetterereignisse mit fast 35.000 Toten und mehr als 158 Milliarden Dollar Schäden. Das Jahresranking wird von Jamaika angeführt – in dem Karibikstaat richtete Hurrikan »Melissa« mit Windgeschwindigkeiten von mehr als 300 Kilometern pro Stunde extreme Verwüstungen an. Auf Platz zwei folgt Sri Lanka nach schweren Überschwemmungen durch Zyklon »Ditwah«.
Hitze sorgt für die meisten Toten, Stürme für Schäden
In der 30-Jahre-Gesamtschau entfielen laut dem Index weltweit rund 40 Prozent der registrierten Todesfälle auf Hitzewellen. Stürme verursachten dagegen 58 Prozent der wirtschaftlichen Schäden.
Germanwatch greift für seinen Bericht auf Zahlen aus der internationalen Katastrophendatenbank EM‑DAT zurück, sowohl absolut als auch im Verhältnis zu Bevölkerung und Wirtschaftsleistung. Der Index zeigt allerdings nicht, welcher Anteil der Katastrophen dem Klimawandel zuzuschreiben ist. Einzelne Wetterereignisse lassen sich zwar nicht pauschal dem Klimawandel zuschreiben, doch die menschengemachte Erwärmung erhöht nach Erkenntnissen der Klimaforschung die Häufigkeit und Intensität vieler Extreme, besonders von Hitzewellen und Starkregen. Wärmere Luft kann mehr Wasserdampf aufnehmen, was Niederschläge verstärkt. Wärmere Meere können mehr und stärkere Wirbelstürme verstärken.
An der Spitze der relativen Schäden durch Extremwetter steht in der 30-Jahre-Bilanz Dominica. Dort richtete Hurrikan »Maria« im Jahr 2017 Schäden von 1,9 Milliarden Dollar an, was fast dem Dreifachen der damaligen jährlichen Wirtschaftsleistung des kleinen Karibikstaates entsprach. Auf Rang zwei folgt Myanmar, wo Zyklon »Nargis« 2008 fast 140.000 Menschen tötete. Honduras auf Platz drei wurde 1998 von Hurrikan »Mitch« verwüstet, der mehr als 14.000 Todesopfer forderte.
Entscheidend ist auch die Verwundbarkeit: Arme Staaten können Zerstörungen schwerer bewältigen als reiche. »Unter den zehn am massivsten getroffenen Staaten der vergangenen 30 Jahre ist in unserem Index mit den Bahamas nur ein einziges reicheres Land«, sagt Germanwatch-Mitautor David Eckstein.
Allein Indien erlebte 436 Wetterextreme mit 78.000 Todesopfern. Auf den Philippinen waren es 373 Ereignisse. Und es zeigt sich: Manche Länder werden wieder getroffen, noch bevor der Wiederaufbau abgeschlossen ist.
Auch Europa wird stark in Mitleidenschaft gezogen. Italien, Frankreich, Griechenland und Spanien finden sich unter den 20 am stärksten betroffenen Ländern des Langfrist-Indexes. Spanien steht im Jahresranking für 2025 sogar auf Platz drei: Fast 3900 Menschen starben dort während der extremen Hitzeperiode von April bis September.
Deutschland auf Rang 34
»Dieses Jahr hat uns auch hier in Deutschland erneut vor Augen geführt, was für eine tödliche Gefahr Hitzewellen sind, die durch die Klimakrise immer häufiger und extremer werden«, sagte Germanwatch-Expertin Laura Schäfer. Insgesamt liegt die Bundesrepublik im 30-Jahre-Index auf Rang 34, für 2025 auf Platz 48. Mehr als 33.000 Menschen starben hierzulande seit 1996 infolge von Wetterextremen. Die direkten Schäden summierten sich auf inflationsbereinigt 133 Milliarden Dollar. Folgekosten, etwa durch Produktionsausfälle, sind nicht enthalten. Die Ahrtal-Flut 2021 zeigte die Grenzen des Katastrophenschutzes selbst in einem wohlhabenden Land.
Der Index liefert Argumente für die aktuellen Verhandlungen auf dem Klimagipfel in Antalya. Neben schnellerem Klimaschutz geht es um Geld für Anpassung und den Umgang mit unvermeidbaren Verlusten. Nach dem jüngsten Bericht des UN-Umweltprogramms benötigen Entwicklungsländer bis 2035 jährlich rund 305 Milliarden US-Dollar für Anpassungsmaßnahmen. Die internationale Unterstützung liegt weit darunter. Das verschärft die Konflikte zwischen Industrie- und Entwicklungsländern.
»Die Hauptverursacher der Klimakrise müssen endlich ihren fairen Beitrag für Anpassung und den Umgang mit Verlusten und Schäden leisten«, sagt Germanwatch-Mitautorin Lisa Schultheiß. Die Organisation fordert, auch fossile Energiekonzerne stärker in die Pflicht zu nehmen. Und es sei notwendig, Deutschlands internationale Klimafinanzierung aus dem Bundesetat bis 2030 auf zwölf Milliarden Euro jährlich mehr als zu verdoppeln.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.
