https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Hassan Herzallah
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
The Second Life of Gaza’s Rubble
The Strip is buried under 61 million tons of rubble. Some people are finding creative ways to use it as a resource.
In mid-October, as the weather began to change, rain fell on the displacement camp where I live in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, in southern Gaza. When I woke up that morning, our tent seemed more fragile than ever. The tarpaulin that shielded us from the rain and wind was old, worn, and torn, and water had seeped into the small kitchen beside our tent. There were still no signs of new tents arriving, reconstruction getting underway, or any recovery plans. It looked like we were in for another winter of rain and cold in a deteriorating tent.
Later that day, on my way to a café near our camp to charge my phone, I saw Abu Omar beside his tent, using a hand-operated machine to straighten iron bars. At 50, Abu Omar had spent most of his life working as a blacksmith. But he was now forced to put his profession to a different use.
As displacement continued and ready-made tents became unaffordable, Abu Omar turned his blacksmithing skills into a way to support his family. Through his connections with scrap dealers, he began buying iron salvaged from destroyed buildings, straightening it and selling it on. He also made complete tents from iron bars and tarpaulins, along with beds, tables, and other items needed by families in the camp.
His work sometimes took him directly to families, where he assembled shelters using the straightened iron. He charged what people could afford. “I don’t pressure people,” he said. “Everyone has their own circumstances, and in the end, we are all displaced.”
Three years into Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza, more than 370,000 housing units have been destroyed by Israeli attacks. But the rubble left behind is no longer merely a symbol of devastation. For many displaced people, it has become a resource.
Some sift through the ruins for iron, wood, and aluminum to sell and earn money for daily necessities. Others reuse these materials to repair tents and make furniture. Then there are those seeking to turn the rubble into building blocks that could be used to construct temporary shelters for displaced families.
“We left with nothing and had to start from scratch,” Abu Omar told me. He salvaged iron bars from the roof of his destroyed home and used them to build a tent for his family. When they were forced to flee again, he took the iron with him, never imagining that it would one day become his only source of income.
Abu Omar’s 20-year-old son, Omar, works alongside his father. He had hoped to continue his education, but Israel’s decimation of Gaza’s schools and universities made that impossible.
Omar explained how iron is salvaged from the rubble, straightened, and reused. First, workers extract iron bars from the ruins of destroyed buildings and sell them to scrap dealers. The dealers then straighten the bent bars using specialized hand-operated machines before selling them to people who need them. (The materials are not cheap; everything has become expensive for people in Gaza given the circumstances we are living in. Even a small iron-framed tent measuring three by three meters can cost around $300.)
The iron is used not only to build tent frames but also to make other items for displaced families. “Beds, kitchens, tables, and everything,” Omar said, listing the many things that can be made from salvaged iron and put to use again.
But the iron that reaches Abu Omar is far from ready to use. Before he can straighten the bars and turn them into tent frames, other workers have already spent hours, sometimes days, breaking apart concrete to extract the iron from the rubble.
Mahmoud al-Mughayir, 21, is in his second year of university. His father, Saleh al-Mughayir, was known in Rafah for his work as a carpenter. But the genocide disrupted his father’s work, leaving the family struggling to meet its basic needs. Mahmoud needed a laptop to continue his studies, but buying one was beyond the family’s means. He found himself breaking up concrete to earn enough money to pay for his education and buy a laptop. “I never thought I would work in this line of work, but the circumstances I’m living through pushed me into it,” he said.
Badr Abu Ansa, 28, from Khan Younis, works alongside a group of men breaking up concrete and salvaging materials from destroyed buildings to sell. The process begins when a scrap dealer arranges with the owner of a destroyed house for the group to work at the site. Badr and the other men then break up the concrete and retrieve iron bars, aluminum, tiles, and wood. They hand over what they collect to the dealer in exchange for a daily wage—around 17 to 20 dollars per day.
The work demands more than physical strength. The men lack proper protective equipment and work amid thick clouds of dust as they break up concrete with sledgehammers. When the dust becomes so dense that it is difficult to breathe, some cover their faces with pieces of cloth in an attempt to protect themselves. They also suffer cuts and other injuries while breaking up concrete.
Badr told me that what he earns each day barely covers his basic needs. “After working for 10 hours [one day], I got injured and had to buy medicine. More than half of what I earned that day went on it,” he said.
Badr has two children, but the exhaustion from his long work leaves him with little time to spend with them.
Gaza is buried under an estimated 61 million tons of rubble, while Israeli restrictions on the entry of construction materials, particularly cement, continue to hinder reconstruction. With the need to rebuild far greater than the available supply of building materials, Suleiman Abu Hassanein is trying to find another use for the rubble itself.

Suleiman told me he began developing machines to produce interlocking building blocks in 2021. “The idea came from a need in the community,” he said. His project, Green Rock, turns rubble from destroyed buildings into building blocks resembling Lego bricks. The blocks can be fitted together without the cement used in the whole process. Unlike traditional building blocks, these blocks are made mainly from recycled rubble. Their design allows them to fit and lock together like Lego bricks, without needing cement to join them.
The project aims to reuse material from destroyed buildings, and, according to Suleiman, a comparison conducted by his team between conventional construction and building with these blocks suggests that the overall cost of construction could be negligible. “We found that we could reduce total construction costs by 60 percent,” he told me.
With Gaza’s labor market in collapse and unemployment reaching 78 percent in 2025, Suleiman sees the project as more than a way to produce alternative building materials. He also hopes it will create jobs for displaced people. By crushing, sorting, and recycling rubble, then producing the blocks and using them to build, he aims to create a local economic cycle. It would also give displaced people a chance to help build the shelters they need.
Still, his idea requires funding. Suleiman told me that his team had made significant progress in developing the blocks, and that the samples and designs were ready. However, they still need financial support. He hopes this funding will allow the project to move beyond small-scale experiments and become a practical approach that can be tested and used to provide shelters for displaced families.
The iron bars did not bring Abu Omar’s home back, but they gave him a shelter he built with his own hands, and while Mahmoud and Badr continue working among the rubble to meet their daily needs, Suleiman is trying to turn it into building materials. Their approaches differ, but all are finding ways to survive amid the Israeli destruction that cost them their homes and livelihoods, hoping that what the war left behind can help them get through today and rebuild tomorrow.

https://citylimits.org/citys-shops-bodeg.title: City’s Shops, Bodegas Get 90 More Days to Meet Federal SNAP Requirements
https://citylimits.org/citys-shops-bodeg.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/citys-shops-bodeg.text:
Share This Article
SNAP purchases account for an estimated 15 to 20 percent of a typical New York City store’s sales, according to the mayor’s office, citing figures from groups representing local bodegas. Some Bronx store owners reported figures as high as 30 percent, officials said.
New York City bodegas and small grocery stores have been given an additional 90 days to comply with stricter federal food stocking requirements, following concerns that neighborhood businesses could lose their ability to accept food stamps.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) agreed to delay enforcement until February 2027, following negotiations between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Trump administration, according to a Friday announcement from City Hall.
The new rules, originally scheduled to take effect Nov. 4, require retailers participating in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) to stock at least seven varieties of food in each of four categories: dairy, grains, proteins, and fruits and vegetables. Previously, stores were required to carry three varieties per category.
The requirements are intended to improve access to nutritious foods for SNAP recipients. But smaller neighborhood stores with limited shelf space, refrigeration and financial resources could face difficulties purchasing additional inventory or finding suppliers, city officials said.
SNAP purchases account for an estimated 15 to 20 percent of a typical New York City store’s sales, according to the mayor’s office, citing figures from groups representing local bodegas. Some Bronx store owners reported figures as high as 30 percent, officials said.
The USDA didn’t release guidance about the new requirements until Sept. 4, leaving retailers approximately two months to prepare. Business owners raised concerns about the limited timeline and uncertainty over which products would qualify.
“Bodega owners keep asking us the same questions: which products count, where to buy them, and where to put them,” said Small Business Services Commissioner Kenny Minaya in a statement Friday.
At Finest Deli Inc., near East 126th Street and Madison Avenue in Harlem, Sami, 27, the store manager, said the business was already prepared for the expanded requirements, with ample space to stock a variety of food products.
“It’s a big store, they sell out things quickly,” Sami said.
He said he isn’t particularly concerned about the SNAP changes, explaining that much of the deli’s clientele consists of teachers, professors, high school students and college students from nearby schools.
Representatives from the city’s Department of Small Business Services also visited the deli Friday, Nov. 13, according to Sami.
“They came inside, looked around the store and took pictures of individual food items,” he said, referring to the four staple food categories covered by the new federal requirements: proteins, dairy, grains, and produce.
The extension comes as New Yorkers face broader challenges accessing affordable food.
A report released Monday by Robin Hood and Columbia University’s Center on Poverty and Social Policy found that nearly 1.3 million New Yorkers, roughly 15 percent of the city’s population, relied on food pantries or other free food providers in 2025.
The report also found that nearly a third of New Yorkers experienced food hardship, meaning they sometimes or often ran out of food or worried about running out before they could afford more. More than half of pantry users worked or lived with a working spouse or partner.
The findings reflect conditions before the full impact of recent federal SNAP cuts and new work rules, and do not measure the effects of the new retailer requirements.
For SNAP recipients, losing access to neighborhood retailers could mean traveling farther to purchase groceries, particularly in communities with limited supermarket options, city officials said.
“In neighborhoods like Corona and East Elmhurst, bodegas are more than small businesses. They are lifelines for working families, seniors, and neighbors who depend on them to put food on the table,” said Councilmember Shanel Thomas Henry, chair of the City Council’s Committee on Small Business.
The city plans to coordinate with federal officials and local agencies to help store owners understand the requirements, while Small Business Services will offer free compliance assistance.
The extension provides additional preparation time, but retailers must still meet the expanded standards when enforcement begins in February.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.title: Louis Vuitton Launches Three Fragrances as Part of Expansive Keith Haring Collection
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.author: Andy Battaglia
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/lo.text:
As part of an expansive collection set to include ready-to-wear fashion, accessories, and a recently touted line of limited-edition Artycapucines handbags, Louis Vuitton announced three new fragrances inspired by the art and life of the late Keith Haring.
“Three fragrances, three ways to let the imagination speak,” reads a somewhat cryptic press release.
A scent named Attrape-Rêves is described as “a radiant, optimistic fragrance that carries the promise embodied by the ‘radiant baby,’ Keith Haring’s emblem.” In another scent named Imagination, “the artist’s celebrated characters come alive through the glass of the bottle and its case. They carry the idea that everyone holds an infinite field of possibilities within, and they also appear on the matching travel case in coated Monogram canvas.”
The final fragrance, Ombre Nomade, is characterized as “a golden labyrinth, with no beginning or end, its lines echoing the swirls of oud wood.” (There’s nary a mention of the smells of a graffiti-strewn 1980s–era subway station, as one might expect.)
The fragrances will be up for sale at Louis Vuitton stores starting January 1, when the rest of the fashion house’s Keith Haring line is made available. The line was inspired in part by a garment case on which Haring painted his radiant baby decades before Nicolas Ghesquière, Louis Vuitton’s artistic director of women’s collections, included it in his Cruise 2027 Show staged at the Frick Collection in New York, as part of a three-year partnership between the brand and the museum.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/van-.title: Chris Van Hollen’s Evolution on Israel and Palestine
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/van-.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/van-.text:
When Chris Van Hollen first ran for Senate in 2016, he was considered the pro-Israel, Democratic establishment pick with the backing of AIPAC-aligned donors. He was a U.S. representative who regularly voted to approve military aid to Israel; his opponent, Rep. Donna Edwards, was an outspoken critic of the Israeli government and the pro-Israel lobby. He outspent her 3 to 1 and won the Maryland Democratic primary by about 130,000 votes.
A decade later, Van Hollen has evolved into one of the harshest critics of Israel in the Senate. He’s staked his criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and apartheid rule of Palestinians as a key argument behind his run against staunch Israel-defending Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate majority leader.
Politicians often update their stances with the times, leaving voters to sort out what’s a genuine change of heart and what’s opportunism. In Van Hollen’s case, advocates for Palestine who seek to end U.S. military support for Israel told The Intercept that his evolution is a sign that he can be pushed by public pressure.
“Before this evolution, Van Hollen had looked a lot more like a mainstream Democrat on Israel,” said Yousef Munayyer, a senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington D.C. and a longtime advocate for Palestinian rights. “Times have changed in a lot of ways, where the Democratic base has changed in a lot of ways, and he has changed along with it — I don’t know that the same can be said for a lot of other folks, like Chuck Schumer.”
Van Hollen was elected to the House in 2002, in the feverish early years of the war on terror, and joined the vast majority of his colleagues from both parties in unconditionally supporting arms transfers to Israel. In 2010 and 2012, he co-sponsored the initial round of funding for U.S. support of Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense systems and called for additional cooperation between Israel and the Pentagon for weapons development, such as enhancing Israel’s F-35 fighter jet program. In 2016, the year he was elected to the Senate, he co-sponsored a House resolution affirming a 10-year memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Israel to continue providing State Department funds for Israel to buy weapons. The MOU, inked by President Barack Obama, was widely seen by observers as a concession to Israel to alleviate pressure over his Iran nuclear agreement — which Van Hollen supported and Schumer famously opposed.
Van Hollen’s Maryland House district had a large pro-Israel voter base, Munayyer pointed out, and some of his pro-Israel stances may have been the product of being responsive to his constituents. But in the Senate, Van Hollen continued to support Israel, backing a 2018 bill that authorized extending military aid to the country until at least 2028, as well as guarantees to loans and access to U.S. military stockpiles until 2023.
His most notable shift has followed the October 7, 2023, attacks. While that year, Van Hollen supported a resolution that “reaffirms Israel’s right to self-defense” and promised military equipment resupply, he has since co-sponsored resolutions and bills that invoked the use of Biden-era sanctions against Israeli settlers in the West Bank, voted several times to block the sale of some weapons to Israel, and is leading an effort to strip a Pentagon spending bill of its provisions that more closely tie the U.S. and Israeli militaries. He also introduced a resolution demanding a State Department report on Israeli detention of Palestinian children and Israeli military and settler killings of American citizens in the West Bank.
Margaret DeReus, executive director of the pro-Palestine lobbying group Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which collaborated with Van Hollen on the recent State Department resolution, said she is supporting his run for majority leader, arguing that he would help rein in some of the least popular excesses of the Trump administration.
“Senate Democrats should be led by a Majority Leader who is committed to fighting the Trump Administration on the Iran war, stopping the lawless ICE raids on American cities, and ending US aid to Israel,” she told The Intercept in a statement. “Senator Van Hollen is a leader in the Senate for enforcing US laws around military assistance to countries committing human rights violations, including in Palestine and Sudan, and for ending this illegal war.”
And unlike Schumer, Van Hollen’s past support for Israel was not unequivocal.
During Israel’s war on Lebanon in 2006, he wrote a letter to then-Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice criticizing the Bush administration’s decision not to push for an end to Israel’s bombing of civilians, which drew backlash from supporters of Israel. In 2019, Van Hollen took to the Senate floor to blast then-Sen. Marco Rubio’s bill to crack down on the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement in the U.S., saying he disagreed with the boycott but wanted to uphold constitutional rights. The following year, he gave a floor speech to oppose Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s plan to unilaterally annex parts of the West Bank, and he introduced a 2021 Pentagon-spending amendment that would have prohibited Israel from using U.S. aid for its annexation efforts. After Israeli forces killed Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, he pushed the Biden administration to seek accountability.
This marks a contrast with Schumer, DeReus said. She said the current minority leader has a “long record of paving the way for this disastrous war [on Iran] as the only current Senate Democrat who voted against Obama’s JCPOA,” which placed agreed-upon restraints on Iran’s nuclear development. And he has continued to support military assistance to Israel.
During recent resolutions to block sales of certain weapons to Israel, Schumer was among the minority of Senate Democrats who voted against it.
Schumer and Van Hollen’s offices did not respond to The Intercept’s requests for comment.
On a press tour over the weekend after announcing his run for the leadership position, Van Hollen differentiated himself from Schumer on Israel and Palestine, criticizing Schumer for siding with the pro-Israel lobby against progressive Senate candidates in the Democratic midterm primaries and speaking against “a blank check” to the Israeli government.
“We’re seeing violent settlers push Palestinians off their land with the complicity of the Israeli government,” Van Hollen said Sunday on Fox News. “I don’t think American taxpayer dollars should be going to that purpose.”
While Van Hollen’s strong stand against Israel appears to be, in part, motivated by personal moral conviction and a desire to “look yourself in the mirror at the end of the day,” whether or not he continues to push for Palestinian rights if elected leader will depend on how much Palestine remains a litmus test in the Democratic Party, said Tariq Kenney-Shawa, an associate fellow at Palestinian think tank Al-Shabaka.
“I really think it’ll come down to whether and how [Van Hollen] continues to be pressured by the movement and the Democratic base,” Kenney-Shawa said.
Munayyer also credits the gains made in Congress to a global organizing movement against Israel’s genocide and apartheid rule, which he said has made the issue into something beyond even Palestine and Israel.
“It’s seen as a proxy for authenticity,” he said. “And if you say that you’re going to do something on this issue, then you back away from it, it looks like you just don’t have the integrity to do the things that you need to do.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Cecilia Nowell
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.
Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.
“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.
The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.
The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.
“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.
Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Viamão: Justiça dá liminar e suspende projeto do Executivo que permitia a venda de débitos dos contribuintes para bancos, inclusive IPTU
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Eugênio Bortolon
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Por decisão do Juiz Cláudio Edel Fagundes foi suspenso liminarmente os efeitos da votação em regime de urgência do Projeto de Lei Projeto de Lei nº 138/2026 pela Câmara de Vereadores de Viamão na terça-feira (10), texto que autorizava a prefeitura a “vender” créditos da dívida ativa municipal (como IPTU, outros tributos e taxas atrasadas) para bancos, fundos e financeiras, em troca de antecipação de receita.
Com a decisão, estão congelados os prazos de sanção pelo Executivo Municipal, veto ou promulgação até o julgamento do mérito. A promulgação implicaria até na perda de bens dos devedores e a inscrição em órgãos de defesa do consumidor, tipo Serasa e SPC.
A decisão do Poder Judiciário foi tomada atendendo mandado de segurança do vereador Diego Petry (Podemos), presidente da Comissão de Orçamento. Ele diz que a presidente da Câmara, Michele Silva (PSDB) atropelou o processo legal na sessão de cinco de novembro, dia em que foi votado o projeto. Na ocasião, Petry teve o pedido regimental de vista por 24 horas negado pela presidência, que alegou a sobreposição dos prazos de urgência da Lei Orgânica sobre o regimento interno da Câmara e colocou a matéria em votação.
Além do cerceamento ao debate, a oposição questiona o quórum da aprovação. Por se tratar de alienação de patrimônio público, os parlamentares argumentam que o projeto exigia maioria qualificada de dois terços (14 votos), mas foi aprovado por maioria simples. A Câmara tem 21 representantes.
Como é o projeto
O projeto autoriza o município a promover a cessão onerosa de direitos creditórios originados de créditos tributários e não tributários, inclusive aqueles inscritos em dívida ativa. Na prática, a proposta permite que o município negocie com instituições privadas ou fundos de investimento o direito de receber valores devidos à administração municipal. Em contrapartida, o município recebe recursos financeiros pela cessão desses direitos, conforme as condições estabelecidas em cada operação.
O projeto abrange créditos já constituídos e reconhecidos pelos devedores ou contribuintes, podendo incluir valores parcelados, vencidos ou em cobrança judicial e extrajudicial. A proposta não permite, entretanto, a transferência de expectativas de arrecadação ou de créditos ainda não constituídos.
Destinação dos recursos
Um dos principais pontos do projeto estabelece a destinação dos valores obtidos com as operações. Conforme o texto aprovado, e suspenso atualmente, pelo menos 50% dos recursos deverão ser aplicados em despesas associadas ao Regime Próprio de Previdência Social (RPPS). O restante deverá ser destinado a despesas com investimentos. A gestão financeira e contábil dos recursos ficará sob responsabilidade da Secretaria Municipal da Fazenda, com controles específicos para identificação e acompanhamento das movimentações.
O texto estabelece que a cessão dos direitos creditórios não altera a obrigação dos contribuintes nem modifica as condições originais dos débitos, como valores principais, juros, multas, prazos e critérios de atualização, conforme informa a assessoria de imprensa da Câmara.
A cobrança judicial e extrajudicial também permanecerá sob responsabilidade dos órgãos municipais competentes. Assim, a instituição que adquirir os direitos não poderá substituir o município na cobrança nem determinar os procedimentos administrativos ou judiciais.
Outro ponto previsto é que o município não poderá garantir o pagamento dos créditos cedidos, assumir a inadimplência dos devedores ou se comprometer a recomprar valores que eventualmente não sejam recuperados. O risco econômico da operação ficará com o adquirente dos direitos creditórios.
Operações dependerão de estudos e fiscalização
O projeto determina que cada operação seja precedida de estudos técnicos, econômicos, financeiros e jurídicos que demonstrem o interesse público e a vantagem econômica para o município.
Também deverá ser justificado o percentual de deságio aplicado na negociação, além da avaliação da expectativa de recuperação dos créditos e dos impactos orçamentários, financeiros e patrimoniais. A proposta prevê ainda a criação de um Conselho Gestor, composto por representantes das secretarias municipais da Fazenda e da Administração, da Procuradoria-Geral do Município, da Contabilidade e por dois fiscais tributários.
Entre as atribuições do colegiado estão acompanhar a gestão financeira das operações, fiscalizar a execução dos contratos, analisar prestações de contas e elaborar relatórios anuais sobre os recursos recebidos e sua destinação.
O Projeto de Lei nº 138/2026 foi encaminhado pelo prefeito Rafael Bortoletti ao Legislativo em 15 de outubro de 2026. Na justificativa, o Executivo argumenta que a medida busca ampliar a eficiência na recuperação de ativos municipais e permitir a obtenção de recursos mediante a negociação de direitos creditórios. Agora, a prefeitura vai tentar anular os efeitos da liminar que suspendeu a promulgação da lei.
A proposta está fundamentada no artigo 39-A da Lei Federal nº 4.320/1964, incluído pela Lei Complementar Federal nº 208/2024, que regulamenta a cessão de direitos creditórios pelos entes públicos.

https://hyperallergic.com/shahzia-sikand.title: Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work
https://hyperallergic.com/shahzia-sikand.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/shahzia-sikand.text:
Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work
With work by Shahzia Sikander and Hylozoic/Desires, “Between Salt and Earth” simultaneously probes and defies the violent and extractive legacies of British imperialism across Asia.
A new joint video exhibition has opened above 14th Street on the High Line, featuring three moving-image works that illustratively dissect and defy the economic legacies of the British Empire's grip on South Asia and China. Screening daily until January 11, Between Salt and Earth presents two animated videos by Pakistani-American artist Shahzia Sikander and one documented performance by artists Himali Singh Soin and David Soin Tappeser, who make up the duo Hylozoic/Desires.
The artists examine British colonial extraction and violence in Asia through the lens of the East India Company's monopolies on salt, opium, and other highly valued goods. A new work by Sikander, “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026), consists of hand-painted images that the artist digitally animated in a research-driven cinematic exploration of trade history between the declining Mughal Empire, the East India Company, and the Qing Dynasty.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: ‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money
Democrats say they plan to investigate Trump’s dealings with Venezuela after winning control of Congress.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump is facing criticism over how it has handled billions of dollars in oil revenue collected from Venezuela.
Since January 3, Trump’s government has controlled Venezuela’s oil exports, gathering the revenue in an account overseen exclusively by the US Treasury.
Last week, the Department of State released a 53-page report aimed at shedding light on the account’s activities. It revealed that at least $12.11bn have passed through the account since the start of the year.
But critics say the report lacks key details about where the money came from and who it is going to.
“There’s been zero transparency on all of the financial engineering associated with how $12bn of Venezuelan oil was changing hands and being utilised,” said Tyson Slocum, the director of the energy programme at Public Citizen, a US-based consumer advocacy nonprofit.
“All we have now is a very barebones narrative of how the funds were used, but not details on what entities were involved.”
Questions of sovereignty
Concerns about Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil sector began late last year, when his government began seizing oil tankers leaving the South American country.
Any oil on board, Trump said, would be kept or sold by the US. He and members of his administration framed the confiscated fuel as compensation for the losses incurred when Venezuela nationalised its oil industry decades ago.
“American sweat, ingenuity and toil created the oil industry in Venezuela,” White House aide Stephen Miller said at the time. “Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property.”
Tensions between the US and Venezuela reached a tipping point on January 3, when Trump authorised a military operation to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
In a speech that morning, Trump highlighted the role oil had played in his decision. “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Trump said.
He proceeded to explain that some of the Venezuelan oil proceeds would go “to the United States of America in the form of reimbursement for the damages caused us by that country”.
Days later, Trump revealed he had spoken to oil companies “before and after” the operation. He also held a meeting with oil industry executives at the White House to discuss plans for Venezuela.
Legal experts have raised concerns that the January 3 operation was an attack on Venezuela’s sovereignty, in violation of international law.
They have also questioned the legality of seizing another country’s natural resources, given that a 1962 United Nations resolution grants nations “permanent sovereignty” over their own natural resources.
But supporters of Trump’s actions have pointed to Maduro’s history of violent repression and anti-democratic actions in Venezuela as justification for the operation.
Maduro has since been replaced by his former vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has largely cooperated with Trump’s demands.
But the focus on Venezuela’s oil revenue has left some critics questioning whether Trump plans to address the human rights issues in the South American country.
Trump has repeatedly downplayed the importance of democratic elections in Venezuela, said John Feeley, a former US ambassador and senior diplomat in Latin America.
“Trump has made patently clear that he has no interest in the democratic future of Venezuela,” said Feeley, calling the US-Venezuela relationship “protectorate neocolonialism”.
‘The biggest oil deal in history’
More recent manoeuvres have also raised speculation about the Trump administration’s commitment to transparency in its management of Venezuelan oil.
In late August, for instance, Trump announced his government would have a direct stake in extracting nearly a fifth of Venezuela’s oil.
Under the terms of the agreement, the US gained “majority control” in a 100-year deal for 17 Venezuelan oilfields, with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels.
North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a company owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, was given the rights to operate the fields.
The Pentagon, meanwhile, took a 35 percent stake in the company, and the US was guaranteed 20 percent of the oil output at cost. Trump called it “the biggest oil deal in history”.
But Betancourt has faced investigations in the US, Spain and Switzerland over accusations of money laundering.
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado also said the contract with NABEP “evidently does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants”.
Venezuela has long struggled to export its oil, so the fact that it will now be sold on the open market is beneficial to the country’s economy, said Luis A Pacheco, a former executive with Venezuela’s state oil company and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute Center for Energy Studies at Rice University.
But Pacheco is sceptical of Trump’s deal with NABEP.
“This is an obscure outfit with no known financial sources, with very little tech wherewithal,” he said. “This so-called mega-deal, without doubt, will certainly yield very little of what’s expected of it.”
Little transparency over billions of dollars
The shroud of secrecy surrounding the Venezuelan oil deals has spurred some Democrats in the US Congress to press for greater accountability.
In September, Democrats in the House of Representatives (PDF) and Senate asked the administration to disclose what had been uncovered by KPMG, an outside accounting firm hired to audit transactions involving Venezuelan oil exports.
The State Department did issue its report last week. But key portions were redacted, including who deposited money into the accounts and who the final recipients of the funds were.
Feeley, the diplomat, said there are also questions about the total sum of the proceeds. Only $12bn is accounted for in the report.
“We have no idea how that money was used, and we have no idea what percent of the total amount of money deposited in the US Treasury that $12bn represents,” said Feeley. “But most experts allege that it is only a fraction.”
In a statement to Al Jazeera, a State Department spokesperson said its report “provides a comprehensive account, down to the cent, of the Venezuelan natural resource revenues deposited in, held by, and disbursed” from the account.
Venezuela’s requests for disbursement are checked against a “list of approved and prohibited expenditure categories”, the spokesperson added.
The funds are then used for “essential public services, macroeconomic stability, and the rebuilding of key sectors such as energy, healthcare and infrastructure”.
But who receives those funds remains unclear. Pacheco said there is no reason the US could not disclose details of the monetary flow.
“Even though this report gives you some information, it still doesn’t give you light into the most important thing, which is what is the Venezuelan regime is doing with the money,” Pacheco said.
“You can affirm with very good certainty, when you talk about billions of dollars, something is draining away.”
Pacheco also questioned the supervisory role the Trump administration has claimed over the Venezuelan government. At one point, Trump even claimed he would “run” the South American country.
“The discourse of the White House is that they exert some sort of tutelage over the Venezuelan regime,” Pacheco said. “But apparently that tutelage doesn’t go as far as to tell the Venezuelans where is the money going to.”
New Congress, new oversight?
But this year’s midterm elections could usher in a wave of oversight into the Venezuelan oil money.
Democrats won majority control in both the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, and lawmakers have already floated the possibility of opening investigations, once the new Congress arrives in January.
“The admin is sending billions to Delcy Rodriguez’s corrupt government where the list of who benefits is kept murky,” Representative Joaquin Castro wrote on social media after the election.
“I will continue to demand answers, and use every tool we will have with the incoming Democratic majority, including congressional hearings, to uncover what the United States is doing in Venezuela.”
One area of exploration might be the role private oil trading companies play in the Trump administration’s deal. Firms like Vitol, a Dutch multinational energy company, could be put under the microscope.
A week before Trump sent troops into Caracas to abduct Maduro, John Addison, a senior trader with Vitol, held a secret meeting with Vice President JD Vance on a tarmac in Montana, according to the news agency Reuters.
Vitol was later able to buy oil from the state-owned Venezuelan oil company at a steep discount. Addison and his wife donated $6m to Trump’s election campaign in 2024.
Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have long been eager to investigate the dealings of firms like Vitol in Venezuela.
“Oversight Democrats will not stop until we know exactly what companies are profiting from these foreign policy decisions, especially in Venezuela,” Representative Robert Garcia said in January.
Garcia is expected to chair the oversight committee next year.

The Trellis Art Fund, a private foundation in New York, has announced its 2026 Stepping Stone cohort. Each of the twenty artists honored will receive $40,000 installments over two years, totalling in $800,000.
The Stepping Stone grant program was founded in 2024 and awarded $20,000 to artists with promising practices. In 2025, it expanded the program to a two year grant, and committed to a second year of funding for the inaugural grantees. https://gothamist.com/news/28-year-old-m.title: 28-year-old man fatally stabbed on Brooklyn street after intervening in fight, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/28-year-old-m.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/28-year-old-m.text:
Police said they are looking for a person who fatally stabbed a Brooklyn man after he intervened in an argument between his attacker and another man with a dog.
NYPD officials said 28-year-old Isaiah Davis, 28, was stabbed around 12:30 a.m. on Tuesday on Wyona Street near Fulton Street in Cypress Hills, Brooklyn. They said Davis' attacker had been fighting with another man and a dog — possibly trying to rob him — when Davis got in the middle of it.
Police said the attacker left, came back and stabbed Davis in the torso. EMS responded and took Davis to Brookdale Hospital Medical Center, where doctors pronounced him dead, police said.
Officials said the attacker and Davis did not appear to know each other. They said Davis lived in Crown Heights, about 3 miles away from the incident. It was not immediately clear what happened to the other man and the dog after the stabbing, or what the argument was about.
The NYPD said the attacker was wearing a blue hoodie.
This is a developing story and may be updated.

When bigots began making Islamophobic demands that Mayor Zohran Mamdani stay away from the 9/11 commemoration events, City Council Speaker Julie Menin rose to his defense, calling the insults "absolutely inappropriate." And when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the mayor of being an antisemite who supports terrorists, Menin suggested Netanyahu's rhetoric was dangerous: "This idea of what the prime minister said can really incite violence. We cannot have this."
But on Monday afternoon, Speaker Menin lent her credibility to a forum that was honoring people who have spent the last several years trading in Islamophobia and anti-Palestinian rhetoric. The event was not included on Menin's public schedule emailed to the City Hall press corps.
Speaker Menin was given headliner treatment at Touro University's annual antisemitism symposium, alongside actor Debra Messing, who said she didn't vote for Zohran Mamdani in the 2025 mayoral primary because he "celebrated 9/11" and who spent Election Day 2025 re-sharing numerous Islamophobic memes that referred to Mamdani as an "actual communist jihadist" and stated that Muslims are "commanded to lie if it means spreading Islam." Messing spoke towards the end of the event, and also received an award. (As did singer and MAGA donor Gloria Gaynor.)
Another speaker at this year's symposium: Mort Klein, the national president of the Zionist Organization of America, who has proudly used the slur "filthy Arab," praised President Donald Trump's plans to level Gaza, and called Mamdani a "Jew-hater."
While New York City's political leaders who marched in this year's Israel Day Parade—including Speaker Menin—rushed to condemn the presence of Israeli finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, Klein defended him. Smotrich has called for the "total annihilation" of Palestinian cities in Gaza.
