https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Sotheby's makes last-minute deal to sell $180m Van Gogh painting following dispute
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Sotheby’s today announced that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in New York.
The Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.
The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).
The Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”
The provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.
Last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he says took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.
In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”
The Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”
No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.
What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.
- Martin Bailey will be analysing the sale result in his weekly Adventures with Van Gogh blog on Friday

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-b.title: A History of Taxing the Rich in California
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-b.author: Fred Glass
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/california-b.text:
A History of Taxing the Rich in California
A look at the history of efforts to tax the rich in California suggests that the recent loss of Proposition 40, the billionaires tax, does not mean the end of progressive tax conflict in California. Prop 40 is a battle lost, not the war.
In the wake of the defeat of Proposition 40, the billionaire tax in California, observers are parsing the loss. The good news is that there were actually two progressive tax ballot measures before the Golden State’s electorate this year, and while we lost Prop 40, we won the other one, Prop 3. This point is key, because it’s not possible to grasp the reasons for the loss of 40 without knowing its intertwined history with Prop 3. Since economic inequality will not be disappearing any time soon, and taxing the rich is an integral aspect of fixing the problem, we need to devise a balance sheet of lessons drawn from these two campaigns to inform the next round.
Prop 3 has made permanent a temporary state income tax in place since 2012 on the top 2 percent of income earners. These are people who make at least $370,000 per year. Prop 3 mostly supports public education but also supports other state-funded services. Last year, it brought in over $14 billion in revenue, close to 6 percent of the entire state budget. Prop 3 passed by a comfortable margin of better than 60–40 percent.
Prop 40 — which lost 52–48 percent — proposed to tax California’s 250 billionaires on their bloated collective wealth (an estimated $2.4 trillion), a 5 percent levy to backfill cuts that Donald Trump and the Republican Congress made to federal Medicaid assistance to the states. Until now, California’s share came to $20 billion a year. Starting January 1, 2027, the loss of Prop 40 means that unless the state’s governor and legislature come up with a Plan B (and there is barely a glimmer of one at the moment), three million of the poorest Californians will lose access to health care.
This goal of Prop 40, to save health care for the state’s indigent, was lost in mainstream media reportage on the campaign, which breathlessly — and in the worst tradition of fawning celebrity journalism — focused on the astronomical sums of money spent against Prop 40 and narcissistic wounds suffered by the ultrarich at the prospect of paying higher taxes.
Example: a New York Times story in the final weekend of the campaign, “Inside the War Against California’s Wealth Tax,” managed to spill ink across two pages without saying a single word about the purpose of the tax that the self-absorbed right-wing billionaires were fighting.
Little attention, too, was devoted to analyzing what the enormous spigot of political action committee (PAC) money against the billionaire tax purchased: a torrent of some of the most deceptive and deliberately confusing paid messaging ever delivered in a state ballot measure campaign (and that’s saying something). Prop 3, by contrast, received generally favorable coverage and flew mostly below the radar, while Prop 40 was being carpet-bombed.
What accounted for the differing treatment? And does the result mean Prop 40 was a first step toward wealth taxes from which we can draw valuable insights and move forward? Or a serious mistake from which it will take a while to recover?
What They’re Saying
One postelection refrain is the assertion that the billionaires have way too much money and will spend so much (which they won’t even feel) that the people don’t stand a chance to tax the rich. The implication is that progressive forces should work on other issues that we can actually win. There is an obvious element of truth here, but it’s only part of the story. It’s also the defeatist lesson the billionaires would like us to internalize.
A more nuanced narrative: Forget a wealth tax. Proposition 3, a top tier income tax, was on the same ballot and won. Only income taxes on the rich stand a chance.
Again, a partial truth: the failure of one wealth tax doesn’t mean all will fail. But the devil is in the details. And income taxes on the superwealthy, as Thomas Piketty pointed out a dozen years ago, are so twentieth century. They are still necessary, but they are a mismatch with the ability of the rich to avoid tax scrutiny. And that focus ignores the big enchilada of where the real money is.
Then there’s Governor Gavin Newsom’s self-serving mantra: You can’t do it in one state. It has to be a federal wealth tax. Which is half right — we do need that. But it’s not an either/or. Fully one-quarter of the country’s billionaires reside in California, and there’s plenty of need for a fair share of their taxes right here.
Finally, for people closer to the labor campaigns for 3 and 40 — they were both led by unions — and tuned into the inside baseball, there are competing stories about why the campaigns did not work together, and crucially, why a handful of important labor and nominally progressive organizations opposed the billionaire tax. The division inflicted real damage on 40 and, with its defeat, perceptions of what’s possible along these lines in the future.
Sorting through these viewpoints and explanations with the goal of doing better next time requires some background in California’s tax wars, beginning with the disastrous Prop 13. Had the major backer of the Prop 40 campaign, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers, absorbed the history and applied its lessons from the outset, things might have gone differently. That knowledge might have also given the leadership of the Prop 3 campaign a more expansive view of the state’s tax needs than the narrow picture they felt compelled to defend.
Prop 13
No examination of California’s tax politics can avoid the legacy of Prop 13. The proposition was placed on the California ballot in 1978 by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, an anti-tax group backed by big business. It turned out to be a small government, anti-tax program replicated by the Right all across the United States.
Prop 13 capped property taxes at 1 percent of assessed value and limited increases in tax rates to no more than 2 percent per year. Although it was sold to the public in a time of high inflation as a measure to “keep grandma in her home” on her fixed income, it applied to both residential and commercial property. This meant, over time, that large commercial property owners would pocket billions of dollars in the difference between what they pay in taxes and what they would be paying if their property, increasing in value over the years, was reassessed upward to market value.
Prop 13 didn’t stop with revisions to the property tax code. A state constitutional amendment, it changed the threshold for the legislature to pass any tax from a simple majority to two-thirds supermajority, and the same for local taxes. Meanwhile, it left a simple majority in place for reducing or eliminating a tax. It mandated that property value reassessments to current market rate could only take place when the property was sold, and even then, with loopholes that allowed corporations to avoid reassessment and thus higher taxes.
Beyond the details of its mandates, two other facets of the measure bear mention. Its dog-whistle racist campaign message pitted white homeowners against renters and welfare recipients: as in, “Your hard-earned tax dollars shouldn’t be wasted on black and brown poor people” — a template for conservative campaigners elsewhere. It represented a backlash, in a time of high inflation, against the last gasps of social movements of the 1960s and ’70s, especially the gains of the civil rights movement and rise of public sector unions.
Prop 13 was a traumatic event from which consultants and politicians couldn’t recover for more than three decades, preventing them from understanding that yes, it was actually still possible to tax the rich. What began as a political defeat morphed into a self-inflicted inhibition and common sense.
Lesson One: Don’t Forget About the Money
The first progressive tax campaign I worked on was in 1992. A combination of upper-tier personal income and corporate tax increases, Prop 167 was placed on the California state ballot by public sector unions seeking to draw business contributions away from support of Republican Governor Pete Wilson’s ballot-box attempt to concentrate power over the state budget into his office. It was the first effort in a decade and a half to tax the rich following passage of Prop 13 but, still suffering below its shadow, the plan was not completely serious.
After raising the money to get the tax on the ballot, the unions directed staff like me — I was communications director for the California Federation of Teachers (CFT) at the time — to work the campaign but spent no money on media. Meanwhile, business interests treated the threat seriously, put together a war chest, and expended millions on media buys.
Yet until three weeks before Election Day, the two sides were polling dead even. At that point, the anti-tax forces pulled out all the stops. You could not turn on a radio or TV without teeth-gnashing boutique owners sobbing about how they were going to lose the businesses they had built with their own two hands. Ultimately, the business coalition outspent the unions by a margin of more than twenty to one.
In actuality, no small businesses would have been affected by the taxes. But the tactic of corporations hiding behind mom-and-pop stores, deployed against progressive taxes since time immemorial, proved effective. That prevarication, coupled with the equally venerable blackmailing canard that all the “job creators” would leave the state — and multiplied by the huge imbalance in political spending — meant that we lost by a wide margin, 59–41. All the smart people said, “You see. We told you. California is an anti-tax state and will remain that way forever.”
Some of us felt the story had a different moral. Studying the campaign timeline, we saw that progressive taxes were at first blush popular. Until the opposition’s river of negative media advertising widened into a flood, with no comparable answer forthcoming from our side, the public was far from convinced how evil Prop 167 was.
We posited that if the unions were to pony up a reasonable amount of campaign funding for media alongside a robust field operation, we could win a future campaign. But that insight — blocked by the common wisdom among the political cognoscenti that California’s electorate had been “anti-tax” since Prop 13 and would remain that way until Judgment Day had to wait for some twenty years to be tested.
Poor consolation: the unions’ feint worked, and Wilson’s measure went down to defeat.
Lesson Two: The Right Message at the Right Time
Two decades later, following the subprime mortgage housing crash and Great Recession, my union organized and led a successful campaign to pass a progressive tax. After three years of massive state budget cuts pummeling public schools and social services, the state still faced a record multibillion-dollar budget deficit.
To ward off further harm, we went on offense, pulling together a coalition that included unions and community and faith-based groups. In our early meetings we came up with three criteria to test in opinion research: What tax would raise the largest amount of revenue, drawn from the most progressive source, with the best chance of winning?
These deliberations and tests resulted in our proposal for a millionaire tax ballot measure to add two top-tier marginal tax rates to the state income tax schedule: an additional 3 percent on income between $1 million and $2 million, and 5 percent on any income above $2 million. We calculated that this would raise $5 billion — not enough to fill the entire state budget hole, but a good start and, following our criteria, winnable. The core of our message: “Tax the rich for schools and services.”
We had tested similar sentiments a year earlier with a march from Bakersfield to Sacramento and found over six weeks that they resonated deeply in the communities of the central valley, supposedly a conservative bastion. Reinforced now by our opinion research, we began circulating petitions to gather the requisite number of voter signatures to place our millionaire tax on the ballot.
Then-Governor Jerry Brown had a different idea. Notoriously averse to opinion research, and with a record of electoral success based on his gut instincts, he rejected our overtures to join the campaign and put a rival petition for signatures into circulation with a mix of progressive and regressive taxes, including increases on the lowest income earners along with a 1¢ sales tax increase. Our research told us (and we told him) that this would not fly with the electorate.
Our proposed measure came out on top of his in five straight opinion polls over several months, but he remained unmoved until the first week of March 2012. During that interval, he shaved away the other unions in our coalition with a razor governors have at their disposal: the threat to veto any legislation sponsored by groups that refused to comply with his will. Despite the loss of these partners (who behind the scenes let us know their hearts were still with us), we retained sufficient resources and coalition partners to put ten thousand marchers carrying millionaire tax signs in the streets of the capital, parading past Brown’s windows.
Two days later, we announced the results of a new poll showing our numbers going up and his going down. Brown finally caved. He called CFT president Joshua Pechthalt, a high school social studies teacher in Los Angeles, and worked out a compromise deal. This became Proposition 30, with two parts: three tiers of additional 1 percent tax bumps on individuals making $250,000, $300,000 and $500,000 a year, coupled with a modest 0.25 percent sales tax. Brown insisted on inclusion of the latter (we negotiated it down from his original 1¢ sales tax) due to his agreement with the Chamber of Commerce that they would stay out of the fight so long as Brown didn’t “demonize the rich.” With the sales tax, he said, everyone had skin in the game.
We didn’t like the sales tax, nor that the Prop 30 tax would be temporary; our millionaire tax proposal had been for a permanent tax. But Brown agreed to limit the sales tax to four years and extend the progressive income tax to seven years. And the Prop 30 package was actually projected to raise more money than our millionaire tax (and it has).
Lesson Three: A Big Coalition
With Brown on board, and all of our former coalition partners returned to the fold, we were set up for success. But first we had to overcome a messaging hiccup.
The governor had been campaigning mostly on the idea that Prop 30 would save education from further cuts. We agreed with that message, but based on our research — and the post–Occupy Wall Street injection of economic inequality into public conversation — we knew that there also had to be a strong emphasis on taxing the rich. Brown’s hodgepodge approach — save education, tear down the state’s wall of debt, shared sacrifice, and reluctantly, fair taxes — had to be redirected to what we knew were the winning messages.
After some internal conversations, he dropped the distracting mishmash and became a disciplined messenger, going straight to stripped-down messages on education, fair share of taxes for the rich, and emphasizing that the sales tax (our biggest worry) represented just one tiny penny on a four-dollar sandwich.
Prop 30 made it across the finish line with votes to spare, 55–45 percent, overcoming more than $50 million in opposition spending and decades of formerly unshakeable warnings that California voters would never ever vote for a tax. Thanks to Brown’s hefty campaign fund, we slightly outspent the rich conservatives who bankrolled the other side. That, plus our robust ground game (door-to-door canvassing and earned media from demonstrations, town halls, and other public events) and late course correction on messaging made the difference. Prop 30 was the largest income tax increase on wealthy Californians since World War II.
Four years later, as the sales tax expired, the coalition brought Prop 55 to the voters to extend Prop 30, this time as a pure progressive tax for another fourteen years. Brown didn’t bother participating, nor did we need him, as the wealthy reactionaries, having had their butts handed to them four years before, stayed home. A unified labor movement, with adequate funding and support from a wide spectrum of progressive community partners, executed well, and Prop 55 won in a landslide, by 64–36, demonstrating the popularity of taxing the rich if an undisturbed electorate makes its choice without a thumb on the scale from a well-heeled opposition.
The above are key pieces of the ancestry to this year’s Proposition 3 victory, which made the Prop 55 tax permanent. But there’s one more election story we should review, the lessons of which help explain Prop 3’s success and the defeat of Prop 40 on November 3.
Split Roll
In March 2020, now retired, and prey to the notion that “idle hands are the devil’s workshop”, I was gathering signatures with my local faculty union for the “Schools and Communities First” ballot measure, ultimately Prop 15. Generated by the same progressive tax coalition behind Props 30 and 55, Prop 15 was the long-anticipated “split roll” tax meant to overcome the choke hold placed over the state budget via property tax limitations in 1978’s Prop 13.
Prop 15 proposed a simple change: resetting the tax basis of commercial property from its last purchase price to current market value. It explicitly excluded residential and agricultural property and, attempting to neutralize small business opposition, set the bar for reassessment to property worth $3 million or more. It would have drawn more than 90 percent of its revenues from less than 10 percent of commercial property holders — entities like Disney and Chevron whose owners paid property taxes based on long-past-shelf-life assessments, robbing the state and its public services of billions of dollars each year.
At the outset, the measure polled well, although not as strongly as the millionaire tax had. But it ran into three problems.
The broad labor/community progressive tax coalition, well prepared, had gathered the most signatures ever for a California ballot measure campaign — 1.7 million — by mid-March. It would have been even more, but the intervention of the COVID-19 pandemic put a premature end to that activity. As it turned out, this represented but the beginning of how the pandemic undercut the yes campaign.
With the imposition of restrictions on public events and face-to-face contact, one of the main tools of labor-community coalitions against big money, grassroots people power, largely evaporated. Door-to-door canvassing and large rallies to draw earned media were out, as was tabling and leafleting in public spaces. The campaign thus developed a decent virtual speakers bureau program, including relational organizing efforts and battalions of letter-to-the-editor writers.
Although Prop 15 phone banking was well staffed with volunteers, it became tough for voters to distinguish volunteers from paid callers funded by oil corporations, realtors, and large commercial property owners like Chevron. Already weeks before Election Day, phone banks had been rendered less effective due to voter fatigue at the tsunami of calls.
A second factor was the problematic role of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). Its president, Alice Huffman, steered the state organization into a no endorsement on the campaign, while her political consulting firm was accepting $740,000 in No on 15 contributions. The Huffman-led NAACP’s endorsement figured prominently in the massive direct mail operation that sent deceptive “No on 15” literature streaming into African American households, which claimed falsely that 15 would tax homeowners. The NAACP position was partly countered by Prop 15 endorsements from other institutional pillars of black communities, but it sowed confusion among African American voters.
Third, Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed the measure late and declined to campaign for it. By contrast, Jerry Brown had been out every day in October 2012 calling for the passage of Proposition 30. Governors are reliable media magnets. The no side outspent the pro-15 forces by some $20 million, most of which went to TV advertising. Newsom missing in action meant the loss of earned media opportunities that could have counterbalanced the negative ads.
Had any one of these factors gone the other way, Prop 15 would have won despite its funding disadvantage. Instead, it lost narrowly, 52–48.
Between Election Campaigns
The defeat of Prop 15 and the pandemic in which it occurred left a nasty dent in progressive tax work and on the general atmosphere of the political left in California. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) played a significant role in the Prop 15 campaign, mounting a coordinated statewide effort among its twenty chapters. Its activists, fresh from the 2020 Bernie Sanders primary victory over Joe Biden in the state, had regrouped after Biden clinched the nomination and enthusiastically staffed phone banks for 15, logging more calls than most unions. But after November, the two major political disappointments in a nine-month span sent the mostly youthful cohort into a demoralized space; membership and activism decayed over the next few years.
A similar dysphoria enveloped the rest of the progressive tax coalition, which largely lost momentum, nursing its wounds through the 2024 election cycle. Beyond the general disorientation and social anomie fostered by the pandemic, the education unions (the California Teachers Association [CTA], CFT, and significant sectors of the Service Employees International Union) leading the coalition had to face unrelenting attacks from the Right for their support of school closures, diluting energy for other commitments.
One of the coalition’s community organizations, California Calls, kept the faith and continued to host sparsely attended meetings. Only CFT, with little active support from the other groups, pushed a new effort in the legislature. The union worked with Alex Lee, a state assemblymember in Alameda and Santa Clara counties (and the only state representative at the time associated with DSA) to promote wealth tax legislation. Since everyone understood Newsom would veto any such bills, a paper Democratic legislative supermajority meant nothing (even if it had been unified on the issue, which it wasn’t) and these bills did not advance.
Limited meetings and deferred decision-making brought no campaign in 2024. But heading toward the 2026 midterms, the coalition got its act together, tested the waters on several proposals, and decided its best move was to make Prop 55 permanent. This would ensure that the funding — an average above $10 billion a year from the progressive tax, or around 5 percent of the entire state budget — would continue, without which the public sector, especially education, would suffer serious budget reductions, and high-end income earners would receive an entirely unnecessary tax cut.
Or so went the plan before Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill.” HR 1 gave federal tax cuts to the rich and paid for it with massive reductions to Medicaid, including a loss of some $20 billion a year for California’s share of that program (called “Medi-Cal” here). The looming threat to Medi-Cal and by extension to health care jobs spurred SEIU-United Healthcare Workers into action.
Enter the Billionaire Tax
A 120,000-member statewide union representing frontline workers across numerous corporate and public health care entities, UHW stood to lose tens of thousands of jobs after January 1, 2027, if nothing changed. Its president, Dave Regan, had used ballot measures in the past — dozens of them — to leverage his union’s interests in Sacramento. Sometimes this meant maintaining the efforts all the way to November,and at other times agreeing to drop them from the ballot if negotiations with employers or the legislature gained improved outcomes.
So no one was sure, when the billionaire tax entered the picture in September 2025 with a filing for title and summary, whether it was a straightforward entry into the ballot measure lists or a bargaining ploy for Regan with Gavin Newsom and the state legislature. What unfolded suggests an initial goal of a negotiating chip that, in failing, forced the union, fatefully, to repurpose it as a real ballot campaign.
The measure itself, despite claims by opponents that it was poorly designed, was put together by a rock-star team of progressive economists and lawyers who fully understood the present and future perils of nonchalant-ing its construction and, at least from this layman’s point of view, gave it a solid foundation on both economic and legal grounds.
Although Regan approached the progressive tax coalition with a request for support, the conversation did not go well. Its leaders felt the measure was ill-timed and could get in the way of Prop 55 renewal. Regan’s position was essentially a pointed question: What about the three million Medi-Cal recipients and thousands of union jobs? To which the coalition leaders gave an unsatisfactory answer predicated on by no means certain budgetary maneuvers and legislative goodwill. Regan’s blunt personality preceded him into the room and was a factor in the discussion, which ended in mutual antagonism.
The Opposition Consolidates
By late December, several of the wealthiest tech moguls in California, having created the “Building a Better California” PAC to oppose the tax, celebrated the season with a party in Marin whose guests included Sergey Brin (Google cofounder, worth $250 billion and a MAGA donor) and Newsom. Brin reportedly cornered the governor and gave him a piece of his mind about the tax, threatening to leave the state if it passed. Newsom promised to try to get rid of it and was as good as his word, quickly becoming its most high-profile non-right-wing billionaire opponent and reliably delivering their false talking points (all the billionaires will leave, innovation will be smothered, California will be left a smoking husk).
As a signal to his left that he didn’t share an entire bed with right-wing sociopaths, he added his own two cents: billionaires do need to pay their fair share, but a) at the federal level, not via the state, and b) it’s a good idea but fatally flawed (repeating a commonly employed argument for campaigns against ballot measures).
The measure received its title and summary around the first of the year (late for this sort of thing; Prop 3 had been gathering signatures already for months), and UHW began campaigning at the same time as the billionaires and their puppet governor danced and sang before an eager audience of mainstream media editors and reporters — none of whom seemed to know how to ask uber-rich people questions like: What impact will passage of this measure actually have upon your life/finances/business?; What is a greater value, your keeping every penny or millions of poor people keeping access to health care?; What does it mean to “leave the state” when you already own multiple mansions all over the country and world?; or Without your tax dollars, what other action do you suggest the government should take to prevent this health care debacle from occurring?
The small coterie of fuming billionaires unearthed and spent the quarters from their couch cushions (piling up close to $400 million to date and counting, the largest sum ever expended on a California ballot initiative) to pay for consulting firms, gather signatures for two poison-pill measures to nullify 40, launch salvos of direct mail. and reserve massive media buys.
Regan met with Newsom and attempted to work out a deal. In exchange for the governor’s support, the UHW president offered to pull the measure from the ballot and drop to a new bottom line: from 5 percent to 2 percent. This would have had the effect of reducing the revenue from $100 billion over five years to $40 billion — enough to get through two years of covering the Medi-Cal cuts before (presumably) a Democratic administration would be in national office, which (again presumably) would restore federal funding for Medicaid. But Newsom declined the deal.
There matters stood until the June midterm Democratic primary. When Tom Steyer, the sole gubernatorial candidate supporting the billionaire tax, failed to make it into the top two for November, the CTA, State Building Trades Council (BTC), and Planned Parenthood, among others, immediately announced their public opposition to the billionaire tax.
CTA was the only organization offering a principled reason for its position. Prop 40 allocated 90 percent of its projected revenues to shoring up Medi-Cal, which violated the state budgetary rules put in place from an earlier voter decision, Prop 98, that mandates 40 percent of the state general fund to public education. CTA’s opposition to the billionaire tax was consistent with their long-standing defense of that line in the sand. If it had stopped there, its hands would have been clean.
Instead its leaders signed onto the scary and false messaging flowing from the billionaires’ playbook: Prop 40 would cause the billionaires to flee. The state would lose substantial tax dollars. Because the tax is temporary, voters should reject it, because it doesn’t meet the long-term needs of the state. The last one took the cake, as CTA with its other breath was urging passage of Prop 3, which it had supported as a temporary tax beginning in 2012 up to this election cycle.
At the time of CTA’s announcement, it posted its recommendations for the full slate of propositions on its website. Next to the no vote on Prop 40, it placed, without explanation, a link to the Building a Better California website. After a few weeks the link was removed.
The public statements from the BTC, Planned Parenthood, and the others simply parroted the billionaires’ talking points and aren’t worth dissecting. It is important to note a common strand among these nominally progressive groups’ decision-making processes: none offered a plebiscite to their members on the question. The BTC is one of the most conservative sectors of the labor movement and reliably tails behind the promises of construction capital for jobs. It was Planned Parenthood’s foundation board, which relies on philanthropy, that voted for opposition.
These moves were amplified by the billionaire media machine, which emphasized the split in the progressive community and labor when it wasn’t simply pretending that “teachers” were opposed. (The lie was exposed, to little media notice, when two of the largest local CTA affiliates, United Teachers Los Angeles and United Educators of San Francisco, came out for Prop 40. Shortly afterward the California Federation of Teachers, which had been neutral, and which has a more democratic governance structure than CTA, switched to a support position.)
Momentum Returns and Recedes
Things looked bad for Prop 40 until three days at the beginning of August. At that point, UHW’s organizing within two of the major institutions of California progressive politics paid off.
First, the state Democratic Party leadership, expressing its displeasure with the governor, voted narrowly to endorse the billionaire tax. The next day, with President Lorena Gonzalez leading the charge, the California Federation of Labor Unions came overwhelmingly on board. As icing on the cake, the California Nurses Association joined the newly expanding coalition the following day.
But this represented the high point of the campaign. Late endorsements and sporadic earned media emanating from such events as enthusiastic rallies featuring Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna and cheerleading by Nobel Prize–winning economists turned out to be no match for the record-setting spending tide of the other side, which all along had been steadily eroding the early advantage in poll numbers among a public disgusted with Trump-supporting oligarchs.
A no campaign has more messaging tools at its disposal than the pro side of a ballot measure. Where the latter has to make and hold its case before the electorate on the merits, the opposition — especially one with an unlimited pocketbook — doesn’t have to convincingly argue on the same ground. It only needs to cast doubt on the enterprise, showing (or claiming) that various trusted messengers are opposed, rolling out “experts” who “prove” it’s all wrong, and muddling the issues through fearmongering and misdirection.
Communications from hell, summoned up by demonic billionaire-backed consultants performed those tasks well.
Homeowners learned that they were the target of unnamed but terrifyingly evil “Sacramento politicians” who wanted their homes (like those in the 2020 split roll campaign). Old people found that their pensions were going to be taken away by Prop 40. “Stanford professors” (usually not identified for who they were: the right-wing Hoover Institute) demonstrated that the tax would strip California of innovation and tax revenues. And so on.
Progressive tax campaigns produce time-tested, predictable reactions from right-wing rich people, which backers of the measures do well to inoculate against. While modulating with circumstances, they fall into three main themes:
- The “job creators” will all leave, taking all the jobs with them in their platinum-lined backpacks. The innovation this time around was substituting wealthy “taxpayers” and “tax revenues” for employers and jobs.
- This is a tax on “you.” This takes two forms: an outright lie making a levy on 250 people into a general tax, and “First they come for the billionaires, then they come for you.”
- Misdirection: pretending small business owners/homeowners/pensions are the targets, obscuring the point of economic inequality and the tax-dodging of the superrich.
Inoculation is possible, but it requires a sufficient timeline before the campaign proper to manufacture the needles and serum and delivery, and sufficient financial resources to pay for it all.
With a relatively popular governor actively opposed, and putatively progressive organizations gravely restating the false messages that billionaires couldn’t have convinced the public to believe on their own, the billionaire tax had too big a mountain to climb. A progressive tax campaign needs three things to have a reasonable shot at winning: the right message at the right time; the largest coalition possible; and sufficient cash for at least a modicum of paid advertising to augment its field campaign and earned media against the most well-funded opposition imaginable. Prop 40 had but one out of three, and it wasn’t enough.
Compare and contrast with Prop 3’s advantages. Built on a long-standing and extensive coalition of unions and community organizations, with the full backing of the Democratic political establishment (including the governor, who otherwise never met a progressive tax he liked), and with a bank account supported by the biggest labor political contributor (CTA) in the state, and facing virtually no opposition spending, it offered a free lunch to the public (“not a tax increase” — technically true, just maintaining an earlier one) along with its backward, modestly progressive tax messaging (“If it fails, rich people will get a completely unnecessary tax cut”).
Prop 3’s victory relied on keeping below the line of fire aimed at Prop 40. It might have been a larger target itself had the billionaire tax not existed. But in that event, as in 2016 with Prop 55, the progressive tax coalition would probably have prevailed anyway, because it was sufficiently prepared and resourced. CTA did not have to hand the billionaires a winning card against a historically justifiable tax on plutocrats for a good cause. Their action dismissed the possibility of a united two-proposition tax the rich campaign that could have provided much-needed consciousness-raising in the electorate about the evils of our New Gilded Age imbalance of wealth and power. Such a dedicated education campaign remains an urgent task.
At one level, it’s pointless to second guess what SEIU-UHW might have done differently to get Prop 40 past the third of a billion dollars a couple dozen sociopathic tech oligarchs spent to keep every speck of their hoard and prevent a few million of the poorest Californians from gaining back the health care Trump stole from them. It’s done. But it’s also essential to understand the mistakes that could have been avoided so as to not commit them again the next time around.
What’s Next
The loss of Prop 40 does not mean the end of progressive tax conflict in California. It’s a battle lost, not the war. We can close this account with a note about the short term and the longer run.
It remains to be seen whether the deal originally offered to the UHW will materialize, and budget maneuvers and modest corporate tax increases or loophole closures backed by the legislature and Governor-elect Xavier Becerra will result in enough revenue to reverse the loss of health care for millions of California residents caused by the cruel actions of Trump and the federal government. It’s within the power of the new governor and legislature, if they are committed to it; the tax increases (on income, since thanks to passage of the billionaires’ deceptive Prop 42, wealth taxes are off the table for the time being) will simply require a legislative supermajority of two thirds. If the “blue wave” of November 3 should mean anything to the legislators, it’s that now is the time to act without fear of electoral retribution on that score.
Beyond the immediate need to plug the funding gap left by the failure of the billionaire tax, those interested in reversing the stratospheric economic inequality that allows a handful of spoiled oligarchs to thwart what would otherwise be the will of an electoral majority must rise beyond the narrow definition of success of the Prop 3 coalition. Future progressive tax victories cannot depend on an “I win, you lose” mindset between what should be coalition partners.
The key here is that all potential interested partners need to get over sectoral myopia and understand the common problem, the common enemy, and common working-class interests. Or, as Martin Luther King Jr noted in another time and place, “The best way to solve any problem, is to remove the cause.” The other side is serious. Are we?

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: NYC Public School Enrollment Falls 3%, With Further Decrease Expected
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Amy Zimmer, Chalkbeat, Alex Zimmerman, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
New York City’s public schools lost about 23,000 students, or nearly 3%, from the year before, according to preliminary numbers the Education Department released Monday.
That leaves the nation’s largest school system with about 766,900 students, from kindergarten through senior year, as of Oct. 31, with several contributing factors leading to the drop: falling birth rates, families leaving the city and a slowdown of immigration into the five boroughs under President Donald Trump.
Over the past decade, the city has lost about 200,000 students, or nearly 20%.
Enrollment in city-funded preschool programs was up slightly, thanks to the rollout of a new program for 2,000 2-year-olds this year as well as an uptick in 4-year-olds signed up for prekindergarten programs.
What the dip means for school budgets remains murky. Historically, when schools have fewer students than projected on their roster, the Education Department claws back money in the middle of the school year. But since the pandemic, the city has largely kept school budgets steady despite enrollment declines. Officials declined to say whether they planned to continue that policy, known as being “held harmless.” Since 2020, New York City has spent nearly $2 billion to prop up budgets at schools with declining enrollment.
Any changes to wind down that policy could be politically explosive, as schools could have to cut back on after-school and other enrichment programs this school year and eventually let go of teachers. When former Mayor Eric Adams proposed phasing it out, the blowback was so intense that City Council members apologized for giving him the green light. (The decision was later rolled back.)
In his first budget deal, Mayor Zohran Mamdani kept school budgets whole, though some experts warn that approach is inequitable because it allows schools with declining enrollment to spend significantly more per student than other campuses.
Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels has repeatedly raised concerns about declining enrollment, saying that the city will need to look closer at closures or mergers for schools too small to offer a full array of courses. Already, the city is floating proposals to close two small schools in Harlem and one in Brooklyn, as well as merge two sets of schools in the Bronx and Brooklyn, according to public documents. Those plans are expected to be voted on by the Panel for Educational Policy over the next two months.
“We’ve started to have conversations in communities,” Samuels told the Chancellor’s Parent Advisory Committee last week. “It doesn’t mean it’s not going to be tough sometimes, but they have been going pretty well.”
Enrollment is projected to continue declining. By the 2034-35 school year, the city is predicting that the student population will fall by another 130,000, according to demographic projections from the School Construction Authority.
The declines in New York City mirror national trends. Thirty states have seen public school enrollment declines since 2014. Many large school systems — including in Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia and Houston — are also grappling with sharp drops.
Mamdani’s administration pointed to some efforts to help bolster city schools, including reducing class sizes, which is required by state law and has likely been aided by declining student headcounts. Aside from continuing some of his predecessor’s initiatives, Mamdani has yet to articulate a vision for the public school system. He has focused more on his affordability agenda and expanding his free 2-K program, which expects to add 10,000 more seats next year.
When the city’s free preschool programs for 2-, 3- and 4-year-olds are included in the enrollment tally, the total is 863,100, according to the Education Department’s preliminary data. That was down about 2.6% from the previous year.
Chalkbeat New York Reporter Michael Elsen-Rooney contributed.
Amy Zimmer is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat New York. Contact Amy at azimmer@chalkbeat.org.
Alex Zimmerman is a senior reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Alex at azimmerman@chalkbeat.org.

Le secteur de l’intelligence artificielle (IA) repose sur la confiance d’investisseurs qui, séduits par la promesse d’une rentabilité future, arrosent les entreprises de milliards de dollars, à un niveau jamais atteint dans l’histoire économique.
Mais pour l’instant, l’IA coûte bien plus qu’elle ne rapporte, et le secteur se heurte à ses propres limites : le coût social et écologique des centres de données, de plus en plus rejetés par les citoyennes et les citoyens. À cela s’ajoute la crainte de voir l’intelligence artificielle prendre le contrôle de nos vies, voire les menacer.
Argument marketing ou risque réel de voir cette révolution technologique nous échapper ?
Une émission présentée par Samia Dechir, préparée avec Mathieu Mialaret et Raphaël Gribe Marquis.
Nos invité·es :
- Nastasia Hadjadji, spécialiste de l’économie numérique, coautrice avec Olivier Tesquet du livre Apocalypse Nerds. Comment les technofascistes ont pris le pouvoir (Divergences, 2025) ;
- Éric Louis, militant contre un projet de centre de données dans les Hauts-de-France et auteur du livre Casser du sucre à la pioche (Éditions du Commun, 2024) ;
- Dan Israel, journaliste à Mediapart, responsable du pôle économie et social et chargé du suivi de l’intelligence artificielle.

https://taz.de/Kontroverse-um-Ex-Bio-Pap.title: Kontroverse um Ex-„Bio-Papst“ Urs Niggli: Bioland kontert Kritik an Ökolandbau
https://taz.de/Kontroverse-um-Ex-Bio-Pap.author: Jost Maurin
https://taz.de/Kontroverse-um-Ex-Bio-Pap.text:
Kontroverse um Ex-„Bio-Papst“ Urs Niggli: Bioland kontert Kritik an Ökolandbau
Agrarforscher Niggli bestreitet, dass Bio die Welt ernähren könne. Die Branche hält dagegen – und muss zugleich um EU-Zuschüsse für Ökohöfe bangen.
Bioland-Chef Jan Plagge hat den Ökolandbau gegen Kritik des Agrarwissenschaftlers Urs Niggli verteidigt. „Im Ökolandbau wird Agrarökologie erfolgreich in die Praxis umgesetzt“, schreibt der Präsident des größten deutschen Biobauernverbands als Reaktion auf ein taz-Interview mit Niggli. Dieser hatte bestritten, dass Bio allein die Welt ernähren könne, und für die Agrarökologie plädiert – einer Mischung aus konventioneller und Ökolandwirtschaft.
„Seit Jahrzehnten zeigen Biobetriebe, wie sich Landwirtschaft an ökologischen Zusammenhängen ausrichten lässt“, ergänzte Plagge. Dazu gehörten vielfältige Fruchtfolgen, an den Standort angepasste Sorten, der Aufbau der Bodenfruchtbarkeit und moderne Technik. Statt auf mineralische Stickstoffdünger und chemisch-synthetische Pflanzenschutzmittel zu setzen, die oft die Artenvielfalt belasten, nutzten sie natürliche Prozesse und stärkten betriebliche Kreisläufe.
Niggli, der lange das Forschungsinstitut für biologischen Landbau geleitet hat, hatte im Interview darauf verwiesen, dass Biolebensmittel durchschnittlich 20 bis 50 Prozent teurer seien. Die Erträge seien im Mittel 25 bis 30 Prozent niedriger. Deshalb habe sich der Biolandbau auch nach mehr als 100 Jahren nur auf einer sehr kleinen Fläche weltweit durchgesetzt.
Plagge hält dagegen, dass hohe Erträge allein kein ausreichender Maßstab seien. „Natürlich sind Erträge wichtig“, schreibt er. Es müsse aber auch berücksichtigt werden, wie viel Energie, mineralischer Stickstoffdünger und andere externe Betriebsmittel für die Erzeugung nötig seien und welche ökologischen Folgekosten entstünden. „Ein hoher Ertrag ist wenig wert, wenn seine Voraussetzungen von importierter fossiler Energie und globalen Lieferketten abhängen, die jederzeit ins Wanken geraten können.“
Skepsis gegenüber Gentechnik
Niggli fordert für die Agrarökologie verbindliche Mindestanforderungen, die sich in weiten Bereichen an der EU-Öko-Verordnung orientieren sollten. Anders als der Ökolandbau solle sie aber beispielsweise die neue Gentechnik nicht ausschließen, so der früher teils als „Bio-Papst“ bezeichnete Forscher.
Plagge betont hingegen, Ökolandbau sei wissenschaftsbasierte Landwirtschaft. „Das bedeutet nicht, jede technische Neuerung möglichst schnell einzusetzen.“ Es gelte, Nutzen und Risiken abzuwägen. „Gerade bei neuen gentechnischen Verfahren müssen mögliche Folgen für Ökosysteme, Züchtungsfreiheit und die Abhängigkeit von patentiertem Saatgut sorgfältig geprüft werden. Wer diese Fragen stellt, handelt nicht ideologisch, sondern verantwortungsbewusst.“
EU-Subventionen unter Beschuss
Unterdessen kämpft die Biobranche dafür, dass die EU den Ökolandbau weiter subventioniert. Denn der Rat der Mitgliedstaaten hat Ende Oktober die verbindliche Bioförderung aus seiner Verhandlungsposition zur Reform der EU-Agrarpolitik ab 2028 gestrichen. Die Mitgliedstaaten sollen künftig selbst entscheiden können, ob sie Biobetriebe bei der Umstellung und der Beibehaltung ihrer Wirtschaftsweise finanziell unterstützen.
„Das französische Beispiel zeigt, was es bedeutet, wenn der Staat den ökologischen Landbau nicht mehr ausreichend honoriert“, teilten der Branchendachverband Bölw und der französische nationale Verband des ökologischen Landbaus mit. Nachdem Frankreich 2018 die Beibehaltungsprämie für Biobetriebe abgeschafft habe, sei die Zahl der neu umgestellten Hektare bis 2025 um rund 60 Prozent eingebrochen. Die Organisationen forderten das EU-Parlament auf, sich für die verpflichtende Förderung des Ökolandbaus einzusetzen.
Vorsichtshalber verlangten die Anbauverbände Bioland, Naturland, Demeter und Biokreis von den Parlamentariern, die geplante Reform der gemeinsamen Agrarpolitik abzulehnen und stattdessen den bestehenden Rechtsrahmen bis 2034 fortzuführen. Mit den aktuell diskutierten Reformvorschlägen drohten erhebliche Verschlechterungen für Agrarumweltmaßnahmen, den Ökolandbau und die Entwicklung ländlicher Räume.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.title: Psychische Erkrankungen | Ein Beinbruch? Lieber wegignorieren!
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.author: Sarah Yolanda Koss
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.text:
- Kommentare
- Psychische Erkrankungen
Ein Beinbruch? Lieber wegignorieren!
Wie oft Menschen mit psychischen Erkrankungen im Arbeitsalltag Diskriminierung erfahren, zeigt, mit wie vielen Stigmen diese verbunden sind. Ein Kommentar.
Stellen Sie sich vor, Sie haben chronische Rückenschmerzen. Anstatt zum Arzt zu gehen, schleppen Sie sich unbehandelt zur Arbeit. Dort darf schließlich niemand von ihrem Leiden erfahren. Sonst könnten Sie bei der nächsten Gehaltserhöhung übergangen-, vielleicht gar gekündigt werden. Oder Sie brechen sich ein Bein – und anstelle von Mitleid gehen Ihre Kolleg*innen auf Abstand. Was, wenn der Beinbruch ansteckend ist?
40 Prozent der Menschen mit psychischen Erkrankungen erfahren in ihrem Arbeitsumfeld Diskriminierung, wenn diese bekannt werden. Das sind erschreckend hohe Zahlen. Insbesondere, wenn man bedenkt, dass je nach Rechnung 25 bis 40 Prozent aller Personen in der Bundesrepublik an einer psychischen Erkrankung – wie beispielsweise Depressionen, Angst-, Zwangsstörungen oder Suchterkrankungen – leiden. Besonders krass: Das Stigma kann auch Jahre später noch Folgen haben, selbst wenn die Erkrankung längst überwunden ist.
Bei diesen Zahlen ist es besonders bedenklich, wenn die Bundesregierung mit jeder Gesetzesänderung aufs Neue aufzeigt, wie wenig Ernst auch sie psychische Erkrankungen nimmt. Plötzlich dürfen Psychotherapiepraxen verwanzt werden, Gespräche in Beichtstühlen bleiben indes Privatsache (Nachrichtendienstreform). Dann sollen die gesetzlichen Therapieplätze verringert werden (Kassenreform). Die Psyche wird künftig also später und schlechter behandelt. Wir kennen es ja schließlich von anderen Krankheiten: Am besten hilft, sie wegzuignorieren.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://citylimits.org/federal-cuts-coul.title: Federal Cuts Could Threaten HIV Prevention, as Latinos Make Up 41% of New Diagnoses in NYC
https://citylimits.org/federal-cuts-coul.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/federal-cuts-coul.text:
Share This Article
“We are invisible when it comes to understanding the challenges related to many health issues. And when we talk about HIV, it is even more alarming,” said Guillermo Chacón, president of the Latino Commission on AIDS.
Funding cuts to HIV prevention programs could make it harder for Latino New Yorkers—who are already disproportionately impacted by the virus—to access testing, treatment and other essential health services, health advocates warn.
The concerns were raised at a press conference last month ahead of National Latino AIDS Awareness Day. This year’s theme, “Knowing Your HIV Status Is a Good Place to Start,” focused on the importance of testing as the first step toward prevention, treatment and care.
Attendees—a mix of elected officials, public health advocates and Latino leaders—also called for greater access to health services and efforts to reduce the stigma that prevents people from seeking care.
“There has been so much stigma in our communities,” City Councilmember Alexa Aviles, who represents Brooklyn’s Sunset Park, said during the event. “This is an epidemic that we have made so much progress in, and yet still Latinos are disproportionately impacted.”
According to the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene’s 2024 HIV Surveillance Report, released in December 2025, the city recorded 1,791 new HIV diagnoses in 2024—up 5.4 percent from the year prior.
Latino residents accounted for 41 percent of those cases, despite making up approximately 30 percent of the city’s population.
For Guillermo Chacón, president of the Latino Commission on AIDS, the numbers reflect deeper structural problems in how public health institutions address the needs of Latino communities.
“We are invisible when it comes to understanding the challenges related to many health issues. And when we talk about HIV, it is even more alarming,” he told City Limits.
Chacón, who has worked with the organization for 32 years, said one of the main challenges is that public health systems often approach health disparities through racial categories, overlooking the specific needs of Latino communities.
He also pointed to barriers affecting immigrants who may struggle to navigate the U.S. health care system, particularly when it comes to sexual health education and access to prevention tools such as pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, which helps prevent HIV infection.
He described how even a negative interaction with clinic staff can discourage someone from returning for care. Limited operating hours can create another barrier for people who work during the day. “If people are working Monday through Friday, it is not going to work. You have to offer services at night and on weekends,” he said.
Those challenges are unfolding as federal funding for HIV prevention faces potential reductions.
Congress funded the Centers for Disease Control’s domestic HIV prevention program at $755.6 million for fiscal year 2026, according to the HIV Medicine Association. The Trump administration’s 2027 budget request would eliminate that core funding, keeping only $220 million for the Ending the HIV Epidemic initiative, and the House Appropriations Committee’s spending bill includes no money for the account.
Fiscal year 2027 began Oct. 1, but Congress has not passed a full-year health spending bill. A stopgap measure signed Sept. 2 keeps funding at 2026 levels through Dec. 11, and the Senate has yet to act. Meanwhile, the Kaiser Family Foundation reports the CDC is ending its direct, five-year grants to community-based organizations—$239.3 million nationwide—and sending supplemental money to health departments instead.
Chacón pointed to a recent three-year contract renewal for the Latino Commission on AIDS’ religious leadership program, which works with churches to provide health education and connect congregations with testing and other resources. Despite securing the contract, the organization faced a 60 percent funding reduction.
New York City’s Health Department warned last year that cuts to Medicaid, and stricter eligibility rules for Medicaid recipients that take effect in January, further threaten the city’s prevention progress. Medicaid is the largest source of insurance coverage for people with HIV in the country, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation.
On the local level, the Health Department says a new program aims to widen access.
“Hook Up and Bridge,” which began this fall, funds 26 clinical and community organizations to provide HIV and sexual health services directly or through referrals.
“Latino communities are among the most affected by HIV in New York City,” Sarah Braunstein, assistant commissioner of the department’s Bureau of Hepatitis, HIV and STIs, told City Limits.
Many groups funded through the new initiative have long served Latino New Yorkers by offering Spanish-speaking staff who are “trusted messengers.” Specific outreach plans are still being developed, she said.
Beyond testing and treatment, the initiative is meant to be a touchpoint for broader needs, according to the department. Braunstein said the program is open about sexual health, with providers trained to take sexual histories in an “affirming, open, stigma-free” way.
For Chacón, addressing the epidemic requires stronger partnerships among government agencies, nonprofits and communities, as well as confronting the stigma that keeps people away from care.
“The stigma, for me, is the fundamental obstacle to making a difference,” he said.
Find a map here of the city’s HIV testing, prevention and treatment services.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fr.title: Amid Legal Controversy, Christie’s Withdraws Frida Kahlo Painting Hours Before Auction
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fr.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/fr.text:
Christie’s pulled a Frida Kahlo painting from an evening sale hours before it was to be auctioned amid a debate over whether the work was legally permitted to leave Mexico.
“In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research. We look forward to selling this work at a later date,” a spokesperson for Christie’s told ARTnews. The work, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $2 million to $3.5 million, was to be included in the 20th Century Evening Sale in New York, scheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m. on November 17.
In the days leading up to the sale, Mexico’s cultural authorities had faced accusations of failing to protect the painting, which is considered part of the nation’s heritage and legally protected. An online campaign argued that the 1952 work, titled Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (Congress of the Peoples for Peace), was part of the trust that Kahlo’s husband, the artist Diego Rivera, created for the Casa Azul after her death in 1954 and that it cannot legally leave the country. It is unclear where the painting was held prior to it coming to New York for this week’s auction.
The Frida Kahlo Museum told ARTnews that the painting is part of an ongoing investigation by Mexican authorities. At the time of publication, the National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL), which is responsible for the country’s patrimony, maintained that Kahlo donated it during her lifetime and that it left Mexico before her work was declared an artistic monument in 1984.
In a statement Monday, the collective behind the campaign, Defendamos la Colección Gelman (Let’s Defend the Gelman Collection), called on INBAL to stop the sale of Congreso de los pueblos por la paz. The collective asserts that the oil-on-masonite work was among the hundreds of artworks and objects at Casa Azul that Rivera inventoried after Kahlo’s death, when he established the trust. The inventory, the collective says, carried explicit instructions from Rivera that the items remain on the premises both during his lifetime and after his death.
Queried on the collective’s claims, a representative for the Frida Kahlo Museum told ARTnews that, “In accordance with established protocols, the auction house Christie’s has been informed that the work is part of an ongoing investigation being conducted by the competent Mexican authorities.” It added, “An investigation file exists that gathers information on several works, including Congreso de los pueblos por la paz.”
According to the museum, INBAL “reported that, through its legal department, it has requested from Christie’s documentation proving the provenance and ownership of the painting.” Christie’s did not address whether it provided INBAL with the documentation in its statement to ARTnews.
A provenance published on Christie’s website, that has since been removed, listed the work’s earliest owner as Galería Ramis Barquet, a the Monterrey-based operation with a New York branch, run by Ramis Barquet, though it did not provide a date when Barquet came into possession of the work. An unnamed collector bought it from the gallery and put it up at auction at Sotheby’s in 2020. The current seller bought it at that sale for $2.6 million and is now consigning it to Christie’s.
INBAL did not respond to ARTnews’s request for comment by publication time. In a statement dated November 16 to the Mexican newspaper Excélsior, however, the institute said that Congress of the Peoples for Peace, “a painting created by Frida Kahlo in October 1952, was donated by the artist during her lifetime and left Mexico before the declaration of her work as an artistic monument.” It is unclear to whom Kahlo would have donated the work.
Kahlo painted Congreso de los pueblos por la paz two months before the Congress of the Peoples for Peace, which met in Vienna in December 1952. INBAL’s statement cited research from art historian Luis-Martín Lozano, who collaborated in cataloguing the painting for Christie’s. According to Lozano, Rivera took the painting to Vienna in late 1953, as recorded in the memoirs of Emma Hurtado, Rivera’s wife from 1955 until his death in 1957. The statement also pointed to Raquel Tibol’s 1977 book Frida Kahlo: Crónica, testimonios y aproximaciones, which reproduces the painting on plate 17.
In its statement, also from November 16, Defendamos la Colección Gelman disputed Lozano’s timeline of events. “The account—attributed to historian Luis-Martín Lozano—that the work was taken to the Congress in 1953 is chronologically impossible, as the Congress had already concluded months earlier. Furthermore, there is no evidence that Rivera returned to Europe that year; his travels were extensively documented—notably in the files that the FBI kept on him,” they wrote.
In its request for comment, ARTnews also asked INBAL about the discrepancy in Lozano’s research.
Furthermore, INBAL said that the export would not have covered Kahlo’s Congreso de los pueblos por la paz, claiming that it had left Mexico prior to July 25, 1984, when a decree declared her art an artistic monument and subject to Mexico’s strict cultural patrimony laws. Once designated “artistic monuments” of the nation, protected works may be bought and sold within Mexico but can leave the country only temporarily, unless INBAL grants an exceptional authorization.
“In previous cases, the INBAL has specified that the definitive export prohibition applies to works that were in national territory when the declaration of July 25, 1984 was published,” INBAL said.
After Kahlo’s death, Rivera notarized an inventory of the couple’s possessions as the basis for a trust administered by the Banco de México. The trust holds the properties and collections and oversees the reproduction rights to both artists’ work. Its proceeds were intended to support the upkeep of two museums: the Frida Kahlo Museum (Casa Azul) and the Museo Anahuacalli. It remains active today.
The inventory became the subject of public controversy in April 2025, when Hilda Trujillo, director of the Museo Anahuacalli and the Frida Kahlo Museum in Mexico City from 2002 to 2020, published a lengthy online post alleging that several works listed in Rivera’s inventory were currently unaccounted for. Among them, she wrote, was Congreso de los pueblos por la paz, which she said appears on Rivera’s list under the number A.F. 18. Defendamos la Colección Gelman provided ARTnews with a reproduction of the inventory including a zoomed-in, but blurry, image that reads, “18. – Congreso de los pueblos por la paz. – Oleo sobre masonite. – 1952. – 0.19 x 0.25.” (Christie’s lot entry gave the dimensions of the work as 18.7 x 24.8 centimeters.)
In her post, Trujillo traced the painting’s later whereabouts through a 2011 list that notes it as belonging to the collection of gallerist Mary-Anne Martin, and through the art historian Helga Prignitz-Poda’s 1988 catalogue raisonné, which attributed ownership to Barquet.
“It is unclear how or why it left the Frida Kahlo Museum,” she wrote. Trujillo accused the trust that manages both museums of mismanagement and negligence, claiming that in two episodes, in 2009 and 2013, its administrators dismissed evidence that works belonging to the Casa Azul may have been stolen and sold to private collectors in the United States. The trust responded to Trujillo’s allegations in a public statement that April that read in part: “The person making these accusations today never filed a formal complaint during their professional association with the trust.”
Defendamos la Colección Gelman described the case of Congreso de los pueblos por la paz as confirming “a troubling trend” that began with the Mexican government’s alleged lack of transparency surrounding the loan of the Gelman Collection to the new Faro Santander museum in Spain. “[W]hat once appeared to be an exception, the indefinite removal from the country of works designated as ‘Artistic Monuments’ with the consent of INBAL, is beginning to become the rule.”
The Gelman collection comprises more than 300 artworks, including a significant number of paintings by Kahlo and Rivera, as well as other important Mexican artists such as José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Markwayne Mullin defends private-jet trip to football game as millions hit by flight delays
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Sam Levine
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
US homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended his decision to fly in a private government to a college football game on Saturday as Americans weathered widespread flight delays and cancellations, saying: “We still got to live our life.”
Mullin, a former US senator from Oklahoma, traveled on a government aircraft on Saturday to watch a football game between Louisiana State University and the University of Texas, the New York Post reported on Tuesday. The trip to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, came about a day after a four-hour ground stop that led to thousands of flights being delayed or cancelled – and an estimated 1.5 million people were stranded.
Evidently, botched maintenance work upgrading telecommunication lines from old copper wire to fiber optic cables in at least one remote location prompted the FAA to implement the ground stop.
Mullin is required to travel on a government aircraft with secure communication systems and pay back the government for personal travel. Still, the homeland security secretary defended his decision to travel for pleasure while many other Americans were stranded.
“We would have never went if the airlines – if the airways – weren’t completely open. [And] they’d been completely open for 21 hours,” Mullin said on an interview on CNBC on Tuesday.
“I would have never taken airspace if the airspace wasn’t open and we still got to live our life at the same time.
“We still have family, friends, and we also have work we do every day.”
Mullin spent part of the game in the box of Ben Bordelon, CEO of Bollinger Shipping, a company that has Department of Homeland Security contracts, the Post reported. Mullin said on CNBC he did not know Bordelon.
He defended his travel as Republicans have sought to cast shift blame away from Donald Trump’s administration for the nationwide ground stop to Congress and the Joe Biden White House prior to Trump’s second presidency.
Democrats have said that characterization is “absurd”, noting that both the Biden administration and Congress have allocated tens of billions of dollars for air traffic control improvements.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Estado precisa reconhecer genocídio e homologar 70 terras indígenas, defende pesquisador
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Larissa Bohrer
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Desde o processo de colonização do Brasil, os povos indígenas são sistematicamente atacados e, ainda assim, resistem em preservar a ancestralidade, seus territórios e o direito de ter a identidade reconhecida e respeitada. O professor e pesquisador Alessandro Martins Prado, da Universidade Estadual de Mato Grosso do Sul (UEMS), debruça-se na realidade dos Guarani Kaiowá, do Mato Grosso do Sul, para entender quais mecanismos da justiça de transição podem ser usados como forma de superar essas graves violações e garantir direitos fundamentais.
O estudo gerou o livro “Justiça de transição e direitos indígenas: o caso dos Guarani e Kaiowá de Mato Grosso do Sul”, em pré-lançamento pela Editora Thoth. Ao Conexão BdF, da Rádio Brasil de Fato, Prado destaca que os direitos fundamentais dos indígenas sempre foram violados, mas há momentos em que essas infrações aprofundam-se, como durante a ditadura. O professor recorda que o agravamento foi validado no relatório oficial da Comissão Nacional da Verdade. “O documento reconhece apenas 490 mortos políticos. Mas são reconhecidos mais de 8 mil indígenas assassinados“, aponta.
Na avaliação de Prado, a ascensão da extrema-direita, por meio do bolsonarismo, “legitimou esses ataques” aos povos indígenas. “No caso do governo Bolsonaro, quase ficou autorizado que houvesse um ataque generalizado aos povos indígenas. Nós tivemos um genocídio dos Yanomami. No caso dos Guarani Kaiowá — que houve, após o segundo turno das eleições, o áudio estimulando o envenenamento da água deles — é um caso de crime contra a humanidade, [passível de ser] julgado pelo Tribunal Penal Internacional”, reforça.
Com relação aos desafios do quarto governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), Alessandro Martins Prado reforça que o princípio de tudo é o reconhecimento formal de que está acontecendo um genocídio. “A palavra assusta, mas, quando você retira esses indígenas das suas terras ancestrais, de forma forçada, desloca-os para pequenas reservas sem espaço suficiente de produzir sua cultura e suas formas de vida, ocorre um desmatamento imenso. Você está promovendo um genocídio porque você está tirando as condições de subsistência de um povo”, defende.
O professor aponta que há, atualmente, cerca de 70 terras indígenas que dependem apenas da assinatura do Executivo para serem homologadas. Esse processo tem um custo financeiro, mas mesmo assim precisa ser feito.
Os impactos vividos pelos indígenas com décadas de violações sistemáticas são muitos. “No caso dos Guarani Kaiowá, eles sofreram um período de expulsão de seu território e espoliação das suas riquezas durante quatro décadas. Isso reflete em uma colonização tardia e que hoje reflete, por exemplo, nos casos de suicídio, que são nove vezes superiores [na comparação com os dados do Brasil]. É um número muito grande. Os índices de mortes violentas por assassinato são comparáveis aos índices de morte no Iraque quando os EUA invadiram o país pela segunda vez.”
Para ouvir e assistir
O jornal Conexão BdF vai ao ar em duas edições, de segunda a sexta-feira: a primeira às 12h e a segunda às 17h, na Rádio Brasil de Fato, 98.9 FM na Grande São Paulo, com transmissão simultânea também pelo YouTube do Brasil de Fato.

https://hyperallergic.com/olivia-reaveys.title: Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality
https://hyperallergic.com/olivia-reaveys.author: Bryan Martin
https://hyperallergic.com/olivia-reaveys.text:
Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality
Everything is a treasured scrap for Reavey to pull from in her unorthodox black-and-white photography.
Olivia Reavey moves at breakneck speed. Her silver-gelatin-analog printing process is frenzied and intense: Black-and-white prints are cut into irregular quadrilaterals with crumpled edges, then hung unframed and loosely fixed to the walls with clips, pins, and other supports. But this is not just slapdash; everything here is intentionally energetic and playful, with images asserting the body’s formal pleasure captured in film.
Many bare their flesh but are often obfuscated or appear with objects: a broken branch covers a male’s buttocks in “Stick” (all works 2026); a wooden lever protrudes from a woman’s pubic area, captured in the reflection of a mirror in “Untitled.” The penetrative and phallic elements here are obvious, but also read neutrally in a recurring tension between eroticism and form — shapes and tonal values outweigh anything provocative.

Kader Attia, curator of the seventh edition of the Kochi–Muziris Biennale (KMB), has announced the focus of the upcoming exhibition will be “the relationship between dreams, memory and repair.” The show will run from December 12, 2027 to March 31, 2028 in the Indian port city of Kochi, Kerala.
In a press release, Attia set the “unpredictability” of dreams and art against AI’s “increasingly predictive logic,” which destroys “our sovereignty over the sources of our dreams.” He also traces the emergence of dreams and memories back through human evolution, where, as a physically weaker species amid the wildness of nature, we began to gather and share memories. According to Attia, the increasing complexity of technology has overtaken human control in how and where our memories develop and are used.
“The art world is one of the last spaces where society co-individuates itself,” Attia says. “Our subjectivity is fragmented, like the internet, an intensely fragmented landscape, yet there we are tracked by the algorithm. Exhibitions are important because they produce emotions, activating new traces in our minds. That is how we produce traces for the future. In the same way we are the traces of our ancestors and of the millions of anonymous subjects who preceded us.”
Attia routes his reflections on thought and subjectivity through the history of Kochi’s harbor—one of India’s largest ports and a historic center for colonial European trade. Despite the lasting “dream of empire” which persists in the mind of Koichi’s residents, the curator argues that it’s possible to reverse exploitative legacies through art.
Dr. Venu V, chair of the Kochi Biennale Foundation, said, “Kader Attia’s multi-layered proposition sets a compelling tone for Kochi–Muziris Biennale 2027. By engaging with history, memory, colonial legacies, and the possibilities of repair, it makes art not merely an aesthetic experience but a means of reflection, dialogue, and understanding.”
