https://gothamist.com/news/woman-arreste.title: Woman arrested after climbing outside of a Manhattan skyscraper's 91st floor, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-arreste.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/woman-arreste.text:
An 18-year-old woman from Portland, Oregon, was pulled off the outside of a Midtown luxury residential tower around its 91st floor Monday evening, police said.
Vivian Warnock was arrested after people called police to report someone climbing the exterior of the Steinway Tower at 111 West 57th St., according to the NYPD. Officers responded just before 5 p.m. and saw her climbing the building's exterior, police said. FDNY firefighters pulled her down, and she was arrested at 5:30 p.m., police said. No injuries were reported.
Police charged Warnock with burglary, a felony, but Manhattan prosecutors reduced the charge to criminal trespassing, a misdemeanor. She pleaded not guilty Tuesday and was released on her own recognizance, according to prosecutors. Court records did not yet include her lawyer information.
The complaint describes her as being inside the building at about 4:30 p.m., but doesn’t say what floor she was on at the time. A building employee watched her go past a sign designating the area for emergencies, according to the complaint. She told an officer she went to the area “for the views,” the complaint states.
The criminal complaint does not describe how Warnock got into the building, how she was able to climb it or how long she was on the outside. Police didn’t provide more information on those matters.
The employee told police Warnock does not live in the building and had no permission to be there, according to the complaint.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Nan Goldin to debut new film exploring nature and extinction in first UK solo museum show in over two decades
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Simon Bainbridge
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
For audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.
What links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.
Rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents new and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.
The show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a new score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.
It accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.
Elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.
For Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas says. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”
• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-
14 March 2027

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-democrat.title: Reject “Electoralism.” Embrace Socialist Electoral Strategy.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-democrat.author: Elliot Lewis
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-democrat.text:
Reject “Electoralism.” Embrace Socialist Electoral Strategy.
Socialists’ recent electoral success has given the US left new life. But socialists need more than elections to achieve major change. Electoral politics must be just one part of a broader strategy to build working-class power inside and outside the state.
In elections this year, 169 (and counting) candidates or ballot initiatives endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) nationally or by its chapters succeeded at city, state, and federal levels. DSA member Zohran Mamdani is the mayor of the largest city in the country, and it seems increasingly possible that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will run for president of the United States in 2028.
These exciting developments raise the question of the role of elections in the socialist project. Today some on the Left refer to socialists running for office as “electoralism.” But that term has a specific historical meaning, which much of the radical left has long viewed with disdain. It’s worth getting clear on what distinguishes electoralism in that sense from a transformative democratic socialist electoral strategy like the one many in DSA are trying to work toward today.
Unlike anarchist or syndicalist approaches to organizing, which view militancy outside of the state as the sole mechanism for bringing about social change, both electoralist and democratic socialist electoral strategies see contesting elections as an important tool for helping bring about socialism. But while electoralism focuses exclusively on winning elections and making change through policy measures, a democratic socialist strategy understands elections and socialist governance as one important means among others of achieving reforms and facilitating the organization of the working class into an agent capable of transforming society.
Electoralism and Social Democracy
Electoralism has existed nearly as long as the socialist movement itself. In Evolutionary Socialism, published in 1899, German socialist Eduard Bernstein argued that capitalism could be gradually overcome through a peaceful electoral path and piecemeal legislative reform. In the early twentieth century, social democratic parties across Western Europe seemingly began making good on this vision, winning state power through elections and attempting to enact pro-worker reforms. Though most early socialists did not think of themselves as “electoralists” and understood the importance of organizing outside the state, particularly in the workplace, over time social democratic strategy focused more and more on winning elections and parliamentary power. Social democrats eventually became electoralists in practice, if not in name.
When social democratic parties were on the rise in the early and mid-twentieth century, the industrial working class was increasingly joining unions and engaging in mass strikes, giving the parties significant political leverage. This combination of power inside and outside the state allowed socialists to pass significant policy measures that improved the lives of millions, like universal health care, vacation for all, and expansive labor rights. The growing power of the working class outside of the state at the time also helped conceal the problems that the social democrats’ increasingly electorally focused strategy would eventually face.
As time wore on, however, social democrats in government found themselves constrained to merely managing capitalist economies — whose center of power lay not in the state but in the hands of private capital owners who could withhold or offshore their investments if they felt sufficiently threatened, causing economic turbulence and eventually leading to socialist electoral defeat. Many social democratic parties began abandoning the end goal of bringing about socialism entirely, focusing on achieving reforms within capitalism instead. The problem was worsened by the fact that the labor movement, social democrats’ traditional base of power, slowly ossified and came to represent an ever smaller proportion of the working class.
In periods of economic stagnation, as in the 1970s and ’80s, this dynamic led socialist governments such as François Mitterrand’s in France to impose austerity measures in an attempt to appease capital and maintain growth. But this too ultimately undermined their popularity and brought about their electoral ousting. In recent decades, declining union density has accelerated this dynamic, leading desperate left-wing parties to try to cobble together broader populist coalitions in order to win a plurality of votes. But these parties have then found that they lacked the organized power outside of the state to overcome the leverage of capital once they entered government, as we saw with the collapse of Podemos in Spain and Syriza in Greece.
The core reason that postwar social democratic parties failed, then, was not that party leaders betrayed their base, but that the structural economic conditions imposed by capitalist social relations give owners of capital significant power over the state, limiting socialists’ ability to implement policy reforms absent independent bases of popular power. Social democrats often took this structural imbalance of power between capital and workers outside of the state as an unchangeable given, adopting an electoralist approach at the expense of reconstituting working-class organization.
An Alternative to Electoralism: a Democratic Socialist Electoral Strategy
Observing the crisis of social democracy in the 1970s, the Marxist philosopher Nicos Poulantzas theorized a democratic socialist electoral strategy as an alternative to both Leninist insurrectionism and social democratic electoralism. For Poulantzas, the state was a terrain of struggle that could be used by socialists to enact transformative change, but only if it was used to help build independent working-class power that would solidify this change and shift power from capital to workers.
Adam Przeworski developed this idea further with the concept of class formation. Przeworski argued that whether proletarians act on their class interests rather than their many other interests (as, e.g., homeowners or college graduates or Catholics) depends on whether a political struggle brings class interests to the fore. This struggle is not just about changing people’s ideas but also about changing the world to materially align people around their shared class interests. For example, socialists in Sweden significantly reduced the wage gap between different types of workers through their “solidaristic wage policy,” thereby not only raising the floor for the lowest-paid workers and reshaping the economy around more efficient industries but also leveling material differences between different segments of the working class.
Today the biggest challenge American socialists face is a politically fragmented working class and a weak labor movement decimated by decades of neoliberal attacks. A democratic socialist electoral strategy aims to use electoral campaigns and socialist governance to slowly rebuild working-class consciousness and organization in order to reconstitute the popular power needed to transform society. Such a strategy situates those efforts within a broader approach alongside equally necessary grassroots organizing in workplaces and neighborhoods.
Using Elections to Agitate and Organize
What does such an electoral strategy, as opposed to mere “electoralism,” look like in practice? For one thing, socialists can use campaign communications to clarify the lines of class struggle. Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaigns exemplified this approach to messaging, with his “Not Me, Us” language, his calls for political revolution, and his frequent finger-pointing at the billionaires who benefit from our current class society.
Once in office, socialists can continue to raise people’s political awareness by pointing out when capital stands in the way of much-needed reform or is otherwise harming the interests of working people. Mayor Mamdani’s “Rental Ripoff Hearings” are an excellent example of this type of us-versus-them line drawing, as are Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s frequent viral denunciations of corporate greed in her House speeches. Electoral campaigns can also be used to build socialist organization, as DSA has done in recent years by building out volunteer-led organizing efforts that engage thousands of volunteers in outreach to the broader working class — not only reaching more voters but also developing activists who may continue organizing in the socialist movement for years to come.
Socialists in office can go beyond changing peoples’ ideas too: they can use their political power to make it easier for workers, renters, and consumers to build collective organization, thereby increasing the potential power of the socialist movement in the long run. One way to facilitate working-class organization is to use the power of the state to bolster organizing directly, for example by helping tenants and workers organize through public offices dedicated to the task, as the Mamdani administration has begun to do with its Office of Tenant Protection and Office of Worker Power.
When socialists have greater political power, they can also pass legislation that directly empowers organizing, like reforming labor law to make it easier to unionize or establishing enforceable collective bargaining rights for tenant unions. With enough power, socialists can start to change the broader structures of the economy to shift power from capital to the working class — for instance, by nationalizing key industries. Even smaller reforms along the way, such as rent freezes and reducing transit costs, can grow support for the socialist project while redistributing resources.
Finally, a democratic socialist electoral strategy recognizes the limited power of elections alone on the road to socialism. While winning elections and passing legislation are an essential part of building political power, democratic socialists must equally prioritize building people power beyond elections through union, tenant, and social movement organizing. Recognizing what elections can’t do is as important as understanding how we can best use them to build power.
Most socialists in the United States today believe in the importance of contesting elections and taking state power to make change. But as the movement grows, socialists should avoid the pitfalls of a pure-and-simple electoralism that focuses on electing candidates and getting policy passed to the exclusion of all else. Such an approach sets the movement up for disaster when capital brings its leverage to bear in the context of a disorganized working class. We should instead be pursuing a democratic socialist electoral strategy, using campaigns and elected office alongside grassroots organizing to help rebuild the independent bases of working-class power that will be needed to achieve socialism in the long run.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Progress Stalls in Reducing 911 Calls for NYC Students in Emotional Distress
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Abigail Kramer, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Crystal Roach felt her hands shake as she ordered an Uber. Her thoughts were racing, imagining her 6-year-old son, Zai, confused and afraid. She pictured his little wrists in handcuffs, and it felt hard to breathe.
Roach had just gotten off the phone with a guidance counselor from Zai’s school — P.S. 11, in Clinton Hill, Brooklyn. Zai had recently been diagnosed with autism. At home, he was funny and affectionate, saying “I love you” and doing silly dances to make Roach laugh, even though he didn’t like being hugged or touched. But for months, he’d been having meltdowns in class and the lunchroom, throwing pencils and books, tearing up papers, hitting other kids or teachers.
School staff called Roach nearly every day, she said, telling her she had to pick up Zai (a family nickname) immediately. Roach told them she couldn’t keep leaving work. She was a single parent and a nanny, and her boss was losing patience.
But this call — in April 2026, near the end of Zai’s first grade — was different: The school had called a mobile crisis team, which in turn called 911. Police and an ambulance were on their way. If Roach didn’t get there first, they’d take Zai to an emergency room. No one could tell her which hospital.
The idea of not knowing where Zai was felt intolerable. Roach frantically dialed her mom and an aunt, trying to find someone who could get to Zai faster.
When she pulled up to the school, there was a police car parked in front. That’s when her fear shifted to disbelief, she said. “I just kept thinking: ‘Cops? For a 6-year-old?’”
New York City schools are only supposed to call 911 on students in the most extreme circumstances. Under city regulations, school staff must do everything they can to de-escalate a student’s behavioral or mental health crisis themselves — only resorting to 911 if someone is at imminent risk of serious physical harm.
When schools do call 911 — incidents known as “child in crisis” calls — police typically show up first, containing students until EMTs arrive. Hundreds of times each year, kids end up in handcuffs — some of them as young as 6 and 7 years old.
In the wake of a 2013 lawsuit, the city adopted rules aimed at reducing child in crisis calls, including quarterly reporting requirements and crisis intervention training for schools. In 2023, after an investigation by ProPublica and The City Reporter, the New York City Council passed a law requiring police to document whether schools had attempted to de-escalate a crisis before involving EMTs or cops.
But while the number of calls dropped after the lawsuit was settled, progress has largely stalled. New York City schools continue to call 911 on students in emotional distress well over 2,000 times a year.
Child in crisis calls are far more likely to happen to students with disabilities and Black students, and they frequently involve very young kids. Since 2016, when the city first started tracking the numbers, schools have called 911 more than 5,000 times on children who were less than 10 years old, according to city data.
Families and mental health providers say that hauling kids to hospitals is traumatic, humiliating and often counterproductive. In most cases, students wait for hours in crowded ERs, only to be evaluated and sent home without treatment, advocates say.
“Calling 911 doesn’t make anything better at school the next day,” said Nelson Mar, a senior attorney at Legal Services NYC who is working with Roach to secure special education services for Zai.
Mar also led the 2013 lawsuit that prompted the city to adopt its first formal limits on schools’ use of 911. But while the settlement led to gains, he said, it failed to address the root causes of child in crisis incidents. Despite federal laws requiring school districts to serve students with disabilities, most city schools lack the training and resources to support kids who’ve experienced serious trauma, or whose disabilities manifest in disruptive behavior.
By the time a situation escalates to the point where school staff consider calling 911, they’ve likely missed countless opportunities to help a kid succeed, advocates and educators say.
In a March 2026 letter to the Mamdani administration, Mar and other advocates urged the city to expand behavioral interventions in city schools. Among their recommendations: Staff each district with specialists who can help schools create detailed behavior plans for struggling kids; train teachers to understand common behavior patterns in neurodivergent students; and expand initiatives like the Path program, which uses evidence-based strategies to support students with emotional disabilities in general education classrooms.
When schools have more tools, they can become more “healing-centered and less punitive,” Mar said. “There needs to be a culture shift.”
How Bureaucracy and Punishment Left a First Grader Without Help
Zai’s troubles started near the beginning of first grade. When school staff first raised concerns about his behavior, Roach trusted they wanted what was best for him, she said. Zai’s big sister had attended P.S. 11 and left with a wall full of achievement awards.
Roach enrolled Zai in therapy and took time off work to sit in his classroom. On the school’s advice, she requested an evaluation for an individualized education program — a document that could entitle Zai to special education services to help him regulate his meltdowns.
But the evaluation was delayed for months, long beyond the legal deadline, despite Roach’s repeated emails pleading with the school to speed up the process. As the delays stretched on, she said, Zai’s meltdowns became more frequent and the school’s response more punitive.
He came home calling himself “a bad kid,” something he heard from a teacher, Roach said. He often had to miss recess or eat lunch alone, as a punishment for something he’d done on a previous day.
Desperate for help, Roach took Zai to a neurologist, who diagnosed him with autism.
Based on that diagnosis, Zai’s school could have provided him services through a “504 plan,” using its discretionary budget to assign him a one-on-one paraprofessional who’d help him calm down when he got agitated. They also could have sought help from the district to create a detailed behavior plan identifying Zai’s triggers and strategies to prevent his meltdowns.
“They didn’t do any of that,” Roach said.
In an occurrence report from April, P.S. 11 Principal Abidemi Hope wrote that the school had tried several interventions for Zai, “including my direct involvement as principal, At-Risk counseling services, and structured morning and afternoon check-ins with support staff.”
Despite these efforts, Hope wrote, Zai’s “behaviors have continued to escalate in both frequency and severity, surpassing the school’s capacity to safely manage them within the general education setting.”
To Roach, it seemed like P.S. 11 just wanted to get rid of Zai, even before completing his assessment or providing him with a full set of services.
“He was just seen as a problem child,” she said.
It’s not unusual for kids with difficult behaviors to be pushed out of general education schools. According to a data analysis released last week by the New York City Independent Budget Office, almost 30% of students classified as having emotional disabilities are placed in separate, special-education schools run by District 75.
Overwhelmingly, they end up concentrated in a handful of schools where attendance and graduation rates are among the poorest in the city — and where they are even likelier to be subject to a 911 call.
A Team Meant To Prevent 911 Calls Made One Instead
In the last decade, the city has launched several initiatives designed to make schools less punitive and more supportive, including healing-centered schools, the “mental health continuum,” and restorative justice programs.
Proponents say those programs benefit all kids, not just those with serious mental health or behavioral struggles. But they remain small and marginal, frequently losing momentum and funding when political priorities shift.
More recently, city officials have encouraged schools to make use of mobile crisis teams — mental health professionals who can respond in anywhere from a few hours to a few days to triage struggling students and help them connect to longer-term services if necessary. One of the teams’ explicit goals is to keep people in crisis away from unnecessary encounters with police and trips to the ER.
When P.S. 11 staff told Roach about the crisis team program, she thought it sounded like a good idea.
On the day the school called the team, Zai had a meltdown after a change in his schedule, flipping tables, throwing classroom materials and punching a teacher in the stomach, according to a school occurrence report. The teacher took Zai on a walk around the school to help “settle his nervous system,” the report said. They encountered another staff member, who began to question Zai about misbehavior on the previous day. Zai ran away and sat on a bench.
Zai was calm and back in class when the crisis team arrived later in the day. When he was pulled out to meet with the two crisis responders, along with Hope and other school staff, however, he got upset again. Zai kicked Hope, then drew a picture of her, scribbled over her face and wrote, “Weak, you should die.”
In the crisis de-escalation plan that P.S. 11 filed with the city last year, staff are instructed to remove distressed students from the environment that is setting them off and attempt to have a conversation “exploring the student’s point of view.”
Those steps were not taken in the incident with Zai. According to the report, staff reprimanded him, instructing him to speak politely as his behaviors began to escalate. Hope — who was the focus of Zai’s behavior — remained in the room as he started to throw erasers and books at her and push away staff members who tried to intervene. That’s when the mobile crisis team called 911.
VNS Health, the nonprofit agency that deployed the crisis team, declined to comment, citing client privacy. Neither the principal nor Education Department officials responded to specific questions about Zai’s experience.
In an emailed statement, spokesperson Onika Richards wrote, “Under no circumstance is 911 ever called simply for a student’s behavior — or to cause student arrest or pressure to transfer out of our schools. 911 is only called as an alternative, when an emotional or behavioral crisis has exceeded the ability of the school staff to address it safely.”
She added, “Our students are children who need support, not children who should be criminalized or handcuffed.”
When Roach arrived at Zai’s school, she found him standing silently, surrounded by two police officers, the two members of the crisis team and Hope. Two more officers were coming through the door.
Her worst fears were relieved: Zai was still in the building, he was unhurt and he wasn’t wearing handcuffs. But he looked scared and small, rocking back and forth and flicking his fingers in the way he does to soothe himself when he’s upset.
“What crime did he commit?” she asked later. “I have a 6-year-old child that was treated more like a criminal.”
After the 911 call, Mar helped Zai transfer to P.S. 20, another school in Clinton Hill, where he was assigned a paraprofessional within weeks. When he got overwhelmed or appeared to be escalating, staff gave him choices about where to go, including rooms stocked with calming tools such as Legos and sensory toys.
In the three months before school broke for summer, Roach said she picked Zai up early only once — after he saw a police car outside the school and panicked.
Abigail Kramer is a New York City-based journalist. You can reach her at: abigailkramer@gmail.com.

Film „La bola negra“: Vom Fragment zum Epos
Der Film „La bola negra“ verwebt drei schwule Lebensgeschichten rund um Federico García Lorca. Vergangenheit und Gegenwart greifen dabei ineinander.
Selbst in einem etwas trägen Kinojahr wie diesem gibt es sie: die wahrlich großen Filme, die etwas genuin Neues schaffen. „La bola negra“ gehört zu ihnen, auch wenn seine Eröffnung zunächst auf eine falsche Fährte führt und ein Kino verspricht, das ganz auf Spektakel setzt. Flugzeuge dröhnen heran, als sich die Bewohner eines abgelegenen Dorfs in der kargen andalusischen Landschaft in dessen Mitte versammeln.
„Willkommen Mussolini!“ steht auf einem Fähnchen, auf einem Podest haben sich Musiker in Stellung gebracht. Immer wieder fokussiert die Kamera einen jungen Trompeter, der in der Menge seine Mutter entdeckt und sie ermuntert, den rechten Arm zu heben, so wie es die Bauern, Frauen und Kinder um sie herum bereits getan haben.
Dann zischt und kracht es, die ersten Bomben schlagen ein. Menschen werden getroffen und zu Boden gerissen, Staub und Trümmer fliegen durch die Luft. Binnen Sekunden verwandelt sich die eigentümliche Versammlung in ein ohrenbetäubendes Inferno.
Der Film
„La bola negra“. Regie: Javier Calvo und Javier Ambrossi. Mit Guitarricadelafuente, Miguel Bernardeau u.a. Spanien/Frankreich 2026, 155 Min.
Dass Spanien im Jahr 1937 in einen Bürgerkrieg verstrickt ist, in dem die Zweite Republik gegen die unter Franco versammelten Putschisten kämpft, und dass Mussolinis Italien aufseiten ebenjener Nationalisten steht, hier also Verbündete im Geiste bombardiert werden: Das muss man sich entweder aus dem eigenen Geschichtswissen erschließen oder sich aus Randbemerkungen im weiteren Verlauf zusammensetzen.
Wie in einem alchemistischen Prozess
Darin liegt eine der großen Besonderheiten von „La bola negra“, in der stillen Raffinesse seiner Details und der Kunst ihrer Verflechtungen. Auf seiner Flucht durch eine zerstörte Kirche erklimmt der Trompeter, der sich wenig später als Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) zu erkennen gibt, etwa die Trümmer einer überdimensionierten Statue des heiligen Sebastian.
Das ist nicht nur wegen seines Namens eine schöne Anspielung, sondern auch, weil der von Pfeilen durchbohrte, für seine Schönheit bekannte Märtyrer als Schutzpatron der Schwulen gilt. Wer um seine Bedeutung weiß, ahnt bereits, welche Sehnsüchte Sebastián auf seinem Weg entdecken wird.
Wie in einem alchemistischen Prozess kristallisiert sich allerdings erst allmählich heraus, worauf eine letztlich fast ein Jahrhundert umspannende Erzählung hinaus will. Bevor Javier Calvo und Javier Ambrossi die Geschichte von Sebastián vertiefen, wechselt der Film erstmals die Zeitebene, zu einem weiteren seiner insgesamt drei Handlungsstränge – in einer fließenden Bewegung, wie sie sich in „La bola negra“ immer wieder vollzieht: Schon Momente zuvor setzt ein Wechsel in der Musik ein, der die Szenen ineinander bluten und einander antworten lässt.
Die Frage der Zugehörigkeit
Im Mittelpunkt des zweiten Kapitels steht der zwanzigjährige Carlos (Milo Quifes), der sich im Granada des Jahres 1932 um die Aufnahme ins örtliche Casino bewirbt, einen exklusiven Gesellschaftsklub, in dem hochrangige Militärs, Geistliche und die wohlhabenden Vertreter der städtischen Oberschicht über seine Zugehörigkeit entscheiden.
Dem speziellen Verfahren, mit dem darüber abgestimmt wird, verdankt der Film zumindest indirekt seinen Titel: Mit weißen und schwarzen Kugeln, bolas negras also, wird über Carlos’ Schicksal geurteilt, während über den Köpfen der versammelten Honoratioren Bauarbeiter an der imposanten Saalkuppel arbeiten.
Der Wille zur Restauration ist schließlich auch unter ihnen ungebrochen: Die Zweite Spanische Republik, der Kultur und dem Schöngeistigen zugewandt, in der auch schwule Männer auf etwas größere Freiheiten hoffen durften, wurde gerade erst ausgerufen, da arbeiten die reaktionären Kräfte schon wieder an ihrem Rückbau. Als sich schließlich die schwarzen Kugeln mehren, ist klar, dass Carlos abgelehnt wurde. Der Grund sind Gerüchte über seine Homosexualität.
Körper liegen aufeinander
Was Carlos noch die Zugehörigkeit kostet, lebt der junge Historiker Alberto (Carlos González), Protagonist der dritten Zeitebene, mit einer Selbstverständlichkeit, die keiner Erklärung mehr bedarf. Im Athen des Jahres 2017 ist er auf der Suche nach den Spuren einer vergangenen queeren Kultur, durchstöbert Märkte nach Musikaufnahmen aus dem Konstantinopel der 1920er Jahre für seine Promotion in Spanien, lässt sich von alten Melodien und den verschlungenen Geschichten ihrer Interpreten in den Bann ziehen.
Sein eigenes Begehren kennt derweil weit weniger Umstände: Über die App „Grindr“ verabredet er sich zu einem schnellen Sexdate mit einem muskulösen Fremden. Nackte Körper liegen aufeinander, ineinander verschlungen.
Nur einen Augenblick später, zurück im Spanien des Jahres 1937, sind es wieder Körper, die übereinanderliegen, nun aber tot oder schwer verwundet, zu einem wimmernden Haufen aus Fleisch und Gliedmaßen geworden. Es ist ein Schnitt von solcher Präzision, dass die Montage in „La bola negra“ selbst zu erzählen beginnt: von der Gewalt, die zwischen diesen Körpern liegt, von acht Jahrzehnten spanischer und schwuler Geschichte und den so unterschiedlichen Graden an Freiheit, die sich in diesem Bild zwischen ihnen auftun.
Gespräche über Theater und Poesie
Unter ihnen befindet sich Rafael Rodríguez Rapún (Miguel Bernardeau), halb nackt, mehr tot als lebendig. Sebastián, der inzwischen auf einem Militärstützpunkt der Nationalisten dient, dienen muss, soll ihn bewachen und den verwundeten Kämpfer der verfeindeten republikanischen Seite aushorchen. Stattdessen verstricken sich die beiden bald in tastende Gespräche über Theater und Poesie. Und die Art, wie Sebastián ihn ansieht, verrät, dass er darüber auch romantische Gefühle für Rafael entwickelt.
Was Sebastián zu diesem Zeitpunkt noch nicht weiß: Der Mann, den er bewachen soll, war einst der Geliebte Federico García Lorcas. Der Dramatiker, der heute zu den bedeutendsten des Landes zählt, war im Jahr zuvor von den Faschisten verhaftet und ermordet worden. Vorher arbeitete er an „La bola negra“, seinem ersten Theaterstück mit einem ausdrücklich schwulen Protagonisten. Es sollte unvollendet bleiben. Was von ihm geblieben ist, vor dem Vergessen zu bewahren, wird nun zu Rafaels letztem Anliegen.
Wie weit die Leben dieser Männer ineinandergreifen, wie sorgsam Javier Calvo und Javier Ambrossi sie über die Jahrzehnte hinweg miteinander verwoben haben und wie kunstvoll sich letztlich alles fügt, macht einen der großen Reize von „La bola negra“ aus. Mehr soll deswegen an dieser Stelle nicht vorweggenommen werden. Nur so viel: Was sich allmählich offenbart, ist nicht allein die Verbundenheit einzelner Schicksale, sondern auch, wie untrennbar die Erfahrungen schwuler Männer mit der Geschichte Spaniens verbunden sind.
Geschichten aus dem kollektiven Gedächtnis getilgt
„La bola negra“ erzählt nicht von einer Geschichte neben der Geschichte, von einer queeren Parallelwelt, die sich abseits der großen historischen Ereignisse entwickelt hätte. Ohne auch nur in die Nähe gut gemeinter, aber ungalanter Repräsentationsgesten zu geraten, führen Javier Calvo und Javier Ambrossi vor, dass schwule Männer immer Teil all dessen waren, von Spanien selbst, von seinen politischen Verwerfungen und gesellschaftlichen Umbrüchen – auch wenn ihre Geschichten aus dem kollektiven Gedächtnis getilgt wurden. Dass sich in dieses große Panorama mit Glenn Close als „Lorca“-Forscherin und Penélope Cruz als Varieté-Tänzerin auch noch zwei Hollywoodstars einfügen, ist angesichts dessen, was das in Cannes mit dem Regiepreis ausgezeichnete Duo hier erzählt und leistet, beinahe eine schöne Zugabe.
Denn mehr als alles andere ist „La bola negra“ ein schwules Epos – womöglich das erste, das diesem Titel in seiner ganzen Bedeutung gerecht wird. Mit einer Größe, die für queere Erzählungen weiterhin selten ist, werden die Vergangenen gewürdigt, die den Mut fanden, ihr Begehren zu leben, zu benennen und zu beschreiben. Javier Calvo und Javier Ambrossi lassen keine Zweifel daran, dass es ihr Mut ist, auf dem die Freiheit heutiger schwuler, lesbischer und trans Menschen gründet.
Doch auch diese Freiheit ist in „La bola negra“ letztlich keine abgeschlossene Geschichte. In der letzten Bewegung des Films finden die drei Zeitebenen noch einmal zusammen. Ein Sonett aus Federico García Lorcas „Sonetos del amor oscuro“, das Rafael bei sich trägt und an Sebastián weitergibt, durchweht die finalen Szenen. Sein letzter Vers wird zugleich zum letzten Satz von „La bola negra“: „¡Mira que nos acechan todavía!“
„Schau, sie lauern uns noch immer auf.“

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.author: Oliver Heidkamp
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.text:
- Kultur
- Politisches Theater
»Inside Bundestag«: Wo ist der Drive hin?
»Inside Bundestag«, fünfte Episode: Flehende Verzweiflung und dilettantische Tänze antworten auf das allgemeine politische Kopfschütteln.
Die Resignation hat seit Trump I, das ist keine allzu gewagte Theorie, vermutlich weltweit zugenommen. Die leeren Blicke, das Kopfschütteln und das hörbare Ausatmen, nicht zu vergessen das leise Fluchen, die Reaktionen also auf die Polarisierungen von rechts. Gut also, dass im Ballhaus Prinzenallee in Berlin eine Art temporärer Bundestag zu besuchen ist, der der Abstumpfung, dem politischen Desinteresse, auf die solche Polarisierungen auch in deutschen Parlamentsdebatten abzielen, etwas entgegenzusetzen weiß.
Anhand ausgewählter Debatten (Regie: Lukas David Schmidt, Dramaturgie: Mia Massmann) werden die Sitzungswochen nicht nur reinszeniert. Im Laufe einer jeden seriell angelegten Episode, catchige Songs mit hohem Wiedererkennungsmerkmal inklusive, präsentieren die Theatermacher auch ein Gegenmittel. Es ist wohl das, was jede und jeder vor den Endgeräten macht: mal mehr und mal weniger clever in Gegenrede treten.
Im Ballhaus Prinzenallee antwortet nicht die Stille der eigenen vier Wände, sondern, im besten Fall, das Lachen der Gemeinschaft. Dabei wird nicht im Stil der Verunglimpfung und des Treffens unter der Gürtellinie gegen die Populisten gewettert. Man passt sich also nicht den Methoden der hegemoniesüchtigen Männer und Frauen an, die aus den Gefühlen des Volks eine giftige Suppe brühen.
Im Weddinger Bundestag persiflierte am Freitagabend Caroline Hanke etwa die Dobrindtschen Tiraden gegen Gen-Z-Demonstranten dergestalt, dass ihr pointiertes Armschwenken genügte, um die Lobhudeleien auf die »Polizistinnen und Polizisten« zur allgemeinen Belustigung zu überzeichnen. Darüber hinaus ließ sie das mangelnde Verständnis des Bundesministers des Innern für die Proteste gegen strukturelle Gewalt und für gute Schulen erkennen.
Solch helle Momente waren an diesem Abend, der fünften Episode, ansonsten rar. Tobias Artner gelangen sie auch. Nele Trebs flehende Verzweiflung, mit der sie die Klagen der Klimaaktivisten unterlegte, mussten auflaufen. Das liegt in der Natur der Kassandrarufe. Dass einiges anderes an diesem Abend keinen Widerhall fand, scheint jedoch weniger mit schauspielerischen Leistungen als eher an einer unausgegorenen Setzung gelegen zu haben, wie sich in der Half-Time-Show dann zeigte. Die Tanzeinlagen von Trash Deluxe fügten sich ungewollt in den übrigen, recht frei drehenden Abend ein, sorgten aber immerhin für Unterhaltung, weil sie eben genau so dilettantisch sein wollten.
Die vergangenen Episoden haben der Wut angesichts der politischen Verhältnisse ein Ventil verliehen. Der Aufführung vom Freitagabend vergangener Woche aber fehlte der drive, das naiv-schrullige, überzeugende Pathos, mit theatralen Mitteln die Fackel der Gerechtigkeit hochzuhalten, mit der die Reihe bisher als modernes Agitprop überzeugen konnte. Vielleicht ist die Luft nach fünf Folgen ja raus, das Theaterexperiment am Ende. Oder wird es in der letzten, sechsten Episode zu einem krönenden Abschluss kommen, wird es wieder gelingen, den Polarisierungen liebevoll kuratierte, freundliche Eingriffe entgegen- und einen common ground herzustellen? Wir werden sehen.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ge.title: Cologne Auction House Moves Forward with Sale of Gothic Paintings as Jewish Dealer’s Heirs Claim They Were ‘Stolen’
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ge.author: Alex Greenberger
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ge.text:
The Cologne-based Lempertz auction house said it still planned to sell two works by Gothic painter Johann Koerbecke after the heirs of a German Jewish art dealer who was persecuted by the Nazis claimed the pieces were “stolen.”
Dealer Max Stern held the paintings in Düsseldorf between 1936 and 1937, the year the Nazis shut down his gallery. Per a provenance supplied by Lempertz, both paintings were then held by Düsseldorf’s Galerie Hans Bammann, which appears to have then sold them.
On Monday, the Dr. Max and Iris Stern Foundation issued a release in which it called on Lempertz to stop the sale of the two works planned for Saturday. According to the foundation, such a sale should not occur “until two distinct ownership claims of different victims are justly resolved according to the Washington Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art.”
Both paintings—The Annunciation and The Vision of Saint Bernard—are likely from Marienfeld high altarpiece, which was completed in 1457. They are being auctioned in a sale of Old Masters art. They carry high estimates of around 300,000 euros each, or about $329,000 apiece, making them the auction’s most expensive works. “For art historical reasons,” the Lempertz lot entries read, “the two important panels (Lots 1005 and 1006) will first be offered individually and then together.”
The Dr. Max and Iris Stern Foundation pointed out that both works appear in several databases of missing artworks, including the Interpol Database of Stolen Art since 2021. On the German Lost Art Database, both are reported as “Nazi-confiscated property”; the foundation registered that claim with the organization in 2018.
The foundation has demanded the return of multiple artworks belonging to Stern over the past decade, and in some cases, it has been successful. In 2017, for example, the FBI returned a painting by Jan Franse Verzijl that had been on view at an US art fair two years earlier.
Potentially complicating the matter is the fact that, prior to Stern’s possession of the Koerbecke paintings, they were owned by Ellen Funke, who, during the Nazi era, was classified as a Mischling, or “mongrel,” because she had Jewish ancestry through her mother. She sold her collection in 1936 to fund her emigration from Germany, and works she once owned have also been the subject of restitution claims—two of which happen to involve the Koerbecke works.
In 2025, Bavaria’s state museums restituted Koerbecke’s Vision of Saint Bernard to Funke’s heirs. At the time, the Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen noted that The Vision of Saint Bernard and The Annunciation were at one point part of a single work, with both images appearing on either side of the same panel, and that Stern had taken them apart with the hope of selling them both. Funke’s heirs are listed as the sellers of The Vision of Saint Bernard on the auction house’s website.
Similarly, Funke’s heirs are also listed as the sellers of the The Annunciation, which entered the Kolumba Art Museum of the Archdiocese of Cologne as a donation in 1996. The museum restituted the work in 2025.
The Dr. Max and Iris Stern Foundation’s release notably does not mention Funke by name. But it does state that the foundation “maintains that the rights and histories of both Jewish victims must be taken into account, and neither claim should be privileged at the expense of the other.” In an email to ARTnews, a spokesperson for the foundation said “the museums restituted the paintings to Ellen Funke’s heirs in accordance with the priority principle set forth in the guidelines established in Germany to apply the Washington Principles,” adding that that restitution ”did not result in a ‘just and fair solution’ in accordance with the Washington Principles.”
In a statement to ARTnews, Lempertz said it would not cancel its planned sale of the paintings by Koerbecke, who is widely considered one of the great painters of the Gothic era in Germany.
“We adhere to current restitution practices and follow the recommendations of the Federal Government,” a representative for the auction house said, claiming that the Stern “had the panels sawn in two” and went on to sell one of them for “double the price.”
“These magnificent paintings were not taken away from Max Stern,” the Lempertz representative said, adding, “Max Stern received compensation after the war; the heirs of the Funke family did not.”
The Stern Foundation spokesperson said the “view that the paintings were not ‘seized’ from Max Stern has long been refuted,” citing a 2019 statement from the now-defunct German Advisory Commission that the persecution of Jewish art dealers began at latest by August 1933, “so that from that point on at the latest, it can in no way be assumed that ‘proper, customary business transactions’ took place.” The spokesperson added that the claim that Max Stern was compensated for the paintings is “incorrect“ and has “no legal basis.”
Lempertz did not dispute the listings for both paintings on the Art Loss Register, but the representative also noted that the listings contain details of the works’ respective restitutions.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: National Security Agency network for internal communications goes down
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down.
In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events.
The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored.
The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily.
The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said.
Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff.
A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong.
The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights, a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services. None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible.
Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.”
He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe.
Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions.
While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly.
“Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week (Outlook, the FAA, the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like.
“What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”
Shrai Popat contributed reporting

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Ato contra negacionismo científico reúne estudantes, políticos e artistas na UFSC
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Vitória Vasconcellos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A União da Juventude Socialista (UJS) organizou um ato em resposta à presença da deputada federal Júlia Zanatta (PL-SC), do deputado federal Guilherme Colombo (PL-SC) e do não eleito deputado estadual Paulo Kogos (PL-SP) na Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina (UFSC), nesta segunda-feira (16). A manifestação ocorreu no varandão do Centro de Comunicação e Expressão (CCE), onde políticos, estudantes e artistas conversaram sobre o negacionismo científico e o contexto político atual.
O deputado estadual Marquito (Psol-SC) enfatizou que a universidade pública representa um espaço de combate à desinformação e não pode ser palco de retrocesso científico e social. Na mesma linha, a deputada federal Giovana Mondardo (PCdoB-SC) reafirmou o compromisso com o debate de ideias, mas explica: “Querem transformar a universidade em palanque para narrativas perigosas para a sociedade”.
A fala da deputada se refere à palestra com os temas “Libertarianismo tropical”, ministrada por Kogos, e “Armando a liberdade: o Direito Natural ao Armamento e o Poder do Estado”, por Zanatta. O último painel foi sobre o tema “Libertarianismo na Política Institucional”, em que Kogos, Zanatta e Colombo se apresentaram juntos. A palestra ocorreu no mesmo dia e horário da manifestação (16) e foi organizada pelo Núcleo Rothbard de Estudos em Escola Austríaca (Nurea), projeto de extensão do curso de Arquitetura e Urbanismo.
A jovem militante Larissa Stephanie (PCdoB-SC) foi uma das convidadas para o ato. Ela diz que militâncias como esta são importantes para ressaltar a participação ativa da juventude na política. Para ela, as palestras no CTC “são movimentos controversos para demonstrar poder e atacar a universidade”.
O vereador Leonel Camasão (Psol-SC) argumenta que o encontro de estudantes e políticos de extrema direita é um contraponto: “Vejo que nós precisamos ignorar, buscar um caminho de ignorar eles, principalmente os mais provocantes, um momento que alguém perde a cabeça e eles colocam isso pra viralizar nas redes, criar fato político”.
Júlia Zanatta e a polêmica da vacinação infantil
A deputada Zanatta é autora de diversas iniciativas legislativas contra a obrigatoriedade da vacinação infantil e defende o perdão de sanções financeiras aplicadas a pais que optaram por não imunizar os filhos contra a covid-19. O Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente traz expressamente que “é obrigatória a vacinação das crianças nos casos recomendados pelas autoridades sanitárias” (§ 1º do Art. 14 do ECA).
Descumprir o calendário de vacinação infantil pode ser entendido como falta de cuidado e negligência dos responsáveis pelos menores, podendo acarretar perda da guarda e do poder familiar dos filhos. Se a criança não vacinada morrer em decorrência de uma das doenças cobertas pela vacinação obrigatória os pais ou responsáveis podem ser penalizados, nos termos do Código Penal, por homicídio culposo.
Após o fim dos discursos, alguns estudantes e professores universitários que estavam no varandão foram até o Centro Tecnológico (CTC) da UFSC, no estacionamento do prédio onde ocorria o evento com Zanatta e Kogos. A Polícia Militar também estava no local, mas ficou em frente à entrada do prédio. Os manifestantes fizeram um protesto pacífico.

https://hyperallergic.com/meet-natalie-w.title: Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer
https://hyperallergic.com/meet-natalie-w.author: Sarah Cascone
https://hyperallergic.com/meet-natalie-w.text:
Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer
The artist is among the few shooting on the company’s 20x24, creating otherworldly double-exposure self-portraits with a rapidly dwindling stock of nearly 20-year-old film.
WHATELY, Mass. — The text message said to head around back to the barn, an only slightly ominous-looking structure with heavily weathered wooden siding, tucked off a winding road in Franklin County, Massachusetts. Inside was one of the world’s only 20x24 Polaroid Land Cameras — sometimes referred to as the Giant Polaroid — and the artist Natalie White, shooting with a rapidly dwindling stock of nearly 20-year-old film long past its expiration date.
A muse and model-turned-photographer, performance artist, and feminist activist, White just debuted 15 of her unique large-format Polaroids in Natalie White: Strange Magick, a selling exhibition at Phillips Los Angeles. The images are colorful and dreamy, close-up portraits of the artist with an otherworldly quality. Each photo is a double exposure, an unpredictable process that creates ghostly effects with White’s hands and fingers overlaid atop her face.
To achieve this, White leaves the film in the camera after pushing the shutter, takes a second shot, and hopes for the best.
“We’re giving all control to the negative,” White told Hyperallergic. “We always joke that there’s a little magical man painting inside the camera who decides what the double exposure is going to look like.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.title: Whistleblower: Deadly drone strike in Kuwait could’ve been avoided
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
Whistleblower: Deadly drone strike in Kuwait could’ve been avoided
Whistleblower accuses the military of dismissing advanced security warnings of a drone strike that killed six US soldiers in Kuwait.
Washington, DC – An American soldier wounded in a deadly Iranian drone attack in Kuwait is accusing senior military officials of ignoring warnings and being ill-equipped ahead of launching the US-Israel war on Iran, according to a whistleblower complaint.
The complaint, obtained by Al Jazeera English on Tuesday, is tied to an Iranian one-way attack drone that evaded air defences at the outpost within the first 48 hours of the war. Six service members were killed, and dozens were injured, including the whistleblower. It remains the deadliest assault on US forces since the war commenced.
The 14-page letter, submitted on Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees, alleges that the army repeatedly brushed aside warnings that the Port of Shuaiba in Kuwait was vulnerable to drone attacks. Though the site was fortified, there was no roof.
“The drone threat to the port was raised directly to the commanding general of the 1st Theater Sustainment Command at least three times in the week before hostilities,” the complaint states.
“Each warning was dismissed.”
The soldier, who is not named, also alleges the installation had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance”, adding that at least one of those killed “could have survived” if there was adequate medical support on site.
The army says it has completed its investigation of the Port of Shuaiba attack but has not publicly released its findings.
In a news conference following the incident, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described the drone as a “squirter” that “happened to hit a tactical operations centre that was fortified”.
But senior military leaders have acknowledged that Iran’s Shahed attack drones, known to fly low and slow, have inflicted more damage on the battlefield than anticipated.
Tehran has repeatedly targeted US and allied assets with attack drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, more than 23 American service members have been killed.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the allegations.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/trending/m.author: MEE staff
https://www.middleeasteye.net/trending/m.text:
Mamdani's moustache sparks meltdown as critics see Saddam Hussein, terrorism and NYC's demise
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has sparked a fresh wave of outrage over what may be his most controversial political statement yet: his moustache.
Facial hair took centre stage on Monday after Mamdani posted a video announcing the disbandment of the New York Police Department's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a controversial police unit responsible for both counterterrorism operations and policing protests.
But while Mamdani was busy explaining the overhaul, some online appeared far more concerned with what was happening directly above his upper lip.
For certain critics, the moustache was apparently all it took to transform New York City's first Muslim mayor into the deceased former Iraqi dictator, Saddam Hussein.
For a moment I thought I saw Saddam.
— Abhijit Chavda (@AbhijitChavda) November 16, 2026

Conservative commentator Will Chamberlain offered an even more elaborate interpretation of the mayor's facial hair.
"Trying to beat the allegations of being an Islamist by adopting the aesthetics of the secular Ba’athists," he wrote on X.
Apparently, the moustache had not only become a political statement but an ideological rebranding exercise, with Mamdani allegedly swapping Islamist imagery for the look associated with the secular Arab nationalist movement that once ruled Iraq under Hussein.
All this from a few millimetres of facial hair.
It looks like Saddam Hussein is running NYC.
— Spencer Pratt (@spencerpratt) November 16, 2026
The timing of Mamdani's announcement only added fuel to the outrage.
Some critics interpreted the disbandment of the SRG as evidence that the Muslim mayor was weakening New York's counterterrorism capabilities, with the moustache seemingly providing all the visual confirmation they needed.
One user took the alarm a step further, writing: "Terrorists have realised it's easier to get elected by Democrats than to fly planes into buildings."
The implication was hardly subtle: New York's first Muslim mayor was not merely dismantling a counterterrorism unit but somehow represented the very threat it was supposed to combat.
By then, the moustache had graduated from a questionable fashion choice to a full-blown national security emergency.
But the NYPD is not abandoning counterterrorism.
Under the restructuring announced by Mamdani and police commissioner Jessica Tisch, the SRG's counterterrorism responsibilities will be transferred to the department's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau, while protest policing will be handled separately.
The changes follow years of criticism over the SRG's aggressive tactics against demonstrators.
Still, the combination of a Muslim mayor, a disbanded police unit and a newly prominent moustache proved irresistible to those inclined to see a national security threat in a grooming decision.
Far-right activist Laura Loomer, who has repeatedly promoted anti-Muslim rhetoric, was quick to offer her own interpretation, once again framing a Muslim politician's actions as evidence of an impending Islamist threat.
Muslim Mayor gets elected in NYC and immediately moves to eradicate the counter terrorism program in NYC. Gee, I wonder why? 🤔 As I said, jihad is coming. Soon Americans will experience their very own October 7th style events in American neighborhoods . The Islamic takeover of America is rapidly accelerating.
— Laura Loomer (@LauraLoomer) November 16, 2026
Apparently, reorganising a police unit was now proof of an imminent terrorist takeover.
And the explanation behind the supposedly ominous new look makes the controversy even more remarkable.
Mamdani had already announced in early November that he was participating in Movember, an annual campaign encouraging men to grow moustaches to raise awareness about prostate cancer, testicular cancer and men's mental health.
He also announced a $4m investment in a new prostate cancer centre at Kings County Hospital in the borough of Brooklyn.
In other words, the moustache that some interpreted as a tribute to Middle Eastern authoritarianism was actually intended to promote cancer awareness.
The reactions also illustrate how quickly familiar anti-Muslim stereotypes can enter the conversation, with a Muslim politician's appearance and decisions on policing being interpreted through the lens of terrorism.
If you’re a brown guy participating in Movember people will immediately start accusing you of becoming a totalitarian dictator.
— Murtaza Hussain (@MazMHussain) November 17, 2026
For now, Mamdani's moustache remains the subject of online debate, while New York's counterterrorism responsibilities remain within the NYPD.
Whether the internet can survive another two weeks of Movember is another question entirely.

Swiss video artist Pipilotti Rist has been named the winner of the 2027 Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts, presented by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Rist will receive the honor in a ceremony taking place April 8, 2027. She will receive a $100,000 cash prize and will undertake a residency at the school that spring.
“Pipilotti Rist has spent four decades using digital tools to dissolve the line between screen, body, building, and landscape,” said MIT Vice Provost for the Arts Keeril Makan in a statement. “Her immersive multimedia installations slow us down, return us to our bodies and the spaces we occupy, and gather us into shared experience, rather than fragmenting our attention.”
Rist is known for her pathbreaking immersive video and light installations investigating the relationships between the body, nature, and technology. Among her most recognized works is 1997’s Ever Is Over All, in which she walks down a city street smashing car windows with a flower; the piece served as the basis for Beyoncé’s 2016 “Hold Up” music video.
“I am kissing your Institute and your feet,” said Rist in a statement. “I am immensely touched and grateful to have this trust and investment in ideas I’ve yet to conceive. I’m honored to receive an award that has been granted to so many of my heroes, and look forward to collaborating closely with the brilliant minds at MIT.”
Established in 1974, the Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts at MIT recognizes important contributions by artists in all fields, and is intended to fund their future creative endeavors. Past winners include David Adjaye, Santiago Calatrava, Agnes Denes, Olafur Eliasson, Isaac Julien, Jeff Wall, Bill Viola, and Pamela Z.
