https://gothamist.com/news/greenpoint-ma.title: Greenpoint man accused of groping jogger stands trial after years of neighborhood concerns
https://gothamist.com/news/greenpoint-ma.author: Samantha Max
https://gothamist.com/news/greenpoint-ma.text:
A Greenpoint man with severe mental illness who has faced repeated accusations of harassing, assaulting and groping people in the neighborhood stands trial this week in Brooklyn.
Christopher Boissard’s allegedly aggressive behavior has divided the North Brooklyn neighborhood for years. Gothamist previously spoke with more than a dozen community members who expressed deep ambivalence about how to balance Boissard’s mental health needs with their own safety.
According to city officials and court records, Boissard, 35, has repeatedly cycled between psychiatric hospitals, substance abuse treatment and incarceration over the years. He is currently detained on Rikers Island.
Boissard’s trial comes just weeks after a man with a documented history of mental illness allegedly stabbed and killed a woman running on a path in South Brooklyn. While it is rare for people with psychiatric conditions to commit violent crimes, the cases that do occur often raise concerns about the city’s ability to properly care for people who need mental healthcare.
Boissard stands trial on sexual abuse and forcible touching charges. He faces up to four years in prison if convicted of the most serious offense.
Assistant District Attorney Taylor Tesher said in her opening statement Monday that Boissard grabbed a runner’s breast as she jogged past him on July 5, 2024. The touch was brief, the prosecutor said, but “it still stripped away her sense of safety.”
“She could not believe this happened to her,” Tesher said.
Greenpoint residents previously told Gothamist that Boissard’s physical aggression made them feel deeply unsettled in their own neighborhood. Similar, random acts of violence or belligerence by people seemingly in mental distress in public places like sidewalks, parks and subway cars have stoked concerns from the East Village to Bed-Stuy.
Amanda Gauthier, the jogger, had never seen Boissard before that day, the assistant DA told jurors. She reported the assault to police to ensure it didn’t happen to anyone else, the prosecutor said. Tesher then told the jury that they would learn other information about Boissard that would make his intent “all the more clear to you.”
Boissard was convicted of forcible touching in 2021, according to the state’s sex offender registry, which classifies him as a “sexually violent offender and predicate sex offender.” Whether jurors find him guilty in this case will likely depend on whether they believe he intended to touch Gauthier in order to gratify himself or degrade her. He has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him.
Defense attorney Natalia Mata didn’t deny that Boissard touched the runner. But she said it was a “hit,” “swipe,” or “swat,” and not a grope.
“On July 5, 2024, Christopher Boissard had no sexual intent. Not to degrade. Not to abuse. Not to fulfill his sexual desires,” the Brooklyn Defender Services attorney said.
Mata said Boissard can’t verbally communicate because he is deaf. She said the runner was moving very quickly and that the encounter happened “in the blink of an eye.” She also told jurors not to judge what Boissard’s intentions were that day based on any testimony they may hear from people who have had encounters with her client in the past.
“No one is saying you have to like Mr. Boissard,” she said.
Boissard, dressed in a checkered, button-down shirt and blazer, followed the proceedings through two American Sign Language interpreters, occasionally groaning or gesturing animatedly. His mother sat behind him in the gallery.
Gauthier, 30, breathed deeply and occasionally dabbed her face with a tissue during approximately three hours of testimony Monday afternoon. She told the jury that she started running in college to cope with anxiety — that when she runs, she feels like she can breathe.
On the day she encountered Boissard, she said she was training for the New York City marathon. It was an “easy run” on a path she knew well, she said, so she was jogging at a slower than usual pace and listening to a podcast.
As Gauthier turned onto Manhattan Avenue near the north end of the neighborhood, a man “put his arm up,” she said. She ran into his arm, she said, and then his hand touched her left breast “almost like the pledge of allegiance.” The jogger said it felt “like his hand was palming my breast” and that she felt “intense pressure afterward.” She recalled shouting “What the hell?” and swatting his hand before running away.
Defense attorney Johnny Castellanos questioned whether Boissard made any sexual gestures, spit at Gauthier or exposed himself before, during or after touching her chest. She said she didn’t remember seeing that.
“To me it wasn’t an accident, because it seemed like he intentionally put his hand up,” she said.
Since the incident, Gauthier said, she has continued to run regularly — both on her own and with a team. But she said she wears headphones less and is more vigilant than she used to be.
“Two years ago, before this happened, I guess I was a little more naive,” she said. “Now I am definitely more attentive.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: New bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Constanza Ontiveros Valdés
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura, a new bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.
Juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration issues, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020).
Though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.
“On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper. “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.
Central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo says, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”
Sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite, which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, launched in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is currently in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.
“A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales says. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”
The Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” says Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.
Sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.
“There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” says Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”
In El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December), curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra says. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”
Independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea, exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo, will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” says Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation, which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff, a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.
Sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta, presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.
Picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other issues. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he says.
Sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo says. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”
- Sutura, 18 November-22 November, various locations, Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, El Paso, United States

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/athens-polyt.title: The 1973 Athens Polytechnic Uprising Still Matters Today
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/athens-polyt.author: Christos Avramidis
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/athens-polyt.text:
The 1973 Athens Polytechnic Uprising Still Matters Today
In November 1973, Greek students occupying the Athens Polytechnic painted “USA Out” and “NATO Out” on its gate, protesting decades of US interference in Greece. Today US bases there still tie the country to Washington’s wars.
A military dictatorship had ruled Greece for more than six years when, in November 1973, hundreds of student occupied the Athens Polytechnic, transforming their university into a center of resistance. Thousands of workers, school students, and ordinary citizens soon joined them.
On the pillars of the Polytechnic’s central gate, a student painted two messages in large letters: “USA OUT” and “NATO OUT.” Within days, on November 17, a military tank would smash through that same gate. Why were young Greeks risking their lives to overthrow the military dictatorship also demanding the withdrawal of the United States and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)?
The answer lies in the three decades preceding the uprising. During those years, Greece experienced Nazi occupation, British military intervention, civil war, and the consolidation of an anti-communist political order that American assistance sustained. The Greek ruling class was all too happy to allow US interference to consolidate its own rule.
The Resistance That Britain Opposed
During World War II, Greece developed one of Europe’s largest resistance movements. The communist-led National Liberation Front (EAM) and its armed wing, the Greek People’s Liberation Army (ELAS), mobilized hundreds of thousands of people and came to control much of the Greek countryside.
EAM was far more than a guerrilla organization. In the territories it liberated from Nazi occupation, EAM established institutions of popular administration, organized schools, and introduced new forms of political participation. In 1944, women were able to vote and stand as candidates in elections the resistance organized, years before they gained equal voting rights in national Greek elections.
By the time German troops withdrew in October 1944, the resistance had become one of the most powerful social and political forces in the country. But Winston Churchill’s government was determined to prevent the communist-led movement from dominating postwar Greece.
The confrontation centered on the future of the armed forces. Under British supervision, the Greek government demanded the disarmament of ELAS while retaining military formations associated with the government in exile. EAM rejected an arrangement that would leave its supporters disarmed in the face of potentially hostile forces.
In practice, the leadership of EAM and of the Communist Party of Greece had an ambivalent stance toward the British army and British agents operating on Greek soil. They had cooperated with the British against the Nazi occupation. But they were deeply skeptical of British intervention in liberated Greece. Events after the German withdrawal from Athens confirmed their suspicions: the forces of liberation (EAM/ELAS and their allies) would have to fight a new battle.
On December 3, 1944, an enormous, initially peaceful demonstration gathered in central Athens. Police opened fire, killing demonstrators and wounding many others.
The Athens police chief, Angelos Evert, later acknowledged ordering the shooting. He had remained in charge of the police during the Nazi occupation, maintaining relations with the occupying authorities as well as contacts with British intelligence. The massacre marked the beginning of the December clashes, which Greeks call the Dekemvriana.
British troops clashed with ELAS in the streets of Athens, using tanks, artillery, and aircraft. Their Greek allies included formations containing former members of the Security Battalions, which had collaborated with the Nazi occupiers in the struggle against the resistance. Militants who had fought the Nazis now faced the British army — and, fighting alongside it, former collaborators of the occupation.
Churchill himself arrived in Athens on Christmas Day to intervene in the political negotiations. The British military campaign eventually defeated ELAS in the capital. The Varkiza Agreement, which the government and EAM signed in February 1945, then required the resistance to surrender its weapons.
The Left had suffered a military defeat and now had to accept a political settlement from a position of profound weakness. Its supporters would soon discover how little protection that settlement provided.
White Terror and the American Takeover
Widespread persecution of the Left, which Greeks remember as the White Terror, followed the disarmament of ELAS. Armed right-wing groups, often operating with the tolerance or cooperation of state authorities, targeted people associated with EAM. They murdered and tortured former resistance fighters or drove them from their homes. State authorities imprisoned many more.
Contemporary figures that EAM compiled recorded 1,289 murders, 31,632 cases of torture and physical abuse, 84,931 arrests, and 265 rapes between February 1945 and March 1946. United Nations documentation later cited these figures, but they originated with the persecuted movement rather than an independent nationwide investigation.
The political climate was hardly conducive to a free electoral contest. The government scheduled elections for March 1946, while thousands of leftists faced imprisonment, displacement, intimidation, and restrictions on political activity. The communist-led left boycotted the vote, arguing that the conditions made meaningful democratic participation impossible.
The Right emerged victorious. A referendum later that year restored King George II to the throne, consolidating the monarchy’s influence in the postwar political order. Greece descended into full-scale civil war.
By 1947, however, Britain could no longer afford to sustain its intervention. The United States took its place.
President Harry Truman requested $400 million in assistance for Greece and Turkey, declaring that Washington would help free peoples resist communist domination. In Greece, this meant massive military assistance to the government fighting the communist-led Democratic Army of Greece (DSE).
American weapons, money, and military advisers helped determine the outcome of the war. During its final stages in 1949, Greek government aircraft dropped American-supplied napalm on Greek territory, targeting communist positions in the mountains of northern Greece. The United States had used napalm during World War II, but its deployment in Greece preceded Washington’s much better-known use of the weapon in Vietnam.
Government forces defeated the DSE in 1949. For their supporters, however, the end of the war did not bring freedom.
The state sent thousands of leftists to prisons and remote island camps. The camp on the island of Makronisos became particularly notorious for its system of torture, beatings, forced declarations of repentance, and ideological reeducation. The contrast with the treatment of Nazi collaborators was striking, with far higher numbers of executions.
One execution became a symbol of that political order. Nikos Beloyannis had been a communist resistance fighter during the Nazi occupation. The authorities arrested him after the civil war, and a military court sentenced him to death. A photograph of him smiling with a red carnation during his trial became famous internationally, while an international campaign demanded that the Greek government spare his life.
Nevertheless, on March 30, 1952, a firing squad executed Beloyannis and three other communists.
Their deaths reflected the determination of the postwar Greek state to eliminate what it regarded as the communist threat, despite the formal restoration of parliamentary institutions. That same year, Greece joined NATO.
Much of Greece’s political elite had fled the country during the Nazi occupation, while significant sections of its economic elite had collaborated with the occupying forces. After liberation, the former returned to power, while much of the latter retained its economic influence. The restored ruling establishment built new mechanisms of repression and presided over a new era for Greek capitalism, keeping wages low and suppressing trade unions. US imperialism, which had taken the reins from its British counterpart, underpinned this new configuration of forces. In the postwar years, US interference would take many forms; at the same time, the Greek left would prove much more resilient than anyone could have predicted.
When the American Ambassador Intervened in Greek Elections
American influence went beyond supplying weapons. Declassified US diplomatic documents reveal direct American intervention in Greece’s electoral arrangements.
In March 1952, US ambassador John Peurifoy informed Washington that the American embassy’s political intervention and a public statement had blocked the introduction of proportional representation. The American ambassador was candidly discussing his government’s efforts to influence the electoral system of a formally sovereign democracy. The elections four years later vividly illustrated the political consequences of Greece’s unusual electoral arrangements.
In the 1956 parliamentary elections, the opposition Democratic Union won 48.15 percent of the popular vote, compared with 47.38 percent for Konstantinos Karamanlis’s conservative National Radical Union.
Yet Karamanlis secured 165 parliamentary seats, while the opposition received only 132. The party that won fewer votes formed the new government.
The opposition alliance was not a communist electoral front. It brought together centrist and left-wing forces against the conservative government. Even this broad parliamentary challenge failed to dislodge the Right.
Two years later, the United Democratic Left (EDA) became Greece’s second-largest parliamentary party, demonstrating the continuing electoral strength of the Left despite years of persecution. The result alarmed the conservative establishment and reinforced its fears about the political consequences of a more open democratic system.
The Monarchy, the Para-State, and the Road to Dictatorship
The Greek monarchy was far from a ceremonial institution. The palace intervened repeatedly in political affairs, exercised substantial influence over the armed forces, and helped shape the composition and survival of governments. Alongside the formal state existed an extensive anti-communist security apparatus and networks of right-wing organizations, some of which maintained close relations with elements of the police, military, and intelligence services.
Greek and American security agencies also cooperated during the Cold War in covert structures, including a clandestine stay-behind network called “Red Sheepskin.” These networks formed part of the country’s anti-communist security architecture, although their existence alone does not establish responsibility for every episode of political violence.
In 1965, King Constantine II’s confrontation with the centrist Prime Minister Georgios Papandreou over control of the military precipitated a government crisis. Papandreou had won a substantial parliamentary majority in 1964, yet his government collapsed amid royal intervention and defections from his own party. Greeks call these defections the Apostasia.
The conflict was particularly revealing because Papandreou was no communist revolutionary. He was a moderate centrist politician operating within the parliamentary system. Nevertheless, his attempt to exercise authority over the military collided with the monarchy and the security establishment.
By April 1967, Greece was approaching another national election. The army intervened before voters could go to the polls.
The Colonels and Their American Allies
On April 21, 1967, a group of military officers seized power. They suspended the constitution, banned political parties, imposed censorship, and arrested thousands of political opponents.
The dictatorship established a system of exile and torture that particularly targeted communists, trade unionists, students, and other opponents. Its leaders justified their seizure of power as necessary to prevent a communist takeover.
The precise extent of American foreknowledge of the coup, and of individual US officials’ involvement in it, remains contested. But the documentary record of Washington’s subsequent military cooperation with the dictatorship is extensive and undisputed.
The Johnson administration suspended deliveries of certain major weapons systems. The suspension, however, was only partial, and restrictions on military deliveries were gradually eased. An October 1969 memorandum for President Richard Nixon acknowledged that the United States had delivered approximately $100 million in military equipment to Greece as grant assistance between April 1967 and June 1969. During the same period, the dictatorship held political prisoners in camps and prisons, and torture and repression continued unabated.
American officials had a clear understanding of the nature of the dictatorship. They also regarded Greece’s position in NATO, its military installations, and its strategic location in the eastern Mediterranean as important to American interests.
The contradiction was evident. Washington publicly called for constitutional government while maintaining significant military ties with a dictatorship that had abolished it.
Greece was not an isolated example. In Spain, the United States had signed military agreements with Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in 1953, securing access to bases in exchange for financial and military assistance. The protection of Western strategic interests could coexist with the survival of authoritarian governments.
The Tank at the Athens Polytechnic Uprising
By November 1973, the Greek dictatorship was facing growing opposition. On November 14, students occupied the Athens Polytechnic and established a makeshift radio station. Their broadcasts called on the population to join the struggle for freedom. The most famous slogan of the uprising was “Bread, Education, Freedom.”
But the messages painted on the pillars of the university gate revealed another dimension of the revolt. They read “USA OUT” and “NATO OUT.”
For the protesters, these demands were inseparable from their struggle against the dictatorship. They had grown up in a country where American military assistance had helped defeat the communist left and where political prisoners had endured years of persecution. US diplomats had intervened in its domestic politics, and Greece’s military dictatorship maintained close relations with Washington. Thousands gathered around the Polytechnic.
In the early hours of November 17, the dictatorship sent tanks against the occupied university. One crashed through the main gate. Police and soldiers violently suppressed the uprising. Historian Leonidas Kallivretakis has documented twenty-four confirmed deaths associated with the events, many of them in the streets surrounding the Polytechnic.
In Greek popular memory, the uprising became the decisive event that brought down the dictatorship. Strictly speaking, however, the dictatorship survived for another eight months.
On November 25, hard-line military officer Dimitrios Ioannidis overthrew dictator Georgios Papadopoulos and established an even more repressive military government. But Greek society had watched police and soldiers kill young people who had demanded freedom. The apparent restoration of military control could not erase the political consequences of the uprising.
American officials continued to maintain diplomatic and military relations with the new junta, despite their awareness of its repressive character.
US diplomatic reporting from 1974 acknowledged the resentment directed at Washington and the widespread Greek belief that American support had contributed to the dictatorship’s survival. The new rulers also maintained their interest in relations with the United States while seeking international support for their rule.
The junta finally collapsed in July 1974, after it organized a coup against Cyprus’s president, Archbishop Makarios III, triggering the crisis that culminated in Turkey’s invasion of the island.
Democracy returned. But the legacy of the Polytechnic uprising extended far beyond the overthrow of the colonels.
The Bases That Never Left
The anger against foreign intervention remained a powerful force in Greek politics after the restoration of democracy. In August 1974, even conservative Prime Minister Karamanlis withdrew Greece from NATO’s integrated military command structure in protest over the alliance’s response to Turkey’s invasion of Cyprus.
The decision reflected both the government’s security concerns and the extraordinary public anger surrounding the Cyprus crisis.
Greece returned to NATO’s military command in 1980.
In October 1981, Andreas Papandreou, the son of Georgios Papandreou, led the Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK) to victory. PASOK won 48.07 percent of the vote, the highest share in the party’s electoral history. Its program had promised a fundamental change in Greece’s relationship with the United States, including the removal of American bases and withdrawal from NATO, but neither happened.
In 1983, Papandreou’s government signed a new agreement regulating the American military presence. The country remained in NATO, and American facilities continued operating.
More than fifty years later, Greece remains an important part of American military strategy. Successive governments have expanded defense cooperation with Washington, including agreements granting American forces access to facilities across the country. Among the most significant is Souda Bay, on the island of Crete, a major logistical and operational hub for the US Navy and Air Force in the eastern Mediterranean.
The implications became particularly visible during the American attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025.
Greek news outlets reported that American KC-135 aerial refueling aircraft operating from Souda Bay supported the mission involving US B-2 bombers. According to these reports, aircraft departing from the base participated in refueling operations over the Mediterranean.
In March 2026, the United States, Israel, and Iran were once again locked in military confrontation. Greece’s defense minister, Nikos Dendias, publicly discussed the possibility of attacks on military facilities and the measures the government had taken to protect Souda Bay and other critical infrastructure.
The Greek government has stated that Greece is not participating in operations against Iran. But the strategic importance of American military facilities on Greek territory has made questions about their use, security, and accountability increasingly consequential.
The Polytechnic Uprising Lives On
Every November 17, tens of thousands of Greeks take to the streets to commemorate the Polytechnic uprising. The annual march traditionally ends outside the American embassy. Even the statue of Harry S. Truman in Athens became a target of protest. Over the decades, demonstrators repeatedly attacked it and attempted to bring it down, sometimes succeeding.
The monument to the president whose doctrine had initiated America’s postwar intervention in Greece became a recurring symbol of opposition to that intervention.
The dictatorship fell in 1974. Parliamentary democracy returned, and governments of different political orientations have held power since then. Yet the country continues to host military facilities that form part of Washington’s wider strategic presence in the Mediterranean and the Middle East.
For generations of Greeks, the Polytechnic has represented not only the struggle against military dictatorship but also the demand that the country’s future should be decided by its own people.
Fifty-three years after the uprising, the words students painted on the pillars of its gate remain part of an unresolved historical debate. A tank smashed the gate. The demands written on its pillars survived.

Alors que les agents publics se sont mobilisés dans tout le pays mardi 17 novembre, les lycéens et les salariés les ont rejoints pour exiger que le gouvernement, drapé dans sa posture attentiste, accède à leurs revendications sur le pouvoir d’achat et l’investissement dans les services publics.
« Du fric pour les services publics ! » Mardi 17 novembre, plus de 500 000 fonctionnaires, étudiants et lycéens, mais aussi des salariés du privé se sont mobilisés à Paris, place de la Nation, et dans plus de 200 villes en France pour dénoncer la précarité les frappant, tout comme l’austérité plombant leur avenir.
Si le bras de fer entamé depuis l’automne dans la rue contre la vie chère et la dégradation des services publics se poursuit, c’est que les miettes octroyées pour la revalorisation du Smic et celles promises aux 5,8 millions d’agents publics la semaine passée ont encore fait monter d’un cran la colère.
Sophie Binet, secrétaire générale de la CGT, a prévenu. « Pour les salariés comme pour les agents publics, le compte n’y est pas. Pourquoi attendre le 11 décembre (fin des élections professionnelles dans la fonction publique, NDLR) pour nous répondre ? C’est maintenant ! »

https://taz.de/Grammy-Nominierungen/!623.title: Grammy-Nominierungen: Das Jahr der Pop Girlies
https://taz.de/Grammy-Nominierungen/!623.author: Ann Toma-Toader
https://taz.de/Grammy-Nominierungen/!623.text:
Grammy-Nominierungen : Das Jahr der Pop Girlies
Sängerinnen Raye, Rosalía und Olivia Dean prägen die Grammy-Nominierungen für 2026. Da wird sogar Klassik mit Techno und Flamenco vermischt.
S ieben von acht. So viele Frauen stehen in diesem Jahr auf der Liste der Grammys, nominiert für das Album des Jahres. Der einzige Mann, Bruno Mars, wirkt zwischen den Sängerinnen Raye, Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers, Olivia Dean und Taylor Swift etwas verloren. Raye führt mit elf Nominierungen und gleicht somit Beyoncés Rekord aus, Rosalía folgt mit neun. Das sollte nicht überraschen: Alle sieben Frauen dominieren nicht nur die Charts, sondern auch das Internet.
Während Britney Spears, Lady Gaga und Katy Perry die weibliche Spitze der Popmusik in den 2000ern abbildeten, konnten sie sich nur selten bei Preisverleihungen gegen ihre männlichen Konkurrenten durchsetzen. Teenie-Schwärme wie die Justins (Bieber und Timberlake) gaben den Ton an, so wie auch die Backstreet Boys oder One Direction.
Mittlerweile hat sich einiges verändert: Wir schauen kein MTV mehr und auch kein Viva, stehen nicht mehr Schlange bei MediaMarkt, um die neuste CD zu ergattern. Und: Die männerdominierte Musikbranche kuratiert nicht mehr unseren Musikgeschmack, da Social Media es Künstler*innen ermöglicht, direkt mit ihren Fans zu interagieren. Internet-Trends entscheiden nun, wer in den Charts die Nase vorn hat.
Da vor allem Tiktok die treibende Kraft hinter der Popularität neuer Pop-Hits ist, hat sich auch die Art, Musik zu konsumieren, verändert. Die „Pop Girlies“, wie Fans große Pop-Sängerinnen auf Social Media bezeichnen, nutzen Trends zu ihrem Vorteil. Die Bezeichnung steht stellvertretend für eine kulturelle Bewegung in der Popmusik, die von weiblicher Kraft, Authentizität und starker Vernetzung über soziale Medien geprägt ist.
Über Nacht zum Phänomen
Zur Vernetzung gehört besonders, dass Hörer*innen einen Ausschnitt aus einem Song aufgreifen und ihn mit originellen Choreografien tanzen oder über Videozusammenschnitte und Memes legen. So kann ein Song zum Trend werden und für mehr Aufrufe und Interaktion mit den Künstler*innen sorgen. Trends sind oft kurzlebig – die Bewährungsprobe für die Künstler*innen besteht darin, virale Momente in nachhaltige Wirkung umzuwandeln. Gleichzeitig bieten Trends die Möglichkeit, für unbekannte Künstler*innen ganz groß zu werden.
So geschah es auch mit Raye's Song „Where is my husband“. Der Song wurde praktisch über Nacht in den sozialen Medien berühmt. Dabei half auch Raye selbst nach. Immer wieder filmte sie sich dabei, wie sie zu dem Song mitsang und dabei auf ihren Ringfinger zeigte (ohne Ring, denn sie sucht im Lied nach einem Mann) oder den Entstehungsprozess im Studio dokumentierte. Auch ihre Live-Auftritte, in denen sie meist barfuß und euphorisch über die Bühne tanzte, gingen viral.
Aber auch Deans Song „Man I need“ wurde auf tausenden Social-Media-Videos unterlegt. Und Rodrigos Auftritt mit The-Cure-Sänger Robert Smith wurde begeistert aufgenommen. Dass Swift bei jeder Veröffentlichung große mediale Aufmerksamkeit genießt, ist nicht neu; spätestens seit ihrer Verlobung mit dem NFL-Star Travis Kelce lassen sich in den sozialen Medien wilde Interpretationen über ihre Beziehung aus den Songtexten ziehen.
Nicht nur bei Swift suchen Fans nach Hinweisen auf ihr Leben: Durch den immer größer werdenden Wunsch nach Authentizität wird es den Künstlerinnen mehr möglich, loszulassen und sie selbst zu sein. Rodrigo und Phoebe Bridgers singen ganz offen über Depressionen, Rosalía steht zu ihren spanischen Wurzeln und zeigt sich auch privat offen queer. So können die Sänger*innen eine Vorbildrolle einnehmen, mit der sich Fans identifizieren.
Pop ist nicht gleich nur Pop
Gleichzeitig schaffen die für den Grammy nominierten Frauen es, den Begriff Pop auszuweiten: Raye lässt Bigband-Einflüsse in ihrem Album groß werden und Dean ist gern mal in Richtung R&B unterwegs. Bei Rodrigo und bei Bridgers darf es rockig und laut werden und Rosalía hat auf ihrem Album „Lux“ erfolgreich Klassik mit Techno und Flamenco vermischt.
Die Sängerinnen lediglich als „Pop Girlies“ abzustempeln, wäre also zu kurz gedacht – und würde ihre Leistungen herabwürdigen. Auch Patti Smith lehnte den Begriff „female artist“, also weibliche Künstlerin, komplett ab. Man nenne ja auch die Männer nur Künstler, ohne ihr Geschlecht zu betonen.
Trotzdem: Ihre Bekanntheit in den sozialen Medien hat ihnen Türen geöffnet, die Frauen lange verschlossen wurden. Bei der medialen Aufmerksamkeit, die die Nominierten durch virale Momente und Tiktok-Trends erlangen, wurde es der Jury der Grammys unmöglich gemacht, wegzugucken.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

Infantino-Herausforderer Diallo: Aufstand der Besitzstandswahrer
Die Uefa präsentiert mit Phillippe Diallo einen Gegenkandidaten für Fifa-Boss Gianni Infantino. Eine Revolution droht also nicht. Ein Kommentar.
Europas Fußballfunktionäre haben ihren Widerstandsgeist entdeckt. Zwei Tage vor Ablauf der Frist haben sie endlich einen Gegenkandidaten für Fifa-Boss Gianni Infantino gefunden: Sie nominierten den französischen Verbandspräsidenten Philippe Diallo – nachdem Uefa-Boss Aleksander Čeferin schon längst abgesagt und auch Trainerlegende Arsène Wenger vor Tagen seinen Verzicht erklärt hatte.
Ein echter Aufbruch sieht anders aus. Denn mit Diallo kommt ein Mann aus dem innersten Zirkel des Fußballgeschäfts. Noch im Juni 2026 hatte der 63-Jährige eine Unterstützungserklärung für Infantino unterschrieben. Nun will er ihn bei der Wahl im März entthronen.
Zwischen Diallos Ja zu Infantino und seinem späteren Nein lagen nur wenige Monate, darin allerdings zum einen die WM mit dem unsäglichen Gebaren der Fifa gegenüber US-Präsident Trump und zum anderen, weitaus gewichtiger wohl: der spätsommerliche Vorstoß Infantinos, sämtliche kommerzielle Aktivitäten der Fifa in eine neue Tochterfirma auszulagern und dafür private Investoren mit ins Boot zu holen, unter anderem den Bruder von Trumps Schwiegersohn.
Erst nach dieser eigenmächtigen Anbahnung eines Milliarden-Deals wurde Infantino für die Besitzstandswahrer aus dem europäischen Dachverband untragbar. Die Uefa-Granden, bis dahin kaum als Vorkämpfer gegen die Kommerzialisierung des Fußballs in Erscheinung getreten, pochten hier nun völlig zu Recht darauf, dass direkte Renditeansprüche auf Fifa-Erlöse weiterhin außen vor zu lassen sind. Die Europäer protestierten, und Infantino ruderte zurück.
Kandidat Diallo, dessen Wahlaussichten angesichts von nur 55 europäischen unter 211 abstimmungsberechtigten Föderationen nicht die besten sind, müsste nun schnell erklären, wie er denn künftig die Fifa zu führen gedenkt. Weniger Präsidentenmacht und unabhängige Kontrollgremien forderte die Uefa unlängst in einer Erklärung vom Weltverband.
Diallo müsste zeigen, wie er das umsetzen will. Ansonsten bliebe vom europäischen Widerstandsgeist nichts übrig außer dem Bestreben, beim nächsten Milliarden-Deal wieder mit am Tisch zu sitzen.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ce.title: Celebrating the Inaugural Art Week NYC, Organized by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ce.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/ce.text:
ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum just wrapped up the inaugural edition of Art Week NYC, a citywide event celebrating all the New York art world’s ecosystem has to offer, from museums and galleries to artists, collectors, and cultural tastemakers from the Lower East Side and Tribeca to Chelsea and the Upper East Side.
Art Week NYC kicked off with an opening party at the Mallory in Chelsea, a 19th-century warehouse building that used to be home to the Tunnel nightclub. Programming took place over four jampacked days, from November 11–14. A launch event at the Metropolitan Museum of Art had in attendance New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, City Council Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal; New York State Senator Jose Serrano, and City Council member Virginia Maloney. David Breslin, the Met’s curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department, referred to Art Week NYC as “a defining tradition in our city’s cultural landscape—and that’s saying a lot.”
On November 13 and 14, ARTnews hosted a slate of programming at PMC’s ground-floor studio across the street from the New York Public Library. The two-day event was presented by Amazon, in partnership with Louis Roederer Champagne, Piaget, and Flying Whale Wines.
Friday featured in-depth conversations with art world insiders, such as dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky on what separates collectors from speculators; Tina Vaz, the MTA’s director of arts and design, speaking about several newly announced public art commissions; and photographer Stephen Shore detailing his new book, The Mental Image, a mix of memoir, pictures, and art history. Top 200 Collectors Larry and Allison Berg discussed the increasing crossover between sports and the art world, while art adviser Sophia Cohen gave insights on how a new generation of collectors is reshaping the market.
On Saturday, ARTnews welcomed two of our sponsors to the PMC Studio: Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s Head of Patrimony, talked about Andy Warhol’s love of timepieces and how the watchmaker came to collaborate with the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, while Frédéric Rouzaud, president of Maison Louis Roederer, discussed lasting ways for private patrons, like the Louis Roederer Foundation, to support contemporary art.
The day also looked back on what has happened to art in the 2020s (so far), synthesizing the impact of the pandemic, the NFT boom and bust, the rise of AI, and social and political upheaval; featured a spirited chat with New York Magazine’s Jerry Saltz on the current state of art criticism and the art world; and explored the importance of art collecting as both a personal passion and a creative practice from the point of view of two fashion executives, Carolina Herrera global creative director Wes Gordon and Oribe cofounder Daniel Kaner.
Before bidding farewell to our very first Art Week NYC, ARTnews revealed the winners of the third annual ARTnews Awards. This year’s jury included top curators from across the United States, and you can read more about the categories and the winners here.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Trump nominates Chris LaNeve as army chief after Hegseth fired predecessor
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: George Chidi
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Donald Trump has nominated Gen Chris LaNeve to be the US army’s top officer, making permanent his interim service after the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, unexpectedly fired his predecessor in April.
LaNeve had been serving as Hegseth’s senior military commander before his nomination for a fourth star and service as vice-chief of staff of the army in February.
Two months later, Hegseth fired the army chief of staff, Gen Randy George. While the firing has never been explained, George had insisted on an official investigation into an unauthorized 28 March army helicopter flyover near the Tennessee home of musician Kid Rock, which Hegseth blocked.
LaNeve’s relatively short tenure as a four-star general has raised questions among Democrats and Republicans, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal.
LaNeve, 59, graduated from the University of Arizona in 1990 and later earned master’s degrees from Central Michigan University and the US Army Command and General Staff College. He has served in a wide variety of command roles, including a rotation as the commander of the 82nd Airborne Division and the 8th Army in Korea.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.title: Os 350 anos da Arquidiocese de Olinda e Recife
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.author: Fabio Potiguar
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/colunist.text:
Eu digo “nossa Igreja” com muito afeto. Digo como padre que faz parte desta história e que tem aprendido tanto com o povo desta terra no ecumenismo, no diálogo inter-religioso e no trabalho de justiça e paz pela promoção dos direitos humanos.
No dia 16 de novembro de 1676, nascia a Diocese de Olinda. São 350 anos de uma história que passa pela Sé de Olinda, pelo Pátio do Carmo, pelas ruas do Recife e por tantas comunidades onde a fé foi transmitida de geração em geração.
Quando penso nessa história, penso nas mulheres que sustentam a vida de tantas comunidades, nas catequistas, nas religiosas, nos padres e em tanta gente cujo nome ficou guardado na memória do povo.
Lembro de Dom Vital, frade franciscano capuchinho e bispo de Olinda. Era ainda muito jovem quando assumiu esta igreja e continuou a viver a pobreza franciscana. Ao chegar ao Palácio da Soledade, pediu que lhe preparassem um quarto simples e concedeu alforria às pessoas escravizadas que ali viviam. Homem de oração, viveu um tempo de fortes tensões entre a Igreja e o Império e chegou a ser preso em 1874, durante a Questão Religiosa. Sua firmeza nas provações faz parte da memória da nossa Igreja.
Penso, com ternura, em Dom Helder Câmara. A memória de Dom Hélder me faz perguntar, também a mim mesmo, se estamos ouvindo os pobres, se aprendemos com eles e se temos coragem de enfrentar, ao lado deles, as injustiças que os fazem sofrer.
Por isso, entre as alegrias deste jubileu, quero destacar o Prêmio Dom Helder Vivo, idealizado pela Comissão de Justiça e Paz e lançado no encerramento do Sínodo Arquidiocesano. É bonito ver o nome de Dom Helder ligado ao reconhecimento de pessoas, coletivos e iniciativas que, hoje, trabalham pela dignidade humana, pelos direitos humanos, pela justiça social, pela cultura da paz e pela ecologia integral.
A Casa das Pastorais Sociais e a Missa no Pátio do Carmo também dizem muito sobre esta festa. A mesma Igreja que se reúne em torno da mesa da Eucaristia é chamada a lutar para que haja pão na mesa de cada família. É ali, na vida concreta, que a nossa oração se faz compromisso com a justiça e a paz.
“Para que todos sejam um” (Jo 17,21). Essa prece de Jesus me toca profundamente. Ela nos pede que atravessemos a rua, que encontremos os irmãos e as irmãs de outras Igrejas, que conversemos com pessoas de outras tradições religiosas e que trabalhemos juntos pelo bem de quem mais precisa.
Dou graças a Deus por esses 350 anos. E peço ao Espírito Santo que nos dê alegria para caminhar juntos, ternura para cuidar uns dos outros e coragem para defender a dignidade dos pobres.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/1.text:
US Navy chief says Iran war has put ‘strain’ on maritime forces
Lawmakers press Hung Cao over expanding war, opaque leadership shake-ups, and low crew morale in confirmation hearing.
United States Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has acknowledged that the Iran war is taxing the maritime service as bipartisan senators questioned him over extended ship deployments, dwindling weapons stockpiles, and resources being shifted away from the Asia-Pacific.
Testifying before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Tuesday at his confirmation hearing to lead the military branch, Cao faced sharp, bipartisan grilling over the mounting human and material costs of the US-Israel war on Iran, which is now deep into its ninth month.
“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” Cao said, while insisting that joint military efforts have “really set China back on their heels”.
Cao, a retired US Navy captain and former Republican Party candidate for the Virginia Senate, has served as acting navy secretary since April 2026 after previously holding the under-secretary post.
The candidate, backed by US President Donald Trump, is now seeking US Senate confirmation for the permanent top civilian job.
The hearing comes amid burgeoning political fallout over the protracted quagmire with Iran, which recently saw a failed US House bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his stewardship of the war.
Voter frustration over the war — and its economic sting — proved decisive in the November midterm elections, which were widely seen as a repudiation of the war and ultimately cost the Republicans control of both the House and the Senate.
The Democratic-controlled 120th Congress is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
Heated Senate exchange
As the ranking Democrat on the committee, Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island questioned Cao during the nearly two-hour hearing, saying he was candidly troubled by his performance so far.
“I am concerned, frankly, about your leadership record as acting secretary,” said Reed, who called on the acting US Navy secretary to speak to Hegseth‘s ongoing and planned dismissals of numerous naval officers over the past year, pressing Cao on whether he would “defend the military leaders in the future from partisan meddling in their careers”.
Democratic lawmakers went on to criticise the US Navy for bypassing standard congressional notification after quietly relieving the entire leadership team — the commander, executive officer and command master chief — of the nuclear-powered attack submarine USS South Dakota following an October underwater collision with the seabed.
“We relieve commanding officers for everything from negligence to even just fraternisation or, you know, harassment,” Cao said, making the case against the US Navy’s traditional policy of publicly announcing the removal of commanders. “I want to make sure that we’re protecting their livelihood afterwards as well.”
His stated intent to safeguard individuals’ careers was promptly rebuked by Reed, who maintained that privacy does not justify shielding information from congressional oversight.
“The squadron commodore [of the USS South Dakota] felt that they did not live up to their honour, courage, and commitment ethos, and therefore, he relieved the commanding officer, the executive officer, and the command master chief,” Cao countered.
Cao’s record on sailor mental health comes under fire
The US Navy chief-nominee also faced intense questioning from lawmakers about low crew morale, severe supply shortages, and mental health strains aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln following its record-breaking 265-day deployment in the Pacific Ocean, South China Sea, Indian Ocean, and North Arabian Sea.
The vessel returned to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, California, in early October after the USS George Washington arrived on station to relieve it. Together with the USS George HW Bush and the newly arrived USS Theodore Roosevelt, the US is temporarily massing three carrier strike groups to bolster regional maritime security and tighten the months-long naval blockade against Iran.
Last week, Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. He noted, however, that the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change.
During Tuesday’s hearing, Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, argued that Cao was “failing these sailors and their families”, and noted that his “confrontation with them leaves me with the clear impression that you simply don’t care”.
Cao pushed back, declaring that he does not control the deployment lengths of US Navy ships that have crept steadily closer to a full year at sea — up from a standard of six to eight months during the US’s so-called “war on terror”.
“Sustained investment in our people will increase readiness, improve retention and recruitment, and enable our ability to support national objectives,” said Cao.
When asked about suicide attempts aboard the ships, Cao told Blumenthal that what he saw “as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicide mitigations”.
Cao faces a rare waiver hurdle for the top spot
In his opening statement, Republican Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker expressed support for Cao’s nomination to lead the US Navy, noting that while the service faces significant challenges during a particularly volatile time, it also has major opportunities.
Beyond fielding tough questions from lawmakers on Tuesday over the strain of the Iran war on fleet readiness, Cao still faces a complex confirmation path to become the permanent secretary of the navy, requiring a rare congressional waiver.
Because he left active-duty service in October 2021, he falls short of the seven-year separation period mandated by federal law to preserve civilian control of the military.
Securing that exemption poses a steep political climb for Cao, who must clear the hurdle by meeting a 60-vote threshold, which may prove tricky in a polarised Washington.
Cao will ultimately need cross-party support from Democrats or independents to avoid a filibuster, while winning over war-sceptical Republicans.

https://www.artforum.com/news/yayoi-kusa.author: Polly Watson
https://www.artforum.com/news/yayoi-kusa.text:
Subscribe to

An “Infinity Net” painting by Yayoi Kusama brought in $15.1 million with fees at Sotheby’s in New York last night, setting an auction record for the late artist. The work had arrived to the block carrying an estimate of $10 million to $15 million; the hammer came down at $12.5 million before fees. Artnews reports that the sale followed a four-minute battle between two unnamed clients, both bidding by phone.
The painting, titled No. 3P.B., 1960, is a rare early example of Kusama’s “Infinity Net” series. Begun in 1958, the series is characterized by dense abstract fields of dots swirling across large-scale monochrome canvases. More broadly, it is emblematic of the artist’s obsessive focus on repetition, also embodied in her “Infinity Mirror Rooms,” which gained popularity with the rise of social media, thanks to their selfie-friendly nature. Kusama painted the rich red No. 3P.B. shortly after moving to New York. It was shown in the Whitney Annual of 1961, a forerunner of the Whitney Biennial.
The artist’s previous record was set in 2022 by another early “Infinity Net” work, the white Untitled (Nets), 1959, which went for $10.5 million with fees at Phillips. Since Kusama’s death this past August at the age of ninety-seven, nearly thirty of her works have come to auction. No. 3P.B. was a highlight of the Now and Contemporary Evening Auction, which raked in $268.7 million with fees, an increase of 50 percent over last year’s event. The sale was followed immediately by a single-lot auction of works from the collection of the late Ted and Ruth Baum, which pulled in nearly $110 million with fees, bringing the night’s total to a whopping $378.7 million with fees. Tomma Abts, Firelei Báez, Sam Francis, and Jonas Wood are among the artists who set records alongside Kusama.

Une semaine après le début de la conférence sociale et alors que la mobilisation ne faiblit pas, les syndicats pressent les employeurs de se conformer à l’injonction.
Sans surprise, le patronat rechigne à ouvrir les négociations de branches. C’était pourtant une promesse de Jean-Pierre Farandou, ministre du Travail, issue de la conférence sociale du 9 novembre.
Sous pression de la mobilisation du 5 novembre, qui a vu 1,6 million de personnes dans les rues, l’exécutif entendait impulser des « négociations flash » de deux semaines dans les branches professionnelles sur les salaires, en plus de la hausse du Smic de 1,6 %.

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://taz.de/Israel-hat-die-Amazon-Clo.title: Israels Besatzungspolitik und Big Tech: Wir sind alle Komplizen
https://taz.de/Israel-hat-die-Amazon-Clo.author: Daniel Bax
https://taz.de/Israel-hat-die-Amazon-Clo.text:
Israels Besatzungspolitik und Big Tech : Wir sind alle Komplizen
Israel hat Millionen von Fotos auf eine Amazon-Cloud hochgeladen, um damit Palästinenser zu überwachen. Soll man den Konzern deswegen boykottieren?
F ür die über fünf Millionen Palästinenserinnen und Palästinenser, die in den besetzten Gebieten leben, ist Israel keine Demokratie, sondern Besatzungsmacht und Überwachungsstaat. Der britische Guardian hat jetzt enthüllt, dass das israelische Militär 3,5 Millionen Fotos von Palästinensern aus Gaza und dem Westjordanland auf eine Cloud-Plattform von Amazon zur Gesichtserkennung hochgeladen hat. Die Datenbank wurde in den ersten Monaten des aktuellen Kriegs im Gazastreifen in die Amazon-Cloud übertragen, wie aus geleakten Dokumenten hervorgeht.
Westliche Firmen sind in diesem Krieg längst Komplizen. Rund 50 Unternehmen hat ein UN-Bericht von Francesca Albanese im vergangenen Jahr namentlich genannt – Rüstungskonzerne, Hersteller von Baustoffen und schwerem Gerät, aber auch Banken und Versicherungen sowie Tech-Konzerne wie Google, Amazon, Microsoft und Palantir. Letztere stellen die digitalen Schlüsseltechnologien bereit, mit denen Israel seine Kriege führen und seine Besatzung aufrechterhalten kann. Menschenrechtler bezeichnen die besetzten Gebiete sogar als „Testlabor für Waffen und Überwachungstechnologien“.
Investigativrecherchen vom Guardian und dem israelisch-palästinensischen „+972 Magazine“ aus Israel haben bewirkt, dass Microsoft vor einem Jahr einer israelischen Militäreinheit zumindest bestimmte Cloud- und KI-Dienste gesperrt hat. Mitarbeiter und Aktionäre des Tech-Konzerns waren empört, dass dieser Millionen von abgehörten palästinensischen Mobiltelefonaten auf einer Microsoft-Cloud gespeichert hatte. Der Dokumentarfilm „Naza“ zeigt, dass solche Daten genutzt wurden, um Luftangriffe im Gazastreifen zu planen. Doch moralische Skrupel wie im Fall von Microsoft sind die Ausnahme. Dafür sind die Geschäfte zu lohnend.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Menschenrechtler fordern Sanktionen gegen Israel und gegen Konzerne, die Profit aus Krieg und Besatzung schlagen. Denn ein individueller Boykott bringt nur wenig: Dazu sind wir alle selbst zu sehr von Google, Amazon & Co abhängig. So gesehen sind wir alle Komplizen.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.author: Andreas Fritsche
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120394.text:
- Kommentare
- Wirtschaft
Kritik an Tesla ohne Energie
Der geplanten Erweiterung der Fabrik in Grünheide steht nichts entgegen – weder unüberwindliche Hindernisse noch wirksamer Widerstand. Ein Kommentar
Knapp 30.000 US-Dollar, umgerechnet etwa 27.000 Euro, sollen Käufer für ein Cybercab von Tesla bezahlen. Es hat kein Lenkrad und keine Pedale für Bremse und Antrieb, denn es fährt autonom. In Deutschland sind derartige Fahrzeuge bislang noch nicht zugelassen. Doch der US-Konzern Tesla will sie genau hier produzieren, in seinem Werk im brandenburgischen Grünheide. Dafür soll ab nächstes Jahr eine neue Fabrikhalle gebaut werden. Tesla benötigt eine Genehmigung. Doch wer die Geschichte des Standorts kennt, braucht wenig Fantasie, um sich vorzustellen, dass kein Problem groß genug wäre, das Vorhaben zu stoppen.
Berichte über einen dramatischen Wassermangel in der Region sind ein Dauerbrenner, seit Tesla in Grünheide ansässig ist. Werksleiter André Thierig versichert vorsorglich, man werde auch mit dem Ausbau innerhalb der vertraglich vereinbarten Wassermengen bleiben. Der Wasserverbrauch des Betriebs konnte zuletzt gesenkt werden, und mit der neuen Halle ist eine neue Abwasserbehandlungsanlage geplant. Doch selbst wenn es nicht so wäre: Die Politik würde irgendwie schon jedes erdenkliche Hindernis beseitigen. Zu verlockend ist die in Aussicht gestellte Investition von drei Milliarden Euro, zu willkommen sind die Arbeitsplätze.
Schließlich stand Brandenburg einige Jahre gegen den Bundestrend fast allein durch die Tesla-Ansiedlung wirtschaftlich gut da, und dieser Effekt könnte erneut eintreten. Aktuell steigt im Vergleich zum Vorjahr Monat für Monat die Arbeitslosenquote.
Widerstand ist daher kaum zu erwarten. In der Gemeindevertretung von Grünheide hat die Landtagsabgeordnete Kathleen Muxel (AfD) jahrelang gegen Tesla gekämpft. Doch sie ist im Januar 2026 verstorben. Ihre Partei hält Elektroautos zwar für eine grüne Spinnerei, spricht im Fall von Tesla jedoch nicht mehr darüber, seit Konzernboss Elon Musk sich offen positiv über die AfD äußert.
Ein scharfer Kritiker nicht der Tesla-Fabrik an sich, aber der Umstände ihrer Ansiedlung war Linksfraktionschef Sebastian Walter. Doch auch diese Stimme fehlt nun im Parlament, weil Walters Partei bei der Landtagswahl 2024 an der Fünf-Prozent-Hürde scheiterte. Freie Bahn also für Elon Musk und seine Cybercabs.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.
